Central cartilage lesion: practical distinction Feature Central ACT / CS1 Cellularity Usually lower Increased; irregular distribution Often markedly increased Chondrocytes Small, relatively uniform Binucleation common Greater atypia and pleomorphism Growth pattern No permeative entrapment Entrapment of pre-existing lamellar bone Destructive/permeative growth Imaging Usually small; no aggressive features Deep endosteal scalloping; often larger Cortical destruction and soft-tissue extension may occur Site terminology All sites ACT: appendicular; CS1: axial Chondrosarcoma grade 2/3 These features are not interchangeable or independently definitive. Age, skeletal site, imaging, and adequate sampling remain essential; phalangeal lesions and lesions before growth-plate fusion require particular caution. Biopsy, sampling, and reporting checklist Review radiographs and cross-sectional imaging before biopsy; document exact bone, compartment, and relationship to cortex and medulla. For central cartilage tumors, sample the tumor-host bone interface to assess permeative entrapment of pre-existing lamellar bone. For osteochondroma-associated lesions, document cartilage-cap thickness measured perpendicular to the bone-cartilage interface. For surface tumors, assess cortical invasion, Haversian canal involvement, medullary extension, and soft-tissue invasion. For suspected dedifferentiated chondrosarcoma, extensively sample the interface between cartilaginous and high-grade components. Preserve non-decalcified or EDTA-decalcified tissue when molecular testing may be needed; acid decalcification can impair IHC and nucleic acids. Report tumor size, site, local extent, margins, and percentage of viable tumor/response when applicable. Scope: Content is organized from the supplied WHO chapter excerpt. Diagnostic criteria and terminology follow that source. Radiologic correlation and multidisciplinary review are emphasized where histology alone is insufficient. Ancillary tests are presented according to their stated diagnostic role, not as universal screening panels.

title: Genetic Tumor Syndromes
content: use client Enchondromatosis (Ollier Disease and Maffucci Syndrome) IDH1, IDH2 Usually non-hereditary; postzygotic somatic mosaicism Multiple cartilaginous neoplasms in the medullary cavity or periosteum, often producing bone expansion and deformity. Maffucci syndrome is defined by associated cutaneous, soft tissue, or visceral vascular lesions. Usually presents in early childhood; Ollier disease commonly causes asymmetric or unilateral enchondromas, limb-length inequality, angular deformity, finger swelling, and growth arrest. Maffucci syndrome includes vascular lesions, often spindle cell hemangiomas, in addition to skeletal enchondromas. Malignant transformation is suggested clinically by new or worsening pain and accelerated growth. Patients are at increased risk for secondary chondrosarcoma; reported risk varies substantially with skeletal distribution and is higher when long bones or pelvis are involved. Ollier disease is also associated with gliomas and juvenile granulosa cell tumors; additional tumors have been reported in Maffucci syndrome. Diagnosis is based on the combination of clinical findings and characteristic radiographic distribution. Essential radiographic/clinical pattern: at least 2 enchondromas plus findings such as growth disturbance, typical hand/foot deformity, or columnar lucencies in long-bone metaphyses. In milder adult presentations, at least 3 usually anatomically related enchondromas may support the diagnosis even without other typical features. Maffucci syndrome requires associated vascular lesions; spindle cell hemangioma is overrepresented. Ollier disease: multiple enchondromas, often involving long and short tubular bones; growth disturbance and deformity are common. Maffucci syndrome: enchondromas plus dermal, subcutaneous, or visceral vascular lesions, particularly spindle cell hemangiomas. Metachondromatosis is a separate inherited disorder with enchondromas and osteochondroma-like lesions; many lesions regress in adulthood. Enchondromas are well-circumscribed cartilaginous nodules and may be hypercellular with enlarged, irregular nuclei. In the setting of Ollier disease or Maffucci syndrome, increased cellularity and some nuclear atypia alone are insufficient for atypical cartilaginous tumor / chondrosarcoma, grade 1. Assessment for malignant transformation requires multidisciplinary correlation with imaging, particularly cortical destruction and soft tissue extension. Most cases harbor postzygotic IDH1 or IDH2 mutations; IDH1 p.Arg132 variants predominate, especially p.Arg132Cys. Identical IDH variants may be present in multiple lesions; low-level variants may also be detectable in non-neoplastic tissue. Rare germline variants involving HIF-pathway genes and rare PTH1R variants have been reported, but are not the usual basis of Ollier disease or Maffucci syndrome. Metachondromatosis is associated with germline heterozygous loss-of-function PTPN11 variants; spondyloenchondrodysplasia is associated with biallelic ACP5 variants. Multiple sporadic enchondromas Use the characteristic distribution, asymmetry, deformity, and associated vascular lesions to establish a syndromic pattern. Metachondromatosis Inherited condition with both enchondromas and osteochondroma-like lesions, often pointing toward adjacent joints and regressing in adulthood. Secondary chondrosarcoma New pain, accelerated growth, cortical destruction, marrow edema, periosteal reaction, or an extraosseous mass raise concern; atypia alone is not sufficient. Do not diagnose ACT/CS1 from increased cellularity or mild nuclear atypia alone in an enchondromatosis background. Do not assume Ollier disease or Maffucci syndrome is inherited; both are usually caused by postzygotic mosaicism. Vascular lesions distinguish Maffucci syndrome from Ollier disease. Li–Fraumeni Syndrome TP53 Autosomal dominant; de novo variants occur Cancer-predisposition syndrome characterized by early-onset multiple primary tumors, especially soft tissue sarcomas, osteosarcoma, breast cancer, brain tumors, and adrenocortical carcinoma. Core tumor spectrum: adrenocortical carcinoma, breast cancer, central nervous system tumors, osteosarcoma, and soft tissue sarcomas. Sarcomas are a substantial component of the tumor spectrum; osteosarcoma, rhabdomyosarcoma, leiomyosarcoma, and liposarcoma are represented. Rhabdomyosarcoma and osteosarcoma occur predominantly before age 19; liposarcoma and leiomyosarcoma occur more often in adults. Classic criteria include a proband with sarcoma before age 45, a first-degree relative with cancer before age 45, and a first- or second-degree relative with cancer before age 45 or sarcoma at any age. The clinical spectrum is broader than the classic family-history definition; Li–Fraumeni-like presentations may not fulfill classic criteria. Essential: demonstration of a germline pathogenic TP53 variant and/or an appropriate family history. Consider germline testing using established clinical criteria, including the Chompret criteria and current hereditary cancer testing recommendations. A TP53 alteration detected by tumor-only sequencing is not, by itself, proof of a germline variant. Distinguish pathogenic germline variants from somatic variants, clonal hematopoiesis, polymorphisms, and variants of uncertain significance. Soft tissue sarcomas and osteosarcoma are defining bone/soft tissue tumor associations. Other core tumors include breast carcinoma, brain tumors, and adrenocortical carcinoma. Additional reported tumors include lymphoma, gastrointestinal malignancies, melanoma, lung cancer, ovarian and endometrial carcinomas, renal and prostate carcinomas, and ocular tumors. Most tumors have no distinctive gross or histopathologic features compared with their sporadic counterparts. Rhabdomyosarcoma and Wilms tumor more often show anaplastic histology in the Li–Fraumeni setting. Abnormal p53 immunostaining, either strong diffuse nuclear staining or complete absence, may occur but does not establish a germline TP53 variant. Caused by germline pathogenic variants in the TP53 tumor suppressor gene; missense variants in the DNA-binding domain are common, but truncating, splice-site, deletion, and other variants occur. Tumors commonly acquire a second hit affecting the wild-type TP53 allele. Germline confirmation requires constitutional testing; tumor sequencing alone cannot reliably establish germline status. Li–Fraumeni-like syndrome A clinical designation for families with a suggestive but less complete tumor/family-history pattern; some cases lack an identifiable TP53 variant. Other hereditary cancer-predisposition syndromes Consider additional cancer-predisposition genes when the phenotype is suggestive but TP53 testing is negative. Somatic TP53 alteration or clonal hematopoiesis A TP53 variant in tumor-only or blood-based testing does not automatically indicate constitutional Li–Fraumeni syndrome. Abnormal p53 immunohistochemistry is not a substitute for germline testing. A negative TP53 result does not explain every Li–Fraumeni-like family; the clinical phenotype and broader genetic context remain important. Radiation-associated second malignancies have been reported, but outcome differences and treatment-response predictions are not definitively established. McCune–Albright Syndrome GNAS Postzygotic somatic activating mosaic variant; not inherited Mosaic disorder classically associated with fibrous dysplasia, hyperpigmented macules, and endocrine hyperfunction, including precocious puberty. The classic triad comprises fibrous dysplasia, hyperpigmented macules, and precocious puberty; any combination may occur. The syndrome is defined by fibrous dysplasia plus at least one extraskeletal feature, or by at least two extraskeletal features. Fibrous dysplasia may be polyostotic or monostotic and commonly affects the appendicular skeleton, craniofacial bones, and spine. Endocrine manifestations include precocious puberty, hyperthyroidism, growth hormone excess, hypophosphatemia, and rarely neonatal Cushing syndrome. Malignancy risk is increased, most often through sarcomatous transformation of fibrous dysplasia; breast and thyroid carcinomas have also been reported. Essential: at least 2 of the 3 classic clinical features, or monostotic fibrous dysplasia with demonstration of a GNAS variant. Demonstration of a somatic activating GNAS variant is desirable when two or more clinical criteria are present. Clinical expression depends on the distribution and extent of mosaicism; not all patients show the complete classic triad. Skeletal: fibrous dysplasia, which may cause pain, fracture, deformity, facial asymmetry, and neurologic compromise from craniofacial involvement. Skin: irregularly bordered hyperpigmented macules that typically respect the midline and may follow Blaschko lines. Endocrine: ovarian estrogen-producing cysts with precocious puberty, thyroid disease, growth hormone excess, and phosphate wasting. Other reported manifestations include hepatobiliary, pancreatic, and cardiovascular abnormalities. Fibrous dysplasia consists of proliferating fibroblast-like marrow stromal cells replacing normal bone and marrow. Irregular, discontinuous trabeculae of woven bone are distributed throughout the lesion and are poorly mineralized and non-functional in orientation. Solid tumors associated with the syndrome generally resemble their sporadic counterparts. Caused by postzygotic activating (gain-of-function) variants in GNAS, which encodes the Gs alpha subunit. Most variants affect p.Arg201; a smaller subset affects p.Gln227. Constitutive Gs alpha activation increases cAMP signaling; the degree and distribution of mosaicism contribute to clinical variability. Detection of a somatic GNAS variant can support diagnosis, particularly in selected or atypical presentations. Isolated fibrous dysplasia Look for additional endocrine or cutaneous features; a GNAS variant can support McCune–Albright syndrome in monostotic disease. Other causes of precocious puberty The ovarian cysts and endocrine findings occur in the setting of postzygotic GNAS mosaicism and may coexist with fibrous dysplasia and hyperpigmented macules. Carney complex Can include lentigines and endocrine neoplasia, but the defining skeletal lesion in McCune–Albright syndrome is fibrous dysplasia. The complete classic triad is not required; presentations are highly variable. A negative result from peripheral blood does not necessarily exclude a postzygotic mosaic variant in affected tissues. New pain, aggressive bone destruction, or an extraosseous mass in fibrous dysplasia warrants evaluation for malignant transformation. Multiple Osteochondromas EXT1, EXT2 Autosomal dominant; variable expressivity Hereditary disorder characterized by multiple benign cartilage-capped surface neoplasms, usually arising near the metaphyses of long bones. Most patients present during the first decade with a painless bony mass, limb deformity, or impingement on adjacent structures. Osteochondromas enlarge during childhood and usually stop growing after physeal closure. Common deformities include ulnar shortening with radial bowing, valgus knee/ankle alignment, limb-length inequality, and short stature. Complications include restricted motion, bursal formation, tendon/nerve/vessel impingement, and spinal cord compression. The major neoplastic complication is secondary peripheral ACT/CS1 or higher-grade chondrosarcoma; new growth after puberty, worsening pain, or an adult cartilage cap thicker than 2–3 cm is concerning. Essential: at least 2 radiographically demonstrated osteochondromas in the juxta-epiphyseal region of long bones and/or a proven germline pathogenic variant in EXT1 or EXT2. Radiographic continuity of the cortex and medullary cavity of the lesion with the parent bone is the hallmark. Germline molecular testing is not mandatory when clinical and radiographic findings are characteristic. MRI is useful for evaluating cartilage cap thickness and suspected complications. Osteochondromas occur in bones formed by endochondral ossification, especially long bones; ribs, spine, and pelvis may also be involved. Langer–Giedion syndrome (TRPS2) may include craniofacial dysmorphism and intellectual disability due to a contiguous deletion including EXT1 and TRPS1. Potocki–Shaffer syndrome may include enlarged parietal foramina and craniofacial abnormalities due to a deletion including EXT2 and ALX4. Individual lesions are histopathologically similar to sporadic osteochondromas. Secondary peripheral chondrosarcoma may be difficult to distinguish from osteochondroma on histology alone; clinical and radiographic findings, including cartilage cap thickness, are essential. Malignant transformation most often produces secondary peripheral ACT/CS1, but grade 2 or 3 chondrosarcoma may occur. Caused by germline inactivating variants or deletions involving EXT1 (8q24.11) or EXT2 (11p11.2). A second somatic hit leads to biallelic inactivation in the developing osteochondroma. EXT1 and EXT2 encode proteins involved in heparan sulfate polymerization and signaling pathways including Hedgehog, BMP, FGFR3, and WNT/β-catenin. Pathogenic variants are identified in approximately 70–95% of affected individuals in the supplied source. May show both enchondromas and osteochondroma-like lesions; associated with PTPN11 rather than EXT1/EXT2. Dysplasia epiphysealis hemimelica (Trevor disease) Distinguished by its characteristic epiphyseal distribution and absence of the EXT1/EXT2 hereditary multiple osteochondroma pattern. Secondary peripheral chondrosarcoma Consider new growth after skeletal maturity, increasing pain, and an adult cartilage cap thicker than 2–3 cm; integrate imaging and histology. Histology alone may not distinguish an osteochondroma from secondary peripheral ACT/CS1. Do not rely on a negative germline test to exclude a clinically and radiographically characteristic case. All patients require follow-up; the source does not identify a reliable protective or risk factor for malignant transformation. Neurofibromatosis Type 1 NF1 Autosomal dominant; de novo and postzygotic mosaic variants occur Tumor-predisposition syndrome characterized by multiple pigmentary, neural, and skeletal findings, with increased risk of benign and malignant tumors in nervous and non-nervous systems. Typical findings include multiple café-au-lait macules, axillary/inguinal freckling, Lisch nodules, and choroidal abnormalities. Skeletal manifestations include scoliosis, sphenoid wing dysplasia, non-ossifying fibromas, and congenital tibial bowing with fracture or pseudarthrosis. Plexiform neurofibromas occur in approximately 30–50% of individuals; the lifetime risk of MPNST is approximately 11.7–15.8% in the cited source. Other associated tumors include GIST, pheochromocytoma, breast cancer before age 50, rhabdomyosarcoma in young children, and optic pathway glioma. A bone or soft tissue tumor may be the sentinel presentation of previously unrecognized NF1. Diagnosis is clinical, based on established NIH criteria and revised criteria for constitutional and mosaic NF1. A pathogenic NF1 variant is detectable in up to approximately 95% of individuals with a clinical diagnosis in the cited source. Consider mosaic NF1 when findings are segmental or limited; the variant may be detectable only in affected tissue and not peripheral blood. In a child with café-au-lait macules and a malignant tumor, constitutional mismatch repair deficiency should also be considered. Peripheral nerve sheath: cutaneous and plexiform neurofibromas; ANNUBP may precede MPNST. Bone: non-ossifying fibromas, tibial dysplasia/pseudarthrosis, and scoliosis. Other soft tissue/systemic tumors: GIST (often multifocal and KIT/PDGFRA/BRAF/SDH-wildtype), glomus tumor, pheochromocytoma, and embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma. CNS: optic pathway glioma and other gliomas, particularly pilocytic astrocytoma in children. Most NF1-associated tumors are histopathologically similar to their sporadic counterparts. MPNST commonly arises from a pre-existing neurofibroma, either abruptly or through ANNUBP. MPNST may show loss of S100/SOX10 and H3K27me3, although loss may be less frequent than in sporadic MPNST. NF1-associated GISTs are usually KIT-, PDGFRA-, BRAF-, and SDH-wildtype and often show spindle cells with skeinoid fibers. NF1 is a tumor suppressor gene at 17q11.2 encoding neurofibromin, a negative regulator of RAS/MAPK signaling. Tumor development may involve a second hit in NF1. ANNUBP may acquire CDKN2A/CDKN2B deletion; progression to MPNST is associated with additional PRC2 gene alterations and, less commonly, TP53 alterations. An NF1 microdeletion including SUZ12 is associated with increased MPNST risk. For mosaic disease, testing affected tissue may be necessary when peripheral blood testing is negative. Legius syndrome Can resemble NF1 clinically with pigmentary findings; NF1-associated neurofibromas and other tumors are generally absent in the specific NF1 genotype–phenotype subsets described in the source. Constitutional mismatch repair deficiency Consider in children with café-au-lait macules and malignant tumors. ANNUBP versus MPNST ANNUBP is a precursor lesion with increased transformation risk; assess morphology and additional molecular alterations, including CDKN2A/CDKN2B and PRC2 pathway changes. A negative blood test does not exclude mosaic NF1; affected tissue may be required. Loss of H3K27me3 or Schwann cell markers is supportive in context but is not independently diagnostic of NF1-associated MPNST. Do not overlook NF1 when a characteristic associated tumor presents before the syndrome has been recognized. Paget Disease of Bone PFN1, SQSTM1, TNFRSF11A, TNFRSF11B, ZNF687 Genetic predisposition; commonly autosomal dominant with incomplete penetrance and variable expressivity Disorder of abnormal osteoclastic and osteoblastic activity producing enlarged, weakened bone with disorganized architecture; a minority of cases have an identifiable hereditary basis. Usually affects adults aged 50 years or older; may be discovered incidentally or through elevated serum alkaline phosphatase. Common sites include pelvis, lumbar spine, long bones, and skull; disease may be monostotic or polyostotic. Symptoms include bone pain, deformity, pathologic fracture, hearing loss, and spinal stenosis. Radiographs may show osteolysis, cortical thickening, coarse trabeculae, bone enlargement, and sclerosis. Malignant transformation is uncommon (<1% in the cited source); Paget-associated sarcomas are usually high-grade osteosarcomas and have poor outcomes. Essential: lamellar bone in a mosaic pattern with prominent cement lines, together with compatible radiographic findings. Osteoclasts and osteoblasts may be prominent in active phases or inconspicuous in the sclerotic phase. Serum total alkaline phosphatase is a first-line biochemical screen for metabolically active disease. Bone scintigraphy can assess disease activity and distribution; CT/MRI evaluate complications. Paget disease may be associated with giant cell tumor of bone, particularly in severe hereditary forms involving ZNF687 or PFN1. Pagetoid sarcoma follows the distribution of Paget disease and is predominantly high-grade osteosarcoma. Secondary sarcoma is rare but should be considered when a previously affected site develops new pain, aggressive destruction, or a soft tissue mass. Three phases are recognized: an initial osteolytic phase, a mixed lytic/sclerotic phase, and a late sclerotic phase. The mixed phase shows disorganized lamellar bone in a mosaic pattern with conspicuous basophilic cement lines. The active lytic phase has numerous osteoclasts in Howship lacunae; osteoclasts may be enlarged and multinucleated. In the late sclerotic phase, bone is thickened and marrow is replaced by fibrovascular tissue. Familial cases are often associated with SQSTM1 variants, particularly in the ubiquitin-binding domain; variants are less frequent in sporadic cases. TNFRSF11A and TNFRSF11B variants are associated with dominant and recessive forms, respectively. PFN1 and ZNF687 variants have been detected in severe Paget disease associated with giant cell tumor of bone. Pathogenesis involves dysregulated osteoclastogenesis and RANKL signaling; SQSTM1/p62 variants may impair CYLD-mediated inhibition of TRAF6 signaling. Fibrous dysplasia Paget disease shows mosaic lamellar bone with prominent cement lines; fibrous dysplasia typically shows irregular woven-bone trabeculae in fibroblastic stroma. Chronic osteomyelitis / reactive remodeling Integrate the characteristic radiographic distribution and mosaic lamellar-bone architecture. Paget-associated osteosarcoma New aggressive destruction or a soft tissue mass in a Paget-affected bone should prompt evaluation for secondary sarcoma. The mosaic pattern with prominent cement lines is the key histologic clue. Do not mistake the enlarged, sometimes hypermultinucleated osteoclasts of Paget disease for a giant cell neoplasm. Malignant transformation is rare, but new symptoms or aggressive imaging findings require further evaluation. title: Adipocytic Tumors
content: use client Lipoma Benign Usually superficial subcutis of upper back, proximal extremity, and abdomen; deep variants include intramuscular, parosteal, and tendon-sheath lesions. Well-circumscribed proliferation of uniform mature adipocytes. Variable paucicellular fibrous septa and fat necrosis may be present; atypical hyperchromatic stromal cells are absent. Intramuscular lipomas may infiltrate skeletal muscle; atrophic entrapped muscle fibers can mimic atypical stromal cells. No routine IHC is required for a typical lipoma. HMGA2 rearrangements involving 12q13–q15 occur in a subset; HMGA2::LPP is a common fusion. MDM2 amplification testing is reserved for selected deep, large, recurrent, or retroperitoneal fatty tumors. ALT/WDLPS Shows at least focal atypical hyperchromatic stromal/adipocytic nuclei, often in septa; MDM2 amplification supports the diagnosis. Intramuscular lipoma Muscle infiltration alone is not malignancy; distinguish atrophic entrapped muscle nuclei from true atypical stromal cells. Lipomatosis A discrete neoplasm versus diffuse regional overgrowth of mature fat. Adipocyte size variation alone does not establish ALT/WDLPS. Deep location and large size warrant careful evaluation but are not independently diagnostic. Diffuse overgrowth; subtype depends on clinical distribution Trunk/extremity, head and neck, abdomen/pelvis, bowel, or symmetric upper-body/neck fat. Diffuse, poorly circumscribed overgrowth of mature adipose tissue in a characteristic anatomic distribution. Histology shows lobules and sheets of mature adipocytes, sometimes infiltrating adjacent structures. Clinical patterns include diffuse, multiple symmetric, pelvic, steroid-associated, and HIV-associated lipodystrophy. No specific IHC profile is established. Multiple symmetric lipomatosis has been associated with mitochondrial DNA variants. Some infiltrating/facial lipomatoses and overgrowth phenotypes harbor somatic PIK3CA variants. Discrete mass versus diffuse regional overgrowth. Lipomatosis lacks atypical hyperchromatic stromal cells and the MDM2-amplified neoplastic phenotype. Massive regional fat accumulation can mimic a neoplasm radiologically; distribution and imaging are important. Lipomatosis of nerve Benign, often progressive hamartomatous overgrowth Appendicular nerves, especially median nerve; upper extremity predominates. Epineurium is expanded by mature adipose tissue, separating and widely spacing nerve fascicles. Perineurial thickening and pseudo-onion-bulb-like hypertrophic change may occur; nerve fiber loss can be present. MRI: coaxial cable-like on cross-section and spaghetti-like longitudinally. EMA, S100, and neurofilament protein may help characterize perineurial and nerve-fiber changes; anatomic relationship is defining. Activating somatic PIK3CA hotspot variants occur in a subset. Intraneural perineurioma A perineurial neoplasm versus epineurial mature fat separating nerve fascicles. Diffuse lipomatosis Nerve-centered epineurial expansion and nerve-territory overgrowth distinguish this entity. Treatment should balance decompression/debulking with preservation of nerve function. Lipoblastoma / lipoblastomatosis Benign; localized or diffuse/infiltrative Predominantly trunk and extremities in infants/young children; also abdomen, pelvis, retroperitoneum, head/neck, and perineum. Lobulated tumor with adipocytic cells at different stages of maturation: primitive stellate/spindled cells, multivacuolated or signet-ring lipoblasts, and mature adipocytes. Fibrovascular septa divide lobules; myxoid zones show plexiform vasculature and primitive mesenchymal cells. Zonal maturation may be present, with immature peripheral myxoid areas and mature central adipocytes. Mitoses are very rare; atypical mitoses and tumor necrosis are absent. Adipocytes may express S100, CD56, and CD34; primitive mesenchymal cells may express CD34 and desmin. Nuclear PLAG1 IHC can support diagnosis but has limited sensitivity and is not a stand-alone test. PLAG1 rearrangement/copy-number gain supports diagnosis in selected cases; 8q11–q13 rearrangements occur in about 60%. HMGA2 alterations are less common; negative PLAG1 does not exclude lipoblastoma. Myxoid liposarcoma Usually older patient/deep extremity; uniform primitive cells, chicken-wire capillaries, DDIT3 alteration. Lipoblastoma shows maturation spectrum and lobular zonation. Mature adipocytes only, without primitive mesenchymal-to-lipoblast maturation. Atypical stromal cells and MDM2 amplification, unlike pediatric lipoblastoma. Lipoblastoma may mature over time and later specimens may show few or no lipoblasts. Lipoblastomatosis is more diffuse/infiltrative and harder to excise, but does not metastasize. Lipoblastoma-like tumor Benign; infrequent local recurrence Often genital/perigenital, especially vulva; also extremities, trunk, pelvis, and retroperitoneum. Multinodular/lobulated growth separated by variably thick acellular fibrous bands. Lobules contain mature adipocytes, small uni-/bivacuolated lipoblasts, and bland spindle cells with fibrillary cytoplasm and blunt-to-tapered nuclei. Matrix is variably myxoid to collagenous, with conspicuous thin-walled plexiform vasculature. Mitoses are infrequent; necrosis is absent. RB1 nuclear expression is often lost or mosaic. Desmin and/or S100 may be expressed; CD34 is positive in a minority. Weak PLAG1, DDIT3, MDM2, or CDK4 IHC may occur without corresponding gene rearrangement/amplification. No recurrent RB1 loss, DDIT3 rearrangement, or PLAG1 rearrangement is established; molecular testing may exclude mimics. LLT spindle cells are bland and mature adipocytes/lipoblasts are admixed; conventional MLPS has uniform primitive cells and DDIT3 rearrangement. Lipoblastoma Usually infancy/early childhood with maturation spectrum; PLAG1 rearrangement in a subset. ASLT Requires atypical hyperchromatic spindle cells; LLT spindle cells are bland. Do not diagnose MLPS from plexiform vessels and myxoid matrix alone. One metastatic case is reported, but dissemination otherwise has not been described in series. Angiolipoma Usually subcutaneous extremities, especially forearm, then trunk. Well-circumscribed nodule of mature adipocytes and clusters of branching capillary-sized vessels. Fibrin thrombi within small vessels are a characteristic clue; vascularity may be peripheral. Cellular angiolipoma may be predominantly vascular. No specific IHC panel is usually required. Low-frequency PRKD2 variants are reported in many cases; no routine molecular test. Ordinary lipoma Lacks conspicuous capillary clusters and fibrin thrombi. Intramuscular hemangioma / visceral vascular lesions Distinct lesions with larger-caliber vessels. Angiosarcoma Angiolipoma lacks endothelial atypia and destructive malignant vascular proliferation. Usually small, painful/tender, and subcutaneous; do not mislabel other vascular lesions as angiolipoma. Myolipoma of soft tissue Usually deep retroperitoneal, abdominal, pelvic, or inguinal soft tissue; less often trunk wall, pleura, or extremities. Intimate admixture of mature adipose tissue and well-differentiated smooth muscle. Smooth muscle forms intersecting fascicles of bland spindle cells with eosinophilic cytoplasm and cigar-shaped nuclei; mitoses absent or rare. Fat lacks atypical hyperchromatic stromal cells, significant fibrous septation, or convincing lipoblasts. Smooth muscle expresses SMA, desmin, and h-caldesmon. ER/PR often positive; HMGA2 nuclear staining in a subset. MDM2, CDK4, and HMB45 are negative in source-described cases. No routine molecular test; HMGA2 alterations reported in some cases. Angiomyolipoma Myolipoma lacks PEComa phenotype/HMB45; angiomyolipoma typically has dysmorphic vessels and melanocytic markers. ALT/WDLPS with smooth muscle differentiation Look for atypical adipocytic/stromal cells and MDM2 amplification. Leiomyoma with entrapped fat Myolipoma has substantial intimate admixture of fat and smooth muscle. Large retroperitoneal lesions can mimic aggressive tumors radiologically; bland cytology and absence of ALT features are important. Chondroid lipoma Usually deep subcutis abutting muscular fascia or skeletal muscle; limbs, limb girdles, and trunk. Circumscribed, usually encapsulated/lobulated mass with mature adipose tissue and chondroid-appearing areas. Chondroid zones contain small lipoblasts at different maturation stages, with uni- to multivacuolated droplets indenting bland or convoluted nuclei. Myxoid/chondroid/hyalinized matrix creates lacuna-like spaces and sharp cell borders; calcification/ossification may occur. S100 reflects maturation: mature adipocytes stain strongly; lipoblastic cells may be weak/negative. Keratin and EMA usually negative; rare focal positivity. ZFTA::MRTFB fusion can confirm selected cases; ZFTA::NCOA1 also reported. A distinct malignant chondroid-lipoma-like sarcoma with ZFTA::RELA has been reported. Chondrolipoma/osteolipoma Mature lipoma with metaplastic cartilage/bone; chondroid lipoma has immature lipoblasts in myxohyaline matrix. Extraskeletal chondrosarcoma Chondroid lipoma is bland and adipocytic; chondrosarcoma shows malignant cytology/destructive growth. Uniform primitive cells and DDIT3 alteration versus chondroid matrix and lipoblastic maturation. Identify the adipocytic/lipoblastic component; use molecular confirmation in atypical cases. Spindle cell lipoma / pleomorphic lipoma Classically subcutaneous posterior neck, back, and shoulder in older men; other sites, particularly in women. Spindle cell lipoma: bland spindle cells, mature adipocytes, and ropey collagen in fibrous or myxoid stroma; mast cells are consistent. Spindle cells are uniform, elongated, randomly distributed or in short fascicles; mitoses absent/rare and necrosis absent. Pleomorphic lipoma additionally contains pleomorphic spindle cells and multinucleated floret-like giant cells. Fat-poor, myxoid, pseudoangiomatous, and plexiform patterns occur. Spindle/floret cells typically CD34-positive; S100 and desmin variable/focal. Nuclear RB1 loss is common and supportive. Heterozygous RB1 loss, often with 13q deletion; molecular confirmation usually unnecessary. ASLT/APLT Require true atypical hyperchromatic spindle cells and/or broader pleomorphism; spindle cell lipoma cells are bland. Atypical stromal/adipocytic cells and MDM2 amplification versus RB1 loss and no MDM2 amplification. DFSP Dermal storiform infiltrative spindle-cell tumor with honeycomb fat entrapment; spindle cell lipoma has ropey collagen, mature fat, CD34-positive bland cells. Floret cells in pleomorphic lipoma do not by themselves indicate malignancy. Avoid obsolete term dendritic fibromyxolipoma. Hibernoma Benign; no malignant subtype Often thigh, trunk, chest, upper extremity, and head/neck; usually deep/intramuscular. Highly vascular tumor of polygonal brown-fat cells with abundant finely multivacuolated cytoplasm. Central round bland nuclei with small nucleoli; scattered univacuolated white-fat cells common. Classic hibernoma contains >70% brown-fat cells; myxoid and spindle-cell patterns occur. Nuclear atypia and mitotic activity are absent. UCP1 strongly highlights brown-fat cells. S100 and CD10 commonly positive; SOX10, CD68, keratin, EMA, and nuclear MDM2 generally negative; Ki-67 low/absent. Rearrangements involving 11q, particularly 11q13; MDM2/CDK4/HMGA2 amplification is not typical. ALT/WDLPS with hibernoma-like areas Atypical hyperchromatic stromal cells and MDM2 amplification versus bland UCP1-positive brown fat. Lacks abundant multivacuolated brown-fat cells and UCP1 expression. Can be intensely FDG-avid and hypervascular; imaging avidity alone does not indicate malignancy. Atypical spindle cell lipomatous tumor (ASLT) / atypical pleomorphic lipomatous tumor (APLT) Intermediate Low local recurrence if incompletely excised; no metastases in source series More often subcutaneous than deep; ASLT more often distal extremities. Lobulated/nodular, often poorly circumscribed lesion, sometimes infiltrative. ASLT: variable mature adipocytes, atypical spindle cells, lipoblasts, and collagenous/myxoid matrix; ropey collagen and mast cells may occur. Essential ASLT feature: at least focal mild-to-moderate spindle-cell atypia with enlarged hyperchromatic irregular nuclei; adipocytes often show marked size variation and focal binucleation/multinucleation. APLT: more extensive bizarre pleomorphic/hyperchromatic cells, often floret-like giant cells and/or pleomorphic lipoblasts; typically more cellular than pleomorphic lipoma. Mitoses generally <1/mm²; necrosis absent. CD34, S100, and desmin variably expressed. RB1 nuclear loss in approximately 50–70%; focal MDM2/CDK4 staining can occur but is not amplification. MDM2/CDK4 amplification absent; 13q14/RB1 loss common; TP53 alterations more frequent in APLT in cited studies. Spindle/pleomorphic lipoma Bland spindle cells and classic posterior neck/back/shoulder site; ASLT requires genuine atypical spindle nuclei; APLT has broader pleomorphism and higher cellularity. ALT/WDLPS or DDLPS MDM2-amplified; ASLT/APLT lack MDM2 amplification and are often superficial. Uniform primitive cells and chicken-wire vessels with DDIT3 alteration; ASLT/APLT show atypical spindle/pleomorphic cells. Adipocyte size variation alone is insufficient; atypical spindle-cell nuclei are essential for ASLT. Floret cells alone do not distinguish APLT from pleomorphic lipoma; assess cellularity and extent of pleomorphism. Rare sarcomatous transformation is reported; significance remains uncertain. ALT / well-differentiated liposarcoma (WDLPS) Locally aggressive; no metastatic potential unless dedifferentiation occurs ALT: deep proximal extremity/trunk. WDLPS: retroperitoneum, spermatic cord, mediastinum. At least focal nuclear atypia in adipocytes and/or stromal cells. Lipoma-like: mature adipocytes with variable fibrous septa and scattered hyperchromatic atypical stromal cells, often in septa or vessel walls. Sclerosing: low-cellularity, extensive fibrillary collagen with scattered bizarre hyperchromatic stromal cells; lipoblasts may be present and fat may be inconspicuous. Inflammatory: chronic lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate, sometimes follicles, may obscure atypical cells and mimic lymphoma. Lipoblasts are not required; patterns may coexist. MDM2 and/or CDK4 typically strong diffuse nuclear expression; staining may be difficult in lipoma-like lesions. MDM2-positive histiocytes in fat necrosis are a pitfall. MDM2 amplification, often with CDK4 co-amplification, is defining; MDM2 FISH is the preferred confirmatory test in difficult cases. Consider testing for recurrent lesions, deep extremity lesions >10 cm, patients >50 years, equivocal atypia, and retroperitoneal/pelvic/abdominal fatty tumors. No atypical stromal/adipocytic nuclei and no MDM2 amplification. Lack MDM2 amplification; often superficial with atypical spindle cells/lipoblasts. Cellular WDLPS vs bland DDLPS Source: 0–4 mitoses/10 HPF favors cellular WDLPS; ≥5 favors DDLPS. HPF diameter was not consistently reported. Perinephric myxoid pseudotumor of fat Mature fat, myxoid degeneration, bland spindle/stellate cells and lymphoplasmacytic inflammation; lacks atypical hyperchromatic stromal cells and MDM2 amplification. Use ALT for surgically amenable sites; WDLPS for retroperitoneum, spermatic cord, and mediastinum. Do not use 'atypical lipoma'. Atypia may be focal; sample thick septa and solid areas. Dedifferentiated liposarcoma (DDLPS) Malignant Malignant; local recurrence and metastatic potential Most often retroperitoneum; also spermatic cord, abdomen/pelvis, mediastinum, and less often extremities. Non-lipogenic malignant mesenchymal component arising with ALT/WDLPS or in a characteristic site with MDM2 amplification. Transition from WDLPS is usually abrupt but may be gradual; WDLPS component may be unsampled or not obvious. High-grade areas commonly resemble UPS/pleomorphic spindle-cell sarcoma; may mimic myxofibrosarcoma, SFT, or inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor. Multiple patterns, including bland and high-grade areas, are common; heterologous myogenic or osteo-/chondrosarcomatous differentiation occurs in a minority. Bland DDLPS may be difficult to distinguish from non-lipogenic cellular WDLPS. Source: 0–4 mitoses/10 HPF favors cellular WDLPS; ≥5 favors DDLPS. 'Low-grade DDLPS' is no longer recommended. MDM2 and/or CDK4 typically strong diffuse nuclear expression. STAT6 can be expressed in a subset due to STAT6 amplification and may mimic SFT. MDM2 amplification is central; FISH is commonly used. High-amplitude copy-number gains involving MDM2 and other 12q13–q15 oncogenes support diagnosis. UPS / pleomorphic sarcoma At characteristic sites, search for WDLPS and test MDM2 amplification. Pleomorphic liposarcoma Has pleomorphic lipoblasts but typically lacks MDM2/CDK4 amplification; DDLPS with homologous lipoblastic differentiation is amplified. Usually superficial and MDM2 non-amplified. Solitary fibrous tumor STAT6 alone is not specific in this setting; integrate morphology and MDM2 amplification. Sample both fatty and solid components; core biopsy may sample only dedifferentiated area. Do not use 'low-grade DDLPS'. Retroperitoneal disease can recur late. Myxoid liposarcoma (MLPS) Malignant; >5% round-cell component defines higher-grade disease in supplied source Deep soft tissue of extremities, especially thigh; primary retroperitoneal MLPS is exceedingly rare. Lobulated tumor with abundant myxoid stroma, uniform small spindle cells, variable lipoblasts, and delicate arborizing chicken-wire capillaries. Tumor cells often cluster around capillaries; mucin pools may create microcystic/pulmonary-edema-like areas. Classic areas are relatively uniform, without substantial atypia or mitotic activity; lipoblasts may be sparse or absent. Higher-grade MLPS: round-cell areas >5% of tumor, usually with diminished myxoid matrix and increased cellularity; record percentage. Pure higher-grade areas may mimic other round-cell sarcomas. Strong diffuse nuclear DDIT3 IHC is highly sensitive/specific in source-cited studies and can be an alternative to molecular testing. Most cases harbor FUS::DDIT3; a small subset has EWSR1::DDIT3. DDIT3 break-apart FISH, RT-PCR, or sequencing can confirm; DDIT3 is more specific than FUS/EWSR1 alone. Infant/young child, maturation spectrum and PLAG1 alteration in subset; MLPS is usually deep extremity tumor with DDIT3 fusion. Bland spindle cells/mature adipocytes; lacks DDIT3 rearrangement. Myxofibrosarcoma Pleomorphic spindle cells/curvilinear vessels versus uniform MLPS cells/chicken-wire network. Other round-cell sarcomas Higher-grade MLPS may be morphologically indistinguishable; demonstrate DDIT3 alteration or diffuse DDIT3 protein. Modest hypercellularity without round-cell morphology is not sufficient for higher-grade MLPS. Adequate sampling is essential; round-cell percentage is prognostically important. Metastases may involve soft tissue and bone/spine rather than predominantly lung. High-grade malignant; substantial local recurrence and metastatic risk Usually deep extremity soft tissue, especially lower limb; also trunk/head-neck; minority subcutaneous. High-grade sarcoma with variable numbers of unequivocal pleomorphic lipoblasts; number varies within tumor, so extensive sampling is essential. Non-lipogenic component often resembles UPS, with markedly pleomorphic spindle cells, giant cells, brisk/atypical mitoses, and frequent necrosis. Myxofibrosarcoma-like areas may occur; approximately one quarter show epithelioid pattern. Epithelioid areas may mimic poorly differentiated carcinoma, renal clear cell carcinoma, adrenocortical carcinoma, or melanoma. MDM2/CDK4 typically negative, separating from DDLPS with lipoblastic differentiation. Epithelioid cases may express keratins and Melan-A; use differential-directed panel. No pathognomonic recurrent rearrangement; absence of MDM2 amplification supports distinction from DDLPS. DDLPS with homologous lipoblastic differentiation DDLPS is MDM2-amplified; pleomorphic liposarcoma typically is not. UPS with entrapped fat Entrapped adipocytes are not pleomorphic lipoblasts; identify tumor-cell lipid vacuoles indenting atypical nuclei. Pleomorphic liposarcoma requires pleomorphic lipoblasts. Carcinoma/melanoma in epithelioid cases Use keratin, melanocytic and organ-specific markers, and demonstrate pleomorphic lipoblasts. Pleomorphic lipoblasts can be focal; generous sampling is mandatory. Do not infer DDLPS from pleomorphic lipoblasts alone; MDM2 status and site matter. Myxoid pleomorphic liposarcoma Extremely aggressive malignant tumor Strong predilection for serosal-lined cavities, especially mediastinum; also abdominopelvic cavity, head/neck, chest wall, trunk, and extremities. Usually children/young adults; often large deep mass in a serosal-lined cavity. Extensively myxoid, relatively hypocellular zones resembling MLPS juxtaposed with hypercellular pleomorphic-liposarcoma-like areas. Myxoid zones may show pseudocysts, elaborate capillaries, and small lipoblasts, but greater spindling, nuclear irregularity, and hyperchromasia than true MLPS. Hypercellular areas show severe atypia, bizarre pleomorphic lipoblasts, increased mitoses, and necrosis. IHC does not play a defining diagnostic role. Widespread loss of heterozygosity with near-haploid or pseudohyperdiploid profiles is characteristic in reported cases. Absence of FUS/EWSR1::DDIT3 helps exclude conventional MLPS; absence of MDM2 amplification helps exclude myxoid WDLPS/DDLPS. Conventional MLPS has uniform primitive cells/chicken-wire capillaries/DDIT3 fusion; myxoid pleomorphic tumor has greater atypia and pleomorphic lipoblast-rich high-grade zones. Pleomorphic liposarcoma with myxoid change Myxoid pleomorphic tumor more often affects younger patients and serosal cavities and has juxtaposed MLPS-like and pleomorphic areas. DDLPS with myxoid morphology DDLPS is MDM2-amplified; myxoid pleomorphic liposarcoma lacks MDM2 amplification and shows widespread LOH. Do not diagnose conventional MLPS from myxoid matrix and delicate vessels alone. Source describes aggressive behavior; adequate sampling and margin assessment are critical. All PathologyGPS / Soft Tissue Tumors / Adipocytic Tumors Adipocytic Tumors A morphology-first diagnostic reference focused on essential criteria, ancillary testing, and practical differential diagnosis. Core rule Interpret atypia, architecture, site, and molecular findings together. Adipocyte size variation alone does not establish ALT/WDLPS. MDM2 amplification is decisive in the appropriate setting. Diagnostic GPS: morphology to classification Establish setting Age, site, depth, size, imaging, circumscribed versus infiltrative/diffuse. Identify dominant pattern Mature fat; maturation spectrum; spindle/myxoid; brown fat; vascular; smooth muscle; or pleomorphic sarcoma. Search for atypia Inspect fibrous septa, vessel walls, and solid areas for hyperchromatic stromal nuclei, lipoblasts, mitoses, and necrosis. Order targeted tests MDM2 for ALT/WDLPS or DDLPS; DDIT3 for MLPS; PLAG1 in selected lipoblastoma; RB1 in selected spindle-cell lesions. Integrate whole lesion Correlate with imaging and sampling; a core may miss WDLPS, dedifferentiation, or focal pleomorphic lipoblasts. Behavior categories are not histologic grade Benign: usually cured by local excision; recurrence is uncommon or related to incomplete removal. Intermediate, locally aggressive: may recur/infiltrate locally but has little or no metastatic potential. ALT/WDLPS at resectable sites is locally aggressive. Intermediate, rarely metastasizing: locally aggressive with a small metastatic risk; the supplied adipocytic excerpt does not assign a principal example. Malignant: destructive growth with metastatic potential; risk varies by histotype and grade. High-yield molecular tests ALT/WDLPS; DDLPS MDM2 amplification (FISH) DDIT3 rearrangement / diffuse DDIT3 IHC PLAG1 rearrangement (supportive; incomplete sensitivity) Spindle cell / pleomorphic lipoma RB1 loss (supportive) UCP1 IHC ZFTA::MRTFB or ZFTA::NCOA1 in selected cases Entity reference Diagnostic criteria and differential diagnosis Search by entity, morphology, site, marker, or gene. e.g. MDM2, DDIT3, RB1, lipoblast... bg-teal-700 text-white border border-slate-300 bg-white text-slate-600 Collapse View diagnostic profile − + Essential morphology / criteria Immunohistochemistry Molecular pathology Differential diagnosis Diagnostic pitfalls No matching entity. High-stakes comparison: lipoma, ALT/WDLPS, ASLT/APLT, and DDLPS Feature DDLPS Atypical nuclei Absent Present, often focal Atypical spindle/pleomorphic cells Variable; malignant non-lipogenic component MDM2 amplification Present Typical site Often superficial Deep extremity / retroperitoneum Often subcutaneous Predominantly retroperitoneal Metastatic potential None Only after dedifferentiation Not established in source series Yes Biopsy, sampling, and reporting checklist Correlate with imaging: exact site, depth, size, and fatty/nonfatty solid components. Sample radiologically enhancing solid nodules, thick septa, and heterogeneous areas. For suspected ALT/WDLPS or DDLPS, target atypical septa/solid areas and consider MDM2 FISH when morphology is equivocal or sampling is limited. In core biopsies, state limitations: a small sample may miss a WDLPS component, dedifferentiation, or focal pleomorphic lipoblasts. For MLPS, quantify round-cell component; >5% defines higher-grade disease in the supplied source. Report histotype, grade where applicable, necrosis, mitotic activity per mm² when feasible, and margins. Scope note: Based on the supplied WHO source excerpt. Ancillary tests described as supportive or selectively useful are not stand-alone criteria. The page does not replace radiologic correlation, adequate sampling, or expert soft-tissue pathology review.
entities: Atypical spindle cell lipomatous tumor (ASLT) / atypical pleomorphic lipomatous tumor (APLT)

title: Chondro Osseous Tumors
content: use client Soft Tissue Chondroma Benign chondro-osseous tumors Benign; local recurrence is reported in approximately 15–20% after marginal excision Approximately 80% occur in the region of the fingers. Other common sites include the hands, toes, and feet; trunk and head and neck are uncommon. Usually a solitary, painless, firm, slowly enlarging mass. Most patients are adults aged 30–60 years (median 34.5 years); men are affected more often than women (M:F approximately 1.5:1). Radiographs typically show a well-demarcated soft-tissue mass separated from bone, with spiculated or ring-like calcifications. Cartilage is bright on T2-weighted MRI. Rare locations reported in the skin, lip, and dura. Essential: a soft-tissue mass composed of nodules of well-delineated cartilage. The cartilaginous matrix is hyaline or myxoid and may show calcification. Chondrocytes show limited atypia and little mitotic activity. Establish the extraosseous and extrasynovial location; imaging should demonstrate separation from adjacent bone. Grossly, a well-circumscribed, nodular, solid, greyish-bluish-white mass, sometimes with focal myxoid areas; most are smaller than 30 mm. Microscopy shows lobules of well-formed hyaline cartilage delineated by fibrous septa. Cartilage is often hypercellular. Chondrocytes occur in clusters within lacunar spaces or may appear to float in a flocculent myxoid matrix. Nuclei are usually small, round, and dark. Larger nuclei with fine or coarse chromatin, small nucleoli, and mild-to-moderate pleomorphism may occur; these changes should be interpreted with the overall bland architecture and limited mitotic activity. Coarse calcification and endochondral ossification may be present. Chondrocytes in mineralized areas may undergo necrosis; heavily calcified lesions may contain histiocytes that obscure the underlying cartilage. A chondroblastoma-like pattern is hypercellular, with grooved or cleaved nuclei and moderate eosinophilic cytoplasm. Grungy calcification may surround individual chondrocytes and mimic chondroblastoma. Calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate crystals may be present in a subset. Mitotic activity is limited. The supplied WHO excerpt does not specify a defining immunohistochemical profile. Do not invent a marker-based diagnosis: the diagnosis rests on the extraosseous location and characteristic lobulated hyaline cartilage with limited atypia and mitotic activity. Diagnostic molecular pathology is not clinically relevant according to the supplied WHO excerpt. Limited cytogenetic studies have reported heterogeneous abnormalities, including 12q13–q15 rearrangements and trisomy 5; HMGA2 transcripts have been identified in a subset with 12q13–q15 rearrangements. Approximately half of cases, particularly those with a chondroblastoma-like pattern, have been reported to harbor FN1 rearrangements with FGFR1 or FGFR2 fusion partners; PDGFRA fusions have also been reported. These reported alterations are pathogenetic observations, not required diagnostic tests. Chondroblastoma-like soft tissue chondroma vs chondroblastoma The chondroblastoma-like pattern can show grooved/cleaved nuclei and pericellular grungy calcification. Correlate with imaging and anatomic location: soft tissue chondroma is extraosseous and extrasynovial, whereas the supplied excerpt describes the mimicry but does not provide a complete bone-tumor differential panel. Heavily calcified soft tissue chondroma vs a nonspecific calcified mass Extensive mineralization, chondrocyte necrosis, and histiocytic infiltrates can obscure the cartilage. Search for residual lobules of hyaline cartilage and fibrous septa. Soft tissue chondroma vs malignant cartilaginous lesion The expected pattern is well-delineated cartilage nodules, limited cytologic atypia, and little mitotic activity. The supplied excerpt does not provide formal criteria for extraskeletal chondrosarcoma; do not overcall malignancy from hypercellularity or focal nuclear variation alone. Do not mistake hypercellularity or mild-to-moderate nuclear pleomorphism alone for malignancy; integrate lobular architecture, limited atypia, and low mitotic activity. The chondroblastoma-like variant may be misleading because of grooved nuclei and grungy pericellular calcification. Heavy calcification can produce necrotic chondrocytes and a histiocytic infiltrate that obscures the cartilaginous nature of the lesion. Confirm that the lesion is separate from bone and is extrasynovial; imaging correlation is important. Molecular alterations reported in small series are not clinically required for diagnosis. Treatment is marginal excision. The reported recurrence rate is approximately 15–20%. The supplied WHO excerpt does not describe metastatic behavior. Extraskeletal Osteosarcoma Malignant chondro-osseous tumors High-grade malignant neoplasm; prognosis is substantially influenced by metastatic status, size, site, and completeness of resection Usually a deep soft-tissue mass, most often in the limbs and particularly the lower extremity. Other frequent sites include buttock, shoulder, trunk, and retroperitoneum; dermal or subcutaneous origin is occasional. Usually presents as a progressively enlarging mass, sometimes painful; some patients have lung metastases at presentation. Typically occurs in midlife or later adulthood, most often between 50 and 60 years, although the reported age range is wide (12–90 years); pediatric cases are uncommon. Accounts for less than 1% of soft-tissue sarcomas and approximately 5% of osteosarcomas. No clear sex predilection is established. Imaging generally shows a large, deep soft-tissue mass with variable mineralization and heterogeneous post-contrast enhancement. By definition, the tumor does not arise from bone and does not represent metastasis from a skeletal osteosarcoma, although secondary involvement of bone may occur. Most cases arise de novo; approximately 5–10% are associated with previous radiation. Essential: malignant cells are directly associated with neoplastic bone/osteoid produced by the tumor. The tumor must have no connection to the skeletal system at origin. Exclude osteoblastic/osteogenic differentiation occurring as a heterologous component of another tumor. There is no minimum amount of neoplastic bone required, but the osteoid/bone must be convincingly neoplastic and intimately associated with malignant tumor cells. Grossly, tumors range from 10 to 500 mm (mean approximately 80–100 mm) and may be circumscribed, tan-white, hemorrhagic, and necrotic. Mineralization ranges from gritty foci to heavily formed bone; extensive hemorrhagic cystic change occurs in a minority. The histology spans the patterns recognized in conventional skeletal osteosarcoma. Osteoblastic morphology is most common; chondroblastic and fibroblastic patterns also occur. Tumor cells may be spindle, polygonal, epithelioid, plasmacytoid, or markedly anaplastic. Mitotic activity is typically brisk, and atypical mitoses may be present; tumor necrosis is common. The defining feature is neoplastic bone intimately associated with malignant cells. Deposition may be lace-like, ribbon-like, trabecular, or sheet-like. In some tumors, bone is more prominent centrally while densely cellular tumor is peripheral. This is the reverse of the zonal pattern described for myositis ossificans. Distinguish true neoplastic osteoid/bone from fibrillary collagen deposition (pseudo-osteoid). Rare well-differentiated examples show abundant well-formed trabecular bone surrounded by a minimally atypical spindle-cell component resembling parosteal or low-grade central osteosarcoma; high-grade transformation/dedifferentiation has rarely been reported. SATB2 immunoreactivity may help identify osteoblastic differentiation when bone is difficult to distinguish from collagenous stroma. SATB2 is not specific. It supports osteoblastic differentiation but cannot establish extraskeletal osteosarcoma independently. MDM2 expression may occur in rare well-differentiated examples, similar to parosteal and low-grade central osteosarcoma; MDM2 amplification in low-grade extraskeletal osteosarcoma has been reported rarely and inconsistently. The supplied WHO excerpt does not define a comprehensive immunohistochemical panel. Use morphology, imaging, and exclusion of another primary tumor as the diagnostic foundation. High-grade tumors show clonal, highly complex chromosomal aberrations. Reported genomic changes include losses involving CDKN2A, TP53, RB1, PTEN, NF1, and LSAMP; gains/amplifications involving RUNX2, CDC5L, COPS3, EGFR, MDM2, CDK4, and PMP22; and mutations in multiple tumor-suppressor, chromatin-remodeling, histone-modifying, WNT/β-catenin, and sonic hedgehog pathway genes. TERT promoter and PIK3CA mutations have also been reported. Genomic profiles overlap with conventional skeletal osteosarcoma and undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma. Rare MDM2 amplification in low-grade examples is not a consistent defining finding and should not be used as a stand-alone diagnostic criterion. Myositis ossificans The supplied WHO excerpt highlights a reverse zonation pattern: extraskeletal osteosarcoma may have more prominent bone centrally and densely cellular tumor peripherally, the reverse of myositis ossificans. Evaluate the architecture and the intimate association of malignant cells with neoplastic osteoid. Pseudo-osteoid / collagen deposition Fibrillary collagen may mimic osteoid. Confirm genuine neoplastic bone/osteoid intimately associated with malignant cells; SATB2 may assist in recognizing osteoblastic differentiation but is not specific. Skeletal osteosarcoma with soft-tissue extension or metastasis Extraskeletal osteosarcoma requires no skeletal connection at origin and must not represent metastasis from an underlying skeletal osteosarcoma. Correlate with imaging and clinical history. Heterologous osteoblastic differentiation in another tumor Exclude osteoblastic differentiation as a heterologous component of another neoplasm; this exclusion is part of the essential diagnostic criteria. Well-differentiated extraskeletal osteosarcoma vs parosteal/low-grade central osteosarcoma Rare extraskeletal examples may resemble these low-grade skeletal osteosarcomas, with abundant trabecular bone and minimally atypical spindle cells. Establish the extraosseous origin and absence of skeletal attachment; MDM2 expression is not by itself decisive. Do not diagnose extraskeletal osteosarcoma merely because a soft-tissue tumor contains calcification or bone; malignant cells must be intimately associated with neoplastic osteoid/bone. Do not mistake fibrillary collagen (pseudo-osteoid) for true osteoid. There is no minimum quantity of neoplastic bone required, but its authenticity and association with malignant cells are essential. Do not overlook the requirement to exclude a skeletal primary, metastasis, or secondary extension from bone. SATB2 is supportive for osteoblastic differentiation but is not specific and cannot replace morphologic assessment. Remember the reverse central-to-peripheral distribution relative to myositis ossificans described in some cases. Do not use rare MDM2 expression/amplification as a general defining feature of extraskeletal osteosarcoma. In non-metastatic patients undergoing complete resection, reported 5-year overall survival is approximately 37–66%; reported 5-year disease-free survival is approximately 43–82%. Adverse or significant prognostic variables identified in multivariable analyses include older age, larger tumor size, positive surgical margins, axial site, metastasis, and chemotherapy status. Simultaneous TP53 and RB1 copy-number losses or CDKN2A loss have been associated with worse overall survival and/or local recurrence in reported studies. UICC/AJCC TNM staging can be applied. All PathologyGPS / Soft Tissue Tumors / Chondro-osseous Tumors Chondro-osseous Tumors A morphology-first diagnostic reference focused on the distinction between benign soft tissue chondroma and malignant extraskeletal osteosarcoma, with emphasis on essential criteria, osteoid recognition, and exclusion of skeletal origin. Core diagnostic rule Cartilage nodules with limited atypia favor soft tissue chondroma; malignant cells producing true osteoid define extraskeletal osteosarcoma. For extraskeletal osteosarcoma, prove the osteoid is neoplastic, intimately associated with malignant cells, and not arising from or representing spread from bone. Diagnostic GPS: morphology to classification 1. Establish the compartment Confirm a soft-tissue-centered lesion. For chondroma, document separation from bone and extrasynovial location; for osteosarcoma, exclude skeletal origin. 2. Identify the matrix Determine whether the lesion contains lobulated hyaline/myxoid cartilage or true neoplastic osteoid/bone. Do not equate calcification or collagen with osteoid. 3. Assess cytology and growth Soft tissue chondroma usually has well-delineated cartilage nodules, limited atypia, and little mitotic activity. Extraskeletal osteosarcoma shows malignant cells, brisk mitoses, and often necrosis. 4. Test the critical distinction In suspected osteosarcoma, establish intimate association between malignant cells and neoplastic osteoid; distinguish pseudo-osteoid and consider the zonal pattern relative to myositis ossificans. 5. Correlate and report Use imaging to assess bone connection, primary skeletal disease, and mineralization. SATB2 may support osteoblastic differentiation but is not specific. High-yield essential diagnostic criteria Soft tissue chondroma: well-delineated cartilage nodules; hyaline or myxoid matrix, sometimes calcified; limited chondrocytic atypia and little mitotic activity. Extraskeletal osteosarcoma: malignant cells intimately associated with neoplastic bone/osteoid; no skeletal connection at origin; exclude heterologous osteoblastic differentiation in another tumor. No minimum amount of neoplastic bone is required for extraskeletal osteosarcoma, but the matrix must be genuine neoplastic osteoid/bone. SATB2 can help identify osteoblastic differentiation when osteoid is difficult to distinguish from collagen, but it is not specific. Critical distinction Feature Soft tissue chondroma Extraskeletal osteosarcoma Biology Benign Malignant Typical setting Digits / hands; adults 30–60 Deep soft tissue; usually age 50–60 Matrix Hyaline or myxoid cartilage Neoplastic osteoid / bone Architecture Well-delineated cartilage lobules Variable osteoblastic, chondroblastic, or fibroblastic pattern Cytology Limited atypia; low mitotic activity Malignant cells; usually brisk mitoses Necrosis May affect chondrocytes in calcified areas Tumor necrosis common Key exclusion Bone connection / synovial origin Skeletal primary, metastasis, or secondary extension Entity reference Diagnostic criteria and differential diagnosis Search by morphology, matrix, site, immunomarker, or diagnostic pitfall. e.g. osteoid, SATB2, pseudo-osteoid, grungy calcification... bg-teal-700 text-white border border-slate-300 bg-white text-slate-600 Collapse − View diagnostic profile + Clinical profile Essential diagnostic criteria Histopathology Immunohistochemistry Molecular pathology Differential diagnosis Prognosis and behavior Diagnostic pitfalls No matching entity. Differential diagnosis: practical decision points Diagnostic problem Key discriminating feature Practical next step Calcified digital soft-tissue mass Well-delineated lobules of hyaline cartilage, limited atypia, low mitotic activity Correlate with imaging to confirm separation from bone and extrasynovial location Chondroblastoma-like chondroma Grooved/cleaved nuclei and grungy pericellular calcification may mimic chondroblastoma Reassess the anatomic compartment and search for the characteristic soft-tissue cartilage lobules Soft-tissue mass with mineralization and atypical cells True osteoid must be intimately associated with malignant cells Distinguish osteoid from fibrillary collagen; SATB2 may assist but is not specific Osteoid-forming soft-tissue malignancy Extraskeletal osteosarcoma requires no skeletal connection at origin Review imaging/history to exclude skeletal primary, metastasis, and secondary extension Ossifying lesion with central bone Extraskeletal osteosarcoma may show central bone and peripheral cellular tumor, reverse of myositis ossificans Evaluate zonation and the cytologic malignancy of the cellular component Osteoid in a tumor with another line of differentiation Heterologous osteoblastic differentiation in another neoplasm must be excluded Classify the primary neoplasm before diagnosing extraskeletal osteosarcoma Reporting checklist Record the precise soft-tissue site, depth, size, and relationship to adjacent bone and joint/synovium. For soft tissue chondroma, describe lobular cartilage architecture, matrix type, calcification/ossification, cytologic atypia, and mitotic activity. For extraskeletal osteosarcoma, document malignant cell morphology, osteoid/bone pattern, necrosis, mitotic activity, and the intimate association of malignant cells with neoplastic matrix. State that imaging/clinical correlation excludes a skeletal primary, metastatic osteosarcoma, and secondary extension from bone. If SATB2 is used, interpret it as supportive but nonspecific evidence of osteoblastic differentiation. For extraskeletal osteosarcoma, report margin status and relevant staging information; UICC/AJCC TNM staging can be applied. Scope note: This reference is based on the supplied WHO excerpt for soft tissue chondroma and extraskeletal osteosarcoma. The excerpt does not provide a comprehensive immunohistochemical differential panel for all mimics; unprovided marker profiles and diagnostic criteria have therefore not been added.

title: Fibroblastic And Myofibroblastic Tumors
content: use client Nodular fasciitis Nodular fasciitis (NF) is a benign mesenchymal neoplasm composed of plump, uniform fibroblastic/myofibroblastic cells that display a tissue culture–like pattern. • NF typically develops on the surface of fascia and extends into the subcutis, although occasional cases are intramuscular • Dermal localization is less common • Essential: bland, myofibroblastic spindle cell proliferation with a feathery, tissue culture–like growth pattern • Variably myxoid stroma with microcystic changes • Extravasated red blood cells • Desirable: assessment of USP6 gene rearrangements can be helpful in selected cases • NF is composed of plump spindle to stellate cells lacking nuclear hyperchromasia or pleomorphism • Mitotic figures may be plentiful, but atypical forms are not observed • Although the tumor may be highly cellular, it typically exhibits cystic discohesion and myxoid stromal changes, imparting a torn, feathery, or tissue culture–like appearance • Hypercellular areas often show S- or C-shaped fascicles, or a storiform growth pattern • Stromal collagen is usually minimal, though keloidal collagen bundles may be present and occasionally prominent • Molecular testing is usually unnecessary in clinically and histologically typical cases • However, in challenging cases, break-apart USP6 FISH or targeted RNA fusion assays or next-generation sequencing techniques may be used to support the diagnosis • USP6 fusion genes are not identified in all cases of NF, and a negative result does not exclude the diagnosis • Myxofibrosarcoma or low-grade myofibroblastic sarcoma: look for infiltrative malignant growth, atypia, and atypical mitoses • USP6 supports nodular fasciitis Proliferative fasciitis and proliferative myositis Proliferative fasciitis is a subcutaneous benign neoplasm characterized by large ganglion-like cells and plump myofibroblastic cells. Proliferative myositis has the same cellular composition but occurs within skeletal muscle. • Proliferative fasciitis develops most frequently in the upper extremities, particularly the forearms, followed by the lower extremities and trunk • Proliferative myositis arises predominantly in the trunk, shoulder girdles, and upper arms, and less often in the thighs • Essential: plump spindle cells admixed with ganglion-like cells • Variable collagenous/myxoid stroma • Subcutaneous/fascial involvement (proliferative fasciitis) • Intramuscular checkerboard growth pattern (proliferative myositis) • These cells usually have one nucleus but may have two or three • They may be evenly or irregularly distributed • Mitotic figures are found in both the spindle cells and the ganglion-like cells and may be relatively numerous but are not atypical • The stroma varies from myxoid to collagenous • The lesional borders are typically infiltrative or poorly defined • The neoplastic ganglion-like cells show FOS rearrangement, which is detectable by FISH, whereas the reactive spindle cells lack FOS rearrangement • Nodular fasciitis: ganglion-like cells favor proliferative fasciitis/myositis • Checkerboard entrapment of muscle favors proliferative myositis Myositis ossificans and fibro-osseous pseudotumor of digits Myositis ossificans and fibro-osseous pseudotumor of digits are self-limited, benign neoplasms composed of spindle cells and osteoblasts associated with bone formation. • Myositis ossificans can occur throughout the body, with common sites including trauma-prone areas, such as the elbow, thigh, buttock, and shoulder • Essential: hypercellular fascicles of uniform spindle cells • Admixed woven bone with zonation, being most mature at the periphery • Myositis ossificans is characterized by a distinctive zonal architecture • In the centre, the lesion is densely cellular, composed of spindle cells oriented randomly or in short intersecting fascicles • The spindle cells have eosinophilic cytoplasm and plump vesicular nuclei with nucleoli • Normal mitoses are often numerous • The stroma is vascular and myxoid and contains fibrin, extravasated erythrocytes, scattered lymphocytes, and osteoclast-like giant cells • Molecular studies for USP6 rearrangement may be useful in the appropriate clinicopathological context • Extraskeletal osteosarcoma: orderly peripheral maturation favors myositis ossificans • Malignant osteoid and absent zonation favor osteosarcoma Ischaemic fasciitis Ischaemic fasciitis is a reactive pseudosarcomatous fibroblastic/myofibroblastic proliferation, often associated with prolonged compression of soft tissue overlying bony prominences. • Ischaemic fasciitis usually arises around the limb girdles, sacral region, and greater trochanter • The chest wall and back may also be affected • Ischaemic fasciitis usually develops in the deep subcutis, but involvement of the deep dermis, skeletal muscle, and tendinous tissue can also occur • Essential: zonal appearance with central fibrinoid degeneration and cystic changes • Periphery with granulation tissue–like vascular component • Admixed plump ganglion-like myofibroblasts • The histological hallmark of ischaemic fasciitis is a distinct zonal appearance • The central part of the lesion is characterized by a hypocellular area of fibrinoid degeneration/necrosis with or without pseudocystic degeneration or infarcted fat • The fibroblastic/myofibroblastic cells vary in size and shape • Fibrosis/fibrohyalinosis or myxoid stromal change, hyalinosis of vessel walls, vessels with fibrin thrombi, an inflammatory infiltrate, and extravasated erythrocytes may be observed • Mitotic activity can be seen, mainly in the granulation tissue–like areas, but is inconspicuous overall • Not clinically relevant • Proliferative fasciitis: central fibrinoid necrosis and pseudocystic change with peripheral granulation tissue favor ischemic fasciitis Elastofibroma Elastofibroma is a benign, poorly defined proliferation of fibroelastic tissue with excessive abnormal elastic fibers. • Elastofibroma most often arises in the deep soft tissue between the lower scapula and the thoracic wall • It may rarely occur in extrascapular locations, including other parts of the thoracic wall, extremities, limb girdles, neck, eyes, oral cavity, and gastrointestinal tract or other viscera • Essential: a bland, hypocellular fibrofatty tumor with excessive abnormal elastic fibers • A focally myxoid matrix is common • Immunohistochemically, the spindle cells are positive for CD34, but negative for SMA, desmin, and S100 • Desmoid-type fibromatosis: elastofibroma contains characteristic abnormal elastic fibers and mature fat • Desmoid shows sweeping fascicles Fibrous hamartoma of infancy Fibrous hamartoma of infancy (FHI) is a benign soft tissue neoplasm of infants and young children, characterized by an organoid, triphasic morphology composed of bundles of bland fibroblastic/myofibroblastic cells, nodules of primitive mesenchyme, and mature adipose tissue. • FHI commonly involves the axillae, trunk, upper extremities, and genital region • Other reported locations include the scalp, foot, hand, orbit, and buttock • Essential: triphasic morphology consisting of fibroblastic/myofibroblastic bundles, primitive mesenchymal nodules, and mature adipose tissue • About 25% of cases show areas resembling giant cell fibroblastoma [[Martos-Cabrera L, Sampedro-Ruiz R, Pérez-González YC, et al • Hamartoma fibroso de la infancia: una serie de 21 casos y revisión de la literatura • Actas Dermosifiliogr • 2021 • 112:520–7 • Lipofibromatosis: the triphasic pattern with primitive mesenchymal nodules favors fibrous hamartoma of infancy Fibromatosis colli Fibromatosis colli is a benign, self-limited fibrous proliferation occurring in the sternocleidomastoid muscle of infants. Some cases progress to shortening of the muscle, resulting in torticollis. • Fibromatosis colli affects the sternocleidomastoid muscle, with a predilection for the right over the left • Most commonly, the middle or distal third of the muscle body is involved • However, about 15% of cases involve the entire muscle • Essential: fusiform mass in the sternocleidomastoid muscle of infants • Bland fibroblastic proliferation with associated atrophic skeletal muscle • Surgical specimens are infrequent, obtained only from the minority of patients requiring tenotomy for persistent torticollis • When histology is obtained, sections demonstrate a paucicellular, scar-like fibroblastic proliferation entrapping skeletal muscle • Infantile fibromatosis: sternocleidomastoid-centered lesion in an infant with atrophic entrapped muscle supports fibromatosis colli Juvenile hyaline fibromatosis Juvenile hyaline fibromatosis is a rare autosomal recessive disorder characterized by painful and disfiguring deposits of hyalinized fibrous material in the dermis, subcutaneous soft tissues, gingiva, and viscera. • Juvenile hyaline fibromatosis is a multisystem disease that involves the skin, subcutaneous tissue, gingiva, bone, and viscera • Juvenile hyaline fibromatosis typically presents in infancy but can also manifest later in childhood, with more severe cases appearing earlier • Essential: subcutaneous nodules and gingival hypertrophy with abundant hyaline-like material • Desirable: confirmation by germline sequencing of ANTXR2 • Lesions are characterized by abundant extracellular eosinophilic, non-fibrillar hyaline-like material that obliterates normal tissue structures • The cellular component comprises plump to spindled, uniform fibroblasts, often arranged in cords mimicking vascular spaces • The extracellular matrix deposits are strongly PAS-positive and diastase-resistant • The identification of a pathogenic germline variant mutation in ANTXR2 (4q21.21) confirms the diagnosis • Other hyaline deposition disorders: PAS-positive, diastase-resistant extracellular hyaline plus gingival and systemic findings support this syndrome Calcifying fibrous tumor Calcifying fibrous tumor is a benign paucicellular fibroblastic neoplasm with dense stromal collagen, chronic inflammation, and variably prominent psammomatous and/or dystrophic calcification, which often arises on serosal surfaces. • In soft tissues, calcifying fibrous tumor may involve subcutaneous fat or deep somatic tissue, and has been reported to occur on the trunk, neck, and extremities • Tumours often arise at serosal sites, specifically pleura, peritoneum, and paratesticular serosal surfaces • Essential: circumscribed hypocellular densely collagenous mass • Scattered bland spindled fibroblasts and a sparse lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate • Desirable: admixed dystrophic or psammomatous calcifications • Calcifying fibrous tumor is characteristically a paucicellular circumscribed mass with abundant hyalinized collagen, within which are scattered, bland, long spindled fibroblasts • These lesional cells have pale eosinophilic cytoplasm and are often inconspicuous among the collagen • There may be clefts or cracks within the collagenous stroma • Admixed calcifications may be of dystrophic or psammomatous type and may be abundant or sparse • Around 20% do not have calcifications and may be more difficult to recognize (non-calcifying calcifying fibrous tumor) • GIST or inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor: dense hyalinized collagen, psammomatous/dystrophic calcification, and lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate • KIT/DOG1 and ALK are typically negative Inclusion body fibromatosis Inclusion body fibromatosis is a benign, sometimes multicentric, myofibroblastic neoplasm with characteristic eosinophilic intracytoplasmic inclusions. • Extradigital examples are reported on the extremities, tongue, and breast • Essential: dermal-based, cytologically bland myofibroblastic proliferation • Eosinophilic intracytoplasmic and paranuclear inclusions • Spindle cells have lightly eosinophilic cytoplasm and an elongated, cytologically bland nucleus, and they exhibit low mitotic activity • Cells proliferate in whorls, interlacing short fascicles, or storiform arrays within a variably collagenous dermis • They characteristically grow perpendicular to the epidermis, surround adnexa, and occasionally infiltrate deeper tissues • By immunohistochemistry, the inclusions are commonly highlighted with actin, calponin, and (occasionally) caldesmon • Digital fibromatosis without inclusions: the characteristic eosinophilic paranuclear inclusions are the key discriminator Fibroma of tendon sheath Fibroma of tendon sheath (FTS) is a benign fibroblastic/myofibroblastic spindle cell neoplasm, usually attached to a tendon sheath. • FTS typically arises on the flexor tendons of the fingers, most commonly affecting the thumb, index, and middle fingers • Intra-articular
