involvement, particularly of the knee, elbow, or wrist, is rare • Essential: a paucicellular or moderately cellular collagen-rich lesion with slit-like vessels • Desirable: occurs most often on the finger tendons • FTS is well circumscribed and lobulated, composed of bland spindle cells embedded in a collagenous stroma • The cellularity is generally low but can be variable, often increasing towards the periphery of the tumor • Characteristic slit-like, thin-walled vessels are typically present and tend to be more conspicuous at the edges • Degenerative changes, including myxoid or cystic alterations, chondroid or osseous metaplasia, and occasional pleomorphic cells, may be observed • The morphological features of FTS can overlap with those of nodular fasciitis, myofibroma, and desmoplastic fibroma, making the differential diagnosis challenging • The identification of USP6 fusion genes or locus rearrangement may be useful • Nodular fasciitis: FTS is collagen-rich and lobulated with slit-like vessels • NF is more myxoid and tissue-culture-like Desmoplastic fibroblastoma Desmoplastic fibroblastoma is a benign, paucicellular, hypovascular neoplasm composed of bland spindle or stellate fibroblasts within abundant collagenous stroma. • The most common sites are the upper arm, shoulder, lower limb, back, and forearm • Tumors may also arise on the hands and feet • The tumor typically presents as an asymptomatic, painless, slow-growing subcutaneous mass, but fascial and skeletal muscle involvement is relatively common • Essential: hypocellular and hypovascular tumor with abundant collagenous stroma • Bland spindled and stellate cells • Although well demarcated grossly, most tumors microscopically infiltrate subcutaneous fat, and approximately 25% extend into skeletal muscle • Rare examples are purely intramuscular • The lesions have abundant collagenous or myxocollagenous matrix with hypovascularity • Cellularity ranges from low to moderate, and the neoplastic cells tend to be uniformly distributed within the extracellular matrix • The lesional cells are stellate, bipolar, and spindled, and they have uniform, bland nuclei with distinct small nucleoli • Fibroma of tendon sheath: diffuse strong nuclear FOSL1 supports desmoplastic fibroblastoma • FTS more often has slit-like vessels Myofibroblastoma Myofibroblastoma is a benign neoplasm composed of myofibroblastic cells and bands of hyalinized collagen, with a variable adipocytic component. • Approximately half of cases occur in the inguinal/groin area, including the vulva/vagina, perineum, and scrotum • However, there is a wide anatomical distribution, including trunk/axilla, breast, extremities, abdominal cavity, retroperitoneum, and viscera • The majority are superficial/subcutaneous • Essential: haphazardly intersecting short fascicles of bland spindle cells • Bands of hyalinized collagen • Variable adipocytic component • Desirable: expression of CD34 and/or desmin • Tumours are unencapsulated and generally well circumscribed • The spindle cells are arranged in variably sized short fascicles, with interspersed broad bands of hyalinized collagen or (less commonly) ropy collagen • Scattered mast cells are often present • Tumours may vary from markedly cellular to paucicellular and hyalinized and usually contain admixed mature adipocytes, which can range from rare to occasionally the dominant component • Schwannoma-like palisading, focal epithelioid or round cell morphology, or degenerative-type nuclear atypia (enlarged hyperchromatic nuclei and multinucleation) can occur • Loss of RB1 can be demonstrated by FISH, although this is usually not necessary to establish the diagnosis • Cellular angiofibroma and spindle cell lipoma: overlap in the RB1-deleted family • Integrate site, vessels, collagen, adipocytes, desmin and CD34 Calcifying aponeurotic fibroma Calcifying aponeurotic fibroma (CAF) is a benign neoplasm with a propensity to arise in the soft tissues of the hands and feet in children and adolescents, characterized by alternating zones of bland spindle cells and less cellular, partly calcified zones with plump to epithelioid cells. • CAF arises most commonly on the palmar surfaces of the hands and fingers, followed by the plantar surfaces of the feet and toes • Wrists and ankles are less commonly involved • Essential: geographical areas of calcified matrix surrounded by palisading epithelioid fibroblasts • Interspersed bland spindle cells in a collagenous stroma • The cellular component has a fibromatosis-like appearance with infiltration of adjacent soft tissue components • Entrapment of nerves and vessels may be seen • The cells show no nuclear atypia or mitotic activity • The cells are often arranged around the calcifications • Osteoclast-type giant cells are frequently seen in these areas, and osseous metaplasia has been described • Detection of the FN1::EGF gene fusion may be helpful in cases of CAF lacking calcification, although this is not required for routine diagnosis as most cases display the salient features • Fibromatosis or soft-tissue chondroma: alternating cellular spindle zones and calcified epithelioid-cell foci support calcifying aponeurotic fibroma SMAD3-rearranged fibroblastic tumor SMAD3-rearranged fibroblastic tumor is a benign spindle cell neoplasm with EWSR1::SMAD3 fusion and a predilection for superficial acral sites, characterized by alternating cellular fascicles and hyalinized areas. • Tumours are superficially located within dermis and/or subcutaneous fat • These lesions occur on the extremities with a large majority located in the hands and feet • Essential: superficial acral nodule • Short intersecting cellular fascicles of bland spindle cells with variably hyalinized areas • Desirable: immunoreactivity for ERG • EWSR1::SMAD3 fusion or EWSR1 gene rearrangement in select cases • The tumors are typically well demarcated but show infiltration into subcutaneous fat • Superficial cases may directly abut the epidermis • The tumors consist of short intersecting cellular fascicles of monomorphic fibroblastic spindle cells lacking nuclear pleomorphism, hyperchromasia, or prominent nucleoli • Mitotic activity is typically low • The stroma is either collagenous or myxoid • The EWSR1::SMAD3 fusion or EWSR1 gene rearrangement may be confirmed by molecular methods • Other superficial acral spindle-cell tumors: correlate the characteristic morphology with SMAD3 rearrangement • Avoid diagnosis by CD34/ERG alone PRRX1-rearranged fibroblastic tumor PRRX1-rearranged fibroblastic tumor is a benign spindle cell neoplasm characterized by PRRX1 rearrangements, most often with NCOA1. • Tumours most commonly arise in subcutaneous tissue of the trunk or proximal extremities, with a smaller subset presenting in the head and neck • Rare dermal and intramuscular cases have been reported • Essential: a paucicellular, circumscribed, bland spindle cell neoplasm • Hyalinized stroma with variably wire-like and ropy collagen • Prominent ectatic and irregular vascular spaces • Demonstration of PRRX1 rearrangement • Tumours present as a circumscribed, occasionally multilobular mass with elongated, irregular, and ectatic vascular spaces evident at low magnification • Closer inspection shows a predominantly paucicellular neoplasm composed of bland spindle cells arranged haphazardly or in short fascicles within a hyalinized background • Focal increased cellularity, myxoid/edematous stromal change, or dense eosinophilic ropy or wire-like collagen are often appreciated • Tumours with KMT2D alterations appear to have especially prominent perivascular hyalinization, and a subset of superficial cases may show scattered clusters of pigmented dendritic cells • The tumor cells have monomorphic ovoid nuclei with small nucleoli and scant pale cytoplasm with tapering processes • Identification of a PRRX1 rearrangement helps differentiate this tumor from other fibroblastic neoplasms • Desmoplastic fibroblastoma and fibroma of tendon sheath: compare cellularity, collagen pattern, site, and defining molecular findings Angiomyofibroblastoma Angiomyofibroblastoma is a benign superficial myofibroblastic neoplasm with a predilection for the vulva and vagina. • Virtually all cases arise in pelviperineal subcutaneous tissue, with the majority arising in the vulva • About 10–15% of cases occur in the vagina • Essential: bland round to spindle cells in a perivascular distribution • Prominent small to medium vessels • Angiomyofibroblastoma is generally well demarcated by a thin fibrous pseudocapsule from surrounding soft tissue • At low magnification, tumors show alternating hypocellular and hypercellular areas and prominent small to medium-sized thin-walled vessels • Thick-walled, often hyalinized vessels, can be seen • The tumor cells, which are set in a variably myxedematous to fibrous stroma and typically concentrated around the vasculature, are round to spindle-shaped, with eosinophilic cytoplasm • Binucleated and multinucleated tumor cells may occur • Cellular angiofibroma: angiomyofibroblastoma has alternating cellularity and perivascular clustering • Cellular angiofibroma has thick-walled vessels Cellular angiofibroma Cellular angiofibroma is a benign, cellular, and richly vascularized fibroblastic neoplasm that usually arises in the superficial soft tissues of the vulvovaginal, inguinoscrotal, or paratesticular regions. • Cellular angiofibromas typically arise in the superficial soft tissues of the vulvovaginal, inguinoscrotal, or paratesticular regions • Rare examples have been described at other sites, including oral mucosa, anorectal region, orbit, male pelvis, prostate, and subcutaneous tissue of the chest wall • Essential: bland spindle cells • Short bundles of delicate collagen fibers • And numerous small to medium-sized thick-walled vessels • Variable adipocytic component • The tumors are generally well circumscribed • Poorly marginated, infiltrative tumors occur rarely in men • The spindle cell component is randomly distributed throughout the lesion, occasionally with a fascicular arrangement or nuclear palisading • Spindle cells have short, oval to fusiform nuclei with inconspicuous nucleoli and scant, palely eosinophilic cytoplasm with poorly defined borders • Mitoses are generally sparse, but they can be more frequent in some cases • Deletion of RB1, located in chromosome band 13q14, can be detected by FISH or other molecular methods but is usually not required for diagnosis • Angiomyofibroblastoma and solitary fibrous tumor: thick-walled hyalinized vessels favor cellular angiofibroma • STAT6 supports solitary fibrous tumor Angiofibroma of soft tissue Angiofibroma of soft tissue is a benign fibroblastic neoplasm composed of uniform spindle cells with abundant fibromyxoid stroma and a prominent network of branching, thin-walled blood vessels. • Angiofibroma of soft tissue typically arises in the lower extremity, sometimes involving or adjacent to the knee • Unusual anatomical locations include the upper extremity, back, abdominal wall, pelvic cavity, and breast • Essential: bland and uniform short spindle cells • Variably myxoid or collagenous stroma • Prominent small, thin-walled branching blood vessels • Desirable: AHRR or NCOA2 gene rearrangements in select cases • Angiofibroma of soft tissue is composed of uniform bland spindle cells in a variably myxoid to collagenous stroma with a prominent vascular network • The lesions are mostly well circumscribed • The architecture is vaguely lobulated, with alternating myxoid and collagenous areas and regional variation in cellularity • The neoplastic spindle cells have inconspicuous palely eosinophilic cytoplasm and short ovoid or tapering nuclei, with irregular nuclear contours, fine chromatin, and indistinct nucleoli • Cytological atypia and nuclear hyperchromasia are generally absent • Detection of AHRR or NCOA2 rearrangement or AHRR::NCOA2 gene fusion (or other rare variant fusion) supports the diagnosis, but it is generally not required • Solitary fibrous tumor: delicate branching vessels and bland short spindle cells • STAT6 nuclear staining favors solitary fibrous tumor Nuchal-type fibroma Nuchal-type fibroma is a benign fibroblastic proliferation that commonly arises in the posterior neck in middle-aged adults. • Nuchal-type fibroma is a superficial lesion that occurs in the dermis and subcutis • Although the majority arise in the posterior neck (70%), they may occur at extranuchal sites, including the upper back, shoulder, head, extremities, and buttock • Essential: a hypocellular collagenous lesion with bland fibroblasts • Entrapped adipose tissue and small nerve bundles • Typically arising at the posterior aspect of neck in adults • Entrapped normal structures, including adipose tissue, skeletal muscle, and nerves, may be seen • Many nuchal-type fibromas contain a localized proliferation of small nerves, in some cases similar to those in traumatic neuroma • This feature is usually absent in Gardner fibroma, which may otherwise be morphologically indistinguishable from nuchal-type fibroma • By immunohistochemistry, the stromal fibroblasts are positive for CD34 and negative for β-catenin (absent nuclear staining), SMA, and desmin • Desmoplastic fibroblastoma: nuchal-type fibroma is markedly hypocellular and entraps fat and nerve bundles Acral fibromyxoma Acral fibromyxoma is a benign fibroblastic neoplasm with a marked predilection for the periungual region of the digits. • Acral fibromyxoma shows a strong predilection for the periungual and subungual regions of the fingers and toes • Other areas of the hands and feet, ankles, wrists, lower legs, and thighs are affected rarely • Essential: acral, usually periungual location • Lobulated architecture with storiform or fascicular growth • Bland spindle cells in a variably myxoid or collagenous matrix • Acral fibromyxomas present in the dermis and subcutis as lobulated tumors, occasionally with a polypoid growth and surrounding epidermal collarettes • Most tumors show an infiltrative growth pattern, with rare invasion of underlying bone • The tumors are composed of bland-appearing spindled or stellate cells arranged loosely in a variably myxoid or collagenous stroma • Alternating myxoid and hyaline zones with wavy fascicles of collagen fibers are frequent • Scattered multinucleated cells may be present • The tumors show deletion of the RB1 gene, but demonstration of this is not required • Superficial acral fibromyxoma versus myxoid DFSP: assess CD34, architecture, and infiltrative pattern Gardner fibroma Gardner fibroma is a benign plaque-like neoplasm composed of coarse, haphazardly arranged collagen bundles with sparsely interspersed fibroblasts, often associated with familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP). • These tumors typically present as painless mass-forming lesions • Essential: plaque-like mass in the paraspinal region or trunk of young children • Haphazard arrangement of coarse collagen fibers with clefts or cracks and few inconspicuous spindle cells • Desirable: expression of CD34 and nuclear β-catenin • A helpful diagnostic feature is entrapment of adjacent adipose tissue and neurovascular bundles at the edge of the lesion • Rare tumors may show abundant intralesional adipose tissue • By immunohistochemistry, CD34 is almost always positive, whereas SMA is negative • Nuclear accumulation of β-catenin is often observed, particularly in cases associated with FAP • Although not necessary for diagnosis, identification of germline APC variants can have important implications for surgical and long-term case management • Desmoid fibromatosis: Gardner fibroma is hypocellular with coarse haphazard collagen • Desmoid is more cellular with sweeping fascicles Palmar fibromatosis and plantar fibromatosis Palmar and plantar fibromatoses are benign nodular fibroblastic/myofibroblastic proliferations typically arising in the volar aspect of the hands and fingers or involving plantar aponeuroses, respectively. • Palmar fibromatosis preferentially involves the volar or flexor aspect of the hands and is bilateral in as many as 50% of cases • Essential: bland, variably cellular nodular proliferation of spindled fibroblasts/myofibroblasts • Collagenous stroma • Involvement of aponeurosis and variably subcutis and dermis in the palmar and plantar aspect • Typically, tumors involve a thickened palmar/plantar tendon or aponeurosis, forming single to multiple discontinuous, moderately cellular spindle cell nodules in a collagenous stroma • Morphologically, there are three phases of growth (proliferative, involutional, and late-stage) • Some plantar lesions are hypercellular and mitotically active and mimic spindle cell sarcomas, but they lack atypia • Mitotic activity may be prominent in pediatric examples • Occasionally, particularly plantar lesions show interspersed multinucleated cells • Scar or reactive fibrous proliferation: nodular fascicular proliferation in palmar/plantar fascia supports fibromatosis Desmoid fibromatosis Desmoid fibromatosis is an intermediate, locally aggressive, deep-seated myofibroblastic neoplasm with infiltrative growth and a propensity for local recurrence. • Desmoid fibromatosis is most commonly diagnosed in the extremities (30–40% of cases) • Lesions also occur in the retroperitoneum or abdominal cavity (15%), abdominal wall (20%), and chest wall (10–15%) • Essential: long, sweeping fascicles of bland myofibroblasts • Infiltrative growth • Desirable: nuclear β-catenin expression • CTNNB1 variant in select cases • Desmoid fibromatosis is characterized by long, sweeping fascicles of bland fibroblasts and myofibroblasts with infiltration into surrounding soft tissues • The fascicles typically span an entire 10× objective field, and lymphoid aggregates are often appreciated at the advancing edge of the lesion • The tumor cells demonstrate pale eosinophilic cytoplasm and lack nuclear hyperchromasia or cytological atypia • Thin-walled blood vessels, occasionally with a gaping or staghorn appearance, are often prominent with variable perivascular edema • Mitotic figures are variable, but atypical mitoses are lacking Not specified in the supplied source. • Scar, nodular fasciitis, and low-grade fibromyxoid sarcoma: long sweeping bland fascicles with infiltrative growth • Nuclear beta-catenin/CTNNB1 supports desmoid Lipofibromatosis Lipofibromatosis (LPF) is an intermediate, locally aggressive pediatric soft tissue neoplasm with a predilection for the hands and feet; it is composed of an admixture of mature fat, short fascicles of bland spindle cells, and lipoblast-like cells in the interface between these components. • LPF preferentially involves the hands and feet, although it can also occur at other locations such as the trunk and the head and neck • LPF typically presents as a slow-growing, poorly demarcated subcutaneous mass, which can also involve skeletal muscle • Essential: an admixture of mature fat, short fascicles of bland spindle cells and lipoblast-like cells • Infiltrative margins • Most often in the hands and feet of young children • Lipofibromatosis is composed of mature adipose tissue traversed by cellular fascicles of spindle cells with bland, uniform, elongated nuclei • Fat usually forms a major proportion of the lesion • In newborn patients, the fat lobules may have an immature appearance with myxoid matrix • Small collections of univacuolated cells may be present in the fibroblastic component, where melanin-laden cells have occasionally been documented • Lipofibromatosis entraps subcutaneous tissue and sometimes skeletal muscle • Fibrous hamartoma of infancy: lipofibromatosis is predominantly infiltrative spindle cells admixed with fat, without the classic triphasic pattern Giant cell fibroblastoma Giant cell fibroblastoma (GCF) is a locally aggressive fibroblastic neoplasm, closely related to dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans (DFSP), arising primarily in children and characterized by the presence of multinucleated giant cells and pseudovascular spaces. • GCF is preferentially located in superficial soft tissues of the trunk and (more rarely) the extremities, and the head and neck region • GCF rarely involves superficial skeletal muscles • Essential: spindle cells and scattered multinucleated cells, often lining pseudovascular spaces • Infiltrative margins within dermis and subcutaneous fat • Hypocellular lesion with myxoid or collagenous stroma • Desirable: COL1A1::PDGFB fusion in select cases • GCF is a dermal and subcutaneous tumor, rarely involving skeletal muscle • Classic GCF infiltrates the subcutaneous fat with a honeycomb pattern and spare cutaneous adnexal structures • This neoplasm is usually hypocellular, composed of loose fascicles of wavy spindle cells in a myxoid to collagenous stroma • Numerous pleomorphic mononucleated and multinucleated giant cells are also present • Tumour cells display an amphophilic cytoplasm and oval hyperchromatic nuclei • The identification of t(17 • 22) Is useful in non-classic cases • DFSP: giant cell fibroblastoma has pseudovascular spaces and multinucleated giant cells • Both may show COL1A1::PDGFB Dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans Dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans (DFSP) is a superficial, intermediate, locally aggressive spindle cell neoplasm with a diffusely infiltrative, storiform growth pattern. Fibrosarcomatous DFSP is characterized by a fascicular growth pattern, increased mitotic activity, and metastatic potential. • These tumors show a predilection for the trunk and the proximal extremities, followed by the head and neck region • Involvement of the genital area, the breast, and acral sites is less common • Essential: storiform architecture and uniform spindle cell morphology • Diffusely infiltrative growth with a honeycomb pattern in the subcutis • For fibrosarcomatous DFSP: fascicular architecture with increased mitotic activity • Desirable: expression of CD34 • Classic DFSP DFSP is a dermal-based tumor typically showing additional diffuse infiltration of subcutaneous adipose tissue, giving rise to the characteristic honeycomb appearance • The tumor is composed of cytologically uniform spindled cells containing plump or elongated wavy nuclei, arranged in storiform, whorled, or cartwheel growth patterns • Cytological atypia is minimal and mitotic activity is low • The collagenous stroma contains small blood vessels • The superficial portion of the neoplasm may be less cellular, causing considerable challenges in the differential diagnosis on small biopsies • However, the COL1A1::PDGFB fusion may be cryptic in about 2% of cases, and another 2% of cases harbour alternative fusions involving PDGFD • Dermatofibroma: DFSP shows honeycomb infiltration of subcutaneous fat and diffuse CD34 • Dermatofibroma is usually more circumscribed and factor XIIIa-positive Solitary fibrous tumor Solitary fibrous tumor (SFT) is an intermediate, rarely metastasizing fibroblastic neoplasm characterized by bland spindle cell morphology; a patternless growth pattern; a prominent branching, thin-walled, dilated (staghorn) vasculature; and NAB2::STAT6 gene fusion. • SFTs may occur at any anatomical site, including superficial and deep soft tissues and within visceral organs and bone • About 30–40% of extrapleural, extrameningeal SFTs arise in the extremities • 30–40% Arise in deep soft tissues, the abdominal cavity, the pelvis, or the retroperitoneum • Essential: spindled to ovoid cells in a patternless architecture with prominent branching and hyalinized vasculature • Variable stromal collagen deposition • Desirable: STAT6 expression by immunohistochemistry • A prominent branching, frequently dilated vascular network is often present (termed staghorn or haemangiopericytomatous) • Scattered smaller or medium-sized hyalinized blood vessels may also be identified • Morphological patterns correlate with the NAB2::STAT6 fusion variant • SFTs most often have low mitotic counts, without substantial nuclear pleomorphism or necrosis • By immunohistochemistry, SFT typically shows strong and diffuse expression of CD34 and nuclear STAT6 • NAB2::STAT6 gene fusions are pathognomonic of SFT, and STAT6 immunohistochemistry is a sensitive and specific surrogate for all fusion types • Synovial sarcoma and other CD34-positive spindle tumors: patternless architecture, branching vessels, and nuclear STAT6 support solitary fibrous tumor Inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor Inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor (IMT) is an intermediate, rarely metastasizing myofibroblastic neoplasm composed of plump spindle cells accompanied by an inflammatory infiltrate of plasma cells, lymphocytes, and/or eosinophils. • Unusual locations include somatic soft tissues, pancreas, liver, CNS, and placenta • Essential: fascicles of plump spindle cells with inflammatory infiltrate and a variable collagenous or myxoid stroma • Desirable: expression of ALK • ALK, ROS1, RET, NTRK, or other gene rearrangements, in selected cases • The morphology of IMT can be heterogeneous • Spindled fibroblastic-myofibroblastic cells and inflammatory cells form three basic histological patterns • The second is a hypercellular pattern, which is characterized by a compact fascicular spindle cell proliferation with variable myxoid and collagenous stroma and inflammatory infiltrate • Dystrophic calcifications and osseous metaplasia are occasionally seen • One or more patterns are often seen within a single tumor • In addition to immunohistochemical detection of ALK protein, molecular assays for ALK may be used to confirm the diagnosis but are generally not required • Exceptional situations such as inversion of ALK on the same chromosome arm may lead to a false negative FISH result • In ALK-negative cases, immunohistochemistry for ROS1 and pan-TRK and/or molecular tests for non-ALK gene rearrangements may be useful • Nodular fasciitis and reactive inflammation: myofibroblastic spindle cells with lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate • Kinase fusion testing supports IMT Low-grade myofibroblastic sarcoma Low-grade myofibroblastic sarcoma (LGMS) is an intermediate, rarely metastasizing spindle cell neoplasm with mild nuclear variability and a diffusely infiltrative growth pattern. • There is a wide anatomical distribution • Essential: diffusely infiltrative growth • Cellular fascicles of spindle cells with pale eosinophilic cytoplasm • Nuclear atypia • Desirable: variable expression of SMA and/or desmin • Histologically, LGMSs are characterized by a diffusely infiltrative growth pattern • In deep neoplasms, cells often grow between individual skeletal muscle fibers • The cytoplasm is sparser and less brightly eosinophilic than that of smooth muscle neoplasms • More rarely, tumors are hypocellular, with more prominent, sometimes hyalinized, collagenous stroma • Mitotic activity is present, while necrosis is relatively rare • There are no specific genetic or molecular markers • Nodular fasciitis and desmoid fibromatosis: infiltrative growth with cytologic atypia and mitotic activity favors sarcoma Superficial CD34-positive pleomorphic fibroblastic tumor Superficial CD34-positive pleomorphic fibroblastic tumor is an intermediate, rarely metastasizing neoplasm of the skin and subcutis, characterized by spindled cells with abundant, granular to glassy eosinophilic cytoplasm, marked nuclear pleomorphism, a low mitotic count, and diffuse CD34 expression. • This tumor most frequently occurs in the lower extremities, especially thigh, followed by arm, buttock, shoulder, and (rarely) vulva • This tumor typically presents as a slow-growing, painless mass of superficial soft tissues • Essential: superficial location • Spindle cells with granular to glassy eosinophilic cytoplasm • Marked nuclear pleomorphism but a low mitotic count • Diffuse CD34 expression • Lipidized tumor cells are commonly present • The neoplastic cells show moderate to marked nuclear pleomorphism, often with bizarre, hyperchromatic nuclei containing prominent nucleoli and intranuclear cytoplasmic pseudoinclusions • Despite these alarming nuclear features, mitotic activity is very low, and necrosis is rarely seen • A mixed inflammatory cell infiltrate is often present • There is morphological overlap with tumors reported as PRDM10-rearranged soft tissue tumors • Atypical fibroxanthoma/pleomorphic dermal sarcoma and DFSP: superficial dermal location, pleomorphism, and CD34 expression guide distinction Myxoinflammatory fibroblastic sarcoma Myxoinflammatory fibroblastic sarcoma is an intermediate, rarely metastasizing neoplasm showing both a predilection for acral sites and variably myxoid and cellular areas with bland spindle cells, a prominent inflammatory infiltrate, and scattered large polygonal cells with macronucleoli. • The tumor presents most often in the acral sites: hands, fingers, and feet, more often on dorsal sides • Rarely it presents in the proximal parts of extremities and trunk wall • Essential: variably myxoid and cellular areas with bland spindle cells, a prominent inflammatory infiltrate, and scattered large polygonal cells with macronucleoli • The tumor contains large polygonal cells with nuclear pleomorphism, pseudoinclusions, and large eosinophilic nucleoli, potentially mimicking Hodgkin cells • Vacuolated pseudolipoblasts and mildly atypical spindle cells are often seen • There is a prominent stromal lymphoplasmacytic and neutrophilic inflammatory component • Cellularity is moderate to high in half of the cases • Stroma is mostly collagenous, usually with at least focal myxoid areas • Tenosynovial giant cell tumor and acral fibromyxoma: bizarre virocyte-like cells in myxoinflammatory stroma favor MIFS Nodular necrotizing fibroblastic tumor Nodular necrotizing fibroblastic tumor is a superficial mesenchymal neoplasm composed of epithelioid cells with a brisk inflammatory infiltrate and, in many cases, central necrosis. • Tumours tend to occur in the skin and subcutis of the limbs, trunk, or acral sites, the latter of which account for less than half of cases • No bone involvement has been reported so far • Essential: well-defined nodules of neoplastic cells with surrounding and/or admixed inflammation • Tumor cells with copious, eosinophilic to amphophilic cytoplasm and enlarged, vesicular nuclei with prominent nucleoli • Often central necrosis • Desirable: evidence of YAP1::MAML2 fusion • Nodular necrotizing fibroblastic tumor shows a nodular or multilobular growth pattern • Tumour lobules are sometimes separated by fibrous septa showing florid lymphoplasmacytic inflammation • Some lobules show central necrosis • The neoplastic cells are large, with copious, dense, amphophilic to eosinophilic cytoplasm, usually with emperipolesis of inflammatory cells • The nuclei are large and vesicular, with prominent red nucleoli • Identification of YAP1::MAML2 fusion can be helpful • Inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor and other inflammatory spindle-cell lesions: assess nodular necrosis, cytologic features, and defining molecular findings Infantile fibrosarcoma Infantile fibrosarcoma (IFS) is a locally aggressive fibroblastic tumor, most frequently occurring in infancy, characterized by an ETV6::NTRK3 fusion or other alterations leading to oncogenic activation of kinase genes. • IFS most commonly involves the soft tissues of the extremities, followed by the trunk and the head/neck • Tumours in intra-abdominal, retroperitoneal, or visceral sites are less frequent but do occur • Essential: a primitive ovoid/round cell or spindle cell tumor, often arranged in sheets or fascicles • Thin-walled, ectatic, branching vessels and/or mixed chronic inflammation • Desirable: ETV6::NTRK3 or other alterations of kinase genes • IFS may demonstrate a spectrum of histological patterns across cases and within a given case • Most frequently, IFS is a cellular, monomorphic neoplasm composed of primitive, ovoid/round to spindled cells, arranged either in compact, haphazard sheets or in long fascicles • Often tumors demonstrate a prominent ectatic or haemangiopericytoma-like vascular pattern • The background stroma may range from myxoid to heavily collagenous • A subset of cases have decreased cellularity with a collagenized matrix • Gene fusions or activating variants involving receptor tyrosine kinase encoding genes (e.g • ETV6::NTRK3) or downstream effector molecule (BRAF) fusions or activating alterations may be demonstrated by various molecular modalities • Fibrous hamartoma of infancy and cellular congenital/infantile fibromatosis: infantile fibrosarcoma is a malignant cellular spindle-cell neoplasm • Test for NTRK fusion when appropriate Myxofibrosarcoma Myxofibrosarcoma is a malignant fibroblastic neoplasm with variably myxoid stroma, nuclear pleomorphism, and a characteristic curvilinear vasculature. • Myxofibrosarcomas usually arise in the superficial soft tissue of the limbs, including the limb girdles, with the lower extremities more commonly involved than the upper extremities • Involvement of the trunk, head and neck, and hands and feet are rare • Essential: multinodular architecture with infiltrative margins • Variably pleomorphic tumor cells with myxoid stroma and curvilinear vasculature • Hypercellular areas in higher-grade tumors • Subcutaneous tumors are highly infiltrative and often extend well beyond the clinically apparent lesion • At the low-grade end of the spectrum, myxofibrosarcoma is relatively hypocellular, composed of scattered hyperchromatic, spindled to stellate cells within a prominent myxoid stroma • The tumor cells are often clustered around the curvilinear vessels with or without associated chronic inflammatory cells • Vacuolated tumor cells resembling lipoblasts (pseudolipoblasts) may be present • In low-grade tumors, mitotic activity is inconspicuous • Nodular fasciitis and other myxoid sarcomas: infiltrative multinodular growth, curvilinear vessels, and atypia favor myxofibrosarcoma Low-grade fibromyxoid sarcoma Low-grade fibromyxoid sarcoma is a malignant fibroblastic neoplasm characterized by alternating collagenous and myxoid areas, deceptively bland spindle cells with a whorling growth pattern, and arcades of small blood vessels. • The most common sites of involvement are the proximal extremities and trunk, usually subfascial in depth • Essential: alternating fibrous and myxoid areas • Bland spindle cells in a whorling or short fascicular growth pattern • Desirable: MUC4 expression • FUS gene rearrangement in select cases • Low-grade fibromyxoid sarcoma is composed of collagenous areas and myxoid nodules • An abrupt transition between these two areas is typical • The tumor cells are bland, spindled, and sometimes plump, and they grow in short fascicles or in a whorling pattern • Mitotic activity is generally inconspicuous • Arcades of small vessels and arteriole-sized vessels with perivascular sclerosis are seen • If MUC4 is negative or not available, identification of FUS::CREB3L2 (or other rare variants) offers molecular genetic support for the diagnosis • Myxofibrosarcoma and desmoid fibromatosis: bland whorled cells with alternating fibrous/myxoid zones • Diffuse MUC4 and FUS::CREB3L2 support LGFMS Sclerosing epithelioid fibrosarcoma Sclerosing epithelioid fibrosarcoma is a rare malignant fibroblastic neoplasm composed of distinctive epithelioid cells arranged in cords and nests and embedded in a densely sclerotic hyalinized stroma. • Tumours are deep-seated and arise most often in the upper or lower extremities or limb girdle, followed by the trunk and the head and neck • Rarely, tumors arise in the pelvis, retroperitoneum, viscera, or bone • Essential: epithelioid cells arranged in cords, nests, or trabeculae and embedded in a dense sclerotic hyalinized stroma • Keratin-negative • Desirable: diffuse strong MUC4 expression (in most cases) • EWSR1::CREB3L1 or other rearrangements • Sclerosing epithelioid fibrosarcoma shows infiltrative growth within the adipose tissue and skeletal muscle in most cases • A characteristic feature is the prominent hyalinized sclerotic collagenous stroma, showing variable degrees of cellularity • The tumor cells usually have clear to pale eosinophilic cytoplasm and uniform round nuclei with inconspicuous nucleoli • Although more than half of the cases may show a spindle cell component, it is usually limited in nature • Pseudoalveolar or acinar growth patterns are occasionally seen • Demonstration of EWSR1::CREB3L1 or other rearrangements can help confirm the diagnosis • For cases with characteristic morphology and MUC4 expression, additional molecular studies are not required • However, in tumors lacking MUC4 staining, sequencing is recommended to demonstrate the alternative fusions involving YAP1 and KMT2A for a definitive diagnosis • Carcinoma and epithelioid sarcoma: epithelioid cords/nests in dense hyalinized stroma • Use keratins, MUC4, and fusion testing Undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma Undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma (UPS) is a malignant pleomorphic mesenchymal neoplasm showing no identifiable line of differentiation and no distinctive molecular aberration when analysed by presently available technology. UPS is a diagnosis of exclusion. • UPS may be found at any location • UPS has no characteristic clinical features that distinguish it from other types of sarcoma • Essential: spindle, pleomorphic, epithelioid morphology • Absence of any morphological or immunohistochemical feature of specific lines of differentiation • UPS is morphologically intermediate- to high-grade and may display pleomorphic, spindle cell, and epithelioid areas, without specific defining features • They lack an identifiable line of differentiation, other than a (myo)fibroblastic appearance • UPS is often patternless, with frequent enlarged, irregular, bizarre, multinucleated tumor giant cells with coarse chromatin and prominent nucleoli • The amount of cytoplasm is variable, and it is pale to eosinophilic • Intracytoplasmic or intranuclear inclusions can be seen • Molecular analysis may help exclude other entities in the differential diagnosis of UPS • The presence of MDM2 and CDK4 amplification may suggest a dedifferentiated liposarcoma • Mutations in BRAF, NRAS, KIT, or NF1 • Exclude specific lineages first: diagnosis requires pleomorphic malignancy without definable differentiation after appropriate IHC/molecular workup Reactive / self-limited and pseudoneoplastic Benign fibroblastic / myofibroblastic Fibromatoses Intermediate / locally aggressive Malignant First establish the compartment and setting Superficial dermis/subcutis versus fascia, tendon/aponeurosis, skeletal muscle, or deep soft tissue; age, site, growth rate, prior trauma/compression, and multiplicity are major discriminators. Look for a defining architecture Tissue-culture-like/myxoid (nodular fasciitis); zonal bone (myositis ossificans); triphasic organoid pattern (fibrous hamartoma of infancy); thick collagen and slit vessels (tendon-sheath fibroma); patternless growth and branching vessels (solitary fibrous tumor); honeycomb fat infiltration (DFSP). Decide whether the lesion is bland, infiltrative, or cytologically malignant Infiltration alone does not equal sarcoma: desmoid fibromatosis and DFSP infiltrate. Conversely, bland cytology does not exclude malignancy in entities such as low-grade fibromyxoid sarcoma. Use immunohistochemistry as a differential-directed panel Choose markers to test a specific hypothesis, not as a broad screening panel. Interpret staining in the lesional cells and in the correct compartment. Use molecular testing to resolve a real diagnostic fork Examples include USP6, CTNNB1, COL1A1::PDGFB, NAB2::STAT6, kinase fusions in IMT/infantile fibrosarcoma, FUS::CREB3L2, and EWSR1::CREB3L1. A negative assay may not exclude a morphologically compatible entity. Integrate margins, grade, and clinical behavior State the biologic category and the feature that drives it. For infiltrative or malignant lesions, correlate sampling and imaging; avoid upgrading a benign lesion solely because mitoses are present when atypical mitoses/necrosis are absent. Small, rapidly growing lesion; tissue-culture pattern, myxoid/microcystic stroma and ordinary mitoses. USP6 supports the diagnosis. Myositis ossificans Extraskeletal osteosarcoma Peripheral maturation and zonal bone formation favor myositis ossificans; malignant cytology and absent zonation favor osteosarcoma. Scar / other spindle cell lesions Long sweeping bland fascicles with infiltrative growth; nuclear beta-catenin or CTNNB1 alteration supports desmoid. DFSP Dermatofibroma Storiform growth with honeycomb infiltration of fat and diffuse CD34 favors DFSP; confirm PDGFB/PDGFD rearrangement when needed. Other bland spindle cell tumors Alternating fibrous and myxoid zones with bland whorled cells; diffuse MUC4 and FUS::CREB3L2 support the diagnosis. Carcinoma / epithelioid sarcoma Epithelioid cords or nests in dense hyalinized stroma; use keratins, MUC4 and fusion testing in context. Infiltrative multinodular growth, curvilinear vessels and cytologic atypia favor myxofibrosarcoma. Other CD34-positive spindle cell tumors Patternless architecture and branching vessels with nuclear STAT6 support solitary fibrous tumor. Reactive inflammation Myofibroblastic fascicles with lymphoplasmacytic inflammation; ALK/ROS1 or other kinase fusion may confirm. SMA / desmin Myofibroblastic differentiation; expression is variable and not entity-specific. Desmin plus CD34 commonly supports myofibroblastoma in the right morphology. CD34 Useful in DFSP, superficial CD34-positive pleomorphic fibroblastic tumor, cellular angiofibroma, myofibroblastoma and several benign lesions; not specific. Distribution and architecture matter. Nuclear beta-catenin Supports desmoid fibromatosis in context; may also occur in Gardner fibroma and cranial fasciitis. Correlate with CTNNB1 testing where appropriate. STAT6 Strong nuclear staining supports solitary fibrous tumor; interpret as nuclear staining in lesional cells. MUC4 Diffuse strong expression supports low-grade fibromyxoid sarcoma and most sclerosing epithelioid fibrosarcomas; not all SEF are positive. ALK / ROS1 / NTRK Can identify kinase-rearranged inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor; negative ALK does not exclude IMT. RB1 Loss may support the RB1-deleted family (myofibroblastoma, cellular angiofibroma, spindle cell/pleomorphic lipoma) but is not independently diagnostic. ERG Can be expressed in SMAD3-rearranged fibroblastic tumor; use with morphology and fusion testing rather than as a stand-alone lineage marker. title: Fibrohistiocytic And Synovial Tumors
content: use client Tenosynovial giant cell tumor (TGCT) Benign / malignant variant Localized and diffuse forms are benign but may recur; rare malignant TGCT is aggressive Localized: fingers (≈85%), tendon sheath/interphalangeal joint. Diffuse: knee (≈75%), then hip/ankle. Extra-articular lesions: knee, thigh, foot. Localized: Slowly growing, usually painless mass; typically age 30–50 years; female predominance. Diffuse: Pain, swelling, tenderness, restricted motion, and often hemorrhagic effusion; usually young adults under 40; slight female predominance. Rare malignant TGCT: Usually adults aged 50–60 years; lower limb, especially knee. Variable admixture of small histiocyte-like cells, larger epithelioid synoviocytes, osteoclast-like giant cells, foamy macrophages, inflammatory cells, and hemosiderin. Localized: Circumscribed, lobulated architecture; giant cells and xanthoma cells are often conspicuous; hemosiderin is virtually always present; stromal hyalinization varies. Diffuse: Infiltrative, expansile sheets; giant cells may be sparse or absent; cleft-like spaces are common; blood-filled pseudoalveolar spaces occur in a minority. Malignant TGCT: Enlarged atypical mononuclear cells, increased mitoses including atypical forms, necrosis, nuclear enlargement/nucleoli, spindle-cell areas, and sometimes myxoid change. Larger mononuclear synoviocytic cells: Clusterin positive; a subset expresses desmin. Smaller histiocyte-like cells: CD68, CD163, and CD45 positive. Desmin highlights dendritic processes in a subset; expression is variable. CSF1 rearrangements occur in approximately 75% of cases; diverse fusion partners are reported. Only a small neoplastic cell population carries the rearrangement; recruited macrophages form most of the tumor bulk. Molecular testing is not routinely clinically required in typical cases. Giant cell tumor of soft tissue TGCT is synovial/tendon-sheath centered and hemosiderin-rich; soft-tissue GCT is usually superficial, multinodular, and lacks the characteristic synovial context. Keratin-positive giant cell–rich tumor KPGCT contains keratin-positive mononuclear cells and often a lymphoid cuff; TGCT shows synoviocytic/histiocytic populations with CSF1-associated biology. Malignant TGCT versus sarcoma Do not equate brisk mitoses alone with malignancy; malignant diagnosis requires overt malignant morphology in a conventional TGCT or sarcomatous recurrence. Localized and diffuse TGCT differ in site, architecture, and recurrence risk. Brisk mitotic activity and occasional necrosis may occur in otherwise conventional TGCT; assess cytologic atypia and atypical mitoses. Avoid the outdated term pigmented villonodular synovitis; use diffuse-type TGCT when appropriate. Localized: Recurrence approximately 4–30%, usually manageable by re-excision. Diffuse: Recurrence approximately 40–60%; repeated recurrence may severely impair joint function. Malignant TGCT: Aggressive; about one third mortality in reported cases, with nodal and lung metastases. Variable proportions of small histiocyte-like cells, larger epithelioid synoviocytes, foamy macrophages, and multinucleated giant cells. Hemosiderin deposition and variable stromal collagenization. Malignant TGCT requires overt malignant areas in a conventional TGCT or sarcomatous recurrence. Chondroid synoviocytic neoplasm Locally aggressive May recur or persist if incompletely excised; metastases have not been reported Temporomandibular joint/temporal bone region in nearly 80%; rare cases in hip, knee, thumb, and spine. Rare; reported age range 17–75 years, mean/median approximately 50 years; no sex predilection. TMJ-region lesions present as expansile, locally aggressive masses; other sites usually present as nonspecific soft-tissue masses. Imaging may show a lytic/expansile lesion, often bone-centered, with calcified matrix on CT. Multinodular tumor with large eosinophilic synoviocytes, small histiocytes, foamy macrophages, siderophages, and osteoclast-like giant cells. Prominent cellular nodules/sheets of synoviocytes admixed with lobules of myxohyaline cartilage. Pericellular (chondroblastoma-like) calcification or calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate deposits may occur. Mitotic activity is usually low; high-grade atypia is absent. Clusterin highlights synoviocytes within and outside the chondroid matrix. CSF1 mRNA may be detected in synoviocytes by chromogenic in situ hybridization. FN1 fusions are frequent, most often with FGFR2; other partners include TEK, FGFR1, PRG4, PLAG1, MERTK, NTRK1, BMPR2, AGFG1, and MALAT1. Other reported fusions include PDGFRA::USP8; rare cases have TIMP3::ZCCHC7 or CSF1::COL6A3. FN1 break-apart FISH can be used; RNA-based next-generation sequencing better identifies the fusion partner. Synovial chondromatosis Chondroid synoviocytic neoplasm has prominent cellular synoviocytic nodules admixed with histiocytes/giant cells; synovial chondromatosis is dominated by cartilaginous nodules. Soft-tissue chondroma Chondroid synoviocytic neoplasm shows synoviocytic and histiocytic components, giant cells, and often an FN1 fusion. Tenosynovial giant cell tumor Chondroid matrix/lobules are a defining additional component in chondroid synoviocytic neoplasm. Chondroblastoma-like calcification / tumoral pseudogout Look for the underlying synoviocytic neoplasm and cartilage; extensive CPPD may mimic pseudogout. High cellularity, synoviocytic overgrowth, atypia, or mitotic activity may be alarming but do not alone establish malignancy. Do not mistake chondroid matrix or CPPD deposits for a separate cartilage-forming neoplasm. Locally aggressive at most; local recurrence or persistence may follow incomplete excision. Metastatic disease has not been reported in the supplied source. Multinodular proliferation of large eosinophilic, moderately pleomorphic synoviocytes. Chondroid/myxohyaline cartilage and calcified matrix with histiocytes, osteoclast-like giant cells, and foamy macrophages. Clusterin expression is supportive in selected cases. Plexiform fibrohistiocytic tumor Intermediate Intermediate; local recurrence and rare metastasis Superficial dermis/subcutis, especially upper extremities; lower extremities next. Trunk and head/neck less common. Usually children and young adults; median age approximately 14.5–20 years; slight female predominance in most series. Slow-growing, poorly defined plaque or nodule, typically 1–3 cm. Infiltrative lesion with plexiform architecture at the dermal–subcutaneous junction. Biphasic pattern: nodules of histiocytoid cells and osteoclast-like giant cells surrounded by fascicles of spindle cells. Hemorrhage, hemosiderin, and chronic inflammatory infiltrates may be present. Mitotic activity is generally low; necrosis is absent. Atypia and lymphovascular invasion are rare. Spindle cells express SMA. Histiocytes in plexiform nodules express CD163 and CD11c. CSF1 mRNA may be detected in interspersed round cells by chromogenic in situ hybridization. No recurrent defining molecular alteration is established. Molecular testing is not clinically relevant in routine diagnosis. Plexiform fibrohistiocytic tumor has characteristic plexiform architecture and biphasic histology; soft-tissue GCT is more uniformly multinodular and giant-cell rich. Plexiform fibrohistiocytic tumor is a superficial dermal/subcutaneous lesion with spindle-cell fascicles and plexiform nodules. Dermatofibroma / other fibrohistiocytic lesions The plexiform architecture and biphasic histiocytoid/giant-cell plus spindle-cell pattern are key. Lymphovascular invasion and cytologic atypia are uncommon but can occur. A small biopsy may not show the full plexiform architecture; correlate with the infiltrative superficial growth pattern. Local recurrence: approximately 12.5–37.5%. Regional lymph-node metastasis: approximately 6%; lung metastasis is exceptional. Plexiform architecture involving dermis and/or subcutis. Biphasic composition of histiocytoid/giant-cell nodules and interspersed myofibroblastic spindle-cell fascicles. Intermediate; local recurrence with very rare metastasis Usually superficial soft tissues of upper/lower extremities (≈70%); trunk (≈20%) and head/neck (≈7%) less often. Rare; predominantly fifth decade, but reported age range 5–89 years; no clear sex predilection. Usually a painless enlarging mass; average symptom duration approximately 6 months. Peripheral mineralization is common. Well-circumscribed, multinodular superficial soft-tissue neoplasm; fibrous septa separate cellular nodules. Nodules contain round-to-oval mononuclear cells and numerous osteoclast-like multinucleated giant cells in a richly vascular stroma. Mitotic activity is readily seen, but nuclear pleomorphism and bizarre giant cells are absent; necrosis is rare. Metaplastic bone formation occurs in approximately 50%, often as a peripheral shell of woven bone; vascular invasion may be present. Lacks the peripheral lymphoid aggregates and keratin expression characteristic of keratin-positive giant cell–rich tumor. Keratin is negative; this helps distinguish keratin-positive giant cell–rich tumor. The supplied source does not define a specific positive immunophenotype. H3-3A variants typical of most giant cell tumors of bone are absent. HMGA2::NCOR2 fusion, characteristic of keratin-positive giant cell–rich tumor, is not present. Giant cell tumor of bone Soft-tissue GCT is superficial and multinodular, often with peripheral metaplastic bone; bone GCT is an osseous-centered lesion and commonly has H3-3A alterations. KPGCT has keratin-positive mononuclear cells and often peripheral lymphoid aggregates; soft-tissue GCT is keratin-negative. TGCT is centered on synovium/tendon sheath and typically contains hemosiderin-rich synoviocytic/histiocytic populations. Mitotic activity alone is not evidence of malignancy; atypia, bizarre giant cells, and necrosis are generally absent. Peripheral bone formation and vascular invasion can occur in this intermediate neoplasm. Local recurrence approximately 12%; metastasis is very rare. Multinodular superficial soft-tissue neoplasm with histiocytoid mononuclear cells and osteoclast-like giant cells. Metaplastic bone formation is common. Absence of keratin expression. Keratin-positive giant cell–rich tumor (KPGCT) Intermediate / uncertain lineage Usually indolent; local recurrence and rare distant metastasis reported Subcutis and bone. Soft-tissue sites include trunk, extremities, and head/neck; rare deep, sinonasal, vocal-cord, and cranial-fossa lesions. Most common in young adults; median age approximately 25 years, with a wide age range; pronounced female predominance (≈72%). Soft-tissue lesions are usually asymptomatic solid masses; some are painful or grow rapidly. Osseous lesions are typically lytic intramedullary masses, sometimes with a soft-tissue component. Nodular polymorphous population of mononuclear cells/histiocytes, mixed inflammatory cells, and Touton-type and osteoclast-type giant cells. Soft-tissue lesions often have a peripheral pseudocapsule with lymphoid cuff/aggregates; hemosiderin, microhemorrhage, and intratumoral lymphoid aggregates are common. Mononuclear cells may have bright eosinophilic or plasmacytoid cytoplasm; giant-cell-rich, xanthomatous, and hybrid patterns occur. A subset shows storiform growth with few giant cells; most are cytologically bland, although moderate atypia may occur. Infarction is common; coagulative necrosis and vascular invasion are uncommon. Keratin is variably positive in the mononuclear cell population; plasmacytoid cells may show a paranuclear dot-like pattern. H3.3 G34W is negative. SMARCB1 (INI1) expression is retained. HMGA2::NCOR2 fusion occurs in most cases; rare HMGA2::COL14A1 has been reported. Fusion testing may support difficult or keratin-poor cases, but false-negative results occur with some methods. CSF1 expression may be increased without CSF1 gene alteration. KPGCT has keratin-positive mononuclear cells and often a lymphoid cuff; soft-tissue GCT is keratin-negative. TGCT is synovium/tendon-sheath centered and commonly hemosiderin-rich; KPGCT is a polymorphous keratin-positive giant-cell/histiocytic neoplasm. Xanthogranulomatous epithelial tumor This term is an acceptable synonym/pattern when the xanthomatous component predominates; it is within the KPGCT spectrum. KPGCT is H3.3 G34W negative and may show HMGA2::NCOR2; bone GCT typically has H3-3A mutation-associated staining. Keratin may be focal or limited to a small mononuclear-cell population; carefully search for positive cells. A negative HMGA2::NCOR2 assay does not exclude KPGCT because false negatives are reported. Do not confuse infarction with coagulative tumor necrosis. Most reported tumors behave indolently; local recurrence may occur. Distant metastases have been reported in two patients; no fatal outcome documented in the supplied source. Polymorphous population of osteoclast-type/Touton giant cells, histiocytes, and inflammatory cells. Keratin-positive mononuclear cells. HMGA2::NCOR2 fusion is desirable in challenging or keratin-poor cases. All Benign Malignant PathologyGPS / Soft Tissue Tumors / Fibrohistiocytic and Synovial Tumors Fibrohistiocytic and Synovial Tumors A morphology-first diagnostic reference emphasizing architecture, cellular composition, immunophenotype, molecular findings, and practical differential diagnosis. Core rule Classify giant-cell-rich lesions by their architecture, site, and defining cell population. Giant cells alone are not diagnostic. Look for synovial association, plexiform growth, keratin-positive mononuclear cells, hemosiderin, and chondroid matrix. Diagnostic GPS: morphology to classification Establish the setting Determine whether the lesion is synovial/tendon-sheath centered, superficial dermal/subcutaneous, or bone-associated. Assess architecture Look for localized nodules, diffuse sheets, plexiform growth, multinodular septated growth, or chondroid lobules. Identify the cell populations Separate synoviocytes, histiocytes, spindle cells, osteoclast-like giant cells, Touton giant cells, and inflammatory cells. Apply targeted IHC Use clusterin, CD68/CD163, SMA, and keratins in the morphologic context; keratin-positive mononuclear cells are a key clue to KPGCT. Use molecular tests selectively CSF1 rearrangement may support TGCT; FN1 fusions support chondroid synoviocytic neoplasm; HMGA2::NCOR2 supports KPGCT. Behavior categories Benign, recurrence-prone: Conventional localized and diffuse TGCT; recurrence risk is substantially higher in diffuse disease. Locally aggressive: Chondroid synoviocytic neoplasm; local recurrence or persistence may follow incomplete excision, but metastases have not been reported. Intermediate, rarely metastasizing: Plexiform fibrohistiocytic tumor and giant cell tumor of soft tissue. Uncertain lineage, usually indolent: KPGCT; local recurrence and rare distant metastases have been reported. Malignant: Malignant TGCT is exceptionally rare and should be diagnosed only when overt malignant morphology is present. High-yield ancillary findings TGCT CSF1 rearrangement in approximately 75%; clusterin in larger synoviocytic cells FN1 fusion, often with FGFR2; clusterin SMA in spindle cells; CD163/CD11c in histiocytes Keratin negative; lacks typical H3-3A variants KPGCT Keratin-positive mononuclear cells; HMGA2::NCOR2 in most cases Entity reference Diagnostic criteria and differential diagnosis Search by entity, site, morphology, immunostain, or gene. e.g. CSF1, clusterin, keratin, giant cells... bg-teal-700 text-white border border-slate-300 bg-white text-slate-600 Collapse − View diagnostic profile + Clinical profile Essential diagnostic criteria Histopathology Immunohistochemistry Molecular pathology Differential diagnosis Prognosis and behavior Diagnostic pitfalls No matching entity. High-stakes comparison: giant-cell-rich lesions Feature Soft-tissue GCT Plexiform FHT Typical setting Synovium / tendon sheath Superficial soft tissue Subcutis or bone Dermis / subcutis Architecture Localized nodules or diffuse sheets Multinodular with fibrous septa Polymorphous nodules / sheets Plexiform, biphasic Key clue Hemosiderin; clusterin Keratin negative Keratin-positive mononuclear cells Histiocytoid nodules with spindle-cell fascicles Molecular clue CSF1 rearrangement subset No defining alteration HMGA2::NCOR2 No recurrent event established Sampling and reporting checklist Correlate with the precise anatomic relationship to joint, synovium, tendon sheath, dermis, subcutis, and bone. Sample heterogeneous, nodular, hemorrhagic, chondroid, and radiologically aggressive areas. For TGCT, document localized versus diffuse growth and assess for overt malignant areas when atypia is present. For giant-cell-rich lesions, specifically assess keratin in mononuclear cells and look for peripheral lymphoid aggregates. For chondroid synoviocytic neoplasm, identify the synoviocytic component and calcified/chondroid matrix; consider fusion testing in difficult cases. For plexiform fibrohistiocytic tumor, demonstrate the plexiform architecture and biphasic cellular composition. Report tumor size, site, growth pattern, margins, mitotic activity, necrosis, vascular invasion, and any malignant component as appropriate. Scope note: Based on the supplied WHO source excerpt. Molecular findings and immunostains are presented as supportive findings where indicated, not as stand-alone diagnostic criteria. The page does not replace radiologic correlation, adequate sampling, or expert soft-tissue pathology review.

title: GIST
content: use client Gastrointestinal Stromal Tumor (GIST) KIT / PDGFRA-driven and other molecular subsets Variable biological behavior; assess risk using site, size, mitotic activity, and tumor rupture rather than soft-tissue sarcoma grade Anywhere in the GI tract: stomach (~55%), small bowel (~32%), colon/rectum (~6%), and esophagus (~1%). Extragastrointestinal examples occur mainly in mesentery, omentum, and retroperitoneum; many represent detached GI primaries or metastases. Most often presents in the sixth decade (median 60–65 years); slight male predominance. Small lesions may be incidental microGISTs. Symptoms include vague abdominal discomfort, bleeding from mucosal ulceration, abdominal mass, or perforation. Advanced disease commonly spreads to peritoneum and liver; bone, skin, and soft-tissue metastases are less frequent and lung metastases are exceedingly rare. About 10% are disseminated at presentation, sometimes preventing confident assignment of the primary site. Syndromic settings account for approximately 5–10%: particularly SDH-deficient GIST, and less commonly NF1-associated or familial KIT/PDGFRA-associated disease. NF1-associated tumors are often multifocal, small-bowel based, and KIT/PDGFRA wildtype. Essential: an intramural, submucosal, or subserosal GI mass with spindle-cell, epithelioid, or mixed morphology and KIT (CD117) and/or DOG1 expression. Desirable: demonstration of a KIT or PDGFRA pathogenic variant (present in approximately 85% of tumors). Molecular testing is particularly important in KIT/DOG1-equivocal cases and for predictive treatment assessment. Interpret KIT and DOG1 with morphology and site. Strong diffuse KIT is typical, but a small minority (<5%), especially PDGFRA-mutant tumors, may be KIT-negative or only minimally positive. A diagnosis of GIST should not be based on KIT positivity alone; integrate the complete phenotype and exclude mimics. Spindle-cell morphology predominates, especially in gastric GIST; epithelioid morphology occurs in approximately 20–25% of gastric cases. Mixed spindle and epithelioid patterns also occur. Nuclear pleomorphism is uncommon. Spindle-cell patterns include conventional fascicular/sheet-like growth, sclerosing (often in small tumors and sometimes calcified), palisaded-vacuolated, and diffuse hypercellular patterns. Epithelioid GIST may be sclerosing, discohesive, hypercellular (occasionally pseudopapillary), or rarely sarcomatous. Myxoid stroma may be present. Small-intestinal and colonic GISTs are usually spindle-cell tumors in diffuse sheets or vague storiform arrays. Skeinoid collagen fibers are particularly associated with tumors of low biological potential. Additional intestinal features include neuropil-like anuclear areas, nuclear palisading, perivascular hyalinization, and regressive vascular changes (dilated/thrombosed vessels, hemosiderin, and fibrosis). Rectal GISTs are usually spindle-cell. Large tumors may show hemorrhage, cystic degeneration, or necrosis. Rarely, high-grade sarcomatoid dedifferentiation develops de novo or after imatinib, sometimes with loss of KIT and heterologous epithelial, myogenic, or angiosarcomatous differentiation. KIT (CD117): usually strong and diffuse; staining may be cytoplasmic, membrane-associated, or perinuclear dot-like. A negative result does not exclude GIST, particularly in PDGFRA-mutant tumors. DOG1 (ANO1): similarly sensitive and specific; can identify a substantial proportion of KIT-negative GISTs. Use as a complementary key marker. CD34: common in spindle-cell GIST, especially gastric tumors; less consistently expressed in epithelioid examples. PDGFRA: often strong/diffuse with paranuclear dot-like accentuation in PDGFRA-mutant GIST. SMA and h-caldesmon may be positive; S100 may be expressed in some tumors. Desmin and keratins are rare. These variable markers should not override the KIT/DOG1-centered profile and morphology. Approximately 85% harbor mutually exclusive activating KIT or PDGFRA variants, causing ligand-independent receptor tyrosine kinase activation and downstream RAS/MAPK and PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling. KIT (~75%): exon 11 is most common (~66% overall; deletions, substitutions, and indels), followed by exon 9 (~6%; usually p.(Ala502_Tyr503dup), enriched in small-intestinal tumors). Exon 13 p.(Lys642Glu) and exon 17 p.(Asn822Lys) are uncommon. PDGFRA (~10%): most commonly exon 18 (~8% overall), especially p.(Asp842Val); exon 12 and 14 variants are rare. PDGFRA-mutant tumors are usually gastric and have a lower metastatic risk overall than KIT-mutant tumors. Rare alternatives include NF1, BRAF, or KRAS alterations; very rare tumors harbor NTRK3, FGFR1, or ALK fusions. KIT/PDGFRA/BRAF-wildtype and NF1-associated tumors are generally not imatinib-sensitive. Progression is associated with stepwise chromosomal losses (14q, 22q, 1p, 15q); higher-risk tumors may acquire CDKN2A, TP53, and RB1 inactivation. DMD inactivation is a late event found in nearly all metastatic GISTs. Secondary KIT mutations in exons 13/14 or 17/18 are important mechanisms of acquired imatinib resistance and may be polyclonal. SDH-deficient GIST Usually gastric, often epithelioid, multinodular/plexiform and sometimes multifocal; KIT and DOG1 remain strong, but SDHB is lost (with SDHA loss only in SDHA-mutant cases). KIT/PDGFRA mutations are absent. See separate profile below. PDGFRA-mutant GIST versus SDH-deficient GIST Both may be gastric and epithelioid. PDGFRA-mutant tumors may show weak/focal or absent KIT and strong PDGFRA; SDH-deficient tumors show loss of SDHB with retained KIT and DOG1. Genotyping and SDH IHC resolve the distinction. Smooth-muscle neoplasm (leiomyoma / leiomyosarcoma) GIST may show SMA or h-caldesmon, but desmin is rare and KIT/DOG1 support GIST. A smooth-muscle phenotype with diffuse desmin and absence of KIT/DOG1 should prompt consideration of smooth-muscle tumor; correlate with the supplied morphology and panel. Schwannian neoplasm S100 can be expressed in a subset of GISTs, so S100 alone is not exclusionary. A diffuse Schwannian phenotype with absent KIT/DOG1 favors a nerve-sheath lesion; the supplied WHO excerpt does not provide a full schwannoma differential panel. Gastric glomus tumor A relevant gastric mesenchymal mimic. Use morphology and a differential-directed panel: GIST is usually KIT/DOG1-positive, whereas glomus tumor shows smooth-muscle differentiation; occasional gastric glomus tumors may express synaptophysin. Other mesenchymal masses / extragastrointestinal GIST For mesenteric, omental, or retroperitoneal lesions, determine whether a GI attachment or primary is present. Many reported extragastrointestinal GISTs may represent detached gastric tumors or metastases rather than a truly de novo extra-GI primary. Do not apply FNCLCC soft-tissue sarcoma grading to GIST. Risk assessment is based principally on mitotic activity, size, and anatomic site, with tumor rupture as an additional adverse factor. Count mitoses in 5 mm², not an assumed number of high-power fields: this commonly corresponds to approximately 20–25 fields with a 40× objective, depending on microscope field diameter. A KIT-negative result does not exclude GIST; add DOG1 and consider PDGFRA-mutant disease. Conversely, KIT positivity alone is not sufficient for diagnosis. Do not infer benign behavior from small size or low mitotic activity without considering site and molecular subtype. Intestinal GISTs are generally more unpredictable than gastric tumors. Tumor rupture is an adverse prognostic factor and must be documented. The best-established risk variables are mitotic activity (per 5 mm²), tumor size, and anatomic site. Gastric and rectal GISTs have higher local recurrence rates than small-bowel GISTs, while small-bowel tumors have higher rates of abdominal dissemination/metastasis. KIT-mutant tumors tend to behave more aggressively than PDGFRA-mutant or triple-wildtype tumors. Mutation subtype also has predictive value: KIT exon 11 has the highest imatinib response; KIT exon 9 may benefit from higher-dose imatinib; PDGFRA p.(Asp842Val) is primarily resistant. Secondary KIT mutations are associated with acquired resistance. Sunitinib, regorafenib, and ripretinib have activity in selected resistant disease; avapritinib has activity in advanced PDGFRA p.(Asp842Val)-mutant disease. Risk models/nomograms may integrate site, size, and mitotic count as continuous variables. SDH-Deficient GIST Distinct molecularly defined GIST type Metastatic potential is not reliably predicted by size or mitotic rate; metastases may nevertheless follow an indolent course Almost exclusively gastric in well-characterized cases. Often multifocal and multinodular/plexiform. A key diagnosis in children, adolescents, and young adults; median age in young-adult series approximately 22 years, with female predominance. It accounts for the overwhelming majority of pediatric GISTs. Multifocality, young age, gastric location, and lymph-node metastases are important clinical clues, although some cases are indistinguishable clinically from other GISTs. May be syndromic: Carney-Stratakis syndrome (germline SDHx pathogenic variant) or Carney triad (SDHC promoter epimutation; GIST, paraganglioma, and pulmonary chondroma). Essential: epithelioid morphology, loss of SDHB expression by immunohistochemistry, and expression of KIT and/or DOG1. Loss of SDHB is required regardless of which SDH-complex subunit is affected. KIT and DOG1 are usually strongly and diffusely expressed, despite absence of KIT and PDGFRA mutations. SDHA IHC helps subclassify: loss of SDHA accompanies SDHA-associated tumors; SDHA is retained in tumors associated with SDHB, SDHC, or SDHD variants and in SDHC epimutation. Confirm that non-neoplastic cells provide an internal positive control before interpreting tumor-cell SDHB/SDHA loss. Typically gastric, centered in muscularis propria, relatively circumscribed but unencapsulated, and often pushes toward mucosal and serosal surfaces. Multifocality and multinodular/plexiform growth are characteristic clues; a rich capillary network and epithelioid predominance (sometimes nested) are common. Lymph-node metastases are more frequent than in conventional GIST and may be present despite a small primary tumor and low mitotic activity. Most tumors retain the general GIST phenotype; rare aggressive dedifferentiated tumors may show focal or complete loss of KIT and DOG1, with sarcomatoid morphology. SDHB: complete loss of granular cytoplasmic staining in tumor cells is the defining IHC finding. Internal non-neoplastic elements must show convincing granular cytoplasmic positivity. SDHA: loss supports an SDHA-associated tumor; retained expression is expected with SDHB/SDHC/SDHD alterations and SDHC epimutation. Beware weak, diffuse, non-granular cytoplasmic blush in tumor cells. This is not equivalent to the strong, granular mitochondrial staining in internal controls and may still represent true SDH deficiency. KIT and DOG1: typically strong and diffuse, helping distinguish SDH-deficient GIST from some PDGFRA-mutant epithelioid GISTs, which often show weak/focal or absent KIT. Interpret SDHB carefully in small biopsies and cell blocks; insufficient internal controls should lead to a cautious/inconclusive interpretation rather than a false call of loss. SDH-deficient GIST lacks KIT and PDGFRA mutations. SDH IHC is considered equally informative as SDH molecular testing for identifying deficiency. Approximately 30% are associated with germline SDHA pathogenic variants; approximately 20% with germline SDHB, SDHC, or SDHD variants; approximately 50% with postzygotic systemic SDHC promoter hypermethylation (epimutation). SDH complex (mitochondrial complex II) comprises SDHA, SDHB, SDHC, and SDHD; SDHAF2 supports SDHA flavination. Dysfunction destabilizes the complex, causing SDHB protein degradation and succinate accumulation. Succinate acts as an oncometabolite and contributes to hypoxic signaling and epigenetic reprogramming, including MGMT promoter hypermethylation. Consider genetic counseling/testing for SDH-associated syndromes, including evaluation for paraganglioma/pheochromocytoma, SDH-deficient renal carcinoma, and pulmonary chondroma. Conventional KIT/PDGFRA-mutant epithelioid GIST Both can be gastric and epithelioid. SDH-deficient GIST shows SDHB loss, often multifocal/plexiform growth and strong KIT/DOG1; KIT/PDGFRA mutations are absent. PDGFRA-mutant tumors may show weak/focal or absent KIT and retain SDHB. PDGFRA-mutant GIST This is the most important molecular/IHC distinction in an epithelioid gastric GIST. Use SDHB (and SDHA) IHC plus KIT/PDGFRA genotyping; morphology alone may not reliably separate them. Both are gastric mesenchymal tumors and can enter the differential. Strong KIT/DOG1 and SDHB loss support SDH-deficient GIST; smooth-muscle marker expression and glomus-cell/perivascular morphology support glomus tumor. Other gastric mesenchymal tumors Use morphology and a targeted IHC panel rather than site alone. The supplied WHO excerpt specifically emphasizes KIT/DOG1 and SDH IHC; it does not provide a comprehensive marker-by-marker differential for all gastric mesenchymal mimics. Dedifferentiated SDH-deficient GIST Rare aggressive sarcomatoid tumors may lose KIT and DOG1. In a gastric sarcoma with suggestive history/morphology, consider dedifferentiation and review prior material; focal loss is reported in aggressive cases. Do not use tumor size and mitotic rate to reassure against metastatic potential: small, mitotically inactive SDH-deficient GISTs may metastasize. Lymph-node spread, uncommon in conventional GIST, is a recognized feature of SDH-deficient GIST. Do not interpret SDHB as lost unless internal non-neoplastic positive controls are present. Distinguish granular mitochondrial staining from weak diffuse cytoplasmic blush. SDHA retention does not exclude SDH deficiency; SDHA is retained in most non-SDHA-associated cases. KIT/DOG1 positivity does not distinguish conventional from SDH-deficient GIST. The SDHB/SDHA profile and mutation status are decisive. Do not equate metastatic spread with rapidly fatal disease; metastases may be indolent and long-term disease-specific survival can remain high. Unlike conventional KIT/PDGFRA-mutant GIST, size and mitotic rate do not reliably predict outcome. Metastatic disease may be indolent despite substantial cumulative metastatic rates. Reported metastatic rates can be high, including lymph-node involvement, while disease-specific survival exceeds 80% at 10 and 15 years in reported series. SDH-deficient tumors do not respond to imatinib. Some activity has been reported with next-generation TKIs such as regorafenib; temozolomide has been explored in the setting of MGMT promoter hypermethylation, with early promising results. Additional KRAS or TP53 mutations and chromosome 1q amplification have been associated with worse outcomes. Because of multifocality, metachronous tumors, and syndromic associations, lifelong surveillance is indicated even when germline sequencing does not identify a pathogenic variant. All PathologyGPS / Gastrointestinal Pathology / Mesenchymal Tumors Gastrointestinal Stromal Tumor A morphology-first diagnostic reference emphasizing essential criteria, KIT/DOG1 immunophenotype, molecular classification, SDH deficiency, and practical differential diagnosis. Core diagnostic rule Establish GIST by morphology and KIT/DOG1, then determine the molecular subtype. In an epithelioid gastric tumor, SDHB IHC is critical: SDH-deficient GIST retains KIT/DOG1 but loses SDHB. Diagnostic GPS: morphology to classification 1. Establish the site Record exact GI segment, mural layer, size, multifocality, and whether the lesion is truly extragastrointestinal or attached to a GI primary. 2. Identify the pattern Spindle, epithelioid, or mixed; note gastric plexiform/multinodular architecture, skeinoid fibers, sclerosis, palisading, and vascular changes. 3. Confirm GIST phenotype KIT and DOG1 are the key markers. Remember that a minority of GISTs, especially PDGFRA-mutant tumors, may be KIT-negative. 4. Separate SDH-deficient GIST In gastric epithelioid or multifocal disease, perform SDHB IHC with internal controls; add SDHA and molecular work-up as indicated. 5. Assess risk and report For conventional GIST, count mitoses per 5 mm² and integrate size, site, and rupture. Do not apply FNCLCC grading or conventional risk rules to SDH-deficient GIST. High-yield diagnostic criteria Conventional GIST: GI mural/submucosal/subserosal mass; spindle, epithelioid, or mixed morphology; KIT and/or DOG1 expression. SDH-deficient GIST: epithelioid morphology; loss of SDHB; KIT and/or DOG1 expression; absence of KIT/PDGFRA mutations. KIT negativity does not exclude GIST. DOG1 can rescue a subset of KIT-negative cases. SDHB loss must be judged against granular cytoplasmic staining in non-neoplastic internal controls.
