Differential diagnosis: practical decision points Diagnostic problem Features favoring GIST Most useful next step KIT-negative suspected GIST Compatible GI mural tumor; DOG1 may remain positive DOG1 IHC; consider PDGFRA mutation testing Gastric epithelioid GIST Epithelioid cells with KIT/DOG1 expression SDHB IHC; add SDHA and KIT/PDGFRA genotyping Gastric mesenchymal tumor with smooth-muscle phenotype KIT/DOG1 expression supports GIST; SMA/h-caldesmon may overlap Use a panel and interpret desmin, KIT, DOG1 with morphology Multifocal gastric GIST in a young patient Plexiform/multinodular growth, epithelioid cells, lymph-node spread SDHB/SDHA IHC and genetic counseling assessment Mesenteric/omental/retroperitoneal GIST-like mass GIST phenotype but no obvious mural primary Search for attachment, detached primary, or occult metastatic GI GIST Risk assessment and reporting checklist Record exact anatomic site, tumor size, multifocality, mural layer, and whether the lesion is primary GI or extragastrointestinal. Document spindle, epithelioid, or mixed morphology and relevant pattern (plexiform, sclerosing, hypercellular, palisaded-vacuolated, skeinoid fibers). Report KIT and DOG1 results; in epithelioid gastric tumors, multifocal tumors, or young patients, assess SDHB and consider SDHA. For conventional GIST, count mitoses in 5 mm² and report tumor size, site, and rupture status. Do not substitute FNCLCC grade. For SDH-deficient GIST, explicitly state that conventional size/mitotic risk models are not reliably predictive; recommend consideration of SDH-syndrome evaluation and lifelong surveillance. In advanced or recurrent disease, mutation subtype and secondary KIT mutations may be relevant to predictive treatment assessment. Scope note: This reference is based on the supplied WHO excerpt. The differential diagnosis emphasizes distinctions supported by that source; it is not an exhaustive catalog of every gastric or intestinal mesenchymal mimic. Ancillary findings must be interpreted with morphology, site, and appropriate internal controls.

title: Pericytic Tumors
content: use client Glomus Tumor Benign / malignant spectrum Usually benign; malignant tumors are aggressive; uncertain malignant potential is a separate category Distal extremities, especially subungual region, hand, wrist, and foot; rare visceral/deep tumors, with an unusual gastric predilection. Cutaneous lesions: usually <10 mm, reddish-blue nodules with longstanding pain, often cold- or touch-triggered. Deep/visceral lesions present as nonspecific masses. Most patients are 20–40 years old; subungual tumors are more common in women. Multiple lesions occur in approximately 10%. Familial multiple glomus tumors (glomuvenous malformations) are autosomal dominant and associated with GLMN inactivation; NF1-associated digital tumors may be multiple. Essential: monomorphic round-to-epithelioid cells with central round nuclei and sharply defined borders, arranged in perivascular nests. Malignant: marked nuclear atypia (irrespective of mitotic activity) OR atypical mitotic figures. A benign-appearing component is often present. If no benign precursor is identified, demonstrate SMA and pericellular collagen IV and/or supportive molecular findings. Tumors with at least one atypical feature other than nuclear pleomorphism, but not meeting malignant criteria, are of uncertain malignant potential. Glomus cells are small, uniform, rounded, with central round nuclei, amphophilic to lightly eosinophilic cytoplasm, and sharp borders; oncocytic/epithelioid change may occur. Solid type (~75%): nests of glomus cells around capillary-sized vessels. Glomuvenous malformation/glomangioma (~20%): cavernous hemangioma-like channels with small clusters of glomus cells. Glomangiomyoma: transition from round glomus cells to elongated mature smooth-muscle-like cells. Glomangiopericytoma pattern: branching hemangiopericytoma-like vessels. Glomangiomatosis: diffuse vascular-malformation-like architecture with glomus cells investing vessel walls. Symplastic glomus tumor: striking nuclear atypia without other malignant features (e.g., large size, deep location, mitotic activity, necrosis). Typically SMA and muscle-specific actin positive; h-caldesmon positive. Pericellular collagen IV is desirable, particularly for malignant tumors without a benign precursor. CD34 is focal or absent. BRAF V600E IHC may be positive in the mutated subset; gastric tumors are commonly synaptophysin-positive. Sporadic soft-tissue/visceral tumors may harbor NOTCH-family rearrangements, commonly CARMN (MIR143HG)::NOTCH1/2/3. NOTCH rearrangements were not detected in subungual glomus tumors or other pericytic tumors in the supplied source. A small subset has BRAF or KRAS variants; BRAF variants have been associated with malignant histology. Familial multiple tumors: germline GLMN inactivation; NF1-associated tumors: biallelic NF1 inactivation. Myopericytoma Round, sharply demarcated glomus cells in nests versus oval/spindle myoid cells in multilayered concentric perivascular cuffs. Angioleiomyoma Mature smooth-muscle bundles around variably sized channels versus uniform round cells around capillaries. Symplastic glomus tumor Marked atypia alone, without atypical mitoses or other malignant features, may be symplastic rather than malignant. Gastric GIST Gastric glomus tumor is usually SMA-positive and may be synaptophysin-positive; interpret a differential-directed panel with morphology. SFT/branching-vessel lesions A branching vascular pattern is not diagnostic; identify the characteristic perivascular round glomus-cell population and myoid phenotype. Size >2 cm and deep location alone do not establish malignancy; these tumors may be of uncertain malignant potential. Infiltrative growth, high cellularity, and spindle-cell morphology are more frequent in malignant/uncertain-potential tumors but require integration with cytology and mitoses. Separate symplastic atypia from malignancy; atypical mitotic figures are a decisive malignant feature. Typical glomus tumors, glomuvenous malformations, and symplastic tumors are benign. Malignant tumors may metastasize; disease-related death has been reported in up to 40%. Some large visceral tumors without other atypical features have behaved aggressively. Usually benign; rare deep-seated malignant tumors may metastasize Usually dermis/subcutis, especially distal extremities; less often proximal extremities, neck, trunk, and oral cavity. Deep, visceral, and intracranial sites are rare. Usually a painless, slow-growing superficial nodule present for years; most are solitary, but multiple lesions/myopericytomatosis occur. Any age, predominantly adults. EBV association has been reported in patients with AIDS. Essential: bland oval-to-spindle myoid cells in multilayered concentric growth around numerous small vessels. SMA, h-caldesmon, and collagen IV support the diagnosis; desmin/CD34 are at most focal. Malignant myopericytoma is exceptionally rare: typically deep, infiltrative, with marked atypia and high mitotic count. Unencapsulated, usually well-circumscribed nodular/lobular lesion; cellularity ranges from solid to hypocellular collagenous/myxoid. Characteristic concentric multilayered cuffs of bland oval-to-spindle myoid cells around numerous small vessels; vessel caliber varies and branching vessels may occur. Fascicular/whorled areas may resemble myofibroma or angioleiomyoma; glomus-like and combined patterns occur. Intravascular examples occur. Degenerative changes include symplastic atypia, hyalinization, and cystic change. Myopericytomatosis describes diffuse dermal/subcutaneous involvement by numerous microscopic nodules. SMA, h-caldesmon, and collagen IV typically positive. Desmin and CD34 usually negative or only focally positive. PDGFRB variants occur in a subset across myopericytoma, myopericytomatosis, and myofibroma; NOTCH3 variants have also been reported. Molecular testing is not clinically relevant for routine diagnosis in the supplied source. Glomus tumor Concentric spindle/ovoid perivascular cuffs favor myopericytoma; round glomus cells in nests favor glomus tumor. Mature eosinophilic smooth-muscle bundles and vascular channels favor angioleiomyoma; layered perivascular cells favor myopericytoma. Myofibroma Biphasic primitive cellular zones plus hyalinized myoid nodules favor myofibroma; uniform concentric cuffs favor myopericytoma. Solitary fibrous tumor Branching vessels overlap; concentric myoid cuffs and SMA/h-caldesmon support myopericytoma. Intravascular growth does not imply malignancy. Degenerative/symplastic atypia may occur in otherwise conventional tumors. Increased cellularity alone is insufficient for malignancy; require convincing atypia, infiltrative growth, and high mitotic activity. Most do not recur, even after marginal/incomplete excision; apparent recurrence may represent persistent growth. Rare malignant tumors have shown aggressive growth, distant spread, and poor outcome. Myofibroma / Myofibromatosis Benign; clinical risk depends on distribution Solitary myofibroma has an excellent prognosis; multicentric/visceral infantile disease may be life-threatening Solitary lesions: skin of extremities, head/neck, and trunk. Infantile myofibromatosis may involve liver, heart, GI tract, brain, and bone. May be congenital, arise in the first 2 years, or occur in adults; adult cases show male predominance. Solitary or multicentric. Congenital/early-childhood lesions may involve viscera or bone. A subset of familial infantile cases is autosomal dominant with variable penetrance; germline PDGFRB variants are established. Essential: biphasic zonation with primitive cellular areas (often branching hemangiopericytoma-like vessels) and peripheral nodules/fascicles of hyalinized myoid spindle cells. Primitive zones may show mitoses, necrosis, and calcification, particularly in infants; these findings alone do not establish malignancy. Both components typically express SMA and collagen IV; desmin and h-caldesmon are usually negative. Well-circumscribed nodule with biphasic architecture. Primitive component: plump immature spindle cells with branching hemangiopericytoma-like vessels; cellularity and mitotic activity may be prominent. Mature component: peripheral nodules/fascicles of variably hyalinized myoid spindle cells; chondroid-appearing matrix may occur. Zonation may be haphazard or reversed in older children/adults. Infantile lesions may consist almost entirely of primitive cellular zones. Intravascular extension is common and does not imply malignancy. Atypical cases may show high cellularity, predominantly fascicular growth, infiltrative growth, or perineurial invasion. Both components express SMA and collagen IV. Desmin and h-caldesmon are usually negative. Germline PDGFRB variants underlie a subset of familial autosomal dominant infantile myofibromatosis. NOTCH3 variants have also been reported in familial myofibromatosis and across the myopericytoma/myofibroma spectrum. Routine molecular testing is not clinically relevant in the supplied source. Biphasic primitive-to-hyalinized zonation favors myofibroma; concentric multilayered cuffs throughout favor myopericytoma. Infantile hemangiopericytoma Historical term for cellular infantile myofibroma; use myofibroma. SFT Branching vessels overlap, but biphasic zonation and SMA/collagen IV support myofibroma. Malignant spindle-cell neoplasm Mitoses/necrosis can occur in primitive zones; integrate atypia, infiltrative pattern, and biphasic architecture. Intravascular extension is common and is not a malignancy criterion. Mitoses, necrosis, and calcification may be present in cellular infantile lesions. Distinguish solitary from multicentric/generalized disease with visceral involvement. Solitary lesions have excellent prognosis and do not recur or metastasize. Infants with generalized disease involving viscera/brain have worse outcomes. PDGFRB-mutant pediatric disease may respond to tyrosine kinase inhibitors such as imatinib. SRF-Rearranged Myoid Neoplasm Usually benign Usually benign; rare metastatic case reported Usually deep soft tissue (skeletal muscle); less often subcutis. Trunk, head/neck, and extremities; rare visceral examples. Painless mass of variable duration; wide age range (infancy–63 years), most in children/young adults; approximately equal sex distribution. Essential: monomorphic ovoid-to-spindle cells with fibrillary cytoplasm in short fascicles, files, or solid growth, showing myoid/immature smooth-muscle differentiation. One or more smooth-muscle markers support myoid differentiation; myogenin and MYOD1 should be negative. Definitive diagnosis requires SRF fusion detection; targeted RNA sequencing or SRF break-apart FISH is recommended. Well-demarcated, unencapsulated, homogeneous tan-white/rubbery mass; most <5 cm, occasional tumors >15 cm. Uniform ovoid-to-spindle cells resembling smooth muscle, with fibrillary cytoplasm and bland nuclei, arranged in short fascicles/files or solid areas. Some show myofibroma-like biphasic growth with primitive round-cell nests and surrounding myoid fascicles; tumor may protrude into dilated vessels. Calcification and collagenous stroma are common. Most have low mitotic activity, but a subset has >10 mitoses/2 mm² and focal necrosis. Most express SMA, desmin, and h-caldesmon; profile varies by fusion partner. SRF::RELA commonly coexpresses SMA/desmin; SRF::ICA1L is often desmin-negative. Cytokeratin expression is variable. Myogenin and MYOD1 are negative. Defining SRF fusion; common partners RELA, ICA1L, CITED1/2, NCOA2; rare partners include MKL2, C3orf62, ARGFXP1, NFKBIE. Most have similar SRF exon 4 breakpoints. Confirm with targeted RNA sequencing or SRF break-apart FISH. SRF fusions also occur in a rare subset of well-differentiated spindle-cell rhabdomyosarcoma in very young children; correlate with skeletal-muscle markers. Leiomyoma/leiomyosarcoma Smooth-muscle markers overlap; SRF fusion and full morphology/context distinguish. High mitotic activity or necrosis warrants careful evaluation. Myofibroma has characteristic biphasic primitive/hyalinized zones; SRF tumor more often has short smooth-muscle-like fascicles and requires fusion confirmation. Spindle-cell rhabdomyosarcoma Myogenin/MYOD1 expression supports skeletal-muscle differentiation; usual SRF-rearranged myoid neoplasm is negative. Other pericytic tumors SMA/desmin/h-caldesmon are not specific; SRF fusion is required for definitive classification. Smooth-muscle phenotype alone is insufficient. High mitotic activity/focal necrosis occur in a minority; integrate fusion, morphology, and clinical behavior. A reported metastatic tumor was 19 cm, highly mitotic, and SRF::ICA1L-positive; this does not establish generally malignant behavior. Most follow a benign course; one lung-metastatic case is reported in the supplied source. Benign Benign; recurrence after excision is very uncommon Usually dermis/subcutis of extremities (lower > upper); also head/neck and trunk. Solid subtype favors lower extremity in women; venous subtype more often head/neck; cavernous subtype more often upper extremity. Firm, well-circumscribed, slow-growing nodule; approximately half are painful, particularly solid type. Broad age range, peaking in third–sixth decades; overall M:F approximately 2:3. Usually solitary and <2 cm. Essential: well-circumscribed tumor of cytologically bland, well-differentiated smooth-muscle cells around variably sized vascular channels. Subtypes by predominant vascular morphology: solid, venous, cavernous; mixed patterns are common. SMA and h-caldesmon are desirable; desmin and calponin are commonly positive. Bundles of bland smooth-muscle cells with intervening vessels of variable caliber. Solid: compact smooth-muscle bundles with thin-walled slit-like channels. Venous: thick-walled muscle-coated vessels; vessel-wall muscle swirls and blends with intervascular bundles. Cavernous: dilated vascular channels with intervascular smooth-muscle bundles that may be difficult to distinguish from vessel walls. Myopericytoma-like concentric perivascular areas may occur. Adipocytic metaplasia, hyalinization, calcification, and degenerative atypia may be present; mitoses are absent. Strong diffuse SMA and calponin; usually diffuse h-caldesmon and desmin. HMB45 and Melan-A are negative, including tumors with adipocytic metaplasia. A subset has NOTCH2 rearrangements or PDGFRB/NOTCH3 variants; rare reports include Xq22/IRS4 rearrangement and CARMN::TXK fusion. Molecular testing is not clinically relevant for routine diagnosis. Mature smooth-muscle bundles/channels favor angioleiomyoma; concentric multilayered cuffs of less eosinophilic myoid cells favor myopericytoma. Uniform round glomus cells in perivascular nests versus mature smooth-muscle fascicles. Angiomyolipoma Do not call angioleiomyoma with adipocytic metaplasia angiomyolipoma; PEComa typically expresses HMB45/Melan-A. Leiomyoma Numerous vascular channels intimately associated with smooth-muscle bundles define angioleiomyoma. Adipocytic metaplasia does not imply angiomyolipoma; HMB45/Melan-A remain negative. Degenerative atypia may occur, but mitoses are absent in conventional angioleiomyoma. The continuum with myopericytoma can complicate classification; focus on mature smooth-muscle bundles versus concentric perivascular layering. Benign; recurrence after surgical excision is very uncommon. All PathologyGPS / Soft Tissue Tumors / Pericytic Tumors Pericytic Tumors A morphology-first diagnostic reference focused on essential criteria, myoid differentiation, molecular confirmation, and practical differential diagnosis. Core rule Read the perivascular architecture before interpreting the immunostains. Round glomus cells, concentric myopericytic cuffs, biphasic myofibroma, and mature smooth-muscle bundles are distinct patterns despite overlapping myoid markers. Diagnostic GPS: morphology to classification Establish the setting Record site, depth, age, multiplicity, and relationship to digits, skin, skeletal muscle, or viscera. Identify the dominant cell Round uniform glomus cells; concentric oval/spindle myoid cells; biphasic myofibroma; or mature smooth-muscle cells. Read the vascular pattern Capillary-centered nests, concentric cuffs, branching vessels, or variably sized muscle-coated channels. Assess atypia carefully Separate symplastic/degenerative atypia from true malignancy; assess atypical mitoses, infiltrative growth, mitotic activity, and necrosis. Use targeted ancillary tests SMA/h-caldesmon/collagen IV for myoid phenotype; SRF fusion for SRF-rearranged neoplasm; molecular tests only where source supports utility. Behavior categories Benign: conventional glomus tumor, glomuvenous malformation, symplastic glomus tumor, most myopericytomas, solitary myofibroma, and angioleiomyoma. Uncertain malignant potential: glomus tumors with atypical features that do not meet malignant criteria; size/deep location alone are insufficient. Rare malignant forms: malignant glomus tumor and malignant myopericytoma; evaluate cytology, mitoses, necrosis, and infiltrative growth. Clinical distribution matters: solitary myofibroma is usually indolent, whereas generalized infantile myofibromatosis with visceral/brain involvement has a worse outcome. High-yield morphology and ancillary tests SMA, h-caldesmon, collagen IV; NOTCH-family fusions in subset Concentric perivascular cuffs; SMA, h-caldesmon, collagen IV Biphasic zonation; SMA and collagen IV SRF-rearranged myoid neoplasm SRF fusion by RNA sequencing or break-apart FISH Mature smooth-muscle bundles; SMA, calponin, h-caldesmon, desmin Entity reference Diagnostic criteria and differential diagnosis Search by entity, morphology, site, marker, or gene. e.g. SMA, collagen IV, PDGFRB, SRF... bg-teal-700 text-white border border-slate-300 bg-white text-slate-600 Collapse − View diagnostic profile + Clinical profile Essential diagnostic criteria Histopathology Immunohistochemistry Molecular pathology Differential diagnosis Prognosis and behavior Diagnostic pitfalls No matching entity. High-stakes comparison: perivascular myoid tumors Feature Dominant cell Round glomus cells Oval/spindle myoid cells Primitive + mature myoid cells Mature smooth-muscle cells Architecture Perivascular nests Concentric multilayered cuffs Biphasic zonation Muscle bundles around vascular channels Key marker pattern SMA, h-caldesmon, collagen IV SMA, collagen IV SMA, calponin, h-caldesmon, desmin Useful distinction Round cells / capillary nests Layered perivascular growth Primitive and hyalinized zones Mature muscle / channel pattern Sampling and reporting checklist Document exact site, depth, size, and relationship to skin, digit, tendon, skeletal muscle, or viscera. Sample heterogeneous areas, especially infiltrative edges, solid nodules, necrosis, and areas with cytologic atypia. For glomus tumors, distinguish symplastic atypia from malignant criteria; record atypical mitoses, mitotic activity, necrosis, and growth pattern. For myopericytoma/myofibroma, assess concentric perivascular cuffs versus biphasic zonation; do not interpret intravascular extension alone as malignancy. For SRF-rearranged myoid neoplasm, obtain molecular confirmation by RNA sequencing or SRF break-apart FISH. For angioleiomyoma, describe predominant solid, venous, or cavernous vascular pattern and document any atypia or mitoses. Scope note: Based on the supplied WHO excerpt. Molecular and immunohistochemical findings are presented within the limits stated by the source; they are not substitutes for morphology and clinicopathologic correlation.

title: Peripheral Nerve Sheath Tumors
content: use client Schwannoma Benign peripheral nerve sheath tumors Benign; recurrence is uncommon after gross total resection Peripheral nerves of skin/subcutis (especially head and neck and flexor surfaces of extremities), spinal intradural extramedullary compartment, and cranial nerves (especially vestibular division of CN VIII). Usually solitary and sporadic (>90%); peak incidence in the fourth to sixth decades, with no sex or race predilection. Slow-growing, often asymptomatic or incidental; pain may occur, especially in schwannomatosis. Spinal lesions may cause radicular sensory or motor symptoms; vestibular tumors may cause hearing loss and vertigo. Multiple tumors, young age, bilateral vestibular schwannomas, or multifocal nerve involvement should prompt consideration of NF2-related or other schwannomatosis. Essential: a benign tumor composed almost entirely of Schwann cells, showing one or more characteristic architectural patterns. Desirable: diffuse S100 and SOX10 immunoreactivity. A capsule and displacement/draping of uninvolved nerve fascicles support schwannoma; intratumoral axons are generally absent or limited compared with neurofibroma. Conventional schwannoma is usually encapsulated and biphasic: compact Antoni A areas alternating with loose Antoni B areas. Antoni A: elongated tapered nuclei, modest eosinophilic cytoplasm, occasional nuclear palisading and Verocay bodies (parallel nuclear rows separated by aligned cell processes). Antoni B: loose cobweb-like tumor processes, lipid-laden histiocytes, thick-walled hyalinized vessels, hemosiderin, and cystic degeneration. Peripheral/subcapsular lymphoid aggregates may occur. Ancient schwannoma: scattered bizarre degenerative nuclei, often with hyalinization or ischemic change; atypia alone does not imply malignancy. Cellular schwannoma: predominantly/exclusively Antoni A, lacks Verocay bodies, may be hypercellular, hyperchromatic and mitotically active, with small necrotic foci. Encapsulation, subcapsular lymphocytes, hyalinized vessels and Schwannian whorls support schwannoma over MPNST. Plexiform schwannoma: thinly encapsulated or unencapsulated multinodular/plexiform growth, often superficial and presenting in childhood; thick-walled vessels may be absent. Epithelioid schwannoma: multilobulated epithelioid cells in myxoid/hyalinized stroma; conventional spindle areas may coexist. Microcystic/reticular schwannoma: interconnected microcyst-rich network of bland spindle cells in myxoid/fibrillary/hyalinized stroma; conventional Verocay bodies and hyalinized vessels are usually absent. S100 and SOX10: diffuse, extensive nuclear and cytoplasmic staining is characteristic across subtypes. GFAP is variable; collagen IV typically outlines pericellular basement membranes. CD34 is commonly limited to subcapsular areas, unlike the lattice-like stromal pattern of neurofibroma. Neurofilament highlights entrapped axons, often at the periphery; EMA may highlight perineurial cells in the capsule. Cellular schwannoma: Ki-67 may show hotspots but remains below 20% in the source description; p16 and H3K27me3 are retained. Epithelioid schwannoma may lose SMARCB1/INI1 in a subset (~40%); this overlaps with epithelioid MPNST and is not independently proof of malignancy. NF2 inactivation is found in approximately 50–75% of sporadic cases; other reported alterations include LATS1/2, ARID1A/B, DDR1 and SOX10. An SH3PXD2A::HTRA1 fusion is reported in roughly 10%. Multiple schwannomas may reflect NF2-, SMARCB1-, LZTR1- or chromosome 22-related schwannomatosis; mosaic/segmental forms occur. Molecular diagnostic testing is not clinically relevant for routine diagnosis according to the WHO excerpt. Neurofibroma Schwannoma is usually encapsulated, composed almost entirely of Schwann cells, and diffusely S100/SOX10-positive; neurofibroma is unencapsulated, infiltrative, mixed-cellular and contains axons. Cellular schwannoma vs MPNST Cellular schwannoma may be hypercellular, hyperchromatic, mitotically active and occasionally show small necrotic foci. Look for encapsulation, subcapsular lymphocytes, hyalinized vessels and Schwannian whorls; retained H3K27me3/p16 and Ki-67 hotspots <20% support cellular schwannoma in the source description. Epithelioid schwannoma vs epithelioid MPNST Both may show epithelioid morphology and SMARCB1 loss. Infiltrative margins, geographic necrosis and significant atypia favor epithelioid MPNST; mild atypia without necrosis may remain challenging. Melanotic lesion Neuromelanin-like pigment can occur in otherwise typical schwannoma; melanocytic markers such as HMB45 are negative, unlike malignant melanotic nerve sheath tumor. Bizarre degenerative nuclei in ancient schwannoma do not by themselves indicate malignancy. Cellular schwannoma may mimic MPNST; assess the overall architecture and ancillary profile, not cellularity alone. Diffuse S100/SOX10 is typical of schwannoma but is not the pattern of conventional MPNST; epithelioid MPNST is an important exception. SMARCB1 loss occurs in both epithelioid schwannoma and epithelioid MPNST. Usually no recurrence after gross total resection; cellular and plexiform tumors may be difficult to remove completely and may require debulking. Malignant transformation of conventional schwannoma is exceptionally rare; reported transformations have most often been epithelioid MPNST. Benign overall; plexiform and sizeable intraneural lesions carry risk of transformation Most often skin; less often deep medium-sized nerves, plexuses, major nerve trunks and spinal roots. Multiple paraspinal tumors are common in NF1. Most are sporadic and solitary; multiple or plexiform tumors strongly suggest NF1. Cutaneous lesions are usually asymptomatic, mobile, soft masses. Deep lesions may cause nerve-distribution motor or sensory symptoms. NF1-associated clues include café-au-lait macules, axillary/inguinal freckling, Lisch nodules, optic pathway gliomas and bone dysplasia. A distinct growing nodule or increased PET activity within a plexiform neurofibroma raises concern for ANNUBP or MPNST. Essential: a low-cellularity spindle-cell neoplasm associated with variably myxoid to collagenous stroma. Desirable: Schwannian cells positive for S100/SOX10, with CD34-positive stromal cells in a lattice-like pattern and neurofilament-positive entrapped axons. In an NF1-associated lesion, at least two ANNUBP features (atypia, hypercellularity, loss of neurofibroma architecture, or specified increased mitotic activity) raise the diagnosis; p16 loss/CDKN2A/B inactivation may support it. Bland spindle cells with thin, wavy nuclei are dispersed in loose myxoid stroma with collagen often described as shredded-carrot-like. Mixed cellular components include neoplastic Schwann cells, perineurial/perineurial-like cells, fibroblasts and mast cells. The tumor is unencapsulated and tends to infiltrate soft tissue and parent nerves. Localized intraneural lesions expand one nerve fascicle; plexiform lesions expand multiple fascicles, each bounded by perineurium, producing a bag-of-worms/ropy pattern. Diffuse cutaneous and massive diffuse soft-tissue forms may extensively involve dermis, subcutis and skeletal muscle. Pseudomeissnerian corpuscles are typical in diffuse and plexiform forms. Ancient neurofibroma: scattered bizarre nuclei and smudgy chromatin without other worrisome features; not a premalignant lesion. Cellular neurofibroma: hypercellularity without cytologic atypia or increased mitotic activity. ANNUBP: at least two of four features—cytologic atypia, hypercellularity, loss of neurofibroma architecture, and mitotic count >1/10 mm² but <3/2 mm². This concept is principally developed for NF1-associated tumors. S100 and SOX10 label the Schwannian component, often less extensively than in schwannoma; collagen IV is also positive in Schwann cells. CD34 highlights stromal cells in a characteristic lattice-like network; EMA/GLUT1 highlight limited perineurial cells. Neurofilament highlights entrapped axons. p16 is usually retained in a subset of tumor cells but may be lost in ANNUBP/MPNST foci; Ki-67 is typically low in conventional neurofibroma. p16 loss can serve as a surrogate for CDKN2A/CDKN2B inactivation in selected ANNUBP cases. Biallelic NF1 inactivation in the neoplastic Schwann-cell population is the recurrent somatic event in conventional neurofibroma. ANNUBP is associated with CDKN2A/CDKN2B deletion; occasional SMARCA2 loss is reported. MPNST more often acquires additional alterations including SUZ12, EED or TP53 inactivation and chromosomal aneuploidy. CDKN2A/CDKN2B inactivation may support ANNUBP in selected cases; it is not a substitute for morphology. Neurofibroma is unencapsulated, infiltrative, mixed-cellular, collagenous/myxoid and contains entrapped axons; schwannoma is usually encapsulated and diffusely S100/SOX10-positive. Ancient neurofibroma vs ANNUBP Scattered bizarre degenerative nuclei alone define atypia/ancient change and are not premalignant. ANNUBP requires at least two specified worrisome features. Cellular neurofibroma vs MPNST Cellularity alone is insufficient for MPNST; assess atypia, mitotic activity, necrosis and loss of architecture. ANNUBP vs MPNST ANNUBP falls short of MPNST criteria but is a precursor/early malignant stage with increased progression risk; MPNST typically shows additional genomic complexity and malignant histology. Do not equate ancient neurofibroma with ANNUBP. Do not diagnose ANNUBP from hypercellularity alone; at least two specified features are required. Plexiform neurofibroma is strongly associated with NF1 and carries increased MPNST risk. A massive diffuse soft-tissue neurofibroma is benign in itself, but an associated intraneural/plexiform component may harbor MPNST. Localized cutaneous neurofibromas are consistently benign; diffuse cutaneous lesions rarely transform. Plexiform and sizeable solitary intraneural neurofibromas carry transformation risk. Lifetime MPNST risk in NF1 is estimated at 9–13%. ANNUBP is considered a precursor lesion; one study reported low recurrence even with positive margins, arguing against automatically aggressive surgery. Perineurioma Benign and rare malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumors Soft-tissue and sclerosing forms are benign; malignant perineurioma is very rare Soft-tissue lesions most often involve lower limbs, then upper limbs and trunk; sclerosing perineurioma commonly affects fingers and palms. Intraneural and mucosal forms occur at other sites. Usually a painless mass; subcutis is more often involved than deep soft tissue. About 10% are dermal. Middle-aged adults are typical, with slight female predominance; sclerosing perineurioma tends to affect young adult men. Essential: storiform, whorled and/or lamellar architecture; elongated slender spindle cells with bipolar cytoplasmic processes; EMA expression. Desirable: variable claudin-1, GLUT1 and CD34 expression. Malignant perineurioma requires malignant cytologic/cellular features, including hypercellularity, atypia/hyperchromasia and high mitotic count. Soft-tissue perineurioma is well-circumscribed but unencapsulated, usually firm/rubbery and yellow-tan-white. Predominantly storiform or whorled growth; long lamellar fascicles and perivascular growth may occur. Cells are slender spindle cells with wavy/tapered nuclei and delicate bipolar processes. Stroma is usually collagenous; approximately 20% show focal myxoid matrix. Mitoses are scarce or absent. Degenerative pleomorphic or multinucleated cells may occur. Sclerosing perineurioma: cords of small epithelioid-to-spindle cells in dense collagen. Reticular perineurioma: elongated interconnected cells in a lacy pattern. Intraneural perineurioma forms circumferential perineurial whorls around nerve fibers (pseudo-onion bulbs); mucosal perineurioma expands lamina propria with swirling delicate spindle cells. Rare malignant perineurioma shows hypercellularity, nuclear atypia/hyperchromasia and high mitotic activity. EMA is consistently expressed, ranging from weak/focal to strong/diffuse; claudin-1 and GLUT1 are often positive. CD34 is positive in about 60%. S100, SOX10 and GFAP are negative, supporting separation from Schwannian tumors. Sclerosing perineurioma may show limited keratin staining. 22q12 deletion and NF2 mutations are recurrent; 17q11 deletion including NF1 is also reported. 10q24 alterations recur in sclerosing perineurioma. Molecular diagnostic testing is not clinically relevant for routine diagnosis in the supplied WHO excerpt. Perineurioma expresses EMA/claudin-1/GLUT1 and lacks S100/SOX10; schwannoma shows diffuse S100/SOX10 and pericellular collagen IV. Perineurioma has a characteristic storiform/whorled/lamellar pattern and EMA-positive perineurial phenotype; neurofibroma has Schwannian S100/SOX10-positive cells and lattice-like CD34 stromal cells. Malignant perineurioma Degenerative atypia alone may occur in benign tumors. Malignancy requires a combination of hypercellularity, significant atypia/hyperchromasia and high mitotic activity. Sclerosing perineurioma vs other sclerosing acral lesions Cords of epithelioid/spindle cells in dense collagen with EMA positivity support sclerosing perineurioma. Degenerative nuclear atypia does not by itself indicate malignancy. Do not expect S100/SOX10 positivity in a conventional perineurioma. EMA can highlight capsule/perineurial cells in other nerve sheath tumors; interpret staining in the lesional cells. Benign soft-tissue and sclerosing perineuriomas rarely recur locally. Malignant perineuriomas may metastasize but appear less aggressive than conventional MPNST in reported cases. Granular Cell Tumor Schwannian tumors with benign and malignant forms Usually benign; malignant tumors are rare (approximately 1–2%) but have substantial metastatic risk Deep dermis/subcutis, especially head and neck, trunk and proximal extremities; tongue is the most common single site (~25%), followed by breast. GI and respiratory mucosa may be involved. Usually an indolent, firm, often asymptomatic lesion; skin/tongue lesions may itch or hurt. Typically adults aged 40–60 years; some series report female predominance. Up to 10% are multifocal. Malignant tumors usually arise in deep soft tissues, especially trunk and extremities, and are often >5 cm. Essential: nests, trabeculae and sheets of epithelioid-to-polygonal cells with abundant intensely eosinophilic granular cytoplasm and diffuse S100 or SOX10 immunoreactivity. For malignant potential, assess the six histologic parameters: spindling, high N:C ratio, vesicular nuclei with prominent nucleoli, pleomorphism, increased mitoses (>2/2 mm²), and geographic necrosis. Three or more are helpful to identify tumors with metastatic propensity; neither mitoses nor necrosis alone captures all metastatic cases. Poorly defined/infiltrative sheets, nests and trabeculae of large polygonal cells with abundant granular eosinophilic cytoplasm. Granularity reflects lysosomal accumulation; granules are PAS-positive and diastase-resistant, sometimes with clear halos. Cell borders may be indistinct and syncytial. Nuclei range from small mildly hyperchromatic to vesicular with prominent nucleoli; mitoses are usually scant in benign lesions. Overlying squamous epithelium, especially tongue and esophagus, may show florid pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia mimicking squamous cell carcinoma. Malignant tumors range from overtly sarcomatous to deceptively bland; assess the complete six-feature panel rather than any single feature. S100 and SOX10 are typically diffuse; α-inhibin and calretinin are commonly positive. CD68, CD63/NKI-C3 and NSE are positive but likely reflect lysosomal content and are nonspecific. Keratin, CD163 and myogenic markers are negative. MITF and TFE3 often show diffuse nuclear staining; HMB45 is consistently negative, while rare focal melan-A may occur. Loss-of-function variants in ATP6AP1 (~61%) and ATP6AP2 (~11%) collectively occur in approximately 72%; other V-ATPase-related genes are altered in a subset. These V-ATPase gene alterations are highly characteristic/pathognomonic in the WHO excerpt, but molecular testing is not designated clinically relevant for routine diagnosis. Squamous cell carcinoma Florid pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia can overlie a granular cell tumor. Identify the subepithelial granular cells and confirm Schwannian phenotype. Histiocytic lesion Granular cell tumor may express CD68/CD63, but diffuse S100/SOX10 and absence of CD163 support granular cell tumor over histiocytic proliferation. Melanocytic tumor Granular cell tumor is typically HMB45-negative and strongly S100/SOX10-positive; MITF/TFE3 nuclear staining is not proof of melanocytic differentiation. Benign vs malignant granular cell tumor Use the constellation of six histologic parameters; three or more are helpful for metastatic propensity. A single feature, including necrosis or mitotic activity, is insufficient. Pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia can be mistaken for invasive squamous cell carcinoma; sample and examine the underlying lesion. CD68 positivity is nonspecific and reflects lysosomes. No single histologic feature reliably identifies every tumor that will metastasize. Benign tumors may recur if incompletely excised. Malignant granular cell tumors have approximately 50% metastatic rate, including regional nodes and distant sites. Older age, size >5 cm, local recurrence and metastasis are adverse factors. The supplied excerpt notes no established prognostic value for AJCC TNM staging. Dermal Nerve Sheath Myxoma Benign; incomplete excision is associated with frequent local recurrence Predominantly distal extremities, especially fingers/toes and lower extremities; fingers account for approximately 36%. Small, superficial, slow-growing, often asymptomatic mass; occasional pain. Rare tumor, peak incidence in young adults (mid-thirties), slight male predominance; reported age range 8–72 years. Essential: a myxoid dermal and/or subcutaneous neoplasm with multilobulated growth, composed of bland spindle and epithelioid Schwann cells; S100 positivity. Desirable: small superficial lesion on distal extremity (often finger/toe) in a young adult. Usually dermal/subcutaneous, often multinodular with abundant myxoid matrix bordered by dense fibrous tissue; rare extension into skeletal muscle. Small epithelioid, ring-like, stellate and spindle Schwann cells form cords, nests and syncytial aggregates. Ring-like cells may mimic lipoblasts. Usually mild atypia and very few or absent mitoses; scattered moderate degenerative pleomorphism may occur. Rare focal palisading or Verocay-like structures; multivacuolated cells and spider-like processes are uncommon. Diffuse S100 and SOX10; GFAP and CD57 often moderate-to-diffuse; collagen IV strongly outlines tumor cells. Rare keratin-positive cells, scattered EMA-positive capsule perineurial cells, occasional CD34-positive fibroblasts; NFP-positive axons are infrequent. No recurrent genetic abnormality identified. Expression profiling resembles dermal schwannoma and differs from cellular neurothekeoma. Molecular diagnostic pathology is not clinically relevant. Cellular neurothekeoma Dermal nerve sheath myxoma is Schwannian (diffuse S100/SOX10) and abundantly myxoid/multinodular; cellular neurothekeoma is biologically and molecularly distinct. Lipoblastoma / liposarcoma mimic Ring-like or multivacuolated cells can resemble lipoblasts; use the diffuse Schwannian immunophenotype and abundant myxoid lobulated architecture. Both are S100/SOX10-positive; dermal nerve sheath myxoma is typically superficial, multinodular and abundantly myxoid, with ring-like/epithelioid cells. Do not use the obsolete term myxoid variant of neurothekeoma; WHO identifies this as a Schwann cell tumor distinct from cellular neurothekeoma. Ring-like cells can mimic lipoblasts. Incomplete excision has a high recurrence rate, particularly in finger lesions. Benign, but local recurrence is common after incomplete removal. In the largest modern series, 47% recurred after local excision; repeated recurrences and persistent disease were reported, especially in finger tumors. Solitary Circumscribed Neuroma Benign; recurrence is exceptional after complete excision Approximately 90% occur on the face (cheek, nose, forehead, lips, eyelids, chin); oral mucosa is the second most common site. Usually a solitary, slow-growing, firm, painless dermal nodule, typically 2–5 mm. Most common in fifth to seventh decades; no sex predilection. Multiple cases are rare. Essential: circumscribed cutaneous lesion composed of Schwann-cell-rich nerve fascicles, with or without partial capsule, focal palisading and artefactual clefting; S100 positivity and NFP-positive axons. Desirable: capsule highlighted by perineurial markers EMA/GLUT1. Well-demarcated dermal proliferation of bland spindle Schwann cells with wavy nuclei in hyalinized collagen; commonly lobular with well-developed microfascicles and variable nuclear palisading. Thin perineurial-derived capsule may be incomplete superficially; a parent nerve may be seen at the base. Artefactual clefting is frequent. No cytologic atypia and inconspicuous mitoses; overlying epidermis is usually normal or attenuated. Spindle cells strongly and diffusely S100-positive and GFAP-negative. NFP highlights intratumoral axons; axon-to-Schwann cell ratio is <1:2. Capsular perineurial cells express EMA, claudin-1 and GLUT1. Pathogenesis unknown; molecular testing is not clinically relevant. Traumatic neuroma Solitary circumscribed neuroma is usually not associated with trauma or histologic evidence of traumatic nerve injury; it is a circumscribed Schwann-cell-rich dermal nodule. SCN contains intratumoral NFP-positive axons and microfascicles; schwannoma is typically encapsulated and composed almost entirely of Schwann cells. SCN is circumscribed and Schwann-cell-rich with hyalinized collagen and palisading; neurofibroma is unencapsulated, mixed-cellular and more diffusely myxocollagenous. The presence of axons is important; use NFP to demonstrate them. Do not assume a traumatic etiology in the absence of history or histologic evidence. Rare multiple lesions have been described, but the source does not establish a consistent syndrome association. Benign; generally no recurrence after complete excision. Only a single recurrence was documented in the cited literature; no metastases reported. Ectopic Meningioma and Meningothelial Hamartoma Other nerve-associated / meningothelial lesions Usually benign; behavior follows meningioma grade and extent of resection Entirely extracranial/extraspinal sites, including scalp, calvarium, sinonasal region and rare visceral sites; meningothelial hamartoma most often involves scalp skin/subcutis. Ectopic meningioma is a rare extra-CNS meningioma; scalp meningothelial hamartoma may present as a congenital or early-life cutaneous lesion. Some lesions are incidental and may represent ectopic rests or metaplastic meningothelial-like cells. Essential: meningothelial rest or neoplasm located entirely outside the CNS, with no connection to the CNS. Establish absence of a primary intracranial/intraspinal connection by imaging and clinical correlation. Ectopic meningiomas resemble their CNS counterparts and may show similar histologic grades; benign meningothelial tumors predominate. Scalp meningothelial hamartomas often show slit-like spaces resembling lymphatics but lined by meningothelial cells, with meningothelial clusters and psammoma bodies. Gross appearance varies; calvarial meningiomas are typically hyperostotic. No highly sensitive/specific marker is available. Most express vimentin, EMA and progesterone receptor; SSTR2A may also be expressed. p63 may be positive in meningioma and is not reliable for distinguishing it from epithelial neoplasms. Molecular studies are limited; PTEN and Gorlin syndrome associations have been reported, but pathogenesis remains uncertain. Primary CNS meningioma with extracranial extension The essential distinction is a lesion entirely outside the CNS with no connection; correlate with imaging. Lymphatic or vascular lesion in scalp Meningothelial hamartoma may form slit-like spaces, but the lining cells are meningothelial rather than endothelial; psammoma bodies and meningothelial clusters may help. Epithelial neoplasm EMA and p63 are not specific; interpret the full morphology and clinical/anatomic setting. Do not diagnose ectopic meningioma without excluding a CNS connection. SSTR2A/EMA/PR positivity supports but does not independently establish the diagnosis. p63 expression is not a reliable discriminator from epithelial tumors. Tumor grade and completeness of resection influence outcome. Intraosseous skull-base cases recur more often than convexity cases. Distant metastases have been reported in approximately 6%, mostly in anaplastic examples; hamartomas are usually cured by surgery with rare recurrence. Neuromuscular Choristoma Benign intraneural lesion; important association with subsequent desmoid fibromatosis Proximal large nerves and plexuses, especially sciatic nerve and brachial plexus; cranial nerve and intraorbital examples reported. Extremely rare (<100 reported cases), usually infancy/childhood but adult presentation occurs; sexes roughly equal. Pain or peripheral neuropathy, often with limb atrophy/undergrowth. MRI signal resembles skeletal muscle; interfascicular fat is limited (<50%), unlike lipomatosis of nerve. Desmoid fibromatosis develops in roughly 80%, often after surgery/biopsy; MRI may show a contrast-enhancing fibroblastic mass. Essential: mature skeletal muscle within nerve fascicles. For neuromuscular choristoma–desmoid fibromatosis: associated invasive fibroblastic/myofibroblastic proliferation with sweeping fascicles. Desirable: validate both myogenic and neural components; EMA-positive perineurium around individual fascicles; nuclear β-catenin may be present. Fusiform enlargement of a proximal nerve with multifascicular involvement; some fascicles appear beefy red on cut surface. Haphazard bundles of mature cross-striated skeletal muscle are intercalated among intraneural Schwann cells, axons and perineurium. Associated desmoid fibromatosis shows invasive fibroblastic/myofibroblastic proliferation with sweeping fascicles. Myogenic component expresses mature skeletal muscle markers including desmin. Residual nerve: neurofilament-positive axons and S100/SOX10-positive Schwann cells; EMA outlines perineurium around individual fascicles. Nuclear β-catenin may be seen in neural and myogenic cells and in associated desmoid fibromatosis. Most cases and associated desmoid components show CTNNB1 exon 3 mutations, commonly p.(Ser45Phe); possible somatic mosaicism is proposed. Molecular testing is not clinically relevant for routine diagnosis. Lipomatosis of nerve Neuromuscular choristoma contains mature skeletal muscle within fascicles and has limited interfascicular fat (<50%); lipomatosis of nerve is characterized by abundant interfascicular adipose tissue. Intraneural rhabdomyoma / other myogenic lesion Demonstrate mature muscle intercalated within native nerve fascicles, with preserved axons, Schwann cells and perineurium. Desmoid fibromatosis A fibroblastic mass may coexist with neuromuscular choristoma; recognize the intraneural muscle component and avoid confusing the primary nerve lesion with the secondary desmoid. Because the lesion involves a functional nerve, biopsy or radical resection can cause morbidity and may trigger desmoid fibromatosis. In classic radiologic settings, a no-touch approach has been advocated due to risk of desmoid development after biopsy. Do not confuse mature intraneural skeletal muscle with a malignant rhabdomyoblastic component. NMC is considered benign, but associated desmoid fibromatosis is frequent and may be locally aggressive. Accurate intraoperative recognition is important to avoid overly aggressive nerve resection; advanced desmoid disease may require radical surgery or amputation. Hybrid Nerve Sheath Tumor Benign; recurrence is uncommon and generally related to incomplete excision Schwannoma-perineurioma usually occurs in superficial soft tissues of extremities, trunk and head/neck; schwannoma-neurofibroma often arises in association with a nerve and may be superficial or deep. Schwannoma-perineurioma: superficial mass, usually asymptomatic or mildly tender; young adults are common, slight female predilection. Schwannoma-neurofibroma: mass with possible pain, paresthesia or paresis; multiple lesions may occur with NF2-related, SMARCB1/LZTR1-related schwannomatosis or NF1. Schwannoma-perineurioma: bland spindle cells with Schwannian differentiation (S100/SOX10) admixed with perineurial-differentiated cells (CD34 and/or EMA); VGLL3 rearrangement is desirable in unusual cases. Schwannoma-neurofibroma: juxtaposed components morphologically and immunophenotypically typical of both schwannoma and neurofibroma. Other combinations include neurofibroma-perineurioma and granular cell tumor-perineurioma, but the supplied WHO excerpt notes these are exceptionally uncommon and does not elaborate. Schwannoma-perineurioma: generally lobulated, composed of vague spindle-cell fascicles with variable cellularity; focal storiform, whorled or microcystic patterns may occur. Low-power appearance often resembles perineurioma. Schwannoma-perineurioma cells have eosinophilic cytoplasm with delicate fibrillar processes, monomorphic ovoid nuclei and inconspicuous mitoses; necrosis has not been reported. Schwannoma-neurofibroma: two distinct components—circumscribed cellular schwannoma-like nodules with fascicular/whorled growth, and hypocellular neurofibroma-like areas with wavy nuclei, myxoid collagenous stroma and capillary-like vessels. There is no consensus on whether schwannoma-neurofibroma is a distinct entity; it may represent a heterogeneous group or Schwann-cell-rich neurofibroma/Antoni B-like areas. Schwannoma-perineurioma: dominant S100/SOX10-positive Schwannian population plus a second slender-cell population variably highlighted by CD34, EMA, claudin-1 and GLUT1. Schwannoma-neurofibroma: schwannoma component diffusely S100/SOX10-positive; neurofibroma component variably S100-positive and consistently CD34-positive. EMA is negative in tumor cells but may highlight a perineurial layer. CD34 and entrapped axons are not independently diagnostic because similar findings may occur in schwannoma. Schwannoma-perineurioma: approximately 50% have CHD7::VGLL3 fusion; other VGLL3 partners and diverse alternative fusions are reported. Schwannoma-neurofibroma: monosomy 22 and chromosome 22q gene alterations (including LZTR1, NF2, SMARCB1) are reported; molecular findings are heterogeneous. Molecular testing is not required for prototypical morphology/immunophenotype; VGLL3 or related fusion may support challenging schwannoma-perineurioma. Hybrid tumor requires a distinct second component with perineurial or neurofibromatous morphology/phenotype; focal CD34 alone is insufficient. Neurofibroma with Schwann-cell-rich nodules Schwannoma-neurofibroma criteria lack consensus; consider the possibility that apparent hybrid areas represent Schwann-cell proliferations within neurofibroma. Myxoid schwannoma / Antoni B areas Some schwannoma-neurofibroma-like lesions may reflect Antoni B areas rather than a distinct hybrid entity; correlate morphology and immunophenotype across the lesion. Schwannoma-perineurioma Look for two immunophenotypically distinct cell populations, S100/SOX10-positive and perineurial-marker-positive. Do not diagnose a hybrid tumor solely because CD34-positive cells or entrapped axons are present. Schwannoma-neurofibroma is a less settled category; document the two components and acknowledge diagnostic uncertainty when appropriate. Prototypical schwannoma-perineurioma generally does not require molecular confirmation. Schwannoma-perineurioma is benign; local recurrence is associated with incomplete excision. Schwannoma-neurofibroma is considered benign, with very rare local recurrence. Malignant Peripheral Nerve Sheath Tumor (MPNST) Malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumors Aggressive sarcoma with poor prognosis; malignant triton tumor is particularly aggressive Often deep, arising from a major nerve or pre-existing plexiform neurofibroma; may occur anywhere in the body. Usually affects adults aged 20–50 years; rare in children and often NF1-associated when pediatric. Associated with NF1 or prior radiation; may present with enlarging mass, pain, neuropathic symptoms or neurologic deficit. In NF1, a distinct growing nodule or increased FDG-PET activity within plexiform neurofibroma is concerning but imaging is not specific. Essential: spindle-cell sarcoma usually arising from a pre-existing nerve sheath tumor or in a patient with NF1. In sporadic/radiation-associated cases, diagnosis integrates morphology and evidence of Schwannian differentiation (often focal S100/SOX10) and/or H3K27me3 loss. Low-grade MPNST: 1.5–4.5 mitoses/mm² without necrosis; high-grade: ≥5 mitoses/mm², or 1.5–4.5 mitoses/mm² with necrosis (criteria cited in the WHO excerpt). Typically fascicles of spindle cells with alternating hypercellular and hypocellular areas (tapestry/marble-like pattern), often with hemangiopericytoma-like vasculature. Cells have monomorphic hyperchromatic wavy nuclei and pale eosinophilic cytoplasm; geographic necrosis and conspicuous mitoses are common. Pleomorphism may be extensive and mimic undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma. Perivascular accentuation may occur; tumor may track along nerve bundles. Heterologous differentiation occurs in ~15%: skeletal muscle (malignant triton tumor), bone, cartilage or endothelium. Rare glandular MPNST, usually in NF1, may produce mucin. S100 is positive in <50%, SOX10 in <70%, and GFAP in 20–30%; staining is usually focal/patchy. Diffuse S100/SOX10 is generally incompatible with conventional MPNST. Complete H3K27me3 loss is a surrogate for PRC2 deficiency and supports MPNST, especially high-grade, sporadic de novo and radiation-associated tumors. Weak/focal staining or mosaic loss is not diagnostically meaningful. Heterologous components stain with their respective lineage markers; glandular areas express keratin and CEA and may express neuroendocrine markers. Complex karyotypes with frequent concurrent inactivation of NF1, CDKN2A/CDKN2B, TP53 and PRC2 components EED or SUZ12. PRC2 loss causes complete H3K27me3 loss in many high-grade tumors; additional copy-number alterations accumulate during progression from plexiform neurofibroma through ANNUBP to MPNST. Rare NTRK fusions have been reported, including in NF1-associated or H3K27me3-loss cases; routine molecular diagnostic testing is not used. Cellular schwannoma Cellular schwannoma may be mitotically active but usually retains H3K27me3/p16 and shows capsule, subcapsular lymphocytes, hyalinized vessels and Schwannian whorls; S100/SOX10 is typically diffuse. ANNUBP ANNUBP is an NF1-associated precursor/early lesion with at least two specified histologic features but falls short of MPNST criteria; assess mitotic count, necrosis, architecture and molecular progression. Undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma MPNST may be markedly pleomorphic; nerve association, NF1 history, focal Schwannian markers and H3K27me3 loss support MPNST. Epithelioid MPNST Epithelioid MPNST is a distinct entity with diffuse S100/SOX10, frequent SMARCB1 loss and retained H3K27me3, unlike conventional MPNST. Malignant triton tumor This is MPNST with skeletal muscle differentiation, including mature rhabdomyoblasts; it is particularly aggressive. S100/SOX10 are often only focal or absent; lack of diffuse staining does not exclude MPNST. Only complete H3K27me3 loss is meaningful; weak/focal staining or mosaic loss lacks diagnostic relevance. H3K27me3 loss is a surrogate, not an entity-specific standalone test; integrate NF1/nerve association and morphology. Distinguish ANNUBP from low-grade MPNST carefully, especially on small biopsies. Aggressive with poor prognosis. Adverse factors include truncal site, size >5 cm, local recurrence and high-grade morphology. NF1-associated MPNST appears to have worse prognosis than sporadic tumors; malignant triton tumors are particularly aggressive. UICC/AJCC TNM staging may be used. Epithelioid Malignant Peripheral Nerve Sheath Tumor Malignant; capable of local recurrence, distant metastasis and disease-related death Usually superficial mass in extremities or trunk; some are deep-seated or visceral. Rare (~1% of soft tissue sarcomas), median age approximately 40 years, equal sex distribution. Usually not associated with NF1; may arise de novo or in a pre-existing schwannoma. Essential: sarcoma with solid/nested architecture and epithelioid cytomorphology, prominent nucleoli, geographic necrosis and often limited nuclear pleomorphism, with diffuse S100/SOX10 positivity. Desirable: loss of SMARCB1/INI1, seen in the majority. Exclude melanoma by appropriate melanocytic markers and clinical correlation. Plump, relatively uniform epithelioid cells with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm and round vesicular nuclei with prominent nucleoli. Characteristic multilobular growth, often with extracellular myxoid or hyalinized matrix; hemorrhage/necrosis may be present. Infiltrative margins, geographic necrosis and/or significant nuclear atypia support malignancy over epithelioid schwannoma; borderline cases can be challenging. Strong diffuse S100 and SOX10, unlike conventional MPNST. Most show loss of SMARCB1/INI1; H3K27me3 is retained. Melanoma markers are absent; keratin may be positive. SMARCB1 genomic inactivation occurs in approximately 70%, usually large arm-level/homozygous deletions, less often intragenic deletions or nonsense variants. Unlike conventional MPNST, NF1/CDKN2A/B alterations are uncommon and EED/SUZ12 alterations are absent. Epithelioid schwannoma Both may show diffuse S100/SOX10 and SMARCB1 loss. Infiltrative margins, geographic necrosis and significant atypia favor epithelioid MPNST. Melanoma Epithelioid MPNST shows Schwannian markers but lacks melanoma marker expression in the source description; use a melanocytic panel and clinical context. Conventional MPNST Epithelioid MPNST has diffuse S100/SOX10 and usually retained H3K27me3; conventional MPNST more often has focal/patchy Schwannian markers and may lose H3K27me3. SMARCB1 loss is not specific: it also occurs in a subset of benign epithelioid schwannomas. Diffuse S100/SOX10 does not exclude malignancy in this epithelioid subtype. Mild atypia without necrosis may make distinction from epithelioid schwannoma difficult. Potential for local recurrence, distant metastasis and death from disease; stage using UICC/AJCC TNM as applicable. Malignant Melanotic Nerve Sheath Tumor Unpredictable malignant behavior; long-term recurrence and metastasis can occur even without overtly malignant morphology Usually spinal or autonomic nerves near the midline; also reported in GI tract, bone, soft tissue, heart, bronchus, liver and skin. Rare, chiefly adults, equal sex distribution. Carney complex-associated cases occur younger (average ~22.5 years) than sporadic cases (~33.2 years). Pain, sensory symptoms or mass effect; multiple tumors occur in approximately 20% and increase suspicion for Carney complex. Carney complex is variably associated across series; psammomatous and non-psammomatous tumors have similar clinical behavior. Essential: fascicular-to-sheet-like proliferation of variably pigmented, relatively uniform plump spindle-to-epithelioid cells; coexpression of S100/SOX10 and melanocytic markers (e.g. HMB45, melan-A). Desirable: loss of PRKAR1A by IHC and/or a PRKAR1A pathogenic variant. Do not rely on psammoma bodies or overt malignant cytology to predict behavior. Short fascicles or sheets of polygonal-to-spindle cells, often syncytial; vague palisading or whorls may occur. Heavy melanin may obscure cytologic detail; pigment is Fontana–Masson-positive and iron/PAS-negative. Less pigmented areas show eosinophilic/amphophilic cytoplasm, round/ovoid nuclei, grooves and pseudoinclusions. Psammoma bodies occur in roughly 50% and may require extensive sampling. Mitoses and necrosis may occur but are not clearly associated with outcome. Strong S100 and SOX10 plus melanocytic markers HMB45, melan-A and tyrosinase. PRKAR1A expression is typically lost; PRAME is not expressed in the source description. Collagen IV/laminin may show increased intercellular deposition compared with melanoma, but exceptions occur. PRKAR1A inactivation/loss is common and underlies many Carney complex cases; PRKAR1A loss also occurs in many apparently sporadic tumors. Unlike primary CNS melanocytoma/melanoma, GNAQ/GNA11 p.Q209, CYSLTR2 and PLCB4 mutations are generally absent; BRAF, NRAS and TERT promoter mutations are also absent in the reported series. Molecular testing may help support diagnosis and exclude melanoma/melanocytoma. Metastatic melanoma Both express melanocytic markers; MMNST arises in association with spinal/autonomic nerves, coexpresses Schwannian markers and often loses PRKAR1A. BRAF/NRAS/TERT promoter and GNAQ/GNA11 pathway findings may help in selected cases. Primary CNS melanocytoma/melanoma MMNST generally lacks GNAQ/GNA11 p.Q209, CYSLTR2 and PLCB4 alterations described in these lesions. Pigmented epithelioid melanocytoma PRKAR1A loss may also occur in pigmented epithelioid melanocytoma; do not use PRKAR1A loss alone. Pigmented schwannoma MMNST coexpresses melanocytic markers; ordinary schwannoma with neuromelanin-like pigment lacks more-specific melanocytic markers such as HMB45. The former term melanotic schwannoma is not recommended; use malignant melanotic nerve sheath tumor. Psammoma bodies do not define a clinically indolent subgroup. Histologic atypia, mitoses and necrosis are not reliable predictors of outcome; metastasis may occur without malignant morphology. PRKAR1A loss is supportive but not entirely specific. Behavior is difficult to predict. Older reports suggested <15% metastatic risk, but more recent series report local recurrence/metastasis rates of 26–44%. Only approximately 53% of patients followed for >5 years remained disease-free in reported series; long-term follow-up is required. UICC/AJCC staging may be applied, although prognostic value has not been established. All PathologyGPS / Soft Tissue Tumors / Peripheral Nerve Sheath Tumors Peripheral Nerve Sheath Tumors A morphology-first diagnostic reference covering benign Schwannian and perineurial neoplasms, hybrid nerve sheath tumors, and malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumors, with emphasis on essential criteria, immunophenotypic patterns, and practical differential diagnosis. Core diagnostic rule Start with architecture and nerve relationship; then map the Schwannian, perineurial, axonal and melanocytic components. Diffuse S100/SOX10 favors Schwannian differentiation, but does not exclude epithelioid MPNST. H3K27me3 and SMARCB1 must be interpreted in the correct morphologic context. Diagnostic GPS: morphology to classification 1. Establish the setting Record superficial vs deep location, relationship to a named nerve, nerve fascicle expansion, multiplicity, NF1/schwannomatosis history and prior radiation. 2. Assess circumscription Encapsulated, displacing nerve fascicles favors schwannoma; unencapsulated infiltrative mixed-cell lesion with entrapped axons favors neurofibroma. 3. Identify the lineage Schwannian: S100/SOX10; perineurial: EMA/claudin-1/GLUT1; axons: neurofilament; stromal CD34 pattern helps separate neurofibroma from schwannoma. 4. Recognize atypical/malignant change In NF1 lesions, distinguish ancient/cellular neurofibroma, ANNUBP and MPNST using architecture, atypia, mitotic activity and necrosis. Interpret H3K27me3 loss carefully. 5. Check special patterns Consider epithelioid MPNST, melanotic nerve sheath tumor, granular cell tumor, neuromuscular choristoma and hybrid tumors when morphology or phenotype departs from conventional patterns. High-yield diagnostic criteria Schwannoma: benign tumor composed almost entirely of Schwann cells; diffuse S100/SOX10 is desirable. Neurofibroma: low-cellularity spindle-cell neoplasm in myxoid/collagenous stroma, with mixed cellular elements and entrapped axons. Perineurioma: storiform/whorled/lamellar spindle-cell lesion with bipolar processes and EMA expression. MPNST: spindle-cell sarcoma usually associated with a nerve sheath tumor or NF1; in sporadic cases, focal Schwannian differentiation and/or complete H3K27me3 loss may support the diagnosis. Epithelioid MPNST: epithelioid sarcoma with diffuse S100/SOX10; SMARCB1 loss is desirable but not specific. MMNST: coexpression of Schwannian and melanocytic markers in a variably pigmented spindle/epithelioid tumor. Critical immunophenotypic distinctions Entity Key phenotype Interpretive caution Diffuse S100/SOX10; collagen IV CD34 usually subcapsular; axons often peripheral S100/SOX10 in Schwannian cells; lattice-like CD34 stroma Mixed cell population; NFP highlights axons EMA; often claudin-1/GLUT1 S100/SOX10 negative in lesional cells S100/SOX10 often focal; H3K27me3 may be completely lost Weak/focal or mosaic H3K27me3 is not diagnostic Diffuse S100/SOX10; frequent INI1 loss; H3K27me3 retained INI1 loss also occurs in benign epithelioid schwannoma MMNST S100/SOX10 plus HMB45/melan-A/tyrosinase; PRKAR1A often lost PRKAR1A loss is not entirely specific Entity reference Diagnostic criteria and differential diagnosis Search by entity, morphology, site, immunomarker, molecular alteration or differential diagnosis. e.g. Antoni A, H3K27me3, ANNUBP, INI1, PRKAR1A... bg-teal-700 text-white border border-slate-300 bg-white text-slate-600 Collapse − View diagnostic profile + Clinical profile Essential diagnostic criteria Histopathology Immunohistochemistry Molecular pathology Differential diagnosis Prognosis and behavior Diagnostic pitfalls No matching entity. Differential diagnosis: practical decision points Diagnostic problem Key discriminator Next step Encapsulated nerve-associated spindle tumor Antoni A/B, Verocay bodies, diffuse S100/SOX10 Assess capsule, nerve displacement and axonal distribution Unencapsulated myxocollagenous spindle lesion Wavy nuclei, mixed cells, lattice-like CD34, intratumoral axons Favor neurofibroma; in NF1 lesions assess ANNUBP criteria Hypercellular NF1-associated nodule Atypia, hypercellularity, architecture loss, mitotic activity and necrosis Separate ancient/cellular neurofibroma, ANNUBP and MPNST Spindle tumor with EMA positivity Storiform/whorled/lamellar pattern; S100/SOX10 negative Consider perineurioma Epithelioid Schwannian malignancy Diffuse S100/SOX10, infiltrative growth/necrosis; INI1 often lost Distinguish epithelioid MPNST from epithelioid schwannoma and melanoma Pigmented nerve-associated tumor Schwannian plus melanocytic phenotype; PRKAR1A often lost Consider MMNST; do not infer benignity from bland histology Reporting checklist Record exact site, depth, relationship to a named nerve, nerve fascicle involvement, multiplicity and relevant syndrome/radiation history. Describe circumscription/encapsulation, growth pattern, cellularity, cytologic atypia, mitotic activity, necrosis and any heterologous differentiation. For Schwannian lesions, report S100/SOX10 distribution; for perineurial differentiation, EMA/claudin-1/GLUT1; document NFP-positive axons when relevant. In NF1-associated neurofibromatous lesions, explicitly assess the four ANNUBP features and distinguish them from MPNST. For suspected conventional MPNST, describe the extent of S100/SOX10 staining and whether H3K27me3 loss is complete with appropriate internal controls. For epithelioid MPNST, assess INI1/SMARCB1 and exclude melanoma; for MMNST, document melanocytic coexpression and PRKAR1A status when tested. Document margins and relevant staging for malignant tumors; UICC/AJCC TNM may be used for MPNST and epithelioid MPNST. Scope note: This reference is based on the supplied WHO excerpt, which covers schwannoma, neurofibroma, perineurioma, granular cell tumor, dermal nerve sheath myxoma, solitary circumscribed neuroma, ectopic meningioma/meningothelial hamartoma, neuromuscular choristoma, hybrid nerve sheath tumor, conventional and epithelioid MPNST, and malignant melanotic nerve sheath tumor. The source provides limited detail for some rare entities; those limitations are preserved rather than filled with unsupported diagnostic criteria.

title: Round Cell Sarcomas
content: use client Ewing sarcoma FET–ETS fusion sarcoma Malignant Diaphysis/metadiaphysis of long bones, pelvis, and ribs; approximately 25–30% are extraskeletal and may arise in viscera. Peak incidence in the second decade; nearly half of patients are younger than 20 years. Male predominance (M:F approximately 1.4:1). Pain and a palpable mass; pathological fracture or fever may occur. Bone imaging: permeative osteolysis with aggressive periosteal reaction; often a large soft-tissue component. Small round cell morphology. Strong, diffuse membranous CD99 expression. Desirable: NKX2-2 expression. Desirable: EWSR1 (rarely FUS) rearrangement or a defining FET–ETS fusion. Uniform small round cells in sheets. Round nuclei with finely stippled chromatin and inconspicuous nucleoli. Scant clear or eosinophilic cytoplasm; indistinct cell borders. Occasional larger cells with prominent nucleoli and irregular nuclear contours (large-cell/atypical pattern). Poorly formed rosettes may be present. Uncommon patterns: pseudoalveolar, clear-cell, mildly spindled, or sclerotic. After chemotherapy: variable necrosis with residual tumor in loose connective tissue. CD99: strong, diffuse membranous staining in approximately 95%; sensitive but not specific. NKX2-2: useful supportive marker; more specific than CD99. PAX7: higher specificity than CD99. Keratin: positive in approximately 25%; may be focal. Neuroendocrine markers and S100: occasionally positive. EWSR1::FLI1: approximately 85%; usually t(11;22)(q24;q12). EWSR1::ERG: approximately 10%; usually t(21;22)(q22;q12). Rare alternative FET–ETS fusions involve EWSR1, FUS, or rarely TAF15 with an ETS-family partner. Confirm with fusion testing or rearrangement testing; EWSR1 rearrangement alone is not specific. Additional alterations may include STAG2, CDKN2A, TP53, ERF, and FGFR1. CIC-rearranged sarcoma Often more pleomorphic, with prominent nucleoli and brisk mitoses; CD99 is usually patchy, while ETV4, WT1, and DUX4 are useful nuclear markers. CIC rearrangement supports the diagnosis. Sarcoma with BCOR genetic alterations Often shows round-to-spindle morphology and delicate vasculature; nuclear BCOR, SATB2, and cyclin D1 are supportive. Molecular confirmation is required. NFATC2-rearranged sarcoma Fibrohyaline stroma with cords, nests, trabeculae, or pseudoacini; CD99 may be diffuse but often dot-like/paranuclear. NFATC2 rearrangement is required. Adamantinoma-like Ewing sarcoma Head and neck tumor with basaloid nests, fibromyxoid/hyalinized stroma, and squamous differentiation; keratin and p63/p40 expression, sometimes keratin pearls. CD99 positivity alone does not establish Ewing sarcoma. FET–ETS fusions are not entirely specific and occur in other tumor types. Do not use the historical term primitive neuroectodermal tumor as a separate entity. NFATC2 fusion sarcoma Predominantly bone (approximately 2.1:1 bone-to-soft-tissue ratio); metaphysis/diaphysis of long bones. Soft-tissue cases involve extremities, head and neck, and chest wall. Wide age range (reported 0–78 years); median approximately 38.5 years. Male predominance in reported cases (M:F approximately 2.6:1). Painful, locally destructive bone lesion; symptoms may precede diagnosis for years. May extend into surrounding soft tissue; occasional surface/periosteal origin. Round-to-spindle cells arranged in cords, nests, and trabeculae. Fibrohyaline or myxohyaline stroma. Genetic confirmation of NFATC2 rearrangement is required. Supportive molecular pattern: EWSR1 break-apart FISH with 5′ probe gain/amplification or direct identification of an NFATC2 fusion. Small-to-medium round and/or spindle cells. Cords, small nests, trabeculae, and pseudoacinar structures. Fibrohyaline or myxohyaline stromal background. Cytoplasm is limited and eosinophilic or clear. Nuclear features range from monotonous small nuclei to marked pleomorphism; chromatin may be dense/hyperchromatic or vesicular. Mitotic activity and necrosis are variable. Focal matrix-poor sheets may occur. CD99: diffuse in approximately half of cases; often paranuclear dot-like rather than classic membranous. PAX7 and NKX2-2: may be positive. NKX3-1: often positive, but results vary between laboratories. Keratin: may show focal dot-like staining. EWSR1::NFATC2 is the common fusion; FUS::NFATC2 also occurs. EWSR1::NFATC2 is often associated with amplification of the rearranged regions and a derivative ring chromosome. FUS::NFATC2 has not shown the same amplification pattern in reported cases. NFATC2 fusions are not specific: similar fusions without partner-region amplification occur in simple bone cysts and vascular malformations/hemangiomas. A rare FUS::NFATC4 fusion has been reported. Ewing typically has monotonous sheets of small round cells without prominent fibrohyaline stroma; classic CD99 is diffuse membranous and FET–ETS fusion is defining. Myoepithelioma Can show cords/nests in myxoid or hyaline stroma; correlate with myoepithelial differentiation and the full immunophenotype. Ossifying fibromyxoid tumor Consider in a bone/soft-tissue lesion with fibromyxoid stroma; assess for characteristic peripheral ossification and its broader morphologic pattern. Osteosarcoma / osteoblastoma Evaluate for tumor osteoid or osteoblastic differentiation in the appropriate bone lesion. NFATC2 fusion alone is not sufficient without the appropriate morphology and context. An unbalanced EWSR1 FISH pattern with 5′ gain/amplification is a useful clue, not a substitute for integrated interpretation. BCOR-altered sarcoma BCOR::CCNB3: pelvis, lower-extremity long bones (metadiaphysis), and paraspinal region; slightly more common in bone. BCOR-ITD: soft tissues of trunk, retroperitoneum, and head/neck; extremity involvement is uncommon. BCOR::CCNB3: predominantly children/adolescents; more than 90% are younger than 20 years. BCOR::CCNB3: marked male predominance (M:F approximately 4.5:1). BCOR-ITD: often congenital or arises during the first year of life; adult cases are rare. Pain and swelling are common. Often a large mass; bone lesions may show cortical destruction and a soft-tissue component. Primitive round-to-spindle cells in nests, sheets, or fascicles. Variably myxoid stroma with delicate vasculature. Expression of BCOR, SATB2, and cyclin D1. Molecular confirmation of a BCOR abnormality (fusion or ITD), YWHAE::NUTM2B fusion, or KDM2B fusion. BCOR::CCNB3: uniform primitive round, ovoid, or short spindle cells in solid sheets or vague nests. Rich capillary network is characteristic. Less common patterns include hypocellular short spindle cells in myxoid matrix or solid fascicles of plump spindle cells. Nuclei have finely dispersed chromatin; nucleoli are usually inconspicuous. Mitotic activity is variable. BCOR-ITD spectrum: cellularity ranges from hypercellular primitive sheets to hypocellular spindle-cell areas in a richly vascular myxoid matrix. Primitive myxoid mesenchymal tumor of infancy (PMMTI) usually has a low-cellularity myxoid phenotype. BCOR: strong, diffuse nuclear staining; supportive but not specific. SATB2 and cyclin D1: commonly positive. Cyclin B3: expressed in BCOR::CCNB3 sarcoma; not typically seen in other BCOR-family tumors. TLE1, KDM2B, and pan-TRK may be positive; pan-TRK expression does not establish a kinase fusion. CD99: positive in approximately 50%. BCOR::CCNB3 is the most common fusion in this group. Other BCOR fusions include YWHAE and less common partners such as MAML3, ZC3H7B, CHD9, KMT2D, CIITA, RTL9/RGAG1, CLGN, MAML1, and AHR. BCOR internal tandem duplication (ITD) defines a subset including undifferentiated round-cell sarcoma and PMMTI. YWHAE::NUTM2B and KDM2B fusions occur in a small subset. Detection: BCOR break-apart FISH; targeted RNA sequencing for fusions and ITD. BCOR sarcoma often has short spindle-cell areas and a rich capillary network; BCOR/SATB2/cyclin D1 expression and a BCOR-family alteration support BCOR sarcoma. CIC tumors more often show nuclear pleomorphism, prominent nucleoli, brisk mitoses, and necrosis; ETV4/WT1/DUX4 are useful markers. Synovial sarcoma BCOR can be positive in synovial sarcoma; BCOR IHC alone is not specific. Integrate morphology and molecular findings. Kinase fusion–positive spindle-cell neoplasm Pan-TRK can be expressed in BCOR-altered sarcoma without a NTRK fusion; confirm a suspected kinase fusion molecularly. Clear cell sarcoma of kidney / high-grade endometrial stromal sarcoma These can share BCOR ITD-related biology; correlate with the primary site and entity-specific morphology. BCOR immunoreactivity is not specific and should not replace molecular confirmation. Pan-TRK positivity may be misleading in this group. BCOR::CCNB3, BCOR-ITD, and other BCOR-family alterations have different clinical settings and should not be treated as interchangeable. CIC fusion sarcoma Usually deep soft tissue of limbs or trunk; less often head/neck, retroperitoneum, or pelvis. Visceral sites include kidney, GI tract, and brain. Primary bone involvement is rare (<5%). Predominantly young adults; reported median age approximately 25–35 years. Wide reported age range, including children and older adults. Presents as a mass, with or without pain. Large tumors; visceral or metastatic symptoms may be the initial presentation. Predominant round-cell phenotype. Mild nuclear pleomorphism. Epithelioid and/or spindle-cell components may be present. Variably myxoid stroma. CIC gene rearrangement or supportive surrogate expression (ETV-family transcription factors).
