Diffuse sheets of undifferentiated round cells, often with lobulated growth separated by fibrotic stroma. Minor spindle, rhabdoid, or epithelioid components may be present. Mild nuclear pleomorphism with vesicular chromatin and prominent nucleoli. Lightly eosinophilic cytoplasm, sometimes with clearing. Necrosis is common; mitotic activity is brisk. Focal myxoid areas occur in approximately one third, with reticular or pseudoacinar architecture. CD99: often positive but usually patchy cytoplasmic/membranous; diffuse membranous staining is less common. ETV4: nuclear staining in approximately 85%; relatively high specificity. WT1: nuclear staining in approximately 83%; specificity is higher than CD99. N-terminal antibody is more sensitive than C-terminal antibody. DUX4: nuclear staining in approximately 97%; highly specific in the cited series. NKX2-2: typically negative. CIC::NUTM1 tumors: NUT positive. Calretinin and ERG may be positive; keratin, S100, and myogenic markers are rarely positive. CIC::DUX4 accounts for approximately 95%; associated with t(4;19) or t(10;19). Less common partners include AXL, CITED1, FOXO4, LEUTX, NUTM1, NUTM2A, and SYK. Trisomy 8 and MYC amplification are reported additional alterations. CIC break-apart FISH may be false negative (reported 14–43%); targeted RNA sequencing can also be false negative. DNA methylation profiling may help distinguish CIC-rearranged sarcoma from other round-cell sarcomas. CIC sarcoma has more nuclear pleomorphism and prominent nucleoli; CD99 is commonly patchy, NKX2-2 is typically negative, and ETV4/WT1/DUX4 are useful. BCOR sarcoma often has a rich capillary network and round-to-spindle/fascicular areas; BCOR, SATB2, cyclin D1, and molecular testing aid classification. NFATC2 tumors characteristically have cords/nests/trabeculae in fibrohyaline stroma and require NFATC2 fusion confirmation. CD99 is highly nonspecific; a patchy pattern is common in CIC sarcoma. A negative CIC break-apart FISH result does not exclude the diagnosis. Do not classify as Ewing sarcoma solely because of small round-cell morphology or CD99 positivity. All PathologyGPS / Soft Tissue and Bone Tumors / Round Cell Sarcomas Round Cell Sarcomas A morphology-first diagnostic reference emphasizing defining criteria, immunophenotype, molecular confirmation, and practical differential diagnosis. Diagnostic principle Small round-cell morphology is a pattern, not a diagnosis. Integrate architecture, cytology, immunophenotype, anatomic setting, and fusion status. CD99 alone is insufficient. Diagnostic GPS: round-cell sarcoma workup 1. Confirm the pattern Round-cell, round-to-spindle, or mixed morphology; assess cytologic uniformity and atypia. 2. Read the stroma Fibrohyaline/myxohyaline (NFATC2); delicate capillary network (BCOR); fibrous septa and focal myxoid change (CIC). 3. Use a focused IHC panel CD99 is not specific. Add NKX2-2/PAX7, BCOR/SATB2/cyclin D1, ETV4/WT1/DUX4 as morphology directs. 4. Confirm the genetic class FET–ETS, NFATC2, BCOR-family, or CIC alteration; choose an assay that covers the suspected event. 5. Reconcile discordance A negative or equivocal result may reflect assay limitations; CIC FISH and RNA sequencing can be false negative. Entity reference Diagnostic criteria and differential diagnosis Search by entity, site, morphology, marker, or gene. e.g. CD99, ETV4, BCOR, NFATC2... bg-teal-700 text-white border border-slate-300 bg-white text-slate-600 Collapse − View diagnostic profile + Clinical Profile Essential Diagnostic Criteria Histopathology Immunophenotype Molecular Pathology Differential Diagnosis Diagnostic Pitfalls No matching entity. High-yield differential: four major molecular classes Feature Ewing NFATC2 BCOR-altered CIC-rearranged Architecture Sheets Cords/nests/trabeculae Sheets/nests/fascicles Sheets; lobulated Stroma Usually scant Fibrohyaline / myxohyaline Delicate capillaries; variable myxoid Fibrous septa; focal myxoid CD99 Strong diffuse membranous Variable; often dot-like Positive in ~50% Often patchy Helpful IHC NKX2-2, PAX7 PAX7, NKX2-2; variable NKX3-1 BCOR, SATB2, cyclin D1; cyclin B3 in BCOR::CCNB3 ETV4, WT1, DUX4 Molecular class FET–ETS EWSR1/FUS::NFATC2 BCOR fusion/ITD; selected YWHAE/KDM2B CIC fusion, usually CIC::DUX4 Scope: Based on the supplied WHO source excerpt. Differential points are organized from the source-described morphology, immunophenotype, and molecular findings. Ancillary markers are interpreted as supportive unless included in the stated essential criteria.

title: Smooth Skeletal Muscle Tumors
content: use client Leiomyoma Smooth muscle tumors Benign Somatic type: deep subcutis or skeletal muscle of the extremities. Gynecological type: pelvis, abdomen, retroperitoneum, abdominal wall, omentum, mesentery, peritoneal surface, and round ligament. Benign smooth muscle tumor of deep somatic soft tissue, including retroperitoneal and abdominal sites. ICD-O 8890/0 Somatic tumors occur mainly in middle-aged adults without sex predilection; gynecological-type tumors occur predominantly in women, often around perimenopause. Somatic lesions are usually solitary and may calcify. Gynecological-type retroperitoneal/abdominal lesions may be multiple and are associated in some patients with concurrent uterine leiomyomas or prior hysterectomy for leiomyomas. Local recurrence is not expected for somatic leiomyoma; recurrence is reported in fewer than 10% of gynecological-type retroperitoneal/abdominal lesions. Essential: intersecting fascicles and bundles of benign, mature smooth muscle with essentially no mitotic activity. Somatic type: essentially no atypia, no necrosis, and less than 1 mitosis/7.95 mm² (equivalent to <1/50 HPF using a 0.45-mm field). Gynecological type: up to 10 mitoses/7.95 mm² may be acceptable only in the absence of necrosis and significant cytological atypia; focal degenerative atypia requires careful search for mitoses and additional sampling. Somatic tumors are circumscribed, tan-grey to white, often rubbery and whorled; stromal hyalinization and calcification are frequent. Occasional mucoid-cystic degeneration occurs. Somatic-type cells closely resemble normal smooth muscle: abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm and uniform blunt-ended, cigar-shaped nuclei in orderly intersecting and perpendicular fascicles. Gynecological-type tumors resemble uterine leiomyoma and are often paucicellular, with richer vascular stroma and sometimes greater cellularity. Macrotrabecular/microtrabecular patterns, fibrosis, hyalinization, calcification, myxoid/cystic change, focal epithelioid or clear-cell change, nuclear palisading, metaplastic bone, and fatty differentiation may occur. Deep leiomyoma should not show tumor necrosis. Focal degenerative nuclear atypia must trigger additional sampling and a deliberate search for mitotic activity. Both types: usually strong, diffuse SMA, desmin, and h-caldesmon; S100 is negative. Gynecological type: ER, PR, and WT1 are almost always expressed. Somatic soft-tissue type: ER and PR are negative. Interpret hormone-receptor status in the context of site and morphology. Routine diagnostic molecular testing is not clinically relevant. Gynecological-type retroperitoneal/abdominal leiomyomas may share uterine leiomyoma alterations: HMGA2 or PLAG1 rearrangements, MED12 exon 2 mutations, and rare KAT6B::KANSL1 or EWSR1::PBX3 fusions. Leiomyosarcoma Any mitotic activity or atypia in a somatic smooth-muscle tumor warrants concern; assess the entire lesion for atypia, mitoses, necrosis, and infiltrative growth. Gynecological-type lesions have a different accepted mitotic range, but necrosis or significant atypia is not acceptable. EBV-associated smooth muscle tumor Consider in immunosuppressed patients, unusual/multifocal sites, or tumors with primitive round-cell areas; EBER in situ hybridization is required. GIST or other spindle-cell neoplasm Use site, morphology, and a context-directed panel; smooth-muscle markers should be interpreted as a panel rather than individually. Do not apply uterine/gynecological-type mitotic thresholds to somatic deep soft-tissue leiomyoma. Focal degenerative atypia in gynecological-type lesions is not automatically malignant, but requires adequate sampling. Recurrence of gynecological-type retroperitoneal leiomyoma has been reported without subsequent progression or metastasis. Benign regardless of type; complete excision is curative. There is no metastatic risk. Rare local recurrences occur in gynecological-type retroperitoneal/abdominal lesions. EBV-Associated Smooth Muscle Tumor Uncertain behavior; clinical course is immune-status dependent Any site. HIV-associated tumors favor intra- or extra-axial CNS; post-transplant tumors most often involve liver, followed by lung, gastrointestinal tract, and spleen. Head/neck and lymph nodes may also be involved. Smooth muscle neoplasm associated with EBV infection, usually in the setting of T-lymphocyte immunosuppression. ICD-O 8897/1 Strongly associated with HIV/AIDS, solid-organ transplantation, and less commonly congenital/primary immunodeficiency (including GATA2 or CARMIL2 deficiency). Rare cases occur in immunocompetent or iatrogenically immunosuppressed patients. May arise months to years after onset of immunodeficiency or transplantation. Presentation depends on site and may include mass effect, neurological deficits, GI obstruction/bleeding/perforation, or endobronchial symptoms. Multicentric distribution is not uncommon. Multiple lesions should not automatically be interpreted as metastases. Essential: clinical history of immunosuppression; neoplasm with smooth-muscle differentiation; EBER-positive tumor cells by in situ hybridization. EBER in situ hybridization is necessary for diagnosis; smooth-muscle immunophenotype alone is insufficient. Intersecting fascicles of spindle cells with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm and elongated nuclei often resemble leiomyoma. A second population of primitive-appearing round/oval smooth-muscle cells is common and may be admixed. Patterns may be epithelioid, tightly packed, or hemangiopericytoma-like. Atypia is usually mild to moderate but may be marked, particularly in HIV-positive patients; mitotic activity is generally low but hotspots may exceed 10/2 mm². Tumor infiltration is common, usually sparse but occasionally more pronounced. Intratumoral lymphocytes are mainly CD8-positive and EBER-negative; the neoplastic smooth-muscle cells are EBER-positive. Neoplastic cells are consistently and diffusely positive for SMA and h-caldesmon; desmin is variable and often focal. EBER in situ hybridization is consistently positive in tumor cells and is essential. Do not mistake EBER-negative intratumoral lymphocytes for the neoplastic population. EBV demonstration, especially EBER in situ hybridization, is the diagnostic molecular pathology test. Multicentric lesions may represent independent EBV infection events rather than metastases from one clone. Post-transplant tumors may be donor- or recipient-derived. MYC overexpression and AKT/mTOR pathway activation have been implicated; these are pathogenetic observations, not routine diagnostic requirements. Leiomyoma / leiomyosarcoma Smooth-muscle morphology overlaps. Clinical immunosuppression and EBER positivity in tumor cells establish EBV-SMT. Metastatic smooth-muscle tumor Multifocality is common and may reflect independent infection events; do not assume dissemination of one clone. Other spindle-cell neoplasm Demonstrate smooth-muscle differentiation and localize EBER signal to neoplastic cells. Do not use the discouraged labels AIDS-associated EBV-positive SMT, post-transplant EBV-positive SMT, EBV-associated leiomyoma, or EBV-associated leiomyosarcoma. Histological grade is not a reliable predictor of behavior or outcome. EBER must be positive in tumor cells; intratumoral CD8-positive lymphocytes are generally EBER-negative. Outcome depends mainly on the patient's immune status; histological grading is not a reliable prognostic indicator. Overall prognosis may be more favorable than conventional leiomyosarcoma, but multifocal organ involvement and intracranial disease correlate with worse survival. Surgery is used for symptomatic or critical-site lesions. Immune restoration (antiretroviral optimization or reduction of immunosuppression when feasible) is central; mTOR inhibitors have shown reported benefit. Chemotherapy and radiotherapy are generally considered ineffective. Malignant Deep soft tissue of extremities and retroperitoneal/intra-abdominal cavities, frequently with vascular origin (especially IVC and tributaries). Visceral LMS arises in smooth-muscle-rich organs and has distinct biology. Malignant mesenchymal neoplasm with smooth-muscle differentiation. ICD-O 8890/3 Usually presents with a mass effect and/or pain. IVC tumors may cause Budd–Chiari syndrome, leg edema, or deep-vein thrombosis. Most cases occur in the fifth to seventh decades. Retroperitoneal tumors are more common in women; extremity tumors show a slight male predominance. Most are sporadic. Predisposition settings include Li–Fraumeni syndrome, retinoblastoma, and genomic-instability syndromes; radiation and cyclophosphamide are reported risk factors. Essential: neoplasm with morphological and/or immunohistochemical evidence of smooth-muscle differentiation, with variable nuclear pleomorphism and mitotic activity. Recognize intersecting fascicles of spindle cells with eosinophilic/fibrillary cytoplasm, blunt-ended nuclei, variable pleomorphism, and usually conspicuous mitotic activity; atypical mitoses and tumor necrosis support malignancy. Any mitoses in an adult smooth-muscle tumor warrant careful evaluation for malignancy in the supplied source. Usually intersecting fascicles of spindle cells; focal storiform or microcystic patterns and rare epithelioid morphology occur. Cells have eosinophilic, sometimes fibrillary cytoplasm, elongated ovoid nuclei with blunt ends, small nucleoli, and variable pleomorphism. Mitotic activity is usually conspicuous and atypical mitoses may be present. Necrosis, hemorrhage, cystic degeneration, lymphovascular invasion, and occasional chronic inflammation may occur. Poorly differentiated/dedifferentiated areas may resemble undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma and may be spindled, polygonal, epithelioid, or rhabdoid with bizarre multinucleated cells and brisk mitoses. A typical LMS component or prior history is needed to support this interpretation. Visceral LMS (uterus, GI tract, dermis) should be considered separately because of distinct biology. Typically positive for desmin, SMA, smooth-muscle myosin, and h-caldesmon. h-Caldesmon is the most specific of these, but no single marker is entirely lineage-specific; concordant expression of multiple markers is more persuasive. Expression may decrease or be lost in poorly differentiated/dedifferentiated areas. Focal or weak CD34, KIT, DOG1, keratin, or EMA can occur and should not override morphology. No consistent disease-defining genetic alteration; routine diagnostic molecular testing is not clinically relevant. Complex genomes commonly show widespread copy-number gains/losses, chromothripsis, and whole-genome duplication. TP53 and RB1 are frequently biallelically inactivated; PTEN, CDKN2A, ATRX, ATM, BRCA2, MYOCD, and other pathway alterations are reported. Gene-expression studies describe molecular groups with smooth-muscle differentiation enrichment, less differentiated/immunogenic features, and visceral/uterine enrichment; these are not routine diagnostic classifiers. Compare mitotic activity, cytological atypia, tumor necrosis, and infiltrative growth; site-specific criteria matter, particularly for gynecological-type leiomyoma. Look for immunosuppression, primitive round-cell component, and EBER positivity in tumor cells. Undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma In poorly differentiated tumors, require a recognizable LMS component or prior LMS history; smooth-muscle markers may be lost in dedifferentiated areas. GIST / other spindle-cell tumors Focal/weak KIT, DOG1, CD34, keratin, or EMA can occur in LMS; interpret the complete panel and morphology. Do not diagnose LMS from SMA positivity alone; use multiple smooth-muscle markers and morphology. Dedifferentiated areas may lose smooth-muscle markers, so sample and search for a conventional component. Visceral LMS is biologically distinct from primary soft-tissue LMS and should not be casually pooled with it. Prognostic variables include age, retroperitoneal location, size (>4–5 cm), bone/neurovascular involvement, prior disruptive surgery, mitotic activity, FNCLCC grade, and intratumoral vascular invasion. Aggressive tumor with significant risk of local recurrence, metastasis, and disease-related mortality. Metastatic risk is associated with older age, retroperitoneal location, larger size, bone/neurovascular involvement, mitotic activity, FNCLCC grade, and intratumoral vascular invasion. Disease-specific survival is associated with age, metastases at presentation, AJCC stage, size >50 mm, FNCLCC grade, and RB1/ATRX alterations. Rhabdomyoma (Adult, Fetal, and Genital) Skeletal muscle tumors Adult and fetal types predominantly head and neck (parapharyngeal space, salivary glands, larynx, oral cavity); other sites include bladder, mediastinum, abdomen/pelvis, extremities, vulva, and scrotum. Genital type arises in genital tract, especially vagina, or paratesticular region. Benign extracardiac mesenchymal tumor with skeletal-muscle differentiation. ICD-O 8903/0 fetal; 8904/0 adult; 8905/0 genital Usually a slow-growing painless mass, although rapid growth and local compressive symptoms may occur. Adult rhabdomyoma may be unifocal or multifocal; fetal tumors are usually solitary. Adult type: median age about 60 years, male predominance. Fetal type occurs at all ages with peaks below 3 years and around 60 years; about one quarter are congenital. Multicentric fetal rhabdomyoma is associated with Gorlin syndrome (PTCH1); cases have also been reported with Birt–Hogg–Dubé syndrome (FLCN). Essential: well-circumscribed mass without invasion, composed of cells showing skeletal-muscle differentiation. Strong desmin, MYOD1, and myogenin expression supports skeletal-muscle lineage; MYOD1 and myogenin label primitive spindle cells. Unencapsulated lobular mass. Adult type: large polygonal cells with abundant granular eosinophilic cytoplasm, small round vesicular nuclei, and distinct borders. Spider-cell vacuoles, rod-like inclusions, or cross-striations may occur; mitoses and clear-cell change are rare. Classic fetal type: irregular bundles of immature skeletal-muscle fibers in myxoid stroma; fetal myotube-like spindle cells have central oblong nuclei and eosinophilic cytoplasm. Intermediate/juvenile lesions are more cellular with less myxoid stroma and differentiated rhabdomyoblasts. Cellular fetal type is more uniform and may show mitoses (up to 5/50 mm²), but lacks atypia, infiltrative margins, atypical mitoses, and necrosis. Female genital type: small polypoid lesions with loose fibrous tissue and differentiated spindle, polygonal, or elongated rhabdomyoblasts; cross-striations may be seen. Vaginal lesions lack a cambium layer. Male genital lesions resemble adult or fetal type and may be markedly sclerotic. Desmin, MYOD1, and myogenin are positive; desmin is generally strong and diffuse. Focal SMA expression may occur. Routine molecular testing is not clinically relevant. Fetal rhabdomyoma may involve Hedgehog pathway activation; PTCH1 loss-of-function underlies Gorlin syndrome-associated cases. A few adult tumors also show evidence of Hedgehog pathway activation. Embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma Rhabdomyoma is circumscribed and lacks invasion; fetal rhabdomyoma may be cellular and mitotically active but lacks atypical mitoses, necrosis, and infiltrative margins. Vaginal embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma Genital rhabdomyoma is polypoid but lacks the subepithelial cambium layer characteristic of botryoid ERMS. Parathyroid adenoma Rare head-and-neck rhabdomyomas may mimic parathyroid lesions; skeletal-muscle markers and morphology clarify lineage. Do not use the discouraged term rhabdomyomatous hamartoma for these extracardiac neoplasms. Mitotic activity in cellular fetal rhabdomyoma does not by itself establish malignancy. Genital rhabdomyoma may show some cytological atypia; correlate with circumscription, lack of invasion, and absence of mitoses. Benign. Local growth may cause site-related symptoms; multicentric fetal lesions may be associated with syndromic disease. Inflammatory Rhabdomyoblastic Tumor Usually indolent; malignant progression is recognized Predominantly deep soft tissue of extremities and trunk; may occur at other soft-tissue sites. A skeletal-muscle-lineage neoplasm with prominent inflammatory infiltrate and distinctive rhabdomyoblastic tumor cells. WHO source lists uncertain-behavior and malignant-progression codes as xxx/1 and xxx/3 Typically presents as a slowly growing mass. The supplied source describes a spectrum from tumors with indolent behavior to rare tumors with malignant progression. Clinical context and adequate sampling are important because the inflammatory background may obscure the neoplastic cells. Recognize a neoplasm with skeletal-muscle differentiation in a conspicuous inflammatory background. Assess cytological atypia, mitotic activity, necrosis, infiltrative growth, and any evidence of progression; do not infer benignity from the inflammatory component alone. Inflammatory background is a prominent component and may obscure the neoplastic population. Rhabdomyoblastic cells show variable size and shape, with eosinophilic cytoplasm and skeletal-muscle differentiation; the supplied source emphasizes the inflammatory and rhabdomyoblastic combination. Near-haploidization or widespread loss of heterozygosity may be demonstrable in selected cases. Use skeletal-muscle lineage markers (desmin, MYOD1, and myogenin) to establish rhabdomyoblastic differentiation, interpreted with the morphology. The supplied source does not establish a single immunophenotypic marker as independently diagnostic. Near-haploidization or widespread loss of heterozygosity is a desirable finding in selected cases, not a universal requirement. Rhabdomyosarcoma Compare the inflammatory-rich architecture and clinical behavior with conventional ERMS, ARMS, and spindle/sclerosing RMS; establish skeletal-muscle lineage. Inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor A dense inflammatory infiltrate can overlap; demonstrate skeletal-muscle differentiation rather than assuming myofibroblastic lineage. Pleomorphic sarcoma with rhabdomyoblastic differentiation Correlate the extent and distribution of skeletal-muscle markers with the characteristic inflammatory-rhabdomyoblastic morphology. Do not equate inflammatory background with reactive lesion. Distinguish the usual indolent course from the recognized malignant-progression category. Ancillary molecular findings are desirable in selected cases, not required in every case. The source recognizes uncertain-behavior and malignant-progression categories; behavior must be assessed in the context of morphology and clinical follow-up. Embryonal Rhabdomyosarcoma Malignant; generally more favorable than other RMS subtypes Common in children and adolescents; can arise at many sites. Botryoid pattern occurs on mucosal surfaces; paratesticular tumors often show spindle-cell morphology. Malignant skeletal-muscle neoplasm recapitulating embryonic skeletal-muscle differentiation. ICD-O 8910/3 Occurs predominantly in children. ERMS is associated with RAS-pathway predisposition syndromes including Costello (HRAS), NF1, and Noonan; associations also include Beckwith–Wiedemann, DICER1-related predisposition, and Li–Fraumeni syndrome. About 7% of patients with RMS may harbor a germline cancer-predisposition variant; ERMS is more likely than ARMS to be associated with one. Essential: primitive round and spindle-cell morphology with scattered differentiated rhabdomyoblasts; desmin positivity with heterogeneous nuclear myogenin and/or MYOD1; absence of FOXO1 fusion. Desirable: exclude MYOD1 p.(Leu122Arg) mutation and recurrent VGLL2/VGLL3- or NCOA2/NCOA3-related fusions, especially in spindle-cell lesions. Primitive mesenchymal cells span stages of myogenesis: stellate cells with sparse amphophilic cytoplasm, differentiating tadpole/spider cells, and occasional terminal differentiation with cross-striations or myotubes. Typical tumors contain variably differentiated rhabdomyoblasts in loose myxoid mesenchyme with alternating dense and loose cellularity. Poorly differentiated dense areas may mimic ARMS. Botryoid ERMS is polypoid and has a subepithelial cambium layer of condensed tumor cells over hypocellular myxoid stroma with radially oriented capillaries. Spindle-cell morphology is particularly seen in paratesticular tumors. Cartilaginous differentiation may occur, especially in female genitourinary tumors and DICER1-altered cases. Anaplastic ERMS contains markedly enlarged atypical cells with hyperchromatic nuclei and often bizarre multipolar mitoses. In children, extensively pleomorphic tumors are classified as anaplastic ERMS rather than pleomorphic RMS. A small subset has neuroectodermal elements ranging from ganglion cells/neuropil to mature ganglioneuroma, ganglioneuroblastoma, or primitive neuroblastoma; this component may be focal and missed in biopsy. Desmin is essentially always positive, with variable extent. Myogenin and MYOD1 are positive in essentially all cases, but the number of positive nuclei is variable and may be extensive in dense-cellular ERMS. SMA and muscle-specific actin are frequently positive. Aberrant keratin, S100, CD56, synaptophysin, or neurofilament expression may occur; do not infer neural differentiation without corresponding morphology and neural-marker profile. p53 IHC may help identify anaplastic cases for further TP53 evaluation. H3K27me3 loss occurs in more than half and does not distinguish ERMS from malignant Triton tumor. Absence of PAX3::FOXO1 and PAX7::FOXO1 distinguishes ERMS from fusion-positive ARMS. RAS-pathway alterations (NRAS, KRAS, HRAS, NF1, FGFR4), PI3K-pathway alterations (PTEN, PIK3CA), and cell-cycle pathway alterations (FBXW7, CTNNB1) are reported. HRAS/KRAS variants are enriched in infants; NRAS variants in adolescents. 11p15.5 loss of heterozygosity and IGF2/H19/CDKN1C imprinting-region dysregulation are common pathogenetic themes. TP53 alterations occur in a subset and may associate with anaplasia. Exclude MYOD1 p.(Leu122Arg) and defining fusions in spindle-cell tumors when indicated. Alveolar RMS ARMS typically has strong homogeneous nuclear myogenin and a PAX3/7::FOXO1 or alternative defining fusion; ERMS has heterogeneous myogenin/MYOD1 and lacks FOXO1 fusion. MYOD1-mutant spindle/sclerosing RMS Requires MYOD1 p.(Leu122Arg); may show spindle/sclerosing morphology and aggressive behavior. Fusion-associated spindle-cell RMS Monomorphic spindle-cell morphology with a defining fusion; test VGLL2/VGLL3, NCOA2/NCOA3-related groups as appropriate. Neuroblastoma / ganglioneuroblastic tumor A true neuroectodermal component requires morphologic and immunophenotypic evidence; aberrant neural-marker expression alone in ERMS is insufficient. Primitive dense-cellular ERMS may mimic ARMS; do not diagnose ARMS by morphology alone. Botryoid ERMS has a cambium layer; genital rhabdomyoma does not. Anaplasia in a child remains an ERMS pattern, not adult-type pleomorphic RMS. Neuroectodermal differentiation can be focal and may be missed in small biopsies. ERMS is highly chemotherapy-sensitive and generally has a more favorable outcome than other RMS types. Risk stratification incorporates fusion status, IRSG group, primary site, stage, size, and age. Ages 1–9 years generally fare better than adolescents or adults. TP53 and MYOD1 alterations are important high-risk features in clinical-trial/risk assessment. Alveolar Rhabdomyosarcoma High-grade malignant; fusion-positive disease has adverse prognosis Most often deep soft tissue of extremities; also head/neck, genitourinary and gynecological tracts, paraspinal tissue, and perineum. Malignant neoplasm of monomorphic primitive round cells with skeletal-muscle differentiation, defined by a recurrent fusion, usually PAX3::FOXO1 or PAX7::FOXO1. ICD-O 8920/3 Rapidly growing and highly aggressive. Approximately 25–30% have locoregional or distant metastases at diagnosis. Peak incidence is around ages 10–25 years (median 15); roughly equal sex distribution. A subset occurs in adults over 40 years. Essential: uniform primitive round-cell morphology, often with rare rhabdomyoblasts; strong homogeneous nuclear myogenin; evidence of PAX3::FOXO1, PAX7::FOXO1, or another qualifying fusion. Absence of PAX3/7::FOXO1 and alternative fusion suggests ERMS with primitive phenotype rather than fusion-negative ARMS. Highly cellular primitive round cells with scant cytoplasm and hyperchromatic nuclei, arranged in nests separated by fibrovascular septa. Central discohesion produces irregular alveolar spaces and variable cystic change. Solid ARMS retains cytomorphology but lacks septa and discohesion. Mitoses are often brisk; wreath-like multinucleated tumor giant cells are common. Rhabdomyoblastic differentiation may be present. Treatment may reduce cellularity and increase rhabdomyoblastic differentiation and stromal fibrosis. Desmin, myogenin, and MYOD1 support skeletal-muscle differentiation. Nuclear myogenin is typically strong and diffuse/homogeneous, unlike the more heterogeneous or focal pattern in ERMS and other RMS subtypes; MYOD1 may be limited. Keratin, MUC4, ALK, OLIG2, and neuroendocrine markers (synaptophysin, chromogranin, CD56, INSM1) may be expressed and are diagnostic pitfalls. PAX3::FOXO1 accounts for approximately 70–90% and PAX7::FOXO1 for 10–30% of fusions. Detect by RNA-based sequencing, other molecular methods, or fusion-protein IHC targeting the junctional region/FOXO1 C-terminus. Rare alternative fusions are reported. Formerly described fusion-negative ARMS is biologically and clinically closer to ERMS; do not retain 'fusion-negative ARMS' as a separate entity. Dense-cellular ERMS ERMS lacks the defining fusion and usually shows heterogeneous myogenin/MYOD1; molecular testing resolves the overlap. Ewing sarcoma / other round-cell sarcoma Use morphology and a lineage-directed panel; ARMS may show aberrant ALK, keratin, MUC4, OLIG2, or neuroendocrine markers. Neuroendocrine neoplasm Neuroendocrine-marker expression can occur in ARMS; establish skeletal-muscle differentiation and defining fusion. Alveolar architecture alone is not sufficient: solid ARMS lacks alveolar spaces, and ERMS can mimic ARMS. Strong diffuse nuclear myogenin is a useful clue but fusion confirmation is essential. Do not use 'mixed embryonal and alveolar RMS' or 'fusion-negative ARMS' as recommended terminology. Fusion-positive ARMS has worse prognosis than fusion-negative RMS/ERMS; PAX3::FOXO1 generally has worse outcome than PAX7::FOXO1. MYCN, CDK4, and MIR17HG amplification and rare pathogenic TP53 alterations correlate with poor outcomes. Pleomorphic Rhabdomyosarcoma Highly aggressive malignant sarcoma of adults Deep soft tissue, most often lower extremity; also chest/abdominal wall, upper extremity, abdomen/retroperitoneum, and head/neck. High-grade pleomorphic sarcoma of adults with variable numbers of bizarre eosinophilic polygonal, round, and spindle cells showing skeletal-muscle differentiation. ICD-O 8901/3 Usually rapidly growing, deep, variably painful mass. Most common in the sixth to seventh decades (mean age about 72 years), with male predominance. Similar tumors in children are considered ERMS. Essential: high-grade pleomorphic sarcoma composed of pleomorphic spindle, epithelioid, round, and/or polygonal cells with a variable population of brightly eosinophilic rhabdomyoblastic cells and variable desmin, myogenin, and/or MYOD1 expression. Markedly atypical spindle, epithelioid, round, and pleomorphic cells with variable focal or extensive multinucleated, polygonal, spindle, or rhabdoid cells containing abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm. Usually large and well-marginated with pseudocapsule; cut surface is whitish/fleshy and often necrotic. Some tumors that resemble pleomorphic RMS represent other tumor types with divergent rhabdomyoblastic differentiation; exclude a definable alternative entity. Desmin is positive to variable extent, sometimes diffuse. MYOD1 and myogenin are positive, sometimes only focally. Interpret skeletal-muscle markers in the context of the pleomorphic sarcoma; focal expression alone should prompt consideration of divergent differentiation in another sarcoma. Complex karyotypes with TP53 mutations, RB1 alterations, and CDKN2A deletions are reported; genomic profiles resemble undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma. Undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma with rhabdomyoblastic differentiation Determine whether skeletal-muscle differentiation is an integral defining component or focal divergent differentiation in another tumor type. Dedifferentiated leiomyosarcoma Search for conventional smooth-muscle component and assess smooth-muscle markers; dedifferentiated LMS may lose lineage markers. Anaplastic ERMS In children, extensively pleomorphic/anaplastic RMS is classified as anaplastic ERMS rather than pleomorphic RMS. Age is critical: pediatric pleomorphic tumors should not be classified as adult-type pleomorphic RMS. Some apparent pleomorphic RMS cases are other sarcomas with divergent rhabdomyoblastic differentiation. Necrosis and atypical mitoses are common; correlate with the high-grade morphology. Highly aggressive. The largest cited study reported median survival of 7.3 months, with approximately 80% dying of disease. Lung metastases are common. Fusion-Associated Spindle Cell Rhabdomyosarcoma Molecularly heterogeneous; behavior varies by fusion group Infantile group: trunk and head/neck. ZFP64::NCOA2/3 group: lower extremities and trunk. VGLL3-rearranged group: head/neck, especially tongue. Other fusions occur at varied sites, including viscera. Heterogeneous group of skeletal-muscle sarcomas with fascicular spindle-cell morphology, defined by recurrent pathognomonic gene fusions. ICD-O 8912/3 Usually rapidly growing, localized, deep-seated mass; pain may result from local compression. Congenital/infantile group presents at birth or within the first year. ZFP64- and VGLL3-associated tumors tend to occur in middle-aged or older adults, with male predilection. Essential: monomorphic spindle-cell morphology; expression of at least two skeletal-muscle markers (e.g. desmin and MYOD1/myogenin); confirmation of the characteristic gene fusion. RNA-based targeted sequencing or FISH can detect the defining fusion. Congenital/infantile tumors: cellular intersecting or herringbone fascicles of monomorphic spindle cells, resembling leiomyosarcoma or infantile fibrosarcoma; hypocellular zones may mimic myofibromatosis. ZFP64::NCOA2/3 tumors: monomorphic spindle cells in long herringbone fascicles; extensive chondro-osseous differentiation may occur. VGLL3-rearranged tumors: bland spindle cells diffusely infiltrate skeletal muscle, usually without significant mitoses or necrosis. Other fusion-defined groups have variable morphology. Large solid masses and necrosis may occur in some groups. Infantile tumors: diffuse desmin with heterogeneous MYOD1 and myogenin. ZFP64::NCOA2/3: variable MYOD1 and desmin; myogenin usually negative. VGLL3-rearranged: diffuse desmin with scattered myogenin/MYOD1; patchy SMA may occur. Infantile group: NCOA2 or CITED2 fusions, commonly SRF::NCOA2, VGLL2::NCOA2, VGLL2::CITED2; less often TEAD1::NCOA2. ZFP64 group: ZFP64 rearranged with NCOA2 or NCOA3. VGLL3 group: VGLL3 fusions with TCF12, EP300, or PPARGC1A. Other reported fusions include MEIS1::NCOA2, MEIS1::FOXO1, DCTN1::ALK, and EWSR1::NF2. EWSR1::TFCP2, FUS::TFCP2, and MEIS1::NCOA2 tumors are discussed separately as TFCP2-rearranged RMS in the source. Infantile fibrosarcoma Infantile spindle-cell RMS expresses skeletal-muscle markers and has a defining fusion; morphology can overlap with fascicular spindle-cell tumors. Smooth-muscle morphology overlaps, but skeletal-muscle markers and a defining RMS-associated fusion establish this category. Myofibroma / myofibromatosis Hypocellular areas may mimic myofibroma; demonstrate skeletal-muscle differentiation and fusion. MYOD1 p.(Leu122Arg) defines a separate aggressive entity; test mutation status in appropriate spindle/sclerosing lesions. Do not classify all spindle-cell RMS as one biologic group; prognosis differs substantially by fusion partner. Infantile tumors may be indolent, whereas ZFP64::NCOA2/3 tumors have substantial recurrence/metastatic potential. Fusion confirmation is essential; morphology and immunostains alone do not define the molecular group. Congenital/infantile tumors usually behave indolently, with exceptional metastases or fatal outcomes. Most VGLL3-rearranged tumors follow an indolent course. ZFP64::NCOA2/3 tumors have high potential for local recurrence, distant metastasis, and death. Outcome data for rarer fusion groups are limited. MYOD1-Mutant Spindle Cell / Sclerosing Rhabdomyosarcoma Aggressive malignant Occurs in children and adults; may arise in soft tissue at varied sites. Spindle-cell and/or sclerosing rhabdomyosarcoma defined by MYOD1 p.(Leu122Arg) mutation. Recognized in both children and adults. The source emphasizes aggressive clinical behavior despite multimodal therapy. Essential: spindle cells in fascicles and/or oval-to-spindle cells with variable sclerotic stroma; typically diffuse, intense MYOD1 immunoreactivity; demonstration of MYOD1 p.(Leu122Arg) mutation. Desirable: variable desmin and myogenin staining. Spindle-cell pattern: hypercellular intersecting fascicles of long spindle cells with pale eosinophilic cytoplasm and oval, fusiform, or blunt hyperchromatic nuclei; herringbone/fibrosarcomatous growth may occur. Sclerosing pattern: round, oval, or short spindle cells in cords, nests, trabeculae, or microalveoli in striking hyaline to pseudochondroid stroma; pseudoangiomatous architecture may mimic osteosarcoma or extraskeletal myxoid chondrosarcoma. Hybrid spindle/sclerosing forms occur. Primitive round-cell areas, lipoblast-like cells, and multinucleated giant cells are rare. Rhabdomyoblastic differentiation may be more evident after chemotherapy. MYOD1 is diffusely positive and is the most consistent marker. Desmin ranges from diffuse to focal; myogenin is usually focal. Do not rely on desmin or myogenin alone; molecular confirmation is required. Demonstration of MYOD1 p.(Leu122Arg) is required for diagnosis. MYOD1-mutant spindle/sclerosing RMS is distinct from fusion-associated spindle-cell RMS; assess defining fusion status when morphology/context warrants. Fusion-defined groups require recurrent fusions (e.g. VGLL2/VGLL3/NCOA2-related); MYOD1-mutant entity requires p.(Leu122Arg). Embryonal RMS with spindle-cell component ERMS lacks MYOD1 p.(Leu122Arg) and defining spindle-cell RMS fusions; it usually shows heterogeneous myogenin/MYOD1. Extraskeletal myxoid chondrosarcoma / osteosarcoma Sclerosing RMS can mimic these through pseudochondroid/hyaline stroma and pseudoangiomatous pattern; establish skeletal-muscle differentiation and MYOD1 mutation. Diffuse MYOD1 staining is supportive but mutation demonstration is required. Spindle and sclerosing patterns may coexist; both belong to the same molecularly defined entity when MYOD1 p.(Leu122Arg) is present. Do not mistake focal myogenin for absence of skeletal-muscle differentiation. Associated with aggressive clinical course, recurrence, metastasis, and fatal outcomes in children and adults despite multimodal treatment. The source reports 5-year event-free survival below 10% in MYOD1-mutant tumors. All PathologyGPS / Soft Tissue Tumors / Smooth and Skeletal Muscle Tumors Smooth and Skeletal Muscle Tumors A morphology-first reference integrating smooth-muscle differentiation, skeletal-muscle lineage, defining molecular alterations, and behavior-specific diagnostic pitfalls. Core rule Establish the lineage, then classify the pattern and molecular subgroup. Smooth-muscle markers overlap across entities; skeletal-muscle markers establish lineage but do not replace fusion or mutation testing when required. Diagnostic GPS: morphology to classification 1. Establish the setting Record age, anatomic site, depth, immune status/transplant history, multiplicity, and whether the lesion is visceral or somatic soft tissue. 2. Identify the muscle lineage Smooth muscle: eosinophilic fascicles and blunt-ended nuclei. Skeletal muscle: rhabdomyoblasts, granular/eosinophilic cytoplasm, cross-striations, or primitive myogenic cells. 3. Read the architecture Mature intersecting fascicles; primitive round/oval EBV-SMT component; embryonal myxoid/dense zones; alveolar nests/septa; spindle fascicles; or sclerosing cords in hyaline matrix. 4. Assess behavior Evaluate atypia, mitoses, atypical mitoses, necrosis, infiltrative growth, vascular invasion, and distribution. Apply site- and entity-specific thresholds. 5. Order defining tests EBER for suspected EBV-SMT; PAX3/7::FOXO1 for ARMS; MYOD1 p.(Leu122Arg) for spindle/sclerosing RMS; targeted RNA/FISH for fusion-associated spindle-cell RMS. High-yield classification Smooth muscle: leiomyoma (benign), EBV-associated smooth muscle tumor (immune-status-dependent, uncertain behavior), and leiomyosarcoma (malignant). Skeletal muscle: rhabdomyoma (benign); inflammatory rhabdomyoblastic tumor; and rhabdomyosarcoma groups—embryonal, alveolar, pleomorphic, fusion-associated spindle-cell, and MYOD1-mutant spindle/sclerosing. Do not collapse molecular groups: infantile and VGLL3-rearranged spindle-cell RMS are usually indolent, whereas ZFP64::NCOA2/3 and MYOD1-mutant spindle/sclerosing RMS have aggressive behavior. Marker and molecular quick guide Smooth-muscle phenotype SMA, desmin, h-caldesmon; use a panel, not one marker Gynecological leiomyoma ER, PR, WT1 usually positive; somatic leiomyoma ER/PR negative EBV-SMT EBER ISH positive in neoplastic cells (required) Skeletal-muscle lineage Desmin, MYOD1, myogenin; distribution/intensity varies by RMS subtype PAX3::FOXO1 / PAX7::FOXO1 or alternative defining fusion MYOD1-mutant RMS MYOD1 p.(Leu122Arg) required Fusion-associated spindle RMS RNA-based sequencing or FISH for recurrent fusion Entity reference Diagnostic criteria and differential diagnosis Search by entity, morphology, site, marker, fusion, or gene. e.g. EBER, MYOD1, FOXO1, h-caldesmon... bg-teal-700 text-white border border-slate-300 bg-white text-slate-600 Collapse − View diagnostic profile + Definition Clinical profile Essential diagnostic criteria Prognosis and behavior Histopathology Immunohistochemistry Molecular pathology Differential diagnosis Diagnostic pitfalls No entities match this search. Practical sign-out checklist Document exact anatomic site, depth, size, and relationship to vessel, organ, mucosal surface, or skeletal muscle. For smooth-muscle tumors, record atypia, mitotic count with area, atypical mitoses, necrosis, and infiltrative/vascular invasion. For suspected EBV-SMT, document immune/transplant history and confirm EBER in tumor cells. For RMS, document age, site, subtype-defining morphology, skeletal-muscle marker distribution, and molecular test status. For ARMS, report FOXO1 fusion status and fusion partner when available. For spindle-cell RMS, consider fusion testing and MYOD1 p.(Leu122Arg) according to morphology and age. For pleomorphic RMS, exclude another sarcoma with divergent rhabdomyoblastic differentiation. Correlate molecular subgroup with behavior; do not infer prognosis from spindle-cell morphology alone. Educational diagnostic reference based on the supplied WHO source excerpt. Ancillary tests and clinical management should be interpreted in the full clinical and radiologic context. This page is not a substitute for institutional protocols or multidisciplinary review.

title: Tumors Of Uncertain Differentiation
content: use client Intramuscular myxoma Benign myxoid neoplasms Benign; cellular subtype may recur locally but is not destructive Large muscles of the thigh, shoulder, buttock, and upper arm; may be multiple with fibrous dysplasia (Mazabraud syndrome). Essential: intramuscular, hypocellular myxoid tumor composed of bland spindle cells. Desirable: GNAS activating variant in selected diagnostically challenging cases. Uniform spindle-to-stellate cells with small oval nuclei, inconspicuous nucleoli, and indistinct pale eosinophilic cytoplasm in abundant myxoid matrix. Hypovascular; sparse capillary-sized vessels. Cystic change and stromal vacuolation may occur. Necrosis and mitotic figures should be absent. Peripheral infiltration between and around individual skeletal muscle fibers is common despite a deceptively circumscribed gross appearance. Cellular myxoma contains hypercellular areas (10–90%) with increased cells and more conspicuous vessels, occasionally thick-walled or in collagenous stroma; mitoses remain very rare and pleomorphism/necrosis are absent. CD34 is commonly positive; SMA is rarely positive. Desmin, S100, and MUC4 are negative. Scattered CD163-positive muciphages may be present. Activating GNAS variants in exons 8 or 9 occur in >90% of sporadic intramuscular/cellular myxomas and in Mazabraud-associated cases. GNAS activation leads to downstream FOS (c-FOS) activation. Copy-number variants are absent in cellular myxoma. GNAS testing can help distinguish cellular myxoma from low-grade myxofibrosarcoma on limited material. Low-grade myxofibrosarcoma Atypia, nuclear hyperchromasia, and infiltrative curvilinear vessels favor myxofibrosarcoma; these are not features of cellular myxoma. GNAS variant supports myxoma but must be interpreted with morphology. Myxoid liposarcoma Search for lipoblasts and characteristic delicate branching vasculature; use DDIT3 fusion testing when morphology/site warrant. The supplied excerpt does not detail this differential. Juxta-articular myxoma Periarticular location, cyst-like spaces, and fibrin/hemosiderin-related reactive change favor juxta-articular myxoma. Cellularity alone does not establish malignancy: cellular myxoma may be substantially hypercellular. Nuclear atypia/hyperchromasia, necrosis, or appreciable mitotic activity should prompt reconsideration of the diagnosis. Do not mistake peripheral entrapment of skeletal muscle fibers for sarcomatous invasion. Classic intramuscular myxoma usually does not recur. Cellular lesions have a small risk of local, non-destructive recurrence. Malignant transformation is not described. Benign but locally recurrent (up to approximately one third) Periarticular soft tissue, most often around the knee (>85%); also hip, shoulder, elbow, and ankle. Essential: bland, paucicellular myxoid tumor arising in soft tissue around a large joint. Poorly circumscribed and infiltrative into periarticular soft tissue; bland spindle cells with uniform ovoid nuclei and inconspicuous nucleoli in myxoid matrix. Few vessels; cellularity may increase, but mitoses remain scarce. Cyst-like spaces lined by delicate fibrin or thicker collagen are common. Hemorrhage, chronic inflammation, hemosiderin, and fibrin may reflect trauma and can also occur in recurrent lesions. IHC is generally not diagnostic. Lesional cells may express CD34 and/or SMA; S100 is negative. Intratumoral muciphages may be CD163-positive. Molecular testing is not clinically relevant according to the supplied WHO excerpt. Both are bland and myxoid. Periarticular location, cyst-like spaces, fibrin lining, and hemorrhagic/hemosiderin reactive change favor juxta-articular myxoma. Ganglion or synovial cyst A cystic lesion without a true bland spindle-cell myxoid neoplasm favors a cyst; correlate with joint relationship and histology. Significant nuclear atypia/hyperchromasia and malignant vascular architecture are not expected in juxta-articular myxoma. Do not interpret infiltrative growth as evidence of malignancy; local infiltration is characteristic. Recurrence may occur more than once, but malignant transformation does not occur. Local recurrence occurs in up to one third of patients; incomplete excision and difficulty defining the border are practical concerns. No malignant transformation is reported. OGT-rearranged mesenchymal neoplasm Molecularly defined / emerging entities Benign; limited follow-up Predominantly acral; occasional more proximal extremity or limb-girdle lesions. Essential: cords/nests of epithelioid cells in hyalinized or fibromyxoid stroma AND an OGT gene rearrangement. Molecular confirmation is required; morphology and CD34 alone are insufficient. Well-circumscribed, often lobulated tumor with alternating moderately cellular and hypocellular zones; two-tone appearance from myxoid cellular areas and hyalinized/fibromyxoid hypocellular areas. Predominantly epithelioid/plump ovoid cells with a minor spindle-cell component, arranged in cords, nests, reticular structures, or perivascular concentric whorls. Uniform nuclei, delicate chromatin, inconspicuous nucleoli, very low mitotic activity, and no necrosis. Some OGT::FOXO1/FOXO3 tumors have vacuolated or signet-ring-like cells. CD34 is focal to diffuse in all reported cases; EMA is focal in some. A minority show keratin (AE1/AE3) and/or ERG. SMARCB1/INI1 is retained; broad endothelial, myoepithelial, nerve-sheath, myogenic, and perineurial markers are generally negative. OGT fusions are defining; reported partners include FOXO1, FOXO3, FOXO4, and CITED1. OGT::FOXO4 and OGT::CITED1 may arise through intrachromosomal rearrangements and can be missed by dual-color break-apart FISH. Use an assay capable of detecting the relevant fusion. Myoepithelioma Myoepithelial tumors show a broader myoepithelial immunophenotype (keratin/EMA with S100, SOX10, or GFAP); OGT-rearranged tumors are typically negative for these lineage markers. Perineurioma Perineurial markers (EMA, claudin-1, GLUT1) support perineurioma; OGT-rearranged tumors are not typically perineurial. Other acral epithelioid mesenchymal tumors The characteristic hyalinized/fibromyxoid stroma is suggestive but not definitive; demonstrate OGT fusion for confirmation. A negative break-apart FISH result does not exclude OGT rearrangement when an intrachromosomal fusion is suspected. CD34 positivity is not specific; do not diagnose this entity without molecular confirmation. No recurrence or metastasis has been reported after excision to date, but follow-up is limited. Deep angiomyxoma Benign / locally recurrent myxoid neoplasms Locally infiltrative; recurrence possible; no metastatic behavior expected Deep pelviperineal soft tissue, especially vulvovaginal, inguinoscrotal, and perianal regions. Essential: poorly demarcated, highly infiltrative, uniformly hypocellular spindle-cell lesion with abundant myxoid matrix and evenly distributed medium-to-thick-walled vessels. Uniformly hypocellular tumor with copious myxoid/fibromyxoid matrix and medium-to-large vessels distributed throughout. Spindle or stellate cells with delicate processes; collagen fibrils and smooth-muscle (myoid) bundles may lie near vessels. Highly infiltrative growth with imperceptible blending into adjacent tissue; margins can be difficult to assess. Focal hypercellularity, collagenous areas, or neurofibroma-like morphology may occur. Desmin is usually diffusely positive. CD34 is positive in a minority; SMA is generally limited to myoid bundles. ER and PR are typically positive in tumors in women and may also be positive in men (more often PR). HMGA2 is sensitive but not specific. Chromosome 12q13–q15 aberrations and HMGA2 rearrangement/upregulation are characteristic in a subset. HMGA2 may be rearranged or aberrantly expressed through other regulatory mechanisms; HMGA2 expression is not specific and is seen in several other mesenchymal tumors. Molecular testing is not considered clinically relevant for routine diagnosis in the supplied WHO text. Angiomyofibroblastoma Usually more circumscribed and superficial, with alternating cellularity and perivascular clustering; deep angiomyxoma is deeply infiltrative and uniformly hypocellular with vessels throughout. Cellular angiofibroma Typically circumscribed and collagenous with conspicuous hyalinized vessels; deep angiomyxoma is extensively myxoid and infiltrative. Adipocytic differentiation and characteristic lipoblasts/vascular pattern favor liposarcoma; deep angiomyxoma shows bland uniform spindle cells and characteristic thick-walled vessels. Other pelvic myxoid neoplasms Integrate depth, infiltrative pattern, vascular caliber/distribution, desmin and hormone-receptor profile; HMGA2 alone is not specific. The term “aggressive” is increasingly avoided; depth and infiltrative local behavior are the defining clinical issues. HMGA2 positivity supports but does not establish the diagnosis. Margins may be difficult to assess because tumor blends with normal tissue. Reported local recurrence ranges widely (approximately 9–50%), likely partly reflecting margin-assessment uncertainty; multiple recurrences are uncommon. Hormone-receptor-positive recurrent tumors have been treated with surgery and GnRH analogues. Acral fibrochondromyxoid tumor Indolent; local recurrence if incompletely excised Exclusively acral, about twice as common in hands (especially fingers) as feet. Essential: acral multinodular tumor with fibrovascular septa and bland spindle/round cells in fibrous, myxoid, or chondroid matrix. Desirable: CD34 and ERG expression; THBS1::ADGRF5 fusion or THBS1 rearrangement in selected cases. Multinodular lesion partitioned by fibrous bands containing numerous small vessels. Spindle or round cells in abundant myxoid, chondroid, or fibrous matrix; cells form poorly defined groups, small clusters, or rows, sometimes in lacunar spaces. Scant eosinophilic cytoplasm; small round, ovoid, or reniform nuclei, occasionally with longitudinal grooves; pleomorphism and mitoses are usually absent. Rare cystic change, calcification, or ischemic necrosis may occur. CD34 and ERG are positive in approximately 94% and 97%, respectively. THBS1::ADGRF5 fusion was identified in 27/29 cases in the cited series. Fusion/rearrangement supports the diagnosis but is generally not required in a morphologically typical lesion. Chondromyxoid fibroma / soft-tissue chondroma Acral location, multinodular fibrovascular septa, bland cells, and THBS1::ADGRF5 support AFCMT; correlate with whether the lesion is soft tissue-based and the characteristic architecture. Low-grade chondrosarcoma Atypia, permeative growth, and destructive bone-centered disease should prompt consideration of chondrosarcoma; mild cortical scalloping can occur with AFCMT. Other acral myxoid tumors CD34/ERG coexpression and fusion testing can support AFCMT, but neither marker alone is specific. Mild cortical scalloping or saucerization does not by itself imply a primary bone malignancy. Rare ischemic necrosis should not be overcalled as malignant necrosis in the absence of other malignant features. Local recurrence is approximately 18%, particularly after incomplete excision. No malignant transformation or distant metastasis has been reported. Angiomatoid fibrous histiocytoma (AFH) Intermediate / rarely metastasizing Intermediate; rarely metastasizing Usually subcutis/deep dermis of extremities; also trunk, head and neck, often near lymph-node basins. Essential: nodules of epithelioid-to-ovoid cells in syncytial-like sheets with peripheral lymphoplasmacytic rims/infiltrates, often with germinal centers. Desirable: blood-filled pseudovascular spaces, fibrous pseudocapsule/hemosiderin, and EWSR1 or FUS rearrangement in selected cases. Usually circumscribed and lobulated, with spindle, epithelioid, or histiocytoid cells in sheets/fascicles/nodules. Blood-filled pseudovascular spaces are not lined by endothelium; thick fibrous pseudocapsule with hemosiderin and peripheral lymphoplasmacytic cuff with germinal centers are characteristic. About one third lack pseudovascular spaces and may be solid, mimicking a lymph node. A rare small-round-cell variant may mimic undifferentiated round-cell sarcoma. Mitotic activity is usually low; atypical mitoses, focal necrosis, pleomorphic cells, or multinucleated giant cells can occur and do not reliably predict aggressive behavior. Desmin and SOX9 are commonly focal or diffuse; membranous CD99 is common. Tumor cells are consistently negative for MYOD1, myogenin, keratins, S100, and CD34. ALK, EMA, pan-TRK, TLE1, synaptophysin, and CD68 may be variable. >90% harbor EWSR1::CREB1; rare cases show EWSR1::ATF1, FUS::ATF1, or EWSR1::CREM. EWSR1::CREB1/ATF1 also occurs in clear cell sarcoma and other FET-CREB tumors; fusion detection must be interpreted with morphology and immunophenotype. AFH lacks the downstream MITF pathway activation characteristic of clear cell sarcoma. Clear cell sarcoma Both may harbor EWSR1::ATF1/CREB1. Clear cell sarcoma shows melanocytic differentiation (S100/SOX10/Melan-A/HMB45); AFH typically lacks these markers and has lymphoplasmacytic cuff/pseudocapsule. Lymph node / nodal metastasis AFH can mimic a lymph node, especially when solid; look for characteristic peripheral lymphoplasmacytic cuff, fibrous pseudocapsule, hemosiderin, and molecular findings. Ewing / other round-cell sarcoma Small-round-cell AFH may mimic sarcoma; integrate desmin/SOX9, negative myogenic markers, architecture, and FET-CREB fusion. FET-CREB family epithelioid mesenchymal tumor Fusion overlap exists. FET-CREB tumors are often keratin-positive and may be cavity-based; AFH is usually desmin/SOX9-positive and keratin-negative. “Angiomatoid malignant fibrous histiocytoma” is not recommended terminology. Pseudovascular spaces are absent in a substantial minority; their absence does not exclude AFH. Atypia or mitotic activity alone does not establish aggressive behavior. Local recurrence is approximately 10–15%; incomplete excision is associated with recurrence. Metastases occur in approximately 1–5%, mainly locoregional lymph nodes; distant metastasis and disease-related death are rare. Ossifying fibromyxoid tumor (OFMT) Intermediate / variable behavior Variable; malignant examples defined by high cellularity, atypia, and mitotic activity Usually subcutaneous on extremities; less often trunk or head and neck. Essential: ovoid/epithelioid cells in cords or sheets within collagenous or myxoid matrix, often with peripheral bone; variable S100 and often focal desmin. Malignant OFMT: high cellularity, high nuclear atypia, and >1 mitosis/6 mm² (>2 mitoses/50 HPF). Desirable: PHF1 rearrangement or other characteristic fusion in selected cases. Often encapsulated or well circumscribed and lobulated; peripheral shell of bone is present in about half but is not required. Uniform ovoid/epithelioid cells arranged in cords or diffuse sheets in collagenous or myxoid matrix. Most have <1 mitosis/6 mm² (<2/50 HPF). Approximately 10% have increased mitotic activity; malignant examples may show osteosarcoma-like bone elements. S100 is variable; desmin and keratin are focal in a minority. CD34, EMA, SMA, and SOX10 are negative in the WHO-described profile. Approximately 80% harbor a fusion involving PHF1; common examples are EP400::PHF1 (up to 40%) and PHF1::TFE3 (about 10%). PHF1 fusions alter chromatin accessibility and are useful in unusual cases; absence does not exclude OFMT. Chondromyxoid fibroma / chondroid lesion OFMT has ovoid/epithelioid cells in cords/sheets and often a peripheral bone shell; well-formed cartilage is not the defining feature. Soft-tissue chondroma Chondroma shows mature hyaline cartilage; OFMT has a fibromyxoid/collagenous matrix with cords/sheets of ovoid cells. Extraskeletal osteosarcoma Malignant osteoid with sarcomatous cells favors osteosarcoma; OFMT may contain bone, including osteosarcoma-like elements in malignant examples, so evaluate the overall architecture and criteria. Myoepithelial tumor Myoepithelial tumors typically express keratin/EMA with S100/SOX10/GFAP; OFMT has a different phenotype and may show PHF1 fusion. Peripheral bone is not obligatory; its absence does not exclude OFMT. Metastases have been reported even in tumors with lower mitotic activity; no single threshold guarantees benign behavior. Delayed metastases may occur up to 20 years after primary excision. Tumors with >1 mitosis/6 mm² recur more often and may metastasize, but metastasis can occur below this threshold. Lung and soft tissue are common metastatic sites; long-term follow-up is warranted. Myoepithelioma, myoepithelial carcinoma, and mixed tumor Myoepithelial / lineage-defined Myoepithelioma and mixed tumor usually benign; carcinoma malignant Soft tissue and subcutis, often extremities; also trunk and head/neck. Essential: trabecular, reticular, nested, and/or solid growth of spindle or epithelioid cells, often in myxoid or hyalinized stroma; keratin/EMA plus S100, SOX10, or GFAP expression. Mixed tumor additionally shows ductal differentiation. Myoepithelial carcinoma shows increased cytologic atypia and mitotic activity. Broad morphologic spectrum: spindle, epithelioid, plasmacytoid, or clear cells in cords, nests, reticular/trabecular arrays, or solid sheets. Myxoid, chondromyxoid, or hyalinized stroma is common; mixed tumors contain ductal structures. Carcinoma is supported by infiltrative growth, increased cytologic atypia, and mitotic activity; no single morphologic pattern alone defines malignancy. Myoepithelial phenotype requires epithelial marker expression (keratin and/or EMA) together with one or more myoepithelial markers: S100, SOX10, or GFAP. Marker expression is variable and no single marker is sufficient; correlate with morphology. EWSR1 rearrangements occur in a subset, with multiple fusion partners; FUS rearrangements also occur. EWSR1::POU5F1 and other fusions are reported; molecular findings support classification but are not independently specific for malignancy. AFH AFH may show syncytial nodules, pseudovascular spaces, peripheral lymphoplasmacytic cuff, and EWSR1::CREB1/ATF1; myoepithelial tumors show keratin/EMA plus S100/SOX10/GFAP. Extraskeletal myxoid chondrosarcoma EMC is usually keratin-negative and defined by NR4A3 rearrangement; myoepithelial tumors have a true myoepithelial phenotype. Myoepithelial carcinoma vs benign myoepithelioma Assess infiltrative growth, atypia, and mitotic activity; molecular alteration alone does not establish carcinoma. Parachordoma Not recommended terminology; use the current myoepithelial tumor classification and demonstrate the appropriate phenotype. Do not use “parachordoma” as a preferred diagnosis. A myxoid matrix or S100 positivity alone is not enough; require the combined epithelial and myoepithelial phenotype. Molecular fusions overlap with other entities; use clinicopathologic correlation. Behavior depends on subtype and malignant features; myoepithelial carcinoma has meaningful risk of local recurrence and metastasis. Pleomorphic hyalinizing angiectatic tumor (PHAT) Intermediate / locally recurrent Locally recurrent; metastatic behavior is not established Usually subcutaneous soft tissue of distal extremities, especially lower limb. Essential: clusters of ectatic, hyalinized vessels surrounded by pleomorphic hemosiderin-laden cells with nuclear pseudoinclusions; very low or absent mitotic activity. A peripheral component of hemosiderotic fibrolipomatous tumor (HFLT) is often present. Distinctive ectatic, thin-walled vessels with conspicuous perivascular hyalinization. Perivascular pleomorphic spindle/epithelioid cells with abundant hemosiderin and characteristic intranuclear pseudoinclusions; mitoses are very low or absent. Often associated with peripheral HFLT-like fatty tissue; infiltrative margins may be present. No single immunophenotype is defining; hemosiderin-laden macrophages and lesional spindle cells must be distinguished. CD34 may label spindle cells in the HFLT/PHAT spectrum. PHAT and HFLT are linked by recurrent TGFBR3::MGEA5 fusion or related rearrangements involving TGFBR3 and/or MGEA5 in a subset. Molecular findings support the HFLT-PHAT spectrum but do not replace characteristic morphology. HFLT HFLT is predominantly adipocytic with bland hemosiderin-laden spindle cells; PHAT shows ectatic hyalinized vessels and more conspicuous pleomorphic perivascular cells. Myxofibrosarcoma Myxofibrosarcoma shows atypical spindle cells and curvilinear vessels in myxoid stroma, often with mitotic activity; PHAT has hyalinized ectatic vessels, hemosiderin, and pseudoinclusions. Angiosarcoma PHAT vessels are ectatic but not lined by malignant endothelial cells; endothelial markers should be interpreted with architecture. Ancient schwannoma Can show degenerative atypia and hemosiderin, but lacks the characteristic ectatic hyalinized vessels and HFLT association. Marked pleomorphism can be striking despite very low mitotic activity; do not equate atypia alone with high-grade sarcoma. Recognize an associated HFLT component and sample the lesion adequately. Local recurrence can occur, particularly after incomplete excision; metastasis is not a defining feature. Hemosiderotic fibrolipomatous tumor (HFLT) Locally recurrent; rare progression/association with sarcoma in the spectrum Acral/distal extremity, especially foot and ankle. Essential: mature adipose tissue admixed with bland hemosiderin-laden spindle cells and macrophages in an acral lesion. Mature adipose tissue with infiltrating bland spindle cells, often in fibrous septa and between fat lobules. Abundant hemosiderin-laden macrophages and spindle cells; chronic inflammatory cells may be present. May coexist with or transition to PHAT, which has ectatic hyalinized vessels and pleomorphic perivascular cells. Spindle cells are often CD34-positive; macrophages are highlighted by histiocytic markers. No single IHC marker is diagnostic. TGFBR3::MGEA5 fusion/rearrangements are reported in HFLT and PHAT, supporting a biologic spectrum. Some tumors in this spectrum may acquire additional alterations; molecular testing is supportive rather than required in classic cases. Ordinary lipoma HFLT has infiltrative growth, hemosiderin-laden spindle cells/macrophages, and acral predilection; ordinary lipoma lacks this component. Atypical lipomatous tumor ALT shows atypical hyperchromatic stromal cells and MDM2 amplification; HFLT spindle cells are typically bland and hemosiderin-rich. PHAT Look for ectatic hyalinized vessels and pleomorphic hemosiderin-laden perivascular cells to diagnose PHAT rather than HFLT. Myxoinflammatory fibroblastic sarcoma Acral site overlaps; MIFS has myxoid/inflammatory background and bizarre virocyte-like cells, whereas HFLT is adipocytic and hemosiderin-rich. Acral location and hemosiderin are clues, not sufficient criteria without the characteristic adipocytic/spindle-cell composition. Sample for a PHAT component or a more cellular atypical area. Local recurrence is possible; careful excision and long-term clinical follow-up are appropriate. Phosphaturic mesenchymal tumor (PMT) Molecularly / clinically defined mesenchymal tumors Usually benign; rare malignant examples Any soft tissue or bone site; often small and difficult to localize. Essential: bland spindle-cell tumor with matrix deposition, grungy calcification and/or rich vascular network, plus clinical hypophosphatemia and/or osteomalacia. Desirable: FGF23 overproduction in serum or tumor (in the absence of tumor-induced osteomalacia, TIO). Malignant examples show frankly sarcomatous morphology. Bland spindle or stellate cells in variable myxoid/chondromyxoid or basophilic matrix, with characteristic “grungy” calcification. Prominent branching vascular network; osteoclast-like giant cells and mature adipose tissue may be present. Malignant tumors show overt sarcomatous cytology and growth rather than merely increased cellularity. FGF23 expression may be demonstrated in tumor, but sensitivity can be limited; use in context with clinical biochemistry. SSTR2A and other markers may be expressed but are not independently diagnostic. Most PMTs harbor FN1::FGFR1 fusion; a smaller subset has FN1::FGF1 fusion. FGF23 overproduction causes renal phosphate wasting, hypophosphatemia, and osteomalacia. Molecular confirmation is useful in difficult cases. Osteosarcoma / chondrosarcoma PMT is generally bland with grungy calcified matrix and clinical TIO; malignant bone-forming/cartilage-forming tumors show overt malignant cytology and destructive growth. Myositis ossificans / reactive fibro-osseous lesion Zonal maturation and clinical/radiologic evolution support reactive lesion; PMT has a spindle-cell neoplasm with characteristic matrix/vascularity and FGF23-related syndrome. Other calcifying mesenchymal tumors The combination of grungy calcification, rich vessels, biochemical hypophosphatemia, and FN1-related fusion is most useful. Do not diagnose PMT from calcification alone; correlate with serum phosphate and evidence of tumor-induced osteomalacia. FGF23 may be difficult to demonstrate by IHC; biochemical and molecular correlation is valuable. The clinical syndrome may be absent in an incidental lesion; the WHO essential criteria emphasize clinical evidence. Complete excision usually resolves the biochemical syndrome. Recurrence or metastasis may occur, particularly in malignant examples. GLI1-altered mesenchymal tumor Variable; local recurrence and metastasis reported in a subset Soft tissue, often deep extremity or trunk; may occur in children and adults. Essential: lobular architecture, spindle-cell or nested epithelioid growth, prominent admixed branching capillaries, and GLI1 rearrangement, amplification, or protein overexpression. Lobulated tumor with spindle-cell fascicles or nested epithelioid cells and conspicuous branching capillary vessels. Cytology ranges from bland to atypical; some tumors show increased cellularity or epithelioid morphology. The entity includes GLI1-rearranged and GLI1-amplified lesions; morphology alone may overlap with other perivascular/epithelioid tumors. GLI1 nuclear immunoreactivity may be present and is supportive, but protein overexpression is not equivalent to a specific fusion. CD34 and S100 may be coexpressed in some kinase-altered/GLI1-spectrum tumors; interpret as a panel. GLI1 rearrangements commonly involve partners such as ACTB or MALAT1; GLI1 amplification is another mechanism. Molecular confirmation by RNA-based fusion assay, FISH, or copy-number analysis is useful when morphology/IHC suggests the entity. PEComa PEComa typically coexpresses melanocytic and smooth-muscle markers and has perivascular growth; GLI1-altered tumors may show GLI1 alteration without the full PEComa phenotype. GIST GIST is usually KIT/DOG1-positive and has a GI mural origin; GLI1-altered tumors require molecular classification. Solitary fibrous tumor SFT shows nuclear STAT6/NAB2::STAT6; branching vessels alone are not specific. Other kinase-altered spindle-cell neoplasms Use a broad fusion panel when morphology and CD34/S100 coexpression raise a kinase-driven differential. GLI1 protein expression alone is not fully specific; integrate morphology, site, and molecular results. Do not assume all GLI1-altered tumors have identical behavior; the category is heterogeneous. Behavior is variable; local recurrence and metastasis have been reported. Long-term follow-up is appropriate. Superficial FET-ETS family neurocristic tumor Usually indolent but recurrence/metastasis may occur Cutaneous or subcutaneous, often superficial extremity or trunk. Essential: cutaneous/subcutaneous lesion of bland small round-to-ovoid cells in nests, cords, and trabeculae; no significant atypia or necrosis; strong diffuse SOX10, S100, and CD99. Desirable: FET::ETS-family fusion. Superficial dermal/subcutaneous, well-circumscribed or multinodular tumor with nests, cords, and trabeculae of uniform small round/ovoid cells. Cells are bland with scant-to-moderate cytoplasm; significant pleomorphism and tumor necrosis are absent in the defining pattern. Some cases may show myxoid or sclerotic stroma; distinguish from malignant clear cell sarcoma and other neurocristic tumors. Strong diffuse S100 and SOX10 with CD99 expression are characteristic. Melanocytic marker expression may overlap with related neurocristic lesions; use the complete profile and fusion context. FET-ETS family fusions are characteristic; molecular testing supports classification and helps separate from other neural crest-derived tumors. CCS is typically deep, infiltrative, and cytologically more conspicuous with prominent nucleoli; shares melanocytic markers but has EWSR1::ATF1/CREB1 rather than the defining FET-ETS family fusion. Melanoma Clinical skin primary, junctional component, and broader melanoma phenotype may favor melanoma; molecular and clinicopathologic correlation is essential. Malignant gastrointestinal neuroectodermal tumor MGNET is deep GI/mesenteric and usually lacks melanocytic differentiation; superficial site and FET-ETS phenotype favor this superficial tumor. Schwannoma Schwannoma has characteristic Antoni A/B and/or Verocay architecture and lacks the defining FET-ETS fusion. Do not classify a bland superficial SOX10/S100-positive lesion solely by immunophenotype; the fusion and clinical site are important. Do not conflate this entity with deep clear cell sarcoma or gastrointestinal neuroectodermal tumor. The supplied WHO text describes generally indolent behavior, but recurrence/metastasis can occur; follow-up data remain limited. Kinase-altered spindle cell neoplasm Variable; includes locally aggressive and malignant tumors Soft tissue of extremities and trunk; may be superficial or deep. Essential: fibrosarcoma-like, MPNST-like, or lipofibromatosis-like morphology; often CD34/S100 coexpression; kinase-pathway fusion or activating alteration (e.g., NTRK1/2/3, RET, RAF1, ALK, FGFR1, EGFR, BRAF). Morphologic spectrum includes infiltrative fascicular spindle-cell tumors resembling fibrosarcoma or MPNST and lipofibromatosis-like lesions. Some tumors are relatively bland; others show increased cellularity, atypia, and mitotic activity. The morphologic pattern does not reliably identify the driver. CD34 and S100 coexpression is a useful clue in selected cases but is not universal. CD34 and S100 may be coexpressed; SOX10 may vary depending on differentiation. Pan-TRK, ALK, and other kinase-related IHC may be useful screening tools, but molecular confirmation is required. Recurrent kinase fusions/alterations involve NTRK1, NTRK2, NTRK3, RET, RAF1, ALK, FGFR1, EGFR, and BRAF. Use RNA-based NGS/fusion testing where possible; DNA panels may miss some intronic fusion events. Identify the actual driver because it may have therapeutic implications. Conventional fibrosarcoma Morphology may overlap; a kinase fusion identifies a molecularly defined subset and may alter treatment. MPNST MPNST may show S100/SOX10 but typically has a different clinical/molecular context; kinase fusion testing is important in atypical spindle tumors. Lipofibromatosis A bland infiltrative fibroblastic tumor with adipose entrapment may overlap morphologically; kinase alteration defines a subset. NTRK-rearranged spindle-cell neoplasm This is within the broader kinase-altered spectrum; confirm the specific kinase fusion rather than relying on pan-TRK staining. Pan-TRK immunostaining is a screening surrogate, not proof of an NTRK fusion. Do not treat all morphologically similar spindle tumors as one entity; molecular driver classification is central. Behavior depends on the specific tumor and molecular driver; targeted therapy may be relevant in advanced disease. Pseudoendocrine sarcoma Malignant; limited case numbers Predominantly soft tissue of extremities; often deep-seated. Essential: nested/trabecular architecture; uniform epithelioid cells with round nuclei and speckled chromatin; nuclear β-catenin in most; keratin and neuroendocrine markers negative. Desirable: CTNNB1 alteration in selected cases. Uniform epithelioid cells in nests and trabeculae, resembling a neuroendocrine neoplasm. Round nuclei with finely speckled chromatin and relatively uniform cytology; architecture may be organoid. The name reflects morphologic mimicry, not true neuroendocrine differentiation. Nuclear β-catenin is present in most cases. Keratins and neuroendocrine markers are negative, helping exclude epithelial and neuroendocrine neoplasms. CTNNB1 alterations are reported and may support diagnosis; molecular testing is desirable in selected cases. Neuroendocrine neoplasm Pseudoendocrine sarcoma is negative for neuroendocrine markers and keratins; nuclear β-catenin supports the diagnosis. Epithelioid sarcoma Epithelioid sarcoma often expresses keratin/EMA and loses INI1; pseudoendocrine sarcoma is typically keratin-negative. Other nested epithelioid sarcomas Integrate site, nuclear β-catenin, negative neuroendocrine/epithelial markers, and CTNNB1 status. Do not infer neuroendocrine differentiation from nested/trabecular morphology alone. Nuclear β-catenin is supportive but should be interpreted with the full phenotype. Malignant potential is recognized; outcome data are limited by rarity. NUT-rearranged sarcoma Malignant Deep soft tissue; may arise in multiple anatomic regions. Essential: monomorphic round, epithelioid, and/or spindle cells in sheets, nests, or fascicles with variable collagenous/myxoid stroma, plus a NUT-family gene fusion with a specific partner. Desirable: nuclear NUT immunoreactivity. Pure or mixed population of round, epithelioid, and spindle cells with monomorphic nuclei. Sheets, nests, or fascicles; variable collagenous or myxoid stroma. Cytologic appearance may be nonspecific. Nuclear NUT staining is a useful surrogate and supports the diagnosis; a negative stain does not replace molecular assessment if suspicion remains. NUTM1 rearrangements occur with different partners; the partner and fusion context matter for classification. Demonstrate the fusion by RNA sequencing or an appropriate rearrangement assay; molecular confirmation is central. Ewing sarcoma / round-cell sarcoma Round-cell morphology overlaps; NUT immunohistochemistry and fusion testing distinguish NUT-rearranged sarcoma. Synovial sarcoma Can be spindle/epithelioid and keratin-positive; SS18::SSX fusion or surrogate IHC supports synovial sarcoma, while NUT fusion supports this entity. Poorly differentiated carcinoma NUT-rearranged sarcoma is a mesenchymal tumor; integrate morphology, NUT, keratin, and fusion testing. NUT staining is a surrogate; molecular confirmation is recommended in diagnostically consequential cases. Do not assume that all NUT-positive tumors are identical without identifying the fusion partner. Aggressive malignant behavior is reported; prognosis varies with site and disease extent. PATZ1-rearranged sarcoma Malignant; clinical behavior variable Soft tissue, including deep extremity and trunk. Essential: monomorphic round-to-spindle cells in fibromyxoid background with thick fibrous capsule and hyalinized vessels; coexpression of skeletal-muscle and myoepithelial markers; PATZ1 rearrangement. Monomorphic round-to-spindle cells in a fibromyxoid stroma, often with thick fibrous capsule and hyalinized vessels. May show variable cellularity and patterns that overlap with other spindle/round-cell sarcomas. Coexpression of skeletal muscle markers and myoepithelial markers is characteristic; interpret the panel rather than a single marker.
