Myogenic markers should be assessed alongside myoepithelial markers to distinguish from conventional rhabdomyosarcoma. PATZ1 rearrangement is defining; fusion partners include EWSR1 and other partners reported in the literature. Molecular confirmation is essential in the appropriate morphologic/immunophenotypic setting. Rhabdomyosarcoma PATZ1-rearranged sarcoma may express skeletal muscle markers but also shows myoepithelial marker coexpression and PATZ1 rearrangement. Myoepithelial phenotype overlaps; the characteristic morphology and PATZ1 rearrangement establish the distinct entity. Ewing/round-cell sarcoma Monomorphic round-cell morphology overlaps; fusion testing is required. Myogenic marker positivity alone is not sufficient for rhabdomyosarcoma. Do not diagnose based on morphology/IHC alone without considering PATZ1 rearrangement. Reported outcomes are variable; long-term data are limited. Established malignant tumors of uncertain differentiation Deep soft tissue of extremities, especially near joints; also trunk, head/neck, and visceral sites. Essential: characteristic monophasic spindle-cell, biphasic epithelial/spindle-cell, or poorly differentiated morphology in the appropriate setting, with SS18::SSX fusion or a highly specific surrogate immunophenotype. Desirable: demonstration of SS18 rearrangement/fusion or validated SS18::SSX surrogate IHC. Monophasic tumors show uniform spindle cells in intersecting fascicles with wiry collagen and branching vessels. Biphasic tumors contain epithelial glands/nests admixed with spindle-cell component. Poorly differentiated areas may be round-cell, epithelioid, or highly cellular and can mimic other sarcomas. Keratin and EMA are variable in monophasic tumors and more conspicuous in epithelial areas of biphasic tumors. TLE1 is sensitive but not specific. SS18::SSX fusion-specific antibody is highly useful when available. Defining t(X;18) rearrangement produces SS18::SSX1, SS18::SSX2, or rarely SS18::SSX4 fusion. Fusion testing by RNA sequencing, RT-PCR, or SS18 break-apart FISH; fusion-specific IHC can serve as a strong surrogate. Both can be spindle-cell tumors; synovial sarcoma often expresses keratin/EMA and has SS18::SSX, whereas MPNST has nerve association and may show H3K27me3 loss. Fibrosarcoma / solitary fibrous tumor Morphology overlaps; SS18::SSX fusion is decisive. SFT is supported by nuclear STAT6. Ewing sarcoma Poorly differentiated synovial sarcoma may be round-cell; keratin/EMA and SS18::SSX distinguish it from Ewing family tumors. Carcinoma Biphasic synovial sarcoma can mimic carcinoma; demonstrate spindle-cell component and SS18::SSX fusion. TLE1 is not specific and should not be used alone. A negative SS18 break-apart FISH result may require RNA-based fusion testing if morphology is compelling. The historical term “synoviosarcoma” is not recommended. Risk depends on size, site, grade, and stage; late recurrence and metastasis may occur. Malignant; regional lymph-node metastases are relatively characteristic Distal type: hands/forearms; proximal type: pelvis, perineum, genital region, and trunk. Essential: nodular epithelioid/spindle-cell tumor with central necrosis or pseudogranulomatous pattern and loss of SMARCB1/INI1 in most cases. Confirm with epithelial marker expression and appropriate clinical/anatomic setting. Distal type: nodules of epithelioid cells with central necrosis, often creating a pseudogranulomatous appearance. Proximal type: larger epithelioid/rhabdoid cells, often with more marked atypia; may show myxoid areas and can mimic extrarenal rhabdoid tumor. Tumor cells may be epithelioid or spindle-shaped; necrosis and infiltrative growth are common. Broad-spectrum keratins and EMA are commonly positive. Loss of nuclear INI1/SMARCB1 is characteristic in most cases; internal non-neoplastic cells must retain staining. CD34 may be positive; S100 and endothelial markers are generally not defining. Biallelic SMARCB1 inactivation/deletion is the central molecular event in most cases. Rare cases may have alternative molecular mechanisms; loss of INI1 is a key surrogate. Extrarenal rhabdoid tumor Both may lose INI1 and express keratin/EMA. Epithelioid sarcoma usually shows nodular/pseudogranulomatous architecture and occurs in characteristic distal/proximal sites; ERT typically affects infants/young children and has diffuse rhabdoid morphology. Epithelioid sarcoma expresses keratin/EMA but is a mesenchymal tumor with characteristic morphology and INI1 loss. Granulomatous inflammation Central necrosis and epithelioid cells can mimic granuloma; demonstrate neoplastic keratin-positive cells and assess INI1. MPNST usually has nerve association and different phenotype; INI1 loss alone is not specific. INI1 loss is not unique to epithelioid sarcoma; correlate with age, site, morphology, and phenotype. Rhabdoid cells in proximal epithelioid sarcoma can mimic extrarenal rhabdoid tumor. The historical distal/proximal subtypes differ morphologically; sample adequately. Local recurrence and distant metastasis are significant risks; regional lymph-node involvement is relatively common. Alveolar soft part sarcoma (ASPS) Malignant; often indolent but metastatic Deep soft tissue of extremities; head and neck in children; also trunk and other sites. Essential: nested/alveolar growth of eosinophilic polygonal cells with prominent sinusoidal capillaries. Desirable: nuclear TFE3 expression and/or ASPSCR1::TFE3 fusion. Uniform large polygonal cells in nests separated by thin fibrovascular septa; central discohesion creates pseudoalveolar pattern. Abundant granular eosinophilic cytoplasm, vesicular nuclei, and prominent nucleoli; glycogen may impart clear-cell appearance. PAS-positive, diastase-resistant crystals are present in approximately 80%, sometimes sparse. Mitotic activity is often low; vascular invasion is common. Nuclear TFE3 (C-terminal antibody) is characteristic; cathepsin K and GPNMB are consistently expressed. Usually negative for epithelial, neuroendocrine, and melanocytic markers. Desmin may be focal; myogenin and MYOD1 are negative. ASPSCR1::TFE3 fusion is the defining alteration in most cases; detection is useful in selected cases. TFE3 IHC is a surrogate and can be interpreted with morphology; confirm fusion when needed. Granular cell tumor Both may have granular cytoplasm; ASPS shows pseudoalveolar nests, sinusoidal vessels, TFE3, and crystals; granular cell tumor expresses S100/SOX10. Paraganglioma Can show nested architecture and vascularity; ASPS is negative for neuroendocrine markers and shows TFE3/fusion. Metastatic renal cell carcinoma Clear/eosinophilic nested tumor with vessels; correlate with clinical history and renal markers, and use ASPSCR1::TFE3 testing. Both can express TFE3; PEComa usually expresses melanocytic markers and often smooth-muscle markers, whereas ASPS is typically negative for melanocytic markers. Low mitotic activity does not imply benign behavior. TFE3 IHC is a useful surrogate but is not by itself fully specific; correlate with molecular testing and exclusion of mimics. Do not confuse ASPS with granular cell tumor or paraganglioma in pediatric head/neck lesions. Distant metastasis at diagnosis, older age, size >10 cm, and truncal location are adverse factors. Metastases may occur late; conventional chemotherapy has limited activity. Targeted and immune therapies have changed treatment options. Molecularly defined malignant epithelioid tumors Malignant; frequent recurrence/progression and metastasis Often mesothelial-lined cavities, especially abdominal/peritoneal; also other sites. Essential: monomorphic epithelioid/round-cell neoplasm with keratin expression and FET-CREB family fusion, after excluding other established entities with the same fusion family. Fusion alone is not specific; clinicopathologic correlation is mandatory. Solid sheets, cords, or nests of medium-sized epithelioid/round cells with eosinophilic-to-clear cytoplasm; some small-round-cell or focal spindle-cell areas. Hyaline sclerosis may separate organoid nests/cords. Abdominal lesions may be encapsulated; other sites may be infiltrative. Lymphoplasmacytic cuffing is common; cystic change frequent, hemorrhage usually absent. Focal necrosis may occur; mitotic activity often low (<4/2 mm²). Broad-spectrum keratin and EMA are commonly positive; peritoneal cases may express WT1 (C-terminal) and occasionally HEG1. Calretinin is almost always negative and BAP1 is retained; S100, SOX10, HMB45, and Melan-A are consistently negative. Desmin is usually negative. Variable ALK, CD99, CD34, synaptophysin, inhibin, and MUC4 can mislead. Fusions involve EWSR1 or FUS with CREB-family genes (CREM, ATF1, CREB1); EWSR1::CREM is most frequent in reported genetically confirmed cases. FET-CREB fusions also occur in AFH, clear cell sarcoma, and other tumors; the fusion is critical but not entity-specific. Epithelioid mesothelioma Can share keratin, WT1, and epithelioid morphology; FET-CREB fusion, retained BAP1, almost always negative calretinin, and lack of classic mesothelioma architecture/course support this tumor. AFH often has desmin/SOX9 and peripheral pseudocapsule/hemorrhagic spaces; FET-CREB epithelioid tumors are keratin-positive and usually desmin-negative. Clear cell sarcoma / MGNET These share FET-CREB fusions but express melanocytic markers (CCS) or arise in GI tract with neuroectodermal phenotype (MGNET); FET-CREB epithelioid tumors are consistently S100/SOX10/HMB45/Melan-A-negative. Sclerosing epithelioid fibrosarcoma MUC4 positivity may overlap; FET-CREB fusion and keratin profile help resolve. Some cases express synaptophysin; chromogranin is rare. Evaluate morphology and broad panel rather than one neuroendocrine marker. Do not equate any FET-CREB fusion with this entity; first exclude AFH, clear cell sarcoma, MGNET, and other established fusion-defined tumors. WT1 positivity alone does not establish mesothelioma. Retained BAP1 and negative calretinin are useful context, not standalone proof. Approximately three quarters recur or progress; about one third develop systemic metastasis or die of disease. Clear cell sarcoma of soft tissue Aggressive malignant tumor with late metastases Deep soft tissue of distal extremities, especially tendons/aponeuroses; may occur elsewhere. Essential: nested/fascicular architecture; plump spindle/ovoid cells with pale eosinophilic cytoplasm and prominent nucleoli; melanocytic marker expression (S100, SOX10, Melan-A, HMB45). Desirable: EWSR1::ATF1 or EWSR1::CREB1 fusion. Nested or fascicular growth partitioned by thin fibrous septa; often infiltrates dense fibrous tissue. Plump spindle/ovoid cells with pale eosinophilic/amphophilic cytoplasm, vesicular nuclei, and macronucleoli; true clear cytoplasm is uncommon despite the name. Melanin pigment is present in >50% but may be subtle; multinucleated wreath-like giant cells may occur. Mitotic activity can be low; necrosis in roughly one third. Consistent S100, SOX10, Melan-A, HMB45, and MITF expression. Diffuse PRAME staining is generally absent; interpret in context. EWSR1::ATF1 is most common; EWSR1::CREB1 is an alternative. EWSR1 rearrangement alone is less specific than identifying the fusion partner. Fusion drives MITF pathway activation and melanocytic differentiation. Metastatic melanoma CCS can be nearly indistinguishable immunohistochemically. Deep soft-tissue/tendon-associated primary, characteristic architecture, and EWSR1::ATF1/CREB1 fusion favor CCS; correlate with skin/mucosal history. Both may harbor EWSR1::ATF1/CREB1; AFH is usually desmin/SOX9-positive and lacks melanocytic markers, with pseudocapsule/lymphoplasmacytic cuff. Superficial neurocristic tumor Usually superficial and cytologically bland, with FET-ETS fusion; CCS is typically deep, infiltrative, and has prominent nucleoli. PEComa coexpresses melanocytic and smooth-muscle markers; CCS has melanocytic markers without the characteristic smooth-muscle phenotype. Despite the name, cells are usually not truly clear. Low mitotic activity does not indicate indolent behavior; late metastases are characteristic. EWSR1 break-apart positivity alone is not sufficient without partner and clinicopathologic context. Recurrence approaches 40%; pulmonary or nodal metastases occur in at least 30–50%, sometimes more than a decade after diagnosis. Large size, necrosis, incomplete excision, and nodal involvement are adverse features. Extraskeletal myxoid chondrosarcoma (EMC) Malignant; often prolonged course with late distant recurrence Deep soft tissue, usually proximal extremities and limb girdles. Essential: generally bland cells with eosinophilic cytoplasm arranged in strands/cords in predominantly myxoid stroma. Desirable: NR4A3 rearrangement in selected cases. Multinodular tumor with fibrous septa and hypocellular lobules containing abundant pale-blue myxoid/chondromyxoid matrix; strikingly hypovascular. Uniform round-to-oval cells form interconnected cords, clusters, trabeculae, or cribriform networks; delicate processes and modest eosinophilic/vacuolated cytoplasm. Well-formed hyaline cartilage is virtually never present. Rare hypercellular, high-grade, pseudopapillary, rhabdoid, or non-myxoid solid variants occur. S100 is positive in no more than 20%; KIT in up to 30%. INSM1/synaptophysin may be positive; pan-TRK can be positive in a subset. Keratin, GFAP, and muscle markers are usually negative. Rhabdoid examples may lose INI1. >90% harbor NR4A3 rearrangement, most often EWSR1::NR4A3, less commonly TAF15::NR4A3; rare alternative partners occur. NR4A3 rearrangement is a hallmark but has rarely been reported in a distinct subset of uterine leiomyosarcomas; interpret in site/context. May show cords in myxoid matrix; keratin/EMA and S100/SOX10/GFAP phenotype favors myoepithelial tumor, while NR4A3 fusion supports EMC. Low-grade fibromyxoid sarcoma LGFMS has alternating fibrous/myxoid zones and MUC4; EMC has multinodular hypovascular myxoid lobules and NR4A3 rearrangement. Chordoma Chordoma expresses brachyury and keratins and is axial; EMC lacks well-formed cartilage and is usually soft-tissue based. Undifferentiated round-cell sarcoma Solid high-grade EMC may mimic round-cell sarcoma; NR4A3 rearrangement is decisive in the correct context. The name is misleading: true cartilage is generally absent. S100 negativity does not exclude EMC; most cases are S100-negative. Pan-TRK, KIT, or neuroendocrine marker positivity can occur and should not redirect diagnosis without molecular context. Older age, large size (>100 mm), metastasis at presentation, and proximal location are adverse factors. Distant recurrence can occur late; variant non-EWSR1 fusions may be associated with more aggressive morphology/behavior. Desmoplastic small round cell tumor (DSRCT) Highly aggressive malignant tumor Usually peritoneal/abdominal cavity in young males; can occur at extra-abdominal sites. Essential: nests of predominantly small round cells in variable desmoplastic stroma with keratin and desmin immunopositivity. Desirable: EWSR1 rearrangement or EWSR1::WT1 fusion. Sharply defined nests and trabeculae of small round cells in prominent desmoplastic collagenous stroma; central necrosis common. Cells have scant cytoplasm, hyperchromatic nuclei, dispersed chromatin, and inconspicuous nucleoli; mitoses frequent. Rhabdoid inclusions, rosettes, or tubular structures may occur. Desmoplasia may be less conspicuous when tumor trabeculae become confluent. Polyphenotypic profile: keratin, EMA, and desmin (often dot-like) positivity. Nuclear WT1 with C-terminal antibody is usually positive; N-terminal antibody is not. Myogenin and MYOD1 are consistently negative. Some cases express neuroendocrine markers, but INSM1 is not typically positive. Characteristic t(11;22)(p13;q12) produces EWSR1::WT1 fusion; detection is useful for confirmation. Tumors are otherwise genomically relatively quiet; secondary alterations are uncommon. Both are small round-cell tumors; DSRCT has desmoplasia, keratin/desmin coexpression, C-terminal WT1, and EWSR1::WT1 rather than EWSR1::FLI1/ERG. Desmin positivity overlaps, but DSRCT is keratin-positive and myogenin/MYOD1-negative. Neuroendocrine carcinoma Nested architecture and occasional neuroendocrine marker expression overlap; keratin/desmin polyphenotype and WT1 C-terminal staining support DSRCT. Wilms tumor / other WT1-positive tumors Use anatomic context, morphology, antibody epitope, and EWSR1::WT1 fusion. Desmin is often dot-like; do not misinterpret as specific skeletal-muscle differentiation. Use WT1 antibody directed to the C-terminus; N-terminal antibody may be negative. EWSR1 break-apart alone is not fully specific; identify the WT1 partner when possible. Overall survival remains poor despite multimodality therapy; reported 5-year survival is approximately 10–23%. Absence of liver or extra-abdominal disease may be associated with better outcome. Extrarenal rhabdoid tumor (ERT) Extrarenal soft tissue and organs, predominantly infants and young children. Essential: infant/young child, rhabdoid cell morphology, and loss of SMARCB1/INI1 expression. Infiltrative hypercellular mass of sheets or solid trabeculae of rhabdoid cells with large vesicular round/bean-shaped nuclei, prominent nucleoli, and abundant cytoplasm. Juxtanuclear eosinophilic PAS-positive, diastase-resistant hyaline inclusions/globules are characteristic. Mitoses and necrosis are prominent. Some tumors are predominantly small round-cell with only scattered rhabdoid cells. Loss of nuclear INI1/SMARCB1 is characteristic; confirm intact internal positive controls. Keratin and EMA are common (often dot-like); synaptophysin, SALL4, and glypican-3 may be positive. CD34 is typically negative. Desmin is unusual; if positive, myogenin/MYOD1 should be checked and are negative in ERT. Most show biallelic SMARCB1 inactivation, including mutation, deletion, or copy-neutral LOH; rare cases have SMARCA4 alteration with retained INI1. Germline SMARCB1/SMARCA4 alterations may indicate rhabdoid tumor predisposition syndrome and warrant genetic evaluation. Both may lose INI1 and express keratin/EMA. Epithelioid sarcoma more often has nodular/pseudogranulomatous architecture and occurs in distal/proximal characteristic sites; ERT is typically in very young children with diffuse rhabdoid morphology. DSRCT Both may express keratin and desmin; DSRCT has desmoplastic nests, dot-like desmin, C-terminal WT1, and EWSR1::WT1. ERT lacks myogenin/MYOD1; these markers support skeletal muscle differentiation. Carcinoma / neuroendocrine tumor ERT may express epithelial and neural markers; age, rhabdoid morphology, and INI1 loss are key. INI1 loss alone does not distinguish ERT from epithelioid sarcoma and other SWI/SNF-deficient tumors. Retained INI1 does not exclude every rhabdoid tumor; consider SMARCA4 in rare cases. Desmin positivity should trigger myogenin/MYOD1 testing, not automatic classification as rhabdomyosarcoma. Outcome is poor across sites; median survival is approximately one year and 5-year survival is <15% in reported series. Variable; malignant PEComa defined by adverse morphologic features Abdominal cavity, pelvis, retroperitoneum, uterus, and GI tract; broad distribution. Essential: epithelioid and/or spindle cells with granular eosinophilic-to-clear cytoplasm, nested/trabecular/sheet-like architecture with perivascular orientation, and variable melanocytic plus smooth-muscle marker expression. Desirable: TFE3 expression/rearrangement when smooth-muscle markers are negative. Nested epithelioid cells with abundant granular eosinophilic or clear cytoplasm and round nuclei; thin-walled capillaries surround nests. Perivascular radial growth is characteristic; sclerosing variant shows cords/trabeculae in dense collagen. A classic triphasic angiomyolipoma pattern may occur but is uncommon outside kidney/liver. Malignant tumors show variable mitoses, necrosis, atypia, and pleomorphism. Melanocytic markers: HMB45 (most sensitive), Melan-A, cathepsin K. Smooth-muscle markers: SMA, desmin, h-caldesmon; SMA is often more extensive. S100 nuclear staining is generally absent. Some tumors lack smooth-muscle markers. Strong nuclear TFE3 in approximately 15–20%; TFE3-rearranged tumors often have epithelioid/alveolar morphology and may lack muscle markers. Most harbor TSC2 variants/16p loss; a small subset has TFE3 fusions (commonly SFPQ, ASPSCR1, or NONO). TFE3-rearranged PEComas generally lack TSC2 alterations and are pathogenetically distinct. A subset is associated with tuberous sclerosis. Both express melanocytic markers; CCS is typically S100/SOX10-positive and lacks smooth-muscle phenotype, with EWSR1::ATF1/CREB1 fusion. Alveolar soft part sarcoma Both can show TFE3; ASPS is typically negative for melanocytic markers and smooth-muscle markers, and has ASPSCR1::TFE3. Melanoma has melanocytic phenotype but lacks characteristic perivascular growth and smooth-muscle coexpression; correlate with clinical primary. Leiomyosarcoma Smooth-muscle markers overlap, but melanocytic marker expression and perivascular epithelioid morphology support PEComa. TFE3-rearranged renal cell carcinoma Can share TFE3 and clear/eosinophilic cells; correlate with renal origin, epithelial markers, and molecular context. HMB45 is sensitive but not entirely specific; use the combined melanocytic/smooth-muscle phenotype and morphology. TFE3-rearranged PEComas may lack smooth-muscle markers; consider TFE3 testing in the appropriate phenotype. Do not rely on the historic terms “sugar tumor of lung” or “clear cell myomelanocytic tumor.” Large size (>5 cm), infiltrative margins, marked atypia/pleomorphism, conspicuous mitoses, and necrosis are associated with aggressive behavior. Common metastatic sites include liver, lymph nodes, lungs, and bone. Intimal sarcoma Large-caliber pulmonary arteries, aorta, and cardiac chambers (often left atrium). Essential: intraluminal growth within a large-caliber blood vessel or cardiac chamber and spindle-cell/variably pleomorphic morphology. Desirable: MDM2 and/or CDK4 amplification in selected cases; amplification is helpful but not specific. Intraluminal mass may resemble thrombus or thromboembolus; can extend along vessel or cardiac chamber. Mildly to severely atypical spindle cells with variable mitoses, necrosis, and nuclear polymorphism; myxoid or epithelioid areas may occur. May show cartilage, osteoid, or focal rhabdomyosarcomatous differentiation. SMA is variable; desmin may be positive; myogenin/MYOD1 mark rhabdomyoblastic areas. MDM2 nuclear expression in at least 70%; CDK4 may be positive. SMA variable, desmin in a subset; myogenin/MYOD1 only with rhabdomyosarcomatous differentiation. MDM2 amplification is frequent, often with CDK4 and PDGFRA coamplification; MDM2/CDK4 amplification is supportive but not specific. Some cases show amplification/high polysomy of receptor tyrosine kinase genes (PDGFRA, KIT, PDGFRB, EGFR). Molecular subsets include copy-number-high and rare MSI-high-like tumors. Thrombus / organized thromboembolus Intimal sarcoma is a true intraluminal neoplasm with atypical spindle/pleomorphic cells; imaging may show heterogeneous intravascular material and FDG uptake. Undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma of heart Can share MDM2 amplification/methylation profile; anatomic intraluminal origin in large vessel/cardiac chamber supports intimal sarcoma. Fascicular spindle morphology and SMA/desmin may overlap; MDM2 amplification and intraluminal origin favor intimal sarcoma. Dedifferentiated liposarcoma MDM2 amplification overlaps; exclude a primary retroperitoneal/soft-tissue DDLPS and use the intraluminal vascular/cardiac origin. Metastatic sarcoma Assess primary site and true vascular intimal origin; MDM2 amplification alone is not diagnostic. MDM2 or CDK4 amplification is not specific; do not diagnose intimal sarcoma without the characteristic intraluminal site and growth. Aortic lesions may mimic atherosclerosis with adherent thrombus or aneurysmal change. Pulmonary artery intimal sarcoma may be misdiagnosed as recurrent pulmonary embolism. Poor prognosis; mean survival reported at 5–9 months for aortic and 13–18 months for pulmonary/cardiac tumors. Multimodal therapy is often used; no established standard of care. Anthracycline-based therapy has some activity. All PathologyGPS / Soft Tissue Tumors / Tumors of Uncertain Differentiation Tumors of Uncertain Differentiation A morphology-first diagnostic reference emphasizing essential criteria, lineage assessment, defining molecular alterations, and practical differential diagnosis across benign, intermediate, and malignant entities. Core diagnostic rule Start with architecture and cytology; use immunophenotype to test lineage, then use molecular findings to establish the entity. Many defining fusions overlap across entities. A rearrangement is not a diagnosis without the correct site, morphology, and immunophenotype. Diagnostic GPS: morphology to molecular classification 1. Establish the setting Record anatomic compartment, depth, relationship to tendon/joint/nerve/vessel/viscera, age, multiplicity, and relevant systemic syndrome. 2. Classify the pattern Myxoid/hypocellular; epithelioid/nested; spindle/fascicular; round-cell; perivascular; adipocytic/hemosiderotic; or intraluminal. 3. Test lineage Use a focused panel: keratins/EMA, S100/SOX10, melanocytic markers, myogenic markers, endothelial markers, INI1, and selected transcription factors. 4. Select molecular test Choose the alteration that resolves the differential: GNAS, OGT, THBS1::ADGRF5, EWSR1/FUS partners, PHF1, NR4A3, SS18::SSX, SMARCB1, TFE3, or MDM2/CDK4. 5. Assign behavior Do not equate atypia, mitoses, recurrence, or a fusion with grade in isolation. Apply entity-specific criteria and document limitations. High-yield diagnostic principles A bland myxoid tumor is not automatically benign: evaluate site, vascular pattern, cellularity, atypia, mitoses, and defining molecular findings. For epithelioid tumors, distinguish true lineage (melanocytic, myoepithelial, smooth muscle, epithelial) from nonspecific marker expression. Fusion testing must identify the partner whenever the same gene family is shared by multiple entities (e.g., EWSR1/FUS–CREB family). INI1 loss occurs in more than one tumor type; age, site, architecture, and phenotype separate epithelioid sarcoma from extrarenal rhabdoid tumor. MDM2 amplification is supportive in intimal sarcoma but is not specific; the intraluminal large-vessel/cardiac origin is essential. Molecular-first triage: practical targets Diagnostic pattern High-value molecular target Key caveat Intramuscular/cellular myxoma GNAS Useful in selected cases; interpret morphology. Acral epithelioid / hyalinized tumor OGT fusion Some intrachromosomal events may evade break-apart FISH. Acral chondromyxoid tumor THBS1::ADGRF5 Supports a typical morphology; usually not required. AFH-like tumor EWSR1::CREB1 / EWSR1::ATF1 / FUS::ATF1 Fusion overlap with CCS and other FET-CREB tumors. OFMT-like tumor PHF1 rearrangement Supports diagnosis; not all cases harbor PHF1 fusion. Myxoid corded tumor NR4A3 rearrangement Rarely occurs in another tumor context. Spindle tumor with neural/myoid markers Kinase fusion panel NTRK/RET/RAF1/ALK/FGFR1/EGFR/BRAF alterations. Round-cell/desmoplastic tumor EWSR1::WT1 EWSR1 break-apart alone is less specific. Melanocytic soft-tissue tumor EWSR1::ATF1 / CREB1 Separate CCS from AFH and FET-CREB epithelioid tumor. Intraluminal cardiac/vascular sarcoma MDM2/CDK4 amplification Supportive but not specific. Critical differential diagnosis: pattern-based checkpoints Diagnostic problem Most useful discriminator Next step Bland but infiltrative myxoid lesion Intramuscular myxoma: hypocellular, hypovascular, bland; deep angiomyxoma: pelvic, infiltrative, thick-walled vessels; juxta-articular myxoma: periarticular cystic/fibrin change. Use site and vessel pattern first; GNAS only for selected intramuscular/cellular myxoma cases. Acral myxoid/chondroid lesion AFCMT: multinodular fibrovascular septa and bland cells; OGT-rearranged neoplasm: epithelioid cords/nests in hyalinized/fibromyxoid stroma. THBS1::ADGRF5 for AFCMT when needed; OGT fusion required for OGT-rearranged neoplasm. EWSR1/FUS-rearranged epithelioid tumor AFH, CCS, and FET-CREB epithelioid mesenchymal tumor can share fusion family members but differ in lineage markers and architecture. Identify exact fusion partner and integrate desmin/SOX9, melanocytic markers, keratin, site, and pseudocapsule/lymphoid cuff. INI1-deficient epithelioid/rhabdoid tumor Epithelioid sarcoma versus extrarenal rhabdoid tumor; age, site, pseudogranulomatous architecture, and rhabdoid morphology matter. INI1 with internal control; keratin/EMA, myogenin/MYOD1, WT1, and clinical context. TFE3-positive epithelioid tumor ASPS, TFE3-rearranged PEComa, and renal cell carcinoma may overlap. Use melanocytic and smooth-muscle markers, epithelial markers, site, and fusion partner. Spindle cell tumor with CD34/S100 Kinase-altered spindle-cell neoplasm is a molecularly heterogeneous group. Use RNA-based fusion panel; do not rely on pan-TRK or CD34/S100 alone. Intraluminal large-vessel mass Intimal sarcoma versus thrombus or metastatic tumor. Demonstrate malignant spindle-cell neoplasm and assess MDM2/CDK4 amplification; amplification alone is not specific. Molecular testing and reporting checklist State the exact anatomic site, depth, relationship to a named structure, and clinical setting; for myxoid lesions, note periarticular versus intramuscular versus pelviperineal location. Describe architecture, cellularity, cytologic atypia, mitotic activity, necrosis, vascular pattern, matrix type, and any distinctive inclusions or pigment. Report the complete immunophenotype, including internal controls for INI1/SMARCB1 and any other loss-based marker. For fusion-driven tumors, identify the fusion partner whenever possible; a generic EWSR1/FUS rearrangement may not be sufficiently specific. For kinase-altered spindle-cell neoplasms, favor RNA-based fusion testing when available; document the actual kinase alteration. For intimal sarcoma, document intraluminal origin and report MDM2/CDK4 results with the caveat that amplification is supportive, not specific. Separate diagnostic certainty from biologic behavior; apply the entity-specific criteria rather than relying on atypia or molecular results alone. title: Vascular Tumors
content: use client Synovial vascular anomalies Site: Knee most common; also elbow, wrist, and ankle. Age/sex: Predominantly children and adolescents; no significant sex predilection. Presentation: Joint swelling, effusion, persistent pain, restricted movement, and sometimes recurrent hemarthrosis. benign vascular anomalies arising in synovium-lined spaces morphologically within the spectrum of venous or arteriovenous malformation. The lesions display variable histological features depending on the subtype. Venous malformations are composed of spongiform, variably sized, dysmorphic venous channels, often associated with thrombosis and phleboliths. Arteriovenous malformations are infiltrative lesions comprising small, medium, and large arteries with loss of the internal elastic lamina, and veins of similar caliber exhibiting thickened walls and intimal hyperplasia. A diffuse or lobular proliferation of small vessels with plump endothelial cells and pericytes may also be observed. Villous hyperplasia of the synovium is present in some cases, particularly in chronic lesions with recurrent hemarthrosis, and may show prominent iron deposition. Venous malformation Spongiform dysmorphic venous channels; no arterial component. Arteriovenous malformation Abnormal arteries and thick-walled veins with arteriovenous shunting. Malformation Vascular malformation Intramuscular vascular anomalies Site: Lower extremities, especially thigh and calf; also head and neck, upper limbs, and trunk. Age/sex: Up to 90% of reported cases occur in older children, adolescents, and young adults; sexes are equally affected. Presentation: Slowly growing, often painful intramuscular mass; pain may worsen after exercise. For VM: spongiform clusters of dysmorphic venous channels For FAVA: prominent fibroadipose tissue, nodules of back-to-back venous channels, and variably thick-walled veins For IFVA: nodular aggregates of small vascular channels along with variably thick-walled veins For AVM: a combination of abnormal arteries with disruption of internal elastic lamina, large thick veins, and indeterminate vessels For PHOST: abundant fibromyxoid and adipose tissue and aggregates of abnormal vessels including arteries, veins, and indeterminate vessels VMs form a spongiform network of irregularly shaped venous channels of varying calibers and have sharply demarcated borders with minimal to no interposed skeletal muscle or fibrofatty tissue (see section Venous malformations). FAVA lesions demonstrate extensive fibrofatty stroma containing nodular clusters of thin-walled venous channels, often budding from larger dysmorphic veins. Peripheral nerves may be surrounded by fibrous tissue and infiltrated by abnormal veins. Lymphoid aggregates are frequent, and occasional foci of metaplastic bone, dysmorphic lymphatic channels, and indeterminate vascular clusters with coiled lumina and concentric muscular layers may be present. IFVA consists of capillary-like vascular channels arranged in lobules or cords associated with large veins and arteries with thick walls and indeterminate vessels. Veins are enlarged, many having irregularly thickened walls. Arteries may show enlargement with loss of internal elastic lamina, intimal cushions, and medial muscular hyperplasia. Venous malformation: Somatic TEK (about 60%) or PIK3CA (about 20%). FAVA: Usually somatic PIK3CA. IFVA and AVM: MAP2K1 or KRAS variants. CM-AVM: RASA1 or EPHB4 variants. PHOST: Germline PTEN; PIK3CA-associated mimics are termed soft-tissue angiomatosis. Spongiform venous channels with sharply demarcated borders and little intervening fibrofatty tissue. Fibroadipose vascular anomaly (FAVA) Prominent fibroadipose stroma with clustered venous channels and possible nerve involvement. Abnormal arteries, veins, and indeterminate vessels; fast-flow shunt. Site: Head and neck most common in extracranial disease; also extremities, trunk, and viscera. Parkes Weber syndrome usually affects a lower extremity. Age/sex: Congenital; often recognized in childhood or early adulthood; no sex predilection. Presentation: Warm, erythematous superficial lesion; pain, ulceration, or bleeding may develop. Deep lesions may present later. vessels of different sizes and types, including both arteries and veins with high-pressure arterial flow features; clinical and radiological evidence of an arteriovenous shunt within a poorly defined vascular lesion. AVMs exhibit variable morphology. The nidus is composed of disproportionately enlarged arteries and veins, along with vessels of indeterminate morphological features. Arteries exhibit tortuosity, irregular calibers, focal fragmentation or duplication of the internal elastic lamina, and focal neointimal hyperplasia. Veins demonstrate intimal hyperplasia, thickened smooth muscle coats, and adventitial fibrosis – changes driven by high-pressure arterial flow. A generalized increase in small vessels resembling small arteries, capillaries, or veins is commonly observed. Many AVMs contain lobular foci of small-caliber vessels, predominantly of capillary type, which may mimic other vascular lesions such as pyogenic granuloma, infantile or congenital hemangioma, or the pseudokaposiform proliferation seen in Stewart–Bluefarb syndrome. The intervascular stroma is variably cellular and shows edema, fibrosis, hemosiderin deposition, and occasional fat entrapment. Sporadic AVM: Somatic MAP2K1; less often KRAS, HRAS, or BRAF. CM-AVM1: Germline RASA1. CM-AVM2: Germline EPHB4. PTEN hamartoma tumor syndrome: Germline PTEN. HHT-associated disease: ENG, ACVRL1, GDF2, or SMAD4 in the relevant syndromic settings. Venous channels only; lacks dysplastic arteries and high-flow shunting. Tufted angioma / kaposiform hemangioendothelioma Lobular capillary tufts and platelet-rich microthrombi rather than an arterial-venous nidus. Venous malformations Site: Skin, mucosa, and subcutis; may extend into muscle, bone, and viscera. Head and neck are common; BRBNS favors palms, soles, and trunk; VVM favors lower extremities. Age/sex: Often present at birth or arise early in life; both sexes are affected. Presentation: Soft, compressible blue-purple lesions; thrombosis may cause swelling and pain. VVM may become hyperkeratotic. For CVM and BRBNs: dysmorphic venous channels For VVM: capillary or venular-type channels with focal or diffuse endothelial immunopositivity for GLUT1 and focal immunopositivity for D2-40 or PROX1 VMs are characterized by haphazardly arranged large, ectatic, irregular, variably sized venous channels in the dermis, subcutis, and deep soft tissues. The vessels are lined by a single layer of flat endothelial cells and display a concentric smooth muscle wall, often discontinuous or thin relative to the luminal diameter. In some areas, the vessel walls show irregular strands or nodules of smooth muscle merging with fibromyxoid stroma, probably representing the sequelae of organized thrombi. Lumina are variably empty or congested, and organizing thrombi, which may evolve into calcified phleboliths, may be seen. Papillary endothelial hyperplasia (Masson phenomenon) is commonly observed. However, lymphatic marker expression has been reported in VMs associated with BRBNs. VMs in BRBNS typically show closely apposed, small, abnormal, and often spongiform veins and organizing thrombi. CD31: Diffuse endothelial positivity. CD34: Variable expression. D2-40 and PROX1: Usually negative; expression may occur in BRBNS-associated lesions. WT1: Negative. Ki-67: Extremely low. Verrucous venous malformation: GLUT1 often focal or diffuse; D2-40 and PROX1 may be focally positive. Common venous malformation: Somatic TEK (about 60%) or PIK3CA (about 20%). Familial multifocal cutaneous/mucosal lesions: Germline TEK with a second somatic event. Blue rubber bleb nevus syndrome: Dual cis-acting TEK variants. Verrucous venous malformation: Somatic MAP3K3. Lymphatic malformation Lymphatic endothelial markers (D2-40/PROX1) support lymphatic differentiation; venous lesions are usually negative. Verrucous venous malformation Dermal/subcutaneous capillary-venular channels with GLUT1 and focal lymphatic-marker expression. Spindle cell hemangioma Site: Dermis or subcutis, especially distal extremities and hands; oral cavity also reported. About half are intravascular. Age/sex: Wide age range (8–78 years; median 32); no sex predilection. Presentation: Slowly developing, usually asymptomatic blue nodule, typically 1–2 cm. cavernous vascular spaces admixed with more solid spindle cell areas; vacuolated endothelial cells; minimal nuclear atypia; and mitotic activity. The tumors are often well-circumscribed, mostly involving the dermis or subcutis. Around half of the tumors are intravascular. They consist of two components: irregular, dilated, thin-walled, congested, cavernous-like vascular channels admixed with more solid areas of spindle cells. The cavernous spaces are lined by bland and flat endothelial cells and may contain thrombi, with or without dystrophic calcification (phleboliths). The solid spindle cell areas contain bland spindle-shaped cells with pericytic and fibroblastic features, and may contain slit-like vascular spaces as well as vacuolated epithelioid endothelial cells (blister cells) that may resemble adipocytes. Spindle cells are also seen in the cavernous vessel septations. Mitotic activity and nuclear atypia are minimal. Endothelial cells: Positive for endothelial markers. Spindle cells: May show focal SMA and/or desmin expression. IDH1 p.Arg132Cys (R132C) in most cases; less often IDH2 p.Arg172. Kaposi sarcoma Kaposi sarcoma shows slit-like vascular spaces and HHV8 positivity; spindle cell hemangioma has cavernous spaces and vacuolated endothelial cells. Kaposiform hemangioendothelioma KHE is infiltrative and associated with platelet-rich thrombi; spindle cell hemangioma is benign and circumscribed. Benign Benign vascular tumor Hemangioma of bone Site: Vertebral bodies most common, followed by calvarium and long bones; multifocal lesions occur. Age/sex: Any age (mean 32 years); slight female predominance. Presentation: Usually incidental and asymptomatic; large vertebral lesions may cause pain, cord compression, or neurologic symptoms. bone tumor with compatible imaging; thin-walled blood vessels lined by a single layer of non-atypical endothelial cells. hemangiomas have variable histological features and comprise different morphologies such as cavernous (gaping vascular spaces), capillary (lobulated small vessels), mixed, venous, and arteriovenous patterns. In general, the vascular spaces are lined by a single layer of flat and cytologically bland endothelial cells. Secondary changes include reactive sclerosis of involved bone, new bone formation, calcification, and thrombosis. EWSR1::NFATC1/2 fusion is present in a small subset of histologically typical hemangiomas of bone , as well as in other osseous vascular tumors displaying epithelioid morphology and nuclear atypia. Endothelial cells: CD31, ERG, FLI1, and CD34 positive. Pericytes: SMA highlights the preserved pericytic network. A small subset harbors EWSR1::NFATC1 or EWSR1::NFATC2 fusions. Epithelioid hemangioma of bone Epithelioid endothelial cells and lobular growth distinguish epithelioid hemangioma from bland conventional vascular channels. Angiosarcoma Cytologic atypia and destructive malignant growth are absent in conventional bone hemangioma. Anastomosing hemangioma Site: Most often kidney; also genitourinary tract, paraspinal region, and other soft tissue/visceral sites. Age/sex: Typically adults; male predominance is reported. Presentation: Often incidental or presents as a localized mass; clinical symptoms depend on site. anastomosing vessels lined by hobnail endothelial cells, often in association with fibrin thrombi, hyaline globules, and extramedullary hematopoiesis. These lesions have a loosely lobulated architecture at low magnification and can be associated with a medium-caliber vessel. There is often focal infiltration into adjoining tissue. The neoplasms consist of anastomosing sinusoidal capillary-sized vessels with scattered hobnail endothelial cells. There may be a lymphocytic infiltrate. Mitoses are absent or rare. Mild cytological atypia can be present, but no multilayering of endothelial cells is seen. Vascular thrombi are typical, and zones of central sclerosis with focal necrosis are common. Endothelial cells: CD34, CD31, and ERG positive. Anastomosing hemangioma has bland hobnail endothelial cells without multilayering or significant atypia. Kaposi sarcoma has spindle-cell proliferation and HHV8 association. Epithelioid hemangioma Site: Bone most common; also skin and soft tissue, especially head and neck, distal extremities, and trunk. Multifocal lesions may be regionally clustered. Age/sex: Wide age range; peak in the fourth decade. No overall sex predilection; bone lesions show slight male predominance. Presentation: Erythematous-violaceous papules or angiomatoid nodules; deep lesions cause localized pain. well-formed vessels with a lobular architecture, lined by epithelioid endothelial cells; variable eosinophilic infiltrate. Conventional EH is typically well demarcated and has a distinctive lobular architecture at low power. The centers of the lobules are the most cellular with solid growth, while an increased maturation of the vascular lumina may be seen at the periphery, surrounded by an intact pericytic layer. The tumor vessels are lined by a single layer of large and polyhedral epithelioid endothelial cells, with occasional nuclear hobnailing and protrusion into the lumen, resembling a tombstone. The lesional cells have oval or kidney-shaped nuclei with vesicular or fine chromatin, which tend to be hyperlobated or cleaved, and abundant, deeply eosinophilic cytoplasm, with variable intracytoplasmic vacuoles (blister cells). Cytological atypia is often mild, and mitotic activity is generally low. Marked lymphoplasmacytic infiltrates, prominent lymphoid follicles, and abundant eosinophils are not uncommon, particularly in head and neck lesions. A subset of EH may display intravascular growth, with centrifugal extension into adjacent soft tissues. Endothelial cells: CD31, FLI1, and ERG consistently positive. CD34: Variable and often diminished. Cytokeratins and EMA: Positive in a subset. SMA: Highlights the pericytic layer. FOS and FOSB: Useful ancillary nuclear markers; interpret cautiously because expression is not entirely specific. Decalcification may reduce FOS expression. FOS rearrangements: Partners include LMNA, MBNL1, and VIM. FOSB rearrangements: Most often ZFP36; rarely WWTR1 or ACTB. GATA6::FOXO1: Subset with head-and-neck cutaneous predilection. TPM3::ALK or TPM4::ALK: Reported in cutaneous hemangioma with epithelioid features. Epithelioid hemangioendothelioma Epithelioid hemangioma shows lobular vascular proliferation with well-formed vessels; EHE shows cords/nests of epithelioid cells in myxohyaline stroma. Epithelioid hemangioma lacks destructive infiltrative growth and marked endothelial atypia. Site: Head and neck are common; also axilla, trunk, extremities, and viscera. Generalized lymphatic anomaly and kaposiform lymphangiomatosis may be multisystemic. Age/sex: Usually congenital or recognized in childhood; no consistent sex predilection stated. Presentation: Soft, often transilluminant or cystic swelling; may enlarge, bleed, or become infected. malformed and usually excessive lymphatic channels; kaposiform clusters of lymphatic endothelial cells in KLA; compatible clinical and imaging features. Macrocystic LM consists of one or more dilated, relatively well-circumscribed cystic spaces, whereas microcystic LM consists of small, anastomosing lymphatic vessels with an infiltrative growth pattern. Many cases show mixed macrocystic and microcystic morphology. The cystic spaces typically contain proteinaceous fluid, sometimes with lymphocytes and histiocytes. In cases with intralesional hemorrhage, vessels are filled with blood, and abundant interstitial hemosiderin is often present. Reactive lymphoid tissue is frequently observed between vessels and may form follicles. Intravascular papillary projections resembling valves may be seen. The endothelium is flat or mildly swollen, but lacks atypia. D2-40, PROX1, and VEGFR3: Useful lymphatic markers, particularly in macrocystic lesions. Large lymphatic channels: D2-40 and LYVE1 may be negative or only focally positive; PROX1 and VEGFR3 are usually positive. ERG and CD31: Positive. CD34: Negative or only focally positive. Somatic PIK3CA variants are common; NRAS variants occur in selected cases. Venous channels have smooth-muscle walls; lymphatic spaces are irregular and lymphatic-marker positive. Kaposiform lymphangiomatosis KLA shows kaposiform clusters of lymphatic endothelial cells and may be associated with coagulopathy. Tufted angioma and kaposiform hemangioendothelioma Site: Usually skin and subcutis of the trunk or extremities; deeper soft tissue and retroperitoneal sites can occur. Age/sex: Predominantly infants and young children; most present in infancy. Presentation: Infiltrative violaceous plaque or mass; KHE may be associated with Kasabach–Merritt phenomenon. cannonball-like distribution of multiple small and variably well-defined intradermal lobules of tightly packed small capillaries; dual positivity of spindled endothelial cells for panendothelial and lymphatic markers; presence of platelet-rich microthrombi. Classic TA histology shows multiple small, well-circumscribed vascular tufts dispersed in a cannonball-like fashion within the dermis, sometimes extending into the subcutis. The tufts are composed of closely packed capillaries with compressed lumina, occasionally accompanied by subtle fascicles of delicate spindled endothelial cells. Dilated thin-walled lymphatic vessels focally form crescentic clefts at the tuft periphery. Classic KHE histology includes the presence of vascular tufts equivalent to those of TA, but accompanied by larger, less defined, coalescing nodules composed of fascicles of spindled endothelial cells forming elongate slit-like lumina containing erythrocytes and curving around epithelioid, pericyte-rich nodules with central microthrombi. Other areas display more typical capillary formation. Dilated lymphatic vessels reminiscent of lymphatic malformation are frequently seen within adjacent desmoplastic stroma. Mitoses are rare. CD31, CD34, and ERG: Strongly positive. Podoplanin (D2-40), LYVE1, and PROX1: Positive in spindled endothelial cells; less extensive in superficial tufted angioma. GLUT1: Negative. WT1: Positive. Lobular capillary hemangioma TA/KHE show lymphatic-marker expression and platelet-rich microthrombi; lobular capillary hemangioma lacks this combination. VM has ectatic venous channels rather than capillary tufts and spindle endothelial proliferation. Intermediate Intermediate / rarely metastasizing Retiform hemangioendothelioma Site: Predominantly dermis and subcutis of distal extremities; trunk and other sites less common. Age/sex: Broad age range, often young to middle-aged adults; no consistent sex predilection. Presentation: Slowly growing, usually painless red-purple plaque or nodule. arborizing branching vascular channels; hyperchromatic endothelial cells with hobnail morphology and no or very low mitotic activity. Scanning magnification reveals characteristic elongated and narrow arborizing vascular channels with a striking resemblance to normal rete testis. Although this pattern is usually readily apparent, if the vascular channels are small or collapsed, the retiform architecture may be less discernible. Monomorphic endothelial cells with prominent protuberant nuclei having a characteristic tombstone or hobnail appearance line the blood vessels. These cells have scant cytoplasm, which seems to blend with the underlying stroma. Pleomorphism is absent and mitotic figures are rare. A prominent sclerotic stroma is noted. Intravascular lymphocytic infiltrates are present in about half of the cases. CD31, CD34, and ERG: Positive; CD34 is often stronger. PROX1: Positive. D2-40 and VEGFR3: Usually negative, but exceptions occur. KSHV/HHV8: Negative. YAP1-rearranged tumors may show loss of the YAP1 C-terminal region. YAP1 rearrangement may support diagnosis in challenging cases. Papillary intralymphatic angioendothelioma PILA shows intraluminal papillary tufts with matchstick-like hobnail endothelial cells. Retiform HE is usually low-grade with retiform architecture and limited atypia; angiosarcoma shows destructive growth and greater atypia. Site: Dermis and subcutis, often of extremities. Age/sex: Broad age range; commonly reported in children and young adults. Presentation: Slow-growing, usually painless cutaneous or subcutaneous nodule. poorly defined lymphatic vessels with stromal and intraluminal lymphocytes and proteinaceous fluid; intralymphatic, intraluminal hobnail proliferation of polarized matchstick-like columnar endothelial cells; expression of panendothelial and lymphatic markers. PILA is a poorly delineated dermal and/or subcutaneous proliferation of lymphatic channels showing variable intraluminal papillary tuft proliferation, with hyaline cores and intermixed lymphocytes with proteinaceous fluid. A lymphatic vascular malformation is often present nearby. The cavernous or slit-like lymphatic vascular channels are lined by columnar, matchstick-like, or hobnail endothelial cells. The lesional cells have eosinophilic cytoplasm and round uniform nuclei with indistinct nucleoli; they lack cytological atypia and mitoses. CD31 and ERG: Positive; CD34 is less consistently positive. Podoplanin, VEGFR3, and PROX1: Lymphatic endothelial markers are positive. PILA has intraluminal papillary projections with hyaline cores and lymphocytes; retiform HE has elongated rete-testis-like channels. PILA lacks high-grade atypia and destructive malignant growth. Composite hemangioendothelioma Site: Usually distal extremities, particularly hands and feet; dermis and subcutis. Age/sex: Usually adults; no consistent sex predilection. Presentation: Slowly growing, painless or mildly symptomatic cutaneous/subcutaneous mass. at least two morphologically distinct vascular tumor elements, most often closely resembling RHE and EHE; demonstration of neuroendocrine marker expression in neuroendocrine CHE. CHE is a poorly circumscribed, infiltrative lesion that is typically centered in the dermis and subcutis, although occasional cases are deep-seated or involve viscera. It comprises a complex admixture of histologically benign and malignant vascular components that vary greatly in their relative proportions. Most often the tumors show mixed morphological features of RHE and epithelioid hemangioendothelioma (EHE), although the characteristic myxochondroid matrix of EHE is not seen. Less often, foci resembling spindle cell hemangioma, angiosarcoma, and benign vascular lesions (lymphangioma, angiomatosis, vascular malformation, and cavernous hemangioma) are present. Most cases contain 2–3 components. Vacuolated, pseudolipoblastic endothelial cells are frequently present. The angiosarcoma-like areas are usually characterized by a low-grade appearance, with complex dissecting vascular channels showing subtle endothelial atypia and relatively few mitotic figures. CD31, ERG, and FLI1: Consistently positive. CD34 and D2-40: Positive in approximately half of cases. CAMTA1: Negative. Neuroendocrine-differentiated cases: Synaptophysin and other neuroendocrine markers may be positive. YAP1::MAML2 occurs in composite hemangioendothelioma and retiform hemangioendothelioma. PTBP1::MAML2 has been reported in composite hemangioendothelioma with neuroendocrine differentiation. Composite HE contains multiple vascular patterns in one lesion, not a purely retiform pattern. Composite HE is generally low-grade/intermediate; angiosarcoma shows overt malignant endothelial atypia and destructive growth. Site: Skin most common; also oral mucosa, lymph nodes, and viscera. Distribution varies with clinical subtype and immune status. Age/sex: Strong male predominance in classic and endemic forms; age distribution varies by subtype. Presentation: Multifocal red-purple macules, plaques, or nodules; visceral disease may cause organ-specific symptoms. proliferation of small slit-like vessels lined by minimally to mildly atypical cells and surrounded by bland spindle cells; extravasated erythrocytes and patchy lymphoplasmacytic infiltrates in the early stage. All five clinical and epidemiological KS subtypes show identical histological features. Early skin lesions show subtle vascular proliferation. In the patch stage, vascular spaces are increased in number, dissecting collagen fibers in the upper reticular dermis. Lining endothelial cells are flattened or oval, with no or minimal atypia. Pre-existing vessels may protrude into lumina of new vessels. Ovoid/spindle endothelial cell proliferations surround pre-existing vessels, and admixed lymphoplasmacytic infiltrates, extravasated erythrocytes, and hemosiderin deposits are common. Rarely, lesions resemble lymphangioma or hemangioma, causing diagnostic confusion. CD31, CD34, and ERG: Positive in lining endothelial cells and spindle tumor cells. Podoplanin (D2-40): Positive. KSHV/HHV8: Almost invariably shows nuclear positivity; staining may be very focal. KSHV/HHV8 detection by PCR or in situ hybridization may be useful when immunohistochemistry is negative in rare cases. Kaposi sarcoma is HHV8-positive; spindle cell hemangioma is HHV8-negative and has cavernous vascular spaces. KHE is typically HHV8-negative and shows platelet-rich microthrombi. Pseudomyogenic hemangioendothelioma Site: Usually distal lower extremities; often involves multiple tissue planes and may be multifocal within one region. Bone may also be involved. Age/sex: Predominantly young adults; male predominance (approximately 3.5:1); mean age about 30 years. Presentation: Slowly growing, often painful or tender soft-tissue mass; multifocal lesions are common. plump spindle or (less commonly) epithelioid cells with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm and vesicular chromatin; fascicular or sheet-like growth pattern; expression of ERG and keratins (AE1/AE3). The tumor is composed of sheets and loose fascicles of plump spindle cells with abundant, brightly eosinophilic cytoplasm, sometimes mimicking rhabdomyoblasts. A minor component of cells with epithelioid cytomorphology is often present, but sometimes epithelioid cells predominate. Intraosseous lesions are often dominated by epithelioid cells with densely eosinophilic cytoplasm, associated with reactive woven bone, hemorrhage, and osteoclast-like giant cells. The tumor cells contain vesicular nuclei with generally small nucleoli. The degree of nuclear atypia is usually mild, and mitotic activity is scarce. About 10% of tumors show notable pleomorphism or large nucleoli. Occasional tumors may contain myxoid stroma. Cytokeratins (AE1/AE3): Diffuse; MNF116 is negative. ERG and FLI1: Positive. CD31: Positive in approximately half of cases. SMA: Focal positivity in about one third. CD34: Negative. INI1 (SMARCB1): Retained. FOSB: Consistent nuclear expression. FOSB rearrangement supports the diagnosis. Epithelioid sarcoma Pseudomyogenic HE expresses endothelial markers and may express keratin; epithelioid sarcoma typically shows loss of INI1. Pseudomyogenic HE has eosinophilic rhabdomyoblast-like cells and FOSB expression; EHE has characteristic fusion-defined epithelioid morphology. YAP1::TFE3 hemangioendothelioma Site: Superficial/deep soft tissue, bone, lung, and liver; virtually any site may be involved. Age/sex: Adults, 20–78 years (median 44); slight female predominance. Presentation: Solitary or multifocal mass; symptoms depend on the involved site. solid growth and/or well-formed vascular channels lined by epithelioid endothelial cells with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm. Desirable (in selected cases): TFE3 rearrangement; YAP1::TFE3 fusion; strong and diffuse immunohistochemical positivity for TFE3. It may also demonstrate cells in coalescing nests, clusters, and discohesive strands, as well as a pseudoalveolar growth pattern. These growth patterns may be present in variable proportions. There is often a myxoid to myxohyaline stroma. An epithelioid cytomorphology usually predominates, with the cells showing well-demarcated cell borders and abundant, glassy eosinophilic to vacuolated cytoplasm. The nuclei are typically vesicular with prominent nucleoli. ERG and CD31: Consistently positive. CD34: Positive in approximately 80%. Low-molecular-weight keratins: Positive in approximately 20%. TFE3: Diffuse nuclear expression; rare conventional EHE may show TFE3 staining. YAP1 C-terminus: Frequently lost. CAMTA1: Usually negative; rare fusion-confirmed positive cases reported. YAP1::TFE3 fusion supports and helps distinguish this entity from other vascular tumors. Epithelioid hemangioendothelioma, WWTR1::CAMTA1 type YAP1::TFE3 type has TFE3 expression and YAP1::TFE3 fusion; conventional EHE has WWTR1::CAMTA1 fusion. YAP1::TFE3 HE lacks the marked cytologic atypia and destructive growth typical of angiosarcoma. Intermediate / locally aggressive, metastatic potential Site: Soft tissue, lung, liver, and bone; soft-tissue lesions are usually solitary, whereas visceral and bone disease is often multifocal. Age/sex: Usually adults (mean about 51 years); rare in children; sexes equally affected. Presentation: Painful soft-tissue or bone mass; large-vessel involvement may cause occlusion, edema, or thrombophlebitis. cords or nests of epithelioid cells with cytoplasmic vacuolization within a myxochondroid or hyaline stroma; absence of vasoformation, showing immunoreactivity for endothelial markers. Epithelioid hemangioendothelioma presents as a solid mass that lacks a lobular architecture. Angiocentric tumors expand the vessel wall, obliterate the lumen, and spread centrifugally into surrounding tissue, where they elicit a sclerotic response. Infiltrative growth into adjacent skeletal muscle or fat may be seen. The tumor is characterized by cords and nests of epithelioid cells in a myxohyaline stroma. tumor cells have moderate amounts of eosinophilic cytoplasm and round nuclei with inconspicuous nucleoli. Intracytoplasmic vacuoles are sometimes present and may contain erythrocytes (blister cells or signet-ring cells). Well-formed blood vessels are not present. ERG and CD31: Typically positive. CD34 and D2-40: Less frequently positive. Cytokeratins: Positive in approximately 40%; EMA is unusual. SMA: Positive in approximately 50%. CAMTA1: Diffuse strong nuclear expression in most WWTR1::CAMTA1-fused tumors. TFE3: Variable in WWTR1::CAMTA1-fused tumors, usually not strong/diffuse; TFE3-fused tumors are CAMTA1-negative. WWTR1::CAMTA1 fusion supports conventional epithelioid hemangioendothelioma. Epithelioid hemangioma is lobular and well-formed; EHE shows cords/nests of epithelioid cells in myxohyaline stroma. EHE typically has characteristic fusion and relatively uniform epithelioid cells; angiosarcoma shows overtly malignant infiltrative vascular growth. Site: Skin of head and neck most common; also breast, soft tissue, bone, liver, heart, and spleen. Radiation-associated cases often involve breast skin. Age/sex: Cutaneous cases peak around the seventh decade and show male predominance; primary breast angiosarcoma favors younger women. Presentation: Purplish-red papules, nodules, or plaques; deep lesions are often rapidly growing, poorly defined, and painful. vasoformative malignant tumor, or poorly differentiated tumor with expression of endothelial markers (CD31, ERG). Angiosarcomas have an infiltrative growth pattern and show variable degrees of cytological atypia and architectural differentiation. Well-differentiated vasoformative areas are composed of atypical endothelial cells lining anastomosing vascular spaces, whereas more solid components show endothelial multilayering and sheets of cellular growth. The cells can range from spindled to large epithelioid with pale eosinophilic cytoplasm and vesicular nuclei. Cytoplasmic vacuoles containing fragmented erythrocytes can be present. Epithelioid angiosarcoma shows predominance of epithelioid cells forming nests or sheets. Most tumors show a high-grade morphology, with nuclear atypia, increased mitotic activity (most prominent in solid areas), and coagulative necrosis. There may be associated blood lakes, extensive hemorrhage, and organizing hematoma that obscure the neoplasm. CD31: Typically membranous positive. ERG: Typically nuclear positive. CD34: Variable. D2-40: May be positive. Epithelioid tumors: Cytokeratin and/or EMA may be positive. Perivascular SMA-positive pericytes: Commonly absent. Radiation- and lymphedema-associated tumors: MYC often strongly positive. CAMTA1, TFE3, and FOSB: Negative; INI1 retained in nearly all cases. MYC amplification, assessed by FISH or MYC immunohistochemistry, can help distinguish radiation-associated angiosarcoma from atypical vascular lesions. EHE shows characteristic fusion and more uniform epithelioid cells; angiosarcoma has marked atypia and destructive infiltrative growth. Anastomosing hemangioma is cytologically bland and lacks endothelial multilayering. Malignant Malignant vascular tumor All PathologyGPS / Soft Tissue Tumors / Vascular Tumors Vascular Tumors and Malformations An outline-based, morphology-first reference. Short diagnostic points support rapid review and sign-out. Diagnostic approach Classify the vascular pattern before interpreting ancillary studies. Integrate architecture, endothelial phenotype, clinical setting, imaging, and diagnostically useful molecular findings. Diagnostic GPS: first-pass classification 1. Malformation or neoplasm? Assess developmental history, flow characteristics, distribution, and architecture. 2. Define the pattern Venous, arteriovenous, lymphatic, capillary-lobular, retiform, epithelioid, or spindle-cell. 3. Assess biologic behavior Look for infiltration, endothelial multilayering, cytologic atypia, mitoses, and necrosis. 4. Order targeted tests Use lineage markers and entity-associated alterations only when they resolve a specific differential.
