High-yield molecular associations TEK, PIK3CA; MAP3K3 in verrucous venous malformation Fast-flow AVM / IFVA MAP2K1, KRAS; selected syndromic cases involve RASA1 or EPHB4 PIK3CA; NRAS in selected cases IDH1, less often IDH2 WWTR1::CAMTA1 or YAP1::TFE3 FOSB-related rearrangements MYC amplification in selected secondary/radiation-associated cases Source and scope: Based on the supplied WHO excerpt. The outline is intentionally concise; only source-supported diagnostic information is included; empty sections are omitted.

title: Adenomas
content: Tubular adenoma Usually young, premenopausal patients Sharply circumscribed, compact proliferation of closely packed, small, uniform round-to-oval tubules. Bilayered tubules with luminal epithelial cells and an attenuated outer myoepithelial layer; bland nuclei and rare mitoses. Very scant, delicate fibrovascular stroma. Prominent epithelial/tubular proliferation with minimal stroma; distinguish from fibroadenoma. Lactating adenoma Pregnancy, especially the third trimester, or breastfeeding Well-circumscribed, closely packed secretory lobules. Cuboidal or hobnail cells with granular or vacuolated cytoplasm, luminal milk-like secretions, bland nuclei, and sometimes binucleation. Sparse, delicate, sometimes edematous connective tissue. Secretory lobules in the appropriate clinical setting; infarction can cause pain and alarming imaging. Ductal adenoma Usually older adults; peripheral small- to medium-sized ducts Organized adenomatous glands within a thick concentric fibroelastotic wall; may be multinodular. Round, oval, elongated, or branched bilayered glands; bland cuboidal, columnar, or occasionally spindled cells. Concentric laminated fibrosclerotic capsule; intralesional fibrosis may compress glands. No arborizing papillary fronds; sclerosis, calcification, and entrapped glands may mimic radial scar or invasion. p63, p40, SMA, calponin, SMMHC Highlight the peripheral myoepithelial layer when needed, particularly in difficult cases. Interpret with architecture and internal controls. EMA, CK19, CK8/18 Luminal epithelial markers may help confirm the ductal component in tubular adenoma. A broad panel is not routinely required in classic cases. ER Ductal adenoma may show heterogeneous expression. Do not use ER alone to establish or exclude the diagnosis. Ki-67 and p53 Ductal adenoma typically shows low labeling indices. Supportive only; not stand-alone diagnostic criteria. α-Lactalbumin / Oil Red O Secretory cells and luminal material in lactating adenoma may show α-lactalbumin and lipid-related staining. Correlate with pregnancy/lactation history and morphology. 01 Confirm a circumscribed glandular lesion Assess the border, gland density, stromal volume, and whether a benign dual-cell pattern is preserved. 02 Identify the dominant pattern Closely packed tubules with scant stroma favor tubular adenoma; secretory lobules favor lactating adenoma; glands in a concentric fibrosclerotic wall favor ductal adenoma. 03 Evaluate the myoepithelial layer Use p63 or p40 with a cytoplasmic marker such as SMA, calponin, or SMMHC when H&E is equivocal. 04 Exclude important mimics Consider fibroadenoma, intraductal papilloma, sclerosing adenosis/radial scar, and invasive carcinoma as appropriate. 05 Check clinical and imaging concordance Review pregnancy/lactation status, growth, imaging, and sampling adequacy. Limited or discordant samples may need additional sampling or excision. bg-slate-50/70 font-semibold text-slate-900 text-slate-700 PathologyGPS / Breast Adenomas Breast Pathology • Diagnostic Reference Breast Adenomas A practical guide to tubular adenoma, lactating adenoma, and ductal adenoma, emphasizing architecture, the epithelial–myoepithelial bilayer, stromal features, and key diagnostic mimics. Benign glandular tumors H&E-first approach IHC when indicated Core concept Breast adenomas are benign glandular epithelial tumors arising from the terminal duct lobular unit. They contain varying proportions of glands, fibrous tissue, and fat. Fibroadenoma is the most common adenoma-type lesion but belongs to the fibroepithelial tumor spectrum and is not the primary focus of this page. Tubular, lactating, and ductal adenomas are benign. Their most useful distinction is architectural: dense tubules with scant stroma, secretory lobules, or glands surrounded by a concentric fibrosclerotic wall. Diagnostic caution A circumscribed mass is not automatically benign. Ductal adenoma may show sclerosis, calcification, or a pseudoinfiltrative edge; lactating adenoma may infarct and enlarge. Interpret morphology together with imaging and clinical findings. Diagnostic GPS A pattern-based approach Side-by-side comparison Three principal adenomas Use the clinical setting as a clue, but make the diagnosis from the overall histologic pattern. Entity Typical setting Low-power architecture High-power features Stroma Key discriminator 01 • Tubular adenoma Dense tubules, scant stroma Low power: sharply demarcated, compact proliferation of small, regular tubules. High power: luminal epithelial cells and an attenuated myoepithelial layer; bland nuclei and rare mitoses. Stroma: minimal delicate fibrovascular tissue, without the prominent stromal component of fibroadenoma. Key distinction: prominent epithelial proliferation and minimal stroma. 02 • Lactating adenoma Secretory lobules Clinical setting: pregnancy or breastfeeding; often diagnosed during the third trimester. Architecture: closely packed hyperplastic secretory lobules separated by sparse connective tissue. Cytoplasm: granular or vacuolated, with luminal milk-like material; binucleated cells may be common. Pitfall: infarction may cause rapid enlargement, pain, tenderness, skin changes, and suspicious imaging. 03 • Ductal adenoma Glands in a fibrosclerotic wall organized glands, often radiating from the center, enclosed by a thick concentric fibroelastotic capsule. Cells: bilayered glands with bland cuboidal, columnar, or occasionally spindled ductal cells. Helpful negatives: no arborizing papillary fronds and no prominent myoepithelial hyperplasia. sclerosis, dystrophic calcification, and entrapped glands can create a pseudoinfiltrative appearance. Immunohistochemistry When a panel helps In classic lesions, morphology is primary. Use immunohistochemistry to resolve a specific uncertainty rather than as a substitute for architectural assessment. Marker(s) Diagnostic use Interpretive caution Differential diagnosis Common mimics and separating features Fibroadenoma Usually has a more conspicuous stromal component and characteristic intracanalicular or pericanalicular fibroepithelial architecture. Tubular adenoma shows dense epithelial/tubular proliferation with very little stroma. Intraductal papilloma Papilloma has arborizing fibrovascular cores. Ductal adenoma is a sclerosing adenomatous lesion without characteristic branching papillary fronds. Sclerosing adenosis / radial scar Sclerosing adenosis retains a lobulocentric pattern of compressed acini. Radial scar has a central elastotic or hyalinized nidus with radiating entrapped glands. Both can mimic invasion. Invasive carcinoma Irregular glands in desmoplastic stroma or a truly infiltrative growth pattern raise concern. Demonstrating a myoepithelial layer supports a benign glandular lesion, but stains must be interpreted with morphology and controls. Sign-out checklist Before finalizing the diagnosis Is the lesion circumscribed, and is the overall architecture appropriate for an adenoma? Is the epithelial–myoepithelial bilayer present where expected? Is the stromal volume and pattern consistent with the proposed subtype? For a secretory lesion, does the clinical history support pregnancy or lactation? Have sclerosis, calcification, or infarction been considered as potential mimics of malignancy? Are the imaging findings concordant with the histologic diagnosis? ✓ Scope: This page focuses on diagnostic morphology, useful immunohistochemistry, and practical differential diagnosis. Management decisions should incorporate radiology–pathology concordance and the full clinical context.

title: Common Invasive Carcinoma
content: nst Invasive Breast Carcinoma of No Special Type (IBC-NST) Common / default category Invasive breast carcinoma that does not show sufficient defining features for classification as a recognized special histological type. Highly variable architecture: tubules and glands, nests, cords, trabeculae, or solid sheets; infiltrative growth is typical. Desmoplastic stroma is common. Cytologic atypia, mitotic activity, and tubule formation vary with grade. An associated in situ component may be present; search for lymphovascular invasion and document the relationship to adjacent in situ disease. Medullary-like, neuroendocrine, or other unusual patterns should be described and classified according to current criteria rather than overcalled as a separate entity. ER, PR, and HER2 are predictive biomarkers. Use morphology-directed stains when needed to distinguish invasion from in situ disease, identify a possible non-breast primary, or characterize a special type. A low-grade morphology with ER negativity or HER2 positivity is discordant and warrants verification. DCIS involving sclerosing adenosis or a radial scar; microglandular adenosis; invasive lobular carcinoma; metastatic carcinoma; and spindle-cell or metaplastic lesions when morphology is unusual. Report histological type, Nottingham grade, invasive size, focality, lymphovascular invasion, associated DCIS, margins, nodal findings, and biomarker results as applicable. microinvasive Microinvasive Carcinoma Small-volume invasion Invasive carcinoma with no invasive focus measuring more than 1 mm. The presence and measurement of invasion must be distinguished from extensive in situ disease. One or more tiny foci of stromal invasion, often adjacent to high-grade DCIS or another in situ lesion. Careful examination is required because invasion may be subtle and may be obscured by inflammation, biopsy-site change, or a sclerosing background. Measure the largest invasive focus for pT classification; do not substitute the overall span of associated DCIS. Myoepithelial markers may help in selected equivocal foci, interpreted with H&E morphology and appropriate internal controls. Cytoplasmic myoepithelial markers can highlight stromal cells and vessels; a nuclear marker such as p63 can provide complementary evidence. DCIS with retraction artifact, DCIS involving a sclerosing lesion, displaced epithelium after biopsy, and tangentially sectioned glands. Extensive sampling of the in situ lesion and suspicious interfaces is important. Use current staging and reporting protocols; the largest invasive focus determines the microinvasive size category. ilc Invasive Lobular Carcinoma (ILC) Special histological type Invasive carcinoma characterized by discohesive cells, commonly infiltrating in single files or dispersed individually, usually associated with loss of E-cadherin pathway function. Classic pattern: small, uniform cells infiltrating in single files, targetoid rings around ducts, or loose sheets. Intracytoplasmic lumina or signet-ring-like cells may occur. Other patterns include solid, alveolar, pleomorphic, tubulolobular, and mixed forms. The tumour can be subtle grossly and radiologically; the infiltrative span may exceed the apparent mass. Associated lobular carcinoma in situ may be present, but its presence is not required for diagnosis. Loss of membranous E-cadherin and p120 catenin redistribution to the cytoplasm support lobular differentiation. Aberrant or retained E-cadherin staining can occur; interpret a panel in conjunction with morphology. Most classic ILCs are ER-positive and HER2-negative. Ductal/NST carcinoma with discohesive areas, histiocytes, lymphoma, metastatic signet-ring carcinoma, and benign cells in fat or around nerves. Consider the possibility of diffuse or multifocal growth when correlating with imaging and measuring extent. Grade and biomarkers are assessed using standard breast carcinoma protocols. tubular Tubular Carcinoma A well-differentiated invasive carcinoma composed predominantly of open, angulated tubules infiltrating desmoplastic stroma. Well-formed tubules with open lumina and sharp angulations, lined by a single layer of low-grade epithelial cells. Tubules lack a surrounding myoepithelial layer and infiltrate fibrous stroma. Nuclear atypia and mitotic activity are usually low; a substantial conventional carcinoma component may preclude classification as pure tubular carcinoma. Usually strongly ER-positive and HER2-negative. Myoepithelial markers may help in difficult cases, but the diagnosis rests on the infiltrative architecture and cytology. Sclerosing adenosis, radial scar/complex sclerosing lesion, microglandular adenosis, and tubular-pattern carcinoma of another type. Typically associated with a favorable prognosis when strict criteria for a pure special type are met. Evaluate the entire tumour to estimate the proportion of tubular morphology. cribriform Invasive Cribriform Carcinoma An invasive carcinoma with a predominant cribriform architecture formed by tumour nests containing multiple punched-out spaces. Uniform low-grade cells form sieve-like nests with rounded, punched-out spaces. True invasion is indicated by infiltrative nests in stroma without a peripheral myoepithelial layer. Exclude an in situ cribriform component and mixed tumours that do not meet criteria for the special type. Typically ER-positive and HER2-negative. Myoepithelial stains can assist when invasion is uncertain. Cribriform DCIS, adenoid cystic carcinoma, and other invasive carcinomas with focal cribriform architecture. Usually has a favorable outcome when pure or nearly pure and correctly classified. Record any associated in situ component separately. mucinous Mucinous Carcinoma An invasive carcinoma in which tumour cell clusters are present in abundant extracellular mucin. Cohesive clusters, nests, or strips of tumour cells float in extracellular mucin pools. Cellularity and nuclear grade vary; classic mucinous carcinoma is usually low grade. Mixed tumours contain a substantial non-mucinous invasive component; assess the proportion and describe mixed morphology. Usually ER-positive and HER2-negative. Correlate with morphology; mucin production alone is not sufficient to classify a tumour as mucinous carcinoma. Mucocele-like lesion with atypia, mucinous DCIS, metastatic mucinous carcinoma, and invasive carcinoma with focal mucin production. The distinction between pure and mixed mucinous carcinoma is clinically relevant. Measure the invasive component and document associated disease. micropapillary Invasive Micropapillary Carcinoma An invasive carcinoma characterized by small tight clusters of tumour cells within clear stromal spaces, often showing reversed polarity. Small nests or morula-like clusters are surrounded by empty-appearing lacunar spaces. Clusters lack true fibrovascular cores; the apical surface may face outward toward the stroma (inside-out polarity). Lymphovascular invasion and lymph node metastases are common associations; distinguish true vascular spaces from retraction artifact. Epithelial markers confirm carcinoma when needed. Endothelial markers can help evaluate suspected lymphovascular invasion, but must be interpreted with morphology and controls. Retraction artifact in NST carcinoma, lymphovascular tumour emboli, papillary lesions, and metastatic carcinoma. Recognize and report the micropapillary component and lymphovascular invasion carefully because of the association with nodal involvement. apocrine Invasive Apocrine Carcinoma Special histological type / phenotype An invasive carcinoma with prominent apocrine cytomorphology; classification requires the appropriate morphology and current diagnostic criteria. Abundant granular eosinophilic cytoplasm, distinct cell borders, and enlarged nuclei with prominent nucleoli. Apocrine morphology can occur in carcinomas that are not a pure apocrine special type; evaluate the tumour as a whole. Most invasive apocrine carcinomas are high grade, although the phenotype and receptor profile are variable. Androgen receptor is often expressed, while ER and PR are frequently negative; HER2 may be positive or negative. AR testing is not a universal predictive standard, so interpret within the clinical context. Apocrine metaplasia, apocrine DCIS, oncocytic lesions, and metastatic carcinomas with eosinophilic cytoplasm. Do not infer a treatment category from apocrine morphology alone. Report ER, PR, and HER2 according to validated protocols. metaplastic Metaplastic Carcinoma A heterogeneous group of breast carcinomas showing squamous and/or mesenchymal differentiation, including spindle-cell and matrix-producing forms. Patterns include low-grade adenosquamous, fibromatosis-like, spindle-cell, squamous, and carcinomas with heterologous mesenchymal differentiation or matrix production. Tumours may be biphasic or monophasic and can show abrupt transitions between conventional carcinoma and metaplastic elements. Extensive sampling may be needed to identify a conventional invasive component or an in situ component. Broad-spectrum cytokeratins and/or p63/p40 can support epithelial differentiation in spindle or squamous areas, but expression may be focal or absent in some components. Use a differential-driven panel to exclude primary sarcoma, malignant phyllodes tumour, and metastasis. Malignant phyllodes tumour, primary breast sarcoma, melanoma, lymphoma, and metastatic malignancy. No single stain should be interpreted in isolation. Many metaplastic carcinomas are triple-negative, but low-grade forms can behave differently from conventional high-grade TNBC. Classification should follow the dominant morphology and established criteria. Tubule formation Score 1: >75% of tumour forms tubules; score 2: 10–75%; score 3: <10%. Nuclear pleomorphism Score 1: small, relatively uniform nuclei; score 2: moderate variation; score 3: marked variation, enlarged vesicular nuclei and often prominent nucleoli. Mitotic count Count definite mitoses in the hotspot. For a standardized tumour area of 2 mm²: score 1 ≤7, score 2 = 8–14, score 3 ≥15; verify the current validated local protocol and microscope field area. Total score / grade Add the three component scores: 3–5 = grade 1; 6–7 = grade 2; 8–9 = grade 3. Report component scores as well as the grade. PathologyGPS / Breast pathology Common Invasive Breast Carcinomas A morphology-first diagnostic guide to invasive carcinoma of no special type, microinvasion, lobular carcinoma, and common special histological types—with practical grading, biomarker, staging, and sign-out checkpoints. Diagnostic GPS Confirm invasion → classify morphology → grade → assess LVI and extent → verify biomarkers → complete structured reporting. H&E-first IHC when indicated ER / PR / HER2 Nottingham grade pTNM essentials 1. Classification at a glance Invasive breast carcinoma is a morphologically heterogeneous group. Use invasive breast carcinoma of no special type (IBC-NST) when the tumour does not meet criteria for a recognized special type. A special-type diagnosis should be based on the defining morphology and the required extent of that pattern under current classification criteria. Common diagnostic groups IBC-NST Microinvasive carcinoma Invasive lobular carcinoma Tubular and invasive cribriform carcinoma Mucinous carcinoma Invasive micropapillary carcinoma Invasive apocrine carcinoma Metaplastic carcinoma High-value prognostic/reporting elements Histological type and Nottingham grade Invasive tumour size and focality Lymphovascular invasion Associated in situ carcinoma Margin status and distance Regional lymph node status ER, PR, HER2; other indicated biomarkers Post-neoadjuvant response when applicable 2. Diagnostic GPS: practical workflow Start with architecture Is the growth truly infiltrative? Look for irregular glands, nests, cords, single cells, stromal response, and destructive growth. Do not diagnose invasion from cytologic atypia alone. Exclude common mimics Consider DCIS involving a sclerosing lesion, sclerosing adenosis, radial scar, microglandular adenosis, biopsy-related epithelial displacement, and retraction artifact. Classify the tumour Decide whether the morphology fits IBC-NST or a recognized special type. If the tumour is heterogeneous, describe the mixed pattern and apply current criteria. Assign Nottingham grade Score tubule formation, nuclear pleomorphism, and mitotic activity independently; add the three scores to derive grade. Assess extent and spread Measure the invasive component, determine focality, inspect margins, search for LVI, and evaluate lymph nodes when submitted. Verify predictive biomarkers Perform ER, PR, and HER2 using validated protocols. Resolve unusual morphology–biomarker discordance before finalizing the report. Integrate and sign out Correlate imaging, gross findings, histology, biomarkers, and treatment history. Use the current CAP/institutional synoptic protocol. 3. Entity profiles: morphology, IHC, and differential Use the entity cards below as a rapid reference. The differential diagnosis is morphology-dependent; immunohistochemistry should answer a specific question rather than replace H&E interpretation. Back to workflow ↑ Definition. Morphology checklist IHC / biomarker notes Key differential Reporting / clinical relevance 4. Nottingham histological grading Grade is based on three independently scored features. Assess the whole tumour when possible, using the highest-grade area for nuclear pleomorphism and the mitotic hotspot for mitotic scoring. Component Practical scoring guide Grading pitfalls Do not count pyknotic or hyperchromatic apoptotic nuclei as mitoses. Calibrate the microscope field area; “per 10 HPF” is not comparable across microscopes without area standardization. Core biopsy grading is useful but may underestimate mitotic activity and overall grade because of sampling. For a very small tumour, document limitations if there is insufficient tissue for reliable scoring. 5. Biomarker interpretation: practical checkpoints ER and PR ER and PR are nuclear stains; interpret with appropriate controls and validated assay procedures. ER staining in 1–10% of invasive tumour cells is reported as ER low positive under current commonly used guidance, with the recommended explanatory comment. When staining is 0–10%, document internal-control status. If controls are absent or unsatisfactory, consider testing another specimen according to protocol. PR adds prognostic information in ER-positive disease; isolated PR positivity with ER negativity is unusual and should prompt review of controls and results. HER2 Score membrane staining as 0, 1+, 2+, or 3+ using the current ASCO/CAP algorithm. Equivocal IHC (2+) requires reflex ISH according to the applicable guideline. Distinguish faint/incomplete membrane staining from absent staining; avoid overcalling 2+ as 3+. Unexpected combinations—such as low-grade morphology with HER2 IHC 3+—warrant verification. Ki-67 Use as an adjunct to morphology and other biomarkers, not as a standalone substitute for grade or genomic assays. Reproducibility is limited, particularly in intermediate ranges; follow validated local scoring procedures. Preanalytic handling and fixation can affect results; core biopsies may provide more standardized material. Additional testing when indicated PD-L1 testing may guide immunotherapy in selected metastatic TNBC settings; use the assay and scoring system specified for the clinical indication. Multigene expression assays may help treatment decisions in selected early-stage ER-positive/HER2-negative cancers. AR, molecular profiling, and other markers are context-dependent and are not universal routine tests for every invasive carcinoma. Biomarker criteria and therapeutic indications evolve. Follow the current validated assay instructions, ASCO/CAP guidance, and institutional protocols. 6. Staging, size, nodes, and margins Invasive tumour size For pT classification, measure the largest invasive focus, not the total span of associated DCIS or LCIS. Integrate gross, microscopic, and imaging findings when needed. For multiple separate invasive foci, document multiplicity and apply the appropriate staging modifier. Lymph nodes Record the number of nodes examined and involved, the size of the largest metastatic deposit, and extranodal extension when applicable. Deposits greater than 2 mm are macrometastases; deposits greater than 0.2 mm and up to 2 mm are micrometastases; isolated tumour cells are no greater than 0.2 mm or 200 cells, using current staging definitions. Assess at the tumour periphery in clearly endothelial-lined spaces. Retraction artifact is a major pitfall. D2-40, CD31, or ERG may help in selected cases, but staining can be misleading and must be correlated with H&E. Margins Record the distance from invasive carcinoma and associated DCIS to relevant margins. Additional shave margins designated as final margins supersede the corresponding margins of the original specimen. Apply current institutional and guideline-specific margin standards. Post-neoadjuvant specimens Correlate with the pretreatment tumour site and marker clip, sample the tumour bed adequately, and document residual invasive carcinoma, in situ disease, nodal disease, and treatment effect. Residual cancer burden (RCB) may supplement ypTNM when used by the institution. 7. Common diagnostic pitfalls Invasion versus in situ disease: DCIS involving a sclerosing lesion can simulate invasion; use myoepithelial markers judiciously and inspect the H&E architecture. Myoepithelial stain interpretation: stromal or vascular staining can mimic a peripheral layer. Pair a nuclear marker (e.g., p63) with a cytoplasmic marker when appropriate. Retraction versus lymphovascular invasion: require convincing endothelial-lined spaces and avoid relying on a single stain. Special type overclassification: confirm the required morphology and proportion; otherwise classify as IBC-NST and describe the pattern. Biomarker discordance: unexpected ER/HER2 results should trigger review of tumour type, grade, controls, fixation, and assay validity. Under-sampling: extensive DCIS, post-treatment tumour beds, subtle lobular carcinoma, and imaging–gross discordance require targeted additional sampling. Metastasis to breast: consider a non-mammary primary when morphology, immunophenotype, or clinical history is unusual. 8. Gross examination and sampling Review imaging and specimen orientation before sectioning; identify clips, calcifications, lesion count, and expected location. Ink margins according to the laboratory's color scheme, serially section the specimen, and map larger or poorly defined lesions. Submit tissue to establish invasive size and focality, evaluate close margins, and investigate possible invasion in extensive in situ disease. After neoadjuvant therapy, sample the entire tumour bed as needed because residual disease may be soft, scattered, or grossly inapparent. Document cold ischemia and fixation parameters according to the laboratory's validated breast biomarker workflow. 9. Sign-out checklist Histological type and any special/mixed pattern Nottingham grade and three component scores Associated DCIS / LCIS and extent when relevant Margins and measured distances Regional lymph nodes and largest deposit ER, PR, HER2 results and required comments Treatment effect / RCB if post-neoadjuvant pTNM elements and any staging modifiers Radiology–pathology correlation Current CAP/institutional synoptic elements completed Related PathologyGPS pages Use the dedicated pages for precursor lesions and other breast tumour families. Non-invasive neoplasia Papillary lesions Fibroepithelial lesions Educational reference for professional use. This page summarizes supplied source material in an organized diagnostic format. Confirm current classification, biomarker interpretation, staging, and reporting requirements against the latest authoritative guidelines and institutional protocols. On this page overview Classification workflow entities Entity profiles grading biomarkers Biomarkers staging Staging / margins pitfalls Pitfalls grossing Gross examination signout Sign-out checklist Key reminder Morphology establishes the diagnosis. IHC resolves a focused differential. Biomarkers guide therapy. Keep each step explicit in the final report.
