title: Non Invasive Neoplasia
content: alh Atypical Lobular Hyperplasia (ALH) Lobular neoplasia A non-invasive low-grade neoplastic proliferation of small, discohesive cells in terminal duct lobular units (TDLUs), with or without pagetoid duct involvement. Fewer than half of the acini in an involved TDLU are filled and expanded. Small, relatively uniform type A cells with hyperchromatic nuclei, or slightly larger type B cells with vesicular nuclei and mild variability. Cells are discohesive and may involve acini and terminal ducts in a pagetoid pattern. The involved acini are not filled and expanded to the extent required for classic LCIS. Usually an incidental microscopic finding; no specific gross abnormality is expected. When needed, loss of membranous E-cadherin supports lobular differentiation. Interpret with morphology; aberrant retained staining can occur in lobular lesions. A bilateral risk marker and a non-obligate precursor. The source describes a roughly 4- to 5-fold relative risk and an estimated absolute risk around 1% per year. For incidental ALH on core biopsy, observation may be appropriate when radiology–pathology findings are concordant and another target lesion explains the imaging. Excision is considered when discordant or when another lesion independently warrants excision. classic-lcis Classic Lobular Carcinoma In Situ (LCIS) A non-invasive proliferation of discohesive cells in TDLUs, with or without pagetoid involvement of terminal ducts. More than half of the acini in an involved TDLU are filled and expanded. Type A cells are small, uniform, and hyperchromatic; type B cells have somewhat larger vesicular nuclei with mild variability. Glandular architecture is absent; mitoses are uncommon. Pagetoid extension into adjacent ducts can occur, as can involvement of other benign lesions. Small foci of apoptosis or minute necrosis may rarely be present. Typically shows loss of membranous E-cadherin, strong cytoplasmic p120 catenin, and loss of membranous β-catenin. Most cases are strongly ER-positive with a low Ki-67 index. Both a bilateral risk marker and a non-obligate precursor, with an ipsilateral predominance and increased association with invasive lobular carcinoma. The source describes approximately 8- to 10-fold relative risk. Management depends on incidental versus targeted disease and radiology–pathology concordance. Incidental classic LCIS with concordant imaging may be managed with high-risk screening and risk-reduction counseling without routine excision in selected cases. Borderline or discordant lesions require further evaluation. florid-lcis Florid Lobular Carcinoma In Situ Non-classic LCIS LCIS with classic-type cytology and marked distention of involved TDLUs or ducts, producing a confluent, mass-like architecture. Markedly expanded acini with little or no intervening stroma between adjacent involved spaces, and/or an expanded acinus or duct approximately 40–50 cells in diameter. Cytology resembles classic LCIS; the defining feature is the extent and confluent architecture. Microcalcifications and comedonecrosis may be present but are not required. Carefully search adjacent tissue for subtle invasive lobular carcinoma. Usually retains the lobular phenotype, including loss of membranous E-cadherin. ER is often strongly positive; interpret any aberrant staining in context. Clinical outcome data are limited. Florid LCIS is more often associated with invasive lobular carcinoma than classic LCIS and warrants careful evaluation. Surgical excision is generally recommended. Margin assessment and further treatment should be discussed in a multidisciplinary setting; optimal margin width and the role of radiation remain uncertain. pleomorphic-lcis Pleomorphic Lobular Carcinoma In Situ LCIS composed of large, discohesive cells with marked nuclear pleomorphism, with nuclei greater than four times the size of a lymphocyte or comparable to high-grade DCIS, with or without apocrine features. Marked nuclear size and shape variation; binucleated or multinucleated cells may occur. Apocrine cytology can be present, particularly in apocrine pleomorphic LCIS. Comedonecrosis and calcifications are common associations but are not required. Search carefully for associated invasive carcinoma, most often invasive lobular carcinoma. E-cadherin is usually lost. ER may be reduced or absent, particularly in apocrine cases; AR, HER2 overexpression/amplification, and a moderate-to-high Ki-67 index may be seen in subsets. Evidence on natural history is limited. Reported recurrence rates after conservative surgery vary widely; invasive carcinoma may be found synchronously or develop subsequently. Excision to negative margins is generally favored when feasible, with margin status reported. Radiation and other adjuvant approaches remain debated and should be individualized. adh Atypical Ductal Hyperplasia (ADH) Ductal low-grade neoplasia An epithelial proliferative lesion with cytologic and architectural features similar to low-grade DCIS, but with less developed architecture, more limited TDLU involvement, or limited contiguous extent. Monotonous, evenly spaced cells with round nuclei, dense chromatin, and distinct cell borders. Rigid bridges, bars, or arcades of uniform thickness; bulbous micropapillae with narrow bases and broad tips; or a cribriform pattern. No intermediate- or high-grade nuclear features. Necrosis is not expected. The distinction from low-grade DCIS is quantitative: limited involvement, generally ≤2 mm contiguous extent, or limited involved spaces; in a papilloma, the source cites ≤3 mm as a practical threshold. Because core biopsies may not show the full lesion, use conservative wording when extent cannot be assessed. Typically diffuse strong ER positivity and absence of high-molecular-weight cytokeratins such as CK5/6 or CK14. Usual ductal hyperplasia more often shows heterogeneous ER and mosaic basal cytokeratin staining. Associated with a 3- to 5-fold increased risk of invasive breast carcinoma in either breast; the source estimates an absolute risk of approximately 1% per year. Core biopsy upgrade rates vary; contemporary series cited in the source report approximately 10–20%. Diagnostic excision or vacuum-assisted excision is commonly recommended, with selective observation considered only in carefully chosen, concordant, limited lesions under local guidance. dcis Ductal Carcinoma In Situ (DCIS) Ductal neoplasia A non-invasive proliferation of cohesive neoplastic epithelial cells confined to the mammary ductal-lobular system, with a range of nuclear grades and architectural patterns. Assess nuclear grade as low, intermediate, or high; grade is based primarily on cytologic features, not architectural pattern alone. Architectures include solid, cribriform, micropapillary, and papillary patterns; mixed patterns are common. Low-grade DCIS shows small, monomorphic cells and often cribriform or micropapillary architecture; necrosis is uncommon but does not exclude it. Intermediate-grade DCIS has moderate nuclear variability and may show mitoses or necrosis. High-grade DCIS shows large, pleomorphic nuclei, irregular contours, coarse chromatin, prominent nucleoli, and usually conspicuous mitoses; comedonecrosis is common but not mandatory. Evaluate for microinvasion, especially with high-grade disease, stromal inflammation/fibrosis, or irregular small clusters beyond involved ducts. ER testing is recommended to inform endocrine risk-reduction discussions. Myoepithelial markers can help in selected difficult cases, but use more than one marker and do not diagnose invasion solely from absent staining. A heterogeneous, non-obligate precursor of invasive carcinoma. Breast cancer–specific survival is excellent overall, but invasive recurrence has greater clinical significance than recurrent in situ disease. Management is individualized and may include breast-conserving surgery with radiation or mastectomy. Margin goals, endocrine therapy, and selected de-escalation approaches depend on current guidelines, patient factors, and multidisciplinary review. ALH Lobular; small discohesive cells Fewer than 50% of acini filled/expanded Risk marker and non-obligate precursor Classic LCIS More than 50% of acini filled/expanded Florid LCIS Lobular; classic-type cytology Marked confluent distention; little intervening stroma and/or 40–50-cell diameter Higher concern; excision generally recommended Pleomorphic LCIS Lobular; marked nuclear pleomorphism Large cells; nuclei >4× lymphocyte size Higher concern; excision and margin assessment ADH Ductal; low-grade monotonous cells Limited extent of a DCIS-like proliferation Risk marker; assess upgrade risk DCIS Ductal; cohesive neoplastic cells More extensive ductal epithelial neoplasia Non-obligate precursor; grade and extent guide management 1. Identify the cell population Discohesive cells suggest lobular neoplasia; cohesive, polarized cells with rigid bridges, micropapillae, or cribriform spaces suggest ductal low-grade neoplasia. 2. Assess extent and architecture For ALH versus classic LCIS, estimate the proportion of acini filled and expanded. For ADH versus low-grade DCIS, assess contiguous extent and the number of involved spaces. 3. Grade the cytology Marked pleomorphism in a discohesive lesion raises pleomorphic LCIS. Intermediate- or high-grade nuclei preclude ADH. 4. Apply a targeted IHC panel Use E-cadherin and p120/β-catenin when lobular versus ductal differentiation is uncertain. Use ER and basal cytokeratins to support ADH versus usual ductal hyperplasia. 5. Correlate with imaging Determine whether the lesion explains the imaging target. Discordance or a target lesion not accounted for histologically warrants additional evaluation. 6. Search for invasion For florid/pleomorphic LCIS and DCIS, thoroughly examine adjacent tissue for subtle invasive carcinoma; use myoepithelial markers as adjuncts, not in isolation. PathologyGPS Breast Adenomas Epithelial-myoepithelial tumors Breast pathology · Diagnostic guide Non-Invasive Neoplasia A practical, morphology-first guide to lobular neoplasia, atypical ductal hyperplasia, and ductal carcinoma in situ—with emphasis on quantitative thresholds, immunohistochemistry, and radiology–pathology correlation. H&E first Quantitative thresholds Risk and upgrade assessment Core diagnostic question Is this lobular or ductal neoplasia—and how far has it developed? Lobular: discohesive cells; E-cadherin pathway abnormality is typical. Ductal: cohesive cells; assess architecture, nuclear grade, and extent. Always: correlate pathology with the imaging target. 01 · Overview Classification at a glance This page groups non-invasive epithelial neoplasia by lobular and ductal phenotype. Lobular neoplasia includes atypical lobular hyperplasia and classic LCIS; florid and pleomorphic LCIS are non-classic forms and are treated separately here because their architecture, cytology, and clinical management differ. ADH is included in this section as a limited low-grade ductal proliferation on the spectrum with low-grade DCIS. Lesion Cell phenotype Key discriminator Clinical framing Interpretive caution These diagnoses are not interchangeable. For ALH versus classic LCIS and ADH versus low-grade DCIS, the distinction depends partly on quantitative extent. Limited core biopsies may not show the full lesion; describe uncertainty explicitly and recommend appropriate correlation when needed. 02 · Diagnostic workflow Diagnostic GPS 03 · Entity profiles Lesion-by-lesion guide Morphology checklist Immunohistochemistry Behavior / risk Clinical correlation 04 · Ancillary studies IHC patterns and practical limitations Lobular versus ductal differentiation E-cadherin: loss of membranous staining supports lobular neoplasia. p120 catenin: diffuse cytoplasmic staining supports a lobular phenotype. β-catenin: membranous expression is often lost in lobular lesions. Some lobular lesions retain aberrant E-cadherin staining; fragmented, diminished, or cytoplasmic staining should not automatically trigger a ductal diagnosis. ADH versus usual ductal hyperplasia ADH: typically strong, diffuse ER positivity and absent CK5/6 or CK14 in the atypical cells. Usual ductal hyperplasia: heterogeneous ER and mosaic basal cytokeratin staining. Interpret stain distribution across the proliferation rather than relying on a single positive or negative focus. Immunohistochemistry supports but does not replace architectural and quantitative assessment. DCIS versus invasion Myoepithelial markers can be useful in difficult cases, including DCIS involving sclerosing adenosis. Use more than one marker when appropriate. Loss of myoepithelial staining alone does not unequivocally establish invasion; evaluate the contour of cell clusters, stromal response, and overall pattern. 05 · Diagnostic pitfalls Common traps Overcalling ALH as LCIS Estimate the proportion of acini filled and expanded; fewer than half supports ALH, more than half supports classic LCIS. Overcalling ADH as DCIS ADH is a limited low-grade DCIS-like proliferation. Extent thresholds are practical and may be difficult to apply on a partial core sample. Calling pleomorphic LCIS from type B cells alone Borderline type B classic LCIS should remain classic LCIS unless the marked nuclear pleomorphism criterion is met. Assuming necrosis is required Comedonecrosis and calcifications may occur in florid or pleomorphic LCIS and DCIS, but they are not mandatory for those diagnoses. Using E-cadherin as a stand-alone answer Aberrant retained or diminished staining can occur. Integrate staining pattern with cell cohesion and morphology. Missing invasion near non-classic LCIS/DCIS Thoroughly sample adjacent tissue, especially when there is a mass, marked distention, high-grade cytology, inflammation, or stromal fibrosis. 06 · Reporting Sign-out checklist Is the proliferation lobular or ductal? Is the cytology low grade, pleomorphic, or high grade? For ALH/LCIS, is less than or more than half of the acini involved? For ADH/DCIS, can the full extent be assessed? Are necrosis, calcifications, or apocrine features present? Has E-cadherin/p120 been used only when needed and interpreted with morphology? Is there radiology–pathology concordance? Has adjacent tissue been examined for invasive carcinoma? For florid/pleomorphic LCIS, is margin status reported when applicable? For ADH on core biopsy, has upgrade risk and sampling adequacy been addressed? Reporting principle State the lesion subtype clearly, document relevant grade/extent and associated findings, and flag radiology–pathology discordance or limited sampling when these affect interpretation. Educational reference for professional use. Management statements summarize the supplied source and are not a substitute for current institutional protocols, multidisciplinary review, or patient-specific clinical judgment. On this page overview Classification workflow entities Lesion profiles ihc IHC patterns pitfalls Diagnostic pitfalls signout Key reminder For borderline low-grade lesions, extent matters. For lobular lesions, cohesion and the E-cadherin pathway matter. For all lesions, concordance matters.

title: Papillary Lesions
content: 01 Confirm true papillary architecture Identify discrete papillary aggregates with fibrovascular cores. Focal papillary features in apocrine metaplasia or usual ductal hyperplasia alone should not be overcalled as papilloma. 02 Map myoepithelial cells Assess the fibrovascular cores and the periphery of the involved duct or lesion separately. Core staining and peripheral staining answer different questions. 03 Characterize the epithelial proliferation Assess cytologic uniformity, nuclear grade, mitotic activity, usual ductal hyperplasia, and any monotonous atypical population. 04 Assess lesion boundary and invasion Look for a cystic space or fibrous capsule, a rounded or pushing border, and unequivocal infiltrative growth beyond the lesion boundary. 05 Use targeted IHC and integrate Select stains to answer a specific morphologic question. Interpret staining distribution, internal controls, and potential mimics before assigning a diagnostic category. Intraductal papilloma Arborescent papillae; often broad fibrovascular cores Present Continuous layer expected Bland or heterogeneous epithelial proliferation without atypia; sclerosis can entrap epithelium and mimic invasion. Papilloma with ADH / DCIS Papilloma containing a monotonous atypical epithelial focus Present along benign papilloma cores; may be absent in atypical foci Usually retained around the papilloma For low-grade atypia, < 3 mm supports ADH and ≥ 3 mm supports DCIS in a papilloma; intermediate/high-grade atypia is classified as DCIS regardless of extent. Papillary DCIS Neoplastic epithelium lining arborizing fibrovascular cores Absent Present around the involved duct Neoplastic papillary proliferation within a duct with a retained peripheral myoepithelial layer. Encapsulated papillary carcinoma (EPC) Delicate papillae in a cystic space, usually with a fibrous capsule and rounded or pushing border Usually absent; may be focally present Usually low/intermediate nuclear grade. Do not infer invasion from absent myoepithelium, high grade, or phenotype alone. Solid papillary carcinoma (SPC) Expansile solid nodules with inconspicuous delicate fibrovascular cores Not the defining criterion Presence/absence alone does not determine in situ status Monotonous round-to-spindle cells; palisading, mucin, and neuroendocrine differentiation may occur. Invasive papillary carcinoma Entirely papillary architecture with unequivocal invasive growth Absent in invasive areas Extremely rare. Exclude EPC/SPC, high-grade carcinoma with pseudopapillary growth, and metastasis when appropriate. Are myoepithelial cells present? p63 plus a smooth-muscle/myoepithelial marker panel, e.g. SMMHC, calponin, or SMA Evaluate the papillary cores and lesion periphery separately. Use morphology and internal controls; no single marker is definitive in every setting. Low-grade atypical proliferation or usual ductal hyperplasia? ER, CK5/6 and/or CK14 Low-grade atypical foci are typically strongly and diffusely ER-positive and lack high-molecular-weight cytokeratin expression, whereas usual ductal hyperplasia typically shows a heterogeneous pattern. Correlate with morphology. Is neuroendocrine differentiation present in a suspected SPC? Synaptophysin, INSM1, chromogranin, as appropriate Neuroendocrine differentiation is common in SPC, but it is a supporting feature rather than a substitute for the characteristic architecture and cytology. What is the phenotype of a suspected EPC? ER, PR, HER2; Ki-67 when appropriate Typical EPC is usually ER-positive, often PR-positive, HER2-negative, and has low-to-moderate proliferation. Phenotype alone must not be used to diagnose invasion. Absence of myoepithelial cells along papillary cores does not by itself establish invasive carcinoma. Reactive myofibroblasts may express calponin and SMA; vascular pericytes may express actin, calponin, or SMMHC; scattered neoplastic cells may express p63. Sclerosing papilloma can entrap epithelium and mimic invasion. A panel of myoepithelial markers may be helpful. On core biopsy, fragmentation may prevent assessment of the full epithelial–stromal interface or lesion boundary. Displaced epithelium at a recent biopsy site may mimic invasion. Myoepithelial IHC can be non-contributory if myoepithelial cells were not displaced. Infarction or poor tissue preservation can obscure architecture; absent staining in compromised tissue should not automatically be interpreted as a true negative. PathologyGPS / Breast / Epithelial Lesions / Papillary Lesions Breast · Epithelial lesions Breast Papillary Lesions A morphology-first diagnostic guide focused on histology, myoepithelial distribution, targeted immunohistochemistry, and the practical differential diagnosis. Educational reference prototype · Requires expert review before clinical deployment Diagnostic GPS Histology table IHC guide Pitfalls Core biopsy Start with H&E architecture. Map where myoepithelial cells are present or absent, then integrate epithelial cytology, lesion boundaries, and targeted IHC. Myoepithelial status is a location-dependent observation—not a stand-alone diagnosis. true Branch A · Myoepithelium on cores Consider papilloma Assess whether the epithelial proliferation is benign, atypical, or DCIS. For low-grade atypia in a papilloma, use extent ( < 3 mm vs ≥ 3 mm ) alongside grade and morphology. Branch B · Myoepithelium absent on cores Classify architecture and boundary Consider papillary DCIS, EPC, SPC, or invasive papillary carcinoma in the appropriate morphologic setting. Assess the peripheral layer and seek unequivocal invasion before diagnosing an invasive component. When the core biopsy is insufficient If fragmentation or limited sampling prevents definitive classification, a qualified category such as “atypical papillary lesion” or “at least papillary carcinoma in situ” may be appropriate, with excision for complete characterization when indicated. Histology: rapid differential table Use this table to organize the differential; the final diagnosis depends on the complete morphology and adequate sampling. Entity Architecture Myoepithelium on cores Peripheral layer Key discriminator IHC: answer a specific question Select stains to resolve a morphologic uncertainty. Interpret staining distribution and quality rather than relying on positive or negative results alone. Markers / approach Interpretation IHC pitfall: Reactive myofibroblasts, vascular pericytes, and occasional neoplastic cells can mimic myoepithelial staining. Correlate with cell location, morphology, and controls. High-yield diagnostic pitfalls ! Core biopsy: minimum review checklist Is a discrete papillary lesion present, rather than focal papillary features in another process? Are myoepithelial cells identified along the cores and at the periphery, where assessable? Is the epithelial proliferation heterogeneous/bland or monotonous and atypical? If low-grade atypia is present in a papilloma, what is its measured extent? Is there a capsule or pushing border, and is frank invasion unequivocally demonstrated? Are the tissue quality and internal controls adequate for IHC interpretation? Does the limited sample require a qualified diagnosis or excision for full classification? Diagnostic focus This page focuses on diagnostic morphology, myoepithelial distribution, targeted immunohistochemistry, and the practical differential diagnosis. Interpret findings in the context of the complete specimen and clinical-radiologic correlation. On this page Diagnostic pitfalls Core biopsy checklist Core principle H&E architecture → map myoepithelium → characterize epithelium → assess boundary/invasion → targeted IHC → integrate or qualify.

title: Precursor Lesions
content: Usual ductal hyperplasia (UDH) Usually TDLU; may involve larger ducts Haphazard, heterogeneous proliferation; fenestrations and irregular slit-like peripheral lumina; thin, stretched bridges Mixed cell population, variable nuclear size/orientation, streaming; grooves and pseudoinclusions may be present CK5/6 or CK14 mosaic/heterogeneous; ER heterogeneous Mixed phenotype and irregular architecture; not the monotonous, rigid pattern of ADH/DCIS Columnar cell change / hyperplasia (CCL) TDLU Enlarged, dilated acini with irregular contours; columnar lining and apical snouts; 1–2 layers in change, stratification/tufting >2 layers in hyperplasia No monomorphic low-grade atypia ER positive; high-molecular-weight cytokeratins such as CK5/6 absent Columnar cells and apical snouts without low-grade cytologic atypia Flat epithelial atypia (FEA) Dilated acini with smooth/rounded contours; one or more layers; no well-developed bridges, arcades, or micropapillae Low-grade, monomorphic atypia; rounded, uniform nuclei Strong diffuse ER; CK5/6 negative Low-grade atypia without intraluminal architecture Atypical ductal hyperplasia (ADH) Usually TDLU; may occur in papilloma or fibroadenoma Rigid bridges/bars/arcades, bulbous micropapillae, or cribriform spaces; partial involvement or limited contiguous extent Monomorphic low-grade cells, evenly spaced round nuclei, distinct borders; no intermediate/high-grade nuclei or necrosis Strong diffuse ER; CK5/6 and CK14 negative Low-grade DCIS-like morphology, but limited extent; quantitative distinction Sclerosing adenosis Lobulocentric TDLU proliferation Small compressed/distorted acini in collagenous stroma; lobular architecture maintained, sometimes extending into fat Bland epithelial and myoepithelial cells Myoepithelial markers may be needed: p63, calponin, SMMHC Lobulocentric growth and retained myoepithelial layer/basement membrane Apocrine adenosis / adenoma Adenosis: lobulocentric acini distorted by sclerosis. Adenoma: well-circumscribed compact glands with little stroma Abundant granular/eosinophilic or foamy cytoplasm, apical snouts, prominent nucleolus; assess nuclear variation Typically AR+, ER−, PR−; EMA and CK8/18 positive; myoepithelium may be attenuated Apocrine phenotype; adenoma is well delineated, while adenosis remains lobulocentric and sclerotic Microglandular adenosis (MGA) Usually unifocal; non-lobulocentric Haphazard small round glands, open lumina with secretions; single epithelial layer; no myoepithelium but continuous basement membrane Classic MGA bland; atypical MGA shows crowding, multilayering, atypia and sometimes mitoses S100+, often EGFR+; ER/PR/HER2 negative; basement membrane highlighted by collagen IV/laminin; myoepithelial markers negative No myoepithelial layer does not equal invasion: confirm continuous basement membrane and assess for atypia/invasive carcinoma Radial scar / complex sclerosing lesion Lobulocentric sclerosing lesion Central hyalinized collagen/elastosis with entrapped irregular benign tubules; stellate and zonal; larger/disorganized lesions termed complex sclerosing lesions Usually bland; associated UDH, apocrine metaplasia, or atypia may occur p63, calponin, SMMHC if myoepithelial layer is difficult to see Central elastotic nidus and radiating architecture; atypia or carcinoma may coexist UDH Heterogeneous / mosaic Heterogeneous Mixed epithelial phenotype supports usual hyperplasia FEA / ADH / low-grade DCIS Negative Strong diffuse Shared low-grade neoplasia phenotype; morphology and extent distinguish entities Sclerosing adenosis / radial scar p63, calponin, SMMHC highlight myoepithelium Not the primary discriminator Use a nuclear and a cytoplasmic marker when invasion is a concern MGA Absent Usually negative Continuous basement membrane (collagen IV/laminin) surrounds glands Apocrine lesions May be attenuated; interpret carefully AR+, EMA/CK8/18+ support apocrine differentiation ← Breast Pathology PathologyGPS · Breast Breast Precursor and Proliferative Lesions A practical diagnostic guide to benign epithelial proliferations, low-grade precursor lesions, adenosis, and selected sclerosing lesions—with emphasis on architecture, cytology, immunohistochemistry, and core biopsy limitations. Morphology first IHC as an adjunct Quantify extent Radiology–pathology correlation Diagnostic GPS 1 · Low power Is the process duct-centered, lobulocentric, or haphazard/non-lobulocentric? 2 · Cytology Heterogeneous cells favor UDH; monotonous low-grade cells raise FEA/ADH/DCIS. 3 · Architecture Look for fenestrations, apical snouts, rigid bridges, cribriform spaces, or sclerosis. 4 · Myoepithelium / BM Use targeted IHC when invasion is in the differential; MGA is BM-positive but myoepithelium-negative. 5 · Extent & concordance For ADH versus low-grade DCIS, quantify extent and integrate sampling and imaging. Core Morphologic Comparison Use the horizontal scroll area on narrow screens. Entity Typical site Architecture Cytology IHC clues Key discriminator bg-slate-50/70 bg-white UDH vs. Low-Grade Neoplasia Feature Cell population Monotonous / clonal-appearing Nuclear orientation Haphazard; overlapping Evenly spaced, regular Irregular fenestrations; thin stretched bridges Rigid bridges, arcades, bulbous micropapillae or cribriform pattern (ADH/DCIS) ER Usually strong and diffuse CK5/6 Mosaic / heterogeneous Selected IHC / Basement Membrane Guide Lesion Useful stains Interpretive point High-Value Diagnostic Pitfalls ADH vs. low-grade DCIS is quantitative The distinction depends on extent and involvement, not a reliable cytologic dividing line. Published thresholds are guidelines; apply cautiously to core biopsies where the full lesion may not be represented. Do not diagnose invasion from sclerosis alone Sclerosing adenosis and radial scar can entrap and distort glands, sometimes extending into fat. Assess lobulocentric architecture and myoepithelial cells. MGA lacks myoepithelial cells Unlike invasive carcinoma, classic MGA retains a continuous basement membrane. Evaluate glandular crowding, atypia, and associated carcinoma. Myoepithelium may be attenuated In apocrine adenosis and sclerosing lesions, a thin or focally inconspicuous layer is not by itself proof of invasion. FEA is not equivalent to ADH FEA has low-grade cytologic atypia but lacks the architectural complexity required for ADH. Imaging concordance and adequate sampling matter. Associated lesions matter Atypia or carcinoma can involve radial scars, sclerosing adenosis, papillomas, and other benign lesions; examine the entire morphologic context. Core Biopsy Review Checklist Confirm the imaging target and radiology–pathology concordance. Identify the dominant pattern at low power before interpreting individual glands. Assess nuclear uniformity, polarity, cell borders, and architectural rigidity. For ADH, document the extent and whether the lesion is fully represented. Use myoepithelial and basement membrane stains selectively, with morphology leading. Look for associated FEA, ADH, DCIS, lobular neoplasia, or invasive carcinoma. For calcification targets, confirm that the sampled histology accounts for the calcifications. Consider a second review for borderline ADH/DCIS or difficult FEA cases. If sampling is limited, use a descriptive diagnosis or qualified interpretation when appropriate. Risk and Precursor Context These lesions do not carry equivalent biologic meaning. UDH and sclerosing adenosis are benign proliferations associated with a modest increase in subsequent breast cancer risk. CCL/FEA belong to the low-grade neoplasia pathway but have a low reported progression risk. ADH is a recognized high-risk lesion and early neoplastic step related to low-grade DCIS. MGA is benign in its classic form but may coexist with atypical MGA and carcinoma, including triple-negative carcinoma. Radial scar/complex sclerosing lesion is benign; concern depends in part on associated atypia, sampling, and imaging concordance. This page is a diagnostic reference, not a substitute for current institutional protocols or multidisciplinary radiology–pathology assessment. PathologyGPS · Breast Diagnostic Reference

title: Rare Invasive Neoplasms
content: acinic Acinic Cell–Like Carcinoma Salivary gland–like carcinoma Granular or clear cells, often with PAS-D-positive cytoplasmic granules; frequently associated with an MGA-like pattern. Architecture ranges from microglandular (MGA-like) growth to solid nests, sometimes with central necrosis; the patterns may merge. At least a subset of tumour cells has abundant, variably eosinophilic and basophilic granular cytoplasm. Paneth-like cells may occur but are uncommon. Cells may have clear cytoplasm, centrally located atypical nuclei, and distinct nucleoli; atypia and mitotic activity are often more pronounced in solid areas. High-grade DCIS may be present. A high-grade invasive component or metaplastic carcinoma may coexist. Often triple-negative, although rare ER- and/or PR-positive cases have been reported. Serous/acinar differentiation: lysozyme and α1-antichymotrypsin; S100, EMA, and low-molecular-weight keratins are commonly positive. PAS-D can highlight intracellular granules. CK5/6, GCDFP-15, and AR may be positive in subsets. NR4A3 immunohistochemistry is generally negative in breast acinic cell–like carcinoma; this helps distinguish it from salivary gland acinic cell carcinoma. The molecular profile is closer to triple-negative breast carcinoma and the microglandular adenosis (MGA) family than to salivary gland acinic cell carcinoma. The NR4A3-associated t(4;9) rearrangement characteristic of many salivary gland acinic cell carcinomas has not been identified in breast acinic cell–like carcinoma. Microglandular adenosis and atypical MGA: basement membrane material surrounds MGA glands; EMA is commonly negative in MGA. The boundary can be difficult in limited samples. Secretory carcinoma: consider ETV6::NTRK3 testing when morphology overlaps; this fusion is not characteristic of acinic cell–like carcinoma. Conventional high-grade triple-negative carcinoma and mixed carcinoma; use cytology and acinar differentiation markers to support classification. Outcome data are limited. Pure acinic cell–like carcinoma often has a relatively favorable course, but nodal and distant metastases have been reported. A coexisting high-grade component is associated with more aggressive behavior. MGA-like and/or solid architecture with granular cytoplasm. Eosinophilic and basophilic cytoplasmic granules, ideally highlighted by PAS-D. Supportive serous/acinar immunophenotype, interpreted with morphology. adcc Adenoid Cystic Carcinoma (AdCC) Dual epithelial–myoepithelial cell populations with true lumina and basement-membrane-rich pseudolumina; MYB pathway alterations are common. Classic AdCC: tubular and cribriform areas with luminal epithelial cells and peripheral/basal myoepithelial cells. True lumina contain epithelial mucin; pseudolumina contain stromal matrix and basement membrane material, sometimes with fibroblasts and small vessels. Classic tumours usually have low mitotic activity, limited atypia, and no prominent necrosis; perineural invasion may occur. Solid-basaloid AdCC (SB-AdCC) shows solid nests or trabeculae of basaloid cells, increased atypia and mitoses, and sometimes necrosis. High-grade transformation is rare. Luminal cells: CK7/CK8 and EMA; KIT (CD117) is often strong in the luminal component. Myoepithelial/basal cells: p63, CK5/6, CK14, calponin, smooth muscle myosin heavy chain, or CD10, depending on the case. Collagen IV and laminin highlight basement membrane material in pseudolumina. MYB is often diffusely positive in classic AdCC. Most cases are ER-negative, PR-negative, and HER2-negative. Classic AdCC commonly harbors MYB::NFIB fusion; MYBL1 rearrangements or MYB amplification may occur in fusion-negative cases. MYB/MYBL1 rearrangements are less frequent in SB-AdCC; alterations involving chromatin modifiers or NOTCH signaling may be found. Tubular carcinoma and invasive cribriform carcinoma: usually strongly ER/PR-positive and lack the characteristic dual cell population and matrix-filled pseudolumina. Microglandular adenosis: lacks the characteristic dual epithelial–myoepithelial composition of AdCC. Collagenous spherulosis: benign intraductal process; correlate with the overall architecture and a generally less supportive KIT/MYB profile. SB-AdCC may mimic basaloid carcinoma or small cell neuroendocrine carcinoma; search for classic AdCC areas and use neuroendocrine markers when appropriate. Classic breast AdCC usually behaves favorably despite a triple-negative phenotype. SB-AdCC has a higher risk of nodal and distant metastasis. Prognosis in high-grade transformation is uncertain because reported cases are few. Classic: invasive tubular/cribriform/solid tumour with dual cell populations and true lumina plus matrix-filled pseudolumina. SB-AdCC: basaloid solid nests/trabeculae, often with increased mitotic activity and atypia. Use immunohistochemistry and, when needed, molecular testing to confirm the diagnosis. secretory Secretory Carcinoma Microcystic/honeycomb, tubular, solid, or papillary growth with abundant intracellular and extracellular secretions; ETV6::NTRK3 is characteristic. Polygonal cells have eosinophilic granular or vacuolated cytoplasm and round-to-oval nuclei. Architectural patterns include microcystic/honeycomb, tubular, solid, and papillary areas, often mixed within one tumour. Intracytoplasmic and extracellular eosinophilic or amphophilic secretions are a key clue; they are commonly PAS-, mucicarmine-, and Alcian blue-positive. Nuclear atypia and mitotic activity are usually mild to moderate and low, respectively; an in situ component may be present. Often positive for S100, mammaglobin, SOX10, MUC4, TRPS1, and polyclonal CEA; CK5/6 and/or EGFR may be positive. Most cases are ER-negative, PR-negative, and HER2-negative, although weak ER/PR expression can occur. Pan-TRK immunohistochemistry can be a useful screening adjunct, but a negative result does not always exclude an NTRK fusion. ETV6::NTRK3 fusion is the defining molecular alteration in most cases and can be confirmed by RNA-based sequencing or an appropriate FISH/RT-PCR assay. Rare NTRK1 fusions have been reported. Molecular confirmation may also identify eligibility for TRK-targeted therapy in recurrent or metastatic disease. Acinic cell–like carcinoma: look for prominent granular cytoplasm and serous differentiation; ETV6::NTRK3 supports secretory carcinoma. Mucoepidermoid carcinoma: identify basaloid/intermediate, epidermoid, and mucous cell populations; MAML2 rearrangement supports MEC. Mucinous cystadenocarcinoma and other mucin-producing lesions, especially in limited biopsies. Usually indolent, with generally favorable long-term outcomes, but late recurrence and rare aggressive cases occur. Nodal metastases are documented; distant metastases are uncommon. Characteristic secretory morphology with intracellular and extracellular secretions. Supportive immunophenotype, commonly including S100 and mammaglobin. ETV6::NTRK3 fusion or another appropriate molecular finding is highly supportive. mec Mucoepidermoid Carcinoma (MEC) Mixture of mucous, intermediate/basaloid, and epidermoid cells in cystic and solid patterns; true keratinization is not a typical feature. Low-grade tumours often have prominent cystic spaces lined by mucous cells admixed with eosinophilic cells. Solid nests show a spectrum from basaloid/intermediate cells to epidermoid and mucous cells. High-grade tumours are more solid and show greater cytologic atypia, increased mitotic activity, and sometimes necrosis. An intraductal component may be present. True keratinization and squamous pearls argue for another diagnosis. CK14 and p63 highlight basaloid and epidermoid cells; CK7 highlights mucous cells, producing a zonal pattern. GATA3, TRPS1, and mammaglobin may be retained. S100, SOX10, and MUC4 are variably positive. Most reported cases are triple-negative; weak ER positivity and rare HER2 amplification have been reported. Low- to intermediate-grade cases may harbor CRTC1::MAML2 or, less often, CRTC3::MAML2 fusion. MAML2 rearrangement supports MEC in the appropriate morphologic setting; it is not reported in high-grade breast MEC in the source material. Secretory carcinoma: overlapping secretions and bland cytology; secretory carcinoma is associated with ETV6::NTRK3 and lacks the characteristic MEC cell mixture. Metaplastic squamous cell carcinoma: true keratinization favors squamous differentiation rather than MEC. Usual ductal hyperplasia and benign cysts can be mimics in limited samples; evaluate the full architecture and cytology. Low-grade MEC can overlap with breast or cutaneous hidradenoma; clinicopathologic correlation may be needed. Grade is the key prognostic feature. Low- and intermediate-grade tumours generally behave indolently; high-grade MEC may metastasize and can be lethal. A convincing mixture of mucous, intermediate/basaloid, and epidermoid tumour cells. Cystic and/or solid architecture with no true keratinization. Consider MAML2 rearrangement testing when morphology is supportive. mca Mucinous Cystadenocarcinoma Other rare invasive carcinoma Large mucin-filled cystic spaces lined by atypical tall columnar cells with abundant intracytoplasmic mucin and no peripheral myoepithelial layer. Well-circumscribed mass with solid and cystic components; cystic spaces may contain gelatinous material. Cysts are lined by tall columnar cells with basally located nuclei, stratification, tufting, and papillary formations. Abundant intracytoplasmic mucin and luminal mucin are present; atypia can vary within the same tumour. Adjacent DCIS may be present but is not required. Most cases are ER-negative, PR-negative, and HER2-negative, although rare ER-positive or HER2-positive cases have been reported. Typically CK7-positive and CK20-negative/CDX2-negative; TRPS1 may support breast origin in the appropriate context. The cystic structures lack a peripheral myoepithelial layer. Molecular data are limited and no clinically established defining molecular alteration is currently identified in the source material. Conventional mucinous carcinoma: usually strongly ER/PR-positive and does not show the same large cystic architecture lined by tall mucinous columnar cells. Encapsulated papillary carcinoma: usually ER/PR-positive and lacks the prominent intracytoplasmic mucin characteristic of mucinous cystadenocarcinoma. Metastatic pancreatobiliary, ovarian, or gastrointestinal mucinous cystadenocarcinoma must be excluded, particularly when adjacent DCIS is absent; use a focused panel and clinical correlation. Reported cases are few. Many patients have had favorable outcomes, but local recurrence, distant metastasis, and disease-related deaths have been documented. Follow-up data remain limited. Invasive carcinoma with large mucin-filled cystic spaces. Atypical tall columnar lining cells with abundant intracytoplasmic mucin. Exclude a metastasis from another primary site when the clinical or morphologic context warrants it. tccrp Tall Cell Carcinoma with Reversed Polarity (TCCRP) Tall columnar cells in solid/solid-papillary nests with nuclei at the apical pole; IDH2 p.Arg172 mutation is common. Circumscribed nests, often in dense fibrous stroma, with delicate fibrovascular cores creating a solid-papillary pattern. Tall columnar cells have abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm and typically bland round-to-oval nuclei, sometimes with grooves or intranuclear inclusions. The defining feature is reversed polarity: nuclei are apical rather than basal. Foamy histiocytes may occur in fibrovascular cores; true papillae or colloid-like cystic material can be present. Mitoses are usually rare. Tumour nests generally lack a myoepithelial layer, supporting classification as invasive even without a conspicuous desmoplastic response. Usually triple-negative, with rare weak or focal hormone receptor expression; almost all reported cases are HER2-negative. CK7 and CK5/6 or CK14 are commonly expressed; basal keratin staining may be mosaic-like. Calretinin may be positive. Chromogranin and synaptophysin are typically negative. IDH2 R172 immunohistochemistry may be useful. Breast markers can be variably positive; TTF-1 and thyroglobulin are expected to be negative. IDH2 p.Arg172 hotspot mutations are common; PIK3CA mutations are also frequent. BRAF mutations and RET/PTC rearrangements characteristic of papillary thyroid carcinoma have not been identified in the cases described in the source material. Tall cell variant of papillary thyroid carcinoma: verify breast origin using clinical history, breast-lineage markers, TTF-1/thyroglobulin, and molecular findings. Solid papillary carcinoma and other papillary breast lesions: pay particular attention to the reversed nuclear polarity and absence of myoepithelial cells. Neuroendocrine neoplasm: chromogranin and synaptophysin are typically negative in TCCRP. Most reported cases have followed an indolent course with favorable outcomes; rare nodal or distant metastases have been described. Published experience remains limited. Predominantly solid-papillary invasive growth composed of tall columnar cells. Unequivocal apical/reversed nuclear polarity. Supportive immunophenotype and, when needed, IDH2 mutation or IDH2 R172 immunohistochemistry. net Neuroendocrine Tumor (NET) of the Breast Neuroendocrine neoplasm Well-differentiated malignant epithelial neoplasm with convincing neuroendocrine morphology and diffuse, uniform neuroendocrine marker expression. Well-differentiated neuroendocrine architecture may include organoid nests, trabeculae, ribbons, or rosettes, depending on the case. Diagnosis requires correlation of morphology with diffuse, uniform expression of neuroendocrine markers and exclusion of mimics. Neuroendocrine differentiation can occur in other breast carcinoma types; do not classify a tumour as a primary breast NET solely because one neuroendocrine marker is positive. Use a panel of neuroendocrine markers, typically including synaptophysin and chromogranin; interpret staining extent and intensity with morphology. Assess ER, PR, and HER2 as for other invasive breast carcinomas. Breast-lineage markers and a comparison with any prior or concurrent neuroendocrine tumour may be useful in determining the primary site. The source material does not identify a single defining molecular alteration for primary breast NET. Metastatic NET to the breast must be excluded using clinical history, imaging, and comparison with a known primary when available. Solid papillary carcinoma can show neuroendocrine differentiation and should be distinguished by its architecture and overall features. IBC-NST with neuroendocrine differentiation should not automatically be classified as a primary breast NET. Primary breast NETs are extremely rare. Prognosis and management depend on tumour grade, stage, and confirmation that the breast is the primary site. Well-differentiated neuroendocrine morphology. Diffuse and uniform expression of neuroendocrine markers. Reasonable exclusion of metastatic NET and breast carcinoma mimics. nec Neuroendocrine Carcinoma (NEC) of the Breast High-grade malignant epithelial neoplasm with neuroendocrine differentiation; small cell and large cell patterns may occur. High-grade cytology, brisk mitotic activity, and necrosis may be present; small cell morphology includes scant cytoplasm, nuclear molding, and finely granular chromatin. Large cell neuroendocrine carcinoma shows larger cells with more abundant cytoplasm and prominent nucleoli, while retaining neuroendocrine architecture. The diagnosis requires convincing morphology and neuroendocrine marker expression; exclude a metastatic neuroendocrine carcinoma. Synaptophysin and chromogranin are commonly used to support neuroendocrine differentiation; use a panel and interpret in context. Evaluate ER, PR, and HER2 and use breast-lineage markers as appropriate. Clinical and radiologic correlation is essential, particularly to exclude a pulmonary or gastrointestinal primary. No single defining molecular alteration is established in the source material for breast NEC; testing should be guided by the differential diagnosis and clinical context. Metastatic small cell lung carcinoma or another extra-mammary NEC: correlate with imaging and history; immunophenotype alone may not establish the site. Solid-basaloid AdCC and other high-grade basaloid carcinomas: seek defining morphology and use neuroendocrine markers. IBC-NST with focal neuroendocrine differentiation: assess the dominant morphology and extent of neuroendocrine features. Breast small cell NEC is associated with a worse prognosis than other breast carcinomas with neuroendocrine differentiation. Localized disease is generally approached using breast cancer principles, while metastatic cases may be considered for regimens used in small cell lung cancer in multidisciplinary care. High-grade neuroendocrine carcinoma morphology. Supportive neuroendocrine marker expression. Exclusion of metastatic neuroendocrine carcinoma from another primary site. 1. Recognize the pattern Start with H&E: secretions, granular cytoplasm, dual cell populations, mucous/intermediate/epidermoid cells, reversed polarity, or neuroendocrine morphology. 2. Choose a focused panel Use morphology-directed immunohistochemistry rather than a broad, indiscriminate panel. Include ER/PR/HER2 for clinical classification and lineage markers when the primary site is uncertain. 3. Confirm when it matters Consider fusion or mutation testing for ETV6::NTRK3, MYB::NFIB/MYBL1, MAML2, or IDH2 when the differential diagnosis or treatment implications warrant it. 4. Exclude metastasis For mucinous cystadenocarcinoma and neuroendocrine neoplasms in particular, correlate with history and imaging and exclude an extra-mammary primary. 5. Report the clinical essentials Document type, Nottingham grade when applicable, invasive size, focality, LVI, margins, nodal findings, associated in situ disease, and predictive biomarkers according to current protocols. Acinic cell–like carcinoma Granular cytoplasm; MGA-like to solid Lysozyme, α1-antichymotrypsin, S100, EMA; PAS-D granules No salivary-type NR4A3 rearrangement/overexpression Adenoid cystic carcinoma Tubular/cribriform; true lumina and pseudolumina Luminal CK7/EMA; basal/myoepithelial p63/CK5/6; MYB MYB::NFIB; MYBL1 alterations in some cases Secretory carcinoma Microcystic/honeycomb; intra- and extracellular secretions S100, mammaglobin, SOX10, MUC4; pan-TRK adjunct ETV6::NTRK3 Mucoepidermoid carcinoma Mucous + intermediate/basaloid + epidermoid cells CK7 in mucous cells; p63/CK14 in basaloid/epidermoid cells CRTC1::MAML2 or CRTC3::MAML2 in some cases Mucinous cystadenocarcinoma Mucin-filled cysts lined by tall mucinous columnar cells CK7+, CK20−/CDX2−; TRPS1 may support breast origin No established defining alteration TCCRP Tall columnar cells with apical nuclei; solid-papillary nests CK7 plus CK5/6 or CK14; IDH2 R172 IHC may help IDH2 p.Arg172; PIK3CA often mutated Breast NET Well-differentiated neuroendocrine morphology Diffuse synaptophysin/chromogranin; ER/PR/HER2 as indicated No single defining alteration in source Breast NEC High-grade neuroendocrine morphology, brisk mitoses/necrosis Neuroendocrine marker panel; breast-lineage markers as indicated PathologyGPS / Breast Pathology Rare Invasive Breast Neoplasms A morphology-first diagnostic guide to salivary gland–like carcinomas, other rare invasive carcinomas, and breast neuroendocrine neoplasms. H&E pattern recognition Focused IHC Molecular confirmation Primary vs. metastatic Core principle Morphology leads Recognize the defining architecture and cytology first. Immunostains and molecular assays should resolve a specific diagnostic question. Clinical caution Triple-negative does not mean one biology Several rare entities are usually triple-negative but can have an indolent course. Accurate classification helps avoid both underdiagnosis and overtreatment. Critical exclusion Rule out an extra-mammary primary This is especially important for neuroendocrine neoplasms and mucinous cystadenocarcinoma when an associated in situ component is absent. Diagnostic GPS A practical workflow Use the smallest panel that answers the morphologic question, and interpret results in context. Quick comparison Morphology, immunophenotype, and molecular clues Markers are supportive, not standalone diagnoses. Use locally validated assays and current interpretive criteria. Use IHC to answer a specific differential diagnosis or lineage question. Order fusion/mutation testing when it can resolve classification or treatment relevance. For NET/NEC and mucinous cystadenocarcinoma, consider whether metastasis from another site has been excluded. Document invasive size, histologic type, grade when applicable, focality, LVI, margins, and nodes. Report ER, PR, and HER2 using current validated protocols; include additional biomarkers only when indicated. Educational reference for pathologists. title: Epithelial Myoepithelial Tumors
content: Pleomorphic adenoma Benign epithelial-myoepithelial tumor A circumscribed biphasic neoplasm with epithelial glands and myoepithelial cells embedded in characteristic chondromyxoid stroma. Usually a well-circumscribed, lobulated nodule, often retroareolar. Glands and epithelial strands show an inner luminal layer and an outer myoepithelial layer. Myoepithelial-like spindle or stellate cells are present in a myxoid, chondromyxoid, or occasionally chondroid/osseous matrix. Significant atypia, atypical mitoses, and tumor necrosis are not expected. Matrix-producing metaplastic carcinoma may also contain abundant matrix, but typically shows malignant cytology, disorganized tumor nests, loss of an orderly peripheral myoepithelial layer, and often stromal invasion/desmoplasia. Benign in most cases. Incomplete excision, especially with extensive polypoid intraductal growth, can lead to recurrence. Rare malignant transformation has been reported. Classic adenomyoepithelioma (AME) Tumor of uncertain malignant potential A biphasic neoplasm with small glandular spaces lined by inner luminal epithelial cells and a conspicuous proliferation of abluminal myoepithelial cells. Often a circumscribed or multilobulated nodule, sometimes with central sclerosis. The myoepithelial population may be clear-cell, spindle, myoid, plasmacytoid, or epithelioid. Patterns include tubular, spindle-cell, lobulated, and papillary forms; mixed patterns are common. Satellite nodules can occur and are not, by themselves, proof of malignancy. Atypical AME may show mild-to-moderate cytologic atypia and increased mitotic activity; atypical mitoses or convincing malignant features warrant concern for malignant transformation. Look for a nodular proliferation of enlarged, plump myoepithelial cells around haphazardly arranged glands. This helps separate AME from papilloma with myoepithelial hyperplasia, adenosis, tubular adenoma, and microglandular adenosis. Most behave indolently after complete excision, but local recurrence, rare metastasis, and malignant transformation have been reported. Classic AME is therefore best regarded as a neoplasm of uncertain malignant potential. Malignant adenomyoepithelioma (M-AME) Malignant epithelial and/or myoepithelial component An AME with malignant transformation of the luminal epithelial component, myoepithelial component, or both, usually with recognizable AME-like architecture somewhere in the tumor. Moderate-to-marked cytologic atypia, increased mitotic activity, and tumor necrosis are common warning features. The tumor may show a focally irregular/infiltrative outline, stromal desmoplasia, and an inflammatory response. Luminal malignancy may resemble invasive carcinoma of no special type or a special type; myoepithelial malignancy may show spindle or epithelioid overgrowth. Metaplastic patterns, including spindle-cell, squamous, low-grade adenosquamous, and matrix-producing carcinoma, have been described. Extensive sampling may be needed to find a residual classic AME component. Atypical AME and M-AME overlap. Do not classify a lesion as malignant from mitotic count or Ki-67 alone; integrate cytology, necrosis, architecture, invasion, and the relationship between the atypical and conventional components. Potentially aggressive. Hematogenous metastases, particularly to the lungs and sometimes the brain, are reported; nodal metastases are uncommon. Management and staging depend on the malignant component and clinical context. p63 / p40 Nuclear myoepithelial markers Use as part of a panel; staining can be variable in AME and may be lost or altered in malignant areas. SMMHC Myoepithelial marker Useful alongside p63 to demonstrate the outer cell population; avoid reliance on a single stain. Calponin / SMA Myoepithelial or myoid differentiation Can support myoepithelial differentiation; SMA is robust but less specific. CK5/6 / CK14 Basal-type cytokeratins May highlight myoepithelial/basal differentiation, but patterns can be paradoxical or heterogeneous in AME. S100 / SOX10 Myoepithelial-associated markers Supportive in context; neither is independently diagnostic. Low-molecular-weight CK / EMA Luminal epithelial component Can help identify the inner epithelial population in a biphasic lesion. ER / PR Hormone receptor status Variable in AME; absence of hormone receptors does not by itself establish malignancy. Ki-67 / p53 Proliferation / tumor suppressor pattern Higher proliferation or aberrant p53 may support concern, but no single threshold reliably separates atypical from malignant AME. HRAS p.Gln61Arg IHC / molecular testing Selected malignant AME work-up A positive result can support an AME relationship in a carcinoma with compatible morphology; use only when clinically/pathologically indicated. Matrix-producing metaplastic carcinoma Atypical malignant cells in nests or aggregates; disorganized architecture; no orderly continuous myoepithelial rim; necrosis, atypical mitoses, and/or invasion may be present. Mucinous carcinoma Neoplastic epithelial cells in epithelial-type mucin; lacks the organized biphasic epithelial-myoepithelial architecture of pleomorphic adenoma. Intraductal papilloma with myoepithelial hyperplasia Papillary fronds and fibrovascular cores are central. In AME, myoepithelial cells are often more numerous, larger, and plumper, with a nodular or multilobulated tumor pattern. Adenosis / tubular adenoma / microglandular adenosis Correlate overall architecture and myoepithelial-cell prominence. Tubular AME typically has conspicuous hyperplastic myoepithelial cells and larger, more irregular tubules than microglandular adenosis. Adenoid cystic carcinoma Can overlap morphologically and may share some marker expression. MYB rearrangements typical of adenoid cystic carcinoma are not characteristic of AME; interpret molecular results with morphology. Invasive carcinoma with metaplastic differentiation Search extensively for a conventional AME component and determine whether the epithelial and/or myoepithelial populations show malignant cytology, destructive invasion, and increased mitoses. PathologyGPS Breast Papillary lesions Adenomas Breast pathology · Diagnostic guide Epithelial-Myoepithelial Tumors A morphology-first approach to biphasic breast neoplasms, with emphasis on recognizing the two cell populations and identifying features that raise concern for malignancy. H&E first IHC panel approach Diagnostic pitfalls Core diagnostic question Is this a true biphasic neoplasm—and is either component malignant? Luminal cells: epithelial differentiation. Abluminal cells: myoepithelial differentiation. Malignancy: assess cytology, mitoses, necrosis, invasion, and component-specific changes. 01 · Overview Classification at a glance Breast epithelial-myoepithelial tumors are a heterogeneous group of biphasic neoplasms. The principal entities covered here are pleomorphic adenoma, classic adenomyoepithelioma (AME), and malignant adenomyoepithelioma (M-AME). Adenoid cystic carcinoma is a separate entity and should be considered in the differential diagnosis when morphology overlaps. Benign Biphasic glands and strands in chondromyxoid stroma. Classic AME Uncertain malignant potential Prominent, often enlarged abluminal myoepithelial proliferation. Malignant AME Malignant Malignancy in luminal cells, myoepithelial cells, or both. Terminology note For breast tumors with malignant epithelial and/or myoepithelial components arising in an AME-like lesion, use malignant adenomyoepithelioma or an appropriate descriptive diagnosis. The term “epithelial-myoepithelial carcinoma” is not recommended for these breast tumors in the source classification. 02 · Diagnostic workflow Diagnostic GPS 1 Start at low power Assess circumscription, lobulation, satellite nodules, sclerosis, matrix, papillary growth, and any irregular infiltrative edge. 2 Confirm the biphasic pattern Look for inner luminal epithelial cells and an outer myoepithelial population. Determine whether the myoepithelial cells are thin and orderly or conspicuous, enlarged, and proliferative. 3 Characterize the architecture Consider glands/strands in chondromyxoid matrix (pleomorphic adenoma) versus a prominent myoepithelial proliferation around glands (AME). Patterns in AME may be tubular, spindle-cell, lobulated, or papillary. 4 Search for malignant features Evaluate nuclear atypia, mitotic activity and atypical mitoses, necrosis, destructive invasion, desmoplasia, and an inflammatory response. Extensively sample heterogeneous or large lesions. 5 Use a targeted IHC panel Combine nuclear and cytoplasmic myoepithelial markers with luminal epithelial markers. Interpret staining distribution and intensity in the context of H&E. 6 Classify and communicate Separate classic AME, atypical AME, and M-AME. If DCIS arises in an AME, report it as DCIS and manage it accordingly. 03 · Entity profiles Key entities and morphology Morphologic checklist Diagnostic pitfall Behavior / clinical significance Atypical AME: mild-to-moderate cytologic atypia and increased mitotic activity may occur without sufficient evidence for malignancy. Atypical mitoses, substantial necrosis, marked atypia, or destructive invasion should prompt careful evaluation for M-AME. 04 · Ancillary studies Immunohistochemistry: use a panel Myoepithelial marker expression in AME can be variable and unpredictable. No single stain should be used in isolation. A practical panel often combines a nuclear marker such as p63 with a cytoplasmic marker such as SMMHC, supplemented by other markers according to the morphologic question and tissue quality. Marker(s) Role Interpretive note Expected pattern in a biphasic lesion Luminal epithelial markers can highlight the inner layer, while a combination of myoepithelial markers supports the outer population. Confirm that the distribution matches the H&E architecture. Important limitation Malignant AME may show an aberrant immunoprofile with loss of a clear distinction between the two cell populations. Negative or patchy staining does not exclude the diagnosis. 05 · Differential diagnosis High-yield differential diagnosis Entity Features that help separate it 06 · Molecular context Molecular findings: supportive, not a substitute for morphology Reported alterations include PIK3CA hotspot mutations in both ER-positive and ER-negative tumors, AKT1 hotspot mutations more often in ER-positive tumors, and recurrent HRAS hotspot mutations particularly in ER-negative tumors. Alterations involving and have also been reported. Detection of an appropriate hotspot alteration, including a compatible p.Gln61 alteration, may support an AME origin in a carcinoma with fitting morphology. These findings are not required for routine diagnosis. Molecular testing should answer a specific diagnostic question and be interpreted with morphology and immunophenotype. 07 · Reporting Sign-out checklist Is the lesion truly biphasic? Are luminal and myoepithelial populations both recognizable? Is the tumor circumscribed or infiltrative? Is there cytologic atypia, and in which component? Are mitoses increased or atypical? Is tumor necrosis present? Is there destructive invasion, desmoplasia, or an inflammatory response? Has the lesion been adequately sampled for a malignant component? Does the IHC pattern support the H&E interpretation? Is any associated DCIS or invasive carcinoma separately described? Reporting principle When malignancy is present, specify whether the luminal epithelial component, the myoepithelial component, or both are malignant, and describe the malignant histologic pattern whenever possible. Educational reference for professional use. Interpret findings in conjunction with the complete specimen, clinical and radiologic context, and current institutional diagnostic standards. title: Fibroepithelial Lesions
content: 01 Confirm a biphasic fibroepithelial lesion Identify both epithelial and stromal components. On core biopsy, integrate the tissue pattern with imaging and clinical findings; a cellular fibroepithelial lesion may not be classifiable with certainty on limited tissue. 02 Look for the dominant architecture Pericanalicular and/or intracanalicular growth with relatively uniform stroma supports fibroadenoma. Exaggerated intracanalicular growth with well-developed, expansile leaf-like stromal fronds raises phyllodes tumor. Disorganized normal ducts, lobules, and fat without a fibroadenoma-like growth pattern supports hamartoma. 03 Assess stromal cellularity and distribution Compare stromal cellularity with the epithelial component and assess whether it is uniform, heterogeneous, or accentuated immediately beneath the epithelium. Periepithelial stromal condensation and stromal heterogeneity support phyllodes tumor in the appropriate architecture. 04 Evaluate atypia, mitoses, overgrowth, and borders For a suspected phyllodes tumor, document stromal cellularity, stromal nuclear atypia, mitotic activity, stromal overgrowth, and tumor border. These features exist on a continuum and must be assessed together, ideally after adequate sampling. 05 Decide what can be concluded on core biopsy A typical fibroadenoma can usually be diagnosed reliably on core. If the lesion is cellular or the distinction from phyllodes tumor is uncertain, consider a qualified diagnosis such as benign fibroepithelial lesion/neoplasm and recommend radiology-pathology correlation and further sampling/excision as appropriate. Hamartoma Well-demarcated, often encapsulated mass with lobules, ducts, fibrous stroma, and adipose tissue in variable proportions Variable fibrous and adipose components; often prominent intralobular fibrosis and atrophic lobules Disorganized but otherwise normal breast components; no characteristic intracanalicular or pericanalicular fibroadenoma pattern. Correlate with imaging and clinical findings. Conventional fibroadenoma Circumscribed biphasic lesion with pericanalicular and/or intracanalicular pattern Usually uniformly low cellularity, without significant atypia; mitoses uncommon No well-developed leaf-like fronds, no stromal overgrowth, no significant stromal atypia, and low stromal mitotic activity. Cellular fibroadenoma Often pericanalicular; mildly to moderately increased stromal cellularity Usually < 1 stromal mitosis/mm² in the cited WHO description; marked atypia and marked heterogeneity are absent Lacks marked stromal atypia/cellularity, exaggerated intracanalicular architecture, periductal subepithelial stromal condensation, and intratumoral heterogeneity. On core, overlap with benign phyllodes tumor may remain. Juvenile fibroadenoma Often pericanalicular, sometimes large and rapidly growing Uniform mild-to-moderate increase in cellularity; fascicular spindle cells without significant nuclear atypia; mitotic activity usually low Age/context plus pericanalicular pattern and usual ductal hyperplasia (often gynecomastoid type) support the diagnosis; increased cellularity alone does not establish phyllodes tumor. Complex fibroadenoma Fibroadenoma with one or more defined additional features Fibroadenoma background; may be smaller than other fibroadenomas At least one of: sclerosing adenosis, epithelial calcifications, papillary apocrine metaplasia, or cysts > 3 mm. Myxoid fibroadenoma Fibroadenoma architecture with extensive myxoid stroma Abundant myxoid change Extensive myxoid stroma is the defining feature; rare cases are associated with Carney complex. Benign phyllodes tumor Exaggerated intracanalicular pattern with expansile leaf-like stromal fronds capped by benign epithelium and myoepithelium Usually more cellular than fibroadenoma; may show periepithelial accentuation and heterogeneity; mitoses usually < 2.5/mm² Well-developed expansile leaf-like fronds and increased stromal cellularity are central. Borders are usually pushing/delimited; stromal atypia is absent or limited and stromal overgrowth is absent. Borderline phyllodes tumor Phyllodes architecture with intermediate or overlapping adverse stromal features Features fall between benign and malignant categories; grading is a combined assessment rather than a single-feature threshold Use when the overall pattern does not meet the threshold for benign or malignant classification. A borderline grade is appropriate when the combined findings fall between benign and malignant categories; tumors may show up to three adverse criteria. Malignant phyllodes tumor Phyllodes tumor, sometimes with marked stromal overgrowth that obscures epithelial elements Marked stromal hypercellularity and atypia, increased mitoses, stromal overgrowth, and/or infiltrative border; malignant heterologous elements may occur At least four of five adverse histological criteria support a malignant grade: marked stromal cellularity, marked stromal atypia, increased mitoses, stromal overgrowth, and infiltrative border. Malignant heterologous elements also support malignancy. Periductal stromal tumor Biphasic pattern with benign ducts surrounded by cellular spindle-cell stroma; lacks typical leaf-like fronds Cellular, variably atypical and mitotically active spindle stroma No distinct tumor outline or obvious fronded architecture, but stromal features resemble phyllodes tumor. It is classified as a subtype of phyllodes tumor. Stromal cellularity Assess degree and distribution; marked and usually diffuse increase supports malignancy. Stromal nuclear atypia Assess degree of pleomorphism; marked atypia is an adverse feature. Mitotic activity Increased mitoses are an adverse feature; a mitotic count of ≥ 5/mm² is an adverse feature supporting a malignant grade. Stromal overgrowth A low-power field containing only stroma and no epithelial elements meets the stated definition. tumor border An infiltrative border is an adverse feature; benign tumors are usually delimited/pushing, although small protrusions may occur. Hamartoma versus fibroadenoma CD34; SMA if a myoid component is suspected Diffuse stromal CD34 staining is often seen in fibroadenoma but is not diffuse in hamartoma; in hamartoma, CD34 is mainly in intralobular stroma. Myoid hamartoma may show diffuse strong SMA. IHC is usually not required for a typical hamartoma. Phyllodes tumor versus metaplastic carcinoma Broad-spectrum cytokeratin and p63, interpreted with morphology; molecular testing may help in selected cases Diffuse epithelial differentiation favors metaplastic carcinoma. Interpret focal keratin expression and p63 positivity cautiously, because these may occur in phyllodes tumors, particularly malignant cases and limited core biopsies. Is a molecular test needed to separate fibroadenoma from phyllodes tumor? Selected molecular assays / targeted sequencing when available and clinically appropriate MED12 alterations occur in both entities and do not independently settle the diagnosis. TERT promoter mutations may favor phyllodes tumor; a five-gene PCR assay may serve as an adjunct on preoperative core biopsy. Do not diagnose phyllodes tumor from stromal cellularity alone. Integrate architecture, periepithelial stromal condensation, heterogeneity, atypia, mitotic activity, overgrowth, and borders. Cellular fibroadenoma and benign phyllodes tumor may overlap, particularly on core biopsy. In uncertain cases, a qualified benign fibroepithelial lesion/neoplasm diagnosis is preferable to false precision. Fibroadenoma-like areas can occur within phyllodes tumors and may be sampled preferentially on core biopsy. Occasional bizarre or multinucleated stromal giant cells in an otherwise benign phyllodes tumor are not, by themselves, a marker of malignancy. Skin ulceration in a large phyllodes tumor does not necessarily imply malignancy; fungating fleshy polypoid growth through skin strongly indicates malignancy. When a malignant phyllodes tumor is suspected, extensive sampling is important because adverse features and malignant components can be focal. For large tumors or those with features suggesting malignancy, sample extensively, with at least two sections per 10 mm of greatest tumor dimension. In a malignant spindle-cell lesion, extensively sample for residual epithelial structures before concluding primary/metastatic sarcoma. Use clinical history and targeted work-up to assess metaplastic carcinoma and other sarcomas. Diagnostic reference · Interpret in conjunction with the complete specimen and clinical context Diagnostic GPS Histology table Phyllodes grading IHC & molecular Pitfalls Core biopsy Start with the biphasic pattern, then decide whether the architecture is fibroadenoma-like, phyllodes-like, or a disorganized collection of normal breast components. For suspected phyllodes tumor, grade the stromal component using the full set of histological parameters rather than one isolated finding. true Branch A Normal components, disorganized Consider hamartoma when ducts, lobules, fibrous tissue, and fat are haphazardly arranged without classic fibroadenoma growth patterns; correlate with imaging. Branch B Uniform biphasic lesion Pericanalicular and/or intracanalicular architecture with relatively uniform, bland stroma supports fibroadenoma. Subtype features may refine the diagnosis. Branch C Leaf-like fronds / stromal concern Consider phyllodes tumor. Evaluate stromal cellularity, atypia, mitoses, overgrowth, and border, then assign benign, borderline, or malignant grade. Biological principle In fibroepithelial tumors, neoplastic progression usually involves the stromal rather than epithelial component. Epithelial atypia, in situ carcinoma, or invasive carcinoma can coexist and should be classified separately. Histology: rapid differential table The table is intentionally wide so the “Key discriminator” column remains readable. On a narrow screen, scroll horizontally. Entity Architecture Stromal pattern Key discriminator row Phyllodes tumor: grading checklist Assess five adverse histological criteria. At least four support a malignant phyllodes tumor diagnosis; document the criteria present and the criterion absent. Parameter What to document Borderline category Tumors with overlapping features require a combined assessment. Tumors with up to three adverse criteria generally fall within the borderline category; document all features and explain any discordance. Sampling matters Phyllodes tumors are heterogeneous. For large tumors or those suspicious for malignancy, submit at least two sections per 10 mm of greatest tumor dimension. IHC & molecular: targeted use IHC is not a substitute for the architecture and stromal assessment. Use ancillary studies only when they address a defined differential diagnosis. Diagnostic question Potential ancillary study Interpretation / limitation Core biopsy: practical approach When fibroadenoma is typical Architecture is characteristic and stromal cellularity is low and uniform. No well-developed stromal fronds, stromal overgrowth, or significant atypia. Core biopsy diagnosis is generally reliable when imaging and pathology are concordant. When phyllodes tumor cannot be excluded Cellular fibroepithelial lesion, stromal heterogeneity, or leaf-like architecture. Limited core may not represent the most diagnostic or highest-grade area. Use clinicoradiologic correlation and consider excision or additional sampling according to the case. Suggested cautious wording when unresolved “Benign fibroepithelial lesion/neoplasm; definitive distinction between cellular fibroadenoma and phyllodes tumor is limited on this core biopsy. Recommend radiologic–pathologic correlation and further evaluation as clinically appropriate.” Example wording for adaptation; not a required reporting template. Diagnostic pitfalls ! On this page Core diagnostic principle The stromal component drives grading in phyllodes tumor. Architecture and the combined stromal criteria matter more than any single feature or ancillary stain.
