title: Genetics
content: brca BRCA-Related Hereditary Cancer BRCA1 / BRCA2 High-penetrance autosomal dominant predisposition to breast and tubo-ovarian cancer; also associated with prostate and pancreatic cancer. Consider with young-onset or bilateral breast cancer, a relevant family history, male breast cancer, or triple-negative disease. BRCA1-associated tumors are more often high-grade, triple-negative, and lymphocyte-rich. BRCA2-associated tumors are more often hormone receptor–positive; no single morphology reliably identifies a carrier. BRCA1-associated tumors may show invasive carcinoma of no special type, a medullary pattern, or metaplastic carcinoma. A pushing border, prominent lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate, marked atypia, and high mitotic activity can support suspicion but are not diagnostic. Pathology cannot establish hereditary status; germline testing is required. A germline pathogenic or likely pathogenic variant establishes the molecular diagnosis. A variant of uncertain significance (VUS) should not be used by itself to direct clinical management. Homologous recombination deficiency may predict sensitivity to PARP inhibitors in an appropriate clinical setting. Do not use morphology, basal markers, or triple-negative status alone to assign BRCA status. pten PTEN Hamartoma Tumor Syndrome PTEN Autosomal dominant syndrome with hamartomas and increased risks of breast, thyroid, endometrial, renal, and other cancers. Cowden syndrome is associated with macrocephaly, mucocutaneous lesions, and multiple hamartomas. Benign breast findings may include hamartomas, fibroadenomas, adenosis, ductal hyperplasia, papillomatosis, and fibrocystic change. Lifetime breast cancer risk in women may be as high as approximately 85% in reported series. Breast cancers are usually conventional invasive carcinoma of no special type, often with associated DCIS. Apocrine differentiation has been reported, but a specific breast cancer morphology is not consistently present. Diagnosis is supported by a germline pathogenic PTEN variant and clinical features within the PHTS spectrum. Clinical criteria and genetics consultation help determine who should undergo testing. A hamartomatous or unusual benign breast lesion may be a clue only when interpreted with the patient's broader phenotype. atm ATM-Related Cancer Predisposition ATM Heterozygous pathogenic variants confer a moderate increase in breast cancer risk. Biallelic pathogenic variants cause ataxia-telangiectasia. Ataxia-telangiectasia features progressive ataxia, telangiectasia, immunodeficiency, and increased malignancy risk. Breast cancer risk is elevated in heterozygous carriers; risk may vary substantially by variant. No reproducible, distinctive breast tumor morphology has been established. Reported tumors are often hormone receptor–positive and may show a luminal phenotype; a BRCA1-like lymphocyte-rich pattern is not typical. Confirm a suspected hereditary predisposition with germline testing and variant-specific interpretation. Do not assume ATM-associated tumors have homologous recombination deficiency or will respond to PARP inhibitors. Distinguish heterozygous breast cancer susceptibility from biallelic ATM-related ataxia-telangiectasia. tp53 Li-Fraumeni Syndrome TP53 Autosomal dominant predisposition to early and multiple primary cancers, including breast cancer, soft-tissue and bone sarcomas, brain tumors, and adrenocortical carcinoma. Very early-onset breast cancer, especially before age 31, may warrant consideration even without a striking family history. Look for multiple primary tumors and a family history of core Li-Fraumeni cancers. Breast cancer risk is high, and many affected patients develop cancer at young ages. Most associated breast cancers are invasive carcinoma of no special type. HER2-positive disease is overrepresented; DCIS and malignant phyllodes tumors are also reported. Consider germline TP53 testing using established clinical criteria and genetics consultation. Germline findings must be distinguished from somatic variants and clonal hematopoiesis when interpreting tumor-only sequencing. A confirmed TP53 germline variant affects surveillance and treatment planning, including careful consideration of radiation exposure. chek2 CHEK2-Related Breast Cancer Predisposition CHEK2 Moderate-penetrance predisposition; risk depends on variant type and family history. The best-studied truncating variant is c.1100del. Risk is more strongly associated with ER-positive than ER-negative breast cancer. Some variants may also be associated with contralateral breast cancer risk. No consistent, pathognomonic morphology has been established. Many reported tumors are hormone receptor–positive; reported luminal A/B associations vary by variant. A germline pathogenic variant supports the diagnosis; interpret missense variants according to current clinical classification. Do not treat every CHEK2 variant as conferring the same level of risk. Variant-specific interpretation matters; a VUS is not equivalent to a pathogenic variant. cdh1 Hereditary Diffuse Gastric and Lobular Breast Cancer CDH1 / CTNNA1 Associated primarily with diffuse gastric cancer and invasive lobular breast carcinoma, particularly with CDH1 pathogenic variants. Consider in families with diffuse gastric cancer and/or lobular breast cancer, especially at younger ages. CDH1 carriers have a substantial lifetime risk of lobular breast cancer. CTNNA1-associated gastric cancer risk is recognized, while the magnitude of lobular breast cancer risk is less certain. The characteristic breast tumor type is invasive lobular carcinoma. Loss of E-cadherin expression is a hallmark of lobular differentiation but does not by itself prove a germline CDH1 variant. Germline testing is guided by personal and family history and appropriate clinical criteria. A pathogenic germline variant should prompt genetics-led assessment of gastric and breast cancer risks. Do not equate loss of E-cadherin in a tumor with hereditary CDH1 syndrome. palb2 PALB2-Related Cancer Predisposition PALB2 Important breast cancer susceptibility gene; pathogenic variants can confer substantial lifetime risk, modified by family history and other factors. Consider in familial breast cancer and in patients meeting criteria for hereditary cancer testing. PALB2 participates in the BRCA-related DNA repair pathway. No specific histologic appearance is sufficient to identify a PALB2 carrier. PALB2-associated tumors are reported more often in ER-negative and/or triple-negative groups than some moderate-risk gene–associated tumors. Diagnosis requires a germline pathogenic or likely pathogenic PALB2 variant. Risk estimates and management should be individualized using current guidance and family history. PALB2 is a key high-risk gene and should not be treated as equivalent to a low-penetrance risk allele. stk11 Peutz-Jeghers Syndrome STK11 Autosomal dominant syndrome with mucocutaneous pigmentation, gastrointestinal hamartomatous polyposis, and increased risk of breast and several other cancers. Characteristic findings include mucocutaneous melanin pigmentation and gastrointestinal polyposis. Breast cancer risk in women is high and may be in the range reported for BRCA1/BRCA2 carriers. Breast cancers do not have a specific, reliably diagnostic histologic phenotype. A germline pathogenic STK11 variant supports molecular confirmation. Management includes syndrome-specific surveillance for breast, gastrointestinal, pancreatic, gynecologic, and other cancers. Recognize the syndromic phenotype; the breast tumor itself may look like a sporadic carcinoma. nf1 Neurofibromatosis Type 1 NF1 Autosomal dominant tumor-predisposition syndrome; women with NF1 have increased breast cancer risk, particularly at younger ages. Look for café-au-lait macules, axillary or inguinal freckling, neurofibromas, optic pathway glioma, Lisch nodules, or characteristic bone lesions. Breast cancer may occur at younger ages and may have a less favorable outcome. Most associated breast cancers are invasive carcinoma of no special type; lobular tumors also occur. No consistent ER, PR, or HER2 phenotype has been established. Diagnosis integrates clinical criteria and/or a pathogenic germline NF1 variant. Breast cancer screening should follow appropriate risk-based guidance. The cutaneous and neurologic phenotype may be more informative than the breast tumor morphology. 1. Recognize the trigger Young age, bilateral or multiple primary cancers, male breast cancer, a relevant family history, or a syndrome-associated phenotype. 2. Interpret the tumor in context Use histologic type, grade, ER/PR/HER2 status, and lymphocytic response as clues—not as proof of a germline variant. 3. Refer for germline assessment Apply current testing criteria and involve genetics professionals. Tumor-only sequencing does not establish germline status. 4. Interpret the result correctly Separate pathogenic/likely pathogenic variants from VUSs. A VUS should not independently determine treatment or preventive surgery. Home / Breast Genetics Breast Pathology • Diagnostic Reference Hereditary Breast Cancer Genetics A concise, pathology-focused guide to inherited breast cancer susceptibility: when to suspect a syndrome, what morphology can—and cannot—tell you, and how to interpret germline findings. Germline risk Morphology clues IHC context VUS interpretation Core principle Histology can raise suspicion. Germline testing and clinical context establish hereditary predisposition. High penetrance BRCA1, BRCA2, PALB2, TP53, PTEN, CDH1, STK11 Risk and management depend on the gene, variant, and family context. Moderate risk ATM, CHEK2 and others Penetrance varies; evidence and recommendations are gene- and variant-specific. Polygenic risk Many common low-penetrance alleles Combined effects may refine risk estimates but do not replace assessment of high-risk variants. Diagnostic workflow From morphology to hereditary risk Use pathology findings as part of a broader assessment—not as a stand-alone genetic test. Quick comparison Genes and the clues that matter These are associations, not diagnostic rules. Tumor phenotype overlaps substantially with sporadic breast cancer. Gene / syndrome Main association Pathology clue BRCA1 Breast, tubo-ovarian, prostate, pancreatic cancers Often high-grade, triple-negative, lymphocyte-rich BRCA2 Often ER-positive; no specific morphology Breast, thyroid, endometrial, renal cancers; hamartomas Benign hamartomatous lesions may be a clue Early multiple primaries; sarcoma, brain, adrenal, breast HER2-positive breast cancer is overrepresented CHEK2 / ATM Moderate breast cancer susceptibility Often hormone receptor–positive; no pathognomonic pattern CDH1 Diffuse gastric and lobular breast cancer Invasive lobular carcinoma Familial breast cancer; DNA repair pathway No specific morphology; ER-negative/TNBC association reported Peutz-Jeghers syndrome; breast and GI/pancreatic cancers Syndromic mucocutaneous pigmentation and polyposis Neurofibromatosis; increased breast cancer risk Often NST; clinical phenotype is key Syndrome profiles Practical diagnostic notes Select the relevant syndrome profile for concise clinical, morphologic, and molecular reminders. Profile Clinical clues Pathology Molecular testing and interpretation Diagnostic pearl: Beyond single genes Polygenic risk scores • Common low-penetrance variants each contribute a small effect; their combined contribution can be meaningful. • A polygenic risk score (PRS) combines weighted risk alleles and may refine risk estimates alongside family history, breast density, and other clinical factors. • The 313-variant PRS has been extensively studied, particularly in people of European ancestry. Performance and calibration may differ across ancestry groups. • PRS is a risk-stratification tool, not a diagnosis of a hereditary cancer syndrome. Sign-out checklist Before you close the case □ Confirm age, personal history, bilateral disease, and multiple primary cancers. □ Review relevant family history, including breast, ovarian, pancreatic, prostate, diffuse gastric cancer, and sarcoma. □ Document histologic type, grade, ER, PR, and HER2 status accurately. □ Recommend genetics evaluation when indicated by current criteria or clinical context. □ Distinguish germline results from tumor-only findings and interpret VUSs cautiously. Key takeaways 1. Hereditary risk is established by germline testing and clinical interpretation—not morphology alone. 2. Tumor subtype can guide suspicion, but phenotype overlaps and is never fully specific. 3. A VUS is not a pathogenic result; management should follow current guidance and expert review. title: Spindle Cell Lesions
content: 01 Confirm a true spindle cell lesion Determine whether the sample contains a predominantly spindle cell proliferation, a biphasic fibroepithelial lesion, or a conventional carcinoma with a spindle cell component. Review the clinical history, imaging, prior procedures, and specimen adequacy. 02 Assess architecture and the lesion boundary Evaluate circumscription versus infiltration, fascicular or storiform growth, collagen quality, myxoid change, entrapped ducts and lobules, adipose tissue infiltration, and any leaf-like architecture or epithelial component. 03 Search carefully for epithelial differentiation Look for overt squamous or glandular elements, in situ carcinoma, or focal epithelial differentiation. A bland-appearing spindle cell lesion can still represent metaplastic carcinoma; absence of an epithelial component in a limited core does not exclude it. 04 Use a targeted immunohistochemical panel Use broad-spectrum cytokeratins and p63 (with additional keratins as needed) to assess epithelial differentiation. Select other markers according to morphology, including CD34, desmin, SMA, nuclear beta-catenin, and RB1. 05 Integrate morphology, stains, and sampling Distinguish metaplastic carcinoma, fibromatosis, myofibroblastoma, nodular fasciitis, scar, pseudoangiomatous stromal hyperplasia, phyllodes tumor, and primary or metastatic sarcoma. If the sample is limited or findings are discordant, use a descriptive diagnosis and recommend additional sampling as appropriate. Spindle cell (metaplastic) carcinoma Often infiltrative; intersecting fascicles, haphazard growth, or fibromatosis-like pattern; may contain squamous, glandular, or other heterologous elements Ranges from bland to markedly atypical; mitoses may be numerous; necrosis may occur Broad-spectrum and high-molecular-weight cytokeratins and/or p63 may be focal; use a panel and appropriate controls Search for overt epithelial differentiation, in situ carcinoma, or focal keratin/p63 expression. A negative single stain does not exclude carcinoma. Desmoid fibromatosis Long, sweeping fascicles infiltrating adjacent fat or skeletal muscle; poorly circumscribed; lymphoid aggregates may occur at the advancing edge Bland slender spindle cells with scant atypia; atypical mitoses absent; mitoses may be present Nuclear beta-catenin in many cases; SMA often positive; CD34 and broad-spectrum cytokeratins typically negative Infiltrative growth with long sweeping fascicles. Exclude fibromatosis-like metaplastic carcinoma with epithelial markers; CTNNB1/APC testing may help in selected cases. Myofibroblastoma Usually circumscribed and unencapsulated; short intersecting fascicles with hyalinized collagen; variable fat and several morphologic variants Bland oval-to-spindle cells; mitoses absent or rare; occasional atypical or multinucleated cells can occur Desmin and CD34 commonly positive; ER/PR/AR may be positive; RB1 expression is lost in many cases; cytokeratins and S100 typically negative Circumscription, short fascicles, collagen bands, and supportive immunophenotype. RB1 loss supports the diagnosis but is not specific by itself. Nodular fasciitis Usually a rapidly growing, relatively circumscribed or poorly defined lesion with short irregular fascicles in myxoid-to-collagenous stroma; extravasated red cells and lymphocytes may occur Plump, tissue-culture-like myofibroblasts; nucleoli may be prominent; mitoses can be numerous but typically lack atypical forms SMA often positive; keratins generally negative. USP6 rearrangement testing can support the diagnosis in selected cases Clinical rapid growth and tissue-culture-like morphology; mitotic activity alone does not establish malignancy. Scar / reactive spindle cell proliferation Fibrosis related to prior surgery, trauma, biopsy, or inflammation; may entrap ducts and lobules at the edge Usually bland fibroblasts and myofibroblasts; hemosiderin, histiocytes, foreign-body giant cells, or fat necrosis may be present depending on context No single defining panel; use epithelial markers if fibromatosis-like metaplastic carcinoma is a concern Correlate with prior procedure and location. In a patient with prior surgery, scar can be difficult to distinguish from fibromatosis on a limited sample. Pseudoangiomatous stromal hyperplasia (PASH) Slit-like pseudovascular spaces in collagenous stroma, often with bland spindle myofibroblasts Usually bland; no true endothelial-lined vascular channels Stromal cells commonly express CD34 and may express SMA; endothelial markers should not outline the pseudospaces as true vessels Pseudovascular clefts are not true vascular channels. Correlate with architecture and endothelial-marker staining when needed. Malignant phyllodes tumor with stromal overgrowth Leaf-like architecture may be focal or absent in a limited sample; stromal overgrowth can obscure epithelial elements Stromal hypercellularity and atypia, increased mitoses, and sometimes heterologous malignant elements CD34 may be positive but is variable; keratin/p63 can be focal in some tumors and must be interpreted cautiously Extensive sampling may be needed to identify residual benign epithelial structures and leaf-like areas. Do not classify a spindle cell lesion as sarcoma without considering phyllodes tumor. Primary or metastatic sarcoma / other spindle cell neoplasm Variable by lineage; may be fascicular, storiform, myxoid, pleomorphic, or show specific differentiation Variable atypia, mitotic activity, and necrosis; some translocation-associated sarcomas may be relatively uniform Use morphology-directed panels; consider lineage-specific markers and molecular testing where indicated Primary breast sarcomas are rare. Exclude metaplastic carcinoma and malignant phyllodes tumor, and consider metastasis and skin/subcutaneous tumors based on history and location. Could this be spindle cell metaplastic carcinoma? Broad-spectrum cytokeratin; high-molecular-weight/basal cytokeratins; p63; additional keratins as indicated Expression can be focal or limited to a minor component. Use more than one epithelial marker when suspicion remains, and assess staining in the morphologically relevant spindle cells. Reactive myofibroblasts and entrapped epithelium can complicate interpretation. Does the pattern support myofibroblastoma? CD34, desmin, ER, PR, AR, RB1; SMA as appropriate Desmin and CD34 are commonly positive; hormone receptors may be expressed. Loss of RB1 supports the diagnosis in the appropriate setting but overlaps with other tumors in the 13q/RB1 family. Could this be desmoid fibromatosis? Nuclear beta-catenin; broad-spectrum cytokeratins and p63; CD34; SMA Nuclear beta-catenin supports fibromatosis but is not fully specific and can be difficult to interpret. Excluding metaplastic carcinoma is essential. CTNNB1/APC mutation analysis may help in selected difficult or small biopsies. Are the spaces true vascular channels? CD31 and ERG, with CD34 as an adjunct Use endothelial markers when PASH or another spindle cell lesion mimics a vascular proliferation. Marker selection should follow the morphologic question; CD34 alone is not endothelial-specific. Is a lineage-specific or molecular workup needed? Morphology-directed immunohistochemistry and selected molecular tests Consider targeted workup for a suspected specific entity, including USP6 testing for selected nodular fasciitis-like lesions. Do not apply a broad panel indiscriminately; interpret all results with morphology and clinical context. Infiltrative growth into adipose tissue or disruption/entrapment of native breast structures, especially with cytologic atypia. Overt squamous or glandular differentiation, an in situ carcinoma component, or focal epithelial-marker expression in spindle cells. Marked stromal atypia, brisk or atypical mitoses, tumor necrosis, or a high-grade pleomorphic component. Leaf-like architecture, residual benign ducts, or heterogeneous stromal areas raising concern for phyllodes tumor with stromal overgrowth. A limited core biopsy that does not adequately show the lesion boundary or the relationship to native breast tissue. A prior history of malignancy or a dermal/subcutaneous epicenter that raises the possibility of metastasis or a non-parenchymal tumor. Record the lesion epicenter: breast parenchyma, pectoral fascia/chest wall, dermis, or subcutis. Review prior surgery, biopsy, trauma, radiation, known malignancy, and relevant hereditary tumor syndromes. Describe circumscription versus infiltration and whether ducts, lobules, fat, or skeletal muscle are entrapped or destroyed. Search for epithelial, in situ, squamous, glandular, leaf-like, vascular, or heterologous components. Assess cellularity, nuclear atypia, mitotic activity, atypical mitoses, necrosis, and myxoid or collagenized stroma. Use a morphology-directed IHC panel and interpret staining in the correct cell population with internal controls. If a core is insufficient to distinguish carcinoma, phyllodes tumor, fibromatosis, or sarcoma, qualify the diagnosis and recommend additional sampling as appropriate. PathologyGPS / Breast / Mesenchymal & Epithelial Lesions / Spindle Cell Lesions Breast · Spindle cell lesions Breast Spindle Cell Lesions A morphology-first diagnostic guide to spindle cell lesions of the breast, emphasizing exclusion of metaplastic carcinoma and malignant phyllodes tumor, targeted immunohistochemistry, and biopsy limitations. Educational reference prototype · Expert review required before clinical deployment Diagnostic GPS Differential table IHC guide Malignant features Sampling checklist Spindle cell morphology is a pattern, not a final diagnosis. In the breast, the most consequential early distinction is between a true mesenchymal lesion, spindle cell metaplastic carcinoma, and malignant phyllodes tumor. Architecture, lesion boundaries, epithelial differentiation, and adequate sampling must be considered together. true First exclude Spindle cell metaplastic carcinoma The spindle cells may show only focal keratin or p63 expression. Search for squamous/glandular differentiation and in situ carcinoma; use a panel rather than relying on one negative stain. Also exclude Malignant phyllodes tumor Stromal overgrowth can obscure the epithelial component. Look for leaf-like architecture or residual benign ducts and consider extensive sampling before diagnosing a primary sarcoma. IHC and molecular tools Choose stains to answer a specific morphologic question. Staining must be assigned to the lesional cells, with internal controls and the possibility of focal expression in mind. Markers / test Interpretation Interpretive caution: Cytokeratin and p63 expression may be focal in spindle cell metaplastic carcinoma. Conversely, focal staining must be localized to the lesional spindle cells rather than entrapped epithelium or reactive elements. Features that raise concern for malignancy ! Core biopsy: minimum review checklist When classification remains uncertain: A descriptive diagnosis such as “spindle cell lesion” with a comment about the differential and the need for additional sampling may be more appropriate than overclassification on a limited core biopsy. title: Vascular Tumors
content: 01 Establish the anatomic compartment Is the lesion dermal/superficial, subcutaneous, or centered in breast parenchyma? In a previously irradiated breast, correlate the exact skin location and radiation field. 02 Assess the vascular architecture on H&E Evaluate vessel caliber, circumscription, distribution, anastomosis, endothelial cytology, multilayering, mitoses, and whether channels dissect through fat or lobules. 03 Look for features of malignancy Infiltrative dissection of adipose tissue or mammary lobules, endothelial atypia, multilayering or papillary projections, solid epithelioid/spindle areas, blood lakes, mitotic activity, and necrosis raise concern for angiosarcoma. 04 Use endothelial and ancillary markers Confirm endothelial differentiation with CD31 and ERG; add CD34 and D2-40 as appropriate. In postradiation skin lesions, MYC IHC/FISH can help distinguish atypical vascular lesion from radiation-associated angiosarcoma. 05 Integrate site, history, morphology, and sampling Distinguish benign hemangioma or angiomatosis, atypical vascular lesion, primary parenchymal angiosarcoma, and postradiation angiosarcoma. If the sample is limited or discordant, use a descriptive diagnosis and recommend further sampling/excision as clinically appropriate. Hemangioma Parenchyma or subcutis; perilobular type is microscopic and intralobular Well-formed vessels, usually non-anastomosing; circumscribed or relatively well defined Single layer of bland endothelial cells; no substantial atypia or mitotic activity Endothelial markers highlight vessels; pericytes surround individual vascular channels Well-formed vascular spaces with bland lining cells and pericytes. Thrombosis or post-biopsy hemorrhage can complicate interpretation. Angiomatosis Diffuse process involving breast interlobular stroma; may extend to skin or pectoralis Diffuse, unencapsulated proliferation of variably sized anastomosing channels; relatively uniform distribution around ducts and lobules Flat, inconspicuous endothelial cells without hyperchromasia; mitoses rare or absent CD31 and D2-40 highlight endothelial channels; Ki-67 is usually very low Lobules are not invaded and disrupted; no endothelial tufting, papillae, blood lakes, necrosis, or meaningful atypia. Complete excision may be needed for diagnosis on limited core. Atypical vascular lesion (AVL) Superficial to mid-dermis in previously irradiated skin; subcutis typically spared Relatively circumscribed, often wedge-shaped; thin branching/anastomosing channels Single layer of flattened or hobnail endothelial cells; hyperchromasia may occur, but no true cytologic atypia or multilayering CD31 and ERG positive; CD34 variable. D2-40 usually positive in lymphatic pattern and typically negative in vascular pattern. MYC IHC/FISH usually negative Dermal circumscription and lack of destructive infiltration, endothelial multilayering, and significant atypia favor AVL. Ensure the biopsy adequately samples the lesion. Postradiation angiosarcoma Usually dermis/subcutis in a prior breast radiation field; breast parenchymal involvement is less common Infiltrative, often multifocal; irregular angulated channels dissect fat and stroma; higher-grade areas may be solid Variable atypia; endothelial multilayering, mitoses, blood lakes and necrosis may be present; epithelioid pattern can mimic carcinoma CD31 and ERG strong; CD34 and D2-40 variable. MYC nuclear overexpression/amplification is characteristic in most cases; PRAME often positive Prior irradiation and dermal/subcutaneous infiltrative growth are key. MYC amplification strongly supports radiation-associated angiosarcoma in the right context; focal keratin can occur. Primary angiosarcoma Usually centered in deep breast parenchyma, with or without skin involvement; no prior radiation association Infiltrative, poorly defined anastomosing channels dissect through fibroadipose tissue and disrupt lobules; poorly differentiated areas may be solid Ranges from relatively bland lining cells to marked atypia, multilayering, mitoses, blood lakes and necrosis Strong membranous CD31 and nuclear ERG; CD34 and D2-40 variable. Keratins may be expressed, especially in epithelioid cases Parenchymal origin and destructive infiltration are central. Well-differentiated areas may look deceptively bland; keratin positivity does not exclude angiosarcoma. Confirm endothelial differentiation CD31, ERG; CD34 as an adjunct CD31 membranous staining and nuclear ERG support endothelial lineage. CD34 is variable and should not be used alone. Assess lymphatic differentiation in a vascular lesion D2-40 (podoplanin) Often highlights angiomatosis and the lymphatic pattern of AVL. AVL with a vascular pattern is typically D2-40-negative and may show a surrounding pericytic layer highlighted by SMA. AVL versus radiation-associated angiosarcoma MYC IHC and MYC FISH AVL typically lacks MYC amplification and MYC overexpression. High-level MYC amplification strongly supports postradiation/lymphedema-associated angiosarcoma in the appropriate morphologic setting. Additional contextual markers PRAME; H3K27me3 when indicated Most secondary angiosarcomas show PRAME immunoreactivity, unlike most AVL. H3K27me3 may be lost in radiation-associated angiosarcoma and retained in benign/atypical vascular lesions; interpret as an adjunct, not a stand-alone test. Irregular angulated vascular channels dissecting adipose tissue or disrupting mammary lobules. Endothelial multilayering, papillary projections, significant cytologic atypia, or increased mitotic activity. Solid epithelioid or spindle-cell areas, blood lakes, or necrosis. A clinically suspicious or enlarging postradiation skin lesion with a biopsy that may not represent the full process. A deceptively bland area in a lesion with infiltrative architecture: some angiosarcomas contain well-differentiated regions. Educational reference prototype · Expert review required before clinical deployment Diagnostic GPS Histology table IHC guide Malignant features Sampling checklist Start with location and architecture. A vascular lesion is not classified by endothelial markers alone: the distribution of vessels, their relationship to lobules and adipose tissue, endothelial cytology, and clinical setting determine the differential. true Benign pattern Bland, organized vessels Well-formed channels, bland single-layer endothelium, low mitotic activity, and no destructive dissection favor hemangioma. Diffuse but uniform vascular proliferation without lobular invasion or endothelial atypia favous angiomatosis. Malignant pattern Infiltration and endothelial atypia Destructive infiltration, endothelial multilayering, cytologic atypia, mitoses, solid growth, blood lakes, or necrosis support angiosarcoma. Well-differentiated areas may be deceptively bland. The final diagnostic column is intentionally wider. IHC and molecular tools Use ancillary tests to answer a specific question raised by the morphology. Markers / test Interpretation Interpretive caution: Angiosarcoma, particularly epithelioid angiosarcoma, can show focal keratin expression and mimic carcinoma. Conversely, endothelial marker expression should be interpreted with morphology and a suitable panel. Features that raise concern for angiosarcoma ! Diagnostic checklist for limited samples Record whether the lesion is dermal, subcutaneous, or parenchymal. Assess circumscription versus destructive infiltration and the relationship to adipose tissue and lobules. Evaluate endothelial layering, atypia, mitoses, solid areas, hemorrhage, and necrosis. Correlate with prior breast irradiation and chronic lymphedema history where relevant. Use CD31/ERG and selected ancillary markers to confirm lineage and resolve the differential. For suspected AVL, ensure the biopsy is representative; sampling error can miss an underlying angiosarcoma. If the lesion is diffuse or a core is insufficient for classification, consider a descriptive diagnosis and additional sampling or excision as appropriate. Scope This page focuses on diagnostic morphology, IHC, key molecular adjuncts, and practical differential diagnosis. Epidemiology, treatment, staging, and general sarcoma background are intentionally minimized. title: Nipple Lesions
content: 01 Start with the anatomic compartment Determine whether the process is centered in the epidermis, superficial nipple ducts and duct orifices, nipple dermis/smooth muscle, or deeper breast parenchyma. Correlate with erosion, scaling, discharge, retraction, a palpable mass, and imaging. 02 Separate an epidermal process from a ductal or infiltrative lesion Paget disease is an intraepidermal malignant glandular proliferation. Nipple adenoma is a superficial ductal/tubular proliferation that often connects to the epidermis and retains myoepithelial cells. Syringomatous tumor forms bland epithelial nests and cords infiltrating dermis and smooth muscle around lactiferous sinuses. 03 Look for the defining architecture For nipple adenoma, assess the nodular or wedge-shaped proliferation, variable adenosis/papillomatosis, and preserved myoepithelium. For syringomatous tumor, look for small irregular nests and comma- or tadpole-shaped cords with squamous and glandular differentiation. For SMOLD, identify keratinizing squamous metaplasia within lactiferous ducts with keratin plugging and inflammation. 04 Use a question-driven IHC panel For suspected Paget disease, use low-molecular-weight cytokeratins (such as CK7), HER2, and selected markers based on the differential. Use p63 or p40/high-molecular-weight keratins for squamous differentiation, and myoepithelial markers around ducts/tubules when evaluating nipple adenoma. Consider melanocytic markers if melanoma is in the differential. 05 Search for associated carcinoma and assess sampling Mammary Paget disease is commonly associated with underlying DCIS and/or invasive carcinoma. Evaluate the ipsilateral breast and correlate with imaging. In a superficial or fragmented biopsy, location and the relationship to the epidermis, lactiferous ducts, and deeper breast tissue may be decisive; recommend additional sampling when necessary. Squamous metaplasia of lactiferous ducts (SMOLD) Lactiferous ducts, usually subareolar Keratinizing squamous epithelium extends into ducts; keratin accumulates and may obstruct the duct. Rupture can produce an abscess, sinus tract, and foreign-body reaction. Squamous metaplasia with keratin debris; acute/chronic inflammation and foreign-body giant cells may be prominent. Usually diagnosed morphologically; no defining IHC panel described in the supplied sources. Clinical context may include smoking, subareolar abscess, or fistula. Keratinizing squamous metaplasia in duct lumina is the key finding; inflammation alone is nonspecific. Nipple adenoma Superficial nipple, often contiguous with epidermis Nodular, often wedge-shaped and relatively circumscribed proliferation of tubular/ductal structures; variable adenosis, papillomatosis, and usual ductal hyperplasia. Benign glandular epithelium with a preserved myoepithelial layer; epidermal replacement can cause erosion, bleeding, and crusting. Myoepithelial markers outline ducts/tubules. Heterogeneous CK5/6 and ER expression supports a benign heterogeneous proliferation in difficult cases. Superficial ductal/tubular proliferation with myoepithelial preservation. Can clinically mimic Paget disease; atypia or loss of myoepithelium requires careful evaluation. Syringomatous tumor of the nipple Nipple/areolar dermis and smooth muscle around lactiferous sinuses Locally infiltrative small nests, cords, and comma- or tadpole-shaped structures; may include keratin-filled cysts and squamous differentiation. Does not invade the epidermis or destructively invade ducts. Cytologically bland, heterogeneous epithelial cells; mitoses rare; necrosis is not a feature. Perineural invasion may occur. Peripheral myoepithelial-like cells commonly express p63 and high-molecular-weight keratins; squamous cells may express p40/p63 and CK10; glandular cells express CK8/18. Usually ER/PR/HER2 negative. Infiltrative but cytologically bland. Distinguish from low-grade adenosquamous carcinoma, which is usually deeper and more atypical with mitoses; limited biopsy may be challenging. Mammary Paget disease Nipple and/or areolar epidermis Malignant glandular cells scattered singly, in clusters, or in small gland-like structures throughout the epidermis (pagetoid spread); epidermal acanthosis/hyperkeratosis may occur. Large cells with abundant pale or weakly eosinophilic cytoplasm, enlarged vesicular often pleomorphic nuclei, prominent nucleoli, and variable mitotic activity. Usually CK7/CAM5.2 positive; HER2 overexpressed in most cases; variable ER/PR, AR, GCDFP-15, GATA3, EMA, and CEA. CK20 typically negative. Search for underlying DCIS and/or invasive carcinoma. Differentiate from Bowen disease, melanoma, Toker cells, and direct epidermal involvement by an underlying carcinoma. Toker cells / Toker cell hyperplasia Basal epidermis of the nipple Scattered single cells or small clusters; rarely small monolayered glands without myoepithelium. Small bland cells with clear or pale cytoplasm and no malignant nuclear features. CK7 and CAM5.2 positive; usually ER/PR positive and HER2 negative. Benign cytology and basal location favor Toker cells. Paget cells are larger and atypical, and are often HER2 positive. Interpret with clinical findings and underlying carcinoma status. Low-grade adenosquamous carcinoma Usually deeper breast parenchyma; nipple involvement is uncommon Glandular and squamous elements, sometimes with an associated spindle cell component; may mimic syringomatous tumor. More nuclear atypia and scattered mitoses than typical syringomatous tumor; lumina may contain necrotic debris. Use a panel and interpret in context; squamous/basal markers may overlap with syringomatous tumor. Depth of origin, cytologic atypia, mitotic activity, and destructive invasion help. Superficial biopsy without orientation may not permit confident distinction. Squamous cell carcinoma in situ (Bowen disease) Nipple epidermis Full-thickness atypical squamous proliferation with disordered maturation; may resemble Paget disease clinically and histologically. Atypical squamous cells, often with enlarged hyperchromatic nuclei and dyskeratosis. Usually high-molecular-weight keratins and p63 positive; low-molecular-weight glandular keratins are generally not the dominant pattern. Squamous morphology and p63/high-molecular-weight keratin profile favor Bowen disease over Paget disease. Melanoma involving nipple epidermis Nipple/areolar epidermis Pagetoid or lentiginous melanocytic proliferation; may be pigmented or amelanotic. Atypical melanocytes; pigment may be absent or subtle. S100, SOX10, Melan-A, and/or HMB45 support melanocytic differentiation; keratins support Paget cells instead. Use a melanocytic panel when morphology or pigmentation raises concern. Pigment alone does not establish melanoma; Paget cells may contain phagocytosed melanin. Paget disease vs. Toker cells CK7, CAM5.2, HER2, ER/PR; correlate with morphology Both can express low-molecular-weight keratins. Toker cells are bland, small, and usually ER/PR positive and HER2 negative; Paget cells are cytologically malignant and commonly HER2 positive. Paget disease vs. Bowen disease CK7 or CAM5.2; p63 and high-molecular-weight keratins Paget disease shows glandular differentiation and typically low-molecular-weight keratin expression. Bowen disease shows squamous differentiation and is usually p63/high-molecular-weight keratin positive. Paget disease vs. melanoma CK7, EMA, HER2; SOX10, S100, Melan-A, HMB45 as indicated Assign staining to the atypical lesional cells. Melanocytic markers highlight melanoma; Paget cells express epithelial markers. Melanin may be present in Paget disease because of pigment transfer or phagocytosis. Nipple adenoma vs. invasive carcinoma p63, smooth muscle myosin heavy chain, calponin or other validated myoepithelial markers; CK5/6 and ER in selected cases A continuous myoepithelial layer around ductal/tubular structures supports nipple adenoma. Evaluate for atypia, destructive invasion, or a coexisting carcinoma; no single stain replaces morphology. Syringomatous tumor vs. low-grade adenosquamous carcinoma p63/p40, high- and low-molecular-weight cytokeratins; ER as appropriate There is overlap in basal/squamous markers. Integrate anatomic location, infiltrative pattern, cytologic atypia, mitoses, necrosis, and the relationship to lactiferous sinuses and deeper parenchyma. Persistent unilateral eczematous, erythematous, scaly, crusted, or ulcerated nipple change, particularly when not resolving with appropriate treatment: exclude mammary Paget disease. Paget disease on biopsy: evaluate for underlying DCIS and/or invasive carcinoma even if no mass is palpable. Nipple adenoma with atypia, loss of myoepithelial cells, or a destructive invasive pattern: do not assume a purely benign lesion; assess for associated or contiguous carcinoma. A bland but infiltrative nipple lesion: consider syringomatous tumor, but exclude low-grade adenosquamous carcinoma and relevant skin adnexal tumors. Subareolar abscess or fistula with keratinizing squamous metaplasia: consider SMOLD; inflammation and foreign-body reaction alone are not specific. Pigmented or pagetoid epidermal lesion: consider melanoma and Bowen disease in addition to Paget disease and benign Toker cells. Confirm the exact biopsy site and whether the specimen includes epidermis, nipple ducts, dermis, and/or deeper breast tissue. Review clinical description: erosion, scaling, crust, bleeding, discharge, retraction, palpable mass, abscess, or fistula. For suspected Paget disease, document whether the epidermal cells are malignant and recommend evaluation for underlying breast carcinoma as clinically appropriate. For nipple adenoma, look for a preserved myoepithelial layer and heterogeneous benign epithelial proliferation; assess any atypia or associated carcinoma. For syringomatous tumor, assess infiltrative nests/cords, squamous and glandular differentiation, bland cytology, and the relationship to lactiferous sinuses and smooth muscle. For SMOLD, identify squamous metaplasia within lactiferous ducts, keratin plugging, rupture, and associated inflammation. Use targeted IHC rather than a broad indiscriminate panel; interpret stains in the correct lesional cell population. If the biopsy is superficial, fragmented, or does not establish the lesion's depth and relationship to normal structures, state the limitation and recommend additional sampling when appropriate. The lesion's compartment and relationship to normal structures often narrow the differential before immunohistochemistry is performed. true Do not miss A malignant intraepidermal glandular proliferation. The absence of a palpable mass does not exclude underlying DCIS or invasive carcinoma. Key benign mimic Can cause erosion, bleeding, and crusting that clinically mimic Paget disease. Look for a benign ductal/tubular proliferation with preserved myoepithelial cells. Histology: rapid differential table Use architecture and anatomic location first. IHC findings overlap in some entities and should support, not replace, morphologic interpretation. 230px 210px 360px 280px 300px 390px Entity Typical location Architecture Cytology / inflammation IHC clues Key discriminator / pitfall On smaller screens, scroll horizontally to view all columns. IHC guide: answer a specific question The stains below reflect the differential diagnoses discussed in the supplied WHO nipple-tumor material and the nipple-disorders chapter of the breast biopsy reference. Markers Interpretation Interpretive caution: CK7 positivity alone does not distinguish Paget disease from Toker cells. A myoepithelial layer supports nipple adenoma, but morphology and adequate sampling remain essential. Marker expression can vary, and staining must be assigned to the correct cell population. ! Biopsy review checklist When the sample is insufficient: If the distinction depends on depth, the relationship to normal ducts, or the presence of an underlying carcinoma, use a descriptive diagnosis and recommend additional sampling or excision as clinically appropriate rather than overclassifying a limited biopsy. Scope and source alignment This page prioritizes diagnostic morphology, differential diagnosis, and targeted IHC. It integrates the supplied WHO material on syringomatous tumor, nipple adenoma, and mammary Paget disease with the supplied breast-biopsy chapter on SMOLD, nipple adenoma, syringomatous adenoma, Paget disease, and Toker cells. Rare skin adnexal and other tumors of the nipple–areola complex are not covered exhaustively.
