title: Choroid Plexus Embryonal Pineal Tumors
content: use client Choroid Plexus Papilloma Choroid Plexus Tumors Well-formed fibrovascular papillae lined by a single layer of bland choroid plexus epithelium; mitoses are absent or very rare. Most common in children, particularly during infancy and early childhood; adults may also be affected. Lateral ventricles are the most frequent site; fourth and third ventricular tumors also occur. Hydrocephalus and raised intracranial pressure are common presenting features. Intraventricular papillary neoplasm with a recognizable choroid plexus epithelial phenotype. Well-developed papillae with delicate fibrovascular cores covered by a single layer of uniform cuboidal-to-columnar cells. Mitotic activity is absent or very low: typically <1 mitosis/mm². No combination of malignant architectural and cytologic features sufficient for carcinoma. Papillae have delicate fibrovascular cores and a continuous epithelial covering. Tumor cells have round-to-oval monomorphic nuclei and moderate cytoplasm. Mitoses are absent or rare; Ki-67 is usually <5%, often <1%. Focal tubular, glandular, oncocytic, mucinous, or stromal metaplastic changes may occur. Cytokeratins, usually CK7, are positive. Vimentin and S100 are commonly positive. Kir7.1 shows apical/membranous staining in most cases and supports choroid plexus differentiation. EAAT1 is commonly positive; transthyretin is variable. GFAP and EMA may be weak or focal. Molecular testing is not routinely required for a morphologically typical case. Copy-number analysis may show hyperdiploidy with whole-chromosome gains. DNA methylation profiling can separate most papillomas from carcinomas in difficult cases. Do not grade a papilloma using Ki-67 alone. CSF seeding can rarely occur despite bland histology; correlate with imaging and clinical staging when indicated. Atypical Choroid Plexus Papilloma Retains papillary architecture but has ≥1 mitosis/mm²; does not meet the ≥4-of-5 histologic criteria for carcinoma. Choroid Plexus Carcinoma At least four of five malignant features, including frequent mitoses, increased cellularity, pleomorphism, loss of papillary pattern, and necrosis; invasion supports malignancy. Choroid plexus papilloma with increased mitotic activity, without the full constellation required for carcinoma. Predominantly affects infants and young children; reported median age is under 1 year in pediatric series. Usually arises in the lateral ventricles. May cause hydrocephalus and raised intracranial pressure; metastatic dissemination can occur. Choroid plexus epithelial neoplasm with recognizable papillary architecture. Mitotic count ≥1 mitosis/mm² (approximately ≥2 mitoses per 10 HPF using a 0.23-mm² field) supports the diagnosis. Increased cellularity, nuclear pleomorphism, blurring of papillary architecture, or necrosis may be present but are not required. Does not meet the threshold of at least four of five defining histologic features of choroid plexus carcinoma. Papillary architecture is generally retained, although focal solid growth or blurring may occur. Mitotic activity is increased and is the defining grading feature. Cellularity and nuclear pleomorphism may be increased focally. Necrosis may be present but is not independently diagnostic of carcinoma. Median Ki-67 is higher than in conventional papilloma; reported median is approximately 9%. Immunophenotype generally parallels choroid plexus papilloma. Cytokeratins, vimentin, and S100 are commonly expressed. Kir7.1 may be retained. Ki-67 supports increased proliferation but does not replace mitotic counting. Usually shares the hyperploid copy-number profile of choroid plexus papilloma. Genome-wide copy-number profiling may help distinguish atypical papilloma from carcinoma in selected cases. Methylation profiling may be useful in diagnostically difficult cases. Count mitoses in an adequately sampled viable tumor and report the area used. Do not diagnose carcinoma based on a single atypical feature. Bland single-layered papillae with <1 mitosis/mm²; lacks the increased mitotic activity of atypical papilloma and the multiple malignant features of carcinoma. A malignant choroid plexus epithelial tumor showing at least four of five characteristic histologic features. Approximately 80% occur in children; many present in early childhood. Most arise in the lateral ventricles. Hydrocephalus, increased head circumference in infants, vomiting, and raised intracranial pressure are common. A substantial subset is associated with germline TP53 pathogenic variants and Li-Fraumeni syndrome. At least four of five features: increased cellular density, nuclear pleomorphism, blurring/loss of papillary architecture with poorly formed sheets, necrosis, and frequent mitoses. Frequent mitoses are usually >2.5/mm² (approximately >5 per 10 HPF using a 0.23-mm² field). Infiltrative growth into adjacent brain strongly supports malignancy. Assess for CSF dissemination and systemic metastasis. Tumor is highly cellular with poorly structured sheets and loss of the orderly papillary pattern. Nuclear pleomorphism and frequent mitotic figures are conspicuous. Necrosis is common. Diffuse brain invasion may be present. Tumors are often highly vascular and may show hemorrhage. Cytokeratins are positive; S100 and transthyretin are less frequently expressed than in papilloma. Kir7.1 is retained in approximately half of cases. p53 may show strong diffuse nuclear accumulation in TP53-mutant tumors. SMARCB1 and SMARCA4 nuclear expression are retained. Ki-67 is usually substantially increased; reported median is approximately 20%. Offer genetic counseling and germline TP53 testing to patients and families. Somatic TP53 mutations occur in approximately half of cases. Copy-number profiling often shows complex alterations and hypoploidy. DNA methylation profiling can support classification in difficult cases. Do not diagnose carcinoma from invasion alone without considering the defining histologic criteria and overall context. Recommend germline TP53 evaluation because of the strong Li-Fraumeni association. Medulloblastoma, WNT-Activated Medulloblastomas Medulloblastoma with WNT pathway activation, usually CTNNB1-mutant and showing nuclear β-catenin. Typically affects children aged 7–14 years; rare in infants. Slight female predominance. Often arises near the cerebellar midline or foramen of Luschka, with close relationship to the dorsal brainstem. Usually presents with obstructive hydrocephalus and raised intracranial pressure. Embryonal cerebellar tumor with compatible medulloblastoma morphology. Demonstrate WNT pathway activation by nuclear β-catenin and/or molecular testing. CTNNB1 exon 3 mutation is common; monosomy 6 is a characteristic supportive finding. DNA methylation profiling is the preferred method for molecular group assignment when available. CNS WHO grade 4. Most show classic medulloblastoma morphology with densely packed small round cells, high N:C ratio, brisk mitoses, and apoptosis. Large-cell/anaplastic morphology is uncommon. Desmoplastic/nodular morphology is not expected in this group. Nuclear β-catenin is a key indicator of WNT pathway activation. YAP1 is commonly positive. GAB1 is generally negative, helping distinguish from SHH-activated tumors. Synaptophysin and other neuronal markers are variable. DNA methylation profiling is preferred for group/subgroup assignment. CTNNB1 exon 3 mutation is present in most cases. Monosomy 6 on an otherwise diploid background is characteristic and supportive. If CTNNB1 is wild-type, consider germline APC-associated disease and evaluate APC as clinically indicated. Nuclear β-catenin must be distinguished from cytoplasmic staining. TP53 mutation in WNT medulloblastoma does not carry the same adverse implication as TP53 mutation in SHH-activated disease. Medulloblastoma, SHH-Activated and TP53-Wildtype GAB1-positive SHH pathway profile with wild-type TP53; desmoplastic/nodular morphology is common. Medulloblastoma, SHH-Activated and TP53-Mutant SHH pathway profile plus TP53 mutation; p53 may show diffuse strong nuclear staining and large-cell/anaplastic morphology is frequent. Medulloblastoma, Non-WNT/Non-SHH Lacks WNT and SHH activation; YAP1 and GAB1 are generally negative; methylation profiling assigns Group 3 or 4. Medulloblastoma, Histologically Defined Morphologic descriptor (classic, desmoplastic/nodular, extensive nodularity, or large-cell/anaplastic); molecular group must be assigned separately when possible. SHH pathway activation with wild-type TP53; desmoplastic/nodular or extensive nodularity patterns are common. Occurs in infants, children, and adults; age distribution is broader than WNT-activated disease. Often arises in the cerebellar hemispheres. Presents with symptoms of posterior fossa mass and obstructive hydrocephalus. Medulloblastoma morphology with molecular evidence of SHH pathway activation. TP53 must be wild-type by appropriate molecular testing. DNA methylation profiling is preferred for definitive group/subgroup assignment. Evaluate SHH pathway alterations, including PTCH1, SUFU, and SMO, as appropriate. Desmoplastic/nodular morphology and medulloblastoma with extensive nodularity are common. Classic morphology may occur; large-cell/anaplastic morphology is uncommon. Internodular areas may show increased cellularity and mitotic activity; nodules show neurocytic differentiation. GAB1 is positive in tumor cells and supports SHH activation. Nuclear β-catenin is absent. p53 typically shows weak-to-moderate staining in scattered cells when TP53 is wild-type. p75-NGFR may highlight internodular areas in desmoplastic tumors. DNA methylation profiling is preferred for molecular classification. Sequence TP53 to establish wild-type status. Assess SHH pathway genes such as PTCH1, SUFU, and SMO when relevant. Consider germline predisposition testing, particularly PTCH1, SUFU, TP53, ELP1, and GPR161, with genetic counseling. Do not infer TP53 status from p53 IHC alone when definitive classification is required. Distinguish true desmoplastic/nodular medulloblastoma from reactive nodularity or other embryonal tumors. Nuclear β-catenin and CTNNB1 alteration support WNT activation; GAB1 is negative. SHH pathway activation with TP53 mutation; large-cell/anaplastic morphology and MYCN amplification are important adverse features. Occurs predominantly in children and adolescents, including older children. Strongly associated with Li-Fraumeni syndrome in a subset. Medulloblastoma with molecular evidence of SHH pathway activation. Demonstrate TP53 mutation by sequencing or validated molecular assay. DNA methylation profiling supports subgroup assignment; TP53-mutant cases commonly map to SHH-3. Large-cell/anaplastic morphology is frequent, with large cells, prominent nucleoli, nuclear pleomorphism, and high mitotic activity. Diffuse anaplasia may coexist with a large-cell phenotype. Other cases may show desmoplastic/nodular architecture with focal anaplasia. GAB1 and YAP1 support SHH pathway activation. Diffuse strong nuclear p53 staining supports TP53 mutation but requires molecular confirmation. Ki-67 is typically high. TP53 sequencing is essential to establish the defining alteration. Assess MYCN amplification; GLI2 amplification and chromosome 17p loss may also occur. DNA methylation profiling can refine subgroup assignment. Offer germline TP53 testing and genetic counseling; evaluate for Li-Fraumeni syndrome. TP53 mutation has context-dependent significance; do not extrapolate the adverse association in SHH tumors to WNT tumors. Distinguish from SHH-activated, TP53-wildtype medulloblastoma using molecular TP53 status. Medulloblastoma lacking WNT and SHH pathway activation; molecular classification resolves Group 3 versus Group 4. Occurs across childhood and adulthood, with most cases in children. Often arises in the cerebellar vermis or hemispheres. May present with hydrocephalus or leptomeningeal dissemination. Embryonal tumor with medulloblastoma morphology. No evidence of WNT or SHH pathway activation by integrated IHC/molecular workup. DNA methylation profiling or validated gene-expression classifier is preferred to assign Group 3 versus Group 4. Classic morphology is common; large-cell/anaplastic morphology occurs in a subset, especially some Group 3 tumors. Tumor is densely cellular with small blue cells, brisk mitoses, and apoptosis. Desmoplastic/nodular morphology is uncommon. YAP1 is generally negative, unlike WNT and SHH groups. GAB1 is negative. OTX2 is commonly expressed; interpret with the full panel. DNA methylation profiling is preferred for Group 3 versus Group 4 assignment. MYC amplification is associated with a subset of Group 3 tumors. MYCN amplification can occur in Group 4 and must be interpreted in molecular-group context. Use copy-number and gene-expression data when methylation profiling is unavailable. Do not assign Group 3 or Group 4 from morphology alone. MYCN amplification is not specific to SHH tumors and must be interpreted with the full molecular profile. Use when describing the morphologic pattern; molecular group should still be established whenever possible. Most common in children, with a median age around 9 years; adults may also be affected. Typically arises in the cerebellum and may extend into the fourth ventricle. Symptoms commonly reflect posterior fossa mass effect and obstructive hydrocephalus. Small-cell embryonal neoplasm of the cerebellum with medulloblastoma morphology. Describe the histologic pattern: classic, desmoplastic/nodular, medulloblastoma with extensive nodularity, or large-cell/anaplastic. Assign WNT-activated, SHH-activated (with TP53 status), or non-WNT/non-SHH molecular type when supported. All medulloblastomas are CNS WHO grade 4. Classic pattern: densely packed small round cells with scant cytoplasm, hyperchromatic nuclei, brisk mitoses, and apoptosis. Desmoplastic/nodular pattern: reticulin-rich internodular zones and pale nodules with neurocytic differentiation. Medulloblastoma with extensive nodularity: prominent interconnected pale nodules with advanced neuronal differentiation. Large-cell/anaplastic pattern: large cells, marked nuclear pleomorphism, prominent nucleoli, and frequent mitoses. Synaptophysin and NeuN are often positive, particularly in differentiated nodules, but may be variable. GAB1 and p75-NGFR support SHH activation in the appropriate context. Nuclear β-catenin supports WNT activation. SMARCB1 and SMARCA4 are retained; loss should prompt consideration of AT/RT. DNA methylation profiling is preferred for molecular group and subgroup assignment. Use β-catenin, GAB1, YAP1, OTX2, p75-NGFR, and p53 as a practical IHC screening panel. Perform TP53 sequencing in SHH-activated tumors and assess MYC/MYCN amplification when clinically indicated. CSF cytology and neuraxis imaging are used for staging. Histologic pattern does not substitute for molecular group assignment. Exclude ETMR and AT/RT in poorly differentiated tumors; LIN28A and SMARCB1/SMARCA4 are useful discriminators. Atypical Teratoid/Rhabdoid Tumor (AT/RT) Other Embryonal Tumors CNS embryonal tumor with loss of nuclear SMARCB1 or, rarely, SMARCA4. Predominantly affects infants and young children, but can occur at any age. May arise anywhere in the CNS, including posterior fossa, cerebral hemispheres, and spinal cord. Often presents with rapidly progressive symptoms related to mass effect. Malignant CNS neoplasm with rhabdoid cells and/or compatible embryonal morphology. Loss of nuclear SMARCB1 (INI1) or SMARCA4 (BRG1) in tumor cells, with retained staining in internal non-neoplastic controls. Molecular confirmation of SMARCB1 or SMARCA4 inactivation is useful, particularly in atypical cases. Rhabdoid cells have eccentric nuclei, prominent nucleoli, and abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm with hyaline inclusions. Primitive small-cell areas, epithelioid areas, and mesenchymal-appearing components may coexist. Mitoses, apoptosis, necrosis, and hemorrhage are common. Rhabdoid morphology may be focal or absent in some molecularly defined cases. Loss of nuclear SMARCB1 is the usual defining finding; SMARCA4 loss defines a small subset. Rhabdoid cells may express EMA, SMA, and vimentin. GFAP, synaptophysin, and cytokeratins are variably expressed. Internal endothelial and inflammatory cells must retain nuclear INI1/BRG1 as positive controls. Assess SMARCB1 and SMARCA4 by IHC; perform sequencing/copy-number analysis when needed. DNA methylation profiling can support classification in diagnostically challenging cases. Consider germline evaluation when age, family history, or multiple tumors suggest rhabdoid tumor predisposition syndrome. Loss of INI1 is not unique to AT/RT; correlate with site and morphology and exclude other SMARCB1-deficient tumors. Do not interpret absent staining without an intact internal positive control. Cribriform Neuroepithelial Tumor (CRINET) Cribriform architecture with SMARCB1 loss; Kir7.1 is generally absent, helping separate it from choroid plexus carcinoma. Embryonal Tumor with Multilayered Rosettes (ETMR) Multilayered rosettes, diffuse LIN28A, and usually C19MC alteration; SMARCB1 is retained. CNS Neuroblastoma, FOXR2-Activated FOXR2 activation/rearrangement with OLIG2 expression; confirm with molecular profiling. CNS Tumor with BCOR Internal Tandem Duplication BCOR exon 15 ITD with diffuse nuclear BCOR, dense capillary network, and spindle/oval cells. CNS Embryonal Tumor, NEC/NOS Diagnosis of exclusion after molecularly defined embryonal tumors and high-grade glioma mimics have been excluded. Cribriform neuroepithelial architecture with SMARCB1 loss; typically lacks choroid plexus marker Kir7.1. Reported mainly in infants and young children. Usually arises in the supratentorial compartment, often near the lateral ventricles. Clinical presentation reflects mass effect and raised intracranial pressure. Embryonal/neuroepithelial tumor with characteristic cribriform or sieve-like architecture. Loss of nuclear SMARCB1 expression in tumor cells. Distinguish from choroid plexus carcinoma using morphology and absence of a convincing choroid plexus phenotype. Methylation profiling may assist in difficult cases. Cribriform and trabecular structures are characteristic, often with pseudoglandular spaces. Tumor cells may be epithelioid with clear-to-eosinophilic cytoplasm. Necrosis and brisk proliferation may be present; reported Ki-67 ranges approximately 5–35%. Nuclear SMARCB1 is lost in tumor cells. EMA, tyrosinase, MAP2, synaptophysin, and vimentin may be expressed. Kir7.1 is generally absent, unlike most choroid plexus tumors. GFAP, S100, and cytokeratins are variable. SMARCB1 loss is a key diagnostic clue. DNA methylation profiling may help distinguish CRINET from AT/RT and choroid plexus carcinoma. Do not classify as choroid plexus carcinoma solely because of ventricular location and epithelial appearance. Confirm SMARCB1 loss with internal controls and assess Kir7.1. Loss of SMARCB1 or SMARCA4; rhabdoid cells may express EMA, SMA, and vimentin. Embryonal tumor with multilayered rosettes, strong LIN28A, and usually C19MC alteration. Predominantly affects infants and very young children. Usually supratentorial, often cerebral hemispheres. Rapidly enlarging mass with seizures, focal deficits, or raised intracranial pressure. Highly cellular embryonal neoplasm with multilayered ependymoblastic or medulloepithelial rosettes and/or tubular structures. Strong diffuse cytoplasmic LIN28A expression supports the diagnosis. C19MC amplification/rearrangement is highly specific and present in approximately 90% of cases. If C19MC is absent, assess DICER1; classify as ETMR only when morphology and molecular findings support it. Primitive small round cells form multilayered rosettes, ependymoblastic rosettes, or tubular structures. Neuropil-like matrix may separate embryonal cell-rich areas. Mitoses and apoptosis are brisk; necrosis may occur. Morphology may be heterogeneous, and classic rosettes may be absent in limited samples. LIN28A shows strong diffuse cytoplasmic staining. Nestin and vimentin are strong in embryonal components. Neuropil-like matrix is positive for synaptophysin, NFP, and NeuN. SMARCB1 expression is retained. Test for C19MC amplification/rearrangement at 19q13.42 by FISH or copy-number profiling. If C19MC-negative, assess DICER1 and consider germline testing because compound heterozygous alterations may occur. DNA methylation profiling can support classification. LIN28A is supportive but not specific by itself. LIN28A positivity alone does not establish ETMR. A DICER1 alteration alone is insufficient; correlate with morphology and methylation profile. Embryonal neuroepithelial tumor with FOXR2 activation, commonly showing OLIG2 and neuronal differentiation. Usually affects children and adolescents; rare adult cases occur. Most often supratentorial, particularly cerebral hemispheres. Presents with seizures, focal neurologic deficits, or raised intracranial pressure. CNS embryonal/neuroepithelial neoplasm with compatible morphology. Demonstrate FOXR2 activation, usually by structural rearrangement or other molecular evidence. DNA methylation or gene-expression profiling can establish the entity when morphology is nonspecific. Exclude other molecularly defined embryonal tumors and high-grade gliomas. Tumor is often well demarcated but may show infiltration. Primitive round-to-oval cells form sheets, nests, or lobules. Neurocytic or ganglion-cell differentiation may be present. Mitotic activity and Ki-67 are high; necrosis may occur. OLIG2 is strongly expressed in most tumor cells. Synaptophysin may highlight neuronal differentiation. GFAP and vimentin are generally absent in tumor cells; GFAP may highlight reactive astrocytes. Detect FOXR2 rearrangement/activation using RNA-based NGS or another assay capable of detecting complex structural variants. Copy-number analysis may show FOXR2 locus alteration and frequent chromosome 1q gain. DNA methylation profiling supports definitive classification. FOXR2 rearrangements may be complex and can be missed by limited DNA panels. Do not diagnose from OLIG2 positivity alone. BCOR exon 15 internal tandem duplication in a tumor with solid growth, spindle/oval cells, and dense capillary network. Predominantly affects infants and young children; reported median age is approximately 3.5 years. Usually arises in cerebral or cerebellar hemispheres. Presents with mass effect, seizures, focal deficits, or raised intracranial pressure. Predominantly solid CNS tumor composed of uniform oval or spindle cells. Dense capillary network and focal perivascular pseudorosettes may be present. Demonstrate BCOR internal tandem duplication in exon 15. Nuclear BCOR IHC is supportive but not specific. Uniform oval-to-spindle cells have round-to-oval nuclei and delicate chromatin. A dense branching capillary network is characteristic. Perivascular pseudorosettes may occur but lack the GFAP-positive processes typical of ependymoma. Mitotic activity and Ki-67 are often increased. Strong diffuse nuclear BCOR is a sensitive supportive marker but is not specific. Vimentin and CD56 are commonly positive. OLIG2, GFAP, and S100 are absent or limited to scattered cells rather than diffusely expressed. Perivascular pseudorosettes are typically GFAP-negative. Demonstrate BCOR exon 15 ITD by sequencing or validated molecular assay. DNA methylation profiling can distinguish this tumor from other BCOR-altered and embryonal neoplasms. BCOR ITD is distinct from BCOR fusion-associated tumors. Nuclear BCOR staining alone is insufficient because other neoplasms can express BCOR. Exclude ependymoma and FOXR2-activated CNS neuroblastoma with molecular testing. Diagnosis of exclusion for a CNS embryonal tumor lacking a defining molecular alteration or lacking adequate molecular workup. Most occur in infancy and childhood, although adults may be affected. Can arise throughout the neuraxis; most are supratentorial. Often present acutely with raised intracranial pressure, seizures, or focal neurologic deficits. CNS neoplasm with embryonal morphology and compatible immunophenotype. Exclude medulloblastoma, ETMR, AT/RT, pineoblastoma, FOXR2-activated CNS neuroblastoma, and BCOR ITD tumor. Use NEC when adequate molecular workup excludes recognized entities but classification remains unresolved. Use NOS when further molecular analysis is unavailable or technically unsuccessful. Sheets of densely packed immature cells with high N:C ratios and round, oval, or angulated hyperchromatic nuclei. Mitoses and apoptosis are typically numerous. Foci of neurocytic or ganglion-cell differentiation may occur. Necrosis and hemorrhage may be present. Synaptophysin and OLIG2 are variably expressed. Ki-67 is high. GFAP and vimentin are generally absent in tumor cells, although reactive astrocytes may stain. SMARCB1 and SMARCA4 status should be assessed to exclude AT/RT. Perform broad molecular profiling, including DNA methylation profiling, when available. Use RNA sequencing or targeted fusion testing to identify rare defining alterations. A diagnosis of NEC/NOS should follow exclusion of molecularly defined mimics. Avoid premature NEC/NOS classification before appropriate molecular testing. A small biopsy may obscure diagnostic differentiation; correlate with imaging and obtain additional tissue when feasible. Pineocytoma Pineal Region Tumors Well-differentiated pineal parenchymal tumor with pineocytomatous rosettes and mature neuronal phenotype. Usually affects adults; median age is approximately 44 years, but a wide age range is reported. Arises in the pineal region. Aqueductal obstruction may cause hydrocephalus; Parinaud syndrome and other neuro-ophthalmologic symptoms may occur. Well-differentiated pineal parenchymal neoplasm. Uniform mature cells arranged in sheets and/or large pineocytomatous rosettes. Low proliferative activity and absence of embryonal morphology. CNS WHO grade 1. Moderately cellular tumor composed of uniform mature pinealocyte-like cells. Large pineocytomatous rosettes contain delicate neuropil-like processes. Nuclei are round with finely stippled chromatin; mitotic activity is low. Pleomorphic/gangliocytic areas may occur but do not imply a separate glial component. Synaptophysin, NSE, and neurofilament proteins are usually strongly positive. CRX supports pineal lineage. Chromogranin A and other neuronal markers are variable. No neoplastic glial component is expected. No recurrent defining genetic alteration is established. DNA methylation profiling shows a distinct profile and may help in difficult cases. KBTBD4 alterations are not characteristic; their presence should prompt consideration of PPTID. Distinguish pineocytomatous rosettes from normal pineal parenchyma and pineal cyst wall. Pleomorphic pineocytoma lacks the neoplastic glial component and tumor-cell CD34 expression expected in ganglioglioma. Pineal Parenchymal Tumor of Intermediate Differentiation (PPTID) Intermediate cellularity and atypia; diffuse sheets/lobules, CRX positivity, and KBTBD4 alteration support the diagnosis. Pineoblastoma Primitive high-grade embryonal sheets with brisk mitoses, diffuse CRX, and retained SMARCB1/SMARCA4. Papillary Tumor of the Pineal Region (PTPR) Epithelial papillary/solid pattern with CK18 and SPDEF; usually Kir7.1-negative, unlike choroid plexus tumors. Desmoplastic Myxoid Tumor of the Pineal Region, SMARCB1-Mutant Collagenized and myxoid matrix with SMARCB1 loss; usually low mitotic activity and no overt malignant morphology. Intermediate-grade pineal parenchymal tumor with moderate-to-high cellularity, neuronal phenotype, and often KBTBD4 alteration. Usually affects adolescents and adults; median age is approximately 33 years. Presents with aqueductal obstruction, hydrocephalus, Parinaud syndrome, or other local mass effects. Pineal parenchymal neoplasm composed of diffuse sheets and/or large lobules of monomorphic round cells. Cellularity and cytologic atypia exceed those of pineocytoma but are less primitive than pineoblastoma. CNS WHO grade 2 or 3, based on histologic features and proliferative activity. KBTBD4 alteration is highly desirable as molecular support. Diffuse neurocytoma-like or oligodendroglioma-like sheets and/or lobulated architecture. Moderate-to-high cellularity with round nuclei, mild-to-moderate atypia, and salt-and-pepper chromatin. Cytoplasm is more discernible than in pineoblastoma. Mitotic activity is variable and contributes to grading. Synaptophysin is usually positive. CRX shows diffuse nuclear expression in most cases. Neurofilament and chromogranin A are variable. NeuN is typically negative, helping distinguish from central neurocytoma. OLIG2 is generally negative. KBTBD4 alteration is highly desirable and supports PPTID. DNA methylation profiling may resolve cases with overlapping morphology. IDH mutation and whole-arm 1p/19q codeletion are not expected. Do not classify a tumor as PPTID solely because it lies in the pineal region; exclude central neurocytoma and oligodendroglioma. A mixed pineocytoma-pineoblastoma tumor should not be labeled PPTID. Well-differentiated mature pinealocytes with pineocytomatous rosettes, low mitotic activity, and strong neuronal marker expression. Highly cellular pineal embryonal tumor with primitive small cells, high mitotic activity, and diffuse CRX expression. Predominantly affects infants and children; median age is approximately 6 years. Aqueductal obstruction, hydrocephalus, and raised intracranial pressure are common; CSF dissemination may occur. Poorly differentiated embryonal neoplasm arising in the pineal parenchyma. Highly cellular sheets of primitive cells with high N:C ratios, brisk mitoses, and apoptosis. Pineal lineage is supported by diffuse nuclear CRX expression. SMARCB1 and SMARCA4 are retained; exclude AT/RT. Patternless sheets of densely packed small cells with scant cytoplasm and hyperchromatic nuclei. Mitotic activity and apoptosis are brisk; necrosis may be present. Homer Wright or Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes may occur; pineocytomatous rosettes are absent. Mixed pineocytoma-pineoblastoma tumors may show sharply demarcated differentiated and primitive components. Synaptophysin and NSE are positive. CRX is typically diffusely nuclear positive in >50% of tumor cells. LIN28A is typically negative, unlike ETMR. Neurofilament and chromogranin A are less frequently positive than in pineocytoma. DNA methylation profiling identifies molecular subgroups. Assess DICER1, DROSHA, and DGCR8 alterations in miRNA-processing subgroups. Evaluate RB1 in infantile tumors and MYC/FOXR2 activation when indicated. Germline assessment may be appropriate for RB1- or DICER1-associated contexts. Confirm pineal location; morphology overlaps with other CNS embryonal tumors. Do not confuse with PPTID; KBTBD4 alteration supports PPTID, not pineoblastoma. Papillary and solid epithelial-like tumor with CK18 expression and a characteristic pineal-region location. Occurs in children and adults; reported median age is approximately 35 years. Symptoms reflect aqueductal obstruction, hydrocephalus, and local mass effect. Neuroepithelial tumor of the pineal region with papillary and solid components. Epithelial-like tumor cells with cytokeratin expression, particularly CK18. CNS WHO grade 2 or 3, depending on histologic features. Papillary structures contain vessels covered by layers of large pale-to-eosinophilic columnar cells. Solid areas may predominate, with ependymal-like rosettes or tubules. Nuclear atypia and mitotic activity are variable. True choroid plexus-type papillae with a conspicuous basement membrane are not typical. CK18 and other cytokeratins are characteristic, especially in papillary areas. SPDEF is frequently positive. Vimentin, S100, NSE, MAP2, and CD56 may be positive. GFAP is less frequent than in ependymoma; dot-like EMA is uncommon. Kir7.1 and E-cadherin are usually absent or limited. DNA methylation profiling distinguishes PTPR from ependymoma and pineal parenchymal tumors. No single recurrent alteration is required for routine diagnosis. Exclude metastatic adenocarcinoma using clinical history, imaging, and a focused IHC panel. Distinguish from choroid plexus papilloma using Kir7.1, E-cadherin, and morphology. Pineal-region tumor with collagenized and myxoid stroma and loss of nuclear SMARCB1. Reported in adolescents and adults; median age is approximately 40 years. All reported cases have arisen in the pineal region. Clinical symptoms reflect local mass effect and aqueductal obstruction. Pineal-region neoplasm with desmoplastic and myxoid stromal components. Cords, nests, or fascicles of oval, spindle, and epithelioid cells in collagenized and myxoid matrix. Loss of nuclear SMARCB1 (INI1) in tumor cells with intact internal controls. Assess SMARCB1 locus alteration to support the diagnosis. Variably dense cords and fascicles of small-to-medium oval, spindle, or epithelioid cells. Heavily collagenized stroma alternates with pale basophilic myxoid matrix. Irregular elongated vessels and prominent fibrosis are common. Rhabdoid cells are rare; mitoses are usually exceptional and overt malignant features are lacking. Loss of nuclear SMARCB1 is defining. CD34 and EMA are often expressed. Interpret staining with internal positive controls. Assess SMARCB1 deficiency by IHC and confirm alteration at the molecular level when feasible. DNA methylation profiling may support classification in difficult cases. Do not confuse with AT/RT: both may lose SMARCB1, but location and characteristic desmoplastic/myxoid morphology support this pineal-region entity. The reported case number is small; interpret biologic behavior cautiously. All Categories Central Nervous System Pathology Choroid Plexus, Embryonal, and Pineal Tumors Morphology-first diagnostic reference integrating histology, immunohistochemistry, molecular classification, and clinically relevant differential diagnosis. CNS Directory Choroid plexus tumors 3 entities 5 entities Other embryonal tumors 6 entities Pineal region tumors Integrated Diagnostic Approach Use anatomic site, morphology, targeted immunohistochemistry, and molecular classification in sequence. Diagnostic setting Key histologic clues Initial IHC / molecular workup Integrated interpretation Intraventricular papillary tumor Single-layered papillae; count mitoses; assess cellularity, pleomorphism, necrosis, papillary blurring, and brain invasion. CK7, Kir7.1, EAAT1, S100, transthyretin, Ki-67; consider copy-number or methylation profiling if atypical. Papilloma: <1 mitosis/mm². Atypical papilloma: ≥1 mitosis/mm². Carcinoma: at least 4 of 5 malignant histologic features. Cerebellar embryonal tumor Small blue cells, brisk mitoses/apoptosis; describe classic, desmoplastic/nodular, extensive nodularity, or large-cell/anaplastic pattern. β-catenin, GAB1, YAP1, OTX2, p75-NGFR, p53; DNA methylation profiling; TP53 sequencing in SHH tumors; MYC/MYCN amplification as indicated. Classify as WNT, SHH with TP53 status, or non-WNT/non-SHH; all medulloblastomas are CNS WHO grade 4. Supratentorial embryonal tumor Assess rosettes, rhabdoid cells, cribriform pattern, capillary network, neurocytic differentiation, and mitotic activity. INI1/SMARCB1, BRG1/SMARCA4, LIN28A, OLIG2, BCOR; broad DNA/RNA profiling and methylation classifier. Identify AT/RT, CRINET, ETMR, FOXR2-activated CNS neuroblastoma, or BCOR ITD tumor before using NEC/NOS. Pineal-region neoplasm Separate mature pinealocyte-like rosettes, intermediate cellularity, primitive embryonal sheets, papillary epithelial growth, and desmoplastic/myxoid pattern. Synaptophysin, neurofilament, CRX, CK18, SPDEF, INI1; KBTBD4, DICER1/DROSHA/DGCR8, RB1, MYC/FOXR2, and methylation profiling as indicated. Integrate morphology and site to distinguish pineocytoma, PPTID, pineoblastoma, PTPR, and SMARCB1-mutant desmoplastic myxoid tumor. Practical Guardrails Do not use Ki-67 as a substitute for mitotic counting in choroid plexus tumors. For medulloblastoma, histologic pattern does not replace molecular group assignment. Loss of INI1 or BRG1 requires an intact internal positive control and clinicopathologic correlation. LIN28A is supportive but not specific for ETMR; C19MC alteration is much more specific. title: CNS Genetic Tumor Syndromes
content: use client Neurofibromatosis Type 1 RAS/MAPK Predisposition Multiple café-au-lait macules, intertriginous freckling, neurofibromas, or an optic pathway glioma. Autosomal dominant NF1-related syndrome with cutaneous, osseous, peripheral nerve, and CNS manifestations. Children and adults; both sexes; skin, peripheral nerves, optic pathways, brainstem, and bone. Cutaneous findings often emerge in childhood; plexiform neurofibromas may be congenital. Clinical diagnosis: at least 2 of 7 features: ≥6 café-au-lait macules (>5 mm prepubertal or >15 mm postpubertal); axillary/inguinal freckling; ≥2 neurofibromas or one plexiform neurofibroma; optic pathway glioma; ≥2 Lisch nodules or choroidal abnormalities; characteristic osseous lesion; pathogenic NF1 variant in normal tissue; or an affected parent with one qualifying criterion. Apply age- and context-specific consensus criteria. Plexiform neurofibroma expands and incorporates multiple nerve fascicles in a multinodular pattern. ANNUBP is supported by at least 2 of cytologic atypia, hypercellularity, loss of neurofibroma architecture, and increased mitotic activity. MPNST shows infiltrative malignant spindle cells, brisk mitoses, and often necrosis. Associated gliomas are commonly pilocytic astrocytomas. Neurofibromas usually express S100 and SOX10 in Schwannian cells; CD34 highlights a subset of stromal cells. MPNST may show reduced/patchy S100 and SOX10; loss of H3K27me3 supports PRC2-deficient MPNST but is not universal. p16 loss may occur in ANNUBP/MPNST. NF2-Related Schwannomatosis Bilateral vestibular schwannomas, multiple meningiomas, and spinal ependymomas favor NF2-related disease; plexiform neurofibromas and the NF1 pigmentary phenotype favor NF1. Schwannomatosis (SMARCB1- or LZTR1-Related) Multiple painful schwannomas without the characteristic NF1 pigmentary findings or plexiform neurofibromas favor schwannomatosis. NF1 loss-of-function; neurofibromin is a RAS-GAP. Tumors commonly acquire biallelic NF1 inactivation. ANNUBP may acquire CDKN2A/B and other 9p alterations; MPNST may show PRC2 (SUZ12/EED), TP53, and CDKN2A/B abnormalities. RAS/MAPK and Chromatin-Related Predisposition Bilateral vestibular schwannomas, multiple meningiomas, and spinal ependymomas. Autosomal dominant tumor predisposition caused by NF2 inactivation; mosaic disease is common among de novo presentations. Adolescents and young adults; both sexes; vestibular nerves, other cranial nerves, spinal roots, meninges, and spinal cord. Hearing loss, tinnitus, imbalance, or multiple nerve tumors. Diagnosis can be established by bilateral vestibular schwannomas; an identical pathogenic NF2 variant in 2 or more anatomically distinct NF2-related tumors; or accepted consensus combinations of major/minor criteria. Major features include unilateral vestibular schwannoma, a first-degree relative with NF2-related schwannomatosis, and multiple meningiomas; minor features include schwannomas, ependymomas, and characteristic ocular/dermal findings. Confirm with germline or mosaic-sensitive testing when possible. Schwannomas may be multinodular or plexiform and may coexist with meningiomas and multiple spinal ependymomas. Hybrid schwannoma-neurofibroma tumors can occur. Meningioangiomatosis and glial hamartias are recognized associated lesions. Schwannomas express S100 and SOX10; mosaic/patchy loss of INI1 may occur but is not specific. Meningiomas may show loss of merlin/NF2 expression. Retinal and lens abnormalities are clinical clues rather than diagnostic tumor stains. Plexiform neurofibromas, multiple café-au-lait macules, and intertriginous freckling favor NF1. Multiple painful schwannomas without bilateral vestibular schwannomas or the characteristic NF2 tumor combination favor SMARCB1/LZTR1-related schwannomatosis. NF2 pathogenic variants; merlin tumor-suppressor loss. Tumors typically show biallelic NF2 inactivation. Mosaicism can cause low variant allele fractions and negative routine blood testing. Multiple schwannomas with chronic pain, usually without bilateral vestibular schwannomas. Predisposition to multiple schwannomas associated with germline SMARCB1 or LZTR1 variants; tumor-specific NF2 inactivation is common. Usually second to fourth decades; both sexes; peripheral nerves, spinal roots, and occasionally cranial nerves or meninges. Pain or a palpable mass is common; neurologic deficits are less frequent. Establish a clinical diagnosis using accepted criteria for multiple pathologically confirmed schwannomas or characteristic imaging plus family history, while excluding NF2-related schwannomatosis. Molecular classification requires a pathogenic germline SMARCB1 or LZTR1 variant; assess NF2 in the differential, especially with vestibular tumors. Schwannomas resemble sporadic counterparts and may be multiple, segmental, or plexiform. Hybrid schwannoma-neurofibroma lesions may occur. SMARCB1-related cases can include meningiomas and rarely malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumors. Schwannomas are diffusely positive for S100 and SOX10. INI1 may show mosaic loss in tumor cells; interpret with internal controls and germline testing. LZTR1-related tumors do not have a defining routine IHC surrogate. Plexiform neurofibromas and pigmentary diagnostic criteria favor NF1. Bilateral vestibular schwannomas, meningiomas, and spinal ependymomas favor NF2-related disease. Germline SMARCB1 or LZTR1 pathogenic variants; schwannomas commonly acquire chromosome 22q/NF2 alterations as part of a multi-hit mechanism. Tumor testing alone cannot establish germline status. Von Hippel-Lindau Syndrome Tumor Suppressor Predisposition Hemangioblastomas with retinal, renal, pancreatic, or adrenal manifestations. Autosomal dominant VHL tumor predisposition syndrome involving highly vascular CNS and retinal hemangioblastomas and multiple visceral neoplasms. Childhood through adulthood; both sexes; cerebellum, brainstem, spinal cord, retina, kidney, pancreas, and adrenal medulla. Symptoms depend on tumor location; renal tumors may be multifocal/bilateral. A heterozygous germline pathogenic VHL variant establishes the molecular diagnosis. Clinical diagnosis can be made using accepted criteria based on a characteristic VHL-associated lesion plus family history, or multiple characteristic lesions in a person without family history. Consider VHL with CNS/retinal hemangioblastoma, clear cell renal cell carcinoma, pheochromocytoma, pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor, or multiple pancreatic/renal cysts. Hemangioblastoma has a rich capillary network and stromal cells with lipid-rich clear cytoplasm. Associated tumors include clear cell renal cell carcinoma, pancreatic neuroendocrine neoplasms, and pheochromocytoma/paraganglioma. Hemangioblastoma stromal cells commonly express inhibin-alpha, S100, and CAIX; endothelial cells express CD31/CD34. VHL-associated paragangliomas may show CAIX and inhibin. Use lineage-specific panels to distinguish metastatic clear cell RCC. Key syndromic differential Sporadic hemangioblastoma: may be morphologically identical; multiplicity, younger age, and associated visceral lesions prompt VHL testing. Metastatic clear cell RCC: epithelial nests express pancytokeratin/PAX8 and lack the typical stromal-cell phenotype. Other vascular lesions: lack the characteristic stromal cell population. Germline VHL inactivation with somatic second hit; HIF pathway dysregulation and angiogenic signaling. Tumor VHL alterations alone do not prove hereditary disease. Tuberous Sclerosis Complex mTOR Pathway Predisposition Subependymal nodules, subependymal giant cell astrocytoma, cortical tubers, and renal angiomyolipomas. Autosomal dominant multisystem disorder caused by TSC1 or TSC2 pathogenic variants and mTOR pathway activation. Often recognized in infancy or childhood; both sexes; cerebral cortex, subependymal region, kidney, heart, skin, lung, and retina. Seizures, developmental delay, and skin lesions are common presentations. Clinical diagnosis: definite TSC with 2 major features or 1 major plus ≥2 minor features; possible TSC with 1 major or ≥2 minor features. Major features include ≥3 hypomelanotic macules, facial angiofibromas or fibrous cephalic plaque, ungual fibromas, shagreen patch, multiple retinal hamartomas, cortical dysplasias, subependymal nodules, SEGA, cardiac rhabdomyoma, LAM, and ≥2 angiomyolipomas. A pathogenic TSC1/TSC2 variant in normal tissue is independently diagnostic. Cortical tubers show disorganized cortex, dysmorphic neurons, and balloon cells. SEGA is a circumscribed subependymal tumor with large ganglioid cells and variable spindle-cell/astrocytic areas. Renal angiomyolipomas contain dysmorphic vessels, smooth muscle, and adipose tissue. SEGA and cortical lesions may express GFAP, neuronal markers, and phospho-S6; HMB45/Melan-A and smooth muscle markers highlight angiomyolipoma cells. No single IHC stain establishes TSC. Nevoid Basal Cell Carcinoma Syndrome (Gorlin Syndrome) Odontogenic keratocysts, early/multiple BCCs, and SHH medulloblastoma favor Gorlin syndrome; cortical tubers and SEGA favor TSC. Germline TSC1 or TSC2 loss with somatic second hit; loss of hamartin/tuberin activates RHEB-mTORC1. Mosaic variants may require deep sequencing. Li-Fraumeni Syndrome DNA Damage Response Predisposition Multiple early-onset primary cancers, especially sarcoma, breast cancer, brain tumors, and adrenocortical carcinoma. Autosomal dominant cancer predisposition syndrome caused by germline TP53 pathogenic variants. Children, adolescents, and young adults; both sexes; multiple organs. Classic tumors include soft-tissue/bone sarcomas, premenopausal breast carcinoma, CNS tumors, and adrenocortical carcinoma. A germline pathogenic TP53 variant establishes the diagnosis. Use modified Chompret criteria to select patients for testing: a core tumor before age 46 plus an affected close relative with a core tumor before age 56 or multiple tumors; multiple primary tumors with the first before 46; rare tumors such as adrenocortical carcinoma or choroid plexus carcinoma; or breast cancer at a young age in appropriate family context. Tumors are histologically diverse and generally resemble sporadic counterparts. CNS tumors include choroid plexus carcinoma, high-grade gliomas, and medulloblastoma. Choroid plexus carcinoma may show marked atypia, brisk mitoses, and necrosis. p53 often shows diffuse strong nuclear overexpression or complete null pattern, but wild-type staining does not exclude germline TP53. Interpret p53 in the context of morphology and molecular testing. Constitutional Mismatch Repair Deficiency Syndrome Childhood malignancies with biallelic MMR deficiency, MMR protein loss, and ultrahypermutation favor CMMRD. Familial Retinoblastoma (RB1-Related Predisposition) Retinoblastoma, especially bilateral or multifocal, and pineoblastoma favor RB1-related predisposition. Germline TP53 pathogenic variant; somatic second hit and genomic instability. Clonal hematopoiesis can complicate blood-based testing; confirm suspected germline findings in nonhematopoietic tissue when indicated. PTEN Hamartoma Tumor Syndrome (Cowden Syndrome) PI3K-AKT-mTOR Pathway Predisposition Macrocephaly, mucocutaneous lesions, hamartomas, and increased breast, thyroid, endometrial, and renal tumor risk. Autosomal dominant PTEN-related syndrome encompassing Cowden syndrome and related phenotypes. Usually recognized in adolescence or adulthood; both sexes; skin, oral mucosa, thyroid, breast, endometrium, kidney, and CNS. Macrocephaly and mucocutaneous lesions are prominent clues. A germline pathogenic PTEN variant establishes the molecular diagnosis. Clinical diagnosis uses accepted operational criteria, including combinations of pathognomonic mucocutaneous lesions, macrocephaly, hamartomatous gastrointestinal polyps, characteristic breast/thyroid/endometrial/renal cancers, and relevant family history. Lhermitte-Duclos disease is a major clue. CNS manifestation includes dysplastic cerebellar gangliocytoma (Lhermitte-Duclos disease), with enlarged cerebellar folia and a characteristic striated or tigroid architecture. Other lesions include hamartomatous polyps and diverse benign/malignant tumors. Lhermitte-Duclos lesions show abnormal neuronal and glial elements; synaptophysin highlights dysplastic ganglion cells and GFAP highlights associated glia. PTEN IHC may be reduced but is not a substitute for germline testing. Tuberous sclerosis: cortical tubers and SEGA with TSC-associated systemic findings. Sporadic cerebellar dysplastic gangliocytoma: morphology may overlap; macrocephaly and mucocutaneous/systemic criteria support PTEN syndrome. Cowden-like phenotypes from other genes require molecular distinction. Germline PTEN loss-of-function; PI3K-AKT-mTOR pathway activation. Tumors may show somatic second hits or pathway alterations. DNA Repair Predisposition Childhood brain tumors, hematologic malignancies, and gastrointestinal cancers with café-au-lait-like skin lesions. Autosomal recessive cancer predisposition caused by biallelic pathogenic variants in an MMR gene. Infancy through adolescence; both sexes; brain, gastrointestinal tract, and hematolymphoid system. Multiple malignancies at unusually young ages are typical. Diagnosis requires biallelic pathogenic variants in MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, or PMS2, or compelling functional evidence of constitutional MMR deficiency. Suspect in children with multiple malignancies, high-grade glioma, hematologic cancer, or early colorectal cancer, particularly with consanguinity or Lynch syndrome in relatives. CNS tumors include high-grade gliomas and other embryonal/neuroepithelial tumors. Histology is variable; extreme tumor mutational burden and lymphocytic response may be encountered in some tumors. Loss of the relevant MMR protein pair by IHC (MLH1/PMS2 or MSH2/MSH6) in tumor is a screening clue; constitutional testing in non-neoplastic tissue is required to establish the syndrome. MSI and tumor mutational burden can support the workup. Germline TP53 alteration and the characteristic sarcoma, breast, brain, and adrenocortical tumor spectrum favor Li-Fraumeni syndrome. Familial Adenomatous Polyposis (APC-Associated) Profuse colorectal adenomas and APC-associated WNT medulloblastoma favor FAP. Biallelic germline MMR gene variants; tumors acquire additional MMR loss and often show microsatellite instability and ultrahypermutation. WNT Pathway Predisposition Colonic adenomatous polyposis with risk of medulloblastoma, especially the WNT-activated subtype. Autosomal dominant APC-associated syndrome; the historical Turcot label should not replace a molecular diagnosis. Childhood through adulthood; both sexes; colon, duodenum, brain, thyroid, and other organs. Hundreds to thousands of colorectal adenomas typically develop in classic FAP. A germline pathogenic APC variant establishes the diagnosis. Clinical diagnosis is supported by ≥100 colorectal adenomas, a known familial pathogenic variant, or characteristic extracolonic manifestations with a compatible family history. Attenuated FAP has fewer adenomas and later presentation. Associated CNS tumor is most often medulloblastoma, particularly WNT-activated medulloblastoma. Desmoid-type fibromatosis, osteomas, and other extracolonic lesions may occur. WNT-activated medulloblastoma typically shows nuclear β-catenin and may show monosomy 6. APC-related tumors may show loss of APC pathway function; correlate with germline testing. Childhood cancers with biallelic MMR loss and no classic adenomatous polyposis favor CMMRD. Multiple early-onset core tumors and germline TP53 alteration favor Li-Fraumeni syndrome. Germline APC pathogenic variant with somatic second hit; constitutive WNT/β-catenin signaling. APC genotype can influence phenotype and desmoid risk. Hedgehog Pathway Predisposition Early/multiple basal cell carcinomas, odontogenic keratocysts, falx calcification, and childhood SHH medulloblastoma. Autosomal dominant PTCH1- or SUFU-related tumor predisposition syndrome. Childhood through adulthood; both sexes; skin, jaw, falx, and cerebellum. Odontogenic keratocysts often arise in childhood/adolescence; BCCs increase with age and sun exposure. Clinical diagnosis requires accepted combinations of major and minor criteria, including multiple BCCs or early-onset BCC, odontogenic keratocysts, palmar/plantar pits, falx calcification, rib anomalies, and first-degree family history. A constitutional pathogenic PTCH1 or SUFU variant establishes the molecular diagnosis. Jaw odontogenic keratocysts resemble sporadic counterparts. Associated medulloblastomas are usually SHH-activated; desmoplastic/nodular morphology is common, particularly in young children. Medulloblastoma may show GAB1/SFRP1 patterns supporting SHH subgroup; β-catenin is generally not nuclear. BCC and odontogenic keratocyst findings are morphologic; PTCH1/SUFU testing is definitive. ELP1-Associated Medulloblastoma Predisposition Both may present with childhood SHH medulloblastoma; ELP1 requires germline ELP1 alteration and loss of ELP1 expression, whereas Gorlin syndrome is supported by PTCH1/SUFU variants and characteristic skin/jaw findings. SEGA and cortical tubers with TSC-associated systemic findings favor TSC rather than Gorlin syndrome. Germline PTCH1 or SUFU loss activates Hedgehog signaling. SUFU-associated cases have particularly increased medulloblastoma risk; avoid radiotherapy when feasible because of secondary BCC risk. Rhabdoid Tumor Predisposition Syndrome SWI/SNF Chromatin Remodeling Predisposition Atypical teratoid/rhabdoid tumor or malignant rhabdoid tumor in an infant or young child, sometimes with multiple primary tumors. Autosomal dominant predisposition caused by germline SMARCB1 (RTPS1) or SMARCA4 (RTPS2) pathogenic variants. Infants and young children; both sexes; CNS, kidney, soft tissue, and other sites. Very early onset and synchronous/metachronous rhabdoid tumors are key clues. Suspect with AT/RT, renal or extrarenal malignant rhabdoid tumor, especially in infancy, multiple tumors, or family history. Tumor loss of INI1 or BRG1 prompts germline evaluation; diagnosis of the syndrome requires constitutional pathogenic variant confirmation. AT/RT and malignant rhabdoid tumors show sheets of primitive cells, eccentric nuclei, prominent nucleoli, and variable rhabdoid cytoplasm. Morphology can be heterogeneous and may lack overt rhabdoid cells. Loss of nuclear INI1 (SMARCB1) or BRG1 (SMARCA4) in tumor cells with retained internal controls is a key screening finding. The absent protein identifies the affected pathway but does not itself prove germline status. SMARCB1-related schwannomatosis shares a gene with RTPS1 but presents with multiple schwannomas rather than infantile rhabdoid tumors; confirm the germline variant and phenotype. Germline SMARCB1 or SMARCA4 pathogenic variant with somatic second hit. AT/RT molecular groups include TYR, SHH, and MYC; subgroup does not by itself define germline predisposition. Carney Complex PRKAR1A / cAMP-PKA Predisposition Spotty pigmentation, cardiac myxomas, endocrine overactivity, and melanotic nerve sheath tumors. Autosomal dominant multisystem syndrome, most often due to PRKAR1A inactivation. Childhood through adulthood; both sexes; skin/mucosa, heart, endocrine organs, and peripheral nerves. Lentigines often become prominent around puberty; cardiac myxomas may occur in childhood. Clinical diagnosis uses accepted major criteria, including spotty pigmentation, cardiac or cutaneous myxomas, primary pigmented nodular adrenocortical disease, acromegaly from GH-producing pituitary adenoma, large-cell calcifying Sertoli cell tumor, thyroid tumors, and psammomatous melanotic schwannoma. A pathogenic PRKAR1A variant supports/establishes the molecular diagnosis. Psammomatous melanotic schwannoma (now often termed malignant melanotic nerve sheath tumor) shows pigmented spindle/epithelioid cells, psammoma bodies, and may show infiltrative growth. Myxomas are hypocellular with abundant myxoid matrix. Melanotic nerve sheath tumors express S100 and SOX10 and melanocytic markers (HMB45/Melan-A); PRKAR1A loss may support Carney complex. Myxomas are typically vimentin-positive and lack a specific diagnostic IHC profile. BAP1 Tumor Predisposition Syndrome Both can include melanocytic/nerve sheath tumors; BAP1 loss, uveal melanoma, mesothelioma, and BAP1-inactivated melanocytic tumors favor BAP1 syndrome, whereas lentigines, cardiac myxomas, and endocrine disease favor Carney complex. Germline PRKAR1A loss disrupts PKA regulation and increases cAMP/PKA signaling. A subset of cases lack an identified PRKAR1A variant. DICER1 Tumor Predisposition Syndrome MicroRNA Processing Predisposition Pleuropulmonary blastoma, cystic nephroma, ovarian Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor, and multinodular goiter. Autosomal dominant predisposition caused by germline pathogenic DICER1 variants, with characteristic tumors across multiple organs. Mostly infants, children, and young adults; both sexes; lung, kidney, thyroid, ovary, CNS, and eye. Pleuropulmonary blastoma is a sentinel manifestation. A heterozygous germline pathogenic DICER1 variant establishes the diagnosis. Offer testing for pleuropulmonary blastoma or other characteristic manifestations, including cystic nephroma, ovarian Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor, thyroid nodular disease, and selected CNS embryonal tumors. CNS tumors include DICER1-associated intracranial sarcoma and other rare embryonal/neuroepithelial tumors. Histology varies by tumor type; correlate with the characteristic extracranial spectrum rather than expecting a single morphology. No single IHC marker is diagnostic. DICER1-deficient tumors may show loss of DICER1 protein in some settings, but germline sequencing and tumor second-hit analysis are required. Gorlin syndrome: SHH medulloblastoma with PTCH1/SUFU alterations. Rhabdoid tumor predisposition: INI1/BRG1 loss and rhabdoid morphology. Sporadic pediatric sarcoma: age/site overlap; DICER1 testing and associated tumor history distinguish. Germline loss-of-function DICER1 variant plus a somatic RNase IIIb hotspot mutation is a common two-hit pattern. Tumor sequencing may identify the second hit. Familial Paraganglioma-Pheochromocytoma Syndromes Mitochondrial / Pseudohypoxia Predisposition Multifocal or early-onset paragangliomas, especially head-and-neck tumors, with possible pheochromocytoma and other SDH-associated tumors. Inherited predisposition involving SDHx genes and other susceptibility genes; includes SDHA, SDHB, SDHC, SDHD, and SDHAF2-related disease. Adolescents and adults; both sexes; head and neck, thorax, abdomen, pelvis, adrenal medulla, and occasionally CNS/cauda equina. Symptoms include catecholamine excess, mass effect, or incidental detection. Suspect with paraganglioma/pheochromocytoma at young age, multifocality, bilateral disease, family history, or associated GIST/renal cancer. Germline testing identifies the syndrome and gene; SDHD often shows parent-of-origin effects. Paragangliomas show nested Zellballen architecture with chief cells and sustentacular cells. SDH-related head-and-neck tumors may have clear/vacuolated chief cells and prominent nests; VHL-related tumors may also show clear cytoplasm. Chief cells express synaptophysin, chromogranin, and INSM1; sustentacular cells highlight with S100/SOX10. Loss of SDHB is a screening marker for SDH deficiency; loss of SDHA suggests SDHA alteration. GATA3 and tyrosine hydroxylase may be positive. Cytokeratins are usually negative. Sporadic paraganglioma: morphology overlaps; germline testing and SDHB/SDHA IHC identify hereditary SDH deficiency. Metastatic neuroendocrine tumor: often keratin-positive and lacks the classic sustentacular pattern. VHL: clear-cell paraganglioma may overlap; assess VHL-associated lesions and molecular findings. Germline SDHx variants cause succinate accumulation, inhibition of α-ketoglutarate-dependent enzymes, and pseudohypoxia. SDHB loss is a useful surrogate but does not identify the specific germline gene. Melanoma-Astrocytoma Syndrome CDKN2A Cell-Cycle Predisposition Multiple dysplastic nevi or melanoma together with astrocytoma or nerve sheath tumors. Rare inherited cancer predisposition associated with germline CDKN2A pathogenic variants, often affecting p16INK4A and/or p14ARF. Adolescents and adults; both sexes; skin, brain, peripheral nerves, and pancreas. Multiple atypical nevi/melanoma may precede CNS tumors. Diagnosis requires identification of a pathogenic germline CDKN2A variant in constitutional DNA. Consider testing with familial melanoma plus astrocytoma, multiple melanomas, or a compatible family history of pancreatic cancer and CNS tumors. Associated astrocytomas include pleomorphic xanthoastrocytoma and diffuse astrocytic gliomas from low to high grade. Nerve sheath tumors may resemble schwannoma or neurofibroma; morphology may not distinguish syndromic from sporadic lesions. Astrocytomas show lineage-dependent markers (GFAP/OLIG2); p16 loss may be present. Melanocytic lesions express SOX10, S100, and melanocytic markers. IHC does not replace germline testing. BAP1 tumor predisposition: BAP1-inactivated melanocytic tumors, mesothelioma, uveal melanoma, and meningioma; BAP1 IHC distinguishes deficient tumors. NF1: neurofibromas and pigmentary signs, with different clinical criteria. Sporadic PXA: BRAF V600E/CDKN2A alterations can occur without germline syndrome. Germline CDKN2A pathogenic variant; tumors commonly inactivate the remaining allele. Somatic BRAF V600E may occur in PXA but is not specific for the syndrome. Cell-Cycle Predisposition Bilateral or multifocal retinoblastoma, early onset, and risk of pineoblastoma (trilateral retinoblastoma). Autosomal dominant cancer predisposition caused by a germline RB1 pathogenic variant; tumors develop after loss of the remaining functional allele. Infants and young children; both sexes; retina, pineal region, and other tissues at risk for secondary malignancies. Leukocoria and strabismus are typical presenting signs. A germline pathogenic RB1 variant establishes hereditary retinoblastoma predisposition. Bilateral, multifocal, or very early-onset retinoblastoma strongly suggests germline disease. Trilateral retinoblastoma denotes bilateral ocular retinoblastoma with an intracranial midline neuroblastic tumor, usually pineoblastoma. Retinoblastoma is a small round blue cell tumor with brisk mitoses, necrosis, calcification, and Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes. Pineoblastoma in trilateral disease resembles retinoblastoma histologically. Tumor cells show loss of RB protein; synaptophysin and other neuronal markers may be positive. RB IHC is a screening aid; germline testing confirms hereditary predisposition. Pineoblastoma without retinoblastoma: may be sporadic or associated with other predisposition syndromes. Medulloblastoma: cerebellar origin and distinct molecular groups. Other small round blue cell tumors: use site, morphology, and lineage markers. Germline RB1 pathogenic variant plus somatic second hit; loss of RB1 function dysregulates G1/S cell-cycle control. Genetic counseling and testing of relatives are important. Chromatin / DNA Repair-Related Predisposition Uveal melanoma, mesothelioma, cutaneous melanoma, BAP1-inactivated melanocytic tumors, and rhabdoid/papillary meningioma. Autosomal dominant cancer predisposition caused by germline BAP1 pathogenic variants. Adolescents through adults; both sexes; eye, skin, pleura/peritoneum, kidney, and meninges. Multiple early-onset primary tumors and characteristic melanocytic lesions are clues. Consider germline testing with ≥2 BAP1-associated tumors, one such tumor plus an affected close relative, or unusually young onset. Loss of BAP1 in a relevant tumor supports testing but is not proof of germline disease. A constitutional pathogenic BAP1 variant establishes the syndrome. BAP1-associated meningiomas may show rhabdoid, epithelioid, or papillary morphology and can behave aggressively. BAP1-inactivated melanocytic tumors show epithelioid melanocytes and may be multiple. Complete loss of nuclear BAP1 in tumor cells with retained internal controls supports BAP1 deficiency. Melanocytic lesions express SOX10/S100 and melanocytic markers; BAP1 loss is the key surrogate stain. Psammomatous melanotic nerve sheath tumor with lentigines, cardiac myxoma, and endocrine overactivity favors Carney complex; nuclear BAP1 loss and BAP1-associated tumor spectrum favor BAP1 syndrome. Germline BAP1 loss with somatic second hit. IHC and sequencing are highly concordant but not completely; interpret missense variants carefully. Fanconi Anemia DNA Interstrand Crosslink Repair Predisposition Congenital anomalies, progressive bone marrow failure, and early cancers including medulloblastoma. Genetically heterogeneous inherited DNA repair disorder, usually autosomal recessive; biallelic BRCA2 or PALB2 variants are particularly associated with CNS tumor predisposition. Infancy through adulthood; both sexes; bone marrow, head and neck, kidney, and CNS. Short stature, thumb/radial anomalies, skin pigmentation, and marrow failure may be present but can be absent. Diagnosis is established by increased chromosome breakage in patient cells after diepoxybutane or mitomycin C exposure and/or biallelic pathogenic variants in an FA pathway gene. Germline BRCA2/PALB2 testing is important in children with medulloblastoma and compatible features. Associated medulloblastomas are often large-cell/anaplastic or desmoplastic/nodular with superimposed anaplasia. Other malignancies include MDS/AML and squamous cell carcinoma of the head and neck. No defining tumor IHC profile. Assess tumor morphology and molecular subtype; constitutional chromosome-breakage testing and germline sequencing establish the predisposition. ELP1 syndrome is characterized by SHH-activated, TP53-wildtype medulloblastoma without the Fanconi chromosome-breakage phenotype. Germline TP53 alteration and the broader Li-Fraumeni tumor spectrum favor Li-Fraumeni syndrome. Defective DNA interstrand crosslink repair; biallelic FANC gene variants. Medulloblastomas may show complex chromosomal rearrangements, SHH activation, and TP53 alterations. Heterozygous BRCA2/PALB2 carriers can also develop medulloblastoma after tumor-specific second hit. RNA Processing / SHH Pathway Predisposition Childhood SHH-activated, TP53-wildtype medulloblastoma, often desmoplastic/nodular. Rare inherited predisposition associated with biallelic or specific pathogenic germline ELP1 variants and a characteristic medulloblastoma phenotype. Children; median diagnosis around 6 years; both sexes; cerebellum. Family history of medulloblastoma may be present. Suspect in childhood SHH-activated, TP53-wildtype medulloblastoma, particularly desmoplastic/nodular morphology or family history. Confirm with germline ELP1 testing and correlate with tumor ELP1 expression. Most tumors are desmoplastic/nodular; a minority are classic or large-cell/anaplastic. Histology overlaps with other SHH-activated medulloblastomas. Loss of ELP1 expression in tumor tissue supports the diagnosis but should be followed by germline testing. SHH pathway markers help establish molecular subgroup; TP53 is typically wild-type. SHH medulloblastoma overlaps; germline PTCH1/SUFU variants and jaw cysts/BCCs favor Gorlin syndrome. Chromosome-breakage phenotype and biallelic FANC variants favor Fanconi anemia; ELP1-associated tumors are typically SHH-activated and TP53-wildtype. Rare germline ELP1 pathogenic variants, usually truncating or canonical splice variants. Tumors commonly show 9q loss and somatic PTCH1 mutation without germline PTCH1 alteration. All categories Central and Peripheral Nervous System CNS Genetic Tumor Syndromes Diagnostic reference to inherited tumor-predisposition syndromes with central or peripheral nervous system manifestations. Recognition of a syndromic pattern should prompt appropriate clinical evaluation and germline testing; tumor findings alone do not establish hereditary status. Practical Diagnostic Approach Recognize tumor multiplicity, unusually young age, characteristic combinations of lesions, and relevant family history. Use morphology and targeted immunohistochemistry to identify pathway-deficient tumors, including loss of INI1, BRG1, BAP1, SDHB, or SDHA when appropriate. Distinguish tumor-level alterations from constitutional variants. A tumor-only pathogenic variant or loss of protein expression does not independently prove a germline syndrome. Recommend genetic counseling and constitutional testing when the clinical or pathologic pattern warrants it; consider mosaicism and nonhematopoietic testing when indicated. Do not use the historical term “Turcot syndrome” as a molecular diagnosis. Evaluate APC-associated FAP and constitutional mismatch repair deficiency as distinct conditions.
