title: Cranial Paraspinal Sellar Tumors
content: use client Schwannoma Peripheral Nerve Sheath Tumors A circumscribed Schwann-cell neoplasm with Antoni A/B areas, Verocay bodies, and diffuse S100/SOX10. A benign nerve sheath tumor composed entirely or almost entirely of differentiated neoplastic Schwann cells. Usually adults in the fourth to sixth decades; no consistent sex predilection. Common in vestibular nerve, spinal nerve roots, and peripheral nerves of the head, neck, and extremities. Typically a slow-growing, painless mass; vestibular lesions may cause hearing loss and vertigo, while spinal lesions may cause radicular symptoms. Multiple tumors or bilateral vestibular schwannomas should prompt evaluation for NF2-related schwannomatosis or another schwannomatosis syndrome. Well-circumscribed, usually encapsulated Schwann-cell neoplasm. Conventional tumors show alternating Antoni A and Antoni B areas; Verocay bodies may be present. Diffuse S100 and SOX10 expression supports Schwannian differentiation. Degenerative atypia alone does not indicate malignancy. Antoni A areas are compact, composed of spindle cells with tapered nuclei and eosinophilic cytoplasm. Verocay bodies consist of nuclear palisades separated by aligned cell processes. Antoni B areas are hypocellular and loosely textured, often with microcystic change and foamy histiocytes. Thick-walled hyalinized vessels and peripheral lymphoid aggregates are useful architectural clues. Ancient change produces scattered bizarre degenerative nuclei, often with hyalinization or ischemic change. Cellular schwannoma is predominantly Antoni A, often hypercellular and mitotically active, but retains circumscription and other schwannoma features. Plexiform schwannoma forms multinodular or plexiform growth, often in dermis or subcutis. Epithelioid schwannoma contains lobules or nests of epithelioid cells in myxoid or hyalinized stroma; a subset loses INI1. Microcystic/reticular schwannoma shows an interconnected network of bland cells in myxoid or collagenous stroma. S100 and SOX10 are usually diffuse and strong in tumor cells. GFAP is variable and less sensitive than S100/SOX10. CD34 may highlight subcapsular stromal cells but is not usually diffusely expressed by the neoplastic Schwann cells. Neurofilament highlights entrapped axons, often concentrated at the periphery. EMA highlights perineurial cells in the capsule. INI1 is lost in a subset of epithelioid schwannomas. Neurofibroma Neurofibroma is usually unencapsulated and infiltrative, with mixed cell populations and intralesional axons; schwannoma is more uniform and diffusely S100/SOX10-positive. Perineurioma Perineurioma is EMA/GLUT1/claudin-1-positive and usually S100/SOX10-negative. Hybrid nerve sheath tumor Hybrid tumors contain two recognizable nerve sheath differentiation patterns rather than a nearly pure Schwann-cell population. Malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumor MPNST typically shows destructive infiltration, significant atypia, brisk mitoses and/or necrosis, with absent or only focal S100/SOX10; retained H3K27me3 does not exclude MPNST. Malignant melanotic nerve sheath tumor MMNST is pigmented and expresses melanocytic markers in addition to Schwannian markers, usually with PRKAR1A loss. NF2 inactivation and chromosome 22q loss are common but not specific. LATS1, LATS2, ARID1A, ARID1B, and DDR1 alterations occur in subsets. A recurrent SH3PXD2A::HTRA1 fusion is present in a minority of cases. Germline NF2, SMARCB1, or LZTR1 alterations may underlie multiple tumors. Cellular schwannoma may mimic MPNST; assess the capsule, lymphoid aggregates, hyalinized vessels, Schwannian whorls, and overall architecture. Do not equate degenerative nuclear pleomorphism with malignant transformation. An unencapsulated, mixed-cell nerve sheath lesion with wavy nuclei, myxoid matrix, collagen bundles, and entrapped axons. A benign peripheral nerve sheath tumor composed of neoplastic Schwann cells admixed with non-neoplastic stromal and perineurial elements. Occurs at any age; cutaneous lesions often emerge in childhood or adolescence in NF1. Most commonly dermal or subcutaneous; deep lesions may involve major nerves, plexuses, spinal roots, or dorsal root ganglia. Usually presents as a soft, painless mass; deep lesions may cause sensory or motor symptoms. Multiple cutaneous tumors, plexiform growth, or massive soft-tissue involvement strongly suggests NF1. Bland spindle cells with thin, wavy nuclei in a loose myxoid to collagenous stroma. Mixed cellular composition, including Schwann cells, fibroblastic cells, perineurial cells, and mast cells. Usually unencapsulated, with infiltration of the parent nerve or adjacent soft tissue. Plexiform neurofibroma involves multiple nerve fascicles, each outlined by perineurium. ANNUBP requires at least two defined worrisome histologic features and must be distinguished from ordinary degenerative atypia. The tumor is composed of slender spindle cells with wavy, comma-shaped, or serpentine nuclei. The background is variably myxoid with characteristic wiry or shredded-carrot collagen bundles. Mast cells and CD34-positive stromal cells are commonly admixed. Intraneural lesions expand individual fascicles; plexiform lesions expand multiple fascicles in a multinodular, rope-like pattern. Diffuse neurofibroma may form plaque-like dermal and subcutaneous infiltrates. Ancient neurofibroma shows scattered bizarre nuclei without hypercellularity, architectural loss, or increased mitotic activity. Cellular neurofibroma is hypercellular but lacks the uniform atypia and mitotic activity expected in MPNST. ANNUBP shows at least two of: cytologic atypia, hypercellularity, loss of neurofibroma architecture, or increased mitotic activity above the specified threshold but below that of MPNST. S100 and SOX10 highlight the Schwann-cell component, usually less uniformly than in schwannoma. CD34 highlights a lattice-like network of stromal cells. EMA and GLUT1 highlight scattered perineurial cells and the perineurial boundaries of nerve fascicles. Neurofilament highlights axons traversing the lesion. H3K27me3 is generally retained in neurofibroma and ANNUBP; loss supports MPNST in the appropriate setting. Complete loss of p16 in a suspicious focus may support progression toward ANNUBP or MPNST. Schwannoma is usually encapsulated, composed almost entirely of Schwann cells, and diffusely S100/SOX10-positive; neurofibroma is mixed-cell and commonly contains axons. Perineurioma shows a dominant EMA/GLUT1/claudin-1-positive perineurial population and lacks the Schwann-cell-rich mixed pattern. Hybrid lesions contain discrete or intermingled components with two nerve sheath phenotypes, often including schwannomatous nodules. ANNUBP ANNUBP has at least two worrisome features such as atypia, hypercellularity, architectural loss, or increased mitotic activity; ordinary neurofibroma does not. MPNST shows overt malignant cytology, destructive growth, brisk mitoses and/or necrosis; H3K27me3 loss and complex genomic alterations may support the diagnosis. Biallelic NF1 inactivation is the central molecular event in conventional neurofibroma. ANNUBP commonly shows CDKN2A and/or CDKN2B deletion. SUZ12 or EED inactivation and associated H3K27me3 loss support MPNST rather than neurofibroma or ANNUBP. Scattered bizarre nuclei without other worrisome features represent degenerative atypia, not ANNUBP. A plexiform neurofibroma is highly associated with NF1 and carries increased risk for progression to MPNST. Perineurial differentiation: EMA, GLUT1, and claudin-1 positivity with absent S100/SOX10 in tumor cells. A benign neoplasm composed of perineurial cells, occurring as intraneural or soft-tissue forms. Intraneural lesions typically affect adolescents and young adults, usually in nerves of the extremities; cranial nerve involvement is rare. Soft-tissue lesions occur most often in middle-aged adults and may arise in deep soft tissue without an identifiable nerve association. Intraneural lesions cause slowly progressive weakness, sometimes with muscle atrophy; soft-tissue lesions present as a mass. Intraneural type shows concentric perineurial cell proliferation around axons, forming pseudo-onion bulbs. Soft-tissue type shows bland spindle cells in storiform, whorled, or reticular patterns. Tumor cells express perineurial markers and lack Schwannian markers. Mitoses are rare and necrosis is generally absent. Intraneural perineurioma expands nerve fascicles with concentric layers of perineurial cells around individual axons. Pseudo-onion-bulb structures are most apparent in cross-section. Advanced lesions may show marked separation or loss of axons and myelin within the expanded fascicles. Soft-tissue perineurioma comprises slender spindle cells with tapering nuclei and delicate bipolar processes. Soft-tissue lesions commonly show storiform or whorled architecture in collagenous stroma. Reticular and sclerosing patterns are uncommon morphologic variants. EMA is positive, ranging from focal/weak to strong/diffuse. Claudin-1 and GLUT1 are commonly positive. CD34 is positive in a subset of soft-tissue perineuriomas. S100, SOX10, and GFAP are negative in the neoplastic perineurial cells. Schwannoma is diffusely S100/SOX10-positive and may show Antoni A/B areas; perineurioma is EMA/GLUT1/claudin-1-positive. Neurofibroma contains a mixed population with Schwannian cells, axons, mast cells, and CD34-positive stroma; perineurioma shows a dominant perineurial phenotype. Hybrid tumors demonstrate both perineurial and Schwannian or neurofibromatous components. Low-grade fibromyxoid sarcoma A malignant fibroblastic tumor with characteristic alternating fibrous and myxoid zones and MUC4 expression; perineurioma lacks this profile. Intraneural perineuriomas frequently harbor TRAF7 missense mutations. Soft-tissue perineuriomas may show chromosome 22q, 17q11, or 2p deletions; sclerosing lesions may have 10q alterations. Hybrid Nerve Sheath Tumor A benign nerve sheath neoplasm with two distinct differentiation patterns, most often schwannoma/perineurioma. A benign peripheral nerve sheath tumor combining features of schwannoma, neurofibroma, and/or perineurioma. Occurs over a broad age range, with a peak in young adults and no consistent sex predilection. Usually dermal or subcutaneous in the extremities; cranial nerve and spinal nerve examples are uncommon. Typically a painless, slowly growing mass; nerve-associated lesions may cause pain or neurologic symptoms. Hybrid neurofibroma/schwannoma is associated with NF1, NF2-related schwannomatosis, and other schwannomatosis settings. Demonstrate two recognizable nerve sheath differentiation patterns within one tumor. Schwannoma/perineurioma contains S100/SOX10-positive Schwannian areas and EMA/GLUT1/claudin-1-positive perineurial areas. Neurofibroma/schwannoma combines a mixed neurofibromatous background with monomorphic schwannomatous nodules. Neurofibroma/perineurioma combines neurofibromatous areas with perineurial differentiation. Mitoses are generally rare and malignant features are absent. Schwannoma/perineurioma shows fascicular or storiform growth with plump Schwann cells admixed with slender perineurial cells. The two components may be intermingled or arranged as separate nodules. Neurofibroma/schwannoma may show discrete schwannomatous nodules within a neurofibroma or Schwann-cell bundles dispersed in a myxoid background. Neurofibroma/perineurioma may show plexiform neurofibroma with focal perineurial areas that are subtle on H&E. Degenerative nuclear atypia may occur without indicating malignancy. Schwannian areas express S100 and SOX10. Perineurial areas express EMA, claudin-1, and GLUT1. Neurofibromatous areas show a mixed profile, including Schwannian cells, CD34-positive stromal cells, and scattered perineurial cells. Neurofilament may highlight entrapped axons in neurofibromatous components. A conventional schwannoma is nearly entirely Schwannian and lacks a substantial second perineurial or neurofibromatous component. A conventional neurofibroma has a mixed-cell composition but lacks discrete, well-developed schwannomatous nodules or a distinct perineurioma component. A conventional perineurioma is dominated by perineurial differentiation without a substantial Schwannian or neurofibromatous component. Hybrid benign tumors lack destructive invasion, significant mitotic activity, and tumor necrosis. A subset of neurofibroma/schwannoma hybrid tumors harbors activating ERBB2 mutations. The molecular profile depends on the component and clinical setting; testing is not routinely required for diagnosis. Malignant Melanotic Nerve Sheath Tumor A pigmented Schwannian neoplasm expressing melanocytic markers, commonly with PRKAR1A loss; biologically malignant despite bland areas. A distinct malignant nerve sheath tumor with Schwannian and melanocytic differentiation, often arising near the spinal or autonomic nerves. Usually adults; patients with Carney complex tend to present at a younger age. Typically arises along spinal nerve roots or autonomic nerves near the midline; other visceral and soft-tissue sites occur. May present with pain, sensory symptoms, or mass effect; metastatic disease can cause systemic symptoms. A subset is associated with Carney complex; psammomatous and non-psammomatous forms have similar clinical significance. Neoplasm composed of pigmented cells with combined Schwannian and melanocytic differentiation. S100/SOX10 and melanocytic markers are typically expressed. Loss of PRKAR1A expression is a strong diagnostic clue. Recognize malignant potential even when cytologic atypia and mitotic activity are limited. Tumor cells grow in short fascicles, nests, sheets, or syncytial groups. Cells range from polygonal to spindle-shaped and contain abundant coarse or finely granular melanin pigment. Less pigmented areas reveal round to oval nuclei, occasional grooves or pseudoinclusions, and eosinophilic to amphophilic cytoplasm. Psammoma bodies are present in approximately half of cases but may require extensive sampling. Necrosis, mitoses, and marked atypia may occur but do not reliably predict behavior. S100 and SOX10 are usually positive. HMB45, Melan-A, and tyrosinase support melanocytic differentiation. PRKAR1A expression is typically lost. Collagen IV and laminin may show prominent intercellular deposition. Conventional schwannoma lacks the diffuse melanocytic phenotype and typically retains PRKAR1A; pigment alone is not sufficient for MMNST. Melanoma Melanoma may express melanocytic markers but usually lacks the characteristic Schwannian context and PRKAR1A-loss pattern; correlate with site and molecular findings. Clear cell sarcoma Clear cell sarcoma is typically associated with EWSR1::ATF1 or EWSR1::CREB1 fusion and usually lacks the nerve-associated/PRKAR1A-deficient profile. Melanotic paraganglioma Paraganglioma shows neuroendocrine chief-cell differentiation with chromogranin/synaptophysin and sustentacular cells; MMNST is Schwannian and melanocytic. PRKAR1A inactivation is present in most tumors and can be assessed by immunohistochemistry. A distinct DNA methylation profile separates MMNST from conventional schwannoma and melanoma. GNAQ/GNA11 and BRAF/NRAS/TERT promoter mutations are generally absent; these findings may help exclude melanocytic mimics. The historical term melanotic schwannoma is discouraged because it understates the malignant potential. Absence of psammoma bodies does not exclude the diagnosis. Malignant Peripheral Nerve Sheath Tumor An infiltrative malignant spindle-cell neoplasm, often NF1-associated; H3K27me3 loss and PRC2-pathway alterations are supportive. A malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumor arising from a nerve, a pre-existing nerve sheath tumor, or in association with NF1. Most often affects adults aged 20–50 years; NF1-associated tumors occur at a younger age. Common sites include extremities, trunk, head and neck, and paraspinal regions. Usually presents as an enlarging deep mass, often painful or associated with neuropathic symptoms. Approximately half are associated with NF1; prior radiation is a recognized risk factor. Malignant spindle-cell neoplasm with a compatible nerve association, precursor neurofibroma, or NF1 context. Conventional high-grade tumors show hypercellularity, cytologic atypia, brisk mitotic activity, and often necrosis. Schwannian markers are often absent or only focally expressed. H3K27me3 loss supports conventional MPNST but is not present in all cases. Epithelioid MPNST is a distinct morphologic subtype, usually with diffuse S100/SOX10 and SMARCB1 loss. Conventional MPNST is composed of hypercellular intersecting fascicles of atypical spindle cells with wavy or buckled nuclei. Alternating hypercellular and hypocellular zones may produce a marbled appearance. Perivascular hypercellularity and tumor cell herniation into vessel lumina are characteristic clues. Brisk mitotic activity and geographic tumor necrosis are common in high-grade tumors. Divergent differentiation may include rhabdomyoblastic, cartilaginous, osseous, or epithelial elements. Epithelioid MPNST comprises lobules or sheets of epithelioid cells with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm and prominent nucleoli. Perineurial MPNST is exceptionally rare and shows malignant spindle cells with perineurial differentiation. S100 and SOX10 are negative or only patchy in most conventional MPNSTs. H3K27me3 is completely lost in approximately half to most conventional high-grade tumors; internal non-neoplastic controls must be retained. Neurofibromin loss may support NF1 pathway inactivation, although a widely reliable commercial antibody is not available. Epithelioid MPNST is usually diffusely positive for S100 and SOX10 and loses INI1/SMARCB1. Epithelioid MPNST generally retains H3K27me3. Perineurial MPNST may express EMA and variably CD34 while lacking S100. Neurofibroma / ANNUBP ANNUBP has limited worrisome features and does not meet criteria for MPNST; overt malignant atypia, mitotic activity, necrosis, and complex genomic changes favor MPNST. Cellular schwannoma Cellular schwannoma is usually circumscribed and retains Schwannian architecture, subcapsular lymphocytes, hyalinized vessels, and H3K27me3. Synovial sarcoma Synovial sarcoma is supported by SS18::SSX fusion and usually shows epithelial marker expression; nerve association and H3K27me3 loss may favor MPNST. Leiomyosarcoma Leiomyosarcoma shows smooth-muscle morphology and expression of desmin, SMA, and h-caldesmon. Epithelioid MPNST Epithelioid MPNST has epithelioid morphology, diffuse S100/SOX10, and frequent INI1 loss; conventional MPNST is usually spindle-cell and often loses H3K27me3. MMNST is heavily pigmented and expresses melanocytic markers with PRKAR1A loss. Conventional MPNST commonly shows NF1 and CDKN2A/CDKN2B inactivation followed by SUZ12 or EED inactivation. SUZ12/EED loss disrupts PRC2 and leads to H3K27me3 loss. Complex copy-number alterations and oncogene amplifications may be present. Epithelioid MPNST is usually driven by SMARCB1 inactivation and has a molecular profile distinct from conventional MPNST. H3K27me3 retention does not exclude MPNST, particularly in paraspinal tumors and epithelioid MPNST. A small biopsy may sample only a low-grade precursor component; correlate with imaging and target the most suspicious region. Cauda Equina Neuroendocrine Tumor Cauda Equina Neuroendocrine Tumors A well-circumscribed intradural cauda equina tumor with Zellballen architecture, neuroendocrine chief cells, and sustentacular cells. A neuroendocrine neoplasm of the filum terminale or cauda equina region, biologically distinct from paragangliomas elsewhere. Usually adults in the fourth to sixth decades, with a slight male predominance. Typically arises intradurally from the filum terminale or a cauda equina nerve root. Common presentations include low-back pain and sciatica; sensory, motor, or sphincter symptoms are less common. Functional hormone secretion is extremely rare. Well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumor composed of chief cells in nests or Zellballen. A delicate sustentacular cell network surrounds tumor nests. Chief cells express neuroendocrine markers; sustentacular cells are highlighted by S100 and/or SOX10. Anatomic location and morphology are essential because the entity is distinct from conventional extra-spinal paraganglioma. Chief cells form nests, lobules, trabeculae, or pseudorosettes in a delicate vascular network. Tumor cells are round or polygonal with finely stippled chromatin and inconspicuous nucleoli. Cytoplasm is eosinophilic and granular, but may be amphophilic or clear. A single layer of attenuated sustentacular cells may be difficult to appreciate on H&E. Gangliocytic examples contain mature ganglion cells and a Schwannian component. Ependymoma-like perivascular arrangements and carcinoid-like patterns may occur. Hemorrhage, scattered mitoses, and degenerative pleomorphism do not by themselves establish aggressive behavior. Chief cells express synaptophysin and chromogranin; INSM1 may also be positive. S100 and SOX10 highlight sustentacular cells, which may be sparse or discontinuous. Cytokeratin expression is common and does not exclude this diagnosis. HOXB13 expression supports cauda equina origin in the appropriate context. Schwannoma is diffusely S100/SOX10-positive and lacks a chief-cell neuroendocrine population expressing chromogranin and synaptophysin. Myxopapillary ependymoma Myxopapillary ependymoma shows perivascular pseudorosettes and myxoid papillary cores; dot-like or ring-like EMA and GFAP support ependymal differentiation. Conventional paraganglioma Both may show Zellballen, but cauda equina tumors are typically HOXB13-positive and lack the usual hereditary paraganglioma molecular profile. Metastatic neuroendocrine tumor Correlate with clinical history and imaging; a filum/cauda equina-centered intradural mass and HOXB13 expression favor the primary cauda equina entity. HOXB13 overexpression is characteristic and supports the distinctive developmental origin. The recurrent molecular drivers remain incompletely defined. The usual SDHx-associated alterations of hereditary extra-CNS paragangliomas are not characteristic. Adamantinomatous Craniopharyngioma Craniopharyngiomas Biphasic epithelial tumor with peripheral palisading, stellate reticulum, wet keratin, and nuclear/cytoplasmic beta-catenin accumulation. A WHO grade 1 epithelial tumor of the sellar/suprasellar region, often cystic and locally adherent to critical structures. Bimodal age distribution, with peaks in children and adults, without a strong sex predilection. Arises in the sellar and suprasellar region, often involving the hypothalamus and third ventricular floor. Common symptoms include visual disturbance, headache, growth failure, and endocrine dysfunction. Cyst fluid may be rich in cholesterol and appear oily or machine-oil-like. Epithelial nests or cords with peripheral palisading and stellate reticulum-like central cells. Wet keratin nodules are a highly characteristic feature. Calcification and cyst formation are common. Nuclear and cytoplasmic beta-catenin accumulation supports the diagnosis. Tumor forms cords, trabeculae, and lobules of stratified squamous epithelium. Peripheral palisading of columnar cells surrounds loosely cohesive stellate reticulum-like cells. Wet keratin consists of compact, eosinophilic, anucleate squamous debris. Cholesterol clefts, foreign-body giant cells, calcification, and hemosiderin may be prominent. Reactive gliosis and inflammation may occur at the tumor-brain interface. Broad-spectrum cytokeratins highlight the epithelial component. Beta-catenin shows nuclear and cytoplasmic accumulation in clusters of tumor cells, often in whorled areas. CK5/6 and p63/p40 support squamous epithelial differentiation. BRAF V600E is not a feature of this subtype. Papillary craniopharyngioma Papillary craniopharyngioma is composed of nonkeratinizing squamous epithelium on fibrovascular cores and usually harbors BRAF V600E; it lacks wet keratin and stellate reticulum. Rathke cleft cyst Rathke cleft cyst is lined by ciliated cuboidal/columnar or mucinous epithelium and lacks invasive epithelial nests, wet keratin, and beta-catenin nuclear accumulation. Pituitary neuroendocrine tumor PitNET is a neuroendocrine neoplasm expressing pituitary lineage transcription factors and hormones rather than squamous epithelium. Epidermoid cyst Epidermoid cyst is lined by mature stratified squamous epithelium with lamellated keratin but lacks the characteristic biphasic architecture and wet keratin nodules. CTNNB1 activating mutations drive WNT/beta-catenin pathway activation. Nuclear beta-catenin accumulation is a useful immunohistochemical surrogate for CTNNB1 pathway activation. Small biopsies may contain only squamous epithelium or keratin; correlate with imaging and seek the characteristic epithelial architecture. Reactive gliosis at the interface should not be mistaken for infiltrative glioma. Papillary Craniopharyngioma Nonkeratinizing squamous epithelium arranged around fibrovascular cores; BRAF V600E is characteristic. A WHO grade 1 epithelial tumor of the sellar/suprasellar region, typically occurring in adults. Usually adults, with a peak in middle age; no strong sex predilection. Typically arises in the sellar/suprasellar region and may cause visual, endocrine, or hypothalamic symptoms. Often presents as a solid or mixed solid-cystic mass. Papillary architecture with nonkeratinizing stratified squamous epithelium covering fibrovascular cores. No wet keratin or stellate reticulum-like component. BRAF V600E mutation is a defining molecular feature in most cases. Delicate fibrovascular cores are covered by multilayered, nonkeratinizing squamous epithelium. Tumor cells have relatively uniform nuclei and eosinophilic cytoplasm. The epithelium may show a basal palisaded layer but lacks the classic adamantinomatous stellate reticulum. Wet keratin, prominent calcification, and cholesterol-rich cyst contents are generally absent. Cytokeratins highlight the squamous epithelium. BRAF VE1 immunohistochemistry typically shows strong cytoplasmic staining in tumor cells. Beta-catenin lacks the characteristic nuclear accumulation seen in adamantinomatous craniopharyngioma. Adamantinomatous craniopharyngioma Adamantinomatous tumors show peripheral palisading, stellate reticulum, wet keratin, calcification, and CTNNB1/beta-catenin pathway activation. Squamous metaplasia of Rathke cleft cyst Metaplastic Rathke cleft cyst retains cyst lining and may show cilia or mucinous epithelium; it lacks the characteristic papillary fibrovascular architecture and BRAF V600E. PitNET shows neuroendocrine morphology and pituitary lineage markers rather than a papillary squamous epithelial proliferation. BRAF V600E is present in the great majority of papillary craniopharyngiomas. BRAF VE1 immunohistochemistry can serve as a useful surrogate; molecular confirmation is appropriate when staining is equivocal. Pituicytoma Other Sellar Tumors A circumscribed spindle-cell sellar tumor with strong nuclear TTF1 and variable S100; usually lacks pituitary hormones. A low-grade tumor of specialized glial cells of the neurohypophysis and infundibulum. Usually adults in the fourth to sixth decades; slight male predominance in some series. Arises in the posterior pituitary, pituitary stalk, or infundibulum. Often presents with visual symptoms, headache, or endocrine dysfunction due to mass effect. Well-circumscribed spindle-cell neoplasm with fascicular or storiform architecture. Tumor cells show strong nuclear TTF1 expression. Pituitary hormones and pituitary lineage transcription factors are generally absent. Bland spindle cells form interlacing fascicles or a storiform pattern. Cells have elongated nuclei, inconspicuous nucleoli, and eosinophilic cytoplasm. A rich vascular network may be present. TTF1 shows strong nuclear staining and is the key lineage marker. S100 is commonly positive; GFAP is variable. EMA may be focal. Pituitary hormones and PIT1, TPIT, and SF1 are negative. Spindle cell oncocytoma Spindle cell oncocytoma is also TTF1-positive but has abundant granular eosinophilic oncocytic cytoplasm and strong mitochondrial marker expression. Granular cell tumor of the sellar region Granular cell tumor shows sheets of large cells with abundant PAS-positive granular cytoplasm rather than fascicular spindle-cell architecture. Schwannoma is diffusely S100/SOX10-positive and typically lacks nuclear TTF1. PitNET expresses pituitary lineage transcription factors and often hormones; pituicytoma is TTF1-positive and pituitary hormone-negative. No recurrent defining molecular alteration is established for routine diagnosis. DNA methylation profiling may support classification in difficult cases. Granular Cell Tumor of the Sellar Region A TTF1-positive posterior pituitary tumor composed of large cells with abundant PAS-positive granular cytoplasm. A low-grade neoplasm of neurohypophyseal pituicytes with prominent lysosome-rich granular cytoplasm. Usually adults, often in middle age; no consistent sex predilection. Typically arises in the posterior pituitary or pituitary stalk. May cause visual field defects, headache, hypopituitarism, or hyperprolactinemia from stalk compression. Sheets or nests of large polygonal cells with abundant finely granular eosinophilic cytoplasm. Granules are PAS-positive and diastase-resistant. Nuclear TTF1 supports neurohypophyseal pituicyte lineage. Tumor is composed of large polygonal cells in sheets, nests, or broad trabeculae. Cytoplasm is abundant, finely granular, and eosinophilic. Nuclei are round to oval, usually bland, with inconspicuous nucleoli. PAS-positive, diastase-resistant cytoplasmic granules correspond to lysosomes. A delicate vascular network may be present; mitoses are usually rare. TTF1 shows nuclear positivity. S100 is variable and often focal. CD68 and other lysosomal markers highlight granular cytoplasm. Pituitary hormones and pituitary lineage transcription factors are generally negative. Pituicytoma is a spindle-cell fascicular tumor; granular cell tumor is composed of large polygonal cells with PAS-positive granular cytoplasm. Spindle cell oncocytoma has spindle or epithelioid cells with dense oncocytic cytoplasm and strong mitochondrial marker expression. Metastatic renal cell carcinoma Metastatic RCC may have clear or granular cytoplasm and a rich vascular pattern but expresses epithelial markers and renal lineage markers rather than TTF1. Conventional granular cell tumor Conventional granular cell tumor is usually S100/SOX10-positive and TTF1-negative, unlike the sellar neurohypophyseal tumor. TTF1 expression is a useful lineage surrogate rather than a specific molecular alteration. Spindle Cell Oncocytoma A TTF1-positive sellar tumor with spindle/epithelioid cells, abundant oncocytic cytoplasm, and mitochondrial enrichment. A rare oncocytic neoplasm of the anterior pituitary region, thought to arise from folliculostellate cells. Typically arises in the sellar region, often attached to the anterior pituitary or stalk. Presents with headache, visual impairment, or endocrine dysfunction due to mass effect. Spindle or epithelioid cells with abundant granular eosinophilic oncocytic cytoplasm. Nuclear TTF1 expression supports pituicyte/f​​olliculostellate lineage. Mitochondrial markers are strongly expressed. Pituitary hormones are generally absent. Tumor cells are arranged in fascicles, sheets, or nests. Cells have abundant granular eosinophilic cytoplasm due to numerous mitochondria. Nuclei are round to oval and may show mild to moderate atypia. A prominent vascular network and variable stromal fibrosis may be present. Mitoses are variable; recurrence may occur after incomplete resection. Anti-mitochondrial antibody and other mitochondrial markers are strongly positive. S100 is variable; EMA may be positive. Pituitary hormones and lineage transcription factors are generally negative. Pituicytoma is usually a bland spindle-cell tumor without the striking oncocytic cytoplasm or diffuse mitochondrial marker expression. Granular cell tumor has PAS-positive lysosomal granules and a polygonal-cell pattern; spindle cell oncocytoma is mitochondria-rich and often spindle-cell. Pituitary neuroendocrine tumor with oncocytic change PitNET expresses pituitary lineage transcription factors and often hormones; spindle cell oncocytoma is TTF1-positive and typically hormone-negative. Metastatic oncocytic carcinoma Use clinical history and site-specific markers to exclude metastatic renal, thyroid, or other oncocytic carcinomas. No single recurrent molecular alteration is established for routine diagnosis. Molecular profiling may be considered in recurrent or diagnostically unresolved tumors. Pituitary Adenoma / Pituitary Neuroendocrine Tumor (PitNET) Pituitary Neuroendocrine Tumors A pituitary neuroendocrine neoplasm classified by lineage transcription factors PIT1, TPIT, and SF1, with hormone expression and granulation pattern. A clonal neuroendocrine neoplasm of adenohypophyseal cells; classify by lineage, hormone profile, and clinicopathologic context. Occurs across adulthood; some subtypes show sex- and age-related clinical patterns. Arises in the anterior pituitary and may be functioning or clinically nonfunctioning. Symptoms include hormone excess, hypopituitarism, headache, and visual field deficits from mass effect. Invasion and aggressive clinical behavior are assessed by imaging, surgical findings, and follow-up rather than histology alone. Neuroendocrine tumor with compatible pituitary morphology and cytokeratin expression. Classify lineage using PIT1, TPIT, and SF1; correlate with pituitary hormone immunostains. Assess proliferation with mitotic count and Ki-67, but do not use a single threshold as a stand-alone predictor of behavior. Distinguish tumor from pituitary hyperplasia by reticulin: tumor shows disruption of the normal acinar reticulin framework. Pituitary carcinoma is defined by craniospinal dissemination and/or systemic metastasis, not by cytologic atypia alone. Tumor cells form sheets, nests, trabeculae, or papillary structures and often show a monotonous appearance. Cytoplasm may be acidophilic, basophilic, or chromophobic depending on lineage and granulation. Nuclei are round to oval with finely stippled chromatin; pleomorphism may be present but is not independently diagnostic of malignancy. Reticulin framework is disrupted compared with the preserved acinar pattern of normal or hyperplastic pituitary tissue. Densely and sparsely granulated patterns may be recognized in selected lineages and can have clinical relevance. Crooke cell change, silent corticotroph phenotype, and plurihormonal PIT1-lineage tumors should be specifically recognized. Synaptophysin and chromogranin support neuroendocrine differentiation; broad-spectrum cytokeratin is usually positive. PIT1 identifies somatotroph, lactotroph, and thyrotroph lineage tumors. TPIT identifies corticotroph lineage tumors. SF1 identifies gonadotroph lineage tumors. Use lineage-appropriate hormone stains: GH, prolactin, TSH, ACTH, FSH, and LH. Ki-67 and mitotic count contribute to proliferation assessment but do not independently establish aggressive behavior. ER, SSTR2A/SSTR5, MGMT, and mismatch repair proteins may have predictive or therapeutic relevance in selected settings. Pituitary hyperplasia Hyperplasia expands acini while preserving the reticulin framework; PitNET disrupts the normal acinar reticulin network. Metastatic carcinoma to the sellar region Metastases generally lack pituitary lineage transcription factors and may show a site-specific immunophenotype; correlate with clinical history and imaging. Sellar paraganglioma Paraganglioma is typically keratin-negative and GATA3/tyrosine hydroxylase-positive, with sustentacular cells; PitNET is keratin-positive and expresses PIT1, TPIT, or SF1. Spindle cell oncocytoma is TTF1-positive with oncocytic spindle-cell morphology and lacks pituitary lineage markers. Pituicytoma / granular cell tumor These posterior pituitary tumors are TTF1-positive and generally lack pituitary hormones and lineage transcription factors. Pituitary blastoma Pituitary blastoma occurs in very young children and contains blastemal cells, Rathke pouch epithelium, and neuroendocrine cells; DICER1 alterations are characteristic. Most PitNETs lack a single defining molecular alteration used in routine classification. GNAS mutations occur in a subset of somatotroph tumors; other subtype-associated alterations may be found but are not required for diagnosis. SSTR expression may inform somatostatin analogue therapy; MGMT and mismatch repair status may be relevant in selected aggressive tumors. Germline predisposition may occur in MEN1, AIP-related familial isolated pituitary adenoma, and other syndromic settings. Do not use the former term atypical adenoma as a histologic grade. Do not diagnose carcinoma based on pleomorphism, mitoses, or Ki-67 alone; metastasis is required. A sellar mass in a patient with known carcinoma requires consideration of metastasis even when it resembles PitNET. Pituitary Blastoma A rare DICER1-associated embryonal sellar tumor in infants, combining blastemal cells, Rathke pouch epithelium, and neuroendocrine cells. An embryonal neoplasm of the sellar region, typically presenting in infancy and associated with DICER1 syndrome. Usually occurs in children younger than 2 years, with a median age around 9 months and slight female predominance. Arises in the sellar region and often extends suprasellarly or into the cavernous sinus. Cushing syndrome from ACTH excess is a common presentation; ophthalmoplegia and other pituitary hormone abnormalities may occur. Patients may have other DICER1-associated neoplasms or a family history suggestive of DICER1 syndrome. Triphasic tumor containing primitive blastemal cells, neuroendocrine cells, and Rathke pouch-type epithelium. Neuroendocrine component may show corticotroph differentiation and ACTH expression. DICER1 alterations, usually germline loss-of-function plus a somatic RNase IIIb hotspot mutation, strongly support the diagnosis. Clinical age and syndromic context are important diagnostic clues. Primitive small blastemal cells are admixed with larger neuroendocrine cells and cuboidal/columnar Rathke pouch epithelium. Rathke pouch epithelium may form rosettes, glands, or follicles. Neuroendocrine cells form lobules or sheets and may show Crooke hyaline change. The tumor may show heterogeneous proliferative activity, with higher Ki-67 in the epithelial component. Necrosis may be present. Neuroendocrine cells variably express ACTH and other pro-opiomelanocortin products; GH and other pituitary hormones may be expressed. Rathke pouch epithelial cells show cytokeratin and EMA expression. Pituitary lineage transcription factors may be present in neuroendocrine cells but are usually absent in blastemal and Rathke pouch components. Ki-67 may be markedly elevated, particularly in the Rathke pouch epithelial component. PitNET is usually monomorphic and lacks the triphasic combination of blastemal cells and Rathke pouch epithelium; DICER1 alterations support blastoma. Sellar teratoma Teratoma contains mature or immature derivatives of multiple germ layers; pituitary blastoma has a characteristic triphasic pituitary/Rathke pouch composition. Germ cell tumor Germ cell tumors show characteristic morphology and markers such as SALL4, OCT3/4, PLAP, or AFP depending on subtype; the triphasic pituitary pattern is absent. Rathke cleft cyst with pituitary hyperplasia A cyst with reactive/hyperplastic pituitary tissue lacks a primitive blastemal component and DICER1-associated tumor profile. DICER1 alterations are present in nearly all tested tumors. The usual pattern is a germline loss-of-function variant with a somatic RNase IIIb hotspot mutation. Germline testing and genetic counseling are important because of the association with DICER1 tumor predisposition syndrome. Consider pituitary blastoma in an infant with ACTH-dependent Cushing syndrome and a sellar mass. Sample the tumor extensively because the three components may be unevenly distributed. All PathologyGPS · Central Nervous System Cranial, Paraspinal, and Sellar Tumors A practical diagnostic reference for peripheral nerve sheath tumors, cauda equina neuroendocrine tumors, craniopharyngiomas, posterior pituitary tumors, and pituitary neuroendocrine neoplasms—with emphasis on diagnostic criteria, immunophenotype, molecular findings, and focused differential diagnosis. Diagnostic Approach: Start Here 1. Establish the anatomic compartment Determine whether the lesion is nerve-associated, intradural cauda equina, sellar/suprasellar epithelial, posterior pituitary, or anterior pituitary in origin. 2. For nerve sheath tumors Separate Schwannian, neurofibromatous, and perineurial differentiation using architecture, axonal distribution, S100/SOX10, EMA, GLUT1, and claudin-1. 3. Exclude malignant progression In NF1-associated lesions, distinguish neurofibroma and ANNUBP from MPNST using cellularity, atypia, mitoses, necrosis, H3K27me3, and molecular context. 4. For pigmented nerve-associated tumors Consider malignant melanotic nerve sheath tumor; evaluate melanocytic markers and PRKAR1A rather than assuming melanoma. 5. For craniopharyngioma Wet keratin, stellate reticulum, and beta-catenin nuclear accumulation favor adamantinomatous type; papillary squamous epithelium and BRAF V600E favor papillary type. 6. For sellar tumors Use TTF1 to identify posterior pituitary lineage tumors; use PIT1, TPIT, and SF1 with hormone stains to classify PitNET. 7. In infants with a sellar mass Consider pituitary blastoma, particularly with ACTH-dependent Cushing syndrome; assess the three tumor components and DICER1 status. Critical principle: In sellar and paraspinal lesions, anatomic location and lineage are central. Avoid diagnosing a tumor from a single marker: interpret morphology, a focused immunohistochemical panel, imaging, and molecular findings together. High-Yield IHC / Molecular Framework Schwannian tumors S100 and SOX10; neurofilament highlights axons; EMA/GLUT1/claudin-1 identify perineurial cells. MPNST H3K27me3 loss supports conventional MPNST; INI1 loss supports epithelioid MPNST. S100/SOX10 plus HMB45/Melan-A; PRKAR1A loss is a key clue. Cauda equina neuroendocrine tumor Synaptophysin/chromogranin in chief cells; S100/SOX10 in sustentacular cells; HOXB13 supports site of origin. Craniopharyngioma Nuclear beta-catenin and CTNNB1 alterations in adamantinomatous type; BRAF V600E in papillary type. PitNET PIT1, TPIT, and SF1 define lineage; correlate with GH, PRL, TSH, ACTH, FSH, and LH. DICER1 germline and somatic alterations; heterogeneous epithelial, blastemal, and neuroendocrine components. Important Diagnostic Guardrails Degenerative atypia in schwannoma or neurofibroma is not equivalent to malignancy. ANNUBP is a defined intermediate category; do not use it as a synonym for any atypical neurofibroma. H3K27me3 retention does not exclude MPNST. Malignant melanotic nerve sheath tumor has malignant potential even when cytology appears deceptively bland. Cauda equina neuroendocrine tumor is biologically distinct from conventional paraganglioma elsewhere. Do not confuse posterior pituitary TTF1-positive tumors with PIT1/TPIT/SF1-lineage PitNETs. content: use client Astrocytoma, IDH-mutant Adult-Type Diffuse Gliomas Astrocytoma, IDH-mutant, is a diffusely infiltrating IDH1- or IDH2-mutant glioma with frequent ATRX and/or TP53 mutation and absence of 1p/19q codeletion (CNS WHO grade 2, 3, or 4). Astrocytomas with IDH1 or IDH2 mutation can be located in any region of the CNS, including the brainstem and spinal cord, but they most commonly develop in the supratentorial compartment and are usually centered near or within the frontal lobes . This localization is similar to that of IDH-mutant and 1p/19q-codeleted o The majority of patients present in their thirties or forties (median age: 38 years) with CNS WHO grade 2 or 3 tumors . CNS WHO grade 2 and 3 astrocytomas have similar age distributions , whereas patients with CNS WHO grade 4 tumors tend to be slightly older . IDH-mutant astrocytomas are uncommon in patients aged > 55 years . There is a slight male predominance among CNS WHO grade 2 and 3 IDH-mutant astrocytomas . One study of CNS WHO grade 4 tumors found that their M:F ratio is significantly lower than that of IDH-wildtype glioblastomas . IDH-mutant astrocytomas range from well-differentiated, low-cell-density, and slow-growing tumors (CNS WHO grade 2) to highly anaplastic, hypercellular, and rapidly progressive tumors (CNS WHO grade 4). CNS WHO grade 2 tumors are composed of well-differentiated fibrillary glial cells that diffusely infiltrate the CNS parenchyma individually, usually without cellular cohesion, generating a loosely structured, often microcystic matrix . Cellularity is mildly to moderately increased compared with that of normal brain, and mild nuclear atypia is characteristic. Tumor cell density and cellular morphology may vary, the latter with respect to cell size, cytoplasmic abundance, and prominence of cellular processes. Histological recognition of neoplastic astrocytes depends mainly on nuclear characteristics. Compared with those in normal astrocytes, the nuclei in IDH-mutant astrocytomas are enlarged, and they display irregular nuclear contours, an uneven chromatin pattern, and hyperchromasia. Overall, monomorphic nuclei and rounded nuclear contours may be seen, occasionally showing morphological overlap with oligodendroglial tumors. Nucleoli are typically indistinct and are most often not visible. Unlike in cells undergoing reactive astrocytosis, cellular processes in IDH-mutant astrocytomas usually vary from one tumor cell to the next. Mitotic activity is absent or uncommon in CNS WHO grade 2 tumors; a single mitosis within a resection specimen is compatible with a CNS WHO grade 2 designation . Many of the signature molecular characteristics of IDH-mutant astrocytoma can be demonstrated immunohistochemically. A routine immunohistochemical panel for the initial diagnostic workup of diffuse gliomas in adults involves IDH1 p.R132H, p53, and ATRX . The principal feature distinguishing CNS WHO grade 3 astrocytomas from CNS WHO grade 2 astrocytomas is increased mitotic activity and histological anaplasia (see Grading, below). However, the threshold for a CNS WHO grade 3 designation has not been established in IDH-mutant astrocytoma cohorts. One mitotic figure may be sufficient for assigning grade 3 within a very small biopsy, whereas more mitoses are required in larger resection specimens . Grade 3 tumors also often display increased cell density and greater nuclear atypia, including variation in nuclear size and shape, chromatin coarseness, and dispersion. Multinucleated tumor cells and abnormal mitoses may be seen. By definition, microvascular proliferation (multilayered endothelia within vessels) and necrosis are absent. CNS WHO grade 4 tumors must manifest necrosis and/or microvascular proliferation in addition to the features of CNS WHO grade 3 lesions, but the designation of CNS WHO grade 4 IDH-mutant astrocytoma is also warranted if the tumor shows homozygous deletion of CDKN2A and/or CDKN2B, even in the absence of necrosis or microvascular proliferation (see Grading and Diagnostic molecular pathology) . For more information about the histopathology of microvascular proliferation, see the Histopathology subsection in Glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype. The term “glioblastoma” is no longer applied to CNS WHO grade 4 IDH-mutant astrocytoma. Morphologically, however, the histology of individual cells of CNS WHO grade 4 IDH-mutant astrocytoma has considerable overlap with that of IDH-wildtype glioblastoma, and distinguishing between them requires testing for IDH mutations. Nevertheless, some features differ. Areas of ischaemic zonal and/or palisading necrosis have been observed in 50% of CNS WHO grade 4 IDH-mutant astrocytomas, considerably less frequently than in IDH-wildtype glioblastoma, where they are found in as many as 90% of cases . Focal oligodendroglioma-like components are more common in CNS WHO grade 4 IDH-mutant astrocytoma than in IDH-wildtype glioblastoma . Individual tumor cells of IDH-mutant astrocytoma reliably express GFAP, although to varying degrees . Gemistocytic tumor cells are typically strongly and uniformly positive for GFAP . OLIG2 is a transcription factor that shows strong nuclear immunoreactivity in most forms of diffuse gliomas, including IDH-mutant astrocytomas. One study concluded that OLIG2 expression was lower in high-grade IDH-mutant astrocytomas than in other IDH-mutant gliomas . Vimentin is often positive in tumor cells, with a labelling pattern similar to that of GFAP . Immunohistochemical assays used as surrogates for genetic alterations (e.g. IDH1 p.R132H, p53, ATRX) are discussed below, in the Diagnostic molecular pathology subsection. For CNS WHO grade 2 tumors, the main differential diagnostic considerations are normal brain and reactive astrocytosis. The cytoplasm of normal human astrocytes, in contrast to that of IDH-mutant astrocytoma cells, is not distinct from the background neuropil. Their nuclei are small and regular, displaying delicate and uniform chromatin patterns. Reactive astrocytes are defined by enlarged nuclei (often with a single prominent nucleolus) and clearly distinguished cytoplasm. Reactive gemistocytes are a specific type of astrocytes that are characterized by abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm, eccentric nuclei, and prominent glial processes. Reactive astrocytes are often uniformly distributed throughout tissue and often show similar nuclear and cytoplasmic features, unlike neoplastic cells. Microcystic change strongly favours neoplasia over reactive astrocytosis. Because most IDH-mutant diffuse astrocytomas have IDH1 p.R132H mutations, the finding of positive immunostaining for IDH1 p.R132H excludes reactive astrocytosis . Prior freezing of tissue for intraoperative diagnosis, however, may abrogate IDH1 p.R132H immunostaining and can distort nuclear cytological features. IDH-mutant astrocytoma has a wide differential diagnosis with other diffusely growing brain tumors. The primary considerations are oligodendroglioma, IDH-mutant and 1p/19q-codeleted; glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype; diffuse midline glioma, H3 K27–altered; diffuse hemispheric glioma, H3 G34–mutant; diffuse astrocytoma, MYB- or MYBL1-altered; diffuse low-grade glioma, MAPK pathway–altered; and high-grade astrocytoma with piloid features. Immunohistochemical staining for IDH1 p.R132H is highly sensitive and specific for the IDH1 p.R132H mutation, and immunopositivity is strong evidence of IDH-mutant glioma . IDH1 p.R132H immunohistochemistry has become a critical initial test for the classification of gliomas and also helps to distinguish true neoplasia from reactive gliosis . The p.R132H variant accounts for approximately 90% of all IDH mutations in supratentorial astrocytomas. Of note, more rarely occurring primary infratentorial IDH-mutant astrocytomas show a distinctively different spectrum of IDH mutations, and about 80% are of the non-p.R132H type . Gene sequencing analysis of IDH1 codon 132 and IDH2 codon 172 is recommended in the event of a negative or indeterminate result with the IDH1 p.R132H immunohistochemical stain, in order to rule out the possibility of a non-p.R132H IDH mutation . Given the low frequency of IDH1 and IDH2 mutations in CNS WHO grade 4 gliomas arising in patients aged ≥ 55 years, sequencing analysis need not follow a negative IDH1 p.R132H immunostain in this patient population . In the setting of an IDH-mutant glioma, the detection of strong and diffuse p53 immunopositivity can be used as a surrogate for TP53 mutations and in support of the diagnosis of IDH-mutant astrocytoma. TP53 mutation often leads to reduced degradation of the protein, and to its nuclear accumulation; however, not all TP53 mutations manifest as strong nuclear immunoreactivity, and nonsense mutations in particular can sometimes be associated with a complete absence of staining. Strong nuclear p53 immunohistochemical positivity in > 10% of tumor nuclei correlates well with TP53 mutations in the setting of an IDH-mutant glioma, but it is best evaluated in the context of morphology and other immunohistochemistry in the diagnostic panel, such as ATRX . Most IDH-mutant astrocytomas show even more widespread (> 50%) p53 expression . Inactivating ATRX alterations commonly co-occur with TP53 mutations in IDH-mutant astrocytomas . These often result in a truncated protein and abrogated protein expression, leading to loss of nuclear ATRX immunoreactivity . ATRX immunopositivity in the nuclei of endothelial cells and neurons serves as an internal positive control because ATRX protein is prone to rapid degradation in tissue with even minimal hypoxic damage, so areas of tissue showing nuclear ATRX immunopositivity in these cells should be assessed. Loss of nuclear ATRX expression in neoplastic cells strongly supports the diagnosis of IDH-mutant astrocytoma but is not a surrogate for IDH assessment because loss of nuclear ATRX is also found in H3-altered diffuse gliomas and occasionally in IDH-wildtype gliomas. In addition, although the rate of ATRX loss is > 90% in supratentorial IDH-mutant astrocytomas, the rate in infratentorial IDH-mutant astrocytomas is only about 50% . The combination of mutations in IDH1 or IDH2 and ATRX in a diffuse glioma (including by immunohistochemistry) is sufficient for the diagnosis of IDH-mutant astrocytoma, obviating the need for 1p/19q testing in order to exclude oligodendroglioma. Oligodendroglioma, IDH-mutant and 1p/19q-codeleted Consider Oligodendroglioma, IDH-mutant and 1p/19q-codeleted when its defining profile is present: Oligodendroglioma, IDH-mutant and 1p/19q-codeleted, is a diffusely infiltrating glioma with IDH1 or IDH2 mutation and codeletion of chromosome arms 1p and 19q (CNS WHO grade 2 or 3). The current diagnosis is favored when its own defining molecular and morphologic criteria are met. Glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype Consider Glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype when its defining profile is present: Glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype, is a diffuse, astrocytic glioma that is IDH-wildtype and H3-wildtype and has one or more of the following histological or genetic features: microvascular proliferation, necrosis, TER The current diagnosis is favored when its own defining molecular and morphologic criteria are met. Reactive astrocytes are defined by enlarged nuclei (often with a single prominent nucleolus) and clearly distinguished cytoplasm. Reactive gemistocytes are a specific type of astrocytes that are characterized by abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm, eccentric nuclei, and prominent glial processes. Oligodendroglioma, IDH-mutant and 1p/19q-codeleted, is a diffusely infiltrating glioma with IDH1 or IDH2 mutation and codeletion of chromosome arms 1p and 19q (CNS WHO grade 2 or 3). Among 5542 histologically defined oligodendrogliomas registered in the Central Brain Tumor Registry of the United States (CBTRUS) database, 59% were located in the frontal lobe, 14% in the temporal lobe, 10% in the parietal lobe, and 1% in the occipital lobe [[Central Brain Tumor Registry of the United States [Internet Among 5542 histologically defined oligodendrogliomas registered in the Central Brain Tumor Registry of the United States (CBTRUS) database, 59% were located in the frontal lobe, 14% in the temporal lobe, 10% in the parietal lobe, and 1% in the occipital lobe [[Central Brain Tumor Registry of the United States [Internet]. Among 470 genetically defined CNS WHO grade 3 oligodendrogliomas of the French national POLA network, 62% were frontal tumors, 16% were temporal, 15% were parietal, and 6% were occipital [[Portail Epidemiologie France: Health Databases [Internet]. Other studies have also shown a clear predilection for the frontal lobes in IDH-mutant and 1p/19q-codeleted oligodendrogliomas . Less common locations include the posterior fossa, basal ganglia, and brainstem. Rare cases of intramedullary spinal oligodendroglioma are on record, but data on genotype are usually lacking . Cellular composition Classic oligodendroglioma cells have uniformly round nuclei that are slightly larger than those of normal oligodendrocytes and show an increase in chromatin density or a delicate salt-and-pepper pattern. A distinct nuclear membrane is often apparent. In formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded tissue, tumor cells often appear as rounded cells with well-defined cell membranes and clear cytoplasm around the central spherical nucleus. This creates the typical honeycomb or fried-egg appearance, which, although artefactual, is a helpful diagnostic feature. This artefact is not seen in smear preparations or frozen sections, and it may also be absent in rapidly fixed tissue and in formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded sections made from frozen material. Reactive astrocytes are scattered throughout oligodendrogliomas and are particularly prominent at the tumor borders. Oligodendrogliomas may contain tumor cells that look like small gemistocytes with a rounded belly of eccentric cytoplasm that is positive for GFAP, which are termed “minigemistocytes” or “microgemistocytes”. Gliofibrillary oligodendrocytes are typical-looking oligodendroglioma cells with a thin perinuclear rim of positivity for GFAP . Gliofibrillary oligodendrocytes and minigemistocytes are more commonly seen in CNS WHO grade 3 tumors. GFAP-negative mucocytes or even signet-ring cells are occasionally present, with individual cases reported to consist largely of signet-ring cells . Eosinophilic granular cells occur in some oligodendrogliomas . Rare cases with neurocytic or ganglioglioma-like differentiation have also been reported . Occasional CNS WHO grade 3 oligodendrogliomas feature multinucleated giant cells , and rare cases contain sarcomatous areas . The presence of these various cellular phenotypes does not preclude an oligodendroglioma diagnosis if the tumor is IDH-mutant and 1p/19q-codeleted. Tumor cells with fibrillary or gemistocytic astrocytic morphology are also compatible with this diagnosis when IDH mutation and 1p/19q codeletion are present. Thus, irrespective of oligodendroglial, oligoastrocytic, astrocytic, or ambiguous features on histology, detection of combined IDH mutation and 1p/19q codeletion indicates an IDH-mutant and 1p/19q-codeleted oligodendroglioma . Mineralization and other degenerative features Microcalcifications are frequent, found within the tumor itself or in the invaded brain. Calcifications were recorded in 71 (45%) of 157 CNS WHO grade 3 IDH-mutant and 1p/19q-codeleted oligodendrogliomas, . Mineralization along blood vessels typically takes the form of small, punctate calcifications, whereas microcalcifications in the brain (called calcospherites) tend to be larger, with an irregular and sometimes laminated appearance. However, this feature is not specific for oligodendroglioma, and because of incomplete tumor sampling, it is sometimes not found histologically even when clearly demonstrated on CT. Areas characterized by extracellular mucin deposition and/or microcyst formation are frequent. Rare tumors are characterized by marked desmoplasia . Oligodendrogliomas are molecularly defined by IDH1 or IDH2 mutations and 1p/19q codeletion. Nearly all tumors have a TERT promoter mutation, lack ATRX mutation, and show preserved nuclear ATRX expression. TP53 mutations are uncommon . Diagnosis of oligodendrogliomas requires demonstration of IDH mutation by IDH1 p.R132H immunohistochemistry and/or sequencing of the IDH1 or IDH2 gene, as well as demonstration of 1p/19q codeletion by FISH, chromogenic in situ hybridization, or molecular genetic testing. In the absence of IDH1 p.R132H-positive immunohistochemistry, sequencing for less common mutations in IDH1 (codon 132) and IDH2 (codon 172) should be performed. No particular method for molecular testing for 1p/19q codeletion is required, but it is recommended that 1p/19q assays be able to detect whole-arm chromosomal losses. Only complete losses of both chromosome arms are diagnostic for oligodendroglioma, because partial or isolated loss of 1p or 19q may be present in some IDH-wildtype glioblastomas and IDH-mutant astrocytomas. FISH probes in commonly deleted regions or loss of only a few PCR probes in loss-of-heterozygosity analysis may not reflect whole-arm losses and thus may lead to false positive results . In addition, any copy-number analysis requires sufficient tumor cell content, preferably > 30%, to avoid false negative results when assessing 1p/19q codeletion. Immunohistochemical detection of IDH1 p.R132H expression and preserved nuclear ATRX expression, without demonstration of 1p/19q codeletion, is not sufficient to diagnose an IDH-mutant and 1p/19q-codeleted oligodendroglioma, even with classic histology. In IDH-mutant gliomas with preserved nuclear ATRX expression by immunohistochemistry, 1p/19q analysis remains critical for accurate molecular diagnosis. Most IDH-mutant and 1p/19q-codeleted oligodendrogliomas carry TERT promoter mutations ; however, detection of a TERT promoter mutation in an IDH-mutant glioma is not sufficient for an oligodendroglioma diagnosis, because rare cases are TERT-wildtype, including tumors in teenage patients . TERT promoter mutations are also observed in a subset of 1p/19q-intact IDH-mutant astrocytomas . DNA methylation array analysis reveals a diagnostic molecular profile by combining the detection of an oligodendroglioma-associated methylation signature and 1p/19q codeletion . Copy-number analysis by FISH also provides information on polysomy of 1q and 19p, which has been detected in subsets of 1p/19q-codeleted oligodendrogliomas of CNS WHO grades 2 and 3 and is associated with shorter survival . Homozygous deletion of CDKN2A has been detected in a small proportion of CNS WHO grade 3 IDH-mutant and 1p/19q-codeleted oligodendrogliomas, but not in those of CNS WHO grade 2, and it was reported to be an independent marker of shorter survival . Vasculature Oligodendrogliomas typically show a dense network of branching capillaries resembling chicken wire. In some cases, the capillary stroma tends to subdivide the tumor into lobules. In CNS WHO grade 3 tumors, focal or dispersed pathological microvascular proliferation is frequent. Oligodendrogliomas have a tendency to develop intratumoral hemorrhages. Growth pattern Oligodendrogliomas grow diffusely in the cortex and white matter; however, some tumors feature distinct nodules of higher cellularity against a background of diffuse infiltration. Occasional tumors show a gliomatosis cerebri–like pattern involving more than two cerebral lobes . Within the cortex, tumor cells often form secondary structures such as perineuronal satellitosis, perivascular aggregates, and subpial accumulations. Circumscribed leptomeningeal infiltration may induce a desmoplastic reaction. Oligodendrogliomas can have a rare spongioblastic growth pattern consisting of parallel rows of tumor cells with somewhat elongated nuclei forming rhythmic palisades. Occasionally, perivascular pseudorosettes are seen, although some of these are a result of perivascular neuropil formation within foci of neurocytic differentiation . These patterns are generally present only focally. Proliferation Mitotic activity is low or absent in CNS WHO grade 2 oligodendrogliomas, but it is usually prominent in CNS WHO grade 3 tumors. Accordingly, the Ki-67 (MIB1) proliferation index is usually low (< 5%) in CNS WHO grade 2 oligodendrogliomas and elevated in CNS WHO grade 3 oligodendrogliomas, being generally > 10% in the large French national POLA cohort of CNS WHO grade 3 tumors . However, a definitive Ki-67 (MIB1) cut-off value has not been established due to marked variability in staining results between institutions and non-uniform counting approaches. One study reported a Ki-67 index of ≥ 15% as an independent marker of shorter survival in patients with IDH-mutant and 1p/19q-codeleted CNS WHO grade 3 oligodendrogliomas . A mitotic count of ≥ 5 mitoses/mm2 was also associated with shorter survival but only on univariate, not multivariate, analysis . Another study showed that mitotic count was not associated with outcome in patients with IDH-mutant and 1p/19q-codeleted oligodendrogliomas . Other proliferation markers, such as PCNA , TOP2A , MCM2 , and MCM6 , also correlate with CNS WHO grade and/or survival but do not provide clear advantages over Ki-67 (MIB1). Most oligodendrogliomas demonstrate immunoreactivity with the antibody against IDH1 p.R132H , which facilitates the differential diagnosis versus other clear cell tumors as well as non-neoplastic and reactive lesions . IDH-mutant and 1p/19q-codeleted oligodendrogliomas retain nuclear expression of ATRX and typically lack widespread nuclear p53 staining, consistent with the near exclusivity of ATRX and TP53 mutation versus 1p/19q codeletion in IDH-mutant gliomas . Oligodendrogliomas are immunopositive for MAP2, S100, and CD57 (LEU7) ; however, these markers are also positive in astrocytic gliomas. Similarly, the oligodendrocyte lineage transcription factors OLIG1, OLIG2, and SOX10 are expressed in oligodendrogliomas but also in astrocytic gliomas . GFAP is detectable in intermingled reactive astrocytes but may also stain neoplastic cells such as minigemistocytes and gliofibrillary oligodendrocytes . Antigens expressed by normal oligodendrocytes, including myelin basic protein (MBP), myelin proteolipid protein (PLP), myelin-associated glycoprotein (MAG), galactolipids (e.g. galactocerebroside and galactosulfatide), certain gangliosides, and several enzymes (e.g. CAII [carbonic anhydrase C], CNP, glycerol-3-phosphate dehydrogenase, and LDH) are not diagnostically useful markers for oligodendrogliomas . Synaptophysin immunoreactivity of residual neuropil between the tumor cells is frequent and should not be mistaken for neuronal or neurocytic differentiation. However, oligodendrogliomas may also contain neoplastic cells that express synaptophysin and/or NeuN and neurofilaments . Immunostaining for α-internexin protein is frequent (e.g. in one study it was found in 88.5% of IDH-mutant and 1p/19q-codeleted CNS WHO grade 3 oligodendrogliomas ), but it cannot be considered a surrogate marker for 1p/19q codeletion . Similarly, NOGO-A positivity is common but not exclusive . Reduced nuclear expression of H3 p.K28me3 (K27me3) has been associated with 1p/19q codeletion in IDH-mutant gliomas , but it cannot substitute for 1p/19q testing . IDH-mutant and 1p/19q-codeleted oligodendrogliomas may histologically mimic various other lesions. Macrophage-rich lesions such as those characteristic of demyelinating diseases or resulting from cerebral infarction are readily distinguished by immunostaining for macrophage markers and lack of IDH mutation. The relative increase of oligodendrocytes sometimes seen in partial lobectomy specimens performed for intractable seizures also lack IDH mutation. IDH-mutant astrocytomas lack 1p/19q codeletion and show frequent nuclear p53 immunostaining and loss of nuclear ATRX. In fact, loss of nuclear ATRX is sufficient to diagnose an IDH-mutant astrocytoma without additional testing for 1p/19q codeletion . TERT promoter mutations are common in IDH-mutant and 1p/19q-codeleted oligodendrogliomas, although rare cases have been reported to lack TERT promoter mutation, and some IDH-mutant but 1p/19q-intact astrocytomas may carry TERT promoter mutations . Other morphological mimics, like neurocytoma, liponeurocytoma, and dysembryoplastic neuroepithelial tumor, can be ruled out by their lack of IDH mutation. Ependymomas containing clear cells differ from oligodendrogliomas by their perivascular pseudorosettes and dot-like or ring-shaped EMA immunoreactivity, as well as a lack of IDH mutation and frequent ZFTA (C11orf95) fusions. Clear cell meningioma can be distinguished by EMA and desmoplakin positivity, IDH-wildtype status, and loss of nuclear SMARCE1 . Metastatic clear cell carcinomas differ from oligodendrogliomas by their sharp tumor borders, cytokeratin and EMA positivity, and lack of IDH mutation. Pilocytic astrocytomas with oligodendroglial features are IDH-wildtype and carry MAPK pathway gene alterations, in particular FGFR1 alterations . However, rare cases of IDH-mutant and 1p/19q-codeleted oligodendrogliomas with KIAA1549::BRAF fusions have been reported . In children, diffuse gliomas with MYB, MYBL1, FGFR1, or BRAF alterations may have histological features of oligodendroglioma or oligoastrocytoma but are biologically distinct tumors . The differential diagnosis of diffuse leptomeningeal glioneuronal tumor is facilitated by the clinical presentation and the combination of MAPK pathway gene alteration (in particular KIAA1549::BRAF fusion) and 1p deletion (or 1p/19q codeletion) but absence of IDH mutation . Malignant small cell astrocytic tumors, including IDH-wildtype glioblastomas and H3 G34–mutant diffuse hemispheric gliomas, must be separated from highly cellular oligodendrogliomas by their IDH-wildtype status and specific alterations, including frequent EGFR amplification and chromosome 10 loss , or mutations leading to H3 p.G35 (G34) variants. Oligodendroglioma NOS, oligoastrocytoma NOS, and oligoastrocytoma NEC Rare cases of diffuse gliomas with classic oligodendroglioma histology in which molecular testing for combined IDH mutation and 1p/19q codeletion failed (e.g. because of limited tissue availability, low tumor cell content, inconclusive test results, or other circumstances impeding molecular testing) or could not be completed can be histologically classified as oligodendroglioma NOS and designated as CNS WHO grade 2 or 3 depending on the presence or absence of histological features of anaplasia. Immunohistochemical demonstration of IDH mutation and retained nuclear positivity for ATRX may support the oligodendroglioma diagnosis. However, unless successfully tested for 1p/19q codeletion, such tumors cannot be classified as oligodendroglioma, IDH-mutant and 1p/19q-codeleted. Immunohistochemical positivity for oligodendroglioma-associated markers such as α-internexin and NOGO-A , reduced nuclear H3 p.K28me3 (K27me3) immunostaining , and immunohistochemical loss of nuclear CIC or FUBP1 expression are not sufficient to substitute for 1p/19q codeletion testing. The diagnosis of oligoastrocytoma NOS is reserved for diffuse gliomas that are composed of a conspicuous mixture of two distinct neoplastic cell types morphologically resembling tumor cells with either oligodendroglial or astrocytic features, and in which testing for IDH mutation, nuclear ATRX expression, and 1p/19q codeletion failed or could not be completed. In such cases, tumor cells with oligodendroglial or astroglial features can be either diffusely intermingled or separated into distinct, biphasic areas. However, the diagnosis of oligoastrocytoma is discouraged because molecular analyses have shown that these tumors carry a genetic profile typical of either IDH-mutant astrocytoma or IDH-mutant and 1p/19q-codeleted oligodendroglioma . Thus, diffuse gliomas with mixed or ambiguous histological features should be evaluated for IDH mutation and loss of nuclear ATRX expression, as well as for 1p/19q codeletion when nuclear ATRX is retained . Rare cases of dual-genotype oligoastrocytomas have been reported. These are characterized by two distinct IDH-mutant tumor cell populations: one showing astrocytoma-associated alterations, such as ATRX loss and TP53 mutation, and the other showing oligodendroglioma-associated 1p/19q codeletion . The WHO Classification of Tumors does not consider these tumors to be a distinct type or subtype of IDH-mutant diffuse glioma, but they may be tentatively classified as dual-genotype oligoastrocytoma NEC . Tumors that cannot be fully analysed for IDH mutation and 1p/19q codeletion but demonstrate classic histological features of oligodendroglioma are classified as oligodendroglioma NOS . This indicates that the tumor is a histologically classic oligodendroglioma that will probably exhibit clinical behavior similar to that of an IDH-mutant and 1p/19q-codeleted oligodendroglioma, but that it could not be molecularly analysed or that its test results were inconclusive or uninformative . Tumors that demonstrate oligodendroglial histology but lack IDH mutation and 1p/19q codeletion should not be classified as oligodendroglioma NOS but must be further evaluated to exclude histological mimics, such as dysembryoplastic neuroepithelial tumor, clear cell ependymoma, neurocytoma, polymorphous low-grade neuroepithelial tumor of the young, and pilocytic astrocytoma, as well as molecularly distinct diffuse gliomas that are characterized by BRAF, FGFR1, MYB, or MYBL1 alterations . The relative increase of oligodendrocytes sometimes seen in partial lobectomy specimens performed for intractable seizures also lack IDH mutation.
