title: Parathyroid Tumors
content: use client Parathyroid Hyperplasia Parathyroid Proliferative Disorders Require involvement of multiple glands and interpret the architecture in the clinical setting of secondary or tertiary hyperparathyroidism. A non-neoplastic increase in parathyroid parenchymal cells, most often a compensatory response to chronic renal disease; advanced tertiary disease may show clonal and highly nodular growth. Any age; secondary disease is common in patients with chronic kidney disease, particularly those receiving long-term dialysis. Both sexes; no consistent sex predilection is established. Multiple eutopic or ectopic parathyroid glands are involved, often asymmetrically. Secondary disease is associated with hypocalcemia, hyperphosphatemia, and reduced active vitamin D; tertiary disease presents with autonomous PTH secretion and hypercalcemia after longstanding secondary disease. Demonstrate increased parathyroid parenchymal cellularity in more than one gland. Show reduced stromal and intracellular adipose tissue relative to normal parathyroid tissue. Correlate with a recognized physiologic stimulus, especially chronic renal insufficiency, vitamin D deficiency, or malabsorption. Classify as secondary when the proliferation is compensatory; classify as tertiary when longstanding secondary hyperparathyroidism has progressed to autonomous PTH secretion. Do not classify MEN-associated or other hereditary multiglandular nodular disease as primary hyperplasia by default; these lesions are generally multiple adenomas. In renal failure-associated disease, do not diagnose carcinoma on the basis of nodularity, fibrosis, pseudoinvasion, cytological atypia, or increased proliferation alone. Chief-cell hyperplasia may be diffuse, nodular, or mixed, with increased parenchymal cells and depletion of stromal fat. Secondary and tertiary hyperplasia commonly involve multiple glands asymmetrically. Growth patterns include diffuse, trabecular, acinar, pseudofollicular, and cord-like arrangements. Increasing disease severity is associated with greater nodularity; advanced glands may show hemorrhage, cyst formation, fibrosis, and chronic inflammation. Water-clear cell hyperplasia is a rare diffuse proliferation composed of clear cells with distinct cell borders. Tertiary hyperplasia may show striking architectural atypia, pseudoinvasion, and a high proliferation index despite the absence of carcinoma-defining invasion. Parathyromatosis may produce multiple fibrotic deposits of parathyroid tissue in the neck or mediastinum, sometimes with a buckshot pattern of fat entrapment. PTH and GATA3 support parathyroid differentiation when the site of origin is uncertain. Loss of menin may support MEN1-associated disease but is not specific and can occur in sporadic lesions. Parafibromin, menin, and p27 may help screen for CDC73-, MEN1-, and CDKN1B-related disease, respectively; interpret in the clinical and morphologic context. No immunohistochemical marker independently establishes carcinoma in a hyperplastic gland. Parathyroid adenoma Adenoma is usually a discrete clonal neoplasm, often with a rim of compressed or atrophic non-neoplastic parathyroid tissue at the vascular pole; hyperplasia requires evidence of multigland involvement and appropriate clinical context. A single gland may not be classifiable with certainty. Parathyroid lipoadenoma Lipoadenoma is a discrete neoplasm with a definite increase in parenchymal tissue despite abundant adipose tissue, usually exceeding 50% of gland volume; hyperplasia is characterized by parenchymal expansion and fat depletion. Atypical parathyroid tumor Atypical parathyroid tumor is a neoplasm with worrisome cytological or architectural atypia but no unequivocal invasive growth; hyperplasia, especially tertiary disease, can mimic it but is supported by multigland involvement and the renal disease history. Parathyroid carcinoma Carcinoma requires unequivocal angioinvasion, lymphatic invasion, perineural invasion, destructive invasion of adjacent structures, or metastasis. These findings are absent in hyperplasia; pseudoinvasion in renal failure-associated disease is not sufficient. Routine molecular testing is not indicated for established secondary or tertiary hyperplasia. For apparently primary multiglandular disease, evaluate for germline predisposition; identification of a syndrome such as MEN1 generally favors classification as multiglandular adenomas. Clonal chromosomal abnormalities and somatic alterations may occur in tertiary disease, reflecting progression along a hyperplasia-to-neoplasia continuum. A single enlarged, cellular gland cannot always be separated from adenoma by morphology alone; examine the hilum and correlate with the other glands and postoperative biochemical response. In chronic renal failure, distant metastasis is exceptional. Reserve carcinoma for unequivocal invasion or metastatic disease. Parathyromatosis may mimic invasive carcinoma locally, but vascular invasion, perineural invasion, and distant spread are not features of parathyromatosis. Parathyroid Adenoma A circumscribed parathyroid neoplasm with depleted intratumoral fat and, in many cases, a rim of suppressed non-neoplastic parathyroid tissue. A benign neoplasm composed of chief, transitional oncocytic, oncocytic, clear cells, or a mixture; the most common cause of primary hyperparathyroidism. Most often diagnosed in adults, with incidence increasing with age. Sporadic tumors show a female predominance (male-to-female ratio approximately 1:2–3). Usually arises in an inferior or superior parathyroid gland; ectopic sites include intrathyroidal, retroesophageal, thymic, and mediastinal locations. Usually causes primary hyperparathyroidism, with hypercalcemia, nephrolithiasis, bone disease, or nonspecific fatigue and weakness; some patients are asymptomatic. Multiglandular adenomas may occur in MEN1, MEN2A, MEN4, CDC73-related disease, and other familial syndromes. Identify a discrete, well-circumscribed or encapsulated parathyroid neoplasm composed of chief, oncocytic, transitional, and/or clear cells. Show absent or markedly reduced stromal fat within the neoplastic component. A rim of compressed or atrophic non-neoplastic parathyroid tissue, particularly at the vascular hilum, supports adenoma over hyperplasia but is not invariably present. Correlate with clinical and biochemical evidence of primary hyperparathyroidism and, when available, intraoperative PTH decline or postoperative biochemical cure. Exclude unequivocal vascular, lymphatic, or perineural invasion, destructive invasion of adjacent structures, and metastasis before diagnosing a benign adenoma. Do not diagnose adenoma versus hyperplasia with certainty from a single gland when the clinical and gross findings do not establish the status of the remaining glands. The tumor is usually well circumscribed or surrounded by a thin fibrous pseudocapsule. Intratumoral stromal fat is absent or sparse. A rim of atrophic non-neoplastic parathyroid tissue is identifiable in more than half of cases and is best assessed by sectioning through the vascular hilum. Chief cells typically form sheets, nests, or lobules in a delicate capillary network; palisading around vessels may be present. Follicular structures may occur, occasionally as the predominant pattern; papillary growth is rare. Oncocytic cells may be focal; an adenoma with more than 75% oncocytic cells is classified as oncocytic (oxyphil cell) adenoma. Water-clear cell adenomas are rare and show a proliferation of cells with abundant clear cytoplasm and distinct borders. Cystic change is present when cysts occupy more than 50% of the tumor; hemorrhage, infarction, fibrosis, cholesterol clefts, and calcification may also occur. Occasional mitoses, multinucleated cells, and patchy endocrine nuclear atypia may be seen and do not independently establish malignancy. PTH and GATA3 are typically positive and support parathyroid differentiation. Chromogranin A and synaptophysin are usually positive. Thyroglobulin, TTF1, and monoclonal PAX8 are negative, helping distinguish parathyroid from thyroid follicular lesions. Nuclear parafibromin expression is retained in the vast majority of sporadic adenomas. Routine immunohistochemistry is not required in an otherwise typical adenoma; parafibromin assessment is useful when morphology or clinical history raises concern for CDC73-related disease. Parathyroid hyperplasia Hyperplasia involves multiple glands and is usually associated with a physiologic stimulus such as chronic renal disease. A single-gland adenoma often has a rim of compressed non-neoplastic tissue, although this feature is not completely specific. Lipoadenoma contains abundant adipose tissue, generally more than 50% of gland volume, together with unequivocal expansion of parathyroid parenchyma; conventional adenoma is usually fat-depleted. Atypical parathyroid tumor has a constellation of concerning architectural or cytological features, such as broad fibrosis, monotonous sheet-like growth, increased mitoses, or capsular extension, but lacks definitive invasion. Carcinoma is defined by angioinvasion, lymphatic or perineural invasion, destructive invasion of adjacent structures, or metastasis—not by size, fibrosis, adherence, or cytological atypia alone. Sporadic adenomas commonly show 11q13 loss of heterozygosity and/or biallelic MEN1 inactivation; CCND1 overexpression is another recurrent pathway alteration. Germline predisposition includes MEN1, RET-associated MEN2A, CDKN1B-associated MEN4, CDC73-related disorders, MAX-related MEN5, and familial isolated hyperparathyroidism. CDC73 alterations are uncommon in conventional adenomas but should be considered in parafibromin-deficient lesions or patients with a compatible family history. Section through the vascular hilum to search for a rim of suppressed non-neoplastic parathyroid tissue. A rim-like area can occasionally be seen in hyperplasia; interpret it with clinical, radiologic, and biochemical findings. Do not mistake an intrathyroidal or ectopic parathyroid adenoma for a thyroid neoplasm; use a focused lineage panel. Parathyroid Lipoadenoma Require unequivocal expansion of parathyroid parenchyma together with abundant adipose tissue, generally more than 50% of gland volume. A rare benign parathyroid neoplasm in which abundant adipose tissue is a major component but the parenchymal component is also genuinely increased. Usually occurs in middle-aged to older adults; reported mean age is approximately 56 years. Slight female predominance. Usually arises in a normally positioned gland, with a reported left-sided predilection; ectopic mediastinal examples occur. Most lesions are functioning and produce mild biochemical hyperparathyroidism with typical symptoms. Two or more affected glands may occur; multiglandular lesions with abundant fat are termed lipohyperplasia. Demonstrate a definite increase in both parathyroid parenchymal tissue and adipose tissue. Adipose tissue should generally comprise more than 50% of the glandular volume. Confirm that the parenchymal component is expanded; enlargement caused solely by increased adipose tissue is not lipoadenoma. A rim of compressed non-neoplastic parathyroid tissue supports a neoplastic process. A significant intraoperative PTH decline or postoperative biochemical cure is desirable supportive evidence. The lesion is usually encapsulated and contains abundant mature adipose tissue admixed with increased parathyroid parenchyma. Adipose tissue generally accounts for more than half of the gland volume. The parenchymal component may be composed of chief cells with variable oncocytic or transitional cells. The stromal component may include brown fat and myxoid or fibrous differentiation. A rim of compressed non-neoplastic parathyroid tissue is usually present. The cut surface is often yellow, reflecting the abundant adipose component. PTH and GATA3 support parathyroid lineage when needed. Chromogranin A and synaptophysin may highlight the parenchymal component. Thyroglobulin, TTF1, and monoclonal PAX8 are negative in parathyroid cells and can help exclude thyroid lesions. No specific immunohistochemical profile distinguishes lipoadenoma from conventional parathyroid adenoma; diagnosis is architectural and quantitative. Hyperplasia shows increased parenchymal cellularity with depletion of stromal fat in multiple glands. Lipoadenoma is a discrete lesion with increased parenchyma despite abundant fat, usually exceeding 50% of gland volume. Conventional adenoma is typically fat-depleted; lipoadenoma requires abundant adipose tissue plus unequivocal parenchymal expansion. A few adipocytes in an otherwise typical adenoma are insufficient. Atypical parathyroid tumor is defined by worrisome cytological or architectural atypia without definitive invasion; lipoadenoma is defined by its distinctive adipose-rich composition and lacks the required atypical features. Carcinoma requires unequivocal invasive growth or metastasis. Abundant adipose tissue does not indicate malignancy; assess specifically for vascular, perineural, and destructive soft-tissue invasion. The molecular pathogenesis is unknown. No established hereditary predisposition or diagnostic molecular test is recognized. Do not use the term lipoadenoma for a gland enlarged solely by adipose accumulation without increased parenchymal tissue. Do not apply the diagnosis when adipose tissue is only a minor component of an otherwise conventional adenoma. The term parathyroid hamartoma is not recommended. Atypical Parathyroid Tumor A parathyroid neoplasm with concerning cytological or architectural atypia but no unequivocal carcinoma-defining invasion. A neoplasm of uncertain malignant potential that occupies the diagnostic boundary between conventional adenoma and carcinoma; the diagnosis requires a constellation of worrisome features. Usually occurs in adults; sporadic cases have a mean age of approximately 48 years, with a broad reported age range. Sporadic cases show a slight female predominance; familial cases have a more equal sex distribution and occur at a younger age. Arises in a parathyroid gland and may be adherent to adjacent structures. Usually presents with primary hyperparathyroidism; calcium elevation is often less marked than in carcinoma. A palpable neck mass is uncommon compared with parathyroid carcinoma. Establish that the lesion is a parathyroid neoplasm. Identify significant atypical cytological and/or architectural features that are worrisome for carcinoma. Document the absence of unequivocal full-thickness capsular invasion with extension into soft tissue, vascular invasion, lymphatic invasion, perineural invasion, destructive invasion of adjacent organs, and metastasis. Base the diagnosis on the overall constellation of findings and clinical context, not on a single minor feature. Small foci of fibrosis, occasional mitoses below 5 per 10 mm², limited extension into but not through a thickened capsule, or minor contour irregularity alone are insufficient. Consider prior biopsy, needle washout, ethanol injection, or other manipulation before interpreting fibrosis, fat necrosis, hemosiderin, and irregularity as neoplastic invasion. The tumor is composed of chief cells with variable oncocytic and transitional cells. Growth may be monotonous and sheet-like, trabecular, or composed of closely packed nests. Broad or band-like fibrosis may be present. Tumor cells may extend into, but not through, a thickened capsule. Adherence to adjacent structures, cytological atypia, and increased mitotic activity may be present. Mitotic activity greater than 5 per 10 mm², Ki-67 greater than 5%, coagulative necrosis, macronucleoli, or atypical mitoses increase concern but do not independently establish carcinoma. Fat necrosis and hemosiderin deposition accompanying fibrosis or contour irregularity favor post-traumatic/reactive change in an appropriately manipulated gland. Definitive carcinoma requires unequivocal invasive growth or metastasis. PTH, GATA3, and chromogranin A support parathyroid differentiation. Parafibromin loss, with an intact internal control, indicates parafibromin deficiency and strongly raises concern for CDC73 inactivation. Ki-67, cyclin D1, p27, RB1, BCL2, MDM2, p53, galectin-3, E-cadherin, and PGP9.5 may contribute to risk assessment, but no single marker reliably separates adenoma, atypical tumor, and carcinoma. Parafibromin deficiency is clinically important because it is associated with increased risk of recurrence or metachronous parathyroid tumors. Hyperplasia is supported by involvement of multiple glands and a physiologic driver, particularly chronic renal disease. Tertiary hyperplasia may be markedly atypical, but pseudoinvasion and high proliferation alone do not establish carcinoma. Conventional adenoma may show focal fibrosis, occasional mitoses, or limited capsular thickening, especially when large. Atypical tumor requires a more substantial constellation of worrisome architectural or cytological findings. Lipoadenoma is defined by abundant adipose tissue with definite parenchymal expansion, usually more than 50% adipose volume; atypical tumor is defined by worrisome atypia without unequivocal invasion. Carcinoma requires at least one unequivocal criterion: angioinvasion, lymphatic invasion, perineural invasion, destructive invasion into adjacent structures, or metastasis. Atypical tumor lacks these findings. CDC73 alterations occur in a subset; parafibromin-deficient tumors should undergo germline CDC73 testing. Other reported alterations include changes involving CDKN1A, CDC73, PTEN, RB1, EZH2, HIC1, and CDKN2A, but no molecular profile independently defines atypical parathyroid tumor. Germline evaluation is particularly important when there is parafibromin deficiency, young age, multiglandular disease, or a suggestive family history. Do not use atypical parathyroid tumor as a substitute for careful assessment of the entire capsule and tumor interface. Do not diagnose carcinoma solely because of adherence, fibrosis, mitotic activity, necrosis, or parafibromin loss. Parafibromin-deficient atypical tumors warrant long-term follow-up and consideration of germline testing. Parathyroid Carcinoma Parathyroid Malignancy Malignancy is defined by unequivocal angioinvasion, lymphatic invasion, perineural invasion, destructive invasion of adjacent structures, or metastasis. A rare malignant parathyroid neoplasm; neither cytological atypia, fibrosis, tumor size, nor adherence alone is sufficient for diagnosis. Usually occurs in middle-aged adults; mean age at diagnosis is approximately 51–57 years, but any age may be affected. Most cohorts show a near-equal sex distribution; parafibromin-deficient tumors have a male predilection and tend to occur at younger ages. May arise in any eutopic or ectopic parathyroid location, including the thyroid, retroesophageal space, thymus, mediastinum, or pericardium. Typically presents with symptomatic primary hyperparathyroidism, marked hypercalcemia, and markedly elevated PTH; nephrolithiasis and bone disease are common. A palpable neck mass, hoarseness, recurrent laryngeal nerve dysfunction, or radiologic/intraoperative invasion raises concern for carcinoma. Rare nonfunctioning carcinomas occur; a history of hyperparathyroidism–jaw tumor syndrome is an important risk factor. Diagnose carcinoma only when at least one unequivocal malignant criterion is present: angioinvasion, lymphatic invasion, perineural invasion, destructive invasion into adjacent structures or organs, or regional/distant metastasis. Angioinvasion should show tumor invading through a vessel wall and/or intravascular tumor admixed with thrombus or fibrin; assess the tumor periphery and capsule. Lymphatic invasion and perineural invasion are independently diagnostic when unequivocal. Direct destructive extension into thyroid, esophagus, skeletal muscle, or other adjacent structures establishes malignancy. Metastatic parathyroid tumor in lymph nodes or distant organs establishes carcinoma. Submit and examine the complete parathyroidectomy specimen, with multiple levels and careful evaluation of the capsule and tumor–soft tissue interface. Record mitotic count and Ki-67 proliferation index in all carcinomas; increased proliferation supports risk assessment but is not a substitute for invasive criteria. Most tumors are large, poorly circumscribed, variably encapsulated, and firm, with broad fibrous bands and a lobulated cut surface. Broad bands of fibrosis are common but are not diagnostic of malignancy by themselves. Angioinvasion is characterized by tumor penetrating a vessel wall and/or intravascular tumor admixed with thrombus or fibrin, often in small veins. CD61 or Martius Scarlet Blue may highlight subtle fibrin–platelet material; ERG, CD31, or CD34 can outline vascular endothelium. D2-40 may help highlight lymphatic channels when lymphatic invasion is suspected. Perineural invasion may be microscopic; gross involvement of a large nerve, including the recurrent laryngeal nerve, may also occur. Cytological atypia is variable; some carcinomas are cytologically bland and resemble adenoma. Coagulative tumor necrosis, atypical mitoses, prominent macronucleoli, and increased mitotic activity are worrisome ancillary features. An increased mitotic count is greater than 5 mitoses per 10 mm²; Ki-67 is often greater than 5%, but neither threshold independently defines carcinoma. CDC73-mutated tumors may show sheet-like growth, eosinophilic cytoplasm with perinuclear clearing, nuclear enlargement, microcystic change, and arborizing vasculature. PTH and GATA3 support parathyroid differentiation; chromogranin A and synaptophysin commonly show neuroendocrine differentiation. Loss of nuclear parafibromin, with a positive internal control, is the most reliable ancillary biomarker associated with malignancy in the appropriate morphologic setting. Parafibromin deficiency can also occur in benign tumors in patients with germline CDC73 alterations; it is not independently diagnostic of carcinoma. Other reported abnormalities include loss of APC, E-cadherin, p27, BCL2, MDM2, and 5-hydroxymethylcytosine; positivity for PGP9.5, galectin-3, and TERT; p53 overexpression; and increased Ki-67. Use a panel rather than a single ancillary marker; integrate results with strict morphologic criteria. Thyroglobulin, TTF1, and monoclonal PAX8 are generally negative and help exclude thyroid follicular carcinoma. Secondary/tertiary hyperplasia may show nodularity, fibrosis, pseudoinvasion, and high proliferation, especially in chronic renal failure. Carcinoma requires unequivocal vascular, lymphatic, perineural, destructive adjacent-organ invasion, or metastasis. Adenomas may be large, fibrotic, hemorrhagic, infarcted, or adherent after manipulation. Without unequivocal invasive growth or metastasis, these findings do not establish carcinoma. Lipoadenoma is a benign adipose-rich neoplasm with definite parenchymal expansion; carcinoma is diagnosed by unequivocal invasion or metastasis, not by adipose content or tumor size. Atypical tumor has worrisome cytological or architectural features but lacks definitive invasion. Any unequivocal angioinvasion, lymphatic/perineural invasion, destructive adjacent-organ invasion, or metastasis upgrades the diagnosis to carcinoma. CDC73 inactivation is the principal molecular alteration; approximately 40–80% of sporadic carcinomas harbor inactivating CDC73 alterations, often with loss of heterozygosity at 1q25–q31. Germline CDC73 alterations are associated with hyperparathyroidism–jaw tumor syndrome and a substantially increased risk of parathyroid carcinoma; germline testing should be considered, particularly in parafibromin-deficient tumors. Other reported alterations include TP53 and RB1 loss, CCND1 amplification, rare TERT promoter mutations, and alterations involving PTEN, NF1, KDR, PIK3CA, and DICER1. Record mitotic count and Ki-67 index for prognostic assessment; molecular profiling may identify potentially actionable alterations in advanced disease. Do not diagnose carcinoma based only on broad fibrous bands, capsular irregularity, adherence, tumor size, cytological atypia, necrosis, or an elevated Ki-67 index. Prior fine-needle aspiration, PTH washout, ethanol injection, or surgical manipulation can cause fibrosis, fat necrosis, hemosiderin, and pseudoinvasion. The upper parathyroid gland may be embedded in the thyroid capsule or parenchyma; this anatomic relationship should not be mistaken for destructive invasion. In chronic renal failure-associated hyperparathyroidism, apply particularly strict criteria because pseudoinvasion and high proliferation can occur in tertiary disease. All Categories ← Home PathologyGPS · Endocrine Pathology Parathyroid Tumors A practical diagnostic reference emphasizing the distinction between multiglandular hyperplasia, benign parathyroid neoplasms, tumors of uncertain malignant potential, and carcinoma. Core Diagnostic Principles Interpret the specimen with serum calcium, PTH, renal function, imaging, operative findings, and the status of other parathyroid glands. Section through the vascular hilum when evaluating a suspected adenoma to identify a rim of suppressed non-neoplastic parathyroid tissue. Hyperplasia is fundamentally a multiglandular diagnosis; MEN-associated multiglandular disease is generally classified as multiple adenomas. Parathyroid carcinoma requires unequivocal invasion or metastasis. Cytological atypia, fibrosis, adherence, tumor size, and proliferation alone are insufficient. Parafibromin immunohistochemistry is particularly useful in atypical tumors and carcinomas and should prompt consideration of germline CDC73 testing when deficient. High-Yield Diagnostic Separation Hyperplasia Multiple glands; clinical stimulus; diffuse/nodular parenchymal expansion with fat depletion. Adenoma Discrete fat-depleted neoplasm; often a rim of compressed non-neoplastic tissue at the hilum. Lipoadenoma Definite parenchymal expansion with abundant fat, generally >50% of gland volume. Concerning cytology/architecture without unequivocal invasive growth. Carcinoma Angioinvasion, lymphatic/perineural invasion, destructive adjacent-organ invasion, or metastasis. parathyroid-search Search diagnoses and diagnostic criteria Search: parafibromin, vascular invasion, lipoadenoma, hyperplasia... parathyroid-group Category Collapse All Expand All entities Expand a diagnosis to review the complete diagnostic card. title: Pituitary Tumors
content: use client Somatotroph PitNET PIT1-Lineage PitNETs Usually adults; sellar; acromegaly, gigantism before epiphyseal closure, headache or visual symptoms. Pituitary neuroendocrine neoplasm with diffuse nuclear PIT1 and GH expression. Classify as densely or sparsely granulated based on cytoplasmic keratin pattern and morphology. Correlate with elevated IGF-1 and failure of GH suppression when clinically functioning. Mammosomatotroph PitNET Mammosomatotrophs coexpress GH and prolactin in the same cells; somatotroph tumors lack the distinct prolactin-producing population. Mixed somatotroph-lactotroph PitNET Separate somatotroph and lactotroph cell populations are present; use hormone and lineage markers to establish distinct populations. Acidophil stem cell PitNET Oncocytic cells, prolactin/ER positivity, minimal or absent GH, and mitochondrial accumulation favor acidophil stem cell tumor. Thyrotroph PitNET Compare lineage transcription factors, hormone profile, cytologic differentiation, and whether the tumor represents a single population or distinct components; the defining features of Thyrotroph PitNET are not present. Mature Plurihormonal PIT1-Lineage PitNET Compare lineage transcription factors, hormone profile, cytologic differentiation, and whether the tumor represents a single population or distinct components; the defining features of Mature Plurihormonal PIT1-Lineage PitNET are not present. Immature PIT1-Lineage PitNET Compare lineage transcription factors, hormone profile, cytologic differentiation, and whether the tumor represents a single population or distinct components; the defining features of Immature PIT1-Lineage PitNET are not present. Lactotroph PitNET Distinguish by the defining lineage, hormone profile, architecture, and cytologic differentiation of Lactotroph PitNET; the current lesion lacks that defining combination. Acidophil Stem Cell PitNET Distinguish by the defining lineage, hormone profile, architecture, and cytologic differentiation of Acidophil Stem Cell PitNET; the current lesion lacks that defining combination. Mixed Somatotroph-Lactotroph PitNET Distinguish by the defining lineage, hormone profile, architecture, and cytologic differentiation of Mixed Somatotroph-Lactotroph PitNET; the current lesion lacks that defining combination. GNAS activating mutations occur in a substantial subset, particularly densely granulated tumors. Young patients with sparsely granulated tumors warrant consideration of germline AIP-associated FIPA; consider syndromic context including MEN1, MEN4, Carney complex, and McCune–Albright syndrome. Densely granulated: acidophilic cells with abundant GH granules and diffuse strong GH. Sparsely granulated: chromophobic/pale cells with fibrous bodies and variable, often focal GH. PIT1 is diffusely nuclear in both subtypes. CAM5.2/CK8/18 shows perinuclear keratin in densely granulated tumors and fibrous bodies in sparsely granulated tumors. Alpha-subunit is commonly strong in densely granulated tumors and usually absent in sparsely granulated tumors. Typically adults; sellar; acromegaly or gigantism, sometimes with hyperprolactinemia. Well-differentiated PIT1-lineage PitNET with mammosomatotroph differentiation. GH and prolactin are expressed in the same tumor cell population. Diffuse nuclear PIT1 supports lineage assignment. GH-positive cells without the characteristic coexpression of prolactin in the same cells favor somatotroph PitNET. Shows distinct GH-positive somatotroph and prolactin-positive lactotroph populations rather than a single coexpressing population. Mature plurihormonal PIT1-lineage PitNET Also expresses TSH and alpha-subunit, in addition to GH and prolactin. Compare lineage transcription factors, hormone profile, cytologic differentiation, and whether the tumor represents a single population or distinct components; the defining features of Acidophil Stem Cell PitNET are not present. Distinguish by the defining lineage, hormone profile, architecture, and cytologic differentiation of Mature Plurihormonal PIT1-Lineage PitNET; the current lesion lacks that defining combination. No defining molecular test is required; consider germline evaluation when clinical or family history suggests inherited predisposition. Usually acidophilic cells resembling densely granulated somatotroph tumors. GH and prolactin show extensive cytoplasmic expression. PIT1 is diffusely nuclear. Alpha-subunit may be expressed; TSH is not a defining hormone. Usually adults, often women of reproductive age; sellar; hyperprolactinemia, amenorrhea, galactorrhea, infertility, hypogonadism, or mass effect. PitNET with lactotroph differentiation and prolactin expression. PIT1 nuclear positivity establishes PIT1 lineage. Correlate serum prolactin with tumor size and exclude stalk effect or medication-related hyperprolactinemia. Coexpresses GH and prolactin; lactotroph tumor is predominantly prolactin-lineage. Contains distinct GH-positive and prolactin-positive cell populations. Stalk-effect hyperprolactinemia Prolactin elevation from impaired dopaminergic inhibition is not accompanied by a prolactin-positive PitNET; interpret with imaging and serum levels. Distinguish by the defining lineage, hormone profile, architecture, and cytologic differentiation of Somatotroph PitNET; the current lesion lacks that defining combination. MEN1, MEN4 (CDKN1B), and AIP-related familial isolated pituitary adenoma are relevant hereditary contexts in selected patients. Densely granulated tumors have acidophilic cytoplasm; sparsely granulated tumors are more chromophobic. Sparsely granulated tumors may show paranuclear fibrous bodies. Prolactin is cytoplasmic; PIT1 is nuclear. ER is commonly expressed; CAM5.2 highlights keratin patterns and fibrous bodies. Adults; sellar; central hyperthyroidism with elevated free thyroid hormones and nonsuppressed TSH, often with headache or visual symptoms. PitNET with thyrotroph differentiation. Diffuse nuclear PIT1 with TSH-beta expression supports diagnosis. Correlate with biochemical evidence of inappropriate TSH secretion. Coexpresses GH, prolactin, TSH, and alpha-subunit rather than predominantly thyrotroph differentiation. Other PIT1-lineage PitNETs Somatotroph, lactotroph, and mammosomatotroph tumors are separated by their dominant hormone profile. Thyroid hormone resistance / TSH-secreting nonpituitary source Use clinical, biochemical, imaging, and pituitary-lineage findings to establish a pituitary source. Compare lineage transcription factors, hormone profile, cytologic differentiation, and whether the tumor represents a single population or distinct components; the defining features of Somatotroph PitNET are not present. Compare lineage transcription factors, hormone profile, cytologic differentiation, and whether the tumor represents a single population or distinct components; the defining features of Lactotroph PitNET are not present. Distinguish by the defining lineage, hormone profile, architecture, and cytologic differentiation of Mammosomatotroph PitNET; the current lesion lacks that defining combination. No recurrent molecular alteration is required for diagnosis; consider syndromic evaluation when clinically indicated. Often chromophobic or weakly acidophilic cells in trabecular, sinusoidal, or papillary arrangements. TSH-beta and alpha-subunit are expressed. PIT1 is nuclear; GATA3 may be positive. Cytokeratin pattern varies with granulation. Usually adults; sellar; acromegaly/gigantism with hyperthyroidism and/or hyperprolactinemia. PitNET with PIT1 nuclear immunoreactivity in all or most tumor cells. Extensive GH expression with variable prolactin, TSH, and alpha-subunit expression. GATA3 and ER expression are supportive. Produces GH and prolactin but not TSH; mature plurihormonal tumors show broader hormone expression. Immature PIT1-lineage PitNET Immature epithelioid or spindle cells, marked atypia, prominent nucleoli, and only patchy hormone expression favor the immature subtype. Shows distinct somatotroph and lactotroph populations rather than a single mature plurihormonal population. Distinguish by the defining lineage, hormone profile, architecture, and cytologic differentiation of Immature PIT1-Lineage PitNET; the current lesion lacks that defining combination. No diagnostic molecular test is required; assess hereditary risk from clinical and family history. Solid or sinusoidal growth composed predominantly of acidophilic cells with interspersed chromophobes. GH is usually extensive; prolactin, TSH, and alpha-subunit vary in extent. PIT1 is diffusely nuclear; GATA3 and ER are often positive. Often younger patients; sellar; variable mass effect and endocrine dysfunction; may be clinically nonfunctioning. PIT1-lineage PitNET with immature cytology and limited differentiation toward thyrotroph, somatotroph, and/or lactotroph cells. Tumor cells show diffuse PIT1 with only limited or patchy pituitary hormone expression. Recognize as a high-risk subtype; morphology alone does not establish metastatic behavior. Mature tumor has more differentiated acidophilic morphology and extensive hormone expression. Shows oncocytic cells, mitochondrial accumulation, and prolactin/ER expression with minimal GH. Well-differentiated somatotroph, lactotroph, mammosomatotroph, and thyrotroph tumors show more mature cytology and lineage-specific hormone profiles. No defining molecular test; evaluate for inherited predisposition when young age, family history, or syndromic features are present. Epithelioid or spindle-shaped chromophobic cells with large pleomorphic nuclei. Prominent nucleoli and intranuclear pseudoinclusions may be present. Hormone expression (GH, prolactin, TSH) is usually patchy. PIT1 is diffusely nuclear; other lineage transcription factors help exclude alternate lineages. Usually adults; sellar; hyperprolactinemia often less marked than expected for tumor size, sometimes acromegaly or mass effect. PIT1-positive PitNET with oncocytic features, variable prolactin, and focal to absent GH. ER positivity is supportive. Consider this subtype in a clinically aggressive or treatment-resistant PIT1-lineage tumor. Conventional lactotroph tumors show more convincing prolactin differentiation and lack the characteristic oncocytic phenotype. Sparsely granulated somatotroph PitNET Fibrous bodies may overlap, but acidophil stem cell tumor shows prominent oncocytic/mitochondrial features and little GH. Immature tumors show pleomorphic chromophobic cells rather than oncocytic cells. Compare lineage transcription factors, hormone profile, cytologic differentiation, and whether the tumor represents a single population or distinct components; the defining features of Mammosomatotroph PitNET are not present. No molecular test is required for diagnosis; clinical context may prompt germline evaluation. Large oncocytic cells with abundant granular eosinophilic cytoplasm from mitochondrial accumulation. Prolactin and ER are variable; GH is minimal to absent. CAM5.2 may highlight scattered paranuclear fibrous bodies. Antimitochondrial staining may highlight increased mitochondria. Adults; sellar; acromegaly with hyperprolactinemia or mass effect. Well-differentiated PIT1-lineage PitNET containing distinct somatotroph and lactotroph cell populations. Demonstrate separate GH-positive and prolactin-positive populations rather than assuming coexpression. PIT1 is nuclear in both populations. A single population coexpresses GH and prolactin; mixed tumor has distinct hormone-producing populations. Lacks a distinct prolactin-positive tumor population. Lacks a distinct GH-positive somatotroph population. No specific molecular test is required; consider inherited predisposition based on age, family history, and syndromic findings. Two recognizable cell populations may be intermingled or arranged in separate areas. Somatotroph cells express GH; lactotroph cells express prolactin. PIT1 is diffusely nuclear; ER may highlight lactotroph differentiation. Cytokeratin patterns reflect the granulation of each component. Corticotroph PitNET TPIT-Lineage PitNETs Adults; sellar; Cushing disease when functioning; silent tumors present with mass effect or visual symptoms. PitNET with corticotroph differentiation and nuclear TPIT expression. ACTH expression supports corticotroph differentiation but may be weak or focal. Distinguish functioning from silent corticotroph tumors clinically and biochemically. Crooke cell PitNET Crooke cell change is extensive and present in most tumor cells; conventional corticotroph tumors lack diffuse Crooke hyaline change. Gonadotroph PitNET SF1-lineage tumor expresses gonadotropins rather than TPIT/ACTH. Metastatic PitNET Metastatic designation requires discontinuous CNS spread or systemic metastasis, not local invasion alone. No defining molecular alteration is required; consider MEN1 and other inherited syndromes when clinically indicated. Densely granulated tumors have basophilic cytoplasm and conspicuous secretory granules. Sparsely granulated tumors are often larger and more invasive, with variable cytoplasm. Crooke cell tumor shows extensive hyaline, ring-like cytoplasmic keratin accumulation. TPIT is nuclear; ACTH is cytoplasmic; CAM5.2 highlights Crooke hyaline material. SF1-Lineage PitNETs Usually middle-aged or older adults; sellar; commonly clinically nonfunctioning with headache, visual field loss, or hypopituitarism. PitNET with nuclear SF1 expression and gonadotroph differentiation. FSH-beta and/or LH-beta expression supports the diagnosis, although hormone staining may be focal. Exclude PIT1 and TPIT lineage with transcription factor panel. Null cell PitNET Null cell tumors lack SF1, TPIT, and PIT1 lineage markers; gonadotroph tumors are SF1-positive. TPIT and ACTH support corticotroph lineage. PIT1 with GH, prolactin, or TSH expression establishes PIT1 lineage. No recurrent molecular test is required; MEN1, MEN4, and other hereditary syndromes may be considered in selected patients. Usually monomorphic cells in diffuse, trabecular, or sinusoidal patterns. FSH-beta and LH-beta may be focal or variable; alpha-subunit may be present. SF1 is nuclear; GATA3 may be expressed. Low-molecular-weight keratin patterns are variable. Null Cell PitNET Other PitNET Categories Adults; sellar; usually nonfunctioning mass with headache, visual impairment, or hypopituitarism. PitNET lacking terminal differentiation along PIT1, TPIT, and SF1 lineages. Exclude lineage-specific PitNETs with a complete transcription factor and hormone panel. Use the diagnosis only after excluding other sellar neoplasms. SF1 positivity establishes gonadotroph lineage, even when gonadotropin hormone staining is limited. PIT1 is positive despite limited hormone differentiation. Metastatic neuroendocrine neoplasm Clinical history, imaging, lineage markers, and pituitary-specific transcription factors help establish a primary PitNET. Plurihormonal PitNET Compare lineage transcription factors, hormone profile, cytologic differentiation, and whether the tumor represents a single population or distinct components; the defining features of Plurihormonal PitNET are not present. Multiple Synchronous PitNETs of Distinct Lineages Compare lineage transcription factors, hormone profile, cytologic differentiation, and whether the tumor represents a single population or distinct components; the defining features of Multiple Synchronous PitNETs of Distinct Lineages are not present. No defining molecular alteration; selected cases may show loss of menin or p27 prompting germline evaluation. Neuroendocrine morphology with diffuse or nested growth may resemble other PitNETs. PIT1, TPIT, and SF1 are negative in tumor nuclei. Pituitary hormones are negative; neuroendocrine markers and keratins support PitNET phenotype. Ki-67 and mitotic activity should be documented but do not independently define grade. Adults; sellar; variable hormone excess or mass effect depending on the lineages represented. Demonstrate adenohypophysial hormones and transcription factors from at least two distinct pituitary cell lineages. Use lineage transcription factors to distinguish true plurihormonal differentiation from nonspecific hormone staining. Exclude multiple separate PitNET components. Restricted to PIT1 lineage; broad hormone expression within PIT1 lineage does not establish cross-lineage plurihormonality. Multiple synchronous PitNETs of distinct lineages Separate tumor nodules/components with distinct lineage profiles indicate multiple PitNETs rather than one plurihormonal tumor. Two distinct PIT1-lineage cell populations do not by themselves constitute cross-lineage plurihormonal tumor. Compare lineage transcription factors, hormone profile, cytologic differentiation, and whether the tumor represents a single population or distinct components; the defining features of Null Cell PitNET are not present. Distinguish by the defining lineage, hormone profile, architecture, and cytologic differentiation of Multiple Synchronous PitNETs of Distinct Lineages; the current lesion lacks that defining combination. No diagnostic molecular test is required; consider germline evaluation based on clinical features and family history. Morphology resembles the individual lineage components represented. Coexpression of PIT1 and SF1, with corresponding hormones, is a recognized pattern; rare tumors express all three lineage factors. Hormone immunoreactivity may vary; interpret with transcription factor profile. Adults; sellar; variable endocrine syndromes or nonfunctioning mass effect. Identify at least two distinct PitNET components belonging to different lineages (PIT1, SF1, TPIT), or a lineage-specific PitNET combined with a null cell tumor. Demonstrate distinct components by morphology and lineage-specific transcription factor staining. Subtype each component independently. A single tumor showing cross-lineage transcription factor/hormone expression is plurihormonal; multiple tumors show spatially distinct components. Both components belong to PIT1 lineage and represent distinct hormone cell populations, not distinct major lineages. Collision tumor with non-PitNET sellar neoplasm Use morphology and lineage markers to identify a separate non-PitNET component. No molecular test is required; consider germline testing in young patients, familial cases, or syndromic presentations. Separate nodules or spatially distinct components may be white to yellow and soft. Each component has morphology and immunophenotype of its respective PitNET subtype. PIT1, SF1, and TPIT are essential to establish distinct lineages; hormone staining alone can misclassify components. Ki-67 may vary between components. Metastatic PitNETs Any adult age; primary usually sellar; cervical lymph nodes, liver, bone, or craniospinal axis; endocrine syndrome may precede metastasis by years. A PitNET with discontinuous CNS spread or metastasis to lymph nodes or distant organs. Local invasion into cavernous sinus, bone, or adjacent structures alone does not qualify as metastatic disease. Retain the specific PitNET subtype in the diagnosis (e.g., metastatic corticotroph PitNET). Locally invasive PitNET Contiguous extension into cavernous sinus, bone, or sinonasal tissue is local invasion, not metastasis. Metastatic neuroendocrine tumor from another site Compare morphology and immunophenotype with the sellar primary and correlate with clinical history. Primary high-grade neuroendocrine carcinoma A poorly differentiated phenotype is not the defining criterion; metastatic PitNET is defined by metastatic spread. No molecular marker reliably predicts metastatic behavior; molecular testing is not required for the diagnosis. Metastatic deposits recapitulate the morphology and immunophenotype of the primary PitNET, although progression-related changes may occur. Lineage transcription factors and pituitary hormones help confirm the tumor phenotype. Ki-67 and mitotic activity may be variable and cannot reliably predict metastasis in isolation. Adamantinomatous Craniopharyngioma Craniopharyngiomas Bimodal age distribution in children and adults; sellar/suprasellar; visual impairment, headache, hypothalamic dysfunction, and endocrine deficits. Craniopharyngioma with adamantinomatous morphology. Identify peripheral palisading, stellate reticulum-like epithelium, and characteristic wet keratin. Nuclear beta-catenin in epithelial clusters supports the diagnosis. Papillary craniopharyngioma Lacks wet keratin and stellate reticulum; papillary squamous epithelium and BRAF V600E favor papillary type. Rathke cleft cyst Cyst lining is usually bland ciliated or cuboidal epithelium without invasive epithelial nests or wet keratin. Pituitary blastoma Occurs in very young children and has primitive mixed neuroendocrine and epithelial components. Papillary Craniopharyngioma Distinguish by the defining lineage, hormone profile, architecture, and cytologic differentiation of Papillary Craniopharyngioma; the current lesion lacks that defining combination. CTNNB1 activating mutations drive nuclear beta-catenin accumulation. Epithelial nests and cords with peripheral palisading and loose stellate reticulum-like areas. Wet keratin, calcification, cholesterol clefts, and cyst formation are common. Nuclear beta-catenin highlights clusters of tumor cells; broad-spectrum keratin is positive. Inflammation and foreign-body giant cells may surround keratin debris. Almost exclusively adults; sellar/suprasellar; visual symptoms, headache, and endocrine or hypothalamic dysfunction. Craniopharyngioma with papillary squamous architecture. Tumor consists of nonkeratinizing squamous epithelium covering fibrovascular cores. BRAF V600E mutation or VE1 immunoreactivity supports the diagnosis. Adamantinomatous craniopharyngioma Shows wet keratin, calcification, peripheral palisading, and nuclear beta-catenin. Squamous metaplasia of Rathke cleft cyst Usually bland, cyst-lining metaplasia without complex papillary tumor architecture or BRAF V600E. Metastatic papillary squamous carcinoma Correlate with clinical history and imaging; a sellar-centered primary lesion and BRAF V600E support papillary craniopharyngioma. Distinguish by the defining lineage, hormone profile, architecture, and cytologic differentiation of Adamantinomatous Craniopharyngioma; the current lesion lacks that defining combination. BRAF p.V600E is characteristic and may be detected by VE1 immunohistochemistry. Well-differentiated nonkeratinizing squamous epithelium forms papillae with fibrovascular cores. Peripheral palisading, stellate reticulum, and wet keratin are absent. Tumor cells express broad-spectrum cytokeratins and often CK5/6/p63. VE1 immunohistochemistry may demonstrate BRAF V600E. Pituitary Blastoma Other Anterior Pituitary Tumors Infants and very young children; sellar/suprasellar; Cushing syndrome or mass effect; consider DICER1 syndrome. Primitive sellar tumor with a mixture of adenohypophysial neuroendocrine cells, primitive Rathke cleft-like cells, and primitive folliculostellate cells. Recognize the characteristic mixed primitive components in the appropriate pediatric setting. Evaluate for DICER1-associated disease. Shows mature squamous epithelium, wet keratin, and beta-catenin nuclear clusters rather than a primitive mixed tumor. Shows mature papillary squamous epithelium and BRAF V600E. Shows PIT1-lineage neoplastic cells without the characteristic primitive Rathke cleft and folliculostellate admixture. Associated with germline DICER1 pathogenic variants; molecular confirmation supports syndrome evaluation. Primitive small cells and neuroendocrine elements are admixed with Rathke cleft-like epithelial structures and folliculostellate components. Neuroendocrine markers highlight adenohypophysial elements; cytokeratin highlights epithelial components. The mixed morphology distinguishes the tumor from conventional PitNET and craniopharyngioma. Pituicytoma Posterior Pituitary and Hypothalamic Tumors Adults, often middle-aged; posterior pituitary/stalk; headache, visual disturbance, and hypopituitarism or diabetes insipidus. Well-circumscribed or infiltrative spindle-cell neoplasm of pituicyte lineage. Show a pituicyte-family immunophenotype and exclude other spindle-cell sellar tumors. Recognize spindle cell oncocytoma, granular cell tumor, and ependymal-pattern pituicytoma as related subtypes in the pituicytoma spectrum. Spindle cell oncocytoma Oncocytic cells with abundant granular eosinophilic cytoplasm and mitochondrial accumulation. Granular cell tumor of sellar region Large polygonal cells with abundant PAS-positive granular cytoplasm. Meningioma Whorls, syncytial cells, and EMA/SSTR2A expression favor meningioma; pituicyte tumors typically show TTF1. Schwannoma Antoni A/B areas and Verocay bodies with diffuse S100/SOX10 favor schwannoma. Gangliocytoma and Mixed Gangliocytoma-PitNET Compare lineage transcription factors, hormone profile, cytologic differentiation, and whether the tumor represents a single population or distinct components; the defining features of Gangliocytoma and Mixed Gangliocytoma-PitNET are not present. Sellar Neurocytoma Compare lineage transcription factors, hormone profile, cytologic differentiation, and whether the tumor represents a single population or distinct components; the defining features of Sellar Neurocytoma are not present. Methylation profiling supports a shared pituicyte-family relationship among pituicytoma subtypes; no routine defining driver mutation is required. Biphasic or fascicular growth of bland spindle cells with delicate vascularity is typical. Pituicytoma: spindle cells with elongated nuclei and fibrillary cytoplasm. GFAP and S100 are commonly positive; TTF1 is a useful nuclear marker of pituicyte lineage. Subtype-specific oncocytic, granular, or ependymal morphology may be present. Adults; sellar/hypothalamic; headache, visual symptoms, endocrine dysfunction; may cause acromegaly through hypothalamic hormone secretion. Mature ganglion cells in a sellar or hypothalamic neuronal neoplasm, with or without an associated PitNET. Identify mature dysplastic ganglion cells and assess carefully for an associated PitNET component. If a PitNET is present, classify its lineage independently. Sellar neurocytoma Composed of relatively uniform small neuronal cells rather than large mature ganglion cells. PitNET A pure PitNET lacks mature ganglion cells; search for a mixed component. Spindle-cell glial morphology and TTF1 support pituicyte lineage. Distinguish by the defining lineage, hormone profile, architecture, and cytologic differentiation of Sellar Neurocytoma; the current lesion lacks that defining combination. No defining molecular alteration is required; molecular findings are not routinely diagnostic. Large mature ganglion cells with abundant cytoplasm, vesicular nuclei, and prominent nucleoli occur singly or in clusters. Neuronal processes and neuropil may be present. Ganglion cells express neuronal markers such as synaptophysin and neurofilament. An associated PitNET shows neuroendocrine markers, pituitary hormones, and lineage transcription factors. Usually adults; hypothalamic/sellar region; visual, endocrine, and hypothalamic symptoms; may be hormonally active. Neuronal neoplasm of hypothalamic differentiation in the sellar region. Show neuronal differentiation and exclude gangliocytoma and neuroendocrine PitNET. Correlate with clinical hormone excess when present. Gangliocytoma Shows large mature ganglion cells rather than a monotonous population of small neuronal cells. PitNET expresses pituitary lineage transcription factors and often pituitary hormones. Shows spindle-cell glial morphology and TTF1 rather than neuronal differentiation. Distinguish by the defining lineage, hormone profile, architecture, and cytologic differentiation of Gangliocytoma and Mixed Gangliocytoma-PitNET; the current lesion lacks that defining combination. No routine defining molecular alteration is established. Uniform round cells with finely stippled chromatin in sheets, nests, or neuropil-rich areas. Neuropil and neuronal processes may be conspicuous. Synaptophysin and other neuronal markers are positive; pituitary lineage transcription factors help exclude PitNET. Ki-67 is generally low in conventional examples. Other Sellar Neoplasms Adults, more often women; tuberculum sellae, diaphragma sellae, or parasellar region; visual loss, headache, or cranial neuropathy. Meningothelial neoplasm centered on the sellar/parasellar meninges. Establish meningothelial morphology and immunophenotype. Distinguish a primary sellar meningioma from a PitNET or pituicyte-family tumor. PitNET shows neuroendocrine differentiation and PIT1, TPIT, or SF1 lineage markers. TTF1-positive spindle-cell tumor favors pituicyte lineage. Antoni A/B pattern, Verocay bodies, and diffuse SOX10 favor schwannoma. Chordoma Compare lineage transcription factors, hormone profile, cytologic differentiation, and whether the tumor represents a single population or distinct components; the defining features of Chordoma are not present. NF2 alterations are common in meningiomas; molecular profiling is used for selected classification and risk assessment, not required for routine diagnosis. Syncytial nests, whorls, and meningothelial cells with intranuclear pseudoinclusions may be present. Psammoma bodies may occur depending on subtype. EMA and SSTR2A are commonly positive; progesterone receptor may be expressed. SOX10 and pituitary lineage transcription factors are generally negative. Adults; clivus with possible sellar extension; headache, diplopia, cranial neuropathies, and destructive skull-base mass. Midline notochordal neoplasm with characteristic physaliphorous cells in myxoid stroma. Demonstrate nuclear brachyury with epithelial marker expression. Correlate with clival-centered destructive imaging. Chondrosarcoma Usually lacks broad-spectrum cytokeratin and nuclear brachyury; chondroid matrix and cartilage morphology favor chondrosarcoma. Metastatic carcinoma Clinical history and broad panel; nuclear brachyury supports chordoma. Usually sellar-centered and lineage-marker positive; chordoma is clival-centered and brachyury-positive. Compare lineage transcription factors, hormone profile, cytologic differentiation, and whether the tumor represents a single population or distinct components; the defining features of Meningioma are not present. Loss of SMARCB1/INI1 may occur in poorly differentiated chordoma; brachyury expression is a key diagnostic marker. Lobules and cords of physaliphorous cells with bubbly/vacuolated cytoplasm in abundant myxoid matrix. Conventional, chondroid, and dedifferentiated patterns may occur. Cytokeratin, EMA, and nuclear brachyury are typically positive. S100 may be positive, particularly in conventional/chondroid areas. All PathologyGPS · Endocrine System Pituitary and Sellar Tumors A morphology-first diagnostic reference to pituitary neuroendocrine tumors, craniopharyngiomas, posterior pituitary and hypothalamic neoplasms, and other primary sellar tumors. Emphasis is placed on lineage assignment, essential diagnostic criteria, immunophenotype, and practical differential diagnosis. Diagnostic Approach: Start Here 1. Establish the tumor family Separate anterior pituitary PitNETs from craniopharyngioma, pituicyte-family tumors, neuronal tumors, meningioma, and chordoma. 2. Assign PitNET lineage Use PIT1, TPIT, and SF1 transcription factors together with pituitary hormones. Hormone stains alone may be misleading. 3. Subtype the PitNET Within PIT1 lineage, distinguish somatotroph, lactotroph, thyrotroph, mammosomatotroph, mixed, mature plurihormonal, immature, and acidophil stem cell tumors. 4. Assess the sellar mimics Use morphology-directed panels: beta-catenin for adamantinomatous craniopharyngioma, BRAF V600E for papillary craniopharyngioma, TTF1 for pituicyte lineage, and brachyury for chordoma. 5. Interpret behavior correctly Local invasion does not equal metastasis. A metastatic PitNET requires discontinuous CNS spread or lymph node/distant metastasis. 6. Document proliferation and extent Record mitotic activity and Ki-67, while recognizing that no universally accepted PitNET grading system is established. Correlate invasion with imaging and operative findings. Critical principle: Accurate PitNET classification requires transcription factor-based lineage assignment (PIT1, TPIT, and SF1) integrated with hormone immunohistochemistry and morphology. No single marker or proliferation index reliably predicts metastatic behavior. Search diagnosis, lineage, morphology, IHC, or molecular marker...
