title: Thyroid Tumors
content: use client Thyroglossal Duct Cyst Developmental Abnormalities A midline or near-midline cyst along the thyroglossal tract, usually near the hyoid bone. Congenital remnant cyst; carcinoma is uncommon and is usually papillary thyroid carcinoma. Usually presents in children or young adults; can occur at any age. No strong sex predilection. Midline anterior neck, most often adjacent to or just below the hyoid bone. Painless, mobile mass that elevates with swallowing or tongue protrusion; infection may cause tenderness. Establish the anatomic site and clinical/radiologic context. Assess the defining architecture and cytology described below. Evaluate the entire tumor interface when invasion is a diagnostic requirement. Use ancillary studies as a panel and interpret them in conjunction with morphology. Usually a mobile, painless midline infrahyoid mass that moves with swallowing or tongue protrusion. Cyst is lined by respiratory, squamous, or mixed epithelium; inflammation may denude the lining. Thyroid follicles are often present in the cyst wall. Papillary thyroid carcinoma may arise in the cyst wall; assess for an associated orthotopic thyroid primary. No routine IHC is required for an uncomplicated cyst. For a suspicious epithelial proliferation, thyroglobulin, TTF-1, and PAX8 support thyroid follicular differentiation. Dermoid or epidermal inclusion cyst Keratin debris and skin appendages favor a dermoid; a squamous-lined cyst without thyroid follicles may be an epidermal inclusion cyst. Branchial cleft cyst Typically lateral rather than perihyoidal; lymphoid-rich wall may be present. Metastatic papillary thyroid carcinoma A cystic lymph node lacks the characteristic thyroglossal tract relationship; search for thyroid primary and nodal architecture. Other Congenital Thyroid Abnormalities Distinguish by the defining pattern: Includes thyroid dysgenesis (agenesis, hypoplasia, hemiagenesis, ectopic thyroid) and dyshormonogenetic goitre. No routinely useful molecular test is required for a benign cyst. A developmental abnormality of thyroid formation, migration, or hormone synthesis. Includes thyroid dysgenesis (agenesis, hypoplasia, hemiagenesis, ectopic thyroid) and dyshormonogenetic goitre. Usually identified in neonates, children, or adolescents during evaluation of congenital hypothyroidism; ectopic thyroid may present later. Thyroid dysgenesis is more common in individuals assigned female at birth. Ectopic tissue most often occurs at the tongue base; dyshormonogenetic goitre affects the thyroid gland bilaterally. May cause hypothyroidism; lingual thyroid can produce dysphagia, dyspnea, or airway symptoms. Ectopic thyroid shows normal thyroid follicles in an abnormal anatomic location, most often at the tongue base. Agenesis is absence of thyroid follicular tissue; hemiagenesis is absence of one lobe; hypoplasia is reduced gland volume. Dyshormonogenetic goitre is typically bilateral and multinodular and may show hypercellular, microfollicular nodules with pale colloid and variable random nuclear atypia. In a lymph node, benign thyroid inclusions require strict anatomic and morphologic criteria: medial to the jugular vein, intracapsular, and cytologically bland. Thyroglobulin, TTF-1, and PAX8 confirm thyroid follicular differentiation when tissue identity is uncertain. IHC does not by itself distinguish benign nodal inclusions from metastatic papillary carcinoma; morphology and location are essential. Nuclear features of PTC, papillae, psammoma bodies, or a lateral cervical node favor metastasis; bland intracapsular follicles in a medial node may be benign inclusions. Thyroid follicular nodular disease Occurs in an orthotopic gland and lacks the defining developmental displacement or congenital absence. Thyroglossal duct cyst A cystic tract remnant near the hyoid, rather than ectopic solid thyroid tissue. Distinguish by the defining pattern: Congenital remnant cyst; carcinoma is uncommon and is usually papillary thyroid carcinoma. Developmental defects may involve NKX2-1, FOXE1, PAX8, HHEX, or TSHR. Dyshormonogenesis may involve TPO, DUOX2, DUOXA2, SLC5A5, SLC26A4, TG, or IYD. Thyroid Follicular Nodular Disease Benign Follicular Lesions Multiple variably sized follicular nodules in a background of nodular thyroid enlargement or nodularity. A benign multifocal proliferation spanning hyperplasia and clonal nodules; multinodular goitre is a clinical term. Incidence increases with age and is highest in older adults. Strong female predominance. One or both thyroid lobes; may extend retrosternally into the mediastinum. Often asymptomatic; large nodules may cause dysphagia, dyspnea, hoarseness, or other compressive symptoms. Nodules show variable macrofollicular, microfollicular, papillary, or mixed architecture. Large colloid-filled follicles and cystic degeneration are common. Hemorrhage, fibrosis, calcification, hemosiderin-laden macrophages, and ossification may occur. Nuclear features of papillary thyroid carcinoma are absent. A dominant encapsulated nodule may resemble follicular adenoma; evaluate the entire gland and the interface. No routine IHC is needed in morphologically typical disease. Thyroglobulin, TTF-1, and PAX8 confirm follicular lineage in an unusual lesion. Follicular thyroid adenoma A discrete, completely encapsulated neoplasm with uniform architecture and no background multinodular pattern; assess the entire capsule. Follicular thyroid carcinoma Requires capsular and/or vascular invasion; cytology alone cannot establish carcinoma. Papillary thyroid carcinoma True PTC nuclear features, particularly diffuse clearing, grooves, and pseudoinclusions, are absent in ordinary nodular disease. Clonal nodules may harbor TSHR, GNAS, EZH1, or other pathway alterations; molecular testing is not required for routine diagnosis. Follicular Thyroid Adenoma Benign Follicular Neoplasms A solitary, usually encapsulated follicular neoplasm, most often in adults and more common in women. A benign clonal follicular-cell neoplasm defined by absence of capsular and vascular invasion. Usually diagnosed in adults; broad age range. More common in women. Usually a solitary intrathyroidal nodule. Typically presents as an incidental or palpable thyroid nodule; some are hyperfunctioning. Usually a solitary, well-circumscribed or encapsulated nodule. Microfollicular, normofollicular, or macrofollicular architecture may be present. The capsule and entire tumor–thyroid interface must be adequately sampled. No capsular invasion, vascular invasion, or tumor necrosis is identified. Papillary-type nuclear features sufficient for PTC are absent. Tumor cells express thyroglobulin, TTF-1, and PAX8. HBME-1, galectin-3, and CK19 are not sufficiently specific to distinguish adenoma from carcinoma in isolation. Capsular penetration and/or unequivocal vascular invasion establishes carcinoma. Often multiple nodules with degenerative change and variable architecture rather than a single discrete clonal neoplasm. NIFTP Requires papillary-like nuclear features and strict noninvasive criteria; adenoma lacks qualifying PTC-type nuclei. Follicular Adenoma with Papillary Architecture Distinguish by the defining pattern: A benign adenoma characterized by papillary infoldings into follicular lumina rather than true invasive papillae. Oncocytic Adenoma of the Thyroid Gland Distinguish by the defining pattern: A benign oncocytic follicular-cell neoplasm without capsular or vascular invasion. RAS-like alterations are common but are not required for diagnosis. A hyperfunctioning or nonfunctioning follicular nodule with intrafollicular papillary structures. A benign adenoma characterized by papillary infoldings into follicular lumina rather than true invasive papillae. Usually occurs in middle-aged or older adults. Female predominance. Intrathyroidal, often in a background of chronic lymphocytic thyroiditis. Presents as a solitary thyroid nodule; functional symptoms are uncommon. Well-circumscribed or encapsulated nodule with follicles containing delicate intraluminal papillary infoldings. Papillary structures lack the complex branching architecture and fibrovascular cores of conventional PTC. Nuclear features of PTC are absent. No capsular or vascular invasion is present. Thyroglobulin, TTF-1, and PAX8 support follicular differentiation. No IHC marker independently establishes this benign entity. True papillae with fibrovascular cores and characteristic PTC nuclear features favor PTC. Usually shows multifocal nodularity and degenerative changes rather than a discrete circumscribed adenoma. Follicular adenoma Lacks the characteristic intrafollicular papillary architecture. Distinguish by the defining pattern: A benign clonal follicular-cell neoplasm defined by absence of capsular and vascular invasion. Activating alterations in the cAMP pathway, including GNAS or TSHR, may be present. A circumscribed oncocytic nodule, usually in an adult and often in a background of chronic thyroiditis. A benign oncocytic follicular-cell neoplasm without capsular or vascular invasion. Tumor is composed predominantly or entirely of oncocytic cells with abundant granular eosinophilic cytoplasm. Architecture may be solid, trabecular, microfollicular, or macrofollicular. The capsule and tumor–thyroid interface must be extensively sampled. No capsular or vascular invasion is identified. Thyroglobulin, TTF-1, and PAX8 support follicular-cell origin. Mitochondrial-rich oncocytic cytoplasm is a morphologic feature; no single IHC stain separates adenoma from carcinoma. Oncocytic thyroid carcinoma Requires unequivocal capsular and/or vascular invasion; extensive sampling is essential. Oncocytic hyperplasia in chronic lymphocytic thyroiditis Usually multifocal and intermixed with lymphocytic inflammation rather than a discrete encapsulated neoplasm. Lacks the predominant oncocytic cytology. Oncocytic tumors may show mitochondrial DNA alterations and genome haploidization; these findings do not replace invasion assessment. Non-Invasive Follicular Thyroid Neoplasm with Papillary-Like Nuclear Features (NIFTP) Low-Risk Follicular Neoplasms An encapsulated or clearly demarcated follicular-patterned lesion with PTC-type nuclei but no invasion. A low-risk neoplasm diagnosed only when strict architectural, nuclear, and exclusion criteria are met. Usually diagnosed in adults, often in middle age. Female predominance, reflecting the epidemiology of thyroid nodules. Usually a solitary encapsulated thyroid nodule. Typically detected as a thyroid nodule on imaging or examination. Completely encapsulated or sharply demarcated, predominantly follicular-patterned tumor. Papillary-like nuclear features are present, including enlargement, chromatin clearing, grooves, and occasional pseudoinclusions. True papillae are absent or extremely limited; psammoma bodies and tumor necrosis are absent. No capsular or vascular invasion is identified after complete examination of the tumor–capsule interface. Exclude high-grade features and disqualifying patterns; adequate sampling of the entire capsule is mandatory. Thyroglobulin, TTF-1, and PAX8 confirm follicular differentiation. HBME-1, galectin-3, and CK19 may be expressed but are not diagnostic by themselves. Invasive encapsulated follicular variant of PTC Shows capsular and/or vascular invasion; NIFTP requires complete absence of invasion. Lacks qualifying PTC-type nuclear features. Classic papillary thyroid carcinoma Usually has true papillae, infiltrative growth, or other exclusionary features. Follicular Tumor of Uncertain Malignant Potential (FT-UMP) Distinguish by the defining pattern: A provisional category for follicular tumors in which invasion cannot be confidently classified as absent or present. Well-Differentiated Tumor of Uncertain Malignant Potential (WDT-UMP) Distinguish by the defining pattern: A low-risk category when papillary-like nuclear features are present but invasion remains uncertain. Hyalinizing Trabecular Tumor Distinguish by the defining pattern: Usually indolent; invasion or vascular invasion is uncommon but must be assessed. RAS-like mutations, particularly RAS-family alterations, are common; molecular findings are supportive and cannot substitute for strict histologic criteria. An encapsulated follicular-patterned tumor with equivocal capsular or vascular invasion. A provisional category for follicular tumors in which invasion cannot be confidently classified as absent or present. Usually occurs in middle-aged adults. Often detected during workup of a thyroid nodule; most behave indolently. Encapsulated follicular-patterned neoplasm with no convincing PTC-type nuclear features. A focus raises but does not establish capsular invasion or vascular invasion after deeper levels and careful review. The equivocal focus must be documented and distinguished from artifact, tangential sectioning, or capsular displacement. IHC does not resolve equivocal invasion; the diagnosis is primarily morphologic. No suspicious focus of capsular or vascular invasion. Unequivocal capsular penetration and/or vascular invasion is present. Requires papillary-like nuclear features and strict absence of invasion. Distinguish by the defining pattern: A low-risk neoplasm diagnosed only when strict architectural, nuclear, and exclusion criteria are met. No defining molecular alteration; molecular results do not adjudicate equivocal invasion. An encapsulated follicular-patterned tumor with PTC-like nuclear features and equivocal invasion. A low-risk category when papillary-like nuclear features are present but invasion remains uncertain. Encapsulated or sharply demarcated follicular-patterned neoplasm with nuclear features of PTC. Capsular or vascular invasion is suspicious but not unequivocal. The lesion does not meet strict NIFTP criteria because invasion cannot be excluded. IHC cannot replace morphologic evaluation of the capsule and vessels. No suspicious invasion is present after adequate sampling. Unequivocal capsular and/or vascular invasion is identified. Lacks convincing PTC-type nuclear features. RAS-like molecular profiles may occur; no molecular test establishes uncertain invasion. A trabecular thyroid neoplasm with distinctive intratrabecular hyaline material and PTC-like nuclear changes. Usually indolent; invasion or vascular invasion is uncommon but must be assessed. Trabeculae and nests of elongated or spindle-shaped cells are separated by abundant hyaline material. Nuclei may show grooves, clearing, and pseudoinclusions resembling PTC. Hyaline material is intratrabecular and often surrounds individual tumor cells. Assess for capsular and vascular invasion; most tumors are circumscribed and noninvasive. Ki-67 (MIB-1) often shows distinctive membranous/cytoplasmic staining, a useful supportive feature. Thyroglobulin, TTF-1, and PAX8 support follicular lineage. Calcitonin is negative, helping exclude medullary carcinoma. PTC shows true papillae or follicular architecture with PTC nuclei; HTT has trabecular growth and intratrabecular hyaline. Medullary thyroid carcinoma Usually calcitonin and neuroendocrine marker positive; HTT is thyroglobulin positive and calcitonin negative. Paraganglioma Usually lacks thyroglobulin and shows neuroendocrine phenotype with sustentacular cells. PAX8-GLIS3 or PAX8-GLIS1 fusions support HTT in a subset. Follicular Thyroid Carcinoma Malignant Follicular-Cell Neoplasms An adult follicular-cell malignancy, often presenting as a solitary thyroid nodule; hematogenous spread may involve lung and bone. Diagnosis requires capsular and/or vascular invasion; lymph node metastasis is less common than distant hematogenous spread. Usually occurs in adults, with incidence increasing with age. Thyroid follicular epithelium; may be widely invasive. Presents as a thyroid nodule; hematogenous metastases may cause bone pain or pulmonary symptoms. Usually an encapsulated or widely invasive follicular-patterned tumor. Capsular invasion shows full-thickness penetration through the capsule into adjacent thyroid or soft tissue. Vascular invasion requires tumor within a capsular or extracapsular vessel, attached to the vessel wall and/or covered by endothelium, often with fibrin. Classify as minimally invasive, encapsulated angioinvasive, or widely invasive based on extent and pattern of invasion. CD31 or ERG can help highlight endothelial lining around suspected vascular invasion but must be interpreted with H&E. No capsular or vascular invasion after complete capsule sampling. Shows PTC-like nuclei but is strictly noninvasive. Has PTC-type nuclear features plus invasion. Oncocytic carcinoma Predominantly oncocytic cytology defines a separate entity. Invasive Encapsulated Follicular Variant of Papillary Thyroid Carcinoma Distinguish by the defining pattern: A RAS-like PTC subtype with capsular and/or vascular invasion. Papillary Thyroid Carcinoma Distinguish by the defining pattern: A differentiated follicular-cell carcinoma defined by characteristic nuclear features, often with papillary and/or infiltrative growth. Oncocytic Thyroid Carcinoma Distinguish by the defining pattern: An oncocytic follicular-cell carcinoma defined by capsular and/or vascular invasion or metastasis. RAS-family mutations are common. TERT promoter mutations are associated with aggressive behavior; assess in clinically advanced disease when relevant. An encapsulated follicular-patterned carcinoma with PTC-type nuclei and demonstrable invasion. A RAS-like PTC subtype with capsular and/or vascular invasion. Usually occurs in older adults. Thyroid gland; may show local invasion or distant spread. Presents as a thyroid mass; invasive tumors may metastasize to lung or bone. Encapsulated or sharply demarcated follicular-patterned tumor. Nuclear features of PTC are present, including enlargement, clearing, grooves, and pseudoinclusions. Exclude true papillae and other patterns that would reclassify the tumor as another PTC subtype. HBME-1, galectin-3, and CK19 may be positive but are not individually specific. Lacks the qualifying PTC-type nuclear features. Often infiltrative, papillary, or not fully encapsulated. Distinguish by the defining pattern: Diagnosis requires capsular and/or vascular invasion; lymph node metastasis is less common than distant hematogenous spread. RAS-like alterations are frequent; TERT promoter or TP53 alterations may accompany progression. Most common thyroid carcinoma; typically affects adults, with female predominance and frequent cervical lymph node presentation. A differentiated follicular-cell carcinoma defined by characteristic nuclear features, often with papillary and/or infiltrative growth. True papillae with fibrovascular cores may be present, but a follicular or solid pattern can occur. Characteristic nuclei show enlargement, overlap, chromatin clearing, grooves, and intranuclear pseudoinclusions. Psammoma bodies may be present. Infiltrative growth, lymphatic invasion, and cervical lymph node metastases are common in classic PTC. Subtypes include classic, infiltrative follicular, tall cell, columnar cell, hobnail, diffuse sclerosing, solid/trabecular, and oncocytic patterns; assess subtype-specific thresholds and high-grade features. CK19, HBME-1, and galectin-3 are often positive but are not specific. BRAF VE1 immunostaining can support BRAF p.V600E when validated. Encapsulated, noninvasive follicular-patterned lesion meeting strict exclusion criteria. Encapsulated follicular lesion with unequivocal invasion. Lacks PTC-type nuclear features and is defined by capsular/vascular invasion. High-grade follicular-cell carcinoma Shows tumor necrosis and/or increased mitotic activity. BRAF p.V600E is common in classic and several aggressive PTC subtypes. RET or NTRK fusions occur in a subset. TERT promoter, TP53, or PIK3CA alterations may accompany progression. Usually occurs in older adults and presents as a thyroid mass; may be locally invasive or metastasize hematogenously. An oncocytic follicular-cell carcinoma defined by capsular and/or vascular invasion or metastasis. Predominantly oncocytic tumor cells with abundant granular eosinophilic cytoplasm. May be minimally invasive, encapsulated angioinvasive, or widely invasive. Capsular invasion requires full-thickness penetration; vascular invasion must be unequivocal and carefully documented. High-grade features include tumor necrosis and increased mitotic activity. Mitochondrial markers may highlight oncocytic differentiation but do not distinguish adenoma from carcinoma. Oncocytic adenoma No capsular or vascular invasion. Oncocytic hyperplasia in chronic thyroiditis Usually multifocal and not a discrete invasive neoplasm. Oncocytic PTC Shows characteristic PTC nuclear features and often BRAF-like molecular profile. Mitochondrial DNA mutations, often affecting complex I genes, and genome haploidization/uniparental disomy are characteristic molecular features. RAS-like or PTC-associated drivers may coexist depending on tumor phenotype. High-Grade Follicular Cell-Derived Non-Anaplastic Thyroid Carcinoma High-Grade Follicular-Cell Carcinomas Usually affects older adults and presents with an invasive thyroid mass; regional or distant metastases may be present. Includes poorly differentiated thyroid carcinoma and differentiated thyroid carcinoma with high-grade features; not anaplastic by definition. Usually occurs in older adults than conventional differentiated thyroid carcinoma. No strong sex-specific pattern is defining. Thyroid gland, often with extrathyroidal extension. Presents as an invasive thyroid mass; cervical nodes or distant metastases may be present. Poorly differentiated thyroid carcinoma often shows solid, trabecular, or insular growth, convoluted nuclei, and loss of conventional differentiation. High-grade features in differentiated carcinoma are tumor necrosis and/or increased mitotic activity. The Turin criteria for poorly differentiated carcinoma require solid/trabecular/insular growth, absence of conventional PTC nuclear features, and at least one of convoluted nuclei, mitotic activity, or tumor necrosis. Document mitotic count and necrosis; distinguish high-grade differentiated carcinoma from anaplastic carcinoma. Thyroglobulin, TTF-1, and PAX8 may be retained, often variably or focally, supporting follicular lineage. Ki-67 helps characterize proliferation but is not a standalone diagnostic criterion. Anaplastic thyroid carcinoma Shows overtly undifferentiated pleomorphic, spindle, or giant-cell morphology and usually loss of thyroid differentiation. Conventional papillary or follicular carcinoma Lacks tumor necrosis and/or high mitotic activity. Calcitonin and neuroendocrine markers support C-cell lineage. Anaplastic Thyroid Carcinoma Distinguish by the defining pattern: Undifferentiated, highly aggressive follicular-cell carcinoma; diagnosis of exclusion after excluding other high-grade malignancies. TERT promoter, TP53, PIK3CA, and PTEN alterations may accompany progression. RAS or BRAF p.V600E may reflect the underlying RAS-like or BRAF-like pathway. Typically presents in older adults with a rapidly enlarging neck mass, compressive symptoms, and often advanced local disease. Undifferentiated, highly aggressive follicular-cell carcinoma; diagnosis of exclusion after excluding other high-grade malignancies. Typically occurs in older adults, often over age 60. Slight male predominance compared with differentiated thyroid carcinoma. Rapidly enlarging thyroid mass with frequent invasion of adjacent neck structures. Rapid neck enlargement, dysphagia, dyspnea, hoarseness, pain, and airway compromise are common. Markedly pleomorphic, spindle-cell, giant-cell, or squamoid morphology; patterns may be mixed. Extensive tumor necrosis and brisk mitotic activity are typical. Infiltrative growth with destructive invasion is common. A differentiated thyroid carcinoma component or adjacent precursor may be present; extensively sample the tumor. Primary squamous cell carcinoma of thyroid is classified as a subtype of anaplastic thyroid carcinoma. Broad-spectrum cytokeratin is often positive, sometimes only focally. PAX8 may be retained in a subset; thyroglobulin and TTF-1 are commonly lost. BRAF VE1 immunostaining and/or molecular testing should be performed to identify actionable BRAF p.V600E. High-grade differentiated thyroid carcinoma Retains recognizable differentiated architecture and follicular lineage features. Primary thyroid lymphoma CD45 and lineage markers are positive; cytokeratin is usually negative. Metastatic carcinoma Clinical history and a directed IHC panel are essential. Primary thyroid angiosarcoma Demonstrates convincing endothelial differentiation with ERG/CD31 and vasoformative growth. Distinguish by the defining pattern: Includes poorly differentiated thyroid carcinoma and differentiated thyroid carcinoma with high-grade features; not anaplastic by definition. BRAF p.V600E occurs in a subset and is therapeutically actionable. TP53 and TERT promoter alterations are common progression events; RAS, PIK3CA, and PTEN alterations may occur. Medullary Thyroid Carcinoma C-Cell Neoplasms Can occur at any adult age; hereditary cases present younger and may be multifocal or bilateral. A calcitonin-producing neuroendocrine carcinoma derived from parafollicular C cells. Sporadic cases usually occur in adults; hereditary cases present at younger ages. No strong sex predilection overall. Thyroid C cells, often in the upper and middle thirds of the lobes. May present as a thyroid nodule or cervical lymphadenopathy; diarrhea and flushing can occur with advanced disease. Tumor may show nested, trabecular, spindle-cell, plasmacytoid, or plasmacytoid morphology. Amphophilic or granular cytoplasm and salt-and-pepper chromatin are typical. Amyloid derived from calcitonin may be present in the stroma. C-cell hyperplasia may accompany hereditary disease; assess multifocality and background thyroid. Calcitonin and CEA are usually positive. Synaptophysin, chromogranin, and INSM1 support neuroendocrine differentiation. Thyroglobulin is negative; TTF-1 may be positive. Usually keratin-negative and has S100/SOX10-positive sustentacular cells; calcitonin is generally negative. Hyalinizing trabecular tumor Thyroglobulin positive, calcitonin negative, and shows intratrabecular hyaline. Metastatic neuroendocrine tumor Correlate with clinical history and use site-directed markers; thyroid C-cell markers support MTC. Mixed medullary and follicular carcinoma Contains distinct calcitonin-positive and thyroglobulin-positive malignant components. RET mutations are common; RAS mutations occur in a subset. Germline RET testing is indicated to identify MEN2-associated disease. High-grade MTC criteria include mitotic count ≥5 per 2 mm², Ki-67 ≥5%, and/or tumor necrosis. Mixed Medullary and Follicular Cell-Derived Thyroid Carcinoma Mixed-Lineage Carcinomas Rare; clinical presentation resembles medullary thyroid carcinoma. A single thyroid neoplasm containing both malignant C-cell and follicular-cell components. Rare; reported across adulthood. No established sex predilection. Thyroid gland. Usually presents as a thyroid mass or cervical lymphadenopathy. Two morphologically and immunophenotypically distinct malignant components are present. The medullary component may show neuroendocrine architecture and amyloid. The follicular component shows follicular or papillary differentiation; demonstrate that it is malignant rather than entrapped benign follicles. Calcitonin, CEA, synaptophysin, and chromogranin label the medullary component. Thyroglobulin labels the follicular component. Use serial sections or double labeling when needed to confirm distinct components. Medullary thyroid carcinoma with entrapped follicles Entrapped follicles are benign and lack a separate malignant follicular component. Collision tumor Separate tumors are juxtaposed without convincing admixture or a unified neoplasm. Lacks a true malignant C-cell component. Molecular testing may demonstrate distinct or shared alterations; interpret by component when possible. Mucoepidermoid Carcinoma Salivary Gland-Type Carcinomas Rare thyroid or perithyroidal tumor; occurs in adults and may arise in association with chronic lymphocytic thyroiditis. A salivary gland-type carcinoma composed of mucous, epidermoid, and intermediate cells. Rare; usually reported in adults. Thyroid or immediately perithyroidal soft tissue. Presents as a thyroid mass; cervical lymph node metastasis may occur. Mixture of mucous cells, squamoid/epidermoid cells, and intermediate cells. Cystic and solid growth patterns may be present. Mucin-producing cells should be confirmed with mucin stains when morphology is subtle. Grade and extent of invasion vary; high-grade tumors may show necrosis and marked atypia. Pancytokeratin and p63/p40 support epithelial and squamoid differentiation. Mucicarmine or PAS-D highlights intracellular mucin. Thyroglobulin is generally negative in tumor cells. Sclerosing mucoepidermoid carcinoma with eosinophilia Prominent sclerosis and dense eosinophilic infiltrate are characteristic of the separate thyroid entity. Anaplastic thyroid carcinoma, squamoid subtype Usually lacks a convincing triphasic mucous/intermediate/epidermoid population. Metastatic salivary mucoepidermoid carcinoma Correlate with a salivary primary and imaging. Secretory Carcinoma Distinguish by the defining pattern: A salivary gland-type carcinoma with secretory differentiation, formerly termed mammary analogue secretory carcinoma. MAML2 rearrangement may be present and supports mucoepidermoid carcinoma in the appropriate setting. Rare primary thyroid or perithyroidal neoplasm; usually presents as a slowly enlarging mass in adults. A salivary gland-type carcinoma with secretory differentiation, formerly termed mammary analogue secretory carcinoma. Thyroid or perithyroidal soft tissue. Presents as a slowly enlarging thyroid-region mass; locoregional recurrence or distant metastasis can occur. Microcystic, tubular, papillary-cystic, or solid architecture. Cells have abundant eosinophilic or vacuolated cytoplasm and luminal secretions. Tumor may show infiltrative borders and lymph node or distant metastasis. S100 and mammaglobin are commonly positive. SOX10 and pan-TRK may be positive. Thyroglobulin is negative; use a panel to exclude thyroid follicular origin. Mucoepidermoid carcinoma Shows mucous, epidermoid, and intermediate cells rather than uniform secretory cells. Metastatic breast secretory carcinoma Clinical/radiologic correlation is required; the same fusion may occur. Follicular-derived thyroid carcinoma Usually expresses thyroglobulin, TTF-1, and PAX8. Distinguish by the defining pattern: A salivary gland-type carcinoma composed of mucous, epidermoid, and intermediate cells. ETV6::NTRK3 fusion is characteristic and diagnostically useful; confirm with molecular testing when needed. Sclerosing Mucoepidermoid Carcinoma with Eosinophilia Thyroid Tumors of Uncertain Histogenesis Usually an adult thyroid mass, often in a background of chronic lymphocytic thyroiditis; female predominance is reported. A distinct thyroid carcinoma with prominent sclerosis and eosinophil-rich inflammation; histogenesis remains uncertain. Usually occurs in adults. Female predominance is reported. Thyroid gland, often in a background of chronic lymphocytic thyroiditis. Presents as a thyroid mass, sometimes with cervical lymphadenopathy. Infiltrative nests, cords, and small groups of squamoid and mucin-producing cells in dense sclerotic stroma. Prominent eosinophils and lymphoplasmacytic inflammation are characteristic. Tumor may involve thyroid parenchyma and adjacent soft tissue; lymph node metastases can occur. Search for a conventional mucoepidermoid carcinoma component but do not assume identical histogenesis. Pancytokeratin and p63/p40 may highlight epithelial/squamoid cells. Mucicarmine highlights mucin-producing cells. Lacks the characteristic dense sclerosis and eosinophil-rich inflammatory background. Usually shows marked pleomorphism, brisk mitoses, and extensive necrosis. Riedel thyroiditis Fibrosing inflammatory lesion lacks an infiltrative malignant epithelial population. No defining recurrent molecular alteration is established. Cribriform-Morular Thyroid Carcinoma Distinctive Thyroid Carcinomas Often affects young women; may be multifocal and can be associated with familial adenomatous polyposis. A distinctive thyroid carcinoma with cribriform and morular architecture and WNT pathway activation. Often occurs in young adults. Marked female predominance. Usually intrathyroidal; may be multifocal. Presents as a thyroid nodule; may be the first clue to familial adenomatous polyposis. Cribriform, solid, trabecular, and morular patterns may coexist. Tumor cells often have elongated nuclei, nuclear grooves, and squamoid morules. Colloid is usually scant or absent. Assess for multifocality and consider clinical evaluation for FAP, particularly in young patients. Nuclear and cytoplasmic beta-catenin staining supports WNT pathway activation. PAX8 may be positive; thyroglobulin and TTF-1 are often absent or limited. CD10 and estrogen receptor may be positive in morules. PTC shows follicular differentiation and characteristic papillary architecture; CMTC has morules and nuclear beta-catenin. Metastatic colorectal carcinoma Clinical history and an IHC panel distinguish; CMTC is a primary thyroid tumor with characteristic morular architecture. Poorly differentiated thyroid carcinoma Usually lacks the distinctive cribriform-morular pattern and nuclear beta-catenin profile. CTNNB1 mutations or APC pathway alterations activate WNT signaling. Germline APC alteration should be considered; evaluate for familial adenomatous polyposis. Thymoma of the Thyroid Intrathyroidal Thymic Neoplasms Rare; usually an adult thyroid mass, sometimes associated with ectopic thymic tissue. An intrathyroidal thymic epithelial neoplasm resembling conventional thymoma. Intrathyroidal ectopic thymic tissue. Presents as a slowly enlarging thyroid mass. Lobulated tumor with fibrous septa and a lymphocyte-rich background. Spindle or oval epithelial cells form a network among immature T lymphocytes. Perivascular spaces and medullary differentiation may be present. Cytokeratin highlights the epithelial network. Immature T cells express TdT and may express CD1a. PAX8 (polyclonal) may be positive in thymic epithelial cells; thyroglobulin is negative. Intrathyroidal thymic carcinoma Shows overt cytologic atypia, destructive invasion, and carcinoma-like epithelial growth. Spindle epithelial tumor with thymus-like elements Often has spindle epithelial and glandular/cystic elements with a different architecture. Lymphoma Lymphoid cells are the neoplastic population and lack a keratin-positive epithelial network. Spindle Epithelial Tumor with Thymus-Like Elements (SETTLE) Distinguish by the defining pattern: A rare biphasic thymic-like tumor with delayed metastatic potential. Intrathyroidal Thymic Carcinoma Distinguish by the defining pattern: A thymic epithelial carcinoma arising within the thyroid, distinct from anaplastic thyroid carcinoma. No defining molecular test is required. Usually affects children, adolescents, or young adults and presents as a slowly enlarging thyroid mass. A rare biphasic thymic-like tumor with delayed metastatic potential. Usually occurs in adults, often middle-aged. Intrathyroidal thymic epithelial rests, often in the lower thyroid region. Presents as a thyroid mass, sometimes with cervical lymphadenopathy or local invasion. Biphasic architecture with spindle-cell and glandular or cystic epithelial components. Spindle cells are bland to mildly atypical and may form fascicles. Glandular structures are lined by epithelial cells; mucin may be present. Long-term follow-up is important because metastases may occur years after diagnosis. Cytokeratin and EMA highlight epithelial components. Vimentin may label spindle cells. Thyroglobulin and calcitonin are negative. Thymoma Usually lymphocyte-rich with a network of thymic epithelial cells; SETTLE is spindle-cell predominant and biphasic. Shows overt malignant cytology and destructive invasion. Synovial sarcoma May show spindle and glandular components; use TLE1 and SS18 rearrangement testing when indicated. Distinguish by the defining pattern: An intrathyroidal thymic epithelial neoplasm resembling conventional thymoma. No single molecular alteration is established; SS18 rearrangement testing can help exclude synovial sarcoma. Usually occurs in adults as a thyroid mass, often with cervical lymphadenopathy. A thymic epithelial carcinoma arising within the thyroid, distinct from anaplastic thyroid carcinoma. Infiltrative nests, cords, or sheets of squamoid epithelial cells in fibrous or lymphocyte-rich stroma. Cytologic atypia and mitotic activity support carcinoma; keratinization may be present. Assess extrathyroidal extension, vascular invasion, and cervical lymph nodes. Pancytokeratin and p63/p40 support epithelial/squamoid differentiation. CD5 and CD117 may support thymic differentiation in the appropriate morphology. Thyroglobulin is negative; PAX8 interpretation depends on antibody clone. Often shows highly pleomorphic undifferentiated morphology and may retain PAX8; clinical context and thymic markers help. Lacks overt malignant cytology and destructive invasive growth. Metastatic squamous cell carcinoma Exclude a head and neck or lung primary clinically and radiologically. No defining molecular alteration is required; molecular testing is usually exclusionary. Thyroblastoma Embryonal Thyroid Neoplasms Extremely rare; may occur in children or adults and presents as a rapidly enlarging thyroid mass. A high-grade embryonal neoplasm with primitive follicular, small-cell, and mesenchymal components. Median age is approximately 43 years; reported cases range from adolescence to older adulthood. Marked female predominance has been reported. One or both thyroid lobes, often with extension into perithyroidal soft tissue. Presents as a rapidly enlarging mid-cervical thyroid mass. Primitive thyroid epithelium, a primitive small-cell/blastemal component, and mesenchymal stroma are present. Conventional thyroid carcinoma and conventional germ cell tumor components are absent. Primitive thyroid follicles express TTF-1 and PAX8, with focal thyroglobulin expression. The primitive small-cell component is commonly SALL4 positive but OCT3/4 and PLAP negative. Rhabdomyoblastic differentiation may be demonstrated by desmin and myogenin in the primitive small-cell or stromal components. Triphasic or mixed morphology includes primitive follicular structures, small undifferentiated cells, and mesenchymal stroma. High-grade cytology, brisk mitotic activity, and necrosis are common. Extensive sampling is required to identify the heterogeneous components. Distinguish from teratoma and anaplastic thyroid carcinoma. Thyroglobulin and TTF-1 may highlight primitive follicular components. Cytokeratin labels epithelial elements; mesenchymal markers label stromal components. No single immunophenotype is specific; interpret the panel by component. Usually lacks the organized embryonal mixture of primitive follicular, small-cell, and mesenchymal elements. Teratoma Shows mature or immature derivatives of multiple germ layers; thyroblastoma has characteristic primitive thyroid-type components. SETTLE Usually a more uniform spindle and glandular biphasic tumor with a different clinical course. DICER1 alterations are characteristic; consider germline DICER1 syndrome evaluation. All PathologyGPS · Endocrine System Diagnostic Reference Thyroid Tumors Home A practical diagnostic reference to developmental lesions, follicular-cell neoplasms, C-cell tumors, distinctive thyroid carcinomas, and thymic and salivary gland-type neoplasms involving the thyroid. Emphasis is placed on defining morphology, invasion, immunophenotype, and diagnostically useful molecular findings. Diagnostic Approach: Start Here 1. Establish lineage Separate follicular-cell, C-cell, thymic, salivary gland-type, embryonal, and metastatic lesions. Use thyroglobulin, TTF-1, PAX8, calcitonin, and morphology as a focused panel. 2. For follicular-patterned tumors The capsule and tumor–thyroid interface are decisive. Distinguish benign adenoma, NIFTP, tumors of uncertain malignant potential, and carcinoma by strict assessment of invasion. 3. Recognize papillary nuclear features Nuclear enlargement, chromatin clearing, grooves, and pseudoinclusions support PTC; interpret them with architecture and invasion. 4. Assess grade separately from differentiation Record mitotic activity and tumor necrosis. High-grade differentiated carcinoma and poorly differentiated carcinoma are distinct from anaplastic carcinoma. 5. Identify C-cell differentiation Calcitonin, CEA, and neuroendocrine markers support medullary carcinoma. Evaluate for hereditary RET-associated disease. 6. Use molecular tests to answer a question BRAF, RAS, RET/NTRK fusions, TERT, DICER1, APC/CTNNB1, and ETV6::NTRK3 can be diagnostically or therapeutically relevant in selected entities. Critical principle: In follicular-patterned lesions, malignancy is established by invasion or metastasis—not by cytologic atypia or a positive immunostain alone. title: Epithelial Tumors
content: use client Serous adenofibroma Benign serous tumors Benign biphasic tumor composed of fibromatous stroma and bland tubal-type epithelium. Fallopian tube; many are microscopic, with the fimbria a common site. Admixed epithelial and mesenchymal components; may be cystic. Dense fibromatous stroma may be nodular or papillary. Papillae or cystic spaces are lined by bland tubal-type epithelium containing secretory and ciliated cells. No significant epithelial atypia or destructive stromal invasion. The supplied WHO text does not specify a required IHC panel. Morphology is generally sufficient when the epithelial lining is bland and the stroma is fibromatous. Serous papilloma: delicate branching fibrovascular papillae predominate, without the prominent fibromatous stromal component. STIC: malignant cytology and aberrant p53; Ki-67 is increased in the atypical focus. HGSC: destructive stromal invasion and high-grade malignant morphology. Bland tubal-type epithelium. Fibromatous stromal component in a benign biphasic tumor. No destructive stromal invasion. The distinction from serous papilloma may show interobserver variation and has no clinical significance in the source. Most lesions are small; many are microscopic. Serous papilloma Benign papillary proliferation lined by bland tubal-type epithelium. Tubal mucosa; may be loosely attached and project into the lumen. Delicate, branching fibrovascular stalks. Papillae lined by bland cuboidal to columnar epithelial cells. No significant cytologic atypia or destructive invasion. May appear as friable intraluminal tissue. The WHO source does not identify a diagnostic IHC panel. Use morphology and careful assessment for atypia and invasion. Serous adenofibroma: has a more conspicuous fibromatous stromal component; distinction is not clinically significant. STIC: malignant cytology with aberrant p53; Ki-67 is generally increased in the atypical focus. Exophytic STIC versus expansile-type HGSC without invasion: outcome-based criteria are not established in the source. Delicate papillary proliferation attached to tubal mucosa. Bland tubal-type epithelial lining. Serous tubal intraepithelial carcinoma (STIC) Malignant epithelial tumors Cytologically malignant serous epithelial proliferation confined to tubal mucosa, without stromal invasion. Tubal mucosa, preferentially the fimbria; usually solitary and unilateral, but may be multifocal or bilateral. Usually microscopic and not grossly visible; reported size 0.1–8 mm. Variable combination of epithelial stratification/mucosal thickening, loss of polarity, loss of cilia, nuclear enlargement, increased N:C ratio, hyperchromasia, pleomorphism, irregular nuclear membranes, prominent nucleoli, nuclear molding, mitoses, and apoptotic bodies. Cellular detachment/exfoliation and an irregular mucosal surface may occur. Some lesions are attenuated or flat and subtle at low magnification; rare pagetoid growth may intermingle with residual ciliated cells. The defining distinction from invasive HGSC is absence of stromal invasion. p53: aberrant/mutation-type expression is essential in the WHO criteria. Patterns include diffuse strong overexpression or complete absence (null pattern), interpreted with internal controls. Ki-67: >10% in the atypical focus supports STIC and improves reproducibility; score only the atypical epithelium. The source cites STIC Consortium consensus that p53 IHC is mandatory; Ki-67 is useful but not mandatory. In pagetoid lesions, do not score admixed non-atypical ciliated cells. p53 signature: aberrant p53 in morphologically bland epithelium with low proliferation (typically Ki-67 <10%); no established clinical significance and not reportable. STIL: atypia that does not meet reproducible criteria for STIC, such as non-aberrant p53 or low Ki-67; an intermediate descriptive category. Invasive HGSC: stromal invasion in the tubal wall in the usual occult-tumor setting. Secondary involvement by endometrial serous carcinoma, endometrioid carcinoma, endocervical adenocarcinoma, or non-gynecologic malignancy must be considered in context. Severely atypical serous-type epithelium in tubal mucosa. Aberrant p53 immunohistochemical expression. No stromal invasion. Perform p53/Ki-67 only in morphologically atypical foci; do not use them as screening stains on entirely unremarkable mucosa. For Ki-67 near 10%, compare the atypical focus with background epithelium. A p53 signature alone is not STIC. High-grade serous carcinoma (HGSC) Invasive high-grade malignant epithelial neoplasm with serous differentiation arising in the fallopian tube. Fallopian tube, commonly fimbria; may coexist with extensive ovarian and/or peritoneal disease. Morphology is the same as ovarian HGSC: high-grade serous carcinoma with marked nuclear atypia and complex architecture. In occult early disease, tumor is often localized to fimbria and distinguished from STIC by invasion into submucosal/tubal wall stroma. Grossly evident disease may replace the tube or be confined to its lumen; microscopic tubal disease may coexist with much larger ovarian/peritoneal tumor. Rarely, malignant tubal epithelium has an exophytic papillary pattern without invasion; criteria separating this from exophytic STIC are not established. The source states that histology and IHC are identical to ovarian HGSC. Typical supportive profile in practice: aberrant p53, often diffuse WT1, PAX8 and epithelial marker expression; interpret as a profile, not a site-of-origin test. The supplied excerpt does not provide a complete required panel; no single stain establishes tubal origin. STIC: intraepithelial mucosal lesion without stromal invasion; occult invasive HGSC invades tubal wall stroma. Ovarian/primary peritoneal HGSC: if tube is involved by STIC and/or HGSC in multiorgan extrauterine disease, consensus assigns tubal origin regardless of relative tumor size. Uterine serous carcinoma: may secondarily involve tube and simulate STIC/tubal HGSC; compare morphology, distribution, clinical findings, and selected molecular profiles. Metastatic non-gynecologic carcinoma: exclude with history, morphology, and site-directed IHC. High-grade carcinoma with serous differentiation growing in the fallopian tube. For occult tubal HGSC, demonstrate stromal invasion to distinguish from STIC. Assess the complete tubo-ovarian/peritoneal specimen and clinical history. SEE-FIM is advised in risk-reducing salpingectomies and cases of extrauterine HGSC. Tubal STIC and/or HGSC establishes tubal origin by consensus in multiorgan extrauterine HGSC, regardless of relative tumor size. Molecular comparison may help clarify clonal relationships in selected synchronous tubal, uterine serous, or disseminated HGSC cases. Endometrioid carcinoma Rare primary tubal carcinoma showing endometrioid differentiation. Usually distal two-thirds of tube; may present as a fimbrial mass or diffuse tubal dilatation. Morphology resembles endometrioid carcinoma of endometrium or ovary, including closely packed endometrioid glands meeting carcinoma criteria. May be associated with endometriosis, sometimes as an endometrioid polyp. Rare examples show prominent spindle-cell morphology, squamous-like differentiation, or osseous metaplasia. The source states that grading criteria and prognostic role for FIGO/Silverberg grading in primary tubal endometrioid carcinoma have not been studied. Usually WT1-negative. Usually p53 wild-type. The source does not specify a complete required panel. ER/PR and PAX8 may be used as supportive Müllerian/endometrioid markers in practice; assess MMR as clinically appropriate. These do not establish tubal origin. Secondary endometrial endometrioid carcinoma: exclude direct extension or metastasis from synchronous/prior endometrial primary. Ovarian endometrioid carcinoma: evaluate distribution and relationship to ovary; a tubal mural-centered lesion supports but does not alone prove tubal origin. HGSC: usually high-grade serous morphology, aberrant p53, and often diffuse WT1; tubal endometrioid carcinoma is usually WT1-negative and p53 wild-type. Endometriosis-associated atypia: establish unequivocal carcinoma architecture and/or invasion rather than relying on atypia alone. Tubal mural proliferation of closely packed endometrioid glands meeting criteria for endometrioid carcinoma in endometrium/ovary. Exclude secondary involvement by endometrial or ovarian carcinoma. Lack of diffuse strong WT1 and usually wild-type p53 are desirable supportive findings. All entities STIC Aberrant / mutation-type Usually >10% in atypical focus Severe atypia; mucosal; no invasion p53 signature Aberrant Low, typically <10% Bland epithelium; not reportable STIL May be non-aberrant/equivocal Often below STIC threshold Atypia insufficient for definitive STIC Tubal HGSC Usually aberrant High Invasive high-grade serous carcinoma Tubal endometrioid carcinoma Usually wild-type Not specified Usually WT1-negative PathologyGPS · Female Genital Tract Fallopian Tube Epithelial Tumors A morphology-centered diagnostic guide to benign serous tumors, STIC, high-grade serous carcinoma, and endometrioid carcinoma—with emphasis on precursor recognition, primary-site assignment, SEE-FIM sampling, and practical immunohistochemistry. WHO-based classification Histology + IHC Differential diagnosis SEE-FIM workflow Classification at a glance The supplied WHO chapter identifies HGSC as the principal malignant tumor of the tube. Endometrioid carcinoma is rare. STIC is the recognized precursor of tubal HGSC and may coexist with ovarian/peritoneal HGSC even without an invasive tubal mass. Core diagnostic principles In risk-reducing salpingectomy and extrauterine HGSC, examine the fimbria carefully using SEE-FIM. Diagnose STIC by integrating atypical morphology with aberrant p53; Ki-67 improves reproducibility but does not replace morphology. Distinguish STIC from occult invasive HGSC by looking for stromal invasion. When the tube is involved by STIC and/or HGSC in multiorgan extrauterine disease, consensus assigns the primary site to the tube regardless of relative tumor size. Consider secondary involvement by endometrial serous/endometrioid carcinoma, endocervical adenocarcinoma, and non-gynecologic malignancy. Diagnostic GPS: specimen-to-diagnosis workflow 1 · Clinical context Risk-reducing salpingectomy, adnexal mass, known tubo-ovarian/peritoneal HGSC, or incidental tubal finding. 2 · SEE-FIM sampling Submit fimbria with longitudinal sections and extensively sample the remaining tube; document laterality and gross findings. 3 · Morphology first Assess epithelial atypia, mucosal stratification, papillary growth, and—critically—stromal invasion. 4 · Targeted IHC For atypical mucosal foci use p53 and Ki-67. For invasive carcinoma or suspected metastasis, select a differential-directed panel. Entity reference Search by entity, morphology, immunophenotype, or differential diagnosis. Search histology, IHC, differential… Collapse − Expand + Localization Histopathology Essential diagnostic criteria Immunohistochemistry Key differential diagnoses Diagnostic pearls No matching entities. Try a broader search term. STIC, p53 signature, and STIL: practical comparison Interpret p53 and Ki-67 in the morphologically atypical epithelial focus—not across the entire tubal mucosa. Lesion p53 Ki-67 Morphologic interpretation STIL is a descriptive intermediate category. A p53 signature is not a reportable precursor diagnosis in the supplied WHO text. SEE-FIM: sampling and examination checklist Identify and separately label right and left fallopian tubes. Amputate the fimbria and section it longitudinally to maximize mucosal evaluation. Serially section the remaining tube transversely at short intervals and submit according to the validated laboratory protocol and clinical indication. Thoroughly examine fimbria in risk-reducing specimens even when grossly unremarkable; STIC is typically microscopic. In extrauterine HGSC, extensively examine tubes to identify STIC or occult invasive tubal HGSC that may establish the primary site. For an atypical focus, obtain deeper levels as needed and perform targeted p53 and Ki-67. Assigning the primary site in extrauterine HGSC Consensus rule If the tube is involved by STIC and/or HGSC, assign the primary origin to the fallopian tube in multiorgan extrauterine HGSC, regardless of relative tumor size in tube, ovary, or peritoneum. Potential mimics include secondary involvement by endometrial serous or endometrioid carcinoma, primary endocervical adenocarcinoma, and non-gynecologic malignancies. In selected difficult cases, molecular comparison may help clarify clonal relationships. Reporting checklist Specify histologic diagnosis and, for carcinoma, extent/distribution. For STIC, document mucosal/fimbrial location and p53 result; include Ki-67 when performed and informative. For invasive HGSC, document tubal wall stromal invasion and relationship to fimbria, ovary, and peritoneum. In multiorgan HGSC, state rationale for assigning tubal primary when STIC and/or tubal HGSC is identified. For endometrioid carcinoma, document tubal mural-centered lesion and evaluation for endometrial/ovarian primary. Record SEE-FIM processing when applicable and note sampling limitations. Scope and source note: Based on the supplied WHO chapter, “Tumours of the fallopian tube.” The excerpt details serous adenofibroma/papilloma, STIC, HGSC, and endometrioid carcinoma. Adenomatoid tumor and leiomyoma are mentioned in the introduction but detailed criteria were not included, so they are not expanded here. Practical IHC context beyond the excerpt is identified as supportive and not site-defining. Educational reference for professional use. Interpret IHC with morphology, clinical history, imaging, and the complete specimen. Follow current local protocols and staging standards.

title: Genetic Tumor Syndromes
content: use client BRCA1-/BRCA2-related cancer predisposition BRCA1 / BRCA2 Autosomal dominant; tumorigenesis generally follows a two-hit model Breast, fallopian tube, ovary, and peritoneum; additional reported sites include prostate, pancreas, and endometrium High-grade serous carcinoma (HGSC), often with a fallopian-tube origin; serous tubal intraepithelial carcinoma (STIC) may be identified in risk-reducing salpingo-oophorectomy specimens. The predominant female genital tract malignancy is HGSC of tubo-ovarian or peritoneal origin. Carcinosarcoma is also associated. Endometrioid, clear cell, and undifferentiated carcinomas have been reported, but the relationship to biallelic BRCA inactivation is less firmly documented. With SEE-FIM examination, localized STIC or STIC with limited invasion/spread is found in approximately 5–10% of risk-reducing salpingo-oophorectomy specimens. The SET (solid, endometrial-like, transitional) architectural pattern, tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes, stromal-infiltrating lymphocytes, and necrosis may correlate variably with homologous recombination deficiency (HRD) or BRCA status. These features are not sufficiently reliable to replace molecular testing. Confirm a pathogenic constitutional (germline) BRCA1 or BRCA2 variant; this is the essential syndrome-level criterion. When evaluating risk-reducing specimens, use the SEE-FIM protocol to thoroughly examine the fimbria and identify occult STIC or early invasive carcinoma. Do not infer germline status from HGSC morphology or an HRD phenotype alone. Tumor testing and constitutional testing answer different questions. Tumor HRD assays may incorporate genomic scar measures such as loss of heterozygosity, telomeric allelic imbalance, and large-scale transitions; assay methods and thresholds vary. SET morphology and lymphocyte-rich stroma are supportive associations, not diagnostic surrogates for a BRCA pathogenic variant. A tumor BRCA alteration does not by itself establish an inherited syndrome. The source describes increased endometrial carcinoma risk in some studies, but the association is less settled than the tubo-ovarian/breast association. The source estimates tubo-ovarian cancer risk at 40–60% for BRCA1 and 11–35% for BRCA2 carriers, with average diagnosis ages around 50–53 and 55–58 years, respectively. Estimates vary by variant and population. DNA repair Lynch syndrome MLH1 / MSH2 / MSH6 / PMS2; also EPCAM-associated MSH2 silencing Autosomal dominant Endometrium most commonly, followed by ovary; rare extraovarian endometriosis-associated tumors. Other associated sites include colorectum and multiple gastrointestinal, urinary tract, skin, and brain sites. Endometrial carcinoma is often the sentinel cancer. Gynecologic tumors are most often endometrioid carcinomas, but clear cell, mixed, undifferentiated/dedifferentiated, and carcinosarcoma histotypes are also reported. Most gynecologic cancers in Lynch syndrome are endometrial or ovarian endometrioid carcinomas. dMMR endometrial carcinomas may show tumor heterogeneity, morphologic ambiguity, and increased tumor-infiltrating or peritumoral lymphocytes. These findings are nonspecific. The histologic spectrum is broad; no single morphology establishes Lynch syndrome. Perform MMR immunohistochemistry (MLH1, PMS2, MSH2, and MSH6) as a screening approach where indicated. Interpret loss patterns in the context of the MMR heterodimers: MLH1/PMS2 and MSH2/MSH6. MLH1/PMS2 loss should prompt MLH1 promoter hypermethylation testing. Methylation is usually associated with a sporadic mechanism, although rare co-occurrence with Lynch syndrome has been reported. If MLH1 methylation is absent, or if MSH2/MSH6, isolated MSH6, or isolated PMS2 loss is present, proceed to constitutional testing directed by the pattern or a broader germline panel. MSI testing is an alternative/adjunct, but the source notes reduced sensitivity in endometrial cancers compared with colorectal cancers, particularly for MSH6-associated disease. Abnormal tumor MMR IHC or MSI does not distinguish a germline syndrome from sporadic MLH1 methylation or biallelic somatic alterations. Somatic sequencing may clarify selected germline-negative cases. MMR protein loss is not synonymous with Lynch syndrome; most dMMR endometrial carcinomas are sporadic. Retained IHC does not absolutely exclude a nonfunctional missense-mutant protein because antigenicity may be preserved. A negative germline result with tumor dMMR may reflect double-somatic events or, in some cases, another molecular mechanism. The source gives cumulative endometrial cancer risks of approximately 40–60% and ovarian cancer risks of 9–17%, with substantial gene-dependent variation; MSH6 carriers have the highest incidence in the cited data. Peutz–Jeghers syndrome STK11 (LKB1) Cervix, ovary, and broad ligament; synchronous mucinous metaplasia/neoplasia may involve multiple genital tract sites Gastric-type cervical adenocarcinoma, sex cord tumor with annular tubules (SCTAT), STK11 adnexal tumor, and Sertoli cell tumor. Gastric-type cervical adenocarcinoma ranges from well-differentiated/minimal-deviation morphology to overtly malignant tumors. The defining cells have abundant apical pale eosinophilic or clear cytoplasm and distinct cell borders. Lobular endocervical glandular hyperplasia (LEGH), including atypical forms, occurs in PJS and is considered a precursor to gastric-type cervical adenocarcinoma. Syndromic SCTATs are typically bilateral and multifocal and may contain microcalcifications, unlike most non-syndromic tumors. STK11 adnexal tumors commonly show interanastomosing cords and trabeculae in a myxoid matrix. Sertoli cell tumors may be oxyphilic or lipid-rich. Gastric-type mucinous lesions may occur synchronously at multiple genital tract sites. Recognize the combination of mucocutaneous pigmentation and gastrointestinal polyposis with the characteristic gynecologic tumor spectrum. Demonstrate a germline STK11 pathogenic variant by sequencing when clinically indicated; the source states that the essential syndrome criterion is fulfillment of clinical PJS diagnostic criteria. For a cervical glandular lesion, evaluate the gastric phenotype and distinguish LEGH/atypical LEGH from invasive gastric-type adenocarcinoma using the full morphologic context. In an ovarian/broad-ligament mass, consider SCTAT, STK11 adnexal tumor, and Sertoli cell tumor in the differential. Gastric-type cervical adenocarcinoma is HPV-independent; do not assume an HPV-associated pathway. Syndromic SCTATs are often bilateral/multifocal, but morphology alone does not establish PJS. The source describes aggressive behavior for gastric-type cervical adenocarcinoma and STK11 adnexal tumor, but generally excellent prognosis for SCTAT. The source reports a cumulative risk of approximately 10% for gastric-type cervical adenocarcinoma and 21% for ovarian tumors; estimates are drawn from cited cohorts. Tumor suppressor DICER1-related tumor predisposition syndrome DICER1 Autosomal dominant; de novo variants and somatic mosaicism are also described Ovary and uterine cervix Sertoli–Leydig cell tumor (SLCT), often moderately/poorly differentiated or retiform, and cervical embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma (ERMS), sometimes with fetal-type cartilage. DICER1-associated SLCTs may be moderately to poorly differentiated or retiform and may contain heterologous elements, including mucinous epithelium, fetal-type cartilage, and/or skeletal muscle. Embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma of the female genital tract most often arises in the cervix. Fetal-type cartilage is a highly characteristic clue to DICER1 association. These tumors are histologically indistinguishable from their non-syndromic counterparts; the syndrome is not diagnosed by morphology alone. Gynandroblastoma is another rare reported gynecologic tumor in DICER1 syndrome. In a young patient with SLCT—especially moderately/poorly differentiated, retiform, or heterologous—or cervical ERMS with fetal-type cartilage, consider DICER1 predisposition. Confirm a constitutional DICER1 pathogenic variant. Tumor sequencing may identify a second somatic missense event, typically affecting the RNase IIIb domain. Interpret the characteristic tumor phenotype as a trigger for genetic evaluation, not as proof of a germline variant. DICER1-associated and sporadic counterparts are morphologically indistinguishable. The characteristic RNase IIIb second hit is a tumor-pathogenesis feature; it does not replace germline confirmation. The source describes generally favorable outcomes for SLCT and genital tract ERMS, while noting that selected SLCT features may confer adverse risk. The source reports higher neoplasm incidence in female carriers than male carriers in one cohort, with gynecologic neoplasms predominating in older female patients; overall incidence remains incompletely defined. RNA processing Hereditary leiomyomatosis and renal cell carcinoma syndrome FH (fumarate hydratase) Autosomal dominant; incomplete penetrance and no established genotype–phenotype correlation Cutaneous and uterine leiomyomas; renal cell carcinoma, predominantly renal cortex FH-deficient uterine leiomyoma with distinctive vascular/stromal patterns and cytologic features; rare FH-deficient STUMP or leiomyosarcoma has been described. Uterine leiomyomas may show staghorn vessels, alveolar-pattern edema, and ovoid smooth muscle cells arranged in chains rather than intersecting fascicles. Tumor cells may have prominent eosinophilic nucleoli with perinucleolar halos and eosinophilic cytoplasmic globules. Bizarre nuclei are common. These features may occur in conventional, cellular, and leiomyoma-with-bizarre-nuclei patterns. Rare FH-deficient STUMP and leiomyosarcoma have been reported, but the source notes that these were not confirmed in carriers with germline FH variants. Use FH immunohistochemistry and 2SC immunohistochemistry when morphology raises suspicion for FH deficiency. Loss of FH staining is specific for FH deficiency but has limited sensitivity; some FH-deficient tumors retain FH expression, including with missense variants. Positive 2SC staining is highly sensitive and specific for FH deficiency and may identify cases with retained FH protein. FH/2SC IHC establishes a deficient tumor phenotype, not hereditary syndrome status. Confirm a germline FH pathogenic variant or deletion for definitive HLRCC diagnosis. Most FH-deficient uterine leiomyomas are caused by sporadic genetic alterations; FH deficiency alone does not prove HLRCC. Retained FH IHC does not exclude FH deficiency; interpret with 2SC and morphology. Atypia or bizarre nuclei in an FH-deficient leiomyoma should not automatically be equated with leiomyosarcoma. Renal carcinomas arising in HLRCC are aggressive. Smooth muscle tumors may be cytologically atypical, but biologically malignant behavior is rarely reported in the source. Metabolic enzyme Li–Fraumeni syndrome TP53 Autosomal dominant; de novo pathogenic variants are reported Broad tumor spectrum; female genital tract involvement is uncommon. Core sites include breast, soft tissue, bone, brain, and adrenal cortex. No single gynecologic histotype is characteristic. Reported tumors include endometrioid and serous endometrial carcinomas, ovarian small cell carcinoma of hypercalcemic type, yolk sac tumor, and fallopian tube/peritoneal carcinomas. Gynecologic tumors are rare and histologically diverse; available evidence is largely from larger tumor-spectrum studies and case reports. Reported lesions include endometrioid endometrial adenocarcinoma, uterine serous carcinoma, mixed endometrioid/serous carcinoma, ovarian small cell carcinoma of hypercalcemic type, yolk sac tumor, undifferentiated and endometrioid carcinomas of fallopian tube/peritoneum, and cervical pleomorphic liposarcoma. Incidental bilateral STIC and distal tubal p53 signatures have been reported, but the natural history and implications in LFS are uncertain. Consider TP53 germline evaluation in the context of early-onset cancers, multiple primary tumors, and a suggestive personal/family history; the source references Chompret and NCCN testing frameworks. Distinguish pathogenic germline variants from somatic variants, polymorphisms, variants of uncertain significance, and clonal hematopoiesis. A pathogenic TP53 variant and/or an appropriate clinical history are the essential criteria stated in the source. Because of the increased risk of radiation-induced secondary malignancies, diagnostic and therapeutic radiation exposure should be minimized or avoided when clinically appropriate, balancing cancer-control needs. A gynecologic malignancy alone does not establish LFS; the syndrome is defined by germline TP53 status and/or appropriate clinical criteria. Tumor-only TP53 sequencing cannot establish constitutional status. The source notes that some individuals meeting clinical criteria may lack a detectable TP53 pathogenic variant. Gynecologic malignancies account for a small fraction of LFS-associated tumors. The source reports earlier median age for ovarian cancer in LFS than sporadic cases, but emphasizes that site-specific histology data are sparse. Genome surveillance Carney complex PRKAR1A-related; listed in the source overview, without a detailed syndrome section in the supplied excerpt. PTEN hamartoma tumor syndrome (Cowden syndrome) PTEN-related; listed in the source overview, without detailed gynecologic pathology criteria in the supplied excerpt. Ataxia-telangiectasia syndrome Listed in the source overview; specific gynecologic tumor details are not provided in the supplied excerpt. Ovarian dysgenesis Listed in the source overview; specific gene/pathology details are not provided in the supplied excerpt. von Hippel–Lindau syndrome VHL-related; listed in the source overview, without a detailed syndrome section in the supplied excerpt. 1. Recognize the tumor phenotype Start with the actual neoplasm and its morphology. Examples include tubo-ovarian HGSC/STIC, endometrioid carcinoma with dMMR, gastric-type cervical adenocarcinoma, bilateral/multifocal SCTAT, cervical ERMS with fetal-type cartilage, FH-deficient leiomyoma, or an unusually early/multiple primary cancer pattern. 2. Ask whether the pattern is syndrome-enriched Integrate age, tumor site, multiplicity, bilateral disease, precursor lesions, associated non-gynecologic tumors, and personal/family history. No single morphologic feature is sufficient for most syndromes. 3. Select the tumor-level ancillary test Use the test matched to the phenotype: MMR IHC ± MLH1 promoter methylation/MSI; FH and 2SC IHC; or appropriate tumor sequencing. For risk-reducing tubes, apply SEE-FIM. 4. Separate tumor phenotype from inherited status Abnormal tumor IHC, HRD, or a tumor-only variant may be somatic. A constitutional/germline pathogenic variant (or the specific clinical criteria stated for PJS/LFS) is required to establish the inherited syndrome. 5. Recommend genetics correlation Communicate the histologic clue and tumor test result, and recommend genetic counseling/constitutional testing when indicated. Do not label a patient as having a hereditary syndrome based only on tumor morphology or IHC. teal amber border-amber-200 violet border-violet-200 border-teal-200 bg-amber-500 bg-violet-500 bg-teal-600 All PathologyGPS / Female genital tract Genetic tumor syndromes Genetic Tumor Syndromes of the Female Genital Tract A morphology-led diagnostic guide to hereditary cancer predisposition: recognize syndrome-associated tumor patterns, choose the appropriate tumor-level tests, and distinguish somatic findings from constitutional disease. Diagnostic principle A tumor phenotype can raise suspicion. Germline testing establishes inherited predisposition. Most syndromes follow a two-hit tumor-suppressor model, but the diagnostic evidence required differs by syndrome. Diagnostic GPS: from morphology to hereditary diagnosis Core diagnostic distinction Tumor-level finding MMR protein loss, HRD, FH loss/2SC positivity, or a tumor sequence variant identifies a pathway or tumor phenotype. It does not, by itself, prove inherited disease. Constitutional finding A pathogenic germline variant (or the syndrome-specific clinical criteria stated in the source) establishes the hereditary predisposition diagnosis. Practical rule: report the tumor finding precisely, then recommend genetic counseling/testing when indicated. Avoid diagnosing a hereditary syndrome from morphology or tumor IHC alone. Try another gene, tumor type, or site. Additional syndromes listed in the source overview The supplied source names the following syndromes as having established gynecologic cancer associations, but the excerpt does not provide detailed entity-level diagnostic criteria for them. They are therefore listed here without adding unsupported pathology details. Reporting and communication checklist State the exact tumor histotype and site; describe the morphology that triggered hereditary consideration. Report tumor-level ancillary findings (MMR IHC, MLH1 methylation, FH/2SC, or tumor sequencing) without equating them with germline status. For STIC/risk-reducing tubo-ovarian specimens, document the examination protocol and relevant tubal findings. Recommend genetic counseling/constitutional testing when the phenotype or tumor testing warrants it. Correlate with age, personal history, family history, multiplicity, and extra-gynecologic tumors. Avoid assigning a hereditary syndrome based solely on a suggestive histologic pattern. Scope note: This page follows the supplied source excerpt. It focuses on BRCA-related cancer predisposition, Lynch syndrome, Peutz–Jeghers syndrome, DICER1-related tumor predisposition, HLRCC, and Li–Fraumeni syndrome. The source excerpt provides only overview-level mentions of several additional syndromes; no unsupported entity criteria have been added. This educational reference does not replace genetic counseling, clinical criteria, or current testing guidelines. PathologyGPS · Female Genital Tract · Genetic Tumor Syndromes
