title: Gestational Trophoblastic Disease
content: use client Partial hydatidiform mole (PHM) Molar gestation Usually a diandric, monogynic triploid gestation with focal villous hydrops and trophoblastic proliferation; embryonic development is usually present. A characteristic biphasic villous population: small, fibrotic villi admixed with enlarged, irregularly contoured villi. Enlarged villi show scalloped or irregular outlines, variable hydropic change, and mild-to-moderate circumferential trophoblastic hyperplasia. Cistern formation and trophoblastic pseudoinclusions are frequent. Fetal vessels and nucleated erythrocytes are commonly present in villous stroma; fetal tissue or a gestational sac may be identified. Morphology overlaps with complete mole, hydropic abortion, chromosomal abnormalities (including trisomy), placental mesenchymal dysplasia, and twin gestation with a coexisting complete mole. p57: usually retained in villous cytotrophoblast and villous stromal cells. This helps distinguish PHM from the usual androgenetic complete mole, but does not establish PHM by itself. STR genotyping: definitive confirmation by demonstrating diandric triploidy (two paternal complements and one maternal complement). SNP-based analysis can provide comparable diagnostic accuracy but may require more tissue and be more costly. Complete mole: usually diffuse villous enlargement and circumferential trophoblastic hyperplasia with absent p57 in villous cytotrophoblast and stroma. Hydropic abortion: may show villous edema but lacks the characteristic constellation; p57 is retained. Genotyping may be needed when morphology is equivocal. Digynic triploidy: can resemble PHM on ploidy analysis or conventional karyotyping; parental-origin testing is needed to distinguish it from diandric PHM. Other abnormal villous lesions: if criteria are not met, use a descriptive diagnosis such as abnormal villous lesion, unknown ploidy/genotype rather than overcalling PHM. Do not equate triploidy alone with partial mole. The parental origin of the extra haploid set matters. The source identifies STR genotyping as essential for a definitive PHM diagnosis. Complete hydatidiform mole (CHM) Usually an androgenetic, paternal-only conception with diffuse villous trophoblastic proliferation and no embryonic development. Well-developed CHM: diffusely enlarged hydropic villi, frequent central cisterns, and pronounced circumferential trophoblastic hyperplasia. Cytologic atypia and mitotic figures are common; detached atypical trophoblastic fragments may be present. Very early CHM may have normal-sized villi with irregular, bulbous, or polypoid contours, hypercellular myxoid stroma, and prominent karyorrhexis; trophoblastic hyperplasia may be subtle. Fetal or non-villous placental tissue is generally absent. Rare exceptions may reflect a coexisting twin/multiple gestation or mosaic/chimeric conception. Marked implantation-site intermediate trophoblastic cells can occur in CHM and do not, by themselves, establish PSTT or choriocarcinoma. p57: absent in villous cytotrophoblast and villous stromal cells in usual sporadic androgenetic CHM. Maternal decidua and extravillous trophoblast provide internal positive controls; absence is interpretable only when controls stain appropriately. STR genotyping: demonstrates an androgenetic genome in sporadic CHM. Rare familial biparental CHM may also lack p57 and requires genetic context. PHM: typically p57-retained and has a mixed population of small fibrotic and enlarged scalloped villi; confirm with STR when needed. Hydropic abortion/non-molar early gestation: may overlap morphologically but usually retains p57 in villous cytotrophoblast and stroma. Very early CHM: may lack classic diffuse villous enlargement; do not exclude CHM solely because villi are not markedly hydropic. CHM-associated trophoblastic hyperplasia/exaggerated implantation site: do not misclassify as a separate trophoblastic neoplasm without a discrete destructive tumour pattern. p57 loss is a powerful discriminator, not a stand-alone diagnosis. Confirm adequate internal controls and remember rare familial biparental CHM. Invasive / metastatic hydatidiform mole Molar gestation / GTN A hydatidiform mole, usually complete and less often partial, with myometrial and/or vascular invasion; metastatic lesions contain abnormal molar villi outside the uterus. Abnormal hydropic chorionic villi with the underlying molar morphology are present within myometrium and/or uterine vessels. Vascular invasion may be conspicuous; uterine perforation can occur. Metastatic disease is diagnosed by identifying molar villi at extrauterine sites, commonly vaginal wall, pelvis, or lung. Degeneration or necrosis may compromise villous morphology; p57 can assist in selected cases. p57 may help characterize degenerated villi and distinguish an androgenetic complete mole from other villous lesions. The source does not specify a defining tumour immunophenotype; diagnosis rests on abnormal villi in an invasive or metastatic distribution. Choriocarcinoma: destructive malignant trophoblastic proliferation without chorionic villi; look for the biphasic cytotrophoblast/intermediate trophoblast and syncytiotrophoblast pattern. Non-invasive molar pregnancy: villi are confined to products of conception and do not invade myometrium or vessels. Placental site trophoblastic tumour: infiltrative intermediate trophoblastic neoplasm, generally without chorionic villi. The presence of villi in myometrium or vessels is the defining clue. Do not diagnose choriocarcinoma when the invasive lesion is composed of molar villi. Placental site trophoblastic tumour (PSTT) Gestational trophoblastic neoplasm A neoplasm of implantation-site-type intermediate trophoblast; serum hCG is often only mildly elevated. Infiltrative aggregates or sheets of large, polyhedral to round, predominantly mononuclear implantation-site intermediate trophoblast. Scattered multinucleated tumour cells are common. At the periphery, tumour cells infiltrate myometrium singly, in cords, or in nests, separating smooth muscle fibres. Abundant amphophilic cytoplasm (occasionally eosinophilic or clear), occasional vacuoles, and often pronounced nuclear atypia with large convoluted hyperchromatic nuclei. Chorionic villi are almost never identified; characteristic vascular invasion may occur, with tumour cells replacing the vascular wall. Usually low mitotic activity: approximately 1–2 mitoses/mm² in the source. Diffuse: hPL, MUC4, HSD3B1, HLA-G, GATA3, and MCAM/CD146. Limited: hCG, inhibin, and SALL4. Ki-67 is generally 10–30%. STR genotyping can establish gestational origin and distinguish PSTT from somatic neoplasms or rare non-gestational ovarian germ-cell-origin tumours. Exaggerated placental site: non-neoplastic implantation-site trophoblastic reaction; interpret the extent and pattern of infiltration, mass formation, cytologic features, and proliferation in context. ETT: chorionic-type intermediate trophoblast; more circumscribed/nodular, nests and cords, geographic necrosis, hyaline-like material, and p63 positivity. Choriocarcinoma: biphasic malignant trophoblast with multinucleated syncytiotrophoblast, haemorrhage/necrosis, brisk mitoses, and typically very high Ki-67. Squamous carcinoma/undifferentiated carcinoma and epithelioid smooth-muscle tumours: use a panel rather than a single marker; genotyping may resolve gestational origin. PSTT is not simply an hPL-positive lesion. The diagnosis requires an invasive, mass-forming intermediate trophoblastic neoplasm and clinicopathologic correlation. Epithelioid trophoblastic tumour (ETT) A malignant neoplasm of chorionic-type intermediate trophoblast, often presenting as a discrete nodule in the lower uterine segment or cervix. Well-circumscribed, nodular, expansile proliferation of medium-sized trophoblastic cells; destructive invasion may be present. Tumour cells form nests and cords, often in a perivascular arrangement, separated by prominent geographic necrosis. Cells are relatively uniform with moderate finely granular eosinophilic-to-clear cytoplasm, distinct cell borders, round nuclei, and small nucleoli. Eosinophilic hyaline-like material resembling keratin is characteristic in the centre of nests or between tumour cells; calcification and hemosiderin may occur. Moderate atypia; mitotic activity is generally low (0–4 mitoses/mm² in the source). Cervical mucosal colonization can mimic HSIL. Positive: p63, α-inhibin, HSD3B1, and GATA3. Scattered cells: MCAM and hPL. SALL4 is negative in ETT (helpful against most gestational choriocarcinomas). Ki-67 is commonly 10–25%; CK/Ki-67 double staining can help assess the tumour-cell proliferation index. STR genotyping can demonstrate unique paternal alleles and support gestational origin. PSTT: implantation-site phenotype; diffuse hPL/MUC4/HLA-G/MCAM and generally limited p63, compared with p63-positive ETT. Choriocarcinoma: biphasic cytotrophoblast/intermediate trophoblast rimmed by syncytiotrophoblast, marked haemorrhage/necrosis, brisk mitoses, Ki-67 often >90%, and usually SALL4 positivity. Cervical squamous carcinoma: may be p63-positive and mimic ETT, especially with surface colonization; assess hyaline-like material, trophoblastic markers, morphology, and gestational history. Atypical placental site nodule: generally a smaller, non-destructive lesion; ETT shows a destructive, mass-forming nodular neoplasm. Epithelioid leiomyosarcoma: use smooth-muscle markers and trophoblastic markers as a panel. p63 is not specific. A p63-positive cervical tumour is not automatically squamous carcinoma or ETT; correlate with morphology and a trophoblastic marker panel. Gestational choriocarcinoma A malignant tumour composed of neoplastic villous cytotrophoblast, intermediate trophoblast, and syncytiotrophoblast; often associated with markedly elevated hCG. Classic biphasic/triphasic pattern: malignant mononuclear villous cytotrophoblast and intermediate trophoblast, rimmed by multinucleated syncytiotrophoblast. Infiltrative, destructive solid aggregates with marked cytologic atypia and brisk mitotic activity. Florid haemorrhage, necrosis, and lymphovascular permeation are common. Chorionic villi are not part of the classic tumour pattern; their presence in an invasive lesion should prompt consideration of invasive mole or a mixed lesion. Intraplacental choriocarcinoma may be subtle, resembling infarct or thrombus; malignant trophoblast may extend from villi into intervillous space. Neoplastic syncytiotrophoblast/intermediate trophoblast may express hCG, HSD3B1, hPL, inhibin, MCAM, HLA-G, MUC4, and p63. GATA3 is a broad trophoblastic marker but is not specific. Most gestational choriocarcinomas express SALL4, unlike ETT and PSTT in the source comparison. Ki-67 is typically very high, often >90%; PD-L1 expression is strong in syncytiotrophoblastic tumour cells. STR genotyping can identify unique paternal alleles and distinguish gestational tumour from germ-cell choriocarcinoma or somatic carcinoma with trophoblastic differentiation. Invasive mole: abnormal chorionic villi invade myometrium/vessels; choriocarcinoma is a malignant trophoblastic proliferation without villous architecture. PSTT: mononuclear implantation-site intermediate trophoblast, infiltrative myometrial growth, diffuse hPL/MUC4, usually low hCG and lower Ki-67. ETT: nodular nests/cords, hyaline-like material, p63+, SALL4−, and lower Ki-67. Non-gestational germ-cell choriocarcinoma: may be morphologically identical; STR genotyping and clinical context establish origin. Somatic carcinoma with trophoblastic differentiation: genotyping can help distinguish it from gestational choriocarcinoma. Do not use serum hCG or one immunostain as the diagnosis. The defining morphologic clue is the malignant biphasic trophoblastic population with syncytiotrophoblast. Mixed trophoblastic tumour A gestational trophoblastic tumour containing two or three distinct components of choriocarcinoma, PSTT, and/or ETT. Discrete areas of two or three recognisable tumour types are present in the same tumour. The most common combination in the source is choriocarcinoma plus ETT; less often choriocarcinoma plus PSTT or ETT plus PSTT. Rare tumours contain all three components. Each component should independently show the characteristic morphology of its corresponding entity. Each component retains the characteristic immunophenotype of its lineage; use morphology-directed immunohistochemistry rather than expecting one uniform profile. STR genotyping can establish gestational origin and help exclude germ-cell or somatic tumour origins. A single trophoblastic tumour with morphologic variation: require distinct, recognisable components rather than minor phenotypic heterogeneity. Choriocarcinoma with prominent intermediate trophoblast: assess whether there is a discrete ETT or PSTT component. Somatic carcinoma with trophoblastic differentiation: consider STR genotyping when origin is uncertain. Sample extensively. A small biopsy may capture only one component and under-classify a mixed tumour. Complete mole vs. partial mole Villous population Usually diffuse, relatively uniform villous enlargement Biphasic: small fibrotic villi plus enlarged irregular villi Villous contour / stroma Marked hydropic change; cisterns; early cases may be bulbous/polypoid with myxoid stroma and karyorrhexis Scalloped irregular outlines; variable focal hydrops; cisterns and pseudoinclusions Trophoblast Pronounced circumferential hyperplasia in well-developed cases Mild-to-moderate circumferential hyperplasia, often focal Fetal elements Usually absent Fetal vessels/nucleated RBCs commonly present; fetal tissue may be present p57 Absent in villous cytotrophoblast and villous stromal cells in usual androgenetic CHM Usually retained in villous cytotrophoblast and stroma Genotype Usually androgenetic (paternal-only) Usually diandric triploid Definitive ancillary test STR genotyping when needed; p57 is highly useful STR genotyping demonstrating diandric triploidy PSTT vs. ETT vs. choriocarcinoma Trophoblast lineage Implantation-site intermediate trophoblast Chorionic-type intermediate trophoblast Villous cytotrophoblast + intermediate trophoblast + syncytiotrophoblast Architecture Infiltrative sheets/aggregates; single cells, cords and nests between myometrial fibres Nodular/expansile nests and cords; perivascular pattern; geographic necrosis Destructive solid aggregates; biphasic/triphasic pattern Cytology Large polyhedral cells, abundant amphophilic cytoplasm, often marked atypia Relatively uniform epithelioid cells, eosinophilic/clear cytoplasm, distinct borders Markedly atypical mononuclear cells plus multinucleated syncytiotrophoblast Signature clue Myometrial infiltration and vascular wall replacement Hyaline-like material in/around nests Syncytiotrophoblast rimming malignant mononuclear trophoblast; haemorrhage hPL / MUC4 Diffuse hPL only scattered; MUC4 not listed as a defining marker in source May be expressed p63 Not a defining diffuse marker Positive May be positive SALL4 Limited Negative Usually positive Ki-67 10–30% 10–25% Typically >90% Serum hCG Often low Often mild-to-moderate elevation Often markedly elevated teal amber rose slate border-teal-200 bg-teal-50/50 border-amber-200 bg-amber-50/50 border-rose-200 bg-rose-50/50 border-slate-200 bg-white All PathologyGPS · Female Genital Tract Gestational Trophoblastic Disease A morphology-first diagnostic pathway for molar gestations, invasive mole, and gestational trophoblastic neoplasms—with focused histology, immunohistochemistry, and differential diagnosis. 1 Identify villi vs. a villus-free tumour 2 Classify the trophoblastic lineage 3 Use p57, IHC, and STR appropriately Placental trophoblast: the lineage map Cytotrophoblast Mononuclear, proliferative, stem-cell-like cells. Syncytiotrophoblast Multinucleated cells with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm; major hormone-producing component. Intermediate trophoblast Mononuclear cells; implantation-site, chorionic laeve, and villous-column subtypes. Classification at a glance Molar gestations: complete mole; partial mole. Invasive / metastatic mole: molar villi invading myometrium/vessels or present at extrauterine sites. Gestational trophoblastic neoplasms: choriocarcinoma, PSTT, ETT, and mixed trophoblastic tumour. Other lesions in the source framework: atypical villous lesions, exaggerated placental site reaction, placental site nodule/plaque, and atypical placental site nodule. Do not confuse GTD with GTN GTD is the broad disease spectrum. GTN is a clinical classification introduced for management and includes persistent mole, invasive mole, choriocarcinoma, PSTT, and ETT. A clinical diagnosis of postmolar GTN is commonly based on serial serum hCG and clinical findings; it does not necessarily identify the exact histologic lesion. Diagnostic GPS Start with the specimen: what are you looking at? A. Chorionic villi are present 1. Assess villous architecture. Diffuse enlarged hydropic villi with marked circumferential trophoblastic hyperplasia → favour well-developed CHM. Biphasic small fibrotic and enlarged scalloped villi with focal hydrops → favour PHM. 2. Look for early-mole patterns. Bulbous/polypoid villi, hypercellular myxoid stroma, and karyorrhexis can indicate very early CHM even without striking villous enlargement. 3. Perform p57 with internal controls. Loss in villous cytotrophoblast and stroma supports usual androgenetic CHM. Retention is expected in PHM and non-molar gestations. 4. Resolve equivocal cases with STR genotyping. Androgenetic genome supports CHM; diandric triploidy confirms PHM. Triploidy alone is insufficient. 5. Ask whether villi are invading. Molar villi in myometrium or vessels establish invasive mole; extrauterine molar villi establish metastatic mole. B. A mass-forming trophoblastic proliferation without villi 1. Is there a classic biphasic pattern? Malignant mononuclear trophoblast rimmed by multinucleated syncytiotrophoblast, with haemorrhage and brisk mitoses → choriocarcinoma. 2. Is the tumour infiltrative and composed of large implantation-site cells? Sheets/aggregates dissecting myometrium, vascular wall replacement, diffuse hPL/MUC4/HLA-G/MCAM → PSTT. 3. Is it a nodular epithelioid tumour? Nests/cords, geographic necrosis, central hyaline-like material, p63+, SALL4− → ETT. 4. Are there distinct components? Identify and map choriocarcinoma, PSTT, and/or ETT separately → mixed trophoblastic tumour. 5. If gestational origin is uncertain, consider STR genotyping. This is particularly important against germ-cell tumours and somatic carcinomas with trophoblastic differentiation. The critical histology comparison bg-slate-50 bg-white Entity reference Histology, IHC & differential diagnosis Search an entity or a diagnostic feature. Expand each card for morphology, immunophenotype, and the most important mimics. Search: scalloping, p57, p63, SALL4, hyaline, vascular invasion... − + Histologic diagnosis Immunohistochemistry / molecular Differential diagnosis GPS pitfall: No matching entity or feature. Try a broader search term. Practical IHC / molecular work-up Suspected molar gestation: p57 on villous cytotrophoblast and villous stromal cells, with maternal decidua/extravillous trophoblast as internal positive controls. Equivocal PHM vs. non-molar gestation or CHM: STR genotyping to establish parental contribution and ploidy; do not rely on ploidy alone. Suspected intermediate trophoblastic tumour: choose a panel that includes lineage-associated markers (e.g., hPL, MUC4, HLA-G, MCAM, p63, GATA3, HSD3B1) and Ki-67; interpret patterns, not isolated stains. Suspected choriocarcinoma: correlate morphology with hCG and other trophoblastic markers; SALL4 and Ki-67 can help in the differential. Uncertain gestational vs. non-gestational origin: STR genotyping can demonstrate unique paternal alleles from the index pregnancy. Reporting and sampling checkpoints For villous lesions, describe the villous population, contour, stromal changes, trophoblastic hyperplasia, fetal vessels/RBCs, and p57 result. If the PHM essential criteria are not met, use a qualified descriptive term such as morphologically abnormal gestation, favour PHM, or abnormal villous lesion—unknown ploidy/genotype, as appropriate to the evidence. For a suspected invasive mole, document the presence of abnormal villi in myometrium and/or vessels; distinguish this from villus-free trophoblastic neoplasm. For a mass-forming tumour, document architecture, cell type, necrosis/haemorrhage, mitotic activity, vascular invasion, and each distinct component. Extensively sample heterogeneous tumours and placentas when intraplacental choriocarcinoma is a concern. High-yield diagnostic safeguards • p57 retention does not prove PHM; it also occurs in non-molar gestations. • Triploidy does not prove PHM unless the extra haploid complement is paternal (diandric). • Early CHM may lack the classic enlarged hydropic villi. • Trophoblastic hyperplasia at the implantation site in CHM is not automatically PSTT or choriocarcinoma. • Invasive mole contains abnormal villi; choriocarcinoma is a villus-free malignant trophoblastic proliferation. • p63, GATA3, hPL, or hCG alone cannot classify a trophoblastic tumour. • GTN is a clinical management category, not a single histologic entity. • The source notes that most postmolar GTN is managed clinically with hCG surveillance; the precise tissue process may not be pathologically defined. Source scope: This page is based on the supplied WHO classification excerpt. It focuses on partial and complete hydatidiform mole, invasive/metastatic mole, PSTT, ETT, gestational choriocarcinoma, and mixed trophoblastic tumour. The source mentions atypical villous lesions, exaggerated placental site reaction, placental site nodule/plaque, and atypical placental site nodule but does not provide full entity-level descriptions in the supplied excerpt; these are therefore identified in the classification map without inventing detailed criteria. Educational reference for pathologists. Interpret morphology and ancillary studies in the clinical and gestational context; management decisions require the treating GTD team.

title: Mesenchymal Tumors
content: use client Leiomyoma (including morphologic patterns) Smooth muscle tumors Benign smooth muscle neoplasm. Cellular, mitotically active, hydropic, ischemic, bizarre-nuclei, lipoleiomyoma, epithelioid, myxoid, dissecting, and diffuse leiomyomatosis are patterns—not separate biological entities in this classification. Usual pattern: well-demarcated, intersecting fascicles of spindle cells with indistinct borders, eosinophilic fibrillary cytoplasm, cigar-shaped nuclei, small nucleoli, and rare mitoses. No tumor cell necrosis. Ischemic/infarct-type necrosis may occur: a band of granulation tissue, with or without hemorrhage or fibrosis, separates viable from nonviable tumor; nonviable cells and vessels appear devitalized/mummified. Cellular pattern: increased cellularity compared with myometrium; diffuse central or fascicular peripheral growth, often thick-walled vessels and cleft-like spaces; scant cytoplasm, no atypia, rare mitoses; border may merge with myometrium. Mitotically active pattern: increased mitoses (up to 8.4/mm² in the source) without cytologic atypia or tumor cell necrosis; associated with reproductive age, secretory endometrium, pregnancy, progestogens, or tamoxifen. Hydropic pattern: zonal watery edema separates cells into delicate cords/nests, sometimes perinodular around thick-walled vessels. Ischemic/apoplectic pattern: stellate hemorrhagic zones with a hypercellular rim and reactive degenerative cells; away from these zones, smooth muscle cells lack atypia. Bizarre nuclei pattern: focal, multifocal, or diffuse bizarre mono-/multinucleated cells, smudged chromatin, pseudoinclusions, or prominent nucleoli; mitotic count typically <2.1/mm²; karyorrhectic nuclei can mimic atypical mitoses. Epithelioid pattern: round/polygonal cells with eosinophilic granular or clear cytoplasm in sheets, cords, trabeculae, or nests; no tumor cell necrosis and usually <0.8 mitoses/mm² for benign epithelioid leiomyoma. Myxoid pattern: well-circumscribed, hypocellular tumor with widely separated bland cells in Alcian blue–positive myxoid matrix; no atypia, mitotic activity, or tumor cell necrosis. Diagnosis is one of exclusion. Other patterns: lipoleiomyoma contains mature adipocytes; dissecting leiomyoma has bland smooth muscle nodules dissecting myometrium, often with hydropic change; diffuse leiomyomatosis consists of innumerable poorly circumscribed bland nodules diffusely involving myometrium. Smooth muscle differentiation: desmin, h-caldesmon, SMA, MSA, calponin, transgelin, and SMMHC. ER, PR, and nuclear WT1 are commonly positive. CD10 may be positive, particularly in cellular leiomyoma; it is not by itself evidence of endometrial stromal differentiation. FH-deficient pattern: 2SC positive; FH may be completely lost, but retained FH does not exclude missense mutation. 2SC is more sensitive in the supplied source. p16 and abnormal p53 are uncommon in usual leiomyoma but may occur in leiomyoma with bizarre nuclei or FH-deficient tumors. Increased p16 may occur in hypercellular areas of apoplectic leiomyoma. ALK should be negative; ALK positivity should prompt consideration of inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor. Leiomyosarcoma: assess the combination of tumor cell necrosis, moderate-to-marked atypia, and mitotic activity using subtype-specific thresholds; benign leiomyoma has no tumor cell necrosis. STUMP: one or more worrisome features exceed the benign range but do not meet criteria for leiomyosarcoma; diagnosis of exclusion. Endometrial stromal tumor: delicate arteriolar vasculature and stromal-type cells; CD10/IFITM1 and hormone receptor profile may support ESS, while h-caldesmon/desmin support smooth muscle differentiation. Some overlap exists. PEComa: clear-to-eosinophilic epithelioid/spindle cells with melanocytic marker expression (HMB45/PNL2, often cathepsin K) in addition to smooth muscle markers. Inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor: consider especially in myxoid lesions; ALK testing is useful. Common leiomyoma alterations include MED12 mutation, HMGA2 aberration, RAD51B alteration, or biallelic FH loss; these are generally mutually exclusive patterns. FH-deficient morphology may include staghorn vessels, alveolar edema, scattered bizarre nuclei, chain-like ovoid nuclei, rhabdoid inclusions, and prominent eosinophilic nucleoli with perinucleolar halos. Correlate with possible HLRCC syndrome; morphology/IHC cannot distinguish germline from somatic FH alteration. Do not call tumor cell necrosis based on infarct-type/ischemic necrosis. Do not use mitotic count alone to diagnose leiomyosarcoma without considering atypia, necrosis, and subtype. Smooth muscle tumor of uncertain malignant potential (STUMP) A smooth muscle neoplasm exceeding the criteria for leiomyoma but insufficient for leiomyosarcoma. It is a diagnosis of exclusion. The category is heterogeneous. A tumor may qualify when one key leiomyosarcoma feature is present—diffuse moderate/severe atypia, tumor cell necrosis, or elevated mitotic activity—but the complete criteria for leiomyosarcoma are not met. Spindle-cell examples may show focal/multifocal/diffuse atypia with 2–4 mitoses/mm² and no tumor cell necrosis. A bland-appearing smooth muscle tumor with unequivocal tumor cell necrosis, or necrosis of uncertain type, may be classified as STUMP after excluding treatment- or pregnancy-related ischemic change. A tumor without atypia or tumor cell necrosis but with ≥8.4 mitoses/mm² (≥20 mitoses/10 HPF using the source field diameter) falls into the STUMP framework. Atypical mitoses, vascular intrusion, and irregular/infiltrative margins may be present but are not independent recurrence predictors in the cited data. Epithelioid and myxoid STUMP are exceedingly rare; exclude inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor, PEComa, and other mimics. No defining immunophenotype or validated diagnostic IHC algorithm. p16, p53, Ki-67, PR, ATRX, and DAXX have been explored for risk stratification, but protocols and cutoffs are not standardized. Abnormal p53 and/or diffuse p16 and loss of ATRX/DAXX may identify higher-risk subsets in published studies; these findings should not independently establish STUMP or dictate management. Leiomyoma with a recognized pattern: exclude bizarre nuclei, FH deficiency, mitotically active, ischemic/apoplectic, cellular, epithelioid, and myxoid patterns before using STUMP. Leiomyosarcoma: apply the specific criteria for spindle, epithelioid, or myxoid subtype; if criteria are met, do not downgrade to STUMP. Treatment-related necrosis: correlate with pregnancy, progestins, GnRH agonists, tranexamic acid, or uterine artery embolization. PEComa and inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor: especially important in epithelioid or myxoid tumors. The source recommends a mitotic threshold of ≥8.4/mm² (≥20/10 HPF) for the high-mitotic-count subset, replacing the older 6.31/mm² threshold. The criteria support, rather than replace, integrated judgment. Leiomyosarcoma (spindle cell / conventional) Malignant smooth muscle neoplasm. For conventional spindle-cell uterine LMS, at least two of three criteria are required. Long intersecting and/or compact, disorganized cellular fascicles of spindle cells with eosinophilic fibrillary cytoplasm. Moderate-to-marked nuclear atypia is common; multinucleated tumor cells or osteoclast-like giant cells may occur. Some tumors are deceptively bland at low power. Mitotic activity is usually high; atypical mitoses are common. Tumor cell necrosis, infiltrative growth, and vascular invasion are common. Diagnostic threshold: at least two of (1) tumor cell necrosis, (2) moderate-to-marked nuclear atypia, and (3) ≥4 mitoses/mm² (≥10 mitoses/10 HPF using the source field diameter). Tumor cell necrosis shows an abrupt transition from viable to necrotic tumor without intervening hyalinization or granulation tissue. Desmin, h-caldesmon, and SMA are usually positive, but may be weak or patchy in poorly differentiated, myxoid, or epithelioid areas. CD10, EMA, and broad-spectrum cytokeratins may be positive; EMA/keratin expression is frequent in epithelioid tumors. ER and PR are frequently positive. Abnormal p53, RB1, ATRX, and PTEN pathways are common molecularly; selected alterations may be reflected by IHC. Diffuse nuclear NR4A3 supports an NR4A3-rearranged subset. Diffuse nuclear PLAG1 may correlate with PLAG1 fusion but is not fully specific. STUMP: fails to meet at least two conventional LMS criteria; sample extensively and distinguish tumor cell necrosis from ischemic/infarct-type necrosis. Mitotically active leiomyoma: increased mitoses without atypia or tumor cell necrosis. Cellular leiomyoma: increased cellularity but bland cytology and rare mitoses. Endometrial stromal sarcoma: delicate arteriolar network, characteristic permeative pattern, and stromal IHC/molecular profile. Dedifferentiated LMS: pleomorphic component may lose smooth muscle markers; consider when a conventional smooth muscle tumor is associated with a high-grade pleomorphic component. A low-power bland appearance does not exclude LMS. Search for the most atypical and mitotically active areas and sample the tumor–myometrium interface. Epithelioid leiomyosarcoma LMS with ≥50% epithelioid cytomorphology; requires at least two of three subtype-specific malignant criteria. At least 50% round/polygonal, often discohesive cells with eosinophilic cytoplasm in nested, corded, nodular, or diffuse arrangements; spindle areas may blend with epithelioid areas. Rhabdoid or signet-ring-like cells, cytoplasmic clearing, pseudoglandular spaces, and stromal hyalinization may occur. At least two of: (1) tumor cell necrosis, (2) moderate-to-marked nuclear atypia, and (3) ≥1.7 mitoses/mm² (≥4 mitoses/10 HPF using the source field diameter). Desmin, h-caldesmon, and SMA may be weak or patchy; smooth muscle differentiation should be assessed with a panel. EMA and broad-spectrum cytokeratins may be positive and can create an epithelial mimic. ER/PR may be positive. NR4A3 or PLAG1 rearrangement testing may be useful in selected morphologically uniform epithelioid/myxoid tumors. Benign epithelioid leiomyoma: usually <0.8 mitoses/mm², no tumor cell necrosis, and no significant atypia. PEComa: HMB45/PNL2 and cathepsin K support melanocytic differentiation; TFE3-rearranged tumors may lack smooth muscle markers. UTROSCT: polyphenotypic sex cord-like architecture and markers. Carcinoma: keratin/EMA positivity can overlap; correlate with smooth muscle markers and morphology. Myxoid leiomyosarcoma Malignant smooth muscle tumor with prominent myxoid stroma; diagnosis requires at least two of four criteria. Myxoid matrix is prominent; two studies cited in the source suggest ≥50% of tumor volume. Spindle and/or epithelioid tumor cells with scant-to-moderate eosinophilic cytoplasm, arranged singly, in bundles/thin fascicles, or broader intersecting fascicles. Bulbous nested, tongue-like, or irregular destructive myometrial infiltration is common, but some tumors are circumscribed. At least two of: (1) tumor cell necrosis, (2) at least focal moderate nuclear atypia, (3) ≥0.8 mitoses/mm² (≥2 mitoses/10 HPF), and (4) infiltrative growth. Desmin, h-caldesmon, and SMA may be weak or patchy in myxoid areas. NR4A3 or PLAG1 rearrangement testing can be helpful in epithelioid and/or myxoid tumors with cytologic uniformity. Diffuse nuclear PLAG1 can occur in PLAG1-rearranged sarcoma but may also occur in a subset without detectable rearrangement. Myxoid leiomyoma: circumscribed, hypocellular, bland cells, no mitoses, no atypia, and no tumor cell necrosis. STUMP: falls below the required two malignant criteria. Endometrial stromal sarcoma: evaluate delicate arterioles, tongue-like permeation, lymphovascular invasion, CD10/IFITM1/ER/PR, and defining fusions. Inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor and other myxoid sarcomas: exclude with appropriate morphology, IHC, and molecular work-up. Intravenous leiomyomatosis (IVL) Benign smooth muscle proliferation growing intravascularly, outside or beyond the confines of a leiomyoma; may extend into pelvic veins, IVC, heart, or pulmonary vessels. Intravascular plugs or worm-like cords of benign smooth muscle cells resembling leiomyoma, sometimes free-floating within vascular lumina. Hydropic change, hyalinization, and thick-walled vessels are frequent. Uncommon patterns include adipocytes (intravenous lipoleiomyomatosis), vascular-rich forms, or benign endometrial glands/stroma (intravenous adenomyomatosis). Desmin and h-caldesmon are generally positive; ER and PR are usually positive. CD10 is negative to variably positive. Leiomyosarcoma with vascular invasion: look for malignant cytology, tumor cell necrosis, and mitotic activity; IVL is cytologically benign. Endometrial stromal sarcoma with vascular invasion: small stromal cells and characteristic arteriolar pattern; CD10/IFITM1 and fusion profile support ESS. Other intravascular spindle-cell lesions: correlate with morphology and smooth muscle lineage markers. The intravascular location does not itself mean malignancy. The defining feature is benign smooth muscle growing within vessels. Metastasizing leiomyoma Extrauterine, well-demarcated proliferation of benign-appearing gynecologic smooth muscle, most often involving lung. Well-demarcated intersecting fascicles of bland spindle cells with moderate eosinophilic cytoplasm and blunt-ended nuclei. Minimal-to-absent mitoses; no significant atypia or tumor cell necrosis. Pulmonary lesions may show a peribronchiolar pattern with peripheral entrapment of alveolar spaces. ER and PR are positive; smooth muscle markers support lineage. Metastatic leiomyosarcoma: history of LMS or STUMP, atypia, mitoses, and/or necrosis argue against metastasizing leiomyoma. Primary pulmonary smooth muscle neoplasm: correlate with gynecologic history and compare with prior uterine tumor. Other spindle-cell pulmonary lesions: use morphology and a lineage-directed panel. The source essential criteria include absence of a history of gynecologic or non-gynecologic LMS or STUMP. Compare the extrauterine lesion with the prior uterine tumor whenever possible. Leiomyomatosis peritonealis disseminata (LPD) Multiple benign smooth muscle nodules studding pelvic/abdominal peritoneal surfaces. Multiple, often miliary, well-circumscribed superficial peritoneal or omental nodules. Nodules resemble typical or cellular leiomyoma, with fascicles of bland smooth muscle, absent-to-mild atypia, and low mitotic activity. No destructive invasion is expected; endometriosis or endosalpingiosis may coexist. Smooth muscle markers confirm differentiation. Peritoneal dissemination of leiomyosarcoma: atypia, mitotic activity, tumor cell necrosis, and destructive invasion argue against LPD. Implantation after morcellation: correlate with surgical history and distribution. Other peritoneal spindle-cell proliferations: confirm smooth muscle lineage and exclude mimics. Endometrial stromal nodule (ESN) Endometrial stromal and related tumors Benign, well-circumscribed endometrial stromal neoplasm; distinction from LGESS requires examination of the entire tumor–myometrium interface. Well-circumscribed nodule composed of densely cellular, uniform small cells resembling proliferative endometrial stroma, with scant cytoplasm and round-to-oval nuclei. Arterioles may be hyalinized and surrounded by whorled tumor cells; scattered large vessels may occur at the periphery. Up to three finger-like projections extending <3 mm from the tumor border have been permitted in the source criteria. Mitotic activity is usually low but an increased count alone does not exclude ESN. Other patterns may include smooth muscle, fibromyxoid, sex cord-like, endometrioid glandular, epithelioid, or rhabdoid differentiation. The immunophenotype mirrors LGESS; CD10, ER, and PR are desirable supportive markers. Molecular fusion (e.g., JAZF1::SUZ12 or PHF1-related) does not distinguish ESN from ESS. LGESS: permeative myometrial invasion and/or lymphovascular invasion; irregularity exceeding the limited ESN border allowance. Cellular leiomyoma: smooth muscle fascicles and h-caldesmon/desmin support smooth muscle differentiation. UTROSCT: sex cord-like patterns without a conventional endometrial stromal tumor component. ESN cannot be reliably separated from LGESS on curettage or a limited biopsy because the tumor–myometrium interface is required. Low-grade endometrial stromal sarcoma (LGESS) Infiltrative neoplasm of endometrial stromal-type cells, typically with low-grade cytology and a delicate arteriolar network. Irregular, densely cellular islands of small uniform spindle cells with scant cytoplasm, oval/fusiform nuclei, inconspicuous nucleoli, and minimal atypia. Delicate arteriolar network; tumor cells may form perivascular whorls. Vessels may be hyalinized or curvilinear. Uterine tumors show tongue-like myometrial permeation and/or lymphovascular invasion. Extrauterine tumors may be multinodular and associated with endometriosis. Even a predominantly circumscribed tumor with >3 finger-like projections exceeding 3 mm is classified as LGESS/limited infiltration in the source framework. Mitotic activity is usually low (<2.1/mm²) but can occasionally be brisk. Variant differentiation includes smooth muscle, fibromyxoid, sex cord-like, epithelioid, skeletal muscle, and fatty patterns. Typically strong/diffuse CD10, IFITM1, WT1, ER, and PR; cyclin D1 absent or limited (<50% of tumor nuclei). Broad-spectrum keratin may be positive. Desmin/SMA/h-caldesmon may highlight smooth muscle-differentiated areas. Sex cord-like areas may express inhibin and calretinin. TSC2-mutant epithelioid areas may express HMB45, Melan-A, or cathepsin K. ESN: sharply circumscribed with only limited permitted finger-like projections; no lymphovascular invasion and no extensive myometrial permeation. HGESS: monomorphic high-grade round/spindle cells, brisk mitoses, often necrosis/LVI, and cyclin D1/BCOR-associated molecular profile. Cellular leiomyoma: smooth muscle phenotype; CD10 can be positive in cellular leiomyoma, so no single marker is definitive. UTROSCT: sex cord architecture with polyphenotypic immunoprofile but without a component of conventional endometrial stromal tumor. JAZF1::SUZ12 is the most common fusion; other JAZF1/PHF1-related fusions occur. Molecular confirmation is useful in unusual morphology but does not separate ESN from LGESS. ESR1 mutation testing is recommended in LGESS with high-grade transformation or altered hormone receptor status. TSC2 alterations may underlie epithelioid/sex cord-like morphology. A low mitotic count does not make a tumor benign. The key distinction from ESN is the infiltrative interface and/or lymphovascular invasion. High-grade endometrial stromal sarcoma (HGESS) High-grade endometrial stromal neoplasm defined by characteristic molecular subsets, including YWHAE-, BCOR-, and BCORL1-altered tumors. Expansile, permeative, or infiltrative growth; more than one invasion pattern may coexist. Round-cell, spindle-cell, or mixed morphology with monomorphic mild-to-moderate atypia and readily identifiable mitoses (>4.21/mm² in the source); lymphovascular invasion and necrosis are usually present. A low-grade component may coexist and can predominate, so extensive sampling is essential. YWHAE::NUTM2 tumors: round cells with eosinophilic cytoplasm, irregular high-grade nuclei, vesicular chromatin, and high mitotic activity; may coexist with fibromyxoid or conventional LGESS. ZC3H7B::BCOR / variant BCOR::BCORL1 tumors: haphazard fascicular spindle cells in fibrous-to-fibromyxoid stroma, mild-to-moderate atypia, and at least focal high mitotic activity. BCOR ITD tumors: round/spindle or haphazard spindle-cell growth; may contain a bland low-grade component. YWHAE::NUTM2 high-grade component: diffuse strong nuclear cyclin D1 and BCOR; may express KIT, CD56, and CD99; DOG1 negative. ZC3H7B::BCOR: strong diffuse cyclin D1 and CD10; ER/PR variable; BCOR positive in only about half of cases; desmin negative, focal SMA/caldesmon may occur. BCOR ITD: diffuse strong nuclear cyclin D1 and/or BCOR; CD10 variable; usually ER/PR negative; may express desmin but is usually SMA/caldesmon negative. Fusion/ITD-defined HGESS is consistently TP53 wild type in the supplied source; a TP53 mutation/high copy-number complexity should prompt reconsideration. LGESS with high-grade transformation: a low-grade component and a characteristic LGESS fusion may be present; ESR1 hotspot mutation may accompany transformation. Undifferentiated uterine sarcoma, NCF: diagnosis of exclusion; lacks defining HGESS fusion/ITD and may show pleomorphic morphology and mutant-pattern p53. Undifferentiated endometrial carcinoma: exclude with epithelial markers and appropriate morphology. SMARCA4-deficient uterine sarcoma: exclude with SMARCA4/BRG1 assessment in the appropriate setting. Defining alterations include YWHAE::NUTM2A/B, ZC3H7B::BCOR, variant BCOR/BCORL1 fusions, and BCOR internal tandem duplication; less common KDM2B fusions are emerging. Molecular confirmation is particularly important when morphology or IHC is equivocal. Diffuse cyclin D1 or BCOR is a surrogate, not a substitute for molecular confirmation when the diagnosis is uncertain. Pan-TRK staining can occur without an NTRK rearrangement in BCOR/YWHAE-altered tumors. Endometrial polyp Mixed epithelial and mesenchymal tumors Benign polypoid endometrial lesion with altered/fibrotic stroma, thick-walled vessels, and disorganized glands. Polypoid architecture with altered, often fibrotic stroma, scattered thick-walled vessels, and embedded disorganized glands. Glands may be proliferative, atrophic, or secretory; endocervical-type mucinous and ciliated/tubal metaplasia are common. Torsion may cause hemorrhagic infarction, epithelial metaplasia, and reactive atypia. Unlike adenosarcoma, there is no atypical mitotically active periglandular stromal cuff and typically no leaf-like projections into cystically dilated glands. Polyps with unusual stromal features overlap with low-grade adenosarcoma but do not meet full criteria; the source describes these as benign if completely excised. No specific IHC profile is required in the supplied source; use targeted stains when evaluating a stromal or epithelial mimic. Adenosarcoma: leaf-like architecture and periglandular cuffing by hypercellular neoplastic stroma, often with mitotic activity. Adenomyomatous polyp: prominent smooth muscle component; do not label an ordinary polyp with only minor smooth muscle as adenomyoma. Atypical hyperplasia/carcinoma: inspect glands carefully, particularly in postmenopausal or tamoxifen-associated polyps. Adenomyoma A mass of endometrioid-type glands, endometrioid-type stroma, and smooth muscle; cervical endocervical-type adenomyoma is a distinct glandular pattern. Corpus, broad ligament, or ovarian adenomyoma: nodules/polyps of predominantly bland endometrioid-type glands/cysts surrounded by endometrioid-type stroma and smooth muscle, with smooth muscle usually predominant. Tubal, mucinous, or squamous metaplasia may occur. Endometrioid stroma may be inconspicuous in parts of the lesion. Smooth muscle is usually bland, without increased cellularity; occasional bizarre nuclei may occur without mitotic activity. Cervical endocervical-type adenomyoma: predominantly or exclusively endocervical-type mucinous glands with intracellular mucin and basal nuclei, surrounded by bland smooth muscle; endometrial stroma is absent. Endometrioid-type stromal component: CD10 positive; SATB2 may be positive. Smooth muscle component: desmin, SMA, and h-caldesmon positive. Endometrial polyp with smooth muscle: a minor smooth muscle component is insufficient for adenomyoma. Adenosarcoma: neoplastic hypercellular periglandular stroma, leaf-like architecture, and mitotic activity. Atypical glandular lesion/carcinoma: evaluate glandular cytology and architecture independently. Müllerian adenosarcoma Biphasic neoplasm with benign or mildly atypical epithelial glands and malignant mesenchymal stroma. Broad leaf-like (phyllodes-like) architecture and/or dilated glands lined by benign endometrial or ciliated epithelium, each surrounded by a distinct cuff of neoplastic stroma hypercellular relative to adjacent stroma. Stromal atypia and mitoses are variable and may be subtle; extensive sampling is important. Sarcomatous overgrowth is defined as pure sarcoma without epithelium occupying ≥25% of tumor volume. Sex cord differentiation does not count as sarcomatous overgrowth. Heterologous rhabdomyosarcomatous differentiation may occur. High-grade sarcoma may show marked pleomorphism, brisk mitoses (often >4.21/mm² in the source), and necrosis; it may occur with or without sarcomatous overgrowth. CD10, ER, and PR are often positive in the stromal component, but may be lost in sarcomatous overgrowth. Myogenin and MYOD1 help confirm heterologous rhabdomyosarcomatous differentiation. High-grade areas may show mutation-type p53. Endometrial polyp with unusual stromal features: lacks the full combination of leaf-like architecture and atypical mitotically active periglandular stromal cuffing. Adenofibroma: the historical category is no longer retained; prior cases should be reconsidered as benign polyp with atypical architecture or low-grade adenosarcoma. Carcinosarcoma: both epithelial and mesenchymal components are malignant; in adenosarcoma the epithelial component is benign or only mildly atypical. Adenomyoma: bland smooth muscle predominates; no neoplastic periglandular stromal cuff. Sarcomatous overgrowth is a quantitative definition (≥25% pure sarcoma). Do not count sex cord differentiation as sarcomatous overgrowth. Genital rhabdomyoma Skeletal muscle tumors Benign mature skeletal muscle neoplasm, typically subepithelial in the lower genital tract. Well-circumscribed subepithelial proliferation of polygonal, spindle, and/or elongated mature rhabdomyoblasts in fibrous stroma. Some cells show cross-striations. A cambium layer and mitotic activity are absent; scattered atypical cells may occur. Desmin positive; myogenin and MYOD1 support skeletal muscle differentiation. Embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma: primitive cells, subepithelial cambium layer, frequent mitoses/apoptosis, and immature rhabdomyoblasts. Atypical smooth muscle tumor: use myogenin/MYOD1 to establish skeletal muscle differentiation. Rhabdomyosarcoma (ERMS, ARMS, PRMS) Malignant skeletal muscle neoplasm; classify by morphology as embryonal, alveolar, or pleomorphic when it arises as a primary rhabdomyosarcoma. Embryonal RMS (ERMS): often polypoid and partly covered by squamous or glandular epithelium; primitive dark ovoid-to-spindled cells in edematous or collagenous stroma. A subepithelial cambium layer or peritheliomatous condensation around glands may be present. Strap cells, rounded rhabdomyoblasts, and rare spider cells may occur; overt rhabdomyoblasts can be inconspicuous. Mitoses and apoptosis are frequent. ERMS may show focal anaplasia; fetal-type cartilage occurs in about 40% in the supplied source and is mostly associated with DICER1 alterations. Alveolar RMS (ARMS): small round blue cells in loose cohesive nests/alveoli separated by collagenous septa; central cells lose cohesion while peripheral cells adhere to septa. A solid pattern may lack fibrous septa. Pleomorphic RMS (PRMS): admixture of round, polygonal, bizarre, and spindle cells with marked atypia, with or without giant cells. When rhabdomyoblastic differentiation occurs within another neoplasm (e.g., adenosarcoma or carcinosarcoma), do not classify the entire tumor as a primary RMS subtype. Myogenin and MYOD1 are specific nuclear markers; often diffuse in ARMS and PRMS, but may be focal in ERMS. Desmin, myoglobin, myosin, and MSA may be positive; SMA is negative in the source description. Benign genital rhabdomyoma: mature cells, no cambium layer, no mitotic activity. Adenosarcoma with rhabdomyoblastic differentiation: identify the biphasic phyllodes-like architecture and benign epithelial component. Carcinosarcoma with heterologous rhabdomyosarcoma: identify malignant epithelial and mesenchymal components. Other small round-cell tumors: establish skeletal muscle differentiation with nuclear myogenin/MYOD1 and use molecular testing as appropriate. DICER1 mutation analysis is recommended when available in uterine and tubo-ovarian ERMS. PAX3::FOXO1 and PAX7::FOXO1 account for most fusion-positive ARMS; fusion testing may be helpful in selected cases. Ovarian myxoma Miscellaneous mesenchymal tumors Benign intraparenchymal ovarian myxoid neoplasm with bland spindle/stellate cells and abundant capillary-type vessels. Typically well-circumscribed but unencapsulated intraparenchymal lesion; abundant myxoid matrix displaces follicles and their derivatives. Spindle-to-stellate cells with long tapering processes and bland oval, sometimes indented nuclei; occasional pseudoinclusions; absent-to-minimal mitoses. Small capillary-type vessels, sometimes plexiform; small cysts/pseudocysts and hemorrhage with or without fibrin may occur. Alcian blue highlights abundant hyaluronic-acid-rich matrix. Tumor cells typically express vimentin and SMA; negative for inhibin, desmin, S100, cytokeratins, and EMA. Sex cord-stromal tumor: inhibin and other sex cord markers support this lineage; ovarian myxoma is typically inhibin negative. Myxoid smooth muscle tumor: desmin/h-caldesmon and smooth muscle morphology support smooth muscle differentiation. Nerve sheath myxoma: S100 positivity would argue against ovarian myxoma. Uterine tumor resembling ovarian sex cord tumor (UTROSCT) Uterine tumor with sex cord-like patterns and no conventional endometrial stromal tumor component; most behave indolently but recurrence is possible. Usually well-circumscribed, but an irregular edge with entrapment of surrounding smooth muscle may occur. Sheets, cords, nests, insulae, trabeculae, or tubules; occasionally retiform. The proportion of sex cord-like morphology varies. Cells have scant-to-abundant pale/foamy or eosinophilic cytoplasm, sometimes rhabdoid; nuclei are usually ovoid with minimal atypia and low mitotic activity. A subset shows atypia, brisk mitoses, necrosis, and vascular invasion—features associated with malignant behavior. Polyphenotypic profile: variable inhibin, calretinin, WT1, CD56, CD99, SF1, FOXL2, Melan-A, epithelial markers, ER/PR, smooth muscle markers, and CD10. GREB1 or ESR1 rearrangements may be detected; absence of recurrent LGESS rearrangements supports distinction in the appropriate context. LGESS with sex cord-like differentiation: look for a conventional endometrial stromal component and characteristic LGESS molecular alterations. Ovarian sex cord-stromal tumor involving uterus: correlate with ovarian primary and clinical/radiologic findings. Epithelioid smooth muscle tumor: smooth muscle morphology and marker profile may predominate. No single sex cord marker is specific. The essential criterion is sex cord pattern without a component of endometrial stromal tumor. Perivascular epithelioid cell tumor (PEComa) Myomelanocytic neoplasm composed of epithelioid and/or spindle cells, often arranged around delicate vessels. Often circumscribed but may show permeative tongue-like or infiltrative growth. Epithelioid and/or spindle cells with clear-to-eosinophilic granular cytoplasm; nests, sheets, cords, or fascicles. Delicate thin-walled vessels and radial/perivascular arrangement are characteristic clues; multinucleated, lipid-rich, rhabdoid, or melanin-containing cells and stromal hyalinization may occur. Atypia, mitoses, and necrosis may be present. Sclerosing PEComa has extensive stromal hyalinization. Rare patterns include LAM-like morphology, PEComa/leiomyosarcoma biphasic tumors, and PEComa/LGESS hybrid morphology. Conventional PEComa: melanocytic markers HMB45 and PNL2 are most sensitive; Melan-A may be focal or negative; cathepsin K often strong/diffuse but not specific. Smooth muscle markers (desmin, h-caldesmon, SMA) are variably expressed. TFE3-rearranged PEComa: uniform epithelioid cells with clear/eosinophilic cytoplasm; diffuse TFE3, HMB45, and cathepsin K; Melan-A and smooth muscle markers often rare/absent. Epithelioid leiomyoma/LMS: smooth muscle markers without melanocytic marker profile; PEComa usually has myomelanocytic differentiation. TSC2-mutant LGESS: may show epithelioid areas expressing HMB45, Melan-A, or cathepsin K; look for conventional LGESS component and stromal markers/fusions. Clear cell carcinoma: epithelial markers and organ-specific context; PEComa usually lacks keratin expression. TFE3-rearranged tumors of other lineages: confirm with morphology, marker panel, and molecular testing. TSC1/TSC2 inactivating alterations support PEComa but their absence does not exclude it. TFE3 rearrangement testing is useful when TFE3 IHC is equivocal or the phenotype is unusual. Undifferentiated uterine sarcoma, not classified further (NCF) High-grade malignant mesenchymal tumor with no identifiable line of differentiation after extensive sampling, IHC, and appropriate molecular exclusion. Destructive myometrial invasion. More often sheets of variably pleomorphic epithelioid and/or spindle cells with brisk mitotic activity; necrosis and lymphovascular invasion are common. Uniform monomorphic tumors should trigger a careful search for HGESS, SMARCA4-deficient uterine sarcoma, or undifferentiated endometrial carcinoma. The entity is heterogeneous and is a diagnosis of exclusion; adequate sampling is essential to exclude a recognizable differentiated component. May show focal nonspecific SMA; should be negative for desmin and caldesmon in the source description. Some cases show ER/PR or variable nonspecific CD10. Many pleomorphic tumors show mutant-pattern p53, unlike molecularly defined fusion-driven HGESS, which is consistently TP53 wild type in the source. HGESS: exclude YWHAE, BCOR/BCORL1 fusions or BCOR ITD; use cyclin D1/BCOR as surrogates and molecular confirmation. SMARCA4-deficient uterine sarcoma: assess BRG1/SMARCA4. Undifferentiated endometrial carcinoma: exclude epithelial differentiation with morphology and IHC. Other fusion-driven sarcomas: exclude JAZF1, PHF1, YWHAE, BCOR, ALK, RET, ROS1, NTRK, TFE3, COL1A1, KAT6A/B::KANSL1, and related alterations as appropriate. No pathognomonic molecular alteration. Molecular work-up is primarily exclusionary and should target alterations defining other recognized or provisional entities. Do not use this label as a shortcut for an unclassified high-grade uterine tumor. Exclude better-defined sarcomas and carcinoma first. at least focal moderate atypia; ≥0.8 mitoses/mm² (≥2/10 HPF); infiltrative growth STUMP high-mitotic subset Threshold-based category No atypia or tumor cell necrosis but ≥8.4 mitoses/mm² (≥20/10 HPF) Interface Well-circumscribed; lineage-directed immunohistochemistry; and molecularly defined mimics. 1 Establish the line of differentiation 2 Apply subtype-specific morphologic thresholds 3 Use molecular testing to resolve defined entities Classification map Leiomyoma and patterns · STUMP · leiomyosarcoma · IVL · metastasizing leiomyoma · LPD Endometrial stromal tumors Endometrial stromal nodule · LGESS · HGESS Endometrial polyp · adenomyoma · adenosarcoma Rhabdomyoma · rhabdomyosarcoma Miscellaneous Ovarian myxoma · UTROSCT · PEComa · undifferentiated uterine sarcoma NCF First-pass diagnostic GPS Identify the dominant morphology: fascicular spindle, stromal-type small cells, myxoid, epithelioid, sex cord-like, myomelanocytic, or rhabdomyoblastic. Assess the interface: circumscribed, limited irregularity, tongue-like permeation, destructive invasion, or vascular growth. Evaluate cytology and mitoses: atypia grade, mitotic density in the hotspot, and atypical mitoses. Classify necrosis: tumor cell necrosis versus ischemic/infarct-type or treatment-related change. Apply a lineage-directed IHC panel and targeted molecular testing where indicated. Sampling is part of diagnosis Sample the tumor–myometrium interface to distinguish ESN from LGESS and to assess destructive invasion. Sample heterogeneous smooth muscle tumors extensively, including soft, hemorrhagic, necrotic, myxoid, and most atypical areas. Look for a low-grade component in suspected HGESS and for a differentiated component before diagnosing undifferentiated sarcoma. For suspected IVL, carefully examine peripheral myometrium, adjacent vessels, and lower uterine segment soft tissue. Smooth muscle malignancy: criteria are subtype-specific Tumor type Diagnostic rule Criteria bg-slate-50 bg-white Mitotic counts are based on the field diameter specified in the supplied source (0.55 mm). Use calibrated microscope area and report the counting method consistently. Endometrial stromal tumor: the interface is decisive Feature ESN LGESS HGESS Entity reference Histologic diagnosis, IHC & differential Search by entity, pattern, marker, or diagnostic feature. Expand each entry for criteria and common mimics. Search: tumor cell necrosis, CD10, BCOR, HMB45, cambium layer... − + Histologic criteria Immunohistochemistry Differential diagnosis Molecular / ancillary studies GPS pitfall: No matching entity or feature. Try a broader search term. Lineage-directed IHC: practical starting panels Smooth muscle: desmin, h-caldesmon, SMA, calponin; add ER/PR and selected p53, p16, FH, and 2SC according to morphology. Endometrial stromal: CD10, IFITM1, ER, PR, WT1; add cyclin D1 and BCOR for suspected HGESS; pursue fusion/ITD testing where indicated. PEComa: HMB45, PNL2, Melan-A, cathepsin K plus smooth muscle markers; TFE3 IHC/rearrangement testing for the TFE3-associated subset. Rhabdomyoblastic: desmin with nuclear myogenin and MYOD1. UTROSCT: broad panel of sex cord markers, epithelial markers, ER/PR, smooth muscle markers, and CD10; interpret the polyphenotypic pattern. Molecular testing: when it changes classification FH-deficient leiomyoma: 2SC/FH IHC prompts consideration of HLRCC and genetic counseling; IHC cannot establish germline status. HGESS: confirm YWHAE, BCOR/BCORL1 fusion or BCOR ITD when suspected; cyclin D1/BCOR are supportive surrogates. LGESS: JAZF1/PHF1-related fusions support the diagnosis in unusual cases but do not distinguish ESN from LGESS. Epithelioid/myxoid smooth muscle tumors: consider NR4A3 and PLAG1 rearrangements in cytologically uniform cases. PEComa: TSC1/TSC2 alterations support the diagnosis; TFE3 rearrangement testing can resolve selected cases. ERMS: consider DICER1 testing; ARMS: evaluate PAX3::FOXO1 / PAX7::FOXO1 in selected cases. High-yield diagnostic safeguards • Separate tumor cell necrosis from ischemic/infarct-type necrosis before classifying a smooth muscle tumor. • Apply different mitotic thresholds to spindle, epithelioid, and myxoid LMS. • STUMP is a diagnosis of exclusion—not a synonym for atypical leiomyoma. • ESN versus LGESS requires the tumor–myometrium interface; curettage cannot reliably settle the distinction. • LGESS can have low mitotic activity and still be malignant because invasion is decisive. • HGESS is a molecularly refined category; exclude defined fusion/ITD tumors before undifferentiated sarcoma NCF. • Adenosarcoma has benign/mildly atypical epithelium and malignant stroma; carcinosarcoma has malignant epithelial and mesenchymal components. • Myogenin/MYOD1 nuclear staining establishes rhabdomyoblastic differentiation, but first determine whether it is a component of another tumor. Source scope: This page follows the supplied WHO mesenchymal-tumor excerpt. It covers the entities with detailed descriptions in that source: smooth muscle tumors and related lesions, endometrial stromal tumors, mixed epithelial/mesenchymal tumors, skeletal muscle tumors, ovarian myxoma, UTROSCT, PEComa, and undifferentiated uterine sarcoma NCF. Provisional fusion-defined entities and SMARCB1-deficient vulvar neoplasms are mentioned in the source introduction but are not expanded here because the supplied excerpt does not provide full entity-level diagnostic descriptions. Educational reference for pathologists. Integrate morphology, immunophenotype, molecular findings, sampling, and clinical context. For rare tumors and borderline categories, expert gynecologic pathology consultation is appropriate.
