title: Epithelial Tumors
content: Serous tumors Tubal-type serous epithelium; the key malignant distinction is low-grade versus high-grade cytology and, above all, the presence or absence of destructive stromal invasion. Serous cystadenoma / adenofibroma / cystadenofibroma Simple, non-stratified cuboidal or columnar epithelium resembling tubal secretory or ciliated cells; flattened lining may occur. Cystadenoma is predominantly cystic. Adenofibroma contains small glands/cysts in prominent fibromatous stroma. Cystadenofibroma combines cysts with broad-based papillary projections and fibromatous stroma. No significant epithelial stratification, tufting, hierarchical branching, or destructive invasion. A cyst should be greater than 1 cm to be designated a cystadenoma rather than a cortical inclusion cyst. A minor focus of borderline-type proliferation involving less than 10% of total tumor volume (or less than 0.5 cm³) may be designated focal epithelial proliferation; surface involvement or micropapillary architecture should prompt consideration of SBT. Tubal-type epithelium typically expresses PAX8 and CK7; WT1 and ER are usually supportive of serous differentiation, but the supplied source does not define an obligatory IHC panel for benign serous tumors. Serous borderline tumor (SBT), including micropapillary/cribriform subtype Usual SBT: hierarchical branching papillae with variable stromal cores, stratified epithelium, tufting, and cell detachment; epithelial cell types may include ciliated, non-ciliated, eosinophilic, hobnail, or mesothelial-like cells. Nuclear heterogeneity is typical, but cytology remains low grade. A 10% threshold is commonly used for the minimum epithelial proliferation required to distinguish an early SBT from cystadenoma/adenofibroma with focal proliferation. Micropapillary/cribriform SBT: elongated micropapillae at least five times longer than wide, usually without stromal cores, arising directly from larger papillae (Medusa-head pattern), and/or punched-out cribriform spaces. At least 5 mm of pure micropapillary/cribriform growth is required for this subtype. Micropapillary cells are more monotonous, with high N:C ratios and small uniform nuclei; high-grade nuclear features and frequent mitoses should not be present. Stromal microinvasion (individual cells/small clusters or simple papillae, usually less than 5 mm) is not equivalent to destructive LGSC invasion and is not associated with adverse prognosis in the source framework. Non-invasive implants involve peritoneal surfaces or submesothelial invaginations. Epithelial implants show branching papillae or detached clusters in smoothly contoured epithelial/mesothelial-lined spaces; desmoplastic implants show cells/clusters in reactive granulation tissue-like or desmoplastic stroma attached to the surface. The supplied source does not define a required IHC profile for SBT. Use morphology and adequate sampling as the primary criteria; molecular alterations in the RAS/MAPK pathway (KRAS or BRAF, usually mutually exclusive) are common but not required for diagnosis. An extraovarian implant with destructive infiltrative growth is LGSC, not an invasive implant. A nodular intraparenchymal lymph-node aggregate resembling LGSC should be classified as LGSC; isolated subcapsular papillary/glandular SBT-like involvement is not equivalent to metastatic carcinoma. Low-grade serous carcinoma (LGSC) and high-grade serous carcinoma (HGSC) LGSC: invasive serous tumor with low-grade nuclear atypia (less than threefold variation in nuclear size) and low mitotic activity, typically no more than 5 mitoses/mm² (approximately 12 mitoses per 10 HPF using the specified field area). Patterns include small nests, glands, papillae/micropapillae, solid sheets, and inverted macropapillae. Psammoma bodies are common; necrosis is rare. Search carefully for stromal invasion in micropapillary SBT-like areas. LGSC may arise de novo, with SBT, or as recurrence/progression of SBT. Destructive extraovarian implants are extraovarian LGSC. HGSC: high-grade serous tumor with marked nuclear atypia (greater than threefold nuclear size variation) and/or high mitotic activity, typically greater than 5 mitoses/mm² (approximately more than 12 per 10 HPF using the specified field area). Solid, papillary, labyrinthine/slit-like, glandular, and cribriform patterns occur; atypical mitoses, necrosis, and multinucleated cells are common. HGSC is commonly bilateral, large, exophytic, and advanced stage. Exclude a tubal primary, including STIC, before assigning an ovarian primary site. A small subset of serous carcinomas is morphologically ambiguous between LGSC and HGSC; integrate nuclear grade, mitotic activity, p53, and clinical/pathologic context. LGSC: typically diffuse CK7, PAX8, ER, and WT1; PR and p16 are variable or patchy; p53 shows a wild-type pattern. HGSC: WT1 is nuclear-positive in about 90%; p53 shows a mutation-type pattern in about 95% (diffuse strong overexpression in at least 80%, null with intact internal control, or rarely cytoplasmic pattern). CK7, CA125, and PAX8 are typically positive; ER is frequent; p16 is often block-positive. CK20, CEA, HNF1β, and napsin A are typically negative. p53 is a surrogate for TP53 status, but a minority of HGSCs show discordance between IHC and mutation testing. SBT and LGSC cannot be reliably separated by cytology alone; invasion is a tissue diagnosis. A high mitotic count or greater than threefold nuclear size variation in a presumed LGSC should trigger evaluation for HGSC. The micropapillary/cribriform pattern alone does not establish invasion. Endometrioid carcinoma Usually forms confluent back-to-back glands with smooth luminal contours; squamous/morular differentiation is common. PAX8 and ER/PR are often positive, but WT1 is usually negative. Endometriosis and a coexisting endometrioid precursor support this lineage. Mesothelial proliferation / mesothelioma May mimic papillary serous tumor on peritoneal surfaces. Use a panel including epithelial/Müllerian markers (PAX8, claudin-4) and mesothelial markers (calretinin, D2-40, WT1); WT1 alone is not discriminatory. Metastatic serous carcinoma Correlate with distribution and history. A tubal STIC or fimbrial mucosal involvement supports tubo-ovarian HGSC; primary peritoneal disease may be morphologically identical and requires clinicopathologic assignment. KRAS/BRAF pathway alterations are common in SBT and LGSC; TP53 mutation and complex copy-number changes characterize nearly all HGSC. The most important prognostic distinction in SBT is non-invasive implant versus destructive invasive extraovarian LGSC. Mucinous tumors Gastrointestinal-type (intestinal or gastric/foveolar) or Müllerian-type mucinous epithelium. Establish primary ovarian origin before diagnosing primary ovarian mucinous carcinoma. Mucinous cystadenoma / mucinous adenofibroma Multiple cysts and glands lined by simple, non-stratified mucinous epithelium resembling Müllerian, gastric foveolar, or intestinal epithelium. Intestinal-type areas may contain goblet cells, neuroendocrine cells, or Paneth cells. Nuclei are small, basally located, and cytologically bland; mitoses are absent or minimal. Rare simple papillae may occur, but there is no architectural complexity or cytologic atypia. Adenofibroma has small glands/cysts embedded in prominent fibromatous stroma. Focal extravasated mucin or mucin granulomas may follow cyst rupture. Usually unilateral (about 95%) and multilocular with smooth outer surface; bilateral or relatively small tumors raise concern for metastasis. The supplied source does not specify a mandatory benign mucinous IHC profile. Interpret intestinal and Müllerian differentiation in context; IHC becomes particularly important when excluding a metastatic gastrointestinal primary. Mucinous borderline tumor Mucinous epithelial proliferation with stratification, tufting, or papillary complexity beyond a benign cystadenoma, but without confluent/expansile or infiltrative/destructive invasion. Extensively sample large multilocular tumors, especially solid areas, mural nodules, and areas of complex glandular crowding, to exclude invasion. The supplied source emphasizes the diagnostic overlap between crowded intraepithelial proliferation in mucinous borderline tumor and confluent/expansile invasion; the distinction can be difficult and has interobserver variability. The source does not provide a dedicated required IHC panel for mucinous borderline tumor. In difficult cases, a mutation-type p53 pattern involving a large proportion of tumor tissue (>30%) favors mucinous carcinoma over borderline tumor with complex epithelial proliferation. Mucinous carcinoma Invasive mucinous neoplasm composed of gastrointestinal-type epithelium. Two invasive patterns are recognized, each requiring at least 5 mm linear extent. Confluent/expansile invasion: marked glandular crowding with little or no intervening stroma, producing a labyrinthine appearance; papillary and cribriform areas may occur. Infiltrative/destructive invasion: irregular glands, nests, and single malignant cells infiltrating stroma, often with desmoplasia. Estimate the proportion of this component among all carcinomatous areas. A minute infiltrative focus in a tumor with expansile invasion should not automatically reclassify the whole tumor as infiltrative/destructive type. The proportion of infiltrative invasion is prognostically important; a 10% threshold separates low from high proportion in the recommended growth-pattern grading approach. Usually large, unilateral, and predominantly ovarian. Bilaterality and/or size below 13 cm should raise suspicion for metastasis; advanced-stage disease is uncommon in primary ovarian mucinous carcinoma. Typically diffuse CK7; CK20, CEA, and CDX2 are variable; CA19-9 is often diffuse. CA125, WT1, napsin A, vimentin, ER, and PR are usually negative. PAX8 is usually focal/weak in a subset. p16 is usually negative or non-block; p53 may be wild-type or mutation-type. Diffuse strong SATB2 is present in fewer than 10% of primary ovarian mucinous carcinomas; in the absence of teratoma, it should raise concern for lower gastrointestinal/appendiceal metastasis. A CK7/SATB2 panel is useful for primary ovarian versus colorectal/appendiceal origin; PAX8 and CDX2 are secondary markers. Upper GI and pancreatobiliary metastases may overlap immunophenotypically. Do not equate mucin extravasation or mucin granulomas with stromal invasion. Infiltrative invasion, especially with bilateral ovarian involvement, should trigger a search for an extraovarian primary. A mutation-type p53 pattern in >30% of tumor tissue favors mucinous carcinoma in borderline-versus-expansile invasion dilemmas. Metastatic colorectal / appendiceal adenocarcinoma Often bilateral and/or smaller; infiltrative glands, single cells, or signet-ring cells may be present. Diffuse SATB2 and CDX2 with absent or limited CK7 support lower GI origin; primary ovarian mucinous carcinoma is usually diffusely CK7-positive and SATB2 is rarely diffuse. Metastatic upper GI / pancreatobiliary carcinoma May be CK7-positive and overlap with primary ovarian mucinous carcinoma. Bilaterality, surface/hilar involvement, multinodular growth, signet-ring cells, and clinical/radiologic evidence of a GI primary are important clues. Endometrioid carcinoma with mucinous differentiation Look for conventional endometrioid glands, squamous morules, endometriosis, and ER/PR expression; diffuse CK20/CDX2 or intestinal morphology alone does not establish a primary mucinous carcinoma. Primary ovarian mucinous carcinoma is usually unilateral, large, and stage I; a bilateral small tumor should be treated as metastatic until proven otherwise. The source defines invasive growth by at least 5 mm linear extent for either expansile or infiltrative pattern. Endometrioid tumors Müllerian endometrioid differentiation, often arising in endometriosis. Evaluate the endometrium because synchronous endometrial hyperplasia/carcinoma is common. Endometrioid adenofibroma Widely spaced, cytologically bland endometrioid glands in a fibromatous stroma. Often associated with endometriosis or an endometriotic cyst. Morular, squamous, and mucinous differentiation may occur; dystrophic stromal calcifications may be present. No glandular crowding, cytologic atypia, confluent growth, or destructive stromal invasion. The source does not specify a mandatory IHC profile for benign endometrioid adenofibroma. In practice, glands generally show Müllerian/endometrioid differentiation; correlate with endometriosis and morphology. Endometrioid borderline tumor Crowded endometrioid glands or simple papillae with low-grade cytologic atypia, but without confluent/expansile growth or infiltrative/destructive stromal invasion. Two patterns: intracystic proliferation protruding into an endometriotic cyst (glandular or simple papillary architecture with pseudostratified columnar cells), and the more common adenofibromatous pattern (crowded, irregular glands in fibromatous stroma with lobular architecture). Mild-to-moderate atypia and usually low mitotic activity. Morular/squamous metaplasia is common; mucinous metaplasia may occur. Confluent morular metaplasia alone does not establish carcinoma. Extensive sampling is recommended to exclude endometrioid carcinoma; these tumors are very rarely encountered without associated endometriosis or another endometrioid lesion. PAX8, CK7, ER, and PR positive; WT1 variable. Morules typically show nuclear β-catenin. Coexisting endometrial hyperplasia or carcinoma is common; evaluate the endometrium. Do not mistake confluent morular metaplasia for confluent glandular invasion. Confluent back-to-back or cribriform glandular proliferation is the most common pattern; less commonly destructive glands/nests with desmoplastic stroma occur. Neoplastic glands have smooth luminal borders and round-to-oval nuclei with open chromatin and low-to-moderate atypia. Solid growth is usually a minor component but may predominate in a subset. Morular or squamous differentiation occurs in about half; mucinous, secretory, clear-cell-like, sex-cord-like, spindle-cell, oxyphilic, ciliated, and corded/hyalinized patterns may occur. Grade using the FIGO grading system for endometrial endometrioid carcinoma. Grade 3 is a diagnosis of exclusion after excluding HGSC and metastasis. Most are unilateral and large, frequently associated with endometriosis/endometriotic cyst. Concurrent endometrial hyperplasia or carcinoma may be present. PAX8 and ER/PR are positive in most cases (approximately 81–85%). WT1 and napsin A are usually negative, although exceptions occur. CDX2 and SATB2 may be expressed in subsets, particularly with intestinal/mucinous differentiation. Nuclear β-catenin may be present with CTNNB1 alterations. MMR IHC should be performed where possible for Lynch syndrome screening. p53, MMR, and POLE testing can classify molecular subgroups; mutation-type p53 suggests a copy-number-high subgroup. High-grade endometrioid carcinoma can overlap with HGSC; HGSC is more common and typically shows WT1 and mutation-type p53. Sex-cord-like endometrioid carcinoma may mimic sex cord-stromal tumors; use PAX8, ER/PR, and appropriate sex cord markers in a panel. Synchronous low-grade endometrial and ovarian endometrioid carcinomas may be clonally related yet behave indolently; apply current FIGO criteria and clinicopathologic correlation. High-grade serous carcinoma Usually marked pleomorphism, brisk mitoses, atypical mitoses, and mutation-type p53; WT1 is commonly diffuse. Endometrioid carcinoma more often has smooth back-to-back glands, squamous morules, and ER/PR positivity. Clear cell carcinoma Hobnail cells, tubulocystic/papillary/solid patterns, hyalinized stroma, and napsin A/HNF1β positivity with ER/PR/WT1 negativity favor clear cell carcinoma. Sex cord-stromal tumor Sertoli-like tubules, cords, or trabeculae may mimic endometrioid carcinoma. Demonstrate epithelial/Müllerian differentiation (PAX8, keratins, ER/PR) and use inhibin, calretinin, SF1, and other sex cord markers as needed. Endometriosis is a common precursor/background association but is not by itself diagnostic. MMR IHC is important not only diagnostically but also for Lynch syndrome screening. Clear cell tumors Müllerian clear cell differentiation, frequently associated with endometriosis. The key borderline-versus-malignant distinction is adenofibromatous architecture without papillary growth or stromal invasion versus a characteristic malignant tubulocystic/papillary/solid tumor. Clear cell adenofibroma Adenofibromatous tumor with variably sized glands in fibromatous stroma; low cuboidal cells have clear or eosinophilic cytoplasm. In the bland form, nuclei are small without chromatin abnormalities or nucleoli and mitoses are typically absent. No papillary architecture, densely aggregated glands, tubulocystic/solid carcinoma-like architecture, or stromal invasion. The source does not provide a required IHC profile for clear cell adenofibroma. ER/PR may be negative or weakly positive in clear cell borderline tumors. Clear cell borderline tumor (CCBT) Adenofibromatous clear cell tumor with variable nuclear atypia but no papillary architecture and no stromal invasion. Glands are embedded in fibromatous stroma; cells are low cuboidal with clear or eosinophilic cytoplasm. Enlarged nuclei and occasional nucleoli are permitted; minimal nuclear stratification may occur. Densely aggregated glands, papillary or tubulocystic architecture, and a stromal response to invasion are absent by definition. Extensive sampling is required to exclude an associated clear cell carcinoma; CCBT is often a component rather than the sole element of a tumor. ER and PR may be negative or weakly positive. The source does not define a required borderline-specific panel. Clear cell carcinoma (CCC) Characteristic admixture of tubulocystic, papillary, and solid architecture. Tubulocystic areas show tubules/cysts, sometimes with dense eosinophilic luminal secretions, lined by hobnail, cuboidal, or attenuated cells. Papillary pattern: simple, non-branching papillae with round stromal cores; some hierarchical branching is permitted. Cells are cuboidal and/or hobnail, usually single-layered with minimal stratification. Solid pattern: sheets of polyhedral cells separated by delicate septa. Cytoplasm is clear (glycogen-rich, PAS-positive and diastase-sensitive) or eosinophilic; targetoid cells may occur. Nuclei are enlarged and monomorphic, with rounded-to-angulated contours, hyperchromasia, and prominent nucleoli. Pleomorphism may be focal; mitotic activity is variable and often low. Stromal hyalinization and myxoid stroma are frequent. Usually unilateral and associated with endometriosis; grading is not applicable. Typically PAX8, napsin A, HNF1β, and AMACR positive. Typically WT1, ER, and PR negative. ARID1A loss occurs in about half and often correlates with ARID1A mutation; PIK3CA alterations are common. p53 mutation is less common than in HGSC; use the full morphologic/IHC profile rather than a single stain. Clear/eosinophilic cytoplasm alone is not enough: require the characteristic architecture and cytology. Endometrioid carcinoma with clear-cell change often retains ER/PR and may show squamous morules; napsin A/ HNF1β support CCC. Endometrioid carcinoma with clear-cell/secretory change Often has conventional endometrioid glands, squamous morules, and ER/PR expression. CCC is typically ER/PR-negative and napsin A/HNF1β-positive, with hobnail cells and tubulocystic architecture. Metastatic renal cell carcinoma Can show clear cells and delicate vasculature. Correlate with renal history/imaging and use PAX8 with renal markers (e.g., CAIX, CD10, RCC marker); ovarian CCC typically expresses napsin A/HNF1β and has Müllerian morphology. Yolk sac tumor Reticular/microcystic and glandular patterns can overlap. Yolk sac tumor typically expresses SALL4, AFP, and glypican-3, whereas CCC expresses PAX8 and napsin A/HNF1β. Endometriosis is present in a substantial proportion of CCCs. ARID1A loss is supportive in context but is not specific to CCC. Seromucinous tumors Müllerian-type epithelial admixture, often associated with endometriosis. WHO classification no longer recognizes a distinct seromucinous carcinoma entity. Seromucinous cystadenoma / adenofibroma Cysts or glands lined by bland Müllerian-type epithelium: endocervical-type mucinous, ciliated/serous, and/or endometrioid cells in varying proportions. Predominantly single-layered lining; occasional mild stratification and broad papillae with no or minimal hierarchical branching may occur. Adenofibroma has widely spaced bland glands in prominent hypocellular fibromatous stroma. If epithelial stratification or hierarchical branching exceeds 10% of the lining, a borderline designation is appropriate. Endometriosis is common; bilateral involvement may occur. PAX8, ER, PR, and CK7 are generally positive; WT1 and CK20 are generally negative. Seromucinous borderline tumor (SMBT) Architecturally complex papillary neoplasm with hierarchical branching papillae and variably edematous or fibrous stromal cores. Low-grade stratified and often tufted epithelium showing an admixture of Müllerian cell types: endocervical-type mucinous, ciliated/serous, endometrioid, hobnail, clear, squamous, and eosinophilic cells. Conspicuous neutrophils may infiltrate edematous papillary cores and epithelium. No confluent/expansile or destructive invasion. Endometriosis and an associated benign serous or mucinous cystadenoma are common. Bilaterality can occur. PAX8, ER, PR, and CK7 generally positive; WT1 and CK20 negative; p53 wild-type pattern. KRAS and PIK3CA mutations are frequent; ARID1A loss occurs in a subset. The previously recognized malignant counterpart, seromucinous carcinoma, is not a distinct entity in the WHO fifth/sixth edition framework; reclassify malignant cases according to morphology and molecular findings, most often as endometrioid carcinoma. Endometrioid borderline tumor / carcinoma with mucinous or serous metaplasia Endometrioid glands, morular/squamous metaplasia, and endometriosis may overlap. The distinction may require architectural review and a panel; the source notes clinicopathologic and molecular overlap. Serous borderline tumor SBT is composed of tubal-type serous epithelium and typically expresses WT1; SMBT shows a Müllerian epithelial admixture, often with endocervical-type mucinous and endometrioid components, and is generally WT1-negative. Gastrointestinal-type goblet-cell/foveolar differentiation supports mucinous borderline tumor; SMBT is defined by Müllerian-type admixture and lacks gastrointestinal-type differentiation. Do not diagnose seromucinous carcinoma as a separate histotype under the supplied WHO framework. SMBT commonly arises in or alongside endometriosis. Brenner tumors Urothelial-type epithelium in fibrous ovarian stroma. Benign and borderline lesions are often associated with a benign Brenner component; malignant Brenner tumor requires unequivocal stromal invasion. Benign Brenner tumor Well-circumscribed nests of bland urothelial/transitional-type epithelium embedded in dense fibrous stroma. Nests may show central lumina or microcysts; nuclei are uniform with longitudinal grooves. No significant atypia, brisk mitoses, complex papillary proliferation, or stromal invasion. Typically p63 and GATA3 positive; ER, PR, and WT1 negative. p53 shows a wild-type pattern; p16 may be lost in a subset. Borderline Brenner tumor Complex papillary growth resembling a low-grade papillary urothelial neoplasm, but without stromal invasion. Cells are usually uniform with elongated nuclei, fine chromatin, and visible nucleoli; moderate-to-severe atypia may occasionally occur. Mucinous or squamous metaplasia is common. Benign Brenner tumor areas are nearly always present. Crowded, tortuous nests and increased mitoses may occur, but invasion must be absent. Typically unilateral and confined to the ovary; often a large cystic tumor with papillary masses projecting into the lumen. Usually p63 and GATA3 positive; ER, PR, and WT1 negative. p53 wild-type; p16 loss may occur. Malignant Brenner tumor Invasive carcinoma resembling urothelial carcinoma, with irregularly shaped masses of atypical urothelial-type cells and often focal squamous differentiation. Cystic areas may be lined by multilayered atypical epithelium with hyperchromatic pleomorphic nuclei, prominent nucleoli, dense eosinophilic cytoplasm, and brisk mitotic activity. Desmoplastic stromal reaction helps identify unequivocal invasion in a densely fibromatous background. A benign or borderline Brenner component is essential. If absent, consider HGSC or endometrioid carcinoma with transitional-cell-like differentiation, primary urothelial carcinoma, or squamous carcinoma. WT1 negative; ER/PR negative or weak. p53 is usually wild-type but variable; p16 may be lost with CDKN2A deletion. GATA3 data are limited and may be positive or negative; p63 may be positive. HGSC with transitional-cell-like morphology Usually has mutation-type p53 and WT1 expression and lacks a convincing benign/borderline Brenner component. Extensive sampling and a broad panel are required. Endometrioid carcinoma with squamous differentiation Look for conventional endometrioid glands, squamous morules, ER/PR expression, and endometriosis; a true Brenner tumor shows urothelial nests in fibrous stroma and GATA3/p63 expression. Metastatic urothelial carcinoma Requires clinical history and exclusion of a urinary tract primary. A benign/borderline Brenner component supports primary ovarian malignant Brenner tumor; GATA3/p63 alone cannot establish ovarian origin. A benign or borderline Brenner component is a required diagnostic anchor for malignant Brenner tumor. Invasion may be subtle in dense fibrous stroma; look for irregular infiltrative nests and desmoplasia. Mesonephric-like carcinoma Adenocarcinoma with mesonephric differentiation but without mesonephric remnants; considered a Müllerian carcinoma with secondary mesonephric transdifferentiation. Usually unilateral, solid or mixed solid-cystic ovarian mass. Histology shows a mixture of tubular, glandular/pseudoendometrioid, ductal (slit-like or angulated glands), papillary, and solid patterns. Eosinophilic colloid-like luminal material may be present. Nuclei are often angulated with open/vesicular chromatin; nuclear overlap and grooves are frequent. No squamous or mucinous elements. Other Müllerian components (e.g., endometrioid carcinoma) may coexist; if distinct, classify as mixed carcinoma. Essential diagnosis is prototypical mesonephric carcinoma morphology; GATA3 or TTF1 expression and reduced/absent ER/PR are desirable. Most cases express GATA3 and/or TTF1; CD10 may show luminal staining; PAX8 may be positive. WT1 is negative. ER/PR are significantly reduced or absent; p53 is typically wild-type and MMR proficient. KRAS codon 12 (most common) or codon 13 mutation may help in challenging cases. The lack of mesonephric remnants is part of the definition; do not require a remnant. Endometrioid carcinoma with tubular/sex-cord-like pattern Usually expresses ER/PR and may show squamous/morular differentiation; mesonephric-like carcinoma is typically ER/PR-negative, WT1-negative, and GATA3/TTF1-positive with angulated nuclei and colloid-like luminal material. CCC has hobnail cells, characteristic tubulocystic/papillary/solid architecture, and napsin A/HNF1β positivity; mesonephric-like carcinoma more often has angulated nuclei, luminal colloid, GATA3/TTF1, and reduced ER/PR. Metastatic mesonephric carcinoma from cervix Review clinical history and cervical pathology; ovarian mesonephric-like carcinoma is defined by ovarian presentation without mesonephric remnants and requires exclusion of a cervical primary. Undifferentiated / dedifferentiated carcinoma High-grade malignant epithelial neoplasm lacking overt differentiation (undifferentiated) or showing an abrupt transition from a differentiated component, usually low-grade endometrioid carcinoma (dedifferentiated). Undifferentiated carcinoma / dedifferentiated carcinoma Undifferentiated carcinoma: sheet-like growth of monotonous, discohesive, round cells with minimal cytoplasm, often with geographic necrosis, brisk mitotic activity, and prominent tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes. Rhabdoid features and focal spindle cells may occur. Dedifferentiated carcinoma: biphasic tumor with a differentiated component (usually FIGO grade 1 or 2 endometrioid carcinoma) and an undifferentiated component; the interface may be abrupt. Large, often advanced-stage solid masses with extensive necrosis are typical. Exclude small cell carcinoma of hypercalcemic type and other mimics. Undifferentiated component often shows only focal EMA, pancytokeratin, and CK18; PAX8 is focal or absent. ER, PR, and E-cadherin are usually negative. Loss of SMARCA4 (BRG1), concurrent ARID1A/ARID1B loss, and sometimes SMARCB1 (INI1) loss occur. dMMR is frequent in a subset. ARID1A loss alone is not evidence of dedifferentiation because it is common in endometrioid and clear cell carcinomas. p53 is usually wild-type unless the differentiated component is HGSC. CD138 can be expressed and should not be used alone to diagnose plasmacytoid differentiation. MMR proficiency may help distinguish from small cell carcinoma of hypercalcemic type, which is typically MMR proficient; correlate with SMARCA4 and clinical context. Small cell carcinoma of the ovary, hypercalcemic type Often occurs in young patients and may show small blue cells, follicle-like spaces, and rhabdoid cells; SMARCA4/BRG1 loss is characteristic. Distinguish with age, morphology, calcium status, and molecular/IHC profile. Usually retains epithelial cohesion and shows mutation-type p53, WT1, and PAX8 more consistently. Undifferentiated carcinoma is discohesive with only focal epithelial markers and often loss of SWI/SNF proteins. Lymphoma / melanoma / sarcoma The undifferentiated morphology may mimic non-epithelial malignancies. Use broad lineage exclusion (CD45, SOX10/S100, desmin, myogenin, etc.) alongside epithelial markers. Carcinosarcoma Biphasic malignant neoplasm of epithelial origin with high-grade carcinoma and sarcoma components; molecular findings support a monoclonal origin. Ovarian carcinosarcoma Distinct but usually intermingled high-grade carcinomatous and sarcomatous components; either may predominate. Carcinomatous component is most often HGSC, but endometrioid and other carcinoma types occur. Sarcomatous component is homologous when nonspecific stromal sarcoma is present; heterologous when rhabdomyosarcoma (most common), chondrosarcoma, osteosarcoma, or rarely liposarcoma/angiosarcoma is identified. Usually a large predominantly solid mass with hemorrhage and necrosis; often advanced stage. IHC should demonstrate epithelial differentiation in the carcinoma component and characterize the sarcomatous component with morphology-directed markers. Concordant TP53 abnormalities in both components support a common clonal origin; no single required panel is specified in the supplied source. Dedifferentiated carcinoma Dedifferentiated carcinoma has an undifferentiated epithelial component, often with focal keratin/EMA, and usually a low-grade endometrioid differentiated component. Carcinosarcoma has a true sarcomatous component, sometimes with heterologous differentiation. Collision carcinoma and sarcoma A collision tumor is spatially distinct and may lack shared molecular alterations. Carcinosarcoma typically has intimately admixed components and concordant molecular abnormalities. Carcinoma with reactive/desmoplastic stroma Reactive stroma lacks a morphologically malignant mesenchymal population and does not show heterologous sarcomatous differentiation. Mixed carcinoma Two or more unequivocally distinct ovarian carcinoma histotypes in one tumor; confirm components morphologically and, when available, immunohistochemically. Mixed ovarian carcinoma At least two clearly recognizable histological types must be present on H&E. Any confidently demonstrable proportion of a second histotype is sufficient; report the types and percentage of each component. Confirm distinct components with IHC when available. The most common combination is endometrioid and clear cell carcinoma; napsin A highlights clear cell differentiation and PR supports endometrioid differentiation. Distinguish from a single histotype with ambiguous/heterogeneous morphology and from independent collision tumors, which are usually spatially distinct and do not share molecular alterations. Dedifferentiated carcinoma and carcinosarcoma are classified separately rather than as mixed carcinoma. Use component-directed panels. Examples: napsin A-positive clear cell component versus PR-positive endometrioid component. MMR deficiency may be present, especially in mixed endometrioid/clear cell carcinoma. Single histotype with morphologic mimicry A single carcinoma may show clear, mucinous, sex-cord-like, or transitional-like areas without representing a second true histotype. Require distinct, reproducible morphologic and preferably immunophenotypic components. Collision tumors Two spatially separate neoplasms without shared molecular alterations favor collision tumors rather than a mixed carcinoma. Carcinosarcoma / dedifferentiated carcinoma Carcinosarcoma contains malignant sarcoma; dedifferentiated carcinoma has a differentiated plus undifferentiated epithelial component. Both are separate diagnostic categories. Serous Tubal-type epithelium; SBT is hierarchical papillary and non-invasive; LGSC requires invasion with low-grade nuclei; HGSC requires high-grade nuclei and/or high mitotic activity, usually with mutation-type p53. Mucinous Simple mucinous lining → benign; epithelial complexity without invasion → borderline; ≥5 mm confluent/expansile or infiltrative/destructive invasion → carcinoma. Always exclude metastasis. Endometrioid Bland spaced glands in fibrous stroma → adenofibroma; crowded glands/simple papillae without invasion → borderline; confluent back-to-back glands or destructive invasion → carcinoma. Clear cell Adenofibromatous glands without papillae/invasion → clear cell adenofibroma/CCBT; characteristic tubulocystic, papillary, and solid patterns with malignant nuclei → CCC. Seromucinous Bland Müllerian admixture → benign; complex hierarchical papillae without invasion → SMBT; no separate seromucinous carcinoma category in current WHO framework. Brenner Bland urothelial nests → benign; complex papillary urothelial proliferation without invasion → borderline; invasive urothelial carcinoma plus benign/borderline Brenner component → malignant. Ovarian epithelial pathology emerald amber rose border-emerald-200 bg-emerald-50 text-emerald-950 border-amber-200 bg-amber-50 text-amber-950 border-rose-200 bg-rose-50 text-rose-950 ( Diagnostic criteria Immunohistochemistry Pitfalls PathologyGPS · Female Genital Tract Ovarian Epithelial Tumors A histotype-based diagnostic guide focused on the distinction between benign, borderline, and malignant ovarian epithelial tumors. The central diagnostic questions are: What is the epithelial lineage? Is the proliferation merely complex, or is there unequivocal stromal invasion? Does the tumor fit a specific molecular and immunophenotypic profile? Step 1 Identify histotype Serous · mucinous · endometrioid · clear cell · other Step 2 Assess architecture Simple lining · epithelial proliferation · stromal invasion Step 3 Use targeted IHC Confirm lineage and exclude metastasis or mimics The diagnostic hierarchy Borderline tumors are not simply 'low-grade carcinomas.' They are epithelial proliferations that lack destructive stromal invasion. Invasion must be assessed in the context of the histotype-specific architecture and cytology. Benign Simple or minimally proliferative epithelium, bland nuclei, absent/minimal mitoses, and no invasion. Fibromatous stroma defines adenofibromatous forms. Borderline Architecturally complex epithelial proliferation with low-grade cytology, but no confluent/expansile or destructive stromal invasion. Adequate sampling is essential. Malignant Histotype-specific malignant cytology and/or unequivocal stromal invasion. The pattern and extent of invasion may carry prognostic significance. Rapid histotype recognition Use these high-yield patterns to orient the differential before applying the benign/borderline/malignant criteria. Histotype Recognition pattern Benign category Not defined by WHO classification. Borderline category Malignant category Differential diagnosis: characteristic findings Diagnostic pearls Practical work-up and sampling strategy The most frequent diagnostic error is under-sampling a large heterogeneous tumor or diagnosing invasion from cytologic atypia alone. Gross examination Document laterality, size, surface involvement, capsule integrity, solid versus cystic components, papillary excrescences, mural nodules, necrosis, and relationship to the ovarian hilum. Bilaterality and smaller size are important warning signs for metastatic mucinous carcinoma. Sampling Extensively sample large multilocular mucinous tumors, solid areas, mural nodules, papillary areas, thickened cyst walls, surface lesions, and interfaces between benign/borderline and suspicious areas. For clear cell adenofibroma/borderline tumor, extensive sampling is specifically required to exclude carcinoma. Determine invasion For serous tumors, distinguish non-invasive implants from destructive infiltrative LGSC. For mucinous carcinoma, identify and measure expansile and infiltrative patterns; each requires at least 5 mm linear extent. For endometrioid tumors, distinguish crowded glands from confluent back-to-back growth or destructive invasion. Select IHC by differential PAX8/WT1/ER for serous lineage; CK7/SATB2/CDX2/PAX8 for mucinous origin; PAX8/ER/PR/β-catenin for endometrioid; napsin A/HNF1β for clear cell; GATA3/TTF1/CD10 for mesonephric-like; p63/GATA3 for Brenner. Interpret panels, not single stains. Exclude extraovarian primary For mucinous tumors, correlate with appendix and GI tract. For HGSC, examine the fallopian tubes, especially fimbria, for STIC or invasive tubal carcinoma. For endometrioid carcinoma, evaluate the endometrium and apply current criteria to synchronous tumors. Report precisely State histotype, grade where applicable, invasion pattern and extent, surface/capsule involvement, implants, laterality, and percentage of each component in mixed carcinoma. Do not use 'microinvasion' for SBT stromal foci under the supplied terminology. Important terminology and classification notes The supplied WHO material uses American spelling in this page: tumor, tumor cells, edema, and tumor-associated terminology. Seromucinous carcinoma is not retained as a distinct entity in the WHO fifth/sixth edition framework described in the source. Reclassify according to the actual morphology, most often as endometrioid carcinoma. For serous borderline tumors, the term 'microinvasion' is no longer recommended for small stromal foci of individual cells or small clusters that are considered biologically inert; describe the finding instead. For serous borderline tumors, an extraovarian lesion with destructive infiltrative growth is designated low-grade serous carcinoma rather than an invasive implant. For mucinous carcinoma, primary ovarian origin must be established; bilateral or relatively small tumors and infiltrative invasion should prompt careful exclusion of a gastrointestinal or pancreatobiliary primary. When a benign or borderline tier is not recognized, it is labeled “Not defined by WHO classification.” Educational use only. This page is a diagnostic reference and does not replace review of the complete clinical history, imaging, gross findings, histologic sampling, immunohistochemistry, molecular testing, and current staging criteria. Apply the current WHO classification and institutional reporting standards. When the source material does not establish a required immunophenotype or a benign/borderline counterpart, this page explicitly avoids creating one.

title: Non Epithelial Tumors
content: use client Sex cord-stromal tumors Pure stromal tumors Ovarian fibroma Firm, white, collagen-rich mass; bland spindle cells. Intersecting fascicles of bland spindle-to-ovoid fibroblastic cells in variably collagenous stroma; hyalinized plaques and calcification may occur. Mitoses are usually uncommon. Cellular fibroma has increased cellularity but only mild atypia. Mitotically active cellular fibroma has >4 mitoses/10 HPF without diffuse significant atypia or coagulative tumor-cell necrosis. Inhibin, calretinin, FOXL2, CD56, and SF1 may be positive, often weakly or focally. Reticulin shows a complete pericellular pattern. FOXL2 and DICER1 alterations are absent; absence of FOXL2 can help when adult granulosa cell tumor is considered. Thecoma: plumper cells with pale or lipid-rich cytoplasm and individual-cell reticulin. Adult granulosa cell tumor: reticulin surrounds nests rather than individual cells; consider FOXL2 testing. Cellular fibroma/mitotically active cellular fibroma should not be upgraded to fibrosarcoma solely for mitotic activity. Benign; surface rupture/adhesions, especially in cellular tumors, may be associated with late local recurrence. Thecoma Yellow-tan tumor with diffuse growth of plump theca-like cells. Diffuse or less often nested/lobulated growth of uniform cells with appreciable pale-gray or clear lipid-rich cytoplasm and indistinct cell borders. Nuclei are bland; mitoses absent or minimal. Hyaline plaques or a minor fibromatous component may occur. Reticulin surrounds individual cells. Typically inhibin, calretinin, SF1, and other sex cord-stromal markers; staining can be focal. No recurrent molecular alteration established. FOXL2/DICER1 are generally absent; a FOXL2 mutation should prompt consideration of adult granulosa cell tumor with thecoma-like morphology. Fibroma: spindle cells and collagen dominate, with less abundant pale cytoplasm. Adult granulosa cell tumor: grooved nuclei, varied sex cord patterns, and loss/reduction of pericellular reticulin. Avoid the non-recommended term fibrothecoma; classify as fibroma or thecoma based on the predominant morphology. Almost always benign; reported malignant examples may represent other tumor types. Luteinized thecoma associated with sclerosing peritonitis Usually bilateral ovarian spindle-cell proliferation with bowel-obstructing sclerosing peritonitis. Bilateral, often cortical spindle-cell proliferation with edema/microcysts, entrapped follicles, and scattered luteinized or weakly luteinized cells. Spindle cells can be mitotically active but bland; ovarian medulla may be relatively spared. Spindle cells usually SF1/FOXL2 positive but inhibin/calretinin negative; luteinized cells are inhibin/calretinin positive. Conventional thecoma is usually unilateral and composed predominantly of plump theca-like cells. Cellular fibroma is typically collagenous and lacks the characteristic bilateral pattern and associated sclerosing peritonitis. Ovarian lesion is benign; morbidity and mortality relate to sclerosing peritonitis and intestinal obstruction. Sclerosing stromal tumor Young patient; pseudolobules, alternating cellular and edematous zones, and prominent vessels. Well-circumscribed pseudolobulated tumor. Cellular nodules contain a haphazard admixture of epithelioid/luteinized and spindle cells, separated by hypocellular edematous, collagenous, or myxoid stroma. Thin-walled dilated, often hemangiopericytoma-like vessels are characteristic. Inhibin, calretinin, and SF1 are usually positive, sometimes focally; cytokeratin and EMA are usually negative. TFE3 expression may occur without a TFE3 rearrangement. FHL2::GLI2 fusion or other GLI2 rearrangements have been reported in a subset. Thecoma: lacks the characteristic pseudolobular architecture and prominent branching/dilated vessels. Adult granulosa cell tumor: lacks the typical alternating pseudolobules and has a different reticulin pattern. Metastatic or primary vascular neoplasms are excluded by the mixed sex cord-stromal cell population and immunophenotype. Benign in nearly all reported cases. Microcystic stromal tumor Solid and microcystic architecture with fibrous septa; nuclear β-catenin. Well-circumscribed, unencapsulated neoplasm with variable proportions of solid cellular zones, small rounded microcysts, and fibrous septa/hyaline plaques. Uniform round-to-epithelioid cells have lightly eosinophilic granular cytoplasm; intracytoplasmic vacuoles and signet-ring-like cells may occur. Mitoses are usually low. Diffuse nuclear/cytoplasmic β-catenin, CD10, WT1, cyclin D1, FOXL2, and SF1. Inhibin and calretinin are typically negative; EMA usually negative. CTNNB1 or APC pathogenic variants, usually mutually exclusive. APC alteration may prompt evaluation for familial adenomatous polyposis. Signet-ring stromal tumor: lacks the characteristic microcystic/solid-septated pattern and is typically β-catenin/cyclin D1 negative. Sex cord-stromal tumors: often inhibin/calretinin positive and do not show the characteristic nuclear β-catenin profile. Metastatic signet-ring carcinoma: mucin-positive and typically epithelial-marker positive. Usually benign; rare pelvic/abdominal recurrence or metastasis is reported, but predictive features are not defined. Signet-ring stromal tumor Bland signet-ring cells in fibromatous stroma; vacuoles are not mucin. Variable numbers of cells with a single large cytoplasmic vacuole in fibroma-like/cellular fibroma-like stroma. Nuclei are eccentric, small, uniform, and bland; mitoses rare or absent. Vacuoles do not contain mucin, glycogen, or lipid. Limited data: often SF1, CD10, and WT1 positive; inhibin/calretinin/cytokeratin variable; EMA consistently negative. Desirable profile includes cyclin D1 negative and no nuclear β-catenin. Metastatic signet-ring adenocarcinoma: mucin-containing vacuoles, epithelial/EMA expression, and often infiltrative growth. Microcystic stromal tumor: nuclear β-catenin and cyclin D1 positivity, with solid/microcystic architecture. Benign. Leydig cell tumor Small hilar-centered steroid-cell nodule; Reinke crystals are a helpful clue. Well-circumscribed nodule centered in or predominantly confined to ovarian hilum. Large polygonal cells have abundant eosinophilic or pale cytoplasm, often with lipochrome pigment; clustered nuclei create intervening eosinophilic nuclear-free zones. Reinke crystals may be present but are often absent. Mitoses rare or absent. Inhibin, calretinin, SF1, and Melan-A usually positive; SATB2 may show cytoplasmic staining. Steroid cell tumor, NOS: involves ovarian parenchyma rather than being hilar-centered. Metastatic renal/adrenal or other clear-cell neoplasms: correlate with clinical history and broader immunophenotype. A hilar location with otherwise classic morphology supports Leydig cell tumor even without Reinke crystals. Almost always benign when strict diagnostic criteria are applied. Steroid cell tumor Distinct ovarian mass composed entirely of steroid-secreting cells; assess malignant-risk features. Tumor consists of cells with steroid-cell morphology, typically abundant eosinophilic, granular, or vacuolated cytoplasm. Solid or solid-cystic, often yellow/orange/red/brown; hemorrhage and necrosis may occur. The supplied classification excerpt does not provide a complete microscopic description. Sex cord markers are desirable; use inhibin, calretinin, SF1, and Melan-A in context. No pathognomonic recurrent molecular alteration established. Leydig cell tumor: hilar-centered, often small, with lipochrome and sometimes Reinke crystals. Adrenocortical/renal metastasis: clinical and immunophenotypic correlation is essential. Distinguish a true discrete tumor from non-neoplastic hilar/stromal steroid cells. Recurrence and disease-specific death are uncommon but documented. Potential adverse features include size >7 cm, >2 mitoses/10 HPF (0.2 mm²), necrosis, hemorrhage, significant atypia, older age, and stage >IA; none is individually definitive. Pure sex cord tumors Adult granulosa cell tumor Grooved nuclei, variable sex cord patterns, Call–Exner bodies, and FOXL2 p.Cys134Trp. Diffuse, trabecular, corded, nested, microfollicular, macrofollicular, tubular, gyriform, or watered-silk patterns; Call–Exner bodies may be present. Cells usually have scant cytoplasm and pale round-to-oval nuclei with irregular contours and grooves. Fibromatous stroma may be prominent. Reticulin is absent/reduced around individual tumor cells but highlights nests. FOXL2, inhibin, SF1, and calretinin usually positive; EMA typically negative. FOXL2 c.402C>G, p.(Cys134Trp), in >90–95% of cases. False-negative testing can occur in low-cellularity/cystic tumors or those with prominent fibromatous stroma. Fibroma/thecoma: complete pericellular reticulin and more uniformly stromal morphology. Juvenile granulosa cell tumor: younger patients, round nuclei without grooves, macrofollicular/nodular pattern, brisker mitoses; lacks the characteristic FOXL2 mutation. Sertoli cell tumor: tubules are often dominant, but focal tubules alone do not establish a mixed tumor. Malignant potential with frequent late recurrence; stage is most important. Long-term follow-up is required. Juvenile granulosa cell tumor Child/young patient; irregular follicles, round nuclei without grooves, and brisk mitotic activity. Nodular or diffuse growth punctuated by follicles of variable size and shape, often intermediate-sized; basophilic secretions may be present. Cells are epithelioid with round vesicular nuclei usually lacking grooves and abundant eosinophilic, gray, or vacuolated cytoplasm. Mitoses and apoptosis are often conspicuous; stroma may be edematous, myxoid, collagenous, or hyalinized. SF1, inhibin, calretinin, WT1, CD99, CD56, and FOXL2 usually positive; cytokeratins may be positive; EMA usually negative. Lacks the FOXL2 p.Cys134Trp mutation characteristic of adult granulosa cell tumor. AKT1, GNAS, and other alterations occur; DICER1 may be present in a subset. Adult granulosa cell tumor: nuclear grooves, Call–Exner bodies, and FOXL2 mutation. Sertoli–Leydig cell tumor: look for Sertoli tubules/Leydig cells and DICER1; a DICER1-altered SLCT with JGCT-like areas should be classified as SLCT. Excellent when confined to ovary; rupture, positive peritoneal cytology, and extraovarian spread increase recurrence risk. Sertoli cell tumor Sertoliform tubules, often with hormonal manifestations; consider DICER1 and Peutz–Jeghers context. Hollow or solid tubules are present at least focally and often predominate; trabecular, diffuse, alveolar, pseudopapillary, retiform, pseudoendometrioid, and spindle patterns occur. Sertoli cells are cuboidal/columnar with pale, lipid-rich, or deeply eosinophilic cytoplasm and bland oval nuclei. Hyalinized stroma may be present. SF1 and WT1 usually positive; inhibin, calretinin, CD99, and broad-spectrum cytokeratin variable. EMA, CK7, PAX8, and chromogranin typically negative. A subset has DICER1 alterations; STK11 may be relevant in Peutz–Jeghers syndrome. Adult granulosa cell tumor: grooved nuclei and variable patterns; tubular areas can occur, so do not overcall gynandroblastoma. Endometrioid carcinoma: PAX8/EMA/CK7 positivity and glandular atypia support epithelial differentiation. SLCT: identifiable Leydig-cell component and mixed differentiation. Typically benign; adverse behavior is very rare and enriched in tumors with increased atypia and ≥5 mitoses/10 HPF. Sex cord tumor with annular tubules (SCTAT) Rounded nests of ring-like tubules encircling hyaline basement-membrane material. Variably sized rounded nests of simple/complex tubules surrounding central hyaline basement-membrane-like material; cells are tall with pale cytoplasm and basally located nuclei often in antipodal distribution. Calcification and sclerosis may be extensive, especially in Peutz–Jeghers-associated cases. Calretinin, WT1, inhibin, SF1, CD56, and SOX9 usually positive; EMA and CD10 almost always negative. STK11 germline alteration in syndromic cases; consider Peutz–Jeghers syndrome. Sertoli cell tumor: tubules lack the characteristic annular rings and central hyaline material. Adult granulosa cell tumor: Call–Exner bodies are small follicle-like spaces with secretions, not the characteristic annular tubules. Tubular areas in AGCT do not alone imply SCTAT. Peutz–Jeghers-associated tumors are typically benign; nonsyndromic tumors may show extraovarian spread. Mixed sex cord-stromal tumors Sertoli–Leydig cell tumor (SLCT) Sertoli tubules with Leydig cells; androgen excess; DICER1 in many moderate/poorly differentiated tumors. Variable proportions of Sertoli and Leydig cells. Well-differentiated tumors show recognizable tubules and Leydig cells; moderate/poor differentiation shows immature Sertoli-cell patterns, solid growth, and less obvious Leydig cells. Retiform architecture and heterologous elements may occur. Grade/differentiation and extensive sampling matter. Sex cord markers including inhibin, SF1, calretinin, and FOXL2; cytokeratin may be positive; EMA almost always negative. DICER1 pathogenic variants common in moderate/poorly differentiated and retiform tumors, often with a second hit; consider germline DICER1 evaluation. Well-differentiated SLCTs are generally DICER1 wild type and represent a distinct group. Juvenile granulosa cell tumor: follicular pattern can mimic SLCT; DICER1 alteration and any true Sertoli component favor SLCT. Pure Sertoli cell tumor lacks a convincing Leydig component. Gynandroblastoma requires two or more distinct tumor components, not focal mimicry within SLCT/AGCT. Behavior varies with differentiation, stage, and adverse histologic features; assess and report heterologous elements and relevant grade. Gynandroblastoma True admixture of at least two distinct sex cord-stromal tumor types. Requires distinct, recognizable components of two or more sex cord-stromal tumor types. A fibromatous component in AGCT, tubular areas in AGCT, or focal JGCT-like areas in DICER1-altered SLCT do not by themselves establish gynandroblastoma. Usually positive for sex cord markers such as inhibin, SF1, calretinin, CD56, and FOXL2. FOXL2 and DICER1 testing may help distinguish from AGCT or SLCT in the appropriate context. Exclude a single tumor with divergent architecture or morphologic mimicry. In particular, AGCT with tubular areas remains AGCT; DICER1-altered SLCT with JGCT-like areas is generally an SLCT variant. Most are benign; rare recurrences reported. Other Sex cord-stromal tumor, NOS Convincing sex cord-stromal differentiation but no definable specific subtype. Use only after adequate sampling and exclusion of recognizable pure stromal, pure sex cord, and mixed subtypes. Describe architecture, cytology, stromal component, mitotic activity, necrosis, and any heterologous differentiation. A panel supporting sex cord-stromal differentiation (e.g., SF1, inhibin, calretinin, FOXL2) is useful but does not reliably subtype the tumor. Revisit AGCT, JGCT, Sertoli cell tumor, SLCT, thecoma/fibroma, and metastatic mimics. IHC confirms lineage more reliably than it separates individual SCST entities. Clinical behavior depends on the specific morphology and stage; avoid assigning a subtype unsupported by the findings. Germ cell tumors Malignant germ cell tumors Dysgerminoma Sheets/nests of large clear germ cells separated by fibrous septa with lymphocytes; KIT/OCT3/4/SALL4. Large uniform polygonal cells with clear-to-granular cytoplasm, distinct cell borders, and central nuclei with prominent nucleoli. Nests/sheets are separated by fibrous septa containing lymphocytes; granulomas may occur. Syncytiotrophoblastic giant cells may be present. SALL4, OCT3/4, KIT (CD117), PLAP, and D2-40 typically positive; CD30 and AFP negative. Syncytiotrophoblastic cells may express hCG. Isochromosome 12p or 12p amplification is common. Yolk sac tumor: reticular/microcystic pattern, hyaline globules, AFP/Glypican-3 positivity, OCT3/4 negative. Lymphoma: leukocyte markers positive, germ-cell markers negative. Clear cell carcinoma: PAX8/keratin positive and OCT3/4 negative. Malignant germ cell tumor; stage is key; often highly treatment-responsive. Yolk sac tumor Reticular/microcystic pattern, Schiller–Duval bodies, hyaline globules, AFP/Glypican-3. Reticular/microcystic, solid, glandular, papillary, hepatoid, or polyvesicular vitelline patterns. Schiller–Duval bodies are characteristic but not always present. Hyaline globules may be intra- or extracellular; cytologic atypia and mitoses vary. SALL4, AFP, Glypican-3, and broad-spectrum cytokeratin typically positive; OCT3/4 negative. Interpret AFP as supportive rather than independently diagnostic. PIK3CA/AKT1 pathway alterations may occur; 12p gain can be seen in germ cell tumor context. Dysgerminoma: OCT3/4 and KIT positive, AFP/Glypican-3 negative. Hepatoid carcinoma/metastatic carcinoma: correlate with PAX8, epithelial markers, clinical history, and other germ-cell components. Somatically derived yolk sac tumor in carcinoma is not a true germ cell tumor and should not be managed as one. Malignant; stage and treatment response are important. Embryonal carcinoma Primitive epithelial sheets/glands with marked atypia; OCT3/4, CD30, SALL4. Primitive, highly atypical epithelial cells in solid, glandular, papillary, or alveolar patterns; brisk mitotic activity, apoptosis, and necrosis are common. May be one component of a mixed germ cell tumor. OCT3/4, CD30, SALL4, and cytokeratins typically positive; distinguish from dysgerminoma (usually CD30 negative) and yolk sac tumor (OCT3/4 negative). Dysgerminoma: uniform clear cells, fibrous septa/lymphocytes, OCT3/4 positive but CD30 negative. Yolk sac tumor: reticular architecture/hyaline globules and AFP/Glypican-3. High-grade carcinoma: use age, morphology, germ-cell markers, and associated components. Malignant; frequently occurs as a component of mixed germ cell tumor. Non-gestational choriocarcinoma Markedly hemorrhagic tumor with cytotrophoblast and syncytiotrophoblast; hCG. Biphasic trophoblastic proliferation with mononuclear cytotrophoblast and multinucleated syncytiotrophoblast, extensive hemorrhage and necrosis. Search for other germ cell components in the tumor. hCG strongly highlights syncytiotrophoblast; cytokeratins and other trophoblastic markers support differentiation. Interpret in clinical context. Gestational choriocarcinoma: clinical/paternity/pregnancy history and molecular genotyping may be needed. Epithelioid trophoblastic tumor and placental site trophoblastic tumor have distinct morphology and immunophenotypes. Somatic carcinoma with trophoblastic differentiation is not automatically a germ cell tumor. Highly malignant; clinical correlation and staging are essential. Malignant mixed germ cell tumor Two or more malignant germ cell components; report each component and its percentage. Any amount of a second malignant germ cell component is sufficient. Components may be intimately admixed or geographically separate. Common combinations include dysgerminoma plus yolk sac tumor, immature teratoma plus yolk sac tumor, and embryonal carcinoma plus yolk sac tumor. Polyembryoma is reserved for tumors with >90% embryoid bodies. Apply component-specific markers: OCT3/4/KIT for dysgerminoma; AFP/Glypican-3 for yolk sac tumor; OCT3/4/CD30 for embryonal carcinoma; hCG for syncytiotrophoblast. Do not label a tumor mixed solely because syncytiotrophoblastic giant cells occur in another component. Identify and quantify each genuine malignant germ cell component; distinguish polyembryoma from a mixed tumor with only scattered embryoid bodies. Malignant; stage is the most important prognostic factor. Teratomas Immature teratoma Immature embryonal tissue, especially neuroepithelium; grade by immature neuroepithelial component. Contains immature tissues, most importantly immature neuroepithelium, in a background of mature teratomatous elements. Sample extensively because immature components may be focal. Report grade and any associated malignant germ cell component. IHC is directed by the immature component and differential; neuroepithelial markers may support primitive neural tissue but morphology remains central. Mature teratoma: mature tissues only. Yolk sac tumor: primitive reticular/solid growth with AFP/Glypican-3 and no organized teratomatous tissue pattern. Somatic-type malignancy arising in teratoma: diagnose and classify the somatic malignancy separately. Malignant germ cell tumor category; prognosis relates to stage and grade. Mature teratoma (including somatic neoplasms arising from teratoma) Mature tissues from multiple germ layers; carefully search for somatic-type neoplasia. Mature differentiated tissues from one or more germ layers, commonly skin/adnexa, neural tissue, respiratory or gastrointestinal epithelium, cartilage, bone, and other tissues. Somatic neoplasms may arise within teratoma; mucinous neoplasms are classified in this section in the current WHO framework. Use lineage-specific IHC for any suspected somatic neoplasm; do not apply a generic teratoma panel. Immature teratoma: immature embryonal tissue/neuroepithelium. Metastatic carcinoma involving a teratoma: assess for transition, anatomic distribution, and clinical history. A somatic malignancy arising in teratoma is not a conventional malignant germ cell component. Mature teratoma is benign; behavior depends on any associated somatic neoplasm. Monodermal teratomas Struma ovarii Thyroid tissue predominates; assess for malignant thyroid-type features. Monodermal teratoma composed predominantly of mature thyroid tissue; may be solid or cystic and may show colloid-filled follicles. Search for other teratomatous elements and for papillary/follicular thyroid-type carcinoma features. Thyroglobulin, TTF-1, and PAX8 support thyroid follicular differentiation. Metastatic thyroid carcinoma: clinical history, bilateral/multifocal ovarian disease, vascular invasion, and absence of other teratomatous elements may raise concern. Benign struma lacks diagnostic malignant nuclear/architectural features. Usually benign; malignant thyroid-type neoplasia may arise and should be classified by its morphology. Ovarian carcinoid Well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumor; exclude metastasis, especially GI primary. Insular, trabecular, strumal, or mucinous patterns. Uniform round-to-oval cells have pink cytoplasm and salt-and-pepper chromatin; argentaffin granules may be seen. Mucinous carcinoid may show crowded glands/cribriforming; carcinoma arising in mucinous carcinoid shows solid/signet-ring growth, severe atypia, brisk mitoses, and mucin depletion. INSM1, chromogranin, synaptophysin, and CD56 positive; Ki-67 typically low. CDX2/SATB2 may be positive and do not independently establish primary ovarian origin. Metastatic GI/lung NET: integrate history, laterality, size, nodularity, teratomatous elements, and LVI. Small unilateral tumor with teratoma favors primary ovarian origin; bilateral large multinodular disease without teratoma favors metastasis. Usually excellent prognosis; advanced stage and poorly differentiated mucinous carcinoid are concerning. Other monodermal teratomas Mature tissue derived predominantly from one germ layer or a specialized tissue type. Includes specialized monodermal teratomas such as thyroid-type and neuroendocrine/pituitary-type lesions. Identify the dominant differentiated tissue and assess for associated teratomatous elements or a somatic neoplasm. Use lineage-specific markers based on the dominant tissue (e.g., pituitary hormones/transcription factors for pituitary-type adenoma). Metastasis from an extraovarian primary should be excluded using clinical history, morphology, and lineage-specific markers. Distinguish a monodermal teratoma from a somatic neoplasm arising in a conventional teratoma. Generally benign unless a specific associated malignant neoplasm is identified. Gonadal dysgenesis-associated tumors Gonadoblastoma In situ mixed germ-cell/sex-cord lesion in dysgenetic gonad; rounded nests with basement membrane deposits. Rounded nests containing heterogeneous germ cells, including germinoma-like cells, admixed with small sex cord cells and rounded basement-membrane deposits. May show calcification. Search for an associated invasive germ cell tumor. Germ cells: SALL4, OCT3/4, PLAP, D2-40. Sex cord cells: inhibin, calretinin, SF1, FOXL2, weak SOX9. Mixed germ cell–sex cord stromal tumor, unclassified: irregular/haphazard admixture without the characteristic rounded gonadoblastoma nests and basement-membrane deposits. Dysgerminoma: lacks the organized sex cord component. In situ malignancy; not staged. Excision is curative for gonadoblastoma, but associated invasive germ cell tumor changes management. Mixed germ cell–sex cord stromal tumor, unclassified Irregular admixture of dysgerminoma-like germ cells and sex cord cells without classic gonadoblastoma architecture. Large germ cells singly or in small clusters, with pleomorphic nuclei and abundant often clear PAS-positive cytoplasm, intermixed haphazardly with sex cord cells in cords, trabeculae, tubules, cysts, or diffuse growth. Germ cells: SALL4, PLAP, OCT3/4, KIT. Sex cord cells: inhibin, calretinin, SF1. Gonadoblastoma: rounded nests, heterogeneous germ cells, sex cord cells, and basement membrane deposits. Pure dysgerminoma lacks the sex cord component. Most are clinically benign, but a malignant germ cell tumor (most often dysgerminoma) develops in a minority. Miscellaneous tumors Hilar epithelial tumors Rete cystadenoma and rete adenoma Hilar location; benign tubulocystic/adenomatous lesion derived from rete ovarii. Located in ovarian hilum. Rete cystadenoma shows cystic spaces; rete adenoma shows adenomatous/tubular proliferation. Correlate with hilar anatomy and exclude other epithelial tumors. Use a panel to exclude mimics; no single profile should override the characteristic site and morphology. Serous or endometrioid epithelial neoplasm: evaluate epithelial cytology, architecture, and relationship to ovarian surface/inclusion cysts. Metastatic tumor: clinical history and distribution. Solid pseudopapillary neoplasm Solid and pseudopapillary architecture with nuclear β-catenin; exclude pancreatic primary/metastasis. Mixture of solid and pseudopapillary patterns, often with degenerative changes and delicate fibrovascular cores. Tumor cells may be uniform with eosinophilic cytoplasm and grooved/indented nuclei. Nuclear and cytoplasmic β-catenin; loss of membranous E-cadherin. Chromogranin, calretinin, ER, and inhibin typically negative. CTNNB1 alteration may assist diagnosis. Ovarian sex cord-stromal tumor: sex cord markers positive, usually no nuclear β-catenin pattern. Metastatic pancreatic solid pseudopapillary neoplasm: clinical/imaging correlation essential. Neuroendocrine tumor: chromogranin/synaptophysin and morphology differ. Most are confined to ovary and behave indolently, but extraovarian spread is reported. Small cell carcinoma of the ovary, hypercalcemic type (SCCOHT) Young patient, hypercalcemia, undifferentiated small-cell malignancy, loss of BRG1/SMARCA4. High-grade undifferentiated malignancy composed of small cells, with or without a large-cell component; brisk mitoses, necrosis, and rhabdoid/epithelioid areas may occur. Hypercalcemia is a major clinical clue but is not universal. Loss of SMARCA4 (BRG1) in tumor cells with retained internal controls is critical; assess SMARCA2 (BRM) as appropriate. Other markers are variable and nonspecific. SMARCA4 inactivation in almost all cases; a substantial subset has germline variants. Rare SMARCB1-mutated cases occur. Other small round blue cell tumors, lymphoma, dysgerminoma, high-grade carcinoma, and metastatic tumors. SMARCA4 loss in the correct morphologic/clinical setting supports SCCOHT; correlate with germline evaluation. Highly aggressive malignancy. Ovarian Wilms tumor (nephroblastoma) Triphasic blastemal, epithelial, and stromal tumor; exclude SLCT, especially if no teratoma. Usually a combination of blastemal, epithelial, and stromal elements, although monophasic/biphasic forms occur. Blastema: densely packed small-to-medium cells with scant cytoplasm, coarse chromatin, mitoses and apoptosis. Epithelium: rosettes, papillae, tubules, glands, or glomeruloid structures. Stroma: spindle cells, sometimes with rhabdomyoblastic, cartilaginous, adipocytic, osseous, or neural heterologous elements. Blastema typically WT1, PAX8, and vimentin positive; epithelial component cytokeratin/EMA positive; stromal component vimentin with variable desmin. Synaptophysin, chromogranin, calretinin, SF1, and inhibin usually negative. DICER1 testing is recommended when pure ovarian Wilms tumor is considered against moderately/poorly differentiated SLCT; DICER1 alterations are common in the latter. Moderately/poorly differentiated SLCT: major diagnostic mimic, often DICER1-altered and may express sex cord markers. Teratoma-associated Wilms tumor supports true nephroblastoma. Consider other sarcomas and embryonal tumors. Rare; stage as a primary ovarian neoplasm rather than automatically applying extrarenal Wilms tumor staging conventions. All PathologyGPS · Female Genital Tract Ovarian Non-Epithelial Tumors A morphology-first diagnostic guide to sex cord-stromal tumors, germ cell tumors, and miscellaneous ovarian neoplasms. 1. Initial classification: start with lineage, not a long differential Sex cord-stromal lineage Spindle, theca-like, granulosa-like, Sertoli-like, or steroid-cell morphology. Ask whether the lesion is stromal, pure sex cord, or genuinely mixed. SF1, inhibin, calretinin, FOXL2; then subtype with morphology, reticulin, and targeted molecular testing. Germ cell lineage Primitive germ cells, clear polygonal cells, reticular/microcystic patterns, immature neural tissue, or mature teratomatous tissues. SALL4, OCT3/4, KIT, PLAP, AFP, Glypican-3, CD30, hCG, and lineage-directed markers selected by morphology. Miscellaneous / other Does not fit the two major lineages, or has a distinctive clinical-molecular signature (e.g., hypercalcemia/SMARCA4 loss). Use morphology-directed panels; exclude metastasis and tumors classified in other WHO chapters. Next: Practical first-pass questions Is the tumor predominantly spindle/stromal, sex cord-like, germ-cell-like, or another lineage? Is it unilateral or bilateral, hilar or parenchymal, and is the patient a child, young adult, or postmenopausal? Are there endocrine manifestations (androgenic, estrogenic), hypercalcemia, or a syndrome clue (DICER1, Peutz–Jeghers, gonadal dysgenesis)? Is there a recognizable second component? Sample extensively before diagnosing a mixed tumor. Use IHC to establish lineage; use morphology and selected molecular tests to resolve subtype. No single SCST marker reliably distinguishes all SCST types. 2. Core immunohistochemical approach Question Useful markers Interpretive point Sex cord-stromal differentiation SF1, inhibin, calretinin, FOXL2, WT1 Supports lineage; usually does not independently distinguish individual SCST entities. FOXL2, inhibin, SF1, calretinin; reticulin FOXL2 p.Cys134Trp is highly characteristic; reticulin around nests rather than individual cells. β-catenin, cyclin D1, CD10, SF1; inhibin/calretinin Nuclear β-catenin with inhibin/calretinin negativity supports this entity. Germ cell tumor SALL4, OCT3/4, KIT, PLAP, D2-40 Dysgerminoma typically OCT3/4+/KIT+; correlate with architecture. AFP, Glypican-3, SALL4, cytokeratin AFP/Glypican-3 support yolk sac differentiation; OCT3/4 is usually negative. OCT3/4, CD30, SALL4, cytokeratin CD30 positivity helps distinguish from dysgerminoma. SCCOHT SMARCA4 (BRG1), SMARCA2 (BRM) Loss of BRG1 in tumor cells with retained internal controls is a key diagnostic clue. Ovarian Wilms tumor WT1, PAX8, cytokeratin/EMA, desmin Interpret by component; exclude DICER1-altered SLCT. 3. Entity atlas and diagnostic differentials bg-teal-700 text-white border-teal-700 bg-white border-slate-300 hover:border-teal-500 Search tumor, morphology, marker, or differential… entities · Histology Description Immunohistochemistry Molecular Pathology Differential Diagnosis Diagnostic / Reporting Note No matching entities. Try a broader search term. 4. High-yield diagnostic separations Diagnostic problem Favor Do not overcall Fibroma vs thecoma Fibroma: bland spindle cells/collagen. Thecoma: plump pale/lipid-rich cells; individual-cell reticulin. Do not use “fibrothecoma” as a default label. AGCT vs fibroma/thecoma AGCT: grooved nuclei, varied patterns, reticulin around nests, FOXL2 mutation. A fibromatous component does not make AGCT a gynandroblastoma. AGCT vs JGCT AGCT: grooved nuclei, Call–Exner bodies, FOXL2 p.Cys134Trp. JGCT: round nuclei, irregular follicles, often brisk mitoses. Tubular areas alone do not establish a Sertoli component. SLCT vs JGCT Look for true Sertoli tubules/Leydig cells; DICER1 supports many moderate/poorly differentiated SLCTs. DICER1-altered SLCT with JGCT-like areas is generally SLCT, not gynandroblastoma. Microcystic stromal vs signet-ring stromal tumor Microcystic stromal: solid/microcystic zones, nuclear β-catenin/cyclin D1. Signet-ring stromal: fibromatous stroma, bland non-mucin vacuoles, EMA negative. Exclude metastatic mucinous signet-ring carcinoma. Dysgerminoma vs yolk sac tumor Dysgerminoma: OCT3/4+/KIT+, fibrous septa/lymphocytes. Yolk sac: AFP/Glypican-3+, reticular pattern/hyaline globules. Do not rely on a single marker without morphology. SCCOHT vs other small round cell tumors Young patient, hypercalcemia, undifferentiated morphology, SMARCA4/BRG1 loss. Consider germline SMARCA4 testing when appropriate. Ovarian Wilms tumor vs SLCT Triphasic nephroblastomatous pattern and/or teratoma; DICER1 testing helps exclude SLCT. Pure ovarian Wilms tumor is exceptionally rare; scrutinize the diagnosis. 5. Sampling and reporting checklist Document laterality, ovarian surface/capsular involvement, rupture, adhesions, hilar versus parenchymal location, and extraovarian disease. Sample heterogeneous solid, cystic, hemorrhagic, necrotic, and firm/white areas; search for small secondary components before diagnosing a mixed tumor. For malignant mixed germ cell tumor, list every component and estimate its percentage of the overall tumor. For AGCT, assess reticulin pattern and consider FOXL2 testing in equivocal cases; remember late recurrence. For SLCT, document differentiation, retiform pattern, heterologous elements, and consider DICER1 testing/genetic referral. For steroid cell tumor, record size, mitotic activity per defined area, necrosis, hemorrhage, atypia, and stage; no single feature reliably predicts behavior. For SCCOHT, assess SMARCA4 expression and consider germline evaluation. For suspected primary ovarian carcinoid, exclude an extraovarian primary. Do not force ovarian mesenchymal tumors, mesothelial tumors, or neuroectodermal tumors into this chapter when they are classified in separate WHO chapters. Educational reference for professional use. Interpret morphology, immunophenotype, molecular findings, and clinical context together. The immunohistochemical profile of sex cord-stromal tumors is supportive but often not subtype-specific. Follow current institutional protocols and the current WHO classification.
