title: Epithelial Tumors
content: use client Squamous Intraepithelial Lesions (LSIL and HSIL) Squamous Precursors Use maturation, nuclear atypia, and the vertical distribution of mitoses—not koilocytosis alone. HPV-associated squamous proliferations confined above the basement membrane. Report HSIL with the CIN qualifier (HSIL/CIN2 or HSIL/CIN3) when appropriate. LSIL: basal/parabasal-like cells with increased N:C ratios are largely confined to the lower one third. Maturation is preserved in the middle and upper thirds. Koilocytosis, binucleation, and multinucleation may be present; superficial nuclear atypia alone does not establish HSIL when abundant cytoplasm and maturation are retained. Condylomatous LSIL may show papillary fronds with fibrovascular cores and pointed epithelial spikes. Papillary immature metaplasia shows slender filiform papillae, usually near the proximal squamocolumnar junction, with mild atypia and low mitotic activity. HSIL: immature basaloid cells extend above the lower third, with nuclear crowding, loss of polarity, increased N:C ratios, and mitotic activity in the middle or upper epithelial layers. Atypical mitoses above the basal compartment strongly support HSIL. HSIL/CIN2 shows atypia and mitoses extending into the upper half to upper two thirds, with some maturation. HSIL/CIN3 shows full-thickness atypia and mitotic activity with minimal superficial maturation. Thin HSIL (10 cell layers or fewer), keratinizing HSIL, and HSIL with immature metaplastic phenotype are recognized patterns. Expansile HSIL/CIN3 may extensively involve and expand endocervical glands, sometimes with central necrosis. Deep gland involvement alone is not stromal invasion; examine the epithelial-stromal interface carefully and obtain deeper levels when needed. p16 is a problem-solving stain, not a screening stain for every biopsy. Block-positive staining is strong, continuous nuclear or nuclear/cytoplasmic staining beginning in basal/parabasal cells and extending upward through at least one third of the epithelium. Patchy, scattered, wispy, blob-like, or cytoplasmic-only staining is non-block-type and does not support HSIL. A block-positive p16 result does not independently convert morphologic LSIL into HSIL; a substantial minority of adjudicated LSILs may show block staining. Use p16 when distinguishing HSIL from immature squamous metaplasia, atrophy, inflammation, repair, tangential sectioning, or when adjudicating a morphologically equivocal CIN2-type lesion. Immature squamous metaplasia Usually retains orderly maturation and lacks convincing diffuse nuclear atypia or suprabasal atypical mitoses; p16 is generally non-block-type. Atrophy / reactive or reparative epithelium Can show crowded small cells, but nuclear contours and chromatin are more uniform; correlate with inflammation, erosion, and tissue orientation. LSIL versus HSIL Judge the level reached by immature atypical cells and mitoses. Koilocytosis or striking superficial nuclei alone do not establish HSIL. HSIL involving endocervical glands versus invasion Glandular involvement preserves a recognizable gland outline; destructive irregular nests, stromal response, or paradoxical maturation raise concern for invasion. Do not diagnose LSIL from perinuclear halos without accompanying nuclear atypia. Do not downgrade morphologically unequivocal HSIL solely because p16 is negative/non-block-type. Use CIN2/CIN3 qualifiers because the distinction can affect management, particularly in younger patients. Cervical Intraepithelial Neoplasia, HPV-Independent A rare, evolving category; require a compatible pattern and usually negative/non-block p16, with HPV testing when feasible. A possible precursor to HPV-independent squamous cell carcinoma. Morphologic patterns and natural history remain incompletely characterized. Differentiated pattern: thickened squamous epithelium with near-normal superficial maturation, elongated or anastomosing rete ridges, basal or suprabasal atypia, and increased mitoses limited mainly to lower layers. Abrupt premature maturation, dyskeratosis, and keratin pearls are characteristic clues. Verrucous/verruciform pattern: exophytic papillary proliferation, often with hyperkeratosis/parakeratosis and loss of the granular layer, but without significant basal atypia or appreciable mitotic activity. Basaloid pattern: immature basaloid proliferation, often involving endocervical crypts, and may closely mimic HSIL. Koilocytosis is absent in the described patterns, although pseudokoilocytosis may occur. p16 is usually negative/non-block-type. Occasional basaloid examples with block-type staining have been reported despite negative HPV testing; interpret cautiously. Differentiated pattern may show mutation-type p53 in atypical basal cells. Verruciform lesions are typically p53 wild-type. For a suspected HPV-independent precursor, correlate morphology with HPV molecular testing when available. HSIL Usually block-type p16 and high-risk HPV-associated; basaloid HPV-independent CIN may be difficult, so HPV testing can be decisive. Condyloma / LSIL Usually shows koilocytosis and HPV cytopathic effect; HPV-independent verruciform lesions lack true koilocytosis. Reactive hyperplasia / lichenified epithelium Look for orderly maturation and absence of convincing basal atypia or atypical mitoses. HPV testing, if performed, should be negative. TP53 alterations may occur in differentiated lesions; PIK3CA, EGFR, or SMARCB1 alterations have been reported in verruciform lesions, but molecular subgroups are not established. The entity is newly described and criteria are not fully validated. Do not overstate biological behavior or progression risk. Squamous Cell Carcinoma, HPV-Associated Squamous Carcinomas Invasive squamous morphology plus block-type p16; direct high-risk HPV testing is useful when results are discordant. The great majority of cervical squamous cell carcinomas are HPV-associated. Invasion is characterized by irregular, angulated nests, anastomosing cords, or solid sheets infiltrating cervical stroma, often with desmoplastic or inflammatory response. Nuclear pleomorphism and mitotic activity are usually present. Early invasion may appear as small, ragged nests arising from HSIL, with paradoxical cytoplasmic eosinophilia, stromal loosening, or desmoplasia. Nonkeratinizing SCC shows polygonal cells in nests or sheets without keratin pearls. Keratinizing SCC shows individual cell keratinization and keratin pearls. Basaloid SCC has immature cells with scant cytoplasm and may closely resemble HSIL. Warty/condylomatous and papillary patterns may be exophytic; invasion can be extremely focal or unapparent in a small biopsy. Lymphoepithelioma-like, spindle cell, and acantholytic patterns are uncommon. Histologic pattern and grade are not established prognostic grading systems; stage is the dominant prognostic factor. Usually strong, diffuse block-type p16 in tumor cells. p40, p63, and CK5/6 support squamous differentiation but do not establish HPV association. If p16 is negative/non-block-type or equivocal, perform high-risk HPV testing; consider low-risk HPV testing in selected warty/papillary lesions. HSIL remains intraepithelial; identify destructive stromal invasion, irregular infiltrative nests, stromal reaction, or paradoxical maturation. HPV-independent SCC Morphology alone cannot reliably separate the two. Use p16 and direct HPV testing. Adenosquamous carcinoma Requires recognizable malignant glandular and squamous components on H&E. Papillary HSIL versus papillary SCC A superficial biopsy may not include the invasive base. Abundant papillary fragments with fibrovascular cores warrant careful assessment and correlation with excision. High-risk HPV E6/E7 RNA in situ hybridization or other validated HPV assays can resolve equivocal p16 results. Do not grade cervical SCC using routine differentiation-based systems. Do not call an exophytic papillary lesion HSIL without adequately assessing the stromal interface. Squamous Cell Carcinoma, HPV-Independent Negative/non-block p16 is not enough by itself: confirm HPV negativity with molecular testing. Rare cervical SCCs arise independently of HPV and may present at a more advanced stage. Morphologically, HPV-independent SCC is generally indistinguishable from HPV-associated SCC. Keratinization is more frequent; extensive necrosis, dense lymphocyte-predominant inflammation, and highly vascular stroma may be encountered. The same invasive patterns seen in HPV-associated SCC may occur. No grading system is established. A differentiated HPV-independent intraepithelial lesion may be present adjacent to the invasive tumor. p16 is negative/non-block-type; direct HPV testing should also be negative before assigning HPV-independent status. p53 shows a mutation-type pattern in approximately half of reported cases; p53 wild-type cases also occur. p40/p63/CK5/6 support squamous differentiation but do not establish HPV status. HPV-associated SCC with unusual p16 loss Rare HPV-associated tumors may lack block p16; direct HPV testing is essential before classifying as HPV-independent. HPV-independent CIN The precursor remains intraepithelial; identify unequivocal stromal invasion to diagnose carcinoma. Use PCR or in situ hybridization covering high- and low-risk HPV types as appropriate. p53 immunohistochemistry and/or TP53 sequencing may further characterize the tumor. Do not infer HPV independence from older age, keratinization, or p16 alone. Squamous Cell Carcinoma, HPV Status Undetermined Use only when HPV status cannot be established; most such tumors are likely HPV-associated. An acceptable designation when tumor testing is unavailable, inconclusive, or not feasible. Diagnose invasive carcinoma with squamous differentiation on morphology. HPV-associated and HPV-independent SCC cannot be reliably distinguished morphologically. Attempt p16 immunohistochemistry when feasible. If p16 is non-block-type or equivocal, direct HPV testing is recommended when available. HPV-associated versus HPV-independent SCC Do not assign either category without adequate ancillary evidence. Document the limitation and use the designation HPV status undetermined when testing cannot resolve the status. Endocervical Polyp Benign Epithelial Lesions A bland endocervical epithelial lining over a vascular, often inflamed stromal core. A common benign exophytic lesion that may contain metaplasia or be secondarily involved by SIL/AIS. A stromal core is lined by bland mucinous endocervical-type epithelium, with glands often invaginating into the central stroma. The stroma is vascular and commonly contains mixed acute and chronic inflammation. Surface erosion and reactive/reparative change may produce hobnail-like cells. Squamous metaplasia (often immature), tubo-endometrial metaplasia, or microglandular hyperplasia may involve surface or deeper glands. Pregnancy-associated Arias-Stella change or decidualization may occur. Rare polyps show focal club-like/phyllodes-like intraglandular stromal protrusions and increased periglandular cellularity; these are usually benign. SIL or AIS may rarely involve a pre-existing polyp; assess the epithelial lining and glands rather than assuming all atypia is reactive. No routine immunohistochemical panel is required for a typical polyp. Use targeted stains only to resolve a specific atypical epithelial or stromal component. Adenosarcoma A polyp may show focal periglandular stromal cellularity, but diffuse stromal atypia, increased mitotic activity, and convincing leaf-like architecture raise concern for adenosarcoma. AIS or HSIL involving a polyp Look for cytologic atypia and abnormal maturation beyond reactive change; use p16 in the appropriate diagnostic context. Microglandular hyperplasia Often has closely packed small glands, mucinous cytoplasm, and inflammation; it lacks the cytologic features of AIS. Do not mistake reactive hobnail cells in an eroded polyp for clear cell carcinoma without evaluating the overall architecture and cytology. Adenocarcinoma in Situ (AIS), HPV-Associated Glandular Precursors Mucin-depleted or mucinous pseudostratified endocervical cells with apical mitoses and apoptotic bodies; usually block-type p16. High-grade glandular intraepithelial neoplasia, commonly associated with HPV18 or HPV16. Atypical endocervical glands are lined by columnar cells with pseudostratified, enlarged, hyperchromatic nuclei, loss of polarity, and increased N:C ratios. Apical mitotic figures and basal apoptotic bodies/karyorrhectic debris are characteristic. Cytoplasm may be mucin-depleted or contain intracytoplasmic mucin. The lesion may involve the transformation zone and proximal endocervical canal, may be multifocal, and can coexist with HSIL. AIS is intraepithelial; destructive stromal invasion, desmoplasia, or irregular infiltrative glands establishes invasive adenocarcinoma. Diffuse block-type p16 is characteristic. Partial loss of RB1 may support an HPV-driven lesion. ER and PR are typically lost, whereas benign glandular mimics tend to retain hormone receptor expression. PAX2 is usually lost in glandular neoplasia but retained in many benign endocervical glands. CAIX can support neoplasia over benign/reactive glands but is not HPV-specific. Benign endocervical glands / tubo-endometrial metaplasia Usually show bland nuclei, preserved polarity, and lack the characteristic apical mitoses and apoptotic bodies; ER/PR may be retained. Lobular endocervical glandular hyperplasia (LEGH) A benign gastric-type glandular proliferation with lobular architecture and gastric mucin; distinguish from HPV-independent gastric-type AIS. Invasive HPV-associated adenocarcinoma Search for destructive stromal invasion. AIS may be present adjacent to invasive tumor. High-risk HPV testing is useful, particularly when morphology or p16 is equivocal. When AIS is found on biopsy, an excision is important because an invasive component may be identified in the subsequent specimen. Do not equate extensive gland involvement with invasion; assess the stromal interface. A negative cytology result does not exclude AIS. Adenocarcinoma in Situ (AIS), HPV-Independent Usually gastric-type; distinguish atypical LEGH from gastric-type AIS using cytology, architecture, and ancillary studies. An HPV-independent intraepithelial glandular neoplasm, predominantly of gastric type. Gastric-type AIS may show atypical glands with gastric differentiation, often in a background of LEGH or atypical LEGH. LEGH typically has a lobular arrangement of small to medium glands with bland gastric-type mucinous cells. Atypical LEGH shows cytologic atypia and/or architectural complexity beyond ordinary LEGH. Gastric-type AIS may show more conspicuous nuclear atypia, stratification, and complex glandular architecture while remaining intraepithelial. A visible mass is not typical of gastric-type AIS itself; LEGH or atypical LEGH may produce a multicystic upper endocervical lesion. p16 is usually negative/non-block-type, although rare block-type cases occur. Gastric differentiation markers such as MUC6 and HIK1083 (where available) may support gastric phenotype; interpret as a panel and in morphologic context. ER/PR are generally not useful as positive markers for gastric-type lesions. LEGH Bland lobular glands with orderly architecture and minimal atypia; no destructive invasion. Gastric-type invasive adenocarcinoma Destructive, haphazard deep glands, irregular infiltration, or desmoplastic response support invasion. HPV-associated AIS Usually block-type p16 and high-risk HPV positive, with characteristic apical mitoses and apoptotic bodies. Multifocal/synchronous gastric-type lesions may occur at different sites in the female genital tract, sometimes in Peutz–Jeghers syndrome. Do not interpret a multicystic upper-cervical lesion as benign without assessing for atypical LEGH and gastric-type neoplasia. Adenocarcinoma, HPV-Associated Invasive Adenocarcinomas Invasive endocervical-type adenocarcinoma with block-type p16 and/or high-risk HPV; assess invasion pattern using Silva classification. The most common category of primary cervical adenocarcinoma; diverse morphologic patterns are not treated as separate subtypes. Tumors show endocervical-type glands lined by columnar cells with pseudostratified enlarged hyperchromatic nuclei, apical mitoses, and basal apoptotic bodies. Mucin may be depleted or evident. Architectural patterns include usual-type glandular, papillary, micropapillary, and other patterns. Pattern-based classification is more useful than older pattern names as prognostic categories. Silva pattern A: non-destructive growth, well-demarcated glands, no lymphovascular invasion. Pattern B: limited destructive invasion. Pattern C: diffuse destructive invasion, often with haphazard glands, solid growth, or desmoplasia. Invasion may be difficult to assess in exophytic lesions or small biopsies. A convincing in situ component and associated HSIL can support cervical origin. Usually block-type p16. High-risk HPV testing can confirm association when needed. CK7 and PAX8 are commonly positive. ER/PR are usually negative. p53 is generally wild-type; mutation-type p53 should prompt consideration of HPV-independent tumors or metastasis. HPV-independent gastric-type adenocarcinoma Often deeply infiltrative glands with abundant pale eosinophilic/foamy cytoplasm, distinct cell borders, and non-block p16; gastric markers may be positive. Endometrial endometrioid carcinoma involving cervix Correlate with endometrial sampling and imaging; ER/PR and vimentin may support endometrial origin, but no single stain is definitive. AIS AIS lacks destructive stromal invasion. Assess the gland-stromal interface and look for desmoplasia or irregular infiltrative glands. Stratified mucin-producing carcinoma A recognized morphologic variant of HPV-associated adenocarcinoma with stratified epithelium and intracytoplasmic mucin; mucicarmine can help highlight mucin. High-risk HPV testing is useful in equivocal cases. Block-type p16 is a reliable surrogate in the appropriate morphology. Silva pattern A has essentially no nodal metastatic potential in reported series; patterns B and C have progressively greater nodal risk. Do not diagnose primary cervical serous carcinoma; that entity is not recognized. Work up serous-like morphology for HPV-associated adenocarcinoma, gastric-type carcinoma, or metastasis. Do not classify an adenocarcinoma as endometrioid solely because it is mucin-poor. Adenocarcinoma, HPV-Independent, Gastric Type Deep, often haphazard infiltrative glands with gastric differentiation; usually non-block p16 and HPV-negative. An HPV-independent cervical adenocarcinoma with gastric/gastrointestinal differentiation; may be deceptively bland (minimal-deviation pattern). Tumors are often centered high in the endocervical canal and may be large, deeply infiltrative, polypoid, ulcerated, or circumferential, producing a barrel-shaped cervix. Glands are irregular, haphazard, and deeply infiltrative, often with abundant pale or eosinophilic mucinous cytoplasm, distinct cell borders, and basally located nuclei. Cytologic atypia may be deceptively mild. Destructive invasion may be difficult to recognize in minimal-deviation areas; look for irregular gland distribution, variable gland size and shape, deep stromal involvement, and focal desmoplasia. A spectrum of differentiation may be present, including intestinal differentiation with goblet cells. p16 is usually negative/non-block-type; HPV testing should be negative. MUC6 and other gastric differentiation markers may be positive; HNF4α can support gastrointestinal differentiation. PAX8 is variable and may be absent. ER/PR are usually negative. p53 may be wild-type or mutation-type. Claudin-18.2 may be expressed in a subset, particularly with intestinal differentiation; it is not required for diagnosis. LEGH / atypical LEGH / gastric-type AIS These show lobular or intraepithelial patterns without destructive deep stromal invasion. Gastric-type carcinoma shows haphazard destructive infiltration. HPV-associated adenocarcinoma Usually block-type p16 and high-risk HPV positive, with more conspicuous apical mitoses and apoptotic bodies. Metastatic pancreatobiliary or gastrointestinal adenocarcinoma Clinical/radiologic correlation is essential; morphology and gastric markers overlap. Assess for a cervical precursor or in situ component and use a focused panel. Peutz–Jeghers syndrome may be associated with multifocal gastric-type lesions of the female genital tract. Do not use the historical terms adenoma malignum or minimal-deviation adenocarcinoma as separate entities. A bland cytology does not exclude deeply invasive gastric-type carcinoma. Adenocarcinoma, HPV-Independent, Clear Cell Type Tubulocystic, papillary, and/or solid architecture with clear or eosinophilic cells and hobnail morphology. A primary HPV-independent cervical adenocarcinoma with clear cell differentiation. Common patterns include tubulocystic, papillary, and solid growth, often in combination. Tumor cells may be hobnail, cuboidal, or polygonal, with clear or eosinophilic cytoplasm. Hyalinized stromal cores may be present in papillary areas. Nuclear atypia and mitotic activity vary; identify the characteristic architectural and cytologic combination rather than relying on clear cytoplasm alone. Napsin A and AMACR are useful positive markers. p16 is generally negative/non-block-type and HPV testing should be negative. PAX8 is commonly positive; ER/PR are usually negative. Gastric-type adenocarcinoma Usually shows gastric mucinous cytoplasm and irregular deeply infiltrative glands; napsin A/AMACR support clear cell differentiation. Metastatic clear cell carcinoma (especially renal) Correlate clinically and use a panel including renal markers as indicated; PAX8 alone does not establish cervical origin. Arias-Stella change / reactive hobnail cells Reactive glands lack destructive invasion and significant malignant cytologic features. Do not diagnose clear cell carcinoma on hobnail morphology alone; assess architecture, cytologic atypia, invasion, and clinical context. Adenocarcinoma, HPV-Independent, Mesonephric Type Small tubules with dense eosinophilic luminal secretions, mixed patterns, and GATA3/TTF1/CD10 support. A rare HPV-independent carcinoma showing mesonephric (Wolffian) differentiation, usually in the lateral cervical wall. A mixture of small tubules, ducts, glands, papillary, retiform, solid, and spindle-cell patterns may be present. Tubules are often lined by cuboidal cells with scant cytoplasm and angulated or grooved nuclei; dense eosinophilic luminal secretions are characteristic. The tumor often infiltrates deep cervical stroma and may show lymphovascular invasion. Cytologic atypia can be variable. GATA3, TTF1, and luminal CD10 are useful markers, often in a complementary or variable pattern. PAX8 is usually positive. ER/PR are typically negative. p16 is generally non-block-type and HPV testing should be negative. Do not rely on GATA3 alone; expression can be variable and the differential is broad. Wolffian tumor / female adnexal tumor of probable Wolffian origin Wolffian tumors usually arise in broad ligament/adnexa, often show multiple tubular/solid patterns, and are generally negative for GATA3, TTF1, PAX8, EMA, and claudin-4; mesonephric carcinoma is invasive and PAX8/GATA3/TTF1 may be positive. Block-type p16 and HPV positivity favor HPV-associated carcinoma; mesonephric carcinoma is HPV independent. Endometrioid adenocarcinoma Usually ER/PR positive and lacks the characteristic mesonephric immunophenotype. KRAS, and less commonly NRAS, mutations may support the diagnosis in challenging cases. Do not equate mesonephric adenocarcinoma with Wolffian tumor; their site, immunophenotype, and biology differ. Other Adenocarcinomas: Endometrioid Type and Adenocarcinoma NOS Endometrioid carcinoma is a diagnosis of exclusion; exclude HPV-associated mucin-depleted carcinoma and endometrial extension. Includes rare primary cervical endometrioid adenocarcinoma and adenocarcinoma NOS. Endometrioid adenocarcinoma shows at least focal low-grade endometrioid glands lined by columnar cells with pseudostratified bland nuclei, with or without squamous or mucinous differentiation. Papillary and solid areas may occur. Morphology is identical to endometrial or ovarian endometrioid carcinoma; the primary site cannot be determined by morphology alone, especially in a biopsy. Primary cervical endometrioid carcinoma may infiltrate cervical stroma deceptively, with bland glands and little desmoplasia. Association with endometriosis may provide a clue. Adenocarcinoma NOS is a diagnosis of exclusion when no specific cervical type can be assigned or HPV status cannot be determined; exclude metastasis and tumors extending from the endometrium. ER and/or PR should be positive in endometrioid adenocarcinoma. p16 is usually patchy/non-block-type and HPV testing should be negative. Evaluate p53, MMR, vimentin, and other markers in a focused panel when distinguishing endometrial origin or other mimics. Endometrial endometrioid carcinoma extending into cervix Review endometrial sampling, imaging, tumor distribution, and precursor lesions; morphology and IHC overlap substantially. HPV-associated mucin-depleted adenocarcinoma Often has characteristic HPV-associated morphology and block-type p16; exclude HPV association before diagnosing endometrioid type. Usually ER/PR negative with gastric differentiation and non-block p16. Metastatic endometrioid carcinoma Clinical history and distribution are essential; do not infer cervical primary from a cervical biopsy alone. If HPV testing is performed, endometrioid adenocarcinoma should be HPV negative. Primary cervical serous carcinoma is not an accepted entity. Serous-like tumors require workup for HPV-associated carcinoma, gastric-type carcinoma, or metastasis. Adenosquamous Carcinoma, HPV-Associated Mixed Epithelial Carcinomas Both malignant glandular and malignant squamous components must be recognizable on H&E. An invasive carcinoma with glandular and squamous differentiation, most often HPV-associated. A mixture of malignant glandular and squamous components is present. The diagnosis is based on H&E morphology; both components should be recognizable without special stains. The required percentage of either component is not defined; recognizable components of any amount may support the diagnosis. Necrosis, inflammation, and lymphovascular invasion are common. Glassy cell morphology is within the spectrum; mucoepidermoid carcinoma is not a separate recognized category. Both components typically show block-type p16. Glandular component: CK7 and PAX8 are typically positive. Squamous component: p40 and p63 are typically positive. ER/PR are usually negative. Adenocarcinoma with squamous metaplasia Metaplastic squamous epithelium is not malignant; require a truly malignant squamous component. A variant of HPV-associated adenocarcinoma; mucin is present within stratified tumor epithelium and the squamous component is not a separate malignant component. Carcinosarcoma Carcinosarcoma has a malignant mesenchymal component, not merely squamous differentiation. High-risk HPV is commonly detected; HPV testing can confirm association in selected cases. Do not diagnose adenosquamous carcinoma from cytology alone; defer definitive classification to tissue. Adenosquamous Carcinoma, HPV-Independent Invasive carcinoma with genuine glandular and squamous differentiation plus negative/non-block p16 and negative HPV testing. A rare HPV-independent mixed epithelial carcinoma of the cervix. Shows invasive malignant glandular and squamous components. The morphology may overlap with HPV-associated adenosquamous carcinoma; the HPV status is determined by ancillary testing. p16 is negative/non-block-type; confirm with HPV testing. Use morphology and lineage markers to document both components; no single lineage stain establishes HPV independence. HPV-associated adenosquamous carcinoma Usually block-type p16 and high-risk HPV positive. A recognized HPV-associated adenocarcinoma variant; assess mucin within stratified cells and HPV status. Published experience is limited; avoid extrapolating prognosis from HPV-associated cases. Adenoid Basal Carcinoma Other Epithelial Tumors Small infiltrative nests or cords of bland basaloid cells with little or no stromal reaction. A low-grade adenoid basal tumor with no known metastatic potential when present in pure form. Small, rounded or angulated nests and cords of bland basaloid cells infiltrate cervical stroma, often with peripheral palisading. The cells have scant cytoplasm and relatively uniform nuclei. Stromal reaction is absent or minimal, and mitotic activity is low. Adenoid cystic-like spaces or squamous differentiation may be present. Carefully search for an associated conventional SCC or another carcinoma component. p16 is often block-type and high-risk HPV may be detected. p63/p40 and basal keratins support basaloid/squamous differentiation but are not specific. Basaloid SCC Usually shows greater cytologic atypia, mitotic activity, and destructive stromal invasion; may have an associated HSIL. Adenoid cystic carcinoma-like lesion Adenoid cystic carcinoma is not a distinct recognized cervical carcinoma category; most historical cases represent basaloid SCC or HPV-associated adenocarcinoma with adenoid cystic-like morphology. Adenoid basal carcinoma with an additional carcinoma component The prognosis is determined by the more aggressive component; extensively sample and report each component. High-risk HPV testing may support the diagnosis but is not usually required when morphology is classic. Pure adenoid basal carcinoma has no known metastatic potential. Clear excision is recommended to exclude a more aggressive admixed component. A true biphasic malignancy with malignant epithelial and malignant mesenchymal components. A rare malignant mixed epithelial and mesenchymal neoplasm of the cervix. The tumor contains a malignant epithelial component (often carcinoma) and a malignant mesenchymal component, which may be homologous or heterologous. The epithelial component may be squamous or glandular; the sarcomatous component may show spindle-cell, pleomorphic, or heterologous differentiation. Extensive sampling is important to identify both components and exclude a pure carcinoma with reactive/desmoplastic stroma. Use a panel to demonstrate epithelial differentiation in the carcinoma component (broad-spectrum cytokeratin/EMA) and mesenchymal differentiation in the sarcomatous component (vimentin and lineage-specific markers as indicated). Some sarcomatous areas may retain focal keratin expression; interpret staining with morphology. Both components in adenosquamous carcinoma are epithelial; the squamous component is not a sarcoma. Sarcomatoid carcinoma May show spindle-cell morphology but represents epithelial malignancy with transition/epithelial marker expression; distinguish from a true biphasic carcinosarcoma. Primary cervical sarcoma Lacks a convincing malignant epithelial component. Do not use historical terms malignant mixed Müllerian tumor or malignant mesodermal mixed tumor. Carcinoma, Unclassifiable A diagnosis of exclusion after extensive morphologic and immunophenotypic evaluation. An invasive primary cervical epithelial malignancy that cannot be assigned to a specific carcinoma category. Shows malignant epithelial phenotype but lacks defining morphologic features of SCC, adenocarcinoma, or neuroendocrine carcinoma. Exclude secondary involvement by gynecologic and non-gynecologic malignancies, including sarcomas and other non-epithelial tumors that may express cytokeratins. A biopsy diagnosis may be refined on a larger excision when additional differentiated components are identified. Diffuse p63, p40, and/or CK5/6 should prompt reconsideration of SCC. Use a broad, morphology-directed panel to exclude glandular, neuroendocrine, melanocytic, mesenchymal, and metastatic tumors. p16 and/or HPV testing may help determine HPV association. Poorly differentiated SCC Look for diffuse squamous markers and block-type p16/HPV association. Poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma Search for glandular differentiation and use epithelial/glandular markers in context. Neuroendocrine carcinoma Assess morphology and neuroendocrine markers; high-grade NEC can be very poorly differentiated. Metastatic carcinoma or non-epithelial malignancy Clinical history, imaging, distribution, and a broad immunohistochemical panel are essential. Use only after extensive evaluation; do not use as a shortcut for a limited biopsy. Well-Differentiated Neuroendocrine Tumor (NET) Neuroendocrine Neoplasms Low-grade cytology with neuroendocrine architecture and a convincing neuroendocrine immunophenotype. An extremely rare primary cervical epithelial neuroendocrine neoplasm; mixed neuroendocrine/non-neuroendocrine neoplasms may occur. Well-differentiated neuroendocrine architecture may include organoid nests, trabeculae, ribbons, and rosettes. Cells are relatively uniform with finely granular chromatin and low-grade cytology. Mitotic activity and necrosis are limited compared with NEC. A mixed neuroendocrine and non-neuroendocrine neoplasm (MiNEN) contains a recognizable non-neuroendocrine component. Use synaptophysin, chromogranin, and INSM1 to establish neuroendocrine differentiation; not every marker must be equally positive. Cytokeratin supports epithelial nature. Interpret markers with morphology and exclude non-neuroendocrine mimics. NEC shows high-grade cytology, brisk mitoses, and usually extensive necrosis. Paraganglioma Typically keratin-negative with sustentacular cells; use a panel including keratin and sustentacular markers. Endometrial stromal or other small round cell tumor Use morphology and lineage-specific markers; focal neuroendocrine marker expression alone is insufficient. HPV association is variable in NET; mixed neuroendocrine/non-neuroendocrine neoplasms are more often HPV-associated. Do not use the historical terms typical carcinoid or atypical carcinoid tumor. Neuroendocrine Carcinoma (Small Cell and Large Cell) High-grade morphology with brisk mitoses and necrosis; confirm neuroendocrine differentiation with a panel. Includes small cell NEC, large cell NEC, and combined carcinomas with a neuroendocrine carcinoma component. Small cell NEC: sheets, nests, or trabeculae of small cells with scant cytoplasm, nuclear molding, finely granular or hyperchromatic chromatin, inconspicuous nucleoli, brisk mitotic activity, and extensive necrosis. Crush artifact is common. Large cell NEC: organoid, nested, trabecular, or rosette-like architecture composed of larger cells with moderate cytoplasm, vesicular nuclei, and prominent nucleoli; mitoses and necrosis are brisk. Combined NEC contains a recognizable small-cell or large-cell NEC component admixed with another carcinoma, commonly squamous or adenocarcinoma. Identify and report the components. Cervical NEC may resemble other high-grade cervical carcinomas; the diagnosis requires integration of morphology and immunophenotype. Synaptophysin, chromogranin, and INSM1 support neuroendocrine differentiation; expression may be heterogeneous, and not all markers are positive in every case. Broad-spectrum cytokeratin supports epithelial differentiation. p16 may be block-type in HPV-associated cases. Ki-67 is typically high in NEC and helps distinguish it from well-differentiated NET, but should not replace morphology. SCC usually expresses p40/p63 and CK5/6; NEC shows neuroendocrine morphology and marker expression. Focal overlap can occur. Lymphoma Usually negative for broad-spectrum cytokeratin; use CD45 and lineage markers. Small cell carcinoma metastatic from lung Clinical/radiologic correlation is essential; HPV testing may support cervical origin in the appropriate setting. Well-differentiated NET NET has low-grade cytology and lower proliferative activity; NEC is high grade with brisk mitoses and necrosis. HPV testing may help support a cervical primary, particularly in a patient with a history or imaging concern for an extra-cervical primary. Do not exclude NEC because one neuroendocrine marker is negative; use a panel and correlate with morphology. Search carefully for a combined non-neuroendocrine carcinoma component. All PathologyGPS · Female Genital Tract Uterine Cervix: Epithelial Tumors A practical diagnostic guide to cervical squamous and glandular precursors, invasive carcinomas, mixed epithelial tumors, and neuroendocrine neoplasms—with emphasis on morphology, HPV status, immunohistochemistry, and differential diagnosis. Diagnostic Approach: Start Here 1. Establish the compartment Is the lesion squamous, glandular, mixed, or neuroendocrine? Is it intraepithelial or invasive? 2. For squamous lesions Separate LSIL from HSIL by maturation, atypia, and mitotic distribution. For invasive SCC, establish HPV association with p16 and/or direct HPV testing. 3. For glandular lesions First distinguish benign glands/metaplasia from AIS and invasive adenocarcinoma. Then classify as HPV-associated or HPV-independent. 4. For HPV-independent adenocarcinoma Consider gastric, clear cell, mesonephric, and endometrioid types. Exclude extension from endometrium and metastasis. 5. For mixed or high-grade tumors Confirm that both components are genuinely malignant. Consider adenosquamous carcinoma, carcinosarcoma, and neuroendocrine carcinoma. 6. Use IHC as a panel p16/HPV status is central, but morphology and site remain decisive. Avoid assigning a subtype from a single positive marker. Critical principle: HPV-associated and HPV-independent cervical carcinomas often cannot be distinguished by morphology alone. Use block-type p16 as a surrogate and direct HPV testing when p16 is negative, equivocal, or discordant with morphology. High-Yield IHC / HPV Framework HPV-associated squamous / glandular lesions Usually block-type p16; confirm with high-risk HPV testing when needed. HPV-independent carcinoma Usually negative/non-block p16 and HPV-negative; p53 may be mutation-type in a subset. Gastric differentiation markers (e.g., MUC6); usually ER/PR negative. Clear cell adenocarcinoma Napsin A and/or AMACR; usually HPV-independent. Mesonephric adenocarcinoma GATA3, TTF1, CD10 (often complementary); KRAS/NRAS may help. Synaptophysin, chromogranin, INSM1; correlate with high-grade morphology. Important Diagnostic Guardrails Primary cervical serous carcinoma is not an accepted entity; work up serous-like tumors for HPV-associated carcinoma, gastric-type carcinoma, or metastasis. Endometrioid adenocarcinoma of the cervix is a diagnosis of exclusion: exclude HPV-associated mucin-depleted carcinoma and endometrial extension. Extensive HSIL involving endocervical glands is not automatically invasion. Pure adenoid basal carcinoma has no known metastatic potential; search for an admixed aggressive component. title: Epithelial Tumors
content: use client Endometrial hyperplasia without atypia Precursor lesions Diffuse-field glandular proliferation without cytologic atypia. Histology Irregularly sized and shaped tubular, branching, and/or cystically dilated glands with a variably increased gland-to-stroma ratio. The epithelium is cytologically bland; staggered nuclei may appear pseudostratified and mitotic activity may be increased. The architectural and nuclear changes are generally distributed throughout the sampled endometrium. EAH/EIN: a geographically defined focus of crowded glands with cytology distinct from the background; the gland area exceeds the stromal area within the lesion. Endometrial polyp: focal gland crowding may occur, but crowded glands should not be cytologically distinct from the other glands in the polyp. Cystic atrophy or disordered proliferative endometrium: interpret gland density in the context of the overall background and hormonal pattern. IHC / molecular No immunohistochemical or molecular test is required for diagnosis. Morphology is primary. Do not diagnose EIN solely because a polyp contains crowded or cystically dilated glands. Tubal/ciliated metaplasia in background endometrium is not, by itself, cytologic atypia. Atypical hyperplasia / Endometrioid intraepithelial neoplasia (EAH/EIN) Clonal-appearing, localized crowded glands with cytology distinct from background endometrium. Essential histology A morphologically defined focus of crowded altered tubular or branching glands in which gland area exceeds stromal area. The epithelial cytology must differ from adjacent or entrapped non-neoplastic glands. Increased stratification and limited cribriforming may occur, but prominent cribriform architecture or high-grade nuclear atypia should prompt consideration of carcinoma or serous carcinoma. The focus must be sufficiently large to exclude artifactual crowding. IHC A panel of PAX2, PTEN, and β-catenin may support the diagnosis; aberrant expression of at least one occurs in more than 90% of cases in reported series. Loss of PAX2 or PTEN and nuclear β-catenin can support clonality, but none replaces the required morphologic criteria. Differential diagnosis Hyperplasia without atypia shows a more diffuse field change with relatively uniform cytology. Basalis, endometrial polyp, dyssynchronous endometrium, and cystic atrophy can mimic focal crowding. High-grade atypia is not a feature of EAH/EIN and raises concern for serous carcinoma. The diagnosis requires the combination of gland crowding and altered cytology, not either feature alone. Squamous morules are common and may be associated with CTNNB1 alteration. Atypical polypoid adenomyoma (APA) Complex atypical endometrioid glands embedded in benign myomatous or fibromyomatous stroma. A polypoid lesion, often in the lower uterine segment, composed of irregular and architecturally complex endometrioid-type glands in bland cellular spindle-cell myomatous/fibromyomatous stroma. Squamous morular metaplasia is almost always present. Glands often show mild-to-moderate atypia and may have a lobular arrangement. Rare foci may show more extensive glandular crowding compatible with low-grade endometrioid carcinoma arising in APA. The stromal cells are commonly positive for desmin, SATB2, and p16 (often moderate-to-strong and diffuse); these are not specific because adenomyoma stroma may share this profile. Stromal h-caldesmon and CD10 are usually negative. Adenomyoma has benign endometrial glands without the characteristic cytologic atypia and morular metaplasia. Endometrioid carcinoma involving myometrium shows destructive/infiltrative growth, confluent glands, or desmoplasia rather than a circumscribed polypoid lesion with benign myomatous stroma. Assess for coexistent EIN and carcinoma. Carefully sample the lesion and its interface; a limited focus of carcinoma may coexist. Endometrioid carcinoma Endometrial carcinomas Endometrioid-type glands with complex architecture, stromal exclusion/invasion, or confluent papillary/solid growth. Histology: recognition and invasion Usually retains at least focal glandular architecture. Glands have smooth luminal contours and are lined by columnar cells with eosinophilic cytoplasm and pseudostratified nuclei; atypia is usually mild-to-moderate in low-grade tumors. Squamous, morular, mucinous, secretory, and tubal/ciliated metaplasia support endometrioid differentiation. Well-differentiated carcinoma is distinguished from EIN by stromal invasion or its architectural equivalent: confluent, cribriform, labyrinthine, or complex papillary growth with loss of intervening endometrial stroma. Desmoplasia supports invasion in the appropriate setting. Myometrial invasion patterns Conventional invasion: irregular glands/nests with desmoplastic stroma. Pushing pattern: broad pushing front. Adenomyosis-like or adenoma-malignum-like pattern: haphazard glands within myometrium without an obvious desmoplastic response or accompanying endometrial stroma. MELF pattern: microcystic, elongated, and fragmented glands with fibromyxoid/inflammatory reaction disproportionate to the small invasive focus; cells may be eosinophilic or histiocytoid and can mimic vascular spaces. FIGO grade Grade 1: ≤5% solid non-glandular, non-squamous growth. Grade 2: 6–50%. Grade 3: >50%. Severe nuclear atypia involving >50% of tumor cells increases the grade by one level. If atypia is disproportionate to architecture, exclude serous carcinoma. Binary grouping: grades 1–2 low-grade; grade 3 high-grade. Low-grade tumors typically show diffuse PAX8, CK7, ER, and PR; p16 is usually patchy/non-block. High-grade tumors may lose ER/PR and show block-type p16 and mutation-type p53. Loss of PTEN, ARID1A, or one or more MMR proteins supports endometrioid differentiation in context but is not specific. GATA3 and napsin A are usually negative. Pilomatrix-like high-grade endometrioid carcinoma is an exception: often PAX8/ER/PR-negative, with aberrant nuclear β-catenin and variable CK7, CDX2, synaptophysin, and p63. Serous carcinoma: marked pleomorphism, high N:C ratio, macronucleoli, brisk mitoses, complex papillary/slit-like glands, mutation-type p53 and usually diffuse p16. Clear cell carcinoma: tubulocystic/papillary/solid patterns, hobnail or polygonal cells, napsin A/AMACR positivity and usually ER/PR negativity. Mesonephric-like carcinoma: mixed tubular/ductal/papillary/solid patterns, angulated grooved nuclei and colloid-like luminal material; GATA3/TTF1/CD10 positive, ER/PR usually absent. Dedifferentiated carcinoma: abrupt transition to a discohesive sheet-like undifferentiated component with loss of epithelial differentiation and possible SWI/SNF protein loss. Do not equate any solid growth with grade 3: exclude squamous areas from the solid-growth calculation. Beware of MELF-associated retraction/displacement artifacts that can mimic LVSI. Report depth of myometrial invasion, cervical stromal involvement, LVSI (focal vs substantial), and molecular subtype. Serous carcinoma High-grade carcinoma with marked nuclear pleomorphism and usually papillary and/or glandular architecture. Often arises in atrophic endometrium or an endometrial polyp. Complex papillary and/or glandular patterns are common; glands may be elongated and irregular with slit-like lumina. Less often, rounded glands or solid growth mimic endometrioid carcinoma. Tumor cells show high-grade cytology, marked pleomorphism, high N:C ratio, macronucleoli, and conspicuous mitoses. Multinucleation and psammoma bodies may occur. Intraepithelial replacement of native surface/glandular epithelium may be present. Myoinvasive tumors may show gaping glands and LVSI. Almost invariably mutation-type p53 (overexpression, null, or cytoplasmic pattern); p16 is typically diffuse/block-type and Ki-67 high. MMR proteins are usually retained. WT1 is positive in up to approximately one third, so it is not required. ER/PR are variable. HER2 overexpression/amplification occurs in approximately 25–30%, sometimes heterogeneously. High-grade endometrioid carcinoma: often retains endometrioid-type glands/metaplasia and may show ER/PR, PTEN/ARID1A loss, or dMMR; however, high-grade endometrioid carcinoma can also be p53-abnormal. Clear cell carcinoma: hobnail/cuboidal cells and tubulocystic pattern, with napsin A/AMACR support. POLE-mutated endometrioid carcinoma can be strikingly pleomorphic and mimic serous carcinoma; perform molecular classification rather than relying on morphology alone. The older labels 'serous endometrial intraepithelial carcinoma' and 'minimal uterine serous carcinoma' are not recommended for routine reporting. A superficially confined or polyp-associated lesion may still disseminate. Mesonephric-like carcinoma Carcinoma with mesonephric differentiation but without associated mesonephric remnants. Usually an admixture of tubular, ductal/glandular, papillary, glomeruloid, and solid patterns; spindle areas may occur. Nuclei are angulated with open/vesicular chromatin, overlap, and grooves. Eosinophilic colloid-like material may be present in lumina. Squamous and mucinous differentiation are absent; mesonephric remnants are not present. Most cases express GATA3, TTF1, CD10 (often apical), and PAX8, with variable extent. ER and PR are usually absent or minimal; p53 is wild-type and MMR proteins are retained. KRAS codon 12 (most often) or codon 13 activating mutation can support difficult cases. Endometrioid carcinoma with tubular/sex cord-like patterns: usually ER/PR-positive and may show squamous/morular differentiation; GATA3/TTF1 generally negative. Clear cell carcinoma: napsin A/AMACR support and hobnail/tubulocystic features; mesonephric-like carcinoma is usually napsin A-negative. Cervical mesonephric carcinoma is associated with mesonephric remnants and arises in the cervix; correlate site and precursor/remnant context. Do not grade this histotype; it is regarded as an aggressive histological type. Clear cell carcinoma Malignant epithelial tumor with tubulocystic, papillary, and/or solid patterns and clear-to-eosinophilic cells. Architectural patterns are often mixed. Papillae are typically short and rounded, often with hyalinized stroma. Tubulocystic areas contain variably confluent glands and cysts. Cells may be cuboidal, polygonal, hobnail, or flat, with clear or eosinophilic cytoplasm. Clear cytoplasm and hobnail cells are not individually required. At least focal moderate-to-severe nuclear atypia is typically present. Tall columnar cells, extensive stratification, tufting, detached budding, and squamous differentiation are absent or only focal. Most tumors have relatively low mitotic activity. Napsin A is positive in approximately 56–93% and AMACR/P504S in 75–88%, often in most tumor cells. ER and PR are usually negative or limited to a minority of cells. No single marker is definitive; interpret the panel with architecture and cytology. Secretory/tubal metaplasia or secretory endometrioid carcinoma: often bland, with endometrioid-type glands and ER/PR expression. Serous carcinoma: marked pleomorphism, brisk mitoses, mutation-type p53 and diffuse p16; clear cell carcinoma may have variable p53 status. Mesonephric-like carcinoma: colloid-like luminal material, angulated grooved nuclei, GATA3/TTF1/CD10 positivity and typically minimal ER/PR. Do not diagnose clear cell carcinoma on cytoplasmic clearing or hobnail cells alone. Mixed carcinoma Two or more distinct histological types, with at least one serous, clear cell, or mesonephric-like component. At least two spatially distinct and unequivocal carcinoma histotypes must be recognizable on H&E. The most common combination is endometrioid and serous carcinoma. Any confidently identified amount of a qualifying aggressive component is sufficient; report each component and its percentage. Do not use this category for morphologic variation within one histotype, ambiguous morphology, dedifferentiated carcinoma, or carcinosarcoma. Use component-directed stains to confirm the distinction when needed. For endometrioid/clear cell combinations, napsin A may highlight the clear cell component and PR the endometrioid component. p53, MMR, ER/PR, and histotype-associated markers can help map distinct components. Heterogeneous endometrioid carcinoma: variation remains within one histotype and does not establish a mixed carcinoma. Dedifferentiated carcinoma: differentiated carcinoma plus an undifferentiated component, not a second defined histotype. Carcinosarcoma: malignant epithelial and mesenchymal components. The highest-grade/aggressive component drives grading; report the histotypes and percentages. Undifferentiated / dedifferentiated carcinoma Undifferentiated carcinoma lacks overt lineage differentiation; dedifferentiated carcinoma combines it with a differentiated carcinoma. Undifferentiated component: diffuse sheets of relatively uniform small-to-intermediate cells, condensed chromatin, small or inconspicuous nucleoli, brisk mitotic activity (often >25 mitoses/2 mm²), and no convincing epithelial differentiation (no glands, cohesive nests, or trabeculae). Rhabdoid morphology and focal myxoid matrix may occur; tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes are often numerous. Dedifferentiated carcinoma has an associated differentiated component, most often FIGO grade 1–2 endometrioid carcinoma, with an abrupt or admixed interface. Epithelial differentiation may be limited: diffuse strong keratin is not typical; CK8/18 and EMA are more likely to be positive than broad keratin cocktails. Vimentin is positive; ER, PR, and E-cadherin are usually negative. PAX8 is usually negative but may be focal. Chromogranin/synaptophysin can label a minority of cells (<10%). dMMR is common. Loss of SMARCA4 (BRG1), SMARCB1 (INI1), or combined ARID1A/ARID1B occurs in a substantial subset (about two thirds). p53 mutation-type staining occurs in a minority. FIGO grade 3 endometrioid carcinoma retains cohesive epithelial architecture, glands, or squamous differentiation and usually more convincing epithelial-marker expression. Lymphoma/plasmacytoma: use CD45 and lineage markers; epithelial markers may be weak/negative in undifferentiated carcinoma, so use more than one epithelial marker. High-grade endometrial stromal sarcoma: assess stromal markers and defining molecular context. High-grade neuroendocrine carcinoma: convincing neuroendocrine morphology and diffuse neuroendocrine marker expression, rather than only rare positive cells. SMARCA4-deficient uterine sarcoma: correlate with morphology, MMR status, and broader molecular findings. Do not exclude undifferentiated carcinoma because pancytokeratin or PAX8 is negative. A differentiated endometrioid component is a key clue to dedifferentiated carcinoma. Other endometrial carcinomas Rare carcinoma categories require recognition of distinctive differentiation and exclusion of mimics. Neuroendocrine carcinoma The source chapter identifies neuroendocrine carcinoma as a separate rare category. Evaluate for high-grade small-cell or large-cell neuroendocrine morphology and confirm with a panel of neuroendocrine markers; do not infer neuroendocrine carcinoma from focal synaptophysin/chromogranin staining in an otherwise undifferentiated carcinoma. Carcinoma with germ cell / trophoblastic component A rare category recognized separately in the source chapter. Identify the specific component morphologically and use component-appropriate immunohistochemistry; the provided source excerpt does not supply a complete marker panel or detailed diagnostic criteria for this entity. Diagnostic caution The source material does not provide enough detailed histologic/IHC criteria to construct a full entity-specific differential for these rare categories. Correlate with the dedicated neuroendocrine and trophoblastic sections and specialist references rather than extrapolating criteria. POLEmut Pathogenic exonuclease-domain POLE mutation Ultramutated; generally excellent prognosis, irrespective of histotype. dMMR Loss of one or more MMR proteins (MLH1, PMS2, MSH2, MSH6) Surrogate for MSI-high; assess MLH1 promoter methylation when MLH1/PMS2 are lost. p53abn Mutation-type p53 IHC: overexpression, null, or cytoplasmic pattern Surrogate for a large subset of copy-number-high tumors; commonly high-grade. NSMP No POLEmut, dMMR, or p53abn classifier Heterogeneous residual group; ER status may further stratify risk. All PathologyGPS Gynecologic Pathology Diagnostic Reference Female Genital Tract · Uterine Corpus Epithelial Tumors of the Uterine Corpus A morphology-first diagnostic guide to endometrial precursors and carcinomas, emphasizing histologic recognition, invasion, immunohistochemistry, and practical differential diagnosis. H&E → Histotype → IHC → Molecular class • American English Initial Diagnostic Approach Begin with architecture and cytology on H&E. Establish whether the specimen shows a precursor lesion or invasive carcinoma, then determine the dominant differentiation pattern. Use IHC to resolve a focused differential—not as a substitute for morphology. Once carcinoma is established, complete the molecular classifier when indicated for prognostic and therapeutic stratification. 1 · Is it neoplastic? Assess gland density, cytologic distinction from background, lesion distribution, and whether crowding is focal or diffuse. 2 · Is there invasion? Look for confluent/cribriform glands, loss of intervening stroma, desmoplasia, destructive myometrial growth, and LVSI. 3 · What is the histotype? Endometrioid, serous, clear cell, mesonephric-like, mixed, or undifferentiated/dedifferentiated; recognize rare categories separately. 4 · Which tests answer the question? Use p53, MMR, ER/PR, PAX8, napsin A, GATA3/TTF1, and SWI/SNF markers according to morphology. A practical morphology-first branching scheme Glands remain separated by stroma Consider benign/proliferative endometrium, hyperplasia without atypia, or EIN according to cytology and distribution. Complex glands / stromal exclusion Consider endometrioid carcinoma; assess grade and myometrial invasion pattern. High-grade, non-endometrioid morphology Use targeted IHC to distinguish serous, clear cell, mesonephric-like, undifferentiated, and other rare carcinomas. Molecular Classification: Apply Across Histotypes The four-class ProMisE/TCGA-surrogate framework is not restricted to endometrioid carcinoma. Risk stratification Interpretation caveats: p53-abnormal IHC captures approximately 85–90% of copy-number-high tumors, not all of them. dMMR and MSI-high are not interchangeable. POLEmut tumors may show secondary p53 and/or MMR abnormalities; these multiple-classifier tumors require hierarchical interpretation. If molecular testing is unavailable, histotype, grade, and anatomic stage remain essential. Entity-Based Diagnostic Guide Select a category or search for a histologic feature, stain, or entity. Search: p53, napsin A, MELF, morules, GATA3… bg-teal-700 text-white bg-white text-slate-700 ring-1 ring-slate-300 hover:bg-slate-100 Immunohistochemistry / Molecular Interpret targeted stains in the context of morphology; no entity-specific panel is provided in this entry. -ddx Differential Diagnosis Diagnostic Pitfalls / Pearls No matching entity or feature. Try a broader search term. Core IHC Panels by Diagnostic Question Endometrioid vs serous ER/PR, p53, p16, MMR; consider PTEN and ARID1A in context. Clear cell vs endometrioid Napsin A and AMACR with ER/PR; integrate tubulocystic/papillary architecture. GATA3, TTF1, CD10 (apical), PAX8, ER/PR, p53, MMR. Undifferentiated component Use multiple epithelial markers (e.g., CK8/18, EMA); ER/PR, E-cadherin, PAX8; BRG1, INI1, ARID1A/ARID1B; MMR. EIN support PAX2, PTEN, β-catenin; morphology remains decisive. Reporting & Sampling Checklist Document histotype and FIGO grade where applicable. Assess depth and pattern of myometrial invasion; identify cervical stromal and serosal involvement. Report LVSI and distinguish focal from substantial/extensive involvement; avoid retraction/displacement artifacts. For mixed carcinoma, list each qualifying histotype and estimate its percentage. For dedifferentiated carcinoma, identify and describe both differentiated and undifferentiated components. Perform the molecular classifier (POLE, MMR, p53, NSMP) according to institutional protocol and clinical context. Consider HER2 testing in appropriate serous or p53-abnormal high-stage/recurrent tumors. ✓ PathologyGPS educational reference. Diagnostic interpretation should integrate morphology, immunohistochemistry, molecular findings, clinical information, and current institutional guidelines. title: Uterine Ligaments Tumors
content: use client papillary-cystadenoma Papillary Cystadenoma Benign epithelial / proposed mesonephric-type tumor Cystic-lobulated mass with complex tubulopapillary growth of bland, non-ciliated cuboidal cells; consider von Hippel–Lindau (VHL) syndrome. Usually uterine ligaments; less commonly fallopian tube or ovary. Cystic, lobulated lesion with a thick fibrotic capsule and internal fibrous bands, creating a solid-cystic appearance. Tubulocystic to papillary growth, with broad-based and delicate branching papillae; focal solid areas may occur. Lining cells are cuboidal to low columnar, non-ciliated, with clear to eosinophilic cytoplasm. Nuclei are uniform with inconspicuous nucleoli. Stromal hyalinization and prominent subepithelial blood vessels are common. Cytologic atypia, mitotic activity, and necrosis are typically absent. Frequently positive: AE1/AE3, EMA, CK7, PAX8, and PAX2. WT1, CD10, and calretinin are variably positive. ER and PR are negative. The profile supports epithelial differentiation and a proposed mesonephric association; no single marker is independently diagnostic. Wolffian tumor Usually shows mixed hollow and solid tubules, sieve-like cysts, and diffuse growth. It is usually negative for EMA, claudin-4, PAX8, GATA3, and TTF1. Müllerian serous or other epithelial neoplasm Assess epithelial atypia, papillary complexity, and destructive invasion. Bland non-ciliated lining cells and the fibrotic cystic-lobulated architecture favor papillary cystadenoma. Secondary / metastatic papillary lesion Correlate with clinical history, distribution, and the complete immunophenotype; no single ancillary marker panel is established for this differential; interpretation should be guided by morphology and clinical context. VHL mutation or allelic loss has been reported; demonstration of a VHL alteration may support the diagnosis in a challenging case. The strong association with VHL syndrome is clinically important; this tumor may be the sentinel manifestation. Occurs in adults and may present with abdominal pain; some lesions are incidental. Extremely rare; most reported patients have VHL syndrome. The vast majority are benign, although rare exceptions have been reported. Do not dismiss this as an incidental benign cystic neoplasm without considering the VHL association. Mesonephric origin is proposed from location and immunophenotype, not definitively established. Essential: cystic / lobulated mass with complex tubulopapillary growth of non-ciliated cuboidal cells. Desirable: personal or family history of VHL syndrome. wolffian-tumor Wolffian Tumor Presumed mesonephric / Wolffian tumor Broad-ligament tumor with hollow-to-solid tubules, sieve-like cysts, and diffuse growth; cytology is usually bland and IHC is variable. Most often broad ligament; rare cases in ovary, fallopian tube, or non-adnexal sites. Usually well-circumscribed and solid or solid-cystic; hemorrhage, necrosis, or focal calcification may be present. Admixture of hollow to solid tubules, sieve-like cysts, and diffuse growth; proportions vary. Hyalinized stromal bands may be prominent and nodular or delicate and interspersed. Cells are cuboidal to ovoid, occasionally spindled, with scant cytoplasm, small nuclei, and inconspicuous to small nucleoli. PAS-positive eosinophilic luminal secretions may be present. Atypia and mitotic activity are usually minimal. Variable expression of sex cord-stromal, epithelial, and mesothelial markers, hormone receptors, and CD10. Usually negative for EMA, claudin-4, PAX8, GATA3, and TTF1. Despite the presumed Wolffian origin, these tumors do not reliably show the GATA3 / TTF1 phenotype of mesonephric carcinoma. STK11 adnexal tumor Important overlap in morphology and IHC. STK11 adnexal tumor is supported by complete cytoplasmic STK11 loss and/or an STK11 genomic alteration; it is often aggressive and may be associated with Peutz–Jeghers syndrome. Mesonephric / mesonephric-like carcinoma KRAS / NRAS alterations may support these mimics in the appropriate setting. Wolffian tumors are usually GATA3- and TTF1-negative and lack recurring genomic alterations. Sex cord-stromal tumor Wolffian tumors may express sex cord markers, so a single positive marker is not diagnostic. FOXL2 or DICER1 alterations may help evaluate mimics. Endometrioid carcinoma Correlate with Müllerian morphology and phenotype; PTEN, PIK3CA, or ARID1A alterations may support endometrioid lineage. Peritoneal mesothelioma Assess morphology and a broader mesothelial panel; BAP1, CDKN2A, or NF2 alterations may help in selected cases. Wolffian tumors lack recurring genomic alterations. In challenging cases, molecular testing may help exclude mimics: KRAS / NRAS (mesonephric carcinoma), STK11 (STK11 adnexal tumor), FOXL2 / DICER1 (sex cord-stromal tumor), PTEN / PIK3CA / ARID1A (endometrioid carcinoma), and BAP1 / CDKN2A / NF2 (mesothelioma). Age range 19–83 years (mean approximately 45); many patients are middle-aged. May present with abdominopelvic pain or abnormal bleeding; incidental detection is common. Usually benign. Rare recurrences have been reported, sometimes after incomplete excision or iatrogenic dissemination. Some historically reported malignant cases may represent morphologic mimics. Do not diagnose mesonephric carcinoma solely from presumed Wolffian origin or tubular morphology. GATA3 / TTF1 negativity alone does not establish Wolffian tumor; integrate site, architecture, full IHC, and molecular findings. Actively exclude STK11 adnexal tumor because behavior and hereditary implications differ. Essential: typically broad-ligament origin with tubular, sieve-like, and/or solid growth. Bland cytology and the characteristic admixture of architectural patterns provide additional support. stk11-adnexal-tumor STK11 Adnexal Tumor Adnexal tumor of uncertain histogenesis Morphologically diverse paratubal / para-ovarian tumor with interanastomosing cords and trabeculae, myxoid-type stroma, and STK11 loss; distinguish from usually indolent Wolffian tumor. Usually paratubal / para-ovarian soft tissue; rarely ovary, fallopian tube, uterine serosa, or abdominopelvic peritoneum. Usually solid or solid-cystic, often with hemorrhage and necrosis. Most common pattern: interanastomosing cords and trabeculae. Other patterns include cribriform, tubular, cystic, acinar, papillary, nested, and solid. Stroma is often myxoid, but may be edematous, hyalinized, or loosely collagenous. Cells are columnar to cuboidal with relatively uniform atypia, round to ovoid nuclei, vesicular chromatin, prominent nucleoli, and eosinophilic to clear cytoplasm. Overt pleomorphism is absent. Spindled cells may occur but are rarely dominant; signet ring-like cells or whorling may occur. Mitoses are variable; necrosis is uncommon in the source description. Complete loss of cytoplasmic STK11 staining is a key finding. Other markers are nonspecific: keratins, sex cord and mesothelial markers, hormone receptors, CD10, and desmin may be variably expressed. PAX8, EMA, GATA3, and SF1 may show limited expression. Claudin-4, FOXL2, and TTF1 are negative; p53 is wild-type. The most consequential differential. Morphology and IHC overlap; STK11 loss and/or genomic alteration supports STK11 adnexal tumor. Wolffian tumors lack recurring genomic alterations and are usually benign. Sex cord markers may be variable or limited. FOXL2 is negative in the source profile; consider FOXL2 / DICER1 alterations when evaluating mimics. GATA3 and TTF1 are usually negative in STK11 adnexal tumor; KRAS / NRAS alterations may support mesonephric carcinoma in the proper setting. Assess for convincing Müllerian epithelial differentiation and alterations such as PTEN, PIK3CA, or ARID1A; STK11 alteration supports this entity. Defined by STK11 loss-of-function alterations, including point mutations, insertions / deletions, structural rearrangements, and deletions. Testing should cover the entire STK11 coding region and assess copy-number alterations. Approximately 30% are associated with Peutz–Jeghers syndrome. Age range 16–74 years (median approximately 40). Most present with a pelvic mass; approximately 10–15% are incidental. Tumors are often large (40–225 mm; median approximately 110 mm). Metastatic disease is present at diagnosis in approximately 50–60%; recurrence has been reported in approximately 80%. Disease-related death occurs in approximately 50% in the cited series, although follow-up is limited. Prognostic features have not been identified. Do not classify as Wolffian tumor based on tubular, trabecular, or sieve-like architecture alone. Interpret STK11 loss with appropriate internal controls; use molecular testing when needed. Recognition has implications for Peutz–Jeghers syndrome evaluation and clinical management because many tumors behave aggressively. Essential: multiple histologic patterns, often interanastomosing cords / trabeculae, with myxoid, edematous, or hyalinized stroma. Essential support: STK11 IHC loss and/or an STK11 genomic alteration, particularly in patients without known Peutz–Jeghers syndrome. Papillary cystadenoma Tubulocystic / papillary PAX8+, PAX2+, CK7+; ER / PR− VHL association; usually benign Hollow / solid tubules; sieve-like cysts; diffuse Variable; usually EMA−, claudin-4−, PAX8−, GATA3−, TTF1− Usually benign; exclude mimics Interanastomosing cords / trabeculae; diverse patterns STK11 cytoplasmic loss; claudin-4−, FOXL2−, TTF1− Often aggressive; PJS association PathologyGPS · Female Genital Tract Tumors of the Broad Ligament and Other Uterine Ligaments Diagnostic guide to uncommon ligament-associated tumors, emphasizing histologic architecture, immunohistochemistry, molecular testing, and clinically important mimics. Most common benign entities Leiomyoma and adenomyoma Most common sarcoma Leiomyosarcoma Syndrome-associated clues VHL · Peutz–Jeghers At-a-Glance Diagnostic Overview High-yield features of the principal uncommon epithelial and adnexal tumors encountered in the uterine ligament region. Look for complete cytoplasmic STK11 loss and confirmatory genomic testing when appropriate. Wolffian tumors are usually benign; STK11 adnexal tumors are often aggressive and may signal Peutz–Jeghers syndrome. Clinical clue: papillary cystadenoma A broad-ligament papillary cystadenoma should prompt consideration of VHL syndrome and may be its sentinel manifestation.
