title: Epithelial Tumors
content: use client overview Overview sil Squamous intraepithelial lesions hpv-scc HPV-associated SCC ind-scc HPV-independent SCC undetermined SCC, HPV status undetermined villous Villous / tubulovillous adenoma intestinal Intestinal-type adenocarcinoma skene Skene gland adenocarcinoma mullerian Müllerian papilloma mixed Mixed tumor fibroepithelial Fibroepithelial stromal polyp workflow Diagnostic approach smooth start PathologyGPS / Female Genital Tract Vagina Diagnostic reference · Epithelial tumors Vaginal Epithelial Tumors A morphology-first guide to vaginal squamous lesions, carcinomas, glandular neoplasms, and selected miscellaneous epithelial or stromal lesions, with practical immunohistochemical workups and differential diagnoses. Diagnostic principle Establish the site of origin before assigning a primary vaginal diagnosis. topic-search Find a topic Search this page... bg-teal-50 font-semibold text-teal-800 text-slate-600 hover:bg-slate-50 hover:text-slate-900 Use the navigation to move between entities. This page is an educational diagnostic aid and does not replace clinicopathological correlation. Classification and key principles Start here Primary vaginal tumor: a diagnosis of exclusion Primary vaginal malignancies are rare. Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) is the most common primary vaginal cancer. Most vaginal SCCs are HPV-associated, but HPV-independent SCCs also occur. Primary vaginal adenocarcinomas are uncommon; most adenocarcinomas involving the vagina represent direct extension or metastasis from another site. Before diagnosing primary vaginal SCC, exclude a concurrent cervical or vulvar SCC and review the history of either malignancy. A cervical or vulvar SCC within the preceding 5 years is generally considered to exclude a new primary vaginal SCC. For glandular tumors, exclude a cervical, endometrial, colorectal, urinary tract, or other primary as appropriate to the morphology and location. HPV-associated squamous lesions may be multifocal across the cervix, vagina, vulva, perineum, and anal/perianal region. The WHO source recognizes vaginal HPV-independent CIN as a category, but does not yet establish a corresponding HPV-independent precursor lesion for HPV-independent vaginal SCC. Entities covered in this page Group Entities Squamous cell tumors and precursors Squamous intraepithelial lesion (LSIL / HSIL); HPV-associated SCC; HPV-independent SCC; SCC, HPV status undetermined Glandular tumors Villous / tubulovillous adenoma; intestinal-type adenocarcinoma; adenocarcinoma of Skene gland origin Miscellaneous tumors Müllerian papilloma; mixed tumor of the vagina; fibroepithelial stromal polyp Other entities, including clear cell carcinoma, gastric-type adenocarcinoma, endometrioid carcinoma, mesonephric adenocarcinoma, carcinosarcoma, adenosquamous carcinoma, adenosarcoma, sarcomas, and germ cell tumors, are addressed in other relevant chapters in the source classification and are not expanded here. Squamous intraepithelial lesions (VaIN) Definition, distribution, and clinical context Vaginal squamous intraepithelial lesions (SILs) are HPV-related proliferations with abnormal nuclear features and disordered maturation that remain above the basement membrane. They most often involve the upper third of the vagina and the fornices and may be multifocal. Most patients are asymptomatic; lesions are frequently detected during colposcopy performed for cervical HPV-associated disease. More than 80% of cases have a concurrent or prior history of cervical SIL or SCC. Smoking, immunosuppression, HIV infection, and a history of cervical SIL are recognized risk factors. Two-tier histologic classification LAST / WHO category Legacy terminology Interpretation LSIL VaIN 1; condyloma (when applicable) Usually productive, transient HPV infection; commonly regresses. HSIL VaIN 2 and VaIN 3 Transforming infection, almost always associated with high-risk HPV. Histologic interpretation and p16 use follow the same principles as cervical SIL. The supplied vaginal source refers the reader to the cervical SIL section for the detailed morphologic and p16 criteria; it does not reproduce those criteria in full. Accordingly, this page does not invent a separate vaginal-specific threshold. LSIL reflects productive HPV infection and may show koilocytotic change with maturation retained in much of the epithelium. HSIL shows greater cytologic atypia and impaired maturation, with atypical cells extending into a substantial portion or the full thickness of the epithelium, depending on grade. Use block-type p16 staining to support HSIL in morphologically equivocal cases, in accordance with LAST principles; interpret p16 in the context of H&E morphology. Do not diagnose invasion unless atypical squamous cells breach the basement membrane and infiltrate stroma. Ancillary studies and clinical behavior HPV16 is the most prevalent genotype in both LSIL and HSIL; its relative contribution increases with lesion grade. Other commonly reported types include HPV33, HPV52, and HPV18. Molecular HPV testing is not considered clinically relevant for routine diagnosis in the source classification. Estimated progression of HSIL (VaIN 2/3) to invasion is approximately 2–6%, lower than in the cervix; risk is greatest for VaIN 3. LSIL has a substantially lower progression risk. Recurrence is more frequent in immunocompromised patients. Squamous cell carcinoma, HPV-associated Morphology and diagnostic setting HPV-associated vaginal SCC is an invasive or exophytic malignant epithelial tumor showing pure squamous differentiation and attributable to persistent high-risk HPV infection. It most often arises in the upper third of the vagina, frequently along the posterior wall. Gross appearances include ulcerated plaques, polypoid masses, and stricturing lesions. Patients may present with vaginal bleeding or discharge, postcoital bleeding, urinary symptoms, pelvic pain, or a sensation of a vaginal mass. Histology is essentially the same as HPV-associated cervical SCC. Morphology alone cannot reliably distinguish HPV-associated from HPV-independent vaginal SCC. The source classification does not recommend grading primary vaginal SCC. IHC and HPV testing Test Typical result Diagnostic use / caveat p16 Block-type (diffuse, strong nuclear and cytoplasmic staining) Surrogate marker supporting transforming high-risk HPV infection. p53 Usually wild-type pattern Supports the typical HPV-associated profile but is not independently diagnostic. High-risk HPV ISH / PCR Positive Desirable confirmation, particularly if p16 is equivocal or discordant with morphology. Essential criteria include invasive carcinoma with squamous differentiation, no qualifying prior or concurrent cervical/vulvar SCC, and block-type p16 staining as a surrogate for HPV association (with occasional exceptions). Positive HPV testing is desirable when p16 is negative, non-block, or equivocal. Differential diagnosis Differential How to distinguish HPV-independent vaginal SCC Cannot be separated reliably by H&E alone. HPV-independent tumors are more often keratinizing and commonly show non-block/negative p16 and mutation-type p53; confirm with HPV testing when needed. Cervical or vulvar SCC involving vagina Use clinical history, imaging, examination, tumor epicenter, and prior pathology. A cervical/vulvar SCC within 5 years generally argues against a new primary vaginal SCC. HSIL / VaIN HSIL is intraepithelial and lacks destructive stromal invasion. Carefully assess the epithelial-stromal interface, especially in tangential or fragmented biopsies. Adenosquamous carcinoma Look for a bona fide malignant glandular component rather than entrapped benign glands or squamous maturation. This entity is not detailed in the supplied vaginal chapter. Prognosis Outcome is driven by stage, tumor size, and patient factors. High-risk HPV positivity is reported as a favorable prognostic indicator; HPV16-positive tumors have been associated with improved survival. The source reports an approximate 5-year overall survival of 50% across stages. Squamous cell carcinoma, HPV-independent Morphology and biology HPV-independent vaginal SCC is an invasive or exophytic malignant epithelial tumor with pure squamous differentiation arising through mechanisms not associated with HPV. It occurs predominantly in postmenopausal patients (reported median age approximately 73 years), often in the upper third and posterior vaginal wall. Compared with HPV-associated SCC, the keratinizing pattern is more frequent. However, there is substantial morphologic overlap, and histology alone cannot establish HPV independence. No established HPV-independent precursor lesion is currently recognized in the vaginal classification. IHC and molecular workup Marker / test Common pattern Negative or non-block staining Does not support transforming high-risk HPV infection. Mutation-type pattern is common May support an HPV-independent pathway; not all cases are p53-abnormal. HPV testing Negative PCR or ISH may establish absence of HPV; ensure assay coverage and adequate tumor. TP53 Mutations reported in a subset Molecular support in selected cases; not required for routine diagnosis. Essential criteria are invasive squamous carcinoma, exclusion of a qualifying cervical/vulvar primary, and negative/non-block p16 and/or negative HPV molecular testing. The source notes worse overall and progression-free survival compared with HPV-associated vaginal SCC in available studies, while evidence remains limited because of rarity. Practical distinction from HPV-associated SCC Do not use keratinization, age, or p53 alone to assign HPV status. Integrate p16 and HPV testing. If p16 is non-block and HPV testing is unavailable or inconclusive, use the HPV-status-undetermined category rather than overcalling HPV independence. Squamous cell carcinoma, HPV status undetermined When to use this designation Use this category for invasive vaginal SCC when HPV status cannot be determined because ancillary testing is unavailable, infeasible, or inconclusive. The source emphasizes that most such tumors are still likely to be HPV-associated, although at a lower rate than cervical SCC. Report the morphologic diagnosis and explicitly state that HPV status is undetermined. Do not infer HPV independence from a non-keratinizing or keratinizing appearance alone. Villous adenoma and tubulovillous adenoma Morphology These are exceptionally rare benign primary vaginal glandular tumors resembling colorectal adenomas. Most reported lesions occur along the lower posterior vaginal wall. They are usually polypoid and may present with a mass or abnormal bleeding. Villiform and/or tubular architecture lined by intestinal-type columnar epithelium. Scattered goblet cells may be present. Nuclei are elongated, hyperchromatic, and pseudostratified; atypia ranges from mild to severe. There is no stromal invasion. Severe cytologic atypia and/or complex architecture should be classified as adenoma with high-grade dysplasia using criteria analogous to colorectal adenomas. IHC and differential diagnosis Marker Use CK20 Usually positive Supports intestinal differentiation. CDX2 Supports intestinal phenotype. CK7 Variable Not sufficiently discriminatory alone. ER Usually negative Consistent with intestinal rather than Müllerian differentiation. Key differential: intestinal-type adenocarcinoma. The decisive distinction is absence versus presence of destructive stromal invasion. Also consider secondary involvement by colorectal adenoma/carcinoma and benign intestinal metaplasia; correlate with lesion epicenter and clinical history. Recurrence has been reported, and a case of intestinal-type adenocarcinoma developing after an adenoma with high-grade dysplasia has been described. Complete sampling is important when high-grade dysplasia or an associated invasive focus is suspected. Adenocarcinoma, intestinal type Definition and location Intestinal-type adenocarcinoma is a rare primary adenocarcinoma of the distal female genital tract with intestinal differentiation. Vaginal primaries usually arise in the lower third, particularly the posterior wall near the vulvar junction. The vulvar counterpart typically occurs in the vestibule close to the vagina. Before diagnosing a primary vaginal tumor, exclude direct extension or metastasis from a colorectal or other gastrointestinal primary. Some tumors are associated with an intestinal-type villous/tubulovillous adenoma or benign-appearing intestinal epithelium, supporting an adenoma–carcinoma sequence. Histologic features Variable tubular/glandular, tubulovillous, and solid architecture. Columnar cells with intracytoplasmic mucin, often including goblet cells. Signet-ring cells, extracellular mucin, and dirty necrosis may occur. Occasional tumors contain prominent neuroendocrine cells. An associated intestinal-type adenoma or benign intestinal-type epithelium may be identified. IHC profile and differential diagnosis Typical profile Intestinal differentiation. Intestinal phenotype. SATB2 Supports lower gastrointestinal/intestinal differentiation; not proof of colorectal origin. CEA Often expressed in intestinal-type adenocarcinoma. Variable expression; do not use alone to determine origin. ER / PR Against conventional Müllerian hormone receptor-positive adenocarcinoma. PAX8 / SOX17 Usually absent in this tumor type. Wild-type or mutation-type Variable; neither pattern excludes the diagnosis. Most important differential: colorectal adenocarcinoma involving vagina. The morphologic and immunophenotypic overlap can be substantial. No single intestinal marker proves a vaginal primary. Establish the anatomic epicenter and exclude a gastrointestinal primary clinically and radiologically. An adjacent vaginal intestinal-type adenoma or metaplastic epithelium supports, but does not by itself prove, local origin. Other considerations include metastatic appendiceal or other GI adenocarcinoma, and HPV-associated cervical adenocarcinoma with intestinal differentiation. The latter should be evaluated with HPV/p16 testing and cervical site correlation. Molecular findings and behavior Reported recurrent alterations include TP53 and KRAS variants. The source describes molecular clustering with vulvar intestinal-type adenocarcinoma and colorectal adenocarcinoma, distinct from HPV-associated intestinal-type and HPV-independent gastric-type cervical adenocarcinomas. Long-term outcome data are sparse; late recurrences and disease-related deaths have been reported. Adenocarcinoma of Skene gland origin Anatomic clue and morphology This extremely rare adenocarcinoma arises from Skene (periurethral) glands, the female homologues of the prostate. Typical sites include the periurethral/paraurethral region, distal urethra, anterior vaginal wall, and bladder neck. Patients may present with a mass; hematuria or incontinence is less common. Serum PSA may be elevated. Morphology resembles prostatic acinar adenocarcinoma: well-formed to poorly formed glands lined by cuboidal or columnar cells with pale or eosinophilic cytoplasm, round nuclei, and prominent nucleoli. Cribriform growth is common; individual glands, solid areas, or single-file growth may occur. Residual benign Skene glands or a focus resembling high-grade prostatic intraepithelial neoplasia may be present. IHC profile Reported pattern Practical point PSA Generally positive Supports prostatic/Skene gland differentiation. PAP / PSAP Useful in combination with other prostatic markers. NKX3.1 Nuclear prostatic lineage marker. P501S / prostein Additional support for prostatic differentiation. AMACR Positive in some cases Variable; not required. Generally negative A supportive pattern, not a stand-alone criterion. Variable. AR May be positive Can provide additional support. Differential diagnosis: primary urethral adenocarcinoma, metastatic prostatic adenocarcinoma (in the unusual context of a patient with relevant history), and other periurethral gland tumors. The diagnosis requires an appropriate anatomic epicenter and a prostatic immunophenotype; no single marker is sufficient in isolation. Behavior Experience is limited. Inguinal or pelvic lymph node metastases have been documented, although the small number of reported patients with follow-up did not show recurrence or disease-related mortality after treatment. Clinical setting and morphology Müllerian papilloma is a benign papillary Müllerian epithelial tumor of the vagina or cervix. Vaginal lesions most often occur in the upper vagina and predominantly affect prepubertal girls, although adolescents and young adults have been reported. Vaginal bleeding or discharge is a common presentation. Exophytic mucosal or, less commonly, intramural lesion. Slender fibrovascular cores lined by bland cuboidal or columnar epithelium. Hobnail morphology may be present. Nuclei are uniform with fine chromatin; atypia is absent or minimal. Mitoses are absent or sparse; squamous metaplasia may occur. The supplied source does not define a specific diagnostic IHC panel or molecular signature. Diagnosis is primarily morphologic. Differential diagnosis and behavior Consider clear cell carcinoma, particularly when hobnail cells are conspicuous. Significant nuclear atypia, mitotic activity, complex destructive growth, and infiltrative invasion argue against benign Müllerian papilloma. Clear cell carcinoma should be evaluated with an appropriate panel (for example, Napsin A and HNF1β in the relevant differential), but the source does not provide a vaginal-specific marker profile. Outcome is generally favorable. Recurrence, including multiple recurrences, has been reported; one case of clear cell carcinoma after multiple recurrences has been described. Clinical follow-up and complete assessment of recurrent lesions are appropriate. Mixed tumor of the vagina Mixed tumor is a benign neoplasm composed of spindled and epithelial (glandular and/or squamous) elements. It is usually a well-circumscribed solid mass in the posterior distal vaginal wall near the hymen. Cellular spindle-cell component often predominates and may grow in fascicles, cords, nests, or reticular arrays. Epithelial elements are sharply demarcated and may be mucinous glands, mature squamous epithelium, or both. Eosinophilic hyaline material or globules may be present in myxomatous or collagenous stroma. Nuclear atypia is minimal; mitotic activity is usually low. IHC profile and differential Reported coexpression includes AE1/AE3, CK7, EMA, CD10, SMA, desmin, h-caldesmon, WT1, calretinin, BCL2, and CD34. The spindle cells may strongly express epithelial markers. S100 and SOX10 are typically negative. Diagnostic pitfall: epithelial marker expression by the spindle component does not by itself indicate carcinoma or carcinosarcoma. The diagnosis rests on a well-circumscribed lesion with morphologically benign epithelial and spindle-cell components, minimal atypia, and generally low mitotic activity. Differential diagnoses include aggressive angiomyxoma, angiomyofibroblastoma, cellular angiofibroma, leiomyoma, and malignant mixed Müllerian tumor/carcinosarcoma. The source does not provide a definitive comparative IHC algorithm for these entities; use morphology, circumscription, vascular pattern, cytologic atypia, mitoses, and site. These are benign lesions. Local recurrence may occur when incompletely excised. Clinical and histologic features Fibroepithelial stromal polyp is a benign polypoid mesenchymal proliferation of the lower female genital tract, most often vaginal and less often vulvar or cervical. It commonly occurs in reproductive-aged women but may arise at any age, including during pregnancy and after menopause. Pregnancy and occasional tamoxifen exposure suggest hormonal influence. Polypoid or pedunculated lesion lined by squamous epithelium. Hypocellular, poorly circumscribed subepithelial stroma directly abuts the surface epithelium, which may be thickened or ulcerated. Spindled to stellate stromal cells with delicate cytoplasmic processes in collagenous to edematous stroma. Multinucleated stromal cells are characteristic, often subepithelial or perivascular, with rosette-like nuclear arrangement and abundant eosinophilic to amphophilic cytoplasm. Dilated capillaries and medium-sized arterioles may be present; larger central vessels occur in some cases. Mitoses are usually rare or absent. IHC and the pseudosarcomatous pitfall Typical finding Desmin Consistently positive Supports lower genital tract stromal differentiation. Supports hormone-responsive stromal phenotype. CD34 Sometimes positive SMA Rarely positive Usually not a dominant marker. Myogenin / MYOD1 Occasional nuclear positivity Coexpression of both has not been reported in the source. HMGA2 Nuclear positivity in a subset, especially large lesions Can be supportive but is not universal. RB1 Loss reported in some cases Potential molecular association; not a universal finding. Pregnancy-associated lesions may be hypercellular and show marked nuclear pleomorphism and increased mitotic activity, including atypical mitoses. These changes can mimic sarcoma. Interpret atypia and mitotic activity in the context of the characteristic architecture, multinucleated stromal cells, clinical setting, and IHC profile; do not equate atypia alone with malignancy. embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma (especially botryoid pattern), leiomyoma/leiomyosarcoma, angiomyofibroblastoma, aggressive angiomyxoma, and other lower genital tract stromal tumors. The source does not provide a full differential-marker matrix. Myogenin/MYOD1 should be interpreted carefully because occasional positive nuclei have been reported in fibroepithelial stromal polyps. Behavior and management context Fibroepithelial stromal polyps are benign but may recur locally. Complete local excision is the treatment of choice for primary and recurrent lesions. Spontaneous postpartum regression can occur. The relationship between incomplete excision and recurrence is not fully established in the source. Stepwise workflow for a vaginal mass or biopsy Confirm the anatomic epicenter. Determine whether the lesion is truly vaginal, cervical, vulvar/vestibular, urethral/periurethral, or represents direct extension from an adjacent organ. Review prior cervical/vulvar neoplasia, especially within 5 years. Classify the dominant morphology. Separate squamous intraepithelial lesion, invasive squamous carcinoma, gland-forming intestinal-type lesion, prostatic-type periurethral adenocarcinoma, papillary Müllerian lesion, mixed epithelial-spindle lesion, and stromal polyp. For squamous lesions, establish invasion. Assess the basement membrane and stromal interface. If invasive SCC is present, use p16 and/or high-risk HPV testing to classify HPV association. Use HPV-status-undetermined when testing is unavailable or inconclusive. For intestinal-type glands, exclude a GI primary. CDX2, CK20, SATB2, and CEA support intestinal differentiation but cannot distinguish a local primary from colorectal metastasis. Correlate with imaging, endoscopy, history, tumor epicenter, and any adjacent intestinal-type adenoma. For anterior vaginal/periurethral tumors, consider Skene gland origin. A prostatic-type morphology plus PSA, PAP, NKX3.1, and P501S expression supports this rare diagnosis. For papillary lesions, assess cytologic grade and invasion. Bland Müllerian papilloma has slender fibrovascular cores and minimal atypia; significant atypia, mitoses, or destructive invasion requires exclusion of carcinoma, including clear cell carcinoma. For spindle-cell or polypoid lesions, evaluate architecture and cytology. Recognize the characteristic multinucleated stromal cells of fibroepithelial stromal polyp and the biphasic epithelial/spindle composition of mixed tumor. Be cautious about pregnancy-related atypia and mitotic activity. Sample adequately. Extensively sample heterogeneous, ulcerated, recurrent, or high-grade lesions to exclude focal invasion or a malignant component. Document margins and the relationship to adjacent structures where relevant. Quick IHC selection guide Morphologic question Useful initial studies HPV-associated vs HPV-independent SCC p16, p53; high-risk HPV ISH/PCR if needed Block p16 supports HPV association; non-block/negative p16 with negative HPV testing supports HPV independence. p53 mutation-type is common but not universal in HPV-independent SCC. Intestinal differentiation CDX2, CK20, SATB2, CEA; CK7, PAX8, ER/PR as context Confirms phenotype, not site of origin. Exclude GI primary. Skene gland / prostatic-type adenocarcinoma PSA, PAP, NKX3.1, P501S; consider AR and AMACR A concordant prostatic marker panel plus periurethral epicenter is supportive. Müllerian papilloma vs clear cell carcinoma Morphology first; consider Napsin A and HNF1β in the differential Source does not define a specific vaginal papilloma IHC panel. Assess atypia, mitoses, and invasion. Desmin, ER, PR; optional CD34, SMA, HMGA2, RB1 as indicated Characteristic stromal phenotype; no single marker substitutes for morphology. Broad epithelial and mesenchymal panel guided by morphology Coexpression may occur in spindle cells; benign biphasic morphology is central. Reporting checklist Specify the exact entity and, for vaginal SCC, HPV association when established. State the basis for primary vaginal origin and document exclusion of a cervical/vulvar or distant primary when clinically relevant. For SIL, use the two-tier LSIL/HSIL terminology and identify invasion if present. For adenocarcinoma, describe the differentiation pattern and summarize the IHC profile without implying that intestinal markers establish a vaginal primary. For unusual benign lesions, document atypia, mitotic activity, necrosis, invasion, and completeness of sampling as appropriate. Correlate with clinical, radiologic, and endoscopic findings for tumors with a plausible secondary source. Source note: This page is structured from the user-provided WHO Classification text on vaginal tumors. Where the source refers to the cervical chapter for detailed criteria or does not provide a specific IHC/differential algorithm, the limitation is stated rather than silently supplemented. Clinical correlation and current institutional protocols remain essential. PathologyGPS · Diagnostic Excellence. Clinical Insight.

title: Epithelial Tumors
content: Squamous Intraepithelial Lesions (SIL): Condyloma and LSIL HPV-associated, non-invasive squamous lesions Condyloma acuminatum: acanthotic squamous epithelium with prominent papillomatous, verrucous, lobulated, or filiform architecture. Koilocytosis is variable and is often most evident in the valleys between papillae. Koilocytes show rigid perinuclear halos, eccentric nuclei, enlarged hyperchromatic nuclei with irregular raisinoid contours, coarse chromatin, and sometimes binucleation. Flat vulvar LSIL is uncommon. Squamous maturation is preserved, with viral cytopathic changes in the middle and superficial epithelial layers; mitoses remain in the lower third. A subset of condylomata and, less often, flat LSIL may resemble seborrhoeic keratosis. Condyloma is commonly associated with low-risk HPV 6 or 11; LSIL may contain low-risk or high-risk HPV. p16 is usually patchy/non-block in LSIL and condyloma; rare high-risk HPV-associated LSIL may show block staining. Ki-67 is increased mainly in the lower epithelium, but may extend into the upper third in LSIL. HPV DNA or RNA in situ hybridization or PCR can detect HPV when needed. HSIL: basal atypia, loss of maturation, suprabasal mitoses, and block-type p16. HPV-independent VIN: evaluate p16 and p53 patterns; morphology alone is not sufficiently reliable for classification. Seborrhoeic keratosis-like lesion: interpret in the context of age, morphology, and HPV testing when relevant. Do not diagnose flat vulvar LSIL from koilocyte-like change alone. The source emphasizes strict criteria because flat LSIL is uncommon at this site. High-Grade Squamous Intraepithelial Lesion (HSIL) HPV-associated precursor Loss of squamous maturation with atypia beginning in at least the basal third and extending variably toward the surface. Atypia includes disorganization, nuclear enlargement and hyperchromasia, increased nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio, and mitotic activity. HSIL-2 retains some maturation; atypical basaloid cells and mitoses extend into the lower two thirds. HSIL-3 shows subtotal or full-thickness loss of maturation. Warty/condylomatous HSIL may show florid exophytic growth, papillomatosis, partial superficial maturation, koilocytosis, and multinucleation. Extension into skin appendages is common and may mimic invasion. Stromal melanophages are frequent; dermal amyloid or mucinous areas may occur. p16: continuous, strong nuclear and cytoplasmic block-type staining, typically involving at least the basal third. p53: wild-type pattern. This may be heterogeneous or show basal-sparing suprabasal staining; the basal-sparing pattern is highly specific for HPV-associated lesions. Ki-67 shows increased proliferation extending above the basal compartment. Validated HPV DNA/RNA testing can be used when required. HPV-I VIN, p53abn: often keratinizing with basal atypia and aberrant p53; an HSIL-like/basaloid pattern can overlap. HPV-I VIN, p53wt: may be verruciform and acanthotic but has non-block p16 and wild-type p53. Invasion: irregular detached nests, loss of polarity, eosinophilic cytoplasm, and desmoplastic stroma support stromal invasion. Appendageal extension by HSIL is common and should not be mistaken for stromal invasion. Assess the epithelial-stromal interface. Vulvar Intraepithelial Neoplasia, HPV-independent (HPV-I VIN) HPV-independent precursor; p53abn or p53wt p53-aberrant/differentiated pattern: keratinizing epithelium with retained but abnormal maturation, conspicuous basal pleomorphism, basal cell disarray, and premature maturation with abortive keratin pearls or dyskeratosis. Additional findings may include irregular elongated/anastomosing rete ridges, hyperkeratosis, confluent parakeratosis, prominent desmosomes, and acantholysis. An uncommon HSIL-like/basaloid p53abn pattern shows loss of maturation, expanded basal cells, nuclear disorganization, pleomorphism, hyperchromasia, and basal/suprabasal mitoses. p53-wildtype VIN most often shows verruciform acanthotic growth, marked acanthosis (often more than 10 cell layers), elongated rete ridges, parakeratosis, hypogranulosis, and superficial cytoplasmic pallor, with minimal cytologic atypia. Clinical correlation with chronic inflammatory dermatosis, especially lichen sclerosus, is important. p16: negative or heterogeneous/mosaic non-block staining. p53-aberrant patterns include basal or diffuse strong overexpression, complete null staining, or aberrant cytoplasmic staining. p53 wild-type pattern shows variable-intensity nuclear staining in basal and suprabasal cells. Basal-sparing wild-type p53 instead supports HPV-associated disease. Basal-only p53 overexpression can occur in inflammatory dermatoses and should not automatically be called mutation-type. TP53 sequencing may help when p53 staining is indeterminate. HSIL: usually block p16-positive with wild-type p53; basal-sparing p53 can be a useful clue to HPV association. Reactive/inflammatory atypia: correlate with dermatosis and avoid overinterpreting basal-only p53 overexpression. Vulvar aberrant maturation: suspicious but insufficiently specific lesions may be described descriptively rather than classified definitively as VIN. Morphology alone is unreliable. The source recommends p16 and p53 at initial diagnosis to establish HPV status and classify HPV-I VIN. Squamous Cell Carcinoma (SCC), HPV-associated Invasive HPV-associated squamous carcinoma Infiltrating islands or nests of malignant squamous cells, sometimes with extensive complex exophytic expansile growth. Basaloid tumors contain cohesive nests of immature basal-type cells resembling HSIL. Warty/condylomatous tumors show conspicuous superficial atypia and koilocyte-like changes; mixed patterns occur. Approximately one third may be keratinizing; morphology overlaps substantially with HPV-independent SCC and cannot reliably establish HPV status. Invasion is supported by irregular nests, nests disconnected from the surface, loss of polarity, eosinophilic cytoplasm in invading cells, and desmoplasia. p16: strong, diffuse, continuous block-type nuclear and cytoplasmic staining. p53: usually wild-type pattern. Confirm HPV with validated p16 surrogate testing and/or HPV molecular testing when appropriate. HPV-I SCC: often keratinizing, but H&E overlap is substantial; use p16 and p53 rather than morphology alone. HSIL: no stromal invasion; appendageal extension can mimic invasion. Basaloid BCC: diffuse BerEP4 and BCL2 support BCC; p16 is usually not block-type. Do not assign HPV association from basaloid, warty, or keratinizing morphology alone. Block p16 is a key surrogate. Squamous Cell Carcinoma (SCC), HPV-independent Invasive HPV-independent squamous carcinoma; p53abn or p53wt Typically keratinizing and infiltrative, with small tumor nests and frequent keratin pearls. Single-cell budding or a spray-like pattern at the invasive front, often with marked desmoplasia, is associated with aggressive behavior. Other patterns include non-keratinizing, basaloid, warty, acantholytic/pseudoglandular, and spindle-cell/pseudosarcomatous areas. Verrucous carcinoma shows broad bulbous pushing invasion, minimal atypia, and abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm; p53 is usually wild type with scattered positive cells. Adjacent precursor lesions may include dVIN in p53abn tumors or vaVIN in p53wt tumors; lichen sclerosus or lichen planus may coexist. p16: usually negative or non-block; p16 is the first-line surrogate to assess HPV association. p53: use a vulvar-specific pattern-based interpretation. Wild-type patterns include variable scattered basal cells and/or mid-epithelial staining with basal sparing. Mutation-type patterns include basal overexpression, diffuse overexpression, null/complete absence, and cytoplasmic staining. If p16/p53 are indeterminate, consider high-risk HPV molecular testing and/or TP53 sequencing. HPV-associated SCC: block p16 and usually wild-type p53; basal-sparing p53 may support HPV association even if p16 is negative. Verrucous carcinoma: broad pushing fronts, minimal atypia, and wild-type p53 pattern. Reactive/inflammatory dermatosis: avoid interpreting isolated basal p53 overexpression as mutation-type without appropriate context. A p16-negative tumor is not automatically HPV-independent in every circumstance. Rare HPV-associated tumors may be p16-negative; correlate with p53 pattern and molecular HPV testing when needed. Mixed Tumor (Vulvar Pleomorphic Adenoma) Benign sweat gland-type tumor Well-circumscribed neoplasm with a mixture of epithelial, myoepithelial, and stromal components. Apocrine-mixed tumors show branching tubular structures, often with decapitation secretion, embedded in chondromyxoid, cartilaginous, or osseous stroma. Follicular or sebaceous differentiation may occur. Prominent myoepithelial differentiation can produce hyaline cell-rich areas. Eccrine-mixed tumors lack decapitation secretion and follicular/sebaceous differentiation; they show simple monolayered tubules, small nests, strands, cords, or single cells in myxohyaline/cartilaginous stroma. A broad panel can demonstrate multiple populations: SOX10, p63, S100, calponin, SMA, EMA, KIT, CEA, and cytokeratins. PLAG1 is overexpressed in most apocrine-pattern tumors; rare cases show HMGA2 expression. TRPS1 immunoreactivity has also been reported. The source notes SOX10 internal tandem duplications in the eccrine pattern; PLAG1 rearrangement is generally associated with apocrine-pattern tumors. Other vulvar adnexal tumors: this chapter's classification does not comprehensively cover adnexal tumors outside the listed entities. Myoepithelial-rich lesions: use the combination of ductal, myoepithelial, and characteristic chondromyxoid stromal components. The vulvar location is rare. Diagnose from the combined epithelial–myoepithelial–stromal pattern rather than a single positive marker. Fibroadenoma of Anogenital Mammary-like Glands Benign biphasic mammary-type neoplasm Well-circumscribed biphasic lesion composed of bland glandular epithelium and relatively uniform hypocellular spindle/stellate stroma without atypia. Stromal mitotic activity is rare or absent. Variants include columnar cell, oxyphilic, cystic, lactational, usual ductal hyperplasia, pseudoangiomatous stromal hyperplasia, and multinucleate stromal giant-cell changes. Pericanalicular pattern: round or oval glandular lumina remain open. Intracanalicular pattern: abundant stroma compresses ducts into slit-like spaces. A three-layer glandular pattern has been described: luminal cells positive for CK14/CK5/6; an intermediate luminal layer positive for ER/PR and focally AR but negative for CK14/CK5/6; and an outer myoepithelial layer positive for CK14/CK5/6 but negative for ER/PR/AR. GATA3 labels all three glandular layers. Stromal cells, including PASH-like areas, may express ER/PR, vimentin, and CD34; actin staining is variable. Phyllodes tumor: leaf-like stromal fronds, stromal hypercellularity, periglandular cuffing, and increased mitoses favor phyllodes tumor. Mammary-type adenocarcinoma: invasive epithelial growth and cytologic malignancy exclude fibroadenoma. Do not confuse the slit-like intracanalicular pattern of fibroadenoma with phyllodes tumor; assess stromal cellularity, leaf-like architecture, and periglandular condensation. Phyllodes Tumor Biphasic mammary-type neoplasm Biphasic lesion with bland mammary-type glandular epithelium and prominent leaf-like stromal fronds projecting into glandular lumina. Regional variability in stromal cellularity is typical, with band-like hypercellular areas and increased mitotic activity around epithelial structures (periglandular cuffing). Classify as benign, borderline, or malignant using criteria analogous to those applied in the breast; the stromal component is the neoplastic component. The source does not specify a diagnostic IHC panel for vulvar phyllodes tumor. The epithelial component is mammary-like; IHC is not presented as the primary discriminator in this source. Fibroadenoma: more uniform hypocellular stroma, without prominent leaf-like fronds or periglandular stromal hypercellularity. Primary mammary-type adenocarcinoma: malignant epithelial rather than stromal proliferation. The source notes limited case numbers and that criteria predicting malignant behavior are not well established specifically for vulvar phyllodes tumors. Adenocarcinoma of Mammary Gland Type Primary invasive mammary-type adenocarcinoma Usually morphologically identical to invasive breast carcinoma of no special type; in situ component and adjacent anogenital mammary-like glands are only uncommonly identified. Rare patterns include lobular, tubulolobular, mixed ductal/lobular, secretory, mucinous, and adenoid cystic-like carcinomas. The lesion must be dermally centered, with absent or only focal overlying epidermal involvement. Extensive epidermal involvement instead favors invasive Paget disease. An associated in situ component or proximity to anogenital mammary-like glands is supportive but not required. Use breast carcinoma biomarkers: ER, PR, HER2/ERBB2, and other markers guided by morphology and differential diagnosis. Reported profiles align with analogous breast carcinomas, including ER, PR, HER2, EGFR, and CK5 expression. Secretory carcinoma is associated with ETV6::NTRK3 fusion. Invasive Paget disease: extensive epidermal involvement favors Paget disease; mammary-type adenocarcinoma is dermally centered. Metastatic breast carcinoma: clinical/radiologic exclusion of a breast primary is essential. Other primary vulvar adenocarcinomas: use morphology, site, and a directed IHC panel. Do not classify a dermally centered mammary-type carcinoma as invasive Paget disease solely because focal epidermal involvement is present. Basal Cell Carcinoma (BCC) Cutaneous-type malignant epithelial tumor Nests of basaloid tumor cells with hyperchromatic nuclei and scant cytoplasm; peripheral palisading is characteristic at the tumor-stromal interface. Stromal changes include fibromyxoid alteration, retraction clefts, calcification, keloidal-type collagen, and amyloid deposition. Desmoplasia is not a feature in the source description. Melanocytes may colonize tumor nests, with melanin pigment. Keratinizing BCC shows central mature keratinization; nodulocystic BCC shows cystic degeneration. Strong p40/p63, CK5/6, BCL2, BerEP4, and CD10. Typically negative for EMA, CEA, and CK20. p16 is usually patchy rather than block-type. Neuroendocrine markers may be positive and should not be overinterpreted. Basaloid SCC: diffuse BerEP4 and lack of block p16 support BCC over basaloid SCC. Other basaloid adnexal neoplasms: correlate with architecture and site; these are not comprehensively covered in this source. BerEP4 positivity is useful but should be interpreted with the classic palisading/retraction morphology and the p16 pattern. Paget Disease of the Vulva Primary intraepithelial adenocarcinoma, with or without invasion Large round Paget cells with abundant pale cytoplasm, enlarged nuclei, and often prominent nucleoli are present within the epidermis. Cells are commonly concentrated in basal epidermal layers, with single cells or small groups extending upward. Skin adnexal epithelium is frequently involved. Intracytoplasmic mucin is demonstrable in most cases by PAS or mucicarmine. Superficial dermal inflammation and neovascularization are common and correlate with the eczematous clinical appearance. Invasive disease may show individual cells, small groups, or glandular structures in the dermis. CK7 is consistently positive and helps distinguish Paget cells from HSIL, HPV-I VIN, and melanoma. EMA, CAM5.2, CEA, and GATA3 are typically diffusely positive. Melanoma markers are negative. p16 may be diffusely expressed despite the absence of HPV. Usually negative for uroplakin-3, CDX2, and CK20; diffuse expression should raise secondary involvement by urothelial carcinoma or rectal adenocarcinoma. ER, PR, AR, and HER2 may be expressed; HER2 is positive in a subset. Breast biomarkers are recommended where available for invasive Paget disease, but are not routinely indicated for completely in situ disease. HSIL: p16 block-positive; CK7 is not the characteristic Paget profile. HPV-independent VIN: squamous morphology and p16/p53 pattern differ; Paget cells are CK7-positive glandular cells. Melanoma: use melanocytic markers; Paget cells are negative. Secondary Paget disease: diffuse CK20, CDX2, or uroplakin-3 should prompt evaluation for colorectal or urothelial primary. Distinguish primary vulvar Paget disease from secondary epidermal spread of urothelial or colorectal carcinoma. CK7 alone is not enough; use a panel and clinical correlation. HSIL Basal-to-full-thickness atypia; loss of maturation Block p16; wild-type p53 (may be basal-sparing) HPV-associated HPV-I VIN, p53abn Basal pleomorphism/disarray; premature maturation; often keratinizing Non-block p16; mutation-type p53 HPV-independent precursor HPV-I VIN, p53wt Verruciform acanthosis; altered maturation; minimal atypia Non-block p16; wild-type p53 HPV-A SCC Invasive basaloid/warty or mixed pattern; invasion Block p16; usually wild-type p53 HPV-associated invasive SCC HPV-I SCC Usually keratinizing, infiltrative; keratin pearls Non-block p16; p53 pattern classifies subtype HPV-independent invasive SCC p16 block-type Supports HPV-associated SIL/SCC when staining is strong, continuous, nuclear and cytoplasmic. p16 patchy/non-block Typical of LSIL/condyloma and HPV-independent VIN/SCC; interpret with p53 and morphology. p53 wild type Heterogeneous basal/suprabasal staining; basal-sparing suprabasal staining is particularly supportive of HPV-associated lesions. p53 mutation-type Basal or diffuse overexpression, null pattern, or cytoplasmic staining; supports HPV-I p53abn subtype. CK7 / GATA3 / CEA Support Paget disease in the appropriate intraepidermal large-cell morphology. BerEP4 / BCL2 Strong expression supports BCC in the setting of basaloid nests and peripheral palisading. ER / PR / HER2 Use breast-type biomarker assessment for mammary gland-type adenocarcinoma and, when invasive, Paget disease. true ← Vulva PathologyGPS · Female Genital Tract · Vulva Epithelial Tumors A morphology-first guide to vulvar epithelial lesions, with emphasis on HPV/p53 classification, invasion, and practical immunohistochemical separation of mimics. Critical safeguard Prove stromal invasion Separate appendageal extension by HSIL from true invasion; seek irregular nests, loss of polarity, and desmoplasia. p16 / p53 Interpretation Guide Marker pattern Practical interpretation Important: basal-only p53 overexpression can occur in inflammatory dermatoses. Do not call a mutation-type pattern from this finding alone. If p53 is indeterminate, TP53 sequencing may be useful. title: Mesenchymal Tumors
content: Prepubertal Fibroma (CALME, Childhood Asymmetry Labium Majus Enlargement) Benign fibroblastic proliferation · usually prepubertal girls Typically presents as unilateral, painless enlargement of the labium majus rather than a discrete mass; the lesion is poorly defined and diffusely infiltrates pre-existing vulvar connective tissue in the submucosa and dermis. The proliferation is hypocellular and patternless, composed of bland spindle or occasional stellate fibroblastic cells in variably collagenous, edematous, or focally myxoid stroma. Collagen ranges from thick bundles to delicate wispy fibres. Cells have ovoid nuclei, fine chromatin, inconspicuous nucleoli, and poorly defined amphophilic cytoplasm. Nuclear atypia, pleomorphism, and necrosis are absent; mitotic activity is sparse or absent. Adnexal structures may be encircled by the infiltrative proliferation. Grossly, there is no discrete mass or discernible border; the cut surface is pinkish-grey to tan. hemorrhage and necrosis are absent. CD34 is typically multifocal to strongly and diffusely positive. S100, SMA, and desmin are consistently negative in the described cases. ER and PR are commonly positive, although staining may be weak or patchy. No clinically relevant diagnostic molecular test is specified. No known predisposing genetic or environmental risk factor is established. Myofibroblastoma: generally a circumscribed mass with short intersecting fascicles and conspicuous hyalinized collagen; desmin and CD34 are commonly coexpressed, with frequent RB1 loss. Cellular angiofibroma: usually circumscribed and more cellular, with numerous thick-walled vessels. Deep (aggressive) angiomyxoma: deep, poorly circumscribed myxoid neoplasm with a characteristic infiltrative pattern and more prominent vascular component. The diffuse infiltrative edge should not be equated with malignancy. The defining combination is a hypocellular, patternless proliferation of cytologically bland fibroblasts in a prepubertal patient with asymmetric labial enlargement. Local recurrence is reported, particularly after incomplete excision. Myofibroblastoma Benign myofibroblastic neoplasm · RB1 / 13q14 family Usually an unencapsulated but well-circumscribed tumour composed of bland spindle cells arranged in variably sized, generally short and haphazardly intersecting fascicles. Broad bands of hyalinized collagen are characteristic; ropey collagen may occur. The spindle cells have short, stubby nuclei with finely dispersed chromatin, small or inconspicuous nucleoli, and eosinophilic to amphophilic cytoplasm with indistinct borders. Cellularity varies widely, from highly cellular lesions to sparsely cellular, extensively hyalinized examples. The cellular variant may show a higher spindle-cell-to-collagen ratio, infiltrative margins, and storiform or herringbone areas. Mature adipocytes are common and may be a minor or predominant component. Other patterns include schwannoma-like palisading and focal epithelioid, deciduoid, or round-cell morphology. Scattered atypical mononuclear or multinucleated cells may represent degenerative-type atypia. Small hyalinized vessels and perivascular lymphocytes are frequent; mast cells may be present. Diffuse coexpression of desmin and CD34 occurs in approximately 90% of cases, although either marker may occasionally be negative. SMA is expressed in about one third of cases. Nuclear RB1 expression is lost in approximately 90% of cases. RB1 loss is supportive in the appropriate morphologic setting, not independently diagnostic. Loss of 13q14, including RB1, is characteristic of the related tumour family. RB1 loss can be assessed by FISH or next-generation sequencing in selected diagnostically difficult cases. Superficial myofibroblastoma is included within the myofibroblastoma spectrum because of overlapping clinicopathological, immunohistochemical, and molecular features. Cellular angiofibroma: has numerous small-to-medium thick-walled vessels and typically lacks the diffuse desmin expression characteristic of many myofibroblastomas. Spindle cell / pleomorphic lipoma: shares RB1-pathway biology and may contain ropey collagen and adipocytes; correlate with the overall architecture and site. Angiomyofibroblastoma: has alternating cellularity and conspicuous vessels with perivascular clustering of tumour cells. Degenerative atypia, occasional infiltrative margins, or a cellular/storiform pattern do not by themselves establish malignancy. The overall circumscribed architecture, bland cytology, hyalinized collagen, and supportive desmin/CD34/RB1 profile are important. Cellular Angiofibroma Benign fibroblastic neoplasm · richly vascularized Usually a well-circumscribed superficial soft-tissue nodule, composed of moderately to highly cellular, uniform short spindle cells in edematous to fibrous stroma. Numerous small-to-medium-sized thick-walled vessels are a defining feature. Vascular lumina may be rounded, irregularly ectatic, or branching. Spindle cells are randomly distributed, occasionally in fascicles or with nuclear palisading. They have short oval-to-fusiform nuclei, inconspicuous nucleoli, and scant pale eosinophilic cytoplasm. Stroma contains wispy collagen, sometimes with short, delicate, densely eosinophilic collagen bundles; edema, hyalinization, or myxoid change may be present. Mast cells and perivascular lymphoid aggregates are common; adipocytes occur in nearly half of cases. Mitoses are generally sparse but may be more frequent. Degenerative nuclear enlargement/hyperchromasia, intravascular thrombi, and cystic change may occur. Rare cases show sarcomatous transformation, sometimes as an abrupt sarcomatous nodule with lipoblast-like, pleomorphic, or hyperchromatic spindle cells. CD34 is positive in approximately 30–60% of tumours. SMA and desmin are variably expressed, each in approximately 10–20% of cases. ER and PR are expressed in many cases. RB1 loss is frequent and can support the diagnosis in a suitable morphologic context. Partial or complete losses of chromosome 13 (including RB1) and/or chromosome 16 have been described, supporting a pathogenetic relationship with myofibroblastoma, spindle cell / pleomorphic lipoma, and vulvovaginal fibroepithelial stromal polyp. Detection of RB1 loss may be helpful in diagnostically challenging cases. Angiomyofibroblastoma: often shows alternating hypo- and hypercellular areas, thin-walled vessels, and tumour cells clustered around vessels; desmin is usually positive. Myofibroblastoma: more characteristically shows short intersecting fascicles and broad hyalinized collagen bands, with frequent diffuse desmin/CD34 coexpression. Deep (aggressive) angiomyxoma: is typically much more hypocellular and myxoid, with infiltrative entrapment of adjacent tissues. Do not overcall malignancy solely because of increased mitoses or focal degenerative atypia. Sarcomatous transformation is rare; evaluate for a discrete morphologically sarcomatous component. Reported transformed cases have recurred but have not shown metastasis in the cited experience. Angiomyofibroblastoma Benign, superficial, well-circumscribed stromal tumour Usually a well-demarcated, unencapsulated superficial tumour, most often vulvar and generally smaller than 5 cm. Alternating hypocellular and hypercellular areas are characteristic, with prominent small-to-medium-sized thin-walled vessels; thick-walled, often hyalinized vessels may also be present. The stroma ranges from myxedematous to fibrous, including fine fibrils or sclerotic plaques. Bland spindle, ovoid, and epithelioid cells occur singly or in small nests and cords and tend to cluster around vessels. Binucleated and multinucleated cells may be present. Mitoses are rare or absent. Mast cells and lymphocytes may be sparse; mature adipocytes can be focal or, rarely, nearly diffuse (lipomatous angiomyofibroblastoma). Most cases show desmin positivity. Desmin may be reduced or absent in postmenopausal patients. SMA and pan-muscle actin are variably expressed. Tumour cells are consistently positive for ER and PR; CD34 is occasionally positive. Most angiomyofibroblastomas harbour recurrent MTG1::CYP2E1 fusion transcripts. Detection of this fusion can support the diagnosis. Cellular angiofibroma: has more uniformly distributed spindle cells and numerous thick-walled vessels; CD34 is more often positive, while desmin is less consistently expressed. Deep (aggressive) angiomyxoma: is poorly circumscribed, deeply situated, paucicellular, and infiltrative, with entrapment of muscle, nerve, and fat. Myofibroblastoma: shows short intersecting fascicles and prominent hyalinized collagen bands, often with CD34/desmin coexpression and RB1 loss. Perivascular clustering of bland tumour cells in alternating cellularity is a key architectural clue. Do not confuse the usually small, circumscribed angiomyofibroblastoma with deep (aggressive) angiomyxoma, in which infiltrative growth is the defining concern. Cutaneous Myxoma (Superficial Angiomyxoma) Benign superficial myxoid tumour · may be syndromic A superficial dermal or subcutaneous lesion, usually polypoid or exophytic, composed of multinodular, relatively circumscribed lobules of myxoid stroma. Lobules contain sparse bland spindle-shaped and stellate cells with delicate cytoplasmic processes and thin-walled, sometimes arborizing vessels. Not every tumour has prominent vascularity, which is why cutaneous myxoma is the preferred term. Tumour cells have ovoid-to-round nuclei and may show nuclear inclusions; cytological atypia and mitotic activity are usually absent. A neutrophilic stromal infiltrate is often present. Entrapment of epithelial structures, especially hair follicles, may occur; follicular induction is less common. The source does not specify a characteristic diagnostic immunohistochemical profile for this entity. Morphology and superficial anatomic limitation are central. Multifocal cutaneous myxomas may be associated with Carney complex, an autosomal dominant syndrome commonly related to PRKAR1A (17q24) alterations. PRKAR1A mutations can be detected in cases associated with Carney complex. Deep (aggressive) angiomyxoma: arises in deep soft tissue, is poorly marginated and infiltrative, and entraps muscle, nerve, and adipose tissue; it commonly expresses desmin and nuclear HMGA2. Angiomyofibroblastoma: has a more cellular perivascular pattern, alternating cellularity, and usually desmin/ER/PR expression. Other superficial myxoid lesions: assess depth, circumscription, lobular architecture, vascular pattern, and stromal inflammatory cells. The lesion should be confined to dermis and/or superficial subcutis and show non-infiltrative lobular growth. If multiple cutaneous myxomas are present, consider Carney complex rather than treating the lesions as unrelated sporadic nodules. Deep (Aggressive) Angiomyxoma Locally infiltrative benign myxoid neoplasm · recurrence-prone A deep, poorly or vaguely circumscribed, unencapsulated tumour composed of uniformly paucicellular bland oval, spindle, and stellate cells in abundant loose myxomatous stroma with delicate collagen fibrils. Nuclear atypia and mitotic activity are typically absent. Despite bland cytology, infiltrative growth is frequent, with entrapment of skeletal muscle, nerve, and adipose tissue. The vascular component includes capillary-like vessels and medium-sized vessels, some with thick muscular walls or hyalinization. Perivascular cuffs of delicate fibrillary collagen and small bundles of smooth muscle, sometimes arranged around vessels, are common. Recurrent lesions may show more fibro-sclerotic stroma and conspicuous vascularity with perivascular hyalinization. Grossly, the tumour is often larger than appreciated clinically, with a glistening gelatinous to fibrogelatinous cut surface; hemorrhage, vascular congestion, or fibrosis may occur. Desmin is often positive. SMA, ER, PR, and CD34 are variably positive. Nuclear HMGA2 immunoreactivity is present in most cases and is a useful supportive marker; it should be interpreted with the characteristic deep infiltrative morphology. HMGA2 locus rearrangements at 12q14.3 have been identified in approximately one third of tumours. Rearrangements may have diverse partners; molecular testing is not described as routinely required for diagnosis. Angiomyofibroblastoma: usually small, superficial, circumscribed, and alternating in cellularity, with perivascular clustering of tumour cells. Cutaneous myxoma: superficial dermal/subcutaneous, lobulated and non-infiltrative, often with stromal neutrophils. Cellular angiofibroma: more cellular, circumscribed, and characterized by numerous thick-walled vessels. Myofibroblastoma: typically circumscribed, with short fascicles and broad hyalinized collagen bands. The tumour is cytologically bland but not biologically innocuous: local recurrence may occur in 30–40% of cases, sometimes decades after excision, particularly after incomplete removal. Its deep infiltrative extent can exceed the clinical impression. Prepubertal fibroma Diffuse, hypocellular, patternless bland spindle cells; collagenous/edematous stroma CD34 usually positive; ER/PR commonly positive; SMA/desmin/S100 negative Poorly defined enlargement; local recurrence especially after incomplete excision Short intersecting fascicles, broad hyalinized collagen bands; variable fat Desmin + CD34 often diffuse; RB1 loss frequent Usually circumscribed; recurrence rare Cellular angiofibroma Cellular bland spindle cells; numerous thick-walled vessels CD34 variable; ER/PR often positive; RB1 loss frequent Usually circumscribed; rare sarcomatous transformation Alternating cellularity; thin-walled vessels; perivascular clustering Desmin, ER, PR usually positive; MTG1::CYP2E1 fusion in most Superficial and well-circumscribed; benign Cutaneous myxoma Superficial lobules of myxoid stroma, bland stellate cells, thin-walled vessels, neutrophils No defining IHC profile specified Non-infiltrative; consider Carney complex if multifocal Deep (aggressive) angiomyxoma Deep, paucicellular myxoid tumour; infiltrates and entraps adjacent tissue Desmin often +; HMGA2 nuclear + in most; ER/PR/SMA/CD34 variable Locally infiltrative; recurrence up to 30–40% Circumscription and depth First establish whether the lesion is superficial/circumscribed or deep/infiltrative. Deep angiomyxoma is defined by infiltrative growth despite bland cytology. Vascular pattern Numerous thick-walled vessels favor cellular angiofibroma; prominent thin-walled vessels with perivascular tumour-cell clustering favor angiomyofibroblastoma. Collagen pattern Broad hyalinized collagen bands with short fascicles support myofibroblastoma; delicate collagen in a hypocellular, patternless proliferation supports prepubertal fibroma. RB1 family RB1 loss can be seen in myofibroblastoma and cellular angiofibroma and is not specific in isolation. Myxoid lesions Superficial lobulated myxoma with neutrophils is distinct from deep infiltrative angiomyxoma with tissue entrapment and frequent desmin/HMGA2 expression. true ← Vulva PathologyGPS · Female Genital Tract · Vulva Mesenchymal Tumors A morphology-first guide to selected vulvar mesenchymal tumors, emphasizing depth and circumscription, vascular architecture, stromal quality, and focused immunohistochemical and molecular findings. Fibroblastic / Myofibroblastic Vascular Architecture Myxoid Tumors RB1 / HMGA2 / Fusion Findings First question Where is the lesion? Separate superficial, circumscribed tumors from deep infiltrative lesions. This distinction is especially important for angiomyofibroblastoma versus deep angiomyxoma. Architecture Read the vessels and stroma Thick-walled vessels, perivascular cellularity, hyalinized collagen bands, and myxoid lobules provide high-value pattern clues. IHC safeguard Use panels, not single markers CD34, desmin, SMA, ER/PR, RB1, and HMGA2 are supportive in context; none should replace assessment of growth pattern. Practical Diagnostic Approach Feature Diagnostic use Side-by-Side Comparison A quick comparison of the six entities covered in this reference section. Interpret immunohistochemical and molecular findings in conjunction with morphology, anatomic depth, clinical context, and validated laboratory assays. Where the source did not specify a defining IHC profile, this page states that limitation rather than supplying an unsupported panel.
