title: Cell Cycle And Apoptosis Pathways
content: use client p53 p53 Pathway The p53 pathway coordinates cellular responses to DNA damage and other forms of stress. Depending on the context, p53 induces cell-cycle arrest and DNA repair, senescence, or apoptosis, thereby limiting the propagation of genetically damaged cells. TP53 TP53 encodes p53, a sequence-specific transcription factor that regulates cell-cycle progression, DNA integrity, apoptosis, metabolism, ferroptosis, and cellular responses to nutrient deprivation. Its effects depend on cell type, stress signal, and the specific p53 protein variant. Li–Fraumeni syndrome results from a heterozygous germline pathogenic TP53 variant. Tumors commonly acquire a second hit affecting the wild-type allele. Some mutant p53 proteins exert dominant-negative effects; gain-of-function activity has been proposed for selected variants, but its molecular basis is not fully established. Li–Fraumeni syndrome and the broader heritable TP53-related cancer syndrome spectrum Li–Fraumeni Syndrome Autosomal dominant; variable penetrance and expression Cancers often arise in childhood, adolescence, or young adulthood, although risk persists throughout life. Core tumor spectrum includes soft tissue sarcoma, osteosarcoma, breast carcinoma, brain tumors, and adrenocortical carcinoma. Breast cancer is a frequent first malignancy, often occurring at a young age. Other reported tumors include leukemia, lymphoma, melanoma, gastrointestinal carcinomas, lung cancer, and tumors of the genitourinary tract. Multiple primary malignancies in one individual and a family history spanning generations are characteristic clues. The tumor spectrum varies with age; adrenocortical carcinoma, choroid plexus carcinoma, rhabdomyosarcoma, and medulloblastoma are important childhood tumors. A pathogenic or likely pathogenic germline TP53 variant establishes the molecular diagnosis in the appropriate clinical context. Consider testing in patients with a core-spectrum tumor at an unusually young age, multiple primary tumors, or a suggestive family history. Osteosarcoma, low-hypodiploid acute lymphoblastic leukemia, and sonic hedgehog–activated medulloblastoma are additional indications for considering TP53 testing. Traditional Chompret criteria are useful but do not identify every carrier; broader testing strategies have increased recognition of individuals who do not meet classic criteria. A tumor TP53 variant alone does not establish Li–Fraumeni syndrome; constitutional testing is required. Most tumors are morphologically indistinguishable from their sporadic counterparts. Breast carcinomas are commonly invasive carcinoma of no special type; ERBB2-amplified tumors are overrepresented in reported series. Soft tissue sarcomas include leiomyosarcoma, rhabdomyosarcoma, liposarcoma, and undifferentiated sarcoma. Osteosarcoma is the most frequent bone malignancy in the syndrome. Brain tumors include diffuse astrocytic gliomas, choroid plexus carcinoma, and medulloblastoma, including SHH-activated/TP53-mutant tumors. Adrenocortical carcinoma is an important component of the childhood tumor spectrum. Abnormal p53 immunostaining patterns may support the presence of a TP53-altered tumor but are not specific for a germline variant. A null pattern or diffuse strong nuclear staining should be interpreted with appropriate internal controls and tumor-specific context. ERBB2 immunohistochemistry and in situ hybridization are used to classify breast carcinoma, not to establish Li–Fraumeni syndrome. Use lineage- and entity-specific immunohistochemical panels to classify each neoplasm; there is no syndrome-specific IHC profile. BRCA1- or BRCA2-associated hereditary breast/ovarian cancer: usually a narrower tumor spectrum; young breast cancer alone does not distinguish these syndromes. Other hereditary sarcoma and brain tumor predisposition syndromes: integrate the specific tumor combination, age, and family history. Sporadic TP53-mutant cancer: somatic TP53 alterations are common; germline testing is needed to establish constitutional predisposition. Clonal hematopoiesis: a TP53 variant detected in blood, particularly after chemotherapy or with increasing age, may be hematopoietic rather than constitutional; confirm using an appropriate nonhematopoietic tissue. TP53 is located at chromosome 17p13.1 and encodes the p53 tumor suppressor. Germline pathogenic variants include missense, truncating, splice-site, indel, and structural alterations. Tumorigenesis commonly involves somatic inactivation or loss of the remaining wild-type TP53 allele. Variant-specific residual function and dominant-negative effects contribute to variable age of onset and phenotype severity. Use germline next-generation sequencing with validated detection of sequence variants and copy-number/structural alterations; assess low-level mosaicism when clinically indicated. Classify variants using TP53-specific ACMG/AMP guidance; do not infer germline status from tumor sequencing alone. A child with adrenocortical carcinoma, choroid plexus carcinoma, embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma, or SHH medulloblastoma. Young patient with osteosarcoma or soft tissue sarcoma, especially with another primary cancer or a family history of early cancers. Very young patient with breast carcinoma, particularly with multiple primary tumors or a family history of sarcoma, brain tumor, or adrenocortical carcinoma. Multiple primary cancers across different organ systems should prompt constitutional TP53 assessment even when classic family-history criteria are not met. rb1 RB1 and G1/S Cell-Cycle Checkpoint The RB pathway controls the G1-to-S transition. Hypophosphorylated RB proteins bind E2F transcription factors and restrain S-phase gene expression. Cyclin-dependent kinases phosphorylate RB, releasing E2F and allowing cell-cycle progression. RB1 · CDKN1B · CDKN2A · CDK4 · CDK6 · CCND1 · CCNE1 · E2F family RB1 encodes pRB, which restrains E2F-dependent transcription. CDKN1B encodes p27, an inhibitor of cyclin E/A–CDK2. CDKN2A encodes p16INK4a, which inhibits CDK4/6, and p14ARF, which antagonizes MDM2 and stabilizes p53. CDK4 is a kinase that promotes RB phosphorylation; specific germline variants impair p16 binding. RB1, CDKN1B, and CDKN2A predisposition generally reflects loss of tumor-suppressor function, often with somatic inactivation of the remaining allele. In contrast, melanoma-predisposing CDK4 variants are activating: they impair p16 binding, permit RB phosphorylation, and drive G1/S progression. PIK3CA is not an RB-pathway gene; its biology belongs to PI3K signaling. Retinoblastoma syndrome · Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 4 · CDKN2A-related tumor predisposition syndrome · CDK4-related melanoma predisposition syndrome Retinoblastoma Syndrome RB1 Autosomal dominant predisposition; tumor development follows a two-hit mechanism Retinoblastoma is the most common primary intraocular malignancy of childhood; median diagnosis is approximately 12 months for bilateral and 24 months for unilateral disease. Heritable disease is usually bilateral and multicentric, but approximately 15% of hereditary cases may present unilaterally. Leukocoria is the most common presenting sign, followed by strabismus. Trilateral retinoblastoma refers to bilateral ocular retinoblastoma with a synchronous or metachronous intracranial pineal or suprasellar tumor. Survivors have a lifelong risk of second primary malignancies, especially osteosarcoma and soft tissue sarcoma. Clinical diagnosis of retinoblastoma is established by ophthalmologic examination and imaging; intraocular biopsy is avoided because of the risk of extraocular tumor dissemination. Germline RB1 testing should be considered in all patients, regardless of unilateral or bilateral presentation. Bilateral or multicentric retinoblastoma, family history, or an associated intracranial primitive neuroectodermal tumor strongly supports heritable disease. Histopathologic assessment of an enucleated eye should document differentiation and high-risk features, including postlaminar optic nerve, choroidal, scleral, or extraocular invasion. A negative blood test does not completely exclude low-level somatic mosaicism. Tumor is composed of small neuroblastic cells with hyperchromatic nuclei and scant cytoplasm. Mitoses, apoptosis, geographic necrosis, and dystrophic calcification are common. Flexner–Wintersteiner rosettes are characteristic; Homer Wright rosettes and photoreceptor-like fleurettes may also occur. High-risk features include postlaminar optic nerve invasion, massive choroidal invasion (at least 3 mm), scleral invasion, and extraocular extension. The intracranial tumor in trilateral retinoblastoma is histologically similar to retinoblastoma. Synaptophysin and other neuronal markers may support neuroblastic differentiation but are not specific. CRX may be expressed and supports photoreceptor-lineage differentiation in the appropriate context. RB protein loss may be demonstrable but is not a substitute for molecular testing. IHC is not required for the clinical diagnosis of a typical intraocular retinoblastoma. Coats disease and persistent fetal vasculature: may cause leukocoria but lack a retinal malignant mass with characteristic calcification. Medulloepithelioma: usually arises from the ciliary body rather than the retina and has a distinct primitive neuroepithelial/tubular pattern. Retinocytoma: may also have biallelic RB1 alterations but shows low proliferative activity and lacks the destructive malignant phenotype. Other small round cell tumors involving the orbit: correlate with the intraocular epicenter and retinal findings. RB1 is located at chromosome 13q14 and encodes the pRB tumor suppressor. Heritable disease begins with a constitutional heterozygous pathogenic variant (first hit); a somatic second hit inactivates the remaining allele in retinal cells. Second hits include loss of heterozygosity, deletion, sequence variants, promoter methylation, and complex rearrangements such as chromothripsis. Somatic mosaicism may cause a milder phenotype and unilateral disease; low-level mosaic variants may be missed in peripheral blood. Testing may include sequencing, deletion/duplication analysis, RNA analysis for suspected splice variants, and assays capable of detecting mosaicism. Large 13q deletions involving RB1 and neighboring genes may be associated with developmental abnormalities. Bilateral or multifocal retinal tumors in an infant, particularly with a family history. A unilateral retinoblastoma does not exclude heritable disease; molecular testing remains relevant. Bilateral retinoblastoma plus a pineal or suprasellar primitive tumor indicates trilateral retinoblastoma. A later sarcoma, especially osteosarcoma, in a retinoblastoma survivor raises concern for a second primary malignancy. Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia Type 4 CDKN1B Autosomal dominant; incomplete penetrance has been reported Very rare syndrome, often recognized in patients with a MEN1-like phenotype but negative MEN1 testing. Primary hyperparathyroidism is the most frequent manifestation, reported in approximately 75% of affected patients. Pituitary neuroendocrine tumors occur in about one third of reported patients. Pancreatic and other gastroenteropancreatic neuroendocrine tumors may occur; pulmonary, thymic, gastric, and small intestinal NETs are less frequently reported. A female predominance has been described in published cases. A germline pathogenic CDKN1B variant together with parathyroid, pituitary, and/or gastroenteropancreatic neuroendocrine neoplasia. Consider MEN4 in a patient with a MEN1-like phenotype and comprehensive negative MEN1 testing. Testing should be capable of detecting sequence variants, small and large deletions, and mosaic variants. The presence of multiple tumors in the MEN4 spectrum is supportive, but individual tumors are not morphologically distinctive. Parathyroid lesions may be uniglandular or multiglandular and are not reliably distinguishable from sporadic disease. Pituitary neuroendocrine tumors may be nonfunctioning or secrete growth hormone, prolactin, or ACTH. Gastroenteropancreatic and thoracic NETs resemble their sporadic counterparts. No specific histologic feature has been established as diagnostic of MEN4. p27 expression may be reduced or altered in some tumors, but retained staining does not exclude MEN4. There is no validated syndrome-specific IHC pattern; classify each endocrine neoplasm using standard lineage and hormone markers. Tumor p27 staining cannot establish a germline CDKN1B variant. MEN1: clinically overlapping and more common; comprehensive MEN1 testing is the first key molecular distinction. CDC73-related hyperparathyroidism-jaw tumor syndrome: consider jaw tumors, atypical parathyroid tumors, or parathyroid carcinoma. Sporadic multiglandular hyperparathyroidism with an incidental pituitary or pancreatic NET: assess the overall phenotype and germline findings. CDKN1B at chromosome 12p13.1 encodes p27KIP1, a cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor. MEN4 is caused by heterozygous germline loss-of-function variants, including missense, frameshift, and nonsense variants. Reduced p27 function weakens inhibition of cyclin E/A–CDK2 and facilitates RB phosphorylation and E2F-mediated G1/S progression. The reported variants are distributed across the coding sequence and 5′ untranslated region; no clear mutation hotspot is established. Somatic second-hit data are less fully characterized than for RB1 and CDKN2A; do not assume a demonstrated two-hit mechanism in every case. Primary hyperparathyroidism plus pituitary or gastroenteropancreatic NET with negative MEN1 testing. A MEN1-like family history with a pathogenic germline CDKN1B variant. Multiple endocrine tumors in a patient whose phenotype is not explained by MEN1. CDKN2A-Related Tumor Predisposition Syndrome CDKN2A (p16INK4a and p14ARF) Autosomal dominant; penetrance varies with variant and modifying factors Multiple cutaneous dysplastic nevi and early-onset melanoma are characteristic. Affected individuals may develop multiple primary melanomas, often approximately a decade earlier than the general population. Some families show melanoma-astrocytoma syndrome, with astrocytomas in the cerebral hemispheres or cerebellum. Pancreatic cancer is an important associated malignancy, particularly in some North American and mainland European families. Nerve sheath tumors and oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma have also been reported. Melanomas are usually cutaneous rather than mucosal, acral, or uveal. A heterozygous germline pathogenic CDKN2A variant establishes the molecular diagnosis. A personal or family history of multiple melanomas and dysplastic nevi supports testing. Consider CDKN2A testing in melanoma-prone families, especially those with at least three melanoma cases. If CDKN2A testing is negative in a strongly melanoma-prone family, evaluate CDK4 and other relevant melanoma predisposition genes. A somatic CDKN2A deletion in a tumor is not evidence by itself of a germline syndrome. Melanomas are often superficial spreading type and may show pigmentation and pagetoid scatter. No histologic feature reliably distinguishes CDKN2A-associated melanoma from sporadic melanoma. Associated astrocytomas include pleomorphic xanthoastrocytoma and diffuse astrocytic gliomas of variable grade. Reported nerve sheath tumors resemble schwannoma or neurofibroma. The morphology of pancreatic and oropharyngeal tumors is generally similar to sporadic counterparts. Loss of p16 expression may occur in tumors with CDKN2A inactivation but is not specific for a germline variant. p14ARF is encoded by an alternative reading frame; routine IHC does not reliably establish constitutional CDKN2A status. Use standard melanoma, glial, and nerve sheath tumor panels to classify the individual neoplasm. CDK4-related melanoma predisposition: clinical phenotype may be indistinguishable; germline testing separates the two. BAP1 tumor predisposition syndrome: consider uveal/cutaneous melanoma, mesothelioma, and BAP1-inactivated melanocytic tumors. Familial melanoma without an identified CDKN2A variant: evaluate other susceptibility genes and environmental factors. Sporadic melanoma with somatic CDKN2A loss: tumor-only loss does not establish inherited predisposition. CDKN2A at chromosome 9p21 encodes two distinct proteins through alternative reading frames: p16INK4a and p14ARF. p16 inhibits CDK4 and CDK6, maintaining RB-mediated G1 arrest. p14ARF antagonizes MDM2 and thereby supports p53 stability. Germline pathogenic variants are generally loss-of-function; tumors may acquire a second hit through loss of heterozygosity, deletion, or another somatic variant. Germline sequencing and deletion/duplication analysis are required; tumor sequencing alone cannot establish constitutional status. UV exposure, smoking, nevus phenotype, hair pigmentation, and MC1R variants may modify risk. Multiple primary cutaneous melanomas with numerous dysplastic nevi, particularly in a family with several affected relatives. Melanoma-prone family with pancreatic cancer or astrocytoma in affected relatives. A young patient with superficial spreading melanoma and a strong family history should prompt germline CDKN2A testing. If CDKN2A is negative, consider CDK4-related melanoma predisposition. CDK4-Related Melanoma Predisposition Syndrome CDK4 Autosomal dominant Very rare syndrome characterized by early-onset multiple primary cutaneous melanomas. Affected individuals often have numerous atypical or dysplastic nevi. Melanomas may occur on the limbs more often than in CDKN2A-associated families. Reported noncutaneous malignancies include pancreatic, breast, ovarian, cervical, gastric, and other cancers, but the strength of these associations is less certain. A germline pathogenic CDK4 variant establishes the diagnosis. Consider testing in melanoma-prone families that are negative for CDKN2A variants. Multiple primary melanomas and atypical nevi are supportive but do not distinguish CDK4 from CDKN2A predisposition clinically. Melanomas are morphologically similar to sporadic melanomas. Low-cumulative-sun-damage superficial spreading melanoma is commonly reported. A precursor nevus, including an intradermal or dysplastic nevus, may be present. No distinctive histologic feature reliably identifies CDK4-associated melanoma. There is no validated IHC marker for germline CDK4-related melanoma predisposition. p16 expression may be retained or altered depending on the tumor context; it cannot establish a germline CDK4 variant. CDKN2A-related tumor predisposition: the phenotype overlaps substantially; germline sequencing distinguishes the syndromes. Sporadic familial clustering of melanoma: assess UV exposure, nevus phenotype, and germline findings. BAP1 tumor predisposition syndrome: consider the associated BAP1-inactivated melanocytic tumors and uveal melanoma spectrum. CDK4 is located at chromosome 12q14.1 and encodes a serine/threonine kinase that phosphorylates RB. Most reported germline variants affect codon 24, particularly p.Arg24His. These variants impair p16 binding, allowing CDK4 activity, RB phosphorylation, E2F release, and cell-cycle progression. This is an activating, functionally gain-of-function mechanism rather than loss of CDK4 function. Germline sequencing is required; tumor IHC or somatic CDK4 amplification is not equivalent to a constitutional pathogenic variant. Multiple primary melanomas and numerous atypical nevi in a family with negative CDKN2A testing. A melanoma-prone family in which germline testing identifies a CDK4 codon 24 variant. Do not distinguish CDK4 from CDKN2A syndrome by melanoma morphology alone. fas FAS-Mediated Apoptosis Pathway The FAS pathway is a major extrinsic apoptosis pathway that maintains immune homeostasis by eliminating activated or autoreactive lymphocytes. FAS receptor engagement recruits intracellular signaling proteins and activates initiator and effector caspases. FAS · FASLG · FADD · CASP8 · CASP10 FAS (CD95/APO-1) is a death-domain-containing TNF receptor family member. Binding of FAS ligand promotes assembly of the death-inducing signaling complex through FADD and activation of caspase-8 and downstream caspases, leading to apoptosis. Pathogenic variants that impair FAS-mediated signaling reduce lymphocyte apoptosis and cause accumulation of autoreactive and double-negative T cells. ALPS may result from germline variants, most often in FAS, or from somatic FAS variants (ALPS-sFAS); the latter is a somatic phenocopy and is not an inherited syndrome. Autoimmune lymphoproliferative syndrome (ALPS-FAS and other FAS-pathway forms) and somatic ALPS (ALPS-sFAS) Autoimmune Lymphoproliferative Syndrome FAS · FASLG · CASP8 · CASP10 · FADD Usually autosomal dominant for heterozygous FAS variants; rare autosomal recessive forms. Somatic FAS variants cause ALPS-sFAS. ALPS-FAS commonly presents in early childhood with chronic, noninfectious lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly. Autoimmune cytopenias may affect multiple lineages and can include hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and neutropenia. Lymph nodes, spleen, and sometimes bone marrow are involved. Patients have an increased risk of B-cell lymphoma, including Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin lymphoma. ALPS-sFAS may present across a broader age range than germline ALPS-FAS. Splenectomy is associated with a substantial risk of severe infection and should be approached cautiously. Chronic (>6 months), noninfectious, nonmalignant lymphadenopathy and/or splenomegaly, or autoimmune cytopenia involving at least two lineages, in the appropriate clinical context. Peripheral blood flow cytometry demonstrates increased αβ T-cell receptor-positive CD4−/CD8− double-negative T cells: greater than 1.5% of total lymphocytes or greater than 2.5% of CD3-positive lymphocytes. Impaired FAS-mediated apoptosis supports the diagnosis. A pathogenic variant in FAS, FASLG, CASP8, CASP10, or FADD supports a genetically defined form; distinguish germline from somatic FAS variants. Elevated soluble FAS ligand, IL-10, and vitamin B12 are supportive biomarkers but are not independently diagnostic. Expanded double-negative T cells in a lymph node do not replace peripheral blood flow cytometry. Lymph nodes show reactive follicular hyperplasia with prominent pale paracortical expansion. The expanded paracortex contains double-negative T cells and polytypic plasma cells. Progressive transformation of germinal centers or Castleman-like changes may obscure the characteristic pattern. Rosai–Dorfman disease-like histiocytic changes may coexist. Similar lymphoid infiltrates may involve spleen and bone marrow. Firm, fleshy, or necrotic areas should be sampled to exclude an overt lymphoma. The expanded double-negative T-cell population is CD3-positive and TCRαβ-positive. Double-negative T cells are CD4-negative and CD8-negative. The population commonly expresses CD45RA and lacks CD45RO. Cytotoxic markers including perforin, TIA1, and CD57 may be expressed. Plasma cells are generally polytypic; assess light-chain expression when plasmacytosis is prominent. Flow cytometry on peripheral blood is essential for quantifying αβ double-negative T cells. Lymphoma: assess architecture, cytologic atypia, aberrant antigen expression, and clonality; ALPS may coexist with lymphoma. Infectious lymphadenitis: ALPS requires chronic noninfectious lymphoproliferation; correlate with microbiology and clinical course. Castleman disease: may show overlapping histology, but clinical immune dysregulation and αβ double-negative T-cell expansion favor ALPS. Rosai–Dorfman disease: S100-positive histiocytes with emperipolesis may be present as a coexisting pattern rather than explaining the entire syndrome. RAS-associated autoimmune lymphoproliferative disorder: can produce an ALPS-like phenotype but has a distinct molecular basis. Other inborn errors of immune regulation: consider when FAS-pathway testing is negative or the phenotype is atypical. FAS is the most frequently altered gene; heterozygous germline variants commonly affect the intracellular death domain and impair signaling. Rare homozygous FAS or FASLG variants are associated with severe, early-onset disease. Pathogenic variants in FADD, CASP8, and CASP10 disrupt downstream apoptotic signaling. ALPS-sFAS is caused by somatic FAS variants, often detectable in the double-negative T-cell compartment; it is not equivalent to germline ALPS-FAS. Use germline and somatic testing strategies appropriate to the phenotype and sample type. T-cell receptor Vβ restriction may occur in ALPS double-negative T cells; a restricted repertoire or apparent clonality should not be interpreted as lymphoma in isolation. FAS death-domain variants can also occur in lymphoma; molecular findings must be interpreted with morphology and clinical criteria. Child with persistent, noninfectious generalized lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, and autoimmune cytopenias. Reactive-appearing lymph node with marked pale paracortical expansion and an increased αβ CD4−/CD8− T-cell population. Polytypic plasmacytosis or Rosai–Dorfman-like changes in a patient with chronic immune dysregulation. A patient with ALPS phenotype but no germline FAS variant may have somatic FAS disease (ALPS-sFAS) or another immune dysregulation disorder. A new enlarging, firm, necrotic, or architecturally destructive node requires evaluation for lymphoma rather than attribution to ALPS alone. all PathologyGPS · Genetic Tumor Syndromes Cell-Cycle and Apoptosis Pathways A practical diagnostic reference to inherited tumor predisposition and immune dysregulation caused by alterations in cell-cycle checkpoints and programmed cell death. Begin with the tumor pattern or lymphoid finding, then connect the phenotype to the responsible gene and molecular mechanism. Pathology Clues Tumor combinations, age, multiplicity, and lymph node patterns that should trigger syndrome-directed evaluation. − + Pathology / Clinical Pattern Consider Diagnostic Direction Childhood adrenocortical carcinoma, choroid plexus carcinoma, rhabdomyosarcoma, or SHH medulloblastoma Li–Fraumeni syndrome Constitutional TP53 testing; distinguish germline variants from tumor-only alterations and clonal hematopoiesis. Young patient with multiple primary cancers, especially sarcoma, osteosarcoma, and breast carcinoma Review age at each diagnosis and family history; classic Chompret criteria do not capture every carrier. Bilateral or multicentric retinal tumors in an infant Retinoblastoma syndrome RB1 germline testing; evaluate for trilateral retinoblastoma and counsel regarding second primary malignancies. Retinoblastoma survivor with a later osteosarcoma or soft tissue sarcoma Heritable RB1 predisposition Consider a second primary malignancy; assess prior radiotherapy field and lifetime cancer risk. Primary hyperparathyroidism plus pituitary or gastroenteropancreatic NET; MEN1 testing negative MEN4 Consider germline CDKN1B testing with methods capable of detecting sequence and copy-number variants. Multiple cutaneous melanomas and dysplastic nevi, especially with pancreatic cancer or astrocytoma in the family CDKN2A-related predisposition Germline CDKN2A testing; if negative, consider CDK4 and other melanoma susceptibility genes. Melanoma-prone family with negative CDKN2A testing CDK4-related melanoma predisposition Germline CDK4 sequencing; codon 24 variants impair p16 binding and activate cell-cycle progression. Chronic noninfectious lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, and autoimmune cytopenias Autoimmune lymphoproliferative syndrome Peripheral blood flow cytometry for αβ CD4−/CD8− double-negative T cells; assess FAS-mediated apoptosis and germline/somatic variants. Reactive-appearing node with pale paracortical expansion, polytypic plasmacytosis, and double-negative T cells ALPS Correlate tissue findings with peripheral blood flow; do not mistake restricted T-cell repertoire alone for lymphoma. title: DNA Repair And Genomic Stability
content: use client Lynch syndrome Mismatch repair MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2; EPCAM-associated MSH2 silencing Autosomal dominant; one germline pathogenic variant followed by somatic inactivation of the remaining allele. Colorectal and endometrial carcinomas; also upper GI, small bowel, ovarian, urothelial, pancreatic, biliary, brain, prostate and other tumors. Often young onset or multiple primaries; family history may be absent, including de novo and mosaic cases. MMR IHC loss pattern directs gene testing: MLH1/PMS2, MSH2/MSH6, or isolated MSH6/PMS2. Internal non-neoplastic nuclei must stain. MSI-high supports dMMR but neither test alone establishes hereditary disease. Sporadic MLH1 promoter-hypermethylated carcinoma (often BRAF V600E in colorectal tumors); double-somatic MMR deficiency; CMMRD; MUTYH or POLE/POLD1-associated polyposis. Germline sequencing plus deletion/duplication analysis; consider EPCAM deletion and epigenetic silencing. For MLH1/PMS2 loss in colorectal carcinoma, assess MLH1 promoter methylation and/or BRAF V600E. Tumor-only dMMR is not synonymous with Lynch syndrome. Muir–Torre syndrome Usually MSH2; also MLH1, MSH6, PMS2; consider MUTYH Usually autosomal dominant Lynch-spectrum MMR predisposition with a sebaceous tumor phenotype. Sebaceous adenoma, sebaceoma, sebaceous carcinoma, or selected keratoacanthomas with visceral Lynch-spectrum malignancy. Multiple lesions, extra-head-and-neck lesions, cystic sebaceous tumors, younger age, and personal/family cancer history are particularly suggestive. MMR IHC on sebaceous neoplasms can screen, but predictive performance is lower than in colorectal carcinoma; periocular sebaceous carcinoma is a special setting with limitations. Confirm with germline testing when indicated. Sporadic sebaceous neoplasm with somatic MMR loss; MUTYH-associated polyposis; ordinary sporadic visceral carcinoma. Germline testing is required to establish inherited MMR predisposition. MSH2 is overrepresented in Muir–Torre phenotype. Tumor MMR loss alone does not prove germline disease. Constitutional mismatch repair deficiency (CMMRD) Biallelic MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, or PMS2 Autosomal recessive; biallelic germline pathogenic variants (homozygous or compound heterozygous) cause constitutional MMR deficiency in normal tissues. Childhood/adolescent cancers: high-grade glioma, T-lymphoblastic lymphoma/leukemia, colorectal and other Lynch-spectrum cancers, embryonal tumors and sarcomas. Multiple adenomas, café-au-lait-like macules, pigmentary changes, and multiple cerebral developmental venous anomalies are clues. Loss of the affected MMR protein may be present in tumor and all normal cells, including lymphocytes. Standard tumor MSI assays may be negative, particularly in brain tumors. Germline MSI assays in blood leukocytes can be useful in specialist laboratories. Lynch syndrome; NF1; sporadic pediatric high-grade glioma; POLE/POLD1 proofreading deficiency; APC-associated Turcot phenotype. Confirm two pathogenic variants in trans or homozygosity; use validated ancillary germline MMR-deficiency assays when sequencing is inconclusive. Absence of tumor MSI does not exclude CMMRD. BRCA-related cancer predisposition Homologous recombination BRCA1, BRCA2 Autosomal dominant germline predisposition; tumorigenesis commonly follows somatic loss/inactivation of the wild-type allele (two-hit model). Early-onset breast cancer, tubo-ovarian/fallopian tube/peritoneal carcinoma, male breast cancer, prostate and pancreatic carcinoma. BRCA1 is enriched in triple-negative breast cancer; BRCA2 has a stronger male breast and prostate association. No single histologic appearance is diagnostic. Tumor genomic evidence of homologous-recombination deficiency (HRD) may support pathway dysfunction but does not distinguish germline from somatic origin. PALB2/RAD51-related predisposition; sporadic HRD tumors; other hereditary breast/ovarian cancer syndromes. Test germline DNA and interpret tumor findings separately. Pathogenic variants include truncating, splice, and other loss-of-function variants. Biallelic tumor inactivation causes HR repair deficiency; PARP inhibitor sensitivity reflects synthetic lethality, but reversion mutations can mediate resistance. PALB2-related cancer predisposition PALB2 Germline heterozygous pathogenic variants confer dominant cancer predisposition; biallelic variants cause Fanconi anemia subtype. Breast cancer predisposition, including male breast cancer; pancreatic and other cancers may occur. Consider in hereditary breast cancer families without BRCA1/2 variants. No pathognomonic morphology or IHC profile; interpret in the clinical and family-history context. BRCA1/2-associated predisposition; other hereditary breast cancer genes; sporadic breast cancer. PALB2 bridges BRCA1 and BRCA2 in homologous recombination. Germline testing establishes inherited predisposition; tumor second-hit/HRD findings are supportive rather than proof of germline status. RAD51-related cancer predisposition RAD51C, RAD51D Germline pathogenic variants, generally heterozygous, predispose to cancer; biallelic defects in related HR genes may cause Fanconi anemia phenotypes. Predominantly tubo-ovarian and breast cancer risk, depending on gene and family context. No distinctive histology; diagnosis is genetic and clinical. BRCA1/2 and PALB2 predisposition; other hereditary tubo-ovarian cancer syndromes. RAD51C/D participate in homologous recombination. Distinguish germline variants from somatic tumor alterations; variant classification and gene-specific penetrance matter. MUTYH-associated polyposis Base excision repair MUTYH Autosomal recessive; biallelic loss-of-function variants impair removal of adenine mispaired with 8-oxoguanine. Multiple colorectal adenomas and colorectal carcinoma; phenotype may overlap attenuated FAP. Sebaceous neoplasms/Muir–Torre-like presentations have been reported. Adenomatous polyposis; colorectal tumors may show characteristic oxidative-damage-associated mutational patterns, but morphology is not specific. APC-associated FAP; NTHL1-related tumor syndrome; Lynch syndrome; polymerase proofreading-associated polyposis. Biallelic germline testing is essential. MUTYH deficiency promotes G:C>T:A transversions; somatic APC and KRAS/PIK3CA alterations may occur. A single MUTYH variant is carrier status, not MAP. NTHL1-related tumor syndrome NTHL1 Autosomal recessive; biallelic inactivating germline variants. Colorectal adenomatous polyposis and a broader multiple-tumor phenotype, including breast and other cancers described in affected individuals. Adenomatous polyposis; no defining histology. MUTYH-associated polyposis; APC-associated FAP; other recessive polyposis syndromes. NTHL1 glycosylase repairs oxidized cytosine derivatives. Biallelic germline testing establishes the syndrome; consider tumor mutational signatures as supportive evidence. MBD4-associated neoplasia syndrome MBD4 Autosomal recessive; biallelic loss-of-function germline variants. Predisposition includes hematologic malignancy, particularly myeloid neoplasia, and colorectal neoplasia; consider in unusual combinations of tumors. No unique morphology; hematologic and colorectal tumors are evaluated by their usual diagnostic criteria. Other inherited myeloid predisposition syndromes; MUTYH/NTHL1 polyposis; sporadic tumors. MBD4 repairs deaminated 5-methylcytosine at CpG sites. Biallelic loss produces excess C>T transitions at CpG dinucleotides; confirm germline biallelic status. Ataxia–telangiectasia DNA double-strand-break response ATM Autosomal recessive biallelic pathogenic variants; heterozygous carriers have a distinct, incompletely penetrant cancer-risk context. Childhood-onset progressive cerebellar ataxia, oculocutaneous telangiectasia, immunodeficiency, recurrent respiratory disease, and lymphoid malignancies. Lymphoid neoplasms are not morphologically unique; correlate with neurologic, immunologic, and cutaneous findings. Nijmegen breakage syndrome; other immunodeficiency-associated lymphoid proliferations; sporadic lymphoma. ATM kinase coordinates DNA double-strand-break signaling, cell-cycle arrest, and repair. Confirm biallelic germline variants; do not equate a somatic ATM alteration or reduced protein staining with the constitutional syndrome. CHEK2-related hereditary cancer predisposition DNA damage checkpoint CHEK2 Usually autosomal dominant heterozygous germline predisposition with moderate, variant-dependent risk. Breast cancer is the principal clinical association; other cancer associations are variable and should not be overstated. No distinctive histology or tumor IHC pattern. BRCA1/2, PALB2 and other hereditary breast cancer syndromes; sporadic breast cancer. CHEK2 encodes a checkpoint kinase downstream of DNA damage signaling. Variant-specific risk and family history guide interpretation; a tumor CHEK2 variant alone does not establish germline predisposition. Nijmegen breakage syndrome NBN Autosomal recessive biallelic pathogenic variants. Growth retardation, microcephaly, immunodeficiency, radiosensitivity, and increased risk of lymphoid malignancies, particularly lymphoma/leukemia. Lymphoid tumors require conventional classification; the syndromic phenotype is the key clue. Ataxia–telangiectasia; other chromosome-instability/immunodeficiency syndromes. NBN (nibrin) is part of the MRN complex involved in double-strand-break sensing and repair. Confirm biallelic germline variants; avoid unnecessary ionizing radiation where clinically feasible. Polymerase proofreading-associated polyposis DNA replication proofreading POLE, POLD1 Autosomal dominant germline pathogenic variants affecting exonuclease proofreading domains. Colorectal adenomas and carcinoma; endometrial cancer is particularly associated with POLD1. May resemble Lynch syndrome clinically but tumors often lack MSI. Adenomatous polyposis; tumors can be ultramutated with characteristic proofreading-defect signatures, often without classic dMMR. Lynch syndrome; MUTYH/NTHL1-associated polyposis; APC-associated FAP; CMMRD. Pathogenic exonuclease-domain variants impair proofreading (not MMR itself), producing ultramutation. Germline testing and tumor mutation signatures help distinguish from dMMR; combined POLE/POLD1 proofreading defect and MMR deficiency can produce distinctive signatures. Bloom syndrome RecQ helicase / replication stability BLM Autosomal recessive loss-of-function variants. Prenatal/postnatal growth deficiency, photosensitivity, characteristic facial features, immunodeficiency, insulin resistance, and markedly increased early-onset cancers including hematologic malignancies. Broad tumor spectrum without a unique histologic pattern; marked chromosomal instability is a mechanistic clue. Werner syndrome; Rothmund–Thomson syndrome; Nijmegen breakage syndrome. BLM is a RecQ helicase maintaining replication-fork and recombination stability. Biallelic germline loss causes increased sister-chromatid exchanges and genomic instability. Werner syndrome WRN Adult-onset progeroid phenotype, short stature, premature aging, cataracts, diabetes, atherosclerosis, and increased malignancy risk, including sarcomas and thyroid cancers. Tumor histology follows the specific neoplasm; the premature-aging phenotype is the syndromic clue. Bloom syndrome; Rothmund–Thomson syndrome; other progeroid disorders. WRN encodes a RecQ helicase/exonuclease involved in DNA replication, repair, and telomere maintenance. Confirm biallelic germline pathogenic variants. Rothmund–Thomson syndrome RECQL4; ANAPC1 Autosomal recessive; RECQL4-associated and ANAPC1-associated forms. Poikiloderma, sparse hair, growth abnormalities, skeletal defects; RECQL4-associated disease carries osteosarcoma risk and other malignancies. Osteosarcoma in a patient with poikiloderma and skeletal abnormalities is a major clue; correlate with characteristic skin findings. Bloom syndrome; Werner syndrome; other poikiloderma and skeletal dysplasia syndromes. RECQL4 is a DNA helicase involved in replication initiation and genome maintenance. Biallelic pathogenic variants establish the molecular diagnosis; not all clinically defined cases are RECQL4-related. DDX41-related hematologic tumor predisposition RNA/DNA processing and hematopoietic predisposition DDX41 Usually autosomal dominant germline predisposition with later-onset myeloid neoplasia; somatic second hits are common. Adult-onset MDS/AML, often in older adults; family history may be subtle or absent. MDS/AML morphology and cytogenetics are not specific. Consider germline predisposition in unexplained cytopenias, myeloid neoplasm, or family history. Sporadic MDS/AML; other germline myeloid predisposition syndromes (e.g., GATA2, RUNX1, CEBPA). DDX41 variants may be germline with an acquired second DDX41 mutation in the tumor. Test nonhematopoietic tissue when possible; blood/saliva can be confounded by clonal hematopoiesis or tumor-derived variants. Mosaic variegated aneuploidy Mitotic spindle checkpoint / chromosome segregation BUB1B, CEP57, TRIP13; provisionally BUB1, BUB3 Genetically heterogeneous; usually autosomal recessive, with inheritance depending on the gene. Growth retardation, microcephaly and variable developmental findings; increased risk of embryonal tumors and other malignancies, including Wilms tumor and rhabdomyosarcoma in reported cases. Mosaic whole-chromosome gains and losses across cells; aneuploidy varies between tissues/cell populations. Other chromosome-instability syndromes; constitutional mosaic aneuploidy; sporadic embryonal tumors. Defective spindle assembly checkpoint or centrosome/chromosome segregation causes mosaic aneuploidy. Confirm the causative germline variant and demonstrate mosaic aneuploidy where appropriate. MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2, EPCAM Recognizes base–base mismatches and insertion/deletion loops generated during DNA replication. Inherited or acquired loss of both functional alleles causes mismatch repair deficiency, microsatellite instability, increased mutation burden, and impaired damage-triggered apoptosis. Lynch syndrome, Muir–Torre syndrome, and constitutional mismatch repair deficiency (CMMRD). BRCA1, BRCA2, PALB2, RAD51C, RAD51D Accurately repairs DNA double-strand breaks using a homologous template, usually the sister chromatid. Loss of homologous recombination produces genomic instability. In hereditary tumor development, a germline variant is commonly followed by somatic inactivation of the remaining allele. BRCA-related cancer predisposition, PALB2-related predisposition, and RAD51-related predisposition. MUTYH, NTHL1, MBD4 Removes small damaged or inappropriate DNA bases through DNA glycosylases, followed by endonuclease processing and repair synthesis. Biallelic loss of specific glycosylases permits characteristic oxidative-damage or deamination-associated base substitutions to accumulate. MUTYH-associated polyposis, NTHL1-related tumor syndrome, and MBD4-associated neoplasia syndrome. Double-strand-break response and checkpoint signaling ATM, NBN, CHEK2 Senses DNA damage and coordinates checkpoint activation, cell-cycle arrest, repair, and apoptosis. Constitutional loss of ATM or NBN causes chromosome instability and syndromic disease; heterozygous CHEK2 variants confer a generally moderate, variant-dependent cancer predisposition. Ataxia–telangiectasia, Nijmegen breakage syndrome, and CHEK2-related hereditary cancer predisposition. Replication proofreading Proofreads newly synthesized DNA through exonuclease activity during replication. Pathogenic exonuclease-domain variants impair proofreading and produce an ultramutated tumor phenotype; this is distinct from primary MMR deficiency. Polymerase proofreading-associated polyposis. RecQ helicases and replication stability BLM, WRN, RECQL4 Maintain replication-fork stability, recombination fidelity, DNA repair, and telomere integrity. Biallelic loss-of-function variants cause chromosome instability and characteristic multisystem syndromes with cancer predisposition. Bloom syndrome, Werner syndrome, and RECQL4-associated Rothmund–Thomson syndrome. Hematopoietic predisposition and mitotic chromosome segregation DDX41, BUB1B, CEP57, TRIP13, BUB1, BUB3 Includes RNA/DNA processing relevant to hematopoiesis and spindle-checkpoint control of chromosome segregation. Germline DDX41 predisposition may acquire a somatic second hit; spindle-checkpoint defects produce mosaic whole-chromosome gains and losses. DDX41-related hematologic tumor predisposition and mosaic variegated aneuploidy. All pathways PathologyGPS · Genetic Tumor Syndromes DNA Repair and Genomic Stability A diagnostic framework connecting tumor phenotype to inherited defects in DNA repair, replication fidelity, damage response, and chromosome segregation. Pathway Overview DNA repair pathways preserve sequence integrity and chromosome structure. Inherited pathogenic variants often create a constitutional first hit; tumor development may require additional somatic events. The inheritance pattern and molecular mechanism differ substantially across pathways. Key genes Normal function Pathogenic mechanism Associated syndromes Pathology Clues Use the tumor pattern as an entry point; none of these findings alone establishes a germline diagnosis. Colorectal or endometrial carcinoma with dMMR Evaluate the paired MMR IHC pattern and MSI. MLH1/PMS2 loss requires assessment for sporadic MLH1 promoter methylation (and BRAF V600E in colorectal carcinoma) before attributing the tumor to Lynch syndrome. Sebaceous adenoma, sebaceoma, or sebaceous carcinoma Multiple lesions, extra-head-and-neck location, younger age, or a visceral cancer history raise Muir–Torre suspicion. MMR IHC is a screen, not germline confirmation. Child or young adult with high-grade glioma, T-lymphoblastic malignancy, or multiple adenomas Consider CMMRD, particularly with café-au-lait-like macules, pigmentary abnormalities, or multiple developmental venous anomalies. Normal tissues may also lack the affected MMR protein. Early-onset breast, tubo-ovarian, pancreatic, or prostate carcinoma Consider BRCA1/2, PALB2, and RAD51C/RAD51D predisposition. Tumor HRD or a somatic BRCA alteration does not by itself establish a germline variant. Multiple colorectal adenomas with a recessive family pattern Consider MUTYH, NTHL1, and MBD4. Biallelic pathogenic variants are central to these recessive syndromes; distinguish them from APC-associated polyposis and Lynch syndrome. Pediatric or young adult tumor with extreme mutation burden Consider POLE/POLD1 proofreading deficiency and CMMRD. A proofreading-deficient tumor can be ultramutated without the usual MSI phenotype. Lymphoid malignancy with ataxia, telangiectasia, immunodeficiency, or microcephaly Consider ATM-related ataxia–telangiectasia or NBN-related Nijmegen breakage syndrome; the syndromic phenotype is often more informative than tumor morphology. Osteosarcoma with poikiloderma or skeletal abnormalities Consider RECQL4-associated Rothmund–Thomson syndrome. Growth deficiency and photosensitivity also suggest the broader chromosome-instability differential. Adult-onset MDS/AML with a personal or family history suggestive of predisposition Consider germline DDX41, particularly when a somatic second DDX41 variant is detected. Confirm germline status using appropriate nonhematopoietic tissue. Growth retardation with mosaic whole-chromosome gains and losses Consider mosaic variegated aneuploidy due to spindle-checkpoint/chromosome-segregation defects. title: Epigenetic Drivers And Chromatin Remodeling
content: use client Genomic imprinting at 11p15 IGF2, CDKN1C, KCNQ1OT1, H19 Parent-of-origin-specific DNA methylation and long noncoding RNAs regulate monoallelic expression of growth-control genes. IGF2 is normally expressed from the paternal allele, whereas CDKN1C and H19 are normally expressed from the maternal allele; KCNQ1OT1 is a paternally expressed long noncoding RNA. Abnormal methylation, copy-number change, paternal uniparental disomy, or a pathogenic CDKN1C variant disrupts parent-specific expression. Increased IGF2 dosage and/or reduced maternal CDKN1C expression promotes fetal and postnatal overgrowth and embryonal tumor risk. Many abnormalities are mosaic. Beckwith–Wiedemann spectrum, with tumor risk varying by molecular subtype. Oncometabolite-driven epigenetic dysregulation IDH1, IDH2 Wild-type IDH1 and IDH2 encode metabolic enzymes involved in isocitrate metabolism. Their normal activity contributes to cellular metabolic and redox homeostasis. Postzygotic mosaic gain-of-function variants, most often IDH1 p.Arg132 substitutions, produce the oncometabolite D-2-hydroxyglutarate (D-2-HG). D-2-HG inhibits α-ketoglutarate-dependent dioxygenases, altering DNA and histone methylation and favoring chondrogenic over osteogenic differentiation. Ollier disease and Maffucci syndrome. These are generally nonhereditary mosaic disorders, distinct from inherited metachondromatosis. SWI/SNF ATP-dependent chromatin remodeling SMARCB1, SMARCA4, SMARCE1, PBRM1 SWI/SNF complexes use ATP to reposition nucleosomes and regulate access of transcriptional machinery to genomic DNA. Different subunits contribute to distinct SWI/SNF complexes and tissue-specific transcriptional programs. Tumor-suppressor inactivation can impair chromatin remodeling and alter cell-cycle, differentiation, and Polycomb signaling. In rhabdoid tumor predisposition, SMARCB1 or SMARCA4 is commonly subject to a two-hit mechanism. SMARCB1-associated schwannomatosis has a distinct multi-hit interaction with chromosome 22 and NF2. Rhabdoid tumor predisposition syndrome, SMARCB1- or LZTR1-related schwannomatosis, and SMARCE1-related clear cell meningioma predisposition. PBRM1 is a SWI/SNF gene associated with hereditary renal cell carcinoma but not with rhabdoid tumor predisposition syndrome. PRC2-mediated histone methylation EZH2, EED, SUZ12 Polycomb repressive complex 2 (PRC2) establishes repressive histone methylation, particularly H3K27 methylation, to regulate developmental gene expression and maintain cell identity. Weaver syndrome is associated with partial loss of EZH2 function, reducing PRC2 methyltransferase activity and altering H3K27 methylation and the epigenome-wide expression program. Postzygotic mosaic variants may produce variable phenotypes. EZH2 gain-of-function variants associated with an undergrowth phenotype represent a distinct molecular and clinical entity. Weaver syndrome / EZH2-related overgrowth. Beckwith–Wiedemann spectrum IGF2, CDKN1C, KCNQ1OT1, H19; 11p15.5/11p15.4 Mechanistically heterogeneous. Most cases are sporadic epigenetic or mosaic events; CDKN1C pathogenic variants may be inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern with parent-of-origin effects. Recurrence risk depends on the underlying molecular mechanism. Overgrowth phenotype in infancy or early childhood: macrosomia, macroglossia, abdominal wall defects, visceromegaly, and lateralized overgrowth/hemihyperplasia. The phenotype is variable; children with low-level somatic mosaicism may have subtle findings and may first come to attention because of an embryonal tumor. Major associated tumors include Wilms tumor/nephroblastoma and hepatoblastoma; neuroblastoma and adrenocortical carcinoma are less common associations. Tumor risk is molecular-subtype dependent: IC1 gain of methylation and paternal uniparental disomy carry higher childhood tumor risk, whereas IC2 loss of methylation generally carries the lowest risk. CDKN1C pathogenic variants are particularly associated with neuroblastoma risk. Establish the clinical overgrowth phenotype and assess the characteristic features, including macroglossia, abdominal wall defects, lateralized overgrowth, and visceromegaly. Demonstrate an 11p15 imprinting abnormality, copy-number alteration, paternal uniparental disomy, or a pathogenic CDKN1C variant when molecular confirmation is pursued. A negative blood test does not exclude the diagnosis because the causal alteration may be mosaic and enriched in affected tissues. Tumor presentation with subtle or absent classic features should prompt consideration of the spectrum, particularly in children with lateralized overgrowth or multiple embryonal lesions. Associated tumors generally resemble their sporadic counterparts; the syndromic diagnosis is based on clinical and molecular context rather than a unique tumor morphology. Perilobar nephrogenic rests may be present in kidneys of affected infants and young children and are considered precursor lesions for Wilms tumor. Medullary ray nodules may also be seen in kidneys associated with Wilms tumor in this setting. No tumor IHC profile independently establishes Beckwith–Wiedemann spectrum. IHC should be selected for the specific tumor diagnosis; imprinting status requires methylation and/or molecular analysis. Other overgrowth syndromes (Sotos, Weaver, Simpson–Golabi–Behmel, Perlman, and Malan): distinguish by characteristic dysmorphism, developmental profile, associated anomalies, and germline testing. PIK3CA-related overgrowth spectrum: often shows segmental or asymmetric overgrowth; confirm by detecting a postzygotic PIK3CA variant, preferably in affected tissue. Isolated hemihyperplasia: evaluate for an underlying 11p15 abnormality when the phenotype or tumor history suggests Beckwith–Wiedemann spectrum. Perform methylation analysis of the 11p15 imprinting control regions: IC1/H19-IGF2 and IC2/KCNQ1OT1. Assess copy number and allelic composition at 11p15.5/11p15.4, including paternal uniparental disomy and deletions/duplications. Sequence CDKN1C when indicated by the phenotype or family history. Because mosaicism is common, consider testing buccal cells, skin, mesenchymal tissue, or tissue from an affected region when blood testing is negative or inconclusive. Interpret methylation subtype in the context of tumor risk; a methylation abnormality is not interchangeable with a CDKN1C sequence variant. Ollier disease and Maffucci syndrome IDH1 (most often p.Arg132), IDH2 (rarely p.Arg172) Usually nonhereditary, caused by postzygotic somatic mosaicism. The same IDH variant may be found in multiple lesions and at low variant allele fractions in non-neoplastic tissue. This is not a conventional germline autosomal dominant syndrome. Multiple enchondromas usually become apparent in early childhood and produce bone expansion, deformity, limb-length discrepancy, and occasionally pathologic fracture. Lesions predominantly involve the metaphyses of short and long tubular bones; distribution is often asymmetric or predominantly unilateral. Ollier disease is characterized by multiple enchondromas without the characteristic vascular lesions of Maffucci syndrome. Maffucci syndrome combines enchondromatosis with vascular lesions, particularly spindle cell hemangiomas and cavernous hemangiomas in skin, soft tissue, or viscera. Both disorders carry increased risk of secondary central chondrosarcoma; Ollier disease is also associated with gliomas and juvenile granulosa cell tumors. Radiographic and clinical demonstration of multiple enchondromas (at least two) causing bone expansion, symptoms, or deformity supports enchondromatosis. The presence of multiple vascular lesions, especially spindle cell hemangiomas, supports Maffucci syndrome rather than Ollier disease. Molecular confirmation of a postzygotic IDH1 or IDH2 variant in an enchondroma, chondrosarcoma, or vascular lesion supports mosaic pathogenesis but is not required for the clinical-radiologic diagnosis. In enchondromatosis, increased cartilage cellularity and nuclear atypia alone are insufficient to diagnose atypical cartilaginous tumor or grade 1 chondrosarcoma; correlate with imaging, especially cortical destruction and soft-tissue extension. Enchondromas are well-circumscribed intramedullary cartilaginous nodules; periosteal lesions resemble periosteal chondroma. Cartilage may be hypercellular with enlarged, irregular nuclei and myxoid matrix; these findings can occur in benign lesions in the setting of enchondromatosis. Spindle cell hemangioma is an important associated vascular lesion in Maffucci syndrome and may recur locally but does not have metastatic potential. New growth, cortical destruction, or soft-tissue extension in an adult lesion raises concern for secondary chondrosarcoma. No IHC stain reliably distinguishes benign enchondroma from secondary chondrosarcoma in this syndrome; radiologic and clinical correlation is essential. IDH1 R132H IHC may detect a subset of IDH1-mutant lesions but does not detect all IDH1 variants and is not a substitute for sequencing. Use vascular-lineage markers as appropriate to classify associated vascular lesions; they do not establish the underlying mosaic syndrome. Metachondromatosis: inherited disorder associated with PTPN11; lesions include enchondromas and osteochondroma-like lesions, often in hands and feet, with lesions tending to point toward the epiphysis and frequently regressing in adulthood. Spondyloenchondrodysplasia: associated with ACP5 and has a distinct skeletal and systemic phenotype. Multiple sporadic enchondromas: consider the characteristic asymmetric distribution and associated vascular lesions when distinguishing from a syndromic mosaic process. Secondary central chondrosarcoma: assess adult growth, pain, cortical destruction, and soft-tissue extension; atypia alone is not sufficient in Ollier/Maffucci lesions. Sequence IDH1 and IDH2 in lesional tissue; IDH1 p.Arg132 substitutions predominate, particularly p.Arg132Cys, with p.Arg132His and other substitutions also reported. IDH2 variants are uncommon; p.Arg172 substitutions have been reported. Identical IDH variants in anatomically separate lesions support a shared postzygotic mosaic event. Variant detection in affected tissue is more sensitive than testing blood; low-level variant detection in nonlesional tissue may occur. Mutant IDH produces D-2-hydroxyglutarate, which inhibits α-ketoglutarate-dependent enzymes and alters DNA/histone methylation, contributing to abnormal chondrogenic differentiation. Rhabdoid tumor predisposition syndrome SWI/SNF chromatin remodeling SMARCB1 (RTPS1); SMARCA4 (RTPS2) Autosomal dominant cancer predisposition due to a germline pathogenic variant, frequently de novo. Postzygotic mosaicism and gonadal mosaicism are documented. Tumor development typically requires a second inactivating event in the remaining functional allele. RTPS1 (SMARCB1) most often presents in infancy or early childhood with atypical teratoid/rhabdoid tumor (AT/RT), renal malignant rhabdoid tumor, or extrarenal malignant rhabdoid tumor. Synchronous, multifocal, or metachronous primary rhabdoid tumors, particularly in different anatomic sites, strongly suggest a germline predisposition. RTPS2 (SMARCA4) is strongly associated with small cell carcinoma of the ovary, hypercalcemic type (SCCOHT), typically in adolescents and young adults; CNS tumors are less common. A young child with a rhabdoid tumor at any site warrants consideration of germline SMARCB1 testing; bilateral renal malignant rhabdoid tumors are particularly compelling. Survivors remain at risk for subsequent primary tumors, supporting long-term surveillance. A pathogenic germline SMARCB1 variant in a patient with AT/RT or malignant rhabdoid tumor establishes RTPS1. A pathogenic germline SMARCA4 variant in a patient with SCCOHT or an appropriate rhabdoid tumor establishes RTPS2. Loss of nuclear SMARCB1 or SMARCA4 in tumor cells supports the corresponding tumor classification but does not distinguish germline predisposition from a sporadic tumor. Multiple rhabdoid tumors, very early onset, or affected siblings/relatives should prompt constitutional testing, including assessment for mosaicism. Malignant rhabdoid tumors and AT/RTs show rhabdoid cytology, but morphology alone does not establish a hereditary syndrome. SCCOHT is a distinct aggressive ovarian neoplasm associated with SMARCA4 deficiency; evaluate in the appropriate age and clinical setting. Rhabdoid morphology in other CNS tumors does not necessarily indicate AT/RT; many composite rhabdoid tumors retain SMARCB1 expression. RTPS1-associated and sporadic SMARCB1-deficient rhabdoid tumors show loss of nuclear INI1 (SMARCB1) in tumor cells, with retained staining in internal non-neoplastic controls. RTPS2/SCCOHT commonly shows loss of nuclear BRG1 (SMARCA4); correlate with morphology and molecular findings. Complete tumor-cell loss of INI1 or BRG1 is a tumor-classification clue, not proof of a germline alteration. Other SMARCB1-deficient neoplasms (e.g., epithelioid sarcoma and selected myoepithelial or nerve-sheath tumors): integrate site, morphology, clinical age, and molecular context; not all are RTPS-associated. CNS tumors with rhabdoid features but retained INI1: consider other tumor entities with secondary rhabdoid morphology rather than classic AT/RT. SCCOHT versus other small-cell ovarian neoplasms: use clinical setting, morphology, BRG1 IHC, and molecular confirmation. Sporadic rhabdoid tumor: tumor suppressor loss may be entirely somatic; constitutional testing is needed to establish predisposition. Perform germline SMARCB1 or SMARCA4 sequencing plus deletion/duplication and structural-variant analysis. Tumor profiling should assess biallelic inactivation, including sequence variants, copy-number loss, and loss of heterozygosity. SMARCB1 tumorigenesis commonly follows a two-hit tumor-suppressor model; the second event is often deletion or loss of heterozygosity. SMARCB1-associated AT/RTs can be classified into molecular groups (AT/RT-TYR, AT/RT-SHH, and AT/RT-MYC); SMARCA4-altered AT/RT is a distinct, less common group. When blood testing is negative despite strong clinical suspicion, consider mosaicism and testing of another normal tissue; distinguish constitutional variants from tumor-only alterations. SMARCB1- and LZTR1-related schwannomatosis SWI/SNF chromatin remodeling / chromosome 22 tumor-suppressor pathway SMARCB1, LZTR1; tumor-associated NF2 alterations Familial cases show autosomal dominant inheritance with incomplete penetrance; most cases are sporadic. Segmental distribution may reflect mosaicism. Tumors typically acquire additional somatic events involving chromosome 22 and NF2. Multiple schwannomas involving spinal nerve roots, peripheral nerves, and less often cranial nerves; unilateral vestibular schwannoma can occur, particularly with LZTR1-related disease. Severe chronic pain is characteristic; major neurologic deficits and polyneuropathy are less common than in NF2-related schwannomatosis. Segmental distribution of tumors occurs in a subset and may reflect mosaic disease. A minority of patients develop meningiomas; multiple meningiomas, including falcine lesions, are reported with SMARCB1-related disease. A unilateral vestibular schwannoma does not by itself establish NF2-related schwannomatosis; LZTR1-related disease is an important differential. Establish the presence and distribution of multiple schwannomas and integrate clinical findings with updated molecular diagnostic criteria. Identify a pathogenic germline SMARCB1 or LZTR1 variant when assigning the corresponding molecular subtype. If blood testing is negative, evaluate tumor tissue and chromosome 22 alterations; some cases remain schwannomatosis not elsewhere classified. Distinguish NF2-related schwannomatosis, including mosaic NF2, because clinical overlap can be substantial. Most lesions are conventional schwannomas; hybrid schwannoma/neurofibroma tumors are common in this setting and may be mistaken for neurofibroma or malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumor. The cytology and architecture of schwannomas are generally similar to those of sporadic counterparts. A malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumor is uncommon; do not infer malignancy from hybrid morphology alone. Many schwannomas show mosaic loss of nuclear SMARCB1/INI1 in a subset of tumor cells, particularly in familial SMARCB1-related disease. Mosaic INI1 staining is not specific for a germline SMARCB1 variant; it can also occur in sporadic schwannomatosis, NF2-related schwannomatosis, and tumors with LZTR1 variants or no identified variant. Reduced or absent LZTR1 staining has been described in LZTR1-associated schwannomas, but it is not a stand-alone germline test. NF2-related schwannomatosis: bilateral vestibular schwannomas, multiple meningiomas, and other characteristic CNS tumors favor NF2; mosaic NF2 can be difficult to exclude with blood testing alone. Solitary sporadic schwannoma: usually lacks the clinical pattern of multiple painful tumors; mosaic INI1 staining is less common but not impossible. Neurofibromatosis type 1: neurofibromas and associated cutaneous/systemic findings differ from the schwannoma-predominant phenotype. Hybrid schwannoma/neurofibroma versus malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumor: assess atypia, mitotic activity, necrosis, infiltrative growth, and clinical behavior rather than relying on hybrid phenotype alone. Use germline sequencing and copy-number analysis for SMARCB1 and LZTR1; consider broader testing when the phenotype remains unexplained. Tumors commonly show inactivation of both copies of SMARCB1 or LZTR1 together with biallelic NF2 inactivation. A proposed four-hit, three-step model includes the inherited or constitutional first hit, chromosome 22 loss affecting the wild-type predisposition allele and one NF2 allele, followed by inactivation of the remaining NF2 allele. Most patients with schwannomatosis do not have a germline NF2 variant; NF2 alterations are typically somatic in the schwannomas. Consider DGCR8 and other 22q-related schwannomatosis categories when multiple tumors share chromosome 22q molecular findings without an identifiable SMARCB1 or LZTR1 germline variant. Clear cell meningioma predisposition syndrome SMARCE1 Autosomal dominant predisposition caused by a germline inactivating SMARCE1 variant. Penetrance is incompletely defined and may be reduced in males. Clear cell meningioma in a child, adolescent, or young adult should prompt consideration of a germline SMARCE1 variant. Spinal canal and cerebellopontine angle are characteristic sites in the predisposition setting. Multiple relatives with clear cell meningiomas are strongly suggestive. Other tumor associations remain insufficiently established; do not assume a broad extracranial tumor spectrum. A pathogenic germline SMARCE1 variant establishes clear cell meningioma predisposition syndrome. One or more clear cell meningiomas and a positive family history are supportive clinical features. Loss of SMARCE1 expression in a clear cell meningioma is a useful screening clue but does not by itself establish germline status. Patternless or sheet-like growth of round to polygonal cells with clear, glycogen-rich cytoplasm. Prominent perivascular and interstitial collagen may form large acellular zones or brightly eosinophilic amianthoid-like collagen. Tumor cells contain PAS-positive, diastase-sensitive cytoplasmic glycogen. Whorls are often inconspicuous and psammoma bodies are usually sparse. Clear cell meningiomas associated with SMARCE1 alteration typically show loss of nuclear SMARCE1 expression. SMARCE1 loss is a screening clue for molecular evaluation, not proof of a germline pathogenic variant. Use a standard meningioma panel and appropriate internal controls to establish lineage and exclude mimics. Other meningioma subtypes with clear-cell change: the characteristic collagen-rich pattern, glycogen, and SMARCE1 loss support clear cell meningioma. Metastatic clear cell carcinoma (especially renal): use epithelial markers and organ-specific markers; meningioma markers and anatomic/radiologic context help resolve the differential. Clear cell tumors of nerve sheath or other mesenchymal lineage: integrate S100/SOX10 and other lineage markers with morphology and site. Confirm a pathogenic germline SMARCE1 variant using constitutional DNA. Most reported germline variants are frameshift or stop-gain variants predicted to cause loss of protein expression. Tumors may show germline plus somatic inactivation or biallelic somatic SMARCE1 alterations. SMARCE1 loss by IHC can select cases for germline evaluation; methylation profiling may assist classification in histologically challenging cases. Do not equate tumor SMARCE1 loss with inherited predisposition without germline testing. Weaver syndrome / EZH2-related overgrowth EZH2; PRC2 complex also includes EED and SUZ12 Usually de novo autosomal dominant, with parental or proband mosaicism reported. Affected individuals have a 50% chance of transmitting a constitutional pathogenic variant; recurrence in unaffected parents is low but not zero because of possible gonadal mosaicism. Tall stature and generalized overgrowth typically begin in childhood; height may be several standard deviations above the mean. Characteristic facial gestalt, advanced bone age, and disharmonic skeletal maturation support the diagnosis. Developmental delay and intellectual disability are common but variable. Tumor susceptibility includes neuroblastoma and reported hematolymphoid malignancies, including ALL, AML, and non-Hodgkin lymphoma. EZH2-related undergrowth caused by gain-of-function variants is a distinct entity and should not be mislabeled as Weaver syndrome. A pathogenic or likely pathogenic EZH2 variant together with tall stature or characteristic facial features supports EZH2-related overgrowth/Weaver syndrome. Advanced or disharmonic bone age is a useful supportive feature. For a variant of uncertain significance, de novo status and exclusion of overlapping overgrowth syndromes may assist interpretation but do not automatically make the variant pathogenic. Clinical interpretation must account for variant mechanism; EZH2 gain-of-function undergrowth is not Weaver syndrome. Associated tumors are generally morphologically similar to their sporadic counterparts. No distinctive tumor histology has been established as diagnostic of Weaver syndrome. Reduced H3K27me3 staining may theoretically support impaired PRC2 activity in a tumor, but it is not a validated stand-alone diagnostic test for Weaver syndrome. Tumor IHC should not be used to infer a constitutional EZH2 variant without germline testing. Sotos syndrome (NSD1): overlapping overgrowth and developmental features; distinguish by phenotype and molecular testing. EED- or SUZ12-related overgrowth syndromes: overlap in PRC2 biology; use gene-specific testing and phenotype. Simpson–Golabi–Behmel and other congenital overgrowth syndromes: distinguish by characteristic congenital anomalies, dysmorphism, and molecular testing. EZH2 gain-of-function undergrowth: distinct phenotype and molecular mechanism; do not group with Weaver syndrome. Confirm a pathogenic or likely pathogenic EZH2 variant by germline sequencing; assess parental samples when useful to establish de novo status. Most Weaver-associated variants impair EZH2/PRC2 function and reduce H3K27 methyltransferase activity, including H3K27me1 and H3K27me3 deposition. Postzygotic mosaic EZH2 variants can produce variable or subtle phenotypes; tissue distribution may influence clinical expression. A distinct subset of EZH2 gain-of-function variants is associated with growth failure/undergrowth and a different epigenetic signature. Epigenome-wide methylation profiling may support classification in selected diagnostically difficult cases. Infant with Wilms tumor, hepatoblastoma, or bilateral nephrogenic rests Look for macroglossia, abdominal wall defects, lateralized overgrowth, visceromegaly, or subtle asymmetry. Molecular subtype matters because tumor risk differs substantially. 11p15 imprinting; IGF2, CDKN1C Multiple asymmetric enchondromas, especially with limb-length discrepancy A unilateral or markedly asymmetric distribution favors a postzygotic mosaic disorder rather than a conventional inherited skeletal syndrome. Ollier disease Mosaic IDH1/IDH2 gain of function Multiple enchondromas plus spindle cell hemangiomas The vascular lesions, particularly spindle cell hemangiomas, distinguish Maffucci syndrome from Ollier disease. Watch for new adult growth or cortical destruction suggesting chondrosarcoma. Maffucci syndrome Mosaic IDH1, usually p.Arg132Cys Rhabdoid tumor in an infant or young child; multiple synchronous or metachronous tumors AT/RT, renal or extrarenal malignant rhabdoid tumor, and loss of INI1 should trigger germline assessment. Tumor INI1 loss alone does not prove a constitutional variant. Rhabdoid tumor predisposition syndrome 1 SMARCB1 Small cell carcinoma of the ovary, hypercalcemic type, in an adolescent or young adult Loss of BRG1 supports SMARCA4 deficiency. Germline testing distinguishes RTPS2 from a tumor-only SMARCA4 alteration. Rhabdoid tumor predisposition syndrome 2 SMARCA4 Multiple painful schwannomas, especially spinal or peripheral nerve tumors Severe chronic pain and absence of the classic bilateral vestibular schwannoma pattern favor schwannomatosis; unilateral vestibular schwannoma can occur in LZTR1-related disease. SMARCB1- or LZTR1-related schwannomatosis SMARCB1, LZTR1; somatic NF2 Clear cell meningioma in a child or young adult, particularly spinal or cerebellopontine angle Clear cytoplasm, PAS-positive diastase-sensitive glycogen, and collagen-rich perivascular stroma are characteristic. SMARCE1 loss should prompt germline evaluation. Childhood overgrowth with advanced bone age and neuroblastoma Tall stature, characteristic facial gestalt, and developmental delay support Weaver syndrome. Confirm the EZH2 variant mechanism; gain-of-function undergrowth is a separate condition. Weaver syndrome EZH2 / PRC2 Genetic Tumor Syndromes Epigenetic Drivers and Chromatin Remodeling A clinicopathologic reference linking imprinting defects, oncometabolite-driven epigenetic changes, chromatin remodeling complexes, and Polycomb regulation to recognizable tumor and multisystem phenotypes. Pathway Overview Epigenetic regulation controls gene expression without changing the underlying DNA sequence. DNA methylation, histone modifications, genomic imprinting, and ATP-dependent nucleosome remodeling establish transcriptionally active or repressed chromatin states. Pathogenic alterations may be constitutional, postzygotic mosaic, or acquired only in the tumor; these categories have different diagnostic and counseling implications. title: Growth Factor Receptor And Related
content: use client growth-factor-receptors Growth Factor Receptors Cell-surface receptors bind extracellular growth factors and transmit signals through intracellular kinase domains to regulate proliferation, survival, migration, and differentiation. MET · RET · ALK · PHOX2B · FGFR1 Constitutive receptor activation is typically caused by germline gain-of-function variants (MET, RET, ALK). PHOX2B is a developmental transcription factor rather than a receptor. FGFR1-related encephalocraniocutaneous lipomatosis is usually caused by postzygotic mosaic activating variants. Hereditary papillary renal carcinoma · MEN2 · Hereditary neuroblastoma · Encephalocraniocutaneous lipomatosis Hereditary Papillary Renal Carcinoma MET Autosomal dominant; incomplete penetrance Usually presents in the fourth to sixth decades. No consistent sex predilection is established. Bilateral, multifocal tumors arise in the renal cortex. Often detected during imaging or evaluation of a family history of renal cancer. Bilateral and multifocal papillary renal neoplasms, or multiple affected relatives with papillary renal cell carcinoma. Confirm a germline activating MET variant. Assess the possibility of additional hereditary renal cancer syndromes when morphology is atypical. Papillary and tubulopapillary adenomas and carcinomas may coexist. Papillae are lined by a single layer of cuboidal cells with scant basophilic cytoplasm. Foamy macrophages are common; psammoma bodies may be present. Biphasic alveolar-squamoid morphology is reported in a subset. Tumors generally show a renal epithelial phenotype; no immunostain substitutes for germline testing. FH-deficient renal cell carcinoma: prominent inclusion-like nucleoli and perinucleolar halos; evaluate FH and 2SC. Other papillary renal neoplasms: integrate morphology, immunophenotype, and molecular findings. Germline activating missense variants cluster in the MET kinase domain. Chromosome 7 gain or trisomy 7 may be present in tumors but is not diagnostic of hereditary disease. Bilateral, multifocal papillary renal tumors, especially with a family history. Multiple papillary adenomas accompanying papillary renal cell carcinoma. Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia Type 2 RET Autosomal dominant; de novo variants occur Medullary thyroid carcinoma may present in childhood or adulthood, depending on the RET variant. Both sexes are affected. Thyroid C-cell disease is central; pheochromocytomas arise in the adrenal medulla. MEN2A may include hyperparathyroidism; MEN2B is associated with mucosal neuromas and a marfanoid habitus. Medullary thyroid carcinoma, C-cell neoplasia, or a characteristic MEN2-associated tumor pattern. Germline activating RET pathogenic variant. Evaluate for pheochromocytoma before thyroid or parathyroid surgery. MEN2B: look for mucosal neuromas, intestinal ganglioneuromatosis, and marfanoid features. Medullary thyroid carcinoma is often bilateral and multifocal, with background C-cell proliferations. MTC may show nested, trabecular, spindle-cell, follicular, or other patterns. Amyloid derived from calcitonin is common but not obligatory. MEN2-associated pheochromocytomas may be bilateral and accompanied by adrenal medullary hyperplasia. MEN2B may show mucosal neuromas and gastrointestinal ganglioneuromatosis. MTC: calcitonin, CEA, synaptophysin, chromogranin, and INSM1 are typically positive. MTC is negative for thyroglobulin; monoclonal PAX8 is generally negative. Pheochromocytoma: chromogranin and synaptophysin positive; sustentacular cells may highlight with S100 or SOX10. Sporadic MTC: hereditary disease is favored by multifocality, bilateral disease, C-cell proliferations, young age, or family history. Parathyroid lesions and other neuroendocrine tumors: use site-specific markers and clinical context. MEN1 and other hereditary endocrine syndromes: distinguish by tumor spectrum and germline testing.
