Gorlin syndrome · Curry–Jones syndrome · ELP1-related medulloblastoma predisposition · Multiple osteochondromas Nevoid Basal Cell Carcinoma Syndrome (Gorlin Syndrome) PTCH1 · SUFU; rare GPR161-related Gorlin-like phenotype Autosomal dominant; de novo variants are common Congenital features may be present; basal cell carcinomas usually emerge in adolescence or adulthood. Skin, jaw, skeleton, ovaries, and CNS are involved. Features include multiple basal cell carcinomas, odontogenic keratocysts, palmar/plantar pits, and falx calcification. Apply established major and minor clinical criteria. Multiple basal cell carcinomas at a young age or odontogenic keratocysts with characteristic skeletal findings should prompt evaluation. Confirm germline PTCH1 or SUFU pathogenic variant when possible. Basal cell carcinomas may be numerous and histologically resemble sporadic tumors. Odontogenic keratocysts show a keratinizing epithelial lining with palisaded basal cells. Associated medulloblastomas are typically desmoplastic/nodular or extensively nodular. No single IHC marker establishes the syndrome. Evaluate individual tumors with standard site-specific panels. Multiple sporadic basal cell carcinomas: age, jaw cysts, skeletal findings, and family history are discriminating. Other inherited BCC predisposition syndromes: correlate phenotype and germline findings. PTCH1 and SUFU are tumor suppressors; germline loss-of-function variants lead to Hedgehog pathway activation. Tumors commonly acquire inactivation of the remaining allele. PTCH1 and SUFU sequencing plus deletion/duplication analysis are important; GPR161 is a rare consideration. Multiple basal cell carcinomas at a young age. Odontogenic keratocysts with palmar pits, falx calcification, or childhood desmoplastic medulloblastoma. Curry–Jones Syndrome SMO Findings include craniosynostosis, polysyndactyly, segmental skin abnormalities, and gastrointestinal anomalies. Asymmetric or mosaic distribution is characteristic. Characteristic combination of craniofacial, limb, skin, and gastrointestinal abnormalities. A postzygotic activating SMO variant in affected tissue supports the diagnosis. Consider mosaicism when blood testing is negative. Cutaneous and skeletal lesions vary with the affected tissue. Associated hamartomatous lesions are not defined by a single histologic pattern. Other craniosynostosis and limb-patterning syndromes: compare polydactyly pattern and associated anomalies. Other mosaic overgrowth syndromes: assess tissue distribution and molecular findings. Postzygotic activating SMO variants cause aberrant Hedgehog signaling. Affected tissue is preferred for detecting low-level mosaicism. Craniosynostosis with polysyndactyly and segmental skin or gastrointestinal abnormalities. ELP1-Related Medulloblastoma Predisposition Syndrome ELP1 Autosomal recessive in the established familial syndrome context Typically presents in childhood. Predisposition is centered on medulloblastoma; associated developmental or neurologic features may occur. A family history or consanguinity may be informative. Medulloblastoma with a compatible family history or clinical context. Confirm biallelic pathogenic ELP1 variants when evaluating the inherited syndrome. Classify the medulloblastoma by current integrated histologic and molecular criteria. Medulloblastoma morphology is determined by the tumor subtype and may not be distinctive of the predisposition syndrome. Use standard medulloblastoma immunohistochemistry and molecular subgrouping; no syndrome-specific IHC marker is established. Sporadic medulloblastoma: inherited predisposition is assessed by age, family history, and germline testing. Other hereditary medulloblastoma syndromes, including APC- and PTCH1/SUFU-related disease. ELP1 encodes a component of the Elongator complex involved in transcriptional regulation and other cellular processes. Germline pathogenic variants are associated with medulloblastoma predisposition; interpret variant phase and inheritance. Medulloblastoma in a patient with a suggestive family history or biallelic ELP1 findings. Multiple Osteochondromas EXT1 · EXT2 Usually presents in childhood, with lesions developing during skeletal growth. Multiple metaphyseal osteochondromas arise from long bones and other skeletal sites. Pain, deformity, restricted motion, and limb-length discrepancy may occur. Multiple osteochondromas with characteristic radiographic continuity of cortex and medullary cavity. A family history or germline EXT1/EXT2 variant supports the diagnosis. Evaluate new pain, growth after skeletal maturity, or cartilage cap enlargement for secondary chondrosarcoma. Osteochondroma shows a cartilage cap with endochondral ossification and continuity with underlying bone. Secondary peripheral chondrosarcoma shows malignant cartilage with permeative growth and entrapment of host bone. No diagnostic IHC profile; morphology and radiology are central. Sporadic solitary osteochondroma: lacks multiple lesions and familial pattern. Bizarre parosteal osteochondromatous proliferation: lacks medullary continuity and has a different anatomic pattern. Secondary peripheral chondrosarcoma: assess cartilage cap, permeation, and clinical growth. EXT1 and EXT2 encode glycosyltransferases required for heparan sulfate biosynthesis. Germline loss-of-function variants reduce heparan sulfate and alter developmental signaling gradients. Tumor formation may involve somatic inactivation of the remaining allele. Multiple osteochondromas in a child or young adult. Cartilage-capped exostosis with new pain or growth after skeletal maturity. nfkb NF-κB Signaling Pathway NF-κB regulates inflammation, cell survival, and proliferation. CYLD is a deubiquitinase that restrains signaling through NF-κB and other pathways. CYLD Germline loss-of-function variants in CYLD impair negative regulation of signaling and predispose to multiple adnexal tumors. Brooke–Spiegler syndrome Brooke–Spiegler Syndrome Autosomal dominant; mosaic forms occur Usually begins in adolescence or early adulthood. Multiple cutaneous adnexal tumors involve the scalp, face, and trunk. Lesions include cylindromas, spiradenomas, and trichoepitheliomas. Multiple histologically confirmed cylindromas, spiradenomas, spiradenocylindromas, or trichoepitheliomas. A germline pathogenic CYLD variant supports the diagnosis. Consider mosaic disease in patients with segmental or limited clusters of lesions. Cylindroma shows a jigsaw-puzzle arrangement of basaloid nests with thick hyaline basement membrane material. Spiradenoma shows basaloid cells with lymphocytes and often a painful clinical presentation. Trichoepithelioma shows follicular germinative differentiation and horn cysts. Malignant transformation is rare but may show infiltrative growth, atypia, and increased mitotic activity. CYLD-associated tumors may show loss of CYLD expression, although staining is not a substitute for molecular testing. Use appropriate adnexal markers to distinguish follicular and apocrine differentiation when needed. Sporadic spiradenoma/cylindroma: multiplicity, family history, and distribution favor inherited disease. Basal cell carcinoma: retraction artifact and stromal features differ; correlate with adnexal morphology. Other adnexal tumor syndromes: assess the combination of lesion types. CYLD encodes a deubiquitinase that negatively regulates NF-κB and other signaling pathways. Germline loss-of-function variants predispose to multiple adnexal tumors; a second hit may occur in tumors. ALPK1 hotspot variants characterize some sporadic spiradenomas and are not the defining alteration in CYLD-associated tumors. Multiple scalp cylindromas or a 'turban tumor' pattern. A mixture of cylindromas, spiradenomas, and trichoepitheliomas in one patient or family. mtor-pi3k mTOR/PI3K Pathway PI3K generates PIP3 to activate AKT and downstream mTOR signaling. The TSC1–TSC2 complex and PTEN restrain this growth-promoting pathway; PI3Kδ is important in immune cells. TSC1 · TSC2 · PTEN · PIK3CD TSC1/TSC2 and PTEN are tumor suppressors whose loss increases pathway activity. Activated PIK3CD variants cause immune dysregulation and lymphoproliferative disease. Tuberous sclerosis complex · PTEN hamartoma tumor syndrome · Activated PI3Kδ syndrome Tuberous Sclerosis Complex TSC1 · TSC2 Usually recognized in infancy or childhood, but manifestations may be diagnosed at any age. Brain, skin, kidneys, heart, lungs, and eyes may be involved. Features include cortical tubers, subependymal nodules, facial angiofibromas, renal angiomyolipomas, and cardiac rhabdomyomas. Apply current clinical diagnostic criteria using major and minor features. A pathogenic TSC1 or TSC2 variant is independently diagnostic. Evaluate renal, CNS, cardiac, pulmonary, and cutaneous manifestations. Renal angiomyolipoma contains variable proportions of dysmorphic vessels, smooth muscle, and adipose tissue. Subependymal giant cell astrocytoma shows large ganglioid cells and may arise near the foramen of Monro. Pulmonary lymphangioleiomyomatosis shows abnormal smooth muscle-like cells around cystic lung spaces. Cardiac rhabdomyoma is composed of enlarged vacuolated myocytes with spider cells. Angiomyolipoma and LAM cells express melanocytic markers such as HMB45 and Melan-A, and smooth muscle markers. SEGA may express GFAP and neuronal markers variably. Rhabdomyoma expresses muscle markers such as desmin. Sporadic angiomyolipoma: multiple or bilateral lesions and other TSC features favor syndromic disease. PEComa: evaluate morphology, melanocytic/smooth muscle phenotype, and clinical context. Other causes of cortical tubers or subependymal lesions: integrate imaging and clinical criteria. TSC1 encodes hamartin and TSC2 encodes tuberin; the complex inhibits RHEB and mTORC1. Germline loss-of-function variants are followed by somatic second-hit inactivation in many tumors. mTOR pathway activation is a central mechanism across the organ manifestations. Multiple or bilateral renal angiomyolipomas with characteristic CNS or skin lesions. Subependymal giant cell astrocytoma in a patient with cortical tubers. Cardiac rhabdomyoma in an infant with other suggestive findings. PTEN Hamartoma Tumor Syndrome PTEN Often recognized in childhood or adulthood. Multiple organ systems are involved, especially skin, thyroid, breast, endometrium, and gastrointestinal tract. Macrocephaly and mucocutaneous lesions are characteristic clues. Apply established clinical criteria for Cowden syndrome/PTEN hamartoma tumor syndrome. A germline pathogenic PTEN variant confirms the molecular diagnosis. Assess for breast, thyroid, endometrial, renal, and colorectal manifestations. Hamartomatous gastrointestinal polyps may show varied histologies. Thyroid lesions include multinodular goiter, adenomas, and carcinoma. Mucocutaneous lesions include trichilemmomas and papillomatous papules. No single IHC stain establishes PTEN hamartoma tumor syndrome. Loss of PTEN staining in a tumor may support pathway inactivation but requires internal controls and molecular correlation. Peutz–Jeghers syndrome: mucocutaneous pigmentation and arborizing smooth muscle in polyps. Bannayan–Riley–Ruvalcaba phenotype and other hamartoma syndromes: assess the full phenotype and PTEN testing. Sporadic thyroid or breast neoplasia: consider age, macrocephaly, and mucocutaneous findings. PTEN is a lipid phosphatase that converts PIP3 to PIP2 and antagonizes PI3K–AKT signaling. Germline loss-of-function variants include sequence variants and deletions. Tumors may acquire a second hit with loss of the remaining functional allele. Macrocephaly with multiple mucocutaneous lesions or mixed gastrointestinal polyps. Breast or thyroid neoplasia accompanied by characteristic PTEN-related features. Activated PI3Kδ Syndrome PIK3CD Autosomal dominant; usually germline activating variants Usually presents in childhood, although diagnosis may be delayed. Immune system and lymphoid organs are primarily involved. Recurrent respiratory infections, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, autoimmunity, and lymphoma risk are characteristic. Recurrent infections with immune dysregulation or lymphoproliferation. Demonstrate an activating germline PIK3CD variant or an appropriate PIK3R1-related phenotype. Correlate with immunologic testing and clinical history. Lymph nodes may show reactive or atypical lymphoid hyperplasia. Lymphoma, particularly B-cell lymphoma, may develop. Interpret lymphoid proliferations in the context of immune dysregulation. Use standard hematolymphoid panels to classify lymphoid proliferations and exclude lymphoma. No single IHC marker establishes APDS. Common variable immunodeficiency and other inborn errors of immunity: molecular and immunologic evaluation is required. Primary immunodeficiency-associated lymphoproliferative disorders: distinguish by the underlying gene and clinical phenotype. PIK3CD encodes the p110δ catalytic subunit of class IA PI3K. Activating variants cause constitutive PI3Kδ signaling and downstream AKT/mTOR activation. PIK3R1 loss-of-function variants can cause a related APDS phenotype. Lymphadenopathy or lymphoma in a patient with recurrent infections and immune dysregulation. Unusual lymphoid hyperplasia with a history of childhood-onset immunodeficiency. transcription-regulators Transcription Factors and Regulators Transcription factors and regulatory proteins control gene expression, lineage differentiation, development, and cell-cycle checkpoints. Germline variants can produce recognizable tumor-predisposition syndromes. MAX · MAFA · FLCN · RUNX1 · TBXT · CDC73 Mechanisms include tumor-suppressor loss, altered transcriptional regulation, and activating variants affecting lineage-specific transcription factors. Variant type and inheritance differ by syndrome. MEN5 · MAFA-related familial insulinomatosis · Birt–Hogg–Dubé syndrome · Familial platelet disorder with myeloid malignancy predisposition · Familial chordoma · Hyperparathyroidism–jaw tumor syndrome Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia Type 5 / MAX-Related Tumors MAX Usually presents in adulthood, although age varies. Adrenal medulla, paraganglia, pituitary, parathyroid, and pancreas may be involved. Pheochromocytoma/paraganglioma may be bilateral or metachronous; ganglioneuroma and neuroblastoma have also been reported. Pheochromocytoma or paraganglioma with a compatible family history or multiple endocrine/neural crest tumors. Confirm a germline pathogenic MAX variant. Evaluate for additional endocrine manifestations based on the phenotype. Pheochromocytoma shows nested (zellballen) architecture with neuroendocrine cells. Paraganglioma morphology varies by site and may be indistinguishable from sporadic tumors. Ganglioneuroma contains mature ganglion cells in Schwannian stroma. Pheochromocytoma/paraganglioma: chromogranin and synaptophysin positive; sustentacular cells may express S100/SOX10. Loss of MAX expression may support MAX pathway involvement but should be correlated with germline testing. Other hereditary PPGL syndromes, especially SDHx, VHL, RET, and NF1: distinguish by associated tumors and molecular testing. MEN1 and MEN2: compare endocrine tumor spectrum and defining gene. MAX is a transcriptional regulator that dimerizes with MYC-family proteins. Germline loss-of-function variants predispose to endocrine and neural crest tumors; tumors may show loss of the remaining allele. MAX is recognized as the susceptibility gene for MEN5. Pheochromocytoma with bilateral disease, metachronous PPGL, or a family history. PPGL accompanied by pituitary, parathyroid, or neural crest tumors. MAFA-Related Familial Insulinomatosis MAFA Usually presents in adulthood, with variable age at onset. Pancreatic islets are involved. Clinical presentation reflects recurrent hypoglycemia from multifocal insulin-producing lesions. Multifocal pancreatic beta-cell proliferations or multiple insulinomas in a familial setting. Confirm a germline activating MAFA variant. Distinguish from sporadic insulinoma and other causes of congenital or familial hyperinsulinism. Multifocal beta-cell hyperplasia and insulin-producing neuroendocrine lesions may be present. Individual insulinomas are well-differentiated pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors. Insulin highlights beta-cell proliferations and insulin-producing tumors. Sporadic insulinoma: usually solitary and lacks the familial MAFA-associated pattern. MEN1-associated pancreatic NETs: assess other endocrine tumors and MEN1 status. Other familial hyperinsulinism: correlate age, biochemical profile, and genetic findings. Germline activating MAFA variants alter transcriptional regulation of pancreatic beta-cell function. The molecular diagnosis distinguishes familial insulinomatosis from sporadic multifocal beta-cell disease. Multiple insulin-producing pancreatic lesions with familial hypoglycemia. Birt–Hogg–Dubé Syndrome FLCN Skin, lungs, and kidneys are principal sites. Features include fibrofolliculomas, pulmonary cysts with spontaneous pneumothorax, and renal neoplasms. Multiple fibrofolliculomas or characteristic pulmonary cysts with renal tumors or family history. Confirm a germline pathogenic FLCN variant. Evaluate renal tumors for hybrid oncocytic/chromophobe morphology. Fibrofolliculoma shows a follicular epithelial component with radiating strands in a fibrous stroma. Renal tumors include hybrid oncocytic/chromophobe tumors, chromophobe RCC, and oncocytoma. Pulmonary cysts are irregular and often basilar or medial. Renal tumors may show variable CK7, CD117, and other renal epithelial marker profiles depending on subtype. FLCN IHC loss can support pathway inactivation but does not independently establish germline disease. Sporadic renal oncocytoma or chromophobe RCC: multiplicity, hybrid morphology, lung cysts, and skin lesions favor BHD. Other hereditary renal tumor syndromes: compare renal tumor morphology and extra-renal manifestations. FLCN encodes folliculin, involved in AMPK/mTOR and cellular energy-sensing pathways. Germline loss-of-function variants predispose to renal tumors; somatic second hits may occur. Sequence and deletion/duplication analysis should be considered. Hybrid oncocytic/chromophobe renal tumor with pulmonary cysts or spontaneous pneumothorax. Multiple facial fibrofolliculomas in a patient with renal neoplasia. Familial Platelet Disorder with Myeloid Malignancy Predisposition RUNX1 May present from childhood through adulthood. Hematopoietic system is involved, with lifelong thrombocytopenia and platelet dysfunction. Predisposition includes myelodysplastic syndrome and acute myeloid leukemia. Personal or family history of thrombocytopenia and abnormal bleeding with a myeloid neoplasm or familial clustering. Confirm a germline pathogenic RUNX1 variant. Distinguish germline variants from somatic RUNX1 mutations in myeloid neoplasms. Bone marrow findings depend on the associated myeloid neoplasm. MDS may show dysplasia in one or more hematopoietic lineages. AML morphology and immunophenotype are classified using standard criteria. Use standard myeloid immunophenotyping; RUNX1 IHC is not a germline diagnostic assay. Other inherited thrombocytopenias with myeloid malignancy risk, including ETV6- and ANKRD26-related disorders. Acquired thrombocytopenia and sporadic MDS/AML: assess family history and germline status. RUNX1 encodes a core-binding factor transcription factor essential for hematopoiesis. Germline loss-of-function variants predispose to platelet dysfunction and myeloid malignancy. Nonhematopoietic tissue may be required for germline confirmation when blood or marrow is affected by a neoplasm. MDS or AML in a patient with longstanding familial thrombocytopenia or platelet dysfunction. Familial Chordoma TBXT Autosomal dominant in reported families Often presents in adulthood, but age varies. Tumors arise along the axial skeleton, particularly the sacrum and skull base. Family history of chordoma may be present. Chordoma in multiple family members or multiple primary chordomas in a compatible setting. Confirm a germline TBXT duplication or other pathogenic variant when indicated. Classify the tumor by site and histologic subtype. Conventional chordoma shows cords and lobules of cells in abundant myxoid matrix. Physaliphorous cells have bubbly, vacuolated cytoplasm. Dedifferentiated chordoma shows an abrupt transition to a high-grade sarcoma. Brachyury (TBXT) is a highly useful nuclear marker for chordoma. Cytokeratins and EMA are typically positive. Chondrosarcoma: usually lacks nuclear brachyury and epithelial marker expression. Metastatic carcinoma: correlate with clinical history and brachyury expression. Chordoid meningioma at the skull base: use anatomic, morphologic, and immunophenotypic context. TBXT encodes the brachyury transcription factor involved in notochord development. Germline TBXT duplication is associated with familial chordoma in a subset of families. Chordoma in a patient with a first-degree relative with chordoma. Axial chordoma with a familial pattern, particularly at the skull base or sacrum. Hyperparathyroidism–Jaw Tumor Syndrome CDC73 Parathyroid glands and jaw are characteristic sites; renal and uterine lesions may also occur. Presentation may include primary hyperparathyroidism, jaw ossifying fibroma, or both. Primary hyperparathyroidism with an ossifying fibroma of the jaw or a compatible family history. Parathyroid carcinoma or atypical parathyroid tumor should prompt consideration of CDC73-related disease. Confirm a germline pathogenic CDC73 variant. Parathyroid tumors may show atypical features or carcinoma, including invasive growth. Jaw lesions are ossifying fibromas rather than brown tumors of hyperparathyroidism. Renal lesions may include cysts and neoplasms. Loss of nuclear parafibromin expression in a parathyroid neoplasm supports CDC73 inactivation. Retained parafibromin does not completely exclude a pathogenic variant; interpret with internal controls. Sporadic parathyroid adenoma: consider CDC73 testing in young patients, atypical tumors, or carcinoma. Brown tumor: reactive giant-cell lesion associated with hyperparathyroidism, not a true ossifying fibroma. MEN1 and other hereditary hyperparathyroidism syndromes: compare associated tumors and molecular findings. CDC73 encodes parafibromin, a tumor suppressor component of the PAF1 transcription complex. Germline loss-of-function variants or deletions predispose to parathyroid and jaw tumors. Tumors often show a second hit and loss of parafibromin expression. Parathyroid carcinoma or atypical parathyroid tumor, especially in a young patient. Primary hyperparathyroidism with a jaw ossifying fibroma. Parafibromin loss in a parathyroid neoplasm. content: use client angiogenesis Angiogenesis and Hypoxia Signaling Cellular oxygen sensing regulates hypoxia-inducible factors (HIFs), which control angiogenic growth factors, erythropoiesis, vascular permeability, and metabolic adaptation. Under normoxic conditions, VHL targets hydroxylated HIF-α for ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation. VHL Heterozygous germline loss-of-function variants in the VHL tumor suppressor gene predispose to tumors. Somatic inactivation of the remaining allele produces HIF stabilization and a pseudohypoxic transcriptional program, including increased VEGFA, PDGFB, TGFA, and EPO expression. Von Hippel–Lindau syndrome Von Hippel–Lindau Syndrome Autosomal dominant; variable expression and age-dependent penetrance Retinal hemangioblastomas may appear in childhood or young adulthood (mean age approximately 25 years). CNS hemangioblastomas most often present in young adults (mean age approximately 29 years). Cerebellum, brainstem, spinal cord, and retina are characteristic sites for hemangioblastomas. Renal cysts and clear cell renal cell carcinomas are commonly bilateral and multifocal; mean age at RCC presentation is approximately 37 years. Pheochromocytomas typically arise in the adrenal medulla and often present around age 30 years. Pancreatic cysts and pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors may occur. Endolymphatic sac tumors may cause hearing loss, tinnitus, or vertigo. CNS or retinal capillary hemangioblastoma together with a characteristic extraneural VHL-associated tumor, or a pertinent family history. Typical associated lesions include clear cell RCC, pheochromocytoma, pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor, and endolymphatic sac tumor. Multifocal or bilateral clear cell RCC, especially in a young patient, should prompt evaluation for VHL. Germline pathogenic VHL variant testing is strongly recommended to confirm the diagnosis and guide family assessment. A negative family history does not exclude VHL. Hemangioblastoma contains a dense capillary network admixed with lipid-rich stromal cells. VHL-associated clear cell RCC resembles sporadic clear cell RCC and may be multifocal. VHL-associated pheochromocytoma may show clear-cell change, a prominent vascular network, and thick vascular capsules. VHL-associated pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors may show clear-cell change and may be multifocal. Pancreatic islet dysplasia and small neuroendocrine proliferations may accompany pancreatic cystic disease. Endolymphatic sac tumors may extend into and destroy the temporal bone. Clear cell RCC commonly shows diffuse membranous CAIX expression; this supports the clear-cell phenotype but is not specific for VHL syndrome. VHL-associated pheochromocytomas may express membranous CAIX and α-inhibin; neither marker is independently diagnostic. VHL-associated pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors may express α-inhibin and/or membranous CAIX. Use standard lineage-specific markers to classify each individual tumor; no single immunostain establishes germline VHL disease. Sporadic clear cell RCC: bilateral or multifocal tumors, young age, and associated VHL-spectrum lesions favor hereditary disease. SDH-deficient pheochromocytoma/paraganglioma: assess SDHB and SDHA; VHL-related tumors may show weak SDHB staining but retain SDHA. Other hereditary RCC syndromes, particularly FH tumor predisposition syndrome: FH-deficient RCC often shows prominent inclusion-like nucleoli and 2SC positivity. Choroid plexus papilloma: an endolymphatic sac tumor at the cerebellopontine angle may mimic it; temporal bone invasion favors endolymphatic sac tumor. VHL is located at chromosome 3p25.3 and encodes a component of an E3 ubiquitin ligase complex. Germline variants include missense, nonsense, frameshift, splice-site, and deletion variants. A somatic second hit inactivates the remaining functional allele in VHL-associated tumors. Loss of VHL function prevents normal HIF-1α and HIF-2α degradation, producing a pseudohypoxic state. Increased HIF signaling drives VEGFA and other target genes, accounting for marked tumor vascularity. VHL subtype correlations: type 1 has a lower risk of pheochromocytoma; types 2A, 2B, and 2C are associated with differing combinations of pheochromocytoma, hemangioblastoma, and RCC. Bilateral, multifocal clear cell RCC, particularly in a young adult. Retinal or CNS hemangioblastoma with a renal, pancreatic, adrenal, or endolymphatic sac lesion. Highly vascular CNS or retinal tumor with a family history of VHL-associated neoplasia. Multifocal pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors or pancreatic cystic disease in a patient with another VHL-associated tumor. krebs-cycle Krebs Cycle and Succinate Dehydrogenase The Krebs (citric acid) cycle generates reducing equivalents for oxidative phosphorylation and supplies intermediates for biosynthetic pathways. Succinate dehydrogenase (SDH, mitochondrial complex II) links the Krebs cycle to the electron transport chain. SDHA · SDHB · SDHC · SDHD · SDHAF2 Germline pathogenic variants in an SDH-complex gene, followed by loss of the remaining functional allele, cause SDH deficiency. Succinate accumulates and acts as an oncometabolite by inhibiting 2-oxoglutarate-dependent dioxygenases, altering hypoxia signaling and epigenetic regulation. SDHC promoter hypermethylation can underlie Carney triad. Hereditary pheochromocytoma–paraganglioma syndromes (SDHA, SDHB, SDHC, SDHD, SDHAF2) · Carney triad SDH-Deficient Tumor Syndromes SDHA, SDHB, SDHC, SDHD, SDHAF2 Usually autosomal dominant for germline SDH pathogenic variants; SDHD and SDHAF2 show parent-of-origin effects. Carney triad is generally non-hereditary and associated with mosaic SDHC epimutation. Pheochromocytomas and paragangliomas may present from childhood through adulthood; age and site vary by gene. Head and neck paragangliomas are often clinically silent and present as a mass. Abdominal extra-adrenal paragangliomas, particularly SDHB-associated tumors, may produce catecholamines and present with hypertension or related symptoms. SDHB-associated disease is enriched among metastatic paragangliomas. SDH-deficient GISTs are usually gastric and are an important cause of pediatric GIST. SDH-deficient RCC typically occurs in younger adults (median age approximately 35 years). Carney triad classically affects young women and combines gastric GIST, pulmonary chondroma, and paraganglioma. A pathogenic or likely pathogenic germline variant in SDHA, SDHB, SDHC, SDHD, or SDHAF2, or a demonstrated SDHC epimutation. More than one confirmed SDH-deficient neoplasm in an individual or family strongly supports syndromic disease. Loss of SDHB expression by immunohistochemistry, with intact internal positive controls, establishes an SDH-deficient phenotype. Loss of both SDHA and SDHB supports SDHA-associated deficiency; loss of SDHB with retained SDHA supports defects involving other SDH components. A single SDH-deficient neoplasm should prompt genetic counseling and evaluation for an underlying predisposition, unless biallelic somatic-only inactivation is demonstrated. Carney triad is used for syndromic disease without an identified germline SDH pathogenic variant; consider SDHC promoter hypermethylation. SDH-deficient paragangliomas may show well-formed nests of epithelioid cells with clear or vacuolated cytoplasm, particularly in the head and neck. SDH-deficient GISTs are commonly gastric, multifocal, multinodular, or plexiform. SDH-deficient GISTs often have epithelioid cells and may show a nested growth pattern. SDH-deficient RCC commonly shows bland eosinophilic cells in sheets or compact nests. Microcystic change is common in SDH-deficient RCC. Eosinophilic or pale bubbly cytoplasmic inclusions may be present in SDH-deficient RCC. High-grade SDH-deficient RCC may show nuclear atypia, necrosis, and sarcomatoid change. SDH-deficient pulmonary chondromas are bland and may show calcification without entrapped respiratory epithelium or other mesenchymal components. SDH-deficient pituitary neuroendocrine tumors are rare; reported tumors may be large and prolactin-producing. SDHB loss in tumor cells, with retained granular staining in endothelial cells or other non-neoplastic elements, is the key screening finding. SDHA loss accompanying SDHB loss supports SDHA-related deficiency. Retained SDHA with SDHB loss is typical of SDHB-, SDHC-, SDHD-, or SDHAF2-related deficiency. SDHB staining may be weak or difficult to interpret in some tumors; compare tumor staining with strong granular internal controls. SDH-deficient GISTs usually retain strong KIT and DOG1 expression. Some VHL-related pheochromocytomas show weak SDHB staining; do not diagnose SDH deficiency without careful internal-control assessment. CAIX and α-inhibin may support a pseudohypoxic PPGL phenotype but lack sufficient sensitivity and specificity to define SDH deficiency. VHL-associated pheochromocytoma: may show clear-cell change and weak SDHB staining, but usually retains SDHA; interpret SDHB against internal controls and correlate with molecular findings. PDGFRA-mutant GIST: often gastric and epithelioid, but KIT may be patchy or absent; SDH-deficient GIST typically retains strong KIT and DOG1. Renal oncocytoma: has finely granular, mitochondria-rich cytoplasm; SDH-deficient RCC often has flocculent eosinophilic cytoplasm, microcysts, or cytoplasmic inclusions. Clear cell RCC: markedly clear cytoplasm can reduce apparent SDHB staining; morphology and internal controls are essential. Carney complex: a distinct PRKAR1A-associated syndrome; it is not synonymous with Carney triad. SDHA and SDHB encode catalytic subunits; SDHC and SDHD encode membrane-anchoring subunits; SDHAF2 is required for SDHA flavination. Biallelic inactivation destabilizes complex II and leads to loss of SDHB protein. Succinate accumulation inhibits 2-oxoglutarate-dependent dioxygenases and promotes pseudohypoxic signaling and epigenetic dysregulation. Most syndromic tumors have a germline first hit and somatic inactivation of the second allele; somatic-only biallelic SDH alterations are rare. SDHC promoter hypermethylation is a common mechanism in Carney triad and may require a dedicated methylation assay. SDHB and SDHA immunohistochemistry can help assess the functional significance of SDH gene variants of uncertain significance. SDHB-associated paragangliomas have a higher metastatic risk than many other hereditary PPGLs. Paraganglioma with loss of SDHB, especially an abdominal or metastatic tumor. Multifocal or plexiform gastric GIST, particularly in a child or young adult. Eosinophilic renal carcinoma with cytoplasmic inclusions and loss of SDHB. Young woman with gastric GIST and pulmonary chondroma, with or without paraganglioma. Multiple SDH-deficient tumors in one patient, even when family history is negative. fumarate-metabolism Fumarate Metabolism Fumarate hydratase (FH) catalyzes the reversible conversion of fumarate to malate in the Krebs cycle. Loss of FH activity causes fumarate accumulation, which alters epigenetic regulation and impairs DNA repair. FH A heterozygous germline loss-of-function FH variant predisposes to tumor development. Somatic inactivation of the remaining allele causes fumarate accumulation and the oncometabolite phenotype. Biallelic somatic FH inactivation can also occur, particularly in uterine leiomyomas. Hereditary leiomyomatosis and renal cell carcinoma syndrome Hereditary Leiomyomatosis and Renal Cell Carcinoma Syndrome Autosomal dominant tumor predisposition; tumors show biallelic FH inactivation Cutaneous leiomyomas often begin in adulthood (mean age approximately 30 years) and increase in number and size with age. Cutaneous leiomyomas may be painful or sensitive to cold or light touch. Uterine leiomyomas are common in affected women and may cause symptoms or require surgery before age 35 years. FH-deficient RCC typically presents in adulthood (median age approximately 44 years). Skin, uterus, and kidney are the principal sites; pheochromocytoma and paraganglioma are uncommon associations. A germline pathogenic FH variant. Multiple histologically confirmed FH-deficient leiomyomas or FH-deficient RCCs. Two or more of the following: FH-deficient leiomyoma, FH-deficient RCC, or a first-degree relative with FH-deficient neoplasms. A single FH-deficient RCC should prompt consideration of germline testing because the proportion attributable to hereditary disease is substantial. Multiple cutaneous leiomyomas warrant genetic evaluation regardless of FH immunostaining. FH-deficient RCC is a distinct renal carcinoma entity and may show varied architectural patterns. FH-deficient uterine leiomyomas may show bizarre or symplastic nuclear atypia. Multinucleated tumor cells may be present in FH-deficient leiomyomas. Prominent eosinophilic nucleoli with perinucleolar halos are a useful morphologic clue. Staghorn-type vessels and stromal edema may be present in FH-deficient leiomyomas. Some FH-deficient cutaneous and uterine leiomyomas are morphologically indistinguishable from conventional leiomyomas. FH-deficient pheochromocytomas and paragangliomas may resemble their sporadic counterparts. Loss of FH expression in tumor cells, with retained staining in non-neoplastic internal controls, is highly specific but not fully sensitive. Aberrant 2-succinocysteine (2SC) positivity is a sensitive marker of fumarate accumulation. 2SC is less specific in renal carcinoma than in leiomyoma and pheochromocytoma/paraganglioma. FH and 2SC immunohistochemistry identify an FH-deficient phenotype but do not establish germline status. Conventional leiomyoma: may lack the characteristic nucleolar and vascular features; FH and 2SC staining can identify an FH-deficient subset. Leiomyosarcoma: atypia in FH-deficient leiomyoma does not by itself establish malignancy; assess mitotic activity, tumor cell necrosis, and other criteria. MET-associated hereditary papillary RCC: usually papillary/tubulopapillary; FH-deficient RCC may show prominent inclusion-like nucleoli and 2SC positivity. SDH-deficient RCC: often has eosinophilic cells, microcysts, and cytoplasmic inclusions; use SDHB/SDHA alongside FH/2SC. FH is located at chromosome 1q43 and encodes fumarate hydratase. Germline pathogenic variants include missense, nonsense, frameshift, splice-site, and deletion variants. Tumor development generally requires somatic inactivation of the remaining FH allele. Fumarate accumulation promotes epigenetic dysregulation and suppression of DNA repair. FH-deficient immunophenotype does not prove a germline variant; purely somatic biallelic inactivation occurs, particularly in uterine leiomyomas. Germline testing is important for risk assessment and family counseling. Multiple cutaneous piloleiomyomas, particularly when painful or cold-sensitive. Young woman with numerous or early-onset uterine leiomyomas. Renal carcinoma with prominent eosinophilic nucleoli and perinucleolar halos. FH loss and/or 2SC positivity in a renal tumor or smooth muscle neoplasm. metabolite-toxicity Metabolite Toxicity and Tyrosine Catabolism Tyrosine degradation prevents accumulation of reactive metabolites. Defects in the pathway can cause chronic hepatocellular injury, regenerative proliferation, fibrosis, and increased risk of hepatocellular carcinoma. FAH Biallelic germline loss-of-function variants in FAH impair fumarylacetoacetate degradation. Fumarylacetoacetate-related metabolites and succinylacetone accumulate, causing hepatocellular injury, cholestasis, fibrosis, and regenerative nodules. The cancer risk is largely a consequence of chronic metabolic liver injury. Hereditary tyrosinemia type 1 Hereditary Tyrosinemia Type 1 Autosomal recessive Usually presents in infancy, commonly within the first 2 years of life. Both sexes are affected. Liver disease predominates, with progressive hepatic dysfunction and cirrhosis. Renal tubular dysfunction is common; neurologic and cardiac manifestations may occur. Hepatocellular carcinoma is a major long-term concern, particularly with delayed or inadequate treatment. Abnormal liver and kidney function in an infant or child with suspected tyrosinemia. Elevated succinylacetone in blood and/or urine is the key biochemical diagnostic finding. Confirm with biallelic pathogenic FAH variants when molecular confirmation is indicated. Assess hepatic nodules for regenerative, dysplastic, and malignant transformation. Treatment with nitisinone should not be delayed while awaiting molecular results when the biochemical diagnosis is established. Untreated liver may show variable macrovesicular steatosis. Severe cholestasis may be present. Trabecular disarray and pseudoglandular formation may occur. Progressive perisinusoidal and septal fibrosis may lead to micronodular, macronodular, or mixed cirrhosis. Nodular lesions span macroregenerative nodules, dysplastic nodules, and hepatocellular carcinoma. HCC diagnosis requires accepted evidence of malignancy, including vascular or stromal invasion, true neocapsule formation, or significant architectural and cytologic atypia. Rare hepatoblastomas have been reported. Glutamine synthetase, glypican-3, and HSP70 may support the diagnosis of HCC in the appropriate morphologic context. No immunohistochemical marker establishes hereditary tyrosinemia type 1. Interpret immunostains together with reticulin, architecture, and evidence of invasion when evaluating well-differentiated hepatic nodules. Other causes of childhood cirrhosis and chronic liver injury: elevated succinylacetone is the key discriminator for tyrosinemia type 1. Regenerative or dysplastic nodules: distinguish from HCC by architecture, reticulin framework, cytologic atypia, and especially vascular or stromal invasion. Other pediatric hepatic malignancies, including hepatoblastoma: integrate age, morphology, immunophenotype, and clinical metabolic findings. FAH is located at chromosome 15q25.1 and encodes fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase. Disease results from homozygous or compound heterozygous germline inactivating variants, including missense, nonsense, frameshift, splice-site, and deletion variants. Deficient FAH activity causes accumulation of fumarylacetoacetate-related metabolites and succinylacetone. Succinylacetone can be measured in blood or urine and is the key biochemical diagnostic marker. FAH sequencing supports confirmation, family testing, and reproductive counseling; it is not a substitute for biochemical diagnosis. Infant or young child with chronic liver dysfunction, renal tubular abnormalities, and elevated succinylacetone. Cirrhotic liver with numerous regenerative and dysplastic nodules in a child with known tyrosinemia type 1. Hepatic nodule suspicious for HCC in a patient with delayed treatment or persistently abnormal AFP. History of hereditary tyrosinemia type 1 even after nitisinone therapy; HCC surveillance remains important. all PathologyGPS · Genetic Tumor Syndromes Oxidative Stress Response and Metabolism A practical diagnostic reference linking oxygen sensing, mitochondrial metabolism, and inherited metabolic disorders to their associated neoplasms. Use the pathology clues to recognize syndromic patterns, then review the relevant pathway, gene, and tumor phenotype. Highly vascular CNS or retinal hemangioblastoma A second VHL-associated tumor or family history supports the syndromic diagnosis. Paraganglioma with loss of SDHB SDH-deficient tumor syndrome Retained internal controls are essential; follow with SDHA and germline SDHx/SDHAF2 assessment. Gastric multifocal, multinodular, or plexiform GIST SDHB loss; KIT and DOG1 are usually strongly positive despite absence of KIT/PDGFRA driver variants. Eosinophilic RCC with cytoplasmic inclusions SDH-deficient RCC SDHB loss, often with SDHA retained; distinguish from oncocytoma and clear cell RCC. Multiple cutaneous leiomyomas or early, numerous uterine leiomyomas FH tumor predisposition syndrome Consider FH and 2SC immunohistochemistry and germline FH testing. RCC with prominent eosinophilic nucleoli and perinucleolar halos FH-deficient RCC / FH tumor predisposition syndrome FH loss and aberrant 2SC positivity support fumarate hydratase deficiency. Infant with liver dysfunction, renal tubular disease, and elevated succinylacetone Blood or urine succinylacetone is the key biochemical diagnostic marker. title: Protein Regulation
content: use client Ubiquitin signaling and deubiquitination BAP1 (3p21.1); interacting partners include ASXL1, ASXL2, FOXK1, FOXK2, HCFC1, and YY1 Ubiquitylation is the covalent attachment of ubiquitin to a target protein. Depending on the ubiquitin linkage and cellular context, this can direct proteins toward proteasomal degradation or alter their activity, localization, and interactions. Deubiquitinases remove ubiquitin and thereby edit or reverse these signals. BAP1 is a nuclear ubiquitin carboxyl-terminal hydrolase (deubiquitinase), not an enzyme that simply labels proteins for degradation. BAP1 has tumor-suppressive functions involving chromatin regulation, transcription, cell-cycle control, cellular differentiation, and the DNA damage response, including homologous recombination repair. Loss of BAP1 function commonly results from a truncating or splice-site variant, a deleterious missense variant affecting its deubiquitinase function, or tumor-acquired loss of the remaining wild-type allele. Nuclear localization and deubiquitinase activity are both required for tumor-suppressive function. BAP1-related tumor predisposition syndrome (BAP1-TPDS), an autosomal dominant cancer predisposition syndrome caused by a heterozygous constitutional pathogenic variant. The associated tumor spectrum includes BAP1-inactivated melanocytic tumors, uveal and cutaneous melanoma, pleural or peritoneal mesothelioma, clear cell renal cell carcinoma, and meningioma. Multiple BAP1-inactivated melanocytic tumors Multiple small, skin-colored to reddish-brown, dome-shaped papules beginning in adolescence or young adulthood are a useful cutaneous clue. Lesions may be numerous and can resemble Spitz or other melanocytic nevi. They are suggestive but not specific for BAP1-TPDS; correlate with personal and family history of uveal melanoma, mesothelioma, or renal cell carcinoma. BAP1-related tumor predisposition syndrome BAP1 Mesothelioma at an unusually young age, especially peritoneal Mesothelioma in a younger patient, without the usual male predominance, or arising in the peritoneum should raise consideration of BAP1-TPDS. BAP1 loss is common in sporadic mesothelioma as well, so tumor immunohistochemistry alone cannot establish hereditary disease. Uveal melanoma, particularly with a personal or family history of other BAP1-associated tumors Uveal melanoma may be the sentinel malignancy in a carrier. A history of multiple melanocytic skin tumors, mesothelioma, clear cell renal cell carcinoma, or meningioma strengthens the rationale for constitutional evaluation. BAP1 mutation in a uveal melanoma is not synonymous with a germline variant. Clear cell renal cell carcinoma with early onset or syndromic context Consider BAP1-TPDS in a patient with clear cell RCC at a young age, multiple primary tumors, or a family history that includes uveal melanoma, mesothelioma, or characteristic melanocytic tumors. The renal tumor morphology alone is not diagnostic of germline BAP1 disease. BAP1-deficient meningioma, especially in a young patient or with aggressive recurrence BAP1-mutant meningiomas are rare but have been associated with aggressive behavior and frequent recurrence. In a BAP1-deficient meningioma, particularly with young age or a personal/family history of other BAP1-associated tumors, consider genetic counseling and constitutional testing. Tumor BAP1 loss does not prove a germline variant. BAP1 nuclear loss by immunohistochemistry in any associated tumor Complete loss of tumor-cell nuclear staining, with retained nuclear staining in non-neoplastic internal controls, supports BAP1 inactivation in the tumor. This is a tumor-level finding: both sporadic tumors and tumors arising in BAP1-TPDS can show loss. Use age, tumor spectrum, family history, and constitutional testing to determine hereditary status. BAP1-related tumor predisposition syndrome (when constitutional variant is confirmed) BAP1-related tumor predisposition syndrome (BAP1-TPDS) BAP1 (3p21.1) Autosomal dominant predisposition caused by a heterozygous germline / constitutional pathogenic BAP1 variant. A tumor commonly acquires inactivation or loss of the remaining wild-type allele, consistent with a tumor-suppressor two-hit mechanism. Tumor-restricted BAP1 alterations are common in several sporadic cancers and must not be equated with inherited predisposition. Tumors often arise earlier than their sporadic counterparts; affected individuals may develop more than one primary malignancy. Characteristic cutaneous manifestation: multiple BAP1-inactivated melanocytic tumors, typically beginning in the second decade and presenting as subtle skin-colored to reddish-brown dome-shaped papules, often on sun-exposed skin. Major associated malignancies include uveal melanoma, cutaneous melanoma, pleural and peritoneal mesothelioma, and clear cell renal cell carcinoma. Mesothelioma in carriers tends to present at a younger age, lacks the usual male predominance, and is more often peritoneal than in the general mesothelioma population. Other reported tumors include meningioma, basal cell carcinoma, cholangiocarcinoma, and hepatocellular carcinoma. Associations with several other tumor types remain less certain. Penetrance is incomplete and individual cancer risk is not precisely established. UV exposure and asbestos exposure may modify melanoma and mesothelioma risk, respectively. Essential: demonstration of a germline / constitutional pathogenic or likely pathogenic BAP1 variant. Supportive: multiple BAP1-inactivated melanocytic tumors, or a personal/family history involving two or more characteristic tumor types, especially uveal melanoma, mesothelioma, cutaneous melanoma, and clear cell RCC. A BAP1-deficient tumor by immunohistochemistry or a BAP1 variant detected only in tumor tissue is not sufficient to diagnose BAP1-TPDS. Refer for genetic counseling and constitutional testing when the tumor type, age, multiplicity, or family history raises suspicion. Interpret variants of uncertain significance separately from pathogenic variants. BAP1-inactivated melanocytic tumors are often small, well-circumscribed, dome-shaped papules clinically; histologically they may show a combined melanocytic proliferation with conventional nevus-like and larger epithelioid / spitzoid-appearing components. The melanocytic lesions may contain large epithelioid melanocytes with abundant cytoplasm and prominent nuclei; morphology can overlap with Spitz-spectrum lesions and other melanocytic nevi. Mesothelioma, uveal melanoma, cutaneous melanoma, clear cell RCC, and meningioma generally resemble their respective sporadic counterparts. In most settings, the syndrome is recognized through the tumor pattern and molecular findings rather than a unique histologic appearance. BAP1-mutant meningiomas are rare and have been reported to show aggressive clinical behavior and frequent recurrence; the prognostic implications specifically for germline carriers remain uncertain. BAP1: complete loss of nuclear staining in tumor cells, with retained nuclear staining in endothelial cells, lymphocytes, stromal cells, or other non-neoplastic elements as internal positive controls, supports BAP1 inactivation. Retained BAP1 staining does not exclude every pathogenic BAP1 alteration; immunohistochemistry and genotyping are highly, but not perfectly, concordant. BAP1 nuclear loss identifies a BAP1-deficient tumor phenotype; it does not distinguish a somatic tumor event from a germline pathogenic variant. Interpret BAP1 immunohistochemistry in the context of tumor type and technical controls. Do not infer hereditary status from staining alone. Sporadic BAP1-deficient mesothelioma or melanoma: these commonly acquire somatic BAP1 alterations. Distinguish hereditary predisposition by constitutional testing and clinical/family history, not by tumor BAP1 loss alone. Spitz nevus / atypical Spitz tumor and other melanocytic nevi: BAP1-inactivated melanocytic tumors may have epithelioid or spitzoid morphology; correlate with BAP1 immunostaining and the clinical pattern of multiple lesions. Other hereditary melanoma syndromes: assess the full personal and family cancer spectrum and use an appropriately selected germline panel rather than assuming BAP1 from melanoma alone. Other hereditary renal cancer syndromes: clear cell RCC is not specific for BAP1-TPDS; age, multiplicity, associated tumors, and constitutional molecular findings guide classification. BAP1 is located at chromosome 3p21.1 and encodes a nuclear ubiquitin carboxyl-terminal hydrolase / deubiquitinase. Constitutional pathogenic variants are most often nonsense, frameshift, indel, or splice-site variants causing loss of function; deleterious missense variants affecting the ubiquitin hydrolase domain are also reported. Many missense variants remain variants of uncertain significance and require careful classification. Tumor inactivation commonly involves a constitutional pathogenic variant plus somatic loss or inactivation of the wild-type allele (two-hit tumor-suppressor mechanism). Somatic BAP1 mutation or deletion can also occur in tumors without a germline predisposition. BAP1 immunohistochemistry is a useful screening tool for tumor protein loss, but constitutional testing is required to establish BAP1-TPDS. Germline testing should include sequence analysis and, when indicated, deletion / duplication analysis. Most reported germline pathogenic variants are small sequence-level variants; large deletions and rearrangements are less common. A variant detected in tumor tissue should be evaluated in a non-neoplastic constitutional specimen when hereditary predisposition is suspected. Consider the possibility of mosaicism if clinical suspicion remains high despite a negative routine blood test; the supplied source does not define a specific mosaic phenotype or testing algorithm. Genetic Tumor Syndromes Protein Regulation A clinicopathologic guide to ubiquitin signaling and deubiquitination, focused on recognizing BAP1-deficient tumors and distinguishing tumor-restricted BAP1 inactivation from constitutional cancer predisposition. Pathway Overview Protein ubiquitylation and deubiquitination regulate protein stability, activity, localization, and molecular interactions. BAP1 is a deubiquitinase with tumor-suppressive functions; its role in this pathway is the removal and editing of ubiquitin signals, together with effects on chromatin and the DNA damage response. title: RNA Regulation
content: use client MicroRNA biogenesis and DICER1-mediated processing DICER1 MicroRNAs are 21–23-nucleotide noncoding RNAs that regulate gene expression after transcription. DICER1 cleaves hairpin-structured precursor microRNAs (pre-miRNAs) into mature 5′ and 3′ strands; one strand is incorporated into the RNA-induced silencing complex and guides sequence-specific repression of target mRNAs. DICER1-related tumors commonly follow a two-hit pattern: a constitutional loss-of-function variant is paired with a tumor-acquired missense variant affecting a metal-binding residue in the RNase IIIb domain. This selectively impairs production of 5p microRNAs, alters the 5p:3p microRNA balance, and derepresses target transcripts. The developmental or endocrine context influences which tissues develop lesions. DICER1-related tumor predisposition syndrome. Postzygotic mosaic RNase IIIb hotspot variants can produce a distinct, often multifocal or overgrowth-associated phenotype and should not be conflated with conventional heterozygous germline loss-of-function disease. Nuclear microprocessor complex DROSHA, DGCR8 DROSHA and DGCR8 form the nuclear microprocessor complex, which cleaves primary microRNAs (pri-miRNAs) to generate precursor microRNAs. The complex contains one DROSHA molecule and two DGCR8 molecules; DGCR8 binds and stabilizes the complex and helps position pri-miRNA for processing. Constitutional heterozygous pathogenic variants are associated with rare, gene-specific tumor predisposition phenotypes. Reported DROSHA variants are predominantly truncating and tumors may acquire a second hit. The reported DGCR8 p.Glu518Lys missense variant is associated with loss of the wild-type allele / chromosome 22q loss. The clinical spectrum and penetrance remain incompletely defined. DROSHA-related predisposition (reported pineoblastoma and Wilms tumor) and DGCR8-related predisposition (reported multinodular thyroid disease and schwannomas). Evidence is currently based on a limited number of families and cases. Pre-mRNA splicing SF3B2; MYT1 has been reported as a candidate gene The spliceosome removes introns from precursor messenger RNA and joins exons to produce mature mRNA. SF3B2 is a component of the U2 small nuclear ribonucleoprotein (snRNP) complex and contributes to spliceosome function. Heterozygous loss-of-function variants in SF3B2 have been reported in a subset of familial and sporadic Goldenhar syndrome / craniofacial microsomia. Most cases remain genetically unexplained; the phenotype is developmentally heterogeneous and cannot be reduced to a single molecular mechanism. Goldenhar syndrome (oculo-auriculo-vertebral spectrum / craniofacial microsomia). The source also lists MYT1 in the syndrome heading and reports it among candidate genes, but identifies SF3B2 loss of function as the more recently established association. Pleuropulmonary blastoma or childhood lung cysts A cystic pulmonary lesion in an infant or young child, particularly with a personal or family history of cystic nephroma, thyroid disease, or characteristic childhood tumors, should prompt consideration of DICER1. Type I PPB may progress to type II/III disease. DICER1-related tumor predisposition syndrome Pediatric cystic nephroma or anaplastic sarcoma of the kidney Cystic nephroma in a child, especially with lung cysts/PPB or other DICER1-associated lesions, is a strong syndromic clue. Progression to anaplastic sarcoma is a recognized pattern; assess for primitive/blastemal and sarcomatous components. Ovarian Sertoli–Leydig cell tumor In a child, adolescent, or young adult, an ovarian SLCT—particularly with androgenic manifestations, multinodular goiter, or a history of PPB—should trigger evaluation for DICER1. Gynandroblastoma-like and juvenile granulosa cell tumor-like areas have also been reported. Embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma of the uterine cervix Cervical ERMS in a young patient is an important DICER1-associated presentation. A botryoid or polypoid lesion should be interpreted in the clinical context, with attention to additional thyroid, ovarian, pulmonary, and renal findings. Pineoblastoma or Wilms tumor with a relevant family history Although these tumors have broad differential diagnoses, reported germline DROSHA-associated cases include pineoblastoma and Wilms tumor. A tumor-acquired second hit was identified in the analyzed DROSHA-associated tumors; consider constitutional testing in an appropriate clinical setting. DROSHA-related microprocessor predisposition DROSHA Multinodular thyroid disease with schwannomas The combination of familial euthyroid multinodular goiter / thyroid neoplasia and multiple schwannomas is a distinctive reported clue for the DGCR8 p.Glu518Lys-associated phenotype. The evidence remains limited; do not generalize this association to all thyroid nodules or schwannomas. DGCR8-related microprocessor predisposition DGCR8 Epibulbar dermoid with preauricular tags and hemifacial asymmetry An inferotemporal limbal dermoid or dermolipoma, especially with mandibular/hemifacial hypoplasia, accessory tragi, and vertebral anomalies, supports Goldenhar syndrome / craniofacial microsomia. The phenotype is usually unilateral but can be bilateral. Goldenhar syndrome SF3B2; other genetic and non-genetic contributors Complex epibulbar choristoma with craniofacial and auricular anomalies A choristoma containing lacrimal gland, cartilage, and smooth muscle should prompt careful examination for associated ocular, auricular, mandibular, and vertebral anomalies. The diagnosis is primarily clinical; genetic testing is not required in most cases. Goldenhar syndrome / oculo-auriculo-vertebral spectrum SF3B2 in a subset; etiology often unresolved DICER1 (14q32) Autosomal dominant predisposition due to a heterozygous constitutional pathogenic variant, most often loss of function. Approximately 84% of germline pathogenic variants in the cited series were inherited. Postzygotic mosaic DICER1 variants are a separate mechanism and may present with single or multiple tumors depending on variant type, tissue distribution, and developmental timing. Most manifestations arise in childhood or early adulthood; thyroid and female genital tract lesions may present later. Hallmark lesion: pleuropulmonary blastoma (PPB). Other major tumors include ovarian Sertoli–Leydig cell tumor, cervical embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma, pediatric cystic nephroma, pineoblastoma, pituitary blastoma, and primary intracranial sarcoma. Thyroid nodules and multinodular goiter are common; differentiated thyroid carcinoma is a recognized association. Multiple primary tumors and bilateral disease in paired organs can occur. Pituitary blastoma may present with infantile Cushing disease. Ovarian SLCT may present with androgen excess. Macrocephaly and subtle ocular, renal, or dental findings have been reported, usually without major functional impairment. Mosaic RNase IIIb hotspot variants may be associated with overgrowth and developmental delay; this phenotype is not a separate, reliably distinct syndrome. Essential: demonstrate a germline / constitutional pathogenic DICER1 variant. Supportive: personal or family history of characteristic DICER1-associated lesions, particularly PPB, pediatric cystic nephroma, ovarian SLCT, cervical ERMS, or other characteristic embryonal tumors. A typical tumor-acquired RNase IIIb hotspot variant strongly supports DICER1-driven tumor biology, but tumor sequencing alone does not establish a germline predisposition syndrome. A negative blood test does not necessarily exclude low-level or tissue-restricted mosaicism; testing an affected tissue may be informative when clinical suspicion remains high. PPB spans cystic type I, mixed cystic/solid type II, and predominantly solid type III; progression is associated with increasing primitive and sarcomatous components. Across several associated tumors, primitive blastemal or embryonal morphology may recapitulate an immature developmental stage of the involved organ. Some tumors show multiple divergent components, including blastemal, rhabdomyosarcomatous, fibrosarcomatous, cartilaginous, or neuroectodermal elements. Cystic or mixed cystic-solid architecture occurs in PPB, cystic nephroma, thyroid lesions, nasal chondromesenchymal hamartoma, and several gynecologic tumors. Progression from a cystic or hyperplastic precursor to an aggressive sarcoma is best established in PPB and cystic nephroma / anaplastic sarcoma of the kidney; anaplasia may correlate with TP53 alteration. Individual lesions may be morphologically indistinguishable from their sporadic counterparts; the pattern across organs and age is often more informative than a single histologic feature. There is no single immunohistochemical stain that establishes DICER1-related tumor predisposition. Interpret immunophenotype according to the specific tumor type; use morphology, site, age, multiplicity, and molecular findings to recognize a possible syndromic pattern. DICER1 immunostaining, where performed, should not be used as a substitute for constitutional molecular testing. Sporadic counterparts of each tumor: the histology of an individual DICER1-associated lesion may be indistinguishable; multiplicity, age, and cross-organ history are key. Other hereditary PPB / pediatric tumor predisposition syndromes: distinguish by the full tumor spectrum and germline findings rather than by lung cysts alone. Non-syndromic multinodular goiter or sporadic ovarian sex cord-stromal tumors: consider DICER1 when these occur at a young age or with characteristic additional lesions. Most constitutional pathogenic variants are nonsense or frameshift loss-of-function variants distributed across DICER1; larger deletions and pathogenic missense variants are less common. The typical tumor second hit is a missense variant affecting one of the metal-binding residues in the RNase IIIb domain; it is usually in trans to the constitutional loss-of-function variant. RNase IIIb mutants selectively impair generation of 5p microRNAs, causing an altered 5p:3p microRNA ratio and derepression of target mRNAs. Postzygotic mosaic RNase IIIb hotspot variants may be present in multiple tissues and are biologically distinct from the usual constitutional loss-of-function-plus-tumor second-hit pattern. Use germline testing that covers sequence variants and copy-number changes; tumor panels focused on RNase IIIb hotspots may miss constitutional variants elsewhere in the gene. Methylation profiling can identify a shared signature in some DICER1-associated high-grade malignancies, but it does not replace germline testing. Tumor anaplasia may be associated with TP53 variants or loss; TP53 alteration is a progression-related finding, not the defining DICER1 syndrome event. DROSHA- and DGCR8-related microprocessor tumor predisposition DROSHA (5p13.3); DGCR8 (22q11.21) Rare autosomal dominant predisposition associated with heterozygous constitutional pathogenic variants. Penetrance and the full tumor spectrum are not established. Do not infer a hereditary syndrome from a tumor-only alteration or from 22q11 deletion alone. DROSHA: reported constitutional variants in children with pineoblastoma and, less often, Wilms tumor. DGCR8: the reported p.Glu518Lys variant has been associated with familial euthyroid multinodular goiter, thyroid hyperplasia / neoplasia, and multiple schwannomas. A papillary thyroid carcinoma has been reported in a DGCR8-associated family; isolated reports of other lesions remain of uncertain significance. The number of reported families is small, and formal penetrance estimates and outcome data are unavailable. Essential: demonstrate a constitutional pathogenic variant in DROSHA or DGCR8. Supportive: pineoblastoma or Wilms tumor in a patient with a relevant DROSHA variant; or the combination of familial multinodular thyroid disease and schwannomas with the reported DGCR8 p.Glu518Lys variant. Tumor histology alone does not distinguish these syndromic tumors from sporadic counterparts. A tumor-acquired DROSHA or DGCR8 alteration, including chromosome 22q loss, is not by itself evidence of a constitutional predisposition. Reported DROSHA- and DGCR8-associated tumors do not show a distinctive histologic phenotype compared with their sporadic counterparts. Pineoblastoma, Wilms tumor, thyroid nodular hyperplasia / carcinoma, and schwannoma should be classified using their standard site-specific morphologic criteria. No validated immunohistochemical pattern is established for identifying DROSHA- or DGCR8-related predisposition. Routine tumor immunophenotyping does not determine whether a DROSHA or DGCR8 variant is constitutional. Sporadic pineoblastoma and Wilms tumor: consider DROSHA only when age, family history, or constitutional testing supports it. NF2-related or other schwannomatosis syndromes: multiple schwannomas require evaluation of the broader clinical and molecular differential; DGCR8 is a rare reported association. Common multinodular goiter and sporadic thyroid carcinoma: the combination with schwannomas and the specific DGCR8 variant is more informative than thyroid morphology alone. 22q11.2 deletion syndrome: deletion may include DGCR8 and LZTR1, but available data are insufficient to define a general cancer risk attributable to DGCR8 haploinsufficiency. DROSHA-associated constitutional variants reported to date are predominantly truncating (nonsense or frameshift) variants; tumor-acquired second hits have been detected in analyzed cases. The reported DGCR8 predisposition variant is NM_022720.7:c.1552G>A, p.(Glu518Lys), located in the double-stranded RNA-binding domain. DGCR8 p.Glu518Lys-associated tumors have shown loss of the wild-type allele, often with loss of the other copy of chromosome 22q. The same DGCR8 p.Glu518Lys alteration has also been reported somatically in Wilms tumors and a small number of thyroid cancers; constitutional testing is needed to establish inherited predisposition. Consider constitutional testing when the phenotype is suggestive. Current evidence does not support broad syndrome attribution based solely on a tumor variant or an incidental 22q11 deletion. Goldenhar syndrome (oculo-auriculo-vertebral spectrum) Pre-mRNA splicing and craniofacial development SF3B2; MYT1 is listed among candidate genes Usually sporadic and genetically unexplained. Familial cases may show autosomal dominant inheritance with variable expressivity. Heterozygous SF3B2 loss-of-function variants have been identified in a subset of familial cases and a smaller proportion of sporadic cases; this does not explain most patients. Congenital craniofacial microsomia involving structures derived from the first and second branchial arches. Classic pattern: mandibular or hemifacial hypoplasia, ocular and auricular malformations (including epibulbar dermoid and accessory tragus), and vertebral anomalies, especially cervical spine abnormalities. Usually unilateral (reported in approximately 70–90%); expression is variable. Ocular findings include limbal dermoid / dermolipoma, eyelid coloboma, microphthalmia, strabismus (including Duane syndrome), ptosis, and less commonly posterior segment abnormalities. Cardiac, genitourinary, and central nervous system anomalies may coexist. Most patients have normal intelligence and lifespan; airway, feeding, hearing, exposure keratopathy, and amblyopia are important early clinical concerns. The source describes essential clinical features as facial asymmetry with preauricular tags and an ocular finding such as epibulbar dermoid or eyelid coloboma. Diagnostic criteria remain debated; diagnosis is primarily clinical and genetic testing is not required in most cases. Assess the full craniofacial, ocular, auricular, vertebral, cardiac, renal, and neurologic phenotype. Epibulbar dermoid: dense subepithelial collagen resembling dermal collagen rather than normal corneal substantia propria. Dermal appendages, including pilosebaceous and apocrine / eccrine structures, may be present. Dermolipoma contains abundant mature adipose tissue. Complex choristoma may contain lacrimal gland tissue, cartilage, and smooth muscle; osseous choristoma is less common. The histology of the ocular choristoma is not independently diagnostic of Goldenhar syndrome; correlate with the craniofacial and auricular phenotype. No syndrome-specific immunohistochemical profile is established for Goldenhar syndrome or its epibulbar choristomas. Use immunohistochemistry only when needed to characterize an unusual component or exclude a separate neoplasm; routine choristoma diagnosis is morphologic. Isolated epibulbar dermoid / dermolipoma: distinguish syndromic disease by associated hemifacial, auricular, and vertebral anomalies. Other craniofacial microsomia / oculo-auriculo-vertebral spectrum presentations: terminology overlaps; phenotype is variable and diagnostic boundaries are not uniform. Encephalocraniocutaneous lipomatosis and linear nevus sebaceous syndrome: consider when additional cutaneous, ocular, or neurologic findings extend beyond the typical Goldenhar pattern. Heterozygous loss-of-function variants in SF3B2 (11q13.1), a U2 snRNP / spliceosome component, have been reported in approximately 25% of familial cases and 3% of sporadic cases in a large cohort. Inheritance in SF3B2-associated families is autosomal dominant with inter- and intrafamilial variable expressivity. Other reported findings include copy-number variants (including 22q11.2 deletions and 14q22.3 duplications involving OTX2) and candidate-gene variants; many are not diagnostic. MYT1 has been reported among candidate genes, but the available evidence in this source does not establish it as the principal molecular cause. Genetic testing is not required for clinical diagnosis, and a negative result does not exclude the syndrome. Genetic Tumor Syndromes RNA Regulation A clinicopathologic guide to microRNA processing and pre-mRNA splicing, connecting characteristic tumor patterns and developmental phenotypes with the relevant constitutional and somatic molecular mechanisms. Pathway Overview RNA regulation controls gene expression through post-transcriptional silencing and transcript processing. MicroRNA biogenesis involves sequential nuclear and cytoplasmic cleavage steps, whereas pre-mRNA splicing removes introns and joins exons. Constitutional variants, postzygotic mosaicism, and tumor-restricted second hits have different implications and should be distinguished during molecular workup.
