title: Telomere Maintenance
content: use client Telomerase biogenesis and telomere elongation DKC1, TERT, TERC, NOP10, NHP2, NAF1, PARN, WRAP53, ZCCHC8 Maintains chromosome-end length by adding TTAGGG repeats to telomeric DNA. Telomerase contains a catalytic reverse-transcriptase subunit (TERT) and an RNA template (TERC), with accessory proteins required for assembly, stability, trafficking, and activity. Germline pathogenic variants impair telomerase assembly, activity, or maintenance and cause age-inappropriate telomere shortening. Inheritance is gene-dependent and may be X-linked, autosomal dominant, or autosomal recessive; de novo variants also occur. Dyskeratosis congenita and the broader telomere biology disorder spectrum, including severe phenotypes such as Hoyeraal–Hreidarsson syndrome. Shelterin-mediated telomere protection TINF2, POT1, ACD (TPP1), TERF2IP Shelterin binds telomeric DNA, protects chromosome ends from being recognized as DNA breaks, regulates telomerase access, and prevents inappropriate end-to-end chromosome fusion and DNA-damage signaling. Pathogenic variants disrupt telomere capping or regulation. TINF2 and other telomere biology genes can cause short-telomere syndromes, whereas inherited POT1, ACD, TERF2IP, and TERT promoter alterations have been implicated in melanoma and other tumor predisposition. The precise oncogenic mechanism remains incompletely defined. Dyskeratosis congenita/telomere biology disorders and POT1- and shelterin-related tumor predisposition syndrome. CST complex, telomere replication, and end processing CTC1, STN1 (OBFC1), RTEL1 Coordinates telomere replication, protects and processes telomeric DNA, and supports appropriate telomerase recruitment and completion of chromosome-end replication. Germline defects can impair telomere replication or protection, producing critically short telomeres and multisystem telomere biology disorders. Biallelic CTC1 variants are a major cause of Coats plus syndrome. Dyskeratosis congenita spectrum, including Coats plus syndrome and other severe telomere biology disorder phenotypes. Dyskeratosis congenita and telomere biology disorders Telomerase, shelterin, and telomere replication DKC1, TERT, TERC, TINF2, NOP10, NHP2, ACD, POT1, CTC1, STN1, WRAP53, RTEL1, PARN, NAF1, ZCCHC8, and other telomere biology genes Genetically heterogeneous: X-linked recessive (classically DKC1), autosomal dominant (including TERT, TERC, and TINF2), autosomal recessive (including CTC1, NOP10, NHP2, WRAP53, and RTEL1), and occasionally de novo. A single inheritance pattern should not be assumed across the syndrome spectrum. Classic mucocutaneous triad: oral leukoplakia (often on the tongue), nail dystrophy, and reticular or lace-like skin hyperpigmentation. Nail changes often begin in childhood, typically between 5 and 13 years; bone marrow failure commonly emerges during the second decade but age and severity vary. Additional complications include myelodysplastic syndrome, acute myeloid leukemia, head-and-neck/upper aerodigestive squamous cell carcinoma, pulmonary fibrosis, and liver disease. Some individuals present with only one component, such as familial pulmonary fibrosis or unexplained marrow failure, without the complete mucocutaneous triad. Severe phenotypes may include Hoyeraal–Hreidarsson syndrome or Revesz syndrome; Coats plus syndrome is associated particularly with biallelic CTC1 variants and may include bilateral retinal Coats disease, intracranial calcifications, leukodystrophy, gastrointestinal bleeding, and poor bone healing. Demonstration of age-adjusted short telomeres in peripheral blood leukocytes; flow-FISH is a commonly used clinical method, with very short telomeres (often below the first percentile) strongly supportive. Compatible clinical findings, particularly the mucocutaneous triad, bone marrow failure, pulmonary fibrosis, or a characteristic severe childhood phenotype. A pathogenic germline variant in a telomere biology gene provides molecular confirmation and helps establish inheritance and family risk. Absence of the full classic triad does not exclude a telomere biology disorder; clinical expression is variable and may be age-dependent. Cutaneous biopsies may show epidermal atrophy, dermal telangiectasia, and pigment incontinence; these findings are nonspecific. Associated MDS/AML and solid tumors are generally morphologically similar to their sporadic counterparts; the syndromic context, rather than a unique tumor pattern, is the diagnostic clue. In a patient with marrow failure or myeloid neoplasia, integrate the hematologic findings with mucocutaneous changes, pulmonary/liver disease, and family history. No tumor immunohistochemical profile is diagnostic of dyskeratosis congenita or a telomere biology disorder. IHC is selected according to the specific neoplasm; it does not substitute for telomere-length assessment or germline testing. Acquired aplastic anemia and sporadic MDS: distinguish using age, physical findings, family history, telomere length, and germline evaluation. Fanconi anemia: may also present with childhood marrow failure and congenital findings, but is caused by defects in the Fanconi anemia DNA interstrand crosslink repair pathway; chromosome-breakage testing can help distinguish it. Other inherited marrow-failure syndromes: use the associated phenotype and targeted germline testing rather than relying on marrow morphology alone. Coats plus syndrome versus isolated Coats disease: bilateral retinal disease with intracranial calcifications, leukodystrophy, marrow failure, or gastrointestinal vascular manifestations should prompt evaluation for CTC1-related disease. Measure telomere length in peripheral blood leukocyte subsets; age-adjusted flow-FISH is a key diagnostic assay. Very short telomeres support the diagnosis but do not identify the causal gene. Use germline sequencing with deletion/duplication analysis across telomere biology genes; the panel should cover the clinically relevant gene spectrum rather than only DKC1 and TERT. Interpret variants according to gene-specific inheritance: for example, DKC1 is classically X-linked, while TERT/TERC/TINF2 may be autosomal dominant and CTC1/RTEL1 and several telomerase accessory genes may be autosomal recessive. Distinguish constitutional germline variants from acquired somatic variants in hematopoietic cells; when a blood-derived result is ambiguous, consider confirmation in an appropriate nonhematopoietic tissue. A pathogenic variant is not required to recognize a strongly supported clinical/telomere-length phenotype; conversely, a variant of uncertain significance alone does not establish the syndrome. POT1- and shelterin-related tumor predisposition syndrome POT1, ACD (TPP1), TERF2IP, and the TERT promoter Cancer predisposition is associated with inherited germline pathogenic variants. POT1-associated families are generally evaluated as an autosomal dominant predisposition pattern; gene-specific penetrance and evidence strength vary. Melanoma-prone families with earlier-than-usual onset and/or multiple affected relatives are an important clinical setting. POT1 pathogenic variants have also been associated with hematologic malignancies, cardiac angiosarcoma, and brain tumors. Some TERT promoter variant carriers have presented with advanced melanoma in their twenties, but the clinical course is not sufficiently defined to predict behavior in an individual patient. There is currently no established evidence that these variants specifically predispose to acral or mucosal melanoma or to melanocytic tumors at other anatomic sites. Identification of a pathogenic germline variant in POT1, ACD, TERF2IP, or the TERT promoter in an appropriate clinical/family context. A personal or family history of melanoma supports the interpretation but is not by itself diagnostic. Tumor morphology is not sufficiently distinctive to establish this syndrome; genetic confirmation is central. Most reported melanomas resemble their sporadic counterparts. A spitzoid pattern has been suggested in some melanomas from POT1 variant carriers, but available data are limited and this morphology is not a diagnostic criterion. No characteristic histologic pattern has been established for the associated hematologic malignancies, cardiac angiosarcomas, or brain tumors. No validated IHC profile establishes POT1-, ACD-, TERF2IP-, or TERT promoter–related germline predisposition. Use lineage-specific IHC to classify the tumor; do not infer a germline shelterin alteration from tumor IHC. CDKN2A-associated familial melanoma: both may present with melanoma-prone families; distinguish by germline testing and the broader family/tumor spectrum. BAP1 tumor predisposition syndrome: consider when melanocytic tumors coexist with BAP1-inactivated melanocytic tumors, uveal melanoma, mesothelioma, or renal cell carcinoma; confirm with germline BAP1 testing. Sporadic or UV-associated familial clustering: UV exposure and common melanoma risk factors may contribute; family history alone does not identify the causal gene. Other hereditary melanoma genes: use a multigene germline panel when the phenotype does not point reliably to one gene. Confirm a pathogenic germline variant in POT1, ACD, or TERF2IP, or a pathogenic TERT promoter variant using constitutional DNA and an appropriately validated assay. Distinguish germline findings from somatic tumor alterations. A tumor-only POT1 or TERT alteration does not establish inherited predisposition. TERT promoter variants affect transcriptional regulation rather than encoding a telomerase protein; do not classify them as coding loss-of-function variants. The mechanism linking shelterin disruption or elongated telomeres to melanoma remains incompletely understood; proposed mechanisms include altered senescence and abnormal DNA-damage signaling at telomere ends. Somatic BRAF V600E or other melanoma driver alterations may assist tumor characterization but do not establish a germline POT1/shelterin syndrome. MDS or AML with unexplained marrow failure, especially in a young patient Consider a telomere biology disorder when cytopenias coexist with nail dystrophy, oral leukoplakia, reticular pigmentation, pulmonary fibrosis, liver disease, or a family history of marrow failure or early cancers. Dyskeratosis congenita / telomere biology disorder DKC1, TERT, TERC, TINF2, CTC1, RTEL1, and others Head-and-neck or upper aerodigestive squamous cell carcinoma at an unusually young age The combination with mucocutaneous abnormalities or a history of marrow failure is more informative than tumor morphology alone. Telomere maintenance genes Familial pulmonary fibrosis or liver disease with otherwise unexplained cytopenias Telomere biology disorders may present without the classic mucocutaneous triad; consider age-adjusted leukocyte telomere-length testing and germline evaluation. Telomere biology disorder TERT, TERC, RTEL1, PARN, and other telomere genes Bilateral Coats disease with intracranial calcifications or leukodystrophy Poor bone healing, gastrointestinal bleeding, or marrow failure further supports a syndromic telomere disorder rather than isolated retinal Coats disease. Coats plus syndrome CTC1 (typically biallelic germline variants) Melanoma at a young age or multiple melanomas in a family Consider POT1/shelterin-related predisposition among the hereditary melanoma differential, particularly when there are associated hematologic malignancies, cardiac angiosarcoma, or brain tumors in the family. POT1- and shelterin-related tumor predisposition POT1, ACD, TERF2IP, TERT promoter Spitzoid melanoma in a patient with a melanoma-prone pedigree Spitzoid morphology has been reported in some POT1 carriers, but it is not specific and should trigger clinical/genetic correlation rather than a histologic diagnosis of the syndrome. POT1-related predisposition (consider) POT1 and other hereditary melanoma genes Genetic Tumor Syndromes Telomere Maintenance A clinicopathologic guide to inherited telomere disorders and shelterin-related tumor predisposition, linking tumor patterns and multisystem findings to telomere biology and germline testing. Pathway Overview Telomeres consist of tandem TTAGGG repeats and associated proteins at chromosome ends. They protect chromosomes from degradation, end-to-end fusion, and inappropriate DNA-damage responses. Telomeres shorten with cell division; telomerase counteracts this shortening, while shelterin and replication-associated complexes preserve telomere structure and integrity. title: Gu Genetic Tumor Syndromes
content: use client Von Hippel–Lindau Syndrome VHL Autosomal dominant | Renal, adrenal, pancreatic, CNS, and retinal lesions Often recognized in young or middle adulthood; manifestations may begin earlier. Renal findings include multiple bilateral cysts and an approximately 30% lifetime risk of renal cell carcinoma, usually clear cell type. Epididymal cystadenomas occur in up to 60% of affected men; bilateral lesions are highly characteristic. Associated findings include retinal and CNS hemangioblastomas, pheochromocytoma, pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors, and endolymphatic sac tumors. Type 1 is not associated with pheochromocytoma; type 2 includes pheochromocytoma and is subdivided by renal cancer risk. In an at-risk relative, one characteristic VHL-associated tumor is sufficient for clinical recognition. Without a positive family history, the presence of two characteristic tumors supports the diagnosis. A heterozygous germline pathogenic VHL variant establishes the molecular diagnosis when clinical findings are inconclusive. Bilateral or multifocal clear cell RCC at a young age, especially with renal cysts or other syndrome-associated lesions, should prompt evaluation. Renal cysts are lined by clear cells with low-grade nuclei; atypical cysts may show two to three epithelial layers and focal papillary tufting. RCC is usually clear cell type, often low nuclear grade, and may be multifocal and bilateral. Some tumors show tubulopapillary or branched tubular architecture resembling clear cell papillary renal cell tumor, but retain a clear cell RCC immunophenotype and 3p loss. Epididymal cystadenoma and pheochromocytoma are histologically similar to their sporadic counterparts. VHL-associated clear cell RCC typically shows diffuse CAIX and CD10, with negative or only focal CK7. A clear cell papillary-like pattern does not establish clear cell papillary renal cell tumor when the immunophenotype and molecular findings support clear cell RCC. Germline VHL pathogenic variants include deletions, truncating variants, and missense variants. Type 1 is more often associated with deletion or truncating variants; type 2 is more often associated with missense variants. Loss of chromosome 3p is characteristic of VHL-associated clear cell RCC and can be assessed by FISH or copy-number analysis. Tumor-only VHL sequencing cannot establish hereditary disease; compare with uninvolved tissue or blood through germline testing. Sporadic clear cell RCC Usually lacks the clinical pattern of early-onset, bilateral/multifocal renal tumors and other VHL-associated lesions; tumor VHL alterations alone do not prove germline disease. Clear cell papillary renal cell tumor Usually shows diffuse CK7 and lacks the typical diffuse CD10/CAIX pattern of VHL-associated clear cell RCC. Sporadic epididymal cystadenoma A unilateral lesion may be sporadic; bilateral epididymal cystadenomas strongly favor VHL. Do not infer VHL syndrome from a VHL alteration detected only in tumor tissue. Correlate renal morphology with immunophenotype and chromosome 3p status when a clear cell papillary-like pattern is present. Birt–Hogg–Dubé Syndrome FLCN Autosomal dominant | Skin, lung, and kidney Usually manifests after age 20; renal tumors occur at a mean age of approximately 45 years. Facial, neck, or scalp papules represent fibrofolliculomas, trichodiscomas, or acrochordons. Basal-predominant pulmonary cysts may be asymptomatic or present with spontaneous pneumothorax. Approximately 15–30% of patients develop renal tumors; lesions are often multiple and bilateral. Renal tumor burden may range from a single lesion to numerous tumors. A characteristic combination of facial/neck papules, pulmonary cysts, and renal tumors should raise strong suspicion. One or more of the following are supportive: characteristic skin papules, lung cysts, hybrid oncocytic/chromophobe renal tumor, or a pathogenic FLCN variant. Germline FLCN testing is used to confirm the diagnosis and guide family counseling. Multifocal or bilateral oncocytic renal neoplasms, particularly with pulmonary cysts or characteristic skin lesions, warrant evaluation. Renal tumors show a spectrum of oncocytic and chromophobe differentiation. Hybrid oncocytic/chromophobe tumors contain intermixed oncocytoma-like cells and chromophobe cells within the same nests. Chromophobe-like cells may have pale or clear cytoplasm, crisp cell borders, perinuclear halos, and round dark nuclei. Tumors are generally well circumscribed, unencapsulated, and composed of solid, nested, alveolar, or sheet-like areas. Oncocytoma-like tumors and clear cell RCC may also occur. PAX8 is positive in renal epithelial tumors. KIT is patchy in hybrid tumors but typically diffuse in oncocytoma. CK7 preferentially highlights clear/chromophobe-like cells and is often absent in oncocytic cells. Ki-67 is usually low; p53 is limited to scattered nuclei. A heterozygous germline pathogenic FLCN variant confirms the syndrome. FLCN alterations include insertions, deletions, and nonsense variants that can truncate folliculin. Copy-neutral loss of heterozygosity/uniparental disomy is a common secondary event in BHD-associated renal tumors. Sporadic renal oncocytoma Usually solitary; multifocal/bilateral oncocytic tumors and hybrid morphology should prompt assessment for BHD. Chromophobe RCC May be morphologically indistinguishable from the chromophobe component of BHD-associated tumors; clinical and germline context is decisive. Clear cell RCC Can occur in BHD but should not be assumed to represent the characteristic hybrid oncocytic/chromophobe phenotype. The renal morphology is heterogeneous; not every BHD-associated tumor is a hybrid tumor. A negative or subtle skin phenotype does not exclude BHD, particularly when pulmonary and renal findings are present. Hereditary Papillary Renal Carcinoma MET Autosomal dominant | Bilateral, multifocal papillary renal tumors Presents with multiple, often bilateral renal cortical tumors. A family history of renal cancer is characteristic, although some relatives may be asymptomatic. No consistent extrarenal tumor spectrum is established. Suspect the syndrome when multiple family members have low-grade papillary RCC. An individual with bilateral, multifocal, low-grade papillary RCC also warrants evaluation. A germline pathogenic MET variant confirms hereditary papillary renal carcinoma. Most tumors show conventional low-grade papillary RCC morphology. Papillae are lined by a single layer of tumor cells with scant pale cytoplasm. Psammoma bodies and hemosiderin deposition are frequent. Papillary adenomas may coexist with invasive papillary RCC. The histologic phenotype is that of conventional papillary RCC; no syndrome-specific immunohistochemical profile is established. Germline missense variants in MET on chromosome 7q31 cause constitutive activation of the MET receptor tyrosine kinase. Tumor MET alterations alone do not establish a germline syndrome; confirmation requires germline testing. Sporadic papillary RCC Usually lacks the family history or bilateral/multifocal pattern; most papillary RCCs overall are sporadic. Other hereditary renal tumor syndromes BHD, VHL, FH-deficient RCC, and SDH-deficient RCC have different morphologic, immunophenotypic, and extrarenal clues. Do not equate a papillary RCC diagnosis with hereditary MET-associated disease. The combination of low-grade papillary morphology and bilateral/multifocal disease is more informative than papillary morphology alone. Hereditary Leiomyomatosis and Renal Cell Carcinoma Syndrome FH Autosomal dominant | Cutaneous and uterine leiomyomas; FH-deficient RCC Cutaneous leiomyomas often appear around age 30 and may be painful or sensitive to cold or light touch. Uterine leiomyomas are common in affected women and may cause symptoms or require surgery before age 35. FH-deficient RCC occurs in approximately 15% of patients, with a median age of onset around 44 years. Rare associations include pheochromocytoma/paraganglioma and testicular or ovarian Leydig cell tumors. A germline pathogenic FH variant establishes the syndrome. Multiple histologically confirmed FH-deficient leiomyomas or FH-deficient RCCs support the diagnosis. Two or more of the following support the diagnosis: FH-deficient leiomyoma, FH-deficient RCC, or a first-degree relative with FH-deficient neoplasia. An FH-deficient RCC, especially in a younger patient, should trigger genetic counseling and germline assessment. FH-deficient RCC is a distinct renal tumor entity and may show variable morphology. FH-deficient uterine leiomyomas may show symplastic nuclear atypia, multinucleation, prominent eosinophilic nucleoli, staghorn vessels, stromal edema, and eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusions. Some FH-deficient uterine leiomyomas and most cutaneous leiomyomas lack distinctive morphology and resemble conventional leiomyomas. Prominent inclusion-like nucleoli, sometimes with a perinucleolar halo, may be a clue in renal tumor cytology. Loss of FH staining with retained staining in internal non-neoplastic controls is highly specific but incompletely sensitive for FH deficiency. Positive 2-succinocysteine (2SC) staining is highly sensitive but less specific, particularly in renal carcinoma. Use both markers in difficult-to-classify renal carcinomas and selected leiomyomas; interpret staining with morphology and clinical context. Germline pathogenic FH variants establish hereditary disease. Biallelic FH inactivation causes fumarate accumulation and an oncometabolite-associated tumor phenotype. FH/2SC immunohistochemistry identifies FH-deficient tumors but cannot distinguish germline from purely somatic biallelic inactivation. Genetic testing is required to establish hereditary HLRCC syndrome and clarify variants of uncertain significance. Conventional leiomyoma May be morphologically identical; multiplicity, young age, associated RCC, and FH/2SC results guide further evaluation. Leiomyosarcoma Symplastic atypia or multinucleation in FH-deficient leiomyoma does not by itself establish malignant behavior; assess mitotic activity, tumor cell necrosis, and overall features. Sporadic FH-deficient neoplasm Somatic biallelic FH loss can occur, especially in uterine leiomyoma; germline testing is needed to diagnose the syndrome. Retained FH does not fully exclude FH deficiency; 2SC is more sensitive. A single FH-deficient uterine leiomyoma in an older patient is less predictive of germline disease than multiple lesions or early-onset disease. Do not diagnose HLRCC from FH/2SC immunohistochemistry alone. Succinate Dehydrogenase–Deficient Tumor Syndromes SDHA, SDHB, SDHC, SDHD, SDHAF2 Usually autosomal dominant | PPGL, GIST, renal carcinoma, and selected other tumors May present at a young age with multifocal or extra-adrenal paragangliomas; hereditary predisposition is common among adult PPGLs. Genitourinary sites include urinary bladder and periaortic sympathetic-chain paragangliomas. Other associated tumors include pheochromocytoma, gastric GIST, renal carcinoma, pituitary neuroendocrine tumor, and pulmonary chondroma. Pulmonary chondromas are particularly associated with Carney triad and are typically seen in young women. SDHB-associated disease has a higher morbidity and mortality than disease associated with other SDH genes. A pathogenic variant in an SDH gene establishes a hereditary SDH-associated predisposition. More than one SDH-deficient neoplasm in an individual or family is strongly supportive. Even a single SDH-deficient neoplasm is a strong indication for genetic counseling and testing. When no germline SDH variant is identified in a patient with syndromic SDH-deficient tumors, consider Carney triad; SDHC epimutation or low-level mosaicism may be present. SDH-deficient paragangliomas may show rounded nests of monotonous epithelioid cells with clear or vacuolated cytoplasm; morphology is variable and cannot replace immunohistochemistry. SDH-deficient GISTs are usually gastric and may be multilobulated or plexiform; lymph node metastases are more frequent than in conventional GIST. SDH-deficient renal carcinomas form a distinct renal tumor entity and may show variant morphology. Pulmonary chondromas are bland and often calcified; they lack entrapped respiratory epithelium and the mixed mesenchymal elements typical of hamartoma. Loss of granular cytoplasmic SDHB staining indicates SDH-complex deficiency; non-neoplastic endothelial cells and fibroblasts should retain staining as internal controls. Loss of SDHA in addition to SDHB supports SDHA-associated deficiency. Weak diffuse SDHB staining relative to strongly granular internal controls should be interpreted as loss. SDHB screening is recommended in pheochromocytomas and paragangliomas and should be considered in gastric GIST. Germline pathogenic variants may involve SDHA, SDHB, SDHC, SDHD, or SDHAF2; SDHC promoter epimutation and constitutional mosaicism are additional mechanisms. Biallelic SDH-complex inactivation causes accumulation of oncometabolites and pseudohypoxic signaling. SDHA/SDHB immunohistochemistry can help assess the pathogenicity of a variant of uncertain significance. A germline SDHA variant identified incidentally has low penetrance and requires careful clinical interpretation. Conventional paraganglioma May be morphologically identical; SDHB/SDHA immunohistochemistry and germline assessment identify SDH-deficient disease. Conventional gastric GIST SDH-deficient GIST is usually gastric, often plexiform/multilobulated, and has loss of SDHB; clinical context and molecular workup distinguish it. Pulmonary hamartoma Hamartoma contains entrapped respiratory epithelium and other mesenchymal elements; SDH-deficient chondroma is a relatively pure bland cartilage lesion. A normal-appearing or nonspecific morphology does not exclude SDH deficiency. Interpret SDHB only when internal non-neoplastic controls are positive. Do not use Carney–Stratakis syndrome or dyad as the preferred terminology; use Carney triad for the non-hereditary syndromic setting. BAP1 Tumor Predisposition Syndrome BAP1 Autosomal dominant | RCC, melanocytic tumors, mesothelioma, and melanoma Tumors often arise earlier than their sporadic counterparts; reported RCC age at onset ranges from 36 to 72 years, with a median around 47 years. Associated tumors include clear cell RCC, BAP1-inactivated melanocytic tumors, uveal and cutaneous melanoma, mesothelioma, basal cell carcinoma, meningioma, and cholangiocarcinoma. Multifocal clear cell RCC and atypical renal cysts have been reported. A heterozygous germline pathogenic BAP1 variant is required to establish the syndrome. Consider germline testing in patients with two or more associated tumors, or one associated tumor plus a first- or second-degree relative with an associated tumor. Loss of nuclear BAP1 expression in an associated tumor can help identify patients who warrant germline testing. There are no formal phenotypic diagnostic criteria; clinical suspicion should be based on the tumor spectrum and family history. Renal tumors are most commonly clear cell RCC, although non-clear cell subtypes have been reported. Multifocal clear cell RCC and atypical renal cysts may occur. The histology of BAP1-associated RCC may resemble sporadic RCC; morphology alone does not establish hereditary disease. Complete loss of nuclear BAP1 expression in tumor cells, with retained nuclear staining in non-neoplastic internal controls, supports BAP1 inactivation. BAP1 loss in tumor tissue is a screening clue, not proof of a germline variant. Germline heterozygous pathogenic BAP1 variant testing is required for syndrome confirmation. Tumor BAP1 loss reflects biallelic inactivation but may also occur in sporadic clear cell RCC. Tumor-only sequencing cannot distinguish somatic from germline BAP1 alteration. Sporadic BAP1-deficient clear cell RCC May show identical BAP1 loss; germline testing and personal/family tumor history distinguish inherited predisposition. Other hereditary clear cell RCC syndromes VHL and other renal cancer syndromes have different associated clinical findings and germline genes. BAP1-inactivated melanocytic tumor A cutaneous sentinel lesion can prompt evaluation, but germline testing is required to diagnose the syndrome. BAP1 loss by immunohistochemistry does not by itself diagnose BAP1 tumor predisposition syndrome. The penetrance and natural history remain incompletely defined. Hereditary Pheochromocytoma–Paraganglioma Syndromes RET, NF1, VHL, SDHx, MAX, TMEM127, FH, and other susceptibility genes Inherited PPGL predisposition | Adrenal medulla, sympathetic chain, and head and neck A substantial proportion of adult pheochromocytomas and paragangliomas are associated with germline pathogenic variants. Presentation may occur at a young age with multifocal, bilateral, or extra-adrenal tumors. Symptoms may include hypertension, tachycardia, sweating, anxiety, palpitations, and headache. Urinary bladder paraganglioma may cause micturition-associated hypertension, syncope, hematuria, or palpitations. Parasympathetic head and neck paragangliomas are usually nonsecretory. A personal or family history of PPGL or a recognized PPGL syndrome is an essential clinical clue. Morphologic and immunohistochemical features suggesting inherited disease should prompt germline evaluation. All patients with PPGL should be considered for germline testing in the context of clinical and pathologic findings. Multifocality, bilateral adrenal tumors, young age, extra-adrenal location, or an associated syndrome strengthens suspicion. Hereditary PPGLs are generally histologically similar to sporadic tumors. MEN2-associated pheochromocytomas may be multifocal and accompanied by adrenal medullary nodules/hyperplasia and hyaline globules. VHL-associated pheochromocytomas may show a thick vascular capsule, edematous stroma, and small-to-medium cells with clear or amphophilic cytoplasm. SDH-associated tumors may show rounded nests or pseudorosettes of monotonous epithelioid cells with vacuolated cytoplasm. NF1- and MAX-associated tumors may show a conventional or composite pattern. Tumor cells express chromogranin A, synaptophysin, INSM1, tyrosine hydroxylase, and dopamine beta-hydroxylase; keratin is usually negative. Sustentacular cells are highlighted by S100 and SOX10. Loss of SDHB supports SDH-complex deficiency; loss of SDHA in addition to SDHB supports SDHA-associated disease. CAIX may be positive in VHL-associated tumors; FH and 2SC can identify FH-deficient tumors. Susceptibility genes include RET, NF1, VHL, SDHA/B/C/D, SDHAF2, MAX, TMEM127, FH, and additional genes. Tumor immunohistochemistry can direct germline testing, but germline analysis is needed to establish inherited predisposition. Consider biochemical assessment of metanephrine, normetanephrine, and 3-methoxytyramine in the appropriate clinical setting. Sporadic pheochromocytoma/paraganglioma May be morphologically identical; young age, multifocality, family history, and pathway-specific IHC support hereditary evaluation. Metastatic neuroendocrine tumor Usually differs by site-specific clinical context and epithelial/neuroendocrine phenotype; correlate with adrenal/paraganglionic location and sustentacular network. SDH-deficient tumor syndrome Overlaps with hereditary PPGL; SDH-deficient tumors are a defined molecular subset and should be assessed with SDHB/SDHA IHC. No single histologic feature or biomarker reliably predicts metastatic behavior. Avoid fine-needle aspiration of suspected PPGL because of bleeding and catecholamine-related hypertensive crisis risk. Do not assume a negative family history excludes germline disease. Tuberous Sclerosis Complex TSC1, TSC2 Autosomal dominant, with frequent de novo cases | Multisystem hamartomatous disorder Neurologic and cardiac manifestations often appear in infancy or childhood; skin lesions may occur at any age. Renal involvement occurs in approximately 60–80% of patients and includes angiomyolipomas, cysts, and rarely renal malignancy. Renal angiomyolipomas are often multiple and bilateral and are more prevalent and clinically consequential in women. Young women may develop pulmonary lymphangioleiomyomatosis. TSC2-related disease often has more clinical manifestations than TSC1-related disease. A pathogenic TSC1 or TSC2 variant is independently diagnostic. Clinical diagnosis can be made with two major features or one major feature plus at least two minor features. Major features include hypomelanotic macules, angiofibromas/fibrous cephalic plaque, ungual fibromas, shagreen patch, retinal hamartomas, cortical dysplasia, subependymal nodules/giant cell astrocytoma, cardiac rhabdomyoma, lymphangioleiomyomatosis, and angiomyolipomas. Minor features include confetti skin lesions, dental enamel pits, intraoral fibromas, retinal achromic patch, multiple renal cysts, and nonrenal hamartomas. One major feature or at least two minor features suggests possible TSC. Renal angiomyolipoma is a PEComa composed of abnormal thick-walled vessels, smooth muscle cells, and adipose tissue. Epithelioid angiomyolipoma may mimic RCC and can show a predominantly epithelioid pattern. A range of renal carcinomas has been reported, including papillary, eosinophilic/cystic, oncocytic/chromophobe-like, and tumors with smooth muscle stroma. Renal cystic disease may be prominent, particularly with contiguous TSC2–PKD1 deletion. Epithelioid angiomyolipoma expresses melanocytic markers such as HMB45 and is typically negative for cytokeratin. Use epithelial and PEComa-directed markers to distinguish an epithelioid renal lesion from RCC. Pathogenic variants in TSC1 or TSC2 establish molecular diagnosis; a negative conventional test does not exclude TSC. TSC1/hamartin and TSC2/tuberin form a complex that suppresses mTOR signaling. Contiguous deletion involving TSC2 and PKD1 can produce a combined cystic renal phenotype. Sporadic angiomyolipoma May be solitary; multiple/bilateral angiomyolipomas with multisystem findings favor TSC. Renal cell carcinoma Epithelioid angiomyolipoma is HMB45-positive and cytokeratin-negative; RCC shows epithelial differentiation. Birt–Hogg–Dubé renal tumors BHD tumors are typically oncocytic/chromophobe-spectrum epithelial neoplasms, not PEComas. Morphologically similar renal tumors may occur sporadically; diagnose TSC by integrated clinicopathologic and genetic criteria. The absence of an identifiable TSC1/TSC2 variant does not exclude the syndrome. Lynch Syndrome MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2; EPCAM deletions Autosomal dominant | Upper urinary tract urothelial carcinoma and multisystem cancer predisposition Upper urinary tract urothelial carcinoma (renal pelvis or ureter) is the most characteristic genitourinary malignancy. Risk of upper tract urothelial carcinoma is substantially increased, particularly with MSH2 pathogenic variants. Affected patients may be younger and more often female than patients with sporadic upper tract urothelial carcinoma. Bladder urothelial carcinoma and prostate carcinoma have also been associated; renal cell carcinoma and testicular germ cell tumors are less established associations. Other common syndrome-associated sites include colorectum and endometrium. A germline pathogenic variant in MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, or PMS2, or an EPCAM deletion, establishes Lynch syndrome. Mismatch repair immunohistochemistry or microsatellite instability testing of upper tract urothelial carcinoma can identify candidates for germline evaluation. Clinical suspicion is strengthened by young age, personal/family history of Lynch-associated tumors, and mismatch repair deficiency. Muir–Torre syndrome is a Lynch syndrome phenotype that includes sebaceous neoplasms. Lynch-associated urothelial carcinomas generally resemble their sporadic counterparts. Tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes, inverted growth, a noninfiltrative stromal interface, limited nuclear pleomorphism, and lack of differentiation have been described but are neither sensitive nor specific. Morphology alone cannot reliably identify Lynch-associated urothelial carcinoma. Perform mismatch repair IHC for MLH1, PMS2, MSH2, and MSH6 in appropriate upper tract urothelial carcinomas. Loss of one or more mismatch repair proteins supports mismatch repair deficiency and should prompt appropriate molecular/genetic evaluation. Interpret loss patterns in the context of internal controls and the possibility of sporadic mechanisms. Germline pathogenic variants involve MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, or PMS2; EPCAM deletions can cause MSH2 silencing. Somatic loss of the second allele produces mismatch repair deficiency and microsatellite instability. Tumor mismatch repair deficiency or MSI-high status does not alone prove germline Lynch syndrome; germline testing is required. Sporadic mismatch repair-deficient urothelial carcinoma May show the same IHC/MSI phenotype; germline testing and clinical/family history distinguish Lynch syndrome. Mismatch repair-proficient sporadic urothelial carcinoma Retains mismatch repair protein expression and lacks the characteristic MMR-deficient phenotype. Muir–Torre syndrome A cutaneous sebaceous tumor phenotype within the Lynch syndrome spectrum, not a separate molecular syndrome. MMR deficiency in a tumor is a screening result, not a germline diagnosis. The described morphologic clues are not sufficiently sensitive or specific to replace MMR IHC. Hereditary Homologous Recombination Repair Gene Syndromes BRCA1, BRCA2, ATM, CHEK2 Germline DNA-repair predisposition | Prostate, urothelial, breast, ovarian, and other cancers There is no single distinctive phenotype; presentation depends on the tumor type and gene involved. BRCA1/BRCA2 variants are associated with breast, ovarian, pancreatic, prostate, urothelial, and selected other cancers. ATM and CHEK2 variants are associated with increased risk of prostate cancer and other malignancies. A first-degree relative with prostate cancer is associated with increased risk, particularly when diagnosed at a younger age. Men with advanced or metastatic prostate cancer are enriched for germline DNA-repair alterations. A pathogenic or likely pathogenic germline variant in BRCA1, BRCA2, ATM, or CHEK2 in the appropriate clinical setting establishes inherited predisposition. Tumor sequencing that identifies an HR-pathway variant should prompt consideration of germline assessment. Personal and family history of prostate, breast, ovarian, pancreatic, or related cancers should guide genetic evaluation. Prostate carcinomas associated with BRCA1/BRCA2 alterations more often have Gleason score 8 or higher, higher stage, and lymph node metastases. A consistent distinctive histologic pattern has not been established; ductal or intraductal morphology is not a reliable discriminator. No syndrome-specific immunohistochemical profile is established for routine histologic diagnosis. IHC findings should not substitute for germline testing or validated tumor molecular assays. Germline testing is generally performed on blood or another uninvolved tissue using targeted or multigene sequencing. Tumor-only HR-gene alterations may be somatic or germline; paired germline assessment is needed to establish inherited predisposition. Tumor HR-pathway alterations may predict response to PARP inhibitors and platinum-based chemotherapy, depending on tumor type and clinical context. Sporadic prostate carcinoma May share the same morphology; germline testing and personal/family cancer history establish inherited predisposition. Somatic HR-deficient tumor A tumor-only BRCA1/2, ATM, or CHEK2 alteration may be acquired; it does not establish a hereditary syndrome. Lynch syndrome Both may involve prostate or urothelial cancer, but Lynch is defined by mismatch repair gene defects and MMR deficiency. Do not classify a tumor as hereditary solely because tumor sequencing detects an HR-pathway mutation. Histologic grade and stage may be higher, but no unique morphology reliably identifies germline HR deficiency. Carney Complex PRKAR1A (most cases) Autosomal dominant | Endocrine, cardiac, cutaneous, and gonadal neoplasms May be diagnosed in infancy but most commonly becomes apparent around puberty. Pigmented lentigines affect the lips, conjunctiva, canthi, and sometimes genital epithelium. Large cell calcifying Sertoli cell tumors occur in approximately one-third of boys and are nearly universal in affected men. Associated findings include cardiac myxomas, blue nevi, pituitary adenomas, thyroid lesions, and primary pigmented nodular adrenocortical disease. Endocrine manifestations may include acromegaly or Cushing syndrome. Diagnosis requires two major criteria, or one major criterion plus one supplemental criterion. Large cell calcifying Sertoli cell tumor, characteristic lentigines, cardiac myxoma, and selected endocrine tumors are important syndrome clues. A germline pathogenic PRKAR1A variant supports molecular confirmation. Loss of PRKAR1A immunoreactivity in an appropriate neoplasm may prompt molecular testing. Large cell calcifying Sertoli cell tumor is a key genitourinary manifestation; detailed tumor morphology is addressed in the dedicated entity reference. Other associated lesions include cardiac myxoma, blue nevus, thyroid follicular lesions, and endocrine neoplasms. The syndrome is characterized by multiple benign neoplasms and hyperplasias, although malignant tumors have been reported. PRKAR1A immunohistochemistry may demonstrate loss in selected associated neoplasms and can guide genetic testing. No single IHC profile is diagnostic across the diverse tumor spectrum. Most cases are associated with inactivating germline PRKAR1A variants at 17q24.2. DNA sequencing and targeted deletion/duplication analysis can detect PRKAR1A alterations. A subset of patients have no identified PRKAR1A variant. Sporadic large cell calcifying Sertoli cell tumor Rare outside Carney complex; assess for lentigines, cardiac myxoma, endocrine lesions, and family history. Peutz–Jeghers syndrome-associated Sertoli cell neoplasia Typically intratubular large cell hyalinizing Sertoli cell neoplasia with prominent basement membrane deposits and gastrointestinal polyposis/pigmentation. Other endocrine tumor syndromes MEN2, VHL, and SDH-associated syndromes have distinct tumor combinations and molecular drivers. Large cell calcifying Sertoli cell tumor is a strong clue but should be interpreted with the broader clinical criteria. Do not conflate Carney complex with Carney triad, which refers to a distinct SDH-deficient, usually non-hereditary tumor association. Peutz–Jeghers Syndrome STK11 (LKB1) Autosomal dominant | GI polyposis, mucocutaneous pigmentation, and testicular Sertoli cell neoplasia Intestinal polyps commonly cause abdominal pain, bleeding, anemia, or intussusception, often in the first two decades. Mucocutaneous melanin pigmentation is characteristic. Prepubertal boys may present with bilateral gynecomastia, elevated estrogen, and advanced bone age due to intratubular Sertoli cell neoplasia. Testicular lesions may cause bilateral enlargement without a discrete mass and may be multifocal and subcentimeter on ultrasound. Genitourinary tumors outside the testis are rare and their relationship to the syndrome is uncertain. A pathogenic germline STK11 variant supports molecular confirmation. The syndrome is recognized clinically by mucocutaneous pigmentation and gastrointestinal hamartomatous polyposis, with characteristic family history. In the testis, expanded seminiferous tubules with thickened basement membranes and intratubular Sertoli cell proliferation are desirable diagnostic findings. Do not diagnose Peutz–Jeghers syndrome from the testicular lesion alone without clinical/genetic correlation. The process is predominantly intratubular, with patchily expanded seminiferous tubules approximately two to four times normal size. Tubules are surrounded by markedly thickened basement membranes that protrude into the lumen as globular eosinophilic deposits. Large Sertoli cells have pale eosinophilic, often fibrillary cytoplasm and round-to-oval nuclei with fine chromatin and visible nucleoli. Mitoses are absent; calcific foci may be present. Rare stromal invasion may occur and can resemble large cell calcifying Sertoli cell tumor. Tumor cells express inhibin, aromatase, and cytokeratin AE1/AE3. Aromatase expression explains estrogen excess and the associated prepubertal gynecomastia. Germline pathogenic variants in STK11 (LKB1) on chromosome 19p13.3 are identified in more than 90% of patients. No specific molecular alteration has been established for the characteristic testicular intratubular lesion beyond the underlying STK11 syndrome. Large cell calcifying Sertoli cell tumor Usually has a more prominent invasive component, dense eosinophilic cytoplasm, neutrophilic infiltrate, and conspicuous calcification. Sporadic Sertoli cell tumor Usually forms a discrete mass rather than patchy intratubular expansion with globular basement membrane deposits. Carney complex-associated Sertoli cell tumor Carney complex is associated with large cell calcifying Sertoli cell tumors and lentigines/cardiac/endocrine lesions; PJS shows GI polyposis and mucocutaneous pigmentation. Do not misclassify the intratubular lesion as an invasive Sertoli cell tumor in the absence of stromal invasion. Reported renal, prostate, and penile carcinomas in PJS cohorts may be incidental; a causal association is not established. PathologyGPS / Genitourinary Pathology / Genetic Tumor Syndromes Genitourinary Genetic Tumor Syndromes A morphology-first diagnostic reference to hereditary tumor predisposition involving the kidney, urinary tract, adrenal gland, testis, and male genital tract. Core diagnostic principle Recognize the tumor, identify the syndrome clue, then confirm germline status. Tumor morphology and immunohistochemistry can trigger hereditary evaluation, but a tumor-only sequence result does not establish a germline diagnosis. Diagnostic GPS: from tumor phenotype to hereditary diagnosis Recognize the pattern Young age, bilateral or multifocal tumors, unusual histology, multiple primary tumors, or a suggestive family history. Review the associated organs Look for characteristic skin, lung, CNS, endocrine, gastrointestinal, and reproductive manifestations. Use targeted IHC Apply pathway-directed markers such as FH/2SC, SDHB/SDHA, BAP1, mismatch repair proteins, and selected lineage markers. Interpret tumor sequencing carefully A pathogenic variant in tumor tissue may be somatic or germline; tumor-only testing cannot resolve constitutional status. Confirm germline status Use genetic counseling and testing of blood or other uninvolved tissue when hereditary predisposition is suspected. High-yield renal tumor associations Clear cell RCC; often bilateral/multifocal FLCN / Birt–Hogg–Dubé Hybrid oncocytic/chromophobe tumors; oncocytoma-like and chromophobe RCC MET / hereditary papillary RCC Bilateral/multifocal low-grade papillary RCC FH / HLRCC FH-deficient RCC; clinically important aggressive potential SDH genes SDH-deficient RCC Most often clear cell RCC; BAP1 nuclear loss TSC1/TSC2 Angiomyolipoma, cysts, and diverse renal epithelial tumors High-yield ancillary tests FH-deficient neoplasm FH loss; 2SC positivity SDH-deficient neoplasm SDHB loss; add SDHA to assess SDHA-associated deficiency Lynch syndrome candidate MLH1, PMS2, MSH2, and MSH6 IHC; MSI testing as appropriate BAP1-associated tumor Loss of nuclear BAP1 VHL-associated clear cell RCC CAIX/CD10 diffuse; CK7 negative or focal; 3p loss BHD-associated renal tumor PAX8, KIT, and CK7 pattern interpreted with morphology Syndrome reference Essential diagnostic criteria and differential diagnosis Search by syndrome, gene, clinical feature, morphology, immunostain, or differential diagnosis. e.g. FH, SDHB, bilateral RCC, MSH2... Collapse View diagnostic profile − + Clinical Profile Essential Diagnostic Criteria Histopathology Immunohistochemistry Molecular Pathology Differential Diagnosis Diagnostic Pitfalls No matching syndrome. Practical reporting and workup checklist Document age, exact anatomic site, laterality, multifocality, and prior or synchronous tumors. Correlate the tumor with characteristic extra-genitourinary findings and personal/family cancer history. Use internal positive controls when interpreting loss of FH, SDHB/SDHA, BAP1, or mismatch repair proteins. State clearly whether a molecular result is from tumor-only sequencing or germline testing. Recommend genetic counseling and germline testing when a syndrome-associated tumor, immunophenotype, or clinical pattern raises suspicion. Do not assign a hereditary syndrome solely from tumor morphology, immunohistochemistry, or a tumor-only pathogenic variant. Scope note: This reference emphasizes morphologic recognition, targeted immunohistochemistry, and criteria for hereditary evaluation. Definitive diagnosis of a germline tumor predisposition generally requires appropriate germline testing and clinical correlation.

title: Penis Scrotum Tumors
content: use client Condyloma acuminatum Benign / HPV-related Penis (especially glans, then foreskin and shaft), scrotum, perineum, and anus; giant lesions may involve the urethra or coronal sulcus. Usually young men in their 20s–30s; multifocal exophytic or flat genital warts, occasionally a giant locally destructive mass. Papillomatosis with prominent fibrovascular cores and bulbous, well-demarcated rete ridges. Acanthosis with hyperkeratosis and parakeratosis. Koilocytic atypia is variable and may be inconspicuous in older lesions. No true epithelial dysplasia should be present in an uncomplicated condyloma. No routine IHC is required; viral cytopathic change is assessed morphologically. Usually associated with low-risk HPV 6 or 11; HPV testing is rarely needed for routine diagnosis. Warty carcinoma — shows significant cytologic atypia throughout the lesion and infiltrative growth, not merely superficial koilocytosis. Verrucous carcinoma — has a broad pushing invasive front and lacks the characteristic benign koilocytosis of condyloma. Treated condylomas — topical therapy may cause vacuolization, nuclear enlargement, necrotic keratinocytes, and increased mitoses that mimic dysplasia. HPV-associated penile intraepithelial neoplasia (PeIN) Precursor / HPV-associated Glans, foreskin, and penile shaft; may be solitary or multifocal. Usually adult men; presents as erythematous, velvety, scaly, pigmented, or papular plaques, sometimes with erosion or pruritus. Basaloid pattern — monotonous immature cells replace most or all epithelial thickness, with high N:C ratios, mitoses, and apoptosis. Warty pattern — pleomorphic cells with koilocytic atypia and mitoses extend through the epithelium. Mixed pattern — basaloid cells predominate basally with warty differentiation toward the surface. Basement membrane remains intact; stromal invasion excludes pure PeIN. Block-type p16 positivity supports high-risk HPV association. Ki-67 extends above the basal layer; p53 is usually negative or variable. Differentiated PeIN — basal/parabasal atypia with retained surface maturation, usually non-block p16. Reactive squamous hyperplasia — lacks convincing cytologic atypia and typically has only basal/scattered Ki-67. Invasive HPV-associated SCC — demonstrates stromal invasion; inspect the epithelial-stromal interface carefully. Differentiated penile intraepithelial neoplasia (dPeIN) Precursor / HPV-independent Most often inner foreskin; frequently associated with lichen sclerosus. Typically older men (mean age about 64 years), often uncircumcised with longstanding lichen sclerosus; white or pink plaque. Hyperplastic squamous epithelium with hyperkeratosis and parakeratosis, often with elongated anastomosing rete ridges. Atypical hyperchromatic keratinocytes are concentrated in basal and parabasal layers despite apparent surface maturation. Dyskeratosis, individual eosinophilic keratinocytes, and prominent intercellular bridges are useful clues. Basement membrane remains intact; all dPeIN is considered high grade and is not graded further. p16 is non-block/negative; p53 is variable and may show abnormal overexpression. Ki-67 forms a continuous basal/parabasal pattern and may extend suprabasally. HPV-associated PeIN — usually block p16-positive, with full-thickness basaloid or warty atypia and koilocytosis. Squamous hyperplasia / lichen sclerosus — lacks convincing non-reactive nuclear atypia; Ki-67 is usually restricted to scattered basal cells. Invasive HPV-independent SCC — identify stromal invasion, often adjacent to dPeIN. HPV-associated penile squamous cell carcinoma Malignant / HPV-associated Glans and foreskin; subtype-specific sites include glans/foreskin for basaloid SCC and multiple penile compartments for warty carcinoma. Adults; basaloid SCC often presents around age 53, warty carcinoma around 48–55; may present with ulcerated or cauliflower-like mass and inguinal nodes. Basaloid SCC — solid nests/sheets of small uniform basaloid cells, brisk mitoses, and frequent comedonecrosis or abrupt keratinization. Warty carcinoma — exophytic/endophytic papillomatous growth with atypical koilocytosis throughout the tumor and infiltrative deep component. Clear cell SCC — nested/confluent large clear cells with PAS-positive, diastase-resistant cytoplasmic material and geographic/comedo necrosis. Lymphoepithelioma-like SCC — syncytial sheets, nests, or cords of poorly differentiated cells obscured by dense lymphoplasmacytic inflammation. Block-type p16 is expected in the appropriate HPV-associated setting; p63 supports squamous differentiation. High-risk HPV in situ hybridization or molecular testing can confirm association; HPV16 is most common. Giant condyloma — lacks the marked atypia and infiltrative malignant architecture of warty SCC. Verrucous carcinoma — has very well-differentiated cytology and broad pushing invasion, without atypical koilocytosis throughout. Urothelial carcinoma of distal urethra — correlate with urethral in situ disease and use GATA3, CK20, and uroplakin-2 as appropriate. Small-cell neuroendocrine carcinoma — evaluate neuroendocrine morphology and markers in basaloid tumors. Lymphoma — lacks epithelial marker expression; lymphoepithelioma-like SCC expresses p63 and commonly p16. HPV-independent penile squamous cell carcinoma Malignant / HPV-independent Usually glans; may involve coronal sulcus and foreskin; pseudohyperplastic pattern often foreskin-associated. Usually men in the sixth to seventh decades; may present as induration, erythema, exophytic mass, ulcer, or slowly enlarging verruciform lesion. Usual-type SCC — invasive keratinizing carcinoma with variable differentiation; growth patterns include pseudohyperplastic, pseudoglandular, superficial spreading, vertical, verruciform, and multicentric. Pseudoglandular pattern — prominent acantholysis creates gland-like spaces within squamous carcinoma. Verrucous carcinoma — very well-differentiated squamous proliferation with hyperkeratotic papillae and broad pushing invasion; koilocytic atypia is absent. Carcinoma cuniculatum — verrucous pattern with deep, branching, keratin-filled sinus tracts and bulbous invasive fronts. Papillary SCC — complex irregular papillae with jagged stromal interface and keratin lakes. Sarcomatoid SCC — atypical spindle-cell fascicles, sometimes with giant, strap, or rhabdoid cells; surface PeIN may be present. p16 is non-block/negative in HPV-independent tumors; p63 and high-molecular-weight cytokeratin can support epithelial differentiation in sarcomatoid cases. High-risk HPV should be excluded when classification is uncertain; TP53 alterations are common in HPV-independent carcinogenesis, but no routine molecular assay is required. Pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia — lacks destructive invasion and a convincing mass-forming infiltrative carcinoma. Distal urethral urothelial carcinoma — history and in situ component support urethral origin; GATA3, CK20, and uroplakin-2 may be positive. Warty carcinoma — shows high-risk HPV association, block p16, and atypical koilocytosis throughout the lesion. Sarcomas or melanoma — sarcomatoid SCC retains epithelial differentiation (p63/34βE12); use a directed panel if conventional SCC is not identified. Penile squamous cell carcinoma, NOS Malignant / HPV status unclassified Usually glans or coronal sulcus; exclusive foreskin involvement is uncommon. Clinical presentation resembles usual-type penile SCC; a nodular, ulcerated, or cauliflower-like mass. Invasive squamous carcinoma with variable keratinization and no defining special histologic pattern. Identify destructive stromal invasion and squamous differentiation. No HPV classification is available because p16/HPV testing is unavailable or not performed. No specific IHC profile can establish HPV status in this category. HPV status is not established; this designation is appropriate when p16 and HPV testing are unavailable. Penile adenosquamous carcinoma / mucoepidermoid carcinoma Malignant / other epithelial Usually glans near the urethral meatus; may extend to coronal sulcus and foreskin. Rare; usually men in their sixth decade presenting with a penile mass. Predominant squamous carcinoma component, often resembling grade 1–2 usual-type SCC. Adenosquamous carcinoma shows true gland formation with columnar/cuboidal cells and intracellular or luminal mucin. Mucoepidermoid pattern may consist of mucin-producing cells without overt glandular structures. Adjacent PeIN may be present; deeply infiltrative growth is typical. Glandular component may express CEA and high-molecular-weight cytokeratin (34βE12). Mucinous cells may express CK7, EMA, MUC5AC, and MUC6; they are typically negative for p40, p63, CK5, CK14, and p16. No diagnostic molecular alteration is established; molecular testing is not routinely relevant. Usual SCC with pseudoglandular/acantholytic pattern — pseudospaces lack true mucin-producing glandular cells. Metastatic adenocarcinoma involving penis — correlate with clinical history and organ-specific markers. Extramammary Paget disease of penis and scrotum Malignant / intraepidermal adenocarcinoma Penoscrotal epidermis; scrotum alone is common, with some cases involving both scrotum and penis. Usually older men (median age about 65–73); chronic pruritic erythematous, scaly, erosive, or exudative plaque, often delayed diagnosis. Large pale cells with abundant pale eosinophilic cytoplasm, enlarged nuclei, and prominent nucleoli occur singly or in clusters within epidermis. Adnexal structures may be involved; dermal invasion occurs in a minority and may form nodules, glands, or sheets. Lymphovascular invasion may be present; assess depth, adnexal involvement, and invasive component. Primary Paget disease typically expresses CK7 and CEA; ERBB2 and GCDFP-15 are variable. Primary lesions are usually CK20-, CDX2-, S100-, and HMB45-negative. No routine molecular test is established; primary lesions are not HPV-associated. Secondary Paget disease from urothelial carcinoma — may express CK20 and urothelial markers; correlate with urinary tract evaluation. Secondary Paget disease from prostatic adenocarcinoma — assess PSA, NKX3.1, and other prostate-lineage markers as appropriate. Melanoma in situ — usually expresses S100/SOX10 and melanocytic markers rather than CK7/CEA. Basal cell carcinoma of the scrotum Malignant / cutaneous epithelial Scrotal skin; may arise from interfollicular epidermis or hair follicle. Usually men aged 42–82; red papule, plaque, or nodule with often delayed diagnosis and local invasion. Basaloid nests and cords show peripheral palisading and stromal retraction clefts. Mucinous stroma is characteristic; focal squamous differentiation or microcysts may occur. Morphology resembles BCC at other cutaneous sites; nodular and superficial patterns are most often reported. No site-specific IHC or molecular profile is established; use standard BCC markers only when needed to resolve a differential. No molecular testing is routinely relevant for scrotal BCC. All PathologyGPS / Genitourinary Pathology / Penis and Scrotum Tumors Penis and Scrotum Tumors A morphology-first diagnostic reference emphasizing precursor lesions, HPV classification, invasive squamous carcinomas, and selected scrotal epithelial tumors. Core diagnostic principle Classify penile squamous lesions by invasion and HPV association. Use block-type p16 as the practical surrogate for high-risk HPV when morphology is equivocal. Report HPV-associated or HPV-independent status when established; use SCC-NOS when testing is unavailable. Diagnostic GPS: from clinical setting to classification 1. Establish the site Separate glans, coronal sulcus, foreskin, shaft, scrotal skin, and distal urethra; correlate with the clinical epicenter. 2. Determine invasion For PeIN, confirm an intact basement membrane; for invasive SCC, identify destructive stromal infiltration. 3. Classify HPV association Block p16 supports high-risk HPV-associated disease; non-block p16 and the appropriate morphology favor HPV-independent disease. 4. Recognize the growth pattern Basaloid, warty, clear cell, lymphoepithelioma-like, usual, verrucous, papillary, or sarcomatoid. 5. Report prognostic features Document subtype, grade, depth/level of invasion, lymphovascular and perineural invasion, margins, and pathologic stage. HPV-associated versus HPV-independent penile disease Feature HPV-associated HPV-independent Precursor HPV-associated PeIN Differentiated PeIN Typical p16 Block-positive Non-block/negative Morphology Basaloid or warty; koilocytic atypia may be present Keratinizing; often associated with chronic inflammation/lichen sclerosus Molecular context High-risk HPV, commonly HPV16 TP53 pathway alterations are common; no routine defining assay HPV classification does not replace histologic subtype, grade, or pathologic stage. High-yield differential diagnosis checkpoints Condyloma versus warty SCC: superficial koilocytosis without invasion versus atypical koilocytosis throughout an infiltrative carcinoma. Verrucous carcinoma versus papillary SCC: broad pushing front versus complex irregular papillae with a jagged invasive interface. Differentiated PeIN versus reactive squamous hyperplasia: true basal/parabasal atypia and a continuous Ki-67 pattern support PeIN. Scrotal Paget disease: exclude secondary urothelial or prostatic involvement before designating a primary cutaneous lesion. Scrotal BCC versus basaloid SCC: palisading and stromal clefting with mucinous stroma versus atypical basaloid nests with brisk mitoses/comedonecrosis. Molecular Pathology No diagnostically useful molecular test is established. Differential Diagnosis No matching entity. Reporting and sampling checklist Penile squamous carcinoma Specify histologic subtype and HPV association when established; use SCC-NOS if HPV testing is unavailable. For mixed carcinomas, identify each component and estimate its percentage when feasible. Report histologic grade, depth/level of invasion, lymphovascular invasion, perineural invasion, and margin status. Document involvement of glans, foreskin, shaft, corpus spongiosum, corpus cavernosum, and urethra as applicable. Assess regional lymph nodes and assign pathologic stage using the applicable current staging system. Scrotal epithelial lesions For extramammary Paget disease, distinguish intraepidermal from dermally invasive disease and document adnexal, lymphovascular, and dartos involvement. Investigate possible secondary Paget disease, particularly from prostate or urothelial carcinoma; use a directed IHC panel. For scrotal BCC, assess peripheral and deep margins carefully; subclinical extension may complicate margin assessment. Scrotal malignancies are uncommon and do not all have a dedicated AJCC staging framework; correlate with the appropriate site-specific protocol.
