title: Prostatic Tumors
content: use client Prostatic Cystadenoma Benign glandular neoplasm Prostate, periprostatic/retrovesical region, or rarely retroperitoneum. Reported across the third to ninth decades; approximately 30 cases have been described. May cause urinary obstruction, constipation, abdominal distention, or pain. Imaging often shows a large multiseptated mass; serum PSA is commonly elevated. Large multiloculated cystic mass in or around the prostate. Cysts lined by bland prostatic secretory cells with an outer basal-cell layer. Fibrous or fibromuscular septa separate the cysts. No marked epithelial atypia. Cysts have a dual epithelial lining: low columnar or atrophic secretory cells and flattened outer basal cells. Focal bland papillae may be present. The surrounding stroma is fibromuscular or fibrotic and may be hyalinized or chronically inflamed. Squamous metaplasia may occur. Secretory epithelium: PSA, PAP, and other prostate-lineage markers are positive. Basal cells: high-molecular-weight cytokeratin and p63 are positive. Ductal adenocarcinoma / cystadenocarcinoma-like carcinoma Prominent intracystic papillary growth and cytologic atypia favor carcinoma rather than bland cystadenoma. Seminal vesicle lesion Use prostate-lineage markers to confirm prostatic epithelial origin when the site is uncertain. No clinically useful diagnostic molecular test is established. Incomplete excision may lead to local recurrence; complete surgical excision is the treatment of choice. Rare coexistence with HGPIN or acinar adenocarcinoma has been reported. High-Grade Prostatic Intraepithelial Neoplasia (HGPIN) Glandular precursor lesion Most often peripheral zone; less commonly central or transition zones. Usually identified incidentally in biopsies obtained during evaluation for prostate carcinoma. Isolated HGPIN does not cause clinical symptoms. Incidence increases with age. Atypical, crowded, stratified secretory cells within pre-existing normal-sized or expanded ducts/acini. Enlarged hyperchromatic nuclei with conspicuous nucleoli. Basal-cell layer remains identifiable, although it may be discontinuous or attenuated. No necrosis, marked nuclear pleomorphism, or brisk mitotic activity. Tufting, micropapillary, and flat patterns are recognized; routine pattern designation is not clinically useful. Cells are multilayered with enlarged hyperchromatic nuclei and amphophilic cytoplasm. Prominent nucleoli are a key diagnostic requirement. Cribriform HGPIN is controversial; atypical intraductal proliferation is preferred for intraductal lesions that fall short of IDC-P. High-molecular-weight cytokeratin and/or p63 can demonstrate residual basal cells. Basal-cell stains may help distinguish HGPIN from PIN-like adenocarcinoma and other mimics. Intraductal carcinoma of the prostate (IDC-P) IDC-P has more complex expansile architecture, dense/solid cribriform growth and/or marked cytologic atypia; comedonecrosis may be present. PIN-like adenocarcinoma PIN-like carcinoma shows crowded discrete glands lacking basal cells; HGPIN retains at least a discontinuous basal layer. Benign glandular hyperplasia HGPIN has stratification, enlarged hyperchromatic nuclei, and conspicuous nucleoli. Somatic alterations overlap with prostate carcinoma, including GSTP1 epigenetic silencing, MYC amplification, TMPRSS2::ERG fusion (reported in 20–30%), and PTEN loss. Molecular testing is not clinically relevant for routine diagnosis. Do not diagnose low-grade PIN as a separate entity; it is not reproducibly distinguishable from benign glandular hyperplasia. Do not use the term cribriform HGPIN on needle biopsy; consider atypical intraductal proliferation when criteria for IDC-P are not met. Intraductal Carcinoma of the Prostate (IDC-P) Intraductal neoplasm Usually peripheral zone, commonly accompanying high-grade and high-volume invasive carcinoma. Most often occurs with high-grade, high-stage invasive prostate cancer. Detected in prostate biopsy or prostatectomy specimens; isolated IDC-P is exceedingly rare. Its presence has adverse prognostic and clinical-management implications. Expansile neoplastic epithelial proliferation within pre-existing ducts/acini, with at least partial basal-cell preservation. Lumen-spanning solid or dense cribriform architecture is the most widely accepted diagnostic pattern. Loose cribriform or micropapillary architecture requires marked cytologic atypia for diagnosis under commonly used criteria. Comedonecrosis strongly supports IDC-P. Atypical intraductal proliferation is preferred when an intraductal lesion falls short of IDC-P criteria. Solid and dense cribriform growth are characteristic; dense cribriform growth has more epithelial than luminal area (>50%). Loose cribriform and micropapillary patterns are more controversial and require careful assessment of cytologic atypia. Tumor cells may show enlarged pleomorphic or hyperchromatic nuclei, mitoses, and apoptotic bodies. Residual basal cells are at least partially retained. Cribriform architecture without cytologic atypia may occur in benign central-zone glands or prostatic hyperplasia. Basal-cell markers (high-molecular-weight cytokeratin and/or p63) demonstrate residual basal cells. Basal-cell IHC is recommended for isolated IDC-P on biopsy without concomitant invasive carcinoma. Prostate-specific and urothelial markers can help in difficult cases involving possible urothelial intraductal spread. HGPIN IDC-P is more architecturally complex and/or cytologically atypical; solid/dense cribriform growth and comedonecrosis favor IDC-P. Atypical intraductal proliferation Use this descriptive category when intraductal atypia is greater than HGPIN but insufficient for IDC-P. Invasive cribriform acinar carcinoma Basal-cell layer is absent in invasive carcinoma; IDC-P retains at least partial basal cells. Urothelial carcinoma involving prostatic ducts Use prostate-lineage and urothelial markers; correlate with urothelial in situ disease. Ductal adenocarcinoma Tall pseudostratified columnar cells and papillae with fibrovascular cores favor ductal adenocarcinoma. IDC-P commonly shares genomic alterations with aggressive invasive prostate carcinoma, including PTEN loss, MYC gain, and ERG rearrangement. PTEN loss is reported in up to approximately 85% of cases; ERG rearrangement is present in a majority of cases. Molecular testing is not routinely required to establish the diagnosis. Report IDC-P when present because it is associated with adverse outcome. Do not grade isolated IDC-P on biopsy; describe its presence and the usual association with aggressive invasive carcinoma. Whether IDC-P should be incorporated into Gleason grading when invasive carcinoma is present remains controversial. Prostatic Acinar Adenocarcinoma Malignant glandular neoplasm Most commonly posterior or posterolateral peripheral zone; less often anterior peripheral or transition zone. Predominantly affects older men; many cases are asymptomatic and detected through elevated serum PSA. May be found incidentally in tissue sampled for benign prostatic hyperplasia. Multifocality is common; urinary symptoms are not specific for carcinoma. Infiltrative malignant glands with secretory differentiation and absence of a substantial component of another prostatic carcinoma type. Basal cells are typically absent in invasive carcinoma. Diagnosis is primarily morphologic; prostate-lineage IHC supports difficult cases but does not replace morphology. Recognize and report adverse patterns including cribriform architecture and associated IDC-P. Architecture ranges from well-formed small glands to fused, poorly formed, cribriform, and solid patterns. Infiltrative growth, variation in gland size/shape, and absence of a basal layer support malignancy. Special morphologic subtypes include signet-ring cell-like, pleomorphic giant cell, sarcomatoid, and PIN-like carcinoma. Additional patterns include atrophic, pseudohyperplastic, microcystic, foamy-gland, and mucinous (colloid) patterns. PIN-like carcinoma shows large discrete flat or tufted glands lined by pseudostratified or cuboidal cells; it lacks basal cells and lacks true fibrovascular papillae, complex cribriform glands, and necrosis. NKX3.1 is generally more sensitive and specific for prostatic adenocarcinoma than PSA. PSA, PAP, PSMA, and other prostate-lineage markers may support prostatic origin; a panel is recommended in difficult cases. ERG is positive in fewer than 50% of cases and is not a universal marker. Basal-cell markers (p63 and high-molecular-weight cytokeratin) help distinguish invasive carcinoma from benign glands and HGPIN. Benign mimics (atrophy, adenosis, crowded benign glands) Assess infiltrative architecture, cytology, basal-cell retention, and a panel of basal-cell markers. HGPIN is confined to pre-existing glands and retains basal cells; invasive carcinoma lacks basal cells. IDC-P IDC-P is intraductal and retains at least partial basal cells; invasive acinar carcinoma lacks basal cells. Ductal morphology shows tall pseudostratified columnar cells with papillary or complex cribriform architecture. Urothelial or non-prostatic carcinoma Use a panel including NKX3.1/PSA/PAP and appropriate urothelial or organ-specific markers, with clinical correlation. PIN-like adenocarcinoma versus HGPIN PIN-like carcinoma has crowded glands without basal cells; HGPIN retains a basal layer. TMPRSS2::ERG fusion is a recurrent molecular event; ERG rearrangement is found in a subset of tumors. DNA-repair gene alterations (including BRCA1, BRCA2, ATM, CHEK2, PALB2, FANCI, and MSH2) are clinically important in aggressive and metastatic disease. Mismatch-repair deficiency and homologous-recombination repair defects may guide therapeutic testing; germline/somatic testing is clinically relevant in selected patients. PIN-like adenocarcinoma frequently shows activating RAF/RAS-pathway mutations, differing from usual acinar and ductal carcinoma. Do not diagnose carcinoma on IHC alone; morphology remains primary. Cribriform architecture and/or IDC-P should be documented because of prognostic and potential genetic-testing implications. Sarcomatoid differentiation is a subtype/pattern of acinar adenocarcinoma, not a separate stromal sarcoma. Prostatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma Often periurethral/central; may involve peripheral prostate and present as an exophytic urethral lesion. Usually affects older men; may present with urinary obstruction or hematuria, but can be asymptomatic. Serum PSA may be elevated or normal. May be mixed with acinar adenocarcinoma; pure ductal carcinoma is less common. Papillary and/or complex cribriform glands lined by tall pseudostratified columnar cells. Papillae have true fibrovascular cores; cribriform lumina are often slit-like. In prostatectomy, report the percentage of ductal component; the WHO criterion uses >50% for ductal adenocarcinoma designation. On needle biopsy, even a pure lesion is termed prostate adenocarcinoma with ductal features. Tall columnar cells have abundant amphophilic or pale cytoplasm and elongated enlarged nuclei with prominent nucleoli. Papillary and large cribriform patterns are most characteristic; solid foci, comedonecrosis, and invasive single glands may coexist. Desmoplastic stroma and intraductal growth are frequent. Ductal carcinoma is graded using Gleason grading; ductal areas are assigned pattern 4 except comedonecrosis, which is pattern 5. Usually positive for PSA, PAP, PSMA, NKX3.1, and AMACR. There is no IHC stain that reliably distinguishes ductal from acinar adenocarcinoma. CK20 is patchy positive in a subset (reported 23–60%). Use basal-cell markers when distinguishing intraductal growth from invasive carcinoma. GATA3 and p63 favor urothelial carcinoma; TTF1 supports lung adenocarcinoma in the appropriate differential. Acinar adenocarcinoma Ductal carcinoma has tall pseudostratified columnar cells, elongated nuclei, and papillary fibrovascular cores; prostate markers overlap. IDC-P / HGPIN Basal-cell markers and architecture are key; ductal carcinoma shows tall columnar epithelium and true papillae. Urothelial carcinoma involving ducts GATA3/p63 positivity and lack of prostate-lineage markers support urothelial origin. Colorectal or bladder adenocarcinoma Correlate with clinical/radiologic findings and use prostate-lineage markers; CDX2/villin are not reliable discriminators by themselves. Molecular findings overlap with acinar adenocarcinoma; shared ERG rearrangements support clonal relationship in many cases. Occasional molecular discordance has been reported; molecular findings are not required for routine diagnosis. Ductal carcinoma may be under-sampled or under-staged on biopsy. Preserve the term ductal adenocarcinoma as a separate type in this WHO edition. Report ductal component percentage in prostatectomy; use 'adenocarcinoma with ductal features' on biopsy. Treatment-Related Neuroendocrine Prostatic Carcinoma (t-NEPC) Treatment-related carcinoma Prostate and metastatic sites; may show heterogeneous involvement. Arises after androgen-deprivation therapy, often in castration-resistant prostate cancer. May present with rapid progression despite androgen-receptor-directed therapy. Accounts for approximately 10–15% of castration-resistant prostate adenocarcinomas. Prostatic carcinoma showing complete neuroendocrine differentiation or partial neuroendocrine differentiation admixed with adenocarcinoma after androgen-deprivation therapy. Correlate with a history of antiandrogen/androgen-deprivation therapy. Confirm neuroendocrine differentiation with synaptophysin and/or chromogranin in the appropriate morphology. Most commonly shows small-cell neuroendocrine carcinoma morphology; large-cell and mixed patterns also occur. May be pure neuroendocrine carcinoma or mixed with poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma. The transition between neuroendocrine and adenocarcinoma components is often abrupt. Metastatic deposits may show marked intratumoral heterogeneity. Synaptophysin and chromogranin support neuroendocrine differentiation. The small-cell component is typically negative for PSA and PAP. AR may be retained in a subset; TTF1 is positive in approximately half of small-cell components. p53 nuclear staining is common in small-cell carcinoma. Conventional acinar adenocarcinoma with focal neuroendocrine differentiation Focal neuroendocrine marker expression alone is common and does not establish t-NEPC; require appropriate morphology and clinical context. Primary small-cell or large-cell NEC Treatment history and clinical evolution support treatment-related disease; morphology/IHC may otherwise be similar. Metastatic small-cell carcinoma from another site Correlate with clinical history and imaging; prostate markers may be absent in the neuroendocrine component. Losses of TP53, RB1, and PTEN and epigenetic alterations are implicated in lineage plasticity. EZH2 overexpression and altered DNA methylation profiles have been reported. Molecular testing is not required for routine morphologic diagnosis. Do not perform routine neuroendocrine IHC on every conventional prostate biopsy; focal neuroendocrine differentiation alone has no established routine prognostic/therapeutic role. Do not include the small-cell component in Gleason grading. Adenosquamous Carcinoma of the Prostate Malignant mixed epithelial neoplasm Prostate. Very rare; median reported age approximately 67–74 years. May arise de novo or after hormonal and/or radiation therapy for prostate adenocarcinoma. Patients commonly present with urinary obstruction/frequency; PSA may be elevated or normal; metastases may be present. Both malignant glandular (acinar) and malignant squamous components must be present. The components may be admixed, distinct, or show transition. Exclude urothelial carcinoma with divergent differentiation. Glandular component is commonly grade group 2 or higher. Squamous component varies widely in proportion and differentiation; nuclear pleomorphism is often more pronounced. A sarcomatous component is reported in a substantial subset (20–57%). The glandular component expresses prostate markers; the squamous component expresses basal-cell markers and is usually PSA-negative. Glandular component: PSA and/or PAP positive; ERG may be strong in the glandular component in ERG-rearranged cases. Squamous component: basal-cell markers positive and usually PSA-negative. NKX3.1 expression is not sufficiently characterized to serve as a defining feature. Urothelial carcinoma with divergent squamous/glandular differentiation Assess morphology and IHC of the non-squamous component, prior history, and radiologic findings. Pure squamous cell carcinoma Adenosquamous carcinoma requires a malignant glandular component as well as squamous carcinoma. Acinar adenocarcinoma with focal squamous differentiation Confirm a bona fide malignant squamous component and correlate with treatment history. Reported alterations include TMPRSS2::ERG fusion, PTEN deletion, and SPOP mutation. A FAM131A::BRAF fusion has been reported in an individual case; molecular testing may help in selected cases. Do not classify as pure squamous carcinoma if a malignant glandular component is present. Document the components and consider a sarcomatous component. Squamous Cell Carcinoma of the Prostate Malignant squamous neoplasm Extremely rare; most reported patients are older than 70 years. Often occurs after hormone or radiation therapy for prostatic adenocarcinoma. Presents with urinary obstruction, dysuria, hematuria, or bone pain; PSA is usually not elevated. Pelvic nodal and osteolytic bone metastases are common. Malignant squamous architecture with keratinization and/or intercellular bridges and cellular anaplasia. No glandular component should be present. Exclude prostatic adenocarcinoma with squamous differentiation, direct extension of bladder carcinoma, and metastatic squamous carcinoma. Keratin pearls, intercellular bridges, and cytologic anaplasia resemble squamous carcinoma at other sites. Glandular elements should be absent. Grade as well, moderately, or poorly differentiated; Gleason grading/grade groups do not apply. Usually positive for p63, 34βE12, CK5/6, and CK14. Usually negative for PSA, PAP, and PSMA. AMACR may be positive. Adenosquamous carcinoma Adenosquamous carcinoma contains a malignant glandular component. Urothelial carcinoma with squamous differentiation Use urothelial markers and assess for associated urothelial carcinoma/in situ disease. Bladder SCC extending into prostate Correlate with tumor epicenter and clinical/radiologic findings. Metastatic SCC Exclude a primary squamous carcinoma elsewhere; TMPRSS2::ERG fusion strongly supports prostatic origin in the appropriate setting. Limited case data report TMPRSS2::ERG fusion in 3 of 4 cases and SPOP mutation in one case. PTEN loss or mutation has also been reported; molecular testing is not routinely established. Do not use PSA level alone to exclude prostate origin; serum PSA is usually not elevated. Gleason grading is not applicable. Prostatic origin should be established by exclusion and, in selected cases, molecular findings. Adenoid Cystic (Basal Cell) Carcinoma of the Prostate Malignant basal-cell neoplasm Reported age range 42–93 years. Often presents with urinary obstruction and is diagnosed on transurethral resection; serum PSA is usually normal unless concurrent acinar carcinoma is present. Basal-cell morphology and immunophenotype. Identify malignant features: cytoarchitectural atypia, stromal infiltration/between benign acini, perineural invasion, necrosis, or extraprostatic extension. Exclude metastatic adenoid cystic carcinoma from another primary site, including Cowper glands. Variable admixture of adenoid cystic/cribriform areas with inspissated secretions and basaloid solid nests. Less commonly, cords or small tubules with hyaline rims are present. Stroma may be desmoplastic; mitotic activity and Ki-67 vary widely. Basal-cell markers highlight the outermost cell layers; CK7 labels adluminal cells. PSA is positive in a minority; AMACR and androgen receptor are negative to weak. ERG is negative; BCL2 may be strongly positive and Ki-67 elevated. ERBB2/HER2 overexpression has been reported, but protein findings are inconsistent. Florid basal-cell hyperplasia Carcinoma shows atypia, infiltrative growth, perineural invasion, necrosis, or extraprostatic extension. Urothelial carcinoma Use morphology and prostate/basal-cell versus urothelial marker profile. High-grade acinar adenocarcinoma or NEC Basal-cell morphology and immunophenotype support adenoid cystic/basal-cell carcinoma. Metastatic adenoid cystic carcinoma Exclude a primary elsewhere, including salivary gland or Cowper gland. MYB::NFIB fusion is detected in approximately 17–47% by FISH and is not found in benign basal-cell proliferations. TMPRSS2::ERG fusion has not been identified in this entity. The term 'basal cell carcinoma' can be confused with cutaneous basal cell carcinoma; use the full prostatic entity name. A subset is locally aggressive and can metastasize. Prostatic Stromal Tumor of Uncertain Malignant Potential (STUMP) Prostate-specific mesenchymal tumor Transition or peripheral zone of the prostate. Rare; median age approximately 57.5 years (range 25–86). Usually presents with lower urinary tract obstruction; less commonly palpable mass, hematuria, hematospermia, or rectal fullness. May be incidental or form a large solid/partly cystic mass. Extensive proliferation of atypical prostatic stromal cells, without the nodularity and thick-walled vessels typical of benign prostatic hyperplasia. One or more characteristic stromal patterns may be present. Exclude prostatic stromal sarcoma and other mesenchymal tumors. Five patterns may occur alone or in combination: hypercellular atypical stromal cells with degenerative-appearing nuclei; hypercellular bland fusiform cells; phyllodes-like architecture; myxoid stroma with bland cells; and epithelioid stromal pattern. Benign prostatic glands may be admixed and may show crowding or other benign/proliferative changes. Extensive sampling is required to assess cellularity, atypia, mitotic activity, and possible sarcoma. Vimentin and progesterone receptor are positive. CD34, SMA, and desmin are variably positive; ER is uncommon. KIT, S100, and STAT6 are negative. Florid benign prostatic hyperplasia STUMP shows extensive hypercellular atypical stroma and lacks the nodularity and thick-walled vessels typical of BPH. Prostatic stromal sarcoma Sarcoma shows increased mitoses, atypical mitoses, necrosis, marked hypercellularity, and non-degenerative nuclear pleomorphism. Other spindle-cell tumors Exclude solitary fibrous tumor, inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor, smooth-muscle tumors, rhabdomyosarcoma, GIST, sarcomatoid carcinoma, and seminal-vesicle tumors. Recurrent losses of chromosomes 13, 14, and 1p have been reported, supporting a distinct neoplastic entity. Molecular testing is not routinely required for diagnosis. Clinical behavior is unpredictable; most cases are not aggressive, but recurrence after resection occurs in approximately 15%. Histologic pattern does not reliably predict clinical behavior or concurrent stromal sarcoma. Prostatic Stromal Sarcoma Malignant prostate-specific mesenchymal tumor Transition and peripheral zones of the prostate. Very rare (<0.1% of prostatic cancers); mean age approximately 51.5 years (range 25–86). Approximately half of reported patients are younger than 50 years. Presents with lower urinary tract obstruction; other symptoms include palpable mass, hematuria, hematospermia, or rectal fullness. Diffuse stromal neoplasm with hypercellularity and cytologic atypia. Increased mitotic activity and/or atypical mitoses; necrosis may be present. Exclude STUMP, sarcomatoid carcinoma, postirradiation sarcoma, and other primary mesenchymal malignancies. May be circumscribed or infiltrate between benign prostatic glands. Patterns include storiform, epithelioid, fibrosarcomatous, leaf-like/phyllodes-like, or patternless growth. Tumor cells show hypercellularity, atypia, increased mitoses, and atypical mitotic figures; necrosis may occur. Vimentin is positive; CD34 is variable. SMA and desmin are usually negative; ER and PR are uncommon. Pancytokeratin is rarely positive. STUMP Sarcoma shows increased/atypical mitoses, necrosis, and more overt non-degenerative cytologic atypia. Sarcomatoid prostate carcinoma Often occurs after prostate carcinoma and treatment; focal pancytokeratin expression in the sarcomatoid component supports epithelial lineage. Postirradiation sarcoma A history of pelvic radiation raises this possibility. Other sarcomas Exclude leiomyosarcoma, rhabdomyosarcoma, and other lineage-defined mesenchymal tumors. Molecular alterations are heterogeneous and largely non-recurrent; chromosome 13/14 losses have been reported. MED12 mutations were not detected in the cited specialized prostatic stromal tumor series. No routine diagnostic molecular test is established. STUMP and stromal sarcoma may coexist; thorough sampling is important. Do not classify a sarcomatoid carcinoma as stromal sarcoma without excluding epithelial differentiation. All PathologyGPS / Genitourinary Pathology WHO Classification of tumors · Prostate Prostatic Tumors A practical, morphology-first reference to epithelial neoplasms and prostate-specific stromal tumors. Emphasis is placed on essential diagnostic criteria, focused immunohistochemistry, and the distinction between closely related entities. Diagnostic profiles Diagnostic priorities Start with architecture and cytology; prostate carcinoma diagnosis is primarily morphologic. Use basal-cell markers to distinguish benign glands, HGPIN, and IDC-P from invasive carcinoma when the distinction is consequential. For suspected prostatic origin in a poorly differentiated or metastatic carcinoma, use a prostate-lineage panel rather than relying on PSA alone; NKX3.1 is particularly useful. Recognize treatment-related neuroendocrine carcinoma in the clinical context of androgen-deprivation therapy and appropriate neuroendocrine morphology. For stromal lesions, assess stromal cellularity, atypia, mitotic activity, necrosis, and the presence or absence of benign prostatic glands. Entity reference Diagnostic criteria and differential diagnosis Expand an entity for clinical profile, essential criteria, histopathology, immunophenotype, molecular pathology, and key mimics. Practical diagnostic workflow Atypical glandular / intraductal proliferation First determine whether the proliferation is confined to pre-existing ducts/acini or shows invasive growth. Use p63 and high-molecular-weight cytokeratin to assess basal-cell retention. HGPIN has atypical stratified secretory cells with prominent nucleoli; IDC-P has more complex architecture and/or greater cytologic atypia. Use atypical intraductal proliferation when the lesion is more complex than HGPIN but does not meet IDC-P criteria. Acinar versus ductal adenocarcinoma Ductal features include true papillae with fibrovascular cores, tall pseudostratified columnar cells, and elongated nuclei. Prostate-lineage IHC overlaps; morphology is the key discriminator. Report the percentage of ductal component in prostatectomy; on biopsy use 'adenocarcinoma with ductal features'. High-grade / treatment-associated carcinoma After androgen-deprivation therapy, consider t-NEPC when rapid progression and small-cell/large-cell neuroendocrine morphology emerge. Confirm neuroendocrine differentiation with synaptophysin and/or chromogranin in the appropriate setting. Do not assign Gleason grade to the neuroendocrine component. Prostate-specific stromal lesions STUMP shows atypical or hypercellular specialized stroma, often with benign glands, but lacks overt sarcomatous features. Sarcoma is favored by increased/atypical mitoses, necrosis, and non-degenerative nuclear pleomorphism. Exclude sarcomatoid carcinoma and other lineage-defined mesenchymal tumors with morphology and targeted IHC. Scope: This section covers prostatic glandular epithelial neoplasms, treatment-related neuroendocrine prostatic carcinoma, squamous and adenoid cystic carcinomas, and prostate-specific stromal tumors. Other genitourinary tumor categories are addressed in their respective sections.

title: Renal Tumors
content: use client Clear cell renal cell carcinoma (CCRCC) Morphologically defined RCC Usually solitary, unilateral renal cortical mass. Most common sporadic RCC (60–75%). Usually adults aged ≥60 years; median age approximately 62 years. More common in men. May present with hematuria or flank pain; many are detected incidentally. May first present with hematogenous metastasis. Renal mass with nested, tubular, or alveolar architecture. Predominantly clear cells with delicate arborizing vasculature. Diffuse membranous CAIX or VHL pathway alteration is supportive, especially in atypical cases. Nested, alveolar, tubular, or cystic architecture. Optically clear cytoplasm is typical; eosinophilic cells may increase with grade. A rich capillary network surrounds tumor nests. High-grade tumors may show necrosis, sarcomatoid change, or rhabdoid differentiation. CAIX: strong, diffuse, circumferential membranous staining. PAX8: positive; supports renal epithelial origin. CD10 and RCC antigen: commonly positive. CK7: usually negative or focal. Vimentin: commonly positive. KIT (CD117): typically negative. Clear cell papillary renal cell tumor CK7 is usually diffuse and CAIX has a cup-shaped pattern; CCRCC usually has diffuse box-like CAIX and limited CK7. MiT family translocation RCC Consider in younger patients or tumors with papillary/nested architecture; use TFE3/TFEB IHC and molecular confirmation. Chromophobe RCC Perinuclear halos and distinct cell borders; usually KIT-positive and CAIX-negative. Metastatic clear cell carcinoma PAX8 supports renal origin but is not specific; correlate with clinical history and organ-specific markers. 3p loss and VHL inactivation occur in >90% of sporadic cases. PBRM1, SETD2, and BAP1 are recurrently altered; BAP1 alteration is associated with more aggressive biology. VHL pathway activation drives CAIX and other hypoxia-inducible proteins. Grade heterogeneity is common; report the highest grade represented by at least one high-power field. Sarcomatoid and rhabdoid differentiation are grade 4 features, not separate RCC entities. Papillary renal cell carcinoma (PRCC) Renal cortex; often well circumscribed. Usually adults; male predominance. May be multifocal or bilateral, particularly in hereditary settings. Often detected as an incidental renal mass. Papillary or tubulopapillary architecture with fibrovascular cores. Foamy macrophages and psammoma bodies may be present. Cellular type: more cellular, mitotically active spindle-cell neoplasm; may show hemangiopericytoma-like vessels. Vimentin commonly positive; SMA may be positive. IHC is not sufficient to subtype. Wilms tumor CMN is predominantly spindle-cell; Wilms tumor has blastemal/epithelial/stromal differentiation. Clear cell sarcoma of kidney CCSK has distinct morphology and BCOR-associated molecular alterations. Cellular CMN is commonly associated with ETV6::NTRK3 fusion; alternative kinase fusions occur. Classic CMN may show EGFR internal tandem duplication. Molecular testing can support diagnosis and identify potential targeted therapy in cellular tumors. Rhabdoid tumor of the kidney Paediatric renal malignant tumors Kidney; often large and infiltrative. Highly aggressive malignant tumor of infancy and early childhood; consider synchronous/metachronous CNS rhabdoid tumor. Malignant renal neoplasm with rhabdoid cytology and loss of SMARCB1/INI1 expression. Large cells with eccentric nuclei, prominent nucleoli, and abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm with hyaline inclusions. Sheets, nests, or infiltrative growth; necrosis and brisk mitotic activity common. Complete loss of INI1/SMARCB1 in tumor cells with retained internal controls; keratin and vimentin often positive. Renal medullary carcinoma Both may lose INI1; clinical context, sickle trait, age, and morphology distinguish. Wilms tumor with rhabdoid features INI1 status and molecular context are essential. Biallelic SMARCB1 inactivation is characteristic; germline evaluation is important in young patients. INI1 loss is not exclusive to renal medullary carcinoma. Clear cell sarcoma of the kidney Kidney; usually unilateral renal mass in children. Typically affects young children; malignant tumor with potential for bone and other metastases. Renal malignant neoplasm with characteristic delicate branching vasculature and cords/nests of uniform cells; confirm BCOR-associated alteration when needed. Classic pattern: uniform cells in cords, nests, or anastomosing trabeculae separated by delicate arborizing vasculature. Variant patterns include myxoid, sclerosing, cellular, epithelioid, and spindle-cell areas. BCOR nuclear expression is commonly strong; cyclin D1 and SATB2 may be positive. PAX8 is generally negative. Lacks typical triphasic nephroblastoma pattern; molecular findings help. Rhabdoid tumor INI1 loss supports rhabdoid tumor; CCSK usually retains INI1. Most cases harbor BCOR internal tandem duplication; a subset has YWHAE::NUTM2 fusion. Do not mistake the delicate vascular pattern for a vascular tumor. Nephrogenic rests Nephroblastic lesions Renal parenchyma; may be perilobar or intralobar. Developmental precursor lesions associated with increased risk of nephroblastoma; may be multifocal or bilateral. Foci of persistent embryonal nephrogenic tissue, classified by location and morphology. Perilobar rests are typically peripheral and sharply demarcated; intralobar rests are embedded within parenchyma and may be fibrous or hyperplastic. WT1 may be positive; immunophenotype overlaps with nephroblastoma and is not independently diagnostic. Nephrogenic rests lack the expansile destructive growth and cytologic features of an established tumor. Molecular findings vary with associated predisposition syndromes; no single routine diagnostic alteration. Nephrogenic rests are precursor lesions, not nephroblastoma. Kidney; multicystic renal mass, usually in young children. Pediatric cystic renal neoplasm; typically presents as an abdominal mass. Multicystic lesion with blastemal cells in septa or as focal aggregates; no expansile solid nephroblastoma component. Cysts lined by flattened or cuboidal epithelium. Septa contain blastemal cells, sometimes with epithelial or stromal differentiation. WT1 may label blastemal/epithelial elements; interpret with morphology. Cystic nephroma lacks blastemal cells in septa. Solid expansile component favors nephroblastoma. DICER1 alterations may be relevant in the cystic nephroma/nephroblastic spectrum; source-specific correlation required. Extensive sampling of septa is mandatory. Nephroblastoma (Wilms tumor) Nephroblastic tumors Kidney; usually unilateral, occasionally bilateral. Predominantly children younger than 10 years; mean age approximately 3–4 years. Often presents as abdominal mass; hematuria, pain, hypertension, or anemia may occur. Embryonal renal malignancy with blastemal, epithelial, and stromal differentiation in variable proportions. Triphasic morphology is characteristic but biphasic and monophasic tumors occur. Blastema: sheets of small blue cells with scant cytoplasm. Epithelial differentiation: primitive tubules and glomeruloid structures. Stromal differentiation: spindle cells and possible heterologous elements. Anaplasia is an important adverse histologic feature. WT1 commonly labels blastemal and epithelial components; cytokeratins label epithelial differentiation. Nephrogenic rest Cannot be distinguished from nephroblastoma by cytology alone; architecture and growth pattern are key. Distinct vascular pattern and BCOR-associated alteration. Rhabdoid cytology and INI1 loss. 1p/16q loss of heterozygosity and 1q gain have prognostic relevance in risk stratification; molecular testing is protocol-dependent. Treatment effect and sampling may alter component proportions; report anaplasia and treatment response where applicable. Germ cell tumors of the kidney Miscellaneous renal tumors Renal parenchyma; primary intrarenal location must be established. Usually prepubertal-type teratoma; yolk sac tumor or mixed teratoma–yolk sac tumor is exceptional. Germ cell tumor arising within renal parenchyma; exclude a metastatic or contiguous primary elsewhere. Teratoma shows mature or immature tissues from multiple germ layers. Yolk sac tumor shows reticular/microcystic, papillary, or other patterns with characteristic tumor cells. Yolk sac tumor: SALL4, glypican-3, and AFP may support diagnosis; use morphology and serum markers as appropriate. Age and primitive morphology overlap; germ cell differentiation markers and teratomatous elements help. Clinical and radiologic exclusion of gonadal/mediastinal primary is essential. The supplied WHO text notes absence of chromosome 12p abnormalities in renal germ cell tumors. Do not assume a renal germ cell tumor is primary without excluding another primary site. Use morphology, IHC, molecular findings, and clinical context together. Diagnostic entities Molecularly defined groups in comparison table Entities in IHC comparison table Diagnostic priorities First establish renal epithelial differentiation (PAX8) and correlate with imaging and clinical history. Use architecture and cytology to orient the differential; avoid diagnosing a subtype from one architectural pattern alone. In eosinophilic or high-grade tumors, actively exclude FH-deficient RCC, SDH-deficient RCC, MiT family tumors, ESC-RCC, and collecting duct carcinoma as appropriate. Apply entity-directed IHC panels and confirm molecularly defined entities with the appropriate genetic assay. WHO/ISUP grading has validated clinical applicability for clear cell and papillary RCC; it is not applicable to chromophobe RCC. Practical differential diagnosis workflow Clear-cell tumors Diffuse box-like CAIX with limited CK7 and CD10 positivity favors CCRCC. Diffuse CK7 with cup-shaped CAIX favors clear cell papillary renal cell tumor. In younger patients or unusual papillary/nested tumors, exclude TFE3/TFEB-rearranged RCC. Eosinophilic / oncocytic tumors KIT and CK7 patterns help separate ChRCC from oncocytoma, but sampling heterogeneity can limit core biopsy. Use SDHB in unusual eosinophilic tumors; loss is required for SDH-deficient RCC. Use FH and 2SC for high-grade, papillary, or tubulocystic tumors suspicious for FH deficiency. CK20 and cathepsin K support ESC-RCC in the appropriate morphology. High-grade medullary tumors CDC is a diagnosis of exclusion; assess PAX8, 34βE12, p63/GATA3, FH, and INI1. INI1 loss in a young patient with sickle cell trait strongly supports renal medullary carcinoma. ALK-positive renal carcinoma requires molecular confirmation of ALK rearrangement. title: Seminal Vesicle Tumors
content: use client Cystadenoma of the Seminal Vesicle Glandular neoplasm Benign Confined to the seminal vesicle. Reported in men aged 23–66 years. Usually presents with obstructive urinary symptoms. May be detected as an asymptomatic mass. Can form a large cystic or partly solid mass. Lesion is centered in and confined to the seminal vesicle. Variably sized cysts and glandular spaces are present. Cysts are lined by bland cuboidal epithelium without significant cytologic atypia. Glands show a lobular arrangement with branching lumina in scant stroma. No destructive stromal invasion or malignant epithelial component is identified. Variably sized glandular spaces form branching lumina and cysts. The glands are arranged in a lobular pattern. The lining consists of bland cuboidal epithelial cells. Cystic spaces often contain granular intraluminal secretions. The intervening stroma is scant. Epithelial cells are positive for cytokeratins. PSA and PAP are negative in the epithelial component. Calretinin is negative in the epithelial component. Focal luminal AMACR positivity may occur. Stromal cells may show weak SMA expression and are negative for S100. No diagnostically useful recurrent molecular alteration is established. Seminal vesicle mixed epithelial and stromal tumor Cystadenoma has scant stroma; MEST has a more prominent, often hypercellular stromal component accompanying benign glands and cysts. Primary seminal vesicle adenocarcinoma Adenocarcinoma shows malignant cytology and invasive growth; cystadenoma has bland cuboidal lining and lacks destructive invasion. Cystic lesions of adjacent organs Establish the anatomic epicenter and relationship to the seminal vesicle, prostate, bladder, and rectum. A large cystic mass may obscure its site of origin; correlate with imaging and operative findings. Focal AMACR staining alone does not establish prostatic adenocarcinoma. Adenocarcinoma of the Seminal Vesicle Malignant Centered in the seminal vesicle; may extend into adjacent structures. Usually occurs in men aged 40–70 years; mean age at diagnosis is approximately 62 years. Common presentations include urinary obstruction and hematuria. Hematospermia occurs less commonly. Often forms a large cystic or solid mass and may be bilateral. Tumor is centered in the seminal vesicle or, in a large mass, has a seminal vesicle epicenter. A malignant gland-forming epithelial neoplasm is present. Papillary-glandular and/or trabecular architecture supports the diagnosis. Clinical and pathologic evaluation excludes direct extension from prostate, bladder, or rectum and excludes metastasis from another site. An immunophenotype supporting seminal vesicle origin is present in the appropriate morphologic and clinical setting. Tumor shows glandular differentiation, often with papillary, trabecular, and complex glandular growth. A papillary clear-cell pattern may occur. Hobnail tumor cells may be present. Goblet cells and mucin production may be identified. Tumor cells are typically positive for PAX8, CK7, CEA, and CA125. PSA, PAP, NKX3.1, P501S, and androgen receptor are typically negative. p63 and GATA3 are typically negative, helping to distinguish from urothelial carcinoma in the appropriate setting. WT1, calretinin, and CDX2 are typically negative. CK20 may be positive or negative. AMACR is usually negative but may show focal positivity. No established recurrent molecular alteration is currently used to define this diagnosis. Serum CA125 may be useful for monitoring recurrence in selected patients; it is not a defining molecular test. Prostatic adenocarcinoma involving seminal vesicle Usually expresses prostate-lineage markers such as NKX3.1, PSA, PAP, and/or P501S; correlate with a prostate primary and pattern of spread. Urothelial carcinoma of bladder involving seminal vesicle Usually shows urothelial differentiation, including GATA3 and/or p63 expression; assess for a bladder primary and direct extension. Colorectal adenocarcinoma involving seminal vesicle Usually expresses intestinal markers such as CDX2 and often CK20; establish whether the tumor is secondary. Primary seminal vesicle squamous cell carcinoma Shows squamous differentiation and keratinization rather than gland-forming architecture. Other clear-cell or papillary adenocarcinomas Use the anatomic epicenter, clinical evaluation, mucin production, and a lineage-directed immunohistochemical panel. Primary seminal vesicle adenocarcinoma is a diagnosis of exclusion; direct extension from prostate is much more common. A PAX8-positive, CK7-positive phenotype supports but does not independently prove seminal vesicle origin. Large tumors may obscure the site of origin; imaging and operative findings are essential. Seminal vesicle involvement by prostatic carcinoma is staged as pT3b and has important prognostic significance. Squamous Cell Carcinoma of the Seminal Vesicle Squamous neoplasm Seminal vesicle; reported cases have been unilateral. Reported in men aged 26–69 years, with a mean age of approximately 52 years. Gross hematuria is the most frequent presentation. Other presentations include hematospermia, dysuria, and bladder outlet obstruction. Serum PSA is typically normal. Tumor is centered in the seminal vesicle. Malignant squamous morphology with keratinization is present. No glandular differentiation or mucin secretion is identified. Direct extension from an adjacent organ and metastasis from another squamous carcinoma are excluded. Keratinizing squamous cell carcinoma may form cystic spaces of variable size. Marked chronic inflammation commonly accompanies the tumor. Foci of squamous metaplasia may be present in adjacent epithelium. Tumor cells are positive for p63. Tumor cells are positive for CK5/6. CK7, CK20, PSA, and CEA are typically negative. Aberrant p53 protein accumulation has been described in metaplastic epithelium and carcinoma in an individual case; this is not an established diagnostic molecular feature. Bladder or prostatic urethral squamous cell carcinoma involving seminal vesicle Look for a primary tumor in the bladder or urethra and determine whether the seminal vesicle is secondarily involved. Prostatic adenosquamous carcinoma May contain a glandular component and arise in the prostate; assess the tumor epicenter and sample extensively. Metastatic squamous cell carcinoma Exclude a primary squamous carcinoma elsewhere through clinical history, imaging, and anatomic distribution. Squamous metaplasia with inflammation Metaplasia lacks destructive invasion, significant malignant cytology, and an infiltrative tumor mass. The diagnosis requires convincing seminal vesicle origin, not simply squamous carcinoma involving the seminal vesicle. Marked inflammation and adjacent squamous metaplasia may provide a clue but are not independently diagnostic. Mixed Epithelial and Stromal Tumor of the Seminal Vesicle Mixed epithelial-stromal neoplasm Usually benign; rare tumors may behave malignantly Centered in the seminal vesicle. Usually occurs in middle-aged or older men; reported age range is 39–82 years. Common presentations include obstructive lower urinary tract symptoms and hematospermia. Fever or abdominal pain may occur. A mass above the prostate may be detected on examination or imaging. Tumor originates in the seminal vesicle. A biphasic neoplasm contains both benign epithelial and spindle-cell stromal components. The stromal component is more prominent and often more cellular than in cystadenoma. Stromal cells commonly express estrogen and progesterone receptors. A prostatic stromal tumor or sarcoma incorporating epithelial elements is excluded. The tumor is well circumscribed and typically solid and cystic. Variably sized cysts are lined by cuboidal or columnar epithelium. Epithelial lining may show hobnailing, papillary infolding, or tufting. The stromal component is prominent and may be hypercellular. Stroma may condense around distorted glandular spaces. Rare tumors show stromal atypia and mitotic activity and may behave malignantly. Stromal cells are positive for ER and PR. Stromal cells may express vimentin, desmin, SMA, h-caldesmon, and CD34. Stromal cells are negative for inhibin, S100, and KIT (CD117). Epithelial cells are positive for CK7. Epithelial cells are negative for CK20, PSA, and PAP. Cystadenoma of the seminal vesicle Cystadenoma has scant stroma; MEST has a conspicuous, often hypercellular spindle-cell stromal component. Prostatic stromal tumor of uncertain malignant potential Establish the epicenter; prostatic stromal tumors arise in the prostate and may entrap or incorporate glands. Prostatic stromal sarcoma Look for a prostatic primary, malignant stromal features, and the relationship of epithelial glands to the stromal neoplasm. Fibroadenoma or adenomyoma of the seminal vesicle These exceedingly rare terms have overlapping features with MEST and should be interpreted in the context of the biphasic morphology. Do not classify a lesion as cystadenoma when the stromal component is substantial and hypercellular. Assess stromal atypia, mitotic activity, and necrosis carefully because rare tumors may behave malignantly. The anatomic epicenter is critical when distinguishing a seminal vesicle MEST from a prostatic stromal neoplasm. All PathologyGPS / Genitourinary Pathology / Seminal Vesicle Tumors Seminal Vesicle Tumors A morphology-first diagnostic reference focused on establishing the site of origin, recognizing the major primary neoplasms, and excluding secondary involvement from adjacent organs. Core diagnostic principle Establish the epicenter before assigning the primary site. Secondary tumors, especially direct extension from prostatic adenocarcinoma, are substantially more common than primary seminal vesicle neoplasms. Diagnostic approach 1. Confirm the epicenter Use imaging, gross examination, and the relationship to the prostate, bladder, and rectum to establish whether the mass arises in the seminal vesicle. 2. Exclude secondary tumors Prioritize direct extension from prostate; also consider bladder and colorectal carcinoma, as well as metastasis from another site. 3. Classify the pattern Separate bland cystic glandular lesions, malignant gland-forming tumors, keratinizing squamous carcinoma, and biphasic epithelial-stromal tumors. 4. Use targeted IHC For suspected primary adenocarcinoma, integrate PAX8, CK7, CEA, and CA125 with prostate, urothelial, and intestinal lineage markers. Important secondary involvement Secondary tumors involve the seminal vesicles considerably more often than primary tumors. Direct extension from prostatic adenocarcinoma is the most common source; seminal vesicle involvement is classified as pT3b. Bladder and colorectal carcinomas may also directly invade the seminal vesicles. Rare urothelial carcinoma may spread in situ along the ejaculatory ducts to the seminal vesicle. Benign mimics and interpretive pitfalls Developmental and acquired cysts, hamartomas, hyperplastic conditions, nodular calcification, and amyloidosis may mimic neoplasia. Seminal vesicle epithelium may show atypia and a small-acinar (adenotic) pattern in prostate needle biopsies. Spotty atypia, cytoplasmic lipochrome pigment, marked hyperchromasia, and intranuclear cytoplasmic inclusions favor seminal vesicle epithelium. Prostate-lineage immunostains can help resolve difficult cases.
