title: Testicular Adnexa Tumors
content: use client Serous Cystadenoma Ovarian-Type Epithelial Tumors Benign Adults, 35–73 years. Testis or paratestis. Usually cystic; may cause mass-effect symptoms or be incidental. Cystic lesion lined by a single layer of bland cuboidal or ciliated columnar epithelium. No epithelial stratification, significant atypia, or mitotic activity. No stromal invasion. Cysts contain serous fluid. Lining cells have abundant pale cytoplasm and bland nuclei. Positive: pancytokeratin, CK7, WT1, PAX8, ER, and PR. Negative: calretinin and OCT3/4. Ki-67 is low. Reactive mesothelial hyperplasia Usually lacks the characteristic Müllerian-type ciliated epithelial lining; calretinin positivity and PAX8 negativity favor mesothelial differentiation. No diagnostically relevant molecular alteration is established. Do not overcall focal epithelial crowding without stratification, atypia, or invasion. Serous Tumor of Borderline Malignancy Noninvasive; borderline Reported age range: 14–68 years, including children. Testis or paratestis; may be intratesticular or paratesticular. Presents as a mass. Hierarchically branching papillae with fibrovascular cores. Papillae are lined by stratified serous epithelium with mild to moderate atypia. No destructive stromal invasion. Irregular papillary formations show hierarchical branching. Stratified ciliated columnar cells have eosinophilic cytoplasm, dense chromatin, and prominent nucleoli. Mitoses are rare; psammoma bodies are uncommon. Positive: pancytokeratin, CK7, WT1, PAX8, ER, PR, CA125, CEA, and CK5/6. Negative: calretinin, CK20, OCT3/4, and TTF1. Usually lacks the organized hierarchical papillary proliferation; correlate with mesothelial markers. Well-differentiated papillary mesothelial tumor Mesothelial phenotype (calretinin, WT1, D2-40) and absence of Müllerian markers such as PAX8/ER favor mesothelial lineage. Epithelioid mesothelioma Invasion, cytologic atypia, and BAP1 loss and/or CDKN2A homozygous deletion support malignancy. BRAF mutations are reported in approximately 50% of cases; testing is not required for routine diagnosis. The defining distinction from mesothelial proliferations is the Müllerian-type epithelial phenotype together with the papillary architecture. Serous Cystadenocarcinoma Malignant Reported age range: 7–67 years. Presents with testicular enlargement from a solid or cystic mass. Serous-type epithelial neoplasm with unequivocal stromal invasion. Infiltrative papillary, tubular, or cribriform growth, often with desmoplasia. Exclude mesothelioma, rete testis carcinoma, epididymal carcinoma, and metastasis. Usually low-grade serous morphology; high-grade cases are uncommon. Papillary, tubular, or cribriform structures infiltrate desmoplastic stroma. Psammoma bodies may be present; an associated serous borderline component may be identified. Positive: PAX8, pancytokeratin, CK7, CK8/18, EMA, WT1, ER, BerEP4, and CA125. Negative: calretinin, CK20, inhibin, PLAP, CD30, OCT4, and AFP. Mesothelioma Mesothelial markers (calretinin, D2-40, WT1) support mesothelioma; PAX8 and ER support serous carcinoma. Adenocarcinoma of rete testis A hilar-centered tumor with transition from rete epithelium favors rete carcinoma; PAX8 may be positive in both. Adenocarcinoma of epididymis Establish an epididymal epicenter and exclude metastatic disease. Metastatic serous carcinoma Clinical history and imaging are essential; primary adnexal serous tumors are exceptionally rare. Invasion, rather than cytologic atypia alone, separates carcinoma from a borderline serous tumor. Mucinous Cystadenoma Reported age range: 11–78 years. Testis, paratestis, or spermatic cord. Usually painless testicular enlargement; occasionally pain, heaviness, or incidental detection. Cystic tumor lined by a single layer of mucinous columnar epithelium. No significant atypia, architectural complexity, necrosis, or stromal invasion. No teratomatous elements or background germ cell neoplasia in situ (GCNIS); extensive sampling is important. Lining resembles intestinal, gastric, or cervical mucosa. Scattered goblet cells may be present. Mucin extravasation and mixed inflammation may occur; invasion is absent. Columnar cells may express CK20 and CDX2; CK7 is variable. Goblet cells express MUC2. Scattered chromogranin-positive neuroendocrine cells may be present. Mucinous borderline tumor Shows epithelial stratification, cytologic atypia, and complex papillary architecture. Mucinous component of postpubertal teratoma Look for teratomatous elements or background GCNIS; 12p gain supports a postpubertal germ cell tumor. Metastatic gastrointestinal adenocarcinoma Clinical and radiologic correlation is required, especially when atypia or invasion is present. Absence of 12p gain can help exclude a postpubertal teratoma when the distinction is clinically relevant; it is not a defining alteration of cystadenoma. Extensive sampling is needed before diagnosing a primary benign mucinous cystadenoma. Mucinous Borderline Tumor Reported age range: 42–69 years. Usually presents with painless or occasionally painful testicular swelling. Noninvasive mucinous neoplasm with cytologic atypia and architectural complexity. Complex papillary projections and epithelial stratification are present. Any microinvasive focus is less than 5 mm in linear extent; exclude GCNIS and germ cell tumor. Usually cystic with papillary projections lined by gastrointestinal-type epithelium. Mild to moderate atypia is typical; severe atypia may qualify as intraepithelial carcinoma. Goblet cells, mucin extravasation, inflammation, dystrophic calcification, or metaplastic ossification may occur. CK20 is commonly positive. CK7 and CDX2 are variable. Mucinous cystadenoma Lacks significant atypia, epithelial stratification, and complex architecture. Mucinous cystadenocarcinoma Shows destructive stromal invasion measuring at least 5 mm in linear extent. Metastatic gastrointestinal tumor May share the same intestinal immunophenotype; imaging and/or endoscopy may be necessary. Somatic malignancy in a germ cell tumor Look for GCNIS, teratomatous elements, or 12p gain. No specific molecular alteration is established; absence of 12p gain may help exclude a postpubertal teratoma. Microinvasion is defined by each invasive focus measuring less than 5 mm in linear extent. Mucinous Cystadenocarcinoma Reported age range: 42–81 years. Presents with painful or painless testicular enlargement; ulceration or erectile dysfunction is occasional. Invasive mucinous carcinoma with cytologic atypia and architectural complexity. Back-to-back cribriform glands and papillary structures with destructive stromal invasion. Invasion measures at least 5 mm in linear extent; exclude metastasis and germ cell tumor-associated somatic malignancy. Cuboidal to columnar mucin-producing cells show mild to severe atypia. Back-to-back cribriform glands and papillary structures are characteristic. Goblet cells and mucin pools containing atypical cells may be present; benign or borderline areas may coexist. Typically positive: CK20, CDX2, and MUC2; CK7 is variable. Can be immunophenotypically indistinguishable; radiologic and endoscopic evaluation may be required. Mesothelioma with mucinous differentiation Calretinin, WT1, and CK5/6 support mesothelial differentiation. Assess for GCNIS and teratomatous elements; 12p gain supports postpubertal germ cell tumor origin. 12p gain testing can help identify a somatic carcinoma arising in a postpubertal teratoma; no defining molecular alteration is established for primary mucinous cystadenocarcinoma. Do not diagnose a primary adnexal primary solely from intestinal morphology and CK20/CDX2 positivity; metastatic gastrointestinal carcinoma must be excluded. Endometrioid Tumors Spectrum: borderline to malignant; stromal tumors also described Reported mean age: 68 years (range: 59–82 years). Intratesticular or paratesticular; one reported case arose in the appendix testis. Usually scrotal swelling; endometriosis may be mass-like or incidental. Establish endometrioid epithelial or endometrial stromal differentiation. Borderline epithelial tumors show atypical proliferation; carcinomas show confluent/maze-like or complex papillary growth. Endometrial stromal sarcoma shows endometrial stromal-type cells in an infiltrative multinodular pattern. Exclude metastasis or direct extension from adjacent organs. Endometriosis-like lesions show endometrioid glands and stroma surrounded by smooth muscle bundles. Borderline tumors are typically cystic with papillary architecture. Carcinomas show glandular, papillary, cribriform, or solid growth with variable atypia; squamous differentiation may occur. Low-grade endometrial stromal sarcoma resembles proliferative-phase endometrial stroma and grows in an infiltrative multinodular pattern. Epithelial tumors: CK7, PAX8, ER, and PR positive; CK20, CDX2, and GPC3 negative. Endometrial stromal sarcoma: CD10, IFITM1, vimentin, ER, and PR positive. Metastatic upper gastrointestinal or colorectal carcinoma Often CK20/CDX2 positive; correlate clinically and radiologically. Endometrioid-type yolk sac tumor GPC3 and CDX2 positivity favors yolk sac tumor. Rete testis adenocarcinoma Usually centered in the testicular hilum; demonstrate or seek transition from rete epithelium. Other ovarian-type epithelial tumors Use morphology and the CK7/PAX8/ER/PR profile to classify the epithelial differentiation. JAZF1::SUZ12 fusion was reported in one paratesticular low-grade endometrial stromal sarcoma; it is not an established routine test for the epithelial tumors. Keep epithelial endometrioid tumors separate from endometrial stromal sarcoma; their morphology and ancillary profiles differ. Clear Cell Adenocarcinoma Reported age range: 43–71 years (mean: 52 years). Intratesticular or paratesticular. Presents as a mass, sometimes with local or abdominal pain. Müllerian-type malignant epithelial tumor with clear and/or hobnail cells. Solid, tubulocystic, or complex papillary architecture. Exclude metastatic renal cell carcinoma and mesothelioma. Polygonal, columnar, or hobnail cells have clear cytoplasm. Growth may be solid, tubulocystic, or papillary. Nuclear atypia may be mild to moderate and mitotic activity may be low despite a high Ki-67 index. Positive: CK7, EMA, PAX8, and AR. Negative: WT1, CA19-9, CK20, calretinin, D2-40, ER, and PR. Ki-67 may be high. Calretinin and D2-40 positivity support mesothelial lineage. Serous carcinoma Often shows more prominent cellular budding and more frequent psammoma bodies. Metastatic renal cell carcinoma Correlate with renal imaging and clinical history; use a renal cell marker panel as appropriate. A low mitotic count does not exclude this carcinoma; the Ki-67 index may be high. Brenner Tumor Benign, borderline, or malignant Reported mean age: 53 years. Presents with scrotal swelling, sometimes with tenderness. Urothelial-type epithelial nests or papillary proliferation within fibromatous stroma. Classify by invasion: absent in benign and borderline tumors; present in malignant tumors. Malignant tumors are usually associated with a benign or borderline component. Benign: bland urothelial-type nests with elongated grooved nuclei in dense fibromatous stroma. Borderline: papillary atypical urothelial-type epithelium in cystic spaces or crowded nests without stromal invasion. Malignant: invasive nests of highly atypical urothelial-type cells with frequent mitoses. Reported ovarian counterpart: CK7, GATA3, p63, and uroplakin positive. Reported ovarian counterpart: CK20, PAX8, WT1, ER, and PR negative. Metastatic urothelial carcinoma Look for a primary urinary tract tumor and absence of a characteristic associated Brenner component. Brenner tumor shows urothelial-type nests and dense fibromatous stroma rather than serous or mucinous epithelium. Do not use cytologic atypia alone to classify a borderline or malignant Brenner tumor; invasion is decisive for malignancy. Adenoma of the Collecting Ducts and Rete Testis Collecting Ducts and Rete Testis Reported age range: 12–79 years. Centered in the rete testis at the testicular hilum. Usually a unilateral painless mass or incidental finding. Rete testis epicenter. Multicystic and/or solid lesion composed of dilated glands, papillae, and/or tubules in fibrous stroma. Bland nuclei, rare mitoses, and no destructive invasion. Usually cystadenomatous, with variably dilated cystic spaces lined by bland cuboidal to low columnar cells; cilia may be present. Transition to normal rete testis epithelium is a useful clue. Stratification, tufting, budding, and papillary structures may occur without significant atypia or invasion. Fibrous stroma may be prominent (cystadenofibroma pattern). No specific diagnostic immunophenotype is established in the described entity. Shows atypia, infiltrative growth, desmoplasia, and often necrosis. Sertoli cell tumor Sertoliform cystadenoma is now classified as a Sertoli cell tumor; assess sex cord stromal differentiation. Metastatic carcinoma A hilar epicenter and transition from normal rete epithelium support a primary rete lesion. Sertoliform cystadenoma should be classified with Sertoli cell tumors rather than as a rete adenoma. Adenocarcinoma of the Collecting Ducts and Rete Testis Usually adults; reported age range is broad. Centered in the testicular hilum/rete testis. Presents with a mass and/or pain, sometimes with hydrocele; local spread and nodal metastases are common. Tumor centered in the testicular hilum and arising from rete epithelium. Malignant gland-forming neoplasm with infiltrative growth. Exclude other testicular/paratesticular primaries and metastasis. Papillary, solid, glandular, cribriform, or glomeruloid patterns may be present. Cuboidal to columnar cells show nuclear pseudostratification and cytologic atypia. Desmoplasia and necrosis are common. Transition from normal to neoplastic rete epithelium is helpful when identifiable. Positive: CK7, AE1/AE3, EMA, vimentin, PAX8, and BerEP4. No specific lineage marker for rete epithelium is established. Use mesothelial markers and BAP1/CDKN2A assessment. Ovarian-type epithelial tumors PAX8 can overlap; correlate with morphology, site, and lineage markers such as WT1/ER or intestinal markers. Epididymal adenocarcinoma Establish the epicenter in the epididymis rather than the testicular hilum. Metastatic adenocarcinoma Clinical history and imaging are essential; bilateral disease, lymphovascular invasion, and interstitial growth raise concern for metastasis. Malignant Sertoli cell tumor Use sex cord stromal markers and morphology to exclude sex cord differentiation. PAX8 positivity is not specific for rete origin; diagnosis requires a convincing hilar epicenter and exclusion of metastasis. Adenomatoid Tumor Paratesticular Mesothelial Tumors Predominantly adults, especially in the fourth decade; any age can occur. Usually epididymis; also tunica vaginalis and other paratesticular sites. Usually a small, solitary, unilateral, well-circumscribed mass; often incidental. Paratesticular location, most often epididymal. Bland gland-like or vascular-like spaces lined by mesothelial cells. Mesothelial immunophenotype with retained BAP1. Rounded nodule composed of tubules and slit-like or microcystic spaces. Attenuated to columnar cells form thin bridging strands across lumina. Intracytoplasmic vacuoles and solid cords/clusters may occur. Fibrous, fibromuscular, or collagenous stroma; lymphoid aggregates are common. Infarction may produce regenerative atypia and mitotic activity. Positive: pancytokeratin, CAM5.2, CK7, calretinin, WT1, HBME1, BAP1, L1CAM, and podoplanin. CK5/6 and h-caldesmon are variable. Negative: endothelial markers, CEA, BerEP4, inhibin, and CD15. BAP1 expression is retained. Lymphangioma Endothelial markers (CD31, CD34, ERG) are positive in lymphangioma; adenomatoid tumor is keratin-positive and mesothelial-marker positive. Adenomatoid tumor is circumscribed and bland; mesothelioma shows destructive invasion and may lose BAP1 or CDKN2A. Metastatic signet-ring cell carcinoma Usually lacks the full mesothelial marker profile and may express epithelial carcinoma markers such as CEA. TRAF7 missense mutations are characteristic; L1CAM immunoreactivity can highlight this pathway. No homozygous CDKN2A deletion is expected. Do not mistake infarct-related regenerative atypia for malignancy; assess the overall circumscribed architecture and retained BAP1. Well-Differentiated Papillary Mesothelial Tumor Indolent; papillary noninvasive lesion Reported age range: 18–70 years. Arises from tunica vaginalis, usually within a hydrocele sac. Often associated with hydrocele; rarely presents as a discrete scrotal mass. Solitary papillary lesion arising from tunica vaginalis. Papillae are lined by a single layer of bland mesothelial cells. Absent or minimal stromal invasion; retained BAP1 and no CDKN2A homozygous deletion. Papillary structures have stromal cores and a single row of bland cuboidal cells. Nuclear pseudoinclusions are usually present. Mitoses are absent or exceptional. Complex architecture or increased mitotic activity argues against this diagnosis. Positive: calretinin, WT1, HBME1, D2-40, pancytokeratin, CK7, and CAM5.2. BAP1 is retained; CDKN2A homozygous deletion is absent. BerEP4 may be focally positive; CEA and CD15 are negative. Usually lacks a discrete papillary neoplasm with fibrovascular cores. Destructive invasion, cytologic atypia, and BAP1 loss and/or CDKN2A deletion support mesothelioma. Serous borderline tumor PAX8/ER positivity and calretinin negativity favor Müllerian-type serous tumor. BAP1 is retained; CDKN2A homozygous deletion and BRAF p.V600E mutation are not characteristic. Cytology alone cannot establish this diagnosis; architecture and invasion must be assessed in tissue. Mesothelioma of the Tunica Vaginalis Usually sixth to seventh decade; occasional pediatric cases. Arises from tunica vaginalis and may extend into testis and paratesticular soft tissue. Often presents with hydrocele; may be a palpable mass or incidental finding. Tunica vaginalis-centered malignant mesothelial neoplasm. Predominantly papillary, tubular, or tubulopapillary growth with stromal invasion; sarcomatoid or biphasic patterns may occur. Positive mesothelial markers; BAP1 loss and/or CDKN2A homozygous deletion are supportive. Usually epithelioid with papillary, tubular, and/or tubulopapillary architecture; solid areas may occur. Desmoplasia, moderate to marked pleomorphism, and mitotic activity are present. Necrosis is common in high-grade tumors. Approximately one third show biphasic epithelioid and sarcomatoid morphology; purely sarcomatoid tumors are rare. Mesothelioma in situ may line the tunica vaginalis. Positive: calretinin, podoplanin (D2-40), HBME1, WT1, thrombomodulin, pancytokeratin, and CK7. CK20 and CEA are negative; BerEP4 may be weak/focal. BAP1 loss and MTAP loss support malignancy; CDKN2A deletion can be assessed by FISH. Reactive/atypical mesothelial hyperplasia Lacks destructive invasion and usually retains BAP1/MTAP without CDKN2A homozygous deletion. Bland single-layer papillae without destructive invasion; BAP1 retained. Ovarian-type epithelial tumor PAX8 and ER support Müllerian differentiation; mesothelioma expresses mesothelial markers. Use clinical history, imaging, and a lineage-directed IHC panel. BAP1 alterations/loss and CDKN2A homozygous deletion are diagnostically useful; MTAP loss by IHC can serve as a surrogate for CDKN2A deletion. Germline BAP1 mutations have been reported. Demonstrate invasion whenever possible; cytologic atypia and mesothelial-marker positivity alone are insufficient to distinguish malignancy from benign/borderline mesothelial proliferations. Cystadenoma of the Epididymis Epididymal Tumors Age distribution is not well established. Usually located in the head (caput) of the epididymis. May present with a scrotal mass, infertility, or pain; bilateral cases occur. Epididymal-centered tubular and cystic lesion, sometimes with papillary areas. Single layer of bland tall columnar cells with eosinophilic cytoplasm. No mitoses, necrosis, pleomorphism, or other malignant features. Unilocular or multilocular cyst with a smooth surface and clear fluid. Tubules and cysts are lined by bland tall columnar epithelium. Papillary, microcystic, cribriform, or microglandular areas may occur without atypia. No specific immunophenotype is established. PSA and PAP are negative, helping exclude prostatic carcinoma. Papillary cystadenoma of the epididymis Shows cuboidal clear cells and papillary fronds; often associated with VHL. Metastatic prostatic carcinoma May mimic microglandular/cribriform areas but shows atypia/prominent nucleoli and PSA/PAP positivity. Shows cytologic malignancy and infiltrative growth. The distinction from papillary cystadenoma rests on tall eosinophilic columnar cells rather than bland cuboidal clear cells. Papillary Cystadenoma of the Epididymis Most often third decade; reported range: 12–81 years. Usually head of epididymis. Painless, slowly growing scrotal mass; may be found during VHL or infertility workup. Bilateral tumors are strongly associated with von Hippel–Lindau (VHL) syndrome. Epididymal location. Papillary fronds with fibrovascular cores and bland clear epithelial cells. No significant atypia, mitoses, or necrosis. Consider VHL, particularly with bilateral lesions. Papillae and cysts are lined by cuboidal to columnar cells with clear or vacuolated cytoplasm. Nuclei are small and round; prominent cell borders and occasional cilia may be seen. Luminal spaces may contain homogeneous eosinophilic colloid-like material. Stroma is fibrous, sometimes with focal hyalinization. Positive: cytokeratin, AE1/AE3, CK7, PAX8, and CAIX (cup-like basolateral pattern). Negative: CD10, calretinin, and WT1. PAS may highlight cytoplasmic glycogen. Clear cell papillary renal cell tumor Papillary cystadenoma may resemble it; CK7 positivity with negative CD10, AMACR, and RCC marker supports epididymal papillary cystadenoma. Epididymal cystadenoma Tall eosinophilic columnar cells rather than cuboidal clear cells and papillary fibrovascular fronds. Metastatic clear cell renal cell carcinoma Assess clinical history and renal imaging; renal cell carcinoma marker profile differs. VHL-associated cases may show 3p25–26 loss of heterozygosity and VHL gene mutations. Consider germline VHL evaluation in bilateral or syndromic cases. Bilateral papillary cystadenomas should prompt evaluation for VHL syndrome. Adenocarcinoma of the Epididymis Reported age range: 24–82 years (mean: 55 years). Arises within the epididymis and may involve paratesticular tissues. Presents with scrotal mass, hydrocele, and/or pain. Epididymal epicenter. Malignant glandular neoplasm with infiltrative growth. Exclude rete testis carcinoma, ovarian-type tumors, mesothelioma, and metastatic adenocarcinoma. Tubular, papillary, tubulopapillary, papillary-cystic, or sheet-like undifferentiated patterns. Cuboidal to columnar cells have clear to amphophilic cytoplasm. Stromal invasion, necrosis, and psammoma bodies may be present. Clear cell or mucinous differentiation may occur. Positive: EMA, CEA, PAX8, PAX2, and villin. Mucinous/clear cell variants may express CK20 and CK7. Negative: WT1, CDX2, AMACR, PSA, and RCC marker. Use calretinin, WT1, D2-40, BAP1, and MTAP/CDKN2A assessment. Ovarian-type serous or mucinous cystadenocarcinoma Compare Müllerian or intestinal phenotype and establish the site of origin. Centered in the testicular hilum rather than the epididymis. Clinical history and imaging are essential; some metastatic tumors share the same immunophenotype. PAX8/PAX2 positivity does not independently establish epididymal origin; the anatomic epicenter and exclusion of metastasis are essential. Squamous Cell Carcinoma of the Epididymis / Paratesticular Region Reported age range: 27–85 years. Reported primary sites include epididymis and tunica vaginalis lining a chronic hydrocele. Presents as a hard scrotal mass, with or without hydrocele. Malignant squamous epithelial neoplasm with cytologic and architectural atypia. Establish an epididymal/paratesticular epicenter. Exclude direct extension from scrotal skin/adnexal carcinoma and metastasis. Pleomorphic squamous cells may occur singly or in groups. Keratinization, nuclear hyperchromasia, and eosinophilic to clear cytoplasm may be present. Mitoses, necrosis, and lymphovascular invasion may occur. Intercellular bridges may be inconspicuous or absent. No specific immunophenotype is established in the described cases; use a squamous differentiation panel as appropriate. Direct extension from scrotal skin or skin adnexal SCC Look for an epidermal/skin adnexal primary and a contiguous route of spread. Somatic-type malignancy in a teratoma Look for associated teratomatous elements and evidence of a germ cell tumor. Metastatic SCC Exclude a primary at another site by clinical and radiologic correlation. Primary epididymal SCC is exceptionally rare; a thorough clinical search for another primary site is mandatory. Melanotic Neuroectodermal Tumor of the Epididymis Intermediate; occasional metastasis Usually infants in the first few months of life; reported up to 8 years. Epididymis or paratesticular tissue; occasional testicular, rete testis, or spermatic cord involvement. Firm, painless, rapidly growing scrotal mass, often with hydrocele. Pediatric tumor with two distinct cell populations in fibrous stroma. Large melanin-containing epithelioid cells and small hyperchromatic neuroblast-like cells. Atypical mitoses and necrosis are absent in typical cases. Catecholamine metabolites and urinary VMA/HVA may be elevated. Biphasic architecture: nests, cords, glands, or pseudoalveolar spaces in fibrocollagenous stroma. Large peripheral epithelioid cells have abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm and variable melanin pigment. Small central neuroblast-like cells have scant cytoplasm and hyperchromatic nuclei. Atypical mitoses and necrosis are absent in typical lesions. Small cells: CD57, NSE, NB84, and synaptophysin positive; weak PAX5, S100, CD99, and calretinin may occur. Large cells: pancytokeratin, vimentin, NSE, HMB45, DBH, and EMA positive. Melanoma Usually lacks the characteristic biphasic epithelial/neuroblast-like pattern; correlate with melanocytic markers and morphology. Neuroblastoma Lacks the melanin-containing epithelioid cell population and epithelial component. Alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma Desmin and myogenin/MyoD1 support rhabdomyoblastic differentiation. Lymphoma Leukocyte markers establish hematolymphoid lineage. DSRCT / Ewing sarcoma Use morphology and lineage-directed immunohistochemistry/molecular testing to exclude these small round cell tumors. No molecular pathology data are established for genitourinary cases. The large melanin-containing cell population is essential; sparse large cells in cytology may lead to misclassification as a malignant small round cell tumor. All PathologyGPS / Genitourinary Pathology Testicular Adnexa Tumors A morphology-first diagnostic reference to epithelial, mesothelial, rete testis, and epididymal tumors, emphasizing essential criteria and practical differential diagnosis. Core diagnostic principle Establish the anatomic epicenter, lineage, and presence or absence of invasion. Primary adnexal carcinomas are rare. Excluding metastasis and direct extension is essential before assigning a primary site. Diagnostic GPS: from anatomic site to classification 1. Establish the epicenter Rete testis/hilum, epididymis, tunica vaginalis, testis, or paratesticular soft tissue. 2. Identify the lineage Müllerian-type epithelial, intestinal-type mucinous, mesothelial, urothelial-type, or other epithelial differentiation. 3. Assess architecture Cystic, papillary, tubular, cribriform, solid, or biphasic; evaluate the stromal interface. 4. Determine behavior Look specifically for destructive stromal invasion, desmoplasia, necrosis, mitotic activity, and lymphovascular invasion. 5. Exclude secondary disease Correlate with clinical history and imaging; consider prostate, gastrointestinal, renal, lung, skin, and other primary sites. High-yield diagnostic distinctions Diagnostic problem Key distinction Useful ancillary findings Serous borderline tumor vs mesothelial proliferation Hierarchical papillae with stratified serous epithelium vs bland mesothelial papillae or reactive proliferation. PAX8/ER/PR support serous lineage; calretinin/D2-40 support mesothelial lineage. Mucinous benign/borderline vs carcinoma No atypia/complexity in cystadenoma; atypical complex noninvasive epithelium in borderline tumor; destructive invasion in carcinoma. CK20, CDX2, and MUC2 commonly support intestinal differentiation but do not distinguish primary from metastatic disease. Rete adenoma vs rete adenocarcinoma Bland, noninfiltrative rete-centered cystic/tubular proliferation vs atypical infiltrative carcinoma with desmoplasia and necrosis. Transition from normal rete epithelium is helpful; no specific rete-lineage marker is established. WD papillary mesothelial tumor vs mesothelioma Bland single-layer papillae without destructive invasion vs invasive, atypical mesothelial neoplasm. BAP1 retention and absence of CDKN2A deletion support WDPMT; BAP1/MTAP loss or CDKN2A deletion supports mesothelioma. Epididymal papillary cystadenoma vs cystadenoma Clear cuboidal cells and papillary fibrovascular cores vs tall eosinophilic columnar lining. Bilateral papillary cystadenomas should prompt consideration of VHL syndrome. Ancillary testing: practical use Müllerian-type epithelial tumors PAX8, ER, and PR support Müllerian differentiation. Calretinin and D2-40 help assess mesothelial lineage. Intestinal markers (CK20, CDX2, MUC2) identify mucinous differentiation but cannot by themselves distinguish a primary adnexal tumor from a gastrointestinal metastasis. Mesothelial proliferations Calretinin, WT1, and D2-40 support mesothelial lineage. BAP1 and MTAP immunohistochemistry and CDKN2A FISH can help distinguish malignant mesothelioma from benign or borderline proliferations. Epididymal papillary cystadenoma Bilateral tumors raise the possibility of VHL syndrome. CAIX with a cup-like basolateral pattern and PAX8/CK7 positivity support the diagnosis in the appropriate morphology. Germ cell tumor exclusion When mucinous tumors raise concern for somatic-type malignancy arising in a postpubertal teratoma, extensively sample the background testis and assess for GCNIS and 12p gain when indicated. Grossing, sampling, and reporting checklist Document the precise anatomic epicenter: rete testis/hilum, epididymis, tunica vaginalis, testicular parenchyma, or paratesticular soft tissue. For cystic lesions, sample the entire epithelial lining when feasible, including papillary excrescences, mural nodules, thickened areas, and solid components. For suspected carcinoma, extensively sample the tumor–stroma interface to identify and document destructive invasion. Submit the interface with testicular parenchyma and rete testis to establish the site of origin and assess transition from native epithelium. For mucinous tumors, search for teratomatous elements and background GCNIS; consider 12p testing when germ cell tumor origin is in the differential. For tunica vaginalis lesions, document papillary versus solid growth, invasion into testis or soft tissue, lymphovascular invasion, and any sarcomatoid component. For bilateral epididymal papillary cystadenomas, communicate the potential association with VHL syndrome. In the final diagnosis, state the tumor type, behavior, anatomic epicenter, invasion status, and relevant ancillary results. Scope note: This reference covers epithelial, mesothelial, rete testis, and epididymal tumors of the testicular adnexa. Paratesticular soft tissue tumors are classified with mesenchymal tumors. Ancillary tests should be interpreted with morphology, anatomic location, and clinical/radiologic findings.

title: Testis Tumors
content: use client Germ cell neoplasia in situ (GCNIS) Germ cell precursor Preinvasive Seminiferous tubules of the postpubertal testis Usually asymptomatic; may be detected during infertility workup or in the background testicular parenchyma adjacent to an invasive germ cell tumor. May be bilateral in a small minority of cases. Atypical gonocyte-like cells occupy the spermatogonial niche along the seminiferous tubular basement membrane. Cells show clear cytoplasm, enlarged angulated nuclei, coarse chromatin, and prominent nucleoli. A reliable diagnosis requires immunohistochemistry in the appropriate clinical setting. Neoplastic cells line the tubules in a characteristic single-layer, string-of-beads arrangement. Affected tubules may show multilayering, luminal floating cells, or pagetoid spread into adjacent tubules and rete testis. OCT3/4, SALL4, PLAP, SOX17, AP-2γ, and KIT are useful positive markers; expression may be heterogeneous. OCT3/4 and SOX17 support GCNIS over normal or maturing germ cells. GCNIS is typically hypomethylated and shares an embryonic germ-cell-like molecular profile. Gain of chromosome 12p is characteristic of invasive germ cell tumors and is generally absent in GCNIS. Normal/delayed-maturation gonocytes Interpret age and developmental context; immature gonocytes may retain embryonic markers in prepubertal testes. Arrested spermatogonia Usually lack the full GCNIS immunophenotype and cytologic atypia. Intratubular seminoma Shows more extensive intratubular growth; correlate with adjacent invasive tumor and immunophenotype. GCNIS can be patchy; a negative small biopsy does not exclude a focal lesion. Pagetoid rete testis involvement remains in situ and should not be mistaken for invasive tumor. Gonadoblastoma Germ cell / sex cord-stromal tumor Potential for malignant germ cell tumor development Dysgenetic gonad, including testis; often associated with disorders/differences of sex development Usually occurs in individuals with a dysgenetic gonad and a disorder/difference of sex development. May present as a gonadal mass; bilateral or multifocal disease can occur. Characteristic nests containing germ cells admixed with sex cord-stromal cells. Calcification is common and may be extensive. Assess for an associated invasive germ cell tumor, particularly dysgerminoma/seminoma. Nests of large germ cells are surrounded by smaller sex cord cells resembling Sertoli or granulosa cells. Hyaline basement-membrane-like material and calcification may be conspicuous. Germ cells express OCT3/4, SALL4, and other germ cell markers. Sex cord cells express inhibin, calretinin, and SF1. Often associated with Y-chromosome material, including TSPY, in the setting of gonadal dysgenesis. Molecular findings depend on the underlying disorder/difference of sex development. Seminoma/dysgerminoma Usually lacks the characteristic intimate admixture of germ cells and sex cord cells in nests. Mixed germ cell tumor Contains distinct germ cell tumor components rather than the characteristic gonadoblastoma nests. Large cell calcifying Sertoli cell tumor Lacks the neoplastic germ cell component and gonadoblastoma-type architecture. Search carefully for an invasive germ cell tumor component; its presence changes classification and clinical implications. Seminoma GCNIS-derived germ cell tumor Malignant Testis; typically young to middle-aged adults Most common invasive testicular germ cell tumor; median age is in the late 30s. Usually presents as a painless testicular mass; serum AFP should not be elevated by pure seminoma. Uniform large germ cells with clear-to-pale cytoplasm and distinct cell borders. Nests, sheets, or lobules separated by fibrous septa containing lymphocytes. GCNIS is usually present in adjacent testicular parenchyma. Syncytiotrophoblastic cells may be present and can account for a modest serum β-hCG elevation. Classic architecture is lobulated with fibrous septa and lymphocytic infiltrates. Tumor cells have round nuclei, prominent nucleoli, and glycogen-rich clear cytoplasm. Granulomatous reaction and scattered syncytiotrophoblastic giant cells may occur. OCT3/4, SALL4, SOX17, PLAP, KIT, and D2-40 are typically positive. CD30 and SOX2 are generally negative, helping distinguish seminoma from embryonal carcinoma. β-hCG highlights syncytiotrophoblastic cells when present. Gain of chromosome 12p, commonly i(12p), supports invasive GCNIS-derived germ cell tumor. KIT, KRAS, NRAS, and other pathway mutations occur in subsets; no single mutation is required for diagnosis. Embryonal carcinoma More pleomorphic cells, epithelial/glandular or papillary architecture, brisk mitoses; CD30 and SOX2 positive. Spermatocytic tumor Older patients, three distinct cell sizes, lack of GCNIS, and absence of typical seminoma immunophenotype. Lymphoma Discohesive cells in older men; leukocyte markers positive and germ cell markers negative. Yolk sac tumor Reticular/microcystic or other characteristic patterns; AFP and glypican-3 positive, OCT3/4 negative. Any elevated serum AFP argues against a diagnosis of pure seminoma and should prompt additional sampling/review for a nonseminomatous component. A small syncytiotrophoblastic component does not convert seminoma into choriocarcinoma. Testis; commonly part of a mixed germ cell tumor Typically affects younger adults than seminoma. Often associated with elevated AFP or β-hCG only when other components are present. Primitive malignant epithelial cells with marked nuclear atypia and brisk mitotic activity. Solid, glandular, papillary, or alveolar architecture; necrosis and hemorrhage may occur. GCNIS is usually present. Cells are crowded with overlapping nuclei, prominent nucleoli, and scant basophilic cytoplasm. Glandular and papillary patterns may show central necrosis; solid areas may mimic lymphoma or seminoma. OCT3/4, SALL4, SOX2, CD30, and cytokeratins are typically positive. SOX17 is generally negative, distinguishing it from seminoma and yolk sac tumor. CD117 is usually negative. Gain of chromosome 12p is characteristic of invasive GCNIS-derived tumors. Recurrent mutations are uncommon; molecular testing is not routinely needed. More uniform cells with clear cytoplasm and lymphocyte-rich septa; CD30/SOX2 negative and SOX17 positive. Usually OCT3/4 negative, often glypican-3 and AFP positive; broader architectural patterns. Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma CD45 and B-cell markers positive; germ cell markers negative. Mixed tumors may contain small embryonal carcinoma foci that are easily missed without generous sampling. Do not classify a tumor as seminoma if a convincing embryonal carcinoma component is present. Yolk sac tumor, postpubertal type Testis; commonly mixed with other germ cell components Usually occurs in young adult men. Serum AFP is commonly elevated and is useful for clinical correlation. Diverse patterns including reticular/microcystic, microcystic, glandular, papillary, solid, and hepatoid patterns. Schiller-Duval bodies, hyaline globules, or intracellular/extracellular basement-membrane-like material may be present. GCNIS is usually present in adjacent parenchyma. Reticular/microcystic architecture is common, with anastomosing spaces lined by primitive tumor cells. Schiller-Duval bodies are highly characteristic but not required. Hyaline globules may be PAS-positive and diastase-resistant. SALL4, glypican-3, and AFP are commonly positive; AFP may be focal. Cytokeratins are usually positive. OCT3/4 and CD30 are negative. Gain of chromosome 12p supports a GCNIS-derived tumor. No specific molecular alteration is required for diagnosis. OCT3/4, SOX2, and CD30 positive; yolk sac tumor is typically glypican-3 positive and OCT3/4 negative. Hepatoid carcinoma/metastasis Use clinical context and germ cell markers; AFP alone is not specific. Prepubertal-type yolk sac tumor Occurs in young children and is generally not associated with GCNIS or 12p gain. AFP immunostaining can be focal; a negative result does not exclude yolk sac tumor. In mixed tumors, estimate and report each component after extensive sampling. Choriocarcinoma Highly malignant Testis; usually a component of a mixed germ cell tumor Usually occurs in young adults. Often presents with markedly elevated serum β-hCG and early hematogenous metastases. Biphasic trophoblastic proliferation composed of mononuclear cytotrophoblasts and multinucleated syncytiotrophoblasts. Prominent hemorrhage and necrosis are characteristic. Pure testicular choriocarcinoma is rare. Biphasic trophoblastic cells surround hemorrhagic areas. Syncytiotrophoblasts have abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm and multiple hyperchromatic nuclei. β-hCG strongly highlights syncytiotrophoblasts. GATA3, inhibin, and cytokeratins may be positive in trophoblastic cells. SALL4 may be variable; interpret with morphology and other components. Usually GCNIS-derived with chromosome 12p gain. No specific molecular assay is required. Seminoma with syncytiotrophoblastic cells Scattered syncytiotrophoblasts are present in a seminoma background without a biphasic trophoblastic tumor or extensive hemorrhagic pattern. Placental site trophoblastic tumor Monomorphic intermediate trophoblasts, usually without the classic biphasic cytotrophoblast/syncytiotrophoblast pattern. Metastatic trophoblastic neoplasm Correlate with clinical history and testicular GCNIS-associated components. Extensive hemorrhage may obscure the viable tumor; thoroughly sample the peripheral viable areas. A few β-hCG-positive giant cells in seminoma are not sufficient for choriocarcinoma. GCNIS-derived trophoblastic tumor Testis; exceptionally rare Extremely rare testicular trophoblastic neoplasm in men. Serum β-hCG may be elevated but is not uniformly markedly increased. Proliferation of intermediate trophoblasts in cords, sheets, or infiltrative patterns. Cells have abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm and irregular nuclei. Distinguish from choriocarcinoma by the absence of a classic biphasic trophoblastic population. Mononuclear intermediate trophoblast-like cells infiltrate testicular tissue. Vascular wall involvement and necrosis may be seen. Cytokeratins and GATA3 are typically positive. Human placental lactogen and inhibin may be positive; β-hCG is variable. No defining molecular test is established for routine diagnosis. Biphasic cytotrophoblast and syncytiotrophoblast with prominent hemorrhage; strong β-hCG in syncytiotrophoblasts. Epithelioid trophoblastic tumor Nodular epithelioid growth with hyaline-like material and a different trophoblastic phenotype. Given the extreme rarity, exclude metastatic trophoblastic neoplasia and other testicular germ cell tumor components. Very rare testicular tumor; clinical presentation is generally an intratesticular mass. Nodular or nested growth of epithelioid intermediate trophoblast-like cells. Hyaline-like material and geographic necrosis may be present. The diagnosis requires exclusion of other trophoblastic tumors and metastatic disease. Tumor cells have distinct borders, eosinophilic cytoplasm, and relatively uniform nuclei. Nests and cords may be surrounded by hyaline-like material. p63 is often positive; β-hCG is usually limited or focal compared with choriocarcinoma. No routinely used defining molecular alteration is established. More infiltrative intermediate trophoblasts with hPL expression; epithelioid trophoblastic tumor is more nodular and often p63 positive. Biphasic trophoblastic cells and extensive hemorrhage with prominent β-hCG. Metastatic carcinoma Use clinical history and a broad epithelial/trophoblastic panel. The testicular occurrence is exceptionally uncommon; do not diagnose without excluding metastasis. Cystic trophoblastic tumor Malignant trophoblastic component Testis; usually encountered in mixed germ cell tumors Usually identified as a component of a testicular germ cell tumor. Cystic spaces lined by trophoblastic cells, often with cytotrophoblastic and syncytiotrophoblastic differentiation. Interpret in the context of associated germ cell tumor components. Cystic architecture is the defining pattern. Trophoblastic lining cells may show variable cytologic atypia and β-hCG expression. β-hCG highlights syncytiotrophoblastic differentiation. Cytokeratins are generally expressed by trophoblastic cells. No specific molecular test is required. Shows a solid biphasic trophoblastic proliferation with hemorrhage rather than a predominantly cystic pattern. May be microcystic but shows yolk sac tumor morphology and glypican-3/SALL4 profile. Assess the complete tumor because cystic trophoblastic areas may coexist with other germ cell components. Teratoma, postpubertal type Malignant potential in postpubertal setting Testis; often mixed with other germ cell tumor components Occurs in postpubertal males, usually young adults. May present as a solid or cystic testicular mass; serum markers depend on associated components. Mature and/or immature tissues derived from more than one germ layer, often with organoid differentiation. In postpubertal patients, teratoma is considered a malignant germ cell tumor even when composed entirely of mature tissues. Heterogeneous admixture of somatic tissues, including epithelial, mesenchymal, neural, and other differentiated elements. Immature neuroepithelium may be present; somatic-type malignancy must be actively sought. IHC is lineage-directed to characterize specific components rather than to establish teratoma itself. SALL4 may highlight associated germ cell components but is not expected in most mature somatic tissues. Chromosome 12p gain supports GCNIS-derived postpubertal teratoma. Somatic-type malignancies may acquire molecular alterations characteristic of the corresponding carcinoma or sarcoma. Prepubertal-type teratoma Occurs in young children, lacks GCNIS, and generally lacks chromosome 12p gain; usually benign. Somatic-type malignancy A distinct expansile malignant component must be identified and classified separately. Identify and quantify any accompanying seminoma, embryonal carcinoma, yolk sac tumor, or trophoblastic component. Do not call a postpubertal testicular teratoma benign solely because all sampled tissues are mature. Extensive sampling is required to identify small malignant components. Teratoma with somatic-type malignancy Testis, usually arising in postpubertal teratoma Usually occurs in adults and may present in a primary testicular tumor or metastatic site. The somatic-type malignancy may become clinically dominant, particularly after chemotherapy. Teratoma-associated component showing unequivocal carcinoma, sarcoma, embryonic-type neuroectodermal tumor, or another somatic malignancy. Classify the somatic malignancy according to its differentiation. Distinguish from ordinary immature teratoma and from a separate primary malignancy. A discrete malignant somatic component is present within or adjacent to teratoma. Common patterns include adenocarcinoma, sarcoma, and embryonic-type neuroectodermal tumor. Use lineage-specific markers according to the somatic malignancy; no single IHC profile defines the entity. Germ cell markers may be absent in the somatic-type malignant component. Chromosome 12p gain or i(12p) can support germ cell tumor origin, especially in a metastatic somatic-type malignancy. Additional alterations may reflect the specific somatic malignancy. Metastatic carcinoma or sarcoma to testis Look for an associated teratoma/germ cell tumor and chromosome 12p gain; correlate with clinical history. Immature teratoma Immature tissue alone is not equivalent to a somatic-type malignancy. Primitive germ cell phenotype with OCT3/4 and CD30, unlike a differentiated somatic malignancy. Do not use the obsolete term PNET; use embryonic-type neuroectodermal tumor for the relevant somatic-type malignancy. A somatic-type malignancy may be the only component sampled in a metastasis. Testis; typically young adult men Commonly presents as a testicular mass in young adults. Serum AFP and β-hCG depend on the component types and proportions. Two or more distinct germ cell tumor components are present. Identify and estimate the percentage of each component. Any seminoma mixed with a nonseminomatous component is managed and classified as a nonseminomatous germ cell tumor. Morphology varies according to the combination of components. Sampling should identify small embryonal carcinoma, yolk sac tumor, trophoblastic, and teratomatous foci. Use component-directed panels; OCT3/4/SOX17 support seminoma, OCT3/4/SOX2/CD30 support embryonal carcinoma, and glypican-3/AFP support yolk sac tumor. Chromosome 12p gain is typical of GCNIS-derived components. No single molecular alteration defines mixed germ cell tumor. A pure seminoma diagnosis requires exclusion of nonseminomatous components and correlation with serum AFP. Requires a distinct somatic malignant component rather than multiple germ cell tumor lineages. Contains germ cells and sex cord elements in a characteristic nested pattern, often in a dysgenetic gonad. Report the percentage of each component; even a small nonseminomatous component changes classification and clinical management. Regressed (burned-out) germ cell tumor Evidence of a regressed malignant germ cell tumor Testicular scar; may present with retroperitoneal or distant metastasis May present with metastatic germ cell tumor despite no obvious viable testicular primary. Often associated with a small scar or calcified focus in the testis. Fibrous scar with tubular atrophy, hemosiderin, coarse calcification, and/or chronic inflammation. Residual GCNIS or viable germ cell tumor may be present at the periphery. Clinical and imaging correlation is essential. A hyalinized scar replaces testicular parenchyma. Germ cell neoplasia in situ may persist in adjacent seminiferous tubules. IHC may identify residual GCNIS using OCT3/4, PLAP, and other germ cell markers. No IHC marker proves regression in the absence of residual tumor. Chromosome 12p gain in a metastatic lesion can support germ cell tumor origin. Nonspecific testicular scar Requires correlation with metastatic germ cell tumor and characteristic regressive changes. Infarct Usually shows geographic coagulative necrosis and reparative change. Granulomatous orchitis Shows granulomatous inflammation rather than a typical regressed tumor scar. A scar may be subtle; extensively sample suspicious fibrotic or calcified areas. Non–GCNIS-derived germ cell tumor Usually indolent; rare sarcomatous transformation Testis; typically older men Usually occurs in men older than 50 years, unlike conventional GCNIS-derived germ cell tumors. Often presents as a slowly enlarging testicular mass. Three characteristic cell populations: small, intermediate, and large cells. Absence of GCNIS and lack of typical 12p gain. Rare cases show sarcomatous transformation, which drives aggressive behavior. Diffuse sheets of cells with variable size and chromatin; intermediate cells predominate. Large cells may have filamentous or thread-like chromatin. Lymphocytes and fibrous septa typical of seminoma are generally absent. SALL4 and OCT2 are commonly positive. OCT3/4, PLAP, KIT, and SOX17 are typically negative, distinguishing from seminoma/GCNIS. DMRT1 and MAGE-A4 may support germ cell differentiation. No chromosome 12p gain; recurrent mutations involving FGFR3 and HRAS have been described. Sarcomatous transformation may acquire additional complex genomic alterations. Younger age, uniform clear cells, lymphocyte-rich septa, OCT3/4 and KIT positivity. Older age overlaps; lymphoma is CD45 positive and lacks germ cell marker expression. Spermatocytic tumor with sarcoma Look for an abrupt or distinct high-grade sarcomatous component. Do not misclassify as seminoma based on the word 'spermatocytic'; it is biologically and immunophenotypically distinct. Metastasis is exceptional in conventional spermatocytic tumor; search for sarcomatous transformation in aggressive cases. Teratoma, prepubertal type Usually benign Testis of infants and young children Typically occurs in infants and prepubertal boys. Usually presents as a painless testicular mass. Mature and/or immature tissues derived from multiple germ layers. No associated GCNIS. Usually lacks chromosome 12p gain. Mature organoid tissues are common; immature elements may occur. A mixed teratoma and yolk sac tumor may occur in the prepubertal setting. IHC is directed at specific tissue components; no single marker defines prepubertal teratoma. Usually lacks chromosome 12p gain, supporting distinction from postpubertal-type teratoma. Postpubertal-type teratoma Occurs in adults, is GCNIS-derived, and has malignant potential regardless of mature morphology. Shows primitive reticular/glandular patterns and AFP/glypican-3 expression. Mixed prepubertal teratoma and yolk sac tumor Identify and separately document both components. Age and absence of GCNIS are critical; do not extrapolate the behavior of postpubertal teratoma to this entity. Yolk sac tumor, prepubertal type Typically occurs in infants and young children. Often presents as a testicular mass with elevated serum AFP. Yolk sac tumor morphology in a prepubertal patient. Reticular/microcystic, glandular, papillary, and other yolk sac patterns may occur. Schiller-Duval bodies and hyaline globules may be present. SALL4, glypican-3, and AFP are commonly positive. OCT3/4 is negative. Usually lacks chromosome 12p gain, distinguishing it from postpubertal-type yolk sac tumor. Postpubertal-type yolk sac tumor Occurs in adults and is generally GCNIS-associated with chromosome 12p gain. OCT3/4, SOX2, and CD30 positive; yolk sac tumor is OCT3/4 negative. Hepatoblastoma/metastatic tumor Use clinical context and a panel including germ cell markers. Age, GCNIS status, and chromosome 12p status are important for classification. Testicular neuroendocrine tumor, prepubertal type Usually indolent; behavior depends on context Testis; commonly associated with prepubertal-type teratoma Rare; may occur in children or adults as a component of prepubertal-type teratoma. Often discovered incidentally within a teratoma. Well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumor morphology. Most cases arise in association with prepubertal-type teratoma. Usually not associated with GCNIS. Organoid nests, trabeculae, or ribbons of uniform neuroendocrine cells. Salt-and-pepper chromatin and granular cytoplasm. Synaptophysin, chromogranin, and INSM1 are typically positive. Cytokeratin is usually positive; assess associated teratomatous elements. No defining molecular test is routinely required. GCNIS-associated neuroendocrine tumor Consider teratoma with somatic-type malignancy and evidence of GCNIS-derived germ cell tumor. Metastatic neuroendocrine tumor Clinical history and imaging are essential; a teratoma association supports a primary testicular lesion. Leydig cell tumor Steroidogenic markers such as inhibin and SF1 support Leydig differentiation rather than neuroendocrine lineage. Do not assume every testicular neuroendocrine tumor is a primary conventional NET; search for an associated teratoma. Mixed teratoma and yolk sac tumor, prepubertal type Malignant because of yolk sac tumor component Occurs in prepubertal boys. Presents as a testicular mass; serum AFP may be elevated. Distinct teratoma and yolk sac tumor components. Classify and report both components. Teratomatous tissues are admixed with yolk sac tumor showing reticular, microcystic, or other patterns. The yolk sac tumor component may be focal and requires adequate sampling. Yolk sac tumor component is typically SALL4 and glypican-3 positive, with variable AFP. IHC in teratoma is component-directed. Usually lacks chromosome 12p gain, consistent with non–GCNIS-derived pathogenesis. Postpubertal mixed germ cell tumor Usually GCNIS-associated and often shows chromosome 12p gain. Pure prepubertal teratoma Lacks a yolk sac tumor component and has a different clinical risk profile. Extensively sample to identify a small yolk sac tumor component. Sex cord-stromal tumor Usually indolent; malignant behavior is established by metastasis Testis; intratesticular interstitial compartment Occurs across a wide age range, with peaks in children and adults. May present with a testicular mass, gynecomastia, precocious puberty, or hormonal symptoms. Bilateral lesions require evaluation for an underlying endocrine cause, including congenital adrenal hyperplasia. Well-circumscribed tumor composed of polygonal cells with abundant eosinophilic or granular cytoplasm. Reinke crystals may be present but are not required. Assess size, necrosis, vascular invasion, infiltrative margins, mitotic activity, and nuclear atypia for risk stratification. Sheets, nests, or trabeculae of steroidogenic cells with round nuclei and prominent nucleoli. Lipofuscin pigment and Reinke crystals may be seen. Reticulin fibers typically surround individual tumor cells. SF1, inhibin, calretinin, and Melan-A are commonly positive. Steroidogenic enzymes such as CYP11A1 may support Leydig differentiation. Cytokeratin is usually negative or only focal. Recurrent molecular alterations are not required for routine diagnosis. Selected cases may show alterations in pathways associated with sex cord-stromal tumors; no single defining test is established. Sertoli cell tumor Tubular/cord-like architecture and Sertoli phenotype; typically lacks the classic steroidogenic cytoplasm and Reinke crystals. Metastatic adrenal cortical neoplasm Clinical history and adrenal markers; correlate with bilateral or multifocal disease. Adrenogenital syndrome-related nodules Often bilateral/multifocal and associated with congenital adrenal hyperplasia; biochemical evaluation is essential. No single histologic feature reliably establishes malignancy; metastasis is the definitive criterion. Use mitotic counts per mm² rather than HPF counts when documenting risk features. Testis; intratesticular Occurs in adults and less commonly in children. Usually presents as a painless testicular mass; some cases are associated with endocrine manifestations. Tubules, cords, trabeculae, or nests of Sertoli-type cells. Cells have pale to eosinophilic cytoplasm and oval nuclei. Evaluate necrosis, vascular invasion, infiltrative margins, atypia, mitotic activity, and tumor size. Tubular or cord-like structures are characteristic, with variable stromal hyalinization. Reticulin generally surrounds groups or nests of tumor cells rather than individual cells. SF1, inhibin, calretinin, and nuclear WT1 are commonly positive. Cytokeratin may be positive, often in a variable pattern. Sertoli tumors are usually negative for germ cell markers such as OCT3/4. Most cases do not require molecular confirmation. Selected subtypes have syndrome associations or characteristic molecular findings; interpret in subtype context. More diffuse steroidogenic cytoplasm, Reinke crystals, and Leydig immunophenotype. Granulosa cell tumor Grooved nuclei and Call-Exner bodies in adult type; juvenile type has distinct follicular architecture. Metastatic adenocarcinoma Epithelial markers and clinical correlation; Sertoli tumor typically expresses sex cord markers. Sertoliform cystadenoma is classified within the Sertoli cell tumor spectrum when no convincing distinction is demonstrated. Do not equate bland cytology with zero metastatic risk. Variable; may be associated with Carney complex or other syndromes Testis; often multifocal or bilateral in syndromic cases Occurs in children and young adults; may be associated with Carney complex or Peutz-Jeghers syndrome. May be multifocal, bilateral, or hormonally active. Large Sertoli cells with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm. Prominent intratumoral calcification, often extensive. Assess for multifocality, bilaterality, and syndromic context. Large polygonal cells form nests, cords, or tubules around calcified material. Calcification may be psammomatous or coarse. Sex cord markers including SF1, inhibin, and calretinin are commonly positive. S100 and other markers may be variable. Consider germline evaluation in the appropriate syndromic setting, including PRKAR1A-associated Carney complex and STK11-associated Peutz-Jeghers syndrome. Leydig cell tumor with calcification Leydig morphology and steroidogenic phenotype; calcification is not typically as defining. Sertoli cell tumor, NOS Lacks the characteristic large-cell and calcifying morphology. Metastatic or paratesticular calcifying lesion Correlate with site and sex cord immunophenotype. Recognize syndromic associations and evaluate for bilateral/multifocal disease. Adult granulosa cell tumor Potentially malignant Testis; adult men Rare testicular tumor, usually in middle-aged or older men. Presents as an intratesticular mass. Microfollicular, trabecular, insular, or diffuse growth of granulosa cells. Grooved nuclei and Call-Exner bodies may be present. Assess size, necrosis, vascular invasion, infiltrative growth, mitotic activity, and atypia. Cells have scant to moderate cytoplasm and characteristic longitudinal nuclear grooves. Call-Exner bodies may be seen but are not required. Inhibin, calretinin, SF1, and FOXL2 are commonly positive. Cytokeratin may be variable. FOXL2 mutation status may be useful in selected cases, but ovarian-type FOXL2 mutation should not be assumed in every testicular tumor. Tubular/cord-like architecture and Sertoli morphology; granulosa tumor shows grooved nuclei and possible Call-Exner bodies. Steroidogenic cytoplasm and Reinke crystals; different marker profile. Metastatic granulosa cell tumor Clinical history and comparison with any prior ovarian or other primary tumor. Histologic features associated with aggressive behavior are imperfect predictors; metastasis remains definitive. Juvenile granulosa cell tumor Predominantly occurs in infants, often in the first year of life. May present as a testicular mass or hydrocele. Macrofollicular or irregular follicular structures filled with eosinophilic or basophilic material. Granulosa cells show round nuclei without the prominent grooves typical of adult granulosa cell tumor. Follicles vary markedly in size and shape and may be cystically dilated. Solid and trabecular areas may be present. Inhibin, calretinin, and SF1 support sex cord differentiation. Reticular/microcystic architecture and glypican-3/SALL4 expression; juvenile granulosa tumor shows sex cord markers. Nuclear grooves and Call-Exner bodies are more characteristic of adult type. More uniform tubular architecture. Age is a major diagnostic clue; avoid misclassifying as yolk sac tumor based on a cystic/follicular pattern alone. Fibroma-thecoma group Testis; rare Rare tumors occurring across a broad age range. Usually present as a well-circumscribed testicular mass. Spindle-cell fibroma or lipid-rich thecomatous differentiation. Reticulin stain helps distinguish thecoma/fibroma patterns from other sex cord tumors. Fibroma shows bland spindle cells in collagenous stroma. Thecoma shows cells with pale or lipid-rich cytoplasm. Reticulin may surround individual cells in this family. SF1 and inhibin may support sex cord-stromal differentiation. SMA and desmin may be variable depending on stromal differentiation. No routine defining molecular test. Sex cord stromal tumor, NOS Reticulin surrounds groups of cells rather than individual tumor cells in many NOS tumors. Myoid gonadal stromal tumor Coexpression of actin and S100 with spindle morphology; SOX9 negativity and lack of hyaline plaques support myoid tumor. Leiomyoma Broad fascicles, cigar-shaped nuclei, and perinuclear vacuoles with smooth muscle marker expression. Use reticulin architecture together with morphology and IHC; no single marker is specific. Mixed sex cord-stromal tumor Variable; malignant cases occur Testis; any age Rare; may occur in children or adults. Two or more recognizable sex cord-stromal components, such as Sertoli, Leydig, or granulosa cell elements. The components should be morphologically distinct and identifiable. Admixture of recognizable sex cord-stromal patterns. Reticulin and architecture may help identify individual components. Use a panel including SF1, inhibin, calretinin, and lineage-directed markers. IHC supports sex cord-stromal differentiation but may not resolve every component. Sex cord-stromal tumor, NOS NOS lacks recognizable specific differentiation; mixed tumor has two or more identifiable components. Germ cells are admixed with sex cord elements in characteristic nests, often in a dysgenetic gonad. Mixed germ cell/sex cord tumor Identify a genuine germ cell component and assess for gonadoblastoma-like architecture. Do not use NOS when distinct Sertoli, Leydig, or granulosa components are recognizable. Signet ring stromal tumor Reported cases have behaved benignly Testis; adults Reported in adults, approximately 29–69 years. Usually an asymptomatic intratesticular mass. Solid, well-circumscribed tumor composed predominantly of signet-ring-like cells. Cytoplasmic vacuoles are mucin-negative. Vimentin-positive and cytokeratin/EMA-negative profile supports the diagnosis. Thick fibrous capsule and thin septa divide the tumor into lobules. Tumor cells form nests and trabeculae in loose edematous stroma. Large cytoplasmic vacuoles displace eccentric nuclei; mucin is absent. Vimentin, nuclear β-catenin, cyclin D1, S100, CD10, NSE, and synaptophysin are reported positive. Inhibin, calretinin, actin, desmin, and Melan-A are typically negative. Cytokeratins and EMA are negative, helping exclude metastatic signet-ring carcinoma. CTNNB1 mutations have been identified. Metastatic signet-ring cell carcinoma Usually cytokeratin/EMA positive and mucin-producing; correlate with gastrointestinal history and imaging. Usually expresses sex cord markers such as inhibin/SF1; signet-ring stromal tumor is typically inhibin negative. Solid pseudopapillary neoplasm metastasis Pancreatic primary history and epithelial/β-catenin profile; testicular stromal tumor is mucin-negative and keratin-negative. Do not diagnose metastatic signet-ring carcinoma from vacuolated cells alone; demonstrate mucin and epithelial phenotype. Benign in reported cases Testis; mainly adults Usually occurs in adults, with a mean age around 40 years; rare pediatric cases are reported. Presents as a small intratesticular mass. Pure spindle-cell tumor lacking sex cord differentiation. Coexpression of actin and S100 supports the diagnosis. No or only mild atypia; lymphovascular invasion and necrosis are absent in reported cases. Short fascicles of fusiform cells with scant to moderate lightly eosinophilic cytoplasm. Residual seminiferous tubules may be surrounded, particularly at the periphery. Broad fascicles, cigar-shaped nuclei, and perinuclear vacuoles of leiomyoma are absent. Actin, S100, FOXL2, SF1, vimentin, and desmin are reported positive. Inhibin may be focal. SOX9 is negative; fibroma-like hyaline collagen plaques are absent. No diagnostic molecular alteration is established. Broad intersecting fascicles, cigar-shaped nuclei, and perinuclear vacuoles; usually lacks S100/FOXL2 coexpression. Fibroma Collagen bundles and hyaline plaques; SOX9 may be positive. Shows recognizable sex cord differentiation and a different architectural pattern. The essential pattern is a pure spindle-cell neoplasm with both actin and S100 positivity. Usually benign in children; malignant cases occur in adults Testis; children and adults Approximately half occur in children; the remainder occur in men of any age. Usually presents as a painless intratesticular mass. Tumor with incomplete or undifferentiated sex cord-stromal elements. Specific Sertoli, Leydig, granulosa, or other defined tumors must be excluded. Assess invasive margins, vascular invasion, atypia, mitotic activity, necrosis, and size. Variable epithelioid, ovoid, or spindle cells in nests, compact sheets, or fascicles. Reticulin fibers typically surround aggregates of cells rather than individual cells. Marked pleomorphism is uncommon in clinically benign tumors. SF1, desmin, vimentin, actin, S100, CD99, FOXL2, inhibin, and calretinin may be positive. Cytokeratins are generally negative in neoplastic cells, with rare focal staining. IHC supports lineage but does not reliably distinguish NOS from other sex cord-stromal tumors. No routinely useful defining molecular test is established. Reticulin may surround individual cells; correlate with collagenous or lipid-rich morphology. Sertoli/Leydig/granulosa cell tumor A specific line of differentiation should be recognizable morphologically and supported by IHC. Pure spindle-cell morphology with actin and S100 coexpression. Do not use NOS until specific sex cord-stromal entities have been excluded. Metastasis is the definitive criterion of malignancy; histologic risk features are not perfectly predictive. GCNIS Single layer of atypical gonocyte-like cells in the spermatogonial niche; string-of-beads pattern. Nests of germ cells admixed with sex cord cells, often with hyaline material and calcification. Uniform clear cells in nests/lobules with fibrous septa and lymphocytes. Pleomorphic primitive epithelial cells; solid, glandular, papillary, or alveolar growth. Postpubertal yolk sac tumor Reticular/microcystic and variable patterns; Schiller-Duval bodies and hyaline globules may occur. Biphasic cytotrophoblast and syncytiotrophoblast with hemorrhage and necrosis. Intermediate trophoblast-like cells in infiltrative cords/sheets. Nodular epithelioid trophoblastic cells with hyaline-like material. Cystic spaces lined by trophoblastic cells. Postpubertal teratoma Mature and/or immature somatic tissues from multiple germ layers; search for somatic-type malignancy. Teratoma with a distinct carcinoma, sarcoma, or embryonic-type neuroectodermal malignant component. Two or more distinct germ cell tumor components; quantify each component. Regressed germ cell tumor Hyalinized scar, tubular atrophy, hemosiderin, calcification, and/or residual GCNIS. Three cell populations of different sizes; diffuse growth, usually without lymphocyte-rich septa. Prepubertal teratoma Mature and/or immature organoid tissues in a young child; no GCNIS. Prepubertal yolk sac tumor Yolk sac tumor patterns in a child; no GCNIS. Prepubertal-type testicular NET Organoid nests, trabeculae, or ribbons; often associated with prepubertal teratoma. Mixed prepubertal teratoma/YST Distinct teratoma and yolk sac tumor components in a prepubertal patient. OCT3/4+, SALL4+, PLAP+, SOX17+, AP-2γ+, KIT+; variable intensity. Germ cells: OCT3/4+/SALL4+; sex cord cells: inhibin+/calretinin+/SF1+. OCT3/4+, SALL4+, SOX17+, PLAP+, KIT+, D2-40+; CD30−, SOX2−. OCT3/4+, SALL4+, SOX2+, CD30+, cytokeratin+; SOX17−, KIT usually−. SALL4+, glypican-3+, AFP often focal+, cytokeratin+; OCT3/4−. β-hCG highlights syncytiotrophoblasts; cytokeratin and GATA3 may be positive. Cytokeratin+, GATA3+, hPL may be+, β-hCG variable. Cytokeratin+, GATA3+, p63 often+; β-hCG usually limited/focal. Cytokeratin+; β-hCG highlights syncytiotrophoblastic differentiation. Teratoma / somatic-type malignancy No single profile; use lineage-directed markers for each differentiated or malignant component. Component-directed: seminoma OCT3/4/SOX17; embryonal carcinoma OCT3/4/SOX2/CD30; YST glypican-3/AFP. OCT3/4/PLAP may identify residual GCNIS; no IHC proves regression by itself. SALL4+, OCT2+; OCT3/4−, PLAP−, KIT−, SOX17−. Component-directed; no single defining IHC profile. SALL4+, glypican-3+, AFP variable/focal+; OCT3/4−. Prepubertal-type NET Synaptophysin+, chromogranin+, INSM1+; cytokeratin usually+. Yolk sac component: SALL4+, glypican-3+, AFP variable; teratoma component is lineage-directed. Sheets/nests of polygonal steroidogenic cells; eosinophilic or granular cytoplasm; Reinke crystals may occur. Tubules, cords, trabeculae, or nests of Sertoli-type cells; reticulin often surrounds cell groups. Large eosinophilic Sertoli cells with prominent intratumoral calcification; may be multifocal/bilateral. Microfollicular, trabecular, insular, or diffuse growth; grooved nuclei and Call-Exner bodies may occur. Irregular, variably sized macrofollicles; round nuclei without prominent grooves. Bland spindle-cell fibroma or lipid-rich thecomatous cells; reticulin may surround individual cells. Two or more recognizable Sertoli, Leydig, or granulosa cell components. Signet-ring-like vacuolated cells in nests/trabeculae, loose edematous stroma, and fibrous capsule; mucin negative. Pure spindle-cell tumor in short fascicles; may surround residual seminiferous tubules. Undifferentiated epithelioid, ovoid, or spindle cells in nests, sheets, or fascicles; reticulin surrounds aggregates. SF1+, inhibin+, calretinin+, Melan-A+; steroidogenic enzymes may support differentiation. SF1+, inhibin+, calretinin+, WT1+; cytokeratin variable; germ cell markers usually−. SF1+, inhibin+, calretinin+; other markers variable. Inhibin+, calretinin+, SF1+, FOXL2+; cytokeratin variable. Inhibin+, calretinin+, SF1+; cytokeratin variable. SF1 and inhibin may support sex cord-stromal differentiation; SMA/desmin variable. Use SF1, inhibin, calretinin and component-directed markers; no single profile. Vimentin+, nuclear β-catenin+, cyclin D1+, S100+, CD10+, synaptophysin+; inhibin−, calretinin−, cytokeratin−, EMA−. Actin+, S100+, FOXL2+, SF1+, vimentin+, desmin+; inhibin focal; SOX9−. SF1, desmin, vimentin, actin, S100, CD99, FOXL2, inhibin, and calretinin may be positive; keratins generally negative. All Entity Key features PathologyGPS / Genitourinary / Testis Tumors Testis Tumors A morphology-first diagnostic reference emphasizing essential criteria, immunophenotypic patterns, and practical differential diagnosis. Core diagnostic principle Classify germ cell tumors by lineage and pathogenesis; classify sex cord-stromal tumors by recognizable differentiation. Age, GCNIS status, chromosome 12p, serum markers, morphology, and targeted IHC must be integrated. Diagnostic GPS: start with age, lineage, and GCNIS status 1. Clinical setting Age, laterality, endocrine symptoms, serum AFP/β-hCG/LDH, and imaging. 2. Germ cell or sex cord-stromal Use architecture and cytology; select lineage-directed IHC rather than a broad indiscriminate panel. 3. GCNIS-related or not GCNIS and chromosome 12p gain support the postpubertal GCNIS-derived pathway. 4. Sample and classify Extensively sample heterogeneous tumors; identify and quantify every distinct component. Germ cell tumor classification GCNIS-derived tumors: seminoma and most postpubertal nonseminomatous germ cell tumors. Non–GCNIS-derived tumors: prepubertal-type teratoma, prepubertal-type yolk sac tumor, spermatocytic tumor, and prepubertal-type testicular neuroendocrine tumor. Any seminoma mixed with a nonseminomatous component is classified and managed as a nonseminomatous germ cell tumor. Postpubertal-type teratoma has malignant potential even when all sampled tissues are mature. Sex cord-stromal tumor behavior Most sex cord-stromal tumors are indolent, but metastasis may occur in tumors with deceptively bland cytology. Metastasis is the definitive criterion of malignancy; size, necrosis, atypia, vascular invasion, infiltrative margins, and mitotic activity are risk features. For mitotic assessment, report mitoses per mm² rather than relying on HPF counts. Bilateral Leydig cell–type lesions warrant biochemical evaluation for congenital adrenal hyperplasia and other endocrine causes. Germ cell tumors: histologic features Germ cell tumors: immunohistochemical profiles Typical profile / diagnostic use Sex cord-stromal tumors: histologic features Sex cord-stromal tumors: immunohistochemical profiles High-yield molecular pathology GCNIS-derived invasive germ cell tumors Gain of chromosome 12p, commonly isochromosome 12p; generally absent in GCNIS itself. KIT, KRAS, NRAS, and PIK3CA mutations occur in subsets; no single mutation is diagnostic. FGFR3 and HRAS mutations have been reported; chromosome 12p gain is typically absent. Consider germline PRKAR1A or STK11 testing when clinical features suggest Carney complex or Peutz-Jeghers syndrome. 12p gain in the malignant component can support germ cell tumor origin; additional alterations may reflect the somatic malignancy. Reporting and sampling checklist Document tumor laterality, size, focality, tunica albuginea, rete testis, epididymis, hilar soft tissue, spermatic cord, and lymphovascular invasion. Sample heterogeneous, hemorrhagic, necrotic, cystic, and solid areas to identify minor germ cell components and somatic-type malignancy. Report each germ cell tumor component and its estimated percentage; identify any seminoma/nonseminoma mixture. Correlate post-orchiectomy serum AFP, β-hCG, and LDH with histology; elevated AFP is incompatible with pure seminoma. For sex cord-stromal tumors, document size, necrosis, mitotic count per mm², atypia, vascular invasion, and infiltrative margins. For bilateral Leydig cell–type lesions, recommend clinical and biochemical correlation when appropriate. Diagnostic note: Immunohistochemical profiles are typical patterns, not absolute rules. Interpret stains with morphology, age, clinical findings, serum markers, and adequate sampling. Risk features in sex cord-stromal tumors are not fully reliable predictors of behavior.
