title: Non Urothelial Neoplasms
content: Squamous Neoplasms Separate benign squamous papilloma from verrucous carcinoma and conventional invasive squamous cell carcinoma by evaluating the epithelial lining and, critically, the deep interface. Squamous Papilloma Benign Exophytic papillary projections contain delicate fibrovascular cores covered by mature, keratinizing squamous epithelium. The squamous lining shows orderly maturation without significant architectural or cytologic atypia. No destructive stromal invasion is identified. p63 positive; CK7 and CK20 negative. Ki-67 is generally limited to basal cells, and p53 shows a wild-type pattern. HPV is generally not implicated. Verrucous carcinoma: papilloma lacks a broad, pushing invasive front and tongue-like downward projections. Conventional squamous cell carcinoma: papilloma lacks infiltrative nests, significant atypia, and destructive invasion. A papillary, keratinizing lesion may appear alarming endoscopically. The diagnosis depends on bland squamous epithelium and absence of invasion. Verrucous Carcinoma of the Bladder Malignant, locally invasive; usually indolent Exophytic, warty architecture with large, hyperkeratotic papillae and prominent acanthosis. The squamous epithelium is well differentiated, with minimal cytologic atypia; mitoses are rare. The deep interface is broad and pushing, with rounded, bulbous or tongue-like downward projections into the underlying stroma. The pushing invasive front contrasts with the small, irregular infiltrative nests and paradoxical maturation of conventional squamous cell carcinoma. IHC is not diagnostic. Focal EGFR and TGF-α expression and increased p53 staining have been reported. Squamous papilloma: no broad, pushing invasive front in papilloma. Conventional squamous cell carcinoma: look for irregular infiltrative nests, marked atypia, and destructive invasion rather than a smooth pushing border. Examine the entire lesion. A conventional invasive squamous cell carcinoma component can coexist and must be excluded before diagnosing pure verrucous carcinoma. Pure Squamous Cell Carcinoma of the Urothelial Tract Malignant Invasive carcinoma forms rounded to irregular nests; poorly differentiated tumors may grow as cords or single cells. Well-differentiated areas show abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm, keratinization, and intercellular bridges. Poorly differentiated areas show marked nuclear atypia and may lack obvious keratinization. Grading is based on differentiation/keratinization and nuclear pleomorphism; no universally accepted grading system is established. Schistosoma-associated tumors may show eggs (sometimes calcified), dense chronic inflammation, foreign body-type giant cells, lymphoplasmacytic inflammation, and numerous eosinophils. IHC is of limited value. Reported positive markers include CK5, CK6, CK14, desmocollin-2, desmoglein-3, and MAC387. GATA3, FOXA1, uroplakin-2, and uroplakin-3 are typically negative. Urothelial carcinoma with squamous differentiation: pure squamous carcinoma requires an exclusively squamous phenotype; search for a conventional urothelial component. Metastatic squamous cell carcinoma: exclude a primary tumor elsewhere. Verrucous carcinoma: conventional SCC shows irregular infiltrative nests and greater cytologic atypia. Do not use p16 as a surrogate for HPV in bladder squamous carcinoma. Urine cytology cannot reliably distinguish pure squamous carcinoma from urothelial carcinoma with squamous differentiation. Glandular Neoplasms The central questions are whether the lesion is benign or invasive, whether it is a primary urinary tract tumor, and which glandular phenotype is present. Villous Adenoma Benign; may coexist with or be associated with carcinoma Villoglandular fronds are lined by pseudostratified columnar epithelium resembling colorectal villous adenoma; tubular and tubulovillous patterns may also occur. Most show low-grade dysplasia. High-grade dysplasia, adenocarcinoma in situ, and invasive adenocarcinoma may be present. Adjacent urothelium may show cystitis glandularis, intestinal metaplasia, or squamous metaplasia. The entire lesion must be examined to exclude invasion and an associated malignant component. An enteric phenotype is common, with CK20 and CDX2 positivity. GATA3, PSA, and PAP are typically negative; P501S and PSMA may be expressed. Primary enteric-type adenocarcinoma: look for destructive invasion, desmoplastic stroma, high-grade areas, necrosis, or malignant glands. Urothelial carcinoma with glandular differentiation: identify any conventional urothelial carcinoma component. Metastatic colorectal adenocarcinoma: correlate clinically and radiologically. Do not diagnose a pure villous adenoma from a limited biopsy if the lesion is not adequately sampled. The source material reports invasive adenocarcinoma in a subset of cases. Urinary Tract Adenocarcinoma, NOS and Subtypes Enteric type: intestinal-type glands lined by pseudostratified columnar cells with nuclear atypia; villoglandular structures, mucin-filled microcysts, intracellular or extracellular mucin, and frequent necrosis may be present. Mucinous type: abundant extracellular mucin, usually comprising more than 50% of tumor volume, dissects the stroma; tumor cells occur singly or in small clusters floating in mucin pools. Signet-ring cell type: diffusely infiltrative cells contain prominent intracytoplasmic mucin vacuoles that displace nuclei to the periphery; linitis plastica-like growth may occur. NOS: malignant glandular growth that does not fit a specific subtype. Tumors with more than one pattern are classified as mixed. Adenocarcinoma in situ may be flat, papillary, glandular, or cribriform, with prominent atypia and frequent mitoses. Usually CK7, CK20, villin, and CDX2 positive. GATA3 may be positive in a subset, particularly signet-ring cell tumors. Nuclear β-catenin is less frequent in primary bladder adenocarcinoma than in colorectal metastases. Metastatic colorectal adenocarcinoma: a critical exclusion because it is more common; use clinical/radiologic correlation and a focused panel. Urothelial carcinoma with glandular differentiation: search for conventional urothelial carcinoma or CIS. Urachal adenocarcinoma: assess tumor epicenter, relationship to the bladder dome/anterior wall, and urachal remnants. A glandular phenotype alone does not establish a primary urinary tract origin. Exclude direct extension or metastasis from colorectal, prostatic, and gynecologic sites. Urachal Carcinoma Malignant; diagnosis of exclusion Most are adenocarcinomas. Enteric tumors resemble colorectal adenocarcinoma, with glandular and cribriform architecture, nuclear pseudostratification, and necrosis. Mucinous tumors show abundant extracellular mucin dissecting the stroma, sometimes with floating tumor cells or small clusters. Signet-ring cell carcinoma shows permeative stromal growth by cells with intracytoplasmic mucin. Cystic urachal tumors span a spectrum: benign mucinous cystadenoma has a single layer of bland mucinous columnar epithelium; low malignant potential tumors show mild epithelial proliferation and mild-to-moderate atypia; intraepithelial carcinoma shows marked stratification and unequivocal malignant cytology. Mucinous cystadenocarcinoma may be microinvasive (stromal invasion less than 2 mm and less than 5% of tumor) or frankly invasive. Rare non-glandular types include urothelial, squamous, and neuroendocrine carcinomas. Non-cystic urachal adenocarcinomas are usually CDX2 and CK20 positive; about half express CK7. CD15 and CEA are often positive; GATA3 is generally negative. Nuclear β-catenin, AMACR, and PTEN loss are uncommon. Non-urachal bladder adenocarcinoma: assess for a dome/anterior-wall or midline supravesical epicenter, sharp demarcation from surface urothelium, and urachal remnant association. Metastatic colorectal adenocarcinoma: exclude a primary elsewhere. Urothelial carcinoma with glandular differentiation: identify a urothelial component or associated CIS. Urachal carcinoma is a diagnosis of exclusion. Helpful features include a bladder dome/anterior-wall location, a deep tumor epicenter or sharp separation from surface urothelium, and exclusion of another primary site. Diverticular Carcinoma Malignant; any urinary tract carcinoma type may occur Histology resembles the corresponding carcinoma elsewhere in the urinary tract; urothelial carcinoma is the most common type. Other carcinoma types may be relatively more frequent in diverticula than in the main bladder. A key anatomic feature is that bladder diverticula lack a true detrusor muscle layer and may instead contain a hypertrophic muscularis mucosae. Non-diverticular bladder carcinoma: establish that the tumor arises within or is predominantly located in a diverticulum. Muscularis propria invasion: do not mistake hypertrophic muscularis mucosae for detrusor muscle. Because the diverticulum lacks detrusor muscle, pT2 cannot be assigned on the basis of invasion into a nonexistent muscularis propria layer. State the anatomic limitation clearly. Urethral Accessory Gland and Müllerian-Type Tumors These rare tumors require close attention to the anatomic site of origin and a differential-directed immunohistochemical panel. Littré Gland Adenocarcinoma Malignant; extremely rare Papillary or tubulopapillary adenocarcinoma. Tumor cells are columnar with abundant cytoplasm and mucinous vacuoles; nuclei are large and oval, without marked pleomorphism. The urethral surface epithelium should lack neoplastic changes; clinical and radiologic correlation is essential. Limited data; reported CK7 positivity and PSA negativity. Urothelial carcinoma with extensive glandular differentiation. Bladder or prostatic adenocarcinoma extending into the urethra. Metastatic colorectal adenocarcinoma. This is a diagnosis of exclusion. Confirm the relationship to the penile urethral glands and exclude a more common primary elsewhere. Skene Gland Adenocarcinoma Architecture and cytology closely resemble prostatic acinar adenocarcinoma. Tumors may show tubular or cribriform growth; cribriform areas may show pseudostratification. Solid, single-file, and occasionally intestinal-like patterns have also been described. The diagnosis depends on establishing a urethral accessory gland origin rather than a primary or extension from another site. Usually positive for PSA, PAP, and NKX3-1; AMACR and P501S may also be positive. Metastatic or directly extending prostatic adenocarcinoma. Other urethral adenocarcinomas. Urothelial carcinoma with glandular differentiation. The prostatic immunophenotype is expected and does not by itself prove a prostate primary. Correlate with the tumor's location and clinical/radiologic findings. Cowper Gland Adenocarcinoma Cribriform, trabecular, and solid patterns are described. Tumor cells may appear deceptively bland, with dark nuclei forming gland-like spaces; true tubules are uncommon. Gland-like spaces often contain mucoid material, and perineural invasion is frequent. Advanced tumors may destroy the gland, making confirmation of the site of origin difficult. CK7 and high-molecular-weight cytokeratin positive. PSA, PAP, CEA, S100, and SMA negative. MYB::NFIB fusion has been reported. Prostatic ductal adenocarcinoma. Basal cell carcinoma of the prostate. Do not assign Cowper gland origin on morphology alone. Confirm the bulbomembranous periurethral location clinically and radiologically; prostatic markers should be negative. Clear Cell Adenocarcinoma of the Urinary Tract Malignant; often clinically aggressive, stage-dependent Variable combinations of papillary, tubulocystic, and solid growth. Papillary fibrovascular cores may be hyalinized; myxoid stromal change is common. Tumor cells may be flat, cuboidal, or hobnail, with clear, glycogen-rich, or eosinophilic cytoplasm. Cytologic atypia is usually moderate to severe; mitotic activity and necrosis are variable. Some tumors may be deceptively bland and resemble nephrogenic adenoma. Usually CK7, PAX8, CA125, AMACR, HNF1β, and napsin A positive; CK20 is variable. Typically negative for GATA3, p63, 34βE12, PSA, ER, PR, and WT1. Nephrogenic adenoma: clear cell adenocarcinoma is favored by significant atypia, mitotic activity, invasive growth (especially muscularis propria involvement), hyperchromasia, and aberrant p53 staining. Clear cell/glycogen-rich urothelial carcinoma: PAX8 positivity and lack of urothelial markers support clear cell adenocarcinoma. Metastatic Müllerian clear cell carcinoma: correlate with clinical history and imaging. The overlap with nephrogenic adenoma can be substantial. Do not rely on clear cytoplasm or PAX8 alone; assess invasion, cytologic grade, mitoses, and p53 in context. Endometrioid Carcinoma of the Urinary Tract Malignant; exceptionally rare Glandular and back-to-back architecture resembling endometrioid carcinoma of the uterus. Glands are lined by large columnar cells with eosinophilic, granular cytoplasm, vesicular nuclei, and prominent nucleoli. Clear cell change, squamous nests, basaloid differentiation, or hobnail cells may occur. A key diagnostic clue is the coexistence of malignant endometrioid glands with benign endometriosis, including benign glands and endometrial-type stroma. Typically ER and PR strongly positive; CK7, CAM5.2, and EMA positive. CA125, PAX8, and PAX2 are variable. Urothelial carcinoma with glandular differentiation: typical urothelial carcinoma and intestinal metaplasia are not expected in endometrioid carcinoma. Urachal adenocarcinoma: endometrioid carcinoma is not characteristically centered at the bladder dome or anterior wall. Metastatic endometrioid carcinoma: exclude an extravesical primary. Look for endometriosis/Müllerianosis and a transition to carcinoma. Correlate with gynecologic history and exclude a uterine or other pelvic primary. Establish the exact site: bladder, urachus, diverticulum, urethra, or periurethral gland. Determine the dominant phenotype: squamous, enteric/glandular, mucinous, clear cell, endometrioid, or other. Assess architecture and cytology, then actively search for stromal invasion, desmoplasia, necrosis, and an in situ component. For warty squamous lesions, evaluate the entire deep interface and exclude conventional invasive squamous carcinoma. For glandular tumors, exclude direct extension or metastasis from colorectum, prostate, gynecologic tract, and other adjacent organs. Use IHC as a differential-directed panel; interpret markers with morphology and anatomic location. Document the tumor epicenter, relationship to surface urothelium or urachal remnants, and anatomic staging limitations. Specify the precise anatomic site and specimen type. State histologic type and subtype, if applicable. Describe the dominant architecture and cytologic features. Document the presence and extent of invasion. Report associated in situ disease or metaplastic background when present. For diverticular tumors, note the absence of a true detrusor muscle layer. For suspected primary adenocarcinoma, document exclusion of an adjacent or distant primary. Report lymphovascular invasion, perineural invasion, margins, and stage-relevant findings when applicable. true ← Urinary Tract PathologyGPS · Urinary Tract Non-Urothelial Neoplasms A morphology-focused guide to squamous, glandular, urachal, diverticular, urethral accessory gland, and Müllerian-type neoplasms of the urinary tract. Histologic Diagnosis Differential Diagnosis Immunohistochemistry Tumor Origin Sign-Out First question Where did it arise? Anatomic epicenter and relationship to the surface mucosa are essential, especially for urachal and accessory gland tumors. Second question What is the phenotype? Define squamous, enteric, mucinous, signet-ring, clear cell, endometrioid, or other differentiation before selecting ancillary studies. Critical safeguard Exclude another primary Primary urinary tract adenocarcinoma is uncommon. Exclude colorectal, prostatic, gynecologic, and other adjacent primaries. Diagnostic Workflow Histology Description • Diagnostic Pitfall Sign-Out Checklist □ Educational reference. Data for some rare tumors are limited; interpret ancillary studies in the context of morphology, anatomic location, and clinical findings.

title: Urothelial Tumors
content: Benign Papillary Neoplasms Recognize bland papillary or endophytic lesions and avoid overcalling carcinoma. Urothelial Papilloma Delicate, slender fibrovascular cores lined by bland urothelium of normal thickness (typically 6–7 cell layers), with preserved polarity and no cytologic atypia. Papillae remain separate without fusion. Exclude papillary/polypoid cystitis and examine the entire lesion, especially with prior urothelial carcinoma. Inverted Urothelial Papilloma Predominantly endophytic growth into the lamina propria, forming anastomosing cords and trabeculae of bland urothelium. Peripheral palisading and a smooth, pushing interface are typical; degenerative atypia may occur. Atypia, atypical mitoses, or an infiltrative interface argues against a benign inverted papilloma. Non-Invasive Papillary Neoplasia Grade is determined by the degree of architectural and cytologic disorder. Papillary Urothelial Neoplasm of Low Malignant Potential (PUNLMP) Complex papillary structures with branching and fusion, increased cellular proliferation, and thickened urothelium. Polarity is maintained, with no significant nuclear atypia. A history of urothelial carcinoma and marked cytologic atypia should prompt reconsideration. Low-Grade Papillary Urothelial Carcinoma Complex branching and fused papillae, usually with increased urothelial thickness and recognizable architectural and cytologic atypia. If the urothelium is not thickened, the diagnosis requires conspicuous cytologic and architectural abnormality. Do not grade by mitotic count alone. Confirm absence of lamina propria invasion. High-Grade Papillary Urothelial Carcinoma High-grade cytologic features may be focal: nucleomegaly, nuclear pleomorphism, irregular nuclear contours, clumped chromatin, and readily identifiable mitotic figures. Architectural disorder is usually marked. Cytology determines grade. Report as high-grade when the high-grade component is ≥5%; describe tumors with <5% as low-grade with a <5% high-grade component. Flat Lesions Distinguish high-grade intraepithelial neoplasia from reactive atypia. Urothelial Carcinoma In Situ (CIS) Flat high-grade malignant urothelial cells with pleomorphic, hyperchromatic nuclei, irregular chromatin, and loss of polarity. CIS may be partial-thickness, pagetoid, or clinging in denuded mucosa; papillary formation is absent. Urothelial Dysplasia Atypia considered neoplastic but insufficient for a definitive diagnosis of CIS. Diagnostic reproducibility is limited. Use cautiously and describe the findings when appropriate. Invasive Urothelial Carcinoma Identify invasion, document subtype and extent, and report treatment-relevant features. Conventional Urothelial Carcinoma Infiltrative urothelial malignancy; assess lamina propria, muscularis propria, lymphovascular invasion, and associated CIS. In TURBT, explicitly state whether muscularis propria is present and involved. Histologic Subtypes and Divergent Differentiation Consider squamous, glandular, trophoblastic, nested/large nested, tubular-microcystic, micropapillary, lymphoepithelioma-like, plasmacytoid, giant cell, lipid-rich, clear cell, and sarcomatoid patterns. Recognize and report subtype components because they may affect prognosis and management. Correlate morphology with a focused immunohistochemical panel. Confirm the anatomic site and specimen type; assess adequacy and orientation. Determine growth pattern: exophytic papillary, inverted/endophytic, flat, or invasive. Assess cytologic grade using nuclear features and architectural disorder—not mitotic count alone. Look carefully for lamina propria and muscularis propria invasion, lymphovascular invasion, and CIS. Use immunohistochemistry or molecular testing as an adjunct when the differential diagnosis requires it; morphology remains the diagnostic foundation. For papillary tumors with grade heterogeneity, estimate the high-grade component and apply the ≥5% reporting threshold described in this reference. CK20 CIS may show full-thickness staining; normal/reactive urothelium typically highlights umbrella cells. p53 An aberrant pattern may support CIS in the right morphologic context; wild-type staining does not exclude it. CD44 Often reduced or absent in CIS; retained basal staining may be seen in normal/reactive urothelium. Ki-67 May be increased in high-grade lesions; not a substitute for morphologic grading. GATA3, p63, uroplakins Can support urothelial differentiation in an appropriate differential diagnosis. true ← Urinary Tract PathologyGPS · Urinary Tract Urothelial Tumors A concise, morphology-first guide to urothelial neoplasia throughout the urinary tract, from benign papillomas to invasive carcinoma. Morphology Grade Invasion IHC Molecular Pathology Core principle Morphology first Histology remains the foundation for classification, grading, and diagnosis. Ancillary tests support—not replace—morphologic assessment. Papillary grade Three-tier system Distinguish PUNLMP, low-grade carcinoma, and high-grade carcinoma by architecture and cytologic atypia. Critical task Document invasion Separate non-invasive disease from lamina propria or muscularis propria invasion and document specimen adequacy. Papillary Lesions: Histologic Comparison The most useful distinction is the combination of papillary architecture, urothelial thickness, polarity, and cytologic atypia. No single feature should be interpreted in isolation. Entity Papillary architecture Urothelial thickness / polarity Cytology Urothelial papilloma Delicate, slender fibrovascular cores; no papillary fusion. Normal thickness, generally 6–7 cell layers; polarity preserved. No atypia; mitoses absent or rare and basal. PUNLMP Complex papillae with branching and fusion. Increased cellularity and urothelial thickness; polarity maintained. No significant nuclear atypia; cells remain relatively uniform. Low-grade papillary urothelial carcinoma Complex branching and fused papillary structures. Usually thickened urothelium with mild architectural disorder and focal loss of polarity. Mild but definite atypia: nuclear enlargement, limited variation, and occasional hyperchromasia. High-grade papillary urothelial carcinoma Often complex, branching, and fused papillae; architecture may vary. Marked architectural disorder and loss of polarity. Nucleomegaly, pleomorphism, irregular contours, clumped chromatin, and readily identifiable mitoses; high-grade features may be focal. Key distinction: papilloma vs PUNLMP Papilloma has delicate, non-fused papillae covered by normal-thickness urothelium. PUNLMP has more complex branching/fused papillae and increased urothelial thickness, but retains orderly polarity and lacks significant nuclear atypia. Key distinction: PUNLMP vs low-grade carcinoma Both may show complex papillae and increased thickness. Low-grade carcinoma is separated by definite, albeit mild, cytologic and architectural atypia, including nuclear enlargement and focal loss of polarity. Umbrella-cell prominence may be reduced in PUNLMP and papillary urothelial carcinoma. This is a supportive observation, not a stand-alone grading criterion. Diagnostic Categories Use the key features and pitfalls as a focused sign-out aid. Key features: Diagnostic pitfall: Practical Diagnostic Workflow Selected IHC Clues Interpret staining patterns with morphology; no single marker independently establishes grade. Marker Practical use Molecular Pathology: What Matters Low-grade pathway FGFR3 and RAS/MAPK pathway alterations are common; TERT promoter mutations may also occur. High-grade pathway TP53, RB1, CDKN2A, chromatin-regulating genes, and DNA damage-response pathways are frequently altered. Clinical translation FGFR3 alterations can guide targeted therapy in eligible advanced disease. Routine molecular classification is not a substitute for histologic diagnosis. Sign-Out Checklist Specify anatomic site and procedure. State histologic type and grade. Document lamina propria invasion. Document muscularis propria presence and involvement. Report CIS, lymphovascular invasion, and recognized subtype components. Describe cautery artifact or other limitations affecting interpretation. □ Educational reference based on the supplied urinary tract tumor material. Use current institutional protocols and clinical guidelines for patient management.

title: Gallbladder Extrahepatic Bile Duct Tumors
content: use client Biliary intraepithelial neoplasia (BilIN) Precursor Non-invasive; microscopic precursor Gallbladder and large intrahepatic / extrahepatic bile ducts Usually microscopic and incidentally identified in resection specimens. Associated settings include cholelithiasis, primary sclerosing cholangitis, choledochal cyst, and pancreaticobiliary maljunction. Microscopic, flat or micropapillary epithelial neoplasm confined to the biliary lining. Grade as low-grade or high-grade based on the highest degree of cytoarchitectural atypia. High-grade BilIN is carcinoma in situ (pTis). Low-grade: predominantly flat epithelium with mild atypia, nuclear pseudostratification, hyperchromasia, and increased N:C ratio. Low-grade lesions generally retain basal polarity; mitoses are rare. High-grade: complex micropapillary or papillary architecture, loss of polarity, marked nuclear atypia, and frequent mitoses. High-grade lesions may extend into Rokitansky–Aschoff sinuses and mimic invasion. Biliary, intestinal, and gastric phenotypes may occur; phenotype does not reliably predict the associated invasive carcinoma. Aberrant p53 overexpression may support BilIN over reactive atypia but is not sufficiently reliable as a stand-alone discriminator. MUC5AC expression may increase with dysplasia but has substantial case-to-case variability. S100 may be increased in high-grade BilIN and can be used as an adjunct. No clinically relevant molecular test is established for routine diagnosis. Reactive epithelial atypia Usually shows gradual transition from normal to reactive epithelium; BilIN is more basophilic, with intercellular clefts and more conspicuous cytoarchitectural atypia. Invasive adenocarcinoma BilIN remains confined to the epithelium; look for destructive stromal infiltration, irregular glands, desmoplasia, or isolated infiltrating cells. High-grade BilIN warrants extensive sampling to exclude an occult invasive component. Rokitansky–Aschoff sinus involvement can mimic invasion; assess the preserved sinus architecture. Intraductal papillary neoplasm of the bile ducts (IPNB) Non-invasive precursor; invasion is common at presentation Extrahepatic and large intrahepatic bile ducts; intraluminal growth Typically adults aged 42–80 years; slight male predominance. May present with intermittent abdominal pain, jaundice, or cholangitis. Risk settings include primary sclerosing cholangitis, hepatolithiasis, liver-fluke infection, and pancreaticobiliary maljunction. Grossly visible intraluminal papillary, villous, or polypoid neoplasm with fibrovascular cores. Neoplastic columnar epithelium; mucin production is variable. Classify as low-grade or high-grade according to the highest degree of cytoarchitectural atypia. Exclude intraductal oncocytic papillary neoplasm and intraductal tubulopapillary neoplasm, now separate entities. Fine fibrovascular cores are lined by neoplastic cuboidal or columnar epithelium; tubular/glandular components may coexist. Three epithelial differentiation patterns are recognized: gastric, intestinal, and pancreatobiliary. Intestinal type often has villous architecture and abundant mucin; pancreatobiliary type commonly shows complex papillae and high-grade atypia. Type 1 resembles pancreatic intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasm; type 2 is more complex, irregular, and commonly high-grade. Approximately 40–80% have associated invasive carcinoma at presentation; search carefully for tubular or colloid carcinoma. MUC5AC and MUC6 support gastric differentiation. MUC2 and CDX2 support intestinal differentiation. MUC1 is commonly expressed in pancreatobiliary-type epithelium. KRAS, TP53, and CDKN2A/p16 alterations occur during progression but are not required for diagnosis. GNAS mutations occur in a subset, particularly intestinal-type lesions with villous architecture and mucin hypersecretion. RNF43 alterations are more prevalent in intestinal-type IPNB; molecular testing is not routinely required for diagnosis. Intraductal tubulopapillary neoplasm ITPN is mucin-poor, predominantly tubular/cribriform, and uniformly high-grade; MUC5AC is typically negative. Intraductal oncocytic papillary neoplasm IOPN has complex arborizing papillae lined by cells with abundant granular eosinophilic cytoplasm and characteristic oncocytic phenotype. Invasive cholangiocarcinoma IPNB is predominantly intraluminal and non-invasive; identify and separately document any destructive stromal invasion. Do not use the older term 'oncocytic subtype of IPNB' for IOPN. Do not assume that high-grade dysplasia alone proves invasion; assess the stromal interface. Intraductal tubulopapillary neoplasm of the bile ducts (ITPN) Non-invasive intraductal neoplasm; invasive carcinoma frequently associated Approximately 70% intrahepatic, 20% perihilar, and 10% extrahepatic Usually affects adults around 60 years; female predominance (approximately 2:1). May be incidental or present with abdominal pain, anorexia, weight loss, or jaundice. Intraductal, mass-forming epithelial neoplasm composed predominantly of back-to-back tubules and cribriform glands. High-grade dysplasia is characteristic. Significant intracellular mucin production is absent; MUC5AC is typically negative. Solid, whitish/tan intraductal nodules partially or completely fill a dilated bile duct. Back-to-back tubular glands fuse into cribriform structures; papillary components are usually minor. Cells are cuboidal to columnar with amphophilic cytoplasm, enlarged nuclei, and prominent nucleoli. Comedo-like or spotty necrosis is common; extensive necrosis is uncommon. Intracytoplasmic mucin is typically absent. Approximately 80% show progression to invasive carcinoma, most often conventional large-duct-type tubular adenocarcinoma. CK7 and CK19 are commonly positive. MUC1 is positive in approximately 80% of cases; MUC6 is variable. MUC2 and MUC5AC are consistently negative in the reported series. Usually lacks common KRAS, GNAS, and IDH1/IDH2 hotspot mutations; CDKN2A alterations may occur. Reported alterations involve cell-cycle regulation, chromatin remodeling (including SWI/SNF genes and BAP1), and receptor tyrosine kinase pathways; no routine diagnostic molecular assay is established. IPNB IPNB more often shows papillary/villous architecture, mucin production, and MUC5AC expression. IOPN IOPN shows conspicuous oncocytic cytoplasm and arborizing papillae rather than predominantly back-to-back tubular/cribriform growth. Conventional cholangiocarcinoma ITPN retains a predominant intraductal growth pattern; evaluate for an associated invasive component. Do not equate high-grade dysplasia with invasion. Absence of mucin and lack of MUC5AC are useful discriminators from IPNB. Intraductal oncocytic papillary neoplasm of the bile ducts (IOPN) High-grade non-invasive precursor; invasive carcinoma in a subset Approximately 70% intrahepatic; 15% extrahepatic; 15% diffuse intrahepatic and extrahepatic Rare; age range approximately 36–84 years, without sex predilection. Often incidental; may present with abdominal mass or jaundice. Non-invasive intraductal papillary neoplasm with complex arborizing papillae. Papillae are lined by oncocytic cells with abundant granular eosinophilic cytoplasm. HepPar1 expression is a desirable supportive finding. Usually a large tan-brown intraductal lesion with friable papillary projections or solid nodules and little intraductal mucin. Thick, complex, arborizing papillae contain delicate myxoid fibrovascular cores. Epithelium consists of cuboidal/columnar cells with abundant granular eosinophilic cytoplasm, large nuclei, and prominent nucleoli. Cribriform structures and intraepithelial lumina may occur; goblet cells may be interspersed. All IOPNs are high-grade by architectural and cytologic criteria; approximately 30–40% show invasive carcinoma. Diffuse MUC5AC and MUC6 expression is characteristic. MUC1 is focal; MUC2 is largely restricted to goblet cells. HepPar1 and KIT (CD117) are consistently reported as positive. Recurrent kinase fusions support the diagnosis in selected cases: ATP1B1::PRKACB, ATP1B1::PRKACA, or DNAJB1::PRKACA. KRAS, BRAF, GNAS, RNF43, PIK3CA, and SMAD4 mutations reported in IPNB/cholangiocarcinoma are generally not observed in IOPN. IPNB, especially pancreatobiliary type IOPN has intensely oncocytic cells, complex cribriform architecture, diffuse MUC6, and HepPar1/KIT expression. ITPN ITPN is predominantly tubular/cribriform, lacks conspicuous oncocytic cytoplasm, and is typically MUC5AC-negative. High-grade cytology does not establish invasion; identify destructive stromal infiltration. Do not classify IOPN as an IPNB subtype; it is a distinct entity. Use molecular fusion testing selectively when a small biopsy limits morphologic assessment. Mass-forming intracholecystic neoplasm (ICN) Non-invasive precursor; invasive carcinoma often associated with ICPN Any gallbladder mucosal site; may be unifocal, multifocal, diffuse, or mural within an adenomyoma Typically adults; mean age approximately 61 years, with female predominance. Approximately half present with right upper quadrant pain; the remainder are detected incidentally. Associated settings include gallstones, primary sclerosing cholangitis, and pancreaticobiliary maljunction. Grossly visible, polypoid/papillary, non-invasive epithelial neoplasm arising in the gallbladder mucosa. Subtypes include intracholecystic papillary neoplasm (ICPN) and intracholecystic tubular neoplasm (ICTN). Extensively sample to exclude associated invasive carcinoma. ICPN: broad-based exophytic masses with predominantly papillary and sometimes tubular architecture; biliary, gastric, or intestinal differentiation may be present. ICPN may extend into Rokitansky–Aschoff sinuses and mimic invasion; adjacent flat BilIN may be present. Gastric-type polypoid pyloric gland metaplasia is not ICPN unless it forms a distinct nodule greater than 10 mm or has high-grade dysplasia. More than half of ICPNs have associated invasive carcinoma at diagnosis; invasion may be eccentric or grossly inapparent. ICTN: usually a solitary pedunculated polyp with complex back-to-back small acinar/tubular units, mucin-poor cells, and occasional morules. ICTN may meet cytologic criteria for high-grade dysplasia, but invasive transformation has not been documented in the supplied source. ICPN immunophenotype follows its epithelial differentiation; interpret mucin markers in the morphologic context. ICTN is usually diffusely MUC6-positive and often MUC1-positive. ICTN is typically negative for MUC2, MUC5AC, and CDX2. ICTN morules may show nuclear β-catenin. Molecular data for ICN are inconsistent; no routine diagnostic molecular test is established. ICTN appears associated with WNT pathway alterations. KRAS and GNAS mutations are relatively uncommon overall but KRAS is more frequent in lesions associated with pancreaticobiliary maljunction. TP53 alterations have been reported in ICPN. BilIN BilIN is microscopic and flat/micropapillary; ICN is a grossly visible mass-forming lesion. Pyloric gland metaplasia Commonly occurs in injured gallbladders; does not qualify as ICPN unless it forms a distinct nodule >10 mm or shows high-grade dysplasia. Rokitansky–Aschoff sinus involvement can mimic invasion; preserve the sinus architecture and seek destructive stromal infiltration. Rare oncocytic ICNs lack the defining arborizing papillae and intraepithelial lumina of IOPN. Do not diagnose invasion solely because dysplastic epithelium extends into Rokitansky–Aschoff sinuses. Do not classify an ICPN-associated carcinoma as T1/early T2 without extensive, preferably complete, sampling. Extrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma (eCCA) Malignant Invasive carcinoma Perihilar ducts (right/left hepatic ducts and confluence) or distal extrahepatic bile duct (common hepatic duct / distal common bile duct) Usually presents in the seventh or eighth decade (median age approximately 72 years); slight male predominance. Obstructive jaundice and pruritus are common; cholangitis, abdominal pain, malaise, anorexia, and weight loss may occur. Risk factors include primary sclerosing cholangitis, bile duct cysts, Caroli disease, cholelithiasis, and liver-fluke infection in endemic regions. Invasive epithelial malignancy with biliary differentiation arising in the extrahepatic bile ducts. Identify the anatomic location as perihilar or distal because staging is location-specific. Document histologic grade, lymphovascular invasion, perineural invasion, and margins. Most tumors are poorly defined; gross patterns include sclerosing (most common), nodular, and papillary. Infiltrative glands, irregular fused tubules, solid nests, or single cells are embedded in desmoplastic, often inflamed stroma. Lymphovascular and perineural invasion are common. Most tumors show pancreatobiliary differentiation; intestinal differentiation may occur, particularly in distal tumors. Subtypes include adenosquamous, mucinous, micropapillary, enteroblastic, hepatoid, and undifferentiated carcinoma. Cytokeratins highlight minute infiltrating tumor nests in small biopsies. p53, S100, and SMAD4 immunostains may assist in selected cases but are not independently diagnostic. ERBB2 (HER2) amplification occurs in approximately 15–20% and may be therapeutically actionable. Mismatch repair deficiency / MSI-high occurs in approximately 2%. IDH1 mutations and FGFR2 fusions are typically absent, unlike small-duct intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma. TP53, SMAD4, and CDKN2A alterations support carcinoma in the appropriate context; isolated KRAS or GNAS alterations may also occur in precursor lesions and are not independently diagnostic. FISH for chromosomal polysomy or 9q loss can increase sensitivity for malignancy in biliary cytology. Reactive cholangiocytes Carcinoma shows pleomorphism, irregular nuclear membranes, coarse chromatin, 3D clusters, loss of polarity, and/or necrotic background. IPNB-associated invasive carcinoma Look for a residual intraductal papillary precursor component; separately assess the invasive component. Metastatic adenocarcinoma Integrate clinical history, imaging, morphology, and site-directed immunohistochemistry to exclude a secondary primary. Small forceps biopsies may be difficult because of scant tissue, mild atypia, and inflammation. An isolated KRAS or GNAS mutation does not establish invasive carcinoma. Carcinoma of the gallbladder Most often fundus (~60–70%), followed by body (~30%) and neck/cystic duct (~10%) Usually older adults; female predominance is prominent in some high-incidence regions, while sex distribution is more balanced in parts of East Asia. Right upper quadrant pain is common and may be indistinguishable from gallstones or cholecystitis. Approximately half are incidental findings after cholecystectomy for presumed gallstones or cholecystitis. Major risk factors include gallstones and chronic inflammation; pancreaticobiliary maljunction is another established risk factor. Invasive epithelial neoplasm arising within the gallbladder. Most are biliary-type adenocarcinomas; classify specific histologic subtypes when criteria are met. Extensively sample incidental carcinomas to determine depth/extent of invasion and separately identify the cystic duct margin. Most are tubular adenocarcinomas resembling cholangiocarcinoma, with glands, fused tubules, micropapillae, nests, or single cells. Mucinous adenocarcinoma requires extracellular mucin comprising >50% of the tumor. Poorly cohesive carcinoma shows diffusely infiltrating single cells, nests, cords, or sheets comprising >50% of the tumor; signet-ring cells are not required. Adenosquamous carcinoma requires >25% squamous differentiation; less extensive squamous differentiation is reported as adenocarcinoma with focal squamous differentiation. Undifferentiated/sarcomatoid carcinoma may show spindle-cell, pleomorphic, giant-cell, or heterologous components. Rare patterns include lymphoepithelioma-like and hepatoid carcinoma; exclude direct extension by hepatocellular carcinoma in hepatoid cases. The glandular and squamous components of adenosquamous carcinoma show corresponding epithelial immunophenotypes. For hepatoid morphology, hepatocellular markers may be expressed; correlate with imaging to exclude hepatocellular carcinoma involving the gallbladder. SMARCB1 (INI1) loss identifies rare SWI/SNF-deficient rhabdoid undifferentiated carcinomas. TP53 alterations occur in more than 50% of cases. Other recurrent alterations include CDKN2A/CDKN2B, ARID1A, PIK3CA, and CTNNB1; ERBB2 amplification occurs in a subset (~16%). MSI is uncommon but may have therapeutic implications; HER2 IHC/testing may guide targeted therapy in selected cases. No molecular test is required to establish the diagnosis. Chronic cholecystitis / reactive atypia Reactive changes lack destructive stromal invasion; correlate with the overall architecture and inflammatory background. Rokitansky–Aschoff sinuses Preserved organoid sinus architecture may mimic infiltrative glands, particularly when involved by high-grade dysplasia. Adenomyoma / metaplastic glands Preserved architecture and relationship to the wall favor a benign malformative or metaplastic process; no reliable IHC or molecular marker separates these from carcinoma. Metastatic colorectal adenocarcinoma Intestinal-type morphology requires exclusion of gallbladder involvement by a colorectal primary. Hepatocellular carcinoma involving gallbladder Use clinical/radiologic correlation and hepatocellular markers to distinguish primary hepatoid carcinoma. Gross examination alone may miss flat, firm, diffuse carcinoma in a background of chronic cholecystitis. Do not call sinus involvement invasive without destructive growth beyond the preserved sinus architecture. Extensively sample ICN-associated tumors before assigning an early T category. All PathologyGPS / Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary / Gallbladder & Extrahepatic Bile Ducts Gallbladder & Extrahepatic Bile Duct Tumors A morphology-first diagnostic reference for biliary epithelial precursors, intraductal neoplasms, and invasive carcinomas. Core rule Separate intraductal growth from destructive stromal invasion. Rokitansky–Aschoff sinus involvement and high-grade cytology alone do not establish invasion. Diagnostic GPS: from site and architecture to classification Establish the site Gallbladder versus extrahepatic duct; perihilar versus distal bile duct. Determine the growth pattern Microscopic flat BilIN; gross intraductal papillary/tubular lesion; gallbladder mass; infiltrative ductal stricture. Assess invasion Look for destructive infiltration, desmoplasia, irregular glands, isolated tumor cells, lymphovascular and perineural invasion. Use targeted IHC Mucin phenotype for IPNB; MUC5AC/MUC6 and HepPar1/KIT for IOPN; MUC6 and β-catenin for ICTN; selective p53/SMAD4. Select molecular tests for purpose HER2 and MMR for therapeutic assessment; selected fusion testing for IOPN; interpret KRAS/GNAS in context. Precursor lesion classification Entity Grossly visible? Defining pattern No Flat / micropapillary microscopic dysplasia Yes Papillary / villous, often mucin-producing Tubular / cribriform, mucin-poor, high-grade Arborizing papillae with oncocytic epithelium ICN (ICPN / ICTN) Gallbladder papillary or tubular mass High-yield immunophenotype and molecular clues Useful profile / alteration MUC5AC/MUC6 (gastric); MUC2/CDX2 (intestinal); MUC1 (pancreatobiliary); GNAS/RNF43 in subsets MUC1/MUC6; MUC2 and MUC5AC negative; KRAS/GNAS/IDH1/2 usually absent MUC5AC/MUC6 diffuse; HepPar1 and KIT positive; PRKACA/PRKACB fusions ICTN MUC6 diffuse, MUC1 often positive; MUC2/MUC5AC/CDX2 negative; nuclear β-catenin in morules eCCA HER2 amplification ~15–20%; MSI-high ~2%; IDH1/FGFR2 typically absent Gallbladder carcinoma TP53 >50%; ERBB2 amplification ~16%; MMR deficiency in a small subset Entity reference Clinical profile, diagnostic criteria, and differential diagnosis Search by entity, morphology, site, immunostain, or gene. e.g. MUC6, HER2, Rokitansky–Aschoff, GNAS... bg-teal-700 text-white border border-slate-300 bg-white text-slate-600 Collapse View diagnostic profile − + Clinical profile Essential diagnostic criteria Histopathology Immunophenotype Molecular pathology Differential diagnosis Diagnostic pitfalls No matching entity. Critical distinction: intraductal precursor versus invasive carcinoma Finding Supports non-invasive precursor Supports invasion Growth Confined to mucosa / duct lumen; preserved architecture Destructive infiltration into stroma or wall Stroma No desmoplastic response around lesional epithelium Desmoplastic, inflamed stroma with irregular glands or single cells Dysplasia extending into a pre-existing, architecturally preserved sinus Destructive growth beyond the sinus wall Cytology High-grade atypia may occur without invasion Cytologic atypia plus unequivocal infiltrative growth Sampling Extensive mapping needed for ICN-associated lesions Invasive component may be small, eccentric, or grossly occult Resection, sampling, and reporting checklist For gallbladder carcinoma, thoroughly sample the tumor and surrounding mucosa; identify and submit the cystic duct margin separately. For incidental gallbladder carcinoma, document exact site, depth of invasion, hepatic versus serosal-side involvement, Rokitansky–Aschoff sinus involvement, and margins. For ICN/ICPN, extensively sample the entire lesion and its interface to exclude small or eccentric invasive carcinoma before assigning an early T category. For bile duct resections, document proximal, distal, and radial margins; assess perineural and lymphovascular invasion. For eCCA, specify perihilar versus distal location because the applicable staging system differs. Report precursor grade, invasive component and histologic subtype, tumor grade, lymphovascular invasion, perineural invasion, nodal status, and margin status. Scope note: Based on the supplied WHO chapter excerpt. Molecular alterations are included only where the source describes diagnostic, classification, or clinically actionable relevance. Supportive IHC findings are not stand-alone criteria; correlate with anatomy, morphology, and adequate sampling.

title: Genetic Tumor Syndromes
content: use client Lynch syndrome Autosomal dominant MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2; EPCAM deletions affecting MSH2 CRC; endometrial/ovarian; stomach, small bowel, biliary tract, pancreas Adult; early CRC/endometrial/ovarian cancers; risk varies by gene; MSH2/MLH1 highest, MSH6 later/female-predominant, PMS2 lower. Germline monoallelic pathogenic variant in an MMR gene (or 3′ EPCAM deletion affecting MSH2). CRC may show tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes, Crohn-like reaction, poor differentiation, mucinous/signet-ring or medullary pattern; none is specific. Loss of paired MMR proteins: MLH1/PMS2 or MSH2/MSH6; isolated PMS2 or MSH6 loss suggests the corresponding gene. Retained internal controls are essential. Germline MMR testing confirms; tumor MMR IHC and MSI-H are screening evidence. MLH1 promoter methylation and BRAF V600E help identify sporadic MLH1-deficient CRC; consider double-somatic causes. Sporadic dMMR CRC often older; MLH1 promoter methylation/BRAF V600E may support sporadic origin. CMMRD: childhood-onset, biallelic MMR variants. Constitutional mismatch repair deficiency (CMMRD) Autosomal recessive Biallelic MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, or PMS2 Colon/rectum, small bowel, stomach; also brain and hematologic malignancies; hepatic adenomas Usually childhood; mean onset under 10 years; broad spectrum including high-grade glioma, T-cell lymphoblastic lymphoma, and GI polyposis/carcinoma. Biallelic germline pathogenic variants in one MMR gene compatible childhood cancer phenotype. Multiple adenomatous polyps may occur in colon, small bowel, and stomach; GI carcinomas can show dMMR/MSI features. Loss of MMR proteins in non-neoplastic tissues may be demonstrable; interpret with appropriate controls and validated testing. Biallelic germline MMR variants establish diagnosis; tumor MSI/dMMR supports pathway involvement. monoallelic variant, typically adult-onset; sporadic dMMR tumors do not explain constitutional biallelic variants. Familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP) APC Colon/rectum; duodenum and stomach; extracolonic sites include thyroid, desmoid, and other lesions Usually adolescence; hundreds to thousands of colorectal adenomas in classic FAP; attenuated FAP has fewer adenomas and later presentation. Germline APC pathogenic variant with colorectal adenomatous polyposis >100 adenomas strongly supports classic FAP 0–100 may fit attenuated FAP. Conventional adenomas, ranging from microscopic aberrant crypt foci to innumerable conventional adenomas; associated upper-GI adenomas. No single IHC pattern establishes FAP; evaluate lesions by standard site-specific criteria. Germline APC testing confirms; variant location may correlate with phenotype. Somatic APC alterations alone do not establish hereditary FAP. MUTYH-associated polyposis recessive, biallelic MUTYH; PPAP: POLE/POLD1 proofreading-domain variants; sporadic multiple adenomas lack germline APC variant. MUTYH-associated polyposis (MAP) MUTYH Colon/rectum; duodenum; associated extraintestinal malignancies may occur Usually adult; multiple colorectal adenomas, often fewer than classic FAP; CRC may occur without hundreds of polyps. Biallelic germline pathogenic variants in MUTYH. Adenomatous polyps resemble conventional sporadic adenomas; associated serrated or other polyp types may coexist. No syndrome-specific IHC profile is established. Biallelic germline MUTYH variants confirm; tumor mutational signatures SBS18 and SBS36 are supportive. FAP APC-related dominant inheritance; PPAP: heterozygous POLE/POLD1 exonuclease-domain variant. Hereditary mixed polyposis syndrome GREM1 duplication involving regulatory elements Colon/rectum Variable age; mixed colorectal polyp burden, often across several colonoscopies; family history may be prominent. Duplication affecting GREM1 and its regulatory region between SCG5 and GREM1. Mixed polyp histology, including adenomatous, hyperplastic/serrated, and juvenile-like components; individual polyps may show mixed histology. No defining IHC profile is described. Demonstration of the characteristic GREM1 duplication is essential. FAP/MAP predominantly adenomatous polyposis; JPS: juvenile-type hamartomatous polyps; serrated polyposis: predominantly serrated lesions. Juvenile polyposis syndrome SMAD4 or BMPR1A Colon, stomach, small bowel; SMAD4 may be associated with hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia Often childhood/adolescence; multiple juvenile polyps, GI bleeding, anemia, prolapse, or intussusception; gastric disease can be prominent. Multiple juvenile polyps and/or a germline pathogenic variant in SMAD4 or BMPR1A interpret clinical/family criteria. Juvenile polyps with cystically dilated mucus-filled glands, inflamed edematous lamina propria, and surface erosion. No syndrome-specific IHC profile is required. Germline SMAD4/BMPR1A testing; SMAD4-associated cases may show combined JPS/HHT phenotype. Peutz–Jeghers arborizing smooth muscle and mucocutaneous pigmentation; PTEN hamartoma syndrome: mixed hamartomatous polyps and characteristic extra-GI findings. Peutz–Jeghers syndrome STK11 Small bowel (especially jejunum), colon, stomach; pancreas and other organs also at risk Often childhood; mucocutaneous lentigines and recurrent intussusception/obstruction or bleeding from hamartomatous polyps. Characteristic Peutz–Jeghers polyps and/or germline STK11 pathogenic variant clinical criteria include mucocutaneous pigmentation and family history. Hamartomatous polyp with branching/arborizing smooth-muscle core extending into polyp; glandular epithelium is usually nondysplastic. No specific IHC required for the polyp diagnosis. Germline STK11 pathogenic variant confirms; loss of the remaining allele may occur in lesions. Juvenile polyp cystically dilated glands in inflamed stroma without arborizing smooth muscle; PTEN-associated polyps have variable histology. PTEN hamartoma tumor syndrome PTEN Colon and stomach; breast, thyroid, endometrium, skin, and CNS are important extra-GI sites Variable age; macrocephaly, mucocutaneous lesions, hamartomatous/mixed GI polyps, and increased breast, thyroid, and endometrial cancer risk. Germline PTEN pathogenic variant or accepted clinical diagnostic criteria. Broad spectrum of GI polyps: hamartomatous, hyperplastic, ganglioneuromatous, inflammatory, and adenomatous lesions; no single pathognomonic polyp type. No single IHC pattern is diagnostic; PTEN IHC may be supportive but does not replace germline testing. Germline PTEN testing establishes molecular diagnosis. PJS arborizing smooth muscle and pigmentation; JPS: classic juvenile polyp morphology; Cowden-like sporadic lesions require clinical/genetic correlation. Polymerase proofreading-associated polyposis (PPAP) POLE or POLD1 exonuclease/proofreading domain Colon/rectum; endometrium and other cancers, depending on gene Adult; adenomatous polyposis and CRC; POLD1 carriers have notable endometrial cancer risk. Heterozygous germline missense variant affecting the POLE or POLD1 exonuclease proofreading domain. Colorectal adenomas and carcinomas generally resemble conventional counterparts; tumor mutation burden may be markedly increased. No defining IHC profile. Germline proofreading-domain variant is essential; characteristic high mutation burden/signature supports diagnosis. Lynch MMR gene defect/dMMR; FAP: APC; MAP: biallelic MUTYH. Variants outside proofreading domain should not automatically be classified as PPAP. Other inherited polyposis syndromes (AXIN2, NTHL1, MSH3) Autosomal dominant or recessive, gene-dependent AXIN2 (AD); NTHL1 (AR); MSH3 (AR) Predominantly colon/rectum; duodenal adenomas and extracolonic tumors in selected syndromes Variable adult presentation. AXIN2 may include oligodontia/ectodermal dysplasia; NTHL1 may include multiple primary tumors; MSH3 may include duodenal adenomas. AXIN2: heterozygous GPV NTHL1: biallelic GPVs MSH3: biallelic GPVs. Adenomatous polyps with variable burden; histology is not specific to the causative gene. No syndrome-specific IHC pattern is established. Gene-appropriate germline testing; NTHL1-associated tumors may show characteristic mutation signatures; MSH3-associated tumors may show EMAST. APC-, MUTYH-, or POLE/POLD1-associated polyposis Distinguish by the specific germline gene and inheritance pattern (AXIN2 dominant; NTHL1 and MSH3 recessive). Hereditary diffuse gastric and breast cancer syndrome (HDGC) CDH1; less commonly CTNNA1 Stomach (diffuse-type gastric carcinoma); breast (lobular carcinoma) Young to middle-aged adults; diffuse gastric cancer, including occult intramucosal signet-ring foci; female carriers have increased lobular breast cancer risk. Germline pathogenic variant in CDH1 or CTNNA1 in an appropriate clinical/family context. Diffuse-type gastric carcinoma with poorly cohesive/signet-ring cells; multifocal intramucosal signet-ring cell foci may be subtle and require extensive sampling. Loss of E-cadherin expression may support CDH1 pathway disruption; interpret with morphology and germline results. Germline CDH1/CTNNA1 testing confirms; somatic second-hit events contribute to tumor development. Sporadic diffuse gastric carcinoma no germline syndrome; other hereditary gastric cancer syndromes such as GAPPS have a different polyp/glandular phenotype. Gastric adenocarcinoma and proximal polyposis of the stomach (GAPPS) APC promoter 1B Proximal stomach (fundus/body), with relative sparing of antrum and duodenum Adult; extensive fundic gland polyposis and risk of gastric adenocarcinoma; family history of proximal gastric polyposis/cancer. Characteristic proximal gastric polyposis with a germline APC promoter 1B pathogenic variant. Numerous fundic gland polyps, sometimes with dysplasia; gastric adenocarcinoma may arise in the polyposis field. No specific IHC profile is diagnostic. Germline APC promoter 1B testing is required; routine APC coding-region testing may miss the promoter variant. Classic FAP colorectal adenomatous polyposis and broader APC-associated phenotype; sporadic fundic gland polyps are usually less extensive and lack the inherited pattern. Hereditary and familial pancreatic cancer Usually autosomal dominant susceptibility; gene-specific BRCA1, BRCA2, PALB2, ATM, CDKN2A, STK11, mismatch-repair genes and others Pancreas; some genes confer breast/ovarian, melanoma, or other cancer risks Usually adulthood; pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma in families with multiple affected close relatives; age and associated cancers vary by gene. Familial pancreatic cancer pedigree (including ≥2 first-degree relatives with pancreatic cancer) and/or germline pathogenic variant in an established susceptibility gene. Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma is morphologically indistinguishable from sporadic PDAC; precursor lesions may be present. No syndrome-specific IHC pattern; use tumor-specific testing as clinically indicated. Germline multigene panel testing identifies actionable susceptibility variants; tumor testing may guide targeted therapy (e.g., homologous recombination deficiency). Sporadic PDAC no strong family history or germline variant; distinguish hereditary syndrome by pedigree and germline testing. Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) NF1 GI tract (especially small bowel), periampullary region; also peripheral nerves and multiple organ systems Usually recognized in childhood; café-au-lait macules, axillary/inguinal freckling, neurofibromas, optic pathway glioma; GI manifestations include GIST and periampullary somatostatinoma. Clinical diagnosis requires at least two accepted NF1 criteria or a heterozygous germline NF1 pathogenic variant. GI lesions include GIST, periampullary neuroendocrine neoplasms, and nerve sheath tumors; morphology follows the corresponding tumor entity. Loss of neurofibromin may be demonstrable in NF1-associated tumors; IHC is not a substitute for clinical/genetic diagnosis. Germline NF1 pathogenic variant; biallelic somatic NF1 inactivation may occur in associated tumors. Sporadic GIST/NET assess multiplicity, anatomic distribution, and syndromic stigmata; other hereditary GIST syndromes involve KIT/PDGFRA or SDH. Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 (MEN1) MEN1 Pancreas, duodenum, stomach; parathyroid and pituitary are major extra-GI sites Often young to middle-aged adults; primary hyperparathyroidism, pituitary tumors, and multiple pancreatic/duodenal NETs; de novo cases occur. At least two MEN1-associated endocrine tumors one such tumor plus an affected first-degree relative or germline MEN1 pathogenic variant. Multifocal pancreatic NETs; duodenal gastrinomas may be multiple and small; gastric type 2 NETs may occur in the setting of MEN1-related hypergastrinemia. Hormone IHC may demonstrate functional differentiation; multifocality and hormone restriction can support clonality but are not independently diagnostic. Germline MEN1 testing confirms; tumor loss of the wild-type allele is a common second hit. Sporadic PanNET/gastrinoma typically solitary; consider MEN1 when multifocal or accompanied by parathyroid/pituitary disease. Glucagon cell hyperplasia and neoplasia (GCHN; Mahvash disease) GCGR Diffuse pancreatic islets throughout the pancreas Reported age 7–68 years; both sexes; abdominal pain, altered bowel habits, fatigue, or pancreatitis despite markedly elevated serum glucagon; typically no glucagonoma syndrome. Markedly elevated serum glucagon glucagon-cell hyperplasia in hypertrophic islets merging with glucagon-positive microtumors/PanNETs germline GCGR variant is desirable. Hypertrophic islets intermixed with multiple microtumors and occasional larger tumors; cells are monomorphic with neuroendocrine morphology. Tumor and hyperplastic islet cells are predominantly or exclusively glucagon-positive; occasional PP coexpression. Biallelic GCGR variants; sequencing of all exons and splice sites is required to exclude variants. MEN1-associated multifocal PanNET assess MEN1 and other endocrine manifestations; sporadic glucagonoma usually causes a glucagonoma syndrome. MAFA-related familial insulinomatosis MAFA Endocrine pancreas Adult-onset recurrent hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia; some carriers develop maturity-onset diabetes of the young; very rare, reported in a few families. Multicentric insulin-positive islet-cell proliferations and a germline pathogenic MAFA variant. Dysplastic beta-cell clusters/cords, trabecular insulin-positive microtumors, and larger insulinomas intermingled with normal islets. Lesional cells show insulin expression; other hormone expression is not defining in the supplied source. Germline MAFA missense variants, particularly p.Ser64Phe and reported p.Thr57Arg, segregate with phenotype. Sporadic insulinoma usually solitary; MEN1: often multifocal but accompanied by other MEN1 manifestations. SDH-deficient tumor syndromes Autosomal dominant predisposition; Carney triad is nonhereditary SDHA, SDHB, SDHC, SDHD, SDHAF2; SDHC promoter hypermethylation in Carney triad Paraganglia, stomach (SDH-deficient GIST), kidney; Carney triad includes pulmonary chondroma Often young; paraganglioma/pheochromocytoma, multifocal gastric GIST, renal carcinoma; phenotype and parent-of-origin effects vary by gene. Germline SDHx pathogenic variant or SDHC promoter hypermethylation multiple confirmed SDH-deficient tumors in an individual/family. A single SDH-deficient neoplasm warrants genetic evaluation. SDH-deficient GIST often gastric, multinodular/plexiform and multifocal; paraganglioma morphology may show distinctive nested growth; assess associated tumors. Loss of SDHB by IHC defines SDH deficiency; SDHA loss points particularly to SDHA inactivation. Retained internal controls are required. SDHB IHC loss; germline SDHx testing; SDHC promoter methylation for Carney triad. Biallelic somatic-only SDHx variants are unusual. Conventional KIT/PDGFRA-mutant GIST usually SDHB-retained; sporadic paraganglioma/GIST must be assessed for SDH deficiency. GIST predisposition syndrome KIT or PDGFRA KIT: throughout GI tract; PDGFRA: stomach; associated lesions vary Often younger patients, multifocal GIST; KIT: dysmotility, pigmentation, mast-cell disorders; PDGFRA: inflammatory fibroid polyps, fibrous tumors, GI fibrosis and lipomas. Germline pathogenic variant in KIT or PDGFRA multifocal GIST and syndrome-specific associated lesions are supportive. GISTs resemble sporadic counterparts; KIT-associated tumors often spindle-cell and multifocal; PDGFRA-associated tumors are gastric and may be epithelioid. GIST phenotype typically KIT/CD117 and DOG1 positive; SDHB is retained in KIT/PDGFRA-associated familial tumors. Germline KIT or PDGFRA variant confirms; variants activate receptor tyrosine kinase signaling. SDH-deficient GIST loss of SDHB, often gastric/multifocal; NF1-associated GIST: clinical NF1 features and often small-bowel distribution. PathologyGPS / GI & Liver / Genetic Tumor Syndromes GI Genetic Tumor Syndromes A clinicopathologic reference linking inherited predisposition, gastrointestinal manifestations, diagnostic morphology, immunophenotype, and germline testing. Core principle Recognize the phenotype. Confirm the inherited mechanism. A tumor phenotype or abnormal IHC result may trigger genetic evaluation, but germline testing establishes most hereditary syndromes. Syndrome comparison: genes, inheritance, and GI tumor spectrum Use this overview to recognize the major syndromic patterns. Gene-specific penetrance and age of onset vary; the table is a diagnostic orientation, not a risk calculator. Syndrome Inheritance Gene(s) Principal GI involvement Practical diagnostic workflow 1. Recognize the pattern Age, multiplicity, polyp type, tumor location, family history, and extra-GI findings. 2. Review morphology Classify each polyp or tumor independently; do not infer a syndrome from nonspecific histology. 3. Apply targeted IHC MMR proteins for suspected Lynch/CMMRD; SDHB (± SDHA) for suspected SDH-deficient neoplasia; other stains only when indicated. 4. Confirm the mechanism Use germline testing and appropriate copy-number, promoter, or structural-variant analysis. 5. Communicate implications Recommend genetics referral and family assessment when a hereditary syndrome is suspected or confirmed. High-yield IHC and molecular triggers Loss of MLH1/PMS2 or MSH2/MSH6; MSI-H; confirm germline MMR variant. CMMRD Biallelic germline MMR variants; constitutional MMR deficiency. FAP / GAPPS Germline APC; GAPPS requires attention to APC promoter 1B. MAP Biallelic MUTYH; SBS18/SBS36 are supportive. PPAP POLE/POLD1 exonuclease-domain germline variant. HDGC Germline CDH1 or CTNNA1; E-cadherin loss may support. NF1-associated tumors Clinical NF1 phenotype; NF1 alteration in appropriate tumor context. SDH-deficient tumors Loss of SDHB; SDHA loss can point to SDHA. Familial GIST Germline KIT or PDGFRA. Important interpretive cautions Abnormal MMR IHC or MSI is a screening result, not by itself proof of Lynch syndrome; sporadic MLH1 promoter methylation and double-somatic MMR inactivation are important alternatives. A single SDH-deficient neoplasm should prompt genetic counseling/testing unless a somatic-only explanation is established. The number and type of polyps overlap among hereditary syndromes; integrate histology, distribution, age, family history, and germline results. A pathogenic variant must be interpreted in the correct gene region and inheritance context (for example, POLE/POLD1 proofreading-domain variants in PPAP). Do not use tumor IHC as a substitute for constitutional testing when the diagnosis is a germline syndrome. Syndrome reference Clinical and pathologic profiles Search by syndrome, gene, organ, phenotype, morphology, or marker. e.g. MSH2, STK11, fundic gland polyps, SDHB... Scope and reporting note This page summarizes digestive-system manifestations of the syndromes in the supplied WHO excerpt; it is not a comprehensive review of their extra-GI manifestations or surveillance protocols. Age ranges and penetrance vary by gene and family. Do not infer a specific germline diagnosis from age, polyp count, morphology, or IHC alone. For suspected hereditary disease, correlate with personal and family history and refer for genetic counseling and germline testing. The summaries preserve the source's diagnostic emphasis; no external risk estimates or surveillance schedules have been added.
