title: Anal Canal Tumors
content: use client Anal squamous intraepithelial lesion (LSIL / HSIL) Precursor Noninvasive squamous neoplasia Occurs in the anal canal, anal transformation zone, perianal skin, or more distant perianal skin. Classic condyloma is most frequent in young adults, particularly young men who have sex with men and people with HIV. Giant condyloma more often affects men in their 40s (reported male-to-female ratio, 2.7:1); pediatric cases also occur. Often asymptomatic; may present with single or multiple warty lesions, pruritus, discomfort, bleeding, or a large locally destructive mass. Risk is increased with HIV or other immunosuppression, transplantation, smoking, and sexual exposure. LSIL: cytologic atypia and mitotic activity are confined to the lower one-third of the squamous epithelium, or unequivocal koilocytic changes are present. HSIL: marked cytologic atypia involves at least two-thirds of the epithelial thickness. HSIL shows loss of nuclear polarity and may contain atypical mitotic figures in the upper epithelial layers. Use the two-tier LAST terminology; historical AIN grades may be added parenthetically when clinically useful. For HPV-independent lesions, recognize differentiated intraepithelial neoplasia and verruciform acanthotic intraepithelial neoplasia; terminology is not yet fully codified. LSIL shows koilocytotic atypia, with enlarged irregular nuclei and perinuclear halos. Condyloma acuminatum is exophytic and papillomatous, with thickened epithelium, broad rete ridges, parakeratosis, and koilocytosis. HSIL shows full-thickness or at least two-thirds-thickness immature atypical squamous cells with increased mitoses and loss of maturation. Anal condylomas may contain both LSIL and HSIL; submit and examine the entire lesion adequately. Differentiated intraepithelial neoplasia shows basal/parabasal atypia and is associated with TP53 mutation. Verruciform acanthotic intraepithelial neoplasia shows hyperkeratosis and hypergranulosis, sometimes with upper epithelial cytoplasmic pallor. HSIL typically shows strong, continuous block-type p16 staining extending from basal cells upward through the epithelium. LSIL may show focal or non-block p16 staining; some high-risk HPV-associated LSILs can be block-positive. HPV-independent TP53-mutant intraepithelial neoplasia may show aberrant p53 overexpression with absent p16 block staining. p53 and p16 do not reliably distinguish HPV-independent TP53-wildtype lesions from their mimics. High-risk HPV, most often HPV16 or HPV18, drives most HSIL; HPV6 and HPV11 account for more than 90% of classic and giant condylomas. High-risk HPV E6/E7 oncoproteins disrupt p53 and RB1 pathways, producing p16 overexpression. HPV genotyping by PCR or RNA in situ hybridization can help distinguish LSIL from reactive/negative lesions in selected cases. TP53 mutation supports HPV-independent differentiated intraepithelial neoplasia; molecular testing is not established for TP53-wildtype verruciform acanthotic lesions. Reactive squamous atypia Lacks convincing koilocytosis or the epithelial maturation/atypia pattern of SIL; p16 is not block-positive. Anal transitional zone Can show immature squamous metaplasia; interpret p16 and atypia in the correct anatomic and morphologic context. Pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia Reactive downgrowth with limited atypia and no destructive invasion; search for an underlying cause such as infection or granular cell tumor. Invasive squamous cell carcinoma Requires stromal invasion; HSIL remains confined to the epithelium. Do not use the obsolete three-tier AIN grading system as the primary diagnostic terminology. A negative p16 stain does not exclude LSIL and does not classify every HPV-independent lesion. Do not diagnose HSIL from p16 positivity alone without compatible morphology. A small biopsy may miss a separate HSIL focus in a condyloma or a focal invasive component. Anal squamous cell carcinoma Malignant Malignant; regional nodal and distant metastatic potential Arises in the anal canal or anal margin. Most patients are diagnosed in the sixth decade or later; immunodeficiency may be associated with younger presentation. Women have higher incidence rates than men in many populations, although HIV-related risk is particularly important in men. Common presentations are anal bleeding, pain, a palpable mass, or an indurated/friable ulcer; pruritus, discharge, altered bowel habits, and tenesmus may occur. Approximately 90% of cases are associated with HPV, most often HPV16. Essential: invasive squamous neoplasia arising from anal squamous mucosa. Demonstrate destructive stromal invasion by atypical squamous cells; an associated in situ component may be present. Correlate with the exact site (anal canal, anal verge, or perianal skin) because regional lymphatic drainage differs. Verrucous carcinoma requires broad pushing invasion and adequate sampling to exclude conventional invasive SCC. Keratinizing tumors contain large eosinophilic cells with squamous maturation and keratinization. HPV-associated tumors may show basaloid morphology, with hyperchromatic nuclei, scant cytoplasm, and peripheral palisading around infiltrative nests or trabeculae. Rare tumors show hyalinized nests with an adenoid cystic-like pattern or urothelial-like morphology. Histologic patterns frequently overlap; routine morphologic subtyping and grading have no established clinical predictive value. Verrucous SCC shows exophytic and endophytic broad bulbous epithelial fronds with a pushing interface, minimal atypia, and rare basal mitoses. Verrucous carcinoma lacks HPV cytopathic effect; conventional SCC may arise within it and must be excluded by thorough sampling. Tumor cells are typically positive for pancytokeratin, CK5/6, and p40. p16 is commonly block-positive in HPV-associated SCC; interpret with morphology because p16 positivity is not entirely specific. Use a differential-directed panel when melanoma, neuroendocrine carcinoma, or another poorly differentiated malignancy is considered. HPV testing is etiologically informative but is not required to establish the diagnosis of invasive SCC. PIK3CA pathway alterations are frequent; FBXW7 and KMT2D alterations are also reported. TP53 mutations are more characteristic of HPV-negative SCC because HPV E6 functionally inactivates p53. PD-L1 expression occurs in approximately half of cases and may inform treatment assessment in the appropriate advanced-disease setting; it is not a diagnostic marker. Shows limited atypia and no destructive invasion; an underlying infection or granular cell tumor may be found. Perianal basal cell carcinoma Often shows stromal retraction and lacks atypical mitoses and an associated squamous in situ component. Giant condyloma (Buschke–Löwenstein tumor) HPV-driven, usually HPV6/11; broad pushing growth but lacks unequivocal conventional SCC unless a malignant component is present. Melanoma / neuroendocrine carcinoma Can mimic poorly differentiated SCC; use melanocytic or neuroendocrine markers with epithelial/squamous markers. The term cloacogenic carcinoma is not recommended; classify these tumors as anal SCC. Do not diagnose verrucous carcinoma on a superficial or limited biopsy without excluding conventional SCC. An in situ component is helpful but not definitive because mimics may colonize the surface epithelium. p16 positivity alone does not establish HPV-driven SCC. Anal adenocarcinoma Malignant glandular neoplasm Rare primary malignancy, accounting for approximately 5–10% of anal cancers; most cases are mucosal-type. Median age is approximately 67 years; women account for about 48% of reported cases. Mucosal tumors resemble distal rectal adenocarcinoma or anal SCC clinically. Anal gland adenocarcinoma may present with bleeding or an anorectal mass. Fistula-associated adenocarcinoma usually arises after a longstanding fistula (often at least 10 years), commonly in Crohn disease; new mucous discharge is an important warning symptom. Primary perianal adenocarcinoma is very rare; reported cases include men and women in their sixth decade. Essential: invasive glandular neoplasm arising from the anal canal or associated anal gland/fistula/perianal structures. Classify as mucosal or extramucosal and specify the subtype when possible: mucosal intestinal/transitional type, anal gland/duct, fistula-associated, or primary perianal. For fistula-associated carcinoma, document a pre-existing chronic fistula and exclude direct extension or metastasis from colorectal or other primary sites. Extramucosal tumors lack a luminal in situ component by definition, although secondary surface involvement may occur by erosion, colonization, or pagetoid spread. Correlate with clinical history, imaging, endoscopy, and examination to establish the primary site. Mucosal intestinal-type adenocarcinoma generally resembles colorectal adenocarcinoma and is usually HPV-independent. HPV-associated mucosal tumors may resemble stratified mucin-producing carcinoma, with infiltrative nests, intracytoplasmic mucin, peripheral palisading, apoptosis, and neutrophilic infiltrates. Another HPV-associated pattern resembles usual-type HPV-related endocervical adenocarcinoma, with papillary fronds, overlapping irregular nuclei, brisk mitoses, and apical apoptotic bodies. Anal gland adenocarcinoma typically forms haphazardly distributed glands lined by cuboidal cells with scant mucin; solid, stratified, and mucinous patterns also occur. Fistula-associated adenocarcinoma is usually mucinous and resembles colorectal-type mucinous adenocarcinoma; an adenoma-like component may be present. Primary perianal adenocarcinoma may arise in association with developmental cysts and may resemble colorectal adenocarcinoma. Any anal adenocarcinoma subtype may spread pagetoidly to anal squamous mucosa or perianal skin, producing secondary Paget disease. Primary anal Paget disease is an intraepithelial carcinoma with skin appendage differentiation and may become invasive. HPV-associated mucosal tumors commonly express CK7 and p16; CK20 and p40 are usually negative in the stratified mucin-producing pattern. Usual-type HPV-associated tumors show CK7 and p16, variable CDX2, and minimal CK20. Anal gland adenocarcinoma typically expresses CK7 and MUC5AC and lacks CK20 and CDX2. Anal gland carcinoma is negative for CK5/6 and p63, which are constitutively expressed in benign anal glands. Fistula-associated tumors show variable phenotype: intestinal-type cases may express CK20 and MUC2, whereas others have an anal gland-like mucin profile. Primary Paget disease typically coexpresses CK7 and GCDFP-15 and lacks CK20 and CDX2; secondary Paget disease often expresses CK20 and may also express CK7. High-risk HPV, most often HPV16, drives a subset of mucosal adenocarcinomas, particularly tumors with transitional-zone/non-intestinal phenotype. KRAS variants are reported in approximately 47% of cases; PIK3CA, NRAS, and BRAF variants are less frequent. Microsatellite instability is very rare; molecular data remain limited and no routine diagnostic molecular test is established. Rectal/colorectal adenocarcinoma extending into the anal canal Assess the epicenter, mucosal precursor, imaging, and continuity with a rectal primary. Anal gland adenocarcinoma CK7+/MUC5AC+, CK20-/CDX2- phenotype with haphazard glands and no luminal in situ component supports anal gland origin. Fistula-associated adenocarcinoma Requires a longstanding fistula and exclusion of a colorectal primary; morphology and IHC may be variable. Metastatic gynecologic, prostatic, or breast carcinoma Exclude a primary elsewhere, particularly for CK7-positive anal gland-like tumors. Primary versus secondary anal Paget disease Primary: CK7+/GCDFP-15+, usually CK20-/CDX2-. Secondary: often CK20+, with possible CK7 coexpression and an underlying anorectal adenocarcinoma. Do not assume every anal adenocarcinoma is colorectal-type; establish mucosal versus extramucosal origin. A pagetoid or surface component does not necessarily indicate a primary cutaneous Paget disease. CK7 positivity alone does not prove anal gland origin; integrate CK20, CDX2, MUC5AC, p63/CK5/6, HPV testing, and clinical findings. For fistula-associated carcinoma, a new mucous discharge or change in a longstanding fistula warrants careful evaluation. Inflammatory cloacogenic polyp Tumor-like Benign mucosal prolapse-related lesion Uncommon polypoid lesion of the anal transitional zone. Reported predominantly in North American and European populations. May present with rectal bleeding, prolapse-related symptoms, or an anal polyp. Polypoid lesion with a mucosal prolapse pattern in the anal transitional zone. Identify epithelial hyperplasia with complex tubulovillous architecture and accompanying inflammatory/stromal changes. Interpret in the setting of mucosal prolapse rather than as an epithelial neoplasm. Hyperplastic epithelium forms complex tubulovillous glands. Active chronic inflammation and granulation tissue are present in the lamina propria. Vascular ectasia and smooth muscle proliferation are characteristic associated findings. Cystically dilated mucosal glands and extravasated mucin pools may be present in the lamina propria. Conventional adenoma A true dysplastic epithelial proliferation lacks the characteristic prolapse-associated inflammatory and stromal pattern. Anal squamous intraepithelial lesion SIL shows squamous cytologic atypia and, in HSIL, block-type p16; inflammatory cloacogenic polyp is a mixed mucosal prolapse lesion. Solitary rectal ulcer / mucosal prolapse polyp Shares the mucosal prolapse spectrum; site and clinical context distinguish the specific presentation. Do not overinterpret reactive epithelial hyperplasia as dysplasia or invasive carcinoma. Recognize the relationship to mucosal prolapse syndrome, which also includes solitary rectal ulcer syndrome, rectal prolapse, and proctitis cystica profunda. Anal fibroepithelial polyp (hypertrophied anal papilla / skin tag) Benign reactive polyp Common benign lesion of the anal transformation zone. Often occurs in the setting of chronic inflammation, hemorrhoids, mucosal prolapse, fissures, or Crohn disease. May present as an anal tag or polyp and can be mistaken clinically for condyloma. Polyp covered by nonkeratinizing stratified squamous or transitional epithelium. Subepithelial stroma contains variable vessels, smooth muscle, and chronic inflammation. Correlate with trauma or chronic inflammatory conditions. Polypoid fibrovascular tissue is covered by squamous or transitional epithelium. Reactive hyperkeratosis or parakeratosis may occur. The stroma shows variable vascular, smooth muscle, and chronic inflammatory components. Condyloma acuminatum Shows papillomatous epithelial proliferation and koilocytosis; a fibroepithelial polyp has a dominant stromal core. Anal SIL Requires squamous epithelial atypia; reactive epithelial changes alone are insufficient. Shows more complex tubulovillous epithelial hyperplasia, granulation tissue, vascular ectasia, and mucosal prolapse changes. Clinical resemblance to condyloma is common; base the diagnosis on epithelial morphology and stromal architecture. Do not interpret reactive hyperkeratosis or parakeratosis as evidence of HPV-associated dysplasia. Hemorrhoids Benign vascular plexus dilation The most common mass-like lesion in the anal region. May be internal (proximal to the dentate line) or external (distal to the dentate line). Associated with elevated intra-abdominal pressure and venous plexus dilation; may coexist with other anal lesions. Dilated venous plexuses in the appropriate anatomic compartment. Internal hemorrhoids are covered by transitional or columnar epithelium; external hemorrhoids are covered by squamous epithelium. Dilated, congested vascular channels form the mass-like lesion. The covering epithelium reflects the location relative to the dentate line. Vascular neoplasm Hemorrhoids show dilated venous plexuses without an atypical or destructive endothelial proliferation. Anal fibroepithelial polyp A fibroepithelial polyp has a dominant fibrovascular stromal core rather than a dilated venous plexus. Hemorrhoids may coexist with a separate epithelial lesion; do not assume they explain all symptoms or the entire mass. Ectopic tissue of the anal canal Benign heterotopia Rare; ectopic gastric mucosa is reported more often in men. Ectopic gastric mucosa may present with rectal bleeding, ulceration, or pain. Ectopic prostatic tissue has also been reported. Identify tissue that is histologically native to another organ but located ectopically in the anal canal. Correlate with the clinical setting and exclude direct extension or metastasis when appropriate. Ectopic gastric mucosa shows gastric-type glands in the anal canal mucosa. Ectopic prostatic tissue shows prostatic-type glands and stroma. Metastatic or directly extending carcinoma Assess cytologic atypia, destructive invasion, clinical history, and imaging; benign ectopic tissue lacks malignant features. Anal gland adenocarcinoma is invasive and typically forms infiltrative glands; benign ectopic tissue lacks destructive growth. Do not diagnose malignancy solely because glandular tissue is present at an unusual site. All PathologyGPS / GI & Liver / Anal Canal Tumors Anal Canal Tumors A morphology-first reference to anal squamous precursors, invasive epithelial malignancies, and common tumor-like lesions. Core diagnostic principle Establish the anatomic site and epithelial lineage before assigning the tumor type. The anal canal contains colorectal-type, transitional, and squamous epithelium. The dentate line and anal transformation zone are important diagnostic landmarks. Diagnostic GPS: anatomic site to classification Define the location Distinguish anal canal, anal verge, perianal skin, and ischiorectal region; document the relationship to the dentate line. Identify the epithelial zone Upper colorectal-type columnar mucosa, middle anal transformation zone, or lower nonkeratinizing squamous mucosa. Establish lineage Squamous, glandular, melanocytic, neuroendocrine, or a benign/reactive tumor-like process. Assess invasion Separate intraepithelial SIL from invasive SCC or adenocarcinoma; assess pushing versus destructive growth in verrucous lesions. Use targeted ancillary tests p16/HPV for SIL and selected SCC; CK7, CK20, CDX2, MUC5AC, p63/CK5/6, and HPV studies for selected adenocarcinomas. Anatomic landmarks with diagnostic impact Anal canal: approximately 30–50 mm long, extending from the anorectal junction to the anal verge. Upper zone: colorectal-type columnar epithelium. Middle zone: transitional epithelium forming the anal transformation zone, which is susceptible to HPV-associated lesions. Lower zone: nonkeratinizing stratified squamous epithelium without skin appendages. Perianal skin: hair-bearing keratinizing squamous epithelium beyond the anal verge. Lymphatic drainage: tumors above the dentate line usually drain to perirectal/internal iliac nodes; tumors below it drain to inguinal/femoral nodes. High-yield ancillary tests Anal HSIL p16: strong, continuous block-type staining; correlate with morphology HPV-associated anal lesions High-risk HPV RNA ISH or PCR in selected equivocal cases HPV-independent differentiated AIN Aberrant p53 with absent p16 block staining supports TP53-mutant disease Anal SCC Pancytokeratin, CK5/6, p40; p16 supports HPV association CK7+, MUC5AC+, CK20−, CDX2−; CK5/6 and p63 negative Primary anal Paget disease CK7+, GCDFP-15+; typically CK20− and CDX2− Entity reference Diagnostic profiles and differential diagnosis Search by entity, site, morphology, immunomarker, or molecular alteration. e.g. p16, HPV16, CK7, fistula, Paget... bg-teal-700 text-white border border-slate-300 bg-white text-slate-600 Collapse − View diagnostic profile + Clinical Profile Essential Diagnostic Criteria Histopathology Immunophenotype Molecular Pathology Differential Diagnosis Diagnostic Pitfalls No matching entity. High-yield distinction: anal gland, fistula-associated, and mucosal adenocarcinoma Feature Mucosal type Anal gland / duct Fistula-associated Origin Luminal mucosa Anal gland or duct Longstanding anal fistula Surface in situ component May be present Absent by definition Typical morphology Intestinal or transitional-zone phenotype Haphazard glands, cuboidal cells, scant mucin Usually mucinous; may resemble colorectal mucinous adenocarcinoma Useful phenotype Variable; HPV-associated subset often CK7+/p16+ CK7+/MUC5AC+, CK20−/CDX2− Variable intestinal or anal gland-like phenotype Key exclusion Direct extension from rectum/colon Genital tract or breast primary Colorectal primary extending into fistula Biopsy, sampling, and reporting checklist Document the precise anatomic site and relationship to the dentate line, anal verge, and perianal skin. For SIL/condyloma, sample the entire lesion when feasible because LSIL and HSIL may coexist. For suspected invasive SCC, establish stromal invasion and distinguish conventional SCC from verrucous carcinoma; superficial biopsies may be insufficient. For anal adenocarcinoma, determine mucosal versus extramucosal origin and correlate with endoscopy, imaging, fistula history, and prior malignancy. For fistula-associated carcinoma, document the duration and clinical history of the fistula and exclude a colorectal primary. For suspected Paget disease, distinguish primary cutaneous disease from secondary pagetoid spread by an underlying anorectal adenocarcinoma using a focused IHC panel. Report histologic type, invasion, margins, lymphovascular/perineural invasion when present, and relevant precursor or associated lesion. Scope note: Content is based on the supplied WHO excerpt. Ancillary tests are presented in their stated diagnostic context and should be interpreted with morphology, anatomic site, and clinical findings. Perianal skin tumors outside the anal canal chapter are not comprehensively covered.

title: Appendiceal Tumors
content: use client Appendiceal Serrated Lesions Benign / Precursor Non-dysplastic or dysplastic epithelial precursor Throughout the appendix; hyperplastic polyps and sessile serrated lesions may be incidental. Usually identified incidentally in appendectomy specimens. Most patients are older adults, generally 60–80 years; men and women are affected at nearly equal frequency. Dysplastic lesions, especially those with traditional serrated adenoma-like dysplasia, may obstruct the lumen and present with appendicitis. Hyperplastic polyp: polypoid proliferation of non-dysplastic serrated crypts with goblet and non-goblet columnar cells containing tiny mucin vesicles. Sessile serrated lesion (SSL): architecturally distorted, serrated crypts with preserved lamina propria and no overt dysplasia. Serrated dysplasia: serrated crypts lined by dysplastic epithelium; dysplasia may be conventional, serrated, traditional serrated adenoma-like, or unclassified. Hyperplastic polyp: elongated crypts with luminal serration and increased goblet cells; deep crypt architecture remains normal. SSL: circumferential mucosal involvement by elongated crypts with serration extending to the bases. SSL crypts may be dilated near the muscularis mucosae and show L-shaped or inverted T-shaped profiles. Dysplastic components may show conventional villous dysplasia, serrated dysplasia, or traditional serrated adenoma-like architecture. Traditional serrated adenoma-like dysplasia shows slit-like serration and villous projections lined by tall eosinophilic columnar cells. Postinflammatory mucosal hyperplasia Goblet cell-rich epithelium, Paneth cells, well-formed crypts, preserved lamina propria, and inflammatory changes favor a reactive process. LAMN LAMN shows mucinous epithelial proliferation with reduced lamina propria and mural changes; SSL retains normal appendiceal wall architecture and lacks mural or extra-appendiceal mucin. Conventional adenoma Conventional adenoma shows intestinal-type dysplasia without the defining serrated crypt architecture. Do not diagnose an SSL or hyperplastic polyp in circumferential reactive mucosal hyperplasia after appendicitis or in diverticular disease. Serrated architecture alone does not establish LAMN; assess cytology, lamina propria, muscularis mucosae, and mural changes. Appendiceal serrated lesions are associated with an increased risk of colorectal neoplasia. Appendiceal Mucinous Adenoma Benign Benign; cured by appendectomy May involve any part of the appendix, focally or diffusely. Usually asymptomatic and found incidentally on imaging or in an appendectomy specimen. When associated with acute appendicitis, patients may have right lower quadrant pain, fever, and leukocytosis. Typically occurs in the sixth decade (median age 55 years; reported range 42–68); men and women are similarly affected. Circumferential proliferation of mucin-containing neoplastic columnar cells confined to the mucosa. Muscularis mucosae remains intact around the entire circumference and is clearly separated from the submucosa. No pushing or diverticulum-like mural growth, mural mucin pools, extensive mural fibrosis, or extra-appendiceal mucin/epithelium. Epithelium may be filiform, villous, undulating, or flat; lamina propria may be markedly reduced. Cells are often tall and mucin-rich, with basally oriented small or mildly enlarged hyperchromatic nuclei. Mitotic figures are infrequent in low-grade areas. Focal high-grade dysplasia may show cribriform glands, micropapillae, nuclear stratification, loss of polarity, necrosis, and increased mitotic activity. LAMN / HAMN Incomplete or disrupted muscularis mucosae, pushing or diverticulum-like growth, mural mucin, fibrosis/hyalinization, or extra-appendiceal mucin favors an appendiceal mucinous neoplasm. Reactive epithelium is goblet cell-rich, often includes Paneth cells, and is supported by well-formed lamina propria. Appendiceal serrated lesion Serrated lesions show complex crypt serration rather than the filiform, villous, or undulating architecture typical of mucinous adenoma. Submit the entire appendix when mucinous adenoma is considered to exclude LAMN or HAMN. Do not use the obsolete terms mucinous cystadenoma or borderline tumor of the appendix. Serosal mucin is incompatible with a diagnosis of mucinous adenoma. Conventional Appendiceal Adenoma Benign epithelial neoplasm; HGD is classified as pTis Appendix proper; distinguish from a cecal adenoma extending into the appendiceal orifice. Almost always asymptomatic and discovered incidentally in a resection specimen. May present with appendicitis; rarely causes intussusception or distal appendiceal dilatation. May occur sporadically or with hereditary syndromes, particularly familial adenomatous polyposis; no characteristic sex or age distribution is specified in the source. Tubular, villous, or tubulovillous glandular neoplasm with conventional intestinal dysplasia. No invasive growth. Enlarged crypts expand the mucosa and show variable size and shape. Columnar neoplastic cells have minimal or absent cytoplasmic mucin, with occasional goblet cells. Low-grade dysplasia shows elongated pseudostratified nuclei near the basement membrane without significant architectural complexity. High-grade dysplasia shows papillary or cribriform complexity, nuclear stratification, loss of polarity, and often prominent nucleoli. Mucin pools and the mural remodeling characteristic of appendiceal mucinous neoplasms are absent. KRAS mutations commonly occur with APC or RNF43 alterations; TP53 mutations are reported, particularly in lesions with high-grade dysplasia. Appendiceal mucinous adenoma Mucinous adenoma has mucin-rich columnar epithelium and an intact circumferential muscularis mucosae. Mucinous neoplasms show characteristic mural remodeling, pushing/diverticulum-like growth, and/or mural or extra-appendiceal mucin. Cecal adenoma involving the appendiceal orifice Establish the epicenter and determine whether the lesion arises in the cecum or the appendix proper. Do not interpret reduced lamina propria alone as evidence of a mucinous neoplasm. Conventional appendiceal adenomas are not precursors of pseudomyxoma peritonei. The source reports insufficient evidence to define progression risk by size, villous component, or HGD. Appendiceal Mucinous Neoplasms (LAMN / HAMN) Neoplasm Non-infiltrative neoplasm; peritoneal spread may occur Often asymptomatic and detected on imaging; some patients undergo appendectomy for presumed acute appendicitis. May present with appendiceal dilatation, right lower quadrant pain, fever, or leukocytosis. Peritoneal dissemination may cause progressive abdominal distension, a new umbilical hernia, or an abdominal/pelvic mass. Usually occurs in the sixth decade; women are slightly more frequently affected in reported series. Circumferential mucinous epithelial proliferation with decreased lamina propria and characteristic appendiceal wall remodeling. At least one of the following: disrupted muscularis mucosae, wall hyalinization/fibrosis, pushing or diverticulum-like epithelial growth, mural mucin pools, or extra-appendiceal mucin with or without neoplastic epithelium. LAMN: low-grade cytologic atypia; HAMN: unequivocal high-grade cytologic features in at least 10% of tumor cells. No infiltrative-type destructive invasion; its presence supports mucinous adenocarcinoma. LAMN: circumferential replacement by mucin-rich columnar epithelium with filiform, villous, undulating, or flat architecture. LAMN cells have abundant cytoplasmic mucin and basally oriented mildly enlarged hyperchromatic nuclei; mitoses and apoptotic debris are usually sparse. Lamina propria and lymphoid tissue are reduced or absent; muscularis mucosae may be focally lost. Mural changes include dissecting mucin, expansile or diverticulum-like epithelial growth, fibrosis, hyalinization, and calcification. HAMN: high-grade epithelium may show micropapillary or cribriform growth, epithelial piling, marked nuclear atypia, loss of polarity, frequent mitoses, and necrosis. Extra-appendiceal mucin may be acellular or contain neoplastic epithelium. LAMN commonly harbors KRAS mutations (approximately 60–90%) and GNAS mutations (approximately 50–60%), often together. KRAS mutations are also common in HAMN; GNAS mutations are more variable. Microsatellite instability is not a characteristic feature; BRAF mutations are rare. Mucinous adenoma Mucinous adenoma retains an intact muscularis mucosae throughout and lacks mural remodeling or extra-appendiceal mucin. Appendiceal diverticular disease / interval appendectomy changes Reactive crypts retain goblet and Paneth cells, lamina propria, lymphoid tissue, and an intact muscularis mucosae. Sessile serrated lesion SSL retains lamina propria and normal wall-layer separation, without mural or extra-appendiceal mucin. Mucinous adenocarcinoma Destructive infiltrative glands or small dissecting cellular mucin pools with desmoplasia establish invasive adenocarcinoma. Peritoneal dissemination alone does not distinguish HAMN from mucinous adenocarcinoma; evaluate the pattern of invasion. Examine the entire appendix when the distinction from infiltrative adenocarcinoma is in question. For peritoneal disease, distinguish acellular mucin from mucin containing neoplastic epithelium. Avoid spreading luminal mucin onto the serosa during gross examination. Appendiceal Adenocarcinoma Malignant Malignant; infiltrative invasion with metastatic potential Can arise anywhere along the appendix; mucinous, non-mucinous, and signet-ring cell types occur. Typically affects adults in the fifth through seventh decades. Mucinous adenocarcinoma shows a slight female predominance; non-mucinous adenocarcinoma a slight male predominance; signet-ring cell adenocarcinoma a female predominance. Common presentations include acute appendicitis or abdominal pain; a mass, obstruction, gastrointestinal bleeding, or metastatic symptoms may occur. Malignant glandular neoplasm with infiltrative invasion and/or mucin production. Mucinous adenocarcinoma: infiltrative malignant glands or tumor cells with extracellular mucin comprising more than 50% of the tumor. Signet-ring cell adenocarcinoma: more than 50% of tumor cells show signet-ring morphology. Non-mucinous adenocarcinoma: infiltrative malignant glands resembling colorectal adenocarcinoma or another less common pattern. Mucinous adenocarcinoma shows infiltrative glands, cribriform or incomplete glands, or single infiltrative cells in extracellular mucin with desmoplastic stroma. Small dissecting pools of cellular mucin containing floating tumor nests, glands, or single cells are an additional invasion pattern. Signet-ring cell adenocarcinoma requires more than 50% signet-ring cells, which may float in mucin pools or infiltrate tissue. Non-mucinous adenocarcinoma shows irregular or jagged infiltrative glands with desmoplastic stroma; morphology may resemble colorectal adenocarcinoma. Undifferentiated carcinoma is rare and resembles its colorectal counterpart. Mucinous adenocarcinoma frequently harbors KRAS (approximately 55–80%) and GNAS (approximately 30–70%) mutations; co-mutation is common. TP53 mutations occur across subtypes and are more frequent in non-mucinous adenocarcinoma. Mismatch repair IHC and/or MSI testing should be performed; deficiency is uncommon overall but may occur, particularly in non-mucinous tumors. LAMN/HAMN show broad pushing or diverticulum-like growth with mural remodeling; adenocarcinoma shows destructive infiltrative invasion and desmoplasia. Goblet cell adenocarcinoma GCA shows intimately admixed goblet-like mucinous, neuroendocrine, and Paneth-like differentiation, often without surface precursor dysplasia. Metastatic colorectal adenocarcinoma Correlate with clinical history, imaging, and distribution; appendiceal primary requires an appropriate appendiceal epicenter. Signet-ring cell adenocarcinoma Use the greater-than-50% signet-ring cell threshold for this subtype. Submit the entire appendix when mucinous neoplasm is in the differential to exclude focal infiltrative invasion. Do not classify broad pushing invasion with wall hyalinization as destructive infiltrative adenocarcinoma. For mucinous tumors, report grade and peritoneal disease characteristics; signet-ring cells have adverse prognostic significance. Appendiceal Goblet Cell Adenocarcinoma Malignant amphicrine-like carcinoma; staged as appendiceal adenocarcinoma Any part of the appendix, with a predilection for the distal appendix. Mean age at diagnosis is approximately 56 years (reported range 23–90); men and women are affected similarly. Most commonly presents with acute appendicitis, followed by nonspecific abdominal pain or an abdominal mass. Metastases most often involve the peritoneum, omentum, abdominal wall, and ovaries. Amphicrine-like carcinoma composed of intimately admixed goblet-like mucinous cells with variable neuroendocrine and Paneth-like differentiation. Low-grade component: cohesive, smooth-contoured tubules or nests with goblet-like mucin, small peripheral nuclei, and no brisk mitotic activity or stromal desmoplasia. High-grade component: loss of cohesive tubules/nests, infiltrative single cells or single-file growth, complex irregular glands, cribriform or confluent growth, desmoplasia, and marked atypia. Tumor commonly involves the appendiceal wall circumferentially; early disease may be grossly inconspicuous. Low-grade tumors form cohesive tubules, nests, or clusters resembling intestinal crypts. Low-grade cells have peripheral small nuclei, intracellular goblet-like mucin, and granular eosinophilic cytoplasm. High-grade tumors show irregular anastomosing tubules/nests, cribriform structures, single-file or single-cell infiltration, and confluent sheets. High-grade areas show marked nuclear pleomorphism, frequent mitoses, stromal desmoplasia, and sometimes necrosis. Perineural invasion is common at all grades; lymphovascular invasion is more frequent in high-grade tumors. Chromogranin and synaptophysin highlight variable numbers of tumor cells but are not required for diagnosis. High-grade GCA retains at least rudimentary clustering and often focal low-grade GCA-like areas; signet-ring cell adenocarcinoma is defined by a predominant signet-ring cell population. Conventional / mucinous adenocarcinoma GCA shows intimately admixed amphicrine-like differentiation and typically lacks precursor dysplasia in the surface epithelium. Neuroendocrine carcinoma GCA has goblet-like mucinous and Paneth-like components; neuroendocrine marker expression is variable and is not required. Mucinous carcinoma peritonei Metastatic GCA usually does not produce abundant mucinous ascites; classify and grade the metastatic tumor as GCA. Do not use the terms goblet cell carcinoid, crypt cell carcinoma, microglandular carcinoma, or adenocarcinoid. Appendicitis-associated inflammation may increase atypia and architectural distortion; avoid overgrading low-grade GCA. Grade GCA using the proportion of low-grade and high-grade components; stage it as appendiceal adenocarcinoma. Perineural invasion is common but is not prognostically significant according to the source. All PathologyGPS / GI & Liver / Appendiceal Tumors Appendiceal Tumors A morphology-first reference emphasizing the distinction between epithelial precursors, non-invasive mucinous neoplasms, infiltrative adenocarcinoma, and goblet cell adenocarcinoma. Core diagnostic rule In appendiceal mucinous lesions, the pattern of wall involvement and invasion is decisive. Distinguish intact mucosa, pushing/diverticulum-like growth, and destructive infiltrative invasion; assess the entire appendix. Diagnostic GPS: classify the appendiceal epithelial lesion Establish the epicenter Appendix proper versus cecal adenoma extending into the appendiceal orifice; note distal versus proximal involvement. Assess the mucosal pattern Serrated crypts, conventional intestinal dysplasia, or mucin-rich columnar epithelium. Evaluate the wall Is the muscularis mucosae intact? Look for fibrosis, hyalinization, loss of tissue planes, mural mucin, and pushing growth. Determine the invasion pattern Broad pushing/diverticulum-like growth favors LAMN/HAMN; destructive infiltrative glands with desmoplasia favor adenocarcinoma. Recognize goblet cell phenotype Intimately admixed goblet-like mucinous, neuroendocrine, and Paneth-like differentiation supports GCA. The critical distinction: mucinous adenoma, LAMN/HAMN, and mucinous adenocarcinoma Feature Muscularis mucosae Intact throughout Often disrupted/lost Variable; infiltrative invasion Wall growth Confined to mucosa Pushing / diverticulum-like Destructive infiltrative glands/cells Mural mucin / fibrosis Absent Often present May accompany infiltrative cellular mucin Desmoplasia Not the defining pattern Supports destructive invasion High-yield molecular pathology Appendiceal serrated lesions KRAS and BRAF alterations are described, but routine diagnostic molecular testing is not clinically relevant. Conventional appendiceal adenoma KRAS with APC or RNF43; TP53 may occur, especially in HGD. KRAS and GNAS are common, particularly in LAMN; MSI is not characteristic. Appendiceal adenocarcinoma KRAS, GNAS, and TP53; perform MMR IHC and/or MSI testing. No clinically relevant diagnostic molecular test is established in the supplied source. Gross examination, sampling, and reporting checklist Document appendiceal length, diameter, dilatation, wall integrity, perforation, and any mucin on the serosal surface. Handle suspected mucinous lesions carefully to avoid iatrogenic rupture and displacement of luminal mucin onto the serosa. Submit the entire appendix when LAMN/HAMN or mucinous adenocarcinoma is in the differential, particularly to identify focal infiltrative invasion. Sample the appendiceal base, tip, areas of wall thickening/fibrosis, perforation, serosal mucin, and any solid or nodular component. For extra-appendiceal mucin, document whether it is acellular or contains neoplastic epithelium and record its anatomic distribution. For adenocarcinoma, report histologic subtype, grade, depth/pattern of invasion, lymphovascular and perineural invasion, margins, and nodal status. For goblet cell adenocarcinoma, report grade and the proportion of low-grade and high-grade components; stage according to appendiceal adenocarcinoma criteria. title: Colorectal Tumors
content: use client Colorectal Hyperplastic Polyp Benign Benign; distal small lesions have negligible malignant potential Predominantly distal colon and rectum (75–90%). Usually diagnosed after age 50; men are affected more often than women. Common and usually asymptomatic; detected during screening or surveillance colonoscopy. Typically a small (<5 mm), discrete sessile polyp. Non-dysplastic serrated epithelial proliferation. Crypt architecture is largely preserved, without basal dilation or substantial distortion. Microvesicular type: superficial serration and stellate crypt lumina, with evenly spaced funnel-shaped crypts and proliferation confined to crypt bases. Microvesicular cells contain fine apical mucin vacuoles; nuclei are small, round to ovoid, and basally located. Goblet cell–rich type: elongated, widened, occasionally branched or tortuous crypts lined predominantly by goblet cells. Goblet cell–rich type may show subtle serration limited to the surface and crypt orifices; cross-sectional crypt lumina remain round. Ki-67 in microvesicular hyperplastic polyps shows symmetric labeling of basal epithelial cells. Sessile serrated lesion Shows unequivocal abnormal crypt architecture, especially basal dilation, horizontal growth, and serration extending to crypt bases. Reactive epithelial hyperplasia Lacks a convincing polypoid serrated proliferation with the characteristic crypt pattern. Microvesicular and goblet cell–rich subtypes do not have established clinical significance. Do not diagnose a sessile serrated lesion on proximal location alone. Colorectal Sessile Serrated Lesion (SSL) Benign precursor; dysplasia identifies a higher-risk progression step Predominantly proximal colon (70–80%), particularly SSLs with dysplasia. Most patients are in their 50s at diagnosis, with a slight male predominance. Usually asymptomatic and detected at screening or surveillance colonoscopy; lesions may be subtle and covered by a mucus cap. Large lesions (>10 mm) are more likely to develop dysplasia and are considered advanced lesions in most surveillance guidelines. Serrated crypt proliferation with unequivocal architectural distortion; one characteristic distorted serrated crypt is sufficient. SSL without dysplasia lacks cytological dysplasia. SSL with dysplasia shows increased architectural complexity and cytological dysplasia of variable morphology. Typical SSL crypts show basal one-third dilation, horizontal growth parallel to the muscularis mucosae, serration extending to the crypt bases, and asymmetric proliferation along crypt sides. Crypt bases may be L-shaped or inverted T-shaped; branching is common but not specific. Lesional epithelium contains goblet cells and non-goblet cells with microvesicular mucin droplets. Dysplasia is often sharply demarcated from the background SSL and may show villous architecture, crowded/branched or cribriform glands, and altered serration. Dysplastic cytology may be conventional adenomatous, serrated with eosinophilic cytoplasm and prominent nucleoli, or subtle hypermucinous/minimal-deviation type. Loss of MLH1 in the dysplastic component supports an SSL-associated dysplasia pattern but is not present in every case. Most SSLs harbor activating BRAF mutations; KRAS mutations are uncommon. Progression is associated with CpG island methylation; MLH1 promoter methylation can cause mismatch repair deficiency in the dysplastic component. A subset of mismatch repair–proficient SSLs with dysplasia has TP53 alterations; rare cases have NTRK rearrangements. Hyperplastic polyp Lacks unequivocal basal crypt distortion, horizontal growth, and serration extending to the crypt bases. Mucosal prolapse / inflammatory polyp Usually lacks the characteristic microvesicular mucin-containing epithelial population and distorted serrated crypt bases. Mucosal herniation SSL elements may herniate through muscularis mucosae, especially near lymphoid aggregates; this is not invasion without destructive growth/desmoplasia. Well-oriented sections including crypt bases are often essential; obtain deeper levels when orientation is poor. Do not use size, location, or endoscopic appearance alone to diagnose SSL. Do not grade SSL-associated dysplasia as low- versus high-grade; report the presence of dysplasia. Colorectal Traditional Serrated Adenoma (TSA) Benign epithelial neoplasm with malignant precursor potential Approximately 70% occur in the distal colon and rectum; proximal lesions also occur. Uncommon (<1% of colorectal polyps). Usually asymptomatic and found at screening or surveillance; larger lesions may bleed. Proximal lesions may be plaque-like; distal lesions are often broad-based and polypoid with a pinecone- or coral-like surface. Non-invasive flat or polypoid lesion with slit-like crypt serrations and/or ectopic crypt foci. Dense eosinophilic cytoplasm and pale pencillate nuclei are desirable supporting features. Usually tubulovillous or villous architecture with slit-like serrations. Tall columnar cells have dense eosinophilic cytoplasm and elongated, pale pencillate nuclei with smooth nuclear membranes. Ectopic crypt foci are rounded epithelial protrusions into lamina propria that are not anchored to muscularis mucosae; they are more common in protuberant lesions. Conventional adenomatous-type dysplasia may coexist; any TSA component warrants classification as TSA. Foci of marked nuclear hyperchromasia or high-grade atypia may occur; grade according to nuclear cytology. Ki-67 highlights the proliferative compartment in ectopic crypt foci. Two major molecular routes involve BRAF or KRAS mutations; BRAF-mutant TSAs often show CIMP and RNF43 alterations. KRAS-mutant TSAs, often distal, may harbor RSPO fusions and tend toward conventional adenomatous dysplasia. Conventional adenoma Usually has hyperchromatic, pseudostratified nuclei rather than the pale pencillate nuclei and dense eosinophilic cytoplasm of TSA. Sessile serrated lesion with dysplasia A distinctive TSA component (eosinophilic cytoplasm and/or ectopic crypts) supports classification as TSA. Lacks villous/tubulovillous architecture, ectopic crypts, and characteristic eosinophilic TSA cytology. Do not use the term mixed adenoma or serrated tubulovillous adenoma; classify lesions with any TSA component as TSA. Ectopic crypts are helpful but may be absent, particularly in flat lesions. Serrated Polyposis Syndrome Intermediate Clinical polyposis syndrome associated with increased colorectal carcinoma risk Multiple serrated polyps throughout the colon and rectum; upper GI tract and small intestine are not involved. Most patients are diagnosed at 50–60 years, although the age range is broad; both sexes are affected approximately equally. Presentation may occur during screening, surveillance, evaluation of symptoms, family-history assessment, or at colorectal carcinoma diagnosis. Polyp burden is often substantial (commonly 30–40 cumulative polyps), with frequent pancolonic distribution. WHO 2019 clinical criterion 1: at least 5 serrated lesions/polyps proximal to the rectum, all ≥5 mm, with at least 2 ≥10 mm. WHO 2019 clinical criterion 2: more than 20 serrated lesions/polyps of any size distributed throughout the large bowel, with at least 5 proximal to the rectum. Counts are cumulative across colonoscopies; all serrated histologic subtypes are included. The histology is that of the associated sporadic serrated lesions: hyperplastic polyps, SSLs with or without dysplasia, and TSAs. Conventional adenomas may coexist and should be included in the overall polyp assessment but not in the serrated-polyp count. No single causative germline alteration is established; pathogenic RNF43 germline variants account for fewer than 2% of cases. Associated serrated polyps generally show molecular profiles similar to their sporadic counterparts. MUTYH-associated polyposis May include multiple serrated lesions but is a defined hereditary syndrome requiring clinical/genetic correlation. Hereditary mixed polyposis syndrome Consider GREM1-associated disease when mixed polyp phenotypes and family history are present. PTEN hamartoma tumor syndrome / juvenile polyposis Look for other polyp types and extraintestinal manifestations. The diagnosis is clinical, not based on a single biopsy or histologic subtype. The polyp count is cumulative across procedures. Consider clinical genetics evaluation in undiagnosed polyposis, while recognizing that most serrated polyposis is not explained by a known germline variant. Colorectal Juvenile Polyp Usually benign hamartomatous polyp; multiple lesions may indicate juvenile polyposis syndrome Usually colorectum, especially rectosigmoid; sporadic lesions may occur in children. Sporadic juvenile polyps most often present in childhood, commonly with painless rectal bleeding or prolapse. A solitary lesion is typical in the sporadic setting; multiple polyps raise concern for juvenile polyposis syndrome. Hamartomatous polyp with cystically dilated, mucus-filled glands in an expanded edematous/inflamed lamina propria. No epithelial dysplasia in a typical sporadic juvenile polyp. Cystically dilated glands are lined by non-dysplastic epithelium and may contain mucin, inflammatory debris, and blood. The lamina propria is expanded by edema, inflammation, and granulation tissue. Surface erosion and regenerative epithelial changes may be present. Inflammatory polyp May show granulation tissue and inflammation but lacks the characteristic cystically dilated mucus-filled glands. Mucosal prolapse polyp Shows fibromuscular obliteration and smooth muscle extension rather than the classic juvenile hamartomatous architecture. Juvenile polyposis syndrome Multiple juvenile polyps and clinical/family-history criteria distinguish the syndrome from a solitary sporadic polyp. Interpret polyp multiplicity and family history clinically; a solitary juvenile polyp is not equivalent to juvenile polyposis syndrome. Conventional Colorectal Adenoma Dysplastic precursor lesion; risk increases with size, villous architecture, and high-grade dysplasia May arise anywhere from the ileocecal valve to the anorectal junction. Incidence increases with age and peaks after 70 years; men are affected more often than women. Most uncomplicated adenomas are asymptomatic; occult bleeding is common. Larger lesions may cause visible bleeding, abdominal pain, or altered bowel habits; large distal villous adenomas may cause secretory diarrhea and electrolyte depletion (McKittrick–Wheelock syndrome). Conventional adenomatous dysplasia with nuclear enlargement, hyperchromasia, pseudostratification, and loss of maturation/polarity. Tubular, tubulovillous, or villous architecture; villous component is <25% in tubular, >25% in tubulovillous, and >75% in villous adenoma. High-grade dysplasia is characterized by marked cytologic atypia and/or complex architecture, including cribriforming. Tubular adenoma: elongated crowded crypts with dysplastic epithelium; a villous component under 25% is acceptable. Tubulovillous adenoma: more than 25% villous architecture. Villous adenoma: more than 75% villous architecture. Low-grade dysplasia shows enlarged, elongated, hyperchromatic, stratified nuclei, usually with preserved polarity and maturation toward the surface. High-grade dysplasia shows marked nuclear enlargement/pleomorphism, loss of polarity, full-thickness stratification, and often complex glandular architecture. Advanced adenoma conventionally includes size ≥10 mm, villous/tubulovillous architecture, and/or high-grade dysplasia; surveillance definitions vary. The conventional adenoma–carcinoma sequence commonly begins with APC/WNT pathway inactivation, followed by alterations such as KRAS, SMAD4, PIK3CA/PTEN, and TP53. In Lynch syndrome, adenomas may show mismatch repair deficiency after a second hit in the remaining functional MMR allele. Traditional serrated adenoma Shows slit-like serrations, eosinophilic cytoplasm, pale pencillate nuclei, and/or ectopic crypts. Has a background of architecturally distorted serrated crypts; dysplasia may be sharply demarcated. Reactive/regenerative atypia Usually retains surface maturation and lacks the persistent cytologic and architectural features of adenomatous dysplasia. Villous subtyping has limited reproducibility; size and grade remain important for risk stratification. Assess the surface epithelium when evaluating IBD-associated dysplasia; basal-only atypia requires caution. Inflammatory Bowel Disease–Associated Dysplasia Colitis-associated neoplasia; dysplasia grade and visibility guide clinical management Colorectal mucosa affected by chronic ulcerative colitis or Crohn colitis. Occurs in the setting of longstanding inflammatory bowel disease; lesions may be endoscopically visible or invisible. Diagnosis and grading of dysplasia are more important for management than assigning a specific morphologic pattern. Active inflammation and ulceration can make distinction from reactive atypia difficult. Dysplasia is characterized by unequivocal epithelial cytologic atypia, preferably involving the surface epithelium. Low-grade dysplasia shows mildly enlarged, elongated, hyperchromatic, stratified nuclei, mostly in the basal half of the cells. High-grade dysplasia shows marked nuclear enlargement/pleomorphism, loss of polarity, full-thickness stratification, and often cribriforming. Use indefinite for dysplasia when active inflammation/ulceration prevents confident distinction from reactive change. Conventional/adenomatous-type dysplasia is the most common pattern and resembles sporadic adenomatous dysplasia. Serrated dysplasia may resemble SSL-associated or TSA-associated dysplasia; mixed patterns can occur in one lesion. Hypermucinous dysplasia shows tubulovillous/villous growth, tall cells with multilayered mucin vacuoles, and often subtle atypia. Goblet cell–deficient dysplasia shows tubular architecture, eosinophilic enterocyte-like cytoplasm, and near-complete absence of goblet cells. Crypt cell dysplasia shows mild nuclear enlargement/hyperchromasia without significant architectural change. Intramucosal carcinoma invades lamina propria or extends into, but not beyond, muscularis mucosae; desmoplasia generally indicates submucosal invasion. Aberrant p53 staining may support selected patterns, including basal crypt dysplasia and hypermucinous or goblet cell–deficient dysplasia; it is not a stand-alone diagnostic criterion. MLH1 loss may occur in selected dysplastic serrated lesions. Hypermucinous dysplasia frequently harbors KRAS mutations; goblet cell–deficient dysplasia may harbor PIK3CA and KRAS mutations. Molecular findings are not required for routine diagnosis or grading. Reactive atypia Usually occurs with active inflammation and lacks unequivocal surface dysplasia; repeat evaluation after inflammation control may be necessary. Sporadic adenoma A lesion in a colitis-unaffected area may be sporadic; correlate with distribution of colitis and endoscopic findings. Serrated epithelial change May be endoscopically invisible and resemble hyperplastic polyp; current evidence does not establish benefit from intensified surveillance based on this finding alone. Do not overemphasize morphologic subtype at the expense of a reproducible dysplasia diagnosis and grade. Basal crypt dysplasia without surface involvement is challenging; an indefinite-for-dysplasia diagnosis may be appropriate. Acellular mucin after neoadjuvant therapy does not establish mucinous adenocarcinoma. Colorectal Adenocarcinoma Malignant Malignant epithelial neoplasm with regional and distant metastatic potential Right/proximal colon (cecum, ascending, transverse), left colon (splenic flexure through sigmoid), or rectum. Most cases occur in older adults, with incidence higher in men; incidence in adults younger than 50 years is increasing, particularly for distal tumors. Common presentations include altered bowel habits, abdominal pain, hematochezia, and symptoms of anemia; screening increasingly identifies asymptomatic disease. Proximal tumors are relatively more common in women and patients older than 60 years. Malignant epithelial tumor of the large bowel with unequivocal invasion. Grade by gland formation: low-grade retains glandular differentiation; high-grade contains a sufficiently extensive focus lacking gland formation. Report lymphovascular invasion, perineural invasion, tumor budding, poorly differentiated clusters, margins, lymph nodes, tumor deposits, and treatment response as applicable. Conventional adenocarcinoma forms infiltrative glands, often with desmoplastic stroma; grading is based on the least differentiated component, not cytologic atypia alone. Mucinous adenocarcinoma: more than 50% of the tumor consists of extracellular mucin. Signet-ring cell carcinoma: more than 50% of tumor cells show signet-ring morphology; classified as high-grade. Serrated adenocarcinoma shows serrated glandular architecture and may be associated with a serrated precursor. Micropapillary adenocarcinoma shows small clusters of tumor cells in clear stromal spaces and is considered high-grade. Medullary carcinoma shows solid/syncytial growth with prominent lymphocytic response; grade is not applicable despite solid morphology. Adenoma-like adenocarcinoma is deceptively well differentiated with minimal cytologic atypia but unequivocal invasion; considered low-grade. Low-grade tubuloglandular carcinoma is a distinctive low-grade pattern, typically associated with inflammatory bowel disease. Lymphoglandular complex–like adenocarcinoma is a distinctive pattern formerly described as dome/GALT carcinoma. Adenosquamous carcinoma contains glandular and squamous components and is high-grade. Squamous cell carcinoma is rare; exclude direct extension or metastasis from another primary site. Undifferentiated carcinoma lacks recognizable glandular or other lineage differentiation. Carcinoma with mesenchymal differentiation contains substantial epithelial and mesenchymal components; heterologous differentiation may include osteosarcomatous or rhabdomyosarcomatous elements. Tumor budding is defined as single cells or clusters of up to four tumor cells at the invasive front; poorly differentiated clusters contain at least five tumor cells without gland formation. Mismatch repair protein IHC (MLH1, PMS2, MSH2, MSH6) is used to assess MMR deficiency and screen for Lynch syndrome. D2-40 may help confirm lymphatic invasion in difficult cases. CD3/CD8 assessment of the immune infiltrate may provide prognostic information but is not a routine histotype-defining panel. RAS (KRAS/NRAS) mutation testing is predictive: mutations in relevant codons indicate lack of benefit from anti-EGFR monoclonal antibodies. BRAF V600E has prognostic and therapeutic relevance and, in an MLH1-deficient tumor, helps distinguish sporadic MLH1 promoter methylation from Lynch syndrome. MMR/MSI testing is essential for Lynch syndrome assessment and predicts potential benefit from immune checkpoint inhibitors. ERBB2 (HER2) amplification/overexpression may guide anti-HER2 therapy, particularly in advanced disease. NTRK fusions are rare but actionable; testing is most relevant in selected advanced, MSI-high, BRAF-wildtype tumors. POLE/POLD1 proofreading-domain mutations define a rare ultramutated subset; testing is context-dependent. Metastatic adenocarcinoma Use clinical history, distribution, morphology, and organ-specific immunophenotype to exclude a non-colorectal primary. Appendiceal adenocarcinoma Correlate with epicenter, gross findings, and appendix involvement; morphology and immunophenotype may overlap. Anal gland / gynecologic / prostate carcinoma involving colorectum Use site-specific markers and clinical-radiologic correlation. Treatment effect After neoadjuvant therapy, fibrosis and acellular mucin may remain; acellular mucin alone is not viable tumor or mucinous histotype. Do not grade tumors after neoadjuvant therapy; report grade as not applicable. Cribriform architecture is glandular differentiation and does not by itself define high-grade carcinoma. High-grade budding and poorly differentiated clusters are assessed separately from overall grade. A positive circumferential resection margin is generally defined as tumor within 1 mm of the margin. For pT1 lesions, depth of submucosal invasion, grade, lymphatic invasion, and tumor budding inform nodal risk. Adenoma-like Adenocarcinoma Low-grade malignant colorectal adenocarcinoma Colorectum; often presents as a polypoid or mass-forming lesion. Clinical presentation overlaps with other colorectal adenocarcinomas; source does not define a distinct age or sex predilection. Unequivocal invasion is required despite deceptively bland cytology and adenoma-like architecture. Pure adenoma-like adenocarcinoma is classified as low-grade. Highly differentiated glands closely resemble conventional adenoma. Cytologic atypia may be minimal; the diagnosis rests on unequivocal invasive growth, including infiltrative glands and/or desmoplastic response. Lacks destructive stromal invasion; adenoma-like carcinoma shows unequivocal invasion. Conventional low-grade adenocarcinoma Adenoma-like carcinoma is unusually well differentiated and may show minimal cytologic atypia. Do not equate bland cytology with benign behavior; establish invasion before diagnosing carcinoma. Carcinoma with Mesenchymal Differentiation Rare aggressive colorectal carcinoma; often presents at advanced stage Colorectum; exact anatomic predilection is not established in the supplied source. Extremely rare; literature consists largely of individual case reports. Often presents at advanced stage and appears to have a poor prognosis. More than 30% epithelial differentiation (gland formation and/or keratin expression). More than 30% homologous or heterologous mesenchymal differentiation with marked atypia and/or spindle-cell morphology. Patterns include pure spindle-cell morphology with keratin expression, admixed glandular and mesenchymal components, or overt sarcomatous differentiation. Heterologous elements may include osteosarcomatous or rhabdomyosarcomatous differentiation. Keratin expression supports epithelial differentiation in otherwise spindle-cell areas. Molecular findings are variable; MSI and SWI/SNF complex abnormalities have been reported in a small number of cases. Primary colorectal sarcoma Demonstration of a substantial epithelial component supports carcinoma with mesenchymal differentiation. Conventional adenocarcinoma with reactive spindle stroma Requires a true malignant mesenchymal component rather than desmoplastic stroma alone. The diagnosis requires substantial components of both epithelial and mesenchymal differentiation; focal spindle-cell change alone is insufficient. All PathologyGPS / Gastrointestinal Pathology / Colorectal Tumors Colorectal Tumors A morphology-first diagnostic reference for colorectal epithelial polyps, dysplasia, and carcinoma, emphasizing essential criteria, targeted ancillary studies, and practical differential diagnosis. Core principle Architecture establishes the precursor; unequivocal invasion establishes carcinoma. For serrated lesions, evaluate crypt bases. For carcinoma, grade by gland formation and assess prognostic features separately. Diagnostic GPS: from polyp to invasive carcinoma Establish the setting Age, symptoms, endoscopic location, polyp size, multiplicity, and inflammatory bowel disease history. Assess crypt architecture For serrated lesions, inspect the crypt bases for dilation, horizontal growth, and basal serration. Classify epithelial phenotype Distinguish conventional adenomatous dysplasia from serrated, hamartomatous, and IBD-associated patterns. Identify invasion Look for infiltrative glands, desmoplasia, submucosal invasion, and other unequivocal evidence of malignancy. Apply targeted testing Use MMR IHC/MSI, RAS/BRAF, HER2, or NTRK testing when clinically indicated; avoid non-contributory panels. High-yield molecular and predictive tests Colorectal carcinoma MMR IHC / MSI: Lynch screening and immunotherapy relevance RAS (KRAS / NRAS) Predicts lack of benefit from anti-EGFR antibodies when mutated BRAF V600E Prognostic/therapeutic relevance; helps assess sporadic MLH1-deficient tumors ERBB2 (HER2) Amplification/overexpression may support anti-HER2 therapy in advanced disease NTRK fusion Rare actionable alteration, enriched in MSI-high / BRAF-wildtype subset SSL / serrated pathway BRAF, CIMP, and MLH1 methylation are biologically informative; not routine diagnostic tests Grading and prognostic features Colorectal adenocarcinoma is graded by gland formation: low-grade versus high-grade; cytologic atypia alone does not determine grade. Use the least differentiated tumor component; a qualifying focus lacking gland formation establishes high-grade morphology. Tumor budding (single cells or clusters of up to 4 cells) and poorly differentiated clusters (at least 5 cells without gland formation) are reported separately. Lymphatic/vascular invasion, perineural invasion, tumor deposits, circumferential margin, nodal status, and treatment response are key reporting elements. Do not assign histologic grade after neoadjuvant therapy. For serrated lesions, ensure orientation and inclusion of crypt bases; obtain deeper levels when needed. For dysplasia in IBD, document visibility, grade, distribution, and background inflammatory activity; use indefinite for dysplasia when reactive change cannot be excluded. For rectal carcinoma, assess the circumferential resection margin; tumor within 1 mm is considered involved in the supplied source. After neoadjuvant therapy, document treatment response and viable tumor; acellular mucin alone is not residual carcinoma and does not define mucinous histology.
