title: Esophageal Tumors
content: use client Esophageal Squamous Papilloma Benign Epithelial Tumors and Precursors Typically presents in middle age (median age approximately 50 years). Often located in the lower esophagus in Western series; middle esophageal location is more frequent in some Asian populations. Most patients are asymptomatic; endoscopy may show a small, white, exophytic, wart-like lesion. Papillomatous proliferation of benign squamous epithelium. Fibrovascular cores are present within the papillary projections. Cytologic atypia is absent. Papillary squamous proliferation supported by fibrovascular cores of lamina propria. Scattered vacuolated cells with koilocyte-like morphology may be present. Atypical nuclear features and viral inclusions are absent. Growth is usually exophytic but may be endophytic or spiked. Squamous dysplasia / squamous cell carcinoma: look for unequivocal cytologic and architectural atypia or invasion. Verrucous squamous cell carcinoma: broad, bulbous pushing invasion and deep keratinization are not features of a benign papilloma. HRAS or KRAS mutations have been reported in a subset of cases. Recent data do not support HPV as a usual etiologic factor. Epidermoid Metaplasia of the Esophagus Usually diagnosed in the seventh decade; no sex predominance. May occur anywhere in the esophagus, with approximately half in the lower third. About half of patients have dysphagia; others are detected incidentally during endoscopic follow-up. Epithelial hyperplasia without atypia. Prominent granular cell layer. Superficial compact hyperorthokeratosis. Sharply demarcated epithelial lesion with an undulating mucosal contour and flattened rete pegs. Prominent granular cell layer beneath compact hyperorthokeratosis. Focal parakeratosis may occur between hypergranulosis and hyperorthokeratosis. Squamous dysplasia or carcinoma may be adjacent to or associated with the lesion. Squamous dysplasia: requires unequivocal cytologic and architectural atypia; epidermoid metaplasia lacks atypia. Surface keratinization from other causes: the sharply demarcated hyperplastic epithelium with a prominent granular layer supports epidermoid metaplasia. TP53 mutations have been identified in epidermoid metaplasia and associated synchronous or metachronous squamous neoplasia; this supports a precursor relationship but is not a routine diagnostic test. Esophageal Squamous Dysplasia Most often affects men in the fifth and sixth decades in many populations; distribution and sex ratio vary geographically. May occur anywhere in the esophagus. Usually asymptomatic and detected incidentally or during surveillance; larger lesions or associated carcinoma may cause dysphagia or bleeding. Unequivocal squamous epithelial neoplasia without invasion. Both cytologic atypia and architectural atypia are required. Low-grade dysplasia predominantly involves the lower half of the epithelium with mild atypia. High-grade dysplasia involves more than half of the epithelium or shows severe cytologic atypia, regardless of epithelial thickness. Cytologic atypia includes nuclear enlargement, pleomorphism, hyperchromasia, loss of polarity, and nuclear overlap. Architectural atypia is characterized by abnormal epithelial maturation. Low-grade dysplasia shows mild atypia, largely maintained nuclear polarity, and no atypical mitoses. High-grade dysplasia shows more extensive epithelial involvement and/or severe atypia. Aberrant p53 expression may support the diagnosis in dysplastic mucosa. Reactive / regenerative atypia: lacks the combination of unequivocal cytologic and architectural abnormalities. Barrett dysplasia: arises in metaplastic glandular epithelium rather than squamous mucosa. Invasive squamous cell carcinoma: requires evidence of stromal invasion. TP53 and CDKN2A alterations are key molecular drivers; molecular testing is not routinely required for diagnosis. Barrett Dysplasia Occurs in metaplastic columnar mucosa of the esophagus, usually in patients with Barrett esophagus. Barrett esophagus is associated with chronic gastro-esophageal reflux, age over 50 years, obesity, male sex, and a first-degree family history. Dysplasia itself has no distinct clinical symptoms; endoscopy may show a flat, plaque-like, nodular, ulcerated, or irregular mucosal area. Unequivocal glandular neoplastic alteration without invasion, arising in metaplastic esophageal columnar epithelium. Classify as negative, indefinite, low-grade, or high-grade when appropriate. High-grade dysplasia may be diagnosed on severe cytologic atypia or marked architectural complexity. Abrupt transition from non-dysplastic to dysplastic epithelium, with loss of surface maturation, glandular crowding, architectural complexity, and cytologic atypia. Intestinal / adenoma-like dysplasia resembles colonic dysplasia, with columnar cells, goblet cells, and enterocyte-like features. Gastric-type dysplasia shows a single layer of cuboidal or short columnar cells with enlarged, hyperchromatic, irregular basal nuclei; goblet cells may be absent. Low-grade dysplasia shows nuclear elongation, enlargement, hyperchromasia, and stratification with largely maintained polarity and minimal architectural change. High-grade dysplasia shows marked atypia, loss of polarity, complex crowded or cribriform glands, back-to-back glands, budding, and sometimes atypical mitoses. Basal (crypt) dysplasia is confined to the basal third of involved glands; additional levels may reveal surface involvement. Aberrant p53 staining (overexpression or complete loss) is common and may support the presence of dysplasia. p53 immunohistochemistry can aid diagnosis, but its role in grading is inconclusive; interpret with morphology and appropriate controls. Reactive / inflammatory atypia: preserved maturation and polarity favor reactive change; dysplasia shows an abrupt transition and disordered maturation. Indefinite for dysplasia: use when atypia does not meet criteria for low- or high-grade dysplasia. Intramucosal adenocarcinoma: requires evidence of invasion, such as fused or anastomosing glands, detached tumor cells, or confluent growth. TP53 inactivation is a key event associated with genomic instability and progression. Nucleic acid–based molecular assays are not recommended for routine screening or surveillance. Adenocarcinoma of the Esophagus and Esophagogastric Junction Malignant Epithelial Tumors Typically presents in the seventh decade and predominantly affects men. Nearly all esophageal cases arise in the lower esophagus or esophagogastric junction. Common symptoms include dysphagia, anemia, reflux, weight loss, and pain. Risk factors include gastro-esophageal reflux disease and obesity; Barrett esophagus is the principal precursor. Invasive carcinoma showing glandular or mucinous differentiation. Exclude squamous and significant neuroendocrine differentiation. Use the tumor epicenter and esophagogastric junction landmarks to distinguish esophageal / junctional from proximal gastric primaries. Tubular pattern is most common, with irregular single or anastomosing glands lined by atypical epithelium. Papillary pattern shows papillary architecture; micropapillary areas are rare. Mucinous pattern shows tumor cells floating in abundant extracellular mucin. Poorly cohesive / signet-ring cell patterns account for a minority of cases; signet-ring cells contain large intracytoplasmic mucin vacuoles displacing the nucleus. Enteroblastic differentiation is rare and may show clear cuboidal or columnar cells in tubular, papillary, solid, or yolk sac–like patterns. Invasion is supported by anastomosing or fused glands, detached single cells in stroma, complex expansile glands, or confluent tumor sheets. Duplicated muscularis mucosae is a staging pitfall; tumor between the two layers is staged as pT1a. After neoadjuvant therapy, residual tumor may show cytoplasmic vacuolation, nuclear enlargement or hyperchromasia, apoptosis, and treatment-related stromal changes. Typical profile: CK7+, CK19+, and CDX2+; CK20 is usually negative. Enteroblastic differentiation may be supported by AFP, glypican-3, and SALL4. Poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma generally expresses CK7 and CDX2 and lacks squamous markers. HER2 immunohistochemistry with in situ hybridization for equivocal (2+) results is used for predictive testing. Mismatch repair protein immunohistochemistry can identify mismatch repair deficiency. Poorly differentiated squamous cell carcinoma: usually positive for CK5/6, p63, and p40; adenocarcinoma supports glandular morphology and CK7/CDX2 expression. Neuroendocrine carcinoma: assess morphology and neuroendocrine markers; distinct components may indicate MiNEN. Undifferentiated carcinoma: consider when lineage-specific morphology and immunophenotype are equivocal. Proximal gastric adenocarcinoma: distinguish by the tumor epicenter relative to the esophagogastric junction. Commonly altered genes include TP53, CDKN2A, ARID1A, and SMAD4; these alterations are not individually specific for diagnosis. ERBB2 (HER2) amplification / overexpression is predictive of response to HER2-targeted therapy. MSI-high / mismatch repair-deficient status is predictive for immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy in advanced disease. PD-L1 combined positive score (CPS) is used as an immunotherapy biomarker. Claudin-18.2 expression in more than 75% of tumor cells is a treatment-selection biomarker. Esophageal Mucoepidermoid, Adenoid Cystic, and Adenosquamous Carcinomas Rare tumors, collectively accounting for less than 1% of primary esophageal carcinomas. Most often occur in men, at a median age of approximately 60 years. Dysphagia is the most common presenting symptom. Mucoepidermoid carcinoma is usually in the middle or distal esophagus; adenoid cystic and adenosquamous carcinomas most often arise in the mid esophagus. Mucoepidermoid carcinoma: variable mixture of malignant mucous, epidermoid, and intermediate cells. Adenoid cystic carcinoma: biphasic epithelial and myoepithelial neoplasm with cribriform, tubular, or solid architecture and punched-out spaces. Adenosquamous carcinoma: distinct malignant squamous and glandular components. Mucoepidermoid carcinoma contains cysts and sheets of mucin-producing cells, epidermoid cells, and intermediate cells; proportions vary with grade. Adenoid cystic carcinoma shows inner epithelial and outer myoepithelial cells in cribriform, tubular, or solid patterns. Adenoid cystic carcinoma pseudolumina contain hyalinized basement membrane material; true glandular lumina contain glycosaminoglycans. Perineural invasion and lymphovascular permeation are common in adenoid cystic carcinoma. Adenosquamous carcinoma contains unequivocally malignant squamous and glandular components, separate or intermingled. Acantholytic change or adenoid / microcystic spaces in otherwise conventional squamous carcinoma do not establish adenosquamous carcinoma. Adenoid cystic carcinoma: myoepithelial cells express p63, p40, S100, SMA, and calponin. Adenoid cystic carcinoma: epithelial cells express cytokeratin, CEA, and KIT (CD117). MYB protein overexpression may support adenoid cystic carcinoma. Basaloid squamous cell carcinoma: may show pseudoglandular spaces but is composed of one cell population rather than the biphasic epithelial–myoepithelial pattern of adenoid cystic carcinoma. Conventional squamous cell carcinoma with acantholysis: pseudoglandular spaces alone do not establish a glandular component. Mucoepidermoid carcinoma versus adenosquamous carcinoma: mucoepidermoid carcinoma has intermediate and mucous cells with a generally bland squamous component; adenosquamous carcinoma has distinctly malignant squamous and glandular components. MAML2 gene rearrangement supports mucoepidermoid carcinoma. MYB gene rearrangement supports adenoid cystic carcinoma. Esophageal Squamous Cell Carcinoma Median age at diagnosis is approximately 67.5 years. Most commonly arises in the middle third, followed by the lower third of the esophagus. Dysphagia is the most common symptom and usually indicates advanced disease; chest pain, odynophagia, and weight loss may occur. Early lesions may be asymptomatic or detected during surveillance. Histological evidence of invasion by neoplastic squamous epithelium. Squamous differentiation is characterized by keratinocyte-type cells with intercellular bridges and/or keratinization. Grading is based on cytologic atypia, mitotic activity, and keratinization. Well-differentiated tumors show abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm and keratin pearls, with minimal atypia and low mitotic activity. Moderately differentiated tumors show more evident atypia, less orderly growth, and readily identifiable mitoses. Poorly differentiated tumors consist predominantly of basal-like cells in nests or sheets, sometimes with central necrosis. Verrucous carcinoma shows minimal atypia, prominent papillary surface projections, abrupt keratinization, and broad bulbous pushing invasion. Sarcomatoid carcinoma is biphasic, with neoplastic squamous epithelium and malignant spindle or pleomorphic cells; heterologous differentiation may occur. Basaloid carcinoma shows nests or solid areas of basaloid cells, sometimes with comedonecrosis, pseudoglandular / cribriform spaces, and basement membrane–like material. After neoadjuvant therapy, look for residual viable tumor, fibrosis, necrosis, keratin debris, inflammatory response, and treatment-related vascular changes. p63, p40, and CK5/6 support squamous differentiation when morphology is poorly differentiated. Neuroendocrine markers or melanocytic markers may be needed to exclude mimics in selected basaloid tumors. Adenocarcinoma: shows glandular or mucinous differentiation and typically expresses CK7 / CDX2 rather than squamous markers. Undifferentiated carcinoma: lacks definite squamous, glandular, or neuroendocrine differentiation. Adenoid cystic carcinoma: has a biphasic epithelial–myoepithelial population and characteristic cribriform architecture. Sarcomatoid carcinoma versus true sarcoma: identify the associated neoplastic squamous component and assess epithelial differentiation. TP53 mutation is a key early driver; additional genetic abnormalities accumulate during progression. Routine molecular testing is not required for the histological diagnosis. Esophageal Undifferentiated Carcinoma Reported cases span 39–86 years, with most patients presenting after the seventh decade; male predominance. Usually located in the lower esophagus or esophagogastric junction. Progressive dysphagia is the most common symptom, followed by reflux, weight loss, and anemia. Malignant epithelial tumor without definite squamous, glandular, or neuroendocrine differentiation. For SWI/SNF-deficient carcinoma, demonstrate loss of one or more SWI/SNF complex proteins. Lymphoepithelioma-like carcinoma shows undifferentiated epithelioid cells in sheets with a dense lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate. Tumor forms variably sized nests and sheets of medium-sized to large cells. Cells have poorly defined amphophilic to slightly eosinophilic cytoplasm, producing a syncytium-like appearance. Nuclei are oval and vesicular; pleomorphic giant cells or rhabdoid cells may occur. Lymphoepithelioma-like carcinoma shows large epithelioid cells with prominent nucleoli and indistinct borders, surrounded by dense lymphoplasmacytic inflammation. Cytokeratin may help establish epithelial lineage. Use chromogranin A, synaptophysin, and INSM1 to exclude neuroendocrine carcinoma. Use p63 and p40 to assess poorly differentiated squamous carcinoma. Assess mucin / glandular differentiation when poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma is in the differential. Loss of ARID1A, SMARCA4 (BRG1), SMARCA2 (BRM), or SMARCB1 (INI1) supports SWI/SNF-deficient carcinoma. Poorly differentiated squamous cell carcinoma: assess p63 and p40 and search for squamous morphology. Poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma: assess mucin and glandular differentiation. Neuroendocrine carcinoma: assess neuroendocrine morphology and chromogranin A, synaptophysin, and INSM1. Melanoma, lymphoma, or sarcoma: exclude with lineage-appropriate studies when cytokeratin expression is absent or equivocal. SWI/SNF complex alterations can be assessed by immunohistochemistry or next-generation sequencing. EBV is only occasionally detected in esophageal lymphoepithelioma-like carcinoma. All Esophageal Adenocarcinoma PathologyGPS / GI, Liver & Pancreas / GI / Esophageal Tumors Esophageal Tumors A morphology-first diagnostic reference focused on essential criteria, histopathology, targeted immunohistochemistry, molecular findings, and practical differential diagnosis. Core rule Establish lineage, assess invasion, and interpret the lesion in its anatomic and clinical context. Distinguish squamous and glandular precursor lesions from invasive carcinoma; use targeted ancillary studies to resolve poorly differentiated tumors. Diagnostic GPS: morphology to classification Establish the clinical setting Age, sex, exact esophageal level, Barrett mucosa, reflux history, dysphagia, and endoscopic appearance. Identify the epithelial lineage Squamous, metaplastic glandular, mixed squamous/glandular, or no definite lineage. Determine whether invasion is present Separate intraepithelial dysplasia from invasive carcinoma; assess depth and lymphovascular invasion in early lesions. Use targeted ancillary studies p53 in selected dysplasia; p40/p63 for squamous differentiation; neuroendocrine markers and mucin studies for poorly differentiated tumors; SWI/SNF IHC when indicated. Integrate biomarkers and treatment context For advanced adenocarcinoma, assess HER2, mismatch repair/MSI, PD-L1 CPS, and CLDN18.2 as clinically appropriate; document treatment effect after neoadjuvant therapy. Precursor lesions: the key distinction Squamous dysplasia: requires both cytologic atypia and abnormal epithelial maturation. High-grade dysplasia involves more than half the epithelium or shows severe cytologic atypia at any thickness. Barrett dysplasia: arises in metaplastic columnar epithelium. Assess glandular cytology and architecture, surface maturation, and evidence of invasion. Epidermoid metaplasia: shows epithelial hyperplasia without atypia, a prominent granular layer, and superficial hyperorthokeratosis. High-yield ancillary studies Barrett dysplasia p53 IHC may support dysplasia; interpret with morphology Squamous dysplasia Aberrant p53 may support the diagnosis Squamous differentiation p40, p63, and CK5/6 Neuroendocrine differentiation Synaptophysin, chromogranin A, and INSM1 SWI/SNF-deficient carcinoma ARID1A, BRG1, BRM, and INI1 IHC Advanced adenocarcinoma HER2, MMR/MSI, PD-L1 CPS, and CLDN18.2 Entity reference Diagnostic criteria and differential diagnosis Search by diagnosis, clinical feature, morphology, immunostain, or molecular alteration. e.g. p53, Barrett, keratinization, HER2... bg-teal-700 text-white border border-slate-300 bg-white text-slate-600 Benign / precursor lesion Malignant Collapse View diagnostic profile − + Clinical profile Essential diagnostic criteria Histopathology Immunophenotype Molecular pathology Differential diagnosis : Diagnostic pitfalls No matching entity. High-stakes comparison: squamous versus glandular neoplasia Feature Invasive carcinoma Epithelium Squamous Metaplastic columnar Squamous or glandular lineage Diagnostic basis Cytologic and architectural atypia Unequivocal glandular neoplasia Histologic evidence of invasion Key pitfall Reactive atypia Inflammation-related atypia Tangential sectioning or duplicated muscularis mucosae can complicate depth assessment Biopsy, sampling, and reporting checklist Record the exact esophageal level, tumor epicenter, relationship to the esophagogastric junction, and presence of Barrett mucosa. For precursor lesions, state the epithelial lineage and grade; distinguish dysplasia from reactive change. For suspected invasion, assess stromal invasion and lymphovascular invasion; in endoscopic resections, document depth of invasion and margins. In adenocarcinoma, document histologic pattern and relevant predictive biomarkers when clinically indicated. After neoadjuvant therapy, assess the entire tumor bed adequately before assigning a complete pathologic response; report tumor regression using the institutional or protocol-specified system. For poorly differentiated carcinoma, use a focused panel to evaluate squamous, glandular, neuroendocrine, and SWI/SNF-associated differentiation. Scope note: This reference is based on the supplied WHO esophageal-tumor material. Ancillary findings should be interpreted with morphology, anatomic site, clinical context, and appropriate controls. The page is a diagnostic aid and does not replace adequate sampling or multidisciplinary correlation.

title: Gastric Tumors
content: use client Fundic Gland Polyp Benign Benign; dysplasia is uncommon Oxyntic mucosa of the gastric body and fundus. Usually detected incidentally in adults in their fifth to sixth decades; a female predominance is reported. Usually asymptomatic; multiple polyps in a young patient should prompt consideration of a polyposis syndrome. Sporadic and syndromic forms occur; associations include FAP, GAPPS, and MUTYH-associated polyposis. Disordered expansion of the deeper epithelial compartment of oxyntic mucosa. Dilatation of one or more oxyntic glands. Parietal cell hyperplasia. Architecturally disordered oxyntic glands with glandular buds and irregular, tortuous profiles. Oxyntic gland cysts and shortened foveolae are characteristic. PPI-associated lesions may show cystic glandular expansion, foveolar cell proliferation, and parietal cell protrusion/hyperplasia. GAPPS-associated lesions may show aberrant hyperproliferative glands, inverted foveolar hyperplasia, and hypermaturation. Dysplasia is uncommon in sporadic lesions and is usually low-grade. Routine immunohistochemistry is not recommended. Nuclear β-catenin staining is uncommon and does not reliably distinguish sporadic from FAP-associated lesions. Sporadic lesions commonly harbor CTNNB1 mutations and generally lack APC mutations. FAP-associated lesions show biallelic APC alterations with wild-type CTNNB1. Sporadic fundic gland polyps with dysplasia may acquire APC mutations. Gastric hyperplastic polyp Shows elongated, tortuous foveolae in an edematous, inflamed lamina propria rather than disordered cystic oxyntic glands. Gastric adenoma/dysplasia Shows unequivocal cytologic and architectural neoplasia rather than the characteristic oxyntic gland expansion. Syndromic fundic gland polyposis Histology may overlap with sporadic lesions; multiplicity, age, family history, and clinical context are important. Erosive/regenerative atypia should not be overcalled as dysplasia; an abrupt transition from atypical to adjacent normal epithelium supports dysplasia. Dysplasia and carcinoma are exceptionally uncommon, even in syndromic lesions. Gastric Hyperplastic Polyp Benign; dysplasia or carcinoma may occur focally Usually antrum in H. pylori-associated gastritis or chemical gastropathy; body/fundus in autoimmune gastritis. Typically occurs in the sixth to seventh decades (median age 66 years); no sex predilection is established. Usually asymptomatic and may be multiple. Surface erosion may cause bleeding and iron-deficiency anemia; large pyloric-channel lesions may rarely cause outlet obstruction. Polyp composed predominantly of elongated, tortuous, or branching foveolae lined by foveolar epithelium. Expanded, edematous, and inflamed lamina propria. Cystically dilated glands and surface erosion/ulceration are supportive. Foveolar compartment is disproportionately expanded relative to other mucosal elements. Foveolae are elongated, distorted, branching, or dilated. Lamina propria is commonly edematous, inflamed, and vascular. Globoid mucinous cells may occur and are not dysplastic. Small, haphazard smooth muscle bundles may be present; larger antral lesions may contain thick-walled vessels and smooth muscle extending from the muscularis mucosae. Dysplasia is reported in 1–20% and carcinoma in approximately 2%, particularly in polyps larger than 10 mm. No routine immunohistochemical panel is required for diagnosis. TP53 mutations and p53 overexpression have been associated with dysplastic/malignant foci; molecular testing is not routinely indicated. Fundic gland polyp Shows disordered, cystically dilated oxyntic glands with parietal cell hyperplasia. Polypoid foveolar hyperplasia Usually smaller, with elongated pits in minimally edematous lamina propria. Gastritis cystica profunda Often arises in a gastric remnant after Billroth II surgery; cystically dilated glands extend into the submucosa. Portal hypertensive polyp Often multiple in the body/fundus, with prominent mucosal vascularity, dilated capillaries, and sometimes organizing thrombi. Shows unequivocal neoplastic cytologic and architectural changes. Globoid mucinous cells in hyperplastic foveolae can mimic signet-ring cells but are not, by themselves, evidence of carcinoma. Carefully examine larger lesions, especially those exceeding 10 mm, for focal dysplasia or carcinoma. Consider mucosal prolapse in large distal antral polyps with smooth muscle bundles and thick-walled vessels. Gastric Dysplasia Precursor Non-invasive neoplasia; low-grade or high-grade Incisura/antrum in atrophic, intestinalized mucosa; foveolar-type lesions in H. pylori-naïve patients favor body/fundus. Usually asymptomatic; large or ulcerated lesions may cause bleeding, anemia, or dyspepsia. Most intestinal-type cases occur in patients older than 60 years, with a male predominance. Endoscopy may show a flat, depressed, or elevated/polypoid lesion with surface color change, erosion, or ulceration. Unequivocal intraepithelial neoplasia with cytologic and architectural atypia. No evidence of stromal invasion. Low-grade or high-grade dysplasia, arising in intestinalized glands or showing a distinctive apical neutral mucin cap in foveolar-type lesions. Diagnosis requires a variable combination of cytologic atypia and architectural complexity. Intestinal-type dysplasia shows intestinal differentiation; foveolar-type dysplasia shows gastric foveolar differentiation with an apical mucin cap. Recognized patterns include intestinal, foveolar, serrated, and crypt dysplasia. High-grade dysplasia shows more pronounced architectural and cytologic atypia than low-grade dysplasia. Irregular fused glands, glandular anastomoses, abortive glands, and discohesive cells raise concern for well-differentiated intramucosal adenocarcinoma. No immunohistochemical marker is validated for routine diagnosis or grading. Mucin phenotype markers may help characterize differentiation in selected cases but are not required. APC mutations are frequent in low- and high-grade dysplasia. TP53 alterations and p53 overexpression are more frequent in high-grade than low-grade dysplasia. Molecular alterations vary by phenotype; no marker is validated for routine clinical diagnosis. Reactive/regenerative atypia Usually shows limited cytoarchitectural change, surface/neck predominance, preserved polarity, and gradual transition to normal mucosa. Indefinite for dysplasia A provisional category used when inflammation, small tissue volume, or poor orientation prevents reliable distinction from reactive change. Intramucosal adenocarcinoma Shows invasion into lamina propria, often with irregular fused/anastomosing glands, abortive glands, or discohesive cells. Forceps biopsies frequently underestimate grade; endoscopic resection may reveal high-grade dysplasia or carcinoma. Invasion into lamina propria changes the diagnosis from intraepithelial neoplasia to intramucosal carcinoma (pT1a). High-grade dysplasia is staged as pTis. Gastric Pyloric Gland Adenoma Non-invasive neoplasm; may contain high-grade dysplasia or carcinoma Usually gastric body/fundus, often in a background of atrophic gastritis or pyloric gland metaplasia. Usually detected incidentally in older adults; mean age approximately 66 years, with similar frequency in men and women. Many sporadic cases occur in elderly women with autoimmune gastritis. Syndromic cases occur at younger ages in patients with polyposis syndromes. Polypoid proliferation of closely packed pyloric/mucous neck-type glands. Glands are lined by uniform cuboidal or low columnar cells with foamy, ground-glass cytoplasm. Neoplastic cells lack a well-defined apical mucin cap. Closely packed glands are composed predominantly of pyloric/mucous neck cell-type epithelium. Cells are cuboidal or low columnar with clear or lightly eosinophilic, ground-glass cytoplasm. Round to ovoid nuclei are basally located with inconspicuous nucleoli. Large lesions may contain dilated glands; chief- or parietal-type cells may be admixed. High-grade lesions show crowded hyperchromatic nuclei, loss of polarity, and increased proliferation. High-grade dysplasia/intramucosal carcinoma may occur; submucosal invasion is uncommon. MUC6 is consistently expressed by the glandular component. Pepsinogen I and MIST1 are partially expressed. MUC5AC is mainly expressed in surface cells and may extend variably into the lesion. Focal MUC2/CDX2 or nuclear β-catenin may occur; mucin immunostains are not required for routine diagnosis. GNAS, KRAS, and APC mutations have been identified in sporadic and FAP-associated lesions. Foveolar-type dysplasia/adenoma Shows a distinctive apical neutral mucin cap; pyloric gland adenoma lacks a well-defined apical mucin cap. Oxyntic gland adenoma Shows chief-cell and/or parietal-cell differentiation rather than predominantly pyloric/mucous neck differentiation. Shows elongated foveolae in edematous, inflamed stroma without a uniform dysplastic pyloric gland proliferation. Pronounced surface foveolar differentiation can make distinction from foveolar-type dysplasia difficult. Look for high-grade dysplasia or intramucosal carcinoma, particularly in larger lesions and in autoimmune gastritis. Oxyntic Gland Adenoma Usually indolent; submucosal invasion is classified as gastric adenocarcinoma of fundic gland type Predominantly non-atrophic oxyntic mucosa of the gastric body/fundus. Usually occurs at 60–70 years, with a slight female predominance. Often detected during endoscopic screening in Japan; patients elsewhere may present with reflux symptoms. Endoscopy typically shows a small nodule, subsurface lesion, or flat whitish area. Small intramucosal neoplasm composed of cells with mild cytologic atypia. Predominant chief-cell differentiation, with variable parietal-cell and mucous neck-cell differentiation. A pushing interface and prolapse-type glandular misplacement do not, by themselves, establish submucosal invasion. Tightly packed glands with variable anastomosis, branching, dilation, and occasional cribriforming. Chief-cell-predominant lesions contain monotonous columnar cells with basophilic cytoplasm. Mixed-cell lesions contain chief cells and scattered parietal cells, often in the superficial tumor. Cytologic atypia is usually mild; mitoses are rare and Ki-67 is typically below 5%. The lesion is usually deep in the mucosa and covered by normal foveolar epithelium. A pushing interface and prolapse-type misplacement are characteristic and should not be mistaken for true invasion. MUC6 is diffusely positive. Pepsinogen I highlights chief-cell differentiation. H+/K+ ATPase highlights parietal-cell differentiation. Diffuse strong cyclin D1 can help distinguish OGA from normal oxyntic glands in biopsy specimens. Synaptophysin may be positive in a subset, but chromogranin A is negative. GNAS mutations are recurrent; available molecular data remain limited. TP53 mutations have not been identified in the cited series. Gastric adenocarcinoma of fundic gland type Requires convincing submucosal invasion with atypical cellular differentiation; prolapse-like misplacement alone is insufficient. Pyloric gland adenoma Shows MUC6-positive pyloric/mucous neck-type glands with ground-glass cytoplasm rather than chief-cell-predominant oxyntic differentiation. Gastric neuroendocrine tumor May share clustered/solid glandular architecture; integrate morphology and neuroendocrine markers, noting chromogranin A is negative in OGA. Do not interpret prolapse-type misplacement as submucosal invasion. In small biopsies, OGA may resemble normal oxyntic glands; cyclin D1 can be helpful. OGA is generally slow-growing and follows a benign course. Gastric Adenocarcinoma Malignant Malignant; behavior and prognosis depend strongly on stage and histologic subtype Occurs throughout the stomach; distal disease predominates in high-incidence regions, whereas proximal/cardia involvement is more common in lower-incidence regions. Usually affects men aged 60–80 years. Early-stage disease is often asymptomatic; advanced disease may cause dyspepsia, upper abdominal pain, fatigue, weight loss, hematemesis, or melena. Metastatic presentations may include ovarian involvement (Krukenberg tumor) or, rarely, pulmonary lymphangitic carcinomatosis. Malignant epithelial neoplasm showing glandular differentiation. Invasion into the lamina propria or deeper layers of the gastric wall. Classify the predominant histologic subtype and report distinct components in mixed tumors. Tubular adenocarcinoma: branching, dilated, slit-like, or acinar glands lined by neoplastic columnar or cuboidal cells. Papillary adenocarcinoma: elongated finger-like papillae with fibrovascular cores, lined by columnar or cuboidal tumor cells. Poorly cohesive carcinoma: individual cells or small clusters without gland formation; signet-ring cells contain abundant intracytoplasmic mucin and eccentric nuclei. Mucinous adenocarcinoma: extracellular mucin comprises more than 50% of the tumor area and contains malignant glands or tumor cells. Mixed adenocarcinoma: two or more distinct histologic components, commonly glandular and poorly cohesive components. Carcinoma with lymphoid stroma: irregular sheets, trabeculae, poorly formed glands, or syncytia of polygonal cells with a prominent lymphocytic infiltrate. Hepatoid adenocarcinoma: large polygonal eosinophilic hepatocyte-like cells; bile or PAS-D-resistant hyaline globules may be present. Micropapillary adenocarcinoma: small tumor-cell clusters without fibrovascular cores floating in clear spaces. Gastric adenocarcinoma of fundic gland type shows oxyntic gland differentiation and requires true submucosal invasion. Sarcomatoid carcinoma contains adenocarcinoma and sarcomatoid components. Mismatch repair proteins (MLH1, PMS2, MSH2, MSH6), p53, and E-cadherin may help characterize tumors and support molecular subtyping. EBER in situ hybridization identifies EBV-associated tumors, particularly carcinoma with lymphoid stroma. Hepatoid/enteroblastic differentiation may express AFP, SALL4, claudin-6, or glypican-3; SALL4 and claudin-6 can help distinguish primary gastric hepatoid carcinoma from metastatic hepatocellular carcinoma. Mucin phenotype markers may support gastric (MUC5AC/TFF1, MUC6/TFF2), intestinal (MUC2, CD10, CDX2), mixed, or null phenotype. HER2 and claudin-18.2 testing may be required for treatment selection in advanced disease; PD-L1 CPS and MMR/MSI status are also clinically relevant. TCGA molecular subtypes: EBV-positive, microsatellite-unstable, genomically stable, and chromosomally unstable. ACRG subtypes include MSI, MSS/EMT, MSS/TP53-active, and MSS/TP53-inactive groups. CDH1 germline alterations are associated with hereditary diffuse gastric cancer; APC promoter 1B alterations are associated with GAPPS. Predictive biomarkers include ERBB2 (HER2), mismatch repair deficiency/MSI, PD-L1 CPS, and CLDN18.2 expression. RHOA mutations and CLDN18::ARHGAP fusions have been identified in crawling-type adenocarcinoma. Gastric dysplasia Lacks stromal invasion; intramucosal carcinoma shows invasion into lamina propria. Retains polarity and shows limited atypia with gradual transition to normal mucosa. Gastric neuroendocrine carcinoma Use morphology and neuroendocrine markers in solid, poorly differentiated tumors. Hepatocellular carcinoma metastatic to stomach Correlate with clinical history and use a differential-directed panel; SALL4/claudin-6 may support primary gastric hepatoid carcinoma. Gastric squamous cell carcinoma Shows pure squamous differentiation without an adenocarcinoma component after thorough sampling. Intratumoral heterogeneity is common; adequately sample the tumor to identify mixed or minor components. Biopsy may underestimate invasion or grade, particularly in depressed, poorly differentiated, or diffuse lesions. Poorly cohesive carcinoma may spread widely along the serosa beyond the grossly visible tumor. For tumors involving the esophagogastric junction, staging depends on the tumor epicenter: more than 20 mm into the proximal stomach is staged as gastric cancer. Pathologic TNM stage is the most important prognostic factor; document lymphovascular invasion and treatment response. Gastric Squamous Cell Carcinoma Rare malignant carcinoma; often presents at an advanced stage Upper stomach is most frequently involved, followed by lower and middle portions. Extremely rare, accounting for approximately 0.04–0.5% of gastric cancers. Clinical presentation is similar to other gastric cancers; advanced cases often have poor outcomes. Histologic evidence of squamous cell differentiation. Proof of invasion. Exclusion of metastasis from another organ and distal extension from esophageal squamous cell carcinoma. Shows uniform squamous differentiation with keratinization and/or intercellular bridges. Thorough sampling must show no adenocarcinoma or other histologic component. Verrucous subtype shows very well-differentiated keratinizing squamous cells with minimal atypia, coarse surface papillary projections, and bulbous downgrowth. Use squamous markers such as p40, p63, and high-molecular-weight keratin/CK5/6 when needed to confirm squamous differentiation. Molecular data are limited; no defining molecular alteration is established in the supplied source. Esophageal squamous cell carcinoma with distal extension Correlate with endoscopy and gross tumor epicenter to exclude direct extension. Metastatic squamous cell carcinoma Exclude a primary tumor in another organ clinically and radiologically. Gastric adenosquamous carcinoma Requires a distinct adenocarcinoma component comprising at least 25% of the tumor. Exhaustive sampling is crucial to exclude an adenocarcinoma component. Do not diagnose primary gastric SCC without excluding metastasis and esophageal extension. Gastric Adenosquamous Carcinoma Rare, aggressive malignant carcinoma May occur in any region of the stomach; exclude distal extension from lower esophageal adenosquamous carcinoma. Usually affects men, with a mean age of approximately 62 years. Often presents as a large mass (mean size approximately 60 mm). Accounts for less than 0.4% of gastric cancers. Carcinoma containing distinct adenocarcinoma and squamous cell carcinoma components. Each component must account for at least 25% of the tumor. Distinct gland-forming adenocarcinoma and squamous cell carcinoma components are present in variable proportions. The squamous component resembles conventional squamous cell carcinoma. Adenoid or microcystic change within an otherwise pure squamous carcinoma is insufficient for this diagnosis. Mucin stains can highlight the adenocarcinoma component. p40/p63 and high-molecular-weight keratin (34βE12) or CK5/6 can confirm and help quantify the squamous component. Pure gastric squamous cell carcinoma Lacks a distinct glandular component meeting the 25% threshold. Gastric adenocarcinoma with focal squamous metaplasia Requires a substantial, distinct squamous carcinoma component (at least 25%). Esophageal adenosquamous carcinoma with distal extension Correlate with gross/endoscopic epicenter and extent. Estimate and report the proportion of each component. Lymph node metastases may contain the adenocarcinoma component, squamous component, or both. Gastric Undifferentiated Carcinoma Highly aggressive malignant carcinoma No specific predilection; diffuse involvement of more than one gastric region is common. Usually affects men, with a mean age of approximately 60 years. Typically presents as a large ulcerated, extensively necrotic mass with synchronous regional metastases. Distant metastases may develop rapidly; many patients die within one year of diagnosis. Malignant epithelial tumor composed of cells without recognizable cytologic or architectural differentiation. Exclude poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma, lymphoma, melanoma, germ cell tumor, and sarcoma. Anaplastic medium-to-large polygonal cells grow in solid or discohesive sheets. Pleomorphic tumor giant cells are frequent. A rhabdoid phenotype with binucleated or multinucleated cells may predominate. Less common patterns include spindle-cell/sarcomatoid morphology and osteoclast-like giant cells; osteoclast-like cells are non-neoplastic. Extensive necrosis is common; myxoid or mucinous stroma may be present. Extensive sampling is recommended to identify a diagnostic adenocarcinoma component. Pankeratin expression is variable and may be limited or absent in keratin-poor examples. EMA may help identify epithelial differentiation in keratin-poor tumors. Vimentin is consistently expressed and may show a perinuclear dot-like pattern. Loss of SWI/SNF proteins (SMARCB1/INI1, SMARCA4/BRG1, SMARCA2, or ARID1A) may define a subset. Inactivation/loss of SWI/SNF chromatin-remodeling complex components is reported, sometimes involving more than one protein. SWI/SNF loss may coexist with mismatch repair deficiency or EBV association. Poorly differentiated/solid adenocarcinoma Extensive sampling and epithelial/glandular markers may reveal otherwise inconspicuous differentiation. EBV-associated carcinoma with lymphoid stroma Shows a prominent lymphoid background and often EBER positivity. Aggressive lymphoma, including anaplastic large cell lymphoma Use leukocyte and lineage-specific markers; epithelial markers may be variable in undifferentiated carcinoma. Metastatic melanoma Use melanocytic markers and clinical history. Epithelioid sarcoma or other sarcoma Integrate morphology, epithelial markers, and SWI/SNF protein expression. Do not diagnose undifferentiated carcinoma until lymphoma, melanoma, germ cell tumor, and sarcoma have been excluded. Keratin may be only focal or absent; EMA can be useful in selected cases. Loss of SWI/SNF proteins should be interpreted with morphology and the full differential diagnosis. All PathologyGPS / Gastrointestinal Pathology / Gastric Tumors Gastric Tumors and Precursor Lesions A morphology-first reference for gastric epithelial lesions, emphasizing essential diagnostic criteria, targeted ancillary studies, and practical differential diagnosis. Core rule Establish invasion, identify differentiation, and interpret the background mucosa. Separate non-invasive dysplasia from intramucosal carcinoma; do not mistake oxyntic gland prolapse for submucosal invasion. Diagnostic GPS: from gastric mucosa to classification Establish the background Assess H. pylori-associated or autoimmune gastritis, atrophy, intestinal metaplasia, prior surgery, and polyposis history. Identify the lesion type Distinguish cystic oxyntic glands, foveolar hyperplasia, intraepithelial neoplasia, pyloric/oxyntic gland neoplasia, and invasive carcinoma. Determine invasion Look for lamina propria invasion in dysplasia-like lesions and true submucosal invasion in oxyntic gland neoplasms. Characterize differentiation Assess glandular, poorly cohesive, mucinous, squamous, hepatoid, lymphoid-stroma, or undifferentiated patterns. Use targeted ancillary tests Select mucin, squamous, neuroendocrine, EBV, MMR, HER2, CLDN18.2, and SWI/SNF studies according to morphology and clinical need. Gastric cancerization field Correa cascade: chronic gastritis → glandular atrophy → intestinal metaplasia → dysplasia → invasive adenocarcinoma. Atrophy: loss of native glandular units; may be non-metaplastic (lamina propria fibrosis) or metaplastic (pseudopyloric or intestinal metaplasia). Risk assessment: incomplete/colonic-type intestinal metaplasia is associated with increased gastric carcinoma risk. OLGA and OLGIM stages III–IV identify higher-risk mucosal fields. Clinical context: H. pylori is the major global driver of metaplastic atrophy and sporadic gastric carcinoma; autoimmune oxyntic atrophy is strongly associated with type I ECL-cell NETs. Key distinction: precursor lesion versus invasive carcinoma Feature Invasion Absent Into lamina propria Intramucosal; pushing/prolapse-like misplacement may occur Differentiation Intestinal or foveolar phenotype Glandular differentiation with invasion Chief-cell predominant, with variable parietal/mucous neck cells Key clue Cytologic and architectural neoplasia without stromal invasion Irregular invasive glands or discohesive cells in lamina propria Mild atypia, low Ki-67, MUC6/pepsinogen I profile Biopsy, sampling, and reporting checklist Document the exact gastric site and endoscopic lesion size, morphology, and relationship to the esophagogastric junction. For dysplasia, assess grade and explicitly state whether lamina propria invasion is identified; superficial biopsies may underestimate the lesion. For gastric polyps, examine the entire lesion when feasible, especially lesions larger than 10 mm or with erosion/ulceration. For suspected oxyntic gland neoplasia, distinguish true submucosal invasion from prolapse-type glandular misplacement. For adenocarcinoma, sample heterogeneous areas to identify mixed histology, poorly cohesive components, lymphoid stroma, or sarcomatoid differentiation. Report histologic subtype, grade where applicable, depth of invasion, lymphovascular invasion, margins, lymph node status, and treatment response.
