title: Small Intestine Tumors
content: use client Non-ampullary Duodenal Adenoma Benign / Precursor Non-invasive epithelial neoplasm Duodenum outside the ampulla; intestinal-type lesions may occur throughout the small intestine, whereas pyloric gland adenomas favor the proximal duodenum. Mean age approximately 62 years; slight male predominance. Usually small, solitary, and asymptomatic; larger lesions may cause obstruction. Approximately one quarter are associated with a hereditary syndrome, most often FAP. Mucosal sessile or pedunculated lesion in a non-ampullary duodenal location. Closely packed, non-invasive tubular, tubulovillous, glandular, or tubulopapillary dysplastic epithelium. Classify dysplasia as low-grade or high-grade; high-grade dysplasia is staged as pTis. Intestinal-type adenomas are most common and usually show tubular or tubulovillous architecture. Low-grade lesions contain tall columnar cells with elongated nuclei and inconspicuous nucleoli. High-grade dysplasia shows greater architectural complexity, nuclear stratification, and cytologic atypia. Serrated lesions include sessile serrated lesions and traditional serrated adenomas; dysplasia or associated carcinoma may occur. Pyloric gland adenomas comprise tightly packed pyloric-type glands lined by cuboidal to low-columnar cells with foamy, ground-glass cytoplasm. Intestinal-type adenomas express CDX2 and MUC2; CK7/CK20 coexpression is common. Pyloric gland adenomas show extensive MUC6 expression and variable MUC5AC. Reactive / regenerative atypia Lacks the crowded dysplastic glandular architecture and cytologic features of adenoma. Ampullary adenoma Arises on the ampullary surface or within the ampullary channel; establish the precise anatomic location. Invasive adenocarcinoma Requires unequivocal stromal invasion; high-grade dysplasia alone is non-invasive. Large size, villous architecture, and high-grade dysplasia increase progression risk. In FAP, lesions may be multiple and predominantly sessile; apply the Spigelman system in the appropriate clinical setting. Ampullary Adenomatous Neoplasm Non-invasive; includes ampullary duodenal adenoma and IAPN Duodenal surface of the major papilla (ampullary duodenal adenoma) or within the intra-ampullary channel (intra-ampullary papillary-tubular neoplasm, IAPN). Mean age approximately 62 years; no clear sex predilection. Often asymptomatic and incidentally detected; FAP-associated cases present younger (mean approximately 39 years). IAPN may cause biliary obstruction, jaundice, cholangitis, or occasionally pancreatitis. Grossly visible intraepithelial neoplasm on the duodenal surface of the ampulla or within the ampullary channel. Dysplastic tubular, tubulovillous, villous, or papillary epithelium without invasion for a purely preinvasive diagnosis. For IAPN, the tumor epicenter and predominant bulk are within the ampullary channel. Ampullary surface adenomas usually show intestinal differentiation and tubular or tubulovillous architecture. Low-grade dysplasia consists of tall columnar cells with elongated nuclei; high-grade dysplasia shows architectural complexity, stratification, and atypia. IAPN is an exophytic intrachannel neoplasm, often with mixed low- and high-grade dysplasia. IAPN may show intestinal, pancreatobiliary, or mixed differentiation; more than 80% contain both low- and high-grade areas. Intestinal phenotype: CDX2 and MUC2 positive, usually MUC1 negative; CK7/CK20 coexpression is common. IAPN pancreatobiliary phenotype often expresses MUC1, MUC5AC, and MUC6; intestinal areas express CDX2 and MUC2. Phenotypic overlap is frequent; IHC supports but does not independently define the subtype. Non-ampullary duodenal adenoma Located away from the papilla; correlate endoscopic and gross anatomy. Ampullary adenocarcinoma Unequivocal stromal invasion is required; invasive carcinoma may be hidden in deeper portions of the lesion. IPMN / intraductal papillary neoplasm of bile duct IAPN is centered within the ampullary channel; establish the epicenter and extent relative to ducts and duodenal surface. Endoscopic biopsies have a high false-negative rate for invasion because carcinoma may be deep. Approximately 75% of resected IAPNs have associated invasive carcinoma; careful grossing and sampling are essential. Non-ampullary Duodenal Adenocarcinoma Malignant Invasive carcinoma Duodenum, most often the first and second portions; by definition, the ampulla is not involved. Median age approximately 60 years; slight male predominance. Presentation is often delayed; abdominal pain is common, with occult bleeding in 30–40%. Intestinal obstruction occurs in approximately one third of patients; advanced disease is common at diagnosis. Invasive gland-forming epithelial malignancy arising in the duodenum outside the ampulla. Demonstrate unequivocal invasion; exclude direct extension or mucosal colonization by pancreatic or ampullary carcinoma. Classify the predominant histologic pattern and assess MMR status. Most tumors are tubular adenocarcinoma, but mucinous, poorly cohesive/signet-ring, medullary, adenosquamous, and undifferentiated patterns occur. Approximately 40–50% show gastric or pancreatobiliary morphology; intestinal-type tumors are less frequent. Gastric differentiation is associated with MUC5AC/MUC6; pancreatobiliary differentiation with MUC1. Intestinal-type tumors resemble colorectal adenocarcinoma and express intestinal markers; mixed morphology and immunophenotype are common. Direct extension from pancreatic or ampullary carcinoma may colonize duodenal mucosa and mimic a primary mucosal neoplasm. Intestinal differentiation: CDX2 and MUC2. Gastric differentiation: MUC5AC and MUC6. Pancreatobiliary differentiation: MUC1. MMR protein IHC is required to assess MMR deficiency and possible Lynch syndrome. MMR deficiency/MSI testing is clinically important for hereditary risk assessment and immunotherapy selection. ERBB2 amplification or mutation and actionable kinase fusions occur in a subset; consider comprehensive profiling in advanced disease. Ampullary epicenter or involvement; careful gross examination and mapping are decisive. Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma extending into duodenum May colonize mucosa; correlate with imaging, gross epicenter, and adjacent pancreatic involvement. Metastatic adenocarcinoma Use clinical history, imaging, and site-directed immunophenotype. Primary jejunoileal adenocarcinoma Establish the exact intestinal segment of origin. Do not assign a duodenal primary solely because tumor involves or colonizes the mucosa. Sample the ampulla and adjacent pancreas/bile duct carefully when the lesion is periampullary. Ampullary Adenocarcinoma Invasive carcinoma; site of origin within ampulla affects classification and staging Ampulla of Vater; distinguish ampullary surface origin, IAPN-associated origin, and ampullary ductal origin. Median age in the 60s; men are slightly more frequently affected. May present with jaundice, abdominal pain, weight loss, or gastrointestinal bleeding; ulcerated lesions may bleed. FAP and Lynch syndrome are relevant hereditary associations. Glandular epithelial malignancy centered in the ampulla with unequivocal invasion. Document the epicenter and distinguish ampullary origin from direct extension by pancreatic or bile duct carcinoma. Report invasive carcinoma size; stage according to the anatomic site and applicable TNM system. Most ampullary carcinomas are tubular adenocarcinomas. Intestinal type resembles colorectal adenocarcinoma, with tall columnar cells and pseudostratified elongated nuclei; goblet, Paneth, or neuroendocrine cells may occur. Pancreatobiliary/gastric type shows small glands separated by desmoplastic stroma, lined by cuboidal to low-columnar cells. Mixed/hybrid intestinal and pancreatobiliary features are common; classify the predominant direction when possible. Mucinous carcinoma has extracellular stromal mucin comprising more than 50% of the tumor; neoplastic glands or strips float in mucin pools. Poorly cohesive carcinoma infiltrates as single cells, small clusters, or cords, often with signet-ring cells. Medullary carcinoma shows syncytial sheets or nodules with pushing borders and prominent lymphocytic inflammation. Adenosquamous carcinoma requires a squamous component exceeding 30%; mention even smaller convincing squamous components. Rhabdoid undifferentiated carcinoma may show dyscohesive cells with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusions and myxoid stroma. Intestinal differentiation: CDX2 and MUC2; CK7/CK20 coexpression is not uncommon. Pancreatobiliary differentiation: MUC1; MUC1/MUC2/CDX2 panels help but are not entirely specific. Squamous component expresses squamous cytokeratins, p63, and p40. Rhabdoid undifferentiated carcinoma may show loss of SMARCB1 (INI1), SMARCA4, SMARCA2, and/or ARID1A. MMR protein IHC is recommended routinely to identify MMR-deficient tumors. MMR deficiency/MSI occurs in approximately 10–15% and informs hereditary evaluation and immunotherapy eligibility. For advanced disease, consider tumor sequencing for actionable fusions (ALK, FGFR2, NRG1, NTRK, RET, ROS1), mutations (BRAF, BRCA1/2, KRAS, PALB2), and ERBB2 amplification. Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma Exclude direct extension; determine the tumor epicenter by careful gross dissection. Distal bile duct adenocarcinoma Map the relationship to the common bile duct and ampullary channel. Non-ampullary duodenal adenocarcinoma Ampullary origin requires a tumor epicenter in the ampulla. Metastatic squamous cell carcinoma A pure squamous carcinoma at the ampulla should prompt exclusion of metastasis. The ampulla's complex anatomy makes staging challenging; a very small invasive focus may still reach a higher T category depending on the compartment involved. Invasive carcinoma may be concealed beneath an adenomatous/polypoid component. Do not force a pure intestinal or pancreatobiliary label when the phenotype is hybrid. Conventional Jejunoileal Adenoma Jejunum or ileum; small intestinal adenomas are less common here than in the duodenum. Usually sporadic; associated hereditary syndromes include FAP and MUTYH-associated polyposis. The supplied source does not provide a specific age or sex distribution. Clinical presentation is not specifically characterized in the supplied excerpt. Non-invasive dysplastic glandular epithelial proliferation in the jejunum or ileum. Establish absence of stromal invasion. Assess architecture and dysplasia grade. The supplied source describes conventional jejunoileal adenoma as an epithelial precursor but provides limited detailed histologic characterization. Adjacent residual adenoma is identified in approximately one quarter of jejunal/ileal adenocarcinomas, supporting an adenoma–carcinoma sequence in a subset. Reactive / inflammatory atypia Requires correlation with architecture and background mucosal injury; the source does not provide a detailed differential. Adenocarcinoma Requires unequivocal invasion. Do not infer detailed subtype-specific IHC or molecular findings from the limited source description. Peutz–Jeghers Polyp Benign / Hamartomatous Hamartomatous polyp; syndromic and sporadic forms Small intestine; classic syndromic polyps are often found in the small bowel. Syndromic lesions occur in Peutz–Jeghers syndrome (PJS); solitary sporadic polyps also occur. The supplied excerpt does not specify a characteristic age or sex distribution. PJS carries increased overall malignancy risk; a solitary sporadic polyp does not appear to confer the same risk. Arborizing smooth-muscle core within the polyp mesenchyme. Epithelial component is usually normal or near-normal, without extensive dysplasia. Correlate with clinical history and consider genetic evaluation to distinguish syndromic from sporadic lesions. Syndromic polyps show branching/arborizing smooth-muscle bundles that divide the epithelium into lobules. The epithelial lining is generally normal or near-normal. Epithelial misplacement from prolapse/peristaltic trauma may extend deeply, even to the serosa, and mimic invasion. Sporadic polyps show more haphazard fibromuscular proliferation wrapping individual glands, without the orderly lobular pattern. Germline pathogenic STK11 variants can be identified by next-generation sequencing in patients with PJS. A solitary sporadic Peutz–Jeghers polyp requires adequate genetic/clinical evaluation before excluding germline or mosaic STK11 alteration. Adenoma with prolapse Dysplasia or epithelial serration suggests an adenomatous/serrated lesion with secondary prolapse. True invasive adenocarcinoma Epithelial misplacement in Peutz–Jeghers polyps can mimic invasion; recognize the arborizing smooth-muscle framework and bland epithelium. Mucosal prolapse polyp May show fibromuscular proliferation but lacks the characteristic organized arborizing architecture of a syndromic Peutz–Jeghers polyp. Epithelial misplacement may extend to the serosa and should not be mistaken for carcinoma without supporting cytologic and stromal features. Small syndromic polyps may lack the classic architecture. Do not label a polyp sporadic until PJS has been adequately evaluated. Jejunoileal Adenocarcinoma Jejunum or ileum; ileal tumors are commonly associated with Crohn disease, whereas jejunal tumors are more frequent in celiac disease. Typically presents in the sixth decade; median age approximately 50–60 years. Abdominal pain, nausea/vomiting, gastrointestinal bleeding, and anemia are common. Obstruction and bleeding are typical presentations; approximately 65% present at stage III or IV. Invasive malignant epithelial neoplasm arising in jejunum or ileum with glandular differentiation and/or mucin production. Demonstrate infiltrative invasion and establish the primary site. Classify histologic subtype and grade; assess MMR status. Most tumors resemble colorectal adenocarcinoma, with infiltrative glands lined by columnar cells with elongated nuclei, often with luminal necrosis. Mucinous adenocarcinoma: more than 50% extracellular mucin with malignant epithelium in clumps, strips, or single cells. Medullary carcinoma: more than 50% syncytial solid growth with vesicular nuclei, prominent nucleoli, and prominent lymphocytes and/or neutrophils. Low-grade tubuloglandular adenocarcinoma: haphazard well-differentiated glands without desmoplastic response; small glands have cuboidal to low-columnar eosinophilic cells. Poorly cohesive carcinoma: more than 50% single cells, small clusters, or cords, with or without signet-ring morphology. Undifferentiated carcinoma may show dyscohesive rhabdoid cells and loss of SWI/SNF proteins. Adenosquamous carcinoma contains both glandular and squamous components and is extremely rare. Tumor budding, lymphovascular invasion, and subserosal/serosal involvement are common. MMR protein loss identifies MMR-deficient tumors and supports hereditary assessment and immunotherapy selection. Mucinous tumors typically express MUC2. CK7 is infrequent in sporadic tumors (20–30%) but is more common in Crohn-associated ileal adenocarcinoma. CDX2-positive/MUC1-negative intestinal phenotype has been associated with better prognosis. SATB2 is expressed in approximately 20%; it cannot reliably distinguish jejunoileal from colorectal origin. Undifferentiated rhabdoid tumors may lose SMARCA2, SMARCA4, SMARCB1, and/or ARID1A. MMR deficiency/MSI occurs in approximately 9–31%; test MMR proteins and/or MSI for hereditary assessment and immunotherapy selection. Crohn-associated ileal adenocarcinoma harbors IDH1 mutations (usually p.Arg132Cys) in approximately 20%; MGMT methylation is also common. Celiac-associated tumors show high MSI/MMR deficiency (50–73%), often related to MLH1 promoter hypermethylation; WNT pathway activation is frequent. Common alterations include TP53, KRAS, APC, PIK3CA, and SMAD4. Colorectal adenocarcinoma involving small bowel May extend into mucosa and mimic an adenoma; correlate with clinical history, imaging, and tumor epicenter. Exclude a secondary primary, particularly colorectal origin. Crohn-related inflammatory stenosis Poorly cohesive carcinoma may diffusely thicken and rigidify the bowel wall, mimicking fibroinflammatory stricture. Neuroendocrine neoplasm Use morphology and neuroendocrine markers when a nested/organoid or small-cell pattern is present. Undifferentiated carcinoma mimics Exclude dedifferentiated carcinoma, lung carcinoma metastasis, sarcoma, and melanoma. Crohn-associated poorly cohesive carcinoma may be diffuse and non-mass-forming; inspect strictures carefully. Grade by the least differentiated component; a focus lacking gland formation of at least 0.196 mm² supports high-grade classification. Medullary carcinoma is not graded as high-grade under the source-described scheme despite its solid growth pattern. Report tumor budding and lymphovascular invasion separately from grade. All PathologyGPS / Gastrointestinal Pathology / Small Intestine Small Intestinal Tumors A morphology-first diagnostic reference for duodenal, ampullary, jejunal, and ileal epithelial neoplasms, emphasizing essential criteria, targeted immunohistochemistry, and diagnostically useful molecular findings. Core rule Establish the anatomic epicenter before assigning the primary site. The ampulla, adjacent pancreas, distal bile duct, and duodenal mucosa are closely related. Gross mapping and clinical-radiologic correlation are essential. Diagnostic GPS: site first, then phenotype Map the site Duodenum outside the ampulla, ampullary surface, intra-ampullary channel, jejunum, or ileum. Establish behavior Separate non-invasive dysplasia/adenoma from unequivocal infiltrative invasion. Recognize the pattern Intestinal, gastric/pyloric, pancreatobiliary, mucinous, poorly cohesive, medullary, or undifferentiated. Use targeted ancillary tests MMR/MSI for hereditary assessment and immunotherapy; phenotype-directed IHC; selected sequencing for actionable alterations. Exclude secondary involvement Consider direct extension from pancreas/bile duct and metastasis, especially colorectal carcinoma. Entity reference Search by entity, site, morphology, immunophenotype, or molecular finding. Search entities and features... Collapse − View diagnostic profile + Clinical Profile Essential Diagnostic Criteria Histopathology Immunophenotype Molecular Pathology Differential Diagnosis Diagnostic Pitfalls No matching entity. High-yield site distinction Site Key anatomic distinction Diagnostic implication Non-ampullary duodenum Tumor does not involve the ampulla. Classify as non-ampullary duodenal adenoma or adenocarcinoma according to invasion. Ampullary surface Lesion arises on the duodenal-facing surface of the papilla. Ampullary duodenal adenoma or ampullary duodenal adenocarcinoma. Intra-ampullary channel Epicenter and bulk lie within the ampullary channel. Consider IAPN and IAPN-associated carcinoma; ductal-origin carcinoma is a separate category. Jejunum / ileum Establish segment and exclude secondary involvement. Apply jejunoileal adenoma/adenocarcinoma criteria and evaluate relevant clinical associations. Biopsy, sampling, and reporting checklist Document the exact segment and, for periampullary lesions, the tumor epicenter and relationship to the ampullary channel, common bile duct, pancreatic duct, pancreas, and duodenum. For ampullary and periampullary resections, submit the ampulla and adjacent structures with a dissection method that demonstrates the epicenter. Sample the full depth of adenomatous/polypoid lesions because invasive carcinoma may be concealed in deeper portions. For jejunoileal strictures, especially in Crohn disease, carefully sample diffuse wall thickening even when no discrete mass is present. Report histologic subtype, grade where applicable, depth/extent of invasion, lymphovascular and perineural invasion, tumor budding when assessed, margins, and lymph node status. Perform MMR protein IHC and/or MSI testing in small intestinal and ampullary adenocarcinoma; consider additional molecular profiling in advanced disease. Scope note: Content is based on the supplied WHO source excerpt. Where the excerpt provides limited clinical or diagnostic detail, the page explicitly avoids adding unsupported specifics. Ancillary tests should be interpreted with morphology, anatomic site, and clinical findings.

title: Liver Tumors
content: use client Focal nodular hyperplasia (FNH) Benign Non-neoplastic; no malignant potential Usually solitary and incidental; may occur at any hepatic site. Predominantly affects middle-aged women (female-to-male ratio approximately 9:1). Large lesions may cause abdominal pain or compression; hemorrhage is not an established risk. Unencapsulated, nodular hepatocellular lesion. Fibrous septa and/or central stellate scar with dystrophic vessels. No cytoarchitectural features of malignancy. A map-like (geographic) glutamine synthetase (GS) staining pattern is desirable. Benign hepatocytes form nodules, usually in plates one to two cells thick. Central scar and radiating fibrous septa contain large dystrophic vessels and numerous small arteries. Arteries are not accompanied by portal veins or bile ducts. Ductular reaction is common at the interface of fibrous septa and hepatocellular nodules. Cholestatic changes, steatosis, or large-cell change may be present. GS shows broad, anastomosing, map-like areas of staining. CK7 and CK19 highlight the ductular reaction. CD34 may show patchy to diffuse sinusoidal staining. SAA and CRP are generally not diffusely expressed; focal or periseptal staining can occur. FNH is polyclonal and lacks the pathogenic driver mutations characteristic of HCA. WNT pathway activation is focal and occurs without CTNNB1 or AXIN1 mutation. Inflammatory HCA Usually lacks map-like GS staining and shows diffuse SAA and/or CRP; sinusoidal dilatation and isolated arteries favor HCA. β-catenin–activated HCA Usually shows diffuse or mutation-pattern GS staining; CTNNB1 mutation supports HCA. Well-differentiated HCC Cytologic/architectural atypia and reticulin disruption favor HCC; diffuse GS and GPC3 support HCC. A limited biopsy may not show the full map-like GS pattern. Do not label a CTNNB1-mutated nodule with diffuse GS as FNH-like; classify it as β-catenin–activated HCA or an atypical hepatocellular neoplasm as appropriate. Hepatocellular adenoma (HCA) Benign; subtype-dependent hemorrhage and malignant transformation risk About 85% occur in women of childbearing age; oral contraceptive exposure is a major risk factor. Associated factors include obesity/metabolic syndrome, anabolic steroids, glycogen storage disease, and other inherited disorders. Usually incidental; may present with abdominal pain, palpable mass, or hemorrhage. Hemorrhage occurs in approximately 20–25%; malignant transformation is uncommon (approximately 4–8%) and occurs mainly in men. Multiple lesions (>10) are termed hepatocellular adenomatosis. Benign hepatocellular neoplasm arising in a non-cirrhotic liver in the usual setting. Hepatocytes are arranged in plates one to two cells thick, often with unpaired arteries. Subtype assignment requires integration of morphology, subtype-defining IHC, and molecular findings when indicated. Assess for atypia, reticulin loss, β-catenin activation, and other features associated with malignant transformation. HCA is generally composed of bland hepatocytes in plates one to two cells thick, with occasional pseudoglands. HNF1A-inactivated HCA: diffuse steatosis, clear or ballooned hepatocytes, and lobulated contours are typical. Inflammatory HCA: sinusoidal dilatation/congestion, inflammation, thick arteries, and variable ductular reaction; steatosis may occur. β-catenin–activated HCA: no specific H&E pattern; pseudoglands, irregular nuclei, pigment, or abnormal vessels may occur. β-catenin–activated inflammatory HCA combines inflammatory morphology with β-catenin pathway activation. Sonic hedgehog HCA: bland, often small hepatocytes with clear or retracted eosinophilic cytoplasm; hemorrhagic foci and blood-filled or empty cavities are frequent. Unclassified HCA lacks defining morphologic, immunophenotypic, or molecular features of the recognized subtypes. HNF1A-inactivated HCA: complete loss of L-FABP in lesional hepatocytes. Inflammatory HCA: diffuse SAA and CRP expression. β-catenin–activated HCA: GS pattern reflects the strength and type of pathway activation; nuclear β-catenin may be focal or absent. Strong β-catenin activation (usually non-Ser45 exon 3 mutation): diffuse homogeneous GS. Moderate activation (e.g., exon 3 Ser45): diffuse heterogeneous, starry-sky GS; peripheral accentuation may occur. Weak activation (often exon 7/8 mutation): weak, patchy GS; a strong peripheral rim may occur. β-catenin–activated inflammatory HCA expresses inflammatory markers and shows a β-catenin activation pattern. Sonic hedgehog HCA: PTGDS is specific but insensitive; ASS1 is more sensitive but not entirely specific. H-HCA: biallelic HNF1A inactivation; accounts for approximately 30–35% of HCA. IHCA: activating alterations in the IL6/JAK/STAT3 pathway; approximately 35–40%. β-HCA: CTNNB1 mutation/deletion activates WNT/β-catenin signaling; approximately 10%. β-IHCA: combined inflammatory-pathway and CTNNB1 alterations; approximately 10–15%. shHCA: INHBE deletions generating INHBE::GLI1 fusions; approximately 5–10%. CTNNB1 exon 3 non-Ser45 mutations carry increased malignant transformation risk; exon 7/8 mutations have low or absent risk in the cited classification. TERT promoter mutations and HCC-like copy-number alterations support progression/malignant transformation in an appropriate β-catenin–activated lesion. Unclassified HCA represents fewer than 5% after exclusion of all recognized subtypes. FNH Map-like GS and ductular reaction/fibrous septa favor FNH; diffuse SAA/CRP and absent map-like GS favor IHCA. HCC Thick plates, frequent pseudoglands, small-cell change, mitoses, and reticulin loss/fragmentation favor HCC; GPC3 may support HCC. Well-differentiated HCC in β-HCA If morphology/IHC is equivocal, assess CTNNB1, TERT promoter, and copy-number alterations. Epithelioid angiomyolipoma / small vessel neoplasm Consider a non-epithelial lesion and use lineage-directed markers rather than assuming hepatocellular differentiation. GS is a surrogate for CTNNB1 mutation class, not a perfect substitute for sequencing when the pattern is equivocal or risk assessment changes management. Nuclear β-catenin can be focal or absent despite pathway activation. Different HCA subtypes can coexist in one liver; multiple nodules may not share the same subtype. SAA/CRP and L-FABP subtyping stains do not distinguish HCA from HCC by themselves. Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) Malignant Malignant; vascular invasion and metastasis may occur Usually arises in a background of chronic liver disease or cirrhosis; chronic viral hepatitis, alcohol-related liver disease, and metabolic dysfunction–associated steatotic liver disease are important settings. Most common primary liver malignancy (approximately 75–85% of primary liver cancers). Symptoms include right upper quadrant pain, weight loss, jaundice, hepatomegaly, and worsening ascites; symptomatic disease is often advanced. No preferential intrahepatic location. Primary malignant epithelial neoplasm with hepatocytic differentiation. Establish malignancy by architecture and cytology, including thickened plates, pseudoglands, stromal invasion, and/or reticulin framework disruption. Integrate background liver, imaging, and appropriate hepatocellular and malignancy-associated markers. Sample heterogeneous areas and assess vascular invasion, satellites, and grade. Architectural patterns include trabecular, pseudoglandular, and solid growth. Thickened trabeculae, often more than two cells thick, and pseudogland formation are common. Cytologic atypia, small-cell change, increased nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio, and mitotic activity support malignancy. Reticulin loss or fragmentation and stromal invasion are important diagnostic features. Recognized patterns include macrotrabecular-massive, steatohepatitic, scirrhous, clear cell, fibrolamellar, lymphocyte-rich, and sarcomatoid forms. Arginase-1, HepPar-1, and canalicular polyclonal CEA/CD10 support hepatocellular differentiation. Glypican-3 supports HCC but has limited sensitivity. GS may be diffuse in β-catenin–activated HCC. CK19 expression occurs in a subset and may be associated with a more aggressive phenotype. TERT promoter and CTNNB1 mutations are recurrent alterations. Other recurrent pathway alterations include TP53 and changes in chromatin-remodeling and oxidative-stress pathways. Copy-number changes may include gains of 1q, 7q, and 8q and losses of 6p and 17q. HCA HCA usually retains a benign reticulin framework and lacks significant atypia, mitoses, and stromal invasion. Map-like GS, ductular reaction, fibrous septa, and absence of malignant cytology favor FNH. Metastatic carcinoma / iCCA Use morphology, clinical/radiologic correlation, and lineage-directed IHC; hepatocellular markers support HCC. Focal reticulin loss can occur in HCA near hemorrhage or steatosis; interpret with the overall architecture. CD34 sinusoidal capillarization is not specific for HCC. GPC3 negativity does not exclude HCC. Hepatoblastoma (HBL) Malignant pediatric liver tumor Predominantly affects infants and young children, usually before 3 years of age. Often presents as an enlarging abdominal mass or distension; serum AFP is commonly elevated. Usually arises in an otherwise non-cirrhotic liver. Primary malignant embryonal liver tumor in the appropriate pediatric setting. Recognize epithelial and/or mixed epithelial-mesenchymal patterns. Correlate morphology with AFP and the characteristic WNT/β-catenin pathway context. Epithelial patterns include fetal, embryonal, and small-cell undifferentiated components. Fetal areas resemble developing hepatocytes and may be well differentiated or mitotically active. Embryonal areas show smaller, more basophilic cells in acinar, trabecular, or rosette-like patterns. Mixed tumors contain mesenchymal elements, including osteoid, cartilage, or fibrous tissue. Post-treatment specimens may show extensive necrosis, fibrosis, and cystic degeneration. Hepatocellular markers support epithelial differentiation. Nuclear β-catenin may be present in tumor cells. IHC should be interpreted with morphology; no single stain is independently diagnostic. CTNNB1 mutations and WNT/β-catenin pathway activation occur in up to approximately 90% of cases. NFE2L2 mutations (approximately 2–5%) and TERT promoter mutations have been associated with poor prognosis in reported studies. HCC in a child HCC generally shows greater genomic complexity and malignant hepatocellular features; molecular context can help in difficult cases. Metastatic neuroblastoma Clinical history and neuroendocrine/neural markers distinguish neuroblastoma from hepatocellular differentiation. Pediatric HCN, NOS Consider when morphology and molecular findings do not meet criteria for HBL or HCC. Small-cell undifferentiated areas require careful exclusion of other pediatric small round cell tumors. Treatment effect can markedly alter morphology; review pretreatment material when available. Bile duct adenoma (BDA) Benign; malignant transformation not established for classic lesions Usually a solitary, incidental, subcapsular nodule (approximately 90%). Occurs predominantly in adults without a specific sex predilection. Often discovered during surgery, autopsy, or examination of a resection specimen. Small, nodular proliferation of benign small bile ducts. Frequent inclusion of portal tracts. No infiltrative or pushing growth margin. Disordered collection of uniform small tubules in fibrous stroma. Tubules have absent or narrow lumina and are lined by bland cuboidal cells. Chronic inflammation and collagenization vary in degree. Portal tracts are typically entrapped within the nodule. Oncocytic and clear-cell patterns have been described. Biliary epithelium expresses CK7 and CK19. Ki-67 is low (average approximately 2%; reported not to exceed 10%). Strong p53 staining is not expected; EZH2 favors carcinoma, whereas p16 expression favors BDA in the cited differential. BRAF p.Val600Glu has been detected in a subset (8 of 15 cases in one cited series); molecular testing is not routinely clinically relevant. Small duct iCCA Invasive growth, larger size, atypia, and higher proliferation favor carcinoma. Reactive ductular proliferation Usually lacks a discrete, circumscribed nodular configuration. Von Meyenburg complex / biliary adenofibroma Look for multiple microhamartomatous cystic ducts or the solid-microcystic architecture and stromal scaffold of adenofibroma. BDA can mimic metastatic adenocarcinoma at frozen section; avoid overcalling a small bland subcapsular nodule. Albumin in situ hybridization and CRP can be positive and do not independently establish malignancy. Biliary adenofibroma (BAF) Benign epithelial neoplasm; rare malignant transformation has been described Very rare; fewer than 35 cases had been reported in the cited literature. May present with abdominal pain or be discovered incidentally. No preferential location within the liver. Solid-microcystic intrahepatic epithelial neoplasm. Variably dilated tubular structures lined by non-mucin-secreting biliary epithelium. Fibrotic stromal scaffolding supports the epithelial component. Tubules and variably dilated cystic spaces are lined by bland biliary epithelium. The intervening stroma forms a conspicuous fibrotic scaffold. Assess carefully for cytologic atypia, complex architecture, and invasive growth when considering malignant transformation. Epithelial cells show biliary differentiation, typically including CK7 and CK19. Use IHC to characterize the epithelial component and exclude mimics; no single defining marker is specified in the supplied excerpt. Bile duct adenoma BDA is a small, solid nodular proliferation of tightly packed ducts and typically lacks the microcystic architecture and prominent stromal scaffold. Von Meyenburg complex Usually consists of multiple small, bile-containing ductal microhamartomas. Mucinous cystic neoplasm MCN has mucinous epithelium and ovarian-type stroma; BAF is lined by non-mucin-secreting biliary epithelium. The supplied source does not identify a clinically useful molecular test; do not add nonvalidated molecular claims. Mucinous cystic neoplasm of the liver (MCN) Benign / potentially malignant Usually non-invasive; invasive carcinoma occurs in a minority Occurs overwhelmingly in women, typically in middle age. Usually a solitary, large, multilocular cystic mass, most often in the left hepatic lobe. May cause abdominal pain, fullness, or be found incidentally. Cyst-forming hepatic neoplasm lined by mucin-producing epithelium. Ovarian-type subepithelial stroma is required for diagnosis. Assess for dysplasia and associated invasive carcinoma. Multiloculated cystic spaces are lined by mucinous columnar or cuboidal epithelium. Subepithelial ovarian-type stroma is the defining feature and may be inconspicuous in limited samples. Epithelial dysplasia ranges from low grade to high grade. Invasive carcinoma, when present, is usually associated with high-grade dysplasia. Ovarian-type stroma commonly expresses ER, PR, and inhibin; stromal markers support the diagnosis. Epithelial cells express biliary markers such as CK7 and CK19. Intraductal papillary neoplasm of the bile duct IPNB communicates with bile ducts and shows intraductal papillary growth; MCN has ovarian-type stroma and usually does not communicate with ducts. Simple hepatic cyst Lacks mucinous neoplastic epithelium and ovarian-type stroma. Biliary adenofibroma BAF has bland non-mucinous biliary epithelium and a fibrotic scaffold, not ovarian-type stroma. Ovarian-type stroma may be focal; extensive sampling is important. Do not use the obsolete terms biliary cystadenoma or cystadenocarcinoma. Small duct intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma (SD-iCCA) Malignant biliary carcinoma Usually a peripheral, mass-forming tumor; often diagnosed at a relatively large size. Approximately half of patients have underlying chronic liver disease or cirrhosis. Mean age for iCCA overall is approximately 55–75 years; iCCA is more frequent in men. May be detected during surveillance or resection for suspected HCC. Malignant epithelial neoplasm with biliary differentiation. Typically composed of small tubules with narrow lumina and no significant mucin production. Demonstrate infiltrative growth or other unequivocal evidence of malignancy. Anastomosing small tubular glands are typical; trabecular, cord-like, solid, or other patterns may coexist. Tubular lumina are small or slit-like and generally lack significant mucin. Tumor cells are cuboidal to low columnar with variable nuclear atypia. Desmoplastic stroma is common; replacement growth can mimic HCC. Subtypes include cholangiolocellular, ductal plate malformation-like, lymphoepithelioma-like, and solid-tubulocystic patterns. CK7 and CK19 commonly support biliary differentiation. Albumin RNA in situ hybridization supports a primary hepatic origin in the appropriate context but is not specific for malignancy. CRP may be expressed and does not by itself distinguish SD-iCCA from benign lesions. IDH1/2 mutations and FGFR2 fusions are characteristic actionable alterations in subsets of small duct iCCA. BAP1 and other chromatin-remodeling gene alterations occur in subsets. Molecular profiling can identify therapeutic targets; no molecular test is required for diagnosis. HCC shows hepatocellular differentiation; SD-iCCA shows small glands and biliary phenotype, although replacement growth can mimic trabecular HCC. BDA is small, circumscribed, bland, and noninfiltrative with low proliferation. Metastatic adenocarcinoma Correlate with clinical history and imaging; albumin ISH may support primary hepatic origin but is not definitive alone. Albumin ISH and CRP positivity do not prove carcinoma. Some SD-iCCAs show trabecular or replacement growth and can mimic HCC. Large duct intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma (LD-iCCA) Often arises in association with large-duct cholangiopathies, including primary sclerosing cholangitis, hepatolithiasis, and liver-fluke infection. May present with abdominal pain, weight loss, jaundice, or biliary obstruction. Upstream bile duct dilatation and periductal growth are more characteristic than in SD-iCCA. Malignant epithelial neoplasm with large-duct biliary differentiation. Mucin-producing glands and/or large-duct morphology are typical. Periductal infiltrative growth and desmoplasia support the diagnosis. Glandular and papillary structures are lined by mucin-producing columnar cells. Periductal infiltrative growth, desmoplastic stroma, and perineural/vascular invasion may be present. Large duct tumors may show biliary intraepithelial neoplasia or intraductal papillary precursor lesions. Tumor cells often show more abundant mucin than SD-iCCA. CK7 and CK19 support biliary differentiation. Mucin markers may be expressed; interpret in conjunction with morphology. KRAS and TP53 alterations are frequent in large duct iCCA. SMAD4 and other alterations may occur; IDH1/2 mutations and FGFR2 fusions are less characteristic than in SD-iCCA. SD-iCCA SD-iCCA typically has small non-mucinous tubules, a peripheral mass-forming pattern, and more frequent IDH1/2 mutations or FGFR2 fusions. Metastatic pancreaticobiliary adenocarcinoma Clinical history, imaging, and anatomic relationship to major ducts are essential. Biliary intraepithelial neoplasia / IPNB Precursor lesions lack destructive stromal invasion. Do not infer large duct type from location alone; integrate growth pattern, mucin production, and clinical context. Combined hepatocellular-cholangiocarcinoma (cHCC-CCA) Malignant primary liver carcinoma Rare; accounts for fewer than 1% of primary liver carcinomas. Clinical setting and imaging overlap with HCC and SD-iCCA. Often arises in a background of chronic liver disease; age and sex distribution resemble HCC. Unequivocal hepatocellular and cholangiocytic differentiation must both be present in the same primary liver carcinoma. Each component must meet the established morphologic criteria for HCC or CCA. IHC may confirm the respective morphologies but cannot establish the diagnosis without supportive H&E findings. Estimate the proportion of each component and grade each separately when possible. HCC and CCA components may be juxtaposed, intermingled, or show a transition zone. Hepatocellular areas show characteristic HCC architecture and cytology. Cholangiocytic areas show glandular differentiation, often with desmoplastic stroma. Stem-cell-like areas may occur but are not required for diagnosis. Use hepatocellular markers (e.g., arginase-1, HepPar-1) to support hepatocytic areas. Use biliary markers (e.g., CK7, CK19) to support cholangiocytic areas. IHC alone, without the corresponding morphologic components, is insufficient. Molecular studies support a shared clonal origin of the two components. The profile is often closer to HCC, with TERT promoter and CTNNB1 alterations more common than typical iCCA alterations such as KRAS and IDH1. HCC with aberrant CK19 expression Biliary-marker expression alone does not establish a CCA component; unequivocal glandular morphology is required. iCCA with hepatocellular marker expression Hepatocellular-marker positivity alone does not establish HCC differentiation; require unequivocal HCC morphology. Collision tumor Careful sampling and assessment of transition/intermingling help distinguish a combined carcinoma from two independent tumors. Do not diagnose cHCC-CCA solely from immunophenotypic co-expression. There is no minimum percentage cutoff for either component; report their estimated proportions. HNF1A-inactivated HCA (H-HCA) Diffuse macro-/microsteatosis; clear or ballooned hepatocytes; lobulated contour; occasional pseudoglands. Complete loss of L-FABP in lesional hepatocytes. Biallelic HNF1A inactivation; approximately 30–35% of HCA. Inflammatory HCA (IHCA) Sinusoidal dilatation/congestion, inflammation, thick arteries, variable ductular reaction; steatosis may occur. Diffuse SAA and CRP expression. Activating alterations in IL6/JAK/STAT3 pathway; approximately 35–40%. β-catenin–activated HCA (β-HCA) No specific H&E pattern; pseudoglands, irregular nuclei, pigment, or abnormal vessels may occur. GS pattern depends on mutation strength; nuclear β-catenin may be focal or absent. CTNNB1 mutation/deletion; approximately 10%. Non-Ser45 exon 3 mutations carry increased malignant transformation risk; exon 7/8 mutations have low/absent risk. β-catenin–activated inflammatory HCA (β-IHCA) Inflammatory HCA morphology combined with β-catenin pathway activation. SAA/CRP positive; GS shows a β-catenin activation pattern. Combined inflammatory-pathway and CTNNB1 alterations; approximately 10–15%. Sonic hedgehog HCA (shHCA) Bland small hepatocytes with clear or retracted eosinophilic cytoplasm; hemorrhagic foci and blood-filled/empty cavities are frequent. PTGDS is specific but insensitive; ASS1 is more sensitive but not entirely specific; L-FABP may be reduced. INHBE deletion generating INHBE::GLI1 fusion; approximately 5–10%; associated with increased hemorrhage risk. Unclassified HCA No defining morphologic pattern after exclusion of recognized subtypes. No defining subtype-specific profile. No defining molecular alteration; fewer than 5%. All PathologyGPS / GI & Liver / Liver Tumors Liver Tumors A morphology-first diagnostic reference to hepatocellular and biliary tumors, emphasizing subtype classification, immunophenotype, molecular findings, and practical differential diagnosis. Core rule Classify the lesion by architecture and differentiation, then use targeted IHC and molecular testing to resolve the subtype. For hepatocellular adenoma, subtype assignment is clinically meaningful because β-catenin activation and sonic hedgehog pathway activation affect risk assessment. Diagnostic GPS: from clinical setting to classification Establish the clinical setting Age, sex, background liver, cirrhosis, metabolic disease, viral hepatitis, hormone/steroid exposure, and imaging. Identify the dominant pattern Hepatocellular nodule; trabecular carcinoma; small-duct glands; mucinous large-duct carcinoma; or cystic epithelial neoplasm. Assess architecture Reticulin framework, plate thickness, stromal invasion, ductular reaction, desmoplasia, and vascular/perineural invasion. Apply targeted IHC GS, L-FABP, SAA/CRP, PTGDS/ASS1, hepatocellular markers, and biliary markers according to the differential. Use molecular testing selectively CTNNB1 subtype/risk assessment, INHBE::GLI1, and actionable iCCA alterations when clinically relevant. Hepatocellular adenoma: integrated subtype classification The table integrates the WHO-described morphology, defining immunophenotype, and molecular basis. Percentages are approximate proportions among HCAs; they are not diagnostic criteria. HCA subtype Histology Defining / useful IHC Molecular basis and clinical relevance Interpretive point: GS is a useful surrogate for the strength/pattern of β-catenin pathway activation, but nuclear β-catenin may be focal or absent. If the GS pattern is equivocal—especially on biopsy—and risk assessment will affect management, perform molecular analysis of CTNNB1. HCA: practical interpretation of the GS pattern GS pattern Likely molecular context Interpretation Diffuse homogeneous Strong β-catenin activation, commonly non-Ser45 exon 3 CTNNB1 mutation or large deletion Higher-risk β-HCA pattern; correlate with molecular testing and morphology. Diffuse heterogeneous / starry-sky Moderate activation, e.g., CTNNB1 exon 3 Ser45 β-catenin activation; assess exact mutation because risk differs by mutation class. Weak patchy Often CTNNB1 exon 7/8 Usually weak pathway activation with low/absent malignant transformation risk in the cited classification. Strong peripheral rim May occur with exon 3 Ser45 or exon 7/8 mutations Can mimic FNH map-like GS; evaluate the overall pattern and CD34 distribution, and consider sequencing. Map-like geographic FNH-associated focal WNT activation without CTNNB1 mutation Supports FNH when the morphology is concordant. Hepatocellular adenoma: risk-oriented checklist Record sex, tumor size, multiplicity, oral contraceptive/anabolic steroid exposure, pregnancy, obesity/metabolic syndrome, and relevant inherited disease. Carefully assess lesions ≥50 mm, hemorrhage, atypia, reticulin abnormalities, and any β-catenin activation. Male sex, androgen-associated HCA, β-catenin activation (particularly exon 3), and borderline features increase concern for malignant transformation. When lesions are multiple, subtype each nodule when possible; different subtypes may coexist in the same liver. If GS is equivocal and subtype assignment will affect management, confirm CTNNB1 status molecularly. Sample heterogeneous and hemorrhagic areas; a limited core may not represent the entire lesion. High-yield molecular and ancillary tests Clinical / diagnostic question Test Use H-HCA L-FABP IHC; HNF1A testing if needed Loss of L-FABP supports HNF1A-inactivated HCA. IHCA SAA and CRP IHC Diffuse expression supports inflammatory pathway activation. β-HCA / β-IHCA GS IHC; CTNNB1 sequencing when equivocal Classifies pathway activation and refines malignant transformation risk. shHCA PTGDS and ASS1 IHC; INHBE::GLI1 testing Supports sonic hedgehog subtype; PTGDS specific but insensitive. HCC vs HCA Reticulin, GPC3, hepatocellular markers; TERT promoter / copy-number analysis in selected cases Integrate morphology and ancillary findings; no single stain is definitive. iCCA Comprehensive molecular profiling May identify actionable IDH1/2 mutations or FGFR2 fusions, particularly in SD-iCCA. Scope note: Prepared from the supplied WHO liver tumor excerpt. Molecular findings are included only where they support classification, differential diagnosis, risk assessment, or targeted treatment. IHC and molecular results must be interpreted with morphology and clinical/radiologic correlation.
