title: Mesenchymal Tumors
content: use client Gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST) Malignant / variable behavior Risk ranges from clinically insignificant to aggressive; use risk stratification, not sarcoma grading Most often stomach (~55%) and small bowel (~32%); less often colon/rectum and esophagus; peak incidence in the sixth decade, median age 60–65 years, slight male predominance. Often presents with vague abdominal symptoms, bleeding, anemia, or an abdominal mass. Small lesions may be incidental; advanced tumors spread within the peritoneal cavity and commonly metastasize to the liver. Intramural, submucosal, or subserosal gastrointestinal mass. Spindle cell, epithelioid, or mixed morphology. KIT (CD117) and/or DOG1 expression. KIT or PDGFRA mutation is desirable for confirmation and therapeutic stratification. Spindle cell morphology predominates, particularly in gastric and intestinal tumors. Epithelioid morphology occurs in approximately 20–25% of gastric GISTs; mixed patterns also occur. Small intestinal tumors may show skeinoid collagen fibers, nuclear palisading, or perivascular hyalinization. Hemorrhage, cystic degeneration, and necrosis may occur in larger tumors. Nuclear pleomorphism is uncommon; mitotic activity is a key risk parameter. KIT is strongly and diffusely positive in most tumors; fewer than 5% are negative or only focally positive. DOG1 is highly sensitive and may identify KIT-negative GISTs. CD34 is common, especially in gastric spindle cell GIST. SMA, h-caldesmon, or S100 may be expressed; desmin and keratins are uncommon. Approximately 85% harbor mutually exclusive activating KIT or PDGFRA mutations. KIT mutations occur in about 75%; exon 11 is most common, followed by exon 9. PDGFRA mutations account for about 10%; exon 18, including p.Asp842Val, predominates. Mutation testing predicts response: KIT exon 11 often responds to imatinib; PDGFRA p.Asp842Val is primarily resistant. Rare alternative drivers include NF1, BRAF, KRAS, and NTRK3, FGFR1, or ALK fusions. Leiomyoma / leiomyosarcoma Smooth muscle markers are more consistent; GIST typically expresses KIT and/or DOG1. Schwannoma S100/SOX10-positive nerve sheath phenotype; usually KIT/DOG1-negative. Desmoid-type fibromatosis Infiltrative bland spindle-cell proliferation with nuclear β-catenin; lacks the usual GIST phenotype. Metastatic melanoma or carcinoma Use clinical context and lineage markers; GIST is typically KIT/DOG1-positive. Do not grade GIST using the FNCLCC system. Record tumor size, mitotic count per 5 mm², site, and tumor rupture; these drive risk assessment. A small core may not represent the mitotic hot spot or heterogeneous tumor. SDH-deficient gastrointestinal stromal tumor Distinct GIST subtype; often indolent but may metastasize, including to lymph nodes Almost exclusively gastric; enriched in children and young adults, median age about 22 years, with female predominance. Young age, gastric location, multifocality, and lymph node metastases are useful clues. Symptoms resemble those of conventional GIST, including bleeding, abdominal pain, and mass effect. GIST morphology in the appropriate clinical setting. Loss of SDHB immunoreactivity in tumor cells, with retained internal controls. Evaluate SDHA expression to help identify SDHA-deficient cases. Often multinodular, multifocal, or plexiform growth centered in the muscularis propria. Epithelioid morphology is common, sometimes with nested architecture and a rich capillary network. Lymph node metastases are more frequent than in conventional GIST. SDHB loss is the defining immunohistochemical feature. SDHA loss supports an SDHA-deficient subset; SDHA is retained in other SDH-deficient tumors. KIT and DOG1 are generally expressed, so they do not distinguish this subtype from conventional GIST. About 30% are associated with germline SDHA pathogenic variants and about 20% with germline SDHB, SDHC, or SDHD variants. Approximately half show SDHC promoter hypermethylation (epimutation), associated with Carney triad. SDH-deficient GIST should prompt evaluation for an SDH-deficient tumor syndrome and genetic counseling. Conventional KIT/PDGFRA-mutant GIST Usually retains SDHB; often has KIT or PDGFRA driver mutation. Other gastric epithelioid tumors Integrate KIT/DOG1, SDHB, keratins, neuroendocrine markers, and clinical setting. SDHB loss is more informative than KIT/DOG1 for subclassification. Do not assume a young patient’s gastric GIST is sporadic; assess syndromic associations. Inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor Intermediate Rarely metastasizing; local recurrence is more common than distant spread Most often small intestine and colon, followed by stomach; children and young adults are commonly affected, but age range is broad. May present with abdominal pain, obstruction, hematemesis, intussusception, or fever. Leukocytosis, anemia, elevated ESR, and hypergammaglobulinemia may occur. Loose fascicles of plump spindle cells without substantial pleomorphism. Prominent lymphoplasmacytic inflammatory infiltrate. SMA expression, often with ALK or, less commonly, ROS1 expression. Uniform plump spindle cells form loose fascicles in myxoid or collagenous stroma. Lymphocytes and plasma cells are prominent; eosinophils may also be present. Epithelioid inflammatory myofibroblastic sarcoma shows a more epithelioid morphology and aggressive behavior. SMA is positive in nearly all cases. ALK is expressed in approximately 60%, often with diffuse cytoplasmic staining. A small subset is ROS1-positive. About two thirds harbor tyrosine kinase receptor gene rearrangements, most often ALK; ROS1 and other kinase fusions occur. ALK or ROS1 immunoreactivity is usually sufficient for diagnosis; fusion testing is useful in selected cases and for targeted therapy. GIST Usually KIT/DOG1-positive and lacks the characteristic inflammatory background. Long sweeping fascicles and nuclear β-catenin; lacks ALK expression and prominent plasma-cell-rich inflammation. Reactive inflammatory pseudotumor No defining kinase fusion; correlate with morphology and clinical context. Epithelioid inflammatory myofibroblastic sarcoma Epithelioid cytology, often intra-abdominal, with more aggressive behavior. ALK-negative disease does not exclude inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor. Do not use inflammatory pseudotumor as a synonym for this neoplasm. Inflammatory fibroid polyp Benign Most often gastric antrum, followed by ileum; slight female predominance and peak incidence in middle-aged adults. Often incidental when small; larger lesions may cause pain, bleeding, or obstruction. Small intestinal lesions may present with intussusception. Hypocellular lesion of short spindle to stellate cells in edematous or myxoid stroma. Prominent eosinophilic and lymphocytic infiltrate. CD34 expression is supportive. Poorly marginated, hypocellular proliferation centered in the submucosa. Short spindle and stellate cells have fine chromatin, inconspicuous nucleoli, and scant eosinophilic cytoplasm. Perivascular concentric or onion-skin arrangement may be present. Eosinophils are a conspicuous component of the inflammatory infiltrate. CD34 and PDGFRA are positive in most cases. SMA is positive in a minority. KIT, DOG1, desmin, S100, SOX10, and keratins are negative. Activating PDGFRA mutations occur in many cases; exon 18 mutations predominate in gastric tumors, whereas exon 12 mutations are common in small intestinal tumors. Routine molecular testing is not required for a typical lesion. GIST is usually KIT/DOG1-positive; inflammatory fibroid polyp is typically negative. More cellular fascicular spindle-cell proliferation; ALK/ROS1 may be positive. Mucosal prolapse / reactive polyp Lacks the characteristic submucosal spindle-cell proliferation and eosinophil-rich infiltrate. Familial PDGFRA-associated cases may be multiple and may coexist with GIST. Do not mistake the perivascular pattern for a vascular neoplasm. Plexiform fibromyxoma Benign; no reported recurrence or metastasis Predominantly gastric, especially the antrum and pyloric region; rarely the duodenum. Reported across a wide age range, including children, with equal sex distribution. May present with gastrointestinal bleeding, ulceration, weight loss, or pyloric obstruction. Usually arises in the muscularis propria and may extend toward the mucosa or serosa. Multinodular and plexiform architecture at low power. Uniform bland spindle cells in myxoid, fibromyxoid, or collagenous stroma. Prominent delicate arborizing capillary network. Low mitotic activity without substantial cytologic atypia. Bland spindle cells, likely myofibroblastic, form interconnected nodules and plexiform fascicles. The stroma is myxoid, fibromyxoid, or collagenous. A prominent arborizing network of thin-walled capillaries is characteristic. Venous extension may occur and is not considered clinically significant. SMA is positive; desmin is occasionally positive. ALK, CD34, KIT, DOG1, and keratins are negative. MALAT1::GLI1 fusion or PTCH1 inactivation may occur, leading to GLI1 overexpression; molecular testing is not routinely required for diagnosis. Usually KIT and/or DOG1-positive; lacks the characteristic plexiform myxoid architecture and arborizing capillary network. Typically submucosal, eosinophil-rich, and often CD34-positive, with concentric perivascular fibrosis. Usually has a prominent lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate and may express ALK or ROS1. Myxoid leiomyoma Shows smooth muscle differentiation and typically expresses desmin and h-caldesmon. Do not interpret venous extension alone as evidence of malignant behavior. The plexiform architecture and delicate arborizing vasculature are more useful than isolated immunostains. Calcifying fibrous tumor Benign; local recurrence in approximately 10%; no metastatic potential GI tract, especially stomach and small intestine; also mesentery and peritoneum. Broad age range, peak in young to middle-aged adults. Usually asymptomatic; occasional anemia or abdominal discomfort. Multifocality occurs in a minority, particularly in the peritoneum. Circumscribed, hypocellular, densely collagenous mass. Sparse lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate. Dystrophic and/or psammomatous calcifications are usually present. Slender bland spindle cells are sparse within abundant hyalinized collagen. Chronic lymphoplasmacytic inflammation is present. Psammomatous and dystrophic calcifications are variably prominent. IHC is not usually required; staining profile is not defining. No clinically useful diagnostic molecular alteration is established. More cellular spindle-cell tumor; KIT/DOG1-positive. Myxoid/cellular spindle-cell proliferation with prominent inflammation; ALK may be positive. Sclerosing mesenteritis Usually broader fibroinflammatory process with fat necrosis and characteristic anatomic distribution. The dense collagen and calcifications may dominate a small biopsy; search for the sparse spindle cells and inflammatory infiltrate. Vascular tumors and malformations of the GI tract and liver Benign / variable Ranges from benign vascular lesions and malformations to malignant vascular neoplasms GI tract and liver; hepatic hemangiomas and vascular malformations are the most common hepatic mesenchymal lesions. GI lesions may present with bleeding or anemia; hepatic lesions are often incidental. Clinical context, multiplicity, syndromic associations, and imaging are important. Classify as a vascular neoplasm versus a vascular malformation using architecture and endothelial proliferation. Assess endothelial atypia, mitotic activity, and destructive growth. Use GLUT1 to support infantile hemangioma in the appropriate setting. Vascular lesions span capillary, cavernous, and other architectural patterns; malformations show abnormal vascular channels without a true proliferative neoplasm. Infantile hemangioma shows a characteristic proliferative vascular lesion with low-to-absent atypia. Evaluate for infiltrative growth, endothelial multilayering, cytologic atypia, and mitotic activity when malignancy is a concern. CD31, ERG, and CD34 support endothelial differentiation. GLUT1 expression supports infantile hemangioma. D2-40 may highlight lymphatic differentiation. Selected vascular anomalies harbor pathway alterations; molecular testing is reserved for cases in which classification or management may change. Epithelioid hemangioendothelioma Epithelioid endothelial cells in cords/nests within myxohyaline stroma; CAMTA1 or fusion testing can support. Angiosarcoma Marked atypia, destructive infiltrative growth, mitoses, and complex architecture. Metastatic vascular tumor Correlate with clinical history and exclude an extrahepatic primary. Do not equate vascular channel complexity with malignancy; assess endothelial cytology and proliferative activity. The supplied chapter distinguishes vascular tumors and malformations by morphology and selected ancillary tests. Malignant Malignant vascular neoplasm with variable clinical course May arise in liver and other organs; clinical presentation depends on site and extent. May be incidental or present with pain, mass effect, or multifocal disease. Clinical and radiologic correlation is essential, particularly for hepatic lesions. Cords or nests of epithelioid cells with intracytoplasmic vacuoles. Myxohyaline or fibrous stroma. Expression of endothelial markers such as ERG, CD31, or CD34. Epithelioid cells form cords, strands, and nests in a myxohyaline stroma. Intracytoplasmic vacuoles may contain erythrocytes and mimic signet-ring cells. Mild-to-moderate atypia is typical; assess mitoses and necrosis. CD31, ERG, CD34, and D2-40 support endothelial differentiation. CAMTA1 is positive in approximately 90% of cases and correlates with the underlying fusion. Keratin may be expressed in a subset and can mimic carcinoma. Most conventional cases harbor WWTR1::CAMTA1 fusion; a smaller subset has YAP1::TFE3 fusion. CAMTA1 IHC or fusion testing is useful in unusual or diagnostically challenging cases. More overtly malignant cytology, destructive vascular channels, and higher mitotic activity. Carcinoma with signet-ring features Epithelial markers may overlap; endothelial markers and characteristic fusion support EHE. Other epithelioid vascular lesions Integrate architecture, cytology, endothelial markers, and molecular findings. Focal keratin expression does not establish carcinoma. Use CAMTA1/fusion testing when morphology and endothelial phenotype are equivocal. Glomus tumor Benign / rarely malignant Usually benign; malignant glomus tumor is rare GI tract, particularly stomach; may occur elsewhere in digestive system. Often presents as a submucosal mass; symptoms may include pain or GI bleeding. Clinical behavior depends on site, size, mitotic activity, and atypical features. Glomus-like morphology with uniform round cells surrounding branching vessels. Smooth muscle differentiation, especially strong SMA expression. Uniform round to oval cells are arranged in nests or cuffs around branching, often dilated vessels. Cytoplasm is pale to eosinophilic; nuclei are generally uniform. Malignant examples show increased mitotic activity, atypia, and/or necrosis. SMA is typically strong and diffuse. Collagen IV and other smooth muscle-associated markers may be supportive. KIT/DOG1 are not expected; use to exclude GIST when needed. No routine diagnostic molecular test is established in the supplied chapter. Usually KIT/DOG1-positive spindle or epithelioid tumor; glomus tumor shows perivascular glomus cells and SMA. PEComa Coexpresses melanocytic markers and smooth muscle markers; glomus tumor lacks melanocytic differentiation. Paraganglioma Zellballen architecture and neuroendocrine markers; glomus tumor is SMA-positive. Recognize the perivascular architecture; avoid classifying a glomus tumor as a generic epithelioid mesenchymal neoplasm. Perivascular epithelioid cell tumor (PEComa) and angiomyolipoma Variable / malignant potential PEComa ranges from benign to malignant; most hepatic angiomyolipomas are benign GI PEComas most often colon, liver, small intestine, and pancreas; hepatic angiomyolipoma predominantly affects middle-aged women. GI lesions may cause abdominal pain or bleeding; hepatic angiomyolipoma is often incidental. Multifocal hepatic and renal lesions may be associated with tuberous sclerosis. PEComa: epithelioid and/or spindle cells with granular eosinophilic-to-clear cytoplasm in nested, trabecular, or sheet-like architecture. Angiomyolipoma: variable admixture of adipocytes, thick-walled vessels, and epithelioid cells. Demonstration of melanocytic and smooth muscle markers is desirable. PEComa cells are arranged in nests, trabeculae, or sheets; sclerosing patterns may show cords in dense collagen. Angiomyolipoma contains variable proportions of lipid-rich cells, conventional perivascular epithelioid cells, and thick-walled vessels. Malignant PEComas may show marked atypia, diffuse pleomorphism, increased mitoses, and necrosis. Melanocytic markers include HMB45, Melan-A, PNL2, MITF, and tyrosinase. Smooth muscle markers include SMA and desmin; expression is variable. Cathepsin K is frequently positive. Hepatocellular markers are negative in hepatic angiomyolipoma; HMB45 is useful in apparent hepatic lipomas. TSC2 biallelic inactivation is common; TSC1 alterations are less frequent and activate mTOR signaling. A minority harbor TFE3 fusions, often involving SFPQ or ASPSCR1. Molecular testing may support classification and identify potential mTOR-pathway therapeutic relevance. May express KIT; PEComa can occasionally be KIT-positive but shows melanocytic and smooth muscle differentiation. Hepatocellular adenoma GS or LFABP patterns alone can mislead; HepPar1 and arginase-1 are negative in angiomyolipoma. Smooth muscle phenotype without melanocytic marker expression. Metastatic melanoma Melanocytic markers overlap; smooth muscle markers and characteristic morphology support PEComa. Hepatic angiomyolipoma can be fat-poor and mimic hepatocellular lesions. Histologic atypia alone is not a reliable criterion for malignancy in hepatic angiomyolipoma. Mesenchymal hamartoma of the liver Benign; excellent prognosis after complete excision Exclusively hepatic, usually right lobe; approximately 85% present before age 3 years, with slight male predominance in children. Usually presents with abdominal distension or an upper abdominal mass; may be detected prenatally or incidentally. Large lesions in infants may cause respiratory or circulatory compromise. May be associated with Beckwith–Wiedemann syndrome or placental mesenchymal dysplasia. Abundant hypocellular fibromyxoid stroma with bland stellate or spindle cells. Bile duct-like structures surrounded by collagen collars. Numerous blood vessels of variable caliber. Lobulated mass with abundant hypocellular myxoid stroma. Anastomosing, tortuous, linear, or branching bile duct-like structures may be cystically dilated. Thick-walled arterioles and thin-walled ectatic capillaries are abundant. Extramedullary hematopoiesis is present in most cases. Cystic degeneration may occur without an epithelial lining. Spindle cells express vimentin and actin; desmin is focal. Bile duct-like structures express CK7 and CK19. Nuclear β-catenin is absent. Glypican-3 may be expressed and can mimic hepatoblastoma. A subset has chromosome 19q13.4 rearrangements involving the MHLB1 breakpoint and activation of the C19MC microRNA cluster. Molecular findings are supportive in selected cases, not required for routine diagnosis. Mixed epithelial-mesenchymal hepatoblastoma Shows malignant epithelial/hepatocellular or embryonal components; correlate with age, morphology, and immunophenotype. Infantile hepatic hemangioma Predominantly vascular proliferation without characteristic bile duct-like structures and fibromyxoid stroma. Undifferentiated embryonal sarcoma Markedly atypical pleomorphic cells in myxoid stroma, often with PAS-positive hyaline globules. Glypican-3 positivity does not by itself establish hepatoblastoma. Cystic degeneration can obscure the characteristic stromal and ductal components. Calcifying nested stromal-epithelial tumor (CNSET) of the liver Malignant / uncertain behavior Low-grade neoplasm; usually cured by excision, but recurrence and metastasis are reported Usually right hepatic lobe; rare; female predominance, often children, adolescents, and young adults. Often incidental; may present with abdominal pain, palpable mass, nausea, or Cushing syndrome. Frequently large at diagnosis. Nested architecture surrounded by cellular myofibroblastic stroma. Bland, uniform epithelioid and spindle cells. Psammomatous calcifications and/or bone formation. Nuclear WT1 and β-catenin expression and cytokeratin positivity are desirable. Ovoid to irregular nests of epithelioid-to-spindle cells separated by cellular myofibroblastic stroma. Psammomatous calcifications and occasional ossification are characteristic. Tumor cells are usually bland, but mitotic activity can be variable and occasionally high. Bile ductular proliferation may surround tumor nests. Tumor cells express broad-spectrum keratins and usually nuclear WT1. Nuclear and cytoplasmic β-catenin expression is typical. CD56, EMA, PR, NSE, and KIT are variable. Hepatocellular markers, synaptophysin, chromogranin, and desmin are negative; stromal spindle cells express SMA. Activating CTNNB1 alterations, including exon 3 deletions and point mutations, have been identified in tested cases. TERT promoter mutations have also been reported. Hepatoblastoma Usually shows recognizable hepatocellular/embryonal differentiation and lacks the characteristic nested calcifying pattern. Neuroendocrine neoplasm CNSET is typically keratin/WT1/β-catenin-positive and chromogranin/synaptophysin-negative. Metastatic carcinoma Correlate with clinical history; CNSET has characteristic stromal and calcification pattern. Do not interpret keratin positivity as proof of carcinoma. Mitotic activity alone does not define behavior; integrate size, invasion, multifocality, and clinical course. Malignant gastrointestinal neuroectodermal tumor (GNET) Malignant; aggressive with metastatic potential Most often small intestine; also stomach and other GI sites; typically adults. May present with abdominal pain, bleeding, obstruction, or an abdominal mass. Metastases may be present at diagnosis or develop during follow-up. Compatible epithelioid, spindle, or round-cell morphology. S100 and SOX10 positivity. EWSR1 gene rearrangement. Tumor cells are arranged in sheets, nests, or fascicles; clear-to-eosinophilic cytoplasm may be present. Melanin is generally absent, unlike clear cell sarcoma of soft tissue. Osteoclast-like giant cells may occur. S100 and SOX10 are typically positive. Melanocytic markers may be variable; the phenotype is not equivalent to conventional melanoma. Neuroendocrine markers are generally not defining. EWSR1 rearrangement is essential; common partners include ATF1 or CREB1. Molecular confirmation is important to distinguish GNET from other S100/SOX10-positive tumors. Clear cell sarcoma of soft tissue / GI clear cell sarcoma Overlapping EWSR1::ATF1/CREB1 and S100/SOX10 phenotype; GNET is a primary GI tumor and usually lacks melanocytic differentiation. Melanoma Clinical history and melanocytic marker profile; GNET often lacks convincing melanocytic differentiation. MPNST Often associated with a nerve or NF1; morphology and molecular profile differ. Do not diagnose melanoma solely from S100/SOX10 positivity. Exclude metastatic clear cell sarcoma and melanoma using clinical history and molecular context. Undifferentiated embryonal sarcoma of the liver High-grade malignant sarcoma Predominantly children, usually 6–10 years; rare adult cases; typically a large hepatic mass. Often presents with abdominal mass, pain, fever, or constitutional symptoms. May be cystic or solid on imaging and can mimic a benign cystic lesion. Spindled, stellate, and pleomorphic giant cells loosely arranged in myxoid stroma. No convincing specific line of differentiation. Exclude other defined hepatic sarcomas and sarcomatoid malignancies. Loose myxoid stroma contains pleomorphic spindle and stellate cells, bizarre giant cells, and rhabdoid forms. Characteristic PAS-positive, diastase-resistant hyaline globules may be present. Mitotic activity and necrosis are often prominent. No single lineage-specific IHC profile is defining. Vimentin is commonly expressed; keratin and other markers may be variable. Complex genomic alterations are described; no single defining recurrent molecular alteration is established in the supplied chapter. Mesenchymal hamartoma Bland hypocellular fibromyxoid stroma with bile duct-like structures and no marked pleomorphism. Demonstrable epithelial/hepatocellular differentiation. Rhabdomyosarcoma / other sarcoma Use morphology and lineage-specific IHC/molecular testing to exclude defined entities. Large cystic appearance does not imply benignity. Sample extensively to identify diagnostic pleomorphic areas and exclude a more specific sarcoma. GLI1-altered neoplasms (including gastroblastoma) Malignant / variable Behavior varies by subtype; some cases metastasize Gastroblastoma is gastric and typically affects adolescents or young adults; other GLI1-altered tumors occur in soft tissue and viscera. Gastroblastoma presents as a gastric mass, often in younger patients. Clinical behavior is variable and long-term data are limited. For gastroblastoma: gastric origin and biphasic epithelial and spindle-cell histology. Cytokeratin expression in the epithelial component. Demonstration of GLI1 fusion is desirable. Gastroblastoma shows a biphasic arrangement of epithelial and spindle-cell components. Other GLI1-altered neoplasms may show nested, epithelioid, or spindle-cell patterns. Cytokeratins highlight the epithelial component in gastroblastoma. GLI1 nuclear expression may support the diagnosis but is not a substitute for molecular confirmation. GLI1 fusions or amplification define the molecular group; fusion partners vary by tumor type. Molecular testing is particularly useful for confirming gastroblastoma and separating it from other biphasic gastric tumors. Usually KIT/DOG1-positive and lacks the characteristic biphasic epithelial/spindle architecture. Synovial sarcoma May be biphasic and keratin-positive; SS18::SSX fusion establishes synovial sarcoma. Carcinoma with sarcomatoid change Look for a conventional carcinoma component and broader epithelial differentiation. Do not classify all GLI1-altered neoplasms as gastroblastoma; site and morphology matter. NUT-rearranged sarcoma Rare; reported in deep soft tissue and visceral sites, including the digestive system; age range is broad. Usually presents as a rapidly enlarging mass; clinical behavior is aggressive. Monomorphic spindle, epithelioid, and rhabdoid cells in a partially hyalinized background. Evidence of NUTM1 or NUTM2 rearrangement. Monomorphic spindle, epithelioid, or rhabdoid cells are arranged in sheets or fascicles. A partially hyalinized or collagenous background may be present. High-grade cytologic features and mitotic activity are common. NUT immunohistochemistry can support the diagnosis; interpret nuclear staining in morphologic context. Cytokeratin expression may occur and can lead to confusion with carcinoma. NUTM1 or NUTM2 rearrangement is defining; identify the fusion by FISH or sequencing when needed. NUT carcinoma Usually epithelial carcinoma with squamous differentiation; sarcoma shows mesenchymal morphology and defining rearrangement. SS18::SSX fusion; morphology and immunophenotype overlap. Ewing sarcoma CD99/NKX2.2 phenotype and EWSR1::FLI1 or related fusion; molecular testing distinguishes. NUT expression is not interpreted in isolation; confirm the defining rearrangement when the diagnosis is uncertain. Undifferentiated sarcoma of the GI tract Malignant; diagnosis of exclusion Primary GI tract; exclude secondary involvement and extra-GI primary tumor. Usually presents as a mass with pain, bleeding, obstruction, or constitutional symptoms. Diagnosis requires exclusion of metastatic sarcoma and a defined line of differentiation. Spindle, pleomorphic, epithelioid, or round-cell tumor, usually high grade. No evidence of specific cellular differentiation by morphology or immunohistochemistry. No defining molecular alteration or translocation of another well-characterized sarcoma. No tumor outside the GI tract. Highly variable morphology, including spindle, pleomorphic, epithelioid, and round-cell patterns. Often high-grade with brisk mitotic activity and necrosis. Extensive sampling is required to exclude a differentiated component. No specific lineage-specific immunophenotype is present. Use a broad, morphology-directed panel to exclude epithelial, melanocytic, myogenic, vascular, neural, and hematolymphoid differentiation. No defining molecular alteration is identified; molecular testing is used to exclude specific sarcoma entities. KIT/DOG1 and/or characteristic KIT/PDGFRA/SDH molecular findings. Leiomyosarcoma Smooth muscle morphology and SMA, desmin, and h-caldesmon expression. Endothelial morphology and ERG/CD31 expression. GNET / clear cell sarcoma S100/SOX10 expression and EWSR1 rearrangement. Metastatic sarcoma Clinical/radiologic exclusion of an extra-GI primary is mandatory. Undifferentiated sarcoma is a diagnosis of exclusion, not a default label for an unclassified biopsy. Exclude metastatic disease and molecularly defined sarcomas before signing out. All benign intermediate malignant PathologyGPS / Digestive System / Mesenchymal Tumors Mesenchymal Tumors of the Digestive System A morphology-first reference integrating clinical setting, architecture, immunophenotype, and defining molecular alterations. Core diagnostic principle Establish lineage before assigning behavior. Integrate site, morphology, targeted IHC, and molecular findings. For GIST, use site, size, mitotic count, and rupture for risk assessment. Diagnostic GPS: from a digestive-system mass to classification Define the setting Confirm the organ of origin, mural versus extramural location, depth, size, multiplicity, and clinical history. Recognize the pattern Spindle cell, epithelioid, round cell, myxoid, inflammatory, vascular, perivascular, or mixed epithelial–mesenchymal. Assess behavior Evaluate infiltrative growth, atypia, mitotic activity, necrosis, vascular invasion, and metastasis; apply entity-specific criteria. Select targeted IHC KIT/DOG1 for GIST; SDHB for SDH-deficient GIST; ALK/ROS1 for IMT; ERG/CD31 for vascular tumors; melanocytic and muscle markers for PEComa. Confirm molecularly Use defining alterations when relevant: KIT/PDGFRA, ALK/ROS1, WWTR1::CAMTA1, EWSR1, GLI1, or NUTM rearrangements. Behavior categories are not interchangeable with grade Benign: usually cured by local excision; recurrence is uncommon or related to incomplete removal. Intermediate, locally aggressive: may infiltrate or recur locally but has little or no metastatic potential. Intermediate, rarely metastasizing: has a low but definite metastatic risk; inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor is an example. Malignant: has destructive growth and metastatic potential. GIST requires a separate risk-stratification approach. High-yield diagnostic IHC and molecular tests KIT, DOG1; KIT / PDGFRA mutation testing SDH-deficient GIST Loss of SDHB; assess SDHA ALK / ROS1; kinase fusion testing when indicated CD34; PDGFRA mutation in selected cases ERG, CD31, CAMTA1; WWTR1::CAMTA1 PEComa / angiomyolipoma HMB45, Melan-A, SMA, desmin; TSC1/TSC2 or TFE3 GNET S100, SOX10; EWSR1 rearrangement NUT IHC; NUTM1/NUTM2 rearrangement Entity reference Clinical profile and diagnostic criteria Search by entity, site, morphology, marker, or gene. e.g. DOG1, SDHB, ALK, CAMTA1, EWSR1... bg-teal-700 text-white border border-slate-300 bg-white text-slate-600 Collapse View diagnostic profile − + Clinical Profile Essential Diagnostic Criteria Histopathology Immunophenotype Molecular Pathology Differential Diagnosis Diagnostic Pitfalls No entities match this search. Practical reporting checklist Document the site Specify organ, exact segment, mural layer, and whether the lesion is primary or secondary. Sample heterogeneity Target viable solid areas, necrosis, hemorrhage, and interfaces; do not rely on a limited biopsy alone. Use a focused panel Select markers to establish lineage and distinguish close mimics; avoid indiscriminate broad panels. State the basis for behavior Apply entity-specific criteria, and include size, mitotic activity, necrosis, invasion, margins, and molecular results as appropriate. This reference summarizes the supplied WHO chapter excerpt. Ancillary testing should be selected in the context of morphology, anatomic site, and clinical findings.

title: Neuroendocrine Neoplasms
content: use client Esophageal neuroendocrine neoplasms Distal esophagus predominates; NETs favor the distal esophagus, whereas NECs may occur at any level. Exceedingly rare; poorly differentiated NECs and MiNENs account for most reported esophageal NENs. NECs and MiNENs show a marked male predominance and usually occur in the sixth to seventh decades. Small NETs are often incidental or cause mild symptoms; larger NECs/MiNENs commonly cause dysphagia, pain, weight loss, weakness, or melena. NETs are usually small (<20 mm), polypoid or nodular submucosal masses; NECs/MiNENs are often bulky, infiltrative, and ulcerated. NET: well-differentiated epithelial neuroendocrine morphology with confirmatory neuroendocrine marker expression; report Ki-67 index and/or mitotic count. NEC: small-cell or large-cell poorly differentiated carcinoma with neuroendocrine marker expression and high proliferative activity. MiNEN: two morphologically distinct components, each usually comprising at least 30% of the tumor; confirm neuroendocrine differentiation in the NEN component. Amphicrine-like carcinoma (ALC): neuroendocrine morphology in at least 30% of tumor cells, confirmed by at least two neuroendocrine markers, without geographically distinct neuroendocrine and non-neuroendocrine zones. NET: nested/insular or trabecular architecture; medium-sized cells with granular cytoplasm, round nuclei, and finely stippled chromatin. NEC: solid sheets, rosettes, or palisades; frequent, often extensive necrosis and brisk mitotic activity. Small-cell NEC: small-to-medium cells, scant cytoplasm, high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio, nuclear molding, and finely dispersed chromatin. Large-cell NEC: larger cells with more abundant basophilic cytoplasm, vesicular/ovoid nuclei, and conspicuous nucleoli. MiNEN: usually NEC admixed with squamous cell carcinoma or adenocarcinoma. ALC: neuroendocrine and non-neuroendocrine differentiation is evenly distributed or present in the same cells, rather than forming separate zones. Confirm epithelial neuroendocrine differentiation with at least two of chromogranin A, synaptophysin, and INSM1. Synaptophysin is sensitive but less specific; chromogranin A is more specific but may be weak or absent in high-grade tumors; INSM1 often provides a useful balance. TTF1 may be positive in esophageal NEC and does not establish pulmonary origin. Basaloid squamous cell carcinoma typically expresses p40, p63, and CK5/6; p63 can occasionally be positive in NEC. Esophageal NEC commonly shows inactivating TP53 and RB1 alterations. NOTCH1, FAT1, FBXW7, PDE3A, PTPRM, and CBLN2 alterations have also been reported; these are not routine diagnostic tests. Basaloid squamous cell carcinoma Look for squamous differentiation and p40/CK5/6 expression; neuroendocrine marker expression alone is insufficient. SMARCA4-deficient undifferentiated carcinoma May mimic NEC and show synaptophysin, but chromogranin A and INSM1 are often absent. Pulmonary NEC metastatic to esophagus TTF1 is not reliable for assigning the primary site; integrate clinical and radiologic findings. Do not classify a carcinoma as ALC based only on scattered neuroendocrine-marker-positive cells. A small biopsy may not represent both components of a MiNEN or establish the evenly intermixed pattern of ALC. Gastric neuroendocrine neoplasms Stomach; gastric NETs include distinct clinicopathologic types associated with different backgrounds. Gastric NETs are commonly detected during endoscopy; clinical context and background mucosa are essential for classification. Type 1 NETs arise with chronic atrophic gastritis and hypergastrinemia and are often multifocal and small. Type 2 NETs occur in the setting of gastrinoma/Zollinger–Ellison syndrome, often with MEN1, and may be multifocal. Type 3 NETs are sporadic, usually solitary, and more often larger and invasive. Gastric NEC and MiNEN generally present as aggressive masses with symptoms related to local invasion or metastasis. Establish well-differentiated NET versus poorly differentiated NEC by morphology, not by Ki-67 alone. For gastric NET, document tumor size, depth, multiplicity, lymphovascular invasion, margins, and background mucosal pathology. Classify gastric NET in the clinical context of autoimmune atrophic gastritis, gastrinoma/MEN1, or sporadic disease. MiNEN requires morphologically distinct neuroendocrine and non-neuroendocrine components, generally each at least 30%. Well-differentiated NETs show organoid nests, trabeculae, or ribbons of uniform cells with granular cytoplasm and stippled chromatin. Type 1 and type 2 NETs are often multifocal and arise in a background of enterochromaffin-like cell hyperplasia/dysplasia. Type 3 NETs are more often solitary and may show deeper invasion, larger size, and higher grade. NEC shows small-cell or large-cell morphology, sheet-like growth, marked atypia, brisk mitoses, and often extensive necrosis. MiNEN shows distinct neuroendocrine and non-neuroendocrine components; ALC lacks separate morphologic zones. Use chromogranin A, synaptophysin, and INSM1 to confirm neuroendocrine differentiation; at least two positive markers are preferred. Gastrin and other hormone stains may help in selected functional or syndromic settings. SSTR2 expression may support a well-differentiated NET phenotype and may have theranostic relevance. For NEC versus NET G3, abnormal p53 and loss of RB1 support NEC; retain morphology as the primary classifier. For NEC, TP53 and RB1 pathway alterations are characteristic in the broader NEC class; use p53/RB1 IHC as supportive surrogates rather than a stand-alone classifier. MEN1-associated context is relevant to type 2 gastric NET; routine tumor molecular testing is not required for typical gastric NET classification. Gastric adenocarcinoma with focal neuroendocrine marker expression Requires convincing neuroendocrine morphology; isolated marker-positive cells do not establish NEN. Gastric glomus tumor Usually perivascular architecture and smooth-muscle marker expression rather than epithelial neuroendocrine phenotype. Paraganglioma Typically keratin-negative and shows a sustentacular-cell pattern; see the separate paraganglioma profile. Do not assign gastric NET type from morphology alone; correlate with background mucosa, gastrin status, and clinical setting. Ki-67 grades NETs but does not distinguish well-differentiated NET G3 from NEC. Duodenal and ampullary neuroendocrine neoplasms Duodenum, including periampullary region and ampulla of Vater. Duodenal NETs may be incidental or present with bleeding, abdominal symptoms, or hormone-related syndromes. Gastrin-producing duodenal NETs may occur in the setting of Zollinger–Ellison syndrome and MEN1. Periampullary tumors may cause biliary or pancreatic duct obstruction. NEC and MiNEN are uncommon and generally present as larger, more aggressive lesions. Confirm epithelial neuroendocrine differentiation and distinguish well-differentiated NET from poorly differentiated NEC morphologically. Document exact site, size, depth, ampullary involvement, lymphovascular invasion, and regional nodal status. For MiNEN, identify two distinct morphologic components and estimate their proportions. NETs show nested, trabecular, or gland-like organoid growth with uniform cells and stippled chromatin. Gastrin-producing tumors may show glandular/tubular architecture and may be associated with multifocality in MEN1. Gangliocytic/neuromatous elements should prompt consideration of composite gangliocytoma/neuroma and neuroendocrine tumor (CoGNET) in the periampullary duodenum. NEC shows poorly differentiated small-cell or large-cell morphology, brisk mitoses, and necrosis. MiNEN has separate neuroendocrine and non-neuroendocrine components. Chromogranin A, synaptophysin, and INSM1 support neuroendocrine differentiation; use at least two markers. Gastrin immunohistochemistry can support a gastrin-producing phenotype in the appropriate clinical setting. SSTR2 may be useful for characterization and theranostic assessment. MEN1 context is relevant in selected duodenal gastrinomas; molecular testing is not routinely required for diagnosis. CoGNET Triphasic composition with neuroendocrine, ganglion-like, and Schwannian/neuromatous components; classically periampullary. Keratin-negative neuroendocrine neoplasm with sustentacular cells. Conventional adenocarcinoma Requires gland-forming carcinoma morphology; focal neuroendocrine marker staining alone is insufficient. Do not overlook CoGNET in a periampullary lesion with mixed cell populations. Small biopsies may undersample a mixed neoplasm. Jejunal and ileal neuroendocrine neoplasms Small intestine, especially ileum; multifocal primary tumors may occur. Small intestinal NETs may be clinically silent or present with abdominal pain, obstruction, or mesenteric fibrosis. Carcinoid syndrome is more likely with hepatic metastases because vasoactive products can bypass hepatic metabolism. Multifocality is an important clinical and grossing consideration, particularly for ileal tumors. Identify a well-differentiated epithelial NET and document multifocality, size, depth, mesenteric involvement, and nodal/metastatic disease. Assess lymphovascular and perineural invasion and the relationship to mesenteric fibrosis. Grade NET using mitotic count and Ki-67 index; use the higher grade when results are discordant. NETs typically show nested, trabecular, or gyriform organoid architecture with uniform cells and finely stippled chromatin. Desmoplastic stromal reaction may accompany infiltrative ileal tumors and contribute to mesenteric retraction. NEC is composed of poorly differentiated small or large cells with sheet-like growth, brisk mitoses, and necrosis. MiNEN requires distinct neuroendocrine and non-neuroendocrine morphologic components. Confirm neuroendocrine differentiation with at least two of chromogranin A, synaptophysin, and INSM1. Serotonin may be expressed by many intestinal NETs; hormone stains are selected according to morphology and clinical syndrome. SSTR2 expression is useful in selected diagnostic and theranostic settings. No routine site-specific molecular test is required for conventional small intestinal NET diagnosis. For NEC, abnormal p53 and loss of RB1 may support poorly differentiated NEC over NET G3. Metastatic pancreatic NET Morphology overlaps; correlate with imaging and clinical history, and use site-directed markers only when indicated. Typically keratin-negative with sustentacular cells. GIST Spindle/epithelioid mesenchymal morphology and KIT/DOG1 expression rather than epithelial neuroendocrine differentiation. Carefully examine the entire small bowel when resection is available because multiple primaries may be present. Do not equate high Ki-67 with NEC without poorly differentiated morphology. Appendiceal neuroendocrine neoplasms Vermiform appendix, often distal tip. Usually discovered incidentally in appendectomy specimens, often in younger patients. Most appendiceal NETs are small and located at the tip; larger lesions and base involvement require careful assessment. NEC and MiNEN are rare and behave more aggressively than conventional appendiceal NET. Report tumor size, location, depth of invasion, mesoappendiceal extension, lymphovascular invasion, perineural invasion, margins, and grade. Distinguish conventional well-differentiated NET from goblet cell adenocarcinoma, which belongs to the amphicrine-like carcinoma spectrum but is classified as a distinct appendiceal adenocarcinoma. Use morphology to distinguish NET from NEC; Ki-67 alone is not sufficient. Conventional NET shows nests, trabeculae, or ribbons of uniform cells with granular cytoplasm and stippled chromatin. NEC shows poorly differentiated small-cell or large-cell morphology, extensive atypia, brisk mitoses, and necrosis. MiNEN contains separate neuroendocrine and non-neuroendocrine components. Goblet cell adenocarcinoma shows infiltrative clusters/tubules of mucin-rich goblet-like cells and is not simply a conventional NET with mucin. Chromogranin A, synaptophysin, and INSM1 confirm neuroendocrine differentiation; at least two positive markers are preferred. SSTR2 and selected hormone markers may be useful in conventional NETs. No clinically useful routine molecular test is established for conventional appendiceal NET in the supplied source. Goblet cell adenocarcinoma Infiltrative goblet-cell morphology with mucin production; classify as adenocarcinoma rather than conventional appendiceal NET. Appendiceal adenocarcinoma Glandular or mucinous carcinoma morphology without the classic well-differentiated NET pattern. NEC Poorly differentiated cytology, sheet-like growth, necrosis, and brisk mitotic activity. Do not use the term carcinoid. Do not conflate goblet cell adenocarcinoma with MiNEN solely because it may show neuroendocrine differentiation. Colorectal neuroendocrine neoplasms Colon and rectum; rectal NETs are a common site-specific presentation. Rectal NETs are often small and detected incidentally or during screening endoscopy. Colonic NETs are less common and may present with nonspecific symptoms. Colorectal NEC and MiNEN more often present as large masses with advanced disease or metastases. Classify as well-differentiated NET, poorly differentiated NEC, MiNEN, or ALC according to morphology and confirmatory immunohistochemistry. For rectal NET, document size, depth, grade, lymphovascular invasion, and margin status. For MiNEN, both morphologically distinct components should generally comprise at least 30% of the tumor. NET shows organoid nests, trabeculae, or ribbons of monotonous cells with granular cytoplasm and stippled chromatin. NEC shows small-cell or large-cell morphology, sheet-like growth, marked atypia, brisk mitotic activity, and often necrosis. MiNEN contains distinct neuroendocrine and non-neuroendocrine components. ALC shows evenly intermixed or same-cell neuroendocrine and non-neuroendocrine differentiation without separate morphologic zones. At least two of chromogranin A, synaptophysin, and INSM1 should support neuroendocrine differentiation. SSTR2 may be expressed in well-differentiated NETs and may be useful for theranostic assessment. Abnormal p53 and loss of RB1 support NEC in the appropriate morphologic setting. For NEC, TP53/RB1 pathway abnormalities are characteristic of the broader NEC class; they are supportive rather than required site-specific tests. Poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma Neuroendocrine morphology and convincing expression of at least two neuroendocrine markers are required. Squamous markers such as p40 and CK5/6 support squamous differentiation. Metastatic NEN Correlate with clinical history and imaging; morphology and common neuroendocrine markers do not establish the primary site. Do not diagnose ALC from focal neuroendocrine marker expression without corresponding morphology. Ki-67 does not separate NET G3 from NEC. Anal neuroendocrine neoplasms Anal canal; tumors may arise at any level. Rare; clinical presentation is often related to local mass effect, bleeding, or advanced disease. Anal NEC may present as an irregular mass with surface depressions or ulceration. Poorly differentiated tumors are often clinically aggressive. Confirm epithelial neuroendocrine differentiation with morphology and at least two neuroendocrine markers. Distinguish NET, NEC, MiNEN, and ALC using the same morphologic criteria applied elsewhere in the digestive tract. For MiNEN, document both components and their approximate proportions. NET shows well-differentiated organoid nests or trabeculae of uniform cells with stippled chromatin. ALC has intermixed neuroendocrine and non-neuroendocrine differentiation without distinct zones. Use at least two of chromogranin A, synaptophysin, and INSM1 to establish neuroendocrine differentiation. p40 and CK5/6 help identify squamous differentiation in the differential diagnosis. Abnormal p53 and loss of RB1 may support NEC. No clinically relevant routine diagnostic molecular test is established for anal NEN in the supplied source. Usually expresses squamous markers, including p40 and CK5/6. Anal adenocarcinoma Gland-forming morphology and mucin production identify the non-neuroendocrine component. Metastatic NEC Clinical and radiologic correlation is required to establish primary site. Neuroendocrine marker expression without neuroendocrine morphology is insufficient for diagnosis. Do not infer primary anal origin from immunophenotype alone. Paraganglioma of the digestive system Extra-adrenal paraganglia in the digestive region, including the periampullary/duodenal region and other abdominal sites. Non-epithelial (neuronal-lineage) NEN; may be functional or nonfunctional. Clinical presentation depends on catecholamine secretion, location, and mass effect. Genetic predisposition is the principal recognized risk factor; evaluate personal/family history and syndromic context. Neuroendocrine neoplasm with characteristic morphology and absence of cytokeratin expression. Demonstrate sustentacular cells around tumor cell nests when present. Assess for metastatic disease; metastatic behavior is established by tumor at sites where paraganglionic tissue is normally absent. Nested (zellballen) architecture with chief cells separated by delicate vascular septa. Chief cells have granular cytoplasm and round nuclei with stippled chromatin. Sustentacular cells outline nests; vascularity is often prominent. Chief cells express neuroendocrine markers such as chromogranin A and synaptophysin. Cytokeratins are negative, helping distinguish paraganglioma from epithelial NET/NEC. S100 and SOX10 highlight sustentacular cells. Germline susceptibility alterations, particularly in SDHx genes and other paraganglioma-predisposition genes, are clinically important; genetic evaluation is recommended in the appropriate setting. Epithelial NET Usually cytokeratin-positive; paraganglioma is typically keratin-negative. Contains ganglion-like and Schwannian/neuromatous components in addition to neuroendocrine cells. Mesenchymal morphology and KIT/DOG1 expression rather than a keratin-negative zellballen neuroendocrine tumor. Do not use the obsolete term extra-adrenal pheochromocytoma. A keratin-negative neuroendocrine tumor should prompt consideration of paraganglioma. Composite gangliocytoma/neuroma and neuroendocrine tumor (CoGNET) Predominantly periampullary duodenum. Uncommon neoplasm, classically arising in the periampullary region of the duodenum. May present with abdominal pain, gastrointestinal bleeding, jaundice, or symptoms related to local obstruction. Recognize a composite neoplasm containing neuroendocrine, ganglion-like, and Schwannian/neuromatous components. Periampullary duodenal location is a desirable supporting feature. Triphasic composition includes epithelioid neuroendocrine cells, ganglion-like cells, and spindle-cell Schwannian/neuromatous elements. The three components may be variably represented; adequate sampling is important. Neuroendocrine component expresses synaptophysin and chromogranin A. Ganglion-like and Schwannian components show neural marker expression, including S100/SOX10 in Schwannian elements. Lacks the characteristic triphasic mixture of neuroendocrine, ganglion-like, and neuromatous components. Duodenal NET Pure NET lacks the ganglion-like and Schwannian/neuromatous components. Ganglioneuroma Lacks a distinct epithelial neuroendocrine tumor component. Avoid the historical terms gangliocytic paraganglioma and duodenal ganglioneuroma as substitutes for the current entity name. Hepatic neuroendocrine neoplasms Liver; primary hepatic NENs are exceptionally uncommon. A hepatic NEN should be regarded as metastatic until a primary extrahepatic site has been excluded. Presentation is usually related to liver mass effect or metastatic disease. Clinical and imaging workup is essential because morphology and immunophenotype may not distinguish primary from metastatic NEN. Establish epithelial NET or NEC by morphology and neuroendocrine immunophenotype. Before diagnosing a primary hepatic NEN, exclude an extrahepatic primary through clinical, radiologic, and endoscopic assessment. Classify any mixed tumor using the criteria for MiNEN or ALC. NET shows well-differentiated organoid nests, trabeculae, or ribbons of uniform cells with stippled chromatin. NEC shows poorly differentiated small-cell or large-cell morphology, brisk mitoses, and often extensive necrosis. TTF1, CDX2, ISL1, and other site-associated markers may be helpful in selected cases but do not replace clinical exclusion of another primary. Metastatic gastrointestinal or pancreatic NET Most important consideration; exclude an extrahepatic primary clinically and radiologically. Hepatocellular carcinoma Hepatocellular morphology and hepatocellular markers support HCC rather than NEN. Cholangiocarcinoma Gland-forming biliary carcinoma lacks the defining well-differentiated neuroendocrine morphology. Do not diagnose primary hepatic NET solely because the liver contains a dominant or solitary mass. No routine diagnostic molecular test is established in the supplied source. Gallbladder and extrahepatic bile duct neuroendocrine neoplasms Gallbladder and extrahepatic biliary tree. Very rare tumors; clinical presentation is commonly nonspecific or related to biliary obstruction. Gallbladder tumors may be associated with abdominal pain or jaundice; extrahepatic bile duct tumors may present with obstructive jaundice. NEC and MiNEN are more commonly encountered than well-differentiated NET in reported biliary NEN series. Confirm epithelial neuroendocrine differentiation and classify as NET, NEC, MiNEN, or ALC. For MiNEN, identify two morphologically distinct components and estimate their proportions. Assess depth of invasion, margins, lymphovascular invasion, and regional nodes in resection specimens. NET shows nested/trabecular organoid growth with uniform cells and stippled chromatin. NEC shows poorly differentiated small-cell or large-cell morphology, marked atypia, brisk mitoses, and necrosis. MiNEN often combines NEC with biliary adenocarcinoma. ALC shows diffuse/intermixed differentiation without separate morphologic components. Use at least two of chromogranin A, synaptophysin, and INSM1 to confirm neuroendocrine differentiation. SSTR2 may support NET characterization; abnormal p53 and loss of RB1 may support NEC. Biliary adenocarcinoma with focal neuroendocrine marker expression Requires neuroendocrine morphology; isolated positive cells do not establish NEN. Correlate with clinical history and imaging to exclude another primary site. Usually keratin-negative, unlike epithelial biliary NEN. The supplied source does not identify a clinically relevant routine molecular test for these site-specific tumors. Nonfunctioning pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor (PanNET) Pancreas; tumors may arise in any region. Most PanNETs are nonfunctioning and present through mass effect, incidental imaging, abdominal pain, or metastatic disease. Larger tumors may cause abdominal pain, weight loss, or biliary/ductal obstruction. PanNETs may occur sporadically or in association with MEN1, VHL, NF1, or tuberous sclerosis complex. Well-differentiated epithelial neuroendocrine morphology with confirmatory neuroendocrine marker expression. Report WHO grade using both Ki-67 index and mitotic count; assign the higher grade if discordant. Report tumor size, extent, vascular/perineural invasion, necrosis, margins, and nodal/metastatic status. Pancreatic neuroendocrine microtumor is a separate designation for very small lesions as defined by the WHO classification. Organoid nests, trabeculae, ribbons, or gyriform structures separated by delicate fibrovascular stroma. Uniform cells with granular eosinophilic cytoplasm and round nuclei showing finely stippled chromatin. Amyloid-like stromal material may be present in some tumors. Well-differentiated G3 PanNET retains well-differentiated morphology despite high proliferation. Synaptophysin, chromogranin A, and INSM1 support neuroendocrine differentiation. PanNETs commonly express cytokeratins and may express pancreatic hormones. DAXX/ATRX loss supports PanNET in the appropriate context and helps distinguish it from PanNEC. MEN1, DAXX, and ATRX alterations are characteristic molecular events in a subset of PanNETs. VHL, NF1, and TSC pathway alterations may occur in syndromic or sporadic cases. DAXX/ATRX immunohistochemistry is a useful surrogate in selected cases; routine sequencing is not required for every typical PanNET. Pancreatic neuroendocrine carcinoma Poorly differentiated morphology, abnormal p53, and RB1 loss favor NEC; DAXX/ATRX loss favors PanNET. Acinar cell carcinoma Acinar architecture and trypsin/chymotrypsin/BCL10 expression; focal neuroendocrine staining may occur. Solid pseudopapillary neoplasm Nuclear beta-catenin and characteristic pseudopapillary morphology; usually lacks diffuse neuroendocrine phenotype. Typically keratin-negative and shows sustentacular cells. Do not use Ki-67 alone to classify a G3 lesion as NET or NEC. Scattered neuroendocrine marker-positive cells in acinar cell carcinoma do not establish MiNEN or ALC. Insulinoma Pancreas; may occur anywhere, often as a small solitary lesion. Functioning PanNET causing inappropriate insulin secretion and hypoglycemia. Symptoms reflect Whipple triad: hypoglycemic symptoms, documented low plasma glucose, and relief after glucose administration. Most are sporadic; a subset is associated with MEN1. Clinical and biochemical evidence of endogenous hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia. Well-differentiated PanNET morphology with neuroendocrine marker expression. Report Ki-67 index and/or mitotic count for grade. Typical well-differentiated PanNET architecture with nests, trabeculae, or ribbons of uniform cells. Cells have granular cytoplasm and round nuclei with finely stippled chromatin. Insulin immunoreactivity is desirable but may be variable; correlate with biochemical findings. SSTR2 expression may be present. No clinically relevant routine diagnostic molecular test is established in the supplied source. Nonfunctioning PanNET Requires clinical/biochemical evidence of insulin excess for functional classification. Islet-cell hyperplasia/nesidioblastosis Diffuse or multifocal beta-cell process rather than a discrete insulin-secreting neoplasm. A negative insulin stain does not independently exclude insulinoma when clinical and biochemical evidence is compelling. Gastrinoma Pancreas and duodenum; duodenal primaries are particularly relevant in MEN1. Gastrin-secreting NET causing Zollinger–Ellison syndrome with gastric acid hypersecretion and recurrent peptic ulcer disease. May present with refractory or multiple ulcers, reflux, diarrhea, and complications of acid hypersecretion. A proportion is associated with MEN1; assess for multifocal disease. Clinical and biochemical evidence of inappropriate hypergastrinemia with acid hypersecretion. Well-differentiated neuroendocrine morphology and confirmatory neuroendocrine markers. Gastrin immunohistochemistry is desirable in selected cases. Well-differentiated NET morphology with nested, trabecular, or gland-like architecture. Duodenal gastrinomas may be small and multifocal; careful sampling is important. Gastrin immunohistochemistry supports the functional phenotype. MEN1 context is clinically relevant in a subset; routine tumor molecular testing is not required for diagnosis. Other functioning PanNET Hormone profile and clinical syndrome distinguish gastrinoma from insulinoma, glucagonoma, VIPoma, and somatostatinoma. Reactive G-cell hyperplasia Interpret gastrin expression in the context of clinical biochemistry and a demonstrable neoplasm. Do not infer gastrinoma solely from gastrin immunoreactivity without the appropriate clinical/biochemical syndrome. VIPoma Pancreas; usually a functioning PanNET. VIP-secreting tumor causing watery diarrhea, hypokalemia, and achlorhydria (WDHA syndrome). May cause dehydration, electrolyte disturbance, and metabolic complications. Most reported tumors are G1 or G2, although G3 tumors occur. Clinical and biochemical evidence of VIP excess. Well-differentiated PanNET morphology and neuroendocrine marker expression. VIP immunohistochemistry may support the diagnosis in selected cases. Well-differentiated PanNET architecture with organoid nests or trabeculae of uniform cells. Grade using Ki-67 index and mitotic count. VIP immunoreactivity may be demonstrated; correlate with serum VIP and clinical syndrome. Other causes of secretory diarrhea Biochemical evidence of elevated VIP and a pancreatic NET establish the functional association. Hormone profile and syndrome distinguish VIPoma from other functional subtypes. A functional diagnosis requires clinical and biochemical evidence; immunoreactivity alone is not sufficient. Glucagonoma Pancreas, often in the body or tail. Glucagon-secreting PanNET associated with glucagonoma syndrome. Characteristic manifestations include necrolytic migratory erythema, diabetes or glucose intolerance, weight loss, anemia, and thromboembolic events. Many patients have metastatic disease at presentation. Clinical and biochemical evidence of glucagon excess. Glucagon immunohistochemistry is supportive. Typical well-differentiated PanNET architecture with nests and trabeculae. Tumor cells are uniform with granular cytoplasm and stippled chromatin. Glucagon immunoreactivity supports the functional phenotype. Clinical syndrome and hormone profile distinguish glucagonoma. Non-neoplastic causes of necrolytic migratory erythema Correlate skin findings with glucagon levels and pancreatic imaging. Glucagon immunoreactivity should be interpreted with the clinical and biochemical findings. Somatostatinoma Pancreas; pancreatic tumors are usually solitary and may be large. Somatostatin-secreting PanNET; classic syndrome includes diabetes, cholelithiasis, steatorrhea/diarrhea, and weight loss. Some tumors are nonfunctioning or present without a complete syndrome. A subset occurs in the setting of NF1 or other syndromic disease. Clinical and laboratory evidence of somatostatin excess. Somatostatin immunohistochemistry and SSTR2 are desirable supporting studies. Well-differentiated neuroendocrine morphology with organoid nests and trabeculae. Cells show granular cytoplasm and round nuclei with finely stippled chromatin. Synaptophysin and INSM1 are usually positive; chromogranin A may be less consistent. Somatostatin immunoreactivity supports the functional subtype. SSTR2 may be positive. DAXX/ATRX assessment may provide prognostic information in selected cases; no routine diagnostic molecular test is established. Hormone profile and syndrome distinguish somatostatinoma. Duodenal somatostatin-producing NET Anatomic site and clinical context distinguish pancreatic from duodenal primary. Not all somatostatin-immunoreactive PanNETs produce a complete clinical syndrome. ACTH-producing pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor Pancreas; reported more often in the tail, followed by head and body. Rare functioning PanNET causing ectopic ACTH-dependent Cushing syndrome. Clinical findings include central obesity, moon facies, violaceous striae, hypertension, insulin resistance/diabetes, and hypokalemia. Reported cases show a female predominance; metastatic disease is common at diagnosis or during follow-up. Clinical evidence of Cushing syndrome with biochemical evidence of ACTH-dependent hypercortisolism. ACTH immunohistochemistry is desirable but may be negative in the primary tumor in some cases. Classic well-differentiated PanNET morphology with nested or trabecular architecture. Most reported tumors are G2, although grade is assigned by the standard PanNET criteria. ACTH and related pro-opiomelanocortin peptides may be expressed. EWSR1::BEND2 fusion has been reported in pancreatic ACTH-secreting NETs; this is a potentially useful molecular association, not a routine required test. Other causes of Cushing syndrome Establish ACTH dependence and localize the source clinically and radiologically. Requires clinical and biochemical evidence of ACTH excess for functional classification. ACTH staining may be absent in the primary tumor despite a convincing clinical syndrome; expression may be detected in recurrence or metastasis. Serotonin-producing pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor Pancreas; no consistent site predilection. Extremely rare; functioning tumors may cause carcinoid syndrome. Carcinoid syndrome usually occurs in the presence of liver metastases, although exceptions are reported. Nonfunctioning serotonin-immunoreactive tumors may behave indolently. For a functioning tumor, document clinical and biochemical evidence of serotonin excess/carcinoid syndrome. Serotonin immunohistochemistry is supportive; SSTR2 is desirable. Classic well-differentiated PanNET architecture with nested, trabecular, or gland-like structures. Tumor cells resemble gastric-type enterochromaffin cells; duct-centered growth may occur in selected non-syndromic cases. Serotonin immunoreactivity supports the subtype. Metastatic intestinal NET Clinical history and imaging are required to exclude an extra-pancreatic primary. Hormone profile and clinical syndrome distinguish serotonin-producing tumors. Do not use the term pancreatic carcinoid. Serotonin immunoreactivity alone does not establish a functioning tumor. Pancreatic neuroendocrine carcinoma (PanNEC) Pancreas, most often the head. Uncommon, high-grade malignancy; most patients are middle-aged or older adults. May present with back/abdominal pain, jaundice, weight loss, or nonspecific symptoms similar to pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma. Advanced stage at presentation is common and prognosis is poor. Poorly differentiated epithelial neuroendocrine carcinoma, small-cell or large-cell type. Sheet-like or trabecular growth with marked cytologic atypia and brisk mitotic activity. Confirm neuroendocrine differentiation with at least two markers; report Ki-67 index and mitotic count. Use morphology to distinguish PanNEC from well-differentiated PanNET G3. Small-cell type: sheets of small cells with scant cytoplasm, high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio, nuclear molding, and finely granular chromatin. Large-cell type: larger cells with more abundant cytoplasm, vesicular nuclei, and conspicuous nucleoli. Extensive necrosis and brisk mitotic activity are common. PanNEC may coexist with a non-neuroendocrine carcinoma component. Cytokeratin expression supports epithelial lineage. Synaptophysin and INSM1 are commonly positive; chromogranin A may be variable. Abnormal p53 and complete loss of RB1 are common and support NEC. SSTR2 is often reduced or absent; DAXX/ATRX loss favors PanNET in the differential. TP53 and RB1 alterations are characteristic; KRAS, BRAF, APC, and SMAD4 alterations may also occur. PanNEC generally lacks the MEN1, DAXX, and ATRX alterations typical of PanNET. p53/RB1 immunohistochemistry is a practical surrogate in the appropriate morphologic context. PanNET G3 Retains well-differentiated morphology; DAXX/ATRX loss supports PanNET, whereas abnormal p53/RB1 loss supports NEC. Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma Gland formation/desmoplasia and ductal phenotype; focal neuroendocrine-marker staining alone is insufficient. Acinar differentiation and trypsin/chymotrypsin/BCL10 expression; scattered neuroendocrine-positive cells may occur. G3 is a grade, not a synonym for NEC. Do not classify a tumor as NEC based solely on a high Ki-67 index or necrosis. Pancreatic mixed neuroendocrine–non-neuroendocrine neoplasm (MiNEN) Pancreas; may arise anywhere, with ductal adenocarcinoma–NEC combinations often in the head. Very rare; symptoms commonly reflect tumor growth or metastasis, including abdominal pain, jaundice, weight loss, nausea, vomiting, and anemia. Mixed ductal adenocarcinoma–NEC tumors often behave aggressively. Mixed acinar carcinoma–NENs generally behave similarly to acinar cell carcinoma. Two morphologically distinct neuroendocrine and non-neuroendocrine components must be present. Each component should generally comprise at least 30% of the neoplasm. Confirm neuroendocrine differentiation in the NEN component with at least two neuroendocrine markers. Grade the NET component or report the Ki-67 index of the NEC component; grade the non-neuroendocrine component separately. Common combinations include ductal adenocarcinoma with NEC, ductal adenocarcinoma with NET, and acinar cell carcinoma with NEN. The ductal component resembles conventional pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma with mucin production and infiltrative glands. The acinar component retains acinar morphology and enzyme expression. The neuroendocrine component shows either well-differentiated NET or poorly differentiated NEC morphology. Use neuroendocrine markers to confirm the NEN component. Use component-directed markers to establish ductal or acinar differentiation; acinar carcinomas may show scattered neuroendocrine-positive cells without meeting MiNEN criteria. Limited molecular data are available; KRAS mutations and TP53 pathway abnormalities have been reported in mixed ductal adenocarcinoma–NEC. No routine molecular test is required for MiNEN classification. Amphicrine-like carcinoma Neuroendocrine and non-neuroendocrine differentiation is intermixed without distinct morphologic zones. Acinar cell carcinoma with focal neuroendocrine staining Scattered positive cells or small clusters do not establish a morphologically distinct second component. PanNEC Pure NEC lacks a qualifying morphologically distinct non-neuroendocrine component. Do not diagnose MiNEN from immunohistochemical co-expression alone; separate morphologic components are required. The 30% threshold is a convention; a minor small-cell NEC component should still be reported because it may affect prognosis. PathologyGPS / Gastrointestinal & Hepatopancreatobiliary / Neuroendocrine Neoplasms Neuroendocrine Neoplasms A morphology-first reference to digestive-system neuroendocrine neoplasms, emphasizing site-specific clinical context, diagnostic criteria, immunophenotype, and clinically useful molecular findings. Core diagnostic rule Classify by morphology first; use immunohistochemistry to confirm lineage. Well-differentiated NET and poorly differentiated NEC are distinct tumor types. Ki-67 grades NET but does not distinguish NET G3 from NEC. Diagnostic GPS: from morphology to classification 1. Establish lineage Identify epithelial versus non-epithelial (neuronal) NEN. Paraganglioma is typically keratin-negative. 2. Confirm morphology Look for organoid nests/trabeculae and stippled chromatin (NET) versus sheets, marked atypia, molding, apoptosis, and necrosis (NEC). 3. Confirm neuroendocrine differentiation Use at least two of chromogranin A, synaptophysin, and INSM1 in the appropriate morphologic setting. 4. Grade and classify For NET, report Ki-67 and mitotic count. Classify mixed tumors as MiNEN or amphicrine-like carcinoma using architecture and distribution. 5. Integrate site and context Correlate with anatomic site, background mucosa, functional syndrome, syndromic history, imaging, and metastatic workup. NET versus NEC: the distinction is morphologic Feature Well-differentiated NET Poorly differentiated NEC Architecture Organoid nests, trabeculae, ribbons Sheets, single infiltrating cells Cytology Relatively uniform; stippled chromatin Marked atypia; molding may occur Cytoplasm Relatively abundant, granular Scant in small-cell NEC; variable in large-cell NEC Necrosis May occur; does not alone establish NEC Common, often extensive Ki-67 G1–G3; G3 may retain well-differentiated morphology Usually very high; NEC is high-grade by definition Supportive IHC DAXX/ATRX loss in selected PanNETs Abnormal p53 and/or RB1 loss NET grading and Ki-67 assessment Grade Mitotic count Ki-67 index G1 <2 per 2 mm² <3% G2 2–20 per 2 mm² 3–20% G3 >20 per 2 mm² >20% Count mitoses in the areas of highest activity and assess Ki-67 in hot spots. Manual counting of at least 500 neoplastic cells remains the reference method. If mitotic count and Ki-67 are discordant, assign the higher grade. Report the actual Ki-67 percentage and number of cells counted whenever possible. Necrosis should be reported separately in digestive NETs; it is not currently part of the grading system. Distinguish true tumor necrosis from infarct-like necrosis. MiNEN versus amphicrine-like carcinoma (ALC) MiNEN Two morphologically distinct components: one neuroendocrine and one non-neuroendocrine. Each component generally accounts for at least 30% of the neoplasm. Confirm the neuroendocrine component with at least two neuroendocrine markers. Report the component types and their approximate proportions; grade each component appropriately. Neuroendocrine and non-neuroendocrine differentiation is evenly intermixed or present in the same cells. At least 30% of tumor cells show morphologic neuroendocrine differentiation, confirmed by at least two markers. There are no geographically distinct zones of divergent differentiation. Name the tumor according to its dominant non-neuroendocrine component (e.g., amphicrine-like adenocarcinoma). A small-cell NEC component should be reported even when it is below 30%, with its estimated proportion, because it may dominate prognosis. Scattered neuroendocrine-marker-positive cells alone do not establish MiNEN or ALC. Practical reporting checklist Specify the primary anatomic site and whether the neoplasm is epithelial or non-epithelial. State the morphologic class: well-differentiated NET, poorly differentiated NEC (small-cell or large-cell), MiNEN, or amphicrine-like carcinoma. For NET, report grade, Ki-67 percentage, number of cells counted, mitotic count per 2 mm², and tumor necrosis status. For MiNEN, name both components and estimate their proportions; report even a minor small-cell NEC component. Document tumor size, depth/invasion, lymphovascular and perineural invasion, margins, nodal status, and distant metastasis as appropriate to the site. For pancreatic lesions, distinguish PanNET G3 from PanNEC using morphology and selected p53, RB1, DAXX, and ATRX immunohistochemistry. For a liver NEN, exclude an extrahepatic primary before diagnosing a primary hepatic neoplasm. For a periampullary duodenal tumor with mixed neural/neuroendocrine elements, consider CoGNET; for keratin-negative NEN, consider paraganglioma. Scope note: Prepared from the supplied WHO digestive-system neuroendocrine neoplasm excerpt. Molecular findings are included only where the source identifies a meaningful diagnostic, classification, or clinical role. Site-specific staging and prognostic details should be interpreted using the applicable current TNM system and complete clinical context.
