title: Pancreatic Lesions
content: use client Simple mucinous cyst Benign / precursor Non-invasive; generally indolent Usually solitary; slight body/tail predilection; predominantly women (mean age ~57 years). Often asymptomatic; may cause abdominal pain or jaundice. Typically a unilocular or paucilocular cyst without main-duct communication. Cystic lesion >10 mm. Flat, predominantly non-papillary gastric-type mucinous epithelium. No ovarian-type stroma. Exclude retention cyst by assessing ductal obstruction and chronic pancreatitis. Usually a single layer of cuboidal-to-columnar gastric-type mucinous epithelium. The lining is predominantly flat with minimal papillary or tufted change. Low-grade dysplasia is typical; focal high-grade dysplasia may show tufting, pseudostratification, and loss of polarity. The fibrotic cyst wall lacks ovarian-type stroma. Background PanIN and periductal fibrosis may be present. CK7 and CK19 are diffusely expressed. MUC5AC and/or MUC6 are usually positive. MUC1 is positive in a subset; CDX2 and MUC2 may be focally positive. ER and PR are negative in the cyst wall. Cyst-fluid KRAS alterations may support a mucinous cyst but are not specific; molecular testing is not clinically relevant in resection specimens. PanIN Microscopic lesion <5 mm; simple mucinous cyst is >10 mm. Gastric-type IPMN Papillary architecture and growth within the ductal system favor IPMN. MCN Requires ovarian-type stroma. Retention cyst Look for ductal stenosis/obstruction, calculi, and obstructive chronic pancreatitis. Correlate morphology with imaging and clinical findings; sample adequately to exclude focal invasion. Serous neoplasm Usually benign; malignancy requires unequivocal distant metastasis Any pancreatic region; body/tail in 50–75%; multifocal disease suggests VHL syndrome. Mean age ~58 years; female predominance (approximately 3:1). About 60% are asymptomatic; larger lesions may cause pain, nausea, vomiting, weight loss, or mass effect. Jaundice is unusual. Neoplasm composed of bland cuboidal cells with clear, glycogen-rich cytoplasm. Cystic, microcystic, macrocystic, or solid architecture may occur. Serous cystadenocarcinoma is diagnosed only with unequivocal distant metastasis beyond the pancreatic/peripancreatic bed. Microcystic tumors show numerous small cysts separated by delicate septa, sometimes with a central fibrous scar. Cysts are lined by a single layer of flat-to-cuboidal cells with clear cytoplasm and small uniform nuclei. PAS-positive, diastase-sensitive cytoplasmic glycogen is characteristic. Macrocystic (oligocystic) lesions may mimic MCN or IPMN. Solid serous adenoma forms tightly packed acini with minute or absent lumina. Cytologic atypia or local invasion alone does not establish malignancy. Tumor cells express inhibin, GLUT1, and MUC6. Neoplastic cells are glycogen-rich; PAS-positive and PAS-D-negative. VHL inactivation / chromosome 3p loss supports serous neoplasia in selected cyst-fluid studies. Germline VHL association is clinically relevant when lesions are multifocal or occur with other syndrome features. MCN has mucinous epithelium and ovarian-type stroma; serous neoplasm has glycogen-rich clear cells. IPMN IPMN communicates with and expands pancreatic ducts; serous neoplasm generally does not. PanNET Solid serous adenoma may mimic PanNET; glycogen, inhibin/GLUT1/MUC6, and neuroendocrine markers help. Metastatic renal cell carcinoma Consider clinical history and renal-lineage markers in clear-cell solid lesions. Pancreatic intraepithelial neoplasia (PanIN) Non-invasive precursor; microscopic Within small pancreatic ducts; often incidental in adult pancreas. Microscopic lesions do not produce symptoms and are generally not detectable by imaging. Prevalence increases with age. Microscopic (<5 mm), non-invasive flat or micropapillary epithelial neoplasm confined to pancreatic ducts. Classify as low-grade or high-grade based on the highest-grade focus. High-grade PanIN shows marked cytologic and architectural atypia without stromal invasion. Low-grade PanIN shows flat or micropapillary mucinous epithelium with mild-to-moderate atypia. High-grade PanIN shows complex papillary/cribriform architecture, nuclear stratification, loss of polarity, and marked atypia. Mucinous cytoplasm is common; mitoses and necrosis may be present in high-grade lesions. No infiltrative glands in desmoplastic stroma should be identified. MUC5AC and other ductal markers may support ductal differentiation but do not independently establish grade or invasion. KRAS alterations are common early events; TP53, CDKN2A, and SMAD4 alterations are enriched in advanced/high-grade PanIN. Molecular testing is not routinely required for diagnosis. Grossly visible, usually >1 cm intraductal mucinous neoplasm; PanIN is microscopic. Cancerization of ducts by PDAC Look for adjacent invasive carcinoma and abrupt transition from dysplastic to normal duct epithelium. Invasive PDAC Requires infiltrative growth beyond the duct, often with desmoplasia, perineural, or vascular invasion. Intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasm (IPMN) Non-invasive precursor; may be associated with invasive carcinoma Main duct, branch ducts, or both; often pancreatic head. Usually adults in later decades; many lesions are incidental. Mucin hypersecretion may cause recurrent pancreatitis; main-duct involvement can cause ductal dilatation. Grossly visible mucin-producing epithelial neoplasm within the pancreatic ductal system. Papillary epithelial proliferation with ductal communication. Grade as low-grade or high-grade dysplasia; separately identify and classify any invasive carcinoma. Specify gastric, intestinal, pancreatobiliary, or oncocytic epithelial subtype when possible. Papillary mucinous epithelium expands main or branch ducts. Gastric type: pyloric/foveolar-like epithelium, usually low-grade. Intestinal type: villous papillae with goblet cells; may be associated with colloid carcinoma. Pancreatobiliary type: complex branching papillae lined by high-grade cuboidal cells. High-grade dysplasia shows marked atypia, architectural complexity, and loss of polarity. Invasion may be tubular or colloid; sample extensively, especially solid areas and mural nodules. MUC5AC is commonly expressed. Intestinal type typically expresses MUC2 and CDX2. Pancreatobiliary type commonly expresses MUC1. Use immunophenotype to support, not replace, morphologic subtyping. GNAS and KRAS mutations are characteristic drivers; RNF43 alterations also occur. TP53, CDKN2A, and SMAD4 alterations are associated with progression/high-grade dysplasia or invasion. Cyst-fluid molecular testing may help distinguish mucinous from non-mucinous cysts in selected cases. ITPN ITPN is usually non-mucinous, tubular/cribriform, MUC5AC-negative, and lacks the usual IPMN molecular profile. MCN has ovarian-type stroma and does not arise within the pancreatic duct system. PanIN is microscopic (<5 mm), whereas IPMN is grossly visible. Retention cyst/pseudocyst No neoplastic papillary mucinous epithelium in pseudocyst; correlate with pancreatitis history. Intraductal oncocytic papillary neoplasm (IOPN) Non-invasive intraductal neoplasm; may be associated with invasive carcinoma Usually main pancreatic duct; often head; may involve branch ducts. Typically presents in adults with abdominal pain or pancreatitis; some are incidental. Often forms a large solid-cystic/intraductal mass with ductal dilatation. Intraductal epithelial neoplasm with papillary architecture and conspicuous oncocytic cytoplasm. Located within a dilated pancreatic duct. Identify and separately report any associated invasive carcinoma. Complex arborizing papillae are lined by multilayered oncocytic cells. Cells have abundant eosinophilic granular cytoplasm and prominent nucleoli. Intraluminal mucin may be scant; cribriform and solid areas may occur. Invasion may be tubular or colloid-like; thorough sampling is important. MUC1, MUC5AC, and MUC6 are commonly expressed. HepPar1 may be positive and is not evidence by itself of hepatocellular origin. PRKACA or PRKACB fusion is characteristic and diagnostically useful in selected cases. KRAS and GNAS mutations typical of IPMN are generally absent or uncommon. Pancreatobiliary-type IPMN IOPN has oncocytic cells with granular eosinophilic cytoplasm and PRKACA/B fusion; IPMN has mucinous papillary epithelium. ITPN is predominantly tubular/cribriform, non-oncocytic, and lacks intracytoplasmic mucin. Acinar cell carcinoma Acinar markers (trypsin, chymotrypsin, BCL10) support acinar carcinoma. Intraductal tubulopapillary neoplasm (ITPN) High-grade intraductal neoplasm; invasion common Approximately half in pancreatic head; diffuse involvement in a minority. Mean age ~60 years; slight female predominance. Abdominal pain is common; obstructive jaundice is uncommon; about one third are incidental. Intraductal nodules of back-to-back glands forming large cribriform structures. High-grade cytologic atypia with absent or minimal intracellular mucin. Demonstrate intraductal location and carefully assess for associated invasion. Solid, fleshy intraductal nodules may completely fill and obliterate the duct lumen. Back-to-back tubular glands form complex cribriform structures; papillae may be present. Tumor cells are cuboidal with eosinophilic-to-amphophilic cytoplasm and uniform but atypical nuclei. Mitotic figures are readily identified; focal comedo-like necrosis is common. Invasive carcinoma occurs in a substantial proportion and may be subtle at the tumor periphery. MUC1 and MUC6 are commonly expressed. MUC5AC is absent or only rarely/focally expressed; MUC2 is consistently negative. Acinar and neuroendocrine markers are negative. BRAF, FGFR2, MAML2/3, NRG1, and RET fusions occur in subsets; some may be therapeutically actionable. KRAS mutations are uncommon; molecular testing is not routinely required for diagnosis. IPMN is mucin-producing, MUC5AC-positive, and shows papillary architecture and a spectrum of dysplasia. Acinar carcinoma expresses trypsin, chymotrypsin, and/or BCL10 and may contain apical zymogen granules. PDAC ITPN is centered within ducts with cribriform intraductal nodules; PDAC shows destructive infiltrative glands in desmoplastic stroma. Mucinous cystic neoplasm (MCN) Non-invasive precursor; ~15% associated with invasive carcinoma Almost exclusively body/tail; >95% in women; median age ~45 years. Small lesions are often incidental; larger lesions cause pain, mass effect, or palpable mass. Usually a well-defined multilocular cyst that does not communicate with pancreatic ducts. Large size, thick irregular wall, mural nodules, and elevated CA19-9 raise concern for invasion. Grossly visible multilocular cystic neoplasm, usually in a woman and in body/tail. No communication with pancreatic ductal system. Mucinous epithelial lining with diagnostic ovarian-type subepithelial stroma. Grade as low-grade or high-grade dysplasia; separately identify invasive carcinoma. Cysts are lined by mucin-producing columnar epithelium, sometimes with non-mucinous cuboidal areas. Ovarian-type stroma is composed of densely packed spindle cells and is required for diagnosis. Low-grade dysplasia shows mild-to-moderate atypia; high-grade dysplasia shows complex papillae, stratification, loss of polarity, and marked atypia. Approximately 15% have associated invasive carcinoma, usually tubular-type; invasion may be focal in cyst septa. Epithelium commonly expresses CK7, CK19, EMA, CEA, and MUC5AC. Ovarian-type stroma commonly expresses PR and variably ER, SMA, and desmin. Luteinized stromal cells may express inhibin, calretinin, and tyrosine hydroxylase. KRAS and RNF43 alterations occur; TP53 alterations are enriched in high-grade dysplasia/invasive carcinoma. Cyst-fluid KRAS/GNAS support a mucin-producing cyst; TP53/SMAD4/CTNNB1/MTOR alterations may support high-grade neoplasia in selected cases. IPMN communicates with the duct system; MCN has ovarian-type stroma and lacks ductal communication. Pseudocyst MCN has epithelial lining and ovarian-type stroma; pseudocyst lacks epithelial lining. Simple mucinous cyst lacks ovarian-type stroma and is usually unilocular/paucilocular. Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) Malignant Highly aggressive invasive carcinoma Usually older adults; pancreatic head ~60%, body/tail less common but often later-stage; no strong sex restriction. Often presents with painless jaundice, weight loss, abdominal/back pain, and new-onset or worsening diabetes. Head tumors cause biliary and pancreatic duct obstruction (double-duct sign) and upstream obstructive chronic pancreatitis. Body/tail tumors often present later and may invade celiac axis, stomach, spleen, or adjacent structures. Infiltrating epithelial malignancy, typically with at least focal glandular differentiation. Haphazard, irregular glands infiltrate pancreatic parenchyma and elicit desmoplastic stroma. Perineural invasion and/or vascular invasion strongly support invasive carcinoma. Desirable: perineural and vascular invasion; assess ductal cancerization versus true invasion. In cytology, look for irregular cell spacing, marked anisonucleosis (4:1 within a group), parachromatin clearing, irregular nuclear membranes, and lacy/vacuolated cytoplasm. Most tumors form irregular duct-like glands haphazardly infiltrating pancreatic parenchyma in dense, hypovascular desmoplastic stroma. Neoplastic glands may contain necrotic debris or show incomplete luminal lining. Nuclear size variation is common; a 4:1 nuclear size ratio within a gland supports PDAC. Perineural invasion is frequent and highly tumor-specific in the appropriate setting. Lymphovascular invasion, especially venous invasion, is common; glands adjacent to muscular vessels are a useful clue. Cancerization of pre-existing ducts may mimic high-grade PanIN; seek adjacent invasive carcinoma and abrupt transition to normal duct epithelium. Large-duct pattern may appear deceptively bland; haphazard arrangement outside normal duct branching is key. Foamy-gland pattern has lacy microvesicular cytoplasm, basally placed hyperchromatic nuclei, and apical brush-border-like condensation. Poorly differentiated areas may form solid/cribriform sheets with pleomorphism, atypical mitoses, necrosis, and little mucin. CK7, CK8/18, and CK19 are consistently expressed but are not specific for PDAC. CEA, CA19-9, CA125, MUC1, and MUC5AC are commonly positive; MUC2 is usually negative in conventional PDAC. SMAD4 nuclear expression is lost in approximately 55%; p16 is lost in approximately 75%. p53 shows an aberrant overexpression or null pattern in approximately 75–80%. Trypsin/BCL10 and synaptophysin/chromogranin are usually negative; use to exclude acinar and neuroendocrine neoplasms. WHO source lists diagnostic molecular pathology as not clinically relevant for routine histologic diagnosis. KRAS, TP53, CDKN2A, and SMAD4 are common drivers but are not diagnostic criteria; molecular profiling may guide targeted therapy. Chronic pancreatitis / reactive ductal atypia Reactive glands are usually lobular and orderly, with small round polarized nuclei, uniform spacing, and no marked anisonucleosis or hyperchromasia. PDAC shows haphazard infiltrative glands, desmoplasia, perineural/vascular invasion, and cytologic atypia. Autoimmune pancreatitis (AIP) AIP can produce dense fibrosis and inflammation that mimic PDAC, especially on EUS-FNA. Look for lymphoplasmacytic inflammation, storiform fibrosis, obliterative phlebitis, and (in type 1) increased IgG4-positive plasma cells; absence of unequivocal malignant glands favors AIP. Correlate with imaging/serology and adequate core tissue. Cancerization of ducts (COD) vs. high-grade PanIN COD is favored by immediately adjacent invasive carcinoma with matching cytology and abrupt transition to non-dysplastic duct epithelium; PanIN is a separate intraepithelial precursor without adjacent invasive carcinoma. Acinar architecture/zymogen granules and trypsin, chymotrypsin, or BCL10 positivity support acinar differentiation. Monotonous organoid/trabecular cells with synaptophysin, chromogranin, and INSM1 positivity; PDAC shows infiltrative desmoplastic glands. Metastatic or adjacent-organ adenocarcinoma No IHC marker reliably separates PDAC from bile duct/duodenal adenocarcinoma; integrate anatomic epicenter, precursor lesions, imaging, and clinical history. Malignant exocrine carcinoma Adults; often large tumors; may arise anywhere in pancreas. Typically presents with abdominal pain, weight loss, or mass; lipase hypersecretion syndrome occurs in a minority. Malignant epithelial neoplasm with acinar differentiation. Demonstrate pancreatic enzyme expression (trypsin, chymotrypsin, BCL10) in tumor cells. Exclude neuroendocrine and mixed acinar-neuroendocrine neoplasms. Acinar, solid, trabecular, or glandular growth with granular eosinophilic cytoplasm. Apical zymogen granules and prominent nucleoli may be present. Intraductal growth can mimic ITPN; enzymatic crystals may be seen. Trypsin, chymotrypsin, and BCL10 support acinar differentiation. Neuroendocrine markers may be focally expressed; interpret in context. APC/β-catenin pathway alterations and DNA-repair gene alterations occur in subsets; molecular testing is not required for morphologic diagnosis. ITPN lacks acinar enzyme expression and typically shows cribriform intraductal growth with minimal mucin. PanNET expresses synaptophysin/chromogranin/INSM1 and lacks convincing acinar enzyme phenotype. Clinical history and renal-lineage markers are useful in clear-cell tumors. Pancreatoblastoma Malignant; predominantly pediatric Usually children, especially first decade; pancreatic head common. Most common malignant pancreatic neoplasm in young children; may present with abdominal mass, pain, or weight loss. Can occur in adults but is rare. Distinctive acinar-type differentiation with squamoid nests/bodies. Recognize mixed acinar, trabecular, and solid patterns. Use β-catenin and acinar markers in the appropriate morphologic context. Lobulated tumor with acinar, trabecular, and solid growth patterns. Squamoid corpuscles are characteristic and may be focal. Tumor cells have granular eosinophilic cytoplasm and acinar differentiation. Necrosis and mitotic activity may be present. Trypsin, chymotrypsin, and BCL10 highlight acinar differentiation. Nuclear β-catenin is common in squamoid corpuscles and may be present in tumor cells. CTNNB1/APC pathway alterations occur; consider germline APC/FAP association in appropriate clinical setting. Pancreatoblastoma has characteristic squamoid corpuscles and usually occurs in children. Solid pseudopapillary neoplasm SPN typically occurs in young women and shows pseudopapillary architecture with nuclear β-catenin/LEF1. Neuroendocrine markers are not the defining phenotype; acinar markers support pancreatoblastoma. Solid pseudopapillary neoplasm (SPN) Low-grade malignant potential; usually indolent but can metastasize Predominantly young women; often body/tail but can occur anywhere. Often presents as a large, well-circumscribed mass with abdominal pain or incidental discovery. Female predominance is striking; commonly occurs in young adults. Solid and pseudopapillary architecture with discohesive cells around delicate fibrovascular cores. Nuclear β-catenin and LEF1 support diagnosis. Exclude PanNET and acinar cell carcinoma with lineage markers. Well-circumscribed solid-cystic tumor with degenerative change, hemorrhage, and pseudocystic spaces. Discohesive uniform cells surround delicate fibrovascular cores, creating pseudopapillae. Cells have grooved nuclei and eosinophilic-to-clear cytoplasm; hyaline globules may occur. Foamy macrophages and cholesterol clefts are common. Nuclear β-catenin and LEF1 are commonly positive. CD10, progesterone receptor, and vimentin are often expressed. Synaptophysin may be focal; chromogranin is usually negative. Acinar markers are negative. CTNNB1 activating mutations with Wnt/β-catenin pathway activation are characteristic. PanNET shows diffuse neuroendocrine marker expression and lacks the characteristic nuclear β-catenin/LEF1 profile. Acinar enzyme markers are positive in acinar carcinoma and negative in SPN. Usually pediatric with squamoid corpuscles and acinar differentiation. All PathologyGPS / GI & Hepatopancreatobiliary / Pancreatic Lesions Pancreatic Lesions A morphology-first diagnostic reference covering benign epithelial neoplasms and precursors, invasive carcinomas, targeted immunohistochemistry, and practical differential diagnosis. Core diagnostic principle Establish the growth pattern and prove invasion. For PDAC, fibrosis and atypical ducts alone are insufficient. Haphazard infiltrative glands, desmoplasia, perineural invasion, and vascular invasion are key findings. Benign epithelial tumors and precursors: classification at a glance The WHO classification emphasizes direction of differentiation and gross configuration. This table summarizes the defining architecture, mucin phenotype, and molecular clues. Entity Configuration / site Defining histology Key IHC Molecular clue Solitary cyst >10 mm; often body/tail Flat gastric-type mucinous lining; no ovarian-type stroma CK7, MUC5AC/MUC6 KRAS in cyst fluid; nonspecific Microcystic, macrocystic, or solid Bland clear glycogen-rich cuboidal cells Inhibin, GLUT1, MUC6; PAS+/PAS-D− VHL / chromosome 3p loss Microscopic ductal lesion (<5 mm) Flat or micropapillary mucinous dysplasia Ductal markers are supportive only KRAS; later TP53/CDKN2A/SMAD4 Grossly visible intraductal lesion Papillary mucinous epithelium; subtype-specific MUC5AC; MUC2/CDX2 intestinal; MUC1 pancreatobiliary GNAS, KRAS, RNF43 IOPN Dilated duct; often solid-cystic Complex papillae with oncocytic cells MUC1, MUC5AC, MUC6; HepPar1 may be positive PRKACA / PRKACB fusion Solid intraductal nodules Back-to-back tubules/cribriform; little or no mucin MUC1/MUC6; MUC5AC absent/focal BRAF, FGFR2, NRG1, RET fusions Multilocular cyst; body/tail; almost all women Mucinous lining with ovarian-type stroma; no duct communication Stromal PR/ER; epithelial MUC5AC KRAS, RNF43; TP53 in advanced lesions Diagnostic GPS: classify before ancillary testing Define configuration Solid mass, true cyst, or ductal dilatation? Does it communicate with the pancreatic duct? Identify differentiation Ductal/mucinous, serous/glycogen-rich, oncocytic, acinar, neuroendocrine, or solid pseudopapillary. Establish grade For PanIN, IPMN, and MCN, report the highest grade; high-grade dysplasia is not invasion. Prove invasion Seek destructive infiltrative glands, desmoplasia, perineural or vascular invasion, or extension beyond normal duct anatomy. Use focused tests Choose IHC/molecular assays to resolve a defined differential; no single marker distinguishes PDAC from reactive ducts. Entity reference Clinical profile and diagnostic criteria Search by entity, morphology, site, marker, or gene. e.g. SMAD4, PRKACA, ovarian-type stroma... bg-teal-700 text-white border border-slate-300 bg-white text-slate-600 Collapse View diagnostic profile − + Clinical profile Essential diagnostic criteria Histopathology Immunophenotype Molecular pathology Differential diagnosis Diagnostic pitfalls No matching entity. PDAC versus chronic pancreatitis: high-stakes morphologic comparison This distinction is primarily morphologic. Fibrosis, duct distortion, and reactive atypia occur in chronic pancreatitis and are not sufficient for carcinoma. Seek destructive invasion and cytologic atypia in the correct architectural context. Feature Chronic / obstructive pancreatitis Gland distribution Haphazard, irregular glands infiltrate parenchyma and fat; glands may be isolated or adjacent to muscular vessels. Lobular/acinar organization is generally preserved; distorted ducts follow native anatomy. Stroma Desmoplastic, hypovascular collagen around infiltrating glands. Fibrosis may be extensive but lacks convincing tumor-associated desmoplasia around destructive atypical glands. Cytology Nuclear enlargement, hyperchromasia, irregular membranes, loss of polarity, and anisonucleosis; 4:1 nuclear size variation within a gland supports PDAC. Small, round, uniform, polarized nuclei; no significant anisonucleosis or hyperchromasia. Perineural invasion Common and highly tumor-specific in the appropriate context. Benign glandular inclusions in nerves are exceedingly rare but can occur in longstanding chronic pancreatitis. Vascular invasion Lymphatic and venous invasion are common; tumor may replace endothelium and line vessel walls. Absent. Ductal changes Cancerization of ducts may mimic high-grade PanIN; adjacent invasive carcinoma and abrupt transition are clues. Reactive atypia may occur, but orderly epithelium with preserved polarity is typical. Background pancreas Obstruction may cause upstream acinar atrophy, fibrosis, and islet aggregation. Chronic inflammation, acinar loss, ductal distortion, protein plugs/calculi, and fibrosis may be diffuse. IHC CK7/CK19 and mucin markers are usually positive; SMAD4 loss and aberrant p53 support carcinoma in subsets. Ductal markers may also be positive; retained SMAD4 does not exclude PDAC; no IHC marker alone resolves the differential. Features strongly favoring PDAC Unequivocal perineural invasion by atypical glands. Venous or lymphatic invasion. Haphazard glands in desmoplastic stroma, especially in peripancreatic fat or adjacent to muscular vessels. Marked nuclear atypia with loss of polarity and irregular nuclear membranes. Focal infiltrative mass with duct cutoff/obstruction on imaging. Features favoring chronic / autoimmune pancreatitis Lobulocentric chronic inflammation and acinar loss with preserved native architecture. Reactive ductal epithelium with small, uniform, polarized nuclei. Type 1 autoimmune pancreatitis: lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate, storiform fibrosis, obliterative phlebitis, and increased IgG4-positive plasma cells. No unequivocal destructive, perineural, or vascular invasion. IgG4-positive plasma cells and SMAD4/p53 immunostains are supportive, not stand-alone tests. A negative or limited EUS-FNA does not exclude PDAC when imaging suspicion remains high; core tissue and clinicoradiologic correlation may be necessary. PDAC: practical approach to a limited biopsy / EUS-guided sample Evaluate architecture before isolated cytology: irregular cell spacing, 4:1 anisonucleosis, parachromatin clearing, irregular nuclear membranes, and lacy/vacuolated cytoplasm support well-differentiated adenocarcinoma. Look for atypical epithelium wrapping around desmoplastic stroma, cribriform architecture, long atypical epithelial strips, and loss of polarity. Reactive ductal cells in pancreatitis usually retain small, round, polarized nuclei and relatively uniform spacing. If autoimmune pancreatitis is considered, assess lymphoplasmacytic inflammation, storiform fibrosis, obliterative phlebitis, and IgG4 immunostaining. Use focused markers to exclude acinar and neuroendocrine neoplasms; CK7/CK19 positivity alone does not prove PDAC. If findings are suspicious but not definitive, communicate the limitation and recommend radiologic correlation or repeat core sampling rather than overcalling reactive atypia. Sampling and reporting checklist For cystic lesions, document duct communication, locularity, mural nodules, solid areas, and presence or absence of ovarian-type stroma. For IPMN, IOPN, ITPN, and MCN, sample mural nodules, thickened walls/septa, and all suspicious solid areas to detect focal invasion. For PDAC resections, map tumor size/location, grade, treatment effect, perineural and lymphovascular invasion, margins (including uncinate/SMA and posterior), lymph nodes, and adjacent organ involvement. Distinguish high-grade dysplasia from invasive carcinoma and diagnose each component separately. For limited biopsies, state when invasion cannot be assessed because representative stroma or architecture is lacking. Scope note: Based primarily on the supplied WHO pancreatic tumor excerpt. Ancillary findings are supportive and must be interpreted with morphology, sampling, and clinical/radiologic correlation.

title: Ear Tumors
content: use client Chondrodermatitis nodularis chronica helicis Non-neoplastic / degenerative Inflammatory and degenerative lesion Most often affects patients in the seventh decade; male predominance (approximately 2:1). Usually involves the helix, which is affected about twice as often as the antihelix; any auricular site may be involved. Presents as an intensely painful, firm red nodule with a central crater and crust; pain is often nocturnal and worsened by pressure on the ear. Cup-shaped epidermal crater containing necrotic debris and fibrin. Underlying dermal collagen is homogenized and eosinophilic, with extension to superficial cartilage. Superficial cartilage shows erosion and degenerative change. A central cup-shaped crater contains necrotic debris, fibrin, and variable inflammatory cells. Parakeratotic and hyperkeratotic crust overlies acanthotic epithelium, often with acute inflammation. An inverted funnel-shaped dermal defect contains homogeneous eosinophilic collagen admixed with fibrin. Superficial cartilage shows erosion, loss of basophilia, fibrosis, and chondrocyte dropout. Squamous cell carcinoma of the external auditory canal Carcinoma shows infiltrative malignant squamous epithelium; this lesion instead shows a crater with necrobiotic collagen and superficial cartilage degeneration. Cystic chondromalacia (auricular pseudocyst) The pseudocyst is an epithelium-free cleft within the cartilage and usually presents as a painless fluctuant swelling; this lesion is a painful crater-forming process. Relapsing polychondritis Relapsing polychondritis is a broader inflammatory cartilage disorder; the localized crater with necrobiotic dermal collagen and superficial cartilage erosion supports this diagnosis. Degenerative intracartilaginous pseudocyst Most often affects young men (mean age approximately 35 years; reported male-to-female ratio about 9:1), although any age and either sex may be affected. Involves the helix, scaphoid fossa, concha, or triangular fossa. Usually presents as a unilateral, rapidly developing, painless, fusiform, slightly fluctuant swelling without overlying skin change. Central cleft within the auricular cartilage without an epithelial lining. Degenerated cartilage with variable hemorrhage, granulation tissue, and fibrosis. Clinical presentation is typically a painless fluctuant auricular swelling. The cartilaginous plate contains a central epithelium-free cleft. The cleft may have an irregular contour and a rim of fibrous or granulation tissue containing plump fibroblasts. Mucoid material, hemosiderin, granulation tissue, and fibrosis vary with lesion duration and prior procedures. That lesion has a painful crater, necrobiotic dermal collagen, and superficial cartilage erosion; a pseudocyst has an epithelium-free cleft within the cartilage. Relapsing polychondritis produces inflammatory cartilage injury in a systemic clinical setting rather than a localized intracartilaginous pseudocyst. Traumatic perichondritis Perichondritis is an inflammatory process; the defining finding here is a central epithelium-free cleft in the cartilage. Exostosis (osteoma) of the ear Non-neoplastic / osseous Benign reactive bony proliferation Occurs in individuals with repeated aquatic exposure; no characteristic age or sex predilection is specified. Usually arises in the bony external auditory canal; middle-ear involvement is extremely rare. Often asymptomatic; may cause conductive hearing loss, recurrent otitis externa, otalgia, or cerumen impaction. EAC lesions are commonly called surfer's ear. Mature-appearing lamellar cortical bone in the appropriate radiologic setting. EAC exostoses are typically bilateral and broad-based, medial to the isthmus. Marrow spaces are absent. Composed of lamellar bone with anastomosing trabeculae and interspersed vascular tissue. Otosclerosis Otosclerosis consists of well-demarcated plaques of immature, vascular otospongiotic bone within the otic capsule; exostosis is mature lamellar cortical bone in the EAC. Osteoma of the external auditory canal EAC osteoma is typically unilateral, may be pedunculated, and arises in the lateral canal; exostoses are usually bilateral, broad-based, and medial to the isthmus. Ceruminous adenoma Benign neoplasms Benign apocrine gland neoplasm Occurs across a wide age range (12–85 years), with a peak in the sixth decade; sexes are affected equally. Arises from ceruminous glands in the outer half of the external auditory canal. Presents as an EAC mass with an intact tympanic membrane; conductive hearing loss, otorrhea, discharge, and otalgia may occur. Lateral EAC location and a circumscribed, noninvasive glandular neoplasm. Bland biphasic population of luminal epithelial and basal/myoepithelial cells. Luminal cells show apocrine differentiation with apical snouting or decapitation secretion. Golden-yellow to brown cytoplasmic pigment granules are a desirable feature. Usually circumscribed and unencapsulated, without destructive invasion. Predominantly glandular growth, often with cystic change; solid back-to-back glands and papillary patterns may occur. Bland luminal cuboidal-to-columnar cells have abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm and apical snouts. Outer basal/myoepithelial cells are often spindled and may have clear cytoplasm. Ceruminous pleomorphic adenoma has chondromyxoid stroma; syringocystadenoma papilliferum shows papillary projections and a stromal plasma-cell infiltrate. Pancytokeratin is strongly and diffusely positive. Luminal cells express CK7, EMA, and KIT (CD117); GATA3 is usually positive in luminal/apocrine cells. Basal cells express myoepithelial or basal-cell markers. Ceruminous adenocarcinoma Carcinoma shows destructive infiltration, cytologic atypia, frequent mitoses, and may show perineural or lymphovascular invasion; adenoma is bland and noninvasive. Middle ear neuroendocrine tumor (MeNET) MeNET coexpresses epithelial and neuroendocrine markers and has characteristic neuroendocrine architecture; ceruminous adenoma is a biphasic apocrine glandular neoplasm. Middle ear papilloma Papilloma shows multilayered transitional epithelium with intraepithelial microcysts and transepithelial inflammatory cells, rather than a biphasic apocrine glandular proliferation. Vestibular schwannoma Schwannoma is a spindle-cell nerve-sheath tumor with diffuse S100/SOX10 expression, not an apocrine glandular neoplasm. Malignant epithelial neoplasms Malignant ceruminous gland neoplasm Usually presents in the sixth decade (range 21–92 years), with a slight female predominance; patients present about a decade earlier than those with ceruminous adenoma. Arises lateral to the bony-cartilaginous junction of the external auditory canal; adjacent parotid origin must be excluded. Common presentations are otalgia, an EAC mass, and hearing change; fullness, discharge, and bleeding may occur. External auditory canal origin, with direct extension from adjacent salivary gland sites excluded. Destructive infiltration by malignant glandular cells, often associated with benign ceruminous glands. Perineural invasion, lymphovascular invasion, comedonecrosis, and atypical mitoses support carcinoma. Classify the morphology as adenocarcinoma NOS, adenoid cystic carcinoma, or mucoepidermoid carcinoma when appropriate. Shows destructive infiltration into surrounding soft tissue; bone and cartilage invasion are less common. Adenocarcinoma NOS shows solid and cystic growth, back-to-back irregular glands, pleomorphism, and frequent mitoses, including atypical forms. Apocrine cells may show cytoplasmic snouts or blebs; ceroid pigment granules are absent. Ceruminous adenoid cystic carcinoma shows cribriform, tubular-trabecular, or solid growth with basaloid cells and basement-membrane-like material. Ceruminous mucoepidermoid carcinoma contains intermingled epidermoid, intermediate, and mucous cells. Biphasic luminal and basal/myoepithelial differentiation may be highlighted focally. CD117 highlights luminal cells in ceruminous adenoid cystic carcinoma. The glandular component of ceruminous mucoepidermoid carcinoma may express CEA. Neuroendocrine markers are nonreactive. Adenoma is circumscribed, bland, biphasic, and noninvasive; carcinoma shows destructive infiltration, atypia, frequent mitoses, and may show perineural or lymphovascular invasion. EAC SCC shows squamous differentiation and keratinization rather than malignant ceruminous glandular differentiation. Middle ear adenocarcinoma Middle ear adenocarcinoma is centered in the middle ear/tympanic cavity and often has cystic-papillary architecture; ceruminous carcinoma arises in the lateral EAC from ceruminous glands. Metastatic or directly extending salivary gland carcinoma Imaging and clinical correlation must exclude direct extension from the parotid or another salivary primary. Favor Middle ear neuroendocrine tumor (MeNET) when its defining pattern is present: primary middle-ear epithelial neoplasm with variable architectural patterns and neuroendocrine differentiation. In contrast, Ceruminous adenocarcinoma is characterized by external auditory canal origin, with direct extension from adjacent salivary gland sites excluded. Endolymphatic sac tumor (ELST) Favor Endolymphatic sac tumor (ELST) when its defining pattern is present: tumor centered on the endolymphatic sac/duct. In contrast, Ceruminous adenocarcinoma is characterized by external auditory canal origin, with direct extension from adjacent salivary gland sites excluded. Middle ear squamous cell carcinoma Favor Middle ear squamous cell carcinoma when its defining pattern is present: infiltrating squamous epithelial proliferation with malignant cytologic and architectural features. In contrast, Ceruminous adenocarcinoma is characterized by external auditory canal origin, with direct extension from adjacent salivary gland sites excluded. Malignant cutaneous-type squamous neoplasm Usually affects adults in the sixth to seventh decades; sexes are affected equally. Arises in the keratinizing squamous epithelium of the external auditory canal; origin in the pinna or periauricular skin must be excluded. May present with chronic otorrhea, otalgia, bleeding, hearing loss, otitis externa/media, or facial palsy; an EAC mass is more suggestive. Infiltrating squamous proliferation with architectural and cytologic features of carcinoma. Establish primary EAC origin and exclude direct extension from pinna/periauricular skin or other adjacent sites. Squamous-lineage immunohistochemistry is useful in selected poorly differentiated tumors. Morphology resembles cutaneous SCC; most tumors are well-differentiated and keratinizing. Carcinoma in situ may be present in adjacent epithelium. Concurrent sinonasal-type papilloma, cholesteatoma, or chronic otitis may be present. Poorly differentiated nonkeratinizing tumors require consideration of translocation-associated entities. Pancytokeratin, p40, p63, and CK5/6 support squamous differentiation. EAC SCC may show 3q, 5p, and 8q amplification, 3p deletion, and alterations involving TP53, CDKN2A, NOTCH, and FAT. In poorly differentiated nonkeratinizing tumors, consider BRD4::NUTM1, DEK::AFF2, EWSR1::FLI1, and EWSR1::ERG rearrangements when morphology and clinical context warrant. Ceruminous carcinoma shows malignant glandular/apocrine differentiation, whereas EAC SCC shows infiltrating squamous differentiation. Cholesteatoma Cholesteatoma has bland keratinizing squamous epithelium with laminated keratin debris and inflammation, without malignant cytology or destructive carcinoma. Both are squamous carcinomas; distinguish by anatomic epicenter and exclude middle-ear primary or direct extension from adjacent sites. Papilloma is a noninvasive multilayered transitional epithelial proliferation without pleomorphism, tumor necrosis, or destructive invasion. Cutaneous basal cell carcinoma Basal cell carcinoma has basaloid nests and characteristic stromal relationships rather than conventional squamous maturation and keratinization. Pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia Reactive epithelial hyperplasia lacks destructive infiltrative growth and malignant cytologic features. Favor Middle ear neuroendocrine tumor (MeNET) when its defining pattern is present: primary middle-ear epithelial neoplasm with variable architectural patterns and neuroendocrine differentiation. In contrast, Squamous cell carcinoma of the external auditory canal is characterized by infiltrating squamous proliferation with architectural and cytologic features of carcinoma. Favor Endolymphatic sac tumor (ELST) when its defining pattern is present: tumor centered on the endolymphatic sac/duct. In contrast, Squamous cell carcinoma of the external auditory canal is characterized by infiltrating squamous proliferation with architectural and cytologic features of carcinoma. Favor Middle ear adenocarcinoma when its defining pattern is present: imaging confirms a middle-ear epicenter and bone-destructive adenocarcinoma, often with papillary growth. In contrast, Squamous cell carcinoma of the external auditory canal is characterized by infiltrating squamous proliferation with architectural and cytologic features of carcinoma. Inherited localized bone remodeling disorder Usually presents in the third decade, with a female predominance (approximately 2:1). Involves the otic capsule, commonly anterior to the oval window and at the stapes footplate; round-window and pericochlear sites may also be affected. Typically causes conductive hearing loss from stapes fixation; sensorineural or mixed hearing loss, tinnitus, and vertigo may occur. Disease is usually bilateral. Well-demarcated plaques of immature bone arising within the otic capsule. Active otospongiotic areas show bone resorption, plump osteoblasts, osteoclasts, and dilated vascular marrow spaces. A sharply demarcated interface between normal and affected bone is characteristic. Active lesions contain spongy immature bone with numerous plump osteoblasts and osteoclastic giant cells. Dilated vascular marrow spaces contain cellular connective tissue. Inactive areas show more sclerotic bone; otosclerotic foci may extend toward the cochlear endosteum. Familial clustering and variable-penetrance autosomal dominant inheritance are described, but no specific molecular test is established for routine diagnosis. Exostosis is mature lamellar cortical bone in the EAC, often bilateral and broad-based; otosclerosis is a well-demarcated plaque of immature, vascular bone within the otic capsule. An EAC osteoma is a focal mature bony proliferation, usually unilateral and lateral in the canal; otosclerosis is centered in the otic capsule. Non-neoplastic / keratinizing lesions Non-neoplastic but locally destructive keratinizing lesion Occurs in children and adults; reported annual incidence is higher in children, with a slight male predominance. Congenital lesions are usually unilateral and medial to an intact tympanic membrane in the anterosuperior or posterosuperior middle ear; acquired lesions commonly involve the posterior mesotympanum or epitympanum. Presents with recurrent foul-smelling otorrhea, tinnitus, and progressive hearing impairment; advanced petrous involvement may cause facial paralysis, vertigo, or diplopia. Keratinizing stratified squamous epithelial matrix with abundant laminated keratin debris. Prominent granular cell layer with keratohyalin granules. Perimatrix of granulation tissue and dense fibrous connective tissue with inflammation. Establish middle-ear origin and correlate with imaging. The matrix is thin-to-atrophic, bland keratinizing stratified squamous epithelium in convoluted formations, typically lacking rete ridges. A prominent granular layer contains abundant keratohyalin granules. Cyst contents consist of abundant laminated, anucleate, desquamated keratin. The perimatrix contains granulation tissue and thickened dense fibrous connective tissue. Hemorrhage, hemosiderin-laden macrophages, and foreign-body giant cells may occur, particularly after rupture. SCC shows malignant cytology and infiltrative growth; cholesteatoma has bland keratinizing epithelium, a prominent granular layer, and laminated keratin. Middle-ear SCC is an infiltrative malignant squamous proliferation; cholesteatoma lacks malignant cytologic and architectural features. Papilloma shows multilayered transitional epithelium with mucocytes/microcysts and transepithelial inflammatory cells; cholesteatoma shows keratinizing squamous epithelium and laminated keratin. Cholesterol granuloma Cholesterol granuloma is a histiocytic/giant-cell reaction to cholesterol clefts and hemorrhage rather than a keratinizing epithelial matrix with laminated keratin. Otic polyp An otic polyp is predominantly inflammatory granulation tissue; identify the keratinizing epithelial matrix and keratin debris to diagnose cholesteatoma. Benign surface epithelial neoplasm; recurrence and malignant transformation may occur Reported age range is 19–81 years (median approximately 56 years), with an overall equal sex distribution. Usually unilateral and centered in the middle ear; the mastoid, Eustachian tube, EAC, and skull base may also be involved. About half have concurrent sinonasal/nasopharyngeal disease. Presents with hearing loss, otorrhea, a mass, otalgia, tinnitus, or otitis media; tympanic membrane rupture is frequent. Multilayered transitional epithelial proliferation, usually with inverted/endophytic architecture. Intraepithelial microcysts containing macrophages, mucin, and cellular debris, with transepithelial inflammatory cells. Intact basement membrane and absence of pleomorphism, tumor necrosis, atypical mitoses, and destructive bone invasion. Assess for concurrent sinonasal tract papilloma. Most lesions are inverted, with thick endophytic growth of nonkeratinizing transitional cells bounded by an intact basement membrane. Intraepithelial microcysts contain macrophages, mucin, and cell debris. Transepithelial inflammatory cells are present; mitotic figures may be readily identified. Oncocytic papilloma shows tall stratified columnar cells with abundant oncocytic cytoplasm; the exophytic subtype is extremely rare. Marked pleomorphism, tumor necrosis, atypical mitoses, and destructive bone invasion indicate malignant transformation to SCC. Low-risk HPV has been identified in a small number of cases; rare tumors show transcriptionally active high-risk HPV. EGFR and KRAS mutations have not been documented in temporal-bone sinonasal-type papillomas. SCC shows malignant cytology and destructive invasion; benign papilloma lacks pleomorphism, tumor necrosis, atypical mitoses, and destructive bone invasion. Middle-ear SCC is an invasive malignant squamous proliferation; papilloma retains an intact basement membrane and lacks malignant cytologic features. Cholesteatoma shows keratinizing squamous epithelium with laminated keratin; papilloma shows multilayered transitional cells, microcysts, and transepithelial inflammatory cells. MeNET has neuroendocrine architecture and epithelial/neuroendocrine marker coexpression; papilloma has multilayered transitional epithelial growth with microcysts and inflammatory cell migration. Favor Ceruminous adenoma when its defining pattern is present: lateral eac location and a circumscribed, noninvasive glandular neoplasm. In contrast, Middle ear papilloma is characterized by multilayered transitional epithelial proliferation, usually with inverted/endophytic architecture. Favor Vestibular schwannoma when its defining pattern is present: tumor arising from the eighth cranial nerve. In contrast, Middle ear papilloma is characterized by multilayered transitional epithelial proliferation, usually with inverted/endophytic architecture. Benign peripheral nerve sheath tumor Most often presents in the fifth to sixth decades; a slight female predominance is reported. NF2-associated cases tend to present before age 30. Arises from the vestibular division of cranial nerve VIII and usually involves the cerebellopontine angle/internal auditory canal; bilateral tumors strongly suggest NF2. Usually causes ipsilateral sensorineural hearing loss; tinnitus, vertigo, and imbalance are common. Facial numbness or pain and hydrocephalus occur with large tumors. Tumor arising from the eighth cranial nerve. Alternating compact spindle-cell areas and loose hypocellular myxoid areas. Spindle cells have elongated, tapered or buckled nuclei, sometimes with nuclear palisading. Strong diffuse S100 and SOX10 expression supports the diagnosis. Encapsulated tumor with compact hypercellular Antoni A areas and loose hypocellular Antoni B areas. Antoni A areas contain spindle cells with modest eosinophilic cytoplasm and elongated, tapered-to-buckled nuclei; nuclear palisading may occur. Perivascular hyalinization is characteristic. Mitoses are usually inconspicuous; ancient-type nuclear atypia may occur in a subtype. Tumor cells show strong, diffuse S100 and SOX10 immunoreactivity. NF2 inactivation and loss of merlin expression are common; germline NF2 alterations are relevant in bilateral tumors and the appropriate clinical setting. Meningioma Meningioma shows meningothelial whorls and may have psammoma bodies; schwannoma shows Antoni A/B areas and diffuse S100/SOX10. Neurofibroma Neurofibroma is a less circumscribed mixed-cell nerve-sheath lesion with wavy nuclei and a different stromal pattern; schwannoma is typically encapsulated with Antoni A/B architecture. Solitary fibrous tumor SFT shows patternless spindle-cell growth and characteristic branching vessels; schwannoma shows Antoni A/B areas and diffuse S100/SOX10. Paraganglioma Paraganglioma has nested Zellballen architecture and neuroendocrine differentiation rather than Antoni A/B spindle-cell architecture. Favor Ceruminous adenoma when its defining pattern is present: lateral eac location and a circumscribed, noninvasive glandular neoplasm. In contrast, Vestibular schwannoma is characterized by tumor arising from the eighth cranial nerve. Favor Middle ear papilloma when its defining pattern is present: multilayered transitional epithelial proliferation, usually with inverted/endophytic architecture. In contrast, Vestibular schwannoma is characterized by tumor arising from the eighth cranial nerve. Neuroendocrine neoplasm with usually low proliferation but recurrence potential Most often affects patients in the fifth decade; both sexes are equally affected, with a broad age range. Arises in any part of the middle ear and may extend into the mastoid, Eustachian tube, or EAC. Presents with hearing change, fullness/pressure, or tinnitus; otoscopy typically shows a gray-white or fibrotic mass behind an intact tympanic membrane. Primary middle-ear epithelial neoplasm with variable architectural patterns and neuroendocrine differentiation. Coexpression of epithelial markers and neuroendocrine markers supports the diagnosis. Exclude a middle-ear adenocarcinoma, endolymphatic sac tumor, and paraganglioma using morphology, IHC, and anatomic localization. Cuboidal-to-columnar cells have distinct borders, eosinophilic cytoplasm, and small central hyperchromatic nuclei. Patterns include glands in fibrous stroma, back-to-back glands, pseudorosettes, trabeculae, sheets, and single-cell infiltration. Swirling ribbons of tumor cells may be prominent; mucin may be present in glandular lumina. Some tumors show nuclear pleomorphism and increased mitotic activity. Tumor cells coexpress pancytokeratin and neuroendocrine markers including synaptophysin, chromogranin, and INSM1. ISL1 and SATB2 are commonly expressed; CDX2 and GATA3 may be focally positive; TTF1 is negative. Ki-67 is usually below 2%, although higher indices, including above 20%, have been reported in aggressive tumors. Adenocarcinoma shows glandular/papillary epithelial differentiation without the characteristic diffuse neuroendocrine phenotype; MeNET coexpresses epithelial and neuroendocrine markers. Endolymphatic sac tumor ELST is centered on the endolymphatic sac/duct and typically expresses PAX8 and CAIX; MeNET is a middle-ear neuroendocrine neoplasm. Ceruminous adenoma arises in the lateral EAC and shows a bland biphasic apocrine glandular proliferation; MeNET is centered in the middle ear and expresses neuroendocrine markers. Papilloma shows multilayered transitional epithelium, intraepithelial microcysts, and transepithelial inflammatory cells rather than neuroendocrine differentiation. Paraganglioma has Zellballen architecture and lacks the epithelial keratin coexpression characteristic of MeNET. Favor Ceruminous adenocarcinoma when its defining pattern is present: external auditory canal origin, with direct extension from adjacent salivary gland sites excluded. In contrast, Middle ear neuroendocrine tumor (MeNET) is characterized by primary middle-ear epithelial neoplasm with variable architectural patterns and neuroendocrine differentiation. Favor Squamous cell carcinoma of the external auditory canal when its defining pattern is present: infiltrating squamous proliferation with architectural and cytologic features of carcinoma. In contrast, Middle ear neuroendocrine tumor (MeNET) is characterized by primary middle-ear epithelial neoplasm with variable architectural patterns and neuroendocrine differentiation. Favor Endolymphatic sac tumor (ELST) when its defining pattern is present: tumor centered on the endolymphatic sac/duct. In contrast, Middle ear neuroendocrine tumor (MeNET) is characterized by primary middle-ear epithelial neoplasm with variable architectural patterns and neuroendocrine differentiation. Favor Middle ear squamous cell carcinoma when its defining pattern is present: infiltrating squamous epithelial proliferation with malignant cytologic and architectural features. In contrast, Middle ear neuroendocrine tumor (MeNET) is characterized by primary middle-ear epithelial neoplasm with variable architectural patterns and neuroendocrine differentiation. Locally destructive epithelial neoplasm; strongly associated with VHL Most often presents between ages 30 and 40 (reported range 10–88 years); female predominance (approximately 1.6:1). VHL-associated patients may be younger. Arises in association with the endolymphatic sac/duct; bilateral tumors are nearly always associated with VHL. Common presentations include progressive unilateral hearing loss, tinnitus, facial nerve palsy, and vertigo. Tumor centered on the endolymphatic sac/duct. Simple, coarse, broad, interdigitating papillary projections lined by a single layer of low cuboidal-to-columnar cells. Cells have clear or slightly eosinophilic cytoplasm and uniform round nuclei with coarse chromatin. PAX8 and CAIX positivity with TTF1, GATA3, and RCC marker negativity are desirable in selected cases. Recommend VHL genetic assessment in all patients with ELST. Papillary and/or cystic tumor with frequent bone invasion or remodeling. Broad, coarse, interdigitating papillae have fibrovascular cores and limited branching. Papillae are lined by a single layer of low cuboidal-to-columnar cells with ample clear/vacuolated cytoplasm and indistinct cell borders. Cystic spaces may contain serum, secretions, erythrocytes, or inspissated colloid-like material. Pleomorphism, increased mitoses, and necrosis are usually inconspicuous. Positive for pancytokeratin, CK7, EMA, HIF1α, GLUT1, membranous CAIX, and nuclear PAX8. Usually negative for TTF1, thyroglobulin, CD10, AMACR, GATA3, synaptophysin, and RCC marker. Germline or somatic VHL pathogenic variants and allelic loss are common; ELST may be the initial presentation of VHL. Genetic testing is clinically important even in apparently sporadic cases. Middle-ear adenocarcinoma is centered in the middle ear without endolymphatic sac involvement and is typically PAX8/CAIX negative; ELST is sac/duct-centered and usually PAX8/CAIX positive. Metastatic clear cell renal cell carcinoma Both may show clear cells and vascularity; renal cell carcinoma typically expresses renal markers such as RCC marker/CD10 and lacks the characteristic ELST profile. VHL context does not by itself distinguish them. Papillary or follicular thyroid carcinoma Thyroid carcinoma is typically thyroglobulin and TTF1 positive; ELST is usually negative for both. MeNET expresses synaptophysin, chromogranin, and INSM1; ELST is typically negative for synaptophysin and shows PAX8/CAIX expression. Choroid plexus papilloma, papillary ependymoma, papillary meningioma, and paraganglioma Use the anatomic epicenter and lineage-specific morphology/IHC; ELST shows sac-centered papillary/cystic growth with PAX8 and CAIX expression. Favor Ceruminous adenocarcinoma when its defining pattern is present: external auditory canal origin, with direct extension from adjacent salivary gland sites excluded. In contrast, Endolymphatic sac tumor (ELST) is characterized by tumor centered on the endolymphatic sac/duct. Favor Squamous cell carcinoma of the external auditory canal when its defining pattern is present: infiltrating squamous proliferation with architectural and cytologic features of carcinoma. In contrast, Endolymphatic sac tumor (ELST) is characterized by tumor centered on the endolymphatic sac/duct. Favor Middle ear squamous cell carcinoma when its defining pattern is present: infiltrating squamous epithelial proliferation with malignant cytologic and architectural features. In contrast, Endolymphatic sac tumor (ELST) is characterized by tumor centered on the endolymphatic sac/duct. Primary malignant squamous neoplasm Mean age at presentation is approximately 60 years (range 21–89 years); sexes are affected equally. Arises primarily in the middle ear; direct extension from pinna, nasopharynx, or sinonasal tract is more common and must be excluded. Presents with hearing loss, otorrhea, otalgia, bleeding, tinnitus, vertigo, or facial nerve palsy. Infiltrating squamous epithelial proliferation with malignant cytologic and architectural features. Confirm a primary middle-ear epicenter and exclude direct extension from adjacent sites. Use EBER, NUT immunohistochemistry, or molecular testing in selected nonkeratinizing tumors. Pleomorphic epithelial cells form sheets with a pavement-like appearance, increased N:C ratio, and coarse nuclear chromatin. Most tumors are keratinizing and well to moderately differentiated. Nonkeratinizing tumors may be EBV-associated or harbor rearrangements such as DEK::AFF2. Pancytokeratin, p40, p63, and CK5/6 are positive. EBER may identify EBV-associated tumors; NUT IHC may help classify selected poorly differentiated nonkeratinizing tumors. DEK::AFF2 rearrangement has been described in a subset of nonkeratinizing tumors; molecular testing may aid classification in selected cases. Both are squamous carcinomas; distinguish by the anatomic epicenter and exclude extension from the EAC or pinna. Papilloma is a multilayered transitional epithelial proliferation without pleomorphism, tumor necrosis, or destructive invasion. Cholesteatoma contains bland keratinizing squamous epithelium and laminated keratin without malignant cytology or infiltrative carcinoma. Metastatic/directly extending sinonasal or nasopharyngeal carcinoma Clinical and radiologic correlation establishes whether the middle-ear lesion is primary or represents extension from an adjacent site; EBER and molecular/IHC studies may aid classification. Favor Ceruminous adenocarcinoma when its defining pattern is present: external auditory canal origin, with direct extension from adjacent salivary gland sites excluded. In contrast, Middle ear squamous cell carcinoma is characterized by infiltrating squamous epithelial proliferation with malignant cytologic and architectural features. Favor Middle ear neuroendocrine tumor (MeNET) when its defining pattern is present: primary middle-ear epithelial neoplasm with variable architectural patterns and neuroendocrine differentiation. In contrast, Middle ear squamous cell carcinoma is characterized by infiltrating squamous epithelial proliferation with malignant cytologic and architectural features. Favor Endolymphatic sac tumor (ELST) when its defining pattern is present: tumor centered on the endolymphatic sac/duct. In contrast, Middle ear squamous cell carcinoma is characterized by infiltrating squamous epithelial proliferation with malignant cytologic and architectural features. Favor Middle ear adenocarcinoma when its defining pattern is present: imaging confirms a middle-ear epicenter and bone-destructive adenocarcinoma, often with papillary growth. In contrast, Middle ear squamous cell carcinoma is characterized by infiltrating squamous epithelial proliferation with malignant cytologic and architectural features. Locally aggressive primary glandular malignancy Usually presents in younger adults (reported range 16–55 years; median approximately 33 years), with a slight female predominance. Arises in the middle ear/tympanic cavity, often filling the middle ear and extending into the petrous apex; endolymphatic sac involvement should be absent. Symptoms are often longstanding and nonspecific, including hearing loss, otalgia, vestibular dysfunction, and otorrhea. Imaging confirms a middle-ear epicenter and bone-destructive adenocarcinoma, often with papillary growth. Exclude endolymphatic sac tumor and metastatic carcinoma, including lung, thyroid, and colon primaries. PAX8 and CAIX negativity supports middle-ear adenocarcinoma over ELST. Cystic-papillary glandular architecture with papillae lying loosely or infiltrating fibrous connective tissue. Papillae are usually lined by a single layer of low cuboidal-to-columnar cells with uniform nuclei, eosinophilic cytoplasm, and indistinct cell borders. Thyroid follicle-like areas may occur; other patterns may resemble oncocytic, mucinous, polymorphous, or salivary duct carcinoma. Tumor cells express CK7 and EMA; S100 may be positive. PAX8 and CAIX are negative, helping distinguish the tumor from ELST. MKRN1::BRAF fusion has been reported in oncocytic and papillary middle-ear adenocarcinomas. EGFR mutations have been reported in experimental models of histologically similar tumors; PRKD1/2/3 mutations have not been established in polymorphous-like cases. ELST is centered on the endolymphatic sac/duct and typically expresses PAX8 and CAIX; middle-ear adenocarcinoma is centered in the middle ear and is PAX8/CAIX negative. MeNET coexpresses epithelial and neuroendocrine markers; middle-ear adenocarcinoma shows glandular/papillary morphology without the defining neuroendocrine phenotype. Metastatic carcinoma (lung, thyroid, or colon) Exclude a distant primary by clinical/radiologic correlation and targeted immunohistochemistry; the diagnosis requires a primary middle-ear tumor. Ceruminous carcinoma arises from apocrine glands in the lateral EAC; middle-ear adenocarcinoma is centered in the tympanic cavity and may extend into the petrous apex. Favor Squamous cell carcinoma of the external auditory canal when its defining pattern is present: infiltrating squamous proliferation with architectural and cytologic features of carcinoma. In contrast, Middle ear adenocarcinoma is characterized by imaging confirms a middle-ear epicenter and bone-destructive adenocarcinoma, often with papillary growth. Favor Endolymphatic sac tumor (ELST) when its defining pattern is present: tumor centered on the endolymphatic sac/duct. In contrast, Middle ear adenocarcinoma is characterized by imaging confirms a middle-ear epicenter and bone-destructive adenocarcinoma, often with papillary growth. Favor Middle ear squamous cell carcinoma when its defining pattern is present: infiltrating squamous epithelial proliferation with malignant cytologic and architectural features. In contrast, Middle ear adenocarcinoma is characterized by imaging confirms a middle-ear epicenter and bone-destructive adenocarcinoma, often with papillary growth. All PathologyGPS / Head and Neck / Ear and Temporal Bone Ear Tumors and Tumor-Like Lesions A site-oriented diagnostic reference covering the external ear, external auditory canal, middle ear, temporal bone, and inner ear. Each entity is organized around clinical profile, essential diagnostic criteria, histopathology, immunophenotype, molecular findings, and focused differential diagnosis. Core rule Establish the anatomic epicenter before classifying an ear lesion. Distinguish external auditory canal, middle-ear, endolymphatic sac, and eighth-nerve origin. Imaging and clinical correlation are often essential. Diagnostic GPS: anatomic site, growth pattern, and targeted studies Confirm the epicenter External ear/EAC, middle ear, endolymphatic sac/duct, otic capsule, or vestibular division of cranial nerve VIII. Separate neoplastic from non-neoplastic Consider degenerative auricular lesions, osseous remodeling, cholesteatoma, benign neoplasms, and malignancies. Assess architecture Look for a keratinizing matrix, biphasic ceruminous glands, papillary/transitional growth, neuroendocrine patterns, or destructive invasion. Use focused immunohistochemistry Apply lineage markers to resolve squamous, apocrine, neuroendocrine, renal/thyroid-like, or nerve-sheath differentiation. Correlate with imaging CT and MRI help establish the epicenter, bone destruction, soft-tissue extent, and possible direct extension from adjacent sites. High-yield site and pattern distinctions Auricular pseudocyst Epithelium-free cleft within auricular cartilage Chondrodermatitis nodularis Painful crater, necrobiotic collagen, superficial cartilage erosion EAC exostosis Usually bilateral, broad-based mature cortical bone Bland biphasic apocrine glands with decapitation secretion Destructive invasion by malignant ceruminous glandular cells Inverted transitional epithelium, microcysts, transepithelial inflammatory cells MeNET Epithelial and neuroendocrine marker coexpression Sac/duct-centered papillary tumor; PAX8 and CAIX positive Middle-ear-centered bone-destructive papillary/glandular carcinoma; PAX8/CAIX negative Antoni A/B pattern with diffuse S100/SOX10 Important diagnostic pitfalls Site matters: a ceruminous neoplasm arises in the lateral external auditory canal; middle-ear adenocarcinoma and MeNET are centered in the middle ear; ELST is associated with the endolymphatic sac/duct. Benign versus malignant ceruminous neoplasm: destructive invasion, marked atypia, atypical mitoses, perineural invasion, lymphovascular invasion, or comedonecrosis support carcinoma. Middle ear papilloma: mitotic figures may be readily identified in benign lesions. Pleomorphism, tumor necrosis, atypical mitoses, and destructive bone invasion raise concern for malignant transformation. ELST versus middle ear adenocarcinoma: use the anatomic epicenter and the PAX8/CAIX profile; ELST is typically positive, whereas middle-ear adenocarcinoma is negative. Primary versus secondary carcinoma: exclude direct extension from the pinna, parotid, nasopharynx, or sinonasal tract as appropriate.
