title: Genetic Tumor Syndromes
content: use client Naevoid basal cell carcinoma syndrome (Gorlin syndrome) Developmental and cutaneous tumor-predisposition syndromes Autosomal dominant Hedgehog-pathway tumor-predisposition syndrome Manifestations begin in childhood; odontogenic keratocysts typically arise after early childhood, while basal cell carcinomas usually develop later, often from adolescence onward. Affects the jaw, skin, skeleton, and central nervous system; jaw cysts and multiple basal cell carcinomas are key head and neck findings. May present with multiple jaw cysts, numerous basal cell carcinomas, palmar or plantar pits, macrocephaly, or skeletal anomalies. Apply the clinical criteria: two major and one minor criterion, or one major and three minor criteria. Major findings include multiple basal cell carcinomas or one before age 20 years, odontogenic keratocysts, palmar/plantar pits, falx cerebri calcification, and bifid or fused ribs. In an equivocal clinical presentation, demonstrate a heterozygous constitutional pathogenic variant in PTCH1 or SUFU. A germline SUFU variant does not typically produce odontogenic keratocysts; most syndrome-associated jaw cysts are linked to PTCH1 inactivation. Basal cell carcinomas show the same histological features as their sporadic counterparts; all major subtypes, including pigmented tumors, may occur. Odontogenic keratocysts resemble sporadic odontogenic keratocysts. Syndromic cyst walls may contain epithelial rests, islands, or microcysts, but these findings are not diagnostic of the syndrome. Constitutional pathogenic variants most often involve PTCH1; less commonly PTCH2 or SUFU. Use sequencing together with deletion/duplication analysis; complex alterations may require transcript-level analysis. PTCH1 or SUFU testing may be negative in a minority of clinically affected patients. Familial adenomatous polyposis, extraintestinal manifestations Jaw osteomas, supernumerary teeth, and odontomas favor FAP; multiple odontogenic keratocysts with basal cell carcinomas, palmar pits, or falx calcification favor Gorlin syndrome. Tuberous sclerosis Facial angiofibromas and oral fibromas with enamel pits favor tuberous sclerosis; multiple odontogenic keratocysts and basal cell carcinomas favor Gorlin syndrome. Neurofibromatosis type 1 Favor Neurofibromatosis type 1 when café-au-lait macules, skinfold freckling, neurofibromas, and Lisch nodules; favor Naevoid basal cell carcinoma syndrome (Gorlin syndrome) when multiple odontogenic keratocysts together with basal cell carcinomas, palmar/plantar pits, or falx calcification. Brooke-Spiegler syndrome Favor Brooke-Spiegler syndrome when multiple cylindromas, spiradenomas, spiradenocylindromas, trichoepitheliomas, or membranous parotid basal cell adenoma; favor Naevoid basal cell carcinoma syndrome (Gorlin syndrome) when multiple odontogenic keratocysts together with basal cell carcinomas, palmar/plantar pits, or falx calcification. Cowden syndrome (PTEN hamartoma tumor syndrome) Favor Cowden syndrome (PTEN hamartoma tumor syndrome) when multiple trichilemmomas, oral papillomatosis, and macrocephaly; favor Naevoid basal cell carcinoma syndrome (Gorlin syndrome) when multiple odontogenic keratocysts together with basal cell carcinomas, palmar/plantar pits, or falx calcification. Autosomal dominant neurocutaneous tumor-predisposition syndrome Cutaneous findings often begin in infancy or childhood; cutaneous neurofibromas commonly emerge around puberty. Neurofibromas may involve the skin, peripheral nerves, orbit, and periorbital tissues; orbitofacial plexiform neurofibromas are a characteristic head and neck presentation. Clinical findings include café-au-lait macules, axillary or inguinal freckling, cutaneous or plexiform neurofibromas, and Lisch nodules. A clinical diagnosis requires at least two established diagnostic features. Features include six or more café-au-lait macules, two or more neurofibromas or one plexiform neurofibroma, axillary/inguinal freckling, optic pathway glioma, two or more Lisch nodules, a characteristic osseous lesion, or an affected first-degree relative. Incorporate molecular testing and choroidal abnormalities where appropriate; Legius syndrome and other disorders may mimic selected features. Neurofibromas resemble their sporadic counterparts and contain neoplastic Schwannian cells with a mixed cellular microenvironment, including mast cells and histiocytes. Atypical neurofibromatous neoplasm of uncertain biologic potential (ANNUBP) is supported by at least two features: cytologic atypia, hypercellularity, loss of neurofibroma architecture, and increased mitotic activity. MPNST is typically a high-grade malignant spindle cell neoplasm with brisk mitotic activity and necrosis; it may arise in a plexiform neurofibroma or de novo. A constitutional pathogenic variant in NF1 is identified in most affected individuals; approximately half of cases are de novo. NF1 loss impairs neurofibromin-mediated RAS inactivation; ANNUBP may acquire CDKN2A/CDKN2B and SMARCA2-region alterations, while MPNSTs often acquire PRC2-complex abnormalities. Tuberous sclerosis is characterized by facial angiofibromas, hypomelanotic macules, shagreen patches, and CNS/renal hamartomas; NF1 is supported by café-au-lait macules, skinfold freckling, neurofibromas, and Lisch nodules. Cowden syndrome Multiple trichilemmomas, oral papillomatosis, and macrocephaly favor Cowden syndrome; neurofibromas, café-au-lait macules, and Lisch nodules favor NF1. Favor Naevoid basal cell carcinoma syndrome (Gorlin syndrome) when multiple odontogenic keratocysts together with basal cell carcinomas, palmar/plantar pits, or falx calcification; favor Neurofibromatosis type 1 when café-au-lait macules, skinfold freckling, neurofibromas, and Lisch nodules. Favor Familial adenomatous polyposis, extraintestinal manifestations when colorectal adenomatous polyposis with osteomas, odontomas, supernumerary teeth, or desmoid-type fibromatosis; favor Neurofibromatosis type 1 when café-au-lait macules, skinfold freckling, neurofibromas, and Lisch nodules. Favor Brooke-Spiegler syndrome when multiple cylindromas, spiradenomas, spiradenocylindromas, trichoepitheliomas, or membranous parotid basal cell adenoma; favor Neurofibromatosis type 1 when café-au-lait macules, skinfold freckling, neurofibromas, and Lisch nodules. Favor Cowden syndrome (PTEN hamartoma tumor syndrome) when multiple trichilemmomas, oral papillomatosis, and macrocephaly; favor Neurofibromatosis type 1 when café-au-lait macules, skinfold freckling, neurofibromas, and Lisch nodules. Autosomal dominant APC-associated polyposis and tumor-predisposition syndrome Colorectal adenomas usually develop in adolescence in classic FAP; attenuated FAP has fewer adenomas and later presentation. Head and neck manifestations include craniofacial osteomas, supernumerary teeth, odontomas, desmoid-type fibromatosis, and cribriform-morular thyroid carcinoma. A painless jaw mass, dental anomalies, an enlarging head and neck soft-tissue mass, or a thyroid nodule may prompt recognition. Classic FAP is characterized by more than 100 colorectal adenomas; attenuated FAP generally has 1–100 adenomas. The essential molecular criterion is a constitutional pathogenic APC variant. In a head and neck presentation, multiple osteomas, supernumerary teeth or odontomas, desmoid-type fibromatosis, or cribriform-morular thyroid carcinoma should prompt evaluation for FAP. Desmoid-type fibromatosis is a locally infiltrative, non-metastasizing fibroblastic/myofibroblastic neoplasm and may arise in head and neck soft tissue, maxillary sinus, nasopharynx, or oral cavity. Osteomas are composed of mature cortical or cancellous lamellar bone, commonly involving the mandible. Cribriform-morular thyroid carcinoma shows cribriform architecture admixed with morules; the cribriform component expresses TTF1 and nuclear β-catenin, while morules express CK5 and CD5. Cribriform-morular thyroid carcinoma: cribriform areas are TTF1-positive and show strong nuclear β-catenin; thyroglobulin is negative. Morules are CK5- and CD5-positive and negative for p63, p40, TTF1, and PAX8; PAX8 is absent or only focal in the cribriform component. Germline pathogenic variants in APC establish the inherited syndrome. FAP-associated desmoid tumors are driven by APC inactivation rather than the CTNNB1 mutations more typical of sporadic desmoid-type fibromatosis; nuclear β-catenin may be present. Hyperparathyroidism-jaw tumor syndrome HPT-JT causes ossifying fibromas of the jaws and parathyroid tumors; FAP is favored by colorectal polyposis, osteomas, supernumerary teeth, odontomas, and cribriform-morular thyroid carcinoma. Gorlin syndrome is associated with multiple odontogenic keratocysts and basal cell carcinomas; FAP is associated with osteomas, odontomas, supernumerary teeth, and desmoid-type fibromatosis. Favor Neurofibromatosis type 1 when café-au-lait macules, skinfold freckling, neurofibromas, and Lisch nodules; favor Familial adenomatous polyposis, extraintestinal manifestations when colorectal adenomatous polyposis with osteomas, odontomas, supernumerary teeth, or desmoid-type fibromatosis. Favor Brooke-Spiegler syndrome when multiple cylindromas, spiradenomas, spiradenocylindromas, trichoepitheliomas, or membranous parotid basal cell adenoma; favor Familial adenomatous polyposis, extraintestinal manifestations when colorectal adenomatous polyposis with osteomas, odontomas, supernumerary teeth, or desmoid-type fibromatosis. Favor Cowden syndrome (PTEN hamartoma tumor syndrome) when multiple trichilemmomas, oral papillomatosis, and macrocephaly; favor Familial adenomatous polyposis, extraintestinal manifestations when colorectal adenomatous polyposis with osteomas, odontomas, supernumerary teeth, or desmoid-type fibromatosis. Favor Tuberous sclerosis when facial and oral angiofibromas, hypomelanotic macules, shagreen patches, ungual fibromas, or cortical tubers; favor Familial adenomatous polyposis, extraintestinal manifestations when colorectal adenomatous polyposis with osteomas, odontomas, supernumerary teeth, or desmoid-type fibromatosis. Autosomal dominant CYLD-associated cutaneous adnexal tumor syndrome Cutaneous tumors often begin around puberty and increase in number throughout life; salivary gland tumors usually present after age 40. Multiple lesions predominantly involve the head and neck skin; trichoepitheliomas favor the nasolabial folds, and membranous basal cell adenomas usually involve the parotid gland. Patients develop multiple skin-colored, reddish, or blue nodules and papules; parotid tumors may be unilateral, bilateral, synchronous, or metachronous. Recognize the characteristic combination of multiple spiradenomas, cylindromas, spiradenocylindromas, and trichoepitheliomas. Membranous-type basal cell adenoma of the parotid gland is a characteristic salivary manifestation. A constitutional heterozygous pathogenic CYLD variant supports the diagnosis; multiple familial trichoepithelioma may represent a skin-limited phenotype. Cutaneous tumors are usually multiple and may coalesce; rapid growth, ulceration, or bleeding raises concern for malignant transformation. Parotid tumors are typically well-circumscribed membranous-type basal cell adenomas and may be multifocal or bilateral. Most classic cases and a substantial proportion of the multiple familial trichoepithelioma phenotype harbor constitutional pathogenic variants in CYLD. CYLD is a tumor suppressor gene; testing is useful in patients with multiple characteristic adnexal tumors and/or membranous basal cell adenoma. Tuberous sclerosis produces facial angiofibromas, shagreen patches, and ungual fibromas; Brooke-Spiegler syndrome produces multiple cylindromas, spiradenomas, trichoepitheliomas, and sometimes membranous parotid basal cell adenomas. Cowden syndrome is characterized by trichilemmomas, mucosal papillomatosis, and PTEN-associated hamartomas; Brooke-Spiegler syndrome is characterized by CYLD-associated adnexal tumors. Favor Naevoid basal cell carcinoma syndrome (Gorlin syndrome) when multiple odontogenic keratocysts together with basal cell carcinomas, palmar/plantar pits, or falx calcification; favor Brooke-Spiegler syndrome when multiple cylindromas, spiradenomas, spiradenocylindromas, trichoepitheliomas, or membranous parotid basal cell adenoma. Favor Neurofibromatosis type 1 when café-au-lait macules, skinfold freckling, neurofibromas, and Lisch nodules; favor Brooke-Spiegler syndrome when multiple cylindromas, spiradenomas, spiradenocylindromas, trichoepitheliomas, or membranous parotid basal cell adenoma. Favor Familial adenomatous polyposis, extraintestinal manifestations when colorectal adenomatous polyposis with osteomas, odontomas, supernumerary teeth, or desmoid-type fibromatosis; favor Brooke-Spiegler syndrome when multiple cylindromas, spiradenomas, spiradenocylindromas, trichoepitheliomas, or membranous parotid basal cell adenoma. Favor Cowden syndrome (PTEN hamartoma tumor syndrome) when multiple trichilemmomas, oral papillomatosis, and macrocephaly; favor Brooke-Spiegler syndrome when multiple cylindromas, spiradenomas, spiradenocylindromas, trichoepitheliomas, or membranous parotid basal cell adenoma. Autosomal dominant PTEN-associated hamartoma and cancer-predisposition syndrome Mucocutaneous manifestations often become apparent in early adulthood; the phenotype may be variable within families. Head and neck findings include facial trichilemmomas, oral mucosal papillomatosis, and multiple small keratotic papules concentrated around facial orifices. Macrocephaly and multiple mucocutaneous lesions are important clinical clues; recognition has implications for cancer surveillance. Consider the syndrome in patients with multiple mucocutaneous lesions, particularly multiple trichilemmomas and oral papillomatosis, in the appropriate clinical context. A constitutional pathogenic PTEN variant supports PTEN hamartoma tumor syndrome. Assess the broader phenotype for macrocephaly, hamartomatous lesions, and associated malignancy risk. Trichilemmomas are benign follicular tumors with outer root sheath differentiation and are a clinically important cutaneous clue. Oral papillomatosis consists of multiple papillary or verrucous mucosal lesions. Constitutional pathogenic variants in PTEN establish the molecular basis of PTEN hamartoma tumor syndrome. PTEN loss activates PI3K–AKT signaling; molecular confirmation is particularly useful when the phenotype is incomplete. Multiple cylindromas, spiradenomas, trichoepitheliomas, and membranous parotid basal cell adenoma favor Brooke-Spiegler syndrome; multiple trichilemmomas and oral papillomatosis favor Cowden syndrome. Café-au-lait macules, skinfold freckling, neurofibromas, and Lisch nodules favor NF1; macrocephaly, trichilemmomas, and mucosal papillomatosis favor Cowden syndrome. Favor Naevoid basal cell carcinoma syndrome (Gorlin syndrome) when multiple odontogenic keratocysts together with basal cell carcinomas, palmar/plantar pits, or falx calcification; favor Cowden syndrome (PTEN hamartoma tumor syndrome) when multiple trichilemmomas, oral papillomatosis, and macrocephaly. Favor Familial adenomatous polyposis, extraintestinal manifestations when colorectal adenomatous polyposis with osteomas, odontomas, supernumerary teeth, or desmoid-type fibromatosis; favor Cowden syndrome (PTEN hamartoma tumor syndrome) when multiple trichilemmomas, oral papillomatosis, and macrocephaly. Favor Tuberous sclerosis when facial and oral angiofibromas, hypomelanotic macules, shagreen patches, ungual fibromas, or cortical tubers; favor Cowden syndrome (PTEN hamartoma tumor syndrome) when multiple trichilemmomas, oral papillomatosis, and macrocephaly. Familial paraganglioma syndromes Paraganglioma and endocrine tumor-predisposition syndromes Hereditary paraganglioma-pheochromocytoma syndromes Presentation ranges from childhood to adulthood depending on the susceptibility gene; head and neck paragangliomas may be the first manifestation. Tumors arise along the parasympathetic and sympathetic paraganglionic system, particularly the carotid body, jugulotympanic region, and vagal paraganglia. Patients may present with a painless neck mass, pulsatile tinnitus, hearing symptoms, lower cranial nerve deficits, or catecholamine-related symptoms. Suspect a hereditary syndrome in patients with multiple, bilateral, multifocal, recurrent, or early-onset paragangliomas, or a relevant family history. Establish the diagnosis by identifying a constitutional pathogenic variant in a paraganglioma susceptibility gene. Consider SDHx-related disease and other established susceptibility genes in the appropriate clinical and tumor context. Head and neck paragangliomas show nests (zellballen) of chief cells separated by a delicate vascular network and sustentacular cells at the periphery. Syndrome-associated tumors generally resemble their sporadic counterparts; multiplicity, bilaterality, and family history are important clues. Chief cells typically express neuroendocrine markers; sustentacular cells can be highlighted by S100 or SOX10. Germline pathogenic variants in SDHD, SDHB, SDHC, SDHAF2, and other susceptibility genes are associated with hereditary paraganglioma syndromes. Loss of SDHB immunoreactivity in tumor cells is a useful screening clue for SDH-deficient tumors; correlate with germline testing. Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 MEN2 is characterized by medullary thyroid carcinoma, pheochromocytoma, and often hyperparathyroidism; familial paraganglioma syndromes are centered on paragangliomas and pheochromocytomas without the defining RET-associated medullary thyroid carcinoma pattern. Von Hippel-Lindau syndrome VHL may cause pheochromocytoma/paraganglioma together with retinal/CNS hemangioblastomas, renal clear cell carcinoma, pancreatic lesions, and ELST; familial paraganglioma syndromes are defined by susceptibility-gene-associated paragangliomas. Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 (MEN2) Favor Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 (MEN2) when RET-associated medullary thyroid carcinoma with pheochromocytoma, hyperparathyroidism, or mucosal neuromas; favor Familial paraganglioma syndromes when multifocal, bilateral, or familial head and neck paragangliomas with a susceptibility-gene variant. Favor Hyperparathyroidism-jaw tumor syndrome when CDC73-associated parathyroid neoplasia with jaw ossifying fibromas; favor Familial paraganglioma syndromes when multifocal, bilateral, or familial head and neck paragangliomas with a susceptibility-gene variant. Autosomal dominant RET-associated endocrine neoplasia syndrome Medullary thyroid carcinoma may develop early, particularly in MEN2B; pheochromocytoma and hyperparathyroidism vary by subtype. Head and neck disease is dominated by medullary thyroid carcinoma; adrenal pheochromocytomas are common associated tumors. Patients may present with a thyroid nodule, cervical lymphadenopathy, symptoms of catecholamine excess, mucosal neuromas, or marfanoid habitus in MEN2B. Suspect MEN2 in patients with medullary thyroid carcinoma, especially with pheochromocytoma, hyperparathyroidism, mucosal neuromas, or a family history. A constitutional activating pathogenic RET variant establishes the molecular diagnosis. Exclude or evaluate pheochromocytoma in patients with suspected MEN2 before thyroid or parathyroid surgery. Medullary thyroid carcinoma is a neuroendocrine carcinoma derived from parafollicular C cells; it may show nested, trabecular, or solid growth and stromal amyloid. MEN2B-associated mucosal neuromas contain enlarged nerve bundles and are often multiple in the lips, tongue, and oral mucosa. Medullary thyroid carcinoma typically expresses calcitonin, CEA, and neuroendocrine markers. MEN2 is caused by activating germline variants in RET. Genotype–phenotype correlations are clinically important, particularly for the timing and aggressiveness of medullary thyroid carcinoma. Familial paraganglioma syndromes present with head and neck paragangliomas and/or pheochromocytomas; MEN2 is distinguished by RET-associated medullary thyroid carcinoma and, in MEN2B, mucosal neuromas. VHL can include pheochromocytoma, but the combination of medullary thyroid carcinoma and a germline RET variant supports MEN2; retinal/CNS hemangioblastomas, renal tumors, and ELST support VHL. Favor Hyperparathyroidism-jaw tumor syndrome when CDC73-associated parathyroid neoplasia with jaw ossifying fibromas; favor Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 (MEN2) when RET-associated medullary thyroid carcinoma with pheochromocytoma, hyperparathyroidism, or mucosal neuromas. Autosomal dominant CDC73-associated parathyroid and jaw tumor syndrome Often presents in young adulthood, although age at onset is variable; no consistent sex predilection is emphasized. Jaw lesions are ossifying fibromas, often involving the mandible or maxilla; parathyroid tumors are a major systemic manifestation. Patients may present with jaw swelling, dental displacement, hypercalcemia, renal or uterine lesions, or a family history of parathyroid disease. A constitutional pathogenic CDC73 variant is an essential diagnostic criterion. Alternatively, multiple histologically confirmed parafibromin-deficient neoplasms in an individual or kindred support the diagnosis. Recognize the combination of parathyroid neoplasia and jaw ossifying fibromas; renal and uterine lesions may also occur. Jaw tumors are usually ossifying fibromas composed of cellular fibroblast-rich stroma, sometimes with a storiform pattern, admixed with bony trabeculae and/or cementum-like spherules. The jaw lesions differ from brown tumors of hyperparathyroidism, which reflect osteitis fibrosa cystica. Parathyroid tumors may show parafibromin loss; however, jaw ossifying fibromas are not reliably identified by parafibromin immunohistochemistry. Parafibromin immunohistochemistry is useful in evaluating parathyroid neoplasms; loss supports CDC73-related disease in the appropriate context. Parafibromin immunohistochemistry is not a reliable screening marker for HPT-JT-associated jaw ossifying fibromas. Germline pathogenic variants in CDC73 (HRPT2) establish the syndrome; large deletions require dedicated deletion/duplication analysis. High-impact CDC73 variants may be associated with increased risk of parathyroid carcinoma and jaw tumors. FAP-associated jaw findings are predominantly osteomas, odontomas, and supernumerary teeth; HPT-JT is characterized by ossifying fibromas with parathyroid neoplasia and CDC73 alteration. MEN2 is associated with RET-driven medullary thyroid carcinoma and pheochromocytoma; HPT-JT is associated with CDC73-related parathyroid tumors and jaw ossifying fibromas. Favor Familial paraganglioma syndromes when multifocal, bilateral, or familial head and neck paragangliomas with a susceptibility-gene variant; favor Hyperparathyroidism-jaw tumor syndrome when CDC73-associated parathyroid neoplasia with jaw ossifying fibromas. Favor Von Hippel-Lindau syndrome when retinal/CNS hemangioblastomas, renal clear cell carcinoma, pancreatic lesions, or endolymphatic sac tumor; favor Hyperparathyroidism-jaw tumor syndrome when CDC73-associated parathyroid neoplasia with jaw ossifying fibromas. Li-Fraumeni syndrome DNA repair, chromosomal instability, and telomere syndromes Autosomal dominant TP53-associated broad-spectrum cancer-predisposition syndrome Cancers characteristically occur at young ages, often in childhood or early adulthood; both sexes are affected. Head and neck tumors are uncommon but may involve the larynx, parotid gland, nasal cavity, nasopharynx, and oral cavity. A personal or family history of early-onset sarcoma, osteosarcoma, breast cancer, brain tumor, or adrenocortical carcinoma is a key clue. Apply established clinical/family-history criteria for Li-Fraumeni syndrome or Li-Fraumeni-like syndrome. The essential molecular criterion is a constitutional pathogenic TP53 variant. A head and neck malignancy, particularly at a young age or in a patient with multiple primary tumors, should prompt consideration in the appropriate family context. Head and neck tumors resemble their sporadic counterparts histologically. Reported head and neck malignancies include squamous cell carcinomas and, particularly in pediatric patients, rhabdomyosarcoma, osteosarcoma, synovial sarcoma, and pleomorphic myxoid liposarcoma. Constitutional pathogenic variants in TP53 establish the molecular diagnosis; some clinically suggestive families lack an identifiable variant. TP53 alterations impair cell-cycle arrest, apoptosis, and senescence, allowing propagation of genetically damaged cells. Fanconi anemia Fanconi anemia is distinguished by congenital anomalies, progressive bone marrow failure, crosslinker-induced chromosome breakage, and multifocal oral/head and neck SCC; Li-Fraumeni syndrome is characterized by a broad early-onset cancer spectrum and germline TP53 variants. Bloom syndrome Bloom syndrome features marked pre- and postnatal growth restriction, sun-sensitive facial rash, and increased sister-chromatid exchange; Li-Fraumeni syndrome is defined by early-onset core cancers and TP53 pathogenic variants. Dyskeratosis congenita Dyskeratosis congenita is characterized by oral leukoplakia, nail dystrophy, reticulate pigmentation, and very short telomeres; Li-Fraumeni syndrome is characterized by a broad spectrum of early-onset malignancies. Ataxia-telangiectasia Favor Ataxia-telangiectasia when progressive cerebellar ataxia, telangiectases, elevated AFP, immunodeficiency, and ATM deficiency; favor Li-Fraumeni syndrome when early-onset sarcoma, osteosarcoma, breast cancer, brain tumor, or adrenocortical carcinoma with germline TP53 variant. Inherited DNA interstrand crosslink repair disorder with marrow failure and cancer predisposition Usually recognized in childhood through congenital anomalies and progressive bone marrow failure; head and neck SCC often develops in young adulthood. Head and neck squamous mucosa is a major solid-tumor site; oral potentially malignant disorders and multifocal SCC may occur. Clinical findings may include short stature, microcephaly, hypoplastic thumbs, skin pigmentation, hearing loss, and cytopenias. Recognize the combination of congenital or developmental abnormalities, progressive bone marrow failure, and cancer predisposition. Chromosome breakage testing after diepoxybutane (DEB) or mitomycin C exposure demonstrates increased triradial and quadriradial figures. Confirm with pathogenic variants in one of the FANC pathway genes; most forms are autosomal recessive, with recognized X-linked and autosomal dominant subtypes. In patients with FA, oral leukoplakia or lichenoid lesions warrant biopsy and close surveillance even when clinically bland. FA-associated HNSCC resembles sporadic HNSCC but is often poorly differentiated and may show epithelial–mesenchymal transition. Multifocal disease may be preceded by oral potentially malignant disorders, including lichenoid keratosis or leukoplakia. The FA/BRCA pathway repairs DNA interstrand crosslinks and maintains genomic stability. DEB- or mitomycin C–induced chromosome breakage is a key functional diagnostic test; use germline testing to define the affected FANC gene. Both disorders cause marrow failure and head and neck SCC; dyskeratosis congenita has the characteristic oral leukoplakia–nail dystrophy–reticulate pigmentation triad and very short telomeres, whereas FA shows DEB/MMC-induced chromosome breakage and congenital anomalies. AT is characterized by progressive cerebellar ataxia, telangiectases, elevated AFP, and ATM-related radiosensitivity; FA is characterized by congenital anomalies, marrow failure, and crosslinker-induced chromosome breakage. Bloom syndrome features severe growth restriction, sun-sensitive facial erythema, and increased sister-chromatid exchanges; FA more typically features congenital malformations and progressive marrow failure. Favor Li-Fraumeni syndrome when early-onset sarcoma, osteosarcoma, breast cancer, brain tumor, or adrenocortical carcinoma with germline TP53 variant; favor Fanconi anemia when congenital anomalies, progressive marrow failure, and DEB/MMC-induced chromosome breakage. Inherited telomere biology disorder with marrow failure and cancer predisposition Mucocutaneous features often emerge in childhood; nail dystrophy commonly becomes apparent between ages 5 and 13 years. Head and neck involvement is characterized by oral leukoplakia, most often on the tongue; skin and nails show reticulate pigmentation and dystrophy. Bone marrow failure commonly develops during the second decade; patients are at increased risk of head and neck SCC and hematologic malignancy. Recognize the classic triad of oral leukoplakia, nail dystrophy, and reticulate skin hyperpigmentation/poikiloderma. Demonstrate markedly shortened telomeres in peripheral blood leukocytes, typically below the first percentile. Pathogenic variants in telomere biology genes are desirable for molecular confirmation and subtype definition. Cutaneous findings are nonspecific and may include epidermal atrophy, dermal telangiectasia, and pigment incontinence. Oral leukoplakia requires assessment for epithelial dysplasia and invasive SCC; the syndrome itself does not define a unique tumor histology. Genes include DKC1, TERC, TERT, TINF2, NOP10, NHP2, WRAP53, CTC1, and others involved in telomere maintenance. Flow-FISH or another validated telomere-length assay can demonstrate telomeres below the first percentile in peripheral blood leukocytes. Fanconi anemia is supported by congenital anomalies, marrow failure, and DEB/MMC-induced chromosome breakage; dyskeratosis congenita is supported by the mucocutaneous triad and critically short telomeres. Bloom syndrome features growth restriction and sun-sensitive facial rash with increased sister-chromatid exchange; dyskeratosis congenita features nail dystrophy, oral leukoplakia, reticulate pigmentation, and telomere shortening. AT features progressive cerebellar ataxia, conjunctival telangiectases, elevated AFP, and immunodeficiency; dyskeratosis congenita features mucocutaneous abnormalities and telomere shortening. Favor Li-Fraumeni syndrome when early-onset sarcoma, osteosarcoma, breast cancer, brain tumor, or adrenocortical carcinoma with germline TP53 variant; favor Dyskeratosis congenita when oral leukoplakia, nail dystrophy, reticulate pigmentation, and critically short telomeres. Autosomal recessive ATM-related DNA double-strand break repair disorder Classic disease begins in early childhood with progressive cerebellar ataxia; variant disease may present later in adulthood. Telangiectases typically involve the bulbar conjunctiva and bridge of the nose; head and neck malignancies may involve Waldeyer ring and the parotid gland. Recurrent sinopulmonary infections, immunodeficiency, hypogonadism, and insulin resistance may accompany the neurologic findings. Characteristic progressive cerebellar ataxia and cerebellar degeneration, with telangiectases when present; telangiectases may be absent in young children and variant cases. Serum alpha-fetoprotein is elevated in more than 95% of patients. Supportive findings include reduced IgA/IgE or selected IgG subclasses, lymphopenia, and increased chromosome breakage after X-ray exposure. Confirm with biallelic pathogenic variants in ATM. Tumors arising in AT generally resemble their sporadic counterparts. B- and T-cell lymphoid neoplasms predominate and may involve Waldeyer ring; myeloid neoplasms are uncommon. Biallelic pathogenic variants in ATM establish the molecular diagnosis; MRE11A variants can cause a rare AT-like disorder. ATM deficiency impairs the response to DNA double-strand breaks and causes hypersensitivity to ionizing radiation. FA is characterized by congenital anomalies, marrow failure, and DEB/MMC-induced chromosome breakage; AT is characterized by early-onset cerebellar ataxia, telangiectases, elevated AFP, and ATM deficiency. Dyskeratosis congenita is defined by mucocutaneous triad and critically short telomeres; AT is defined by neurologic degeneration, telangiectases, immunodeficiency, and elevated AFP. Bloom syndrome presents with severe growth restriction and sun-sensitive rash; AT presents with progressive ataxia and telangiectases. Favor Li-Fraumeni syndrome when early-onset sarcoma, osteosarcoma, breast cancer, brain tumor, or adrenocortical carcinoma with germline TP53 variant; favor Ataxia-telangiectasia when progressive cerebellar ataxia, telangiectases, elevated AFP, immunodeficiency, and ATM deficiency. Autosomal recessive BLM-related chromosomal instability syndrome Growth restriction is prominent from early life, with reduced height, weight, and head circumference; both sexes are affected. A sun-sensitive rash commonly appears during infancy on the cheeks and nose; head and neck cancers include oropharyngeal carcinoma. Other clues include a long narrow face, prominent nose and ears, small mandible, recurrent respiratory infections, and male infertility. Recognize marked pre- and postnatal growth restriction with characteristic facial features and sun-sensitive facial rash. Confirm with biallelic pathogenic variants in BLM. Increased sister-chromatid exchange frequency on specialized cytogenetic studies supports the diagnosis. There is no unique histologic appearance for Bloom-associated tumors; tumors are evaluated according to their site-specific diagnostic criteria. Oropharyngeal carcinomas and other epithelial malignancies resemble their sporadic counterparts. BLM encodes a RECQ-family DNA helicase; loss of function causes replication errors, chromosomal rearrangements, and genomic instability. Biallelic BLM pathogenic variants and increased sister-chromatid exchanges are diagnostically useful. Both are chromosomal instability syndromes with cancer predisposition; FA is characterized by congenital anomalies and marrow failure with DEB/MMC-induced chromosome breakage, whereas Bloom syndrome is marked by severe growth restriction and sun-sensitive rash with increased sister-chromatid exchanges. Dyskeratosis congenita shows oral leukoplakia, nail dystrophy, reticulate pigmentation, and telomere shortening; Bloom syndrome shows growth restriction, facial erythema, and BLM-related sister-chromatid exchange. Li-Fraumeni syndrome is defined by early-onset core tumors and germline TP53 variants; Bloom syndrome has characteristic growth restriction, sun sensitivity, and BLM-related chromosomal instability. Favor Ataxia-telangiectasia when progressive cerebellar ataxia, telangiectases, elevated AFP, immunodeficiency, and ATM deficiency; favor Bloom syndrome when marked growth restriction, sun-sensitive facial rash, and increased sister-chromatid exchanges with BLM variants. Autosomal dominant VHL tumor-predisposition syndrome Most patients present between ages 30 and 40 years, although presentation ranges from childhood to late adulthood; there is a female predominance in reported series. Head and neck manifestations include endolymphatic sac tumors of the temporal bone and occasional head and neck paragangliomas; retinal and CNS hemangioblastomas are major associated tumors. Hearing loss may be the presenting symptom of an endolymphatic sac tumor; visual loss, cerebellar ataxia, spinal cord compression, or hormone-excess symptoms may occur. A constitutional pathogenic VHL variant with at least one associated neoplasm is an essential diagnostic combination. In the absence of an identified VHL variant, retinal and/or CNS hemangioblastomas together with another characteristic VHL-associated neoplasm support the diagnosis. Genetic testing should be considered in every patient with an endolymphatic sac tumor; patients with VHL require radiographic screening for these tumors. Endolymphatic sac tumors are papillary and/or cystic, often with temporal bone remodeling; bland cuboidal-to-columnar cells form broad interdigitating papillae with fibrovascular cores. Tumor cells have abundant clear or vacuolated cytoplasm and relatively uniform nuclei; mitoses, necrosis, and marked pleomorphism are inconspicuous. CNS hemangioblastomas contain neoplastic stromal cells with abundant reactive vasculature; cellular and reticular patterns occur. VHL-associated paragangliomas may show clear, vacuolated tumor cells in myxoid, edematous, or hyalinized stroma. Endolymphatic sac tumor: pancytokeratin, CK7, EMA, HIF1α, GLUT1, membranous CAIX, and nuclear PAX8 are positive; TTF1 and thyroglobulin are negative. VHL-associated paragangliomas often show membranous CAIX and may express alpha-inhibin. Constitutional pathogenic variants in the VHL tumor suppressor gene establish the syndrome; somatic second hits inactivate the remaining allele in tumors. Type 1 disease is commonly associated with deletion or truncating variants; type 2 disease is commonly associated with missense variants. Both may produce head and neck paragangliomas; VHL is favored by retinal/CNS hemangioblastomas, renal clear cell carcinoma, pancreatic lesions, and endolymphatic sac tumors, while SDHx-related syndromes are centered on paragangliomas. MEN2 is characterized by RET-associated medullary thyroid carcinoma with pheochromocytoma; VHL is distinguished by hemangioblastomas, renal clear cell carcinoma, pancreatic cystic/neuroendocrine lesions, and endolymphatic sac tumors. Favor Hyperparathyroidism-jaw tumor syndrome when CDC73-associated parathyroid neoplasia with jaw ossifying fibromas; favor Von Hippel-Lindau syndrome when retinal/CNS hemangioblastomas, renal clear cell carcinoma, pancreatic lesions, or endolymphatic sac tumor. Autosomal dominant TSC1/TSC2-related multisystem hamartoma syndrome Cutaneous and oral manifestations may begin in childhood; cardiac rhabdomyomas often present in newborns and infants younger than 2 years. Head and neck findings include facial angiofibromas, fibrous cephalic plaques, shagreen patches, poliosis, oral angiofibromas, and dental enamel pits. Angiofibromas favor the centrofacial cheeks, nasolabial folds, chin, anterior gingiva, lips, tongue, and palate. A constitutional pathogenic variant in TSC1 or TSC2 is independently sufficient for a definitive diagnosis. Clinical diagnosis is based on established major and minor features; evaluate the skin, oral cavity, CNS, heart, kidneys, and lungs. Do not diagnose the syndrome from a single facial angiofibroma or other isolated feature because individual manifestations may occur sporadically. Angiofibromas are well-circumscribed nodules of bland oval cells with delicate collagen and evenly distributed small-to-medium-sized vessels. Fibrous cephalic plaques show thickened collagen bundles with decreased or absent elastic fibers; dilated vessels may mimic angiofibroma. Constitutional pathogenic variants in TSC1 (hamartin) or TSC2 (tuberin) establish the diagnosis. Loss of the hamartin–tuberin complex leads to mTOR pathway activation; TSC2 deletions may extend into PKD1 and cause a contiguous-gene phenotype. NF1 is characterized by café-au-lait macules, skinfold freckling, neurofibromas, and Lisch nodules; tuberous sclerosis is characterized by facial angiofibromas, hypomelanotic macules, shagreen patches, ungual fibromas, and CNS/renal hamartomas. Brooke-Spiegler syndrome produces multiple cylindromas, spiradenomas, and trichoepitheliomas; tuberous sclerosis produces facial/oral angiofibromas and fibrous cephalic plaques. Gorlin syndrome is characterized by basal cell carcinomas, odontogenic keratocysts, palmar/plantar pits, and falx calcification; tuberous sclerosis is characterized by angiofibromas, enamel pits, cortical tubers, and renal angiomyolipomas. Favor Familial adenomatous polyposis, extraintestinal manifestations when colorectal adenomatous polyposis with osteomas, odontomas, supernumerary teeth, or desmoid-type fibromatosis; favor Tuberous sclerosis when facial and oral angiofibromas, hypomelanotic macules, shagreen patches, ungual fibromas, or cortical tubers. Favor Cowden syndrome (PTEN hamartoma tumor syndrome) when multiple trichilemmomas, oral papillomatosis, and macrocephaly; favor Tuberous sclerosis when facial and oral angiofibromas, hypomelanotic macules, shagreen patches, ungual fibromas, or cortical tubers. All PathologyGPS / Head and Neck / Hereditary Tumor Syndromes Head and Neck Genetic Tumor Syndromes A diagnostic reference to inherited tumor-predisposition syndromes with head and neck manifestations, emphasizing clinical recognition, essential diagnostic criteria, morphology, immunophenotype, molecular findings, and focused differential diagnosis. Core diagnostic principle Recognize the syndrome from the tumor pattern and the accompanying phenotype. Multiplicity, bilaterality, unusually young age, characteristic associated lesions, and family history should prompt consideration of germline testing. Diagnostic approach: when to consider a hereditary syndrome Look for multiplicity Multiple, bilateral, multifocal, recurrent, or metachronous tumors may indicate an inherited predisposition. Check the age Tumors arising unusually early, multiple primary cancers, or childhood malignancies warrant attention. Connect the phenotype Correlate the tumor with skin, oral, dental, skeletal, neurologic, endocrine, hematologic, and visceral findings. Confirm the mechanism Use syndrome-directed germline testing, functional assays, and tumor immunohistochemistry where appropriate. Entity reference Diagnostic profiles and differential diagnosis All 15 syndromes are independently expandable. Same-group syndromes are included in one another’s differential diagnosis. title: Nasal Paranasal Skull Base Tumors
content: use client Sinonasal papilloma, inverted Sinonasal papilloma Benign; locally recurrent; malignant transformation risk Typically affects older adults, with peak incidence in the sixth decade. Marked male predominance (approximately 3–5:1). Usually arises from the lateral nasal wall and/or ethmoid or maxillary sinus. Presents with unilateral nasal obstruction; rhinorrhea, epistaxis, facial pressure, headache, anosmia, or epiphora may occur. Predominantly endophytic, non-destructive epithelial growth. Rounded nests and ribbons of hyperplastic immature squamous (Schneiderian) epithelium within edematous, hypocellular stroma. Intact basement membrane around epithelial nests. Prominent transmigrating intraepithelial neutrophils are a characteristic clue. Assess carefully for severe dysplasia or an associated invasive carcinoma. Architecture Endophytic ribbons and rounded nests; broad mucosal attachment; basement membrane remains intact. Epithelium Hyperplastic immature squamous/transitional-type epithelium; scattered ciliated or mucous columnar cells may be present superficially. Inflammation Prominent transmigrating intraepithelial neutrophils are characteristic. Dysplasia Uncommon; may be keratinizing or nonkeratinizing. Severe dysplasia / carcinoma in situ should be identified and reported. Carcinoma warning Basaloid growth, conspicuous atypia, increased or atypical mitoses, and loss of intraepithelial neutrophils raise concern for nonkeratinizing SCC. High-risk HPV RNA ISH Usually negative for transcriptionally active high-risk HPV; useful when distinguishing from high-risk HPV-associated nonkeratinizing SCC. Low-risk HPV A subset shows transcriptionally active low-risk HPV; not required for diagnosis. EGFR No routine diagnostic IHC marker; EGFR mutation testing is molecular rather than immunohistochemical. Nonkeratinizing squamous cell carcinoma May also grow endophytically but more often shows basaloid cytology, pleomorphism, increased/atypical mitoses, predominantly exophytic growth, and loss of transmigrating neutrophils; high-risk HPV RNA ISH is often positive in HPV-associated SCC. Oncocytic sinonasal papilloma Shows multilayered oncocytic cuboidal-to-columnar cells and characteristic mucinous microcysts / neutrophilic microabscesses. Exophytic sinonasal papilloma Predominantly papillary, exophytic fronds with fibrovascular cores, usually arising from the anterior nasal septum. Somatic EGFR mutations, usually exon 20 in-frame insertions/deletions, occur in a large subset. A subset is associated with transcriptionally active low-risk HPV; EGFR mutation and low-risk HPV appear mutually exclusive. TP53 and/or CDKN2A alterations are associated with malignant progression. Do not equate endophytic growth alone with carcinoma; assess cytology, mitoses, neutrophilic inflammation, and invasion. High-risk HPV negativity does not establish inverted papilloma without the characteristic morphology. Recurrence and synchronous/metachronous carcinoma are clinically important; thoroughly sample suspicious solid or atypical areas. Sinonasal papilloma, oncocytic Benign; recurrence and malignant transformation may occur Typically occurs in older adults, peaking in the sixth to seventh decades; uncommon below age 30. Sex distribution is approximately equal. Usually involves the lateral nasal wall and/or paranasal sinuses, most often the maxillary sinus. Presents with unilateral nasal obstruction; rhinorrhea, epistaxis, and anosmia may occur. Noninvasive papillary epithelial neoplasm with mixed exophytic and endophytic growth. Multiple layers of cuboidal-to-columnar cells with abundant oncocytic cytoplasm. Intraepithelial microcysts containing mucin and/or neutrophilic microabscesses are characteristic. Dysplasia is uncommon; assess for increased atypia and mitotic activity. Mixed exophytic and endophytic papillary growth. Multilayered cuboidal-to-columnar cells with abundant oncocytic cytoplasm and centrally placed, mildly enlarged / irregular nuclei. Intraepithelial neutrophils are common. Microcysts Mucin-containing microcysts and/or neutrophilic microabscesses are characteristic. Uncommon; increased nuclear atypia and mitotic activity warrant careful evaluation. Diagnostic IHC No defining immunohistochemical profile is specified; morphology is central to diagnosis. HPV HPV is not considered an etiologic factor. Inverted sinonasal papilloma Predominantly endophytic ribbons/nests of immature squamous epithelium with prominent transmigrating neutrophils; oncocytic cells and mucinous microcysts favor oncocytic papilloma. Anterior septal origin and multilayered squamous/respiratory-type epithelium without oncocytic cytoplasm or characteristic microcysts. Papillary squamous cell carcinoma Shows cytologic malignancy, destructive invasion, and/or atypical mitotic activity rather than bland noninvasive papillomatous epithelium. Activating KRAS mutations in exon 2 or 3 are reported. TP53 and CDKN2A alterations are associated with malignant progression. Do not diagnose carcinoma based on papillary complexity alone; assess cytologic atypia and invasion. Recurrence and malignant transformation are reported; thoroughly sample large, heterogeneous, or atypical areas. Sinonasal papilloma, exophytic Benign; malignant change is extremely rare Typically affects adults aged 20–50 years, with a range extending from childhood to old age. Male predominance (approximately 2–10:1). Usually arises from the lower anterior nasal septum; paranasal sinus origin is extremely rare. Presents with epistaxis and unilateral nasal obstruction. Exophytic papillary proliferation with broad fronds and delicate fibrovascular cores. Fronds are covered by multilayered sinonasal-type epithelium, approximately 5–20 cells thick. No high-grade squamous dysplasia and no destructive infiltrative growth. Low-risk HPV, especially types 6 and 11, is present in most cases. Broad exophytic papillary fronds with delicate fibrovascular cores. Maturing multilayered epithelium, ranging from squamous to ciliated pseudostratified respiratory type; transitional forms occur. Additional cells Scattered mucocytes and intraepithelial neutrophils are common. Keratinization Absent or scant unless secondary to trauma or drying. Cytology Mitoses are rare and nonatypical; high-grade dysplasia is not a feature. No defining IHC profile is specified; diagnosis is based on architecture and epithelial maturation. Low-risk HPV (usually types 6 and 11) is detected in most tumors; this is generally assessed by molecular / in situ methods rather than routine IHC. Cutaneous squamous papilloma More often arises in the nasal vestibule and shows keratinizing cutaneous-type squamous epithelium. Shows endophytic nests/ribbons of immature squamous epithelium rather than broad exophytic fronds. Shows significant cytologic atypia, increased / atypical mitoses, and destructive invasion. Most cases harbor low-risk HPV, predominantly types 6 and 11. Confirm the site of origin; a vestibular lesion may be a cutaneous squamous papilloma. Do not overcall scant surface keratinization as dysplasia when it is attributable to trauma or drying. Sinonasal glomangiopericytoma Mesenchymal tumor Usually indolent; locally recurrent in a subset Can occur at any age but peaks in the sixth to seventh decades. Slight female predominance. Usually unilateral in the nasal cavity, involving the turbinates or septum; may extend into ethmoid or maxillary sinuses. Typically presents with nasal obstruction and/or epistaxis. Well-delineated submucosal proliferation of ovoid-to-spindle myoid cells in a richly vascularized stroma. Complex branching thin-walled vessels, including staghorn-like channels, with characteristic perivascular hyalinization. Tumor cells show a syncytial arrangement with blunt-ended nuclei and eosinophilic-to-clear cytoplasm. Mild atypia and limited mitotic activity are typical; necrosis is usually absent. Actin and nuclear beta-catenin expression support the diagnosis in the appropriate morphologic setting. Growth pattern Unencapsulated but well-delineated submucosal tumor, often separated from intact surface epithelium by a tumor-free zone. Tumor cells Syncytial ovoid-to-spindle cells with blunt-ended nuclei, coarse chromatin, and slightly eosinophilic-to-clear cytoplasm. Vasculature Ramifying capillary-sized to large, patulous staghorn vessels. Vessel walls Peritheliomatous hyalinization is a characteristic clue. Background Extravasated erythrocytes, mast cells, and eosinophils are common. Cytologic grade Usually mild pleomorphism, few mitoses, and no necrosis; marked atypia, atypical / increased mitoses, or necrosis suggest aggressive behavior. Late local recurrence may occur; prolonged follow-up is appropriate. Low-grade malignant; locally recurrent; metastasis not reported Occurs in adults, mean age approximately 53 years (reported range 24–85). Notable female predominance. Primarily involves the nasal cavity and ethmoid sinus; any sinonasal site may be affected. Presents with nasal obstruction, pain, epistaxis, or rhinorrhea; orbital or skull-base extension may cause diplopia or neurologic complications. Unencapsulated, infiltrative, monotonous spindle-cell neoplasm with medium-to-long fascicles, often in a herringbone pattern. Tumor cells have uniform ovoid or wavy nuclei, fine chromatin, inconspicuous nucleoli, and scant pale eosinophilic cytoplasm. S100 and SMA are consistently positive; SOX10 is consistently negative. Mitotic activity is usually low (<2/mm²); necrosis is absent. PAX3 rearrangement is desirable for confirmation in selected cases. Infiltrative, unencapsulated spindle-cell proliferation in medium-to-long fascicles, often herringbone. Uniform ovoid or wavy nuclei with fine chromatin and small / inconspicuous nucleoli; scant pale eosinophilic cytoplasm. Entrapped epithelium Hyperplastic respiratory epithelium is commonly entrapped within the tumor. Vessels / stroma Hypocellular fibrous areas and thin-walled hemangiopericytoma-like vessels are common. Invasion Bone infiltration is common; extension to the orbit, anterior skull base, cribriform plate, and brain may occur. Proliferation Mitotic activity is consistently low, usually <2/mm²; necrosis is absent. S100 Consistently positive, sometimes heterogeneous. SOX10 Consistently negative; an important distinction from schwannian tumors. Consistently positive. Desmin Positive in approximately one-half to two-thirds of cases. MYOD1 / myogenin Usually negative or only patchy / focal; rhabdomyoblastic differentiation is uncommon. PAX3 Nuclear staining is present in most cases with an appropriate antibody clone. Pan-TRK Commonly positive but not specific. Focal nuclear staining may occur. Synovial sarcoma Can be spindle-cell and keratin / EMA positive; SS18::SSX fusion or specific fusion IHC supports synovial sarcoma. Cellular schwannoma Usually diffuse SOX10 and S100 positivity; BSNS is SOX10 negative and SMA positive. Shows a prominent branching vascular network, perivascular hyalinization, and nuclear beta-catenin; BSNS is infiltrative and PAX3-rearranged. Nuclear STAT6 and NAB2::STAT6 fusion favor SFT. PAX3::MAML3 is the most common fusion (approximately 60%). Alternative PAX3 partners include NCOA1, NCOA2, FOXO1, and WWTR1. The bland cytology belies malignant behavior; local infiltration and recurrence are important. S100 positivity alone may suggest a neural tumor; the combination of SMA positivity and SOX10 negativity is highly useful. Decalcification can cause FISH failure; consider RNA-based sequencing when tissue permits. Arises in the nasal cavity (septum or lateral wall) and/or paranasal sinuses. Central loosely arranged stellate reticulum-like material. Peripheral palisading with reverse nuclear polarity and subnuclear vacuolization. Stellate reticulum Loose microcystic stellate reticulum-like areas intermingle with denser epithelial areas and wet keratin. Classify the architecture Papillary / inverted epithelial, basaloid, spindle-cell, perivascular myoid, or small round-cell. Practical biopsy and reporting checklist Document the exact anatomic epicenter and correlate with CT / MRI, especially for cribriform plate, skull-base, orbital, and intracranial extension. For papillomas, sample the attachment and all areas with altered architecture, atypia, or suspected invasion. For spindle-cell lesions, assess infiltrative growth, bone involvement, mitotic activity, and necrosis; use a focused panel rather than a broad indiscriminate panel. For suspected olfactory neuroblastoma, document Hyams grade and evaluate for sustentacular cells, neuropil, and high-grade areas. State limitations when decalcification or small biopsy material may compromise fusion testing or assessment of invasion. Diagnostic note: Immunohistochemical and molecular findings should be interpreted in the context of morphology and anatomic site. A marker result alone is not a substitute for adequate sampling and clinicoradiologic correlation.

There is a peak incidence in the fourth and fifth decades of life and a slight male predilection. RCs are located at the apex of a tooth root, or on the lateral aspect of the root associated with a lateral root canal. The most common site is the anterior maxilla, where 40–50% arise, followed by the lower molar area. RCs are always associated with a non-vital tooth. Deposits of cholesterol crystals (clefts) with foreign body giant cells are often seen and may form luminal nodules. Residual and longstanding cysts are less inflamed and have a more regular thin epithelium. Residual cyst (residual radicular cyst) is a radicular cyst that is retained in the jaw after removal of the causative tooth.
