title: Pharyngeal Laryngeal Tracheal Parapharyngeal Tumors
content: use client Hairy polyp Nasopharyngeal hamartoma Benign developmental lesion Usually presents in neonates or young children; adult cases are exceptionally rare. Marked female predominance (male-to-female ratio approximately 1:6). Most often arises from the lateral nasopharyngeal wall; may also involve the oropharynx, palate, tongue, lip, or middle ear. Symptoms reflect size and mobility: airway obstruction, stridor, feeding or swallowing difficulty, hypersalivation, and vomiting. Polypoid lesion with an external ectodermal covering resembling skin. Underlying tissue contains mesodermal elements, with fibroadipose tissue consistently present. No endodermal tissue is identified. Clinical and radiologic correlation may show a smooth fat-containing polyp with a fibrovascular stalk. Surface Keratinizing stratified squamous epithelium with skin adnexa, including hair follicles and sebaceous units. Stroma Fibroadipose tissue is uniformly present. Additional mesodermal elements Cartilage, bone, skeletal muscle, and/or smooth muscle may be present. Uncommon elements Meningothelial, minor salivary gland, or odontogenic elements are rarely encountered. IHC No diagnostic immunohistochemical panel is required; diagnosis is based on the characteristic ectodermal and mesodermal components. Dermoid cyst A cystic lesion with keratinizing squamous lining and skin adnexa; hairy polyp is a polypoid, predominantly solid structure with mesodermal tissue. Teratoma Contains derivatives of all three germ layers; endodermal elements are not a component of hairy polyp. Other nasopharyngeal polyps Lack the combination of skin-like ectodermal covering and underlying mesodermal tissues. Molecular testing is not diagnostically relevant. Do not use the obsolete terms dermoid polyp or teratoid polyp. Recognize that congenital airway symptoms may be the dominant clinical presentation. Salivary gland anlage tumor Benign; recurrence has not been reported after excision Predominantly affects infants, usually diagnosed by 3 months of age. Male predominance; prenatal presentation has been reported. Arises in the posterior nasal septum or posterior nasopharyngeal wall. May cause feeding difficulty and respiratory distress from nasal airway obstruction; polyhydramnios may be detected prenatally. Polypoid lesion showing a complex network of ducts and solid-cystic squamous nests. Ducts and squamous nests are continuous with the surface squamous epithelium. Subepithelial stroma ranges from hypocellular to cellular and spindle-cell rich. Cytologic atypia and mitotic activity are absent. Cytokeratin and SMA expression in stromal spindle cells is supportive in selected cases. Ductal architecture Complex network of tubules and ducts in the submucosa. Squamous component Solid and cystic squamous nests show variable keratinization and continuity with surface epithelium. Subepithelial stroma is often hypocellular, with more cellular stromal nodules centrally. Cytology Atypia and mitoses are absent. Cytokeratins Highlight epithelial ducts and nests; stromal spindle cells may also be positive. SMA Positive in the myoepithelial-like stromal cells; supports the diagnosis in selected cases. Pleomorphic adenoma Usually occurs in older patients and shows a conventional salivary neoplasm with ductal and myoepithelial components in chondromyxoid stroma. Embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma Shows malignant primitive cells, mitotic activity, and skeletal muscle differentiation; these features are absent in salivary gland anlage tumor. Sinonasal teratoma Contains a broader range of mature or immature tissue types rather than the characteristic epithelial-stromal pattern. Whole-exome sequencing of a small number of cases has not identified plausible driver mutations; no diagnostic molecular test is established. The term congenital pleomorphic adenoma is not recommended. The combination of surface continuity, bland squamous nests/ducts, and characteristic stroma is more useful than any single immunostain. Low-grade nasopharyngeal papillary adenocarcinoma Nasopharyngeal carcinoma Low-grade malignant; indolent Occurs across a wide age range, from the first through eighth decades. No sex predilection. Most often involves the posterior nasopharyngeal wall or roof; may arise elsewhere in the nasopharynx. Common presentations include nasal obstruction and blood-stained rhinorrhea. Unencapsulated epithelial neoplasm with complex papillary and glandular architecture. Papillae show arborization and fibrovascular cores; complex glands may be back-to-back, cribriform, or microcystic. Tumor infiltrates the submucosa and shows low-grade cytology. A transition from surface epithelium to tumor supports a primary nasopharyngeal origin. TTF1 positivity with negative thyroglobulin and PAX8 supports the diagnosis in selected cases. Architecture Complex arborizing papillae with fibrovascular cores, admixed with glandular, cribriform, and microcystic patterns. Pseudostratified columnar to cuboidal cells with round-to-oval nuclei, vesicular or optically clear chromatin, and eosinophilic cytoplasm. Atypia / mitoses Mild-to-moderate nuclear pleomorphism; scattered mitoses may occur, but atypical mitoses are absent. Invasion Infiltrative growth into the submucosa; surface epithelial transition may be seen. Pancytokeratin / EMA Diffuse positivity. TTF1 Positive, including in spindle and squamous components when present. Thyroglobulin / PAX8 Negative; useful in excluding metastatic papillary thyroid carcinoma. EBER Negative. p16 / p40 / p63 / S100 Negative in the described profile. Ki-67 Consistently low, typically below 5%. Papillary thyroid carcinoma Usually expresses thyroglobulin and PAX8; nasopharyngeal papillary adenocarcinoma is negative for both and may show surface epithelial transition. Sinonasal papilloma Usually lacks the extensive submucosal infiltrative growth and complex glandular architecture of this carcinoma. Metastatic thyroid-like carcinoma Correlate with thyroid imaging and use a thyroid-lineage panel; TTF1 alone is not specific. A ROS1::GOPC fusion has been reported in an individual case; no recurrent defining molecular alteration is established. TTF1 positivity alone does not establish thyroid origin. Demonstrating submucosal invasion is important in distinguishing this carcinoma from a benign papillomatous lesion. Malignant epithelial neoplasm Occurs across age groups; incidence is strongly influenced by geographic and ethnic background. Nonkeratinizing carcinoma is associated with EBV and is common in endemic regions; keratinizing carcinoma is more strongly associated with tobacco and alcohol exposure. Most often arises from the lateral nasopharyngeal wall, especially the fossa of Rosenmüller. Common presentation is a painless enlarging upper neck mass; nasal obstruction, blood-stained postnasal drip, epistaxis, otologic symptoms, and cranial neuropathies may occur. Infiltrative poorly differentiated carcinoma, usually with limited overt squamous differentiation, for nonkeratinizing carcinoma. Variable admixture of lymphocytes and plasma cells is common in nonkeratinizing carcinoma. Pancytokeratin confirms epithelial differentiation; EBER positivity strongly supports nonkeratinizing nasopharyngeal carcinoma. Keratinizing carcinoma shows invasive squamous cell carcinoma with overt keratinization. Basaloid squamous cell carcinoma shows invasive high-grade basaloid nests with comedonecrosis and an identifiable squamous component. Nonkeratinizing, undifferentiated Syncytial sheets, irregular islands, trabeculae, or discohesive cells; large vesicular nuclei and prominent nucleoli. Nonkeratinizing, differentiated More cellular stratification and pavementing, often with plexiform growth; smaller cells and more distinct borders. Inflammatory background Variable lymphocytes and plasma cells may fragment tumor nests into tiny clusters or single cells. Keratinizing Invasive squamous carcinoma with intercellular bridges and variable keratinization, often with desmoplastic stroma. Basaloid High-grade basaloid nests, often with comedonecrosis; abrupt keratinization or an associated conventional SCC / surface dysplasia establishes squamous differentiation. Pancytokeratin Strong tumor-cell positivity. p40 / p63 / high-molecular-weight cytokeratins Usually positive and support squamous differentiation. EBER ISH Positive in practically all nonkeratinizing carcinomas; variable in keratinizing and basaloid carcinomas. CK7 / CK20 Usually negative. SOX10 May be positive in basaloid nasopharyngeal carcinoma; interpret in morphologic context. Lymphoma Tumor cells are epithelial and pancytokeratin-positive; lymphoma expresses lineage-specific hematolymphoid markers. Oropharyngeal HPV-associated SCC metastatic to nasopharynx / node Use p16 and high-risk HPV testing as appropriate, and correlate with the primary site; EBER supports EBV-associated NPC. Sinonasal undifferentiated carcinoma May be poorly differentiated but lacks the characteristic EBV association in most cases; use a broad lineage-directed panel and EBER. Metastatic carcinoma Correlate with imaging and clinical history; EBER positivity in tumor cells supports NPC in the appropriate setting. Hodgkin lymphoma Large NPC cells may resemble Reed–Sternberg cells, but epithelial markers and EBER pattern establish carcinoma. EBER in situ hybridization is diagnostically useful, particularly in nonkeratinizing carcinoma and metastatic specimens. Plasma EBV DNA is useful for disease assessment and surveillance but is not a tissue-based histologic diagnostic test. Somatic alterations frequently affect CDKN2A, NF-κB signaling, chromatin modifiers, PI3K/MAPK, NOTCH, and TGF-beta pathways; these are not individually diagnostic. Do not diagnose NPC from a lymphocyte-rich background alone; demonstrate epithelial tumor cells. EBER is usually positive in nonkeratinizing NPC but may be variable or negative in keratinizing and basaloid subtypes. The historical distinction between differentiated and undifferentiated nonkeratinizing carcinoma has no established clinical or prognostic value. Squamous papilloma and papillomatosis Precursor and benign epithelial lesions Benign; recurrence may occur, especially with multifocal disease Can occur at any age; recurrent respiratory papillomatosis often begins in childhood, while adult-onset disease also occurs. Larynx is the most common site; lesions may involve the hypopharynx, trachea, and other respiratory mucosa. Presents with hoarseness, dysphonia, cough, stridor, or airway obstruction depending on site and burden. Exophytic papillary proliferation with fibrovascular cores covered by mature squamous epithelium. Koilocytosis may be present, particularly in HPV-associated lesions. No destructive stromal invasion or high-grade cytologic atypia. Papillomatosis is characterized by multiple or recurrent papillomas involving the respiratory tract. Papillary fronds with fibrovascular cores. Epithelium Mature stratified squamous epithelium, often with orderly maturation. Viral cytopathic effect Koilocytosis may be present. Destructive stromal invasion is absent in benign papilloma. p16 Not a reliable stand-alone surrogate for HPV in laryngeal papilloma; interpret with morphology and, when needed, HPV-specific testing. HPV testing Low-risk HPV, particularly types 6 and 11, is associated with respiratory papillomatosis; molecular or in situ testing may be used in selected cases. Papillary squamous cell carcinoma Shows cytologic atypia, loss of maturation, and invasive growth. Verrucous carcinoma Shows broad pushing invasion and a verruciform architecture rather than delicate benign papillary fronds. Squamous dysplasia Shows disordered maturation and cytologic atypia rather than orderly maturation in a benign papilloma. Low-risk HPV, especially types 6 and 11, is associated with recurrent respiratory papillomatosis. Assess the epithelial-stromal interface carefully in fragmented or superficial biopsies. Extensive or recurrent disease warrants evaluation for dysplasia or invasive carcinoma. Laryngeal and hypopharyngeal epithelial dysplasia Precursor lesion with variable risk of progression Occurs predominantly in adults, with strong association with tobacco and alcohol exposure. Most commonly involves the true vocal folds; hypopharyngeal mucosa may also be affected. Presents with persistent hoarseness, dysphonia, or a mucosal white or erythematous lesion. Squamous epithelial atypia and disordered maturation without stromal invasion. Grade according to the extent and severity of architectural disorder and cytologic atypia. Exclude reactive atypia, tangential sectioning, and inflammation-related changes. No stromal invasion is present; any suspicious interface requires deeper levels or additional sampling. Low-grade dysplasia Atypia and disordered maturation are predominantly confined to the lower epithelial layers. High-grade dysplasia More extensive architectural disorder and cytologic atypia involve much of the epithelial thickness. Keratinization Hyperkeratosis and parakeratosis may accompany dysplasia. Basement membrane remains intact; stromal invasion establishes carcinoma. p53 Aberrant overexpression or null pattern may support dysplasia in selected cases but is not independently diagnostic. Expansion of proliferative activity above the basal/parabasal compartment may support dysplasia; interpret with morphology. Not a universal grading marker for laryngeal / hypopharyngeal dysplasia. Reactive / inflammatory atypia Usually retains maturation and lacks the degree of architectural disorder seen in true dysplasia. Carcinoma in situ Full-thickness severe atypia without stromal invasion; distinguish from invasive SCC by the epithelial-stromal interface. Invasive squamous cell carcinoma Irregular nests or single cells infiltrate the stroma, often with desmoplasia. No single molecular alteration is required for histologic diagnosis; molecular testing is not routinely necessary. Tangentially sectioned epithelium can simulate loss of maturation. Do not use p16 or p53 in isolation to assign dysplasia grade. Conventional squamous cell carcinoma Squamous cell carcinoma Malignant Predominantly affects adults, especially older adults; strong association with tobacco and alcohol exposure. Most often arises in the true vocal cords; supraglottic, subglottic, and hypopharyngeal sites are also involved. Glottic tumors commonly present with hoarseness; advanced lesions may cause dysphagia, odynophagia, airway symptoms, or neck mass. Invasive malignant squamous epithelial proliferation. Irregular nests, cords, or single cells infiltrate the stroma. Cytologic atypia, mitotic activity, and variable keratinization / intercellular bridges support squamous differentiation. Assess depth, extent, cartilage involvement, lymphovascular invasion, perineural invasion, and margins. Well differentiated Prominent keratinization, intercellular bridges, and recognizable squamous maturation. Moderately differentiated Infiltrative nests with variable keratinization and cytologic atypia. Poorly differentiated Marked atypia and limited overt squamous maturation; immunohistochemistry may be needed to establish epithelial / squamous lineage. Desmoplasia, inflammation, necrosis, and perineural or lymphovascular invasion may be present. Positive in tumor cells. p40 / p63 Support squamous differentiation, especially in poorly differentiated tumors. High-molecular-weight cytokeratins Usually positive. Should not be interpreted as an automatic surrogate for HPV-driven disease at laryngeal / hypopharyngeal sites. Broad pushing fronts, bland cytology, and minimal atypia; conventional SCC shows destructive infiltrative nests. Basaloid SCC Predominantly basaloid nests with comedonecrosis and a demonstrable squamous component. Spindle cell SCC Malignant spindle-cell component, often with a conventional SCC or dysplastic surface component. Adenosquamous carcinoma Distinct malignant glandular and squamous components, often with mucin production. Reactive pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia Lacks destructive invasion and significant cytologic atypia; correlate with underlying inflammation or infection. No single molecular alteration is required for diagnosis; molecular testing is not routinely needed for conventional laryngeal / hypopharyngeal SCC. Small superficial biopsies may not include the invasive front. Evaluate cartilage and deep soft tissue when imaging suggests extension beyond the mucosa. Low-grade malignant; locally destructive, metastasis exceptionally uncommon Usually affects older adults, with a strong association with tobacco exposure. Occurs in the larynx, hypopharynx, trachea, and rarely parapharyngeal space. Presents as a slowly enlarging, exophytic or verruciform lesion; hoarseness and dysphagia depend on site. Highly differentiated squamous proliferation with a verruciform / papillomatous surface. Broad bulbous pushing invasion at the base rather than jagged infiltrative nests. Cytologic atypia is minimal and mitoses are generally inconspicuous. Adequate deep sampling is essential to demonstrate the pushing interface and exclude conventional SCC. Marked hyperkeratosis and parakeratosis with papillomatosis. Thick, well-differentiated squamous epithelium with minimal cytologic atypia. Broad, bulbous, pushing rete-like fronts extend into underlying stroma. Inflammation Chronic inflammation may be present at the tumor-stroma interface. Pancytokeratin / p40 Positive but not specific; diagnosis is architectural and requires assessment of the deep interface. May show a basal/parabasal distribution; not a substitute for morphologic evaluation. Conventional SCC Shows irregular destructive infiltrative nests and greater cytologic atypia. Papilloma Lacks broad pushing invasion into underlying stroma. Pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia Usually associated with inflammation or infection and lacks a well-developed pushing tumor front. No defining molecular alteration is established for routine diagnosis. A superficial biopsy may be indistinguishable from papilloma or hyperkeratosis; obtain deep tissue. Hybrid lesions with conventional SCC must be excluded because their behavior and management differ. Basaloid squamous cell carcinoma High-grade malignant Occurs predominantly in adults and is rare in the nasopharynx / laryngeal region. May arise in the larynx, hypopharynx, or nasopharynx. Presents with site-dependent symptoms such as hoarseness, dysphagia, odynophagia, or a neck mass. Invasive high-grade basaloid carcinoma with nested growth. Comedonecrosis is frequent. A squamous component must be identified as abrupt keratinization within basaloid nests, conventional invasive SCC, or surface dysplasia / carcinoma in situ. Variable myxoid-to-hyaline stroma may be present. Nests and lobules of basaloid cells, often with peripheral palisading. Small-to-intermediate cells with scant cytoplasm and hyperchromatic nuclei. Necrosis Comedonecrosis is common. Squamous differentiation Abrupt keratinization, conventional SCC, or surface dysplasia / carcinoma in situ provides evidence of squamous lineage. Positive. Usually positive and supports squamous differentiation. May be positive in basaloid nasopharyngeal carcinoma; interpret in the appropriate anatomic and morphologic context. May be positive in nasopharyngeal basaloid SCC, particularly in high-incidence populations. Small cell neuroendocrine carcinoma Shows neuroendocrine morphology and marker expression; basaloid SCC has demonstrable squamous differentiation. Adenoid cystic carcinoma Shows cribriform / tubular architecture and a biphasic ductal-myoepithelial phenotype. Basal cell adenocarcinoma / other basaloid carcinoma Use site, ductal differentiation, and a directed IHC panel; establish a squamous component for basaloid SCC. Nonkeratinizing NPC Often has lymphoplasmacytic background and EBER positivity; basaloid SCC requires basaloid morphology with a squamous component. EBV may be present in nasopharyngeal basaloid SCC; no defining molecular alteration is established. Basaloid morphology alone is insufficient; demonstrate squamous differentiation. SOX10 positivity does not exclude basaloid NPC; interpret with EBER and the complete phenotype. Usually affects adults, often older adults. Most often involves the larynx; may occur at other upper aerodigestive mucosal sites. Presents with hoarseness or a papillary / exophytic mucosal mass. Exophytic papillary tumor with fibrovascular cores. Papillae are lined by dysplastic or frankly malignant squamous epithelium. Identify invasion when present; a superficial biopsy may not show the invasive component. Distinguish from benign squamous papilloma by cytologic atypia and loss of orderly maturation. Papillary fronds with fibrovascular cores; may be predominantly exophytic. Dysplastic or malignant squamous epithelium with nuclear atypia and disordered maturation. Invasive nests or irregular epithelial tongues may be present beneath the papillary surface. Positive and supports squamous differentiation. p16 / HPV Use only when clinically indicated; do not infer HPV-driven biology from morphology alone. Squamous papilloma Shows orderly maturation and lacks significant cytologic atypia or destructive invasion. Shows broad pushing invasion and highly differentiated cytology rather than malignant papillary epithelium. Conventional SCC with papillary surface May show an exophytic component, but the dominant architecture and invasive pattern may be conventional rather than papillary. A superficial biopsy may sample only the papillary surface; assess the base for invasion. Papillary architecture alone does not establish a papillary SCC. Spindle cell squamous cell carcinoma Malignant; often high grade Predominantly affects older adults, with strong association with tobacco and alcohol exposure. Most often arises in the larynx, especially the glottic region. Presents with hoarseness, dysphonia, or an exophytic / polypoid mass. Malignant spindle-cell neoplasm arising in a mucosal site. A conventional SCC, surface dysplasia / carcinoma in situ, or transition between epithelial and spindle-cell components is desirable but may be absent in a limited sample. Demonstrate epithelial differentiation with keratin and/or p40 when possible; expression may be focal or lost in the spindle component. Exclude a primary mesenchymal sarcoma and a reactive spindle-cell proliferation. Polypoid or infiltrative spindle-cell proliferation, often with fascicular or storiform growth. Atypical spindle cells with variable pleomorphism and mitotic activity. Epithelial component Surface dysplasia, carcinoma in situ, conventional SCC, or transition to spindle cells may be present. Heterologous elements Benign or malignant cartilage / bone differentiation may occur. May be focal or absent in the spindle component; a negative result does not exclude the diagnosis. May be focal and support squamous differentiation. Vimentin Usually positive but nonspecific. Differential-directed markers Use a panel to exclude melanoma, vascular, neural, and specific mesenchymal neoplasms when morphology warrants. Undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma Lacks an epithelial component and usually lacks convincing keratin / p40 expression; correlate with mucosal origin and surface dysplasia. Leiomyosarcoma Shows smooth muscle differentiation with desmin, SMA, and h-caldesmon. Melanoma Expresses melanocytic markers such as SOX10, S100, and Melan-A. Reactive granulation tissue / inflammatory myofibroblastic proliferation Usually lacks marked malignant atypia and destructive growth; correlate with clinical setting. Keratin and p40 may be focal or absent in the spindle component. A superficial or ulcerated biopsy may contain only spindle cells; search for an epithelial component and use a focused exclusionary panel. Occurs in adults, usually older adults. May arise in the larynx or hypopharynx. Presents with hoarseness, dysphagia, odynophagia, or a mucosal mass. Invasive carcinoma with unequivocal malignant squamous and glandular components. The glandular component shows true gland formation and/or mucin production. Both components must be malignant; entrapped benign glands or focal mucin alone are insufficient. Extensive sampling may be required to identify both components. Conventional invasive SCC, often moderately or poorly differentiated. Glandular component Malignant glands, duct-like structures, and/or mucin-producing cells. Relationship The two malignant components may be intermingled or present in separate areas. Destructive stromal invasion is present. Positive in both components. Highlights the squamous component. Mucin stains Can demonstrate intracellular or extracellular mucin in the glandular component. Glandular markers CK7 and other glandular markers may highlight the glandular component; interpret in context. Conventional SCC with focal mucin Does not show a distinct malignant glandular component. Mucoepidermoid carcinoma Typically shows a mixture of mucous, intermediate, and squamoid cells; assess architecture and, when needed, MAML2 rearrangement. Salivary-type carcinoma Consider site and salivary differentiation; establish whether the tumor is a primary mucosal adenosquamous carcinoma. No defining molecular alteration is established for routine diagnosis; MAML2 testing may help in the differential with mucoepidermoid carcinoma. Do not diagnose adenosquamous carcinoma from focal mucin alone. Adequate sampling is necessary to establish unequivocal malignant glandular and squamous components. Lymphoepithelial carcinoma of the larynx Malignant; rare Very rare; reported in adults. Arises in the larynx, often supraglottic. May present with hoarseness, dysphagia, or a laryngeal mass. Undifferentiated carcinoma with syncytial epithelial cells in a dense lymphoplasmacytic background. Tumor cells show epithelial differentiation by pancytokeratin. EBER status should be assessed; unlike nasopharyngeal lymphoepithelial carcinoma, laryngeal cases are generally EBV-negative in the described entity. Exclude metastatic nasopharyngeal carcinoma and lymphoma. Tumor cells Large undifferentiated cells with syncytial growth, vesicular nuclei, and prominent nucleoli. Background Dense lymphocytes and plasma cells intimately admixed with tumor cells. Sheets, nests, or irregular islands may be obscured by the inflammatory infiltrate. Positive in carcinoma cells and establishes epithelial lineage. May support squamous differentiation. Typically negative in reported laryngeal lymphoepithelial carcinoma; positive staining should prompt careful exclusion of NPC. CD45 Highlights background lymphocytes; carcinoma cells are negative. Usually arises in nasopharynx and is EBER-positive in nearly all nonkeratinizing cases; correlate with imaging and clinical examination. Tumor cells express hematolymphoid markers and lack pancytokeratin. Conventional poorly differentiated SCC Usually has more obvious squamous differentiation and less prominent lymphoepithelial morphology. A dense lymphoid background can obscure the epithelial nature of the tumor. Assess EBER and the nasopharynx to exclude metastatic or contiguous NPC. Laryngeal cartilaginous tumors Mesenchymal tumors Chondroma benign; chondrosarcoma malignant Usually affects middle-aged to older adults, with male predominance in reported series. Most often arises in the cricoid cartilage; thyroid and arytenoid cartilages are less common sites. Presents with hoarseness, dyspnea, dysphagia, or airway obstruction. Chondroma: lobular cartilaginous tumor without pleomorphism, binucleation, or destructive growth; size 20 mm or less is supportive. Chondrosarcoma: malignant cartilaginous neoplasm with lobular disarray and destructive invasion of native cartilage and/or bone. Chondrosarcoma shows increased cellularity, binucleation, nuclear pleomorphism, and hyperchromasia. Imaging may show an expansile destructive intracartilaginous mass with ring-like, arc-like, or popcorn calcifications. Chondroma Mature hyaline cartilage, hypocellular, with evenly distributed bland chondrocytes; one cell per lacuna; no mitoses or binucleation. Grade 1 chondrosarcoma Lobular disarray and destructive invasion; increased cellularity, binucleation, mild pleomorphism, and hyperchromasia. Grade 2 chondrosarcoma Greater cellularity and nuclear pleomorphism; scattered mitoses may be present. Grade 3 chondrosarcoma High cellularity, marked pleomorphism and multinucleation, increased mitoses, and tumor necrosis. Dedifferentiated subtype Biphasic tumor with conventional chondrosarcoma juxtaposed to high-grade noncartilaginous sarcoma. S100 Positive in chondroid tumor cells. SOX9 D2-40 May be positive. Keratin / EMA Negative in chondroid cells; helps distinguish epithelial tumors with cartilaginous differentiation. Bland hypocellular cartilage without binucleation, pleomorphism, or destructive invasion. Chondrosarcoma Destructive growth, lobular disarray, increased cellularity, binucleation, and nuclear atypia; size greater than 20 mm favors but does not establish malignancy. Chondrometaplasia Usually multiple elastic cartilage nodules in the vocal cord blending with adjacent stroma. Spindle cell SCC with cartilage Cartilage is embedded within a malignant spindle-cell epithelial population. Molecular testing is not considered diagnostically relevant in the described laryngeal cartilaginous tumors. A size cutoff greater than 20 mm is supportive but not definitive for chondrosarcoma. Incisional biopsies may not capture destructive invasion; correlate with imaging and sample the tumor-cartilage interface. Do not use atypical cartilaginous neoplasm terminology for laryngeal lesions without a site-specific evidence basis. All PathologyGPS / Head and Neck Pathology / Pharyngeal, Laryngeal, Tracheal, and Parapharyngeal Tumors Pharyngeal, Laryngeal, Tracheal, and Parapharyngeal Tumors A practical, morphology-first diagnostic reference covering nasopharyngeal, hypopharyngeal, laryngeal, tracheal, and parapharyngeal lesions. Diagnostic priority Establish the anatomic site, epithelial phenotype, and invasive pattern. Use targeted immunohistochemistry to establish lineage or resolve a specific differential; do not substitute marker panels for adequate sampling of the invasive interface. Diagnostic GPS: practical sequence Confirm the site Nasopharynx, hypopharynx, larynx, trachea, or parapharyngeal space; correlate with imaging and endoscopy. Classify the lesion Hamartomatous, papillary, dysplastic, conventional squamous, basaloid, spindle-cell, glandular, or cartilaginous. Find the interface Distinguish orderly maturation, pushing invasion, and destructive infiltrative growth. Apply focused IHC Use epithelial / squamous markers, EBER, thyroid-lineage markers, or cartilage markers according to morphology. Use molecular tests selectively EBER is especially useful in NPC; other molecular tests are not routinely required for most entities on this page. Nasopharyngeal lesions: high-yield distinction Entity Key morphology Useful discriminator Skin-like ectoderm over mesodermal tissue No endodermal elements Surface-connected ducts and squamous nests in spindle-cell stroma Stromal cytokeratin and SMA Low-grade papillary adenocarcinoma Complex papillary / glandular growth with submucosal invasion TTF1+, thyroglobulin−, PAX8− Poorly differentiated carcinoma with variable lymphoplasmacytic background EBER+ in nearly all cases Squamous carcinoma: invasion-pattern comparison Growth pattern Diagnostic anchor Destructive infiltrative nests / cords Cytologic malignancy and invasion Broad pushing fronts Highly differentiated cytology; deep biopsy High-grade basaloid nests Comedonecrosis plus squamous component Papillary SCC Malignant papillary fronds Dysplastic epithelium / invasion Malignant spindle-cell proliferation Epithelial component or focal keratin / p40 Malignant squamous and glandular components True malignant glands / mucin production Entity reference Diagnostic criteria and differential diagnosis Search by entity, morphology, immunomarker, or molecular alteration. e.g. EBER, pushing invasion, TTF1, cartilage... bg-teal-700 text-white border border-slate-300 bg-white text-slate-600 Collapse − View diagnostic profile + Clinical Profile Essential Diagnostic Criteria Histopathology Immunophenotype Differential Diagnosis Molecular Pathology Diagnostic Pitfalls No matching entity. Biopsy, sampling, and reporting checklist Document the precise anatomic epicenter and correlate with endoscopy and cross-sectional imaging. For verrucous carcinoma, papillomatous lesions, and suspected invasion, obtain tissue deep enough to evaluate the epithelial-stromal interface. For nasopharyngeal carcinoma, use EBER in situ hybridization in the appropriate morphologic setting, particularly for metastatic lymph node specimens. For low-grade nasopharyngeal papillary adenocarcinoma, use TTF1, thyroglobulin, and PAX8 as a focused panel when thyroid origin is in the differential. For spindle-cell and poorly differentiated lesions, establish lineage with a focused panel and do not exclude spindle cell SCC solely because keratin is focal or absent. For laryngeal cartilaginous lesions, correlate biopsy findings with imaging and assess destructive invasion at the cartilage interface. Diagnostic note: Interpret immunohistochemical and molecular findings in conjunction with morphology, anatomic site, and imaging. Ancillary tests described as supportive are not stand-alone diagnostic criteria.

title: Salivary Gland Tumors
content: use client Nodular oncocytic hyperplasia Non-neoplastic epithelial lesions NOH is almost exclusively found in the parotid gland; it is rarely seen in the submandibular gland Patients with NOH present with a palpable painless mass, often present for years NOH constitutes < 1% of salivary tumors but accounts for approximately 7% of bilateral salivary lesions The peak incidence is in the fifth and sixth decades of life, and there is a slight female predilection Essential: circumscribed but unencapsulated nodules of oncocytic and/or clear cells Desirable: multifocality NOH consists of irregularly shaped unencapsulated nodules of oncocytes in solid to tubulotrabecular patterns distributed throughout the salivary parenchyma Lobular architecture is preserved Clear cell change is frequent and can form small satellite foci that mimic invasive clear cell tumors Unifocality and encapsulation can separate NOH from oncocytoma Entrapped normal acini, ducts, and adipocytes within nodules and non-perivascular p63-positive basal cells distinguish NOH from acinic cell carcinoma or metastatic renal cell carcinoma Pancytokeratin highlights native ductal structures and helps demonstrate the relationship of oncocytic nodules to residual salivary parenchyma. p63 may highlight non-perivascular basal cells within nodules; interpret the distribution rather than isolated positive cells. SOX10 and S100 are generally not diffuse in the oncocytic nodules; use a focused panel only when acinic cell carcinoma or a myoepithelial neoplasm is considered. Absence of MAML2 rearrangement can rule out oncocytic mucoepidermoid carcinoma Negativity for SOX10, S100, and PLAG1 rearrangement helps distinguish NOH from pleomorphic adenoma and myoepithelioma with oncocytic metaplasia Lymphoepithelial sialadenitis Typically, all salivary (and other mucosal) glands are affected Minor glands are affected mostly microscopically, without enlargement, whereas the parotid glands often show bilateral enlargement Clinical symptoms of sicca syndrome (dry mouth, dry eye), frequently associated with bilateral parotid swelling Patients are predominantly female (M:F ratio: 1:4) and in their sixth or seventh decade of life Essential: a dense benign lymphocytic infiltrate, in salivary glands, with lymphoepithelial lesions Early lesions show a minor to moderate degree of T cell–dominated periductal lymphocytic infiltration, rarely with reactive follicles and usually without lymphoepithelial lesions They are typically encountered in minor labial glands and sampled for diagnostic purposes in cases of suspected Sjögren disease A positive focus is defined as ≥ 1 dense periductal aggregate of > 50 lymphocytes, representing a histological criterion within a diagnostic score Focus score is calculated as the number of lymphocytic foci per 4 mm² Advanced lesions typically manifest as a tumorous enlargement of parotid (or, rarely, the submandibular or lacrimal) glands They show intense, B cell–dominated, lymphoplasmacytic infiltrates with preserved lobular architecture; a variable (often massive) degree of parenchymal atrophy; multiple reactive follicles; and multiple, densely aggregated, partly cystic lymphoepithelial lesions A keratin stain can be helpful for pattern analysis of preserved glandular architecture, including the frequency and distribution of lymphoepithelial lesions Immunohistological staining for kappa/lambda light chains or, alternatively, in situ hybridization detecting corresponding mRNA may demonstrate their polyclonal nature in lymphoepithelial sialadenitis, while molecular evidence of B-cell monoclonality may occur, but in the absence of further histological evidence it does not necessarily represent a malignant transformation There is no association with EBV Cases with ductal dilatation, predominantly diffuse lymphocytic infiltration, and fibrosis represent nonspecific (e.g. traumatic or obstructive) sialadenitis of minor/labial glands Sclerosis, obliterative phlebitis, and numerous IgG4-positive plasma cells, as seen in IgG4-associated sialadenitis of the submandibular glands, are absent HIV-associated cystic lymphoepithelial lesion is histologically similar but is usually bilateral, characterized by bizarre, enlarged follicles and massive cystically dilated lymphoepithelial lesions Salivary lymphoepithelial carcinoma may show irregular lymphoepithelial lesions in a lobular arrangement but represents a bluntly infiltrating neoplasia with increased proliferation, cellular atypia, and the presence of EBV in a significant subset of cases Clinical information is usually indispensable for correct differential diagnosis Pleomorphic adenoma Benign epithelial tumors Most PAs arise in the parotid gland (~70–80%), followed by the oral cavity and submandibular gland In the oral cavity, the palate is the most common location Generally, PA presents as a slowly growing, painless mass Deep parotid lobe tumors present as parapharyngeal space masses; parotid tail tumors present as level II neck lesions; and minor salivary gland PAs may present with dysphagia, airway obstruction, or obstructive sleep apnoea PA is the most common salivary gland neoplasm worldwide, accounting for 50–70% of all salivary gland tumors Essential: an admixture of bilayered ducts, myoepithelial cells, and chondromyxoid/fibrous stroma; absence of invasion and malignant cytomorphological features Desirable: PLAG1 or HMGA2 alterations (in selected cases) Well circumscribed and often encapsulated; the capsule may be incomplete or absent, particularly in minor salivary gland and stroma-rich tumors. Characteristic admixture of bilayered ducts, myoepithelial cells, and chondromyxoid or fibrous stroma. Ducts typically have an inner luminal layer and an outer myoepithelial layer. Myoepithelial cells show broad morphology: plasmacytoid, spindle, epithelioid, basaloid, clear, stellate, or oncocytic. They may merge imperceptibly into the myxoid stroma. Stroma ranges from myxoid and chondromyxoid to hyalinized, collagenous, osseous, or lipomatous. Either cellular or stromal components may predominate. Squamous, mucinous, sebaceous, adipocytic, and osseous metaplasia may occur. Cellular pleomorphic adenoma can be very cellular but should lack destructive invasion. Pseudopodia, satellite nodules, capsular irregularity, and multinodular growth alone do not establish malignancy. Bizarre degenerative (ancient) atypia and post-biopsy infarct-type necrosis may occur. The histological hallmark of PA is its morphological diversity derived from an admixture of bilayered ducts, myoepithelial cells, and stroma PAs are well delineated and/or encapsulated The capsule may be absent in minor salivary gland and chondromyxoid-predominant PAs The ductal and myoepithelial cells are commonly arranged in bilayered tubular structures, with the myoepithelial cells melding with the stroma The cellular phenotype, particularly of the myoepithelial cells, is broad and includes epithelioid, basaloid, stellate, spindled, clear, oncocytic, and plasmacytoid morphology The stroma can be mucoid, myxoid, hyalinized, chondroid, osseous, or lipomatous A variable admixture of bilayered ducts, myoepithelial cells, and myxoid, chondroid, chondromyxoid, fibrous, or hyalinized stroma. Metaplastic changes can include adipose, osseous, squamous, sebaceous, or mucinous differentiation. Pseudopods and satellite nodules may extend beyond the main contour. Luminal/ductal cells: pancytokeratin, CK7, CAM5.2. Myoepithelial cells: calponin (sensitive), SMA, S100, SOX10, p40 (often more useful than p63), CK5/6. GFAP often highlights myxoid and myoepithelial areas. PLAG1 or HMGA2 immunohistochemistry can support the diagnosis; interpret in the morphologic context. PLAG1, and HMGA2, respectively, are emerging as sensitive immunohistochemical markers for PA There is usually strong and diffuse reactivity for pancytokeratin, AE1/AE3, CAM5.2, and CK7, which is often accentuated in the ductal or luminal cell areas, with various muscle, myoepithelial, and basal markers reactive, including calponin (most sensitive), SMA, S100, SOX10, p40 (better than p63), and CK5/6 GFAP is usually more strongly expressed in myxoid and myoepithelial areas The immunoexpression of S100 and SOX10 helps to differentiate oncocytic PA from other oncocytic tumors Ductal cells express epithelial markers; myoepithelial cells may express S100, SOX10, p63, calponin, and SMA. Interpret staining by cell compartment rather than treating the tumor as uniformly positive or negative. Basal cell adenoma: more monotonous basaloid cells, peripheral palisading, basement-membrane-like material, and no characteristic chondromyxoid matrix. Myoepithelioma: almost exclusively myoepithelial cells, with absent or very rare ducts and usually no classic ductal–myxoid admixture. Adenoid cystic carcinoma: cribriform architecture may overlap; look for infiltrative growth, perineural invasion, and characteristic basement membrane material rather than a benign pleomorphic pattern. Mucoepidermoid carcinoma: mucous, intermediate, and epidermoid cells with infiltrative growth; MAML2 rearrangement supports MEC. PA may show squamous or mucinous metaplasia but retains myoepithelial differentiation and lacks destructive invasion. PAs can show squamous metaplasia and mucocytes, and mimic squamous cell carcinoma or mucoepidermoid carcinoma PA can be distinguished from squamous cell carcinoma by the absence of infiltrative growth, marked pleomorphism, and increased mitoses, and it can be separated from mucoepidermoid carcinoma by the identification of well-formed keratin pearls, the presence of myoepithelial differentiation, and the absence of MAML2 rearrangements PA can exhibit cribriform architecture mimicking adenoid cystic carcinoma, as well as areas of compact biphasic tubular structures reminiscent of epithelial-myoepithelial carcinoma Myoepithelial carcinoma is often cytologically bland and may therefore be underrecognized as malignant and misclassified as a myoepithelial-rich PA Not applicable PLAG1 rearrangements are reported in more than half of cases; HMGA2 rearrangements occur in a smaller subset. PLAG1 or HMGA2 alterations are useful in selected cases. Biphasic ductal–myoepithelial tumor with variable chondromyxoid stroma Do not mistake hyalinized PA stroma for AdCC pseudocysts. Seek the broader chondromyxoid/myoepithelial context and true ductal component. Epithelial/ductal groups admixed with plasmacytoid or spindle myoepithelial cells. Fibrillary or chondromyxoid matrix is a major clue. When matrix is scant, distinction from AdCC or other basaloid lesions can be difficult. Basal cell adenoma BCAs are largely restricted to major salivary glands, especially the parotid gland (> 80%) BCA usually presents as a well-defined, mobile, solitary mass, although syndromic cases may be multiple and associated with dermal cylindromas or trichoepitheliomas BCAs account for about 1–4% of all salivary gland tumors They present more frequently in the sixth and seventh decades of life, with a slight female predilection Essential: non-invasive; biphasic basaloid morphology; peripheral palisading; variable amount of collagenous stroma Desirable: dual population immunophenotype; nuclear β-catenin reactivity Well circumscribed or encapsulated tumor with solid, trabecular, tubular, cribriform, or membranous architecture; more than one pattern commonly coexists. Basaloid cells form nests, trabeculae, or tubules. Darker peripheral cells often show palisading, while inner/luminal cells are paler. Tubules contain a central lumen and one or two layers of cuboidal/basaloid cells; luminal secretions may be eosinophilic and PAS positive. Hyaline basement-membrane-like material may be present between nests or as rounded droplets. In the membranous subtype, thick eosinophilic hyaline material surrounds and separates tumor nests; a membranous pattern involving more than 50% supports this subtype. Cystic change is common. A chondromyxoid matrix is not a feature. There should be no destructive or perineural invasion. BCAs are encapsulated or well circumscribed and show tubulotrabecular, cribriform, membranous, or solid growth A subset show a distinct spindled S100-positive myoepithelial cell-derived stromal component The tumor shows peripheral palisading of dark cells with luminal paler cells and ducts Nuclei are vesicular Tumors demonstrate stroma of variable amount and collagenous density, sometimes in drop-like hyaline material A lipomatous subtype has been described Darker peripheral basaloid cells often show palisading, with paler inner cells and ducts. Tubules may have central lumina with eosinophilic/PAS-positive secretion. Luminal cells express epithelial markers, including keratins, EMA, CEA, and CD117. Basaloid/abluminal cells may express p63, calponin, SMA, actin, S100, and GFAP. Nuclear β-catenin and LEF1 coexpression supports BCA, particularly in the appropriate morphologic setting. A stromal spindle-cell component, when present, may be S100 positive and p63 negative. Epithelial and myoepithelial markers highlight the dual cell composition Coexpression of nuclear β-catenin and LEF1 is detected in BCAs Cellular pleomorphic adenoma: lacks the monotonous basaloid pattern and prominent peripheral palisading; often shows myxochondroid stroma and blending myoepithelial cells. Basal cell adenocarcinoma: the decisive feature is invasion, including infiltrative growth beyond the circumscribed border or perineural invasion. Adenoid cystic carcinoma: may show cribriform architecture and hyaline material, but is infiltrative and may show perineural invasion. BCAs are distinguished from cellular pleomorphic adenoma by their basaloid appearance, peripheral palisading, and lack of blending with associated myoepithelial-type stroma BCAs are differentiated from basal cell adenocarcinoma by the absence of invasion CTNNB1/β-catenin pathway alterations are relevant; a subset has CYLD alterations. No single molecular test independently establishes benign behavior. Biphasic basaloid and luminal cells; peripheral palisading On FNA or a small biopsy, BCA may not be separable from BCAC or AdCC. If invasion cannot be assessed, use a descriptive diagnosis such as basaloid neoplasm and recommend excision/correlation. Often markedly cellular, with small sheets and round, trabecular, or solid fragments of monomorphic small basaloid cells. Cells have scant cytoplasm, uniform fine hyperchromasia, and frequent naked nuclei in a relatively clean background. Thin dense hyaline material may surround or interdigitate with fragments; small rounded stromal droplets may be present. Squamoid or sebaceous foci can occasionally be seen. Warthin tumor Tumors are almost exclusively restricted to parotid glands, especially the inferior pole, and periparotid lymph nodes; < 1% are found in the deep lobe Tumors are multifocal in 12–20% of patients, either synchronously or metachronously, and are bilateral in 5–17% Patients present with painless, slow-growing, and fluctuant swellings Pain or facial nerve palsy may occur in metaplastic/infarcted variants Warthin tumor accounts for 5–20% of all salivary tumors, except in Black Africans, in whom it is rare Essential: a circumscribed mass with spaces lined by papillary bilayered oncocytic cells; lymphoid stroma Well-circumscribed, often cystic tumor with papillary-cystic spaces lined by a characteristic bilayered oncocytic epithelium. The luminal layer consists of tall columnar oncocytes; the outer layer is composed of smaller cuboidal/basal cells. Underlying lymphoid stroma commonly contains well-formed germinal centers. The combination of bilayered oncocytic lining and lymphoid stroma is the key diagnostic pattern. Focal squamous, mucous, ciliated, or sebaceous metaplasia may occur. In infarcted/metaplastic Warthin tumor, the bilayered lining may be replaced by bland squamous metaplasia, with necrosis, ghost papillary architecture, granulation tissue, and granulomatous reaction. Warthin tumor is composed of varying proportions of papillary-cystic structures lined by bilayered oncocytic epithelial cells, surrounded by a lymphoid stroma including germinal centers The epithelial component comprises inner columnar and outer cuboidal cells Limited foci of squamous, mucous, ciliated, and sebaceous cells can be present Subtype In the infarcted/metaplastic subtype of Warthin tumor, the bilayered epithelium is replaced by squamous metaplastic epithelium without atypia Mucinous metaplasia may also be present The infarcted/metaplastic subtype, which may follow FNA or trauma, shows areas of necrosis, in which a ghost papillary architecture may be discerned (highlighted with reticulin staining) The oncocytic luminal and basal epithelial layers are cytokeratin positive; basal cells can be highlighted by p63/p40. IHC is usually not required in classic cases. MAML2 rearrangement supports mucoepidermoid carcinoma rather than Warthin tumor. Warthin-like mucoepidermoid carcinoma: may have cysts, lymphoid stroma, and squamous/mucinous epithelium, but lacks the orderly bilayered oncocytic lining; MAML2 rearrangement supports MEC. Oncocytic cystadenoma: lacks the prominent lymphoid stroma with germinal centers and characteristic bilayered oncocytic epithelium. Metaplastic Warthin tumor vs. MEC: seek residual classic bilayered oncocytic epithelium and infarct-related ghost papillae; do not diagnose MEC from squamous metaplasia alone. The main differential diagnosis of the metaplastic Warthin tumor subtype is Warthin-like mucoepidermoid carcinoma; however, Warthin tumors lack MAML2 gene rearrangement Diagnostic molecular pathology is not directly relevant, but an absence of MAML2 alteration can exclude mucoepidermoid carcinoma Bilayered oncocytic epithelium in lymphoid stroma After FNA or trauma, infarction and extensive squamous metaplasia can obscure the classic appearance. Search for residual bilayered oncocytic epithelium and lymphoid stroma. Oncocytoma More than 80% of cases occur in the parotid, approximately 10% occur in the submandibular gland, and the rest occur in minor salivary glands and the sublingual gland Symptoms depend on anatomical location Oncocytoma usually presents as a unilateral painless swelling Oncocytomas represent < 1.5% of salivary gland tumors The incidence peak is in the seventh decade of life, with no sex predilection Essential: a circumscribed mass composed of large oncocytic epithelial cells; lack of entrapped normal parenchyma Desirable: basal cells positive for p63; absence of SOX10 and S100 (in selected cases) Well-circumscribed, usually encapsulated tumor composed of large oncocytes arranged in nests and sheets separated by delicate fibrovascular stroma. Cells have abundant, dense, finely granular eosinophilic cytoplasm; nuclei are centrally placed, uniform, and vesicular, often with a single prominent nucleolus. Scattered dark cells with pyknotic nuclei may represent degenerating oncocytes. Unlike nodular oncocytic hyperplasia, a true oncocytoma forms a discrete mass and lacks entrapped normal salivary parenchyma. Clear cell change may occur due to glycogen and fixation-related effects. AdCC consists of two main cell types: ductal cells and myoepithelial cells Mitotic figures are infrequent AdCC shows three growth patterns: tubular, cribriform, and solid The tubular pattern consists of well-formed ducts and tubules lined with luminal ductal and abluminal myoepithelial cells Tubular areas contain well-formed ducts. Cribriform areas contain pseudocystic spaces filled with hyaline or basophilic matrix contiguous with the stroma; identifying both true glandular lumina and pseudolumina is highly useful. Perineural invasion is a characteristic clue but is sampling-dependent. A solid component, particularly when substantial, is associated with more aggressive behavior; high-grade transformation shows a pleomorphic, mitotically active component that may lose myoepithelial markers. Luminal cells: CK7 and KIT/CD117. Abluminal cells: p63, p40, calponin, and SMA. Pancytokeratin is strong in ductal cells and weaker in myoepithelial cells. MYB overexpression is common but not sufficiently specific by itself. CK7 and KIT (CD117) are typically positive in ductal cells, whereas p63, p40, calponin, and α-SMA are positive in myoepithelial cells MYB protein overexpression is common in AdCC, but its diagnostic value is limited by its suboptimal specificity p63, p40, calponin, and α-SMA highlight the abluminal myoepithelial component. MYB protein overexpression is common but has suboptimal specificity; interpret with morphology and, when needed, molecular testing. Pleomorphic adenoma (PA) — PA usually has a circumscribed or pushing border and characteristic chondromyxoid/myxoid or fibrillary stroma. Ductal and myoepithelial cells may be present, but the angular hyperchromatic basaloid cells and basement-membrane-like pseudocysts of AdCC are not the defining pattern. Infiltration and perineural invasion favor AdCC. Polymorphous adenocarcinoma (conventional PmA) — PmA is usually a minor-gland tumor with cytologic uniformity but striking architectural diversity (single-file, fascicular, tubular, trabecular, and microcystic patterns). Its cells are generally bland with open chromatin; targetoid perineural growth may occur. AdCC more typically has angular hyperchromatic basaloid nuclei, a true biphasic ductal/abluminal population, and hyaline basement-membrane-like pseudocysts. Cribriform polymorphous adenocarcinoma (CASG) — CASG often shows multinodular growth, clear nuclei, glomeruloid and papillary structures, peripheral palisading, and clefting. Do not call a cribriform tumor AdCC on architecture alone; assess the cell population, nuclear quality, stromal material, and PRKD-family alteration when needed. Epithelial-myoepithelial carcinoma (EMC) — EMC has conspicuous, well-formed ducts with an inner eosinophilic luminal layer and an outer layer of larger clear myoepithelial cells. The outer cells are usually more abundant and cytologically clear than the abluminal cells of AdCC. AdCC more often shows compact basaloid nests and cribriform pseudocysts. Basal cell adenoma (BCA) / basal cell adenocarcinoma (BCAC) — These tumors show basaloid nests with peripheral palisading, often with paler central cells and ducts; membranous or hyaline material may be present. Cribriform BCA is a particularly important benign mimic. Look for a circumscribed border in BCA versus destructive infiltration, perineural/vascular invasion, or other unequivocal invasive features in BCAC. AdCC has characteristic true ducts plus pseudocysts and more angular hyperchromatic myoepithelial-type cells. Solid-pattern AdCC versus other basaloid tumors — Solid AdCC may lack recognizable cribriform or tubular structures and can be difficult on a limited sample. Search for focal conventional AdCC, basement-membrane-like matrix, ductal differentiation, and perineural invasion; use a compartment-specific panel (luminal CK7/KIT; abluminal p63/p40/calponin/SMA) and MYB/MYBL1 testing in unresolved cases. The main salivary gland tumors to be distinguished from AdCC include pleomorphic adenoma, polymorphous adenocarcinoma, epithelial-myoepithelial carcinoma, and basal cell adenoma/adenocarcinoma Because AdCC often shows mild cytological atypia and a cribriform pattern, its distinction from benign tumors with a cribriform pattern, especially the cribriform subtype of basal cell adenoma, is critical Demonstration of MYB/MYBL1 rearrangements or gene fusions by FISH or other methods can help establish a diagnosis of AdCC MYB::NFIB is a key recurrent fusion; MYBL1 rearrangements/fusions or MYB amplification may occur in cases without the canonical fusion. Selected tumors also show alterations involving NOTCH, chromatin-remodeling, and growth-signaling pathways. Tubular / cribriform / solid basaloid tumor with pseudocysts Cribriform architecture or hyaline globules alone do not establish AdCC. Look for true ducts plus pseudocysts, infiltrative growth, and the overall cytologic pattern. Usually cellular, with cohesive sheets, tubular/complex fragments, or cribriform groups containing hard-edged stromal balls. Uniform basaloid cells have high N:C ratios, oval-to-angulated hyperchromatic nuclei, and usually limited atypia in conventional tumors. Romanowsky–Giemsa-type stains can highlight discrete spheres and branching tubules of magenta matrix. Solid-basaloid cases may be difficult to distinguish from other basaloid neoplasms on FNA. Acinic cell carcinoma About 90–95% of cases arise in the parotid gland The remainder involve intraoral sites, the submandibular gland, and (exceptionally) the sinonasal tract Patients typically present with slow-growing, painless masses High-grade tumors may be rapidly growing and fixed to adjacent structures, with facial nerve paralysis Acinic cell carcinoma represents 10% of all salivary gland malignancies and as many as 18.7% of parotid carcinomas Essential: a salivary gland carcinoma with serous acinar differentiation Desirable: nuclear staining for NR4A3 (NOR1) or NR4A2 (NURR1), or molecular demonstration of NR4A3 rearrangement (in selected cases) Architectures include solid, microcystic, follicular, and less commonly papillary-cystic patterns, sometimes with prominent lymphoid stroma. The most characteristic cells are serous acinar-type cells with basophilic, granular cytoplasm containing PAS-positive, diastase-resistant zymogen granules. Nuclei are small and often eccentrically placed; cell borders may be indistinct. Intercalated duct-like, vacuolated, oncocytic, clear, and nonspecific glandular cells may be admixed. High-grade transformation adds a high-grade adenocarcinoma or poorly differentiated component with nuclear enlargement, pleomorphism, necrosis, increased mitoses, and increased Ki-67. Neoplastic cells are heterogeneous with the most common cell type being the serous acinar cell which features PAS-positive, diastase-resistant basophilic cytoplasmic zymogen granules, with variable intercalated duct–type, nonspecific glandular, vacuolated, oncocytic, and (rarely) clear cells Cytoplasmic borders are poorly defined and nuclei are small and peripherally placed High-grade (HG) tumors exhibit, in addition to conventional areas, a component of high-grade adenocarcinoma (with variable cribriform, solid, trabecular growth patterns) or poorly differentiated/undifferentiated carcinoma Acinic cell carcinomas with high-grade transformation show nuclear enlargement and pleomorphism, coarse chromatin, necrosis, increased mitotic activity and Ki-67 index, and more frequent perineural and lymphovascular invasion Increased expression of cyclin-D1 and membranous β-catenin have been described SOX10 and DOG1 are typically positive. p40/p63, mammaglobin, and S100 are generally negative (S100 may label intercalated cells). Nuclear NR4A3 (NOR1) is highly sensitive and specific in the reported series; NR4A2 is rarely positive. Nuclear staining for NR4A3 (NOR1) or NR4A2 (NURR1) have been identified in 98% and 2% of cases, respectively The sensitivity and specificity of immunohistochemistry for NR4A3 are 94.4% and 99%, respectively Secretory carcinoma — The key distinction is the nature of the secretory material. Acinic cell carcinoma has intracellular PAS-positive, diastase-resistant zymogen granules and serous acinar differentiation; secretory carcinoma has abundant luminal eosinophilic/bubbly secretions that are PAS-positive before and after diastase and Alcian blue-positive, but lacks true zymogen granules. DOG1 (often apical/luminal) and nuclear NR4A3 support acinic cell carcinoma; mammaglobin and S100 support secretory carcinoma. Warthin tumor — A prominent lymphoid background can be misleading. Warthin tumor has bilayered oncocytic epithelium lining cystic spaces with lymphoid stroma, rather than a neoplastic serous acinar population with zymogen granules. Metastatic carcinoma in an intraparotid lymph node — Consider a nodal location, residual lymphoid tissue, and clinical history; lymphoid stroma can accompany acinic cell carcinoma but does not by itself establish a primary salivary tumor. High-grade transformation — Identify conventional acinic cell carcinoma, if present, and look for abrupt or recognizable high-grade adenocarcinoma/poorly differentiated areas with pleomorphism, necrosis, brisk mitoses, and increased Ki-67. Molecular pathology is typically not needed for diagnosis However, demonstrating NR4A subfamily rearrangements or positive immunohistochemistry for NR4A3 or NR4A2 may be confirmatory in challenging cases Serous acinar differentiation with zymogen granules Do not confuse PAS-D-positive cytoplasmic zymogen granules with the luminal secretions of secretory carcinoma. DOG1 highlights apical luminal membranes in acinic cell carcinoma; NR4A3 nuclear staining is a useful confirmatory marker. Secretory carcinoma The most common site of occurrence is the parotid gland, followed by the oral cavity and submandibular gland In the oral cavity, the lip, soft palate, and buccal mucosa are the most commonly affected subsites SC most commonly presents as a painless, slowly growing mass SC with high-grade transformation is associated with an aggressive clinical behavior, a high propensity for cervical lymph node metastasis, a risk of distant metastasis, and a poor prognosis SC usually occurs in adults, with a mean patient age of 46.5 years (range: 10–86 years) and an equal sex distribution Essential: a malignant salivary gland neoplasm of a single cell type with vacuolated, colloid-like secretory material; no zymogen cytoplasmic granules; immunohistochemical positivity for S100, SOX10, and mammaglobin; lack of immunohistochemical staining for p40 and/or p63 Desirable: ETV6 or RET rearrangement demonstrated by FISH, RNA sequencing, or PCR (in selected cases) Usually well-circumscribed but unencapsulated and lobulated, with fibrous septa. Patterns include microcystic, tubular, follicular, solid, and papillary-cystic growth; macrocystic areas may occur. Tumor cells are relatively uniform, with round-to-oval vesicular nuclei, finely granular chromatin, distinct central nucleoli, and pale pink granular-to-vacuolated cytoplasm. Luminal secretions are abundant, eosinophilic to bubbly, and PAS-positive before and after diastase digestion as well as Alcian blue-positive. True zymogen granules are absent. Atypia and mitoses are usually limited; infiltrative growth and occasional perineural invasion can occur. The tumors have a lobulated growth pattern separated by fibrous septa and are composed of microcystic/solid, tubular, follicular, and papillary-cystic structures with distinctive luminal secretions It may have an infiltrative pattern with occasional perineural invasion and may show abundant fibrosclerotic stroma with prominent, thick, hyalinized septa Some SCs show a macrocystic morphology The tumor cells have low-grade vesicular round to oval nuclei with finely granular chromatin and distinctive, centrally located nucleoli The pale pink cytoplasm is granular to vacuolated CK7, S100, SOX10, vimentin, and mammaglobin are typically positive. p63, p40, NR4A3, and DOG1 are negative. Acinic cell carcinoma — The most important mimic. Acinic cell carcinoma shows serous acinar cytoplasm with PAS-D-positive zymogen granules, often apical membranous DOG1, and nuclear NR4A3. Secretory carcinoma has vacuolated/granular cells and extracellular/luminal bubbly secretions, lacks zymogen granules, and is typically mammaglobin/S100/SOX10-positive and DOG1/NR4A3-negative. Mucoepidermoid carcinoma — MEC is heterogeneous and contains mucous, intermediate, and squamoid cells; secretory carcinoma is usually monophasic. Mucous cells in MEC contain intracellular mucin, whereas SC shows characteristic luminal secretions and a mammaglobin-positive phenotype. Microsecretory adenocarcinoma — MSA has monotonous intercalated duct-like cells, abundant basophilic (blue) secretions, fibromyxoid stroma, and a p63-positive/p40-negative/mammaglobin-negative phenotype. SC more often has abundant vacuolated cytoplasm, pink/bubbly secretions, and mammaglobin positivity. Other microcystic tumors — Correlate cytology and secretions with the full architecture; a microcystic pattern alone is not specific. ETV6 or RET fusion testing can resolve selected cases. In contrast to SC, acinic cell carcinomas demonstrate intense apical membranous staining for DOG1 around lumina and variable cytoplasmic positivity in most cases Approximately 90% of SCs harbour a characteristic chromosomal rearrangement, t(12;15)(p13;q25), resulting in an ETV6::NTRK3 fusion A small subset of cases demonstrate divergent molecular findings, with alternate ETV6::RET, ETV6::MET, ETV6::MAML3, and VIM::RET gene fusions Monophasic vacuolated cells with eosinophilic luminal secretions The pale vacuolated cytoplasm can resemble acinic cell carcinoma. Focus on the nature and location of secretions, absence of zymogen granules, DOG1/NR4A3 negativity, and mammaglobin positivity. ETV6 or RET fusion testing is useful in selected cases. Microsecretory adenocarcinoma Almost all MSAs have arisen in the oral cavity, with palate and buccal mucosa being the most frequently affected subsites A single case involved the parotid gland Patients present with a painless, slow-growing mass Fewer than 30 cases have been reported The mean patient age is 49.5 years (range: 17–83 years), and there is a slight female predominance Essential: a salivary gland malignancy with a microcystic-predominant growth pattern; bluish secretions; fibromyxoid stroma; monotonous tumor cells; positivity for S100 and p63 but not p40 or mammaglobin Desirable: SS18 rearrangement demonstrated by FISH, RNA sequencing, or PCR (in selected cases) A highly consistent pattern: microcystic-predominant architecture with occasional cribriform structures or cords; uniform intercalated duct-like cells with attenuated eosinophilic-to-clear cytoplasm; monotonous oval hyperchromatic nuclei with indistinct nucleoli; abundant basophilic luminal secretions; and variably cellular fibromyxoid stroma. Rounded borders may show subtle infiltration into skeletal muscle, fat, or minor salivary glands. Perineural invasion is rare, necrosis is absent, and mitotic activity is low. MSA has very consistent morphological features: (1) a microcystic-predominant growth pattern with occasional cribriform structures or cords (2) uniform intercalated duct-like tumor cells with attenuated eosinophilic to clear cytoplasm (3) monotonous oval hyperchromatic nuclei with indistinct nucleoli (4) abundant basophilic luminal secretions (5) a variably cellular fibromyxoid stroma S100, SOX10, and p63 are positive. p40, mammaglobin, and calponin are negative; SMA may be focally positive. MSA has a consistent immunophenotype It is positive for S100, SOX10, and p63, and negative for p40, mammaglobin, and calponin Occasional cases are focally positive for SMA Secretory carcinoma — SC has more abundant granular/vacuolated cytoplasm and eosinophilic or pink bubbly luminal secretions, with mammaglobin positivity and usually ETV6::NTRK3 (or an alternate ETV6/RET-related fusion). MSA has monotonous intercalated duct-like cells, basophilic/blue secretions, fibromyxoid stroma, p63 positivity, and is typically p40- and mammaglobin-negative. Polymorphous adenocarcinoma — PmA shows much greater architectural diversity (single-file, fascicular, tubular, trabecular, and targetoid perineural patterns) and often targetoid perineural invasion; MSA is predominantly microcystic with a more uniform cell population and basophilic luminal material. PRKD alterations support PmA; MEF2C::SS18 supports MSA. Adenoid cystic carcinoma — AdCC is biphasic, with ductal and basaloid myoepithelial cells, basement-membrane-like pseudocysts, and typically more extensive infiltrative growth/perineural invasion. MSA is more monotonous and lacks the characteristic biphasic AdCC pattern. Sclerosing microcystic adenocarcinoma — This is less cellular, has more abundant sclerotic/fibrous stroma and cord-like growth, and may show a subtle biphasic population; MSA is microcystic-predominant with basophilic secretions and monotonous cells. Secretory carcinoma has more abundant cytoplasm, pink secretions, mammaglobin positivity, and harbours different fusions (usually ETV6::NTRK3) Polymorphous adenocarcinoma shows more architectural diversity and different genetic alterations (mutations or rearrangements of PRKD1, PRKD2, or PRKD3) Adenoid cystic carcinoma has two cell populations, is far more infiltrative, and harbours rearrangements of MYB, MYBL1, and/or NFIB Sclerosing microcystic adenocarcinoma is less cellular, with more stroma, more cord-like growth, and a subtly biphasic tumor population MEF2C::SS18 fusion can be demonstrated by RNA sequencing, RT-PCR, or SS18 break-apart FISH Microcystic-predominant intercalated duct-like tumor with blue secretions The p63-positive/p40-negative phenotype is useful. Do not mistake MSA for secretory carcinoma solely because both are microcystic and S100/SOX10-positive. MEF2C::SS18 fusion supports MSA. Polymorphous adenocarcinoma More than 95% of PmAs involve minor salivary glands or seromucous glands of the upper aerodigestive tract The palate is the most common site PmA typically presents as a slowly growing, painless mass of variable duration Very few patients with PmA present with lymph node metastasis, but cervical lymph node metastases are common in CASG PmA is the second most common intraoral salivary gland carcinoma, with an incidence rate of 0.051 cases per 100 000 person-years Essential: a salivary gland malignancy with cytological uniformity; architectural diversity; infiltrative border Desirable: immunopositivity for S100; PRKD1 hotspot mutation (for PmA) or translocation of PRKD1, PRKD2, or PRKD3 (for CASG) in selected cases Conventional PmA is an unencapsulated infiltrative tumor composed of uniform cells with scant cytoplasm, bland oval nuclei, open chromatin, occasional small nucleoli, and sometimes nuclear grooves. Architecture is diverse: single-file, fascicular, trabecular, tubular, microcystic, solid, and occasionally papillary-cystic. Stroma may be myxoid, mucinous, or hyalinized. Perineural invasion is frequent and often targetoid; perivascular targetoid growth may also occur. Cribriform PmA (cribriform adenocarcinoma of salivary glands, CASG) shows multinodular growth, solid/cribriform/microcystic patterns, optically clear nuclei, glomeruloid and papillary structures, peripheral palisading, and clefting. The conventional subtype of PmA is typically an unencapsulated submucosal mass The tumors are characterized by cytological uniformity, histological diversity, and an infiltrative growth pattern Streaming or eddy-like formations can be present at the peripheral boundary of the tumor Foci of oncocytic, clear, squamous, apocrine, or mucous cells and microcalcifications can be observed Usually a single tumor-cell population positive for cytokeratins (including CK7) and S100. p63 is often positive, whereas p40 is typically negative. Mammaglobin and KIT may also be positive. PmA is immunoreactive as a single population for cytokeratins (e.g CK7, in 100% of cases) and S100 (97–100%) Staining for p63 is reported in 78–100% of cases, whereas p40 is typically negative; this pattern is helpful in the differential diagnosis Other positive immunomarkers include mammaglobin (67–100%), KIT (CD117) (60%), CEA (54%), GFAP (15%), MSA (13%), and EMA (12%) Adenoid cystic carcinoma — AdCC typically has a biphasic ductal/abluminal population, angular hyperchromatic basaloid nuclei, and cribriform pseudocysts containing basement-membrane-like material. PmA is cytologically uniform with open chromatin and a broad range of patterns; targetoid perineural growth is common. Pleomorphic adenoma — PA generally has chondromyxoid or fibrillary stroma and a circumscribed/pushing interface. PmA is infiltrative, often with single-file or targetoid growth and without the characteristic chondromyxoid matrix. Secretory carcinoma — SC usually has more abundant vacuolated cytoplasm and eosinophilic/bubbly secretions, with mammaglobin positivity. PmA has scant cytoplasm, open chromatin, architectural diversity, and typically p40 negativity despite p63 positivity. Microsecretory adenocarcinoma — MSA is microcystic-predominant with basophilic secretions and fibromyxoid stroma; it is typically p63-positive/p40-negative and mammaglobin-negative. PmA has a wider range of architectures and often targetoid perineural growth. Cribriform adenocarcinoma of salivary glands (CASG) — Recognize the cribriform subtype by multinodular growth, clear nuclei, glomeruloid/papillary structures, peripheral palisading, and clefting. Cervical nodal metastases are more common than in conventional PmA; PRKD rearrangement is frequent. Metastatic papillary thyroid carcinoma — In a limited cytology sample, nuclear grooves and pseudopapillary fragments may be misleading. Correlate with the clinical/radiologic thyroid evaluation and use a directed thyroid-lineage panel when indicated. Detection of a PRKD1 p.E710D hotspot mutation or translocation of PRKD1, PRKD2, or PRKD3 is highly specific for the diagnosis of PmA Cytologic uniformity + architectural diversity + infiltrative growth Do not equate bland cytology with benignity. The combination of cytologic uniformity, architectural diversity, infiltrative edges, and targetoid perineural growth is highly characteristic. PRKD1 hotspot mutation or PRKD1/2/3 rearrangement can support diagnosis. Hyalinizing clear cell carcinoma Most HCCCs arise from oral minor salivary glands in locations including the soft palate, tongue, floor of the mouth, lips, buccal mucosa, retromolar trigone, and gingival sites A minority develop in other sites including the oropharynx, nasopharynx, parotid, sinonasal tract, larynx, and hypopharynx Most HCCCs present with localized swelling The overlying mucosa may be ulcerated HCCC has a slight female predominance Essential: a salivary gland malignancy with nests, cords, and trabeculae of clear and/or eosinophilic cells in a hyalinized stroma Desirable: EWSR1 fusion (in selected cases) Composed of clear and/or eosinophilic cells arranged in nests, cords, and trabeculae; ducts and small cysts may be present. Squamous differentiation and mucocytes are common. Tumors are unencapsulated and infiltrate surrounding tissue, especially skeletal muscle; oral tumors may connect with surface epithelium and show pagetoid spread. Perineural invasion occurs in about half of cases. Stroma ranges from dense basement-membrane-like hyalinization to desmoplastic or fibrocellular areas; juxtaposition of these stromal types is a useful clue. Clear cells are PAS-positive and diastase-sensitive. HCCC is composed of clear or eosinophilic cells Despite its name, tumors composed entirely of clear cells are rare, and some completely lack clear cells The tumor is arranged in nests, cords, and trabeculae Ducts and small cysts may be seen Increased mitoses, marked atypia, and necrosis are rare; when seen, they represent high-grade transformation Epithelial markers include CK7, CK19, CK14, CAM5.2, and EMA. p63, p40, and CK5/6 are usually positive. Myoepithelial markers (S100, MSA, SMA, calponin) are negative. p16 may be positive in oropharyngeal tumors, but transcriptionally active HPV is absent. The tumor cells express epithelial markers including CK7, CK19, CK14, CAM5.2, and EMA They also usually express p63, p40, and CK5/6, supporting squamous differentiation Myoepithelial markers including S100, MSA, SMA, and calponin are negative Some tumors express p16, which can be a diagnostic dilemma when the tumor arises in the oropharynx; however they lack transcriptionally active HPV Clear cell mucoepidermoid carcinoma — Search for mucous, intermediate, and squamoid cells and mucicarmine-positive intracellular mucin; HCCC is typically a monophasic clear/eosinophilic cell tumor with hyalinized stroma and squamous differentiation. Epithelial-myoepithelial carcinoma — EMC has a conspicuous biphasic duct with inner eosinophilic luminal cells and an outer clear myoepithelial layer; HCCC lacks this organized ductal double layer and is negative for myoepithelial markers. Myoepithelial carcinoma / myoepithelioma — These show myoepithelial differentiation and commonly express S100, SOX10, and/or muscle markers; HCCC typically expresses p63/p40/CK5/6 but lacks S100, SMA, and calponin. Metastatic clear cell carcinoma (especially renal) — Correlate with history and imaging; a directed renal-lineage panel is appropriate when clinically indicated. Clear cell odontogenic carcinoma — Consider a primary intraosseous jaw lesion; it is morphologically and genetically related to HCCC, so anatomic origin is essential. The entities include clear cell mucoepidermoid carcinoma, epithelial-myoepithelial carcinoma, myoepithelial carcinoma, oncocytoma, myoepithelioma, and metastatic clear cell carcinoma, with distinction sometimes requiring molecular studies Demonstration of an EWSR1 fusion gene is helpful in selected cases Clear/eosinophilic nests and cords in hyalinized stroma Despite the name, tumors composed entirely of clear cells are uncommon. Do not infer HPV-driven carcinoma from p16 positivity alone. EWSR1::ATF1 is the typical fusion; EWSR1::CREM has also been described. Basal cell adenocarcinoma Most BCACs occur in the parotid gland (> 90%) BCAC usually presents as a slow-growing nodule in the parotid gland Patients with syndromic BCAC may also have multiple skin adnexal tumors BCAC accounts for < 3% of malignant salivary tumors Most affected patients are in their sixth or seventh decade of life Essential: a salivary gland malignancy with invasive growth; basaloid morphology; peripheral palisading with paler inner cells and ducts; dual population immunophenotype Tubulotrabecular, membranous, or solid growth, with membranous and solid patterns common.
