Nests show peripheral palisading of dark basaloid cells, paler inner cells, and centrally located ducts. Squamous and sebaceous elements may occur. Invasion is the defining distinction from basal cell adenoma; perineural and vascular invasion are reported. Anaplasia is uncommon. About 25% show perineural and vascular invasion; anaplasia is rare Often unencapsulated and infiltrative; tubulotrabecular, membranous, or solid patterns may be present. Perineural and vascular invasion are reported. Cytologic atypia may be modest; invasion is the decisive feature. Epithelial and myoepithelial markers demonstrate the dual cell composition. Nuclear beta-catenin is present in a subset. Nuclear β-catenin is present in a subset; this does not distinguish benign from malignant behavior. Basal cell adenoma (BCA) — The key distinction is invasion. BCA is generally circumscribed/encapsulated and lacks destructive infiltration. BCAC shows infiltrative growth; perineural or vascular invasion and tumor necrosis support malignancy. Increased mitotic activity (particularly >4 mitoses/2 mm² in some diagnostic criteria) is concerning. Adenoid cystic carcinoma — AdCC more typically has angular hyperchromatic basaloid cells, true ducts plus basement-membrane-like pseudocysts, and often perineural invasion. BCAC commonly shows peripheral palisading, paler inner cells, and ducts; squamous or sebaceous differentiation may be present. Cribriform BCA versus cribriform AdCC — Do not diagnose AdCC from cribriform architecture alone. Evaluate the tumor border, cell morphology, true lumina versus pseudocysts, stromal material, and invasion. A circumscribed cribriform lesion may be BCA. Pleomorphic adenoma — PA has characteristic chondromyxoid/fibrillary stroma and a mixed epithelial-myoepithelial phenotype rather than a predominantly basaloid tumor with peripheral palisading. The presence of peripheral palisading and focal squamous metaplasia can help to separate BCAC from adenoid cystic carcinoma BCAC is distinguished from BCA by infiltration, necrosis, and mitoses (especially when > 4 mitoses/2 mm²) A subset shows CYLD or CTNNB1 alterations. No defining molecular alteration has been established for BCAC. Infiltrative basaloid tumor with peripheral palisading and ductal differentiation Do not diagnose BCAC from cytologic atypia or β-catenin alone. Establish infiltrative growth, perineural invasion, or vascular invasion. Can closely resemble BCA, with basaloid fragments and hyaline material. Squamoid or sebaceous features may provide a clue, but FNA generally cannot demonstrate destructive invasion or reliably separate BCA from BCAC. Intraductal carcinoma IDC arises predominantly in the parotid gland, with uncommon involvement of the intraparotid lymph nodes, submandibular gland, and oral cavity Patients present with longstanding painless swellings IDCs are indolent neoplasms, but rare cases of invasive carcinoma ex IDC have been reported IDC is rare It affects adults, with a wide age range (25–93 years) and an even sex distribution Essential: a salivary gland malignancy with rounded lobules of ductal neoplastic cells; a surrounding rim of myoepithelial cells; ductal cells positive for S100, SOX10, and mammaglobin and/or AR Desirable: a cystic component; identification of RET fusion (for intercalated duct, oncocytic, or mixed IDC), BRAF p.V600E mutations (for oncocytic IDC), or PI3K pathway mutations (for apocrine IDC) in selected cases Rounded cysts and lobules contain variable solid, cribriform, micropapillary, or Roman-bridge-like ductal proliferations, surrounded by a continuous flattened myoepithelial layer. Intercalated duct type has small amphophilic-to-eosinophilic cells with oval nuclei. Apocrine type has large cells with bubbly eosinophilic cytoplasm, apical snouts, and decapitation secretion. Oncocytic type has abundant granular eosinophilic cytoplasm and round nuclei with prominent nucleoli. Mixed tumors combine patterns. Intercalated duct and oncocytic types are generally low grade; apocrine components may be low or high grade. Invasive carcinoma is indicated by loss of the peripheral myoepithelial layer. The ductal cells vary with each subtype (see #25851Table 4.03) Intercalated duct and oncocytic ductal cells: S100, SOX10, and mammaglobin positive; AR and GCDFP-15 negative. Apocrine IDC shows the reciprocal apocrine profile. Myoepithelial rim: p40/p63, CK14, SMA, and calponin positive. Mixed IDC shows mixed immunoprofiles of the components present Carcinoma ex pleomorphic adenoma — Look for residual pleomorphic adenoma with chondromyxoid stroma and characteristic ductal/myoepithelial components; this background is not a feature of a pure IDC. Sclerosing polycystic adenoma — Look for its characteristic sclerosing/polyclonal acinar and ductal background rather than a discrete intraductal neoplastic proliferation. Cystadenoma — Cystadenoma lacks the fenestrated/cribriform ductal proliferation and complete surrounding myoepithelial layer characteristic of IDC. Mucoepidermoid carcinoma, secretory carcinoma, and salivary duct carcinoma — These do not show a continuous circumferential myoepithelial layer around the neoplastic ducts. Epithelial-myoepithelial carcinoma — EMC has larger, more conspicuous outer myoepithelial cells and an invasive biphasic ductal pattern; in IDC the myoepithelial rim is flattened and confines the intraductal proliferation. Invasive carcinoma arising in IDC — Loss of the peripheral myoepithelial layer with stromal invasion identifies an invasive component; assess each focus separately. Intraductal proliferations seen in carcinoma ex pleomorphic adenoma and sclerosing polycystic adenoma are distinguished by their background elements (chondromyxoid stroma and acinar cells, respectively) Demonstration of molecular alteration can assist in diagnosis Routine break-apart FISH is often falsely negative in IDC with NCOA4::RET, which is a tight inversion due to an intrachromosomal rearrangement Ductal proliferation enclosed by a continuous myoepithelial rim The continuous myoepithelial layer is the key feature supporting intraductal status. Carefully examine the entire lesion for focal invasion. Routine break-apart FISH may be falsely negative for NCOA4::RET because of its intrachromosomal inversion. Salivary duct carcinoma Most tumors involve major salivary glands SDC presents as a rapidly growing tumor, with facial nerve palsy, pain, and cervical lymphadenopathy If arising from pleomorphic adenoma, a rapid increase in size of a longstanding pre-existing mass is common SDC has a distinct male predilection and a peak incidence in the fifth to seventh decades of life Essential: a high-grade carcinoma, most typically with apocrine features Desirable: AR expression Complex solid, cribriform, and papillary-cystic architecture with frequent comedonecrosis. Cells have large pleomorphic nuclei, coarse chromatin, prominent nucleoli, and abundant eosinophilic, often apocrine cytoplasm. Lymphovascular and perineural invasion are common. A residual or hyalinized pleomorphic adenoma component may be present. Variants include sarcomatoid, mucin-rich, micropapillary, basal-like, and oncocytic patterns. Micropapillary SDC shows small nests without fibrovascular cores, retraction spaces, and an inside-out EMA pattern. Rarely, SDC may be purely in situ Subtypes The sarcomatoid subtype of SDC contains areas of highly atypical spindle cells, occasionally with foci of heterologous differentiation (e.g. osteoid production) AR is positive in about 90%; strong diffuse ERBB2/HER2 immunoreactivity occurs in about one third. CK7 is consistently positive; S100 and SOX10 are negative. p63 may highlight basal/myoepithelial cells around an intraductal component. AR is expressed in about 90% of SDCs, indicative of an apocrine immunophenotype Diffuse and strong immunoreactivity for ERBB2 is identified in about one third of SDCs CK7 is consistently positive, whereas S100 and SOX10 are negative Staining for p63 may help to identify the intraductal component by highlighting basal/myoepithelial cells surrounding neoplastic cells Carcinoma ex pleomorphic adenoma — Search for residual PA, including hyalinized/chondromyxoid nodules and PLAG1/HMGA2-associated background. SDC may arise in PA, but the high-grade apocrine carcinoma component should be recognized separately. High-grade mucoepidermoid carcinoma — MEC should contain at least focal mucous and intermediate cells; extensive keratinization favors SCC. SDC more often shows apocrine cytoplasm, marked pleomorphism, complex cribriform/papillary-cystic growth, and comedonecrosis. Adenoid cystic carcinoma with high-grade transformation — Conventional AdCC may be present at the periphery or in a separate component; the high-grade transformed area loses myoepithelial marker expression. Look for residual classic cribriform/tubular AdCC. Metastatic breast carcinoma — SDC resembles apocrine breast carcinoma morphologically and immunophenotypically. Clinical history and imaging are essential; no single marker establishes salivary origin. Metastatic cutaneous SCC or other carcinoma — Exclude a non-salivary primary based on clinical history, examination, and imaging, especially for parotid tumors. The differential diagnosis includes other salivary carcinomas with high-grade transformation Because systemic therapies targeting AR, ERRB2 amplification, the PI3K pathway (including PIK3CA mutations and PTEN loss), and BRAF p.V600E are being investigated, molecular analysis may be warranted High-grade apocrine carcinoma with cribriform/comedonecrotic architecture A rapidly enlarging mass in a longstanding PA is a clinical clue. Do not overlook comedonecrosis, marked cytologic atypia, and infiltrative growth. AR/HER2 testing has therapeutic relevance but does not replace morphologic classification. Myoepithelial carcinoma Most tumors occur in the parotid gland, followed by the palate and the submandibular gland Patients often present with a painless mass, sometimes with recent rapid growth MECA is underrecognized It may present at any age and has no sex predilection Essential: a salivary gland malignancy showing nearly exclusively myoepithelial differentiation; invasive growth Desirable: a zonal pattern with a hypercellular periphery and a hypocellular center May arise de novo or in pleomorphic adenoma. Cells may be spindle, epithelioid, plasmacytoid, vacuolated, oncocytic, or clear, in solid, trabecular, or reticular patterns. Stroma may be myxoid, myxochondroid, or hyalinized. A uniform myoepithelial proliferation with multinodular architecture and transition from peripheral hypercellular zones to central hypocellular areas is characteristic and helps distinguish it from pleomorphic adenoma. Focal duct-like or squamous differentiation may occur. MECA may arise de novo or within a pre-existing PA and is the second most common histological subtype of carcinoma ex PA The uniform cellular myoepithelial proliferation with the multinodular pattern and the transition from peripheral hypercellular zones to central hypocellular areas are characteristic and help to differentiate MECA from PA The presence of PA and tumor necrosis correlates with a worse outcome Cytokeratins, SOX10, S100, and myoepithelial markers including SMA, calponin, and p63/p40 are expressed. Myoepithelioma — A circumscribed lesion without destructive infiltration supports myoepithelioma; myoepithelial carcinoma requires unequivocal invasion and/or malignant cytologic features in the appropriate context. Pleomorphic adenoma — PA shows chondromyxoid/fibrillary stroma and a mixed ductal/myoepithelial population. Myoepithelial carcinoma may show myxoid or hyalinized stroma but is infiltrative and may show plasmacytoid, epithelioid, spindle, or clear cells. Epithelial-myoepithelial carcinoma — EMC has a recognizable biphasic duct with inner ductal cells and outer clear myoepithelial cells. Myoepithelial carcinoma is often predominantly or entirely myoepithelial without the orderly ductal double layer. Hyalinizing clear cell carcinoma — HCCC is typically p63/p40/CK5/6-positive but S100/SMA/calponin-negative and often has EWSR1 rearrangement; myoepithelial carcinoma usually expresses one or more myoepithelial markers. Metastatic melanoma or clear cell carcinoma — Use clinical history and a directed lineage panel when morphology is clear-cell or epithelioid and epithelial differentiation is uncertain. MECA is often cytologically bland and may therefore be underrecognized as malignant and misclassified as a myoepithelial-rich PA Infiltrative myoepithelial proliferation with multinodular architecture Myoepithelial carcinoma can be intracapsular or minimally invasive in the setting of PA and still show clinically significant behavior. Necrosis and an associated PA component are adverse features. Epithelial-myoepithelial carcinoma The majority of EMCs develop in the parotid gland; the remainder affect the other major or minor salivary glands, sinonasal tract, and bronchus EMC usually presents as a slow-growing, painless mass Lymphadenopathy is rare EMC is an uncommon neoplasm, accounting for 1% of all salivary gland tumors It mostly occurs in the sixth and seventh decades of life, with a slight female predilection Essential: a salivary gland malignancy, usually with multinodular invasive growth; at least partly with a dual arrangement of inner ductal cells and outer prominent, usually clear, myoepithelial cells Usually multinodular and invasive. The hallmark is a biphasic arrangement of inner luminal eosinophilic ductal cells and outer abluminal, often clear, myoepithelial cells. The outer component may be a single layer, multilayered, or solid. Nuclear atypia is usually mild to moderate. Patterns include cribriform, basaloid, sebaceous, apocrine/oncocytic, and double-clear appearances; squamous differentiation may occur. High-grade transformation is rare. EMC generally exhibits multinodular invasive growth The myoepithelial component may be single-layered, multilayered, or solid. Clear cells are common, but cribriform, basaloid, sebaceous, apocrine/oncocytic, double-clear, and squamous patterns can occur. Nuclear atypia is often mild to moderate. High-grade transformation is rare. Luminal cells: CK7. Abluminal cells: SMA, calponin, and p63/p40. RAS p.Q61R staining is reported in a subset. The luminal cells are positive for CK7, whereas abluminal cells are usually positive for SMA, calponin, and p63/p40 Diffuse and membranous/cytoplasmic RAS p.Q61R expression is observed in 65% of EMCs RAS p.Q61R immunoreactivity has been reported in a substantial subset, but it is not a substitute for morphology or sequencing. Adenoid cystic carcinoma — AdCC has compact basaloid abluminal cells with angular hyperchromatic nuclei and cribriform pseudocysts containing basement-membrane-like material. EMC shows conspicuous ducts with an inner eosinophilic luminal layer and a thick outer layer of clear myoepithelial cells. Myoepithelial carcinoma — Myoepithelial carcinoma lacks the orderly, repeated inner ductal/outer myoepithelial configuration and is often predominantly myoepithelial. Pleomorphic adenoma — PA is usually circumscribed and has characteristic chondromyxoid/fibrillary stroma; EMC is infiltrative and has a more consistently organized biphasic ductal pattern. Basal cell adenoma/adenocarcinoma — These are basaloid tumors with peripheral palisading and may show ducts, but the typical broad clear-cell outer myoepithelial layer of EMC is a key distinction. Assess invasion to separate adenoma from adenocarcinoma. The differential diagnosis includes other salivary gland tumors with biphasic and/or clear cell morphology, such as adenoid cystic carcinoma, basal cell adenocarcinoma, pleomorphic adenoma, myoepithelial carcinoma, and clear cell carcinoma Assessment of HRAS mutations is useful for discriminating EMC from mimics HRAS mutations, commonly involving codon 61, occur in a significant subset and can help distinguish EMC from mimics. Biphasic ducts with inner luminal and outer clear myoepithelial cells Do not call a tumor EMC merely because it is biphasic. Demonstrate the characteristic inner ductal/outer myoepithelial tubular arrangement and assess invasion. Classically shows three-dimensional clusters with dual epithelial and myoepithelial populations. The two populations may be less obvious in scant or crushed samples; correlate with the tubular biphasic pattern in tissue. Mucinous adenocarcinoma MA is most common in intraoral minor salivary glands Most patients have painless masses or swellings Nodal metastases are occasionally seen at presentation MA has a peak incidence in the eighth decade of life and a relatively equal sex distribution Essential: a salivary gland malignancy with abundant intracellular or extracellular mucin; CK7+, CK20−; no features of other mucin-producing salivary gland neoplasms Desirable: AKT1 p.E17K mutation (in selected cases) Abundant mucin occurs as goblet-like vacuoles, apical caps, foveolar-type droplets, or extracellular stromal pools. Patterns include papillary, colloid, and signet-ring; mixed patterns are common. Papillary fronds often project into cystic spaces. In the colloid pattern, tumor nests are suspended in pools of mucin. Discohesive signet-ring cells are uncommon. Cytologic atypia varies. MA is defined by abundant intracellular and/or extracellular mucin production in multiple forms, including goblet cell–like vacuoles, apical caps, foveolar-type cytoplasmic droplets, or stromal pools Tumors show variable papillary, colloid, or signet-ring architecture, with 40% displaying mixed patterns CK7 positive; CK20, CDX2, p63, p40, TTF1, S100, calponin, SMA, and AR negative. AKT1 p.E17K may support the diagnosis. Mucoepidermoid carcinoma — MEC contains mucous, intermediate, and squamoid cells, often with cystic and solid components. Mucinous adenocarcinoma is dominated by extensive extracellular mucin pools containing floating tumor cells; look for absence of a defining MEC cell mixture. Metastatic mucinous adenocarcinoma — Exclude gastrointestinal, breast, lung, and other mucinous primaries with clinical history, imaging, and site-directed immunohistochemistry. A salivary location alone does not prove primary origin. Mucin-producing adenocarcinoma NOS — If the tumor has significant mucinous differentiation but does not meet criteria for a defined entity, classify only after excluding MEC and metastasis. To diagnose MA, other mucin-producing salivary gland carcinomas must be excluded, including mucin-rich mucoepidermoid carcinoma (epidermoid/intermediate cells; p63/p40+), mucinous and rhabdoid variants of salivary duct carcinoma (apocrine cytology; AR+), and the mucinous/secretory pattern of myoepithelial carcinoma (nested/corded pattern; S100, calponin, or SMA+) Metastasis from gastrointestinal, pancreaticobiliary, or lung adenocarcinomas should be ruled out clinically The identification of AKT1 p.E17K mutation can support the diagnosis Prominent intracellular and/or extracellular mucin with papillary/colloid patterns Do not classify a mucin-producing tumor as primary salivary MA until other salivary carcinoma types and metastatic adenocarcinoma have been excluded. Colloid and signet-ring predominant patterns are associated with recurrence/metastasis. Sclerosing microcystic adenocarcinoma SMA arises from intraoral minor salivary glands in sites including the tongue, lip mucosa, floor of the mouth, and buccal mucosa A single case was reported in the nasopharynx Patients most commonly present with a painless mass or swelling; less common symptoms include dysphagia, numbness, and diplopia SMA is more common in women than men and occurs from the fifth to the eighth decades of life (mean age: 56 years) Essential: an infiltrative low-grade adenocarcinoma embedded in a dense sclerotic stroma; a biphasic cell population with an attenuated myoepithelial cell layer Desirable: perineural invasion Deeply infiltrative ducts/tubules, strands/cords, nests, and occasionally single cells are embedded in dense collagenous stroma. A biphasic population is present: bland luminal ductal cells with round-to-oval monotonous nuclei and eosinophilic-to-clear cytoplasm, surrounded by flattened peripheral myoepithelial cells. Mitoses are inconspicuous. Perineural invasion is common; apposition to or invasion of minor salivary glands may occur. The tumor is composed of a biphasic cell population including luminal-lining bland-appearing ductal cells with round to oval monotonous nuclei, evenly dispersed chromatin, occasional nucleoli, and eosinophilic to clear cytoplasm Ductal lining cells are peripherally surrounded by flattened myoepithelial cells Luminal cells: pancytokeratin and CK7. Peripheral myoepithelial cells: p40/p63, S100, SMA, and calponin. KIT/CD117 is negative; Ki-67 is low. Duct lining cells are positive for pancytokeratin and CK7, and the peripheral myoepithelial cell population expresses p40/p63, S100, SMA (smooth muscle actin), and calponin Low proliferation indexes are seen with Ki-67 (MIB1) staining Microsecretory adenocarcinoma — MSA is more cellular and microcystic-predominant, with monotonous intercalated duct-like cells and abundant basophilic secretions; it is typically S100/SOX10/p63-positive and p40/mammaglobin-negative. Sclerosing microcystic adenocarcinoma has more abundant sclerotic stroma, more cord-like growth, and a subtly biphasic population. Secretory carcinoma — SC has more abundant vacuolated cytoplasm, pink/bubbly secretions, and mammaglobin positivity; correlate with ETV6/RET fusions when needed. Adenoid cystic carcinoma — AdCC shows a true biphasic basaloid/ductal population and basement-membrane-like pseudocysts, often with more overt infiltrative and perineural growth. The biphasic cell population, bland cytology, immunoreactive staining pattern, and lack of keratinization are helpful features in the differentiation from squamous cell carcinoma, polymorphous adenocarcinoma, adenoid cystic carcinoma, mucoepidermoid carcinoma, and hyalinizing clear cell carcinoma Deeply infiltrative ducts and cords in dense collagenous stroma Despite bland cytology and low mitotic activity, the tumor is deeply infiltrative and commonly perineural. Do not mistake it for a benign sclerosing process or a noninvasive ductal lesion. Carcinoma ex pleomorphic adenoma Most CXPAs arise in the parotid gland, but they may originate from the submandibular gland or minor salivary glands The typical clinical presentation is that of a longstanding painless mass with recent rapid progression, or of a previous diagnosis of a PA Occasionally, the tumor may be asymptomatic CXPA accounts for 3.6% of all salivary gland tumors and 12% of all salivary gland malignancies It occurs in the setting of a recurrent PA in about 12% of cases Essential: evidence of a pre-existing PA, clinically or histologically, with a carcinoma (epithelial and/or myoepithelial) A residual PA component may be intermixed with carcinoma or form a discrete, often hyalinized/sclerotic nodule. The malignant component may be any carcinoma type, most commonly salivary duct carcinoma, followed by myoepithelial carcinoma and adenocarcinoma NOS. Classify invasion relative to the PA capsule: intracapsular (including in situ growth retaining myoepithelial cells), minimally invasive (<4–6 mm beyond PA borders), and invasive (≥6 mm beyond the capsule, in commonly used criteria). Report the histologic type of the carcinoma and extent of invasion. In most cases, the carcinoma component constitutes > 50% of the tumor volume CXPA can be subclassified according to the extent of invasion beyond the PA borders as follows: (1) intracapsular, when the carcinoma is confined within the PA capsule in situ intracapsular, when the malignant tumor cells replace the ductal cells while retaining an intact myoepithelial layer (2) minimally invasive, when the carcinoma invades < 4–6 mm beyond the PA borders and (3) invasive, when the invasion beyond the PA capsule measures ≥ 6 mm PLAG1 and HMGA2 may help identify the PA component. AR may support a salivary duct carcinoma component. Additional markers should be selected according to the carcinoma subtype. Staining for AR may be indicative of salivary duct CXPA Pleomorphic adenoma — A conventional PA is usually circumscribed and contains chondromyxoid/fibrillary stroma. CXPA requires carcinoma arising in or associated with PA; identify residual PA and carefully assess for invasive carcinoma beyond the PA boundary. Metastasizing pleomorphic adenoma — This may look cytologically benign, but requires a history of PA and documented metastasis; it is distinct from CXPA, which contains a malignant epithelial component. De novo salivary carcinoma — If no residual PA is identified, use morphology and molecular findings to assess whether a specific carcinoma type is present; PLAG1/HMGA2 alterations may support PA lineage but do not alone prove invasion. SDC, AdCC, MEC, and myoepithelial carcinoma — These may represent the malignant component of CXPA. Classify the carcinoma component by its own morphology rather than using CXPA as a substitute for subtype designation. Myoepithelial carcinoma and epithelial-myoepithelial carcinoma ex PA can mimic cellular PA especially when intracapsular or minimally invasive The invasive multinodular pattern helps to differentiate these tumors from PA PLAG1 or HMGA2 rearrangements detected by FISH serve as a marker of pre-existing PA and can assist in the diagnosis of CXPA Carcinoma arising in a demonstrable pleomorphic adenoma Sampling may capture only PA or only carcinoma. Extensive sampling is essential, especially in a longstanding or recurrent mass with recent rapid enlargement. State the carcinoma subtype and measure invasion beyond the PA boundary. Carcinosarcoma of the salivary glands Most cases of carcinosarcoma manifest in major salivary glands (parotid, 70%; submandibular, 19%); minor gland occurrences are rare Carcinosarcomas are typically rapidly growing, large, and infiltrative tumors The mean age at presentation is 58 years (range: 14–87 years), with no sex predilection Essential: a combined salivary gland tumor with malignant epithelial and mesenchymal components; exclusion of sarcomatoid subtypes of other salivary gland malignancies A combined malignancy with carcinomatous and sarcomatous components. The epithelial component is most often SCC or adenocarcinoma; the sarcomatous component is commonly chondrosarcoma and may dominate. About half arise in a pre-existing PA, often with a residual sclerotic PA nodule. Both components should be identified and sampled; a purely intracapsular carcinosarcoma ex PA is very rare. The sarcomatous components frequently dominate Approximately half of the tumors show a pre-existing, often sclerotic pleomorphic adenoma, usually with a carcinomatous (rarely sarcomatous) intracapsular component Pure intracapsular carcinosarcoma ex pleomorphic adenoma is very rare Use immunohistochemistry to characterize the sarcomatous component and distinguish true carcinosarcoma from other salivary carcinomas with high-grade transformation. Select epithelial and mesenchymal markers according to the morphology. Sarcomatoid carcinoma — Usually shows a malignant epithelial neoplasm with spindle-cell or heterologous sarcomatoid transformation; demonstrate epithelial differentiation in the spindle component and assess whether there are truly distinct malignant epithelial and mesenchymal components. Carcinoma ex pleomorphic adenoma — A residual pleomorphic adenoma or convincing history supports carcinoma ex PA; a separate malignant mesenchymal component is required for carcinosarcoma. High-grade transformation of a salivary carcinoma — High-grade areas retain or evolve from the epithelial lineage rather than forming a distinct malignant sarcomatous component. Metastatic carcinosarcoma or sarcoma involving the salivary gland — Correlate with clinical history, imaging, and evidence of a primary tumor elsewhere. Malignant epithelial and malignant mesenchymal components A spindle-cell or heterologous component alone does not establish carcinosarcoma. Confirm malignant mesenchymal differentiation and exclude a sarcomatoid subtype of another salivary carcinoma. Sebaceous adenocarcinoma Most (~70%) arise in the parotid gland, but they may occur in the sublingual, submandibular, or minor glands Patients present with painful masses, varying degrees of facial nerve paralysis, and occasional skin fixation Rare patients present with tumor metastasis (head/neck or lung) or a non-tender mass Sebaceous adenocarcinoma is rare and shows two peak incidences, in the third and seventh/eighth decades of life (age range: 6–93 years) There is a slight female predominance Essential: an invasive salivary gland malignancy; neoplastic sebaceous cells of varying maturity Desirable: tumor necrosis Multiple invasive nests and/or sheets of variably sized cells with hyperchromatic nuclei and abundant clear, vacuolated-to-eosinophilic sebaceous cytoplasm. Cellular pleomorphism ranges from mild to marked; necrosis is frequent. Perineural invasion occurs in a subset; vascular invasion is rare. A lymphocytic infiltrate is common. Oncocytes and foreign-body giant cells are uncommon. Necrosis is frequent Sebaceous/basal cells: CK5/6, CK7, CK14, and EMA. Sebocytes: CD15, lactoferrin, GCDFP-2, and adipophilin. Sebaceous/basal epithelial cells are positive for CK5/6, CK7, CK14, and EMA; sebocytes are positive for CD15, lactoferrin, GCDFP-2, and adipophilin Sebaceous adenoma or sebaceoma — Benign sebaceous neoplasms are generally circumscribed and lack destructive invasion, significant atypia, and tumor necrosis. Sebaceous adenocarcinoma shows invasive nests/sheets of sebocytes with variable pleomorphism and often necrosis. Metastatic or directly extending cutaneous sebaceous carcinoma — Correlate with skin examination, prior history, and anatomic relationship to the gland; morphology and sebaceous markers alone do not establish a primary salivary origin. Other salivary carcinomas with lymphoid stroma — Recognize the dual population of basaloid/basal epithelial cells and sebocytes; the sebaceous component should be confirmed morphologically and with adipophilin/CD15/lactoferrin/GCDFP-2 as appropriate. The differential diagnosis includes other salivary carcinomas with dense lymphoid reaction and sebaceous differentiation Loss of MSH2 expression is uncommon and may characterize tumors in Muir–Torre syndrome Invasive sebocytic nests with vacuolated cytoplasm and pleomorphism Recognize both sebaceous and basaloid cell populations. In patients with suspected Muir-Torre syndrome, mismatch-repair protein loss (MLH1, MSH2, MSH6) may be relevant; this is not typical of sporadic tumors. Lymphoepithelial carcinoma The majority (> 90%) of LECs arise in the major salivary glands, with the parotid gland predominating (> 75%), as well in the larynx (see section Lymphoepithelial carcinoma of the larynx) and sinonasal cavities (see section Sinonasal lymphoepithelial carcinoma) Patients present with a mass of varying duration; pain (occurring in ~5% of cases) and nerve findings (~2.5%) are rare Cervical lymphadenopathy is noted in about 17% of cases In some ethnic groups (in particular, in Inuit, southern Chinese, Japanese, northern African, and Mongolian populations), LEC accounts for 3.6–92% of malignant tumors, but in non-endemic regions it represents only 0.3–0.7% of malignancies It affects a wide age range (median: 46 years; patients in non-endemic regions tend to be a decade older) Essential: a salivary gland malignancy of undifferentiated morphology with lymphoid stroma; exclusion of other tumors with associated lymphoid proliferation; exclusion of metastasis Desirable: EBER positivity Morphology resembles nonkeratinizing nasopharyngeal carcinoma: nests of large anaplastic carcinoma cells embedded in a dense lymphoid stroma. A basaloid variant may show sclerotic stroma, less lymphoid tissue, and angulated cords or syringoma-like nests. Adjacent salivary parenchyma may show lymphoepithelial sialadenitis. EBER in situ hybridization establishes EBV status. No defining immunohistochemical panel has been established; use stains to characterize the specific tumor components and exclude mimics. Metastatic nasopharyngeal carcinoma — This is the critical exclusion because the morphology may be indistinguishable from salivary LEC. Examine the nasopharynx and correlate with imaging/clinical history; EBER positivity supports EBV association but does not by itself prove the salivary gland is the primary site. Large-cell undifferentiated carcinoma — LEC has a prominent non-neoplastic lymphoplasmacytic stroma accompanying nests/syncytia of undifferentiated carcinoma cells. If the lymphoid background is absent or scant, consider other undifferentiated carcinomas. High-grade MEC — Look for mucous and intermediate cells or other recognizable MEC differentiation; a dense lymphoid background alone is not sufficient for LEC. Lymphoepithelial sialadenitis — Shows reactive lymphoepithelial lesions and lymphoid infiltrates involving ducts, but lacks destructive nests of malignant epithelial cells with marked cytologic atypia. LEC must be distinguished from large cell undifferentiated carcinoma and from metastasis from the nasopharynx In situ hybridization for EBV-encoded small RNA (EBER) establishes EBV status Undifferentiated carcinoma nests in prominent lymphoplasmacytic stroma The lymphoid background can obscure the epithelial component. Do not diagnose LEC without excluding metastatic/non-salivary primary carcinoma; consider the patient's geographic/ethnic and EBV context without using it as a substitute for testing. Squamous cell carcinoma Approximately 80% of cases occur in the parotid gland, with the remainder primarily in the submandibular gland Patient presentations include a mass (with or without pain) and facial nerve palsy Primary salivary SCC is very rare The majority of reported cases of salivary SCC are cutaneous SCC with secondary invasion or metastasis to the salivary gland Essential: a primary salivary gland malignancy with exclusively squamous differentiation; no history of another primary SCC Desirable: presence of salivary duct dysplasia Usually infiltrating well- to moderately differentiated carcinoma with desmoplasia, intracellular keratin, keratin pearls, and intercellular bridges. Poorly differentiated tumors may contain spindle/sarcomatoid cells. Acantholytic (adenoid) features are uncommon. Invasion may involve gland parenchyma, extraglandular soft tissue, nerves, vessels, or bone. Ductal squamous metaplasia/dysplasia with transition to carcinoma may occasionally be seen. Intracellular keratin, keratin pearl formation, and intercellular bridges are seen Invasion includes infiltration of salivary gland parenchyma, infiltration of extraglandular fibroconnective tissues, neurotropism, lymphovascular invasion, and/or osseous invasion Direct invasion and/or metastasis to intraparotid lymph nodes may be present Cytokeratins and p63/p40 are positive. AR, S100, mammaglobin, and DOG1 are negative. p16 may be overexpressed, but High-risk HPV RNA is generally negative. SCCs are immunoreactive for cytokeratins and p63/p40 and are negative for AR, S100, mammaglobin, and DOG1 SCCs may overexpress p16 but are negative for high-risk HPV RNA Metastatic cutaneous SCC — This is the most important exclusion in a parotid-region tumor. Review history and examine the scalp, face, and ear; intraparotid lymph node involvement may represent metastasis. Morphology and p40/p63 positivity cannot distinguish primary from metastatic SCC. Metastatic mucosal SCC — Exclude an oral cavity, oropharyngeal, laryngeal, or other mucosal primary by clinical examination and imaging. p16 expression alone is not proof of transcriptionally active HPV in this setting. High-grade mucoepidermoid carcinoma — MEC contains mucous and intermediate cells, even if sparse in high-grade tumors; mucicarmine/PAS-D may help identify mucous cells. Extensive keratinization and absence of mucous/intermediate cells favor SCC. Adenoid cystic carcinoma with high-grade transformation — Search for a conventional AdCC component; the transformed component may be pleomorphic and lose myoepithelial markers. Primary salivary SCC — A diagnosis of exclusion. A transition from normal/squamous-metaplastic duct epithelium through dysplasia to carcinoma may support salivary origin, but clinical exclusion of another primary remains essential. Primary SCC must be distinguished from metastases (cutaneous or mucosal), as well as from high-grade transformation of adenoid cystic carcinoma with squamoid pattern A lack of mucous and intermediate cells and the presence of keratinization are most helpful in differentiating SCC from a mucoepidermoid carcinoma Infiltrative keratinizing squamous carcinoma; primary diagnosis of exclusion Primary salivary SCC cannot be reliably distinguished from metastasis by morphology or immunohistochemistry alone. Clinical history, skin and mucosal examination, and exclusion of another primary are mandatory. Sialoblastoma Other malignant tumors The majority (two thirds) of tumors arise in the parotid gland, followed by the submandibular gland; there are only rare reports of tumors in the minor salivary glands Patients present with painless facial swelling; rare cases show nerve involvement or skin ulceration Other tumors (naevi and hepatoblastoma) may be coexistent The vast majority of tumors are identified at birth or within the first few months of life, with only rare reports in adults There is no sex predilection Essential: a salivary gland malignancy showing primitive solid organoid nests; basaloid epithelial cells with vesicular chromatin; cuboidal to columnar ductal cells Desirable: dividing fibrous stroma and peripheral palisading Usually a lobulated tumor composed of solid organoid nests of primitive basaloid epithelial cells separated by dense fibrous stroma. Cells have indistinct borders, scant cytoplasm, a high N:C ratio, and round-to-oval vesicular nuclei, sometimes with nucleoli. Differentiated budding ducts lined by cuboidal-to-columnar cells with basophilic luminal secretions or cribriform structures may be present. Peripheral palisading is occasional. Apoptosis, necrosis, pleomorphism, and increased mitoses may occur. The tumor is not graded. Sialoblastoma is not graded SOX10, p63, and beta-catenin are reactive. Cytokeratins (CK5/6, CK7, CK19), S100, SMA, KIT/CD117, and calponin are variable. Tumors are reactive for SOX10, p63, and β-catenin, and variably reactive with cytokeratins (including CK5/6, CK7, and CK19), S100, SMA, KIT (CD117), and calponin Basal cell adenoma/adenocarcinoma — These occur predominantly in adults and show more mature basaloid architecture; sialoblastoma occurs characteristically in neonates or very young children and has primitive organoid nests with budding ducts. Adenoid cystic carcinoma — AdCC shows a more recognizable biphasic ductal/myoepithelial population and basement-membrane-like pseudocysts; sialoblastoma has primitive basaloid cells with ductal budding and immature organoid architecture. Adamantinoma-like Ewing sarcoma — Consider in a primitive basaloid tumor; use an appropriate immunohistochemical and molecular workup to exclude Ewing sarcoma rather than relying on morphology alone. Cellular pleomorphic adenoma — May show basaloid cells and hyaline matrix, but usually has chondromyxoid/fibrillary stroma and lacks the characteristic neonatal presentation and primitive duct-budding pattern. The primitive histological features and the patients’ young age help to differentiate sialoblastoma from other basaloid salivary gland tumors such as basal cell adenoma/adenocarcinoma, adenoid cystic carcinoma, and adamantinoma-like Ewing sarcoma Primitive basaloid organoid nests with budding ducts in an infant/child The neonatal/early childhood presentation is highly informative. Avoid overcalling based only on mitotic activity; the entity is not graded. Careful pediatric biopsy planning is important. Salivary gland carcinoma NOS More than 50% of cases arise in the parotid gland, and 40% arise in minor glands, most often in the hard palate, buccal mucosa, and lips Patients with tumors of major glands usually present with asymptomatic, solitary, firm or cystic masses Occasionally, they may be painful Because of morphogenetic identification of new types of salivary gland adenocarcinoma, the entity adenocarcinoma NOS now accounts for only 5–10% of salivary gland carcinomas The average patient age is 58 years, with a wide age range Essential: a salivary gland carcinoma lacking the morphological, immunohistochemical, and molecular features of other salivary carcinomas; exclusion of metastasis is mandatory A diagnosis of exclusion for tumors with variable ductal or glandular patterns, with or without cystic change or necrosis. Architecture may include small confluent nests or cords, large islands, and densely cellular stroma. Tumor cells may be cuboidal, columnar, polygonal, clear, mucinous, oncocytoid, or plasmacytoid. Ductal/glandular structures are more common in low- and intermediate-grade tumors and less frequent in high-grade tumors. Oncocytic and intestinal-type variants are described. Proof of an intraductal component supports a salivary gland origin Subtypes These include oncocytic adenocarcinoma and intestinal-type adenocarcinoma, the latter of which is often positive for CK20 and CDX2 Use a directed panel to exclude specific salivary entities: NR4A3 and DOG1 for acinic cell carcinoma; calponin, CK5/6, and p63 for basal/myoepithelial differentiation; site-specific markers to evaluate metastasis. Intestinal-type tumors may express CK20 and CDX2. Immunohistochemistry is helpful in distinguishing adenocarcinoma NOS from acinic cell carcinoma (NR4A3, DOG1), tumors with myoepithelial/basal cell composition (calponin, CK5/6, p63), and metastatic adenocarcinoma (site-specific markers) Salivary duct carcinoma — Look for apocrine cytoplasm, marked nuclear pleomorphism, complex cribriform/solid or papillary-cystic architecture, and comedonecrosis; assess AR and HER2 as appropriate. Mucoepidermoid carcinoma — Search for mucous, intermediate, and squamoid cells; MAML2 rearrangement may support MEC in selected cases. Polymorphous adenocarcinoma — Characterized by cytologic uniformity, architectural diversity, infiltrative growth, and often targetoid perineural invasion; S100-positive/p63-positive/p40-negative phenotype is supportive. Acinic cell carcinoma — Look for serous acinar differentiation, PAS-D-positive zymogen granules, DOG1, and nuclear NR4A3. Myoepithelial/basal cell neoplasms — Determine whether there is a basal/myoepithelial population using p63/p40, CK5/6, calponin, SMA, and other directed markers; assess the architecture and invasion. High-grade transformation of a defined salivary carcinoma — Search extensively for a conventional low-grade component at the tumor edge or in less pleomorphic areas. Metastatic adenocarcinoma — Exclude lung, gastrointestinal, breast, renal, and other primaries with clinical history, imaging, and site-directed markers. An intraductal component may support salivary origin but is not a substitute for clinicopathologic correlation. For the diagnosis of adenocarcinoma NOS to be rendered, other primary carcinoma types must be excluded, including salivary duct carcinoma, mucoepidermoid carcinoma, polymorphous adenocarcinoma, and high-grade transformation of other types of salivary carcinoma Tumors with significant mucinous differentiation may be better regarded as mucinous adenocarcinoma Molecular alterations are heterogeneous and not diagnostic Malignant glandular/ductal carcinoma lacking defining features of a specific entity NOS should be reserved for cases in which morphology, immunophenotype, and molecular findings do not support a defined entity. Exclusion of metastasis is mandatory. Sialolipoma Benign mixed epithelial and adipocytic tumors Conventional lipomas (see section Lipomas) predominate in parotid glands (≥ 80%), whereas sialolipoma and oncocytic lipoadenoma manifest in minor glands (50%) and in parotid glands (40%) In the oral cavity, the lower lip and tongue are the most common locations Patients typically present with a slow-growing swelling The salivary gland location is verified by radiological or intraoperative localization and/or by histological demonstration of a rim of salivary parenchyma The mean age at presentation regardless of site is 51.5 years, with an equal sex distribution Essential: a lipoma with benign salivary epithelial components Combined lipoepithelial salivary gland lesions comprise a spectrum of morphological subtypes from sialolipoma to oncocytic lipoadenoma Sialolipoma combines lobules of salivary parenchyma with dominating and evenly interspersed adipose tissue The salivary parenchyma rarely shows focal sebaceous differentiation and is usually devoid of oncocytic epithelium The term “sialolipoma” indicates that the adipocytic component is regarded as neoplastic Subtype The rare oncocytic lipoadenoma subtype typically demonstrates a predominance of epithelial elements with a varying oncocytic component, reminiscent of oncocytoma A minor sebaceous component may occur Pancytokeratin and CK7 highlight the entrapped salivary ducts and acini within the mature adipose tissue. p63 and smooth muscle actin may outline the basal/myoepithelial layer of native ducts when confirmation is needed. IHC is usually unnecessary when mature adipose tissue and well-formed native salivary elements are readily identified. Lipoma with entrapped salivary tissue — Sialolipoma shows a substantial, organized salivary gland component distributed within the adipose lesion; a few peripheral entrapped ducts in an ordinary lipoma are insufficient. Diffuse lipomatosis of the salivary gland — Lipomatosis is a diffuse replacement or infiltration of gland parenchyma by fat rather than a circumscribed tumor-like lesion. Pleomorphic adenoma with lipomatous or adipocytic metaplasia — Look for the characteristic epithelial-myoepithelial neoplasm and chondromyxoid matrix rather than a predominantly mature adipocytic lesion. Adenoid cystic carcinoma (AdCC) Malignant Ductal + abluminal basaloid/myoepithelial Tubular, cribriform, solid; true ducts plus pseudocysts Basophilic/hyaline basement-membrane material Infiltrative; perineural invasion is an important clue MYB::NFIB; MYBL1-related alterations Basal cell adenoma (BCA) Benign Luminal + basaloid/abluminal Solid, trabecular, tubular, cribriform, membranous Hyaline basement-membrane-like material; no characteristic chondromyxoid matrix Circumscribed/encapsulated; no destructive invasion CTNNB1/β-catenin pathway; subset with CYLD Basal cell adenocarcinoma (BCAC) BCA-like tubulotrabecular, membranous, or solid growth Hyaline material may be present Infiltrative growth; PNI/LVI may occur Subset with CYLD or CTNNB1 alterations; no defining molecular test Epithelial-myoepithelial carcinoma (EMC) Inner ductal + prominent outer myoepithelial, often clear Biphasic tubules; may be solid, cribriform, or multinodular Variable; not defined by extensive AdCC-like pseudocysts Usually multinodular invasive growth HRAS, commonly codon 61 Pleomorphic adenoma (PA) Ductal + diverse myoepithelial cells Ducts, nests, sheets, trabeculae Myxoid/chondromyxoid, hyalinized, or fibrous Usually circumscribed; pseudopods/satellites can occur PLAG1 or HMGA2 alterations Myoepithelioma Predominantly / almost exclusively myoepithelial Solid, nested, cords, trabeculae, reticular Myxoid, hyalinized, collagenous, or vascular Well circumscribed; no destructive invasion Rare EWSR1; selected oncocytic cases with PLAG1 fusions Intercalated duct adenoma Cuboidal luminal cells + attenuated myoepithelial layer Small nodular or multinodular ductal proliferation Usually inconspicuous Circumscribed or encapsulated HRAS hotspot variants reported Intercalated duct hyperplasia Benign proliferation Ductal + myoepithelial Small ducts blending with native acini Native gland tissue intermingled No discrete expansile border CTNNB1 mutations often reported Single-layered ductal cells Closely packed small ducts, minimal stroma Minimal; may be vascular or hyalinized Circumscribed/encapsulated IDH2 p.R172 reported in tested cases Monomorphic ductal cells; no true outer myoepithelial layer Beaded, branching, anastomosing cords/canaliculi Loose, edematous, highly vascular stroma Usually well circumscribed No defining recurrent alteration has been established. Polymorphous adenocarcinoma (PAC) Usually cytologically uniform, not a classic biphasic tumor Architectural diversity; cords, tubules, targetoid patterns Variable Infiltrative; perineural invasion may occur Not established as a routine diagnostic test. Biologic behavior Malignant carcinoma Benign neoplasm The key distinction is not cytologic atypia alone; it is the presence or absence of destructive invasion. Border / interface Typically infiltrative; perineural invasion is a characteristic, sampling-dependent clue. Well circumscribed or encapsulated; no destructive or perineural invasion. A limited core or FNA may not include the interface. Do not infer benignity from a bland sample. Overall architecture Tubular, cribriform, and/or solid patterns; mixed patterns are common. Solid, trabecular, tubular, cribriform, or membranous patterns; more than one may coexist. Cribriform architecture occurs in both and is not independently diagnostic. Cell populations Ductal luminal cells plus abluminal myoepithelial/basaloid cells; in classic AdCC, the two populations are usually recognizable. Luminal cells plus basaloid/abluminal cells; darker peripheral cells commonly show palisading and inner cells are paler. Both are biphasic. Identify the arrangement and correlate with the matrix and tumor border. Cribriform spaces True glandular lumina coexist with pseudolumina; pseudolumina are filled with hyaline/basophilic stromal matrix and are contiguous with the stroma. Cribriform spaces may be present; hyaline basement-membrane-like material may occur between nests or as rounded droplets. In AdCC, look for both true ducts and matrix-filled pseudocysts, not just round spaces. Hyaline material Often conspicuous within pseudocysts; represents stromal matrix/basement membrane material. May be present as thick bands, droplets, or membranous material around and between nests. Hyaline globules are not specific for AdCC. Cytology Basaloid cells in tissue fragments, often surrounding larger, rounder, more numerous hyaline balls; stripped oval myoepithelial nuclei may be present in the background. Markedly cellular smears with small sheets and round, trabecular, or solid fragments of monomorphic small basaloid cells; scant cytoplasm, frequent naked nuclei, and thin dense hyaline material around/interdigitating with fragments. There is overlap. Cytology may favor one entity but cannot always separate AdCC from BCA. IHC: luminal compartment CK7 and CD117/KIT typically highlight luminal ductal cells. Luminal cells express keratins; EMA, CEA, and CD117 may be positive. CD117 is supportive in the right pattern, not a stand-alone discriminator. IHC: abluminal compartment p63, p40, calponin, and α-SMA highlight myoepithelial cells. Basaloid/abluminal cells may express p63, calponin, SMA/actin, S100, and GFAP. The shared basal/myoepithelial phenotype means a basic dual-cell panel does not by itself distinguish them. Additional IHC MYB protein overexpression is common but has suboptimal specificity. Nuclear β-catenin and LEF1 coexpression supports BCA in the appropriate morphologic context. Interpret MYB and β-catenin/LEF1 as supportive patterns, not substitutes for morphology and invasion assessment. Molecular MYB::NFIB is a key recurrent fusion; MYBL1 rearrangements or MYB amplification occur in some cases lacking the canonical fusion. CTNNB1 pathway alterations and CYLD alterations are reported; no single molecular test independently establishes benign behavior. A defining AdCC-associated fusion supports AdCC; molecular results must be interpreted with the histology. Most important pitfall Do not diagnose AdCC from cribriform architecture or hyaline globules alone. Do not call BCA solely because the cells are bland or the lesion appears circumscribed in a limited sample. If invasion cannot be evaluated, a descriptive diagnosis such as basaloid neoplasm may be safer, with excision recommended for definitive classification. Cellularity Moderately to highly cellular; cohesive tissue fragments are common. Usually markedly cellular; many small sheets and round, trabecular, or solid fragments. High cellularity is common to both and is not a reliable separator. Cell groups Basaloid cells form tissue fragments and may surround hyaline balls; cribriform/tubular fragments can be present. Monomorphic small basaloid cells form compact sheets, round groups, trabeculae, and solid fragments. Look for the relationship between the basaloid cells and the stromal material, not merely the presence of basaloid groups. Hyaline / stromal material Often larger, rounder, and more numerous hyaline balls; basaloid epithelium may rim or surround the balls. Dense, thin hyaline material often wraps around or interdigitates with fragments; small rounded stromal droplets may occur. This is a useful tendency, not an absolute rule. Both tumors can yield hyaline material. Nuclei and cytoplasm Small basaloid cells with high N:C ratio; oval-to-angulated hyperchromatic nuclei; stripped oval myoepithelial nuclei may lie in the clean background. Uniform round nuclei with fine hyperchromasia, scant cytoplasm, and frequent naked nuclei; cytology is often monotonous. Angulated hyperchromatic nuclei and stripped oval nuclei may favor AdCC, whereas a monotonous population favors BCA, but overlap is substantial. Background Often relatively clean; hyaline matrix is conspicuous. A proteinaceous background is not required. Usually clean background with frequent naked nuclei; myxofibrillary stroma is absent. Absence of chondromyxoid/myxofibrillary matrix argues against PA, but does not by itself distinguish AdCC from BCA. Cell-block IHC KIT/CD117 typically highlights luminal cells; p63/p40 and calponin/SMA highlight abluminal cells. MYB may be positive but is not fully specific. Basal/myoepithelial markers may highlight abluminal cells; nuclear β-catenin and LEF1 coexpression supports BCA in context. Shared biphasic marker expression limits the value of a small panel. Interpret staining by compartment and correlate with the smear pattern. Molecular testing MYB::NFIB or MYBL1-related rearrangement supports AdCC when morphology is equivocal. CTNNB1 or CYLD alterations may be encountered, but testing is not a routine stand-alone cytologic classifier. Use molecular testing selectively; a negative result does not resolve the differential. What FNA cannot establish Cannot reliably demonstrate the full infiltrative interface; absence of sampled PNI does not exclude AdCC. Cannot establish absence of invasion or reliably exclude basal cell adenocarcinoma. If the distinction remains unresolved, report a basaloid neoplasm with AdCC/BCA in the differential and recommend histologic evaluation of the excision. Define the cell layers Is there a true luminal/abluminal arrangement? Separate true biphasic tumors from monophasic ductal tumors and predominantly myoepithelial lesions. Read the matrix Chondromyxoid/fibrillary matrix favors PA; basement-membrane-like hyaline material raises BCA or AdCC; loose vascular stroma with beaded cords favors canalicular adenoma. Assess the interface Destructive infiltration, perineural invasion, or vascular invasion changes the diagnostic category. Cytologic blandness does not exclude malignancy. Map IHC by compartment Use CK7/CD117 for luminal differentiation and p63/p40/SMA/calponin for basal-myoepithelial differentiation. Interpret β-catenin, LEF1, MYB, S100, and SOX10 in context. Use molecular testing to answer a defined question MYB/MYBL1 for AdCC; HRAS for EMC or intercalated duct adenoma in the appropriate morphology; CTNNB1 for selected BCA/hyperplasia; IDH2 p.R172 for striated duct adenoma. CK / pancytokeratin Ductal and often basaloid cells Luminal + basaloid cells Both compartments Ductal cells; myoepithelial cells also keratin-positive Positive Luminal ductal cells CK7 Luminal cells Inner ductal cells Ductal cells CD117 / KIT Typically luminal positive May label luminal cells Not defining Not established p63 / p40 Abluminal myoepithelial cells Basaloid/abluminal cells Abluminal cells Outer myoepithelial layer Myoepithelial cells Often positive Myoepithelial layer Scattered cells only SMA / calponin Typically negative S100 / SOX10 Variable / often supportive Myoepithelial component Not specified S100 often strong Both commonly positive β-catenin / LEF1 Nuclear coexpression supports BCA β-catenin in a subset; not discriminating MYB Often overexpressed; limited specificity AdCC MYB::NFIB; MYBL1 rearrangements/fusions; MYB amplification Supports AdCC in a compatible morphologic setting; canonical fusion is not present in every case. BCA CTNNB1 / β-catenin pathway; subset with CYLD Supports pathway biology; not a stand-alone benignity test. BCAC Subset with CYLD or CTNNB1 alterations No defining molecular test; invasion remains decisive. EMC Useful in selected cases to distinguish EMC from mimics. PA Helpful in selected cases. Rare EWSR1 rearrangements; selected oncocytic cases with PLAG1-related fusions Supportive in selected morphologic contexts. HRAS hotspot variants Reported in adenomas; not routinely required. CTNNB1 mutations Reported more often in hyperplasia; not a routine diagnostic requirement. IDH2 p.R172 Reported in all tested cases in one study; evidence base remains limited. No defining alteration specified Molecular testing is not established as a routine diagnostic tool. All entities Non-neoplastic lesions Benign tumors Malignant tumors Biphasic / ductal focus Non-neoplastic min-w-40 font-semibold text-slate-900 dark:text-slate-100 min-w-44 text-slate-600 dark:text-slate-300 No additional feature-specific details listed. ← Salivary Glands PathologyGPS · Head & Neck · Salivary Glands Salivary Gland Tumors A unified, morphology-first reference to non-neoplastic epithelial lesions, benign neoplasms, and malignant salivary gland tumors, with focused comparison of biphasic and related ductal tumors. Diagnostic priority Architecture, cell lineage, matrix, and invasion drive classification. Assess the tumor interface whenever possible. In limited biopsies and FNA, the absence of sampled invasion does not establish benignity. Clinical Profile Essential Criteria Histopathology IHC Differential Diagnosis Molecular Pathology First question What is the dominant architecture? Recognize biphasic, oncocytic, acinar, papillary-cystic, cribriform, tubular, solid, and mucin-producing patterns. Second question What is the matrix and cell lineage? Separate chondromyxoid stroma, basement-membrane-like hyaline material, loose vascular stroma, and true ductal or myoepithelial differentiation. Third question Is there destructive invasion? Evaluate the interface, perineural invasion, lymphovascular invasion, and infiltrative growth before assigning biologic behavior. Diagnostic workflow A practical morphology-first approach Use a small number of high-yield observations to narrow the differential before ordering a broad ancillary panel. Cross-cutting diagnostic focus Biphasic and related ductal tumors These entities are grouped here because they share a practical differential diagnosis involving luminal, abluminal, basal, or myoepithelial differentiation. This is a diagnostic comparison group, not a separate biologic category. Entity Behavior Architecture Matrix / stroma Interface Molecular clue Critical basaloid differential Adenoid cystic carcinoma vs. basal cell adenoma Both tumors may be biphasic, cribriform, and contain hyaline material. Cribriform architecture or hyaline globules alone are not diagnostic; evaluate the cell arrangement and tumor interface. Feature Diagnostic point Fine-needle aspiration Cytologic distinction: AdCC vs. basal cell adenoma These are pattern-recognition clues, not absolute criteria. FNA cannot reliably demonstrate the complete invasive interface or exclude basal cell adenocarcinoma. FNA feature Practical interpretation Suggested wording when unresolved: “Basaloid neoplasm. The differential diagnosis includes adenoid cystic carcinoma and basal cell adenoma. Cytologic material cannot reliably assess invasion; definitive classification requires histologic evaluation of the lesion and its interface.” Compartment-based interpretation IHC comparison matrix Use staining to map compartments rather than as a binary checklist. Expression varies by tumor and antibody; correlate with H&E. Marker Intercalated duct lesion Molecular pathology Alterations that may resolve a defined differential Molecular results are supportive in the appropriate morphologic context; no alteration replaces assessment of invasion when behavior is the key question. Reported alteration Diagnostic interpretation Complete entity reference Diagnostic criteria and differential diagnosis All entities appear once. Search by morphology, immunomarker, molecular alteration, anatomic site, or differential diagnosis. e.g. PLAG1, ETV6, cribriform, oncocytic... bg-teal-700 text-white border border-slate-300 bg-white text-slate-600 hover:border-teal-500 dark:border-slate-700 dark:bg-slate-900 dark:text-slate-300 Showing of entities . Collapse − View diagnostic profile + Essential Diagnostic Criteria Immunohistochemistry Diagnostic Pitfall No matching entity. Specimen handling Sampling and reporting checklist Record the exact gland and anatomic subsite; distinguish major from minor salivary gland origin. Sample heterogeneous tumors extensively, including solid, cystic, papillary, hemorrhagic, necrotic, and firm areas. Document tumor size, margins, extraparenchymal extension, perineural invasion, lymphovascular invasion, and nodal status as applicable. For biphasic neoplasms, assess the entire tumor–host interface when distinguishing adenoma from carcinoma. For carcinoma ex pleomorphic adenoma, extensively sample the interface between residual PA and carcinoma and document the extent of invasion beyond the PA border when applicable. Use tumor-specific grading only where validated; report high-grade transformation explicitly. Correlate morphology with targeted IHC and molecular testing; do not overinterpret isolated marker positivity. Diagnostic note: Interpret ancillary findings with morphology, anatomic site, and clinical context. A negative molecular result does not exclude an entity unless the alteration is required by its diagnostic definition.

title: AML
content: use client AML with PML::RARA Fusion AML with Defining Genetic Abnormalities Adults; acute bleeding, bruising, cytopenias or leukocytosis; DIC is a critical presentation. Abnormal promyelocytes with heavy granulation or bilobed nuclei; bundles of Auer rods; microgranular variant may be hypogranular with bilobed nuclei. Hypergranular promyelocytes have abundant azurophilic granules and folded/bilobed nuclei. Microgranular APL may show leukocytosis and inconspicuous granules. MPO is typically strong. CD33, CD13, MPO, and CD117 are common. HLA-DR and CD34 are usually absent in classic APL, but may be variable in microgranular cases. CD64 may be expressed; no single marker replaces fusion testing. Demonstrate PML::RARA by FISH, RT-PCR, or RNA sequencing. Suspected APL is a hematologic emergency; start ATRA when clinically indicated before molecular confirmation. Use an orthogonal assay if morphology is compelling but initial FISH is negative. PML::RARA, usually t(15;17); monitor fusion transcript for MRD. AML with other RARA fusions morphology may overlap, but ATRA response varies by partner. AML with RUNX1 :RUNX1T1: maturation and Auer rods may occur, but PML::RARA is absent. AML with NPM1 mutation cup-like nuclei may mimic APL, but NPM1 mutation/cytoplasmic NPM1 defines that entity. AML with RUNX1::RUNX1T1 Fusion Often younger adults, but any age; cytopenias, infection, bleeding, or extramedullary disease. Myeloblasts with granulocytic maturation, frequent Auer rods, and sometimes aberrant B-cell antigens. Marrow often shows blasts with maturation through granulocytic stages. Auer rods may be numerous. Abnormal eosinophils can occur but are more characteristic of CBFB::MYH11 AML. MPO, CD13, CD33, CD117, and often CD34 are positive. Aberrant CD19, PAX5, or CD79a may occur and does not by itself establish B-lineage. CD56 may be aberrantly expressed. Demonstrate RUNX1::RUNX1T1, usually t(8;21). Classify by the defining fusion even when blast percentages are below the conventional AML threshold, according to the applied classification. RUNX1::RUNX1T1; KIT and RAS-pathway co-mutations may affect relapse risk; fusion transcript supports MRD monitoring. AML with CBFB :MYH11: abnormal eosinophils and myelomonocytic differentiation favor CBFB::MYH11. AML with maturation lacks RUNX1::RUNX1T1. B-ALL aberrant CD19 alone is insufficient; require a coherent B-lineage phenotype. AML with CBFB::MYH11 Fusion Often younger or middle-aged adults; leukocytosis, tissue infiltration, or cytopenias. Myelomonocytic proliferation with abnormal marrow eosinophils and inv(16)/t(16;16). Myelomonocytic differentiation is common. Abnormal eosinophils contain coarse basophilic-purple granules and may be most apparent in marrow. Auer rods may be present. MPO highlights granulocytic cells. CD64, CD14, CD11c, and lysozyme support monocytic differentiation. CD34/CD117 highlight blasts; aberrant CD2 may occur. Demonstrate CBFB::MYH11, usually inv(16)(p13.1q22) or t(16;16). Identify abnormal eosinophils and quantify blasts. Evaluate extramedullary myeloid sarcoma when present. CBFB::MYH11; KIT and RAS-pathway co-mutations may affect relapse risk; fusion transcript supports MRD. :RUNX1T1: Auer rods and maturation may overlap, but abnormal eosinophils favor CBFB::MYH11. AML with myelomonocytic differentiation lacks the defining fusion. CMML persistent monocytosis with blasts below AML threshold. AML with DEK::NUP214 Fusion Usually adults, often younger to middle-aged; cytopenias, leukocytosis, or basophilia. t(6;9), often with basophilia, multilineage dysplasia, and adverse-risk biology. Hypercellular marrow with increased blasts and variable multilineage dysplasia. Basophilia may be present. Auer rods may occur. MPO, CD13, CD33, CD117, and CD34 are variable. CD123 may be increased. Use flow cytometry to characterize blasts and exclude basophilic leukemia. Demonstrate DEK::NUP214, usually t(6;9)(p22;q34). Fusion defines the AML category; assess blast count and co-mutations. DEK::NUP214; FLT3-ITD and other mutations may coexist. AML with MECOM rearrangement often abnormal megakaryocytes and inv(3)/t(3;3), not t(6;9). AML-MR dysplasia may overlap, but DEK::NUP214 defines a distinct entity. CML blast phase requires BCR::ABL1 and compatible history. AML with RBM15::MRTFA Fusion Predominantly infants; hepatosplenomegaly, cytopenias, and marrow failure may occur. Infantile megakaryoblastic leukemia with t(1;22). Marrow may be fibrotic with a dry tap. Megakaryoblasts show basophilic cytoplasm and cytoplasmic blebs. Blasts may be small lymphoblast-like or large and pleomorphic. CD41, CD61, and CD42b establish megakaryocytic differentiation. CD34/CD117 are variable. MPO is usually negative; factor VIII-related antigen is less sensitive. Demonstrate RBM15::MRTFA, usually t(1;22)(p13;q13). Confirm megakaryocytic lineage with platelet glycoproteins. Exclude Down syndrome-associated myeloid proliferation. RBM15::MRTFA fusion. AML megakaryoblastic differentiation, NOS Transient abnormal myelopoiesis neonatal Down syndrome setting with GATA1 mutation and frequent spontaneous regression. Acute undifferentiated leukemia lacks megakaryocyte-lineage markers. AML with BCR::ABL1 Fusion Usually adults; de novo presentation or possible previously unrecognized CML; splenomegaly/basophilia may be clues. Myeloid blasts with BCR::ABL1 after excluding CML in myeloid blast phase. Blasts may show granulocytic differentiation. Basophilia, dwarf megakaryocytes, and chronic-phase CML features raise concern for blast-phase CML. No morphology alone reliably separates de novo AML from CML blast phase. MPO supports myeloid lineage; CD34/CD117 assess blasts. CD13/CD33 are common. Flow phenotype cannot independently distinguish de novo AML from CML blast phase. Demonstrate BCR::ABL1. Review prior CBCs, marrow history, basophilia, splenomegaly, and chronic-phase features. Apply classification-specific blast criteria. BCR::ABL1; determine transcript type and additional cytogenetic abnormalities. CML in myeloid blast phase antecedent chronic phase, basophilia, and dwarf megakaryocytes. B-ALL with BCR :ABL1: coherent B-lineage markers. AML with other defining genetics lacks BCR::ABL1. AML with KMT2A Rearrangement All ages; infants/children and adults; leukocytosis, gingival/skin infiltration, or cytopenias. Often monoblastic or myelomonocytic morphology; fusion partner influences phenotype. Monoblasts/promonocytes may have folded nuclei and abundant gray-blue cytoplasm. Myelomonocytic differentiation and extramedullary infiltration are common. Morphology varies with fusion partner. CD33, CD64, CD11c, CD14, lysozyme, and CD4 support monocytic differentiation. CD34 is variable; CD117 may be positive. NG2/CSPG4 may be expressed in some cases. Demonstrate KMT2A rearrangement and identify fusion partner when possible. Exclude MPAL if B/T lineage-defining criteria are met. KMT2A fusion; RNA-based fusion testing may identify cryptic partners. often monocytic but NPM1 mutation/cytoplasmic NPM1 distinguishes it. MPAL with KMT2A rearrangement requires B/myeloid or T/myeloid lineage criteria. AML with monocytic differentiation, NOS lacks KMT2A rearrangement. AML with MECOM Rearrangement Usually adults; cytopenias, leukocytosis or thrombocytosis; often adverse-risk disease. inv(3)/t(3;3), abnormal megakaryocytes, multilineage dysplasia, and increased blasts. Marrow may show multilineage dysplasia and increased blasts. Megakaryocytes may be small with separated nuclear lobes or monolobated forms. Erythroid and granulocytic dysplasia may coexist. CD34/CD117 highlight blasts; MPO supports myeloid differentiation. CD61/CD42b demonstrate dysplastic megakaryocytes. MECOM/EVI1 IHC may be supportive but does not replace genetic confirmation. Demonstrate MECOM rearrangement, classically inv(3)(q21.3q26.2) or t(3;3). Recognize genetic AML entity even with lower blast percentages when classification criteria permit. MECOM rearrangement; classic enhancer relocation leads to MECOM overexpression. AML with DEK :NUP214: t(6;9), not MECOM. MDS/MPN with thrombocytosis lacks AML-defining MECOM rearrangement. MDS with increased blasts MECOM rearrangement defines a distinct category when criteria are met. AML with NUP98 Rearrangement Children, adolescents, and adults; acute marrow failure, leukocytosis, or tissue infiltration. Often immature morphology; phenotype varies with NUP98 fusion partner. Blasts often show limited maturation. Some cases show monocytic or megakaryoblastic differentiation. No single histologic pattern is specific. CD34/CD117 often positive; MPO variable. CD13/CD33 support myeloid lineage. Apply lineage-specific markers when monocytic or megakaryocytic differentiation is suspected. Demonstrate NUP98 rearrangement and identify fusion partner, preferably by RNA-based testing. Exclude other defining fusions and ambiguous-lineage leukemia. NUP98::NSD1, NUP98::KDM5A, and other fusions. AML with KMT2A rearrangement distinct fusion, often monocytic. classify by specific lesion. lacks convincing lineage-specific differentiation. AML with NPM1 Mutation Usually adults, especially middle-aged/older; cytopenias, leukocytosis, or monocytic tissue infiltration. Cup-like nuclear invaginations, often monocytic differentiation, and cytoplasmic NPM1 protein. Blasts may show deep nuclear invaginations/cup-like nuclei. Monocytic/myelomonocytic differentiation is common. Auer rods may occur; morphology is not specific. NPM1 IHC shows cytoplasmic mislocalization in most mutation-positive cases. MPO and CD33 commonly positive; CD34/HLA-DR may be absent or dim but exceptions occur. CD64/CD11c/CD14 may be positive in monocytic cases. Demonstrate pathogenic NPM1 mutation by sequencing or validated assay. Cytoplasmic NPM1 IHC is a useful surrogate, not a substitute for molecular confirmation when needed. Assess FLT3-ITD and other co-mutations. NPM1 mutation, usually exon 12; FLT3-ITD, DNMT3A and other co-mutations; NPM1 is useful for MRD. lacks NPM1 mutation. often monocytic but has KMT2A fusion. apply current hierarchy when NPM1 defines a more specific category. AML with CEBPA Mutation Often younger/middle-aged adults; familial cases can occur; acute cytopenias or leukocytosis. Granulocytic differentiation and maturation; occasional bilobed blasts and Auer rods. Blasts may show granulocytic maturation. Morphology alone cannot establish CEBPA subtype. CD7 may be aberrant. No IHC stain establishes CEBPA mutation. Demonstrate qualifying in-frame bZIP CEBPA mutation under the selected classification. Assess germline status when family history or age suggests predisposition. Qualifying CEBPA bZIP mutation; distinguish germline from somatic variants. :RUNX1T1: may show Auer rods/maturation but fusion differs. AML with maturation, NOS lacks defining CEBPA lesion. Familial CEBPA-associated myeloid neoplasm germline variant and family history. AML, Myelodysplasia-Related Usually older adults; antecedent MDS/MDS-MPN or de novo disease; cytopenias common. Multilineage dysplasia and qualifying MR cytogenetic/molecular abnormalities or antecedent disease. Dysmegakaryopoiesis includes micromegakaryocytes and hypolobated forms. Granulocytes may be hypogranular or pseudo-Pelger-Huët. Dyserythropoiesis and increased blasts may be present. CD34/CD117 assess blasts; MPO supports myeloid lineage. CD61/CD42b highlight megakaryocytic dysplasia. No unique IHC phenotype defines AML-MR. Meet AML criteria and establish qualifying MR genetic abnormalities and/or antecedent MDS/MDS-MPN under the selected classification. Exclude AML-defining genetic entities that take precedence. MR-associated genes include ASXL1, BCOR, EZH2, SF3B1, SRSF2, STAG2, U2AF1, ZRSR2; qualifying cytogenetics are classification-specific. hierarchy may favor the NPM1-defined entity. specific genetic entity takes precedence. Post-cytotoxic therapy AML exposure qualifier may coexist. AML with Other Defined Genetic Abnormalities Age and presentation vary by lesion; acute marrow failure, leukocytosis, or extramedullary disease. Morphology varies; assign the specific genetic category whenever a recognized lesion is identified. Describe blast morphology, maturation, dysplasia, and tissue involvement. Some lesions have characteristic patterns but none is independently diagnostic. Quantify blasts and assess lineage. Use MPO, CD34/CD117, monocytic markers, and lineage-specific markers as indicated. No universal IHC phenotype defines this residual group. Identify the exact recognized genetic lesion and apply current entity hierarchy. Do not use this residual label when a more specific named entity applies. Karyotype, FISH, RNA fusion testing, and myeloid NGS guided by phenotype. Named AML genetic entities assign the specific category. AML defined by differentiation use only when no genetic entity supersedes morphology. AML with Minimal Differentiation AML Defined by Differentiation Usually adults; cytopenias, infections, bleeding, or leukocytosis. Lymphoblast-like blasts with absent or very limited MPO and no convincing maturation. Blasts have high N:C ratio, fine chromatin, scant agranular cytoplasm, and inconspicuous nucleoli. Granulocytic maturation is absent. Auer rods are generally absent. CD34, CD117, CD13, and CD33 support immaturity/myeloid phenotype. MPO is negative or present only in a small subset. CD7 may be aberrant; exclude B/T lineage with lineage-defining markers. Meet AML criteria and establish myeloid lineage despite absent/very limited MPO. Exclude acute undifferentiated leukemia and MPAL. No defining molecular lesion; perform comprehensive cytogenetic and molecular testing. AML without maturation MPO-positive myeloid differentiation is demonstrable. no lineage-defining evidence. MPAL requires two lineage-defining programs. AML without Maturation Usually adults; acute marrow failure, cytopenias, or leukocytosis. Predominantly myeloblasts with little maturation and demonstrable myeloid lineage. Marrow is replaced by myeloblasts with scant cytoplasm, fine chromatin, and nucleoli. Granulocytic maturation is minimal. MPO is positive in blasts. CD13, CD33, CD117, and often CD34 are positive. CD7/CD56 may be aberrant. Meet AML criteria and show myeloid differentiation with minimal granulocytic maturation. Exclude genetically defined AML. No defining molecular lesion; karyotype and myeloid NGS guide classification. AML with minimal differentiation MPO absent/very limited. appreciable granulocytic maturation. lacks MPO and other lineage evidence. AML with Maturation Usually adults; anemia, thrombocytopenia, neutropenia, infection, or leukocytosis. Myeloblasts accompanied by substantial granulocytic maturation. Blasts coexist with promyelocytes, myelocytes, and metamyelocytes. Dysplasia may coexist but does not alone define subtype. MPO positive in blasts and granulocytic precursors. CD13/CD33/CD117 common; CD34 variable. Monocytic markers are not dominant unless mixed differentiation is present. Meet AML criteria and show appreciable granulocytic maturation. Exclude defining genetic AML categories and AML-MR as applicable. No defining molecular alteration; perform cytogenetic and molecular workup. few maturing granulocytes. MPO absent/limited. substantial monocytic component. Acute Basophilic Leukemia Rare; mainly adults; cytopenias, leukocytosis, basophilia, skin lesions, or organ involvement. Predominant basophilic blasts with coarse metachromatic granules. Blasts show basophilic differentiation and coarse metachromatic cytoplasmic granules. Granules may obscure nuclear detail. Immature and mature basophils may be increased. CD123, CD203c, FcεRI and metachromatic stains support basophilic lineage. CD34/CD117 variable; MPO often negative/weak. Use tryptase and KIT studies when mast-cell neoplasm is in the differential. Demonstrate predominant basophilic differentiation and acute blast burden. Exclude CML with basophilia, systemic mastocytosis, and other myeloid neoplasms. No single defining molecular lesion; test BCR::ABL1 and relevant myeloid alterations. CML BCR::ABL1-positive chronic myeloproliferation with left shift. Systemic mastocytosis/mast-cell leukemia tryptase-positive, KIT-mutated mast cells. lacks basophil-specific granules/markers. Acute Myelomonocytic Leukemia Children and adults; cytopenias, leukocytosis, gingival/skin infiltration, or hepatosplenomegaly. Substantial granulocytic and monocytic differentiation, with both components represented. Both granulocytic and monocytic lineages are increased. Monoblasts/promonocytes show folded nuclei and abundant gray-blue cytoplasm. Auer rods may be present in myeloid component. CD64, CD14, CD11c, lysozyme and CD163 support monocytic differentiation.
