CD34/CD117 variable; promonocytes are part of blast-equivalent count. Demonstrate both granulocytic and monocytic differentiation and meet AML criteria. Count promonocytes as blast equivalents where applicable. Exclude CBFB::MYH11 and KMT2A-defined entities. CBFB::MYH11, KMT2A rearrangement, and NPM1 mutation are important subsets. Acute monocytic leukemia monocytic component predominates. no substantial monocytic component. persistent monocytosis with blasts plus promonocytes below AML threshold. Acute Monocytic Leukemia All ages; gingival hypertrophy, skin lesions, CNS involvement, leukocytosis, or cytopenias. Predominant monoblasts/promonocytes with strong monocytic differentiation. Monoblasts have round nuclei, delicate chromatin, prominent nucleoli, and abundant basophilic cytoplasm. Promonocytes have folded/convoluted nuclei. Gingival and skin infiltration are characteristic. At least two monocytic markers: CD11c, CD14, CD64, lysozyme, CD163, or nonspecific esterase. MPO often negative in monoblasts. CD4/CD36/CD68 may be expressed; CD34 often absent. Establish monocytic lineage with at least two accepted markers/cytochemical stains. Include monoblasts and promonocytes in blast-equivalent counts. Exclude BPDCN, histiocytic neoplasms, and MPAL. KMT2A rearrangement and NPM1 mutation occur in subsets; perform broad molecular testing. Acute myelomonocytic leukemia substantial granulocytic component. BPDCN CD4/CD56/CD123/TCF4 positive, without monocytic lineage program. Histiocytic sarcoma mature histiocytic phenotype and destructive mass. Acute Erythroid Leukemia Usually older adults; severe anemia, pancytopenia, transfusion dependence, and aggressive course. Predominantly immature erythroid proliferation, often with TP53 abnormalities and complex karyotype. Marrow often shows sheets of immature erythroid precursors and marked erythroid predominance. Proerythroblasts have deeply basophilic cytoplasm, round nuclei, prominent nucleoli, and vacuoles. Multinucleation, nuclear irregularity, and maturation arrest may occur. E-cadherin, CD71, CD36, and glycophorin A support erythroid lineage; very immature cells may lack glycophorin A. MPO is negative in erythroid blasts. Use a panel because no single marker is fully sensitive across maturation stages. Apply current classification-specific criteria and quantify immature erythroid cells relative to total marrow cellularity. Distinguish from erythroid-predominant MDS. Assess TP53 allelic status and complex karyotype. TP53 multi-hit and complex karyotype are common. Erythroid-predominant MDS lacks acute erythroid leukemia criteria. Acute megakaryoblastic leukemia platelet glycoproteins positive, erythroid markers absent. may show dysplasia but not the defining erythroid-predominant pattern. Acute Megakaryoblastic Leukemia Adults and children; Down syndrome-associated cases in young children; pancytopenia, hepatosplenomegaly, or dry tap. Megakaryoblasts expressing platelet glycoproteins; marrow fibrosis is common. Blasts show cytoplasmic blebs and basophilic cytoplasm. Marrow reticulin fibrosis is common and aspirate may be unobtainable. Blasts may be small lymphoblast-like or large with abundant cytoplasm. CD41, CD61, and CD42b establish megakaryocytic lineage; ensure staining is in blasts, not adherent platelets. CD34/CD117 variable; factor VIII-related antigen may be positive. MPO usually negative; CD36 may be positive. Demonstrate acute blast burden and megakaryocytic differentiation by platelet glycoproteins. Exclude metastatic carcinoma, lymphoma, and erythroid leukemia. In children, assess Down syndrome and GATA1 mutation. GATA1 mutation in Down syndrome-associated disease; RBM15::MRTFA in a distinct infantile subset. AML with RBM15 :MRTFA: defining fusion. neonatal Down syndrome, GATA1-mutated, often regresses. Acute erythroid leukemia erythroid markers rather than platelet glycoproteins. Myeloid Sarcoma Any age; skin, bone, lymph node, soft tissue, orbit, GI tract, or other sites; may precede or accompany marrow AML. Mass-forming tissue infiltration by myeloid blasts, with or without concurrent marrow AML. Destructive mass of blasts in diffuse sheets or nodules. Cells may be myeloblastic, monoblastic, or poorly differentiated. Crush artifact can mimic lymphoma; architecture is replaced by tumor. MPO supports granulocytic differentiation. Lysozyme, CD68, CD163, CD64, and CD14 support monocytic differentiation. CD34/CD117/CD33/CD13 variable; exclude lymphoma, carcinoma, melanoma, BPDCN. Establish myeloid lineage by morphology and IHC/flow. Correlate with blood/marrow and molecular profile. Can occur without overt marrow AML. May share NPM1, KMT2A, RUNX1::RUNX1T1, CBFB::MYH11, or other AML lesions. Lymphoma CD45/lineage markers; myeloid markers support sarcoma. CD4/CD56/CD123/TCF4 positive, usually MPO-negative. Small round cell tumor use keratin, desmin, myogenin, and site-specific markers. Myeloid Neoplasm Post Cytotoxic Therapy Secondary Myeloid Neoplasms Usually adults/older adults; latency varies; cytopenias, MDS, or AML after chemotherapy/radiation. A myeloid neoplasm arising after qualifying cytotoxic exposure; morphology is that of the underlying MDS/AML. May range from MDS with multilineage dysplasia to overt AML. Complex karyotype and increased blasts are common. No single histologic pattern defines the therapy-related context. IHC follows the underlying neoplasm; CD34/CD117 assess blasts and lineage markers characterize differentiation. No IHC marker identifies therapy-related disease. Document qualifying prior cytotoxic exposure and classify the current neoplasm separately. Apply current post-cytotoxic therapy qualifier/category and entity hierarchy. TP53, PPM1D, complex karyotype, and chromosome 5/7 abnormalities are enriched. De novo AML/MDS same morphology without qualifying exposure. may coexist with therapy-related context. Metastatic prior malignancy epithelial markers and clinical correlation. Myeloid Neoplasm with Germline Predisposition Children or adults; lifelong cytopenias, congenital features, family history, or multiple affected relatives may be clues. Myeloid neoplasm arising in a patient with a pathogenic germline predisposition variant. Morphology is determined by the acquired neoplasm: MDS, AML, or MDS/MPN. Hypocellularity, dysplasia, increased blasts, or fibrosis may occur. Review prior CBCs and extrahematologic phenotype. IHC is directed by the acquired neoplasm; no stain establishes germline predisposition. CD34/CD117 and lineage markers assess the acquired neoplasm. Confirm germline variant using nonhematopoietic tissue when needed; blood/marrow may be confounded by clonal hematopoiesis. Classify acquired neoplasm and append predisposition qualifier. Genetic counseling and family assessment are important. Germline genes include DDX41, RUNX1, GATA2, CEBPA, ETV6, ANKRD26, SAMD9/SAMD9L. CHIP somatic mutation without germline status. GATA2 deficiency monocytopenia, B/NK-cell deficiency and infections. Familial platelet disorder with RUNX1 lifelong thrombocytopenia/platelet dysfunction. Myeloid Proliferations Associated with Down Syndrome Neonates and young children with constitutional/mosaic trisomy 21; blasts, hepatosplenomegaly, effusions, or cytopenias. Transient abnormal myelopoiesis or myeloid leukemia associated with trisomy 21 and GATA1 mutation. Transient abnormal myelopoiesis shows circulating/marrow megakaryoblasts, often with cytoplasmic blebs. Myeloid leukemia of Down syndrome often has megakaryoblastic differentiation and fibrosis. Blasts can mimic non-Down syndrome AMKL. CD41/CD61/CD42b support megakaryocytic differentiation. CD34/CD117 variable; MPO generally negative in megakaryoblasts. GATA1 mutation testing is important. Establish trisomy 21 and GATA1 mutation in the appropriate setting. Distinguish neonatal transient abnormal myelopoiesis from persistent/progressive myeloid leukemia of Down syndrome. GATA1 truncating mutations; constitutional or mosaic trisomy 21. Non-Down syndrome AMKL no trisomy 21. neonatal and often self-limited. JMML monocytosis/RAS-pathway lesion rather than GATA1-mutated megakaryoblasts. Myeloid/Lymphoid Neoplasm with Eosinophilia and Tyrosine Kinase Gene Fusions Myeloid/Lymphoid Neoplasms with Eosinophilia and Tyrosine Kinase Gene Fusions All ages, often adults; eosinophilia, splenomegaly, cytopenias, MPN-like disease, lymphadenopathy, or organ injury. Clonal fusion-driven neoplasm; eosinophilia may be absent and presentation may be myeloid or lymphoid. Marrow may show eosinophilic proliferation, myeloproliferation, mast-cell increase, or blasts. Some cases present as lymphoblastic lymphoma/leukemia. Morphology may mimic MPN, MDS/MPN, AML, or ALL. IHC follows lineage: MPO, CD34/CD117, B/T markers, and mast-cell markers as indicated. No IHC stain defines the fusion category. Demonstrate defining kinase fusion by karyotype, FISH, RT-PCR, or RNA sequencing. Do not require eosinophilia if a defining fusion is present. Identify fusion partner for classification and targeted therapy. PDGFRA, PDGFRB, FGFR1, JAK2, FLT3, ETV6::ABL1, and other kinase fusions. CEL no defining kinase fusion. Reactive eosinophilia no clonal fusion and secondary cause identified. MPN/AML/ALL may be presenting phenotype of fusion-defined neoplasm. Myeloid/Lymphoid Neoplasm with PDGFRA Rearrangement Usually adult men; eosinophilia, splenomegaly, cardiac injury, skin/GI symptoms, or mast-cell mediator symptoms. Often FIP1L1::PDGFRA with eosinophilia and increased marrow mast cells. Marrow shows eosinophilic proliferation and variable myeloid hyperplasia. Spindle-shaped mast cells may be increased; fibrosis can occur. May mimic systemic mastocytosis. CD117/tryptase highlight mast cells; CD25 is usually not the defining aberrancy of systemic mastocytosis. MPO/CD34 assess myeloid proliferation/blasts. Fusion requires molecular/FISH testing. Demonstrate PDGFRA rearrangement, commonly FIP1L1::PDGFRA. CHIC2 deletion FISH or RNA fusion assay may be used. Exclude systemic mastocytosis and other kinase fusions. FIP1L1::PDGFRA; many cases are highly imatinib-sensitive. Systemic mastocytosis KIT mutation and aberrant CD25/CD2/CD30. lacks PDGFRA fusion. PDGFRB-rearranged neoplasm distinct locus, often monocytosis. Myeloid/Lymphoid Neoplasm with PDGFRB Rearrangement Adults, often middle-aged men; eosinophilia, monocytosis, splenomegaly, leukocytosis, or lymphadenopathy. CMML-like or eosinophilic MPN phenotype with PDGFRB fusion, commonly ETV6::PDGFRB. Marrow shows myeloproliferation with eosinophilia and monocytosis. May resemble CMML; fibrosis and atypical megakaryocytes can occur. Blast or lymphoblastic transformation may develop. CD34/CD117 assess blasts; MPO highlights myeloid cells. CD14/CD64/CD163 may highlight monocytic component. No IHC marker identifies PDGFRB fusion. Demonstrate PDGFRB rearrangement, commonly ETV6::PDGFRB. Perform karyotype/FISH or RNA fusion testing. ETV6::PDGFRB and other PDGFRB fusions; many respond to imatinib. no PDGFRB fusion; fusion-positive disease is classified here. PDGFRA rearrangement often FIP1L1::PDGFRA. excludes defining PDGFRB fusion. Myeloid/Lymphoid Neoplasm with FGFR1 Rearrangement Usually adults; eosinophilia, MPN-like disease, lymphadenopathy, T/B-lymphoblastic lymphoma, or AML. Aggressive stem-cell neoplasm with myeloid and/or lymphoblastic presentations. Marrow may show MPN, MDS/MPN, or acute leukemia. Lymph nodes may show T-lymphoblastic lymphoma with concurrent myeloid neoplasm. Multiple lineage phenotypes may occur over time. Myeloid component: MPO/CD33/CD117. Lymphoblastic component: TdT, CD34, and B/T lineage markers. IHC identifies phenotype, not the fusion. Demonstrate FGFR1 rearrangement and identify partner. Consider multi-lineage disease; assess marrow and extramedullary lesions. FGFR1 fusions include ZMYM2::FGFR1 and others. requires simultaneous lineage-defining criteria in acute leukemia; FGFR1 fusion defines underlying neoplasm. PDGFRA/B neoplasms different fusion and therapeutic profile. De novo T-ALL lacks FGFR1 rearrangement. Myeloid/Lymphoid Neoplasm with JAK2 Rearrangement Adults; anemia, eosinophilia, splenomegaly, leukocytosis, or lymphoblastic lymphoma/leukemia. MPN-like disease or lymphoblastic neoplasm with JAK2 fusion, commonly PCM1::JAK2. Marrow resembles MPN with granulocytic proliferation, eosinophilia, and atypical megakaryocytes. Fibrosis may be prominent. Lymphoblastic transformation may occur. MPO/CD34/CD117 assess myeloid blasts. TdT and B/T markers characterize lymphoblastic lesions. Molecular confirmation is required. Demonstrate JAK2 rearrangement, commonly PCM1::JAK2. Do not confuse rearrangement with JAK2 V617F mutation. PCM1::JAK2 and other JAK2 fusions; JAK inhibition may be relevant. PMF with JAK2 V617F point mutation, not rearrangement. FGFR1-rearranged neoplasm distinct fusion. lineage criteria are independent of JAK2 fusion. Myeloid/Lymphoid Neoplasm with FLT3 Rearrangement Adults; eosinophilia, cytopenias, leukocytosis, or lymphoid neoplasm. Rare fusion-driven neoplasm with variable myeloid/lymphoid presentation. Marrow shows variable myeloid proliferation, eosinophilia, or increased blasts. Morphology is nonspecific. Document lineage and blast burden. IHC follows lineage; MPO, CD34/CD117, TdT, and B/T markers as appropriate. No IHC assay substitutes for fusion testing. Demonstrate FLT3 rearrangement by cytogenetic or RNA-based assay. Distinguish fusion from FLT3-ITD/TKD mutations. FLT3 fusion; identify exact partner. AML with FLT3-ITD mutation, not rearrangement. Other kinase-fusion neoplasms classify by fusion partner. lineage criteria are independent. Myeloid/Lymphoid Neoplasm with ETV6::ABL1 Fusion Adults/children; leukocytosis, eosinophilia, splenomegaly, or B-lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma. MPN-like or lymphoid presentation with ETV6::ABL1 fusion. Marrow may resemble CML with granulocytic hyperplasia and left shift. Lymphoblastic transformation or concurrent lymphoid disease may occur. Eosinophilia is variable. Myeloid phenotype: MPO/CD13/CD33. Lymphoid phenotype: TdT and B-lineage markers as appropriate. Fusion confirmation is molecular/cytogenetic. Demonstrate ETV6::ABL1 fusion. Exclude BCR::ABL1-positive CML and other ABL-class fusions. ETV6::ABL1; ABL-class inhibitor sensitivity may be relevant. BCR::ABL1 rather than ETV6::ABL1. Other kinase fusion neoplasms distinct partner. assess underlying fusion-defined disease. Myeloid/Lymphoid Neoplasm with Other Tyrosine Kinase Gene Fusions All ages; chronic MPN, AML, lymphoblastic neoplasm, or eosinophilia may be presenting features. Fusion-driven myeloid/lymphoid neoplasm involving another kinase gene. Morphology is fusion- and lineage-dependent. May show MPN, MDS/MPN, AML, or lymphoblastic disease. Assess marrow and extramedullary sites. Use lineage-directed panel: MPO, CD34/CD117, CD13/CD33, TdT, B/T markers, monocytic markers. No universal IHC phenotype. Demonstrate qualifying kinase fusion and identify partners. Exclude named PDGFRA/B, FGFR1, JAK2, FLT3, and ETV6::ABL1 categories. RNA fusion sequencing is useful when karyotype/FISH is unrevealing. Named kinase-fusion entities assign specific category. De novo AML/ALL exclude underlying fusion-defined disease. no defining fusion. MPAL, BCR::ABL1-Positive Acute Leukemias of Mixed or Ambiguous Lineage Usually adults; acute marrow failure, lymphadenopathy, or organomegaly. Acute leukemia meeting both B-lineage and myeloid lineage criteria with BCR::ABL1 fusion. Bilineal disease has separate B-lymphoblast and myeloid blast populations. Biphenotypic disease has one population coexpressing lineage-defining markers. Morphology may be lymphoblast-like or myeloblast-like. B-lineage: strong CD19 plus additional B markers (CD10, CD79a, cytoplasmic CD22) at qualifying intensity. Myeloid: MPO or at least two monocytic markers. BCR::ABL1 detected in leukemic clone. Fulfill MPAL lineage criteria and demonstrate BCR::ABL1. Exclude CML blast phase and B-ALL with aberrant myeloid antigens. BCR::ABL1; determine transcript and additional genomic lesions. :ABL1: lacks definitive myeloid lineage criteria. antecedent chronic phase/basophilia/dwarf megakaryocytes. MPAL KMT2A-rearranged different defining lesion. MPAL, KMT2A-Rearranged Infants, children, and adults; acute cytopenias, leukocytosis, organomegaly, or tissue infiltration. MPAL meeting B/myeloid or T/myeloid criteria with KMT2A rearrangement. Bilineal or biphenotypic populations may be present. Monocytic morphology and tissue infiltration may occur. Document whether markers are on the same or separate populations. B-lineage requires CD19 plus additional B markers; T-lineage requires cytoplasmic/surface CD3. Myeloid requires MPO or monocytic marker combination. CD34/CD117/CD33/CD64/TdT variable. Meet MPAL lineage criteria and demonstrate KMT2A rearrangement. Identify B/myeloid versus T/myeloid phenotype. Exclude AML with aberrant lymphoid antigens. KMT2A rearrangement; identify fusion partner. lacks B/T lineage-defining criteria. B-ALL with KMT2A rearrangement lacks myeloid lineage criteria. MPAL BCR :ABL1: different genetic category. MPAL with Other Defined Genetic Abnormalities Age/presentation vary by genetic lesion; acute marrow failure or extramedullary disease. MPAL with lineage-defining B/T and myeloid differentiation plus another recognized genetic lesion. Bilineal or biphenotypic morphology. Describe each blast population and marker distribution. Genetic lesion may define a distinct biologic subgroup. Apply strict B-, T-, and myeloid-lineage criteria. Flow cytometry is central; IHC complements tissue assessment. Nonspecific CD13/CD33/CD7 alone does not establish lineage. Fulfill MPAL criteria and demonstrate the specific genetic abnormality. Exclude named BCR::ABL1 and KMT2A categories. Karyotype, FISH, RNA fusion testing, and NGS guided by phenotype. AML with aberrant lymphoid markers lacks B/T lineage criteria. B/T-ALL with aberrant myeloid markers lacks MPO/monocytic criteria. Named MPAL genetic subtypes use specific category. MPAL, B/Myeloid All ages; cytopenias, circulating blasts, lymphadenopathy, or hepatosplenomegaly. Unequivocal B-lineage and myeloid lineage in same or separate blast populations. Bilineal cases show distinct B-lymphoblast and myeloid populations. Biphenotypic cases show coexpression in one population. Morphology may be lymphoblastoid or myeloblastic. Strong CD19 plus additional strong B marker(s) per current criteria. Myeloid lineage requires MPO or at least two monocytic markers. CD34/CD117/CD13/CD33 alone are not lineage-defining. Fulfill both B-lineage and myeloid-lineage criteria. Exclude B-ALL with aberrant myeloid antigens and AML with aberrant CD19. Test BCR::ABL1, KMT2A, and other recurrent lesions. B-ALL with aberrant CD13/CD33 no MPO/monocytic lineage program. AML with aberrant CD19 no qualifying B-lineage phenotype. MPAL with BCR :ABL1/KMT2A: classify genetically. MPAL, T/Myeloid Children/adults; cytopenias, mediastinal mass, lymphadenopathy, or organomegaly. Unequivocal T-lineage and myeloid lineage differentiation. Bilineal or biphenotypic populations. Mediastinal mass may accompany T-lineage component. Morphology alone cannot distinguish T-ALL with aberrant myeloid markers. T lineage requires cytoplasmic or surface CD3. Myeloid lineage requires MPO or monocytic marker combination. CD7/CD2/CD5/CD13/CD33 alone are not defining. Fulfill T-lineage and myeloid-lineage criteria. Exclude T-ALL with aberrant CD13/CD33 but no myeloid-defining marker. Perform cytogenetic and molecular testing, including BCR::ABL1 and KMT2A. T-ALL with aberrant myeloid antigens no MPO/monocytic lineage criteria. AML with aberrant CD7 no cytoplasmic/surface CD3. MPAL B/myeloid B markers rather than CD3 define lymphoid component. MPAL, Rare Types Any age; presentation depends on lineage combination and genetic lesion. Rare lineage combinations such as B/T or other combinations meeting strict MPAL criteria. Distinct or overlapping blast populations may be present. Document morphology and distribution of lineage markers. Multiple antigens without lineage-defining criteria do not establish MPAL. Apply strict B-lineage, T-lineage, and myeloid definitions. Cytoplasmic/surface CD3 defines T lineage; CD19 plus additional B markers defines B lineage. MPO or monocytic marker combination defines myeloid lineage. Demonstrate at least two lineage-defining programs. Exclude lineage infidelity in otherwise defined AML/ALL. Karyotype, FISH, and RNA fusion testing. B/T-ALL with aberrant myeloid antigens no myeloid criteria. AML with aberrant lymphoid antigens no B/T criteria. no lineage-defining markers. Acute Leukemia of Ambiguous Lineage, NOS All ages; acute marrow failure, circulating blasts, or extramedullary disease. Acute leukemia that does not meet criteria for a specific genetically defined MPAL category or lineage-defined leukemia. Blasts may be morphologically undifferentiated or show limited nonspecific features. No reliable morphology assigns lineage. Requires exclusion of AML, B-ALL, T-ALL, and MPAL. No lineage-defining MPO, monocytic combination, cytoplasmic/surface CD3, or qualifying B-lineage combination. CD34/CD117/TdT/CD7/CD13/CD33 alone are insufficient. Meet acute leukemia criteria and lack lineage-specific criteria after comprehensive testing. Exclude genetically defined AML/ALL and MPAL. No defining lesion; comprehensive genomic workup. no lineage differentiation at all. AML/ALL with aberrant antigens a single aberrant marker is insufficient. Acute Undifferentiated Leukemia Any age; rare; cytopenias, circulating blasts, or marrow replacement. Blasts lack definitive myeloid, B-cell, or T-cell lineage markers. Monomorphic blasts, usually medium-sized with scant-to-moderate cytoplasm. No convincing granules, Auer rods, monocytic morphology, or lymphoid differentiation. Marrow is replaced by undifferentiated blasts. CD34/CD117/HLA-DR may be positive but are not lineage-specific. MPO, cytoplasmic CD3, and B-lineage criteria are negative. Exclude epithelial, melanocytic, and other nonhematolymphoid tumors in tissue. Meet acute leukemia criteria and lack lineage-defining markers after extensive evaluation. Exclude MPAL and genetically defined AML/ALL. No defining molecular alteration; broad cytogenetic and molecular studies are required. myeloid lineage markers support AML. two lineage programs are present. B/T-ALL lineage-defining lymphoid markers are present. All Granulocytic MPO-positive blasts; azurophilic granules; Auer rods; maturation through promyelocytes, myelocytes, and metamyelocytes. MPO supports myeloid lineage. Minimal maturation suggests AML with minimal differentiation/without maturation; substantial maturation suggests AML with maturation. Abnormal eosinophils suggest CBFB::MYH11. Monocytic Folded or convoluted nuclei; abundant gray-blue cytoplasm; fine chromatin; vacuoles; promonocytes; tissue infiltration. Use at least two monocytic markers (CD11c, CD14, CD64, lysozyme, CD163, or nonspecific esterase). Promonocytes count as blast equivalents. Gingival/skin infiltration suggests monocytic AML or myeloid sarcoma. Erythroid Proerythroblasts with deeply basophilic cytoplasm, round nuclei, prominent nucleoli, vacuoles, multinucleation, and maturation arrest. E-cadherin, CD71, CD36, and glycophorin A support erythroid differentiation. Immature erythroid proliferation with TP53/complex karyotype raises acute erythroid leukemia. Megakaryocytic Blasts with cytoplasmic blebs, basophilic cytoplasm, variable granularity; marrow reticulin fibrosis and dry tap. CD41, CD61, and CD42b are lineage-defining when expressed by blasts. In infants, consider RBM15::MRTFA; in Down syndrome, assess GATA1. Basophilic Coarse metachromatic cytoplasmic granules; basophilic immature forms; granules may obscure nuclear detail. CD123, CD203c, FcεRI, and metachromatic stains support basophilic differentiation. Exclude CML and mast-cell neoplasms. Undifferentiated / ambiguous Monomorphic blasts without convincing lineage-specific morphology; lymphoblast-like and myeloblast-like patterns may overlap. CD34/CD117/TdT are not lineage-defining. Apply strict MPO, monocytic, cytoplasmic/surface CD3, and B-lineage criteria; CD13/CD33/CD7 alone are insufficient. PathologyGPS · Hematopathology Acute Myeloid Leukemia and Related Acute Leukemias A morphology-first reference to genetically defined AML, AML classified by differentiation, secondary myeloid neoplasms, kinase-fusion myeloid/lymphoid neoplasms, and acute leukemias of ambiguous lineage. Integrate marrow morphology, flow cytometry, immunohistochemistry, cytogenetics, and molecular testing. AML Classification: Practical Diagnostic Sequence 1. Establish acute leukemia Quantify blasts in blood and marrow. Account for classification-specific genetic AML entities that may be diagnosed below the conventional 20% blast threshold. 2. Assign lineage Use MPO for granulocytic lineage; at least two monocytic markers for monocytic lineage; CD41/CD61/CD42b for megakaryocytic lineage; and an erythroid marker panel for erythroid differentiation. 3. Exclude genetically defined AML first Prioritize PML::RARA, RUNX1::RUNX1T1, CBFB::MYH11, KMT2A, MECOM, NUP98, NPM1, CEBPA, BCR::ABL1, and other recognized defining lesions. 4. Evaluate myelodysplasia-related status Review antecedent MDS/MDS-MPN, multilineage dysplasia, cytogenetics, and myelodysplasia-related mutations. Apply the selected classification hierarchy. 5. Consider secondary context Document prior cytotoxic therapy, germline predisposition, and Down syndrome-associated myeloid proliferation. 6. Assess tissue disease and ambiguous lineage Myeloid sarcoma may precede marrow AML. For MPAL, require strict lineage-defining criteria rather than nonspecific antigen coexpression. Classification note: WHO-HAEM5 and ICC differ in some names, blast thresholds, and entity hierarchies. State the classification framework used and report the exact genetic lesion. Lineage-Specific Histology and Immunophenotype Pattern-recognition guide for identifying lineage and selecting confirmatory tests. Lineage Histologic Features IHC / Diagnostic Direction High-Yield Genetic Associations APL PML::RARA; urgent ATRA-sensitive leukemia. Core-binding factor AML RUNX1::RUNX1T1 or CBFB::MYH11. Other recurrent fusions DEK::NUP214, RBM15::MRTFA, KMT2A, MECOM, NUP98. Mutation-defined AML NPM1 and qualifying CEBPA mutation. Myelodysplasia-related AML MR gene mutations and/or qualifying cytogenetic abnormalities. TP53 multi-hit and complex karyotype are frequent. Down syndrome-associated disease Trisomy 21 with GATA1 mutation. Kinase-fusion neoplasms PDGFRA/B, FGFR1, JAK2, FLT3, ETV6::ABL1, and other kinase fusions. Immunophenotypic Guardrails CD13, CD33, CD7, CD34, and CD117 are not individually lineage-defining. MPO establishes myeloid differentiation when convincingly expressed in blasts. Monocytic lineage requires at least two accepted monocytic markers. MPAL requires strict B-, T-, and myeloid-lineage criteria; aberrant antigen expression alone is insufficient. CD41/CD61/CD42b must label blasts, not merely adherent platelets. title: Genetic Tumor Syndromes
content: use client Bloom Syndrome DNA Repair / Chromosomal Instability Syndromes Marked growth deficiency, photosensitivity, characteristic facies, and early-onset multiple cancers; confirm biallelic BLM variants. Autosomal recessive DNA-repair disorder with immune dysfunction and a broad predisposition to early-onset hematolymphoid and solid malignancies. Perinatal and postnatal growth deficiency; feeding difficulties may be prominent. Photosensitive skin changes and characteristic facial features are typical. Both sexes are affected; malignancies often arise in childhood or young adulthood. AML, ALL/LBL, and B- or T-cell lymphoma are reported; solid tumors and multiple primary cancers are also common. Mean reported ages: 18 years for AML, 20 years for ALL/LBL, and 22 years for lymphoma. Recognize the characteristic combination of growth deficiency, photosensitivity, facial features, and immune dysfunction. Establish the diagnosis by demonstrating biallelic pathogenic variants in BLM. Classify any associated leukemia or lymphoma using the standard entity-specific morphologic, immunophenotypic, and genetic criteria. There is no syndrome-specific histologic appearance; associated AML, ALL/LBL, lymphoproliferative disorders, and lymphomas resemble their corresponding sporadic counterparts. The spectrum may include more than one hematolymphoid malignancy or multiple cancers of different histologic types. No immunophenotypic profile defines Bloom syndrome itself. Apply the standard lineage and entity-specific IHC panel to the associated hematolymphoid neoplasm. Other inherited DNA-repair disorders Compare the clinical phenotype and confirm the causative germline gene; ataxia–telangiectasia is associated with progressive ataxia and telangiectasia, whereas Bloom syndrome features marked growth deficiency and photosensitivity. Sporadic leukemia or lymphoma The neoplasm may be morphologically indistinguishable; the syndromic phenotype and germline BLM testing establish the predisposition. Biallelic pathogenic loss-of-function variants in BLM are diagnostic. BLM encodes a RECQ DNA helicase; loss of function causes chromosomal instability and increased sister-chromatid exchange. Do not expect a unique leukemia or lymphoma morphology or IHC phenotype. Patients may experience substantial treatment-related toxicity; treatment planning requires recognition of the underlying syndrome. Ataxia–Telangiectasia Progressive childhood cerebellar ataxia, oculocutaneous telangiectasia, immunodeficiency, and lymphoid malignancy; confirm biallelic ATM variants. Autosomal recessive multisystem disorder caused by defective ATM-mediated DNA-damage response, with a strong predisposition to lymphoid neoplasms. Usually manifests in infancy or early childhood; both sexes are affected approximately equally. Progressive cerebellar ataxia, abnormal eye movements, dysarthria, and oculocutaneous telangiectasia are characteristic. Immunodeficiency and recurrent sinopulmonary infections are common; growth retardation, hypogonadism, and elevated serum AFP may occur. Lymphoid malignancies arise from childhood; ALL/LBL is common, and T-prolymphocytic leukemia may occur in young adulthood. DLBCL and Burkitt lymphoma are reported; Hodgkin lymphoma is uncommon. Myeloid malignancies are distinctly uncommon. Lymphoid malignancies show a male predominance (reported M:F ratio approximately 1.4–2:1). Demonstrate homozygous or compound heterozygous pathogenic ATM variants. Establish the associated leukemia or lymphoma using the same diagnostic criteria applied to patients without ataxia–telangiectasia. Elevated AFP is supportive but is not diagnostic. The associated lymphoid neoplasm has the same histologic features as its sporadic counterpart. Common associated entities include lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma, T-prolymphocytic leukemia, DLBCL, and less often Burkitt and Hodgkin lymphoma. In T-prolymphocytic leukemia, correlate blood and marrow findings with lymphocytosis and splenomegaly. The immunophenotype is the same as that of the corresponding sporadic lymphoid neoplasm. Select lineage and entity-specific markers according to the suspected leukemia or lymphoma; no IHC stain independently establishes ataxia–telangiectasia. Other childhood-onset ataxia syndromes Correlate neurologic findings with telangiectasia, immunodeficiency, AFP, and biallelic ATM testing. Nijmegen breakage syndrome and other DNA-repair disorders These may share radiosensitivity and chromosomal instability but have distinct clinical and molecular profiles. Sporadic lymphoid neoplasm Morphology and IHC may be indistinguishable; the constitutional phenotype and germline ATM testing identify the predisposition. Biallelic pathogenic variants in ATM at 11q22.3 establish the inherited disorder. ATM deficiency impairs double-strand DNA-break signaling and promotes chromosomal instability. Recurrent T-cell receptor or immunoglobulin-locus rearrangements may be seen; T-PLL may show TCL1A-associated inv(14)/t(14;14) or MTCP1-associated t(X;14), but these are features of the neoplasm rather than diagnostic tests for the syndrome. High AFP is frequent but is not sufficient for diagnosis. The phenotype of the associated lymphoma is not altered simply because the patient has ATM deficiency. Neurofibromatosis Type 1 (NF1) RASopathies Café-au-lait macules, intertriginous freckling, and neurofibromas with a predisposition to JMML and other tumors. A common RAS/MAPK pathway disorder caused by germline NF1 alteration; associated hematologic risk is particularly relevant to juvenile myelomonocytic leukemia. Usually recognized in childhood; affects both sexes. Café-au-lait macules, freckling, characteristic bone abnormalities, and learning difficulties are common. Neurofibromas may be localized, diffuse, or plexiform; plexiform neurofibromas carry an approximately 10% lifetime risk of malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumor transformation. Optic pathway glioma/pilocytic astrocytoma often develops in the first decade; other CNS tumors, sarcomas, gastrointestinal tumors, and breast cancer are increased. JMML and other myeloid neoplasms are recognized hematologic associations. Establish a compatible NF1 phenotype and/or identify a pathogenic germline NF1 variant. In a patient with a myeloid proliferation, assess persistent peripheral blood monocytosis, leukocytosis, circulating immature myeloid cells, and marrow findings. Do not attribute a MAPK-pathway variant to germline NF1 without genotype–phenotype correlation and appropriate germline testing. RASopathy-associated myeloid proliferations may show hypercellular marrow with myeloid hyperplasia and occasional erythroid hyperplasia. Dysgranulopoiesis is often minimal; pseudo–Pelger–Huët forms or hypogranular granulocytes may occur. Megakaryocytes are often decreased with minimal dysplasia; monocytes are increased, and blasts remain below 20% in the described proliferative pattern. Reticulin fibrosis may be present. No IHC profile diagnoses NF1 or its germline status. Use standard marrow and flow-cytometric studies to characterize the myeloid proliferation and exclude alternative myeloid neoplasms. Legius syndrome May closely mimic NF1 with café-au-lait macules and freckling but lacks neurofibromas and generally has lower oncologic risk. Sporadic JMML The hematologic phenotype may overlap; evaluate for a constitutional NF1 phenotype and germline NF1 alteration. Childhood myelodysplastic neoplasm RASopathy-associated marrow may be hypercellular but typically has minimal dysplasia; assess blasts and integrated clinical/genetic criteria. Germline NF1 pathogenic variants support the diagnosis. NF1 is one of the RAS/MAPK pathway genes implicated in JMML; distinguish constitutional variants from acquired somatic variants. A specific NF1 variant, c.2970_2972del (p.M992del), is associated with absence of neurofibromas. A somatic NF1 or other MAPK-pathway variant in a myeloid neoplasm does not by itself prove a germline RASopathy. Legius syndrome can mimic the pigmentary findings of NF1 but does not produce neurofibromas. Legius Syndrome NF1-like pigmentary findings without neurofibromas; confirm a pathogenic SPRED1 variant. A RAS/MAPK pathway syndrome that can be clinically mistaken for NF1 but generally carries less oncologic risk. Typically recognized in childhood; affects both sexes. Café-au-lait macules and freckling may closely resemble NF1. Neurofibromas are absent, a key distinction from classic NF1. The overall oncologic risk is generally lower than in NF1. Identify an NF1-like pigmentary phenotype without neurofibromas. Confirm the diagnosis with a pathogenic germline SPRED1 variant. Reassess the diagnosis if neurofibromas or other defining NF1 manifestations develop. There is no characteristic hematolymphoid histology attributable to Legius syndrome. A hematolymphoid neoplasm, if present, requires independent classification using standard criteria. No syndrome-specific IHC profile is established. Use standard lineage-specific IHC for any associated neoplasm. Neurofibromatosis type 1 NF1 is favored by neurofibromas, plexiform neurofibromas, characteristic bone lesions, and other NF1 manifestations; Legius syndrome lacks neurofibromas. Other pigmentary disorders Use the complete phenotype and germline molecular testing rather than café-au-lait macules alone. Pathogenic germline variants in SPRED1 establish the molecular diagnosis. Do not diagnose NF1 from café-au-lait macules alone when neurofibromas are absent. Noonan Syndrome Characteristic facies, congenital heart disease, short stature, and lymphatic or skeletal abnormalities; consider JMML in a child with monocytosis. A RAS/MAPK pathway disorder with variable germline causes and a recognized predisposition to myeloid proliferations, especially JMML. Characteristic facial features, congenital heart defects, short stature, coagulopathy, and neurodevelopmental differences may occur. Undescended testes, ocular, lymphatic, and skeletal abnormalities are additional clues. Hepatosplenomegaly may reflect an associated subclinical myeloid proliferation. JMML and other myeloid neoplasms are particularly associated with PTPN11- and CBL-related disease; lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma and AML are also reported. Establish a characteristic Noonan phenotype and identify a pathogenic germline RAS/MAPK pathway variant when possible. In suspected JMML, document sustained peripheral blood monocytosis of at least 1 × 10⁹/L, leukocytosis, and fewer than 20% blasts, then apply full JMML diagnostic criteria. Correlate the genotype with the hematologic phenotype; PTPN11 variants at codons 61, 71, 72, and 76 are associated with particularly increased risk. Marrow may be hypercellular with myeloid hyperplasia and occasional erythroid hyperplasia. Dysplasia is often limited; megakaryocytes may be reduced and monocytes increased. Blasts are increased but remain below 20% in the described RASopathy-associated proliferative pattern. Peripheral blood may show leukocytosis, left-shifted granulopoiesis, sustained monocytosis, and nucleated red blood cells. No IHC profile establishes Noonan syndrome. Use standard flow cytometry and immunophenotyping to characterize blasts and exclude other myeloid or lymphoid neoplasms. The marrow and blood findings may be indistinguishable; the syndromic phenotype and germline testing establish the constitutional predisposition. RASopathy-associated proliferations often show less conspicuous dysplasia; integrate blast percentage, monocytosis, and molecular findings. Other RASopathies Facial, cardiac, cutaneous, developmental, and molecular features overlap; assign the specific syndrome by genotype–phenotype correlation. Germline variants may involve PTPN11, CBL, SOS1, RAF1, RIT1, KRAS, NRAS, and other RAS/MAPK pathway genes. PTPN11 and CBL are particularly relevant to JMML risk; some CBL-associated myeloid proliferations may regress spontaneously. A MAPK-pathway variant found in tumor-only sequencing requires germline confirmation when constitutional predisposition is suspected. A RAS/MAPK mutation alone does not distinguish germline RASopathy from a somatic driver in a myeloid neoplasm. Do not diagnose AML unless the applicable blast threshold and entity-specific criteria are met. Noonan Syndrome with Multiple Lentigines Multiple lentigines with Noonan-like facial and cardiac findings; consider RAF1- or PTPN11-associated disease. A Noonan-spectrum RASopathy formerly termed LEOPARD syndrome, with a distinct pigmentary and cardiac phenotype. Usually becomes apparent during childhood; affects both sexes. Multiple lentigines, characteristic facial features, ocular hypertelorism, and cardiac conduction abnormalities may occur. Pulmonary stenosis, abnormal genital development, growth retardation, and sensorineural deafness are recognized features. The source describes enrichment of lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma and AML in PTPN11- and RAF1-related disease. Recognize the multiple-lentigines phenotype in a patient with Noonan-spectrum features. Confirm a pathogenic germline RAS/MAPK pathway variant, particularly in the appropriate PTPN11 or RAF1 context. Classify any hematolymphoid neoplasm independently using standard diagnostic criteria. No syndrome-specific hematolymphoid morphology is defined. Associated leukemia or lymphoma is evaluated according to its conventional morphologic and genetic criteria. Use standard entity-specific IHC and flow cytometry for any associated hematolymphoid neoplasm. Classic Noonan syndrome Both share facial and cardiac features; multiple lentigines and the associated pigmentary phenotype favor Noonan syndrome with multiple lentigines. Clinical overlap is substantial; molecular findings and the characteristic lentigines phenotype support subclassification. Germline variants in PTPN11 and RAF1 are associated with this phenotype. Genotype–phenotype correlation is important because several RASopathies share overlapping clinical features. Do not treat all Noonan-spectrum syndromes as genetically or clinically interchangeable. Costello Syndrome A distinctive multisystem RASopathy with the greatest malignancy risk among the RASopathies described. A rare RAS/MAPK pathway disorder with increased risk of malignancy; reported cancer risk is approximately three times that of Noonan syndrome. Usually presents in childhood; affects both sexes. Clinical features overlap with Noonan and cardio-facio-cutaneous syndromes. The relative rarity of the syndrome limits precise estimates of individual tumor risks. Among the RASopathies described, Costello syndrome is associated with the greatest malignancy risk. Establish a compatible multisystem phenotype. Confirm a pathogenic germline variant in a RAS/MAPK pathway gene, with genotype–phenotype correlation. Evaluate any hematolymphoid or solid neoplasm as a separate diagnostic entity. No syndrome-specific hematolymphoid histology is defined. Any associated neoplasm should be classified using its standard morphologic criteria. Apply standard lineage-specific IHC to any associated neoplasm. Noonan syndrome Both are RASopathies with overlapping clinical features; molecular testing and the complete phenotype support distinction. Cardio-facio-cutaneous syndrome Clinical overlap is substantial; distinguish by the specific phenotype and germline molecular findings. Pathogenic germline variants in RAS/MAPK pathway genes establish the molecular basis; interpret the specific gene in the context of the phenotype. Do not infer the specific RASopathy from a shared RAS/MAPK pathway variant without considering the full clinical phenotype. Cardio-Facio-Cutaneous Syndrome Cardiac, craniofacial, cutaneous, and developmental findings in a child; confirm a RAS/MAPK pathway variant. A rare multisystem RASopathy that overlaps clinically with Noonan and Costello syndromes. Cardiac, facial, cutaneous, and neurodevelopmental abnormalities are characteristic components of the syndrome. Clinical overlap with Noonan and Costello syndromes can complicate phenotypic classification. The rarity of the syndrome limits reliable estimates of hematolymphoid malignancy incidence. Identify a compatible multisystem phenotype. Demonstrate a pathogenic germline variant in a RAS/MAPK pathway gene when possible. Classify any associated hematolymphoid neoplasm independently. Associated hematolymphoid tumors retain the morphology of their respective entities. Use the standard IHC and flow-cytometric workup for the associated neoplasm. Overlapping cardiac and facial features require genotype–phenotype correlation for distinction. Costello syndrome Both are rare RASopathies with overlapping multisystem findings; molecular testing and the complete phenotype are required. Pathogenic germline variants in RAS/MAPK pathway genes are causative; interpret variants with the clinical phenotype. Do not assign a specific RASopathy solely from a nonspecific somatic MAPK-pathway mutation. All Categories Hematopathology · Predisposition and Inherited Disorders Genetic Tumor Syndromes Associated with Hematolymphoid Neoplasms Diagnostic recognition of inherited cancer predisposition, with emphasis on syndromic features, associated hematolymphoid neoplasms, germline confirmation, and implications for classification and clinical management. When to Consider Germline Predisposition Familial clustering alone does not prove inherited predisposition; shared infections, environmental exposures, or antigenic stimulation may contribute. Consider genetic counseling and germline evaluation when clinical, family, or laboratory findings suggest a constitutional disorder. A hematolymphoid neoplasm strongly associated with an inherited predisposition. A known familial pathogenic germline variant or established cancer-predisposition syndrome. Dysmorphism, congenital anomalies, developmental delay, or other syndromic findings. Two first- or second-degree relatives with hematolymphoid neoplasms. Two independent hematolymphoid neoplasms in one person, or a non–therapy-related hematolymphoid neoplasm with multiple or early-onset solid tumors. Unusually early disease onset or unexplained excessive treatment toxicity. A pathogenic or likely pathogenic variant on tumor sequencing in a gene associated with germline cancer predisposition, with findings compatible with constitutional origin. Germline Testing: Practical Diagnostic Points A germline predisposition can affect diagnostic classification, treatment tolerance, surveillance, and family counseling. Some inherited disorders confer increased treatment toxicity; TP53 germline variants also increase the risk of radiation-associated secondary malignancies. Blood, marrow, tissue, and buccal samples may contain neoplastic cells and therefore may not reliably represent the constitutional genotype. When contamination is a concern, consider nonhematopoietic sources such as hair follicles or fingernail clippings. A tumor-associated variant should not be called germline without appropriate testing of a suitable non-neoplastic specimen. Predisposition Framework Syndromic and nonsyndromic forms may be monogenic or multifactorial. Syndromic predisposition Recurrent extrahematologic manifestations such as growth abnormalities, dysmorphism, congenital malformations, neurologic findings, or immune dysfunction. Examples include Bloom syndrome, ataxia–telangiectasia, and RASopathies. GATA2 deficiency, selected bone marrow failure syndromes, telomere disorders, Fanconi anemia, and constitutional chromosomal abnormalities such as trisomy 21 are also recognized contexts. Nonsyndromic predisposition Monogenic predisposition includes TP53-associated Li–Fraumeni syndrome, CHEK2-associated Li–Fraumeni-like predisposition, and many inborn errors of immunity. Polygenic or multifactorial susceptibility is also relevant, particularly in mature lymphoid neoplasms; selected pathogen-related genetic traits have been associated with entity-specific risk. Syndrome-to-Neoplasm Overview Syndrome Gene / Pathway Key Hematolymphoid Associations Clinical Recognition Clue Bloom syndrome BLM AML, ALL/LBL, B- and T-cell lymphomas Growth deficiency and photosensitivity Ataxia–telangiectasia ATM ALL/LBL, T-PLL, DLBCL, Burkitt lymphoma Progressive ataxia and telangiectasia NF1 NF1 / RAS-MAPK JMML and other myeloid neoplasms Neurofibromas and café-au-lait macules SPRED1 / RAS-MAPK Lower oncologic risk than NF1 Pigmentary findings without neurofibromas RAS-MAPK genes JMML, other myeloid neoplasms, ALL/LBL, AML Facial features and congenital heart disease Noonan syndrome with multiple lentigines Often PTPN11 / RAF1 ALL/LBL and AML reported Multiple lentigines and cardiac findings RAS-MAPK pathway Increased overall malignancy risk Distinctive multisystem phenotype Malignancy risk is not well quantified Cardiac, facial, cutaneous findings Interpreting Marrow Findings in RASopathy-Associated Myeloid Proliferation A typical pattern includes hypercellularity, myeloid hyperplasia, sustained peripheral blood monocytosis (often at least 1 × 10⁹/L), leukocytosis, left-shifted granulopoiesis, and fewer than 20% blasts. Dysplasia is often limited. The distinction from a childhood myelodysplastic neoplasm or AML requires integrated assessment of morphology, blood counts, blast percentage, clinical phenotype, and germline versus somatic molecular findings. genetic-syndrome-search Search syndromes, genes, neoplasms, and diagnostic features Search: ATM, BLM, JMML, photosensitivity, lentigines... genetic-syndrome-group Category Collapse All Expand All syndromes Expand a syndrome for clinical and diagnostic details. title: Histiocytic Dendritic Cell Neoplasms
content: use client Mature Plasmacytoid Dendritic Cell Proliferation Associated with Myeloid Neoplasm Plasmacytoid Dendritic Cell Neoplasms Older adults, predominantly men; skin and marrow, rarely lymph nodes; associated most often with CMML, but also AML, MDS, and MPN. Nodular or interstitial aggregates of medium-sized cells with eccentric round-to-oval nuclei, clumped chromatin, moderate amphophilic cytoplasm, and few mitoses. CD123, TCF4, CD303, CD304, SPIB, CD2AP, and MX1 support pDC differentiation CD56 is usually absent/low; CD34, TdT, or CD56 may be aberrant, particularly in AML-associated cases. Identify mature pDCs in a defined myeloid neoplasm confirm with CD123 plus additional pDC markers assess maturation, CD56, and CD34 exclude reactive pDC aggregates in infection, autoimmune disease, Kikuchi–Fujimoto disease, and Castleman disease. No specific molecular test is required. Clonal findings may overlap with the associated myeloid neoplasm; RUNX1 and RAS-pathway mutations occur in subsets. BPDCN: blastoid cytology, high proliferation, often strong CD56 AML with pDC differentiation: immature CD34-positive pDCs may form a continuum with AML blasts Reactive pDC proliferation: inflammatory/autoimmune setting without convincing clonal association. Blastic Plasmacytoid Dendritic Cell Neoplasm Usually older adults (median roughly 62–70 years), marked male predominance; skin most common, followed by marrow and lymph nodes. Violaceous/brown plaques or nodules, cytopenias, and dissemination. Diffuse monotonous medium-sized blastoid cells with scant cytoplasm, eccentric nuclei, fine chromatin, and inconspicuous nucleoli skin infiltrate is dermal/subcutaneous with epidermal and adnexal sparing. CD123 and nuclear TCF4 are highly useful; CD303, CD304, TCL1, CD2AP, CD4, and CD56 commonly support pDC phenotype CD34 is usually negative MPO, lysozyme, CD14, and lineage-defining B/T markers are generally absent CD123 alone is not specific. Establish blastoid hematolymphoid neoplasm with pDC differentiation demonstrate CD123 plus TCF4 and/or other pDC markers exclude AML with pDC differentiation, mature pDC proliferation, and NK/T-cell neoplasms. No single defining alteration. Complex karyotypes and losses involving CDKN2A/B and RB1 are common; TET2 and ASXL1 mutations recur. AML with pDC differentiation: CD34-positive immature pDCs and myeloid blasts; assess MPO/myeloid phenotype Mature pDC proliferation: bland mature cells and low proliferation Extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma: cytotoxic markers and EBER positivity Acute monocytic leukemia: CD64, CD14, lysozyme, and often MPO. Langerhans Cell Histiocytosis Langerhans Cell Neoplasms Most common in children but occurs at any age; bone, skin, lymph nodes, lung, and hypothalamic-pituitary region. Bone pain, lytic lesions, rash, or multisystem symptoms. Large cells with abundant pale eosinophilic cytoplasm and grooved, folded, or convoluted coffee-bean nuclei eosinophils, lymphocytes, plasma cells, and multinucleated giant cells variably admixed. High-grade pleomorphism is absent. CD1a membranous and CD207 (langerin) granular cytoplasmic are defining; S100 nuclear/cytoplasmic and CD68 Golgi-dot may be positive CD207 is a surrogate for Birbeck granules Cyclin D1 and phospho-ERK may be positive but are not specific. Identify characteristic grooved histiocytes in the correct tissue context demonstrate CD1a and CD207 in lesional cells distinguish neoplastic cells from reactive CD1a-positive dendritic cells correlate with site and systemic distribution. MAPK-pathway alterations are common, especially BRAF p.V600E; MAP2K1 and other pathway mutations occur. Validated BRAF VE1 IHC may complement sensitive molecular testing. Indeterminate dendritic cell tumor: CD1a/S100 positive but CD207 negative Langerhans cell sarcoma: high-grade pleomorphism and atypical mitoses Juvenile xanthogranuloma: CD1a/CD207 negative, CD163/CD68/factor XIIIa positive Reactive Langerhans cells: branching dendritic cells in a site-specific reactive pattern. Langerhans Cell Sarcoma Usually adults; skin, lymph nodes, and extranodal sites; rapidly enlarging mass, ulcerated lesion, or systemic disease. High-grade pleomorphic tumor with large atypical cells, plump or elongated nuclei, high mitotic activity, and atypical mitoses characteristic LCH grooves may be inconspicuous and eosinophils variable. Retains Langerhans phenotype: CD1a, CD207, and S100; staining may be focal CD68, cyclin D1, and HLA-DR may be positive Evaluate staining specifically in high-grade tumor cells. Demonstrate high-grade malignant cytology and increased mitoses confirm Langerhans differentiation with CD1a/CD207/S100 (sometimes focal) exclude histiocytic sarcoma and interdigitating dendritic cell sarcoma with a broad panel. MAPK-pathway mutations, including KRAS and less commonly BRAF p.V600E, occur in a subset. LCH: bland cytology and low mitotic activity Histiocytic sarcoma: CD163/CD68/lysozyme positive but CD1a/CD207 negative Interdigitating dendritic cell sarcoma: CD1a/CD207 negative, often strong S100 Undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma: lacks Langerhans phenotype. Indeterminate Dendritic Cell Tumor Other Dendritic Cell Neoplasms Usually adults (median around 48 years), slight male predominance; usually skin-limited papules or nodules, often generalized; arms and scalp common for solitary lesions. Medium-to-large histiocytoid cells with oval, indented, or grooved nuclei and pale-to-eosinophilic cytoplasm epithelioid or spindle forms pleomorphism usually limited and atypical mitoses absent. CD1a and S100 positive; CD207 (langerin) negative CD68/CD163 variable CD21/CD35 generally negative. Establish clonal dendritic-cell proliferation with CD1a and S100 demonstrate absence of CD207 exclude LCH, Langerhans cell sarcoma, and reactive Langerhans-cell proliferations assess atypia, Ki-67, extracutaneous disease, and associated hematologic neoplasm. MAPK-pathway alterations, including BRAF p.V600E, reported in a subset; molecular testing is useful in disseminated or atypical cases. LCH: CD207 positive Langerhans cell sarcoma: high-grade pleomorphism/atypical mitoses Interdigitating dendritic cell sarcoma: usually CD1a negative and strongly S100 positive Juvenile xanthogranuloma: CD1a negative, CD163/CD68/factor XIIIa positive. Interdigitating Dendritic Cell Sarcoma Usually adults; lymph nodes common, with extranodal skin, soft tissue, and visceral sites; enlarging lymphadenopathy or mass. Spindle-to-epithelioid cells in sheets, fascicles, or storiform patterns, with abundant pale eosinophilic cytoplasm, indistinct borders, elongated irregular nuclei, vesicular chromatin, and conspicuous nucleoli. S100 typically strong/diffuse; fascin often positive; CD45 and variable CD4/CD68 may be expressed CD1a/CD207 and CD21/CD35 are negative Exclude epithelial and melanocytic markers. Demonstrate malignant spindle/epithelioid dendritic-cell proliferation support interdigitating phenotype with S100 and ancillary markers exclude Langerhans-cell, follicular dendritic-cell, histiocytic, melanocytic, and epithelial neoplasms. No single defining molecular alteration. MAPK-pathway alterations and clonal relationship to prior lymphoid neoplasms occur in subsets. Histiocytic sarcoma: CD163/CD68/lysozyme macrophage profile; S100 usually absent/patchy Langerhans cell sarcoma: CD1a/CD207 positive Follicular dendritic cell sarcoma: CD21/CD23/CD35/clusterin positive Melanoma: SOX10/Melan-A/HMB45 positive. Juvenile Xanthogranuloma Histiocyte/Macrophage Neoplasms Usually infants and young children, but adults occur; slight male predominance. Skin most common; eye, CNS, and viscera less common. Yellow-orange papules or nodules. Circumscribed dermal/subcutaneous proliferation of foamy histiocytes Touton giant cells may be present, especially in mature lesions. Early lesions may be non-xanthomatous significant pleomorphism is generally absent. CD68, CD163, CD4, factor XIIIa, and fascin commonly positive CD1a/CD207 negative; S100 usually negative or weak/focal; ALK negative. Identify circumscribed non-high-grade histiocytic proliferation with macrophage phenotype demonstrate CD68/CD163 and factor XIIIa exclude LCH, ALK-positive histiocytosis, and systemic ECD when indicated. No defining molecular alteration required; MAPK-pathway mutations occur in a subset, including disseminated cases. LCH: CD1a/CD207 positive with grooved nuclei/eosinophils ALK-positive histiocytosis: ALK positive, often JXG-like ECD: systemic xanthogranulomatous infiltrates and characteristic skeletal/organ involvement Lipidized dermatofibroma: collagen trapping, epidermal/adnexal changes, and hemosiderin. Erdheim-Chester Disease Usually middle-aged to older adults, male predominance; long bones, retroperitoneum, cardiovascular system, CNS, lungs, and skin. Bone pain, diabetes insipidus, perirenal/periaortic infiltration, and neurologic/cardiac symptoms. Foamy/xanthomatous histiocytes in fibrotic inflammatory background lesions may be patchy. Touton giant cells and variable inflammatory cells may occur. Radiologic distribution is an important diagnostic clue. CD68, CD163, CD14, and factor XIIIa commonly positive CD1a/CD207 negative; S100 usually negative or weak/focal; ALK negative BRAF VE1 may be positive in BRAF-mutated cases. Integrate tissue morphology with characteristic multisystem clinical/radiologic distribution establish macrophage phenotype and absence of Langerhans markers test BRAF and other MAPK alterations using sensitive assays. BRAF p.V600E occurs in approximately half of cases; MAP2K1, KRAS, NRAS, ARAF, and other MAPK-pathway alterations occur. Molecular results guide targeted therapy. JXG: usually localized cutaneous lesion in children; ECD has systemic distribution and long-bone involvement LCH: CD1a/CD207 positive RDD: S100/OCT2 positive with emperipolesis ALK-positive histiocytosis: ALK positive with ALK fusion. Rosai-Dorfman Disease Nodal disease often affects children/young adults, especially cervical nodes; extranodal disease more often in adults. Painless massive lymphadenopathy, fever, or site-specific symptoms. Sinuses expanded by large histiocytes with round nuclei, prominent nucleoli, and abundant pale cytoplasm. Emperipolesis of intact lymphocytes, plasma cells, neutrophils, or erythrocytes is characteristic but may be subtle extranodally. Plasma-cell-rich background and fibrosis may occur. S100 strongly positive and highlights emperipolesis; OCT2 positive; cyclin D1 and phospho-ERK frequently positive CD1a/CD207 and ALK negative. Identify large S100-positive histiocytes with emperipolesis in appropriate architectural context use OCT2/cyclin D1 in difficult cases exclude LCH, ALK-positive histiocytosis, ECD, infection, and IgG4-related disease. About half harbor MAPK/ERK mutations, including KRAS, NRAS, MAP2K1, ARAF, CSF1R, and rarely BRAF p.V600E. Consider germline SLC29A3 or FAS testing in familial syndromic settings. ALK-positive histiocytosis: ALK positive, usually lacks classic emperipolesis ECD/JXG: xanthomatous macrophages, usually S100 negative IgG4-related disease: storiform fibrosis/obliterative phlebitis and appropriate IgG4/IgG ratio; IgG4-positive plasma cells alone are insufficient. ALK-Positive Histiocytosis Infants with multisystem disease may have hepatosplenomegaly, anemia, and thrombocytopenia; single-system/multifocal disease at any age, with female predilection. CNS/PNS, bone, skin, breast, lung, and soft tissue. Large epithelioid, foamy, and spindle histiocytes abundant eosinophilic or multivacuolated cytoplasm irregular indented/folded/lobulated nuclei. Touton cells, hemosiderin, and emperipolesis may occur. Spindle cells may be fascicular or storiform significant pleomorphism is usually absent. ALK positive in lesional histiocytes, usually cytoplasmic; rarely membranous/Golgi-dot and exceptionally nuclear CD68, CD163, CD14, CD4, lysozyme variable; factor XIIIa/fascin common CD1a/CD207 and CD30 negative; Ki-67 generally low. Identify histiocytic proliferation without high-grade atypia demonstrate ALK in lesional histiocytes plus at least two histiocytic markers confirm ALK rearrangement when feasible correlate with systemic distribution and exclude ALK-positive lymphoma/IMT. ALK rearrangements define the entity, most often KIF5B::ALK; other partners include CLTC, TPM3, TFG, EML4, DCTN1, COL1A2, and TRIM33. JXG: similar morphology but ALK negative ALK-positive ALCL: strong CD30 and lacks macrophage phenotype Inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor: myofibroblastic morphology/SMA-desmin profile, not histiocytic ECD: systemic xanthogranulomatous disease, ALK negative. Histiocytic Sarcoma Wide age range (median around mid-40s), slight male predominance; lymph nodes, GI tract, spleen, soft tissue, skin, and CNS. Mass, obstruction, splenomegaly, fever, weight loss, or night sweats. Diffuse sheets of large noncohesive oval/round or spindle cells sinusoidal growth may occur. Abundant eosinophilic often finely vacuolated cytoplasm vesicular, indented/grooved/folded nuclei with prominent nucleoli and variable pleomorphism. Multinucleation and hemophagocytosis may occur atypical mitoses/destructive growth support malignancy. At least two histiocytic markers should label tumor cells: CD163, CD68, lysozyme PU.1, CD4, CD45/CD45RO common; S100 variable/patchy CD1a/CD207, CD21/CD35, MPO, ALK, cytokeratins, ERG, SOX10, HMB45, CD20/PAX5, and CD3 are negative in tumor cells. Demonstrate malignant noncohesive large-cell neoplasm with macrophage morphology confirm at least two histiocytic markers in tumor cells exclude Langerhans, follicular/interdigitating dendritic, lymphoid, epithelial, melanocytic, vascular, and myeloid neoplasms exclude acute monocytic leukemia. MAPK-pathway mutations (KRAS, NRAS, BRAF, MAP2K1, PTPN11, NF1, CBL) recur; TP53/CDKN2A alterations are common. Some cases share IG rearrangements or mutations with antecedent B-cell neoplasms. Interdigitating dendritic cell sarcoma: strong S100, macrophage markers less convincing ALCL: CD30 and often ALK positive DLBCL: CD20/PAX5 positive; histiocytic markers may label reactive macrophages Melanoma: SOX10/HMB45; carcinoma: cytokeratins; UPS: lacks coherent histiocytic phenotype. All PathologyGPS · Hematopathology Histiocytic and Dendritic Cell Neoplasms A practical diagnostic reference emphasizing morphology, lineage-specific immunophenotyping, and the distinction among macrophage, Langerhans-cell, conventional dendritic-cell, and plasmacytoid dendritic-cell proliferations. Diagnostic Approach: Establish the Lineage Lineage Core markers Morphologic clue Langerhans cells CD1a+, CD207+, S100+ Grooved/convoluted nuclei; eosinophil-rich background in LCH. Indeterminate dendritic cells CD1a+, S100+, CD207− Langerhans-like cells without langerin. Interdigitating dendritic cells Strong S100; CD1a−, CD207− Spindle-to-epithelioid cells, often nodal. Macrophages/histiocytes CD163+, CD68+, lysozyme+, PU.1+ Foamy or eosinophilic cytoplasm; variable emperipolesis. Plasmacytoid dendritic cells CD123+, TCF4+, CD303/CD304+ Mature pDCs are bland; BPDCN is blastoid and high grade. Interpretive caution: Confirm that staining is present in lesional cells. Reactive histiocytes may be abundant in lymphoma, carcinoma, melanoma, and inflammatory lesions; a single positive marker is rarely sufficient. High-Yield IHC Panel Macrophage/histiocyte: CD163, CD68, lysozyme, PU.1, CD4. Langerhans: CD1a, CD207 (langerin), S100. Plasmacytoid dendritic: CD123, TCF4, CD303, CD304, TCL1, SPIB. Interdigitating dendritic: S100, fascin; exclude CD1a/CD207 and follicular dendritic markers. Exclusion panel: MPO, CD20/PAX5, CD3, CD30, ALK, cytokeratins, SOX10, HMB45, ERG. Classification Notes Follicular dendritic cell sarcoma and fibroblastic reticular cell tumor are classified among stromal-derived neoplasms of lymphoid tissues, not in this group. BPDCN is included here as a plasmacytoid dendritic-cell neoplasm. Secondary histiocytic/dendritic neoplasms are classified by their current phenotype; compare molecular findings with any antecedent lymphoma/leukemia. Acute monocytic leukemia is not classified as histiocytic sarcoma. hd-search Search diagnoses, markers, morphology, or mutations Search: CD1a, langerin, CD163, TCF4, emperipolesis, ALK... hd-group Category Collapse All Expand All diagnostic entities Expand a diagnosis for full details. − Hide ＋ Details Clinical Profile Essential Diagnostic Criteria Histopathology Immunophenotype Molecular Pathology Differential Diagnosis No matching entities.
