title: Mature T And Nk Cell Neoplasms
group: Mature T And Nk Cell Neoplasms
content: use client T-Cell Prolymphocytic Leukemia Mature T-cell leukemia Older adults; median ~65 years; slight male predominance. Marked lymphocytosis, hepatosplenomegaly, generalized lymphadenopathy, skin or serous involvement. Persistent/progressive mature T-cell lymphocytosis with compatible morphology and phenotype. Small-to-medium prolymphocytes with visible nucleoli and basophilic cytoplasm; cytoplasmic blebs are characteristic. CD2+, surface/cytoplasmic CD3+, CD5+, usually CD7+; CD4+, CD8+, or double-positive; TdT−, CD1a−; TCL1A commonly positive; CD52 usually bright. Sézary syndrome: cerebriform nuclei and skin-predominant disease. ATLL: HTLV-1 association and flower cells. T-LGLL: granular cytoplasm, cytopenias, indolent course. T-lymphoblastic leukemia: TdT+/immature phenotype. TCL1A or MTCP1 rearrangement involving TCR loci is defining; complex karyotype, ATM, JAK1/JAK3/STAT5B alterations may occur. T-Cell Large Granular Lymphocytic Leukemia Mature cytotoxic T-cell leukemia Adults, median ~60 years; no sex predilection. Neutropenia, anemia/PRCA, recurrent infections, rheumatoid arthritis; spleen and marrow, rarely nodes. Persistent clonal cytotoxic T-cell expansion, typically with absolute lymphocytosis >2 × 10⁹/L; integrate count, phenotype, clonality, and clinical context. Large granular lymphocytes have abundant pale cytoplasm with azurophilic granules and round-to-slightly irregular nuclei. Marrow shows subtle interstitial/intrasinusoidal infiltrates. Usually CD3+, CD8+, CD57+, CD16+, CD45RA+, TCRαβ+; CD5/CD7 dim or lost; CD4−; cytotoxic proteins positive. Reactive cytotoxic T-cell expansion: polyclonal/transient and linked to infection. NK-LGLL: surface CD3− and no TCR rearrangement. T-PLL: marked lymphocytosis with prolymphocytes. STAT3 mutations common, especially CD8+ cases; STAT5B enriched in CD4+ cases. NK-Cell Large Granular Lymphocytic Leukemia Mature NK-cell lymphoproliferation Older adults; often incidental persistent lymphocytosis or cytopenias, particularly neutropenia; blood, marrow, spleen. Persistent clonal/oligoclonal NK-cell expansion with compatible phenotype and clinical course; exclude reactive NK expansion and aggressive NK-cell leukemia. Large granular lymphocytes resemble T-LGLL; marrow involvement is often subtle and interstitial/intrasinusoidal. Surface CD3−, cytoplasmic CD3ε+, CD2+, CD7+, CD16 and/or CD56+, cytotoxic proteins+; restricted KIR expression supports clonality. T-LGLL: surface CD3+, TCR expression and clonal TCR rearrangement. Aggressive NK-cell leukemia: acute systemic illness, EBV association, high tumor burden. No TCR gene rearrangement; restricted KIR repertoire; STAT3/STAT5B pathway alterations may occur. Adult T-Cell Leukemia/Lymphoma HTLV-1-associated mature T-cell neoplasm Adults from HTLV-1-endemic regions or with exposure risk; skin, blood, nodes, marrow, bone, and viscera. Hypercalcemia and skin lesions are important clues. Demonstrate HTLV-1 association in a mature T-cell neoplasm; classify clinical subtype (acute, lymphoma, chronic, smoldering). Pleomorphic cells with multilobated “flower” nuclei; diffuse tissue infiltrates or nodal effacement; skin may show epidermotropism. CD2+, CD3+, CD4+, CD25+, CCR4+, often FOXP3+; CD7 frequently lost; CD8 usually negative; CADM1 supports phenotype. Sézary syndrome/mycosis fungoides: no HTLV-1. PTCL-NOS: lacks HTLV-1 integration. T-PLL: TCL1-family rearrangement and typical prolymphocytes. HTLV-1 proviral DNA and monoclonal integration are central; recurrent alterations include PLCG1, PRKCB, CCR4, and immune-evasion genes. Sézary Syndrome Leukemic cutaneous T-cell lymphoma Adults, usually older; erythroderma, severe pruritus, lymphadenopathy, and circulating atypical T cells. Generalized erythroderma plus clonal circulating neoplastic T cells; quantify blood tumor burden and establish clonality. Cerebriform lymphocytes in blood; skin shows epidermotropic atypical lymphocytes, often with minimal spongiosis, and may form Pautrier microabscesses. Usually CD3+, CD4+, CD45RO+ with loss of CD7 and/or CD26; CD4:CD8 ratio increased; TCR clonality in blood/skin. Erythrodermic mycosis fungoides: prior patch/plaque disease and less prominent blood involvement. Inflammatory erythroderma: no matching clonal aberrant T-cell population. T-PLL: prolymphocytes, TCL1. Clonal TCR rearrangement; genomic alterations overlap with MF, including copy-number changes and epigenetic regulator mutations. Aggressive NK-Cell Leukemia Aggressive NK-cell leukemia Adults, often Asian; acute fever, hepatosplenomegaly, cytopenias, liver failure, coagulopathy, and hemophagocytic syndrome. Systemic aggressive NK-cell proliferation, usually EBV-associated, with leukemic blood/marrow involvement. Medium-sized atypical lymphoid cells with azurophilic granules; sinusoidal/interstitial marrow and hepatic/splenic infiltration; necrosis and hemophagocytosis may occur. Surface CD3−, cytoplasmic CD3ε+, CD2+, CD56+, cytotoxic proteins+, usually CD16 variable; EBER positive in most cases. Extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma: localized extranodal destructive mass, often nasal, angiocentric/angiodestructive. NK-LGLL: indolent, usually EBV−. EBV+ T-cell lymphoma: surface CD3/T-cell lineage. Clonal EBV; JAK/STAT, RAS/MAPK, TET2, DDX3X, CREBBP and immune-checkpoint pathway alterations. Primary Cutaneous CD4-Positive Small/Medium T-Cell Lymphoproliferative Disorder Primary cutaneous T-cell lymphoproliferative disorder Adults; solitary small nodule or plaque, commonly head/neck or upper trunk; usually localized and indolent. Solitary localized lesion with small/medium pleomorphic CD4+ T cells and no evidence of systemic lymphoma; exclude MF and primary cutaneous peripheral T-cell lymphoma. Dense nodular or diffuse dermal infiltrate with small/medium pleomorphic lymphocytes, scattered larger cells, histiocytes and plasma cells; epidermis usually spared. CD3+, CD4+, often PD1+, ICOS+, BCL6 variable; CD8−, CD30 usually limited; retain at least some pan-T markers. Primary cutaneous marginal zone lymphoma: B-cell follicles/plasma cells. TFH lymphoma: systemic nodes and broader TFH phenotype. Primary cutaneous PTCL-NOS: destructive, cytologically overt malignant infiltrate. Clonal TCR may be present but is not independently diagnostic; no defining recurrent molecular alteration. Primary Cutaneous Acral CD8-Positive T-Cell Lymphoproliferative Disorder Primary cutaneous cytotoxic T-cell proliferation Adults; solitary slowly growing papule/nodule on ear, nose, or other acral site; indolent. Localized acral lesion with bland monomorphic CD8+ cytotoxic T cells and low proliferative activity. Dense nodular dermal infiltrate of monomorphic small/medium cells; grenz zone may be present; epidermis and adnexa usually spared. CD3+, CD8+, TIA1+, often granzyme B variable; CD4−, CD30−; CD68 may be expressed; low Ki-67. Primary cutaneous CD8+ aggressive epidermotropic lymphoma: epidermotropism, cytotoxic phenotype, high proliferation. Primary cutaneous ALCL: large cells, strong CD30. Clonal TCR rearrangement can occur; no defining genetic abnormality. Mycosis Fungoides Primary cutaneous T-cell lymphoma Adults, often middle-aged/older; patches and plaques in sun-protected areas, progressing in some cases to tumors or erythroderma. Clinicopathologic diagnosis requiring persistent/progressive characteristic lesions and atypical epidermotropic T cells; early biopsies may be subtle. Epidermotropism disproportionate to spongiosis, basal alignment, haloed atypical lymphocytes, Pautrier microabscesses in established lesions; band-like superficial dermal infiltrate. Usually CD3+, CD4+, CD45RO+; loss of CD7 and/or CD5; CD8+ variants occur; assess CD30 in large-cell transformation. Inflammatory dermatitis: spongiosis and mixed reactive cells without convincing atypical epidermotropism. Sézary syndrome: erythroderma and significant blood disease. Primary cutaneous CD30+ LPD: cohesive CD30+ large cells. Clonal TCR supports but does not establish diagnosis; recurrent alterations include TP53, CDKN2A, and epigenetic regulators in advanced disease. Lymphomatoid Papulosis Primary cutaneous CD30-positive lymphoproliferative disorder Adults; recurrent crops of papules/nodules, often ulcerating and spontaneously regressing; trunk/extremities. Recurrent self-healing papulonodular lesions with CD30+ atypical cells; clinical course is essential. Type A: wedge-shaped mixed infiltrate with scattered/clustered large CD30+ cells. Type B: epidermotropic cerebriform cells. Type C: cohesive sheets of CD30+ large cells. Additional patterns include D/E and folliculotropic variants. Large atypical cells strongly CD30+; T-cell markers variable/lost; ALK usually negative; cytotoxic phenotype in some variants. Primary cutaneous ALCL: persistent solitary tumor without spontaneous regression. MF with CD30+ transformation: established MF background. Systemic ALCL: systemic staging and clinical presentation. TCR clonality may be shared with associated MF/ALCL; no single molecular test separates entities. Primary Cutaneous Anaplastic Large Cell Lymphoma Primary cutaneous CD30-positive T-cell lymphoma Adults, usually older; solitary or localized rapidly growing ulcerated skin tumor, usually without systemic disease. Primary skin-limited CD30+ large-cell lymphoma; exclude systemic ALCL and LyP by clinical staging and course. Dermal/subcutaneous cohesive sheets or nodules of large anaplastic cells with hallmark horseshoe/kidney-shaped nuclei; epidermal ulceration common. Strong diffuse CD30 in >75% tumor cells; ALK−; T-cell markers variable; EMA usually negative; cytotoxic markers variable. LyP: recurrent self-regressing lesions. Systemic ALK− ALCL: nodal/extranodal systemic disease. MF with large-cell transformation: known MF and residual MF phenotype. DUSP22 rearrangement occurs in a subset; no rearrangement is required for diagnosis. Subcutaneous Panniculitis-Like T-Cell Lymphoma Primary cutaneous cytotoxic T-cell lymphoma Adults, often young-to-middle-aged; subcutaneous nodules/plaques on extremities/trunk, fever and hemophagocytic syndrome may occur. Lobular panniculitis-like infiltrate of atypical cytotoxic αβ T cells rimming adipocytes; exclude γδ phenotype. Atypical lymphocytes rim adipocytes with lace-like growth; karyorrhexis, fat necrosis and histiocytes; epidermis/dermis often spared. CD3+, CD8+, βF1+, TIA1+, granzyme B+, perforin+; CD4−, CD56−, usually CD30−; EBER−. Cutaneous γδ T-cell lymphoma: γδ TCR, often CD4−/CD8−, epidermal/dermal involvement and worse course. Lupus panniculitis: reactive lymphoid follicles, plasma cells, interface change. Clonal TCR; HAVCR2 mutations in a subset, particularly with hemophagocytic syndrome. Primary Cutaneous Gamma-Delta T-Cell Lymphoma Primary cutaneous cytotoxic γδ T-cell lymphoma Adults; plaques, nodules, ulcerated tumors; may involve epidermis, dermis, and subcutis; systemic symptoms/HLH possible. Clonal mature γδ T-cell lymphoma with cytotoxic phenotype and primary skin presentation. Epidermotropic, dermal, and/or panniculitic infiltrates; angioinvasion, necrosis and adipocyte rimming may occur. CD3+, γδ TCR+, TIA1+, granzyme B/perforin+; βF1−; CD4−, CD8 variable, CD56 variable; often CD5−. S panniculitis-like αβ lymphoma: βF1+, CD8+, CD56− and restricted to subcutis. Primary cutaneous CD8+ aggressive epidermotropic lymphoma: αβ phenotype and marked epidermotropism. SETD2 mutations recurrent; clonal TCRγ/δ rearrangement. Primary Cutaneous CD8-Positive Aggressive Epidermotropic Cytotoxic T-Cell Lymphoma Aggressive primary cutaneous cytotoxic T-cell lymphoma Adults; rapidly progressive multifocal plaques, tumors and ulcers; skin, mucosa, and sometimes lung/CNS involvement. Aggressive epidermotropic CD8+ cytotoxic T-cell neoplasm with destructive epidermal/adnexal involvement. Marked pagetoid epidermotropism by atypical cells, often with keratinocyte necrosis, ulceration, adnexal involvement and angiocentricity. CD3+, CD8+, βF1+, TIA1+, granzyme B+, perforin+; CD4−, CD56 variable; high Ki-67. Mycosis fungoides: less cytotoxic, slower course. γδ T-cell lymphoma: βF1−/γδ TCR+. S panniculitis-like lymphoma: predominantly subcutaneous adipocyte rimming. Clonal TCR; no single defining molecular alteration. Primary Cutaneous Peripheral T-Cell Lymphoma, NOS Primary cutaneous mature T-cell lymphoma, NOS Adults; skin-limited or multifocal plaques/tumors, often rapidly progressive; diagnosis of exclusion. Malignant cutaneous T-cell lymphoma that does not meet criteria for a defined cutaneous T-cell entity. Diffuse destructive dermal/subcutaneous infiltrate of atypical pleomorphic T cells; epidermotropism variable; exclude specific entities. Mature T-cell phenotype with variable CD4/CD8 and frequent antigen loss; CD30 variable; exclude ALK+ disease and EBV-associated NK/T lymphoma. MF, primary cutaneous ALCL, γδ T-cell lymphoma, CD8+ aggressive epidermotropic lymphoma, and systemic PTCL involving skin. Clonal TCR supports neoplasia; no defining genetic signature. Indolent T-Cell Lymphoma of the Gastrointestinal Tract Indolent intestinal T-cell lymphoma Adults; chronic diarrhea, abdominal pain, malabsorption; small bowel/colon; often long-standing. Clonal mature T-cell infiltrate confined predominantly to GI mucosa, without destructive mass-forming growth or systemic aggressive disease. Monomorphic small/medium lymphocytes infiltrate lamina propria, often with preserved architecture and minimal epitheliotropism. CD3+, CD4+ or CD8+ (subset CD4−/CD8−), CD5 variable; CD56 usually negative; low Ki-67. MEITL: monomorphic epitheliotropism and aggressive course. EATL: pleomorphic cells, inflammation, celiac association. Reactive inflammation: polytypic/non-clonal. Clonal TCR; recurrent STAT3-JAK1 pathway alterations in a subset. Indolent NK-Cell Lymphoproliferative Disorder of the Gastrointestinal Tract Indolent intestinal NK-cell proliferation Adults; incidental or mild chronic GI symptoms; stomach, small bowel or colon. Persistent NK-cell proliferation in GI mucosa with indolent course; exclude EBV-associated aggressive NK/T-cell neoplasms. Mucosal expansion by relatively bland medium-sized lymphocytes, usually without destructive mass or angioinvasion. Surface CD3−, cytoplasmic CD3ε+, CD56+, CD2+, cytotoxic markers+; EBER negative. Extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma: EBER+, angioinvasion/necrosis and destructive growth. Aggressive NK-cell leukemia: systemic leukemic disease. No TCR rearrangement; KIR restriction may support clonality. Enteropathy-Associated T-Cell Lymphoma Intestinal T-cell lymphoma associated with celiac disease Adults, often older; small intestine, especially jejunum/ileum; abdominal pain, obstruction, perforation, malabsorption. Intestinal lymphoma in the setting of celiac disease/refractory celiac disease; integrate clinical enteropathy and morphology. Pleomorphic medium/large cells with abundant pale cytoplasm, prominent inflammation, necrosis and destructive mucosal/submucosal growth; adjacent enteropathy may be present. Usually CD3+, CD7+, CD103+, cytotoxic markers+; CD4−, CD8 usually−, CD56−; aberrant phenotype common; EBER−. MEITL: monomorphic epitheliotropic cells, often CD8+/CD56+. Intestinal PTCL-NOS: no celiac association. Indolent T-cell lymphoma: bland mucosal infiltrate. JAK/STAT and epigenetic alterations; associated celiac disease HLA-DQ2/DQ8 background. Monomorphic Epitheliotropic Intestinal T-Cell Lymphoma Aggressive intestinal cytotoxic T-cell lymphoma Adults; often Asian; small intestine, multifocal ulcerated lesions, obstruction/perforation. Monomorphic epitheliotropic intestinal T-cell lymphoma, typically without celiac disease. Monomorphic medium-sized cells with striking epitheliotropism, often forming nests within epithelium; mucosal ulceration and transmural invasion. CD3+, CD8+, CD56+, CD7+, CD5−; cytotoxic proteins+; CD4−; EBER−. EATL: pleomorphic inflammatory background and celiac association. Indolent T-cell lymphoma: bland cells, low proliferation and no destructive epitheliotropism. NK-cell intestinal LPD: surface CD3−. SETD2, STAT5B, JAK3 and GNAI2 alterations reported; clonal TCR rearrangement. Intestinal T-Cell Lymphoma, NOS Intestinal mature T-cell lymphoma, NOS Adults; intestinal mass, ulceration, pain, obstruction or perforation. Intestinal T-cell lymphoma that does not meet criteria for EATL, MEITL, or indolent T-cell lymphoma. Variable pleomorphic or monomorphic infiltrate with destructive growth; morphology and phenotype lack defining pattern of another entity. Mature T-cell markers with variable CD4/CD8; cytotoxic markers variable; assess CD56, CD103, and EBER to exclude defined entities. EATL, MEITL, indolent T-cell lymphoma, extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma, and systemic PTCL involving bowel. Clonal TCR supports T-cell lineage; no defining molecular alteration. Hepatosplenic T-Cell Lymphoma Systemic cytotoxic T-cell lymphoma Young adults, male predominance; hepatosplenomegaly, cytopenias, no or minimal lymphadenopathy; liver, spleen, marrow. Sinusoidal infiltrate in liver/spleen/marrow by clonal γδ or less often αβ T cells, typically with isochromosome 7q and/or trisomy 8. Sinusoidal infiltration of red pulp, hepatic sinusoids and marrow; medium-sized cells with scant cytoplasm and inconspicuous nucleoli. CD2+, surface CD3+, CD7+, CD56 often+, TIA1+; usually CD4−/CD8−, CD5−, CD57−; βF1− in γδ cases. T-LGLL: mature granular cells and indolent course. γδ T-cell lymphoma of skin: primary cutaneous disease. T-PLL: marked blood lymphocytosis and TCL1. i(7q), trisomy 8; SETD2 mutations common; clonal TCRγδ. ALK-Positive Anaplastic Large Cell Lymphoma Systemic CD30-positive T-cell lymphoma Children and young adults, male predominance; lymph nodes, soft tissue, bone, skin, lung; systemic symptoms. Large-cell lymphoma with hallmark cells, strong uniform CD30 and ALK expression; demonstrate ALK rearrangement. Sinusoidal, cohesive or diffuse sheets of large pleomorphic cells; hallmark cells with horseshoe/kidney-shaped nuclei and perinuclear eosinophilic Golgi region. Strong membranous/Golgi CD30; ALK+ (pattern reflects fusion partner); EMA often+; T-cell markers frequently lost; cytotoxic markers variable. ALK-negative ALCL: ALK− but same CD30 pattern. DLBCL/CHL: B-cell markers or weak PAX5/CD15 pattern. ALK+ large B-cell lymphoma: plasma-cell phenotype and ALK expression with B lineage. ALK rearrangement, most commonly NPM1::ALK; other ALK fusion partners occur. ALK-Negative Anaplastic Large Cell Lymphoma Adults, median ~54 years; slight male predominance; nodes and extranodal sites; often advanced-stage disease and B symptoms. Large pleomorphic hallmark-cell lymphoma with uniform strong CD30; ALK protein and rearrangement absent; EBV negative. Diffuse cohesive infiltrate of large pleomorphic cells, hallmark and wreath-like cells; DUSP22-rearranged cases may show doughnut cells and sheet-like growth. Strong uniform membranous/Golgi CD30; ALK−; T-cell antigens often lost; clusterin and MUM1 commonly+; cytotoxic markers variable; EBV−. ALK+ ALCL: ALK expression/rearrangement. Primary cutaneous ALCL: skin-limited. CHL: CD15+, weak PAX5+, CD45−. PTCL-NOS: CD30 less uniformly strong. DUSP22 rearrangement (20–30%), TP63 rearrangement (~5%), JAK1/STAT3 alterations. Nodal T Follicular Helper Cell Lymphoma, Angioimmunoblastic Type Nodal TFH-cell lymphoma Middle-aged/older adults; slight male predominance; generalized lymphadenopathy, B symptoms, hepatosplenomegaly, rash and immune dysregulation. Nodal lymphoma with TFH phenotype, polymorphous infiltrate, arborizing high endothelial venules and expanded FDC meshworks. Polymorphous background with atypical clear-cell T cells, prominent arborizing HEVs and expanded CD21/CD23+ FDC networks; residual follicles often regressed. CD4+, at least 2 (preferably 3) TFH markers among PD1, ICOS, CXCL13, CD10, BCL6; often strong PD1/ICOS; CD7 loss common; EBV+ B immunoblasts may be numerous. nTFHL follicular type: follicular growth pattern. nTFHL-NOS: lacks classic vascular/FDC pattern. PTCL-NOS: insufficient TFH phenotype. Reactive hyperplasia: no clonal atypical TFH population. RHOA G17V, TET2, DNMT3A, IDH2 R172; TET2/DNMT3A may be shared with clonal hematopoiesis. Nodal T Follicular Helper Cell Lymphoma, Follicular Type Adults; nodal disease, sometimes localized; less well characterized than angioimmunoblastic type. Nodal mature CD4+ T-cell lymphoma with TFH phenotype and follicular/nodular growth pattern. Neoplastic TFH cells expand or colonize follicles; follicular dendritic cell meshworks are expanded; classic AITL-type arborizing vessels may be less conspicuous. CD4+, at least 2 TFH markers (PD1, ICOS, CXCL13, CD10, BCL6); CD10/BCL6 often highlight follicular localization; CD21/CD23 outline FDC networks. nTFHL angioimmunoblastic type: polymorphous background, HEVs and extrafollicular FDC expansion. nTFHL-NOS: no follicular architecture. Follicular lymphoma: clonal B cells. RHOA, TET2, DNMT3A and other epigenetic alterations overlap with other nTFHLs. Nodal T Follicular Helper Cell Lymphoma, NOS Nodal TFH-cell lymphoma, NOS Adults; nodal presentation, variable systemic symptoms; diagnosis after excluding AI and follicular types. Nodal CD4+ mature T-cell lymphoma expressing at least 2 TFH markers, without defining AI or follicular architecture. Variable nodal effacement by atypical small/medium clear T cells; lacks the characteristic prominent HEVs/FDC expansion of AI type and follicular pattern of follicular type. CD4+, at least 2 TFH markers; PD1 and ICOS are common but less specific; assess broader panel and distribution. nTFHL-AI and follicular type: defining architecture. PTCL-NOS: lacks convincing TFH phenotype. Reactive TFH expansion: preserved architecture and no convincing atypical clone. TET2/DNMT3A/RHOA alterations may support classification in context but are not individually diagnostic. Peripheral T-Cell Lymphoma, NOS Mature T-cell lymphoma, diagnosis of exclusion Adults, usually older; generalized lymphadenopathy, extranodal disease and B symptoms. Mature clonal T-cell lymphoma that does not meet criteria for a defined T/NK entity; exclude TFH lymphoma, ALCL, EBV-associated and site-specific types. Architectural effacement by polymorphous infiltrate of atypical small-to-large T cells; clear-cell, epithelioid, or inflammatory patterns may occur. Mature T-cell phenotype; CD4 more common than CD8; loss of CD5/CD7 frequent; CD30 variable; exclude ALK, TFH markers and EBER-defined entities. nTFHL: TFH phenotype. ALCL: uniform strong CD30 and hallmark cells. ATLL: HTLV-1. EBV-positive nodal T/NK lymphoma: EBER+ tumor cells. Clonal TCR rearrangement; recurrent epigenetic and TCR/JAK-STAT pathway mutations, but no defining alteration. EBV-Positive Nodal T- and NK-Cell Lymphoma EBV-associated nodal T/NK-cell lymphoma Adults, often older; generalized lymphadenopathy, systemic symptoms; usually no nasal primary. Nodal lymphoma with EBV-positive neoplastic T or NK cells; identify lineage and exclude extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma and EBV-positive B-cell lymphoma. Nodal effacement by polymorphous or diffuse infiltrate with atypical lymphoid cells; angiocentricity/necrosis may be variable; EBER labels tumor cells. EBER strongly positive in neoplastic cells; CD3 and TCR for T lineage; surface CD3−/cytoplasmic CD3ε+ and CD56 often+ for NK lineage; cytotoxic markers+. Extranodal NK/T lymphoma: extranodal destructive nasal/other site and angioinvasion. EBV+ B-cell lymphoma: PAX5/CD20 lineage. PTCL-NOS: tumor cells EBER− or only background B cells positive. Clonal EBV; TCR rearrangement in T-cell cases; no single universal genetic lesion. Extranodal NK/T-Cell Lymphoma EBV-associated cytotoxic NK/T-cell lymphoma Adults, more common in East Asia and Latin America; nasal cavity/upper aerodigestive tract, skin, GI tract and other extranodal sites; destructive mass. EBV-associated extranodal cytotoxic lymphoma with angiocentric/angiodestructive growth and tissue necrosis; demonstrate EBER in tumor cells. Angiocentric and angiodestructive infiltrate with coagulative necrosis; atypical cells variable in size and may be obscured by inflammation. CD2+, cytoplasmic CD3ε+, surface CD3− in NK cases, CD56+, cytotoxic markers+; EBER+; T-cell cases may show surface CD3/TCR. Aggressive NK-cell leukemia: systemic leukemic presentation. EBV+ nodal T/NK lymphoma: primarily nodal. EBV-positive B-cell lymphoma: B-cell markers. Infection: no clonal EBER+ tumor population. Clonal EBV; JAK/STAT, DDX3X, TP53 and epigenetic pathway alterations. Severe Mosquito Bite Allergy EBV-associated NK-cell lymphoproliferative disorder Children/adolescents, particularly in East Asia; exaggerated local reactions to mosquito bites with fever, ulceration, systemic symptoms. Recurrent severe mosquito-bite reactions with EBV-infected NK-cell proliferation; evaluate for systemic CAEBV and lymphoma. Dense infiltrate of atypical lymphocytes at bite sites, often with necrosis and angiocentricity; systemic organs may be involved. EBER+ NK cells; CD56+, cytoplasmic CD3ε+, surface CD3−; cytotoxic markers+. Hydroa vacciniforme LPD: photosensitive vesiculopapules on sun-exposed skin. Extranodal NK/T lymphoma: destructive mass and persistent aggressive tumor. Reactive bite: no EBV+ clonal NK population. Clonal/oligoclonal EBV; germline susceptibility may contribute. Hydroa Vacciniforme Lymphoproliferative Disorder EBV-associated cutaneous T/NK-cell lymphoproliferative disorder Children, often in Latin America/Asia; recurrent vesicles and crusted scars on sun-exposed skin, sometimes systemic disease. Photosensitivity-associated recurrent cutaneous lesions with EBV-positive cytotoxic T/NK-cell infiltrate; distinguish classic skin-limited from systemic disease. Vesiculonecrotic epidermal lesions with atypical lymphocytes, interface change, angiocentricity and dermal infiltrates; scarring may occur. EBER+ atypical lymphocytes; CD8+ cytotoxic T cells common, or NK phenotype; CD56 variable; cytotoxic markers+. Severe mosquito bite allergy: lesions at bite sites, not UV-exposed distribution. Extranodal NK/T lymphoma: destructive mass. Polymorphic reactive hydroa vacciniforme: lacks substantial EBV+ atypical clonal population. Clonal EBV; TCR rearrangement in T-cell cases; assess blood EBV DNA and systemic involvement. Systemic Chronic Active EBV Disease Systemic EBV-positive T/NK-cell lymphoproliferative disease Children/adolescents or adults; persistent/recurrent mononucleosis-like illness, fever, hepatosplenomegaly, hepatitis, cytopenias, vasculitis and organ dysfunction. Persistent systemic symptoms with elevated EBV DNA and EBV-infected T or NK cells; establish infected lineage and exclude overt lymphoma. Variable polymorphic infiltrates in liver, spleen, nodes, marrow and other organs; may progress to destructive lymphoma. EBER+ T or NK cells; lineage defined by surface CD3/TCR versus CD56/cytoplasmic CD3ε; cytotoxic markers often positive. Systemic EBV+ T-cell lymphoma of childhood: overt destructive malignant disease. EBV+ nodal T/NK lymphoma: nodal tumor. Aggressive NK leukemia: acute leukemic presentation. High EBV DNA burden; clonal/oligoclonal EBV-infected T/NK populations; somatic mutations variable. Systemic EBV-Positive T-Cell Lymphoma of Childhood Aggressive EBV-associated systemic T-cell lymphoma Children/adolescents, often after primary EBV infection; fulminant fever, hepatosplenomegaly, cytopenias, liver failure and HLH. Systemic clonal EBV-positive T-cell proliferation with destructive organ involvement and aggressive clinical course. Diffuse infiltrates of atypical small-to-medium T cells in liver, spleen, marrow and nodes; hemophagocytosis and necrosis may be prominent. EBER+ neoplastic T cells; usually CD3+, often CD8+, cytotoxic markers+; CD56 variable; NK lineage must be excluded. Systemic CAEBV: persistent inflammatory disease without overt destructive lymphoma. Aggressive NK-cell leukemia: NK phenotype. EBV+ nodal T/NK lymphoma: nodal-predominant adult disease. Clonal EBV; TCR rearrangement supports T-cell lineage; genomic abnormalities variable. B-cell Small mature lymphocytes, centrocytes/centroblasts, immunoblasts, plasmablasts or plasma cells depending on entity; assess architecture, cytologic spectrum and plasmacytic differentiation. CD20, PAX5, CD79a, CD19; OCT2/BOB1; surface/cytoplasmic immunoglobulin with light-chain restriction. Plasma cell differentiation: CD38, CD138, MUM1. Some aggressive B-cell neoplasms lose CD20/PAX5; plasmablastic neoplasms may be CD20− and require plasma-cell markers and EBER/HHV8 context. T-cell Variable small-to-large atypical lymphocytes; assess architectural pattern, epidermotropism, angioinvasion, cytotoxicity, TFH-like clear cells and background inflammatory cells. Surface/cytoplasmic CD3, CD2, CD5, CD7; CD4/CD8; TCRβF1 or TCRγδ; TIA1, granzyme B, perforin; subset markers such as PD1, ICOS, CXCL13, BCL6. Loss of one or more pan-T antigens is common. CD3ε alone may be cytoplasmic in NK neoplasms; establish surface CD3/TCR and TCR gene rearrangement when needed. NK-cell Often cytotoxic medium-sized cells; assess sinusoidal, angiocentric/angiodestructive or mucosal infiltrates, necrosis and EBV association. Surface CD3−, cytoplasmic CD3ε+, CD2+, CD56 often+, CD16 variable, cytotoxic proteins+; EBER in EBV-associated entities; KIR restriction may support clonality. NK cells lack rearranged TCR genes. CD56 is not lineage-specific; integrate CD3 localization, TCR phenotype, EBER and clinical distribution. 1. Recognize the morphology Large pleomorphic cells, hallmark cells with horseshoe/kidney-shaped nuclei, cohesive sheets or sinusoidal growth. A compatible large-cell anaplastic pattern raises ALCL; morphology alone is insufficient. 2. Confirm CD30 pattern Strong, uniform membranous and Golgi staining in essentially all tumor cells. Uniform strong CD30 is central; patchy CD30 favors other PTCLs or reactive activation. 3. Determine ALK status ALK IHC positive versus negative; confirm rearrangement if equivocal. ALK-positive ALCL is a distinct entity; ALK-negative ALCL requires exclusion of systemic mimics. 4. Establish lineage and exclude mimics T-cell markers may be lost; assess EMA, clusterin, MUM1, cytotoxic markers, PAX5, CD15, EBER and myeloid/germ-cell markers as indicated. Null phenotype does not exclude ALCL, but B-cell, Hodgkin, myeloid or germ-cell differentiation must be excluded. 5. Integrate clinical distribution Systemic nodal/extranodal disease versus skin-limited disease or breast implant-associated effusion/capsule. Clinical staging separates systemic ALCL from primary cutaneous ALCL and breast implant-associated ALCL. Angioimmunoblastic type Polymorphous infiltrate; arborizing HEVs; expanded extrafollicular FDC meshworks; regressed follicles. CD4+ atypical TFH cells; strong PD1/ICOS; ≥2 TFH markers, ideally ≥3; CD21/CD23 highlight FDC expansion. Systemic immune dysregulation, EBV+ B immunoblasts, hypergammaglobulinemia, rash and generalized nodes. Follicular type Neoplastic TFH cells expand/colonize follicles; follicular or nodular architecture with FDC meshworks. CD4+ and ≥2 TFH markers; CD10/BCL6 often highlight follicular localization; assess PD1/ICOS/CXCL13. Follicular growth pattern without the characteristic diffuse polymorphous/HEV-rich pattern of angioimmunoblastic type. NOS Variable nodal effacement; neither diagnostic angioimmunoblastic architecture nor follicular pattern. CD4+ with ≥2 TFH markers; PD1 and ICOS alone are less specific and require careful interpretation. Diagnosis of exclusion after evaluating architecture, full TFH panel, clonality and molecular context. Mycosis fungoides Patch/plaque; epidermotropism disproportionate to spongiosis; basal alignment/Pautrier microabscesses. Usually CD3+ CD4+; loss of CD7/CD5; CD8 variant possible. Chronic patch/plaque course; assess blood involvement before classifying Sézary syndrome. Sézary syndrome Erythroderma with cerebriform circulating cells; skin epidermotropism may resemble MF. CD4+ with loss of CD7 and/or CD26; aberrant blood T-cell population and matching TCR clone. Blood tumor burden and clonality are essential; not simply erythrodermic MF. CD30-positive LPD: LyP Recurrent self-healing papules; variable type A–E histology with atypical CD30+ cells. Large atypical cells strongly CD30+; T-cell markers variable; ALK usually negative. Spontaneous regression and recurrent crops distinguish from persistent primary cutaneous ALCL. Primary cutaneous ALCL Persistent solitary/localized ulcerated tumor; cohesive dermal sheets of large hallmark cells. Strong CD30 in >75% tumor cells; ALK−; T-cell markers often reduced. Skin-limited after staging; exclude systemic ALCL and LyP clinically. CD4+ small/medium T-cell LPD Solitary dermal nodule; dense nodular infiltrate, epidermis usually spared. CD3+ CD4+; PD1/ICOS and other TFH markers variable; low proliferation. Localized indolent behavior; exclude nodal TFH lymphoma and systemic disease. Acral CD8+ T-cell LPD Solitary acral papule/nodule; monomorphic dermal infiltrate, epidermis spared. CD3+ CD8+ TIA1+; low Ki-67; CD30−. Indolent localized lesion versus epidermotropic, highly proliferative aggressive CD8+ lymphoma. Subcutaneous panniculitis-like T-cell lymphoma Lobular panniculitis with atypical lymphocytes rimming adipocytes. CD3+ CD8+ βF1+ cytotoxic; CD56−; EBER−. αβ phenotype and subcutaneous restriction distinguish from γδ lymphoma and lupus panniculitis. Primary cutaneous γδ T-cell lymphoma Epidermal, dermal and/or panniculitic infiltrates; angioinvasion/necrosis may occur. γδ TCR+, βF1−, cytotoxic; CD4− and CD8 variable. Often broader skin compartment involvement and more aggressive behavior than αβ panniculitis-like lymphoma. CD8+ aggressive epidermotropic cytotoxic lymphoma Marked pagetoid epidermotropism, keratinocyte necrosis, ulceration and adnexal involvement. CD3+ CD8+ βF1+ cytotoxic; high Ki-67. Rapid destructive course distinguishes from MF and indolent acral CD8+ LPD. Primary cutaneous PTCL, NOS Destructive pleomorphic dermal/subcutaneous infiltrate not classifiable as a defined entity. Mature T-cell phenotype, variable CD4/CD8, antigen loss and variable CD30. Use only after excluding MF, CD30+ LPD, γδ, aggressive CD8+ and systemic lymphomas. All PathologyGPS · Hematopathology Mature T-Cell and NK-Cell Lymphomas Integrated diagnostic reference for mature T-cell and NK-cell lymphoid proliferations. Diagnosis requires correlation of clinical distribution, tissue architecture, cytology, lineage, viral studies and molecular findings. Lineage Assignment: B Cells vs T Cells vs NK Cells Use a panel and the location of CD3 staining; no single antigen should be interpreted in isolation. title: Precursor B And T Neoplasms
content: use client B-Lymphoblastic Leukemia/Lymphoma (B-ALL/LBL) B-Cell Precursor Neoplasms A monotonous immature B-lineage population with marrow/blood disease or a dominant tissue mass; confirm lineage and immaturity, then classify genetically. A precursor B-cell neoplasm involving bone marrow and usually blood (B-ALL), or presenting primarily in nodal/extranodal tissue (B-LBL). Predominantly children; peak before age 6, with a smaller adult peak. Marrow failure, cytopenias, leukocytosis or leukopenia, bone pain, lymphadenopathy, and hepatosplenomegaly. CNS, testes, skin, soft tissue, liver, spleen, and lymph nodes may be involved; mediastinal masses are uncommon. Abnormal lymphoblasts in blood/marrow or an architecture-effacing tissue infiltrate. B-lineage supported by CD19, CD22, cytoplasmic CD79a, and/or PAX5; interpret markers as a panel. Immaturity supported by TdT and/or CD34, bright CD10, low CD45, low/absent CD20, and absent surface light chains; rare cases lack TdT or CD34. Establish the genetic subtype with appropriate karyotype, FISH, DNA/RNA sequencing, copy-number, and/or expression studies; use NOS only after comprehensive exclusion of defined types. Blasts range from small cells with scant cytoplasm and condensed chromatin to larger cells with dispersed chromatin and visible nucleoli. Nuclei are round, oval, indented, or convoluted; mitoses are variable and macrophages may produce a starry-sky pattern. Marrow shows diffuse sheets or loose collections that replace or intermingle with hematopoiesis; tissue lesions often efface architecture. PAX5 is the most sensitive tissue B-lineage marker; CD79a and CD19 support lineage but are not individually specific. TdT is present in most cases; CD34 is variable. CD10 is often positive, CD20 is usually dim/negative, and CD45 is dim. Compare with hematogones: leukemia shows aberrant antigen intensity/coexpression, including increased CD58/CD10/CD19 or decreased CD38/CD81; use flow cytometry for MRD. CD13/CD33 may be aberrantly expressed, especially in selected genetic subtypes, and do not establish myeloid lineage. T-Lymphoblastic Leukemia/Lymphoma T-lineage requires cytoplasmic or surface CD3; CD7/CD2/CD5 support T differentiation. B-lineage markers in combination favor B-ALL/LBL. Hematogone-rich marrow Normal B-cell precursors show orderly maturation with a spectrum of phenotypes; leukemia forms an aberrant, relatively uniform population. AML with t(8;21) May express CD19, PAX5, or cytoplasmic CD79a; establish myeloid differentiation with MPO and the full phenotype/genetic context. B/myeloid mixed-phenotype acute leukemia Requires convincing lineage-defining myeloid differentiation, particularly moderate/strong MPO or monocytic differentiation; isolated CD13/CD33 is insufficient. Mature B-cell neoplasms (including Burkitt lymphoma) Mature B-cell markers and surface immunoglobulin/light-chain restriction, absent precursor phenotype, and entity-specific morphology/genetics favor a mature neoplasm. Genetic classification is essential: evaluate aneuploidy and recurrent fusions/rearrangements, including BCR::ABL1, KMT2A, ETV6::RUNX1, TCF3::PBX1, and TCF3::HLF. RNA sequencing or expression profiling may be required for cryptic fusions and BCR::ABL1-like or ETV6::RUNX1-like disease. Consider germline predisposition testing (e.g., PAX5, ETV6, TP53) when family history or phenotype raises concern. Risk-adapted therapy has produced long-term remission in more than 90% of children in contemporary settings; outcomes in adults are less favorable. Adverse factors include age under 1 or over 10 years, WBC above 50,000/µL, hypodiploidy, CNS disease, slow early response, and measurable residual disease (MRD). Genetic subtype and MRD at defined treatment time points are central to risk assignment; CNS/testicular involvement has treatment implications. Do not use B-ALL/LBL for mature B-cell neoplasms. A blast percentage threshold is not an absolute prerequisite for diagnosis; interpret low-level disease cautiously and in context. B-ALL/LBL with High Hyperdiploidy A childhood B-ALL phenotype with 51–65 chromosomes and characteristic whole-chromosome gains. A genetically defined B-ALL/LBL with recurrent non-random gains of whole chromosomes. Most common in children; approximately 25–35% of pediatric B-ALL and 7–8% of adult cases. Often presents with a relatively low WBC count. Meets criteria for B-ALL/LBL. Demonstrate 51–65 chromosomes with characteristic non-random gains. Exclude a doubled hypodiploid clone (masked hypodiploidy) and other defining genetic lesions. No distinctive morphology; the appearance is that of conventional B-lymphoblasts. No defining immunophenotype; use the B-ALL/LBL precursor B-cell panel. Flow cytometric DNA index may show increased DNA content. Hypodiploid B-ALL/LBL with masked doubling A doubled hypodiploid clone may mimic hyperdiploidy; SNP array/copy-neutral LOH and DNA-index analysis reveal the underlying monosomies. Other genetically defined B-ALL/LBL Exclude subtype-defining fusions and rearrangements before assigning high hyperdiploidy. Karyotype demonstrates 51–65 chromosomes, often with gains of X, 4, 6, 10, 14, 17, 18, and 21. FISH, DNA index, and SNP array help when metaphases are unavailable or pseudohyperdiploidy is suspected. Very favorable in children; long-term overall survival exceeds 90% in many series, particularly with favorable clinical risk and low MRD. Specific chromosome-gain patterns, age, WBC count, and MRD modify risk. B-ALL/LBL with Hypodiploidy A B-ALL clone with 43 or fewer chromosomes; actively exclude a doubled, deceptively hyperdiploid clone. Includes near-haploid, low-hypodiploid, and high-hypodiploid subgroups. Near-haploid disease is rare and mainly pediatric; low-hypodiploidy becomes more frequent with age. Low-hypodiploid disease accounts for more than 10% of adult B-ALL in some series. Demonstrate ≤43 chromosomes. Assess for masked hypodiploidy when the karyotype appears near-triploid/pseudohyperdiploid. No distinctive morphology; conventional B-lymphoblast morphology. No defining IHC profile beyond precursor B-lineage markers. p53 staining may be aberrant in low-hypodiploid cases but does not replace genetic testing. High-hyperdiploid B-ALL/LBL A doubled hypodiploid clone can mimic high hyperdiploidy; SNP array demonstrates copy-neutral LOH across chromosomes that were originally monosomic. Near-diploid B-ALL Cases with 44–45 chromosomes are not included in the ≤43 chromosome hypodiploid category. Near-haploid: 24–31 chromosomes; low-hypodiploid: 32–39; high-hypodiploid: 40–43. Near-haploid cases often have RTK/RAS pathway alterations, IKZF3 deletions, and 6p22 histone-cluster deletions. Low-hypodiploid cases show TP53 alterations in more than 90%; approximately half may be germline, associated with Li-Fraumeni syndrome. IKZF2 and RB1 alterations also occur. Use karyotype, FISH, DNA index, and SNP array to detect masked doubling. Poor prognosis across hypodiploid subgroups; lower chromosome number generally correlates with worse outcome. Germline TP53 findings have major hereditary cancer implications. B-ALL/LBL with Intrachromosomal Amplification of Chromosome 21 (iAMP21) Multiple RUNX1 signals clustered on abnormal chromosome 21 in a B-ALL case, often with a relatively low blast burden. A rare B-ALL subtype defined by complex intrachromosomal amplification of chromosome 21. Usually occurs in children, often school-age; uncommon in adults. May have a relatively low WBC count. Demonstrate characteristic amplification of chromosome 21/RUNX1, typically with at least five RUNX1 signals in the abnormal clone, interpreted with the assay pattern and cytogenetics. Distinguish from simple trisomy/tetrasomy 21 in high-hyperdiploid B-ALL. No reliable morphologic distinction from other B-ALL. No defining IHC phenotype; standard precursor B-cell markers apply. Usually shows whole-chromosome gains; iAMP21 has complex intrachromosomal RUNX1 amplification. B-ALL with ETV6::RUNX1 ETV6::RUNX1 FISH shows fusion and residual ETV6/RUNX1 signals; multiple RUNX1 signals can also flag iAMP21, which requires targeted confirmation. FISH using RUNX1 probes is central; karyotype and chromosomal microarray can characterize the complex chromosome 21 structure. Historically associated with poor outcome, particularly with standard-risk treatment; risk-adapted intensification improves outcomes. B-ALL/LBL with BCR::ABL1 Fusion B-ALL with Philadelphia chromosome/BCR::ABL1; test even without a known history of CML. A genetically defined B-ALL subtype with constitutive ABL1 tyrosine kinase signaling. Occurs in children and adults; frequency increases with age. May present with high WBC count and occasionally a CML-like blood picture. Demonstrate BCR::ABL1 fusion by karyotype, FISH, or molecular testing. Distinguish de novo B-ALL from CML in lymphoid blast phase using clinical history, marrow background, and genomic context. Morphology is variable and not specific; some cases show increased myeloid-associated antigen expression. Precursor B-cell phenotype; CD13, CD33, and CD66c may be expressed. CRLF2 or other aberrancies may be present but are not defining. BCR::ABL1-positive CML in lymphoid blast phase Prior CML, basophilia, splenomegaly, granulocytic hyperplasia, and BCR::ABL1 in non-blast hematopoietic cells support CML blast phase. BCR::ABL1-like B-ALL Similar expression profile but lacks BCR::ABL1 fusion; has alternative kinase-activating lesions. Detect BCR::ABL1 by karyotype, FISH, RT-PCR, or RNA sequencing; characterize transcript type when clinically relevant. Historically adverse, but outcomes have improved substantially with addition of ABL1 tyrosine kinase inhibitors to ALL therapy. MRD response and kinase-domain resistance mutations influence management. B-ALL/LBL with BCR::ABL1-Like Features A Ph-like expression profile without BCR::ABL1 fusion, often with CRLF2 overexpression or another kinase-activating lesion. A heterogeneous B-ALL group that molecularly resembles BCR::ABL1-positive disease but lacks the defining fusion. Occurs in children, adolescents, and adults; often associated with high-risk clinical features. CRLF2-rearranged cases are enriched in patients with Down syndrome and in some populations. Demonstrate a BCR::ABL1-like gene-expression profile or a defining kinase-activating genetic lesion. Exclude actual BCR::ABL1 fusion. No distinctive morphology. CRLF2 overexpression by flow cytometry or IHC can screen for a substantial subset, but a negative result does not exclude the group. Standard precursor B-cell phenotype. BCR::ABL1-positive B-ALL BCR::ABL1-like disease lacks the BCR::ABL1 fusion and instead carries alternative kinase lesions. Other B-ALL with defined genetic alterations Assign a more specific genetic entity when a defining lesion is identified. Diverse lesions activate ABL-class or JAK-STAT signaling, including ABL1, ABL2, CSF1R, PDGFRB, JAK2, EPOR, and CRLF2 rearrangements or mutations. RNA sequencing, targeted fusion panels, and gene-expression profiling are often required. Generally associated with an unfavorable outcome and increased relapse risk, particularly with persistent MRD. Potential sensitivity to kinase inhibitors depends on the specific kinase lesion; molecular definition is essential. B-ALL/LBL with KMT2A Rearrangement Infant B-ALL with very immature phenotype and KMT2A rearrangement; consider also in older patients with a compatible fusion. A genetically defined B-ALL subtype driven by KMT2A rearrangement with numerous possible fusion partners. Strongly associated with infancy; can occur at other ages. Often presents with high WBC count and aggressive disease. Demonstrate KMT2A rearrangement by break-apart FISH, karyotype, or RNA sequencing. Blasts may be larger with more abundant cytoplasm and variable monocytic-like features; morphology is not diagnostic. Often a pro-B phenotype: CD10 negative or dim, CD34 variable, and strong CD19/cytoplasmic CD79a. Aberrant myeloid/monocytic markers may occur. B-ALL with ZNF384 rearrangement Both may show lineage plasticity and myeloid/monocytic antigen expression; defining fusion testing separates them. AML with KMT2A rearrangement Establish lineage using the complete phenotype; B-lineage-defining marker combination supports B-ALL. KMT2A has more than 90 reported fusion partners; break-apart FISH detects rearrangement, while RNA sequencing identifies the partner. Generally adverse, especially in infants; age, fusion partner, treatment response, and MRD affect outcome. B-ALL/LBL with ETV6::RUNX1 Fusion Childhood B-ALL with ETV6::RUNX1 fusion, often with a favorable-risk profile. A common pediatric B-ALL subtype defined by t(12;21)(p13;q22.1). Predominantly young children; rare in infants and adults. Demonstrate ETV6::RUNX1 fusion by FISH, RT-PCR, or RNA sequencing. No specific morphology; blasts resemble conventional B-lymphoblasts. Often CD10-positive/common B phenotype; no IHC marker substitutes for fusion detection. ETV6::RUNX1-like B-ALL Similar phenotype/expression profile but lacks ETV6::RUNX1 fusion and carries alternative genetic lesions. High-hyperdiploid B-ALL Chromosome 21 gains may produce multiple FISH signals; assess the actual fusion pattern and chromosome copy number. Cryptic t(12;21) is commonly detected by ETV6/RUNX1 dual-fusion FISH or molecular assays. Favorable prognosis in children, with high cure rates; relapse can occur late and requires appropriate follow-up. B-ALL/LBL with ETV6::RUNX1-Like Features ETV6::RUNX1-like expression pattern without the fusion, often with IKZF1 or other B-cell developmental lesions. A heterogeneous group phenocopying ETV6::RUNX1-positive B-ALL at the expression level. Primarily pediatric and adolescent; clinical risk varies with the underlying lesion. Demonstrate ETV6::RUNX1-like gene-expression profile without ETV6::RUNX1 fusion. Identify the underlying genetic alteration when possible. No defining morphologic pattern. No specific IHC surrogate reliably establishes this entity; use standard B-ALL panel. ETV6::RUNX1-positive B-ALL The defining fusion is absent in the like-feature group. Both are expression-defined heterogeneous groups; use the relevant expression classifier and kinase/genetic testing. Gene-expression profiling defines the phenotype; underlying lesions may include alterations in genes involved in B-cell development and signaling. Outcome is heterogeneous; some cases have adverse features. Risk assessment requires the specific genomic lesion and MRD. B-ALL/LBL with TCF3::PBX1 Fusion B-ALL with t(1;19), often showing strong CD9 and a pre-B phenotype with cytoplasmic μ. A recurrent fusion-defined B-ALL subtype. Occurs mainly in children but also in adults. May show CNS involvement at presentation. Demonstrate TCF3::PBX1 fusion, typically t(1;19)(q23;p13.3). No specific histologic pattern; occasional convoluted nuclei or cytoplasmic vacuoles may be seen. Often CD10-positive and CD34-negative; cytoplasmic μ may be expressed. CD9 is commonly strong; interpret with the full phenotype. Other pre-B ALL Cytoplasmic μ and CD9 are supportive but not specific; demonstrate TCF3::PBX1 fusion. B-ALL with TCF3::HLF fusion Both involve TCF3 but have distinct partners and markedly different prognoses; fusion testing is decisive. Detect t(1;19)/TCF3::PBX1 by karyotype, FISH, or RNA-based testing. Historically associated with adverse outcome, particularly with CNS disease, but modern risk-adapted therapy has improved survival. B-ALL/LBL with IGH::IL3 Fusion Marked eosinophilia with a B-lymphoblastic population and an apparent myeloproliferative presentation. A rare B-ALL subtype in which IGH regulatory elements drive IL3 overexpression. Usually presents in adolescents or adults; marked peripheral blood eosinophilia is a major clue. May mimic a myeloproliferative neoplasm. Demonstrate B-lineage lymphoblasts. Confirm IGH::IL3 rearrangement. Marrow may show prominent eosinophilia and features that resemble a myeloproliferative process. Establish B-lineage with PAX5/CD19/cCD79a/CD22 and immaturity markers. Eosinophils are reactive and do not represent the neoplastic lineage. Myeloid/lymphoid neoplasm with eosinophilia and tyrosine kinase fusion These are myeloid neoplasms with characteristic kinase fusions; molecular testing and lineage assessment distinguish them. T-ALL/LBL with eosinophilia T-lineage is defined by cCD3; IGH::IL3 supports the rare B-ALL subtype. FISH or RNA sequencing identifies IGH::IL3 fusion; assess IL3 rearrangement in the appropriate eosinophilic presentation. Rare entity with limited outcome data; prognosis and treatment should be guided by specialist hematologic evaluation and response. B-ALL/LBL with TCF3::HLF Fusion Rare B-ALL with t(17;19), often with severe coagulopathy, hypercalcemia, or unusual immunophenotype. A rare, distinct TCF3-rearranged B-ALL subtype. Usually occurs in children and adolescents. May present with hypercalcemia, coagulopathy, disseminated intravascular coagulation, or thrombosis. Demonstrate TCF3::HLF fusion, typically t(17;19)(q22;p13). Morphology is variable and may show unusual blast features; no single pattern is diagnostic. Precursor B-cell markers are present, but CD10/CD34 may be absent and myeloid-associated antigens may be aberrantly expressed. B-ALL with TCF3::PBX1 Different fusion partner; TCF3::HLF has a much more adverse clinical course. AML or MPAL Aberrant myeloid markers alone do not establish myeloid lineage; evaluate MPO and monocytic differentiation. Confirm TCF3::HLF by karyotype, FISH, or RNA sequencing. Very poor-risk subtype with frequent treatment resistance and relapse; early specialist-directed risk-adapted therapy is essential. B-ALL with DUX4 Rearrangement B-ALL with Other Defined Genetic Alterations Often CD2-positive B-ALL with a characteristic DUX4 expression signature; ERG deletion is a supportive associated finding. A molecularly defined subtype within B-ALL with other genetic alterations. Usually occurs in children and adolescents; can occur in adults. Demonstrate DUX4 rearrangement or a validated DUX4-associated expression signature. No defining morphology. CD2 may be aberrantly expressed; CD371 (CLEC12A) can be a useful surrogate in some settings. ERG protein expression may be reduced or absent in association with ERG deletion. Other B-ALL with aberrant CD2 CD2 alone is not diagnostic; confirm DUX4-associated molecular findings. ZNF384-rearranged B-ALL May share lineage plasticity; defining fusion/expression profiling distinguishes the entities. DUX4 rearrangement is often cryptic and may require RNA sequencing or expression profiling; ERG deletion is frequent. Generally favorable outcome in children in contemporary series, despite some adverse presenting features; MRD remains important. B-ALL with MEF2D Rearrangement Often older children/adolescents with CD10-dim/negative phenotype and strong cytoplasmic/nuclear MEF2D expression. A recurrent fusion-defined B-ALL subtype, commonly involving MEF2D::BCL9 or other partners. Often affects older children, adolescents, and young adults. Demonstrate MEF2D rearrangement/fusion or a validated molecular signature. No specific morphology. CD10 may be dim or absent; CD38 may be bright. MEF2D immunohistochemistry can be a useful screening adjunct where validated. Both may show reduced CD10; molecular testing defines the subtype. B-ALL NOS A defined MEF2D lesion excludes NOS. Common fusions include MEF2D::BCL9 and MEF2D::HNRNPUL1; RNA sequencing is useful. Often associated with an unfavorable outcome and increased relapse risk; MRD response is important. B-ALL with ZNF384 Rearrangement CD10-negative/dim B-ALL with myeloid or monocytic antigen expression and potential lineage plasticity. A fusion-defined B-ALL subtype with a broad range of fusion partners. Occurs across pediatric and adult age groups. Demonstrate ZNF384 rearrangement by molecular testing. No specific morphology; some cases show monocytic differentiation or mixed morphologic features. CD10 is often absent or dim. CD13, CD33, CD65, or monocytic markers may be expressed; interpret in context of lineage-defining markers. KMT2A-rearranged B-ALL Both may show lineage plasticity and myeloid/monocytic antigens; fusion testing separates them. B/myeloid MPAL Aberrant myeloid markers alone do not meet MPAL criteria; establish a second lineage-defining component. Rearrangements involve multiple partners, including EP300, TAF15, and other genes; RNA sequencing is often required. Outcome is variable; some cohorts show intermediate or adverse outcomes. Lineage switch/phenotypic change may complicate MRD monitoring. B-ALL with PAX5 Alterations (PAX5alt) B-ALL with a PAX5-altered genomic profile, often with reduced expression of B-cell differentiation markers. A heterogeneous genetic subtype defined by diverse PAX5 alterations. Occurs in children, adolescents, and adults. Demonstrate a qualifying PAX5 alteration profile; do not infer the subtype from reduced PAX5 staining alone. PAX5 expression may be reduced or heterogeneous; retained PAX5 does not exclude a genomic PAX5 alteration. Use the complete precursor B-cell panel. PAX5 p.P80R B-ALL PAX5 p.P80R is a distinct subtype and should not be subsumed under PAX5alt. A qualifying PAX5 alteration excludes NOS after adequate molecular characterization. Includes diverse PAX5 rearrangements, amplifications, deletions, and other structural alterations; DNA/RNA sequencing and copy-number analysis may be required. Heterogeneous; outcome depends on the specific genomic profile, age, and MRD response. B-ALL with PAX5 p.P80R B-ALL with the recurrent PAX5 p.P80R missense mutation and characteristic altered B-cell differentiation program. A distinct PAX5-mutant B-ALL subtype. Predominantly pediatric and adolescent, but can occur in adults. Demonstrate PAX5 p.P80R mutation; distinguish from other PAX5 alterations. PAX5 staining may be retained; immunohistochemistry cannot establish the specific mutation. Interpret aberrant B-cell maturation markers as supportive only. PAX5alt B-ALL PAX5 p.P80R is a separate molecular subtype, not simply a member of the broader PAX5alt category. The defining mutation assigns the case to this subtype. PAX5 p.P80R is the defining missense alteration; targeted DNA sequencing or broader sequencing can detect it. Reported outcomes are generally intermediate to favorable in pediatric cohorts, but risk is modified by MRD and coexisting lesions. B-ALL with NUTM1 Rearrangement Infant B-ALL with NUTM1 fusion; often retains CD10 and may show a distinctive immature phenotype. A rare fusion-defined B-ALL subtype, frequently involving ZNF or other partners. Most often described in infants and young children. Demonstrate NUTM1 rearrangement/fusion. Precursor B-cell phenotype; CD10 is often expressed. NUT immunohistochemistry may support a rearrangement in selected contexts but molecular confirmation is preferred. Both occur in infants; defining rearrangement testing is required. A NUTM1 fusion establishes a defined genetic subtype. NUTM1 rearrangements have multiple partners; RNA sequencing or targeted fusion testing is useful. Reported pediatric outcomes are often favorable, but data are limited and depend on age, partner, and treatment response. B-ALL with MYC Rearrangement A precursor B-cell phenotype with MYC rearrangement; distinguish carefully from mature Burkitt lymphoma. A rare B-ALL subtype defined by MYC rearrangement in an immature B-cell neoplasm. Occurs in children and adults; adult cases have particularly poor reported outcomes. Demonstrate precursor B-cell lineage and immaturity rather than a mature B-cell phenotype. Confirm MYC rearrangement and exclude mature B-cell lymphoma. May show medium-sized blasts and a starry-sky pattern, overlapping morphologically with Burkitt lymphoma. TdT and other immaturity markers support B-ALL; CD34 may be variable. Mature surface immunoglobulin/light-chain expression and a mature phenotype favor Burkitt lymphoma. Burkitt lymphoma/leukemia Burkitt lymphoma is a mature B-cell neoplasm, typically with surface light-chain expression and no precursor phenotype; MYC rearrangement alone does not distinguish it. Other B-ALL genetic subtypes Assign MYC-rearranged subtype only when MYC rearrangement is demonstrated and precursor phenotype is secure. Confirm MYC rearrangement by karyotype, FISH, or sequencing; identify partner where possible. Adults have a very poor reported outcome, with 5-year overall survival below 20% in cited series. Children treated with Burkitt-type regimens have reported better outcomes; treatment strategy is evolving. B-ALL/LBL, Not Otherwise Specified (NOS) Use only after comprehensive testing excludes all currently defined genetic subtypes. A diagnosis of exclusion for B-ALL/LBL without an assignable defining genetic abnormality. Clinical features are heterogeneous and reflect the underlying unclassified biology. Meets general diagnostic criteria for B-ALL/LBL. Exclude all defined and provisional genetic subtypes with appropriate cytogenetic, FISH, DNA/RNA sequencing, and/or gene-expression studies. If testing is incomplete, use 'not further classified' rather than NOS. Precursor B-cell phenotype as described for B-ALL/LBL; no specific IHC profile defines NOS. All genetically defined B-ALL/LBL subtypes NOS requires comprehensive exclusion; an identified defining lesion takes precedence. B-ALL/LBL, not further classified Use when comprehensive genetic testing has not been completed or is unavailable. No defining alteration; comprehensive testing is required before assigning NOS. In children, reported outcome is intermediate, with 5-year event-free survival around 86%; the category is biologically heterogeneous. T-Lymphoblastic Leukemia/Lymphoma (T-ALL/LBL) T-Cell Precursor Neoplasms Immature T-lineage blasts with cytoplasmic CD3; commonly a mediastinal/thymic mass in an adolescent or young adult. A precursor T-cell neoplasm involving marrow/blood (T-ALL) or primarily nodal/mediastinal/extranodal sites (T-LBL). Predominantly adolescents and young adults, with male predominance. T-LBL commonly presents with an anterior mediastinal/thymic mass, often with lymphadenopathy or pleural/pericardial effusions. Marrow/blood disease may cause cytopenias, leukocytosis, and circulating blasts. Demonstrate an aberrant population of T-lineage hematopoietic precursors. Cytoplasmic or surface CD3 establishes T-lineage; the phenotype must not meet ETP-ALL criteria. A blast percentage above 20% is desirable in blood/marrow but is not an absolute prerequisite; interpret low-level involvement cautiously. Diffuse sheets of monotonous medium-sized lymphoblasts with scant cytoplasm, fine chromatin, and inconspicuous nucleoli. Frequent mitoses, apoptosis, lymphoglandular bodies, and tingible-body macrophages may be present. Thymic involvement may efface architecture; cytologic appearance overlaps with B-ALL. Cytoplasmic CD3 is the most lineage-specific marker; surface CD3 is less often expressed and may be dim. CD7 is usually bright; CD5 and CD2 are variable. TdT is present in most cases. CD1a, CD34, CD99, and KIT/CD117 are variably expressed; CD4/CD8 coexpression is common in cortical-stage cases. CD79a, CD19, CD13, or CD33 may be aberrantly expressed; none alone changes lineage assignment. ETP-ALL ETP phenotype has absent CD1a/CD8, absent or dim CD5, and stem-cell/myeloid marker expression; classify separately. T/myeloid mixed-phenotype acute leukemia Requires myeloid lineage-defining MPO or monocytic differentiation; isolated CD13/CD33 is insufficient. Mature T-cell lymphoma/leukemia Usually lacks TdT/CD34/CD1a and has a mature antigen profile; use morphology, flow, and molecular context. Indolent T-lymphoblastic proliferation Usually preserves architecture, shows normal maturation spectrum and polyclonal TR rearrangements, and lacks LMO2. NK-lineage neoplasm cCD3 (epsilon chain) can overlap; assess true lineage-specific cCD3, surface CD3, phenotype, and clonality. Common alterations include NOTCH1/FBXW7, TAL1/TAL2, TLX1, TLX3, HOXA, LMO1/LMO2, and NKX2-1 pathway lesions. Additional alterations affect JAK/STAT, PI3K/AKT, RAS/MAPK, epigenetic regulators, and cell-cycle genes including CDKN2A/B and PTEN. Long-term response rates approach 85% in children/adolescents and about 60% in adults. MRD at the end of consolidation is the strongest outcome predictor; relapse remains difficult to treat. NOTCH1/FBXW7 mutations have been associated with better outcomes, whereas PTEN alterations and some other genomic lesions may be adverse. Early T-Precursor Lymphoblastic Leukemia/Lymphoma (ETP-ALL) cCD3-positive blasts lacking CD1a/CD8, with dim/absent CD5 and stem-cell or myeloid markers. A distinct T-precursor neoplasm with an immature phenotype and multilineage/stem-cell features. Occurs in children and adults; often presents with marrow disease and may have a high-risk clinical profile. The phenotype reflects an early thymic precursor with retained stem-cell/myeloid differentiation potential. Morphology consistent with lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma. cCD3 positive. CD1a and CD8 absent in fewer than 5% positive blasts. CD5 absent or dim in fewer than 75% positive blasts. At least one myeloid marker (CD11b, CD13, CD33, CD65, KIT/CD117) and/or stem-cell marker (CD34, HLA-DR) expressed in at least 25% of blasts. MPO negative; the source-defined ETP threshold is less than 3% positive. Morphology overlaps with other T-ALL; blasts may be small to medium-sized with scant cytoplasm and fine chromatin. No unique histologic pattern; immunophenotype is essential. cCD3 is required, although expression may be heterogeneous; surface CD3 is usually absent. CD7 is consistently positive. CD1a and CD8 are absent; CD5 is absent or dim. CD34, CD117/KIT, HLA-DR, CD13, CD33, CD11b, or CD65 may be expressed. CD123 may be expressed in a subset. T-ALL, not otherwise specified ETP-ALL meets the specific primitive immunophenotypic criteria; conventional T-ALL more often expresses CD1a and/or CD8 and stronger CD5. ETP-ALL is MPO-negative by the defined threshold and lacks definitive myeloid lineage assignment; carefully apply MPAL criteria. AML with aberrant T-cell markers True cCD3 is required for T-lineage; myeloid lineage is established by MPO/monocytic differentiation. Gene-expression profile resembles early thymic progenitors and hematopoietic stem/myeloid progenitors; MEF2C is often increased and BCL11B/GATA3 decreased. Mutations commonly affect FLT3, RAS pathway, IL7R/JAK signaling, GATA3, ETV6, RUNX1, IKZF1, and chromatin modifiers (EZH2, EED, SUZ12, SETD2, EP300). NOTCH1 mutations are less common than in conventional T-ALL. Initially reported as adverse risk, but later studies show outcomes can approach those of other T-ALL with contemporary intensified therapy. MRD after induction may remain positive more often; response after consolidation and treatment strategy are important. All PathologyGPS · Hematopathology B- and T-Precursor Neoplasms Diagnostic reference focused on lineage assignment, defining genetic abnormalities, immunophenotypic mimics, differential diagnosis, and prognostic implications in precursor B- and T-cell neoplasms. Diagnostic Workflow Establish precursor morphology and determine whether disease is marrow/blood-predominant or tissue-predominant. Assign lineage with lineage-defining markers: B-lineage panel or cytoplasmic/surface CD3 for T-lineage. Confirm immaturity and compare with normal precursors (hematogones or thymocytes). Perform comprehensive genetic classification; use NOS only after exclusion of defined entities. Integrate genetic subtype with MRD, clinical risk factors, and treatment response for prognosis. High-Yield Diagnostic Distinctions B-ALL vs T-ALL: PAX5/CD19/CD22/cCD79a in combination versus cCD3. B-ALL vs hematogones: orderly maturation spectrum versus aberrant uniform phenotype; flow cytometry is essential. High hyperdiploidy vs masked hypodiploidy: use SNP array/copy-neutral LOH and DNA index. BCR::ABL1-like vs BCR::ABL1: similar biology, but only the latter carries the defining fusion. ETP-ALL vs T/myeloid MPAL: apply strict MPO and monocytic lineage criteria; myeloid-associated antigens alone are insufficient. MYC-rearranged B-ALL vs Burkitt lymphoma: precursor phenotype, not MYC status alone, establishes the distinction. B-ALL Genetic Subtypes: Defining Features and Prognosis Prognostic labels are broad group-level summaries. Age, presenting WBC count, CNS status, treatment response, and MRD remain essential for individual risk assignment. Subtype Defining feature Prognosis High hyperdiploidy 51–65 chromosomes; non-random whole-chromosome gains, commonly X, 4, 6, 10, 14, 17, 18, and 21. Exclude doubled hypodiploidy. Favorable in children; long-term survival often exceeds 90%, especially with favorable clinical factors and low MRD. Hypodiploidy ≤43 chromosomes: near-haploid 24–31; low-hypodiploid 32–39; high-hypodiploid 40–43. Adverse; lower chromosome number generally correlates with worse outcome. Low-hypodiploid disease often has TP53 alterations; consider germline predisposition. iAMP21 Intrachromosomal amplification of chromosome 21; typically ≥5 RUNX1 signals with characteristic clustering/pattern on abnormal chromosome 21. Higher relapse risk with standard-risk therapy; treatment intensification improves outcome. BCR::ABL1 Philadelphia chromosome, t(9;22), producing BCR::ABL1 fusion. Historically adverse; outcomes substantially improved with addition of ABL tyrosine kinase inhibitors, but MRD remains important. BCR::ABL1-like Ph-like gene-expression profile without BCR::ABL1; kinase-activating lesions include ABL-class and JAK-STAT pathway alterations, often CRLF2-associated. Generally higher risk and heterogeneous; depends on the kinase lesion, targeted treatment availability, and MRD. ETV6::RUNX1 t(12;21) with ETV6::RUNX1 fusion, often cryptic by conventional karyotype. Very favorable in children; chemosensitive, although late relapse can occur. MRD and clinical factors still matter. ETV6::RUNX1-like Expression profile resembles ETV6::RUNX1-positive disease but the defining fusion is absent. Do not assume the favorable prognosis of ETV6::RUNX1; risk varies with underlying lesions and MRD. KMT2A-rearranged KMT2A rearrangement with variable fusion partners; particularly associated with infant B-ALL. Usually adverse, especially in infants; age, partner, WBC count, and treatment response modify risk. TCF3::PBX1 t(1;19), producing TCF3::PBX1 fusion; often pre-B phenotype with cytoplasmic μ. Modern treatment has improved outcome; assess CNS status and MRD rather than automatically assigning very-high risk. TCF3::HLF t(17;19), producing TCF3::HLF fusion. Very poor prognosis; early relapse and resistance to conventional therapy are concerns. IGH::IL3 IGH::IL3 fusion; may cause marked eosinophilia and mimic a myeloproliferative neoplasm. Very rare; outcome data are limited. DUX4-rearranged DUX4 rearrangement/signature, often with ERG deletion; CD371 may be expressed. Generally favorable relative to many other subtypes; TP53 mutation is an adverse feature. MEF2D-rearranged MEF2D fusion, commonly MEF2D::BCL9 or other partners. Often unfavorable/intermediate-to-poor; outcome varies by age and treatment context. ZNF384-rearranged ZNF384 fusion; often CD10-dim/negative with myeloid/monocytic antigen expression. Heterogeneous; lineage plasticity and lineage switch are clinically important concerns. PAX5alt Diverse PAX5 alterations, including rearrangements and intragenic amplification; excludes PAX5 p.P80R category. Heterogeneous; depends on specific alteration, co-lesions, and MRD. PAX5 p.P80R Recurrent PAX5 p.P80R missense mutation affecting the DNA-binding domain. Outcome data continue to evolve; avoid assigning risk from this mutation alone. NUTM1-rearranged NUTM1 fusion, often in infant/young-child B-ALL; identify by RNA-based testing/FISH as appropriate. Rare with limited outcome data; age, fusion partner, and treatment response matter. MYC-rearranged MYC rearrangement in a demonstrably immature B-cell neoplasm; distinguish from mature Burkitt lymphoma. Poor in adults in reported series; pediatric outcomes may be better with Burkitt-type treatment approaches. B-ALL/LBL, NOS Meets B-ALL/LBL criteria but lacks a defined genetic subtype after comprehensive testing. Heterogeneous/intermediate-risk group; pediatric 5-year EFS reported around 86% in the cited classification data. Precursor vs. Mature Lymphoid Neoplasms: Histology and Immunophenotype No single marker is sufficient. Interpret immaturity, lineage, maturation-associated antigens, surface immunoglobulin/TCR, morphology, and molecular findings together. B-cell lineage Feature Precursor B-cell neoplasm (B-ALL/LBL) Mature B-cell neoplasm Cells / nuclei Lymphoblasts; usually monotonous, high N:C ratio, fine chromatin, inconspicuous nucleoli. Variable: small mature lymphocytes, centrocyte-like cells, immunoblasts, plasmacytoid or plasmablastic cells; chromatin and nucleoli depend on entity. Cytoplasm / architecture Scant cytoplasm; marrow often shows diffuse sheets or interstitial collections; tissue lesions may efface architecture. Variable cytoplasm; may show follicular, marginal-zone, mantle-zone, diffuse, sinusoidal, or other entity-specific patterns. TdT / CD34 TdT usually positive; CD34 variable; both may be absent in a minority. Usually negative; aberrant expression can occur in selected mature neoplasms. CD10 Often positive; common B-ALL frequently expresses CD10. Can also be positive in follicular lymphoma and Burkitt lymphoma; not a precursor-specific marker. B-lineage markers CD19, CD22, cCD79a, PAX5 support B-lineage; use a panel. Usually express mature B-cell markers such as CD20, CD79a, PAX5, and CD19, with entity-specific exceptions. CD20 / CD45 CD20 often dim/negative; CD45 typically dim. CD20 usually positive (may be lost in plasmablastic differentiation); CD45 generally stronger. Surface immunoglobulin Usually absent; surface light chains typically absent. Usually present; flow cytometry may demonstrate monotypic κ or λ light chain. Ki-67 Often increased, but variable and not independently diagnostic. Highly variable; may be extremely high in Burkitt lymphoma, so proliferation alone does not establish precursor status. Most useful distinction Immature phenotype with TdT/CD34 and absent surface Ig, interpreted with morphology and B-lineage markers. Mature differentiation with surface Ig/light-chain restriction and entity-specific architecture/phenotype. T-cell lineage Precursor T-cell neoplasm (T-ALL/LBL) Mature T-cell neoplasm Lymphoblasts, usually small to medium; fine chromatin, inconspicuous nucleoli; nuclei may be convoluted. Mature small lymphocytes or atypical pleomorphic cells; nuclear irregularity, chromatin, and nucleoli vary by entity. Growth pattern Diffuse sheets of blasts; T-LBL commonly forms an anterior mediastinal/thymic mass. Variable patterns including diffuse, vascular/perivascular, sinusoidal, or TFH-associated patterns. TdT / CD34 / CD99 TdT usually positive; CD34 in a subset; CD99 often expressed. TdT and CD34 usually absent; CD99 is not a general mature T-cell marker. cCD3 / sCD3 cCD3 is the key lineage-defining marker; sCD3 often absent or dim, although some cases express it. Usually show mature surface CD3 and TCR expression. CD7 / CD5 CD7 often bright/uniform; CD5 often dimmer than mature T cells or absent. CD7 and/or CD5 may be aberrantly dim or lost; pattern depends on entity. CD1a / CD4 / CD8 CD1a may be positive; CD4/CD8 coexpression is common in cortical-stage cases; ETP-ALL lacks CD1a and CD8. Usually mature subset phenotype; CD4 or CD8 single-positive patterns common, but exceptions occur. TCR May show an immature/partial TCR program; clonality can support neoplasia but must be interpreted in context. Usually express mature TCR; clonal TR rearrangement supports a clonal T-cell process. Key distinction Immaturity markers plus cCD3 and aberrant thymocyte maturation pattern. Mature surface T-cell phenotype, absence of a convincing precursor program, and entity-specific morphology/genetics. B-cell vs. T-cell Precursor Neoplasms: Histology, IHC, and Prognosis B-ALL/LBL T-ALL/LBL Typical age Predominantly children, especially young children; adults also affected. Children, adolescents, and young adults; male predominance. Typical sites / presentation Marrow and blood; cytopenias, bone pain, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly; CNS/testes are important sites. Mediastinal mass uncommon. Marrow and blood or thymic/anterior mediastinal mass; may cause dyspnea, chest pain, pleural/pericardial effusions; lymphadenopathy common. Histology Monotonous lymphoblasts; high N:C ratio, fine to variably condensed chromatin, scant cytoplasm; diffuse marrow replacement or tissue effacement. Small-to-medium lymphoblasts; high N:C ratio, fine chromatin, inconspicuous nucleoli, sometimes convoluted nuclei; diffuse sheets, often mediastinal mass. Lineage-defining IHC CD19, CD22, cCD79a, PAX5 in a coherent B-lineage profile. cCD3 is the most lineage-specific marker; CD7, CD2, and CD5 commonly support T-lineage. Immaturity markers TdT, CD34 (variable), CD10; CD45 dim, CD20 often dim/negative, surface light chains absent. TdT, CD1a (subset), CD34 (about one third), CD99 and/or CD117; sCD3 often absent/dim; CD7 often bright. Phenotypic pitfalls CD10 also occurs in mature follicular and Burkitt lymphomas. CD13/CD33 do not independently establish myeloid lineage. CD13/CD33/CD117 may be expressed without MPAL; cCD3 establishes T-lineage. Exclude thymoma and T/myeloid MPAL. Genetic classification Defined primarily by recurrent genetic abnormalities; subtype and MRD strongly influence risk. NOTCH1/FBXW7, RAS/PTEN and other pathway alterations; ETP-ALL has a more stem-cell/myeloid-like mutation profile. Children: contemporary long-term survival often >90%, but strongly subtype- and MRD-dependent. Adults generally have less favorable outcomes. Children/adolescents: long-term response around 85%; adults around 60% in reported series. Relapsed disease has poor outcomes. Most important prognostic considerations Genetic subtype, age, WBC count, CNS status, early response, and MRD at protocol-defined time points. MRD, particularly after consolidation, is highly informative; NOTCH1/FBXW7 with wild-type RAS/PTEN may identify a favorable group. ETP-ALL diagnostic phenotype: cCD3 positive; CD1a and CD8 absent (<5% blasts); CD5 absent/dim (<75% blasts); at least one stem-cell marker (CD34/HLA-DR) and/or myeloid-associated marker (CD11b/CD13/CD33/CD65/CD117) in ≥25% blasts; MPO negative (<3%). Contemporary outcomes may approach those of other T-ALL despite more frequent MRD positivity after induction. precursor-search Search diagnoses, markers, genes, and differential points Search: TdT, PAX5, CD3, BCR::ABL1, hypodiploidy, MRD... precursor-group Category Collapse All Expand All entities Expand an entity for diagnostic criteria, morphology, IHC, molecular findings, and prognosis.
