title: Special Lymphomas
content: use client Burkitt Lymphoma (BL) Aggressive Mature B-Cell Lymphomas Monomorphic medium-sized cells, starry-sky pattern, germinal-center phenotype, Ki-67 typically ≥95%, and IG::MYC rearrangement. An extremely aggressive mature B-cell neoplasm driven by MYC dysregulation. Bimodal age distribution, with peaks in childhood and older adulthood; male predominance. Endemic disease often involves the jaw/facial bones; sporadic disease commonly involves the abdomen, ileocecal region, ovaries, kidneys, or other extranodal sites. Rapidly enlarging masses, high tumor burden, elevated LDH, and risk of CNS and marrow involvement are characteristic. HIV-associated and other immunodeficiency-associated cases may show nodal disease and plasmacytoid differentiation. Diffuse proliferation of monomorphic medium-sized lymphoid cells with basophilic cytoplasm, multiple small nucleoli, brisk mitotic activity, and abundant apoptosis. Typical germinal-center B-cell phenotype: CD20/PAX5+, CD10+, BCL6+, strong MYC, and absent or weak BCL2. Ki-67 is usually at least 95% and often approaches 100%. Demonstrate an IG::MYC rearrangement in the appropriate morphologic and immunophenotypic context. In adults, evaluate for concurrent BCL2 and BCL6 rearrangements; MYC/BCL2 double-hit disease is not classified as BL. Diffuse sheets of monotonous medium-sized cells with round nuclei and multiple small, basophilic nucleoli. Cytoplasm is deeply basophilic and may contain lipid vacuoles. Numerous mitoses and apoptotic bodies create a very high turnover rate. Tingible-body macrophages produce a classic starry-sky pattern. Coagulative necrosis is common in bulky lesions. Strong pan-B-cell markers: CD20, PAX5, CD79a, CD19, and CD22. Germinal-center markers: strong CD10 and BCL6; HGAL and MEF2B are often positive. MYC is intensely nuclear in most tumor cells. Ki-67 is typically ≥95%. BCL2 is usually negative; weak staining may occur in a minority but strong diffuse expression argues against BL. TdT, CD34, CD5, CD23, and CD138 are usually negative. EBER identifies EBV-associated cases; EBV status is reported as a biologically relevant subtype. High-grade B-cell lymphoma with MYC and BCL2 rearrangements Concurrent MYC and BCL2 rearrangements exclude BL, even when morphology is Burkitt-like; BCL2 is usually strong. High-grade B-cell lymphoma, NOS Often shows greater cytologic variability, less uniform germinal-center phenotype, stronger BCL2, or a Ki-67 index below the typical BL range. High-grade B-cell lymphoma with 11q aberration Usually lacks MYC rearrangement and shows characteristic 11q gain/loss; morphology may closely mimic BL. B-lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma TdT and often CD34 positivity, finer chromatin, and an immature phenotype support lymphoblastic disease. Pediatric-type follicular lymphoma Usually localized and follicular, with a different architecture; small biopsies may overlap cytologically. Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma Usually has larger and more pleomorphic cells, less uniform proliferation, and often BCL2 expression. IG::MYC rearrangement is defining; IGH::MYC is most common, with IGK::MYC and IGL::MYC less frequent. EBV-positive and EBV-negative BL have distinct pathogenetic profiles; EBER is used to establish EBV status. Recurrent mutations include ID3, TCF3, CCND3, TP53, and genes affecting PI3K/B-cell receptor signaling. A starry-sky pattern and near-100% Ki-67 are not specific for BL. Do not diagnose BL from MYC rearrangement alone; integrate the phenotype and exclude double-hit lymphoma. Strong BCL2, cyclin D1, or TdT expression should trigger reconsideration. Primary Effusion Lymphoma (PEL) and Extracavitary PEL KSHV/HHV8-Associated Lymphoid Neoplasms Large-cell lymphoma with plasmablastic/anaplastic morphology and nuclear HHV8 LANA positivity; classic PEL presents as a serous cavity effusion. A KSHV/HHV8-driven large B-cell lymphoma with a terminally differentiated phenotype and frequent EBV coinfection. Usually adults with HIV/AIDS or other substantial immunosuppression; also occurs in older patients with immunosenescence. Classic PEL involves pleural, pericardial, or peritoneal cavities without a solid mass or disseminated nodal disease. Kaposi sarcoma and HHV8-associated multicentric Castleman disease may coexist. Extracavitary PEL presents as solid nodal or extranodal masses, including gastrointestinal tract, skin, lung, or rarely CNS. Classic PEL: malignant large cells in a pleural, pericardial, or peritoneal effusion, usually without an associated solid tumor mass or other nodal/extranodal lymphoma. Extracavitary PEL: a morphologically and virologically related solid lymphoma without a defining effusion. Tumor cells show plasmablastic, immunoblastic, or anaplastic morphology and a terminal B-cell/plasma-cell differentiation phenotype. Demonstrate KSHV/HHV8 infection by nuclear LANA immunohistochemistry; this is essential. Assess EBV by EBER in situ hybridization; EBV is frequent but is not required. Large pleomorphic cells occur singly or in loose groups in effusions, often with abundant basophilic or amphophilic cytoplasm. Nuclei are irregular with coarse chromatin and prominent nucleoli; multinucleated and Reed–Sternberg-like forms may occur. Apoptotic debris and necrosis may be conspicuous. Extracavitary lesions form sheets of large immunoblastic, plasmablastic, or anaplastic cells and may show diffuse, partial, or sinusoidal nodal involvement. Nuclear HHV8 LANA is positive in tumor cells and is the defining diagnostic stain. Plasma-cell/activation markers commonly include CD30, CD38, CD138, MUM1/IRF4, EMA, and HLA-DR. CD20, PAX5, CD79a, OCT2, BOB1, CD19, and surface/cytoplasmic immunoglobulins are usually absent in classic PEL. CD45 is variable and may be absent; aberrant T-cell antigen expression can occur. EBER is frequently positive, particularly in HIV-associated PEL; LMP1 is usually negative. Fluid overload-associated large B-cell lymphoma Usually HHV8-negative and occurs in older patients with fluid overload; B-cell markers are more often retained. KSHV/HHV8-positive DLBCL Usually nodal/splenic, expresses cytoplasmic IgM (often lambda), and often retains CD20 or other B-cell markers; LANA is positive in both. KSHV/HHV8-positive germinotropic lymphoproliferative disorder Usually localized nodal disease with germinal-center colonization and retained nodal architecture rather than a cavity-based lymphoma. ALK-positive large B-cell lymphoma Often plasmablastic and CD20-negative, but ALK is positive and HHV8/EBV are negative. Anaplastic large cell lymphoma May mimic PEL cytologically, but is a T-cell/null-cell lymphoma and is HHV8-negative. Pyothorax-associated lymphoma Associated with chronic pyothorax and EBV, but lacks HHV8 and usually retains a conventional B-cell phenotype. KSHV/HHV8 infection is defining; LANA immunohistochemistry is the routine tissue assay. EBV coinfection is common and is demonstrated by EBER. IGH rearrangement studies may establish B-cell clonality when phenotype is markedly attenuated. Do not diagnose PEL from effusion cytology and plasma-cell markers alone; establish HHV8 positivity. HHV8 positivity does not by itself distinguish PEL from HHV8-positive DLBCL or GLPD; clinical distribution and architecture are critical. KSHV/HHV8-Positive Diffuse Large B-Cell Lymphoma Sheets of plasmablasts/immunoblasts with cytoplasmic IgM, usually lambda, and nuclear HHV8 LANA positivity, often in an MCD setting. An aggressive HHV8-driven large B-cell lymphoma, frequently arising in association with HHV8-positive multicentric Castleman disease. Most often adults, particularly men with HIV infection and substantial immunodeficiency. Usually presents with generalized lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly; MCD is commonly concurrent or antecedent. Extranodal dissemination and peripheral-blood involvement may occur. Demonstrate a clonal large B-cell proliferation with sheets of plasmablastic or immunoblastic cells. Tumor cells are HHV8 LANA-positive. Cytoplasmic IgM, usually lambda-restricted, supports the diagnosis. Correlate with nodal/splenic disease and evaluate for concurrent HHV8-associated MCD. EBV is usually negative; if positive, interpret in the context of profound immunosuppression and the broader differential. Coalescent sheets of intermediate-to-large cells efface nodal or splenic architecture. Cells have vesicular, often eccentric nuclei, one or more prominent nucleoli, and amphophilic cytoplasm. Plasmablastic and immunoblastic cytology is typical; rare cases show intravascular or Hodgkin-like patterns. Necrosis may be present. Nuclear HHV8 LANA is positive. Cytoplasmic IgM, usually lambda, is characteristic; surface immunoglobulin may be absent. MUM1/IRF4 and vIL-6 are commonly positive. CD20 and PAX5 are variable; CD79a, CD38, CD27, and CD138 are often negative or variable. EBER is usually negative, unlike many HIV-associated PEL cases. Primary effusion lymphoma / extracavitary PEL PEL usually lacks cytoplasmic IgM and has a more complete terminal plasma-cell phenotype with loss of B-cell markers; effusion-based presentation favors classic PEL. GLPD is usually localized and germinal-center centered, with preserved architecture and often polyclonal plasmablastic aggregates. Plasmablastic lymphoma Usually HHV8-negative and often EBV-positive; commonly expresses CD138/MUM1 and lacks conventional B-cell markers. EBV-positive DLBCL Usually HHV8-negative and retains a more complete B-cell phenotype; EBER is typically diffuse in tumor cells. Lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma LPL is composed of small B cells, plasmacytoid lymphocytes, and plasma cells, often with MYD88 L265P and IgM paraprotein rather than sheets of HHV8-positive blasts. HHV8 LANA positivity is defining. IGH genes are generally unmutated, consistent with a naive IgM-producing B-cell origin. EBV coinfection is uncommon; MYD88 L265P is not a defining feature. Do not use the obsolete designation 'large B-cell lymphoma arising in HHV8-associated MCD' as the entity name. LANA positivity must be interpreted with architecture, IgM expression, and clinical distribution because multiple HHV8-associated entities are LANA-positive. KSHV/HHV8-Positive Germinotropic Lymphoproliferative Disorder (GLPD) HHV8-positive, usually EBV-positive plasmablasts colonizing germinal centers in a usually preserved lymph node. A usually localized, often polyclonal HHV8-associated lymphoproliferation, classically arising in older immunocompetent adults. Usually older adults; no consistent sex predilection. Typically localized lymphadenopathy, often without systemic immunodeficiency. May be multifocal or associated with immunosenescence; systemic symptoms are often absent. Retained or largely preserved lymph-node architecture. Germinal centers are partially or completely colonized by clusters or sheets of plasmablastic, immunoblastic, or anaplastic cells. Demonstrate HHV8 LANA positivity in the atypical germinotropic cells. EBER positivity and polyclonal B-cell gene rearrangement are desirable supportive findings. Exclude HHV8-positive DLBCL and extracavitary PEL, particularly when plasmablastic aggregates are extensive. Atypical large cells are concentrated within germinal centers, producing a germinotropic distribution. Cells may be plasmablastic, immunoblastic, or anaplastic, with prominent nucleoli and abundant cytoplasm. Nodal architecture is generally retained, although involved follicles may be extensively replaced. Plasmablastic aggregates may overlap morphologically with extracavitary PEL. Atypical germinotropic cells show nuclear HHV8 LANA positivity. EBER is usually positive in the large cells. Plasma-cell differentiation markers and MUM1 may be expressed; phenotype is variable. B-cell markers may be attenuated; light-chain restriction is not consistently demonstrable. LANA staining distinguishes GLPD from EBV-positive germinal-center colonization by other lymphomas. DLBCL shows destructive sheets of clonal plasmablasts/immunoblasts, often with cytoplasmic IgM/lambda; GLPD is germinal-center centered with retained architecture and often polyclonal cells. Extracavitary PEL EC-PEL forms a mass with destructive sheets of large cells and a terminal B-cell phenotype; GLPD is usually localized and follicle-centered. EBV-positive DLBCL is HHV8-negative; LANA positivity in the atypical cells supports GLPD. Polymorphic lymphoproliferative disorder Polymorphic LPD shows a broad spectrum of B-cell maturation and architectural disruption in an established immune deficiency/dysregulation setting. HHV8 LANA positivity is essential. EBER positivity is common and supportive. Polyclonal IG rearrangement supports GLPD over a clonal large B-cell lymphoma, but clonality results must be interpreted with morphology. Do not diagnose GLPD on cytology alone; an adequate tissue biopsy is needed to assess germinal-center localization and architecture. The boundary with EC-PEL may be indistinct in lesions with extensive plasmablastic aggregates; clinical context and multidisciplinary review are important. Polymorphic Lymphoproliferative Disorder in Immune Deficiency/Dysregulation Immune Deficiency/Dysregulation-Associated Lymphoproliferations A destructive, polymorphous lymphoid proliferation in an immune deficiency/dysregulation setting, often with EBV-positive B immunoblasts and HRS-like cells. A spectrum of EBV-associated or other virus-associated lymphoproliferations that does not meet criteria for a defined lymphoma. Occurs in patients with HIV, solid-organ or hematopoietic transplantation, iatrogenic immunosuppression, inborn errors of immunity, or immunosenescence. Can involve lymph nodes or extranodal sites, including gastrointestinal tract, skin, lung, and other organs. Clinical presentation ranges from localized masses to disseminated disease; the immune-deficiency setting is integral to classification. Establish a relevant immune deficiency/dysregulation setting, including the specific clinical background. Show a polymorphous lymphoid proliferation with variable architectural effacement and a spectrum of B-cell maturation, without diagnostic features of a defined lymphoma. Assess EBV by EBER in situ hybridization; assess HHV8 when morphology or clinical setting warrants it. Exclude infectious mononucleosis-like hyperplasia, EBV-positive mucocutaneous ulcer, classic Hodgkin lymphoma, EBV-positive DLBCL, and HHV8-associated entities. Use integrated three-part nomenclature where appropriate: lesion type, viral status, and immune-deficiency/dysregulation setting. Broad polymorphous spectrum includes small lymphocytes, plasma cells, immunoblasts, plasmablasts, and HRS-like large cells. Architecture may be partially or extensively effaced by a mixed infiltrate. EBV-positive cells may be scattered or form aggregates; no validated numerical cutoff separates polymorphic LPD from lymphoma. T-cell/histiocyte-rich or Hodgkin-like backgrounds may occur. An adequate excisional or incisional biopsy is preferred because architecture is essential. Small and large B cells show variable CD20, CD79a, PAX5, OCT2, and BOB1 expression according to differentiation. Large cells may variably express CD30, CD15, MUM1, and CD45; HRS-like cells may show an attenuated B-cell phenotype. EBER highlights variable proportions of cells; the distribution of EBV-positive cells is diagnostically important. Light-chain expression may be polytypic, restricted, or discordant between sites. Flow cytometry may be nondiagnostic because the proliferation can be polymorphous and tissue architecture is required. EBV-positive mucocutaneous ulcer Usually a sharply localized, superficial mucocutaneous ulcer with a circumscribed polymorphous infiltrate and no disseminated mass-forming disease. Confluent sheets of large B cells with a destructive mass-forming pattern support DLBCL rather than polymorphic LPD. Classic Hodgkin lymphoma CHL has characteristic HRS cells in a typical reactive milieu with CD30+, weak PAX5+, and usually CD15+ phenotype; clinical setting and distribution are critical. Infectious mononucleosis-like hyperplasia Usually preserves architecture more effectively and shows a broad polytypic EBV-positive immunoblastic response, often with prominent CD8-positive T cells. KSHV/HHV8-associated GLPD or PEL Demonstration of LANA in the atypical cells redirects classification to an HHV8-associated entity. Plasmacytic small B-cell lymphoma A pre-existing clonal lymphoma with characteristic architecture and phenotype should be classified as that lymphoma, with EBV status and immune context appended as appropriate. EBER in situ hybridization is preferred for tissue assessment of EBV; blood EBV viral load alone does not establish tissue involvement. IG or T-cell receptor clonality studies may assist in selected cases but do not replace morphology and clinical context. HHV8 LANA immunohistochemistry is required when HHV8-associated disease is in the differential. Do not apply a fixed percentage of large cells as a threshold for lymphoma; no validated cutoff exists. Do not classify every EBV-positive polymorphous lesion as DLBCL or CHL. A polymorphous proliferation should prompt evaluation for an unrecognized immune deficiency when the clinical history is incomplete. EBV-Positive Mucocutaneous Ulcer (EBVMCU) A sharply circumscribed mucosal or cutaneous ulcer with EBV-positive atypical B cells in a polymorphous inflammatory background. A localized EBV-driven B-cell lymphoproliferation arising in age-related or iatrogenic immune impairment and selected immune dysregulation settings. Usually older adults with immunosenescence; may occur with methotrexate or other immunosuppressive therapy, transplantation, or inborn errors of immunity. Typically affects oropharyngeal mucosa, skin, or gastrointestinal tract. Presents as a solitary, sharply demarcated ulcer; systemic symptoms and disseminated disease are uncommon. A localized, sharply circumscribed ulcerative lesion involving skin or mucosa. Polymorphous infiltrate with EBV-positive atypical B cells, including immunoblasts and HRS-like cells. Demonstrate EBV in atypical cells by EBER in situ hybridization. Correlate with immune senescence, immunosuppressive medication, transplantation, or another immune dysregulation setting. Exclude systemic EBV-positive DLBCL and polymorphic LPD by clinical staging and distribution. Ulcer bed contains a sharply circumscribed polymorphous infiltrate, often with a rim of small T lymphocytes at the base and sides. Large immunoblasts, plasmablasts, and HRS-like cells are scattered or form small aggregates. Necrosis and a prominent inflammatory background may be present. The lesion is usually localized without destructive extension into adjacent deep tissue. EBER is positive in atypical B cells, often in a broad spectrum of cell sizes. Large cells commonly express CD20, PAX5, CD30, and MUM1; CD15 may be positive in a subset. B-cell marker expression may be attenuated in HRS-like cells. T cells at the ulcer base are usually CD3-positive and may form a rim. LANA is negative unless a separate HHV8-associated process is present. Polymorphic LPD Usually more extensive or mass-forming, often with broader tissue involvement; EBVMCU is characteristically a localized, sharply circumscribed ulcer. Shows destructive sheets of large cells and a mass-forming lesion, often with systemic disease rather than a solitary superficial ulcer. HRS cells may be present, but EBVMCU has a localized ulcerative pattern and often stronger B-cell marker expression. Usually forms a destructive mass, often expresses CD138 and MUM1 with loss of CD20/PAX5, and is frequently associated with HIV; EBVMCU is more circumscribed and polymorphous. EBER in situ hybridization is required to demonstrate EBV in the atypical cells. Clonal IG rearrangements may be detected and do not by themselves establish aggressive lymphoma. Do not diagnose EBV-positive DLBCL solely because large EBER-positive cells are present. The localized clinical distribution is central to the diagnosis; investigate for systemic disease when lesions are multiple or atypical. Diffuse Large B-Cell Lymphoma in Immune Deficiency/Dysregulation A destructive mass-forming proliferation with diffuse sheets of large B cells in a defined immune deficiency/dysregulation setting. A DLBCL-pattern lymphoma classified with explicit documentation of the underlying immune context and viral status. Occurs after solid-organ or hematopoietic transplantation, with HIV, iatrogenic immunosuppression, inborn errors of immunity, or immunosenescence. Can involve lymph nodes or extranodal organs, including gastrointestinal tract, skin, lung, and CNS. May present with a rapidly enlarging mass, systemic symptoms, elevated LDH, or organ dysfunction. Confirm an immune deficiency/dysregulation setting and document the specific cause. Demonstrate diffuse destructive sheets of large atypical B cells. Apply the same morphologic and immunophenotypic criteria used for DLBCL in immunocompetent patients. Assess EBV by EBER and HHV8 by LANA when indicated; report viral status explicitly. Distinguish a monomorphic DLBCL pattern from polymorphic LPD, EBVMCU, and CHL-like proliferations. Diffuse sheets of large centroblastic, immunoblastic, or plasmablastic cells efface tissue architecture. Necrosis, apoptosis, and a variable inflammatory background may be present. HRS-like cells may occur in a subset and should not automatically redirect the diagnosis to CHL. Some cases show a T-cell/histiocyte-rich background resembling THRLBCL. Tumor cells usually express B-cell markers such as CD20, PAX5, CD79a, OCT2, and BOB1, although expression may vary with plasmablastic differentiation or prior therapy. MUM1/IRF4 is commonly positive; CD30 may be expressed. EBER may be positive in tumor cells; LMP1 and occasionally EBNA2 may be expressed in latency patterns associated with the clinical setting. HHV8 LANA should be performed when HHV8-associated lymphoma is considered. Use a standard large B-cell lymphoma panel and cell-of-origin studies as appropriate. Polymorphic LPD contains a broad spectrum of B-cell maturation without confluent sheets of large lymphoma cells; sheets support DLBCL. EBVMCU is a localized superficial ulcer without a destructive mass-forming pattern or systemic disease. CHL has sparse HRS cells, a characteristic inflammatory milieu, weak PAX5, and usually CD30/CD15; DLBCL retains a stronger B-cell program. HHV8 LANA positivity and cytoplasmic IgM support the HHV8-defined entity. T-cell/histiocyte-rich large B-cell lymphoma THRLBCL is defined by sparse large B cells in a T-cell/histiocyte-rich background and is not diagnosed solely because an IDD-associated DLBCL has abundant reactive T cells. EBER in situ hybridization establishes tumor-cell EBV association; peripheral-blood EBV load is not a substitute. Perform entity-directed molecular studies as in immunocompetent patients when indicated. Clonality studies may be helpful in difficult cases but require caution in immune dysregulation. Do not use 'monomorphic PTLD' as a generic substitute for a specific lymphoma diagnosis. The immune context modifies classification and reporting but does not replace the morphologic diagnosis. Inborn Error of Immunity-Associated Lymphoid Proliferations and Lymphomas A mass-forming or infiltrative lymphoid proliferation arising in a genetically defined inborn error of immunity. A clinicopathologic framework encompassing hyperplasia, polymorphic LPD, EBVMCU, and defined lymphomas in patients with inherited immune defects. Often presents in childhood or young adulthood, although CVID-associated disease may present in adulthood. Male predominance occurs in X-linked disorders; distribution depends on the underlying immune defect. Common sites include lymph nodes, gastrointestinal tract, skin, lung, and bone marrow. Associated manifestations may include recurrent infections, autoimmunity, lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, granulomatous disease, or HLH. Establish or strongly suspect an underlying inborn error of immunity; document the specific immune defect when known. Classify the tissue lesion using standard criteria for reactive hyperplasia, polymorphic LPD, EBVMCU, or a defined lymphoma. Assess EBV status in tissue and evaluate HHV8 when clinically or morphologically indicated. Exclude infection and occult malignancy in granulomatous or CD8-rich lesions. Use germline testing to confirm the underlying immune disorder; do not use tumor tissue alone for germline classification. The spectrum is heterogeneous and may include poorly formed germinal centers, reduced plasma cells, T-zone hyperplasia, plasmacytosis, or granulomatous/CD8-rich infiltrates. EBV-associated lesions range from hyperplasia and polymorphic LPD to EBVMCU and overt lymphoma. Common lymphomas include DLBCL, classic Hodgkin lymphoma, Burkitt lymphoma, and marginal zone lymphoma. T- and NK-cell lymphomas are uncommon but may occur, particularly in disorders with chromosomal instability or impaired immune surveillance. Immunophenotype is determined by the specific underlying lesion; use the corresponding lymphoma-specific panel. Flow cytometry may reveal B-cell, T-cell, or NK-cell abnormalities that suggest the underlying immune defect. EBER should be performed in suspected EBV-associated proliferations. HHV8 LANA is indicated when the morphology or clinical context suggests an HHV8-associated process. Granulomatous or CD8-rich lesions require exclusion of infectious organisms and occult lymphoma. Secondary immune deficiency/dysregulation-associated LPD The defining distinction is an inherited immune defect rather than HIV, transplantation, medication-related immunosuppression, or immunosenescence. Sporadic lymphoma The same histologic lymphoma may occur sporadically; the underlying germline immune defect changes the clinical classification and management context. Infectious lymphadenitis Organism-directed stains, cultures, molecular testing, and clinical correlation are essential, especially in granulomatous lesions. CVID-associated granulomatous disease Granulomatous/CD8-rich lesions require exclusion of infection and THRLBCL or overt T-cell lymphoma. Germline testing is recommended to establish the specific inborn error of immunity. EBER and lesion-directed molecular studies should be performed as indicated. Interpret somatic sequencing cautiously because germline variants may be detected in tumor specimens; confirm germline findings in non-neoplastic tissue. Do not diagnose lymphoma from clonality alone; restricted lymphocyte populations may occur in immune dysregulation. Do not perform germline classification using tumor tissue alone. The final diagnosis should name the specific histologic lesion and append the immune-deficiency context. Classic Hodgkin Lymphoma (CHL) Hodgkin Lymphomas Scattered Hodgkin/Reed–Sternberg cells in a characteristic inflammatory microenvironment; CD30+, weak PAX5+, usually CD15+ and CD45−. A germinal-center B-cell neoplasm with profound downregulation of the B-cell program and a prominent tumor microenvironment. Bimodal age distribution, commonly young adults and older adults; male predominance is modest overall. Usually presents with painless lymphadenopathy, especially cervical, supraclavicular, and mediastinal nodes. Mediastinal bulk is particularly associated with nodular sclerosis CHL; B symptoms may occur. Primary extranodal disease or atypical distribution should prompt evaluation for immune deficiency/dysregulation and alternative entities. Identify Hodgkin and Reed–Sternberg (HRS) cells or variants in an appropriate polymorphous inflammatory microenvironment. HRS cells are typically CD30-positive, PAX5-positive with weak-to-moderate intensity, and CD20-negative, weak, or heterogeneous. CD15 positivity, CD45 negativity, and downregulation of OCT2/BOB1 support the diagnosis. Correlate with primary nodal or mediastinal presentation and exclude mimics, particularly NLPHL, EBV-positive B-cell proliferations, mediastinal grey zone lymphoma, and T-cell lymphomas. Assign a histologic subtype when adequate tissue is available: nodular sclerosis, mixed cellularity, lymphocyte-rich, or lymphocyte-depleted. HRS cells are scattered large mono- or multinucleated cells with prominent eosinophilic nucleoli, often in an inflammatory background. The background contains variable small lymphocytes, eosinophils, histiocytes, plasma cells, and neutrophils. Nodular sclerosis: broad or delicate collagen bands divide tissue into nodules; lacunar cells are characteristic. Mixed cellularity: diffuse effacement with numerous HRS cells in a mixed inflammatory infiltrate; granulomas may occur. Lymphocyte-rich: nodular or diffuse small-lymphocyte-rich background with few eosinophils/neutrophils; reactive B-cell nodules may be present. Lymphocyte-depleted: numerous pleomorphic HRS cells with sparse background lymphocytes, often with diffuse fibrosis or histiocytes. CD30 is strongly positive in nearly all HRS cells, often with membranous/Golgi accentuation. CD15 is positive in most cases, often focally. PAX5 is positive but characteristically weaker than in background B cells. CD20 is negative, weak, or heterogeneous; CD79a, OCT2, and BOB1 are usually reduced or absent. MUM1/IRF4 is strongly positive; CD45 and CD138 are usually negative. EBER is positive in a subset, particularly mixed-cellularity and lymphocyte-depleted patterns; EBV shows type II latency. PD-L1 is often expressed; STAT6 may be positive and can support CHL in selected differentials. Nodular lymphocyte-predominant Hodgkin lymphoma LP cells retain a strong B-cell program (CD20, OCT2, BOB1, BCL6), are usually CD30−/CD15−, and are surrounded by PD1-positive TFH rosettes. Mediastinal grey zone lymphoma Mediastinal mass with sheets or clusters of large cells and stronger preservation of the B-cell program favors grey zone lymphoma over classic CHL. Tumor cells usually retain CD20/PAX5/OCT2/BOB1 and CD45; sheets of large cells favor DLBCL rather than sparse HRS cells. Infectious mononucleosis Usually preserves more architecture, has numerous CD20+/CD45+ polytypic immunoblasts, and a CD8-rich background. Large cells retain a full B-cell phenotype and are usually CD45+/BCL6+, CD30−, and CD15−. Nodal TFH-cell lymphoma HRS-like B cells may be EBV-positive, but the background contains neoplastic TFH cells; RHOA G17V or IDH2 R172 mutations support TFH lymphoma. ALK-negative anaplastic large cell lymphoma Tumor cells show a T-cell/null phenotype, strong CD30, and lack PAX5; TR clonality may resolve difficult cases. EBER establishes EBV association in HRS cells. Recurrent 9p24.1 gains/amplification involve PD-L1, PD-L2, and JAK2 and may have predictive relevance for checkpoint blockade. Recurrent alterations affect NF-κB and JAK/STAT signaling, including TNFAIP3, SOCS1, STAT6, and related pathway genes. HRS-like cells are not specific for CHL; interpret them in the context of the background population and complete phenotype. PAX5-negative CHL is rare; confirm lineage and exclude T-cell lymphoma or other mimics before making this diagnosis. Do not diagnose CHL from cytology alone when a primary tissue diagnosis is required. Nodular Lymphocyte-Predominant Hodgkin Lymphoma (NLPHL) Scattered popcorn-like LP cells in B-cell-rich nodules with FDC meshworks and PD1-positive TFH rosettes; strong B-cell phenotype. A germinal-center-derived B-cell neoplasm with six recognized nodular and diffuse growth patterns and a risk of large B-cell transformation. Usually adults aged 30–60 years, but may occur from childhood to older adulthood; male predominance. Typically presents with localized, painless peripheral lymphadenopathy, often cervical, axillary, inguinal, or iliac. Most patients have early-stage disease; B symptoms are less common than in CHL. Liver, spleen, and marrow involvement are uncommon and may be associated with variant growth patterns. Identify scattered large LP cells with multilobated nuclei and one or more nucleoli in a characteristic nodular or mixed nodular/diffuse architecture. LP cells retain a strong B-cell phenotype, typically CD20+, PAX5+, OCT2+, BOB1+, and BCL6+. Nodules contain small B cells and expanded follicular dendritic cell meshworks. PD1-positive TFH cells typically form rosettes around LP cells. At least one unequivocal NLPHL nodule is required when a diffuse pattern E/THRLBCL-like component predominates. Assess for transformation when sheets or confluent aggregates of large B cells develop with loss of the typical NLPHL architecture. LP cells are large with multilobated or folded nuclei, vesicular chromatin, prominent nucleoli, and abundant pale cytoplasm; they resemble popcorn. LP cells are usually scattered singly and constitute a small fraction of the lesion. Background contains abundant small B and T lymphocytes, histiocytes, and FDC networks; eosinophils and neutrophils are typically absent. Pattern A: classic B-cell-rich nodules with scattered LP cells. Pattern B: serpiginous/interconnected nodules with numerous LP cells. Pattern C: extranodular LP cells in a T-cell-rich background. Pattern D: T-cell-rich nodules with increased LP cells. Pattern E: diffuse THRLBCL-like pattern with few B cells; a typical NLPHL nodule must be found. Pattern F: diffuse variant with abundant small B cells and scattered LP cells. LP cells strongly express CD20, PAX5, CD79a, OCT2, BOB1, and PU.1. Germinal-center markers BCL6, LMO2, and HGAL are usually positive; CD10 is usually negative. CD30 is usually negative; CD15 is usually negative or only rarely positive. IgD is expressed in a subset, particularly in young men and selected growth patterns. Background FDC meshworks are highlighted by CD21 and CD23. PD1, CD57, ICOS, and other TFH markers highlight rosetting T cells around LP cells. EBER is usually negative; EBV positivity is exceptional. Classic Hodgkin lymphoma, lymphocyte-rich subtype CHL has CD30+, weak PAX5+, often CD15+, and reduced OCT2/BOB1; NLPHL has strong pan-B-cell markers and PD1-positive rosettes. THRLBCL lacks the characteristic B-cell-rich nodules and FDC meshworks; a convincing NLPHL nodule is required to classify pattern E. Progressive transformation of germinal centers PTGC has enlarged serpiginous follicles with mantle-zone B cells but lacks LP cells with the characteristic neoplastic phenotype. TFH lymphoma has an aberrant clonal TFH-cell population and may show RHOA G17V or IDH2 R172 mutations; NLPHL has a reactive TFH rosette pattern. Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma arising by transformation Transformation shows loss of nodular/FDC architecture and confluent sheets or substantial aggregates of large B cells without a residual diagnostic NLPHL pattern. LP cells are clonal germinal-center B cells with ongoing somatic hypermutation; whole-tissue IG clonality assays may be insensitive. BCL6 rearrangements or amplifications are recurrent. Aberrant somatic hypermutation may target PIM1, RHOH, PAX5, MYC, SOCS1, JUNB, DUSP2, and SGK1. EBV is not a significant etiologic driver and is detected only exceptionally. Do not diagnose NLPHL from LP-cell morphology alone; the immunoarchitecture is essential. Core biopsies may not adequately distinguish pattern E NLPHL from de novo THRLBCL; excisional tissue is preferred. Do not mistake increased LP cells in variant patterns for transformation without assessing architecture and large-cell distribution. Burkitt lymphoma MYC-driven; EBV-associated in most endemic cases and a subset of sporadic/immunodeficiency-associated cases; malaria is a cofactor in endemic regions. Mature germinal-center B cell. Monomorphic medium cells, basophilic vacuolated cytoplasm, starry-sky pattern, brisk apoptosis/mitoses. CD20+, PAX5+, CD10+, BCL6+, MYC strong+, Ki-67 ≥95%, BCL2−/weak, TdT−. Primary effusion lymphoma KSHV/HHV8-driven; frequent EBV coinfection; usually HIV-related or other immunosuppression. Post-germinal-center/terminally differentiated B cell with plasmablastic phenotype. Large immunoblastic, plasmablastic, or anaplastic cells in serous effusion; extracavitary form forms solid sheets. LANA+, CD30+, MUM1+, CD38/CD138 often+; CD20/PAX5/OCT2/BOB1 usually−; EBER often+. KSHV/HHV8-driven; often associated with HHV8-MCD and profound immunodeficiency. Naive IgM-producing B cell. Destructive sheets of plasmablasts/immunoblasts, often with eccentric nuclei. LANA+, cytoplasmic IgM/lambda+, MUM1+, vIL-6+; CD20/PAX5 variable; EBER usually−. KSHV/HHV8-positive GLPD KSHV/HHV8 infection, usually with EBV; often immunocompetent older adults. B-cell lineage with plasmablastic/germinotropic differentiation. Large atypical cells colonize germinal centers; nodal architecture usually retained. LANA+, usually EBER+; variable B-cell/plasma-cell markers; clonality often polyclonal. Polymorphic LPD in IDD Immune deficiency/dysregulation with frequent EBV-driven B-cell expansion. Polyclonal or oligoclonal B-cell proliferation; variable T-cell/plasma-cell admixture. Polymorphous spectrum from small lymphocytes to immunoblasts, plasmablasts, and HRS-like cells; variable effacement. Variable CD20/PAX5/OCT2/BOB1, CD30, CD15, MUM1; EBER highlights variable cell populations. Localized EBV-driven proliferation in immunosenescence or iatrogenic/other immune suppression. EBV-infected mature B cells. Circumscribed superficial ulcer with polymorphous infiltrate and scattered large immunoblasts/HRS-like cells. EBER+, CD20/PAX5 often+, CD30+, MUM1+; CD15 variable. IDD-associated DLBCL Underlying HIV, transplantation, iatrogenic immunosuppression, IEI, or immunosenescence; EBV may be present. Mature B cell, often activated/post-germinal-center phenotype. Diffuse destructive sheets of large centroblastic, immunoblastic, or plasmablastic cells. CD20/PAX5/CD79a usually retained; MUM1 and CD30 variable; EBER variable; LANA− unless HHV8-defined. Inborn error of immunity-associated LPD/lymphoma Germline immune defect affecting immune surveillance, EBV control, or DNA repair. Variable B, T, or NK lineage, depending on the lesion and inherited defect. Hyperplasia, polymorphic LPD, EBVMCU, DLBCL, CHL, BL, MZL, or rare T/NK lymphoma. Entity-specific; EBER and LANA as indicated; flow may reveal underlying immune phenotype. Usually sporadic; EBV contributes in a subset, especially mixed-cellularity and lymphocyte-depleted forms; immune dysregulation increases risk. Germinal-center B cell with defective B-cell transcriptional program. Sparse HRS cells in a rich inflammatory background; subtype-specific sclerosis or inflammatory composition. CD30+, weak PAX5+, CD15 often+, CD45−, MUM1+; CD20 variable/weak; OCT2/BOB1 reduced. NLPHL Unknown; germinal-center selection and somatic hypermutation; EBV is not a significant driver. Germinal-center B cell. Scattered LP/popcorn cells in nodules with mantle-zone B cells and FDC meshworks; variable A–F patterns. CD20/PAX5/OCT2/BOB1/BCL6+, CD10−, CD30−, CD15−; PD1+ TFH rosettes. All PathologyGPS · Hematopathology Selected Special Lymphomas and Lymphoproliferative Disorders A practical diagnostic reference covering selected aggressive B-cell lymphomas, virus-associated lymphoid neoplasms, immune deficiency/dysregulation-associated proliferations, and Hodgkin lymphomas. Emphasis is placed on etiologic context, lineage, tissue architecture, defining immunophenotype, and the differential diagnosis. Diagnostic Approach 1. Establish the clinical setting Age, immune status, viral risk, anatomic distribution, and whether disease is effusion-based, ulcerative, nodal, or mass-forming are often decisive. 2. Identify lineage and differentiation Separate germinal-center B-cell, terminally differentiated B-cell, HRS-cell, and T/NK-cell phenotypes. 3. Assess architecture Determine whether the lesion is follicle-centered, destructive and sheet-forming, polymorphous, ulcer-limited, or associated with a serous effusion. 4. Perform virus-directed studies Use EBER for EBV and LANA for HHV8 when indicated; viral positivity must be localized to the atypical cells. 5. Apply entity-specific criteria Do not let a single marker override the combined morphology, immunophenotype, viral status, and clinical context. 6. Exclude overlapping entities The boundaries among HHV8-associated lesions and immune dysregulation-associated proliferations can overlap; adequate tissue and multidisciplinary correlation may be needed. Core principle: For these entities, etiology and clinical setting are not optional annotations. They may be integral to the diagnosis, particularly for HHV8-associated and immune deficiency/dysregulation-associated lesions. title: Tumor Like Lymphocytic Lesions
content: use client Reactive B-Cell-Rich Lymphoid Proliferations Mimicking Lymphoma Reactive Lymphoid Proliferations Consider this category when an atypical or architecturally distorted lymphoid proliferation is polymorphous, clinically reactive, and lacks convincing evidence of a clonal lymphoma. Variable age; nodal or extranodal disease. Patients may have lymphadenopathy, tonsillar or salivary-gland enlargement, mucosal ulceration, or symptoms related to infection, autoimmunity, drugs, or immunodeficiency. Identify the dominant reactive pattern: florid follicular hyperplasia, progressive transformation of germinal centers, genital-tract lymphoma-like lesion, EBV-associated immunoblastic proliferation, or hematogone hyperplasia. Evaluate architecture, cytology, distribution of cell populations, and the clinical setting together. Use flow cytometry, immunohistochemistry, EBER, microbiology, and/or immunoglobulin or T-cell receptor gene-rearrangement studies as indicated. Do not diagnose lymphoma solely because of architectural distortion, large immunoblasts, or an occasional clonal/oligoclonal rearrangement. Establish an underlying infection, autoimmune disease, immunodeficiency, or drug-related trigger whenever possible. Florid follicular hyperplasia: follicles are variably sized and widely spaced, with polarized germinal centers and tingible-body macrophages. Progressive transformation of germinal centers: large, sharply circumscribed nodules show mantle-zone B cells progressively infiltrating and dismantling germinal centers. Female genital-tract lymphoma-like lesion: superficial polymorphous infiltrate, often with epithelial erosion, polytypic plasma cells, and neutrophils; a mass and sclerosis are typically absent. Infectious mononucleosis: paracortical expansion with a polymorphous mixture of small lymphocytes, plasma cells, and numerous immunoblasts; architecture is often incompletely effaced. Hematogone hyperplasia: small precursor B cells involve paracortex and/or medulla, particularly in children. Florid follicular hyperplasia: germinal-center B cells are BCL2 negative with a high Ki-67 index and preserved polarization. Progressive transformation: CD20-positive mantle-zone B cells express IgD and BCL2; germinal-center cells are admixed; lymphocyte-predominant cells and PD1-positive rosettes are absent. Genital-tract lymphoma-like lesions: large cells are predominantly B cells; plasma cells are polytypic. Infectious mononucleosis: immunoblasts are usually MUM1 positive, CD10 negative, and BCL6 negative; light chains are polytypic. HRS-like cells usually retain CD45 and lack CD15. Infectious mononucleosis typically has a CD8-predominant T-cell background; classic Hodgkin lymphoma more often has an increased CD4:CD8 ratio. Hematogones show an orderly spectrum of B-cell maturation by flow cytometry rather than a uniform aberrant blast population. IGH or TR gene-rearrangement studies may help in equivocal cases, but occasional clonal or oligoclonal results can occur in otherwise reactive lesions, particularly genital-tract lymphoma-like lesions and infectious/inflammatory settings. EBER or pathogen-specific molecular testing may identify an infectious trigger. Follicular lymphoma: monotonous crowded follicles, loss of polarization/tingible-body macrophages, and aberrant BCL2 expression in germinal centers. Nodular lymphocyte-predominant B-cell lymphoma: LP cells and PD1-positive T-cell rosettes are absent in progressive transformation of germinal centers. Classic Hodgkin lymphoma: HRS cells typically lack CD45 and express CD15 in many cases; EBV is concentrated in HRS cells rather than a broad spectrum of immunoblasts. B-lymphoblastic lymphoma: larger, more uniform blasts with a coherent immature B-cell phenotype and often aberrant antigen expression; correlate with flow cytometry and clinical course. IgG4-Related Disease Think of IgG4-RD in an adult with tumefactive, often multiorgan disease and a lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate accompanied by storiform fibrosis; isolated IgG4-rich lymphadenopathy is not sufficient. Usually adults in the fifth or sixth decade, with male predominance. Pancreas, biliary tract, salivary glands, orbit, retroperitoneum, aorta, and lymph nodes are common sites; mass effect or organ-specific dysfunction is typical. For extranodal disease, identify a lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate rich in IgG4-positive plasma cells, an IgG4:IgG plasma-cell ratio greater than 40%, and storiform fibrosis. Exclude well-defined mimics, including ANCA-associated vasculitis, rheumatoid arthritis, multicentric Castleman disease, Rosai-Dorfman disease, infection, lymphoma, and plasma-cell neoplasia. For a primary nodal diagnosis, require established extranodal IgG4-RD (prior, concurrent, or subsequent), polytypic IgG4-positive plasma cells exceeding 400/mm², and an IgG4:IgG ratio greater than 40%. Interpret IgG4 counts and ratios in the context of organ site and morphology; serum IgG4 elevation is supportive but not specific. Demonstrate polytypic plasma cells with kappa/lambda studies. Extranodal lesions show a lymphoplasmacytic and eosinophil-rich infiltrate with storiform fibrosis; the inflammatory component may predominate early and fibrosis later. Obliterative phlebitis is a characteristic supportive feature; an elastic stain can highlight obliterated veins. Reactive lymphoid follicles are common, particularly in head and neck lesions. Nodal patterns include Castleman-like changes, follicular hyperplasia, interfollicular expansion, progressive transformation of germinal centers, and inflammatory pseudotumor-like fibrosis. Nodal inflammatory pseudotumor-like fibrosis with IgG4-positive plasma cells and eosinophils in fibrotic/interfollicular areas is more specific than isolated intrafollicular IgG4-positive cells. Necrosis, abscesses, neutrophilic infiltrates, granulomas, and necrotizing vasculitis are atypical and should prompt another diagnosis. IgG4-positive plasma cells are increased, with an IgG4:IgG ratio greater than 40% in the appropriate morphologic and clinical setting. Plasma cells should be polytypic for kappa and lambda. Nodal germinal centers may show BCL2-negative germinal-center B cells; interfollicular plasma cells are polytypic. No single immunostain establishes IgG4-RD; correlate with fibrosis, phlebitis, organ distribution, and laboratory findings. No defining molecular test is required. Idiopathic multicentric Castleman disease: prominent systemic inflammation, elevated IL-6/CRP, anemia, hypoalbuminemia, and often sheet-like plasma cells; storiform fibrosis and obliterative phlebitis favor IgG4-RD. Rosai-Dorfman disease: S100/OCT2-positive histiocytes with emperipolesis rather than an IgG4-rich fibrosing lymphoplasmacytic lesion. Lymphoma or plasma-cell neoplasm: assess architecture, cytologic atypia, light-chain restriction, and clonality; IgG4 expression does not exclude malignancy. ANCA-associated vasculitis: necrotizing vasculitis and granulomatous inflammation are not typical of IgG4-RD. Unicentric Castleman Disease Castleman Disease Consider UCD when imaging shows a solitary enlarged lymph node or one nodal station, especially a hypervascular mediastinal, cervical, abdominal, or retroperitoneal mass. Any age, typically the fourth decade, with slight female predominance. Usually an incidental solitary nodal mass; symptoms may reflect compression. Mixed/plasmacytic cases can produce inflammatory symptoms. Confirm involvement of a single lymph node or multiple nodes confined to one lymph-node station by clinical and radiologic correlation. Hyaline-vascular subtype: regressed germinal centers, hyalinized vessels penetrating follicles, expanded mantle zones, and hypervascular fibrotic stroma. Mixed/plasmacytic subtype: dense interfollicular plasma-cell aggregates extending toward the cortex, with variable follicular hyperplasia or regression. Demonstrate polytypic plasma cells in most cases; investigate rare monotypic cases for an associated plasma-cell or lymphoid neoplasm. Exclude HHV8-associated disease and systemic multicentric Castleman disease. Hyaline-vascular: numerous follicles with regressed, lymphocyte-depleted germinal centers and radially penetrating hyalinized vessels (lollipop follicles). Mantle zones form concentric onion-skin rings; twinning of germinal centers within a single mantle zone may occur. Interfollicular zones contain prominent high endothelial venules, plasmacytoid dendritic-cell clusters, and fibrosis; sinuses are compressed or obliterated. Mixed/plasmacytic: architecture is often better preserved, with expanded interfollicular zones containing groups or sheets of mature plasma cells. The mixed/plasmacytic subtype may have less conspicuous hyaline-vascular follicles than the classic subtype. Follicular dendritic-cell networks are expanded and highlight with CD21, CD23, and CD35; CD106/VCAM1 is often positive. Residual germinal-center B cells express CD10 and BCL6 and are BCL2 negative; mantle-zone B cells express IgD and BCL2, sometimes dim CD5. Interfollicular plasma cells are usually polytypic. Interfollicular plasmacytoid dendritic cells may express CD123, TCL1, and CD68. KSHV/HHV8 LANA is negative; EBER is negative or highlights only rare bystander lymphocytes. Molecular testing is generally not required. A subset of hyaline-vascular UCDs harbor stromal-cell alterations, including PDGFRB mutations. Idiopathic multicentric Castleman disease: two or more nodal stations with systemic inflammation and characteristic laboratory abnormalities. KSHV/HHV8-associated MCD: LANA-positive plasmablasts in mantle zones and systemic inflammatory flares. Follicular lymphoma: neoplastic follicles with aberrant BCL2 expression and loss of normal germinal-center compartmentalization. Mantle cell lymphoma: cyclin D1/SOX11 and/or CCND1 rearrangement with mantle-zone expansion by neoplastic cells. Nodal marginal zone lymphoma: monocytoid B-cell expansion, follicular colonization, and clonal B-cell population. Idiopathic Multicentric Castleman Disease Think of iMCD in a patient with lymphadenopathy in at least two nodal stations plus systemic inflammation, cytopenias, hypoalbuminemia, edema, or organ dysfunction after exclusion of HHV8 and other mimics. Any age, median around 50 years, with similar frequency in men and women. Multistation cervical, mediastinal, axillary, and abdominal lymphadenopathy; fever, fatigue, edema/anasarca, effusions, hepatosplenomegaly, renal dysfunction, and laboratory inflammation are common. Document enlarged lymph nodes in at least two nodal stations. Biopsy must show compatible Castleman-like morphology, particularly grade 2–3 regressed germinal centers and/or plasmacytosis. Fulfill the required clinical and laboratory criteria for iMCD and exclude HIV, KSHV/HHV8, autoimmune disease, infection, lymphoma, POEMS-associated MCD, and other causes of cytokine-driven lymphadenopathy. Recognize iMCD-TAFRO when thrombocytopenia, anasarca, fever/inflammation, renal dysfunction or marrow reticulin fibrosis, and organomegaly predominate; otherwise classify as iMCD-NOS. Correlate histology with systemic findings; morphology alone is insufficient. Nodal architecture is variably distorted, with regressed or hyperplastic follicles and prominent interfollicular expansion. Regressed germinal centers may be penetrated by hyalinized vessels and surrounded by expanded mantle zones. Interfollicular regions show increased vascularity, mature plasma cells, immunoblasts, and variable fibrosis. Plasmacytic areas may contain sheets or aggregates of mature plasma cells; TAFRO cases may show marrow reticulin fibrosis and megakaryocytic hyperplasia. CD20-positive B cells and CD3-positive T cells retain recognizable compartmental distribution, although regressed germinal centers are B-cell depleted. LANA is negative; this is essential to exclude KSHV/HHV8-associated MCD. Phospho-S6 and phospho-4EBP1 may be increased in interfollicular cells, supporting mTOR-pathway activation but are not required for diagnosis. No convincing aberrant T-cell phenotype or clonal B-/T-cell population should be identified. Antigen-receptor gene rearrangements are typically polyclonal; molecular testing is not a defining diagnostic test. KSHV/HHV8-associated MCD: LANA-positive plasmablasts and viral association. UCD: disease restricted to one nodal station, often without systemic inflammatory syndrome. IgG4-related lymphadenopathy: polytypic IgG4-rich plasma cells and compatible extranodal IgG4-RD; clinical inflammatory profile differs. POEMS-associated MCD: neuropathy, organomegaly, endocrinopathy, monoclonal plasma-cell disorder, and skin changes. Lymphoma: evaluate for destructive clonal populations, aberrant phenotype, and disease-specific molecular findings. KSHV/HHV8-Associated Multicentric Castleman Disease Consider HHV8-MCD in a patient—often with HIV or another immunodeficiency—with episodic fever, generalized lymphadenopathy, inflammatory laboratory abnormalities, and plasmablasts in mantle zones. Usually adults; most patients are HIV-positive, with male predominance. HIV-negative patients tend to be older. Generalized lymphadenopathy, fever, fatigue, weight loss, hepatosplenomegaly, edema, effusions, anemia, and hypoalbuminemia are typical; Kaposi sarcoma may coexist. Identify multicentric Castleman-like nodal morphology in a patient with systemic inflammatory symptoms. Demonstrate KSHV/HHV8-infected plasmablasts by nuclear LANA immunostaining. Recognize plasmablasts in mantle zones, with possible intrafollicular/perifollicular extension and occasional aggregates. Correlate with HIV/immunosuppression, viral load, systemic inflammatory flares, and associated Kaposi sarcoma. Do not equate monotypic cytoplasmic IgM-lambda expression with a clonal B-cell neoplasm; these plasmablasts may be polyclonal by molecular studies. Nodal and splenic morphology resembles iMCD, usually plasmacytic or mixed pattern. Plasmablasts are medium to large cells with one or two nucleoli and moderate amphophilic cytoplasm. Plasmablasts are concentrated in mantle zones but may occur within or around follicles; they may be scattered or form aggregates. Kaposi sarcoma foci may be present in the same specimen. LANA shows nuclear positivity in infected plasmablasts and is the key diagnostic stain. Plasmablasts express MUM1/IRF4 and BLIMP1 and often show cytoplasmic IgM-lambda restriction. CD20 and other B-cell markers are dim or negative; CD138 is typically negative; T-cell markers are negative. vIL-6 is expressed in a subset; EBV is generally negative in HHV8-infected plasmablasts. Background interfollicular plasma cells are usually polytypic and HHV8 negative. KSHV/HHV8 infection is etiologic; viral molecular testing is not usually required when LANA immunohistochemistry is diagnostic. iMCD: LANA negative and lacks HHV8-infected mantle-zone plasmablasts. Plasmablastic lymphoma: destructive sheets of plasmablasts, usually strong plasma-cell phenotype and often EBV-positive; assess clinical context and HHV8 status. Classic Hodgkin lymphoma: HRS cells are scattered in a characteristic inflammatory background and show a different immunophenotype; LANA identifies HHV8-MCD plasmablasts. HIV-associated reactive lymphadenopathy: lacks the characteristic LANA-positive plasmablast population. Kikuchi-Fujimoto Disease T-Cell-Predominant Lesions Think of Kikuchi-Fujimoto disease in a young adult—often an Asian woman—with acute or subacute cervical lymphadenopathy, fever, and paracortical necrotizing foci rich in karyorrhectic debris but lacking neutrophils. Young adults, median age approximately 23–30 years, with female predominance; pediatric cases more often affect boys. Usually unilateral cervical lymphadenopathy with fever, fatigue, weight loss, rash, or arthralgia. Identify circumscribed paracortical foci of karyorrhexis, apoptosis, and variable necrosis. Recognize a mixed population of crescentic histiocytes, plasmacytoid dendritic cells, immunoblasts, and predominantly CD8-positive T cells. Granulocytes are notably absent and plasma cells are sparse. Exclude infection, lymphoma, and autoimmune disease—particularly systemic lupus erythematosus—using clinical and ancillary findings. Do not overcall T-cell lymphoma based solely on partial loss of CD5/CD7 or an occasional oligoclonal T-cell receptor rearrangement. Paracortical lesions are non-expansile, circumscribed, pale, and sometimes wedge-shaped. Proliferative phase: abundant karyorrhectic debris with crescentic or twisted histiocytes, immunoblasts, and plasmacytoid dendritic cells. Necrotizing phase: discrete or confluent coagulative necrosis among the cellular infiltrate and nuclear debris. Xanthomatous phase: foamy macrophages become prominent. Neutrophils and eosinophils are absent or strikingly inconspicuous; plasma cells are scarce. Histiocytes express CD68, CD163, CD4, and characteristically myeloperoxidase. Plasmacytoid dendritic cells express CD123, TCL1, TCF4, CD4, and CD68 and often cluster around necrotic foci. The lymphoid component is predominantly CD8-positive cytotoxic T cells; CD30 may be expressed. Partial or complete loss of CD2, CD5, or CD7 may occur and is not by itself evidence of T-cell lymphoma. TR gene rearrangements are usually polyclonal; occasional monoclonal or oligoclonal results have been reported and must be interpreted cautiously. Lupus lymphadenitis: hematoxylin bodies, plasma cells, vascular changes, and clinical/serologic lupus support; correlate with ANA and other studies. Infectious lymphadenitis: neutrophils, granulomas, organisms, or pathogen-specific studies may identify infection. Peripheral T-cell lymphoma: atypical destructive T-cell population, aberrant phenotype, and convincing clonality favor lymphoma. Hodgkin lymphoma: diagnostic HRS cells and characteristic microenvironment; KFD instead shows karyorrhexis with crescentic histiocytes and no granulocytes. Autoimmune Lymphoproliferative Syndrome Immune Dysregulation-Associated Proliferations Consider ALPS in a child or young adult with chronic noninfectious lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, autoimmune cytopenias, and expanded peripheral-blood αβ double-negative T cells. Usually recognized in early childhood in germline FAS disease; somatic FAS disease can present across a broad age range. Persistent lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, autoimmune cytopenias, and increased lymphoma risk are characteristic. Document chronic, noninfectious lymphadenopathy and/or splenomegaly for more than six months. Peripheral-blood flow cytometry must show αβ double-negative T cells exceeding 1.5% of total lymphocytes or 2.5% of CD3-positive lymphocytes. Demonstrate a pathogenic defect in FAS-mediated apoptosis, commonly involving FAS; other genes include FASLG, CASP8, FADD, and CASP10. Assess autoimmune cytopenias, polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia, family history, vitamin B12, soluble FAS ligand, and IL-10 as supportive findings. Do not substitute lymph-node DNT-cell expansion for the required peripheral-blood flow-cytometric assessment. Lymph nodes show reactive follicular hyperplasia with prominent pale paracortical expansion. Expanded paracortical areas contain double-negative T cells and polytypic plasma cells. Progressive transformation of germinal centers, Castleman-like changes, or marked plasmacytosis may obscure the underlying pattern. Rosai-Dorfman-like histiocytic changes may coexist; similar reactive infiltrates can involve spleen and bone marrow. DNT cells are CD45RA positive and CD45RO negative. DNT cells express cytotoxic markers including perforin, TIA1, and CD57. The proliferating population should be correlated with flow cytometry demonstrating αβ TCR-positive CD4−/CD8− T cells. Immunohistochemistry alone cannot establish ALPS; peripheral blood flow cytometry and clinical/genetic criteria are central. Evaluate germline and/or somatic FAS-pathway alterations, including FAS, FASLG, CASP8, FADD, and CASP10. DNT cells may show a restricted TCRVβ repertoire; restricted repertoire alone should not be mistaken for lymphoma clonality. RAS-associated leukoproliferative disease: overlapping immune dysregulation phenotype; distinguish by the underlying RAS-pathway defect and clinical/genetic criteria. iMCD/UCD: Castleman-like histology may overlap, but ALPS is defined by chronic immune dysregulation and expanded peripheral αβ DNT cells. Lymphoma: destructive atypical clonal population and disease-specific phenotype/genetics; ALPS carries increased lymphoma risk, so a new focal or progressive lesion requires evaluation. IgG4-related disease and Rosai-Dorfman disease may coexist with ALPS rather than simply mimic it. Indolent T-Lymphoblastic Proliferation Immature T-Cell Proliferations Consider iT-LBP when TdT-positive T-cell clusters are found in an otherwise indolent lymph node or around another tumor, especially Castleman disease, without marrow disease or destructive atypia. Usually adults in the fourth or fifth decade, with possible slight male predominance; children can be affected. Often an incidental nodal or extranodal finding in an otherwise indolent clinical course, sometimes associated with Castleman disease or carcinoma. Identify confluent clusters or sheets of TdT-positive T cells without cytologic atypia or tissue destruction. Demonstrate a developmentally appropriate immature thymocyte phenotype, most often CD4/CD8 double positive. Establish an indolent clinical course and absence of clinical evidence for precursor T-cell neoplasia. Show polyclonal TR gene rearrangements; bone marrow involvement is generally absent. Distinguish from T-lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma before considering treatment. Overall nodal architecture is preserved, with clusters or confluent sheets in interfollicular and paracortical regions. Cells are small to medium sized, with open immature chromatin, inconspicuous nucleoli, and no significant atypia. Mitoses may be frequent; scattered histiocytes are common. In Castleman disease, lymphoblasts are usually interfollicular; in association with carcinoma, they may be interspersed among malignant epithelial cells. Cells express TdT and CD3; most are CD4/CD8 double positive, although double-negative cases occur. CD2, CD5, and CD7 are usually present but may show decreased intensity. CD1a, CD10, and CD99 are variable; CD34 is frequently negative. LMO2 is negative in iT-LBP and is often positive in T-lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma. B-cell markers and cytokeratin are negative; cytokeratin helps exclude ectopic thymic epithelial cells. Ki-67 may be high (approximately 40–90%) and does not by itself establish malignancy. TR gene-rearrangement studies show a polyclonal population; a clonal TR rearrangement supports T-lymphoblastic neoplasia in the appropriate context. T-lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma: cytologic atypia, aberrant antigen expression (e.g., CD34, CD33, or CD79a), loss of normal T-cell markers, clonal TR rearrangement, and often marrow involvement or rapid progression. Ectopic thymic tissue: contains thymic epithelial cells highlighted by cytokeratin; iT-LBP lymphoblasts are cytokeratin negative. Reactive thymocyte-like T cells: assess whether there are organized confluent aggregates and whether the clinical setting supports a persistent proliferation. All PathologyGPS · Hematopathology Tumor-Like Lymphocytic Lesions A practical diagnostic reference for reactive, immune-mediated, and virus-associated lymphoid proliferations that may mimic lymphoma. Diagnosis requires integration of tissue architecture, cytology, immunophenotype, molecular studies, and clinical distribution. Diagnostic Orientation: When to Consider These Lesions Clinical / morphologic clue Consider Key discriminator Polymorphous B-cell-rich infiltrate; reactive follicles or immunoblasts Reactive B-cell-rich proliferation Preserved maturation/polarization, polytypic cells, pathogen or immune trigger Multiorgan mass lesions with lymphoplasmacytic inflammation and fibrosis IgG4-related disease Storiform fibrosis, obliterative phlebitis, increased IgG4+ plasma cells and IgG4:IgG ratio Single nodal station with lollipop follicles / onion-skin mantle zones Unicentric Castleman disease Hyaline-vascular follicles and vascular/fibrotic stroma Multistation nodes plus systemic inflammation, edema, cytopenias iMCD or HHV8-MCD LANA separates HHV8-MCD from iMCD; clinical/lab criteria establish iMCD Young adult with tender cervical nodes and paracortical necrosis Kikuchi-Fujimoto disease Karyorrhexis, crescentic MPO+ histiocytes, pDCs; absence of neutrophils Chronic adenopathy, splenomegaly, autoimmune cytopenias ALPS Peripheral blood αβ double-negative T cells and FAS-pathway defect TdT+ T-cell clusters in a bland node or around another tumor Indolent T-lymphoblastic proliferation Maturely patterned thymocyte phenotype, polyclonal TR, indolent course Core principle: Architectural distortion, high Ki-67, immunoblasts, or limited antigen loss do not independently establish lymphoma.
