title: Plasma Cell Neoplasms
content: use client Cold Agglutinin Disease Monoclonal Gammopathies Complement-mediated hemolysis with a monoclonal IgM cold agglutinin and a characteristic marrow B-cell clone, without overt lymphoma. Typically presents in the late 60s; slight female predominance. Hemolytic anemia, acrocyanosis, Raynaud phenomenon, or livedo reticularis, often worsened by cold exposure. Usually a small serum IgM paraprotein, most often kappa-restricted. Demonstrate chronic complement-mediated hemolytic anemia attributable to a cold-reactive autoantibody. Identify a monoclonal cold agglutinin, usually IgM, with clinically significant thermal amplitude. Exclude an associated infection or overt lymphoid malignancy; the marrow clone must not meet criteria for lymphoma. Bone marrow involvement is typically subtle and does not show an extramedullary lymphoma. Peripheral blood may show red-cell agglutination, anisocytosis, and polychromasia. Marrow contains small lymphoid cells in nodular aggregates and a sparse interstitial infiltrate. The lymphoid cells have round to slightly oval nuclei, condensed chromatin, and scant clear cytoplasm. Mature plasma cells are usually fewer than 5% and surround or are scattered between lymphoid aggregates. Paratrabecular growth, prominent lymphoplasmacytic differentiation, increased mast cells, and fibrosis are not typical. The clonal B cells express CD19, CD20, PAX5, CD79a, CD22, and CD79b. Surface IgM and monotypic light chain are present, most often kappa. CD5 is positive in a subset; CD23, CD10, BCL6, MUM1, and cyclin D1 are generally negative. The accompanying plasma cells show IgM and the same light-chain restriction. Lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma / Waldenström macroglobulinemia Usually shows a more substantial lymphoplasmacytic marrow infiltrate, often with plasmacytoid cells and MYD88 p.L265P; CAD lacks the typical LPL pattern. Secondary cold agglutinin syndrome Occurs with infection or an overt lymphoma; identify and classify the underlying condition rather than diagnosing primary CAD. Other small B-cell lymphomas CLL/SLL, marginal zone lymphoma, and mantle cell lymphoma have their own architectural and immunophenotypic signatures and may produce secondary cold agglutinins. MYD88 p.L265P is absent in typical CAD and helps distinguish it from lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma. Recurrent gains of chromosome 3 and mutations including KMT2D and CARD11 are reported but are not required for diagnosis. Do not diagnose lymphoma solely from the presence of a clonal marrow B-cell population. A cold agglutinin associated with infection or overt lymphoma is a secondary syndrome, not primary CAD. IgM Monoclonal Gammopathy of Undetermined Significance Serum IgM M protein below 3 g/dL, less than 10% marrow lymphoplasmacytic involvement, and no attributable disease manifestations. Usually identified incidentally in older adults; incidence rises with age and is higher in men. No symptoms attributable to the clone at diagnosis. Potential IgM-related complications include neuropathy or Schnitzler syndrome, even without overt lymphoma. Serum monoclonal IgM protein is less than 3 g/dL. Clonal lymphoplasmacytic cells comprise less than 10% of bone marrow cellularity. No anemia, constitutional symptoms, hyperviscosity, lymphadenopathy, or hepatosplenomegaly attributable to the lymphoproliferative clone. No other attributable end-organ injury or criteria for lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma, plasma cell myeloma, or another B-cell neoplasm. Marrow shows less than 10% involvement by clonal lymphoplasmacytic or plasma-cell-differentiated cells. The infiltrate may be subtle; quantify the combined clonal B-cell and plasma-cell component. A typical small B-cell phenotype and absence of a lymphoma-defining pattern are essential to classification. B cells typically express surface IgM, CD19, CD20, and PAX5. CD5 may be positive or negative; CD10 and CD23 are generally negative. Plasma cells may show IgM and monotypic kappa or lambda light chain. At least 10% marrow lymphoplasmacytic involvement or attributable clinical manifestations support LPL; MYD88 p.L265P is common but not specific. Cold agglutinin disease Requires clinically significant cold agglutinin-mediated hemolysis; CAD may have a small marrow clone but is defined by the hemolytic syndrome. IgM plasma cell myeloma Usually has a plasma-cell phenotype and myeloma-defining features; t(11;14) may be present, while MYD88 is generally absent. MYD88 p.L265P may be present at the MGUS stage and does not by itself establish LPL. Use molecular findings as supportive evidence in conjunction with marrow morphology, immunophenotype, and clinical criteria. Do not equate any MYD88 mutation with Waldenström macroglobulinemia. Assess IgM-related organ manifestations separately; a small clone can cause clinically important paraprotein-mediated disease. Non-IgM Monoclonal Gammopathy of Undetermined Significance Non-IgM M protein below 3 g/dL, fewer than 10% clonal marrow plasma cells, and no attributable myeloma-defining event. Usually an incidental finding in adults over 50; prevalence increases with age and is higher in men. Most patients are asymptomatic and have no myeloma-related organ damage. May be associated with monoclonal gammopathy-related renal, neurologic, or dermatologic disorders. Serum non-IgM M protein (usually IgG or IgA) is less than 3 g/dL. Clonal bone marrow plasma cells are less than 10% of total nucleated marrow cells. There is no attributable CRAB end-organ damage: hypercalcemia, renal impairment, anemia, or osteolytic bone disease. There is no other myeloma-defining event or biopsy-proven plasmacytoma. Light-chain MGUS requires an abnormal serum free light-chain ratio with an increased involved light chain, no heavy-chain expression on immunofixation, and no attributable end-organ damage. Marrow contains fewer than 10% mature clonal plasma cells. Plasma cells may be scattered or form small aggregates; extensive sheets or a substantial tumor mass should prompt evaluation for myeloma. Assess plasma-cell burden on the core biopsy as well as aspirate because focal disease may be underestimated in aspirates. Plasma cells express CD38, CD138, and MUM1/IRF4. Clonality is established by kappa or lambda light-chain restriction using immunohistochemistry, in situ hybridization, or flow cytometry. Clonal plasma cells commonly show CD19 loss and dim or absent CD45. Smoldering multiple myeloma Smoldering myeloma has 10–60% clonal marrow plasma cells and/or an M protein at least 3 g/dL, without myeloma-defining events. Active plasma cell myeloma Requires at least 10% clonal marrow plasma cells or a biopsy-proven plasmacytoma plus a myeloma-defining event. Monoclonal gammopathy of renal significance Renal biopsy demonstrates injury caused by the monoclonal immunoglobulin, even when the clone does not meet criteria for malignancy. Primary abnormalities include IGH translocations (including t(11;14), t(4;14), t(14;16), and t(14;20)) and hyperdiploidy. FISH may identify a plasma-cell clone but is not required to establish MGUS. Do not classify a patient as MGUS until renal, neurologic, or other monoclonal immunoglobulin-mediated injury has been considered. A normal marrow aspirate does not exclude a small or focally distributed clonal plasma-cell population. Monoclonal Gammopathy of Renal Significance Monoclonal Immunoglobulin-Mediated Disorders A small B-cell or plasma-cell clone produces a monoclonal immunoglobulin that causes biopsy-proven kidney injury without meeting criteria for overt malignancy. Usually presents around the sixth decade, with male predominance; younger adults can be affected. Proteinuria, hematuria, acute or chronic renal insufficiency, hypertension, or hypocomplementemia. Some patients have systemic manifestations such as neuropathy, cardiomyopathy, purpura, or liver involvement. Kidney biopsy demonstrates a lesion attributable to a monoclonal immunoglobulin or its fragment. The responsible B-cell or plasma-cell clone does not meet accepted criteria for a hematologic malignancy requiring treatment on tumor-burden grounds. Characterize the renal lesion by light microscopy, immunofluorescence, and electron microscopy, with amyloid typing when indicated. Identify the responsible clone with serum and urine electrophoresis/immunofixation, serum free light chains, and bone marrow or lymph-node evaluation. The source chapter lists proteinuria greater than 1 g/day and progressive acute or subacute kidney injury as essential clinical features; interpret these in the full clinical context. Renal morphology depends on the mechanism and subtype: immunoglobulin deposition, organized deposits, complement-mediated injury, or vascular occlusion. Common associated lesions include AL amyloidosis, monoclonal immunoglobulin deposition disease, light-chain proximal tubulopathy, proliferative glomerulonephritis with monoclonal immunoglobulin deposits, and cryoglobulinemic glomerulonephritis. The renal biopsy is the defining tissue examination; marrow findings may be minimal or absent. Immunofluorescence should establish restriction to a single immunoglobulin heavy-chain class/subclass and/or light-chain type when present. Use kappa and lambda, IgG subclasses, IgA, IgM, and complement stains as indicated by the renal pattern. Correlate tissue restriction with the circulating paraprotein and the phenotype of the marrow or B-cell clone. Plasma cell myeloma with cast nephropathy Cast nephropathy in a patient with a plasma-cell neoplasm is a myeloma-defining event, not MGRS. AL amyloidosis Shows Congo red-positive fibrillar deposits; MGRS is the broader clinicopathologic category and includes AL amyloidosis when the clone is below malignancy thresholds. Monoclonal immunoglobulin deposition disease A specific non-amyloid MGRS lesion with linear basement-membrane deposits and powdery electron-dense material. Non-monoclonal immune-complex or complement-mediated glomerulopathy Evaluate immunoglobulin restriction, ultrastructure, complement profile, and correlation with the circulating paraprotein. No single molecular alteration defines MGRS; molecular studies should target the identified B-cell or plasma-cell clone. FISH and mutation testing may help classify the clone and guide therapy but do not replace renal tissue diagnosis. Do not dismiss a small clone as clinically insignificant when the monoclonal immunoglobulin is causing kidney injury. Do not label cast nephropathy associated with overt myeloma as MGRS. Immunoglobulin-Related Amyloidosis (AL Amyloidosis) Congo red-positive amyloid with apple-green birefringence, definitively typed as immunoglobulin-derived, in a patient with compatible organ dysfunction. Usually affects older adults; systemic disease may involve multiple organs. Cardiac restrictive physiology, proteinuria/nephrotic syndrome, renal dysfunction, peripheral or autonomic neuropathy, hepatomegaly, or soft-tissue involvement. Macroglossia, periorbital purpura, and submandibular soft-tissue enlargement are characteristic but uncommon. Demonstrate amyloid deposition in tissue by Congo red or an equivalent validated method, or identify typical amyloid fibrils by electron microscopy. Document organ dysfunction attributable to amyloid. Demonstrate a monoclonal protein in serum or urine or an abnormal serum free light-chain profile. Type the amyloid protein; laser microdissection followed by mass spectrometry is preferred when available. A plasma-cell clone or monoclonal protein alone is insufficient: prove that the tissue amyloid is AL rather than ATTR, AA, or another amyloid type. Amyloid is extracellular, amorphous, eosinophilic, and waxy, often involving vessel walls, basement membranes, and interstitium. Congo red stains deposits salmon-pink to red; polarized microscopy shows characteristic apple-green birefringence. Electron microscopy demonstrates randomly arranged, nonbranching fibrils approximately 9–12 nm in diameter. Marrow may show a small clonal plasma-cell population; amyloid is detectable in marrow in a subset of cases. Localized AL may show plasma cells adjacent to deposits; systemic disease may involve heart, kidney, liver, nerves, soft tissue, gastrointestinal tract, skin, or lymph nodes. CD138 and MUM1 highlight plasma cells; kappa/lambda in situ hybridization or immunohistochemistry may demonstrate light-chain restriction. The clone is often lambda-restricted, but kappa-restricted AL also occurs. Immunohistochemical amyloid typing can be supportive, but equivocal or discordant results require mass-spectrometric typing. Transthyretin amyloidosis (ATTR) Commonly involves the heart and/or nerves in older adults; tissue typing is essential because a coincidental monoclonal gammopathy does not prove AL. AA amyloidosis Usually occurs with chronic inflammatory disease or infection; type the deposits rather than inferring the type from clinical history. Non-amyloid deposits are Congo red negative and appear powdery and granular by electron microscopy rather than fibrillar. Incidental MGUS with non-AL amyloid A monoclonal protein may coexist with ATTR or another amyloid type; establish the deposited protein directly. There is no defining molecular test for AL amyloidosis. If hereditary amyloidosis is in the differential, evaluate relevant genes (including TTR and other amyloid-associated genes) rather than assuming a monoclonal protein establishes AL. Never assign AL type solely from serum/urine monoclonal protein or marrow light-chain restriction. Congo red positivity establishes amyloid, not its protein type. A negative fat-pad or marrow biopsy does not exclude organ-limited or systemic AL amyloidosis. Monoclonal Immunoglobulin Deposition Disease Non-amyloid monoclonal immunoglobulin deposits, typically linear along renal basement membranes, with powdery electron-dense material. Usually presents in middle-aged or older adults, with kidney involvement in nearly all cases. Proteinuria, hypertension, progressive renal insufficiency, or nephrotic syndrome. May involve heart, liver, lung, gastrointestinal tract, skin, or peripheral/autonomic nerves, especially with myeloma. Demonstrate monoclonal immunoglobulin deposition in tissue. In renal disease, establish the deposit pattern by immunofluorescence and electron microscopy. Classify as light-chain deposition disease, light- and heavy-chain deposition disease, or heavy-chain deposition disease according to the deposited immunoglobulin. Exclude amyloid by Congo red and ultrastructural assessment. Correlate with a plasma-cell or, less commonly, B-cell clone; the clone may be small. Kidney commonly shows nodular glomerulosclerosis, often resembling diabetic nodular sclerosis. Immunofluorescence shows diffuse linear staining along glomerular and tubular basement membranes and vessel walls. Electron microscopy shows punctate, powdery, nonfibrillar electron-dense deposits along basement membranes. Unlike amyloid, deposits are not composed of randomly arranged fibrils. Extrarenal deposits may occur; inflammatory or lymphoplasmacytic infiltrates are not a characteristic renal feature. Immunofluorescence demonstrates restriction to one light chain, one heavy chain, or a paired light/heavy chain pattern. Use IgG subclasses and heavy-chain stains as needed to define the deposited immunoglobulin. Correlate tissue immunoglobulin restriction with serum/urine immunofixation and the clonal population. Congo red positive with fibrillar ultrastructure; MIDD is generally Congo red negative with powdery nonfibrillar deposits. Diabetic nodular glomerulosclerosis May resemble LCDD on light microscopy; monoclonal linear light-chain staining and powdery deposits support MIDD. Fibrillary or immunotactoid glomerulopathy Shows organized fibrillar or microtubular deposits rather than the nonorganized powdery deposits of MIDD. Light-chain proximal tubulopathy Predominantly involves proximal tubular epithelial cells, often with crystalline inclusions, rather than diffuse basement-membrane deposition. A t(11;14) may be identified in a substantial subset of cases associated with a plasma-cell neoplasm; it is supportive, not diagnostic. Do not diagnose MIDD from nodular glomerulosclerosis alone. Distinguish nonfibrillar deposition disease from amyloid using Congo red and electron microscopy. Mu Heavy Chain Disease Heavy Chain Diseases A rare small B-cell neoplasm producing truncated monoclonal mu heavy chains without associated light chains, often resembling CLL/SLL. Typically occurs in older adults; both sexes may be affected. May present with lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, cytopenias, or marrow involvement. A paraprotein may be detected, but the abnormal mu chain lacks associated light chains. Demonstrate a monoclonal truncated IgM heavy chain without associated kappa or lambda light chain. Establish a clonal B-cell lymphoproliferative disorder and characterize its tissue distribution. Exclude conventional CLL/SLL, lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma, and other small B-cell lymphomas with intact immunoglobulin. The marrow and tissue infiltrate often resembles CLL/SLL, with small mature lymphocytes and occasional plasmacytoid differentiation. Cytoplasmic vacuoles or inclusions may be present in lymphoid or plasma-cell-differentiated cells. The morphology is not independently diagnostic; demonstration of the abnormal heavy chain is required. B cells express pan-B-cell markers such as CD20 and PAX5; the phenotype may resemble CLL/SLL. Intracellular mu heavy chain is demonstrable without corresponding light-chain expression. Use flow cytometry and immunohistochemistry to exclude a conventional light-chain-producing B-cell clone. CLL/SLL May have similar morphology and phenotype, but does not produce a truncated mu heavy chain without light chains. Lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma Usually shows plasmacytoid differentiation and intact monoclonal immunoglobulin; MYD88 p.L265P is common in LPL. Other heavy chain diseases Gamma and alpha heavy chain diseases differ in heavy-chain class and typical clinicopathologic pattern. The abnormal heavy chain results from acquired immunoglobulin heavy-chain gene alterations, including deletions, insertions, and point mutations that remove portions of the variable and CH1 domains. A monoclonal IgM paraprotein alone does not establish mu heavy chain disease; demonstrate the truncated heavy chain and absent light-chain association. Gamma Heavy Chain Disease A clonal B-cell disorder producing truncated gamma heavy chains without light chains; tissue morphology may mimic several indolent B-cell lymphomas. Usually affects older adults, with a female predominance reported. May present with lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, constitutional symptoms, or autoimmune disease. Some patients have an associated autoimmune disorder or an overt lymphoma-like clinical presentation. Demonstrate a monoclonal truncated gamma heavy chain without associated light chains in serum, urine, or tissue. Establish a clonal B-cell lymphoproliferative disorder. Integrate morphology and immunophenotype because the tissue pattern may resemble lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma, marginal zone lymphoma, or another small B-cell lymphoma. The infiltrate is variable and may be lymphoplasmacytic, marginal-zone-like, or resemble another small B-cell lymphoma. Plasmacytoid cells and plasma cells may be present, but morphology alone cannot establish gamma heavy chain disease. The abnormal heavy-chain product is the defining feature. B-cell markers identify the clonal population; plasma-cell markers highlight plasmacytic differentiation when present. Cytoplasmic or extracellular gamma heavy chain may be demonstrated without associated kappa or lambda light chain. A complete panel is needed to classify any coexisting lymphoma-like component. Often has a similar lymphoplasmacytic pattern but produces intact immunoglobulin; MYD88 p.L265P supports LPL rather than gamma HCD. Splenic or extranodal marginal zone lymphoma Can show plasmacytic differentiation; demonstrate the abnormal truncated gamma chain to establish gamma HCD. Mu or alpha heavy chain disease Distinguished by the heavy-chain class and characteristic clinical/pathologic context. Truncating IGH alterations disrupt the variable and CH1 regions and permit secretion of unpaired gamma heavy chains. Do not classify the case solely by its lymphoma-like morphology; heavy-chain analysis is essential. Alpha Heavy Chain Disease An IgA heavy-chain-producing B-cell neoplasm, classically involving the small intestine and associated with immunoproliferative small intestinal disease. Typically affects young adults in regions where chronic intestinal infections are prevalent; historically reported more often in the Mediterranean, Middle East, and North Africa. Chronic diarrhea, malabsorption, weight loss, abdominal pain, and nutritional deficiency. Usually involves the small intestine, particularly the proximal small bowel; mesenteric nodes may also be involved. Demonstrate a monoclonal truncated alpha heavy chain without associated light chains. Establish the characteristic intestinal B-cell lymphoproliferative process and correlate with the clinical syndrome. Exclude conventional extranodal marginal zone lymphoma/MALT lymphoma and other intestinal B-cell neoplasms. Intestinal mucosa shows a dense, often diffuse or nodular infiltrate of mature plasma cells and lymphoplasmacytoid cells in the lamina propria. Villous architecture may be distorted or blunted, with extension into deeper bowel wall or regional lymph nodes in advanced disease. The infiltrate may range from relatively mature plasmacytic proliferation to more atypical lymphoma-like disease. The neoplastic cells show B-cell and plasma-cell differentiation markers, with cytoplasmic alpha heavy chain. Kappa and lambda light chains are absent from the abnormal heavy-chain-producing population. Phenotype overlaps with extranodal marginal zone lymphoma; correlate with the heavy-chain product. Extranodal marginal zone lymphoma of MALT May involve small bowel and show plasmacytic differentiation, but does not produce the characteristic truncated alpha heavy chain without light chains. Reactive plasma-cell-rich enteritis Usually polytypic, lacks a clonal heavy-chain product, and does not show the characteristic persistent lymphoproliferative process. Gamma and mu heavy chain diseases Differ in immunoglobulin heavy-chain class and usual clinical distribution. Acquired IGH alterations truncate the alpha heavy chain, commonly removing the CH1 domain and preventing normal light-chain association. Do not diagnose alpha HCD from intestinal plasmacytosis alone; demonstrate the abnormal alpha heavy chain and absence of associated light chains. Plasmacytoma Plasma Cell Neoplasms A solitary clonal plasma-cell tumor in bone or soft tissue, with no systemic myeloma-defining disease and less than 10% clonal marrow plasma cells. Solitary bone plasmacytoma usually occurs in adults in the fifth to sixth decades and involves the axial skeleton. Extramedullary plasmacytoma most often involves the upper aerodigestive tract, particularly the sinonasal region and upper airway. Presents as a localized mass; systemic symptoms or CRAB features should prompt evaluation for myeloma. Biopsy demonstrates a clonal plasma-cell neoplasm in a single bone or extramedullary site. Bone marrow sampled away from the lesion contains less than 10% clonal plasma cells. Whole-body imaging and clinical evaluation show no additional bone or soft-tissue lesions. There is no attributable CRAB end-organ damage or other myeloma-defining event. If minimal clonal marrow involvement is present, distinguish solitary plasmacytoma with minimal marrow involvement from systemic myeloma. Tumor consists of sheets, nests, or diffuse infiltrates of plasma cells with eccentric nuclei, clock-face chromatin, basophilic cytoplasm, and perinuclear hof. Cytologic spectrum ranges from mature plasma cells to atypical, immature, plasmablastic, or pleomorphic forms. Extramedullary lesions may show more mature plasma-cell differentiation; amyloid deposition may be present. In bone, the lesion replaces marrow and may cause destructive lytic change. Tumor cells express CD138, CD38, and MUM1/IRF4. Kappa or lambda restriction establishes clonality; RNA in situ hybridization may be useful when immunohistochemistry has high background. CD56 and cyclin D1 may be aberrantly expressed; CD19 is usually absent in neoplastic plasma cells. Exclude a B-cell lymphoma with plasmacytic differentiation using CD20, PAX5, and other markers guided by morphology. Plasma cell myeloma Multifocal marrow disease, at least 10% clonal marrow plasma cells, multiple lesions, or a myeloma-defining event excludes solitary plasmacytoma. Plasmablastic lymphoma Often EBV-positive, highly proliferative, and MYC-rearranged, particularly in immunosuppressed patients; most plasmacytomas are EBV-negative. B-cell lymphoma with plasmacytic differentiation Retention of B-cell markers or an associated clonal B-cell component supports lymphoma rather than a pure plasma-cell neoplasm. Neuroendocrine neoplasm Can mimic plasmablastic plasma cells; use CD138, MUM1, light chains, and neuroendocrine markers in the morphologic context. Clonal IG gene rearrangement can support clonality when light-chain studies are inconclusive. FISH abnormalities may overlap with plasma cell myeloma; molecular findings do not replace systemic staging. A biopsy diagnosis of plasmacytoma requires systemic evaluation to exclude multiple myeloma. Do not use a targeted lesion biopsy to estimate marrow plasma-cell burden; obtain a separate, non-targeted marrow sample. Plasma Cell Myeloma / Multiple Myeloma Clonal marrow plasma cells or a biopsy-proven plasmacytoma plus at least one myeloma-defining event (SLiM-CRAB). Predominantly affects older adults, with a slight male predominance. Bone pain, pathologic fractures, anemia, renal impairment, hypercalcemia, recurrent infections, or incidental paraproteinemia. Most cases produce an IgG, IgA, or light-chain paraprotein; a small minority are nonsecretory. Demonstrate at least 10% clonal plasma cells in bone marrow or a biopsy-proven bony/extramedullary plasmacytoma. In addition, demonstrate at least one myeloma-defining event (SLiM-CRAB): S — clonal bone marrow plasma cells at least 60%. Li — involved/uninvolved serum free light-chain ratio at least 100, with involved free light chain at least 100 mg/L. M — more than one focal lesion on MRI, each at least 5 mm. C — hypercalcemia attributable to the plasma-cell disorder. R — renal impairment attributable to the plasma-cell disorder. A — anemia attributable to the plasma-cell disorder. B — one or more osteolytic bone lesions on radiography, CT, or PET/CT; osteoporosis or compression fracture alone without lytic lesions is insufficient. Smoldering myeloma has 10–60% clonal marrow plasma cells and/or serum IgG/IgA M protein at least 3 g/dL or urinary monoclonal protein at least 500 mg/24 hours, without a myeloma-defining event. Marrow plasma cells range from mature forms with eccentric nuclei and clock-face chromatin to immature, plasmablastic, multinucleated, or pleomorphic forms. Growth patterns include interstitial, nodular, band-like, diffuse sheet-like, and nearly complete marrow replacement. A focal nodular aggregate or sheet of clonal plasma cells strongly supports myeloma over a small background population. Peripheral blood may show rouleaux; circulating plasma cells are seen in advanced disease and are prominent in plasma cell leukemia. Renal cast nephropathy shows intratubular eosinophilic casts, often fractured and associated with tubular injury and inflammation. Plasma cells express CD138, CD38, and MUM1/IRF4; use these markers to quantify the infiltrate. Kappa or lambda restriction establishes clonality; RNA in situ hybridization may improve interpretation when background immunoglobulin is high. Neoplastic plasma cells commonly lose CD19 and show dim/absent CD45. CD56 is expressed in a majority but is not universal; CD117, CD20, CD28, CD33, or other aberrant markers may occur. Flow cytometry is useful for detecting small abnormal plasma-cell populations and measurable residual disease. MGUS Less than 10% clonal marrow plasma cells, M protein below 3 g/dL, and no myeloma-defining event. Higher clonal burden (10–60% marrow plasma cells and/or specified M-protein burden) but no SLiM-CRAB event. Solitary plasmacytoma Single tissue or bone lesion, less than 10% clonal marrow plasma cells, no additional lesions, and no myeloma-defining event. Often EBV-positive and highly proliferative, with frequent MYC rearrangement; clinical setting and viral studies are important. Reactive plasmacytosis Usually polytypic, retains a normal plasma-cell phenotype, and lacks a destructive clonal infiltrate. Primary genetic groups include hyperdiploidy and IGH translocations, including t(11;14), t(4;14), t(14;16), and t(14;20). Important secondary abnormalities include gain/amplification of 1q, del(17p)/TP53, del(1p), del(13q), and MYC rearrangements. Perform plasma-cell-enriched FISH when possible; cytogenetic findings contribute to risk stratification and treatment planning. Do not diagnose active myeloma from marrow plasma-cell percentage or M protein alone; a myeloma-defining event is required. Do not count osteoporosis or vertebral compression fracture alone as a lytic bone lesion. A hemodilute or focal aspirate can underestimate plasma-cell burden; correlate aspirate, core biopsy, imaging, and flow cytometry. Plasma Cell Neoplasms with Associated Paraneoplastic Syndromes Recognize the syndrome clinically: POEMS, TEMPI, and AESOP have distinct defining feature combinations and may have only a small plasma-cell clone. POEMS: usually presents around age 50, with distal symmetric sensorimotor polyneuropathy, lambda-restricted IgA or IgG paraprotein, and often osteosclerotic lesions. TEMPI: typically affects adults in the fourth or fifth decade; telangiectasias, erythrocytosis with elevated erythropoietin, monoclonal gammopathy, perinephric fluid, and intrapulmonary shunting. AESOP: rare presentation of solitary plasmacytoma with adenopathy and an extensive overlying violaceous or erythematous vascular skin patch. POEMS requires both mandatory criteria: polyneuropathy and a monoclonal plasma-cell proliferative disorder, usually lambda-restricted. POEMS additionally requires at least one major criterion (sclerotic bone lesions, Castleman disease, or elevated VEGF) and at least one minor criterion (organomegaly, extravascular volume overload, endocrinopathy, skin changes, papilledema, or thrombocytosis/polycythemia). TEMPI requires the characteristic major features: telangiectasias, elevated erythropoietin with erythrocytosis, monoclonal gammopathy, perinephric fluid collections, and intrapulmonary shunting; minor features may support an evolving presentation. AESOP is defined by adenopathy and an extensive skin patch overlying a plasmacytoma; confirm the underlying plasma-cell tumor and exclude mimics. A low marrow plasma-cell percentage does not exclude these syndromes. POEMS marrow often has fewer than 5% clonal plasma cells; osteosclerotic lesions show plasma cells within sclerotic marrow. TEMPI usually has no specific marrow morphology; erythroid hyperplasia and a small clonal plasma-cell population may be present. AESOP skin biopsy shows diffuse reactive vascular hyperplasia in the dermis, sometimes with dermal mucin; subcutis is typically spared. AESOP lymph nodes may show nonspecific sinusoidal lymphoplasmacytic infiltrates and endothelial proliferation. Demonstrate plasma-cell differentiation with CD138, CD38, and MUM1/IRF4. Establish light-chain restriction; POEMS-associated clones are characteristically lambda-restricted. Skin and lymph-node findings in AESOP are often reactive and nonspecific; IHC is used to exclude a primary vascular or lymphoid neoplasm rather than to establish the syndrome. Conventional plasma cell myeloma May share a plasma-cell clone but lacks the defining clinical constellation; POEMS often has low marrow burden and osteosclerotic rather than typical lytic lesions. CIDP and other neuropathies POEMS neuropathy is typically associated with a monoclonal plasma-cell disorder, elevated VEGF, and systemic features; evaluate the full criteria. Polycythemia vera or secondary erythrocytosis TEMPI requires the associated monoclonal gammopathy, telangiectasias, perinephric fluid, and intrapulmonary shunting; elevated erythropoietin favors secondary erythrocytosis. Reactive vascular proliferation / lymphoproliferative disorder In AESOP, the defining context is a plasmacytoma with an overlying extensive vascular skin patch; skin histology alone is not diagnostic. No single molecular alteration defines POEMS, TEMPI, or AESOP. Plasma-cell cytogenetic abnormalities may overlap with other plasma-cell neoplasms; VEGF is a clinically useful biomarker in POEMS rather than a defining tumor mutation. Do not require extensive marrow plasmacytosis for POEMS or TEMPI. Do not diagnose POEMS from neuropathy plus an M protein alone; apply the mandatory, major, and minor criteria. AESOP skin biopsy is typically reactive; the underlying plasmacytoma and clinical distribution establish the syndrome. All PathologyGPS · Hematopathology Plasma Cell Neoplasms and Other Diseases with Paraproteins A practical diagnostic reference for monoclonal gammopathies, monoclonal immunoglobulin-mediated organ injury, heavy chain diseases, plasma-cell tumors, and associated paraneoplastic syndromes. Emphasis is placed on quantitative diagnostic thresholds, tissue findings, clonality, and reciprocal differential diagnosis. Diagnostic Approach: Start with the Clinical and Laboratory Category 1. Identify the paraprotein Use serum and urine electrophoresis with immunofixation and serum free light chains. Determine heavy-chain class, light-chain type, and M-protein burden. 2. Determine whether the clone is clinically significant Separate asymptomatic precursor states from overt lymphoma or myeloma, and recognize organ injury caused by a small clone. 3. Apply the marrow thresholds MGUS: less than 10% clonal cells and no attributable end-organ injury. Smoldering myeloma: 10–60% clonal plasma cells and/or defined M-protein burden without a myeloma-defining event. Active myeloma requires SLiM-CRAB. 4. Let the affected tissue define deposition disease For renal lesions, integrate light microscopy, immunofluorescence, and electron microscopy. Distinguish Congo red-positive fibrils from nonfibrillar monoclonal immunoglobulin deposits. 5. Prove clonality and lineage Use plasma-cell markers, B-cell markers, light-chain restriction, and flow cytometry. A monoclonal protein alone does not identify the underlying neoplasm. 6. Recognize syndrome-level diagnoses POEMS, TEMPI, and AESOP are clinicopathologic syndromes; marrow plasma-cell burden may be low and tissue findings may be nonspecific. Critical principle: A monoclonal gammopathy is not synonymous with myeloma or lymphoma. The diagnosis depends on the clone, its burden, the paraprotein, tissue injury, and the presence or absence of myeloma-defining events. High-Yield Diagnostic Thresholds Use these thresholds with the full clinical and laboratory criteria; none should be interpreted in isolation. Category M-protein / marrow Required clinical status IgM MGUS IgM < 3 g/dL; marrow lymphoplasmacytic cells < 10% No attributable symptoms, cytopenias, hyperviscosity, adenopathy, or organomegaly Non-IgM MGUS M protein < 3 g/dL; clonal marrow plasma cells < 10% No attributable CRAB feature or myeloma-defining event Smoldering myeloma Marrow plasma cells 10–60%, and/or IgG/IgA M protein ≥ 3 g/dL or urine monoclonal protein ≥ 500 mg/24 h No SLiM-CRAB myeloma-defining event Active myeloma ≥ 10% clonal marrow plasma cells or biopsy-proven plasmacytoma At least one SLiM-CRAB myeloma-defining event Single lesion; marrow clonal plasma cells < 10% No additional lesions or myeloma-defining event plasma-search Search diagnoses and diagnostic criteria Search: SLiM-CRAB, Congo red, MYD88, IgM, lambda... plasma-group Collapse All Expand All diagnoses / syndromes Expand a diagnosis for clinical profile, criteria, morphology, IHC, and differentials. content: use client Follicular Dendritic Cell Sarcoma (FDCS) Mesenchymal Dendritic Cell Neoplasms Spindled-to-ovoid syncytial cells in whorls, fascicles, or storiform arrays with at least two follicular dendritic cell markers. A malignant stromal neoplasm showing follicular dendritic cell differentiation; it is not a B-cell lymphoma despite its frequent lymphocyte-rich background. Median age approximately 50 years; occurs across a broad age range. No consistent sex predilection. Nodal and extranodal disease; common extranodal sites include abdomen/retroperitoneum and upper aerodigestive tract. Usually a slowly enlarging, painless mass or isolated lymphadenopathy; abdominal tumors may cause pain. A subset is associated with hyaline-vascular Castleman disease or autoimmune/paraneoplastic syndromes. Identify a spindle, ovoid, or epithelioid neoplasm with a storiform, fascicular, whorled, or syncytial growth pattern. Look for indistinct cell borders, unevenly spaced nuclei, vesicular chromatin, small nucleoli, and intranuclear pseudoinclusions. Recognize admixed small lymphocytes, which may be T-cell predominant, B-cell predominant, or mixed; this background does not establish lymphoma. Confirm follicular dendritic differentiation with at least two FDC markers, preferably including CD21, CD23, CD35, or CXCL13. Show that the atypical spindle/epithelioid cells themselves express FDC markers; do not mistake reactive FDC meshworks for tumor-cell staining. Exclude a lymphoid neoplasm by demonstrating that the lesional spindle cells are not a clonal B- or T-cell population and by correlating lineage markers with morphology. Tumor cells are spindle, ovoid, or epithelioid and may vary in morphology within one tumor. Growth patterns include whorls, fascicles, syncytial sheets, nodules, and storiform arrays. Moderate eosinophilic cytoplasm and indistinct cell borders produce a syncytial appearance. Nuclei are elongated with vesicular chromatin, delicate membranes, and small but distinct nucleoli. Intranuclear pseudoinclusions and binucleated cells resembling benign FDCs are useful clues. Pleomorphism, multinucleation, necrosis, and increased mitotic activity occur in more aggressive examples. Small lymphocytes are typically interspersed; peripheral or perivascular lymphoid aggregates may be present. CD21, CD23, and CD35 highlight follicular dendritic differentiation; expression may be variable or focal. CXCL13 and clusterin are among the most frequently expressed and useful FDC markers. D2-40, SSTR2, fascin, FDCSP, and serglycin (SRGN) may provide additional support. Vimentin and EGFR are commonly expressed but are not lineage-specific. Cytokeratin, CD20, and TTF1 are usually negative; rare aberrant expression is reported. S100 is generally negative or only occasional/focal; interpret with a panel. Ki-67 is variable and is not independently diagnostic. EBV-positive inflammatory FDCS Usually liver or spleen, marked lymphoplasmacytic inflammation, EBER positivity, and often less extensive/variable FDC-marker expression; compare the separate entity below. Fibroblastic reticular cell tumor May overlap morphologically, but favors cytokeratin, SMA, and desmin; lacks the usual FDC marker profile and is generally S100-negative. Lymphoma (including Hodgkin lymphoma and large B-cell lymphoma) The neoplastic cells of FDCS are spindle/ovoid stromal cells expressing FDC markers, not a population expressing a coherent B- or T-cell lineage phenotype. Background lymphocytes may be reactive. Inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor Typically has myofibroblastic cytology and SMA expression; ALK or other kinase alterations may be present, while FDC markers are absent. Meningioma, thymoma, carcinoma, GIST, or undifferentiated sarcoma Use site, architecture, and a focused epithelial, mesenchymal, and FDC-marker panel; no single morphology mimic is reliably excluded by appearance alone. Recurrent alterations involve NF-κB pathway genes (including BIRC3, NFKBIA, TRAF3, CYLD, and TNFAIP3) and tumor suppressors such as CDKN2A, RB1, and TP53. BRAF p.V600E and other alterations occur only in subsets and are not required for diagnosis. Do not diagnose lymphoma solely because the lesion contains numerous lymphocytes. Require FDC-marker expression in the neoplastic spindle/epithelioid cells, not merely in entrapped reactive follicles. A single positive FDC marker is insufficient when morphology is atypical; use a panel. EBV-Positive Inflammatory Follicular Dendritic Cell Sarcoma EBER-positive spindle/oval tumor cells in a prominent lymphoplasmacytic background, usually in liver or spleen. An EBV-associated, generally indolent stromal neoplasm distinct from conventional FDCS, with characteristic inflammatory and clinicopathologic features. Predominantly young- to middle-aged adults; median age approximately 50–58 years. Marked female predominance in hepatic and splenic cases; sex distribution is less distinctive in colonic cases. Almost always liver or spleen; rare sites include colon, tonsil, bronchus, pancreas, and mesentery. Often asymptomatic or presents with abdominal pain/distention; fever, weight loss, malaise, anemia, or inflammatory laboratory abnormalities may occur. Identify atypical spindle-to-oval cells dispersed singly or in loose whorls/fascicles within a prominent lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate. Demonstrate EBV in the neoplastic cells by EBER in situ hybridization; both bland and pleomorphic tumor cells may be positive. Show FDC differentiation with CD21, CD23, CD35, CXCL13, D2-40, or CNA.42; staining may be focal or variable. Recognize rare cases with an SMA-positive fibroblastic/myoid phenotype and absent conventional FDC markers. Exclude lymphoma by confirming that the atypical spindle cells, rather than background lymphocytes, are EBER-positive stromal cells; background B cells, T cells, and plasma cells are usually mixed/polytypic. Spindle-to-oval tumor cells are singly dispersed or form loose whorls and fascicles. A dense lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate is a defining background feature; reactive follicles may be present. Tumor cells have indistinct borders, scant-to-moderate cytoplasm, vesicular nuclei, stippled chromatin, and small central nucleoli. Atypia is variable, with bland cells admixed with enlarged, folded, or hyperchromatic forms; Reed–Sternberg-like cells may occur. Mitotic figures are usually rare; hemorrhage and necrosis may be present. Fibrinoid vascular wall deposits, granulomas, eosinophils, xanthomatous histiocytes, or monocytoid B-cell aggregates may be seen. CD21, CD23, CD35, CXCL13, D2-40, and CNA.42 are variably positive in tumor cells. SMA may be positive in rare cases with a fibroblastic/myoid phenotype. LMP1 is frequently expressed in tumor cells. EBER in situ hybridization is consistently positive in the neoplastic spindle/oval cells. Background lymphocytes comprise mixed CD20-positive B cells and CD3-positive T cells. Plasma cells are polytypic; IgG4-rich plasma cells may be conspicuous in some cases. Conventional follicular dendritic cell sarcoma Usually more tumor-cell-rich with classic syncytial, whorled, fascicular, or storiform growth; EBV is not a defining feature. Inflammatory EBV-positive FDCS is typically liver/spleen-centered and lymphoplasmacytic. May show spindle cells and inflammation, but usually expresses cytokeratin/SMA/desmin and lacks the consistent tumor-cell EBER positivity characteristic of this entity. EBV-positive lymphoma Lymphoma shows EBV-positive atypical lymphoid cells with B-, T-, or other hematolymphoid lineage markers; here EBER labels the spindle stromal tumor cells and the background lymphocytes are mixed and generally non-atypical. Often has well-defined amphophilic cytoplasm and SMA expression, may harbor ALK or another kinase rearrangement, and is generally EBER-negative. Florid lymphoid hyperplasia / inflammatory polyp Predominantly lymphoid without a significant atypical spindle-cell component; usually lacks tumor-cell EBER and FDC-marker expression. EBER in situ hybridization is the key diagnostic assay; clonal EBV is consistently associated with the neoplastic cells. LMP1 alterations have been reported, but broader genomic findings are not sufficiently established for routine diagnosis. Interpret EBER at the cellular level: positivity must involve the spindle/oval tumor cells, not only scattered background lymphocytes. A lymphoplasmacytic background does not establish lymphoma; assess the lineage and clonality of the atypical cells. Fibroblastic Reticular Cell Tumor (FRCT) Spindle-to-ovoid stromal tumor with myofibroblastic differentiation, often cytokeratin-positive, but negative for FDC markers and S100. A rare neoplasm of putative fibroblastic reticular cell origin with morphologic overlap with other dendritic stromal tumors. Usually presents in the sixth to seventh decade; reported age range is broad (13–80 years). No sex predilection. Most often an isolated lymph node mass; extranodal sites include spleen, soft tissue, liver, lung, kidney, breast, adrenal gland, and bone. Typically presents as lymphadenopathy or a newly developed mass. Identify a spindle-to-ovoid cell neoplasm arranged in whorls, fascicles, sheets, or storiform arrays. Look for an accompanying lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate and variable nuclear pleomorphism or multinucleated tumor cells. Demonstrate one or more of cytokeratin, actin/SMA, or desmin in the lesional cells, often accentuating delicate cell processes. Show absence of the usual FDC markers (CD21, CD23, CD35, CXCL13) and interdigitating dendritic cell marker S100. Exclude metastatic carcinoma when cytokeratin is positive by integrating site, morphology, and a focused epithelial panel. The diagnosis is stromal, not lymphoid: the spindle cells should not show a coherent B- or T-cell lineage phenotype. Spindle-to-oval cells form whorled, fascicular, sheet-like, or storiform patterns. A lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate commonly accompanies the tumor cells. Nuclear pleomorphism is variable; multinucleated or giant cells may be present. Intercellular collagen fibrils are a helpful but neither constant nor specific feature. Morphology overlaps with FDCS and interdigitating dendritic cell sarcoma. Cytokeratin is positive in approximately two thirds of cases and may highlight delicate cell processes. SMA/actin and desmin are variably positive. Vimentin, fascin, L-caldesmon, and EMA are often positive. CD21, CD23, CD35, and CXCL13 are typically negative, arguing against FDC differentiation. S100 is typically negative, arguing against interdigitating dendritic cell differentiation. Follicular dendritic cell sarcoma Shares spindle/ovoid morphology and lymphocytes, but FDCS expresses FDC markers (CD21, CD23, CD35, CXCL13, clusterin); FRCT generally does not. Usually EBER-positive in tumor cells with a prominent lymphoplasmacytic background; FRCT lacks consistent EBV association and favors a myofibroblastic/cytokeratin phenotype. Interdigitating dendritic cell sarcoma Typically S100-positive and often expresses other histiocytic/dendritic markers; FRCT is usually S100-negative and may express cytokeratin, SMA, and desmin. Metastatic carcinoma Can be cytokeratin-positive; use clinical history, epithelial differentiation markers, and the characteristic stromal spindle-cell morphology. Cytokeratin alone does not establish carcinoma. Lymphoma Lymphoma is composed of neoplastic lymphoid cells expressing lineage markers; FRCT is a spindle-cell stromal proliferation with myofibroblastic/reticular-cell markers. Cytokeratin positivity does not automatically indicate metastatic carcinoma. Do not diagnose FRCT without excluding FDCS and interdigitating dendritic cell sarcoma with appropriate lineage markers. Intranodal Palisaded Myofibroblastoma Myofibroblastic Tumors Benign intranodal spindle-cell lesion with palisading around amianthoid-like collagen bodies and a myoid immunophenotype. A benign lymph node-based smooth muscle/myofibroblastic stromal neoplasm, usually involving an inguinal node. Usually adults in the fifth or sixth decade; reported age range 19–78 years. Male predominance (approximately 2:1). Predominantly inguinal lymph nodes; rare axillary, cervical, submandibular, mediastinal, and retroperitoneal sites. Solitary, slowly growing, mobile, usually painless mass. Confirm that the lesion is centered in a lymph node and forms a benign spindle-cell proliferation. Identify short fascicles and whorls of bland spindle cells with variably shaped dense collagenous (amianthoid-like) bodies. Look for focal vague nuclear palisading around hyalinized vessels or collagenous bodies. Demonstrate myoid differentiation with SMA and muscle-specific actin; nuclear beta-catenin and cyclin D1 are desirable supportive findings. Exclude Kaposi sarcoma and other vascular lesions with HHV8 and endothelial markers when indicated. The lesion is not lymphoma: the proliferating cells are bland myofibroblastic spindle cells rather than a clonal lymphoid population. Tumor nodules are composed of moderately to highly cellular short fascicles and whorls of spindle cells. Dense, variably shaped collagenous bodies are characteristic. Hyalinized blood vessels may be surrounded by vague nuclear palisading. Tumor cells have scant, lightly eosinophilic cytoplasm and bland elongated or focally wavy nuclei. Perinuclear vacuoles and rounded salmon-colored intracytoplasmic inclusions are common. Extravasated erythrocytes and hemosiderin are frequent; mitotic activity is usually low. Diffuse vimentin, SMA, and muscle-specific actin support myofibroblastic differentiation. Calponin, D2-40, factor XIIIa, nuclear beta-catenin, and cyclin D1 are variably positive. Desmin is usually focal or variable. Ki-67 is typically low (less than 5%). Cytokeratins, S100, CD21/CD23/CD35, CD31/CD34, factor VIII, and HHV8 are negative. Kaposi sarcoma Shows slit-like vascular spaces and HHV8 positivity; intranodal palisaded myofibroblastoma is HHV8-negative and contains characteristic collagenous bodies. Usually has syncytial spindle/ovoid cells with FDC-marker expression and greater cytologic variability; this lesion is bland and myoid-marker-positive. Schwannoma / other nerve sheath tumor Usually expresses S100 and/or SOX10 and shows characteristic nerve-sheath architecture; intranodal palisaded myofibroblastoma is generally negative. Vascular neoplasm Endothelial markers (CD31, ERG, CD34) highlight lesional cells in vascular tumors; they are negative in this myofibroblastic lesion. Lymphoma replaces nodal tissue with atypical lymphoid cells and lineage-marker expression; here the lesional component is a bland spindle-cell myofibroblastic proliferation. CTNNB1 exon 3 gain-of-function mutations have been reported and may explain nuclear beta-catenin expression; molecular testing is not required for routine diagnosis. Do not mistake extravasated erythrocytes and hemosiderin for a vascular neoplasm. The collagenous bodies and myofibroblastic phenotype are more diagnostically useful than focal palisading alone. Littoral Cell Angioma Splenic Vascular-Stromal Tumors Anastomosing, variably dilated splenic sinus-like channels with a dual endothelial and histiocytic phenotype. A benign vascular tumor unique to the spleen, derived from or resembling red-pulp littoral cells. Usually adults in the fourth to seventh decades; any age is possible. Unique to the spleen; often multiple and associated with splenomegaly. Usually incidental; symptomatic cases may show abdominal pain, fever, anemia, thrombocytopenia, or hypersplenism. Concurrent malignancy or immune dysregulatory conditions have been reported, although ascertainment bias may contribute. Identify a circumscribed splenic red-pulp lesion composed of variably sized, blood-filled anastomosing channels, often cystically dilated. Recognize plump cuboidal or tall endothelial lining cells with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm and possible intraluminal sloughing. Look for hemophagocytosis, hemosiderin, and hyaline globules within tumor cells. Confirm dual endothelial and histiocytic differentiation: CD31/ERG/von Willebrand factor together with CD163/CD68/lysozyme. Exclude lymphoma by confirming a vascular channel-forming lesion rather than a mass of atypical lymphoid cells; the lesional cells express endothelial/histiocytic markers, not B- or T-cell lineage markers. Discrete red-pulp lesion with blood-filled anastomosing channels resembling expanded splenic sinuses. Channels vary markedly in caliber and may be cystically dilated. Lining cells are plump cuboidal or tall, with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm and protrusion into the lumen. Tumor cells may slough into lumina and show hemophagocytosis, hemosiderin, or eosinophilic hyaline globules. Papillary fronds may project into vascular spaces. Atypia, necrosis, and mitotic figures are generally absent; extramedullary hematopoiesis may coexist. Endothelial markers: CD31, ERG, and von Willebrand factor are positive. Histiocytic markers: CD163, CD68, and lysozyme are positive. SIRP-alpha is a useful littoral-cell-associated marker. CD8 and CD34 are often negative in tumor cells; WT1 is also often negative. CD207, CD21, claudin-5, and VEGFR2 may be expressed; interpret in the context of the dual phenotype. Splenic hamartoma Hamartoma is disorganized red-pulp tissue with mixed sinus, capillary, and venous channels and macrophages; it lacks the characteristic expansile anastomosing littoral-cell channels with dual endothelial-histiocytic tumor-cell phenotype. Sclerosing angiomatoid nodular transformation (SANT) Shows multiple angiomatoid nodules separated by dense fibrosclerotic stroma and a characteristic mixture of sinusoidal, capillary, and venous vessels. Splenic hemangioma Usually comprises one predominant vessel type (commonly CD31+/CD34+/CD8− capillaries) and lacks the characteristic histiocytic marker expression of littoral cell angioma. Littoral cell hemangioendothelioma / angiosarcoma Consider when there are solid areas, cytologic atypia, mitotic activity, destructive growth, or metastases; ordinary littoral cell angioma is cytologically bland and benign. Splenic lymphoma Lymphoma forms a lymphoid infiltrate or mass with B-/T-cell lineage markers and often architectural effacement; littoral cell angioma forms vascular channels with endothelial and histiocytic differentiation. Do not interpret CD31 positivity alone as proof of conventional hemangioma; the histiocytic component is a defining clue. Atypia, solid growth, or metastatic behavior should prompt reconsideration of littoral cell hemangioendothelioma or angiosarcoma. Splenic Hamartoma Circumscribed but microscopically often ill-defined nodule of disorganized red pulp without well-formed white pulp. A benign splenic parenchymal lesion composed of disorganized red-pulp elements. Can occur at any age, including childhood; median age approximately 40 years. Spleen only. Usually incidental; a minority present with mass-related discomfort, rupture, splenomegaly, or hypersplenism-related cytopenias. Identify a circumscribed splenic nodule composed of disorganized red-pulp elements. Confirm the absence of a well-formed white-pulp component. Recognize irregular sinusoidal channels lined by plump endothelium with loose macrophage aggregates and fibrovascular stroma. Use CD8 to highlight splenic sinusoidal endothelium; CD31 highlights the vascular channels, while CD68/CD163 highlight admixed macrophages. Exclude lymphoma by identifying disorganized but recognizable red-pulp vascular and macrophage components rather than a monomorphic or atypical lymphoid proliferation. Grossly circumscribed nodule, although the microscopic interface may be less sharply defined. Irregularly distributed sinusoidal channels are lined by plump endothelial cells. Loose aggregates of macrophages and fibrovascular stroma reproduce disorganized red-pulp architecture. A well-formed white-pulp component is absent; small lymphoid aggregates may still be present. Additional findings may include sclerosis, calcification, hemorrhage, peliosis, plasmacytosis, extramedullary hematopoiesis, and xanthomatous histiocytes. Rare bizarre stromal/reticulum cells may show cytokeratin, actin, or desmin expression. Splenic sinusoids: CD8-positive, CD31-positive, CD34-negative. Capillaries: CD34-positive and CD31-positive, CD8-negative. Small veins: CD31-positive, CD34-negative, CD8-negative. Admixed macrophages are CD68-positive and CD163-positive. CD8 is particularly useful to demonstrate disorganized splenic sinusoidal elements. Littoral cell angioma Shows more discrete, often multiple anastomosing and dilated vascular channels lined by cells with dual endothelial-histiocytic phenotype; hamartoma recapitulates disorganized red pulp. Sclerosing angiomatoid nodular transformation Has discrete angiomatoid nodules with concentric collagen/fibrinoid rims and intervening fibrosclerotic stroma; hamartoma lacks this nodular architecture. Usually a proliferation of one vessel type, commonly CD31+/CD34+/CD8− capillaries, rather than mixed disorganized red-pulp elements. Contains atypical spindle cells in a lymphoplasmacytic background with tumor-cell EBER and FDC markers; hamartoma is a vascular-red-pulp lesion. Shows a clonal lymphoid population with lineage-marker expression and often architectural replacement; hamartoma retains a disorganized red-pulp vascular framework. A few lymphoid aggregates do not constitute a white-pulp component or establish lymphoma. Assess the vascular subtypes with CD8, CD31, and CD34 rather than relying on a single endothelial marker. Sclerosing Angiomatoid Nodular Transformation (SANT) of the Spleen Multiple angiomatoid nodules with concentric collagenous/fibrinoid rims and intervening fibrosclerotic stroma. A benign, circumscribed splenic lesion characterized by a multinodular vascular architecture and central stellate fibrosis. Most often middle-aged adults; median age approximately 46 years, but any age may be affected. Female predominance. Usually incidental on imaging; symptomatic cases may have abdominal discomfort, a palpable mass, or hypersplenism-related cytopenias. Identify a circumscribed splenic lesion composed of multiple round or convoluted angiomatoid nodules. Look for concentric collagenous or fibrinoid material surrounding the nodules and intervening fibrosclerotic stroma. Demonstrate a mixture of splenic red-pulp vessel types: sinusoidal, capillary, and venous channels. Use CD31 with CD8 and CD34 to characterize the three vascular components; the mixed profile supports SANT. Exclude lymphoma by recognizing a structured angiomatoid vascular lesion with sclerosis rather than a clonal lymphoid proliferation. Multiple round or convoluted angiomatoid nodules may coalesce. Nodules are surrounded by concentric layers of collagen or fibrinoid material. Vascular spaces are slit-like, ectatic, or irregular and contain abundant erythrocytes. Lining endothelial cells are attenuated or plump without significant cytologic atypia or mitotic activity. Intervening stroma is densely fibrotic or fibromyxoid and may contain lymphocytes, plasma cells, eosinophils, and hemosiderin-laden macrophages. All vascular components express CD31. Sinusoidal vessels: CD8-positive and CD34-negative. Capillaries: CD8-negative and CD34-positive. Venous channels: CD8-negative and CD34-negative. The characteristic mixed vascular immunophenotype is more informative than any single marker. Lacks discrete angiomatoid nodules and concentric collagenous rims; instead shows disorganized red-pulp tissue without a well-formed white-pulp component. Shows anastomosing, often cystically dilated sinus-like channels with dual endothelial-histiocytic phenotype; SANT has nodules with concentric sclerosis and mixed vessel types. Usually comprises a single vessel type, commonly capillaries (CD31+/CD34+/CD8−), rather than the three-vessel pattern of SANT. Lymphoma is a lymphoid proliferation with lineage-marker expression; SANT is a non-lymphoid vascular-stromal lesion with angiomatoid nodules and fibrosis. CTNNB1 exon 3 deletions have been reported in a subset, but molecular testing is not established as a routine diagnostic requirement. Do not call SANT a multinodular hemangioma; the defining architecture is angiomatoid nodules with intervening sclerosis and a mixed vascular phenotype. IgG4-related disease and EBV infection are not established etiologies. Conventional FDCS Spindle/ovoid syncytial cells; whorls, fascicles, storiform sheets; admixed small lymphocytes CD21/CD23/CD35, CXCL13, clusterin; often D2-40/SSTR2; usually S100− Tumor cells are stromal and FDC-marker-positive, not a clonal B-/T-cell population. Spindle/oval cells singly or in loose fascicles amid dense lymphoplasmacytic inflammation EBER+ in tumor cells; variable CD21/CD23/CD35/CXCL13/D2-40; LMP1 often+ EBER labels atypical spindle cells; background lymphocytes are mixed and plasma cells polytypic. Spindle/ovoid cells in whorls, fascicles, sheets; lymphoplasmacytic background; collagen fibrils may occur Variable cytokeratin, SMA/actin, desmin; often vimentin/fascin/EMA; CD21/CD35/CXCL13−, S100− Myofibroblastic/reticular stromal phenotype rather than lymphoid lineage; exclude metastatic carcinoma if keratin+. Anastomosing, dilated red-pulp sinus-like channels; plump lining cells; hemophagocytosis/hemosiderin Endothelial: CD31/ERG/vWF+; histiocytic: CD163/CD68/lysozyme+; often CD34−/CD8− Dual endothelial-histiocytic phenotype in vascular channels; no clonal lymphoid mass. Disorganized red-pulp sinusoids, macrophages, and fibrovascular stroma; no well-formed white pulp Sinusoids CD8+/CD31+/CD34−; capillaries CD34+/CD31+; macrophages CD68+/CD163+ Mixed red-pulp architecture with sinusoidal CD8; not a monomorphic lymphoid proliferation. SANT Multiple angiomatoid nodules with concentric collagen/fibrinoid rims and fibrosclerotic septa All vessels CD31+; sinusoids CD8+/CD34−; capillaries CD34+/CD8−; veins CD8−/CD34− Three-vessel phenotype in a sclerosing multinodular architecture, not lymphoma. Entity Typical histology Key immunophenotype How to distinguish from lymphoma bg-slate-50 bg-white font-semibold text-slate-900 text-slate-700 All Categories PathologyGPS · Hematopathology Stroma-Derived Neoplasms of Lymphoid Tissues Diagnostic reference to mesenchymal dendritic cell neoplasms, intranodal myofibroblastic tumors, and splenic vascular-stromal lesions. These entities arise from stromal or vascular elements rather than hematopoietic lymphoid cells. Diagnostic Framework: Stromal Neoplasm or Lymphoma? The key distinction is the identity of the neoplastic cells. In stromal tumors, the lesional cells express follicular dendritic, fibroblastic/myofibroblastic, endothelial, or histiocytic markers. Lymphocytes may be numerous in the background but should be separately characterized rather than assumed to be the tumor population. 1 · Identify the lesional cell Determine whether the atypical population is spindle/epithelioid stromal, endothelial, histiocytic, or lymphoid. 2 · Apply lineage-directed IHC Use FDC markers, SMA/desmin/cytokeratin, endothelial markers, and histiocytic markers according to morphology. 3 · Exclude lymphoma Assess CD45, B- and T-cell markers, light-chain pattern, EBER localization, and clonality when indicated; interpret these in the actual atypical cells. Mesenchymal Dendritic Cell Neoplasms: Histology, IHC, and Exclusion of Lymphoma Splenic Vascular-Stromal Tumors: Histology, IHC, and Exclusion of Lymphoma Practical IHC Strategy Spindle-cell lesion with lymphocytes: start with CD21, CD23, CD35, CXCL13, clusterin, S100, cytokeratin, SMA, and desmin; add EBER when inflammatory FDCS is considered. Splenic vascular lesion: use CD31/ERG with CD8 and CD34 to map vessel types; add CD163/CD68/lysozyme when littoral cell angioma is considered. Possible lymphoma: apply CD45, CD20/PAX5, CD3, and appropriate subtype markers to the atypical population. EBER must be localized to tumor cells, not simply reported as positive in the section. Do not overinterpret isolated markers: CD31 alone does not classify a splenic vascular lesion; cytokeratin alone does not prove carcinoma; CD21 in reactive follicles does not prove FDCS. stroma-search Search diagnoses and diagnostic features Search: CD21, EBER, CD8, SANT, lymphoma... stroma-group Category Collapse All Expand All entities Open an entity for clinical profile, diagnostic criteria, histology, IHC, and differential diagnosis.
