title: Conjunctiva Caruncle Tumors
content: use client Epithelial conjunctival inclusion cyst Tumor-like lesion Any age; bulbar conjunctiva or caruncle; transparent/cloudy, compressible cyst. Benign cyst within substantia propria; lining matches conjunctival or caruncular epithelium. Nonkeratinizing stratified squamous lining, with or without goblet cells; proteinaceous contents; possible stromal fibrosis/inflammation. Conjunctival crypts of Henle lack a true cystic epithelial inclusion; lymphangiectasia is endothelial-lined; filtration bleb lacks epithelial lining; caruncular infundibular cyst/steatocystoma have cutaneous-type lining. None. Reactive epithelial hyperplasia Children or adults; often limbal/bulbar or fornix/tarsal conjunctiva; fleshy or white thickening. Reactive proliferation in an irritative/inflammatory setting; cytology remains benign and maturation is preserved. Pseudoepitheliomatous pattern: acanthosis with orderly maturation, sometimes surface keratinization. Pseudoglandular pattern: prominent glands of Henle lined by squamous epithelium with goblet cells and mucin. Papilloma has fibrovascular fronds; CSIN shows dysplasia and loss of maturation; SCC with mucinous differentiation shows atypia, mitoses, intracytoplasmic mucin, and often invasion. No established recurrent molecular alteration. Papillary and follicular conjunctivitis Inflammatory lesion All ages; papillary pattern usually upper tarsal conjunctiva (often allergic/contact lens); follicular pattern palpebral, forniceal, or bulbar; discharge and irritation. Papillae have vascular fibrovascular cores; follicles are discrete reactive lymphoid aggregates with no central vascular core. Papillary: edematous fibrovascular stromal cores with perpendicular capillaries, covered by non-dysplastic epithelium; mixed inflammatory cells including eosinophils/mast cells. Follicular: reactive lymphoid follicles in substantia propria. Reactive lymphoid hyperplasia forms a mass rather than multiple follicles; conjunctival lymphoma may mimic follicular conjunctivitis and requires clonality/IHC workup. Sarcoid may form nodules. Molecular studies only if lymphoma is suspected. Pterygium and pinguecula Degenerative lesion Usually adults with chronic UV exposure; interpalpebral bulbar conjunctiva; often nasal; irritation or cosmetic concern. Pinguecula is confined to paralimbal conjunctiva; pterygium crosses limbus and extends onto cornea; actinic elastosis is characteristic. Basophilic elastotic degeneration of substantia propria with fibrosis and telangiectasia; overlying epithelium may show acanthosis, metaplasia, or goblet cell hyperplasia; pterygium may efface peripheral Bowman layer. CSIN/SCC may arise in or mimic these lesions; look for epithelial dysplasia or stromal invasion. Pinguecula does not cross onto cornea. No routine diagnostic molecular test. Epibulbar choristoma Choristoma Usually congenital and recognized in childhood; inferotemporal limbus (dermoid), superotemporal conjunctiva (dermolipoma); firm white or soft yellow mass. Mature ectopic tissue at conjunctival/corneal surface; classify as dermoid, dermolipoma, or complex choristoma by tissue composition. Dermoid: collagenous tissue with squamous epithelium and skin appendages. Dermolipoma: abundant mature adipose tissue. Complex choristoma: combinations of lacrimal gland, cartilage, muscle, nerve, bone, or other mature tissues. Dermolipoma vs orbital fat prolapse: conjunctiva is tethered in dermolipoma but mobile over prolapsed orbital fat; lacrimal gland hamartoma may mimic glandular complex choristoma. Epibulbar osseous choristoma Congenital, often detected before age 20; slight female predominance; usually superotemporal episcleral/conjunctival mass, firm and yellow-white. Mature lamellar bone in an ectopic episcleral location; no atypia or destructive growth. Compact lamellar bone with normal osteocytes and possible Haversian canals; periosteum and osteogenic layer; marrow usually absent. Complex choristoma may contain bone but has additional heterotopic tissues; extraskeletal osteosarcoma shows cytologic atypia, malignant osteoid, and destructive infiltration. Conjunctival squamous papilloma Benign epithelial tumor Often men aged 21–40; also children/adolescents; bulbar or palpebral conjunctiva, frequently caruncle; red-pink, vascular, pedunculated or sessile papillary lesion. Exophytic or inverted squamous proliferation with fibrovascular cores and goblet cells; no high-grade dysplasia or destructive invasion. Exophytic fronds lined by nonkeratinizing squamous epithelium with goblet cells; inverted lesions are circumscribed endophytic proliferations; koilocytic change or low-grade dysplasia may occur. CSIN shows disordered maturation and cytologic atypia; SCC shows high-grade atypia and/or invasion; inverted papilloma can mimic SCC but lacks significant atypia and destructive infiltration. Low-risk HPV6/11 common; HPV testing is not required. Block p16 suggests high-risk HPV, not a universal feature. Conjunctival oncocytoma Usually older adults; caruncle, arising commonly from accessory lacrimal glands; circumscribed reddish, brown, or bluish nodule. Well-circumscribed solid/cystic oncocytic epithelial neoplasm without significant atypia, mitoses, or infiltrative margins. Sheets, nests, or microcysts of columnar oncocytes with abundant granular eosinophilic cytoplasm and central nuclei; PAS-positive luminal material may be present. Oncocytic mucoepidermoid, secretory, acinic cell, or apocrine carcinoma show atypia, mitoses, or infiltration; clinical mimics include melanoma, papilloma, and cyst. Mitochondrial DNA mutations have been reported in accessory lacrimal gland oncocytoma; not routinely needed. Hereditary benign intraepithelial dyskeratosis Inherited epithelial disorder Usually children/families from Haliwa-Saponi ancestry in North Carolina; bilateral limbal conjunctival plaques with possible oral mucosal lesions. Sharply demarcated acanthotic epithelium with prominent dyskeratosis but no epithelial dysplasia or invasion. Marked acanthosis and multilayered parakeratosis; numerous dyskeratotic cells with pyknotic nuclei; intact basement membrane; chronic stromal inflammation/telangiectasia. CSIN/CIS shows nuclear pleomorphism, increased N:C ratio, atypical mitoses, and loss of maturation; NLRP1-associated multiple self-healing palmoplantar carcinoma may have similar mucosal lesions but characteristic skin tumors. Autosomal dominant; locus mapped to 4q35 with copy-number duplication; no established causative protein-coding gene. Conjunctival squamous intraepithelial neoplasia Preinvasive epithelial neoplasm Usually middle-aged/older adults; sun-exposed interpalpebral limbus and bulbar conjunctiva; gelatinous, leukoplakic, or papilliform lesion. Squamous dysplasia confined to epithelium; basement membrane intact; grade by epithelial thickness involved. Atypical squamous cells, nuclear enlargement/hyperchromasia, increased N:C ratio, loss of polarity/maturation, and mitoses above basal layer; mild lower third, moderate middle third, severe upper third, CIS full thickness. Reactive hyperplasia retains orderly maturation and bland nuclei; papilloma has fibrovascular cores; invasive SCC breaches basement membrane; sebaceous intraepithelial neoplasia is a consideration in basaloid lesions. UV-associated TP53/TERT promoter alterations; high-risk HPV in a subset; p16 block staining may support HPV association but is not specific. Conjunctival squamous cell carcinoma Malignant epithelial tumor Usually older adults, more common in men in temperate regions; HIV/immunosuppression-associated disease may occur younger and in women; interpalpebral limbus/nasal bulbar conjunctiva. Invasive squamous malignancy with basement membrane breach and stromal invasion; assess depth, margins, PNI/LVI, and adjacent cornea/orbit. Conventional keratinizing or nonkeratinizing SCC; basaloid, spindle, mucinous, pigmented, or acantholytic patterns; desmoplasia and perineural/vascular invasion may occur. CSIN lacks stromal invasion; reactive hyperplasia lacks atypia; basaloid lesions: sebaceous carcinoma or BCC; spindle lesions: melanoma or atypical fibroxanthoma; mucinous pattern: adenosquamous carcinoma. UV-associated TP53 and TERT promoter mutations; EGFR alterations reported; HPV-associated subset. Molecular testing is not required for routine diagnosis. Adenosquamous carcinoma Rare; adults; conjunctiva, often ocular surface; mass may resemble invasive SCC. Invasive carcinoma showing both squamous and true glandular/mucin-producing differentiation. Intermixed malignant squamous areas and glandular structures lined by mucin-producing cells; destructive stromal invasion; mucin stains highlight glandular component. SCC with mucinous differentiation has intracytoplasmic mucin but no true gland formation; reactive pseudoglands are bland and noninvasive; metastatic adenocarcinoma requires clinical exclusion. No routinely established diagnostic molecular alteration. Benign epithelial melanosis of the conjunctiva Benign melanocytic lesion Often younger or middle-aged individuals with darker complexion; usually bilateral, diffuse or patchy flat brown pigmentation, often perilimbal. Increased basal epithelial melanin without increased melanocyte number or atypia. Melanin pigment in basal epithelial cells; melanocyte density and morphology remain essentially normal; melanophages may be present in stroma. C-MIL shows increased atypical intraepithelial melanocytes; nevus shows nests; oculodermal melanocytosis involves deeper ocular tissues and often periocular skin. Junctional, compound, and subepithelial conjunctival nevi Benign melanocytic tumor Usually children or young adults; commonly bulbar conjunctiva near limbus; often stable, circumscribed, sometimes cystic pigmented lesion. Benign nevus cells arranged in junctional, compound, or subepithelial compartments; maturation with depth and absence of destructive invasion. Junctional nests along epithelial-stromal junction; compound lesions include epithelial nests and stromal nevus cells; subepithelial nevi lack junctional component; epithelial inclusion cysts are common. C-MIL is a flat atypical intraepithelial proliferation; melanoma shows destructive stromal invasion, atypia, mitoses, necrosis, or loss of maturation; inflamed juvenile nevus may show alarming atypia. BRAF mutations occur in a subset; molecular testing is not routine. Inflamed juvenile conjunctival nevus Children/adolescents; often bulbar conjunctiva near limbus; rapidly changing, red, raised, inflamed pigmented or amelanotic lesion. Junctional/compound nevus with prominent inflammation and reactive atypia; interpret age, architecture, maturation, and deep component together. Large epithelioid or spindle nevus cells with prominent nucleoli may occur; dense lymphocytic inflammation; maturation with depth and lack of deep mitoses/necrosis favor benignity. Conjunctival melanoma shows destructive invasion, deep mitoses, necrosis, marked atypia, or atypical mitoses; C-MIL is intraepithelial without a stromal nevus component. No routine molecular test. Blue nevus of the conjunctiva Usually adults; often caruncle or bulbar conjunctiva; blue-gray to slate-colored, well-circumscribed lesion. Dermal/subepithelial dendritic or cellular melanocytes containing melanin; no junctional atypia or destructive invasion. Dendritic blue nevus: pigmented spindle/dendritic melanocytes in collagenous stroma. Cellular blue nevus: cellular fascicles/nests of heavily pigmented spindle cells, usually circumscribed. Melanoma shows significant atypia, mitoses, necrosis, infiltrative growth; melanocytoma/combined nevus may show additional components; melanoma metastasis requires clinical correlation. No routinely useful molecular testing; WNT/β-catenin distinction is relevant to deep penetrating melanocytoma, not conventional blue nevus. WNT-activated deep penetrating / plexiform melanocytoma (nevus) Benign/intermediate melanocytic tumor Usually presents as a component of a combined conjunctival nevus; rare; often pigmented lesion. Deep plexiform melanocytic proliferation with WNT/β-catenin pathway activation; assess for atypia, mitoses, and destructive growth. Plexiform/nested deep dermal melanocytes with pigmented dendritic and epithelioid cells; nuclear β-catenin supports pathway activation; may coexist with conventional nevus components. Conventional blue nevus lacks nuclear β-catenin; melanoma shows destructive growth, significant atypia, mitoses, or necrosis; combined nevus contains separate conventional components. WNT pathway activation, commonly involving CTNNB1/β-catenin signaling; nuclear β-catenin is diagnostically useful. Combined nevus Usually young to middle-aged; conjunctiva; pigmented lesion with mixed clinical/microscopic appearance. At least two morphologically distinct nevus components in one lesion; exclude melanoma arising in a nevus. May combine conventional nevus with blue, granular cell, balloon cell, or deep penetrating melanocytoma components; evaluate each component and deep base for atypia. Melanoma ex nevus shows a discrete atypical proliferative component, destructive invasion, mitoses, or necrosis; single-component nevi lack the mixed architecture. Molecular testing is not routinely required; β-catenin IHC may help identify WNT-activated component. Conjunctival melanocytic intraepithelial lesion Preinvasive melanocytic neoplasm Usually middle-aged/older adults; unilateral, often multifocal flat irregular brown pigmentation of bulbar/limbal conjunctiva; may wax and wane. Increased atypical melanocytes confined to conjunctival epithelium; classify low-grade, high-grade, or melanoma in situ; no stromal invasion. Increased basal melanocytes with atypia; single-cell, nested, confluent, or pagetoid spread; melanoma in situ often severe atypia involving most/full epithelial thickness; basement membrane intact. Benign epithelial melanosis has pigment without melanocytic hyperplasia; nevus has nested maturation; invasive melanoma breaches basement membrane; pigmented CSIN is keratinocytic dysplasia with melanocytic colonization. TERT promoter mutations reported in a minority; FISH copy-number changes (RREB1, MYB, CCND1) may help in difficult cases; melan-A/SOX10/HMB45 confirm lineage. Conjunctival melanoma Malignant melanocytic tumor Usually adults >50; no clear sex predilection; most often bulbar conjunctiva near limbus; pigmented or amelanotic nodular/flat lesion with feeder vessels. Severe melanocytic atypia with stromal invasion; document thickness, ulceration, mitotic activity, margins, and LVI/PNI. Radial intraepithelial component may be pagetoid, nested, or lentiginous; invasive component forms atypical melanocytic nests/sheets in stroma; ulceration, mitoses, satellites, and neurotropism may occur. C-MIL/melanoma in situ has no stromal invasion; nevus may show junctional activity/pagetoid spread but matures with depth and lacks destructive growth; pseudoglands of Henle involvement is not invasion. NF1, BRAF, and NRAS are common drivers; TERT promoter mutations and 10q loss associate with adverse behavior; test advanced/metastatic tumors for actionable alterations. All Tumor-like / Reactive Benign Epithelial Premalignant / Malignant Epithelial Benign Melanocytic Premalignant / Malignant Melanocytic Pathology GPS Head & Neck Home / / Eye & Conjunctiva Ocular Surface Pathology Tumors and Tumor-Like Lesions of the Conjunctiva and Caruncle A morphology-first guide to conjunctival and caruncular cysts, reactive and degenerative lesions, choristomas, epithelial neoplasms, and melanocytic proliferations. Diagnostic approach 1. Establish the compartment. Distinguish epithelial, stromal, melanocytic, and choristomatous lesions; note limbal, bulbar, forniceal, palpebral, or caruncular location. 2. Assess epithelial integrity. For squamous lesions, separate reactive hyperplasia, intraepithelial dysplasia, and invasive carcinoma by cytology, maturation, and basement-membrane breach. 3. For pigmented lesions, map the cells. Determine whether melanocytes are increased within epithelium, nested as a nevus, or invading substantia propria. Quick diagnostic comparison Core morphologic distinction for the major conjunctival lesion groups. Group Key histology Diagnostic boundary Reactive / degenerative Bland epithelium, reactive follicles, or actinic elastosis No epithelial dysplasia or destructive invasion Mature ectopic tissue, including skin appendages, fat, cartilage, gland, or bone Mature tissue in an abnormal location; no malignant cytology Squamous epithelial Papillary benign proliferation → dysplasia → invasive SCC Maturation/cytologic atypia and basement-membrane breach Melanocytic Basal pigment → nevus nests → atypical intraepithelial growth → invasive melanoma Melanocyte density, atypia, maturation, and stromal invasion Search diagnosis, morphology, IHC, or differential... of entities Expand all Collapse all − + Clinical Profile Essential Diagnostic Criteria Histopathology and Immunophenotype Differential Diagnosis Molecular Pathology No matching entities. title: Eyeball Tumors
content: use client Ectopic tissue Benign developmental lesion Usually congenital; infancy or childhood; iris/ciliary body, often nasal, temporal, or inferior; well-circumscribed nonpigmented mass, sometimes cystic. Normal lacrimal or thyroid tissue in an abnormal intraocular location; no cytologic atypia or mitotic activity; low Ki-67. Lacrimal tissue forms acini with eosinophilic granules and may contain ducts; thyroid tissue forms follicles with or without colloid; architecture resembles the native gland; bland epithelial cells. Medulloepithelioma: primitive neuroepithelial cords and rosettes; metastatic carcinoma: atypia, destructive growth, and clinical history. No established diagnostic molecular test. Implantation cyst Benign cystic lesion Congenital cases are incidental; acquired cysts occur months to years after penetrating trauma or intraocular surgery; typically inferior or superonasal midperipheral iris. Cyst lined by non-atypical surface-type squamous epithelium, with or without keratinization or goblet cells; correlate acquired lesions with prior trauma or surgery. Concentric layers of stratified squamous epithelium; variable epithelial thickness; keratinization may be present; goblet cells may be present. Pigmented epithelial cyst: single layer of pigmented posterior iris epithelium; uveal melanoma: solid atypical melanocytic proliferation; inflammatory cyst: fluid accumulation without a squamous epithelial lining. No diagnostic molecular alteration established. Pigmented epithelial cyst Usually young adults; peripheral iris, occasionally free-floating in anterior chamber or vitreous; dark-brown cysts may be incidental or detected after dilation. Cyst lined by bland posterior iris pigment epithelium; distinguish from a solid melanocytic lesion by imaging and histology. Single layer of cuboidal or columnar pigmented epithelial cells; no stromal melanocytic proliferation. Implantation cyst: multilayered squamous lining; cystic nevus or melanoma: stromal melanocytic component; drug-associated cysts may be small and pupillary-margin based. Lisch nodule Benign hamartoma Usually children with NF1; multiple, bilateral, small, minimally elevated tan-to-cream nodules, often on the inferior iris. Bland spindle and/or ovoid melanocytes on the anterior iris surface; no mitoses or prominent nucleoli; at least two nodules are a diagnostic feature of NF1. Dome-shaped plaques of haphazardly arranged spindle melanocytes; occasional rounded cells and melanophages; S100-positive; low proliferative activity. Iris mammillations: more regular, diffuse surface elevations; iris nevus: usually a more discrete cellular melanocytic proliferation. Germline NF1 inactivation with RAS pathway dysregulation underlies the syndrome; lesion testing is not routinely indicated. Ocular melanocytosis Benign developmental melanocytic proliferation Congenital, usually unilateral; sclera, uvea, and sometimes periocular skin/orbit; iris heterochromia and slate-blue/gray scleral pigmentation; may be associated with glaucoma. Increased numbers of heavily pigmented, cytologically bland melanocytes in sclera and uvea; no mitotic activity; assess thickened areas for melanoma. Spindle, bipolar, or dendritic melanocytes between scleral lamellae and within uveal stroma; melanocytes may be heavily pigmented; no destructive growth. Diffuse uveal melanoma: atypia, increased cellularity, mitoses, and destructive growth; conjunctival melanosis: limited to conjunctival tissues. GNAQ or GNA11 mutations have been identified in some cases; these are not by themselves evidence of melanoma. Iris nevus Benign melanocytic neoplasm Usually detected in young or middle adulthood; mean age about 51 years; often inferior iris; small, circumscribed pigmented or nonpigmented spot/nodule; no strong sex predilection. Bland iris stromal melanocytic proliferation, usually spindle-cell predominant; low mitotic activity; retained nuclear BAP1 supports nevus but does not exclude melanoma on its own. Spindle to rounded polygonal melanocytes with small nuclei and inconspicuous nucleoli; Melan-A, S100, and SOX10 positive; HMB45 usually focal; Ki-67 low; nuclear BAP1 retained in most. Iris melanoma: greater cellularity, spindle B or epithelioid cells, prominent nucleoli, mitoses, angle invasion; metastasis and nonmelanocytic iris tumors are clinical alternatives. GNAQ/GNA11 and less commonly NRAS, PTEN, KIT, or TP53 alterations; BAP1 or EIF1AX alterations may occur in borderline/uncertain-potential lesions. Iris melanoma Malignant melanocytic neoplasm Usually adults; most often inferior iris; enlarging pigmented or amelanotic nodule, diffuse color change, corectopia, ectropion uveae, hyphema, or secondary glaucoma; 3–5% of uveal melanomas. Atypical, highly cellular melanocytic tumor arising in iris; spindle B and/or epithelioid cells, mitotic activity, stromal invasion, angle seeding, or circumferential growth support malignancy. Spindle B cells show clumped peripheral chromatin and prominent nucleoli; epithelioid cells are discohesive with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm and prominent nucleoli; may be spindle, mixed, or epithelioid; Melan-A, S100, HMB45, and SOX10 positive; BAP1 nuclear loss may occur. Iris nevus: bland cells, low cellularity, no destructive invasion; metastatic melanoma: clinical history and often different immunophenotypic/molecular context; melanocytoma: heavily pigmented bland polygonal cells. GNAQ, GNA11, EIF1AX, SF3B1, and BAP1 alterations; monosomy 3 and 8q gain may occur. Prognostic meaning of some copy-number changes in iris melanoma is less established. Choroidal and ciliary body nevus Usually asymptomatic; choroid, commonly postequatorial; typically under 5 mm diameter and under 1 mm thick; ciliary body lesions are often clinically occult. Small, flat or shallow dome-shaped melanocytic lesion; drusen/halo and minimal subretinal fluid or orange pigment favor nevus; no cytologic malignancy if sampled. Bland spindle and polygonal melanocytes with inconspicuous nucleoli; variable pigmentation; may show drusen-related RPE changes, choriocapillaris attenuation, and photoreceptor/RPE alterations. Uveal melanoma: thickness over 2 mm, subretinal fluid, orange lipofuscin, symptoms, optic-disc proximity, hollowness, or growth; metastasis and melanocytoma are additional considerations. GNAQ or GNA11 mutations are common but do not distinguish nevus from melanoma; BAP1 nuclear expression is generally retained. Uveal melanocytoma Any age; iris, ciliary body, choroid, or optic nerve head; deeply pigmented dark-brown to black lesion, sometimes with secondary glaucoma or cataract. Deeply pigmented melanocytic tumor composed of large polygonal cells with abundant melanin; bland nuclei after bleaching; absent or very low mitotic activity and Ki-67. Large polygonal cells with dense intracytoplasmic melanin obscuring nuclei; bleaching reveals small bland central nuclei and inconspicuous nucleoli; melanocytic markers positive; BAP1 retained; Ki-67 very low. Uveal melanoma: nuclear atypia, mitoses, higher Ki-67, possible BAP1 loss; pigmented epithelial neoplasm: cytokeratin-positive and melanocytic-marker negative. GNAQ mutations have been reported; BAP1 alterations may accompany rare malignant transformation but are not typical. Bilateral diffuse uveal melanocytic proliferation Paraneoplastic syndrome Usually older adults, median age approximately 58–65 years; bilateral diffuse choroidal involvement, often pan-uveal; rapidly progressive bilateral visual loss, exudative retinal detachment, cataracts; associated with extraocular carcinoma. Bilateral diffuse proliferation of bland melanocytes in a patient with an extraocular malignancy; choriocapillaris is spared; low mitotic activity and low Ki-67; correlate with characteristic RPE changes. Predominantly spindle melanocytes with elongated nuclei, inconspicuous nucleoli, and scant pigment; melan-A, HMB45, and SOX10 positive; PRAME negative and nuclear BAP1 retained in reported cases. Diffuse uveal melanoma: cytologic atypia, choriocapillaris effacement, mitoses, and melanoma-type molecular changes; metastatic carcinoma: epithelial tumor cells. No consistent defining genomic alteration; GNAQ, GNA11, and BRAF V600E mutations have not been reported in this syndrome. Choroidal and ciliary body melanoma Usually adults, predominantly fair-skinned populations; choroid most common, ciliary body often occult; may be asymptomatic or cause photopsia, floaters, visual loss, retinal detachment, or secondary glaucoma. Primary malignant uveal melanocytic tumor; spindle B and/or epithelioid cytology, mitoses, destructive growth, and characteristic clinical/imaging findings; assess extrascleral and optic nerve extension. Spindle A/B and epithelioid cell types; epithelioid cells have abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm and prominent nucleoli; variable pigmentation; Melan-A, S100, HMB45, and SOX10 positive; BAP1 loss may be seen in high-risk tumors. Nevus: smaller, thinner, chronicity features, bland cytology; metastasis: often creamy, multiple/bilateral, and systemic primary; melanocytoma: heavily pigmented bland polygonal cells. GNAQ/GNA11 driver mutations; BAP1 loss/alteration, monosomy 3, and 8q gain are associated with metastatic risk; SF3B1 and EIF1AX define additional molecular subsets. Astrocytic tumors of the retina Glial neoplasm/hamartomatous spectrum Often children or young adults; retinal or optic-disc-based lesions; may be incidental, calcified, yellow-white, or associated with tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC). Astrocytic proliferation with appropriate clinical/radiologic context; distinguish circumscribed retinal astrocytic hamartoma from infiltrative or diffuse glioma. Mature astrocytes with fibrillary processes in hamartoma; calcification may be prominent; GFAP and other glial markers support lineage; assess atypia and mitotic activity in suspected neoplasm. Retinoblastoma: small round blue cells and necrosis; reactive gliosis: associated retinal injury and no discrete neoplastic mass; retinal vascular lesions: prominent vascular channels. TSC1/TSC2 pathway alterations are relevant to syndromic retinal astrocytic hamartomas; no single routine molecular test is required. Nodular and massive retinal gliosis Reactive glial proliferation Usually adults with longstanding retinal disease, trauma, inflammation, or retinal detachment; unilateral nodular or mass-like retinal lesion, sometimes mimicking malignancy. Well-circumscribed or massive reactive glial proliferation in a chronically damaged retina; no convincing malignant cytology or infiltrative neoplastic pattern. Dense proliferation of reactive astrocytes with fibrillary processes; GFAP positive; variable Rosenthal fibers and degenerative changes; mitoses and significant atypia are generally absent. Retinal astrocytic tumor: more discrete neoplastic architecture; retinoblastoma: primitive neuroblastic cells; medulloepithelioma: primitive neuroepithelial tubules/rosettes. No established diagnostic molecular alteration. Retinocytoma Benign/low-grade retinoblastoma-spectrum lesion Usually children or young adults; unilateral or bilateral retinal lesion, often discovered incidentally or in relatives of patients with retinoblastoma; may be calcified and partially regressed. Retinoblastoma-like lesion with benign cytology, photoreceptor differentiation, and extensive regression; absence of active proliferative malignant component is key. Small round cells with bland nuclei, fleurettes/photoreceptor differentiation, calcification, and areas of necrosis or gliosis; low proliferative activity. Retinoblastoma: viable small blue cells, brisk mitoses, apoptosis and necrosis; retinal astrocytic hamartoma: glial cells and calcification without photoreceptor rosettes. RB1 pathway inactivation is central; germline RB1 status has implications for the patient and family. Retinoblastoma Malignant embryonal retinal tumor Almost exclusively young children; usually presents before age 5; unilateral or bilateral; leukocoria and strabismus are classic findings. Malignant small round blue-cell tumor of retina; Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes or fleurettes may be present; necrosis, calcification, and high mitotic/apoptotic activity support diagnosis. Sheets of small cells with scant cytoplasm, hyperchromatic nuclei, brisk mitoses and apoptosis; rosettes and photoreceptor differentiation may occur; necrosis and dystrophic calcification common; synaptophysin and other neuronal markers may be positive. Retinocytoma: bland cells and regression; medulloepithelioma: ciliary body origin and neuroepithelial tubules; metastatic neuroblastoma: clinical context and distinct pattern. Biallelic RB1 inactivation; germline RB1 variants in heritable cases. MYCN amplification can drive a subset of RB1-wildtype tumors. Hamartoma of the retinal pigment epithelium Usually congenital or detected in childhood; focal, sharply circumscribed, deeply pigmented retinal lesion, often juxtapapillary or macular; may cause visual disturbance if central. Localized disorganized proliferation of RPE with associated retinal and choroidal changes; sharply demarcated lesion with no malignant cytology. Hypertrophic, heavily pigmented RPE cells with irregular multilayering; associated retinal gliosis and architectural disorganization; no destructive malignant invasion. Congenital hypertrophy of RPE: flat, uniform RPE enlargement with lacunae; RPE adenoma: expansile tumor mass with feeder vessels and retinal invasion. No routinely useful diagnostic molecular alteration. Congenital hypertrophy of the retinal pigment epithelium Congenital or recognized in childhood/adulthood; usually solitary, flat, sharply demarcated, pigmented fundus lesion, commonly peripheral; often incidental. Flat, well-circumscribed RPE lesion with enlarged pigmented cells and characteristic depigmented lacunae; no mass-forming growth. Uniformly enlarged, densely pigmented RPE cells; outer retina may be attenuated; lacunae show reduced or absent pigmentation; no significant atypia or mitoses. RPE hamartoma: irregular multilayered RPE with retinal disorganization; reactive RPE hyperplasia: irregular pigment clumps associated with underlying injury; RPE adenoma: elevated mass. Reactive hyperplasia of the retinal pigment epithelium Reactive lesion Any age; any retinal location; associated with trauma, inflammation, retinal detachment, hemorrhage, degeneration, or radiation; dark pigmented deposits, sometimes spiculated along vessels. Non-neoplastic RPE proliferation associated with an identifiable or occult retinal/choroidal insult; lack of a destructive expansile tumor is important. Irregular clusters, cords, or nodules of pigmented RPE cells; variable epithelial metaplasia and fibrosis; cytologic atypia is generally limited. RPE adenoma/adenocarcinoma: discrete expansile mass, atypia and invasion; choroidal melanoma: melanocytic tumor beneath retina. Adenoma and adenocarcinoma of the retinal pigment epithelium Benign or malignant epithelial neoplasm Usually adults; solitary unilateral dark gray/black or occasionally amelanotic retinal mass, often peripheral; blurred vision or incidental finding; may mimic choroidal melanoma. RPE-derived epithelial neoplasm; adenocarcinoma shows destructive invasion, significant atypia, and/or metastasis; correlate with characteristic elevated mass and retinal vascular supply. Pigmented epithelial cells in nests, cords, tubules, or gland-like structures; adenomas are more circumscribed and bland; carcinomas show pleomorphism, mitoses, necrosis, and invasion; cytokeratin and RPE markers support lineage. Choroidal melanoma: melanocytic markers and choroidal origin; reactive RPE hyperplasia: associated injury and non-expansile pattern; ciliary epithelial tumor: ciliary body origin. No single defining molecular alteration established for routine diagnosis. Reactive epithelial hyperplasia of the ciliary epithelium Usually in severely injured, inflamed, operated, or chronically detached eyes; pars plana/pars plicata; typically incidental in enucleated eyes. Increased ciliary epithelial cells in response to injury or inflammation; often accompanied by fibrous metaplasia; no destructive tumor growth. Hyperplastic ciliary epithelial layers with variable papillary or gland-like configuration; fibrous metaplasia may be prominent; cytologic atypia is absent or mild. Ciliary epithelial adenoma: discrete expansile mass; nodular hyperplasia: localized, well-circumscribed proliferation without preceding injury. Nodular hyperplasia of the ciliary epithelium Benign hyperplasia Older adults; usually incidental, small lesion confined to one ciliary process in pars plicata; rarely causes sectoral cataract or mimics a ciliary body mass. Well-circumscribed proliferation of inner nonpigmented ciliary epithelium without antecedent injury; no infiltrative growth or significant atypia. Nodular epithelial proliferation of nonpigmented ciliary epithelium; may form papillary or adenoma-like structures; bland cytology and low proliferative activity. Reactive ciliary epithelial hyperplasia: history of injury/inflammation and more diffuse changes; ciliary body adenoma: larger expansile neoplasm. Glioneuronal hamartoma of the ciliary body Benign developmental hamartoma Congenital or detected in infancy; usually temporal ciliary body, often extends to iris/retina; may accompany chorioretinal coloboma, microphthalmia, cataract, or elevated IOP. Developmental glioneuronal lesion at the optic cup margin; identify both glial and neuronal differentiation and associated ocular malformation. Mature glial and neuronal elements in a disorganized hamartomatous proliferation; glial component GFAP-positive; neuronal markers highlight neuronal elements. Medulloepithelioma: primitive multilayered neuroepithelial cords/tubules; retinoblastoma: malignant small round cells; optic nerve glioma: nerve-centered infiltrative glial tumor. No defining molecular alteration; not associated with NF1 or NF2. Adenoma and adenocarcinoma of the ciliary body Usually adults; ciliary body, often hidden behind iris; visual disturbance, cataract, lens subluxation, inflammation, or secondary glaucoma; pigmented or nonpigmented mass. Neoplasm arising from pigmented or nonpigmented ciliary epithelium; adenocarcinoma supported by invasion, significant atypia, mitoses, or extraocular extension. Epithelial nests, cords, tubules, or papillary structures; variable pigmentation; adenomas are bland and circumscribed; adenocarcinomas show infiltrative growth, atypia, mitoses, and necrosis; cytokeratin positive. Medulloepithelioma: primitive neuroepithelial tubules and rosettes; melanocytoma/melanoma: melanocytic markers; reactive/nodular epithelial hyperplasia: noninvasive and usually smaller. No routinely established defining molecular alteration. Medulloepithelioma of the ciliary body Embryonal neuroepithelial tumor Usually children, commonly diagnosed before age 10; ciliary body, often unilateral; leukocoria, poor vision, cataract, glaucoma, or painful red eye. Primitive neuroepithelial tumor resembling the embryonic medullary epithelium of the optic cup; distinguish nonteratoid from teratoid forms and assess malignant features. Multilayered neuroepithelial cords, tubules, and rosettes; hyaluronic-acid-rich stroma; heterologous tissues may occur in teratoid tumors; malignant cases show atypia, mitoses, necrosis, and invasion. Retinoblastoma: retinal origin and small round-cell phenotype; ciliary epithelial adenoma: mature epithelial differentiation; glioneuronal hamartoma: mature, non-embryonal elements. DICER1 alterations are associated with some cases; consider germline DICER1 predisposition in appropriate clinical settings. Optic nerve choristoma Rare; reported from childhood to adulthood; optic nerve intraorbital, intracanalicular, or intracranial segments; painless progressive visual loss and optic atrophy; MRI may show fat signal suppressed by fat-saturation. Heterotopic smooth muscle and adipose tissue within or around optic nerve; developmental/malformative lesion rather than a glial or meningeal neoplasm. Mature adipose tissue and well-differentiated smooth muscle bundles; no atypia or mitotic activity. Optic nerve glioma: glial neoplasm; meningioma: meningothelial whorls and calcification; lipoma: mature fat without smooth muscle component. Gliomas of the optic nerve Glial neoplasm Usually children for pilocytic astrocytoma, often associated with NF1; optic nerve/chiasm; visual loss, proptosis, strabismus, or optic atrophy; bilateral disease suggests NF1. Optic pathway glioma most often pilocytic astrocytoma; evaluate for diffuse high-grade glioma when atypia, mitoses, necrosis, or microvascular proliferation are present. Pilocytic tumors show biphasic piloid and microcystic areas, Rosenthal fibers, and eosinophilic granular bodies; GFAP and OLIG2 positive; high-grade gliomas show increased cellularity, mitoses, necrosis, and vascular proliferation. Optic nerve sheath meningioma: meningothelial cells and whorls; choristoma: mature fat/smooth muscle; metastatic tumor: clinical history and epithelial/other lineage markers. Pilocytic astrocytoma often shows MAPK pathway activation, including KIAA1549::BRAF fusion; NF1-associated tumors have NF1 pathway loss; IDH status is relevant in adult-type diffuse gliomas. Medulloepithelioma of the optic disc and optic nerve Very rare; usually orbital optic nerve in children; presents as a large orbital mass, sometimes with visual loss or proptosis; may extend to orbital apex/CNS. Primitive embryonal neuroepithelial tumor with multilayered cords and tubules; optic nerve location is unusual and should prompt careful distinction from optic pathway glioma. Multilayered neuroepithelial cords, tubules, and rosettes resembling optic cup medullary epithelium; teratoid lesions contain heterologous mesenchymal elements; malignant lesions show atypia, mitoses, necrosis, and invasion. Optic nerve glioma: astrocytic morphology and GFAP/OLIG2 phenotype; retinoblastoma: small round-cell tumor of retina; metastatic embryonal tumor: clinical and molecular context. DICER1 alterations may be relevant; evaluate for DICER1 tumor predisposition when clinically indicated. Meningioma of the optic nerve Meningothelial neoplasm Usually middle-aged women; typically unilateral intraorbital optic nerve sheath; progressive visual loss, optic atrophy, optociliary shunt vessels, sometimes proptosis/strabismus; bilateral pediatric cases may be associated with NF2. Meningothelial tumor centered on optic nerve sheath; distinguish primary sheath tumor from secondary extension of intracranial meningioma. Meningothelial whorls, syncytial cells, psammoma bodies in some cases; EMA, SSTR2A, and progesterone receptor may be positive; low-grade lesions generally show low mitotic activity. Optic nerve glioma: GFAP/OLIG2-positive glial tumor; lymphoma/metastasis: cytologic and lineage-marker differences; optic nerve choristoma: mature adipose and smooth muscle. NF2 alterations are common in meningiomas; assess relevant molecular grade-defining alterations when indicated. Melanocytoma of the optic disc and optic nerve Usually adults; typically unilateral optic disc or adjacent anterior optic nerve; deeply pigmented black-brown lesion, usually asymptomatic but may cause visual-field defect or rarely vision loss. Densely pigmented melanocytic tumor composed of bland polygonal cells; melanin bleaching is often needed to assess nuclei; absent or very low mitotic activity. Large polygonal cells with abundant coarse melanin obscuring small bland nuclei; melanocytic markers positive; low Ki-67; BAP1 generally retained. Uveal melanoma: atypia, mitoses, necrosis, BAP1 loss; optic nerve sheath meningioma: nonpigmented meningothelial proliferation; metastatic melanoma: clinical history and morphology. GNAQ/GNA11 pathway mutations may occur; BAP1 alterations are reported in rare malignant transformation. clinical Clinical Profile criteria Essential Diagnostic Criteria histo Histopathology and Immunophenotype diff Differential Diagnosis molecular Molecular Pathology ; All Ophthalmic Pathology Eyeball Tumors A practical diagnostic reference to tumors and tumor-like lesions of the uveal tract, retina, retinal pigment epithelium, ciliary epithelium, optic disc, and optic nerve. Diagnostic Overview by Anatomic Category Intraocular tumors are best approached by their site of origin. The three anatomic groups below differ in their dominant cell lineages, biologic behavior, and key diagnostic considerations. 1. Tumors of the Uveal Tract Iris, ciliary body, and choroid; melanocytic lesions predominate. Tumor group Overview Representative entities Developmental lesions, cysts, and hamartomas Usually benign; include ectopic glandular tissue, epithelial cysts, and NF1-associated iris hamartomas. Ectopic tissue, implantation cyst, pigmented epithelial cyst, Lisch nodule Benign melanocytic proliferations Common in the uvea; range from flat nevi to heavily pigmented melanocytoma. Ocular melanocytosis is a risk factor for uveal melanoma. Ocular melanocytosis, iris nevus, choroidal/ciliary body nevus, uveal melanocytoma Malignant melanocytic tumors Uveal melanoma arises in the iris, ciliary body, or choroid. Metastatic risk is substantially greater for ciliary body and choroidal tumors than for iris melanoma. Iris melanoma, choroidal and ciliary body melanoma Paraneoplastic proliferation Bilateral diffuse, usually bland melanocytic proliferation associated with an underlying extraocular malignancy and progressive visual loss. 2. Tumors of the Retina and Neuroepithelium Neurosensory retina, retinal pigment epithelium, and iris/ciliary body neuroepithelium. Retinal glial lesions Astrocytic tumors are generally indolent and may be syndromic; reactive retinal gliosis can form a mass and mimic a neoplasm. Astrocytic tumors of the retina, nodular and massive retinal gliosis Retinoblastoma spectrum Retinocytoma is a regressed or low-proliferation lesion in the RB1-associated spectrum; retinoblastoma is the principal malignant intraocular tumor of childhood. Retinocytoma, retinoblastoma Retinal pigment epithelial lesions Include congenital and hamartomatous proliferations, reactive hyperplasia, and very rare true epithelial neoplasms. RPE hamartoma, congenital hypertrophy of RPE, reactive RPE hyperplasia, RPE adenoma/adenocarcinoma Ciliary epithelial lesions Span reactive or nodular hyperplasia, developmental hamartoma, and true epithelial neoplasms. Reactive/nodular ciliary epithelial hyperplasia, glioneuronal hamartoma, ciliary body adenoma/adenocarcinoma A rare congenital tumor, usually arising in the ciliary body, with primitive neuroepithelial differentiation. 3. Tumors of the Optic Disc and Optic Nerve Includes developmental lesions and tumors of glial, meningeal, melanocytic, and neuroepithelial origin. Developmental choristoma Rare benign malformative lesion composed of heterotopic mature tissues within or around the optic nerve. Glial tumors Most are low-grade astrocytic tumors in children and are frequently associated with NF1; high-grade gliomas are uncommon. Exceptionally rare; may arise in the optic disc or nerve and show primitive neuroepithelial differentiation. Meningeal tumor Arises from the optic nerve sheath; often presents with slowly progressive visual impairment. Optic nerve meningioma Melanocytic tumor Usually a benign, deeply pigmented lesion of the optic disc; rare malignant transformation has been described. Molecular findings should be interpreted in the appropriate clinicopathologic context.

title: Eyelid Tumors
content: use client Epidermal inclusion cyst Cyst / tumor-like Adolescents to older adults; eyelid skin, brow, or lash line; slow-growing, mobile dermal/subcutaneous nodule, sometimes with a central pore. Dermal/subcutaneous cyst lined by epidermal-type squamous epithelium with a granular layer and laminated keratin; no atypical squamous proliferation. Stratified squamous lining with a well-formed granular layer; laminated orthokeratin fills the lumen; rupture may cause granulomatous inflammation. Pilar cyst lacks a granular layer and has trichilemmal keratinization; dermoid contains skin appendages; intratarsal cyst has a thin corrugated cuticle and no granular layer. No routine molecular testing; multiple lesions may prompt evaluation for Gardner or Muir–Torre syndrome. Intratarsal keratinous cyst Usually adults in their 50s–70s; upper tarsus; painless, firm nodule fixed to tarsal plate, visible on lid eversion. Intratarsal cyst with 4–6-cell-thick squamous lining, corrugated eosinophilic cuticle, and no keratohyalin granules. Basal hyperchromatic cells; brightly eosinophilic luminal cuticle; keratinous contents; CK17 is typically strong. Epidermal inclusion cyst has granular layer and laminated keratin; chalazion is inflammatory and lipid-rich; cystic neoplasms show epithelial complexity. No established routine molecular test; multiple or atypical-age lesions may be associated with PTCH1-related Gorlin syndrome. Phakomatous choristoma Choristoma Congenital; infancy; slight male predominance; deep medial lower eyelid, presenting as a firm subcutaneous mass. Ectopic lenticular tissue with lens-like epithelial cells and bladder cells surrounded by a thick PAS-positive lens-capsule-like membrane. Islands of cuboidal/polygonal lens epithelium; bladder (Wedl) cells; thick PAS-positive basement membrane; cells express vimentin, S100, PAX8, and crystallins. Dermoid/epidermoid cysts are keratin-lined; ectopic lacrimal tissue forms acini/ducts; other congenital masses lack lens-type cells and capsule. No routine molecular testing. Molluscum contagiosum Viral / tumor-like Most often children; either eyelid; one or multiple small, waxy, umbilicated papules; may cause follicular conjunctivitis. Crateriform epidermal hyperplasia containing characteristic intracytoplasmic molluscum bodies. Endophytic acanthotic lobules; large eosinophilic Henderson–Paterson inclusions displacing nuclei peripherally; inflammation may follow rupture. Verruca shows papillomatosis, koilocytosis, and hypergranulosis; keratoacanthoma has crateriform squamous proliferation without molluscum bodies. Molluscum contagiosum poxvirus; molecular testing is rarely needed. Verruca vulgaris Viral / benign epithelial Children and adolescents, but any age; eyelid or eyebrow; keratotic papule, plaque, or filiform lesion; more frequent with immunosuppression. Papillomatous epidermal proliferation with hyperkeratosis, hypergranulosis, parakeratosis, and koilocytosis. Papillary projections with parakeratotic columns; coarse keratohyalin granules; koilocytes in superficial layers; elongated rete ridges. Squamous papilloma is more exophytic with fibrovascular cores and less acanthosis; seborrheic keratosis has horn cysts and lacks convincing viral cytopathy. Low-risk HPV types, particularly 1, 2, 4, and 7; testing is not routinely required. Squamous papilloma Benign epithelial Any age; eyelid skin or margin; soft, skin-colored, sessile or pedunculated papule, often multiple. Exophytic squamous proliferation with fibrovascular cores and no significant dysplasia or invasion. Finger-like or broad-based papillary fronds; orderly squamous maturation; fibrovascular cores; occasional koilocytosis. Verruca has hypergranulosis and parakeratotic columns; seborrheic keratosis has horn cysts; SCC shows dysplasia and/or invasion. Some lesions are HPV-associated, but molecular testing is not routine. Seborrheic keratosis Usually over age 50; periocular skin and lid margin; tan-to-brown, stuck-on papule or plaque. Well-demarcated intraepidermal squamous proliferation with a flat base and no dysplasia. Acanthosis of basaloid keratinocytes; horn cysts/pseudohorn cysts; surface hyperkeratosis; rare mitoses. Verruca has viral cytopathic change; inverted follicular keratosis is endophytic with squamous eddies; SCC shows cytologic atypia and destructive invasion. Common alterations include FGFR3, PIK3CA, HRAS, KRAS, EGFR, and AKT1; not needed for routine diagnosis. Inverted follicular keratosis Benign follicular Middle-aged to older adults; eyelid; usually a small pink or skin-colored dome-shaped papule; men affected about twice as often. Symmetric endophytic follicular infundibular proliferation of basaloid and squamoid cells with squamous eddies and no destructive invasion. Central keratin-filled crypts; peripheral basaloid cells and central squamoid cells; concentric squamous eddies; bland nuclei and non-atypical mitoses. SCC shows atypia, dysplasia, and destructive invasion; irritated seborrheic keratosis has horn cysts and lacks characteristic follicular architecture. Multiple lesions may be associated with PTEN-related Cowden syndrome. Actinic keratosis Premalignant epithelial Usually adults over 60; sun-exposed eyelid skin and margin; erythematous, scaly patch or plaque. Intraepidermal squamous dysplasia that does not involve the full epidermal thickness, with solar elastosis. Atypical keratinocytes with disordered maturation; hyperkeratosis/parakeratosis; dyskeratosis; dermal solar elastosis; p53 and Ki-67 may support difficult cases. SCC in situ shows full-thickness atypia; invasive SCC breaches basement membrane; pigmented AK may mimic lentigo maligna. UV signature with TP53, NOTCH1/2, and FAT1 alterations; molecular testing is not routine. Basal cell carcinoma Malignant epithelial Older adults with chronic UV exposure; lower eyelid most common, then medial canthus; pearly or ulcerated nodule, rolled edge, lash loss; pain/numbness may indicate advanced spread. Basaloid nests, nodules, or infiltrative cords with peripheral palisading and stromal retraction; subtype and margin status require excision assessment. Hyperchromatic basaloid cells with scant cytoplasm; peripheral palisading; stromal retraction; infiltrative/morpheaform patterns show narrow cords in desmoplastic stroma. BerEP4, BCL2, and CD10 are commonly positive. Trichoepithelioma has CK20-positive Merkel cells and stromal CD10; basaloid SCC is BerEP4-negative and more atypical; sebaceous carcinoma expresses adipophilin/AR; Merkel carcinoma is neuroendocrine. PTCH1/SHH pathway alterations are common; PTCH1 germline testing when Gorlin syndrome is suspected. Squamous cell carcinoma Usually older fair-skinned men with chronic sun exposure; lower eyelid and medial canthus; indurated keratotic or ulcerated plaque/nodule; pain or paresthesia suggests perineural invasion. Atypical squamous cells infiltrating dermis as nests/islands with variable keratinization; in situ lesions show full-thickness epidermal atypia. Polygonal atypical cells, intercellular bridges, dyskeratosis, keratin pearls; p40, p63, and CK5/6 support squamous differentiation. Keratoacanthoma-like SCC may overlap with keratoacanthoma; BCC is basaloid with palisading/retraction; sebaceous carcinoma has vacuolated sebocytes and adipophilin positivity. UV-associated TP53 and NOTCH pathway alterations; EGFR/PD-L1 expression may have therapeutic relevance. Merkel cell carcinoma Malignant neuroendocrine Older adults (median about 74 years), more often men; sun-exposed eyelid/head and neck; rapidly enlarging red-blue dermal nodule, often mistaken for chalazion. Dermal small blue cell neuroendocrine carcinoma with characteristic dot-like CK20 and neuroendocrine marker expression; assess MCPyV status. Sheets of monotonous small cells with finely granular chromatin, scant cytoplasm, brisk mitoses and apoptosis; CK20 paranuclear dot-like; synaptophysin, chromogranin, INSM1 positive; TTF1 and CD45 negative. Metastatic small-cell lung carcinoma is usually TTF1-positive/CK20-negative; lymphoma is CD45-positive; melanoma expresses SOX10; other carcinomas lack the typical CK20 dot pattern. MCPyV integration in most cases; virus-negative tumors show UV signature and frequent TP53/RB1 alterations. Ductal hidrocystoma Benign adnexal Usually adults in their 50s–60s; lower eyelid and canthi; small, smooth, translucent or blue-tinged compressible cyst. Sweat duct cyst with bilayered cuboidal/columnar lining and serous contents; apocrine type shows decapitation secretion. Apocrine type: tall eosinophilic luminal cells with apical snouts and outer myoepithelial layer; eccrine type: low cuboidal bilayer without snouts; apocrine epithelium may express GCDFP-15/CK7 and myoepithelium SMA. Epidermal inclusion cyst contains laminated keratin and granular layer; EMPSGC or mucinous carcinoma shows cellular proliferation, mucin, and complex papillary/cribriform architecture. Sebaceous hyperplasia, adenoma, and sebaceoma Benign sebaceous Usually older adults; eyelid/periocular skin; well-circumscribed yellow-tan papules or nodules; multifocal lesions raise Muir–Torre concern. Hyperplasia retains central follicular connection and thin peripheral germinative layer; adenoma has more sebocytes than basaloid cells; sebaceoma has more basaloid cells than sebocytes. Mature foamy sebocytes admixed with bland basaloid germinative cells; adenoma shows central sebocytes/peripheral basaloid cells; sebaceoma has scattered sebocytes among basaloid cells. Sebaceous carcinoma shows infiltrative growth, atypia, mitoses, and pagetoid spread; BCC shows palisading/retraction and lacks sebaceous differentiation. Muir–Torre-associated lesions may show loss of MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, or PMS2; consider mismatch-repair evaluation. Syringoma Most often middle-aged women; lower eyelids/periorbital skin; multiple small skin-colored or yellow papules. Circumscribed superficial dermal proliferation of benign eccrine ducts and tubules in sclerotic stroma. Small ducts/tubules with double-layered cuboidal lining and tadpole-shaped tails; keratin-filled cysts; dense collagenous stroma. Microcystic adnexal carcinoma is deeply infiltrative with perineural invasion; morpheaform BCC shows basaloid cords and retraction; desmoplastic trichoepithelioma has follicular differentiation. No established diagnostic molecular alteration. Mixed tumor Usually adults around 50 years; upper eyelid more common; solitary, slow-growing, smooth, well-circumscribed nonulcerated nodule; male predominance. Well-circumscribed biphasic epithelial/myoepithelial neoplasm with ductal structures and myxoid, chondroid, or hyalinized stroma. Branching ducts with inner luminal and outer myoepithelial cells; variable chondromyxoid, osseous, or adipocytic stroma; SOX10, S100, p63, SMA/calponin support components. Myoepithelioma lacks ducts; chondroma lacks epithelial elements; malignant mixed tumor shows destructive invasion and significant atypia. PLAG1 or EWSR1 rearrangements occur in a subset; PLAG1 is typically absent in eccrine subtype. Tubular adenoma Adults, mean age about 47 years; upper or lower eyelid; solitary, smooth, asymptomatic small nodule. Lobulated dermal apocrine neoplasm composed of multiple irregular tubules with epithelial and myoepithelial layers in fibrous stroma. Double-layered tubules with luminal columnar cells and peripheral myoepithelial cells; focal decapitation secretion; bland cytology; luminal CEA/EMA and peripheral SMA/calponin/SOX10/p63. Syringocystadenoma papilliferum has epidermal connection and plasma-cell-rich stroma; apocrine carcinoma shows atypia and invasion; hidrocystoma is predominantly cystic. BRAF p.V600E in a subset; HRAS/KRAS mutations, especially in nevus sebaceus-associated lesions. Syringocystadenoma papilliferum Often children or adults; lower eyelid margin; papillary, verrucous, cystic, crusted, or oozing lesion; slight female predominance. Endophytic epidermally connected apocrine neoplasm with papillary/cystic structures, bilayered epithelium, and plasma-cell-rich stroma. Papillary projections lined by columnar apocrine cells with decapitation secretion; outer myoepithelial layer; abundant stromal plasma cells; CEA/EMA luminal and SMA/calponin/SOX10/p63 peripheral. Tubular adenoma lacks prominent plasma-cell-rich stroma and epidermal connection; hidradenoma papilliferum is not connected to epidermis and lacks plasma cells. BRAF p.V600E in approximately half of cases; MAPK-pathway alterations include BRAF, KRAS, and HRAS. Pilomatricoma Bimodal: children/young adults and adults 50–65; upper eyelid/medial eyebrow; firm, mobile, often blue-red subcutaneous nodule with gritty calcification. Matrical follicular tumor with peripheral basaloid cells, transition cells, and central ghost/shadow cells, often calcified. Basaloid matrical cells at periphery; abrupt transition to anucleate shadow cells; calcification and foreign-body giant-cell reaction; nuclear beta-catenin may be present. Epidermal inclusion cyst lacks matrical cells; basal cell carcinoma lacks ghost cells; pilomatrix carcinoma shows infiltrative growth, atypia, and atypical mitoses. CTNNB1/beta-catenin pathway alterations are characteristic. Trichilemmoma Adults; central face, eyebrow, and eyelid; small, slow-growing, skin-colored papule; multiple lesions suggest Cowden syndrome. Lobulated follicular tumor with trichilemmal differentiation, peripheral palisading, and thick basement membrane. Clear glycogen-rich cells with peripheral palisading; thick eosinophilic basement membrane; desmoplastic variant has central sclerosis and cords of bland cells. BCC lacks thick basement membrane and shows stromal retraction; desmoplastic trichoepithelioma has follicular papillae/keratin cysts; SCC shows atypia and invasion. Multiple lesions may be associated with germline PTEN alterations (Cowden syndrome). Sebaceous carcinoma Malignant sebaceous Older adults (median about 73 years); upper eyelid often from Meibomian glands; yellow-pink immobile nodule or diffuse thickening, recurrent chalazion, or chronic blepharoconjunctivitis. Malignant sebaceous differentiation with infiltrative growth; pagetoid intraepithelial spread may involve conjunctiva or epidermis. Lobules/sheets of atypical cells with foamy or vacuolated cytoplasm; comedonecrosis and brisk mitoses; pagetoid spread; adipophilin, androgen receptor, and EMA support sebaceous differentiation. BCC is BerEP4-positive and lacks sebaceous vacuoles; SCC is p40/p63-positive without lipid; sebaceoma is circumscribed and cytologically bland; metastatic clear-cell tumors require clinical correlation. TP53, RB1, NOTCH-family, and ZNF750 alterations; Muir–Torre syndrome warrants mismatch-repair IHC (MLH1/MSH2/MSH6/PMS2). Adenoid cystic carcinoma Malignant adnexal Usually middle-aged or older adults, male predominance; upper/lower eyelid or periocular skin; slow-growing firm nodule, sometimes lash loss or pain. Infiltrative basaloid epithelial/myoepithelial carcinoma with cribriform/tubular architecture and prominent perineural invasion. Cribriform pseudolumina with basement-membrane-like material; tubular and solid patterns; dual epithelial/myoepithelial phenotype; perineural invasion common. Basal cell carcinoma lacks true cribriform pseudolumina; primary cutaneous adenoid cystic carcinoma must be distinguished from lacrimal gland or metastatic AdCC. MYB rearrangement/fusion, including MYB::NFIB, in a substantial subset. Signet-ring cell / histiocytoid carcinoma Usually older men (median about 66 years); diffuse eyelid dermis/subcutis, often both lids; painless progressive swelling with possible monocle-like appearance. Diffuse infiltrative adnexal carcinoma with signet-ring/histiocytoid cells; exclude metastatic carcinoma, particularly breast and gastrointestinal primaries. Discohesive cells with intracytoplasmic mucin/vacuoles displacing nuclei; infiltrative dermal/subcutaneous spread; epithelial markers and mucin stains support carcinoma. Metastatic signet-ring carcinoma requires clinical workup; sebaceous carcinoma has lipid vacuoles and adipophilin; lymphoma is CD45-positive. CDH1 alterations and other changes including NTRK3, CDKN1B, ERBB2, TP53, and PIK3CA have been reported. Mucinous carcinoma Usually older adults; lower eyelid or brow; slowly growing, often long-standing firm/cystic or papillomatous nodule; may mimic chalazion or BCC. Dermal carcinoma composed of epithelial nests/islands floating in abundant extracellular mucin; exclude metastasis from breast or gastrointestinal tract. Pools of extracellular mucin with floating nests/cords of bland-to-atypical epithelial cells; neuroendocrine markers may be expressed variably; mucicarmine/PAS-D highlight mucin. Metastatic mucinous carcinoma requires clinical correlation; EMPSGC has neuroendocrine differentiation and often an in situ component; hidrocystoma is cystic and benign. No single routinely diagnostic molecular alteration; molecular testing is not standard. Endocrine mucin-producing sweat gland carcinoma Usually women in their 60s–70s; eyelid/periorbital skin; slow-growing skin-colored or bluish papule, nodule, or cyst; may be multifocal. Low-grade mucin-producing sweat gland carcinoma with neuroendocrine differentiation; assess for associated invasive mucinous carcinoma. Well-demarcated solid, papillary, cribriform, or cystic nodules; uniform cells with neuroendocrine chromatin; mucin production; synaptophysin/chromogranin/INSM1 and hormone receptors often positive. Mucinous carcinoma lacks the characteristic neuroendocrine phenotype; hidrocystoma lacks neoplastic solid/papillary proliferation; metastatic neuroendocrine carcinoma requires exclusion. No defining recurrent molecular test; associated mucinous carcinoma may represent progression. Microcystic adnexal carcinoma Usually middle-aged adults, female predominance; lower eyelid/canthus; indurated skin-colored or yellow plaque/nodule, often slowly progressive; pain/numbness suggests perineural invasion. Deeply infiltrative adnexal carcinoma with bland cytology, keratin cysts, ductal structures, and frequent perineural invasion. Superficial keratin-filled microcysts; deeper infiltrative cords and ducts in desmoplastic stroma; ductal lumina may contain eosinophilic cuticle; perineural/intraneural invasion. Syringoma is circumscribed and superficial; desmoplastic trichoepithelioma is smaller and more symmetric with follicular structures; morpheaform BCC shows basaloid palisading/retraction. Low mutation burden; reported TP53 and JAK/STAT pathway alterations; no routine diagnostic molecular marker. Apocrine carcinoma Adults 44–91 years, male predominance; upper or lower eyelid; solitary bluish-brown nodule with ulceration, bleeding, lash loss, discharge, or chalazion-like presentation. Infiltrative carcinoma with apocrine differentiation, including decapitation secretion and/or zymogen granules. Glandular, tubular, papillary, or solid infiltrative growth; abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm; apical snouts and intracytoplasmic granules; CK7, GCDFP-15, androgen receptor often positive. Sebaceous carcinoma has lipid-rich vacuoles/adipophilin; metastatic breast carcinoma requires clinical correlation; EMPSGC shows neuroendocrine differentiation and mucin. No established defining molecular alteration for routine diagnosis. Eyelid melanocytic nevi Benign melanocytic Any age; eyelid skin or margin; usually small, symmetric, well-circumscribed pigmented or skin-colored papule; congenital or acquired. Benign melanocytic proliferation with maturation, symmetry, and no significant atypia; classify junctional, compound, or dermal pattern. Nests of bland melanocytes; maturation with depth in compound/dermal nevi; congenital nevi may involve adnexa; melan-A/SOX10 highlight melanocytes; HMB45 often decreases with maturation. Melanoma shows asymmetry, cytologic atypia, lack of maturation, mitoses, or destructive growth; pigmented BCC is epithelial and BerEP4-positive. Common acquired nevi may harbor BRAF or NRAS pathway mutations; testing is not routine. Spitz nevus Rare on eyelid; usually children/young patients; rapidly growing solitary pink-red vascular papule or nodule. Symmetric, circumscribed proliferation of epithelioid/spindle melanocytes with maturation and no high-grade atypia or deep atypical mitoses. Large epithelioid/spindle cells in nests/fascicles; clefting, epidermal hyperplasia, maturation; S100/SOX10/Melan-A positive; p16 retained; HMB45 may be superficial. Spitzoid melanoma shows asymmetry, ulceration, deep mitoses, atypia, and/or genomic complexity; conventional nevus lacks characteristic large spitzoid cells. Spitz lineage may show HRAS mutation or kinase fusions (ALK, ROS1, NTRK, RET); molecular testing can help in atypical cases. Cutaneous melanoma in situ Premalignant melanocytic Usually older adults for lentigo maligna; chronically sun-damaged eyelid/periocular skin; flat asymmetric irregularly pigmented macule. Atypical melanocytes proliferate within epidermis and adnexal epithelium without dermal invasion. Lentiginous single-cell growth and/or pagetoid spread; atypical melanocytes along basal/suprabasal epidermis and follicles; SOX10 highlights cells; PRAME positivity/loss of p16 may support diagnosis. Benign lentigo/nevus lacks significant atypia and confluent growth; pigmented actinic keratosis has atypical keratinocytes and melanocyte hyperplasia; invasive melanoma shows dermal invasion. No routine molecular testing for in situ disease. Invasive cutaneous melanoma Malignant melanocytic Usually older adults (median about 71 years); lower eyelid more often than upper; asymmetric variably pigmented or amelanotic macule/nodule, sometimes ulcerated. Malignant atypical melanocytes with dermal invasion; report Breslow thickness, ulceration, mitotic rate, lymphovascular/perineural invasion, satellites, and margins. Atypical melanocytes in nests/sheets or single cells; pagetoid/lentiginous epidermal component may be present; SOX10, S100, Melan-A, and HMB45 support lineage; PRAME may assist. Nevus shows maturation and symmetry; Spitz nevus has uniform spitzoid cytology and limited mitoses; melanoma in situ lacks dermal invasion; metastatic melanoma requires clinical correlation. BRAF, NRAS, NF1, and TERT promoter alterations are relevant; test actionable mutations, especially in advanced disease. All Ophthalmic Pathology · Diagnostic Reference Eyelid Tumors and Tumor-Like Lesions A practical guide to the clinicopathologic features, diagnostic criteria, immunophenotype, and molecular findings of common and distinctive eyelid lesions. Diagnostic Approach Anatomic compartment Determine whether the lesion is epidermal, follicular, sebaceous, sweat gland, melanocytic, or dermal/subcutaneous. Growth pattern Assess circumscription, symmetry, depth, infiltrative growth, perineural invasion, and pagetoid spread. Cytologic features Evaluate maturation, atypia, mitotic activity, necrosis, and differentiation. Clinical context Correlate age, location, recurrence, chronic sun damage, immunosuppression, and possible hereditary syndromes.
