title: Genetic Tumor Syndromes
content: use client Retinoblastoma Syndrome Hereditary cancer predisposition Retinal and intracranial tumors Usually recognized in infancy or early childhood through unilateral or bilateral retinoblastoma; bilateral disease is common in heritable cases, although approximately 15% are unilateral. Retinal tumors may be followed by pineal or suprasellar primitive neuroectodermal tumors (trilateral retinoblastoma); survivors remain at lifelong risk for second primary malignancies. Secondary malignancies include osteosarcoma, soft-tissue sarcoma (especially leiomyosarcoma and rhabdomyosarcoma), melanoma, and epithelial cancers; risk is increased after external-beam radiotherapy. Retinoblastoma in a patient with a germline heterozygous pathogenic RB1 variant, a relevant family history, or bilateral/multifocal disease strongly supports heritable retinoblastoma. Confirm germline RB1 status using blood-based molecular testing; evaluate for mosaicism when clinical suspicion remains despite negative standard testing. Trilateral retinoblastoma requires retinoblastoma with a synchronous or metachronous pineal or suprasellar intracranial embryonal tumor. Document optic nerve, extrascleral, and intracranial involvement because these findings affect staging and management. Ocular retinoblastoma shows the characteristic morphology of retinoblastoma, including primitive neuroblastic cells; differentiation may include Flexner-Wintersteiner or Homer Wright rosettes. Intracranial tumors in trilateral retinoblastoma are embryonal tumors with histology resembling retinoblastoma; pineoblastoma is a high-grade embryonal tumor. Histology of subsequent sarcomas, melanomas, and epithelial malignancies is generally the same as that of their sporadic counterparts. Retinoblastoma commonly shows loss of nuclear RB protein expression, although interpretation requires appropriate internal controls. Immunophenotype of secondary malignancies is determined by the specific tumor type; no single IHC profile defines the syndrome. Nonheritable retinoblastoma: often unilateral and unifocal; germline RB1 testing and family history distinguish heritable disease. Other pediatric retinal tumors or mimics: correlate morphology with retinal location, imaging, and RB1 status. Primary pineal or suprasellar embryonal tumor unrelated to retinoblastoma: assess for current or prior retinoblastoma and germline RB1 alteration. Germline heterozygous pathogenic RB1 variant establishes heritable retinoblastoma predisposition. Tumorigenesis follows biallelic RB1 inactivation; the second hit may involve sequence variants, deletion, loss of heterozygosity, complex rearrangement, or promoter methylation. Use sequencing with deletion/duplication analysis; RNA analysis may detect deep intronic splice variants. Consider mosaicism when blood testing is negative. BAP1 Tumor Predisposition Syndrome Melanocytic and multisystem tumors Autosomal dominant syndrome; tumors often arise at younger ages than their sporadic counterparts, and affected individuals may develop multiple primary malignancies. Key associated tumors include uveal melanoma, mesothelioma (often peritoneal and without male predominance), cutaneous melanoma, renal cell carcinoma, and meningioma. BAP1-inactivated melanocytic nevi / melanocytomas may occur in childhood and are a useful clinical clue, but are not specific for the syndrome. Definitive diagnosis requires a heterozygous pathogenic germline BAP1 variant. Consider genetic counseling and germline testing in patients with two or more BAP1-associated tumors, or one such tumor plus an affected first- or second-degree relative. Loss of nuclear BAP1 expression in a relevant tumor supports BAP1 inactivation and can help select patients for germline evaluation, but does not independently establish a germline syndrome. Histologic features of syndrome-associated uveal melanoma, mesothelioma, renal cell carcinoma, and other tumors generally resemble their sporadic counterparts. BAP1-inactivated melanocytic tumors often show epithelioid melanocytes, frequently with a spitzoid or nested growth pattern. Histologic appearance alone cannot reliably distinguish germline-associated tumors from sporadic tumors. BAP1-deficient tumor cells show loss of nuclear BAP1 staining, with retained staining in non-neoplastic internal control cells. BAP1 immunohistochemistry is a screening tool; concordance with germline status is high but incomplete. Sporadic BAP1-deficient tumor: may show the same loss of nuclear BAP1; germline testing distinguishes tumor-restricted from inherited alteration. Other atypical or spitzoid melanocytic nevi: morphology overlaps with BAP1-inactivated melanocytoma; correlate with BAP1 IHC and clinical/family history. Metastatic or multiple primary tumors: consider the full personal and family tumor spectrum rather than assuming a single metastatic process. Pathogenic germline BAP1 variants, usually loss-of-function sequence variants or deletions, establish the syndrome. Confirm with germline sequencing and deletion/duplication analysis on peripheral blood or another appropriate non-neoplastic specimen. Somatic BAP1 alterations are common in sporadic mesothelioma and metastatic uveal melanoma; tumor-only mutation does not prove hereditary disease. Von Hippel-Lindau Syndrome Retinal and multisystem tumors Autosomal dominant disorder; retinal capillary hemangioblastomas often appear in young adulthood (mean age approximately 25 years) and may be the earliest manifestation. Other characteristic lesions include CNS hemangioblastomas, bilateral/multifocal clear cell renal cell carcinoma, pheochromocytoma, pancreatic cysts or neuroendocrine tumors, and endolymphatic sac tumors. Retinal lesions may cause visual symptoms through exudation, hemorrhage, or retinal detachment; endolymphatic sac tumors may cause hearing loss, tinnitus, or vertigo. Diagnosis is established by a pathogenic germline VHL variant in the appropriate clinical context. Retinal or CNS hemangioblastomas together with characteristic visceral lesions strongly support VHL. Assess personal and family history for multifocal or bilateral renal lesions, pheochromocytoma, pancreatic lesions, and endolymphatic sac tumors. VHL-associated tumors generally have the same histology as their sporadic counterparts. Retinal capillary hemangioblastoma contains a dense capillary network with endothelial cells, pericytes, and characteristic vacuolated or foamy stromal cells. Clear cell renal cell carcinoma shows nests or alveoli of clear cells with delicate vasculature; correlate with renal findings and VHL status. Retinal hemangioblastoma stromal cells may express inhibin-alpha, S100, and other stromal markers; endothelial cells highlight with CD31 and ERG. No single immunohistochemical profile establishes VHL syndrome; IHC should be tailored to the specific tumor and differential diagnosis. Sporadic retinal hemangioblastoma: may be morphologically identical; germline VHL testing and evaluation for multifocal/systemic lesions distinguish syndromic disease. Other retinal vascular lesions: hemangioblastoma has a characteristic capillary-rich pattern with stromal cells rather than a simple vascular malformation. Metastatic clear cell renal cell carcinoma to the eye or orbit: correlate with known renal primary and systemic evaluation. Germline pathogenic VHL variant, detected by sequencing and deletion/duplication analysis, confirms the syndrome. Biallelic VHL inactivation leads to HIF stabilization and a pseudohypoxic transcriptional program, including increased VEGF signaling. VHL alterations also occur in sporadic hemangioblastomas and clear cell renal cell carcinomas; tumor testing alone does not establish hereditary VHL. Sturge-Weber Syndrome Mosaic neurocutaneous vascular syndrome Ocular and neurocutaneous vascular lesions Congenital, usually sporadic condition with no established hereditary pattern; affects individuals of either sex. Typical findings include unilateral facial capillary malformation (port-wine birthmark) in the trigeminal distribution, leptomeningeal vascular malformation, and ocular vascular abnormalities. Ocular manifestations include diffuse choroidal capillary malformation, episcleral and conjunctival vascular dilation, glaucoma, iris heterochromia, and secondary retinal/RPE changes. Clinical diagnosis is supported by the characteristic combination of facial capillary malformation, glaucoma or elevated intraocular pressure, and leptomeningeal capillary-venous malformation. Two of the three major features support the diagnosis; isolated leptomeningeal involvement is recognized as type 3 Sturge-Weber syndrome. Imaging is important for defining intracranial and ocular involvement; evaluate for choroidal thickening and secondary retinal detachment. Choroidal, episcleral, and conjunctival lesions consist of unencapsulated collections of variably dilated, thin-walled vascular channels. Choroidal involvement may produce diffuse choroidal thickening and dilated draining vortex veins. Secondary changes may include retinal pigment epithelial alterations, subretinal fibrosis, and exudative retinal detachment. Endothelial cells express vascular markers such as CD31 and ERG. Immunohistochemistry is not usually required; morphology and clinical/radiologic correlation are central. Isolated facial port-wine birthmark: lacks the characteristic intracranial and ocular manifestations of Sturge-Weber syndrome. Other diffuse choroidal vascular lesions: correlate with facial capillary malformation, episcleral vascular changes, and glaucoma. Hereditary vascular malformation syndromes: distinguish by distribution, associated organ involvement, and molecular context. Most cases harbor a postzygotic activating somatic mosaic GNAQ variant, commonly p.R183Q, in affected tissue. Rare GNA11 or other pathway variants have been reported; a negative result does not exclude the syndrome because mosaic variant allele fractions may be low. Testing should use affected tissue when available; GNAQ p.R183Q is not specific to Sturge-Weber syndrome and also occurs in some isolated port-wine birthmarks. Neurofibromatosis Type 1 Autosomal dominant tumor predisposition syndrome Neural and ocular manifestations Usually recognized in childhood; birth incidence is approximately 1 in 3,000, with equal sex distribution. Characteristic findings include multiple café-au-lait macules, axillary/inguinal freckling, cutaneous and plexiform neurofibromas, and iris Lisch nodules. Ocular/orbital manifestations include optic pathway glioma (usually in young children), choroidal abnormalities, Lisch nodules, sphenoid wing dysplasia, and orbitofacial plexiform neurofibroma. Clinical diagnosis requires at least two accepted diagnostic features, including café-au-lait macules, axillary/inguinal freckling, neurofibromas, optic pathway glioma, Lisch nodules or choroidal abnormalities, characteristic bone lesion, a pathogenic NF1 variant, or an affected parent. Use current age-adjusted size thresholds for café-au-lait macules: greater than 5 mm in children and greater than 15 mm in adults. Consider NF1 testing when clinical criteria are incomplete, atypical, or difficult to assess; sequencing and deletion/duplication analysis are used. Lisch nodules are dome-shaped iris hamartomas composed of bland spindle-shaped melanocytes in a disorganized arrangement. Neurofibromas contain bland Schwannian cells, fibroblastic cells, mast cells, and axons in a collagenous or myxoid stroma. NF1-associated optic pathway gliomas are usually pilocytic astrocytomas. Malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumor shows malignant spindle cells, increased mitotic activity, and often necrosis; it may arise in a plexiform neurofibroma. Neurofibromas typically show S100 and SOX10 expression in Schwannian cells, with variable staining in the overall lesional population. Loss of neurofibromin expression may support NF1-associated tumorigenesis but is not a stand-alone germline diagnostic test. Optic pathway glioma immunophenotype is that of the corresponding low-grade glioma, commonly including GFAP positivity. Legius syndrome: café-au-lait macules and freckling may overlap, but neurofibromas, optic pathway glioma, and Lisch nodules are generally absent. Schwannoma: typically shows diffuse strong Schwannian marker expression and lacks the mixed cellular composition and axons characteristic of neurofibroma. Other low-grade gliomas: correlate optic pathway location and clinical findings; NF1-associated optic pathway glioma is usually pilocytic. NF1 is an autosomal dominant tumor suppressor gene at 17q11.2; a heterozygous germline pathogenic variant establishes molecular diagnosis. Somatic second-hit inactivation of the remaining allele drives many NF1-associated lesions through increased RAS/MAPK and PI3K/AKT signaling. Testing should include sequencing and deletion/duplication analysis; RNA/cDNA analysis may improve detection of splice-altering variants. Large 17q11.2 microdeletions involving NF1 and neighboring genes occur in approximately 5–11% of cases. Goldenhar Syndrome (Craniofacial Microsomia) Congenital craniofacial developmental syndrome Ocular and craniofacial developmental anomalies Congenital condition, usually sporadic; approximately 1 in 5,000 births. Many series report a male predominance, although this is not consistent. Usually unilateral (70–90%) and characterized by hemifacial/mandibular hypoplasia, auricular anomalies or preauricular tags, and vertebral abnormalities. Ocular findings include inferotemporal limbal dermoid or epibulbar choristoma, upper eyelid coloboma, lipodermoid, microphthalmia, strabismus, and occasionally lacrimal drainage obstruction. Clinical diagnosis is based on craniofacial microsomia with facial asymmetry and characteristic auricular findings, together with ocular and/or vertebral anomalies. Look specifically for epibulbar dermoid/choristoma, eyelid coloboma, preauricular tags, mandibular hypoplasia, and cervical vertebral anomalies. Genetic testing is not routinely required because the syndrome is genetically heterogeneous and most cases lack an identifiable diagnostic variant. Epibulbar dermoid is composed of dense collagen resembling dermis, often with pilosebaceous and eccrine/apocrine adnexal structures. Dermolipoma contains abundant mature adipose tissue beneath conjunctival epithelium. Complex choristoma may contain lacrimal gland tissue, cartilage, and smooth muscle. Histology reflects the specific ocular choristoma and is not independently diagnostic of Goldenhar syndrome. Immunohistochemistry is generally unnecessary for typical epibulbar dermoid, dermolipoma, or choristoma. Use lineage-directed markers only when an unusual component raises a specific differential diagnosis. Isolated epibulbar dermoid or dermolipoma: lacks the broader craniofacial, auricular, and vertebral phenotype. Other craniofacial microsomia syndromes: distinguish by associated ear, mandibular, vertebral, cardiac, renal, and ocular findings. Encephalocraniocutaneous lipomatosis and linear nevus sebaceous syndrome: consider when characteristic cutaneous or CNS abnormalities accompany ocular choristomas. Most cases are multifactorial and no single molecular alteration is diagnostic. SF3B2 loss-of-function variants have been identified in a subset, particularly familial cases; reported frequencies are approximately 25% of familial and 3% of sporadic cases. Other reported candidate alterations include copy-number variants and variants involving OTX2 and MYT1; these findings are not required for diagnosis. Muir-Torre Syndrome Lynch syndrome variant / hereditary cancer syndrome Sebaceous and visceral neoplasms Usually presents in adults, but associated visceral malignancies may arise at a relatively young age; no consistent sex predilection is established. Characterized by sebaceous neoplasms, especially sebaceous adenoma and sebaceoma, together with Lynch syndrome-associated visceral malignancy. Ocular adnexal sebaceous neoplasms, including eyelid lesions, may occur but are uncommon; colorectal, endometrial, gastric, small bowel, ovarian, urinary tract, and other cancers are associated. Suspect the syndrome in a patient with sebaceous neoplasms and a personal or family history of Lynch-associated visceral malignancy, particularly with multiple sebaceous tumors. Assess mismatch repair protein expression by IHC and/or microsatellite instability in an appropriate tumor, recognizing that periocular sebaceous carcinoma has limited screening sensitivity. Definitive diagnosis requires identification of a germline pathogenic variant in an MMR gene or an EPCAM deletion causing MSH2 silencing. Sebaceous adenoma and sebaceoma show well-differentiated sebaceous lobules; sebaceous carcinoma shows infiltrative growth and cytologic atypia. The histology of sebaceous and visceral tumors is generally indistinguishable from their sporadic counterparts. MMR-deficient sebaceous neoplasms may show loss of one or more mismatch repair proteins by immunohistochemistry. Evaluate MLH1, PMS2, MSH2, and MSH6; paired loss patterns may suggest the affected MMR pathway. Loss of MSH2 and MSH6 is frequently encountered in Muir-Torre-associated sebaceous tumors; isolated MSH6 or PMS2 loss can also occur. Retained MMR protein expression does not completely exclude the syndrome, particularly in periocular sebaceous neoplasms. Sporadic sebaceous adenoma/sebaceoma: may be morphologically identical; multiple lesions, visceral cancer history, MMR IHC, and germline testing aid distinction. Isolated Lynch syndrome: shares the visceral cancer predisposition but lacks the characteristic sebaceous neoplasm phenotype. MUTYH-associated polyposis: can rarely produce overlapping sebaceous and visceral tumor findings; inheritance pattern and germline testing distinguish it. Most cases result from germline pathogenic variants in MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, or PMS2; EPCAM deletions can cause epigenetic silencing of MSH2. Biallelic MMR inactivation produces mismatch repair deficiency and microsatellite instability. Somatic MMR alterations are common in sebaceous tumors; confirm suspected hereditary disease with germline testing rather than tumor-only sequencing. Retinal and intracranial tumor predisposition Retinoblastoma syndrome Germline RB1 inactivation predisposes to unilateral or bilateral retinoblastoma, trilateral retinoblastoma, and lifelong risk of second primary malignancies. Melanocytic and multisystem tumor predisposition BAP1 tumor predisposition syndrome Germline BAP1 alteration is associated with uveal and cutaneous melanoma, mesothelioma, renal cell carcinoma, meningioma, and BAP1-inactivated melanocytic tumors. Retinal and multisystem tumor predisposition Von Hippel-Lindau syndrome Germline VHL alteration predisposes to retinal and CNS hemangioblastomas, clear cell renal cell carcinoma, pheochromocytoma, and pancreatic and endolymphatic sac lesions. Sturge-Weber syndrome Postzygotic mosaic GNAQ-pathway activation causes capillary malformations involving the face, leptomeninges, and eye, with risk of glaucoma and diffuse choroidal involvement. Neural and ocular tumor predisposition Neurofibromatosis type 1 Germline NF1 inactivation is associated with optic pathway glioma, Lisch nodules, choroidal abnormalities, neurofibromas, and characteristic skeletal findings. Craniofacial and ocular developmental syndrome Goldenhar syndrome (craniofacial microsomia) A developmental disorder involving first- and second-arch structures, typically with hemifacial microsomia, auricular anomalies, epibulbar choristomas, and vertebral defects. Sebaceous and visceral tumor predisposition Muir-Torre syndrome A Lynch syndrome variant caused by germline mismatch repair pathway defects, characterized by sebaceous neoplasms and an increased risk of visceral malignancies. All Ophthalmic Pathology Genetic Tumor Syndromes Associated with Eye and Orbit Tumors Hereditary and mosaic disorders with characteristic ocular, orbital, and systemic manifestations. Recognition of these syndromes can prompt germline evaluation, family counseling, and surveillance for associated malignancies. Diagnostic Overview The table summarizes the principal genetic mechanism, associated ocular findings, and broader tumor spectrum for each syndrome. title: Lacrimal Gland And Drainage Tumors
content: use client Lacrimal gland Lacrimal drainage system Both / site-dependent Dacryops cyst Benign cystic lesion Usually adults in the fourth to fifth decades, but any age; no consistent sex predilection. Most often arises in the palpebral lobe; typically presents as painless eyelid fullness, localized swelling, or mild irritation. Cyst lined by nonkeratinizing, two-layered columnar-to-cuboidal epithelium with scattered goblet cells. Residual lacrimal acini and variably dilated ducts are present in the cyst wall. Imaging typically shows a well-defined fluid-filled lesion without a solid enhancing nodule. The lining is composed of two layers of bland columnar or cuboidal cells. Scattered goblet cells and apical projections may be present. The lumen may contain eosinophilic or mucoid secretions. The cyst wall may show residual acini, dilated ducts, chronic inflammation, and fibrosis. CK7 and CK18 highlight the lining epithelium. The lining is generally negative for CK17, SMA, S100, and GCDFP-15. Conjunctival inclusion cyst: usually squamous epithelial lining and no residual lacrimal acini in the wall. Respiratory epithelial cyst: ciliated respiratory-type lining. Lymphoma or epithelial neoplasm: solid tissue component or nodular enhancement rather than a simple cyst. No established diagnostic molecular alteration. Pleomorphic adenoma Benign epithelial-myoepithelial neoplasm Mean age approximately 40 years; broad age range; no established sex predilection. Usually arises in the orbital lobe and presents as a slowly enlarging, painless superotemporal mass with proptosis or globe displacement; diplopia may occur. Well-circumscribed lacrimal fossa mass, usually with smooth bony remodeling rather than destructive erosion. Admixture of ductal epithelial cells, myoepithelial cells, and variable chondromyxoid or fibrous stroma. No destructive invasion or overt malignant cytology. Intact excision is important; avoid incisional biopsy when pleomorphic adenoma is strongly suspected clinically. Bilayered ducts are admixed with variable epithelial and myoepithelial components. Myoepithelial cells may be spindle, plasmacytoid, clear, epithelioid, or squamoid. Stroma may be myxoid, chondroid, hyaline, fibrous, or osseous. Pseudocapsular protrusions and satellite nodules explain the risk of recurrence after incomplete excision. Luminal cells express CK7 and CAM5.2. Myoepithelial cells express p40, p63, SMA, and calponin. Nuclear PLAG1 and/or HMGA2 expression may support the diagnosis; Ki-67 is usually very low. Myoepithelioma: predominantly or exclusively myoepithelial cells with little or no ductal component. Adenoid cystic carcinoma: infiltrative biphasic growth, basaloid cytology, and frequent perineural invasion. Carcinoma ex pleomorphic adenoma: malignant component, atypia, and/or invasion in association with pleomorphic adenoma. PLAG1 rearrangements are common; HMGA2 rearrangements occur in a subset. These alterations can help establish a pleomorphic adenoma component in selected cases. Lacrimal gland oncocytoma Benign oncocytic epithelial neoplasm Typically adults in the sixth to eighth decades; slight female predominance. May arise in main or accessory lacrimal glands; presents as a well-defined mass, proptosis, eyelid fullness, caruncular enlargement, or lacrimal drainage obstruction depending on site. Well-delineated epithelial neoplasm composed of oncocytes with abundant granular eosinophilic cytoplasm. Solid, papillary, or cystic architecture may be present. Absence of destructive invasion, significant atypia, and brisk mitotic activity supports oncocytoma rather than oncocytic carcinoma. Polygonal cells have abundant finely granular eosinophilic cytoplasm rich in mitochondria. Cells form sheets, nests, trabeculae, or papillary/cystic structures. Nuclei are generally bland with vesicular chromatin and a conspicuous nucleolus. Oncocytic carcinoma shows atypia, mitoses, and invasion of adjacent soft tissue or bone. Antimitochondrial staining may highlight the abundant mitochondria. CK7 and other ductal cytokeratins and EMA are typically positive. Ki-67 is usually very low in oncocytoma. Oncocytic carcinoma: destructive invasion, cytologic atypia, and mitotic activity. Ductal adenocarcinoma: malignant ductal growth with pleomorphism and often comedonecrosis, without the characteristic mitochondrial accumulation. Metastatic oncocytic neoplasm: exclude a nonocular primary clinically. No recurrent, diagnostically established molecular alteration is defined for lacrimal oncocytoma. Myoepithelioma and myoepithelial carcinoma Myoepithelial neoplasms Rare; broad age range; both sexes are affected. Usually a slow-growing, painless superotemporal orbital mass causing proptosis, globe displacement, or ptosis; carcinoma may show more rapid growth or fixation. Myoepithelial neoplasm composed of a relatively uniform population of cells with myoepithelial differentiation. Myoepithelioma is circumscribed and lacks destructive invasion. Myoepithelial carcinoma is diagnosed by invasion into gland, orbital soft tissue, bone, or perineural spaces; cytologic atypia may be variable. Cells may be spindle, plasmacytoid, epithelioid, or clear and grow in sheets or trabeculae. Ducts, microcysts, mucinous foci, and hyalinized fibrous areas may occur. Carcinoma may be cytologically bland; infiltrative growth is the key malignant feature. Tumor cells express cytokeratins, including CK7 and CK14. S100, p63, SMA, muscle-specific actin, and calponin are variably positive. GFAP may be positive in a subset. Pleomorphic adenoma: conspicuous chondromyxoid stroma and a more evident ductal component. Adenoid cystic carcinoma: dual ductal/myoepithelial population with characteristic cribriform or tubular architecture and hyaline basement-membrane material. Epithelial-myoepithelial carcinoma: distinct inner ductal and outer myoepithelial cell layers. No validated lacrimal-specific molecular test is established; EWSR1 rearrangements and 12q alterations are described mainly in salivary counterparts and should be interpreted cautiously. Intraductal carcinoma In situ / intraductal carcinoma Exceptionally rare in the lacrimal gland; only isolated cases reported. Reported presentation includes proptosis and inferomedial globe displacement. Well-circumscribed lobules of neoplastic ductal cells are completely surrounded by a continuous peripheral myoepithelial layer. No stromal invasion should be identified. Round lobules show solid, cribriform, papillary-cystic, or micropapillary architecture. Ductal cells are large and polygonal with amphophilic or oncocytic cytoplasm and usually low-grade atypia. Eosinophilic secretions may fill cystic spaces. Intercalated-duct and oncocytic types may express CK19, S100, SOX10, and mammaglobin. Apocrine-type tumors may express AR and GCDFP-15. The peripheral myoepithelial layer expresses p63, p40, CK5/6, calponin, and SMA. Invasive carcinoma: loss of the continuous peripheral myoepithelial layer and stromal invasion. Adenoid cystic carcinoma: infiltrative growth and characteristic basement-membrane-rich cribriform pattern. Pleomorphic adenoma: mixed epithelial-myoepithelial proliferation with chondromyxoid stroma. RET rearrangements, including NCOA4::RET, are described in salivary intraductal carcinoma; molecular confirmation may support the diagnosis, but FISH can be falsely negative. Carcinoma ex pleomorphic adenoma Malignant epithelial neoplasm arising in pleomorphic adenoma Median age approximately 56 years; no clear sex predilection. A longstanding or recurrent lacrimal fossa mass may suddenly enlarge, become painful or fixed, or cause proptosis, globe displacement, or skin ulceration. Malignant epithelial and/or myoepithelial component arising in association with a primary or recurrent pleomorphic adenoma. Identify residual or hyalinized remnants of pleomorphic adenoma; extensive sampling may be required. Document capsular and extracapsular invasion when assessable. A transition between residual pleomorphic adenoma and carcinoma may be demonstrable. The malignant component may show ductal adenocarcinoma, squamous, mucoepidermoid, myoepithelial, or adenoid cystic differentiation. Perineural, lymphovascular, and bone invasion may be present. PLAG1 and HMGA2 may highlight the underlying pleomorphic adenoma component. The carcinoma component may show increased Ki-67, p53, or MYC expression. AR may support ductal/apocrine differentiation. De novo ductal adenocarcinoma or other primary carcinoma: lacks an associated pleomorphic adenoma component or convincing molecular evidence of one. Recurrent benign pleomorphic adenoma: lacks malignant cytology and destructive invasion. Metastatic carcinoma: correlate with clinical history and imaging. PLAG1 or HMGA2 rearrangements support an underlying pleomorphic adenoma and may help distinguish carcinoma ex pleomorphic adenoma from de novo carcinoma. Adenoid cystic carcinoma Malignant epithelial neoplasm Most often middle-aged adults, with a smaller childhood peak; slight female predominance. Usually orbital lobe; rapidly progressive superotemporal mass with proptosis and inferomedial globe displacement. Pain or paresthesia strongly raises concern for perineural invasion. Malignant biphasic epithelial and myoepithelial neoplasm with tubular, cribriform, and/or solid-basaloid growth. Basophilic or hyalinized basement-membrane-like material is characteristic. Perineural invasion is common and should be actively sought. Cribriform architecture contains pseudocystic spaces filled with basophilic or hyaline material. Tubular areas show small glandular structures with dual cell populations. Solid-basaloid areas are associated with more aggressive behavior. High-grade transformation may show comedonecrosis, marked atypia, and increased mitoses. Luminal cells express cytokeratins; abluminal cells express myoepithelial markers. MYB and KIT may be positive but are not fully sensitive or specific. Ki-67 is often increased, particularly in solid areas. Pleomorphic adenoma: circumscribed, noninvasive, with chondromyxoid stroma. Myoepithelial carcinoma: lacks the characteristic dual ductal/basaloid pattern and basement-membrane-rich cribriform structures. Basal cell adenocarcinoma and epithelial-myoepithelial carcinoma: compare architecture and immunophenotype. MYB::NFIB or MYBL1::NFIB fusions are recurrent and diagnostically useful in selected cases. NOTCH pathway alterations occur in a subset and are associated with more aggressive, often solid-pattern tumors. Primary ductal adenocarcinoma High-grade malignant epithelial neoplasm Typically older adults, mean age approximately 58 years; reported male predominance. Presents with a painless or painful lacrimal fossa mass, proptosis, ptosis, diplopia, or visual decline; imaging often shows an irregular heterogeneous mass with possible bone erosion. Invasive adenocarcinoma with ductal differentiation arising de novo in the lacrimal gland. Exclude carcinoma ex pleomorphic adenoma and metastasis, particularly breast carcinoma. Comedonecrosis and an apocrine phenotype support the diagnosis. Polygonal cells with granular eosinophilic cytoplasm, pleomorphic vesicular nuclei, and prominent nucleoli. Glandular, cribriform, and solid ductal patterns are common. Central comedonecrosis is frequent; perineural, lymphovascular, and bone invasion may occur. Tumor cells express pancytokeratin, CK7, EMA, AR, and GCDFP-15. ERBB2/HER2 may be overexpressed or amplified. Myoepithelial markers are usually negative; ER and PR are generally negative. Carcinoma ex pleomorphic adenoma: residual PA component or PLAG1/HMGA2 alteration. Metastatic breast ductal carcinoma: clinical/radiologic correlation and appropriate breast markers. Adenocarcinoma NOS: lacks the characteristic ductal/apocrine phenotype and comedonecrosis. ERBB2 amplification is present in a subset and may have therapeutic relevance. Secretory carcinoma Rare malignant epithelial neoplasm Reported lacrimal gland cases include adults in the third to sixth decades; sex distribution is uncertain. May present as a circumscribed lacrimal fossa mass with painless proptosis or diplopia; also reported in eyelid/accessory lacrimal tissue. Monophasic carcinoma with secretory/vacuolated cytoplasm and luminal secretions. S100, mammaglobin, and pan-TRK/NTRK immunoreactivity support the diagnosis. Confirm an ETV6-related fusion when needed. Papillary-cystic, solid, and microfollicular patterns may coexist. Cells are round to ovoid with pale eosinophilic, often focally vacuolated cytoplasm. Intracytoplasmic zymogen granules and goblet cells are absent. S100, mammaglobin, CK18, and NTRK are typically positive. p63, CK5, DOG1, and AR are generally negative. Ki-67 is often low in reported cases. Acinic cell carcinoma: zymogen granules and NR4A3 expression/rearrangement; usually lacks the secretory carcinoma immunophenotype. Myoepithelial neoplasm: broader myoepithelial marker expression. Metastatic secretory carcinoma: exclude a primary elsewhere. ETV6::NTRK3 is the characteristic fusion in most cases; other ETV6 partners are possible. NTRK fusion identification may guide TRK inhibitor therapy in unresectable or metastatic disease. Mucoepidermoid carcinoma Lacrimal gland cases typically present around the fifth decade; younger patients may be affected. Usually a slowly enlarging lacrimal fossa mass; occasionally painful proptosis. Drainage-system tumors typically cause unilateral epiphora and a medial canthal mass. Mixture of mucous, epidermoid/squamoid, and intermediate cells in variable proportions. Low-grade tumors are often cystic and mucous-cell rich; high-grade tumors are more solid with increased squamoid/intermediate cells. Use mucin stains when mucous cells are inconspicuous. Mucous cells form glands and cysts containing mucin. Epidermoid cells have eosinophilic cytoplasm and intercellular bridges; keratinization is variable. Intermediate cells have oval nuclei and scant to faintly eosinophilic cytoplasm. Grade using architecture, cystic component, necrosis, mitoses, atypia, and invasion. CK5/6, CK7, and CK14 are commonly positive. Mucin markers may highlight mucous cells; p63 may be focal. Myoepithelial markers are generally negative. Squamous cell carcinoma: lacks a convincing mucous-cell component. Adenosquamous carcinoma: true glandular and squamous differentiation, often with an in situ component. Pleomorphic adenoma with mucous/squamous metaplasia: bland architecture and myoepithelial/chondromyxoid component. CRTC1::MAML2 is a useful recurrent alteration in lacrimal gland mucoepidermoid carcinoma. A CRTC1/3::MAML2 fusion has not been identified in reported lacrimal sac tumors; do not assume the fusion is present in drainage-system cases. Epithelial-myoepithelial carcinoma Low-grade malignant biphasic epithelial neoplasm Usually middle-aged or older adults; reported median age approximately 60 years, with slight male predominance. Slow-growing painless orbital mass with proptosis; some cases show pain, diplopia, or restricted ocular motility. Usually multinodular invasive tumor with a biphasic ductal and myoepithelial arrangement. Inner ductal cells are surrounded by larger outer myoepithelial cells, often clear. Assess for high-grade transformation, necrosis, and perineural invasion. Tubules have inner eosinophilic ductal cells and outer clear or pale myoepithelial cells. The outer layer may be single or multilayered; solid areas and variant patterns may occur. Invasion is often multinodular; high-grade transformation is uncommon. Inner cells express pancytokeratin and CK7. Outer cells express p63, SMA, calponin, and S100. RAS p.Q61R immunoreactivity may be present in the myoepithelial component. Adenoid cystic carcinoma: basaloid cells and basement-membrane-rich cribriform/tubular structures, often MYB altered. Pleomorphic adenoma: chondromyxoid stroma and lack of infiltrative growth. Myoepithelial carcinoma: lacks the orderly inner ductal/outer myoepithelial arrangement. HRAS mutations, particularly codon 61 alterations, support the diagnosis. MYB fusion testing may help exclude adenoid cystic carcinoma in difficult cases. Acinic cell carcinoma Malignant epithelial neoplasm with acinar differentiation Extremely rare; most reported patients are in their fifties, with slight female predominance. May be asymptomatic or present as a slowly growing painless lacrimal fossa mass with proptosis or globe displacement. Malignant epithelial tumor showing serous acinar differentiation. Look for basophilic cytoplasmic granules that are PAS-positive and diastase-resistant. In challenging cases, exclude secretory carcinoma with immunohistochemistry and molecular testing. Solid, acinar, microcystic, papillary-cystic, or follicular patterns may occur. Cells are polygonal with abundant basophilic granular cytoplasm and small central or eccentric nuclei. High-grade transformation shows pleomorphism, increased mitoses, necrosis, and possible perineural or vascular invasion. DOG1 and SOX10 may be positive, particularly with acinar/intercalated duct differentiation. Nuclear NR4A3 or NR4A2 is highly useful in difficult cases. p63, S100, and mammaglobin are usually negative. Secretory carcinoma: often S100/mammaglobin positive and ETV6::NTRK3 fusion-positive; NR4A3 usually negative. Normal lacrimal acini: preserved lobular architecture without an infiltrative neoplasm. Mucoepidermoid carcinoma: mucous, epidermoid, and intermediate cell populations. NR4A3 rearrangement is diagnostically useful; NR4A3 immunohistochemistry is a practical surrogate. Salivary acinic cell carcinoma commonly shows enhancer-hijacking rearrangements involving NR4A3; apply molecular findings in the appropriate lacrimal context. Adenocarcinoma, NOS Lacrimal gland cases usually affect older adults, mean age approximately 50–52 years, with reported male predominance. Presents with upper eyelid swelling, ptosis, nonaxial proptosis, diplopia, pain, or visual decline; imaging may show irregular margins and bone erosion. Drainage-system cases typically present in the sixth to seventh decades with epiphora and an immobile medial canthal mass; bloody tearing is concerning. Invasive gland-forming malignant epithelial neoplasm that does not meet criteria for a more specific carcinoma type. Exclude metastasis and carcinoma arising in pleomorphic adenoma or oncocytoma. For drainage-system tumors, document mucosal relationship, invasion, and any associated precursor lesion. Glands, tubules, cribriform structures, cords, nests, or single infiltrating cells may be present. Cytologic atypia ranges from mild to marked; eosinophilic granular cytoplasm and prominent nucleoli may occur. Mucin production, oncocytic/apocrine features, mitoses, perineural invasion, and lymphovascular invasion are variable. Pancytokeratin and CK7 are commonly positive. AR and GCDFP-15 support apocrine/ductal differentiation, particularly in drainage-system tumors. ERBB2 expression is variable; use a panel to exclude specific salivary-type carcinomas and metastases. Primary ductal adenocarcinoma: more characteristic apocrine phenotype, comedonecrosis, and possible ERBB2 amplification. Carcinoma ex pleomorphic adenoma: residual PA or PLAG1/HMGA2 alteration. Metastatic carcinoma: clinical history, imaging, and site-directed immunohistochemistry. No defining alteration; fusion testing or targeted sequencing may help exclude fusion-defined carcinomas such as adenoid cystic or mucoepidermoid carcinoma. Squamous and inverted papillomas Benign epithelial neoplasms with recurrence / malignant potential considerations Usually adults; often presents with epiphora, recurrent dacryocystitis, or a medial canthal/lacrimal sac mass. May extend along the nasolacrimal duct; unilateral obstruction is typical. Papillary or inverted epithelial proliferation arising from the lacrimal sac or nasolacrimal duct mucosa. Evaluate the entire lesion for dysplasia, carcinoma in situ, and invasive squamous cell carcinoma. Inverted lesions show endophytic epithelial growth into the underlying stroma. Squamous papilloma shows exophytic papillary fronds with fibrovascular cores. Inverted papilloma shows broad endophytic nests and ribbons of squamous/transitional epithelium. Mucocytes, microcysts, and variable inflammation may be present; atypia and invasion indicate progression. Broad-spectrum cytokeratins and p40/p63 highlight squamous differentiation. Ki-67 and p53 may be increased in dysplastic or malignant areas but are not independently diagnostic. Invasive squamous cell carcinoma: destructive stromal invasion, atypia, and mitotic activity. Reactive epithelial hyperplasia: lacks organized papillomatous or inverted architecture. Sinonasal papilloma extending into the drainage system: assess anatomic epicenter and sinonasal involvement. HPV has been investigated in papillomatous lesions, but no single molecular test is required for routine diagnosis. Squamous cell carcinoma of the lacrimal drainage system Usually middle-aged or older adults; often presents with unilateral epiphora, recurrent dacryocystitis, and a firm medial canthal mass. Bloody tearing, pain, fixation, or extension beyond the sac raises concern for malignancy. Malignant squamous epithelial tumor arising from lacrimal sac or nasolacrimal duct mucosa. Distinguish keratinizing from nonkeratinizing morphology and assess invasion, grade, and extent. Exclude direct extension from conjunctival, cutaneous, or sinonasal carcinoma. Keratinizing tumors show nests and tongues of atypical squamous cells, intercellular bridges, and variable keratinization. Nonkeratinizing tumors show large nests, lobules, or ribbons of malignant cells with less overt keratinization. Comedonecrosis, desmoplasia, mitoses, and inflammatory background may be present. Pancytokeratin, CK5/6, p40, and p63 are typically positive. BerEP4, CK20, adipophilin, and melanocytic/neuroendocrine markers are generally negative. Mucoepidermoid carcinoma: contains mucous and intermediate cells. Sebaceous carcinoma: adipophilin-positive sebaceous differentiation. Lymphoepithelial carcinoma: prominent accompanying lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate. Metastatic or directly extending SCC: establish the primary site clinically and radiologically. HPV testing is not routinely used to classify squamous cell carcinoma at this site. Lymphoepithelial carcinoma Malignant epithelial neoplasm with lymphoid stroma Typically adults; limited case numbers preclude a reliable sex or age profile. Often presents over 1–24 months with epiphora and a hard, nontender, immobile mass above the medial canthal tendon. Undifferentiated malignant epithelial cells occur in a dense, heterogeneous lymphoid and plasma-cell background. Confirm epithelial lineage and assess for EBV association. Exclude metastasis or direct extension from a nasopharyngeal or other primary lymphoepithelial carcinoma. Large polygonal malignant cells form sheets, clusters, and isolated cells. Tumor cells have vesicular nuclei and prominent central nucleoli. The background contains mixed lymphocytes, plasma cells, and macrophages. Tumor cells express pancytokeratin, CK5/6, CK14, EMA, and p63. EBER in situ hybridization may demonstrate EBV in tumor cells. Lymphoma: lymphoid cells are the neoplastic population and lack epithelial marker expression. Chronic dacryocystitis: reactive mixed inflammation without malignant epithelial cells. Metastatic nasopharyngeal carcinoma: correlate with nasopharyngeal examination and imaging. EBER in situ hybridization is useful for establishing EBV association; no other defining molecular test is established. Other salivary gland-type carcinomas of the lacrimal drainage system Salivary-type malignant epithelial neoplasms Usually adults; often presents with unilateral tearing and a firm, immobile medial canthal/lacrimal sac mass. Sanguineous reflux on irrigation, a noncompressible mass above the medial canthal tendon, or persistent dacryocystitis is concerning for malignancy. Classify according to the specific salivary-type carcinoma morphology: adenoid cystic, epithelial-myoepithelial, carcinoma ex pleomorphic adenoma, ductal adenocarcinoma, oncocytic carcinoma, or sebaceous carcinoma. Determine whether the lesion is primary to the drainage system or represents direct extension/metastasis. Assess perineural, lymphovascular, and bone invasion. Ductal adenocarcinoma shows pleomorphic polygonal cells in glandular, cribriform, or solid patterns, often with comedonecrosis. Adenoid cystic carcinoma, epithelial-myoepithelial carcinoma, and carcinoma ex pleomorphic adenoma reproduce their characteristic counterparts at other sites. Oncocytic carcinoma shows atypical oncocytes with invasion; sebaceous carcinoma shows sebaceous differentiation. Ductal adenocarcinoma often expresses CK7, AR, GCDFP-15, and may express ERBB2. Use subtype-directed panels: MYB for adenoid cystic carcinoma, myoepithelial markers for biphasic tumors, and adipophilin for sebaceous differentiation. Adenocarcinoma NOS: lacks defining morphology of a specific salivary-type carcinoma. Oncocytic carcinoma versus ductal adenocarcinoma: the former shows abundant abnormal mitochondria. Direct extension from conjunctival or caruncular sebaceous carcinoma must be excluded. MYB or MYBL1 rearrangements/fusions may support adenoid cystic carcinoma. ERBB2 amplification and AR expression may have therapeutic relevance in ductal adenocarcinoma. Melanoma involving the lacrimal drainage system Malignant melanocytic neoplasm Extremely rare; mean age approximately 59 years. Usually arises in the lacrimal sac and presents with unilateral epiphora, medial canthal mass, bloody discharge, or epistaxis; may be mistaken for dacryocystitis. Malignant melanocytic neoplasm involving the lacrimal sac/duct mucosa. Demonstrate melanocytic differentiation and exclude a previous or synchronous melanoma elsewhere. Assess extension into nasolacrimal duct, adjacent soft tissue, bone, and sinonasal structures. Mucosa and adjacent soft tissue are infiltrated by atypical spindle and/or epithelioid melanocytes. Cells contain variable granular melanin and show nuclear pleomorphism, prominent nucleoli, and mitotic activity. Tumor cells express SOX10, S100, Melan-A, and HMB45. Pigmented epithelial carcinoma: cytokeratin-positive and melanocytic-marker negative. Metastatic melanoma: exclude a cutaneous, uveal, or other mucosal primary. Benign melanosis: lacks destructive invasion and malignant cytology. BRAF p.V600E has been reported in an individual case; molecular testing may help guide therapy but is not defining. Cystic and benign epithelial lesions Usually localized, slow-growing or incidental lesions. Diagnosis relies on the epithelial lining or the combination of ductal, myoepithelial, and stromal components. Dacryops cyst; pleomorphic adenoma; oncocytoma; myoepithelioma Intraductal and low-grade biphasic neoplasms Show organized ductal and myoepithelial populations. Demonstrating an intact peripheral myoepithelial layer or an invasive interface is central to classification. Intraductal carcinoma; epithelial-myoepithelial carcinoma Primary lacrimal gland carcinomas A heterogeneous group ranging from indolent secretory and acinic cell carcinomas to aggressive adenoid cystic and ductal adenocarcinomas. Molecular findings can be highly useful for selected subtypes. Carcinoma ex pleomorphic adenoma; adenoid cystic carcinoma; primary ductal adenocarcinoma; secretory carcinoma; mucoepidermoid carcinoma; acinic cell carcinoma; adenocarcinoma NOS Lacrimal drainage epithelial tumors Usually arise in the lacrimal sac or nasolacrimal duct and commonly present with unilateral epiphora or a medial canthal mass. Persistent obstruction, bloody tearing, or a firm immobile mass warrants tissue diagnosis. Squamous/inverted papillomas; squamous cell carcinoma; lymphoepithelial carcinoma; mucoepidermoid carcinoma; salivary gland-type carcinomas; adenocarcinoma NOS Lacrimal drainage melanocytic tumor Exceptionally rare mucosal melanoma, most often involving the lacrimal sac; exclude a primary melanoma elsewhere. All sites All categories Ophthalmic Pathology Lacrimal Gland and Drainage System Tumors A practical diagnostic reference for epithelial, myoepithelial, and melanocytic lesions of the lacrimal gland, lacrimal sac, and nasolacrimal drainage pathway. The anatomic site is essential because the tumor spectrum, presentation, and differential diagnosis differ between the gland and drainage system. Diagnostic Overview Major groups, their typical behavior, and representative entities. Tumor group Overview Representative entities Search diagnoses, morphology, markers, or molecular findings e.g. MYB, epiphora, PLAG1, perineural invasion Anatomic site Tumor category Showing of entities Expand all Collapse all − + Clinical Profile Essential Diagnostic Criteria Histopathology Immunophenotype Differential Diagnosis Molecular Pathology No entities match the current search and filters. Diagnostic interpretation should integrate morphology, immunophenotype, molecular findings, imaging, and clinical history. Lacrimal drainage tumors should be distinguished from lacrimal gland primaries and from direct extension or metastasis.

title: Orbital Tumors
content: use client Orbital dermoid cyst and other developmental cysts Developmental cyst / choristoma Choristomas and cysts Usually congenital or recognized in infancy and childhood; superficial lesions may present before 1 year of age. Deep lesions are often detected later, from childhood through young adulthood. Typically occurs near a cranial suture, most often superotemporally at the frontozygomatic suture; presents as a painless, slowly enlarging, sometimes bone-fixed mass. Deep lesions may cause globe displacement or visual symptoms. Cyst lined by keratinizing stratified squamous epithelium. Epidermal appendages, including hair follicles and sebaceous and/or sweat glands, are present in the cyst wall. Rupture may produce a prominent foreign-body granulomatous reaction and fibrosis. The cyst is lined by keratinizing stratified squamous epithelium. Hair shafts and sebaceous glands are common within the wall or lumen. Eccrine sweat glands may be present in the cyst wall. Rupture may lead to keratin or hair-associated granulomatous inflammation with multinucleated giant cells. Immunohistochemistry is generally unnecessary for diagnosis. Epidermoid cyst: squamous epithelial lining without skin appendages in the cyst wall. Conjunctival inclusion cyst: usually nonkeratinizing conjunctival-type lining, often with goblet cells. Microphthalmia with cyst or encephalocele: developmental ocular or intracranial connection should be assessed clinically and radiologically. Other orbital cysts: correlate epithelial lining, anatomic location, and imaging findings. No diagnostic molecular alteration is established. Cavernous vascular malformation Benign venous vascular malformation Vascular malformations Usually presents in adults in the fourth to fifth decades; approximately 60% of patients are women. Typically intraconal and located in the mid or posterior orbit; causes slowly progressive axial proptosis, sometimes with pain or visual impairment from optic nerve compression or hyperopic shift. Well-circumscribed, usually encapsulated orbital mass composed of large, dilated cavernous venous channels. Vascular spaces are lined by bland, flattened endothelial cells. Clinical and imaging findings typically show a slowly enlarging, well-defined lesion with progressive contrast enhancement. The lesion is circumscribed and commonly surrounded by a fibrous capsule. Large, dilated, blood-filled cavernous vascular spaces are arranged in clusters. The channels are lined by bland endothelial cells without significant atypia. Organizing thrombi and focal small-vessel proliferation may be present. Endothelial cells express CD31 and ERG; CD34 is commonly positive. No specific immunophenotype is required when the morphology is characteristic. Orbital venous malformation: typically unencapsulated, distensible, and composed of communicating venous channels; may enlarge with Valsalva. Combined lymphatic-venous malformation: contains irregular lymphatic channels, often with lymphoid aggregates and prior hemorrhage. Angiosarcoma: destructive infiltrative growth, endothelial atypia, mitoses, and complex anastomosing channels. GJA4 mutations have been reported in a subset of cavernous vascular malformations; testing is not required for routine diagnosis. IDH1 or IDH2 hotspot mutations may occur in lesions associated with Maffucci syndrome. Combined lymphatic-venous malformation Combined low-flow vascular malformation Usually presents in infancy or childhood, with a female predominance; lesions may become symptomatic at any age. May involve superficial and deep orbit, with conjunctival or eyelid components; presents with proptosis, ptosis, motility disturbance, or visual impairment. Acute painful enlargement, proptosis, or ecchymosis may follow intralesional hemorrhage or thrombosis; lesions may expand during intercurrent illness. Unencapsulated, infiltrative malformation composed of variably sized lymphatic and venous channels. Channels are separated by fibrous septa and may contain proteinaceous fluid, blood, or both. Lymphatic endothelial differentiation is supported by D2-40 expression. Malformed endothelial-lined channels of variable caliber permeate the orbital soft tissue. Lymphatic spaces may contain proteinaceous material, blood, or both. Venous channels are variably dilated and may show organizing thrombi. Fibrous septa may contain lymphocytes or well-formed lymphoid follicles. Hemosiderin-laden macrophages indicate previous hemorrhage. CD31 and ERG highlight endothelial cells in both vascular components. D2-40 highlights the lymphatic endothelial component. CD34 may highlight the vascular endothelium but does not independently distinguish the two components. Orbital venous malformation: predominantly venous channels without a substantial D2-40-positive lymphatic component. Cavernous vascular malformation: circumscribed and encapsulated, with large cavernous venous spaces. Lymphoma: cellular lymphoid infiltrate rather than malformed endothelial-lined spaces. Rhabdomyosarcoma: malignant small round or spindle cell proliferation rather than a vascular malformation. Somatic PIK3CA mutations occur in a subset of lymphatic-venous malformations and may support consideration of pathway-directed therapy in selected patients. Orbital venous malformation Slow-flow venous malformation Can present at any age, often becoming apparent later in childhood or adulthood; no consistent sex predilection is established. May involve superficial or deep orbit and adjacent facial, temporal, or intracranial spaces. Superficial lesions are soft and compressible; deep lesions may cause intermittent proptosis or globe displacement. Lesions may enlarge with Valsalva or dependency and become painful with thrombosis; chronic filling and emptying may cause intermittent proptosis and enophthalmos. Slow-flow lesion composed of abnormal, variably dilated venous channels. Channels have variable smooth-muscle walls and lack a normal internal elastic lamina. Thrombi, recanalization, and phleboliths may be present. The lesion consists of enlarged, irregular venous channels of variable caliber. The venous walls show variable smooth-muscle thickness and inconspicuous endothelium. The internal elastic lamina is absent. Thrombosis, recanalization, and phlebolith formation are common. Intravascular papillary endothelial hyperplasia (Masson phenomenon) may occur within organizing thrombi. Endothelial cells express CD31 and ERG; CD34 is variable. In glomuvenous lesions, the perivascular glomus cells are highlighted by SMA. Cavernous vascular malformation: usually a discrete, encapsulated intraconal mass with clustered cavernous spaces. Combined lymphatic-venous malformation: has a demonstrable lymphatic component, often D2-40 positive. Arteriovenous malformation: high-flow lesion with arterial and venous channels, clinical pulsation, bruit, or thrill. Angiosarcoma: infiltrative endothelial neoplasm with cytologic atypia and destructive growth. TEK (TIE2) mutations are common in venous malformations overall; PIK3CA mutations occur in a subset. Orbital-specific molecular data are limited. GLMN mutations are associated with glomuvenous malformations. Arteriovenous malformation High-flow vascular malformation Usually congenital and may be evident at birth; deep or low-grade lesions can become apparent later. No established sex predilection. May cause pulsatile proptosis, warmth, bruit, thrill, chronic pain, visual decline, or cosmetic deformity; hemorrhage can be serious. High-flow vascular lesion with direct communication between arterial and venous channels without an intervening capillary bed. Histology shows abnormal arteries and veins of variable caliber, often with venous intimal and adventitial fibrosis. Clinical examination and Doppler imaging demonstrate arteriovenous shunting. Numerous large-caliber arteries and thick-walled veins are present in a disorganized arrangement. Arteries may be tortuous, while veins often show intimal and adventitial fibrosis. Smaller arterioles, venules, capillaries, and dilated lymphatic channels may be admixed. The background is often fibrous or fibromyxoid. Endothelial cells express CD31 and ERG. Smooth-muscle actin highlights the muscular walls of arterial and venous channels. Immunohistochemistry is supportive but does not establish the high-flow nature of the lesion. Venous malformation: slow-flow lesion without direct arterial-to-venous shunting. Combined lymphatic-venous malformation: contains malformed lymphatic channels and is typically low-flow. Angiosarcoma: malignant endothelial proliferation with infiltrative growth, atypia, and mitotic activity. Somatic RAS-pathway alterations, including MAP2K1, have been reported in sporadic AVMs. RASA1 and EPHB4 alterations are associated with inherited vascular-malformation syndromes. Orbital glial heterotopia Developmental heterotopia Hamartomas and heterotopias Usually presents before 5 years of age, including in neonates; adult cases are rare. Usually unilateral. Presents as a slowly enlarging orbital mass with swelling, proptosis, or strabismus; microphthalmia or anophthalmia may coexist in some cases. Imaging and clinical assessment should establish the absence of a skull defect or intracranial connection. Mature, non-neoplastic CNS tissue is present in the orbit without connection to the intracranial or intraspinal compartments. There is no skull defect to support encephalocele. The lesion is not associated with microphthalmia with cyst. The lesion is composed of mature, benign glial tissue with variable neural elements. Microcalcifications or psammoma bodies may be present. Ependymal or choroid plexus elements are uncommon. Glial cells express GFAP and S100. Neurofilament highlights axons when neuronal elements are present. Encephalocele: demonstrates a skull defect and continuity with intracranial contents or meninges. Microphthalmia with cyst: associated with a malformed, small globe and a cystic connection. Optic nerve or other glial neoplasm: shows a true neoplastic growth pattern and must be distinguished by anatomic relationship and morphology. Mesenchymal hamartomas of the orbit Developmental mesenchymal lesions Predominantly congenital or pediatric lesions; fibrous hamartoma of infancy usually presents before 2 years of age. No consistent sex predilection across the group. Usually presents as a painless orbital mass with variable proptosis, ptosis, or restricted ocular motility. Chondromesenchymal hamartoma may extend from the sinonasal tract into the orbit. Rhabdomyomatous mesenchymal hamartoma: haphazard mature skeletal muscle fibers admixed with benign fibrous, adipose, vascular, and neural elements. Chondromesenchymal hamartoma: irregular islands of mature hyaline cartilage in a variable mesenchymal background. Fibrous hamartoma of infancy: characteristic triphasic admixture of mature adipose tissue, fibroblastic/myofibroblastic fascicles, and primitive mesenchymal nodules. Rhabdomyomatous mesenchymal hamartoma contains randomly arranged mature striated muscle fibers with collagen, fat, vessels, and peripheral nerves. Chondromesenchymal hamartoma contains irregular islands of hyaline cartilage with variable fibrous, myxoid, and fibro-osseous tissue. Fibrous hamartoma of infancy shows mature adipose tissue, bland fibroblastic/myofibroblastic fascicles, and primitive-appearing stellate mesenchymal nodules. Skeletal muscle fibers in rhabdomyomatous mesenchymal hamartoma express desmin, myogenin, and MyoD1. SMA may highlight myofibroblastic cells in fibrous hamartoma of infancy. Immunophenotyping is generally subordinate to the characteristic triphasic or tissue-specific morphology. Rhabdomyosarcoma: atypical proliferating cells, mitotic activity, and destructive growth rather than mature, randomly arranged skeletal muscle fibers. Chondrosarcoma: cytologic atypia and permeative growth rather than bland, mature cartilage islands. Fibromatosis or other infantile fibrous tumors: lack the characteristic triphasic pattern of fibrous hamartoma of infancy. Nasal chondromesenchymal hamartoma extending into the orbit: identify the sinonasal epicenter on imaging. DICER1-associated pathogenic variants are reported in nasal chondromesenchymal hamartoma; diagnosis should prompt consideration of genetic counseling and DICER1 testing. EGFR exon insertion/deletion mutations have been reported in fibrous hamartoma of infancy, but are not established as a routine diagnostic test for orbital cases. Teratoma Germ cell tumor Germ cell tumors Congenital orbital teratoma presents in a newborn; adult orbital teratomas are exceptionally rare. No established sex predilection. Infantile lesions cause rapidly progressive, massive unilateral proptosis, eyelid distension, chemosis, and exposure keratopathy. Adult lesions are more often slow-growing and circumscribed. Imaging may show a complex cystic and solid mass containing fat, calcification, cartilage, or bone; assess for intracranial extension. Tumor contains tissues derived from at least two, and typically all three, germ layers. Mature teratoma contains differentiated adult-type tissues; immature teratoma contains embryonal immature elements, commonly neuroectodermal tubules or rosettes. Extensively sample solid areas to identify immature or malignant components. Ectodermal derivatives include squamous epithelium, skin appendages, hair, and neural tissue. Mesodermal derivatives include adipose tissue, cartilage, bone, and smooth or skeletal muscle. Endodermal derivatives include gastrointestinal, respiratory, thyroid, pancreatic, or salivary-type epithelium. Immature teratoma contains immature neuroepithelial tubules, rosettes, or other embryonal tissue. Keratin or other cyst contents may elicit fat necrosis and a foreign-body reaction. Immunohistochemistry is directed by the tissue components present and is not required to establish a conventional mature teratoma. Immature neuroepithelial components may express neural markers such as synaptophysin and GFAP, depending on differentiation. Dermoid cyst: predominantly ectodermal tissue with skin appendages, without the broad representation of multiple germ-layer derivatives. Developmental orbital cyst: lacks the complex admixture of differentiated tissues. Yolk sac tumor: malignant germ cell neoplasm with reticular/microcystic architecture and AFP/GPC3 expression. No diagnostic molecular alteration is established for conventional orbital teratoma. Yolk sac tumor Malignant germ cell tumor Almost exclusively affects young children; reported mean age is approximately 27 months. A slight female predominance has been reported in the small published series. Usually arises in the extraconal orbit and presents with rapidly progressive proptosis, ptosis, ophthalmoplegia, visual loss, or exposure keratopathy. Serum alpha-fetoprotein is typically elevated when measured. Malignant germ cell neoplasm with variable patterns resembling extraembryonic yolk sac differentiation. Reticular/microcystic, macrocystic, glandular, or myxomatous architecture may be present. Hyaline globules are PAS-positive and diastase-resistant. AFP, glypican-3, and SALL4 support the diagnosis. Reticular or microcystic spaces are lined by flattened to cuboidal malignant cells. Tumor cells show cytologic atypia and mitotic activity. Schiller-Duval bodies may be present but are not required. Intra- and extracellular hyaline globules are characteristic and are PAS-positive, diastase-resistant. Tumor cells show cytoplasmic AFP expression, although staining may be variable. Glypican-3 is commonly positive. SALL4 shows nuclear expression and supports germ cell differentiation. Low-molecular-weight cytokeratin, including CAM5.2, is commonly positive. Teratoma: contains differentiated tissues from multiple germ layers rather than a malignant yolk sac pattern. Embryonal carcinoma: typically shows more primitive solid or glandular growth and a different immunophenotype, including OCT3/4 expression. Metastatic or direct extension of another pediatric malignancy: correlate with imaging, clinical history, and lineage-specific markers. No defining molecular alteration is established for routine diagnosis of orbital yolk sac tumor. Primary orbital melanoma Malignant melanocytic neoplasm Melanocytic tumors Reported age range is 5–91 years, with a median of approximately 45 years; slight male predominance. Arises in orbital soft tissue and may be intraconal or extraconal. Common presentations include unilateral proptosis, decreased vision, periorbital pain, and diplopia. May be associated with oculodermal melanocytosis, nevus of Ota, or a blue nevus; a prior conjunctival, uveal, or cutaneous melanoma must be excluded. Malignant melanocytic neoplasm centered in orbital soft tissue. No prior or concurrent conjunctival, uveal, or nonocular primary melanoma after clinical and imaging evaluation. Melanocytic differentiation is confirmed by an appropriate immunohistochemical panel. Background orbital melanocytosis or blue nevus may support a primary orbital origin. Tumor may be composed of spindle cells, epithelioid cells, or a mixture of both. Mitotic activity is present; necrosis may occur. Tumor cells may show a nested or packeted arrangement separated by extracellular matrix. Melanophages are common in the tumor and adjacent soft tissue. Background orbital melanocytosis or conventional/cellular blue nevus may be present. Tumor cells express S100 and SOX10. Melan-A and HMB45 support melanocytic differentiation. A subset shows loss of nuclear BAP1 expression. Secondary orbital melanoma: exclude extension or metastasis from uveal, conjunctival, cutaneous, or other melanoma. Clear cell sarcoma: may express melanocytic markers but is supported by an EWSR1::ATF1 or related fusion. Melanocytosis or blue nevus: bland melanocytes without destructive growth, significant atypia, or mitotic activity. A panel including GNAQ, GNA11, BRAF, NRAS, TERT promoter, SF3B1, and EIF1AX may help characterize the tumor in the appropriate clinical context. GNAQ and GNA11 alterations overlap with uveal melanoma and do not independently establish an orbital primary; clinical exclusion of another primary site is essential. SF3B1 and EIF1AX alterations have been associated with more favorable outcomes in limited data; prognostic interpretation should be cautious. Always correlate morphology with the anatomic epicenter, imaging findings, and clinical history to distinguish primary orbital lesions from secondary involvement. Glial heterotopia; rhabdomyomatous, chondromesenchymal, and fibrous hamartomas Mature or developmentally patterned tissue; exclude intracranial connection and true malignancy. Teratoma; yolk sac tumor Teratoma shows multiple germ-layer derivatives; yolk sac tumor is malignant and typically AFP/GPC3/SALL4 positive.
