content: use client Fibroadenoma Fibroepithelial Tumors Circumscribed biphasic tumor with intracanalicular and/or pericanalicular growth, without well-developed leaf-like fronds or stromal overgrowth. A benign biphasic neoplasm of the terminal duct-lobular unit, composed of epithelial and stromal components. Most common solid breast tumor in adolescent girls; may occur from approximately 8–9 years of age. Predominantly affects females. May arise in any breast quadrant; multiple and bilateral lesions can occur. Usually presents as a palpable, mobile mass; large lesions may cause breast distortion or asymmetry. Circumscribed biphasic proliferation of stromal and epithelial elements. Intracanalicular and/or pericanalicular architecture. No stromal overgrowth. No well-developed leaf-like stromal fronds. No significant stromal atypia and low stromal mitotic activity. The lesion is composed of benign ducts and a proliferating specialized stroma. Pericanalicular growth preserves rounded duct profiles. Intracanalicular growth compresses ducts into elongated, slit-like spaces. Stromal cellularity is usually mild but may be increased in pediatric lesions. Small leaf-like projections and increased stromal mitoses may occur in pediatric fibroadenomas without establishing phyllodes tumor. The epithelial component retains an inner luminal cell layer and an outer myoepithelial cell layer. p63 and smooth muscle myosin heavy chain can highlight the preserved myoepithelial layer. Stromal CD34 may be expressed but is not specific. Juvenile Fibroadenoma Shows more cellular stroma, often with conspicuous gynecomastia-like usual ductal hyperplasia and micropapillary tufting; it still lacks well-developed leaf-like fronds and stromal overgrowth. Phyllodes Tumor Shows exaggerated intracanalicular growth with well-developed leaf-like stromal fronds and stromal hypercellularity; assess atypia, mitoses, stromal overgrowth, and tumor borders. A subset harbors MED12 exon 2 mutations. TERT promoter mutations were not identified in the pediatric fibroadenomas discussed in the chapter. Increased stromal cellularity and occasional small leaf-like projections can occur in pediatric fibroadenoma and do not alone establish phyllodes tumor. Cytology may not reliably separate a cellular fibroadenoma from phyllodes tumor; correlate with architecture in a core or excision specimen. Circumscribed biphasic lesion with cellular stroma, pericanalicular growth, and gynecomastia-like usual ductal hyperplasia. A fibroadenoma variant occurring predominantly in adolescents, characterized by increased stromal cellularity and prominent usual-type epithelial hyperplasia. Usually occurs in adolescent girls, most often after menarche; prepubertal cases also occur. May occur in any part of the breast and can be multifocal or bilateral. Presents as a rapidly enlarging, sometimes large mass; lesions larger than 50 mm are termed giant juvenile fibroadenomas. May cause breast distortion and asymmetry. Circumscribed biphasic neoplasm with epithelial and stromal components. Predominantly pericanalicular growth, sometimes mixed with intracanalicular areas. Cellular stroma with usual-type ductal hyperplasia showing gynecomastia-like micropapillary tufting. No prominent, well-developed leaf-like fronds. No stromal atypia, stromal overgrowth, or malignant heterologous elements. Stromal mitotic activity is usually low and should not exceed 5 mitoses/mm². The tumor has circumscribed borders and a predominantly pericanalicular architecture. The stroma is more cellular than in conventional fibroadenoma. Usual ductal hyperplasia often forms gynecomastia-like micropapillary tufts. Focal tubular adenoma-like areas may occur. Rare stromal multinucleated giant cells may be present. Well-developed leaf-like fronds, stromal overgrowth, and stromal atypia are absent. The epithelial component retains a dual luminal and myoepithelial cell population. p63 and smooth muscle myosin heavy chain can confirm the preserved myoepithelial layer. The usual ductal hyperplasia shows a mosaic basal cytokeratin pattern, including CK5/6, and heterogeneous ER expression. Usually has less cellular stroma and lacks the conspicuous gynecomastia-like micropapillary usual ductal hyperplasia typical of juvenile fibroadenoma. Shows well-developed leaf-like stromal fronds and more pronounced stromal hypercellularity; juvenile fibroadenoma lacks the characteristic frond architecture, stromal overgrowth, and stromal atypia. MED12 mutations occur in a subset of juvenile fibroadenomas. TERT promoter mutations were absent in the juvenile fibroadenomas discussed in the chapter; reported alterations in other genes remain insufficiently established for routine diagnosis. Do not diagnose phyllodes tumor based only on increased stromal cellularity or a few small leaf-like projections. Reserve the term giant for lesions larger than 50 mm; size alone does not define a distinct biologic category. Biphasic fibroepithelial neoplasm with exaggerated intracanalicular growth, hypercellular stroma, and characteristic leaf-like stromal fronds. A fibroepithelial neoplasm classified as benign, borderline, or malignant according to stromal features. Uncommon in children and adolescents; may occur in adolescent girls. Pediatric cases have been reported more often in Black than in White patients in the United States. Usually presents as a solitary, enlarging breast mass; very large tumors may distort the breast and thin the overlying skin. Benign, borderline, and malignant categories occur; malignant phyllodes tumor is an important malignant breast tumor in adolescent girls. Biphasic fibroepithelial neoplasm with a dominant intracanalicular growth pattern. Well-developed leaf-like stromal fronds are lined by luminal epithelial and myoepithelial layers. Stromal hypercellularity is present. Classify as benign, borderline, or malignant using stromal cellularity, atypia, mitotic activity, stromal overgrowth, and tumor border characteristics. Evaluate the entire lesion when possible because grading may be heterogeneous. Exaggerated intracanalicular growth produces leaf-like stromal projections into epithelial-lined spaces. The stromal fronds are capped by benign luminal and myoepithelial cells. Stromal cellularity is increased, with degree varying by grade. Benign, borderline, and malignant tumors are distinguished by the degree of stromal atypia, mitotic activity, stromal overgrowth, and border infiltrativeness. Malignant tumors may show hemorrhage and necrosis. The epithelial-lined fronds retain luminal and myoepithelial layers. p63 and smooth muscle myosin heavy chain can highlight the myoepithelial layer. Stromal immunostains are not independently diagnostic; morphology remains central to classification. Lacks the prominent, well-developed leaf-like stromal fronds and characteristic stromal hypercellularity of phyllodes tumor. May be cellular and show small leaf-like projections, but lacks well-developed fronds, stromal overgrowth, and stromal atypia; gynecomastia-like usual ductal hyperplasia favors juvenile fibroadenoma. MED12 mutations have been reported in a subset of benign phyllodes tumors. TERT promoter mutations were not identified in the benign pediatric phyllodes tumors discussed in the chapter. Small leaf-like fronds and increased stromal cellularity can be seen in pediatric fibroadenomas; interpret the complete architectural pattern. Core biopsy may under-sample heterogeneous lesions and underestimate grade. Periductal stromal tumor is regarded as a phyllodes tumor subtype with a predominantly pericanalicular pattern. Juvenile Papillomatosis Benign Proliferative Epithelial Lesions Combination of duct papillomatosis, multiple apocrine and non-apocrine cysts, duct stasis, and other benign proliferative changes. A benign proliferative breast lesion of young patients, characterized by a distinctive constellation of cystic and papillary epithelial changes. Usually affects young women younger than 30 years; median age in the largest series was approximately 21 years. Female predominance is marked; male cases are extremely rare. Often arises in the upper outer quadrant but can occur elsewhere in the breast. Typically presents as a firm, mobile, palpable breast mass; pain and nipple discharge are uncommon. A positive family history of breast carcinoma is frequent in reported series, particularly in patients with recurrent bilateral lesions. Duct papillomatosis involving multiple ducts. Multiple apocrine and non-apocrine cysts or ectatic ducts. Papillary apocrine hyperplasia. Duct stasis with inspissated secretions and/or foamy macrophages. Sclerosing adenosis and other benign proliferative changes may accompany the lesion. Multiple cysts and ectatic ducts are present, often containing inspissated secretions or foamy macrophages. Papillary epithelial hyperplasia or papillomatosis commonly involves the ducts. Cyst linings frequently show flat or papillary apocrine metaplasia. Usual ductal hyperplasia may be florid and show cribriform or micropapillary patterns. Apocrine metaplasia and usual ductal hyperplasia merge within lesional cysts. Dense fibrous stroma, sclerosing adenosis, and fibroadenomatoid change may be present. Atypical ductal hyperplasia may occur. Usual ductal hyperplasia shows a mosaic staining pattern with basal cytokeratins such as CK5/6. ER expression is heterogeneous in usual ductal hyperplasia. p63 highlights preserved myoepithelial cells around ducts and within papillary proliferations. Intraductal Papilloma Usually forms a localized papillary lesion with fibrovascular cores; it does not show the characteristic widespread combination of multiple cysts, apocrine metaplasia, duct stasis, and multifocal benign proliferative changes. Is a biphasic stromal and epithelial neoplasm; cysts may occur, but the florid duct papillomatosis, apocrine change, and duct stasis of juvenile papillomatosis are absent. PIK3CA and AKT1 hotspot mutations have been reported in some cases, particularly in the setting of a positive family history, but these alterations are not specific for juvenile papillomatosis. Atypical epithelial proliferation can be present; assess carefully for a coexisting in situ or invasive carcinoma. Cytology alone may not establish the diagnosis; correlate with the clinical setting and tissue architecture. Incomplete excision may lead to recurrence. Papillary epithelial proliferation within a breast duct, supported by fibrovascular cores and a preserved myoepithelial layer. A benign papillary breast lesion included in the pediatric differential diagnosis of a palpable mass or nipple discharge. Uncommon in the pediatric age group. Can occur in either sex, although breast lesions are predominantly encountered in females. Arises within a breast duct, often in a central or subareolar location. May present with a palpable mass or nipple discharge. Papillary proliferation within a dilated duct. Papillae contain fibrovascular cores. A myoepithelial cell layer is retained along papillary cores and around the involved duct. Exclude atypical or malignant epithelial proliferation by assessing cytology and architecture. Papillary fronds project into a ductal lumen. Each papilla contains a fibrovascular core. Myoepithelial cells are present within fibrovascular cores and along the duct periphery. The epithelial proliferation is usually cytologically bland. p63 and smooth muscle myosin heavy chain highlight myoepithelial cells within papillary cores and at the duct periphery. CK5/6 and ER can help characterize usual-type epithelial proliferations when atypia is in question. Shows multiple cysts, duct ectasia, apocrine metaplasia, duct stasis, and widespread papillary hyperplasia rather than a single localized papillary lesion. Do not diagnose a benign papilloma solely from papillary architecture; confirm the distribution of myoepithelial cells and assess for atypia or carcinoma. Secretory Carcinoma Primary Breast Carcinomas Microcystic, solid, tubular, and papillary growth with eosinophilic intracellular and luminal secretions; ETV6::NTRK3 fusion is characteristic. A rare primary breast carcinoma and the most frequently described primary carcinoma in the pediatric age group; it usually follows an indolent course. Can occur at any age but is the most frequently described primary breast carcinoma in children and adolescents. Occurs in both sexes, with a strong predominance in females among breast carcinoma patients. Arises in the breast and usually presents as a palpable mass. Often has an indolent clinical course, particularly in children and young adults. Characteristic microcystic, solid, tubular, and/or papillary architecture. Polygonal tumor cells with granular or vacuolated eosinophilic cytoplasm. Intracytoplasmic and luminal eosinophilic colloid-like secretions. Demonstration of an ETV6::NTRK3 fusion strongly supports the diagnosis. Tumor growth may be microcystic, solid, tubular, or papillary. Polygonal cells have pink granular or vacuolated cytoplasm. Eosinophilic colloid-like secretions are present within the cytoplasm and lumina. Most tumors are histologic grade 1 or 2. S100 and mammaglobin are commonly expressed. Pan-TRK immunoreactivity may support the diagnosis but should be confirmed molecularly when needed. The immunophenotype should be interpreted with the characteristic morphology and molecular finding. Is a benign multicystic and papillary proliferation with preserved myoepithelial cells; secretory carcinoma shows infiltrative carcinoma and lacks a continuous myoepithelial layer around invasive tumor. Retains myoepithelial cells in papillary cores and around the duct; secretory carcinoma is an invasive epithelial malignancy with characteristic secretory cytoplasm and ETV6::NTRK3 fusion. ETV6::NTRK3 fusion is the characteristic, defining molecular alteration. The fusion may be therapeutically relevant because it involves NTRK3. Before diagnosing a primary breast carcinoma in a child, exclude metastasis or direct extension from an extramammary malignancy. Consider hereditary cancer predisposition when breast carcinoma occurs at a young age. Tumor Classification at a Glance Most pediatric breast masses are benign; architecture and stromal features are central to separating fibroepithelial lesions. Entity Category Typical Pattern Key Diagnostic Point Practical Diagnostic Framework 1. Start with the clinical and radiologic context. Ultrasound is generally preferred in children and adolescents; correlate the mass with age, pubertal status, and imaging. 2. For a biphasic lesion, assess architecture. Separate conventional and juvenile fibroadenoma from phyllodes tumor by looking for well-developed leaf-like fronds, stromal overgrowth, atypia, and mitotic activity. 3. For papillary/cystic lesions, assess distribution. Juvenile papillomatosis is a constellation of multifocal cystic and benign proliferative changes; intraductal papilloma is usually a localized ductal lesion. 4. For a malignant epithelial lesion, confirm primary origin. Exclude metastasis or direct extension from an extramammary tumor; secretory morphology and ETV6::NTRK3 support secretory carcinoma. ICD-O coding 9351/1 Adamantinomatous craniopharyngioma ICD-11 coding 2F7A.Y & XH15X9 Other… Adamantinomatous craniopharyngioma is a mixed solid and cystic squamous epithelial tumor with stellate reticulum and wet keratin, usually localized to the hypothalamic–pituitary axis and characterized by activating CTNNB1 mutations. The well-differentiated tumor epithelium forms cords, lobules, ribbons, nodular whorls, and irregular trabeculae. Demonstration of CTNNB1 mutation, as well as an absence of BRAF p.V600E, may be helpful in selected cases. The well-differentiated tumor epithelium forms cords, lobules, ribbons, nodular whorls, and irregular trabeculae. Peripheral crowding and palisading are prominent. The well-differentiated tumor epithelium forms cords, lobules, ribbons, nodular whorls, and irregular trabeculae. Peripheral crowding and palisading are prominent. Degenerative features such as fibrosis, calcification, and nodules/whorls of anucleate remnants of ghost-like squamous cells (termed “wet keratin”) are common. p63 is expressed in all epithelial layers of adamantinomatous craniopharyngiomas ; high–molecular weight cytokeratins (34βE12 [K903], CK5/6) and low- to intermediate-molecular-weight cytokeratins (CK7, CK17, and CK19) are also expressed . p63 is expressed in all epithelial layers of adamantinomatous craniopharyngiomas ; high–molecular weight cytokeratins (34βE12 [K903], CK5/6) and low- to intermediate-molecular-weight cytokeratins (CK7, CK17, and CK19) are also expressed . In contrast to Rathke cleft cysts, craniopharyngiomas in some studies lack CK8 and CK20… The differential diagnosis includes papillary craniopharyngioma, xanthogranuloma, Rathke cleft cyst, epidermoid and dermoid cysts, and pilocytic astrocytoma. Xanthogranuloma of the sellar region is a reactive lesion resulting from leakage, rupture, or hemorrhage of a Rathke cleft cyst, indicated by strips of columnar or ciliated columnar epithelium in the resected material . Pituitary blastoma: Pituitary blastoma is an embryonal neoplasm of the sellar region, composed of primitive blastemal cells, neuroendocrine cells, and Rathke pouch epithelium. content: use client Hepatoblastoma Liver — Epithelial Tumors Embryonal hepatocytic tumor in early childhood; fetal and/or embryonal epithelium, with or without mesenchymal differentiation. A malignant embryonal liver tumor that recapitulates hepatic development and may contain epithelial elements alone or epithelial and mesenchymal components. Usually diagnosed between 6 months and 5 years (median, approximately 18 months); may be congenital. Male predominance (approximately 2:1). Usually a solitary, right-lobe-predominant hepatic mass; multifocal disease occurs. Typically presents as an abdominal mass; serum AFP is markedly elevated in most cases. Lung metastases may be present at diagnosis. Recognize fetal and/or embryonal hepatocytic differentiation in a primary hepatic malignancy. Classify as epithelial or mixed epithelial and mesenchymal according to the components present. Fetal, embryonal, macrotrabecular, pleomorphic, cholangioblastic, and small-cell undifferentiated patterns may occur; mixed tumors contain stromal/heterologous elements. Pure fetal HBL with low mitotic activity can be diagnosed only in a completely evaluated primary resection, not on biopsy or posttherapy tissue. A tumor with small-cell morphology and loss of nuclear INI1/SMARCB1 should be classified as malignant rhabdoid tumor, not HBL. Consider hepatocellular neoplasm, NOS (HCN-NOS) when a pediatric hepatocellular tumor has overlapping/intermediate HBL and HCC features, particularly in an older child. Well-differentiated fetal areas show uniform polygonal cells with low N:C ratios in 2–3-cell-thick trabeculae; light and dark cell populations may be present. Crowded fetal areas show increased cellularity and mitotic activity, dense eosinophilic/amphophilic cytoplasm, and round central nuclei without marked pleomorphism. Embryonal areas contain smaller cells with high N:C ratios, angulated nuclei, frequent mitoses, and rosette or tubular formations. Macrotrabecular HBL has trabeculae more than five cells thick and may mimic HCC. Pleomorphic areas show nuclear enlargement, giant cells, or anaplasia, sometimes after therapy. Small-cell undifferentiated areas show scant cytoplasm and stippled chromatin; evaluate INI1 to exclude rhabdoid tumor. Cholangioblastic areas show biliary-type differentiation and nuclear β-catenin; distinguish from reactive posttherapy bile ducts. Mixed HBL contains epithelial elements with spindle-cell/blastemal, osteoid, cartilage, rhabdomyoblastic, or adipocytic components; teratoid tumors contain heterologous endodermal and neuroectodermal elements. Posttherapy specimens may show necrosis, hemorrhage, peliosis-like change, fibrosis, histiocytic reaction, and extensive bone formation. Nuclear β-catenin is common and supports WNT-pathway activation. AFP highlights tumor cells; arginase-1 and HepPar-1 are generally positive but do not distinguish tumor from non-neoplastic hepatocytes. INI1/SMARCB1 is retained in HBL; loss supports malignant rhabdoid tumor. Use component-directed stains to characterize epithelial and mesenchymal elements; nuclear β-catenin in cholangioblastic areas helps separate them from reactive ducts. CTNNB1 mutations occur in approximately 90% of cases; APC or other WNT-pathway alterations occur in some remaining cases. NFE2L2 mutations occur in a subset and are associated with aggressive biology. TERT promoter mutations are particularly relevant to HCN-NOS and aggressive hepatocellular tumors. Fibrolamellar hepatocellular carcinoma Usually occurs in older children/adolescents; large oncocytic polygonal cells, lamellar fibrosis, diffuse CK7/CD68, and DNAJB1::PRKACA fusion favor fibrolamellar HCC. Pediatric hepatocellular carcinoma Usually occurs in older children and/or diseased liver; conventional HCC shows hepatocellular carcinoma morphology rather than fetal/embryonal developmental patterns. Macrotrabecular HBL and HCN-NOS may overlap, requiring clinicopathologic and molecular correlation. Hepatocellular Neoplasm, NOS (Pediatric) Pediatric hepatocellular tumor with overlapping or intermediate features of hepatoblastoma and hepatocellular carcinoma. A provisional category for difficult-to-classify pediatric hepatocellular neoplasms showing hybrid morphology and biology between hepatoblastoma and hepatocellular carcinoma. Can occur at any age but is more frequent in children older than 8 years. No consistent sex predilection is established. Arises in the liver, often without recognized underlying liver disease. Usually behaves aggressively; clinical presentation resembles a hepatic mass. Use for a pediatric hepatocellular neoplasm that cannot be confidently classified as conventional HBL or HCC and shows intermediate/hybrid features. Tumor may show crowded fetal-like morphology, macrotrabecular architecture, or distinct areas with HBL-like and HCC-like features. Integrate morphology with CTNNB1 and TERT promoter testing and other HCC-associated alterations. Do not equate this category with conventional HBL showing only a macrotrabecular pattern. Tumor may be monotonous and resemble crowded fetal hepatoblastoma. Macrotrabecular architecture may be present. Distinct areas may show hepatoblastoma-like and hepatocellular carcinoma-like morphology. HCC-like features may become more evident in posttherapy specimens. Nuclear β-catenin may be present, reflecting WNT pathway activation. Use hepatocellular markers to establish lineage; no single immunophenotype alone defines this provisional category. CTNNB1 mutations are common. TERT promoter mutations and other HCC-associated alterations support this provisional category and are associated with aggressive behavior. Conventional HBL shows recognizable fetal/embryonal or mixed epithelial-mesenchymal patterns; HCN-NOS has intermediate or hybrid HBL/HCC morphology and may harbor TERT promoter alterations. Pediatric Hepatocellular Carcinoma Conventional HCC is classified as hepatocellular carcinoma based on its morphology and clinical context; HCN-NOS is reserved for tumors with overlapping/intermediate HBL-HCC features. Fibrolamellar Hepatocellular Carcinoma Large oncocytic hepatocytes in dense lamellar fibrosis, usually in a noncirrhotic liver of an older child or adolescent. A distinct hepatocellular carcinoma characterized by oncocytic cytoplasm, lamellar fibrosis, and usually DNAJB1::PRKACA-mediated PKA activation. Occurs in older children and adolescents; generally older than patients with HBL. No clear sex predilection. May arise anywhere in the liver, with a tendency toward the left lobe and hilum. Presents with abdominal mass, hepatomegaly, pain, nausea, or weight loss; usually arises without chronic liver disease and without AFP elevation. Hepatocellular malignancy composed of large polygonal cells with abundant granular eosinophilic cytoplasm and prominent nucleoli. Dense collagenous stroma arranged in parallel lamellae. CK7 and CD68 are typically strongly and diffusely expressed. Demonstration of DNAJB1::PRKACA fusion is desirable and strongly supports the diagnosis in a primary hepatic neoplasm. Large polygonal cells have abundant granular eosinophilic oncocytic cytoplasm, vesicular nuclei, and prominent single nucleoli. Tumor cells form trabeculae, cords, and nests separated by dense parallel lamellar fibrosis. Pale eosinophilic cytoplasmic bodies and hyaline bodies may be present but are not specific. Binucleation, multinucleation, calcification, bile production, and pseudoglandular areas may occur. HepPar-1 and arginase-1 support hepatocellular differentiation; albumin mRNA ISH may be positive. CK7 and CD68 are characteristically strong and diffuse in most cases. Polyclonal CEA may show a canalicular pattern; AFP is usually negative. Glypican-3 is variably positive and is not required for diagnosis. DNAJB1::PRKACA fusion is present in the vast majority of cases and can be detected by RT-PCR or FISH. Rare fusion-negative cases may harbor PRKAR1A mutations, particularly in Carney complex; loss of PRKAR1A expression may be demonstrable. Conventional HCC-associated TP53 and CTNNB1 alterations are generally absent. Usually affects infants and young children and shows fetal/embryonal architecture, often with markedly elevated AFP; lamellar fibrosis and the characteristic fusion favor fibrolamellar HCC. Conventional pediatric HCC lacks the defining combination of oncocytic cells, lamellar fibrosis, and DNAJB1::PRKACA fusion; it more often arises with underlying liver disease. Hepatocellular carcinoma in a patient younger than 18 years; assess background liver disease and exclude HBL/HCN-NOS. A primary malignant hepatocellular neoplasm arising before age 18 years, including conventional and clear-cell patterns. More common in older children and adolescents; approximately two thirds are diagnosed after age 10 years. No single sex tendency is emphasized. May arise anywhere in the liver as a solitary or multifocal mass. Presents with abdominal pain, distension, mass, fatigue, weight loss, or jaundice; may arise in chronic liver disease. AFP is elevated in most, but not all, cases. Establish malignant hepatocellular differentiation in a primary liver tumor. Evaluate for underlying congenital/metabolic/chronic liver disease and viral hepatitis. Recognize conventional and clear-cell patterns; distinguish from HBL and HCN-NOS in younger patients or tumors with mixed morphology. Do not rely on AFP alone; marked AFP elevation may occur with liver regeneration, including in tyrosinemia. Conventional HCC shows malignant hepatocellular growth with trabecular, pseudoglandular, or solid architecture and cytologic atypia. Clear-cell HCC contains tumor cells with clear cytoplasm. Vascular invasion and multifocality may be present and are clinically important. In pediatric tumors with fetal-like or macrotrabecular areas, carefully assess for HBL and HCN-NOS. Use arginase-1 and HepPar-1 to support hepatocellular differentiation. Glypican-3 may support malignancy in the appropriate morphologic context. Canalicular polyclonal CEA/CD10 staining may support hepatocellular differentiation. Interpret immunostains with morphology and background liver findings. The chapter emphasizes a heterogeneous spectrum rather than a single defining pediatric HCC alteration. In suspected fibrolamellar HCC, test for DNAJB1::PRKACA; in HCN-NOS-like tumors, TERT promoter and other HCC-associated alterations may aid classification. HBL usually occurs before age 5 and shows fetal/embryonal components; pediatric HCC more often affects older children and may arise in chronically diseased liver. Fibrolamellar HCC shows oncocytic cells, dense lamellar fibrosis, diffuse CK7/CD68, and usually DNAJB1::PRKACA fusion. Mesenchymal Hamartoma of the Liver Liver — Mesenchymal and Vascular Tumors Benign, often cystic pediatric liver mass composed of loose mesenchyme and irregular bile ducts. A benign developmental lesion of the liver, usually presenting in infancy or early childhood. Usually presents in infants and young children, most often before 2 years of age. No consistent sex predilection is emphasized. Typically arises in the right hepatic lobe as a large, often multicystic mass. Presents with abdominal distension or a palpable mass; large lesions may cause respiratory or feeding compromise. A well-demarcated but non-encapsulated lesion composed of loose myxoid mesenchyme and irregularly distributed bile ducts. Cystic spaces of variable size are common. Recognize that rare malignant transformation or association with embryonal sarcoma has been reported; extensive sampling is important when atypia or solid areas are present. Loose, edematous or myxoid mesenchymal stroma contains irregular, branching bile ducts. Cystic spaces may be lined by flattened or cuboidal epithelium. Hepatocytes may be entrapped at the periphery or within the lesion. Vascular structures and variable fibrosis may be present. Bile duct epithelium expresses cytokeratins. Mesenchymal cells typically express vimentin; immunophenotype is generally nonspecific. Use immunohistochemistry to investigate suspicious solid or atypical areas rather than to establish the diagnosis alone. No single defining molecular alteration is required for diagnosis. Embryonal Sarcoma of the Liver Embryonal sarcoma is a malignant, highly cellular spindle/stellate-cell neoplasm with pleomorphism, mitoses, and characteristic PAS-positive hyaline globules; mesenchymal hamartoma is bland and duct-rich. Calcifying Nested Stromal-Epithelial Tumor CNSET is a solid nested epithelial-stromal neoplasm with calcification/ossification and a distinctive nested architecture, unlike the loose myxoid, cystic, bile-duct-rich hamartoma. Hepatic Congenital Hemangioma Congenital hemangioma is a vascular endothelial proliferation, usually solid and hypervascular, rather than a duct-rich myxoid developmental lesion. Hepatic Infantile Hemangioma Infantile hemangioma is an endothelial tumor with GLUT1-positive vascular channels and possible multifocality/vascular shunting; mesenchymal hamartoma lacks this endothelial proliferation. Rare pediatric liver tumor with nested epithelioid cells, prominent desmoplasia, and calcification/ossification. A rare primary hepatic neoplasm of uncertain differentiation, typically occurring in children and young adults. Usually affects children and young adults; reported age range is broad. Arises within the liver, often as a solitary, well-circumscribed mass. Presents with abdominal pain, distension, or a palpable mass; imaging may show calcification. Nested or trabecular epithelioid tumor cells embedded in dense fibrous/desmoplastic stroma. Calcification and/or ossification is a prominent clue. Confirm the diagnosis by integrating morphology and the characteristic immunophenotype; exclude hepatocellular and other epithelial neoplasms. Tumor cells form nests, cords, and trabeculae separated by dense fibrous stroma. Psammomatous or dystrophic calcification and metaplastic bone may be present. Tumor cells are epithelioid with variable clear to eosinophilic cytoplasm. Necrosis and mitotic activity are variable. Immunophenotype is variable and should be interpreted as a panel in context. Hepatocellular markers are generally not a defining feature; evaluate for epithelial and mesenchymal differentiation as appropriate. No recurrent molecular alteration is established as a routine diagnostic test in this chapter. Mesenchymal hamartoma is predominantly cystic/myxoid with irregular bile ducts; CNSET is a solid nested tumor with dense stroma and calcification. Embryonal sarcoma shows pleomorphic malignant mesenchymal cells and PAS-positive hyaline globules rather than organized epithelial nests with calcifying stroma. Hepatic Angiosarcoma Angiosarcoma shows malignant vasoformative channels and endothelial marker expression, unlike the nested epithelial architecture of CNSET. Malignant pediatric hepatic mesenchymal tumor with pleomorphic stellate cells, myxoid stroma, and PAS-positive hyaline globules. A rare malignant mesenchymal neoplasm of the liver, often presenting in older children. Typically occurs in school-age children, with a peak in later childhood. Usually presents as a large solitary hepatic mass. Abdominal pain, fever, distension, and a palpable mass are common presentations. A malignant mesenchymal neoplasm with markedly variable cellularity and cytologic atypia. Identify pleomorphic spindle, stellate, or polygonal cells in a myxoid background. PAS-positive, diastase-resistant hyaline globules are a characteristic supportive feature. Extensively sample to exclude an associated mesenchymal hamartoma and identify any epithelial component. Tumor is often highly heterogeneous, with alternating hypocellular myxoid and hypercellular areas. Pleomorphic spindle and stellate cells have hyperchromatic nuclei and conspicuous nucleoli. Eosinophilic hyaline globules may be present intracellularly and extracellularly and are PAS-positive, diastase-resistant. Multinucleated giant cells, bizarre cells, and atypical mitoses may be seen. Entrapped bile ducts or residual hamartomatous areas may be present. Vimentin is typically positive. Desmin, muscle-specific actin, and other lineage markers may be variably expressed; no single marker is specific. Hepatocytic and endothelial markers help exclude competing diagnoses. No defining molecular alteration is established for routine diagnosis. Hamartoma is bland, cystic/myxoid, and contains numerous irregular bile ducts; embryonal sarcoma is overtly malignant with pleomorphism, mitoses, and hyaline globules. CNSET has organized epithelial nests and calcifying/desmoplastic stroma rather than a pleomorphic myxoid sarcoma. Angiosarcoma demonstrates malignant endothelial differentiation and irregular anastomosing vascular channels. Fully formed vascular tumor present at birth; GLUT1-negative, with rapid involution or persistent/noninvoluting behavior. A benign vascular tumor that is fully developed at birth and follows a congenital hemangioma growth pattern. Present at birth; may be detected prenatally or in the neonatal period. May be focal, multifocal, or diffuse in the liver. May cause high-output cardiac failure, anemia, thrombocytopenia, or consumptive coagulopathy when large or extensive. Vascular tumor is fully developed at birth. Classify clinical behavior as rapidly involuting, partially involuting, or noninvoluting congenital hemangioma. GLUT1 negativity supports congenital rather than infantile hemangioma. Correlate with imaging and clinical course; distinguish from vascular malformation and infantile hemangioma. Well-formed vascular channels of variable caliber are lined by bland endothelial cells. Lobular vascular architecture may be present. Thrombosis, infarction, fibrosis, and involutional change may be seen depending on subtype and age. Endothelial cells express CD31 and ERG. GLUT1 is negative, helping distinguish congenital hemangioma from infantile hemangioma. No molecular test is routinely required for diagnosis. Infantile hemangioma is usually absent or subtle at birth, proliferates postnatally, and is GLUT1-positive; congenital hemangioma is fully formed at birth and GLUT1-negative. Angiosarcoma shows infiltrative, cytologically malignant endothelial cells and destructive vasoformative growth rather than bland vascular channels. Hamartoma is a myxoid, bile-duct-rich developmental lesion rather than a true endothelial neoplasm. Postnatally proliferating vascular tumor with GLUT1-positive endothelial cells; may be multifocal or diffuse. A benign vascular tumor of infancy that may be focal, multifocal, or diffuse in the liver. Typically presents in infancy; lesions may become apparent after birth as they proliferate. More common in girls in the general infantile hemangioma population. May be focal, multifocal, or diffuse within the liver. Large or diffuse lesions may cause high-output cardiac failure, hepatomegaly, hypothyroidism, or abdominal compartment effects. Clinical course is consistent with postnatal proliferation of an infantile hemangioma. Endothelial cells show GLUT1 expression. Distinguish focal, multifocal, and diffuse patterns and assess for associated vascular shunting or cardiac effects. Lobules of capillary-sized vascular channels are lined by plump endothelial cells during the proliferative phase. Involuting lesions show increasing fibrosis, sclerosis, and reduced vascular spaces. Endothelial cells are cytologically bland. CD31 and ERG highlight endothelial cells. GLUT1 is characteristically positive and distinguishes infantile hemangioma from congenital hemangioma. Congenital hemangioma is fully developed at birth and GLUT1-negative; infantile hemangioma proliferates after birth and is GLUT1-positive. Angiosarcoma is infiltrative and cytologically malignant, with destructive vascular channels and atypia. Hamartoma is a cystic/myxoid lesion with bile ducts and lacks a lobular GLUT1-positive endothelial proliferation. Rare aggressive malignant endothelial tumor with infiltrative, anastomosing vascular channels and endothelial atypia. A highly aggressive malignant vascular neoplasm of the liver; exceptionally rare in children. Extremely rare in children; reported across a broad pediatric age range. No reliable sex predilection is established. Arises in the liver, often as multifocal or diffuse infiltrative disease. May present with hepatomegaly, abdominal pain, anemia, hemorrhage, or liver dysfunction. Infiltrative malignant endothelial neoplasm with irregular, anastomosing vascular channels dissecting hepatic plates. Endothelial cytologic atypia, multilayering, and/or solid areas support malignancy. Confirm endothelial differentiation with a panel of markers. Distinguish from benign congenital and infantile hemangiomas. Irregular, interconnected vascular spaces dissect and replace hepatic parenchyma. Endothelial cells show hyperchromasia, pleomorphism, and multilayering. Solid spindle or epithelioid areas may occur. Hemorrhage and necrosis may be present. Tumor cells express endothelial markers such as CD31 and ERG. CD34 may be positive but is less specific. Use morphology and endothelial marker expression together to distinguish from nonvascular sarcomas. Congenital hemangioma has bland endothelial cells and a circumscribed/lobular vascular architecture; angiosarcoma is infiltrative and malignant. Infantile hemangioma is GLUT1-positive and cytologically bland; angiosarcoma shows endothelial atypia and destructive growth. Embryonal sarcoma is a pleomorphic mesenchymal tumor without true malignant endothelial differentiation; angiosarcoma expresses endothelial markers and forms vascular channels. Pancreatoblastoma Pancreas — Epithelial Tumors Pediatric pancreatic embryonal neoplasm with multiple lines of pancreatic differentiation and characteristic squamoid nests. An embryonal pancreatic neoplasm that recapitulates pancreatic development and shows acinar, squamoid, and sometimes ductal and neuroendocrine differentiation. Usually occurs in young children, with a second peak in older children/adolescents; congenital cases occur. No strong sex predilection is emphasized. May arise in any part of the pancreas; large tumors may extend into adjacent organs. Presents with abdominal mass, pain, or nonspecific gastrointestinal symptoms; AFP may be elevated. A pancreatic epithelial neoplasm showing more than one line of pancreatic differentiation. Squamoid nests are the defining diagnostic feature, although they may be sparse and missed in small biopsies. Acinar differentiation is usually dominant; neuroendocrine, ductal, and primitive round-cell components may be present. Correlate with WNT/β-catenin pathway immunophenotype and clinical context. Tumor forms variably sized epithelial lobules separated by broad fibrous septa. Acinar areas contain uniform polygonal cells with basophilic cytoplasm, central nuclei, prominent nucleoli, and small lumina. Squamoid nests are often centrally located within lobules and may show whorled architecture, abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm, and optically clear nuclei. Ductal/mucinous and primitive round-cell components are usually focal. Neuroendocrine cells may be scattered or form nests/trabeculae. Fibrous stroma may be hypercellular; rare heterologous cartilage or bone may occur. Acinar cells express trypsin, chymotrypsin, lipase, and BCL10; PAS-diastase-positive cytoplasmic granules support acinar differentiation. Neuroendocrine areas express chromogranin A and synaptophysin. Squamoid nests often show abnormal cytoplasmic and nuclear β-catenin, with nuclear LEF1 and cyclin D1. AFP may be expressed. CTNNB1 or APC alterations activate WNT/β-catenin signaling. Loss of heterozygosity at 11p15.5 with IGF2 dysregulation is frequent and may relate to Beckwith–Wiedemann syndrome. Association with familial adenomatous polyposis (APC) is reported. Pancreatic Acinar Cell Carcinoma Acinar cell carcinoma is usually a more monotonous malignant acinar neoplasm without characteristic squamoid nests or the multiple-lineage embryonal pattern of pancreatoblastoma. Solid Pseudopapillary Neoplasm SPN typically occurs in adolescent girls and shows poorly cohesive cells around delicate vessels with pseudopapillary degeneration; it lacks acinar differentiation and characteristic squamoid nests. Malignant acinar neoplasm with granular zymogen-rich cytoplasm and trypsin/chymotrypsin/BCL10 expression. A malignant pancreatic epithelial neoplasm showing acinar cell differentiation. Rare in children; average reported age is approximately 9–10 years (range, 3–16 years). Slight male predominance. May arise throughout the pancreas, most often in the tail, followed by the head. Presents with nonspecific abdominal pain, swelling or mass, nausea, vomiting, fever, or anemia; jaundice is uncommon. AFP may be elevated. Highly cellular malignant epithelial neoplasm with lobular growth and scant fibrous stroma. Cells have moderate to abundant granular eosinophilic cytoplasm and uniform nuclei with prominent nucleoli. Demonstrate acinar differentiation with specific markers, preferably using more than one of trypsin, chymotrypsin, and BCL10. Necrosis and mitotic activity are often prominent. Tumor is highly cellular with scant stroma and a lobular growth pattern. Acinar pattern shows small gland-like lumina and basally located nuclei. Solid areas may mimic pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor. Cytoplasm contains PAS-positive, diastase-resistant zymogen granules. Necrosis is often abundant; mitotic activity is generally high. Trypsin, chymotrypsin, and BCL10 are the most sensitive markers of acinar differentiation; two-marker combinations improve detection. CK7, CK19, and PDX1 may be positive. Scattered neuroendocrine cells may express chromogranin A and/or synaptophysin; diffuse neuroendocrine marker expression is not the expected pattern. AFP may be focally positive. Pediatric molecular data are limited; no clinically established recurrent alteration is required for diagnosis. Adult acinar carcinomas may show BRAF/RAF1 fusions, APC/CTNNB1 pathway alterations, and TP53 changes, but these should not be assumed to define pediatric cases. Pancreatoblastoma shows squamoid nests and multiple lines of pancreatic differentiation; acinar cell carcinoma is typically more uniform and lacks defining squamoid nests. SPN shows pseudopapillary structures, nuclear β-catenin, and loss/abnormal E-cadherin; it lacks acinar enzyme expression and zymogen granules. Adolescent-predominant pancreatic tumor with poorly cohesive cells, delicate vessels, pseudopapillae, and nuclear/cytoplasmic β-catenin. A low-grade malignant pancreatic neoplasm composed of poorly cohesive polygonal cells around delicate vessels, often with cystic degeneration and hemorrhage. Predominantly affects adolescent girls; mean age approximately 14 years. Strong female predominance. Often arises in the body or tail of the pancreas in children. Presents with abdominal pain, dyspepsia, early satiety, nausea, vomiting, or a palpable mass; serum tumor markers are usually negative. Characteristic patient demographic and a well-circumscribed, often encapsulated solid-cystic pancreatic mass. Solid and pseudopapillary architecture with loosely cohesive cells attached to delicate capillaries. Nuclear and cytoplasmic β-catenin expression is characteristic. Exclude pancreatoblastoma and acinar cell carcinoma with acinar markers; exclude PanNET with an appropriate panel. Recognize rare high-grade carcinoma transformation with diffuse atypia and increased mitotic activity. Solid areas contain relatively uniform polygonal cells with numerous delicate capillary-sized vessels. Degeneration causes pseudopapillae, hemorrhage, foamy macrophages, and cholesterol clefts/crystals. Tumor cells have eosinophilic, clear, or vacuolated cytoplasm and uniform round-to-ovoid nuclei with finely stippled chromatin and frequent grooves. PAS-positive hyaline globules may be present but are nonspecific. Mitoses are usually rare; a high-grade transformed component shows diffuse atypia and increased mitotic activity. Abnormal nuclear and cytoplasmic β-catenin and nuclear LEF1 are characteristic. E-cadherin shows loss or abnormal cytoplasmic localization. Cyclin D1, CD10, CD99 (dot-like), progesterone receptor, androgen receptor, glutamine synthetase, TFE3, and SOX11 may be positive. Cytokeratins, synaptophysin, and CD56 may be variably expressed; chromogranin A, PDX1, trypsin, and BCL10 are generally negative. Activating CTNNB1 exon 3 mutations or inactivating APC alterations are characteristic. KRAS, GNAS, CDKN2A, SMAD4, and VHL alterations are typically absent. Pancreatoblastoma has characteristic squamoid nests and acinar differentiation with trypsin/BCL10 positivity; SPN shows β-catenin pathway activation and pseudopapillary degeneration. Acinar cell carcinoma shows zymogen granules and strong trypsin/chymotrypsin/BCL10; SPN lacks acinar markers and has characteristic β-catenin/E-cadherin abnormalities. Gastroblastoma Gastrointestinal — Gastric Tumors Rare gastric biphasic tumor with bland epithelial and spindle-cell components and MALAT1::GLI1 fusion. A rare low-grade gastric epitheliomesenchymal neoplasm with metastatic potential, composed of epithelial and spindle-cell components. Reported age range is 9–56 years; mean age approximately 24 years, median 27 years. Reported cases show male predominance. Intramural gastric tumor, most often in the antrum, but the body may be involved. Presents with abdominal pain/discomfort, palpable mass, gastrointestinal bleeding, or anemia. Establish gastric origin and a biphasic neoplasm composed of epithelial and spindle-cell components. Epithelial component expresses cytokeratins. MALAT1::GLI1 fusion strongly supports the diagnosis. Neither component is usually overtly malignant cytologically; metastatic potential nevertheless exists. Multinodular tumor with variable proportions of epithelial and mesenchymal components. Mesenchymal component consists of bland ovoid-to-spindle cells with pale, clear, or eosinophilic cytoplasm, often in a reticular pattern. Epithelial component forms rosettes with eosinophilic secretions, cords, or solid epithelioid nests. Mitoses are usually rare and marked atypia/pleomorphism is generally absent. Epithelial component expresses pancytokeratin (AE1/AE3 and CAM5.2). Mesenchymal component expresses CD10, CD56, and vimentin. Both components show strong diffuse GLI1 expression. SMA, calretinin, CD34, desmin, and S100 are typically negative; KIT is rarely positive. Recurrent in-frame MALAT1::GLI1 fusion is characteristic and can be detected by molecular testing or FISH. GLI1 pathway activation is a key biologic feature. Plexiform Fibromyxoma Plexiform fibromyxoma is a gastric myofibroblastic tumor with plexiform growth and myxoid stroma; it lacks the characteristic biphasic epithelial component, although GLI1-related fusions may overlap. Gastrointestinal Stromal Tumor GIST is typically a spindle or epithelioid mesenchymal neoplasm with KIT/DOG1 expression and lacks the biphasic keratin-positive epithelial component of gastroblastoma. Appendiceal Neuroendocrine Tumor Appendix — Neuroendocrine Tumors Usually small, well-differentiated enterochromaffin-cell NET at the appendiceal tip, incidentally found after appendectomy. A well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumor arising in the appendix; pediatric cases are predominantly serotonin-producing enterochromaffin-cell tumors. Mean age at presentation is approximately 11–12 years. Girls are more commonly affected than boys. Most arise at the appendiceal tip; the body is less often involved and the base is uncommon. Approximately 85% are discovered incidentally during appendectomy for acute appendicitis; carcinoid syndrome is very uncommon. Uniform neuroendocrine cells with organoid, nested, trabecular, acinar, or ribbon-like architecture. Finely stippled neuroendocrine chromatin and low proliferative activity; most pediatric cases are WHO grade 1. Expression of synaptophysin and chromogranin A or B supports neuroendocrine differentiation. Carefully examine the appendiceal tip microscopically, as small tumors may be grossly occult. Uniform polygonal cells form nests, trabeculae, ribbons, and occasional acini. Nuclei show coarsely stippled chromatin and inconspicuous nucleoli. Mitoses are infrequent to absent; necrosis is very uncommon. Peripheral nuclear palisading and luminal formations may be present. Tumor often involves deep muscularis propria and subserosa with limited mucosal involvement; mesoappendiceal extension may occur. Acute appendicitis may distort architecture and produce focal cytologic atypia. Synaptophysin and chromogranin A/B are positive. Serotonin expression supports enterochromaffin-cell differentiation. S100-positive sustentacular-like cells may surround nests in some cases. Molecular testing is not clinically relevant for routine diagnosis in this entity. Gastrointestinal Lymphoma Lymphoma forms a lymphoid infiltrate or mass and expresses lineage-specific lymphoid markers rather than synaptophysin/chromogranin; correlate with morphology and immunophenotype. GIST is a mesenchymal spindle/epithelioid tumor expressing KIT and DOG1, not a well-differentiated neuroendocrine epithelial neoplasm. All groups Pediatric Pathology Digestive System Tumors Diagnostic classification of pediatric and young-adult digestive system neoplasms, integrating clinical presentation, essential morphologic criteria, immunophenotype, and diagnostically relevant molecular findings across hepatic, pancreatic, and gastrointestinal tumors. Tumor Classification at a Glance Start with the organ, age, dominant architecture, and lineage-specific differentiation. Entity Group Characteristic Pattern Essential Diagnostic Clue Practical Diagnostic Framework 1. Confirm the organ of origin. Separate primary hepatic, pancreatic, gastric, and appendiceal lesions from metastases and adjacent-organ tumors. 2. Use age and clinical setting. An infantile hepatic mass, an adolescent pancreatic mass, and an appendiceal incidentaloma have very different prior probabilities. 3. Identify the dominant lineage and architecture. Assess hepatocytic, biliary, endothelial, mesenchymal, acinar, neuroendocrine, or biphasic differentiation. 4. Apply focused immunohistochemistry. Use lineage-specific panels: hepatocellular markers, endothelial markers/GLUT1, acinar enzymes, neuroendocrine markers, and β-catenin pathway markers as appropriate. 5. Reserve molecular testing for classification. Prioritize CTNNB1/APC, DNAJB1::PRKACA, TERT promoter, MALAT1::GLI1, and other alterations when they resolve a defined diagnostic question. 6. Sample heterogeneous tumors adequately. Look for focal squamoid nests in pancreatoblastoma, mixed components in hepatoblastoma, and distinct malignant or transformed areas. Search entities, criteria, morphology, markers, or genes...
