Try a different search term or category. Diagnostic interpretation should be integrated with age, clinical history, imaging, tumor sampling, and appropriate ancillary studies. Molecular findings should be interpreted in the context of morphology and the specific diagnostic question.

title: Endocrine Tumors
content: use client Follicular Adenoma of the Thyroid Thyroid Tumors Completely encapsulated, noninvasive follicular-cell neoplasm without papillary thyroid carcinoma-type nuclei. A benign, encapsulated thyroid follicular-cell neoplasm. The diagnosis depends on thorough assessment of the entire tumor–capsule interface to exclude invasion. Usually presents in children and adolescents around 11–12 years; mean age is younger than in adults. Female predominance (approximately 3–4:1). May arise anywhere in the thyroid; usually a solitary or dominant palpable nodule. Most patients are euthyroid; compressive symptoms occur in a minority. Hyperfunctioning adenomas cause thyrotoxicosis. A well-circumscribed, encapsulated neoplasm distinct from the surrounding thyroid. No capsular or lymphovascular invasion after adequate examination of the entire tumor periphery. No convincing papillary thyroid carcinoma-type nuclear features. Follicular-cell differentiation is supported by thyroglobulin, TTF1, and PAX8 expression. A thin, well-formed fibrous capsule separates the tumor from adjacent thyroid. Follicular architecture ranges from microfollicular to macrofollicular, often mixed. Tumor cells are cuboidal with pale to eosinophilic cytoplasm and small, round, regular nuclei. Mitotic figures are rare; true tumor necrosis and invasion are absent. Papillary hyperplasia may produce pseudopapillary projections, but nuclei remain polarized, regular, and non-overlapping. Toxic adenomas may show columnar cells, vacuolated cytoplasm, and scalloped colloid. Tumor cells express thyroglobulin, TTF1, and PAX8. Calcitonin and PTH are negative. HBME1 and CD56 may support distinction from malignant follicular lesions; galectin-3 may be positive in benign lesions and is not independently diagnostic. Loss of nuclear PTEN may prompt evaluation for PTEN hamartoma tumor syndrome in the appropriate setting. Papillary Thyroid Carcinoma Shows characteristic papillary thyroid carcinoma nuclear features; papillary architecture alone is insufficient. PTC may also be infiltrative or show lymphatic invasion. Cribriform-Morular Thyroid Carcinoma Shows complex cribriform and morular architecture with aberrant nuclear/cytoplasmic β-catenin, rather than a conventional encapsulated follicular adenoma. Medullary Thyroid Carcinoma Shows C-cell differentiation with calcitonin, CEA, and neuroendocrine marker expression; amyloid may be present. Spindle Epithelial Tumor with Thymus-Like Elements Has a biphasic spindle-cell and glandular epithelial pattern, diffuse keratin and p40/p63 expression, and lacks thyroglobulin. No molecular marker reliably distinguishes follicular adenoma from follicular carcinoma, follicular-variant PTC, or NIFTP. Activating TSHR or GNAS mutations, sometimes with EZH1 mutations, may occur in hyperfunctioning adenomas. Examine the entire capsule and tumor–parenchyma interface; minimally invasive follicular carcinoma may be missed in a limited sample. Distinguishing adenoma from a hyperplastic nodule may be difficult; a discrete capsule and clear demarcation favor adenoma. A pediatric follicular carcinoma may be a sentinel finding for a hereditary tumor-predisposition syndrome. Thyroid follicular-cell tumor with characteristic nuclear features, regardless of its predominant growth pattern. The most common pediatric thyroid malignancy. Pediatric tumors show a relatively high frequency of gene fusions and may present with cervical lymph-node metastases. Most often presents during the second decade; adolescent girls are affected more often than boys. Female predominance is pronounced in adolescents but less evident in younger children. Arises anywhere in the thyroid; may also occur in ectopic thyroid tissue or a thyroglossal duct cyst. Typically presents as a thyroid nodule or cervical lymphadenopathy; hoarseness and dysphagia are uncommon presentations. A malignant follicular-cell neoplasm with characteristic papillary thyroid carcinoma nuclear features. Nuclear enlargement and elongation, chromatin clearing, grooves, and intranuclear cytoplasmic inclusions are key findings. Architecture may be papillary, follicular, solid/trabecular, or diffuse sclerosing; well-formed papillae are not required. Assess tumor capsule, lymphovascular invasion, extrathyroidal extension, and cervical lymph nodes. For an encapsulated follicular-patterned tumor, evaluate the entire tumor periphery for invasion before considering NIFTP. Classic PTC has papillae with fibrovascular cores lined by cuboidal to low-columnar cells. Psammoma bodies, stromal fibrosis, cystic change, and lymphatic invasion may be present. Follicular-variant PTC is composed of follicles without well-formed papillae but retains PTC-type nuclei. Diffuse sclerosing PTC diffusely involves one or both lobes and shows numerous papillary foci, psammoma bodies, fibrosis, lymphocytic thyroiditis, and squamous morules. Solid/trabecular PTC shows predominant solid, nested, insular, or trabecular growth while retaining PTC-type nuclei; necrosis and high mitotic activity are not typical. Tall-cell PTC has cells at least two to three times taller than wide in at least 30% of the tumor. Oncocytic PTC shows abundant granular eosinophilic cytoplasm while retaining PTC nuclear features. Papillary microcarcinoma is defined by a maximum tumor diameter of 10 mm. Tumor cells express thyroglobulin, TTF1, PAX8, and cytokeratins. Galectin-3 and HBME1 are commonly expressed and may support the diagnosis in selected cases. Loss of CD56 expression is frequent, particularly in classic PTC. Calcitonin, CEA, and neuroendocrine markers are generally negative. VE1 immunohistochemistry can identify BRAF p.V600E-mutated tumors. Lacks PTC-type nuclear features and is noninvasive; papillary hyperplasia in adenoma retains polarized, regular nuclei. Shows cribriform architecture and morules with strong nuclear β-catenin; often associated with APC-related familial adenomatous polyposis. Shows C-cell phenotype with calcitonin, CEA, and neuroendocrine markers; thyroglobulin is absent. Shows long spindle-cell fascicles merging with complex glands; diffuse keratin and p40/p63 positivity with thyroglobulin negativity. Gene fusions are more frequent in pediatric PTC than in adult PTC; RET fusions are particularly common, especially after radiation exposure. Other recurrent fusions involve NTRK1, NTRK3, BRAF, ALK, PAX8, and MET. BRAF p.V600E is the most common point mutation but is less frequent in children than in adults and is uncommon in the youngest patients. RAS, PTEN, DICER1, and PIK3CA alterations occur in a subset; these are not uniformly specific for PTC. Do not diagnose PTC from papillary architecture alone; evaluate the nuclear features. Solid/trabecular PTC retains PTC-type nuclei and usually lacks the necrosis and elevated mitotic activity expected in poorly differentiated thyroid carcinoma. In pediatric thyroid nodules, a fusion or BRAF alteration can strongly support PTC, whereas RAS, PTEN, and DICER1 alterations are less specific. Cribriform and morular architecture with diffuse nuclear β-catenin; consider APC-associated familial adenomatous polyposis. A distinctive thyroid carcinoma driven by WNT/β-catenin pathway activation. It may be the first manifestation of familial adenomatous polyposis. Usually affects young women; most patients are younger than 40 years, but pediatric cases occur. Marked female predominance. Often multifocal and bilateral in familial adenomatous polyposis; sporadic cases are usually solitary. May present as a painless thyroid mass, hoarseness, or dysphagia, or be detected incidentally. A well-circumscribed or locally invasive thyroid neoplasm with complex cribriform architecture and squamoid morules. Diffuse nuclear β-catenin expression is a hallmark diagnostic feature. Cribriform, follicular, papillary, trabecular, and solid patterns may be admixed. Evaluate for APC-associated familial adenomatous polyposis and recommend germline assessment when appropriate. Tumors are circumscribed or encapsulated and may be lobulated by fibrous septa. Cribriform structures consist of anastomosing bars and arches without intervening fibrous stroma. Follicle-like structures typically lack colloid. Squamoid morules are whorls of spindle-to-ovoid cells without keratinization. Papillary, pseudopapillary, trabecular, and solid patterns may be present. Capsular and vascular invasion can occur; high-grade tumors may show increased mitoses and necrosis. Strong nuclear and cytoplasmic β-catenin staining is characteristic. Cribriform areas commonly express TTF1, keratins, ER, and PR. Thyroglobulin is typically negative; PAX8 is absent or only weak/focal. Morules express CD10, CDX2, CD5, and CK5 and are negative for TTF1, PAX8, thyroglobulin, ER, and PR. Ki-67 is usually below 5% in conventional tumors; high-grade examples may show substantially higher indices. Usually shows classic PTC nuclear features and lacks the characteristic morules and diffuse nuclear β-catenin pattern of cribriform-morular carcinoma. Lacks the complex cribriform/morular architecture and diffuse nuclear β-catenin expression. Shows calcitonin-positive C-cell differentiation and may contain amyloid; cribriform-morular carcinoma is calcitonin-negative. Shows spindle-cell fascicles merging with complex glands and diffuse keratin/p40/p63 expression rather than cribriform growth with morules and nuclear β-catenin. Germline APC pathogenic variants underlie familial cases; somatic APC second hits drive individual tumors. Sporadic tumors also show WNT/β-catenin pathway activation. BRAF alterations are absent in this entity. Do not assume every case is sporadic; identify the association with familial adenomatous polyposis. Morules have a different immunophenotype from the cribriform component and should be interpreted separately. Invasive parafollicular C-cell neoplasm expressing calcitonin, often with amyloid stroma. A malignant thyroid C-cell neoplasm. Pediatric cases are frequently hereditary and may be the presenting manifestation of MEN2A or MEN2B. Can occur from infancy through adolescence; MEN2B-associated disease may arise during the first year of life. Overall sex distribution is approximately equal. Usually a solitary thyroid nodule when sporadic; familial tumors are often bilateral and multicentric. May present with a thyroid nodule or cervical lymphadenopathy; advanced disease can cause diarrhea, flushing, or ectopic hormone syndromes. An invasive neoplasm showing parafollicular C-cell differentiation. Confirm calcitonin expression and correlate with serum calcitonin when appropriate. Amyloid stroma supports the diagnosis but is not obligatory. In hereditary cases, assess for associated primary C-cell hyperplasia and multifocal/bilateral disease. Recommend germline RET testing and genetic counseling for every pediatric patient. Growth patterns include solid, trabecular, and insular arrangements; numerous variant patterns may occur. Tumor cells may be epithelioid, spindle-shaped, plasmacytoid, or small, with finely granular cytoplasm. Nuclear atypia may be variable, but overt anaplasia is usually absent. Amyloid stroma is present in approximately 90% of cases. Familial tumors are often small, bilateral, and multicentric, with associated primary C-cell hyperplasia. Invasive growth beyond the follicular basement membrane, with stromal sclerosis or amyloid, distinguishes carcinoma from C-cell hyperplasia. Tumor cells express calcitonin, CGRP, synaptophysin, chromogranins, and CEA. Keratins, TTF1, and PAX8 are typically positive. Calcitonin may be absent in a small subset of tumors, including some small-cell examples; correlate with other markers and morphology. Shows PTC-type nuclear features and thyroglobulin expression; MTC is calcitonin- and CEA-positive with neuroendocrine differentiation. Shows morules and diffuse nuclear β-catenin; it lacks the C-cell marker profile of MTC. Shows follicular-cell differentiation with thyroglobulin expression and no invasive C-cell neoplasm. Parasympathetic Paraganglioma Usually lacks keratins and CEA and has sustentacular cells; MTC is epithelial and typically expresses calcitonin, CEA, TTF1, and keratins. Germline activating RET variants cause MEN2A, MEN2B, and familial medullary thyroid carcinoma. RET p.M918T is strongly associated with MEN2B and very early, aggressive disease. Somatic RET mutations occur in a subset of apparently sporadic tumors; germline testing is required to establish hereditary status. A presumed sporadic pediatric MTC may still carry a germline RET pathogenic variant. Interpret calcitonin carefully in infants because physiologic serum levels are higher during the first two years of life. Biphasic tumor with spindle-cell fascicles merging into complex glandular structures; diffuse keratin and p40/p63. A rare, slow-growing malignant tumor of the thyroid or mediastinum with a characteristic biphasic epithelial architecture and potential for late metastasis. Predominantly affects children and young adults; median age is approximately 19 years. Slight male predominance. Usually arises in the thyroid; rarely occurs in the lateral neck or superior mediastinum. Typically presents as a painless thyroid mass; cervical nodal disease may be present, and distant metastases can occur after long latency. A biphasic neoplasm composed of spindle-cell fascicles merging with complex glandular elements. Spindle cells are cytologically bland in most cases. Reticulated or sieve-like areas may be present. Diffuse keratin expression, particularly high-molecular-weight keratins, supports epithelial differentiation. Absence of SS18 or SS18L1 rearrangement helps exclude synovial sarcoma in selected cases. Tumor is highly cellular and vaguely lobulated by fibrous septa. Long interlacing or reticulated spindle-cell fascicles merge imperceptibly with tubulopapillary and gland-like structures. Glandular elements may form tubules, papillae, glomeruloid structures, cords, or cystic spaces. Spindle cells have elongated nuclei, fine chromatin, inconspicuous nucleoli, and scant cytoplasm. Mitoses are usually rare; necrosis and increased mitotic activity are uncommon but may occur. Mucinous or ciliated glandular cells and focal squamous differentiation may be present. Both spindle and glandular components show diffuse pancytokeratin expression. High-molecular-weight cytokeratins are often more extensive than low-molecular-weight keratins. p40 and/or p63 are commonly positive. Thyroglobulin, calcitonin, CEA, TTF1, S100, and CD5 are negative. Synovial Sarcoma Usually has a higher-grade spindle-cell component and is defined by an SS18::SSX fusion; SETTLE lacks SS18/SS18L1 rearrangement and shows its characteristic complex glandular component. Ectopic Type A Thymoma Shows jigsaw-puzzle lobulation, haphazard spindle fascicles, more frequent pericytomatous vessels, and less complex glandular elements. Shows follicular-cell nuclear features and thyroglobulin expression; SETTLE lacks thyroglobulin and has spindle-cell/glandular biphasic architecture. Expresses calcitonin and neuroendocrine markers; SETTLE is keratin-positive but calcitonin- and neuroendocrine-marker negative. Is an encapsulated follicular-cell neoplasm with thyroglobulin expression and no biphasic spindle-cell/glandular architecture. Shows cribriform and morular architecture with diffuse nuclear β-catenin rather than the biphasic spindle-cell/glandular pattern of SETTLE. SETTLE lacks the SS18 or SS18L1 rearrangements characteristic of synovial sarcoma. The GTF2I mutation characteristic of type A/AB thymoma is absent. Rare cases have reported KRAS, NRAS, SMYD1, or KMT2C mutations; these are not defining diagnostic alterations. Late metastases may occur; long-term clinical follow-up is important. Do not mistake extracellular metachromatic material on cytology for amyloid. Parathyroid Adenoma Parathyroid Tumors Enlarged, hypercellular, stromal fat-depleted parathyroid tissue in a patient with primary hyperparathyroidism. A benign parathyroid epithelial neoplasm. Pediatric parathyroid adenomas warrant consideration of hereditary hyperparathyroidism syndromes. True adenomas are more typical in older adolescents; infancy more often raises consideration of calcium-sensing receptor disorders. Childhood hyperparathyroidism affects both sexes approximately equally. May be orthotopic or ectopic, including thyroid, mediastinum, retroesophageal space, and thymus; multigland disease is relatively common. Children are more likely than adults to present symptomatically with marked hypercalcemia and hypercalciuria. Enlarged, hypercellular parathyroid tissue with depletion or absence of stromal fat. A rim of normal or compressed, atrophic parathyroid tissue supports adenoma over hyperplasia. A marked postoperative fall in PTH (greater than 50%) is a desirable clinical correlate. Malignancy requires unequivocal invasive growth and/or vascular space invasion; atypia alone is insufficient. A parathyroid adenoma or hyperplasia in a child should prompt genetic evaluation. Most tumors are composed predominantly of chief cells with reduced or absent stromal fat. Oxyphil or water-clear cell predominance may occur. A rim of normal or suppressed parathyroid tissue may be present at the periphery. CDC73-associated tumors may show sheet-like growth, eosinophilic cells, perinuclear clearing, nuclear enlargement, and arborizing or staghorn vessels. Biopsy-related change or renal secondary hyperplasia may cause fibrosis and reactive atypia that mimic invasion. PTH and GATA3 support parathyroid differentiation. Loss of parafibromin expression supports CDC73 pathway inactivation and should prompt evaluation for hyperparathyroidism-jaw tumor syndrome. Parafibromin immunohistochemistry is not completely sensitive or specific and does not replace germline testing. Parathyroid Hyperplasia Often involves multiple glands and lacks a discrete adenoma with a rim of compressed or normal parathyroid tissue; clinical and operative correlation is essential. Parathyroid Carcinoma Requires unequivocal invasive growth and/or vascular space invasion; cytologic atypia or fibrosis alone is insufficient. May mimic parathyroid adenoma architecturally but expresses thyroglobulin, TTF1, and PAX8 rather than PTH; thyroid follicles contain colloid. Germline CDC73 variants are associated with hyperparathyroidism-jaw tumor syndrome; parafibromin loss is a useful screening clue. MEN1 and MEN4 are important hereditary associations; somatic alterations in CCND1, MEN1, and CDC73 have been reported. Molecular testing does not replace morphologic assessment or germline evaluation. Do not diagnose parathyroid carcinoma on atypia or fibrosis alone. A single gland may be difficult to classify as adenoma versus hyperplasia without clinical and operative correlation. Adrenal Cortical Adenoma Adrenal Cortical Tumors Well-circumscribed, noninvasive cortical neoplasm with low mitotic activity and no tumor necrosis. A benign adrenal cortical neoplasm. Pediatric adrenal cortical tumors are strongly associated with germline predisposition, particularly TP53 and chromosome 11p15 abnormalities. Pediatric cases cluster in the first five years of life, with a smaller adolescent peak. No consistent sex predilection is emphasized. Usually a unilateral adrenal mass. Often presents with hormone excess, especially virilization; cortisol, estrogen, or aldosterone excess may also occur. Nonfunctioning tumors are more common in adolescents. Tumor is usually small and well circumscribed, without extra-adrenal extension or vascular invasion. No capsular invasion, tumor necrosis, or atypical mitoses. Mitotic count is generally no more than 3 mitoses/mm² in 5 mm². Tumor weight below 400 g and size below 105 mm support adenoma but are not absolute criteria. Integrate all morphologic parameters; tumors with an intermediate number of adverse features may be of uncertain malignant potential. Nested or trabecular architecture with a mixture of lipid-rich and lipid-poor cortical cells. Nuclei are relatively small and uniform. Mitotic activity is absent or low. True tumor necrosis and invasive growth are absent. Reticulin framework is generally preserved. Tumor cells express SF1, α-inhibin, Melan-A, and synaptophysin. Chromogranin is negative. p53 usually shows a wild-type pattern with weak nuclear staining. Ki-67 below 10% supports a benign clinical course but should not be used in isolation. Adrenal Cortical Carcinoma Shows a constellation of adverse features, including invasion, necrosis, atypical mitoses, elevated mitotic activity, and often increased Ki-67; no single feature should be interpreted alone. Pheochromocytoma Shows nested chromaffin-cell architecture and neuroendocrine markers; adrenal cortical tumors are SF1-positive and chromogranin-negative. Germline TP53 alterations (Li-Fraumeni syndrome) and chromosome 11p15 abnormalities with IGF2 overexpression are important pediatric associations. Somatic CTNNB1 and ATRX alterations may occur during tumor progression. Pediatric adrenal cortical tumors should be evaluated using pediatric criteria such as the Wieneke/AFIP algorithm rather than adult criteria alone. Some histologically malignant-appearing tumors may have favorable outcomes after complete resection; stage is a major prognostic determinant. Genetic counseling and testing are recommended for pediatric adrenal cortical tumors. Adrenal cortical malignancy supported by invasion, necrosis, atypical mitoses, and increased proliferative activity. A rare but important pediatric malignancy with a strong association with germline TP53 and 11p15 abnormalities. Hormone secretion frequently leads to early clinical detection. Most often occurs in children younger than five years, with a second peak during adolescence. Arises in the adrenal cortex, usually as a unilateral mass. Commonly causes virilization; Cushing syndrome, feminization, and mineralocorticoid excess may occur. Nonfunctioning tumors tend to be larger at detection. Assess tumor size and weight, extra-adrenal extension, vena cava and venous invasion, capsular invasion, necrosis, mitotic count, and atypical mitoses. Invasion, tumor necrosis, and atypical mitoses are major adverse findings. Mitotic count greater than 3 mitoses/mm² in 5 mm² supports carcinoma. Tumor weight above 400 g and size above 105 mm support carcinoma but are not sufficient alone. Ki-67 above 15% correlates with malignant behavior; interpret with morphology and stage. Architecture becomes disorganized, with loss of the normal reticulin framework. Tumor cells may show enlarged, hyperchromatic, and markedly pleomorphic nuclei. Mitotic activity is increased and atypical mitoses may be present. Tumor necrosis is common. Oncocytic and myxoid changes may occur. Aberrant p53 staining (diffuse strong expression or complete loss) correlates with TP53 mutation. Ki-67 above 15% correlates with malignant behavior but is not a stand-alone criterion. Lacks invasion, tumor necrosis, atypical mitoses, and substantial proliferative activity; assess the complete tumor and apply pediatric criteria. Shows chromaffin-cell morphology and neuroendocrine markers; adrenal cortical carcinoma is SF1-positive and typically chromogranin-negative. Germline TP53 pathogenic variants are a major association, particularly in Li-Fraumeni syndrome. Chromosome 11p15 abnormalities and IGF2 overexpression are frequent in pediatric adrenal cortical tumors. TP53 and ATRX alterations are associated with adverse biological behavior in molecular subgroups. Do not apply adult size, weight, or mitotic thresholds to pediatric tumors without considering the pediatric algorithm. Stage is the strongest predictor of outcome; completely resected localized tumors may have a favorable course despite adverse histology. Sympathetic Paraganglioma Pheochromocytoma and Paraganglioma Extra-adrenal sympathetic paraganglionic tumor with Zellballen architecture and neuroendocrine phenotype. A neuroendocrine neoplasm arising from sympathetic paraganglia. Correctly establishing an extra-adrenal location is important because it has genetic and clinical implications. Pediatric cases typically present in the second decade, with reported median ages around 12–13 years. Sex distribution is approximately equal in children. Usually arises in the abdomen, retroperitoneum, pelvis, or thorax; cervical sympathetic-chain sites are less common. May be catecholamine-secreting and present with sustained hypertension, headache, diaphoresis, or an abdominal mass. A neuroendocrine neoplasm with nested (Zellballen) architecture. Tumor cells have stippled neuroendocrine chromatin. Establish that the tumor is extra-adrenal and arises in sympathetic paraganglia. Use neuroendocrine immunohistochemistry and sustentacular-cell markers to support the diagnosis. Consider germline testing, particularly for SDHB and VHL alterations. Small nests of chief cells are separated by delicate fibrovascular stroma. Tumor cells have basophilic, amphophilic, or clear cytoplasm and stippled to coarse chromatin. Marked nuclear pleomorphism may occur but is not independently predictive of metastatic behavior. Necrosis and increased mitoses are uncommon. Capsular extension and lymphovascular invasion may be present. Chief cells express chromogranin, synaptophysin, and INSM1. Tyrosine hydroxylase, DBH, and GATA3 are commonly positive. S100 and SOX10 highlight sustentacular cells. Keratin is generally negative. Loss of granular cytoplasmic SDHB staining supports an SDH-deficient tumor; SDHA loss may indicate SDHA alteration. Arises in head and neck parasympathetic-associated paraganglia and is usually nonfunctional; sympathetic tumors more often arise in the thoracoabdominal compartment and secrete catecholamines. Has the same basic morphology and immunophenotype but arises in the adrenal medulla; confirm the anatomic site. Composite Pheochromocytoma/Paraganglioma Requires a second, well-developed neural or nerve-sheath tumor component comprising at least 5% of the tumor. Germline pathogenic variants are common in pediatric cases; SDHB and VHL are frequent associations. SDHB immunohistochemistry is a useful screening surrogate for SDH-pathway alterations. Do not use benign or malignant terminology; all paragangliomas have metastatic potential. Do not classify a tumor as pheochromocytoma without confirming adrenal medullary origin. Fine-needle aspiration is generally avoided because of hemorrhage and catecholamine-related hypertensive crisis risk. Parasympathetic Paraganglioma (Head and Neck Paraganglioma) Zellballen-pattern tumor associated with carotid body, jugulotympanic region, or vagal paraganglia. A head and neck paraganglionic neoplasm, usually nonfunctional. Pediatric cases have a strong hereditary association, particularly with SDH gene variants. Pediatric cases may present in childhood or adolescence; a reported pediatric series had a median age of approximately 13 years. Female predominance is reported. Common sites are carotid body, jugulotympanic region, and vagal paraganglia; laryngeal and other head and neck sites are less common. Usually presents as an asymptomatic mass; carotid body tumors cause a neck mass, jugulotympanic tumors cause pulsatile tinnitus or hearing symptoms, and vagal tumors may cause cranial nerve deficits. Only a small minority are biochemically functional, often producing dopamine. A neuroendocrine neoplasm with nested architecture and round nuclei with stippled chromatin. Establish the anatomic association with parasympathetic-related head and neck paraganglia. Confirm neuroendocrine differentiation and assess epithelial markers in the differential diagnosis. Consider SDHB immunohistochemistry and germline evaluation, particularly for SDHD and SDHB. Carotid body tumors show prominent Zellballen nests separated by delicate, sometimes cavernous, vascular channels. Chief cells range from epithelioid to spindled and have amphophilic to eosinophilic cytoplasm. Nuclei show hyperchromatic, stippled chromatin. Sustentacular cells may be inconspicuous on H&E. Necrosis, pleomorphism, or local invasion may occur and do not independently establish aggressive behavior. Glands and mucin are absent. Chromogranin and synaptophysin are variably expressed; INSM1 may be positive when chromogranin is negative. GATA3 is useful in distinguishing paraganglioma from many epithelial neuroendocrine tumors. Tyrosine hydroxylase may be focal or absent, especially in nonfunctional tumors. Keratins are generally negative. Arises in thoracoabdominal sympathetic paraganglia and is more often catecholamine-secreting; head and neck parasympathetic tumors are usually nonfunctional. Arises in the adrenal medulla and has a similar Zellballen pattern; anatomic localization distinguishes the entities. Usually expresses calcitonin, CEA, TTF1, and keratins; paraganglioma is typically keratin-negative and GATA3-positive. Epithelial Neuroendocrine Tumor Usually expresses keratins; paraganglioma is generally keratin-negative and often has a sustentacular-cell network. Hereditary predisposition is common; SDHD, SDHB, and SDHC are frequent susceptibility genes. SDHB loss supports an SDH-deficient pathway and is associated with increased metastatic risk. Do not use the terms glomus tumor or chemodectoma as diagnostic names. Metastasis may occur after a long latency, particularly in SDHB-associated disease; lifelong surveillance may be needed. Avoid fine-needle aspiration when possible because of hemorrhage and catecholamine-related risk. Adrenal medullary chromaffin-cell neoplasm with Zellballen architecture and neuroendocrine marker expression. An adrenal medullary neuroendocrine neoplasm. Pediatric cases have a high rate of germline susceptibility and are frequently bilateral or multifocal. Usually presents in the second decade; reported pediatric median ages range from 11 to 16 years. A slight male predominance is reported in some pediatric series. Arises in the adrenal medulla; bilateral and multifocal tumors are relatively common in hereditary disease. Sustained hypertension is the most common presenting sign, often with headache and diaphoresis; abdominal pain, palpitations, tremor, or incidental detection may occur. A neuroendocrine neoplasm arising in the adrenal medulla with nested architecture. Tumor cells have basophilic to amphophilic granular cytoplasm and neuroendocrine marker expression. Keratin negativity supports the diagnosis in selected cases. Assess mitotic count and Ki-67 index for risk stratification, but no single histologic feature reliably predicts metastasis. Consider germline testing in all pediatric patients; SDHB immunohistochemistry and other pathway markers can guide triage. Most tumors show a nested Zellballen pattern; trabecular or diffuse patterns may occur. Chief cells resemble normal chromaffin cells and have granular basophilic to amphophilic cytoplasm. Clear-cell change, intracytoplasmic vacuoles, and eosinophilic cytoplasm may occur. Adrenal medullary hyperplasia may accompany hereditary disease; medullary tissue extending into the alae or involving more than one third of gland thickness supports hyperplasia. Metastasis is defined by tumor at sites where normal paraganglia are absent, such as lymph nodes or bone. Tumor cells express chromogranin A, synaptophysin, INSM1, tyrosine hydroxylase, DBH, and GATA3 in most cases. Loss of granular cytoplasmic SDHB staining supports SDH deficiency; SDHA loss correlates with SDHA mutation. Membranous CAIX may support VHL-associated disease; 2-succinocysteine and fumarate hydratase can support FH-pathway evaluation. Has similar morphology and immunophenotype but is extra-adrenal; confirm adrenal medullary origin for pheochromocytoma. Arises in head and neck paraganglia and is usually nonfunctional; pheochromocytoma is adrenal and commonly catecholamine-secreting. Shows cortical differentiation with SF1, inhibin, and Melan-A expression; pheochromocytoma expresses neuroendocrine markers and lacks SF1. Shows cortical differentiation and may have necrosis, invasion, and atypical mitoses; pheochromocytoma has Zellballen architecture and neuroendocrine phenotype. Contains a second well-developed neural or nerve-sheath component, not merely scattered ganglion cells or limited Schwannian stroma. Germline pathogenic variants are identified in a large proportion of pediatric cases; common genes include VHL, SDHB/SDHD, RET, NF1, and MAX. Pseudohypoxia-pathway alterations (including SDHx, VHL, FH, and EPAS1) and kinase-signaling alterations (including RET and NF1) define major molecular groups. SDHB loss by immunohistochemistry is a useful surrogate for SDH-pathway alteration. Germline testing is recommended because apparently sporadic pediatric tumors may carry pathogenic variants. Do not diagnose metastasis solely from a liver or lung lesion; primary paraganglia can occur at unusual sites. Do not use PASS, GAPP, or other adult scoring systems as validated pediatric prognostic tools. Avoid aspiration biopsy because catecholamine release can precipitate a life-threatening hypertensive crisis. Pheochromocytoma or paraganglioma with a second, morphologically distinct neural or nerve-sheath tumor component. A rare composite neoplasm combining a chromaffin-cell tumor with a developmentally related neural tumor, most often neuroblastoma in pediatric patients. Extremely rare; only a small minority of reported cases occur in children. Slight female predominance is reported in pediatric cases. Most pediatric examples are adrenal composite pheochromocytomas; extra-adrenal composite paragangliomas may occur in the retroperitoneum or mediastinum. Often functional, with hypertension, headache, diaphoresis, or an abdominal mass; VIP secretion may cause watery diarrhea, hypokalemia, and achlorhydria. Both a recognizable pheochromocytoma/paraganglioma component and a second developmentally related neural or nerve-sheath tumor component must be present. Each component should show convincing cytologic and architectural features of its respective tumor type. The minor component should constitute at least 5% of tumor volume. A few isolated ganglion cells or limited Schwannian stroma in an otherwise typical pheochromocytoma/paraganglioma does not qualify. Sample the tumor extensively to identify and characterize each component. The chromaffin component shows conventional Zellballen architecture. The neural component may be neuroblastoma, ganglioneuroblastoma, ganglioneuroma, or a peripheral nerve sheath tumor. Neuroblastoma shows immature neuroblastic cells, focal rosette-like arrangements, and neuropil. Ganglioneuroma/ganglioneuroblastoma shows Schwannian stroma and maturing or mature ganglion cells. A malignant peripheral nerve sheath component may show streaming fascicles of elongated cells in myxoid stroma. Metastases may contain one or both components. The pheochromocytoma/paraganglioma component expresses neuroendocrine markers. Sustentacular cells in the chromaffin component may express S100 and GFAP. The neural component is characterized with lineage-appropriate neuronal, Schwannian, or nerve-sheath markers. VIP immunoreactivity may be demonstrable in tumors associated with WDHA syndrome. Lacks a second well-developed neural or nerve-sheath tumor component; scattered ganglion cells or limited Schwannian stroma are insufficient. Is an extra-adrenal chromaffin tumor without a qualifying second neural component. Arises in head and neck paraganglia and lacks a distinct second neural tumor component. Germline testing is indicated because any pheochromocytoma/paraganglioma component warrants evaluation for hereditary susceptibility. NF1, MAX, and SDHB alterations have been reported in composite tumors. MYCN amplification may be present in the neuroblastoma component and should be assessed in that component when clinically indicated. Do not overcall a composite tumor based on a few ganglion cells or scant Schwannian stroma. Metastatic deposits may contain only one of the two components; sample and characterize metastatic lesions when feasible. Other Neuroendocrine Tumors Epithelial Neuroendocrine Tumors Well-differentiated epithelial neuroendocrine neoplasm; classify by site, differentiation, grade, and hormone/cell type. A site-diverse group of well-differentiated epithelial neuroendocrine neoplasms. Pediatric examples most often involve the gastrointestinal tract and pancreas, but may arise in other organs. Most gastroenteropancreatic cases present in adolescence, with an average age of approximately 12–15 years. A female predominance is reported for pediatric gastroenteropancreatic NETs. Most commonly arise in the gut and pancreas; lung, thymus, pituitary, thyroid, parathyroid, gonads, and teratomas are additional sites. Symptoms depend on site and hormone production: obstruction or intussusception, hypoglycemia (insulinoma), gastrin-related symptoms, carcinoid syndrome, or rarely ectopic ACTH-related Cushing syndrome. A well-differentiated epithelial neoplasm with neuroendocrine morphology. Confirm epithelial nature and neuroendocrine differentiation by immunohistochemistry. Grade as G1, G2, or G3 using site-appropriate mitotic count and Ki-67 criteria. Assess site-specific hormone production and cell lineage where relevant. Examine adjacent non-neoplastic parenchyma or mucosa for hyperplasia, dysplasia, multifocal microtumors, or syndromic changes. Use the site-specific AJCC/UICC staging system. Most tumors show nested or insular architecture composed of polygonal cells. Nuclei are round to oval with finely stippled salt-and-pepper chromatin. Peripheral palisading may be present. Gastric type 2 enterochromaffin-like cell NETs are common in children; classify with clinical context, serum gastrin, and background mucosal changes. Ampullary duodenal NETs may show tubuloacinar architecture and psammoma bodies, often with somatostatin-producing D cells. Ileal NETs show enterochromaffin-cell differentiation and may have brightly eosinophilic cytoplasm. Rectal NETs often show trabecular architecture and infiltrate mucosa and submucosa. Pancreatic NETs may be functional; insulinoma is an important pediatric functional subtype. Pulmonary and thymic NETs may be spindle-cell or polygonal; atypical carcinoid is assessed using mitotic activity and necrosis. General neuroendocrine markers include INSM1, synaptophysin, and chromogranins. Keratins support epithelial differentiation and help distinguish NET from paraganglioma. Gastric ECL-cell tumors express VMAT2 and histidine decarboxylase. Ileal enterochromaffin-cell tumors may express serotonin, substance P, CDX2, and VMAT1. Rectal L-cell tumors may express glicentin, GLP-1/GLP-2, pancreatic polypeptide, PYY, SATB2, and prostatic acid phosphatase. Pancreatic NETs may express ISL1, PDX1, PAX6, polyclonal PAX8, CDX2, and site-appropriate hormones. Pulmonary NETs may express TTF1; hormone markers vary with site and cell type. A chromaffin-cell neoplasm with Zellballen architecture, sustentacular cells, GATA3/tyrosine hydroxylase expression, and usually absent keratin; epithelial NETs are keratin-positive. Is an extra-adrenal neural crest-derived paraganglionic neoplasm, usually keratin-negative; epithelial NETs show epithelial differentiation. Usually arises in head and neck paraganglia and is keratin-negative; GATA3 and sustentacular cells support paraganglioma. Pancreatoblastoma Shows acinar differentiation and characteristic squamoid nests; trypsin, chymotrypsin, and BCL10 support acinar lineage. Pancreatic Acinar Cell Carcinoma Shows acinar architecture and zymogen granules with trypsin, chymotrypsin, and BCL10 expression. Solid Pseudopapillary Neoplasm Shows discohesive cells around delicate vessels, pseudopapillary structures, and nuclear β-catenin; lacks a true neuroendocrine phenotype. Molecular testing is not required to establish the diagnosis. Germline testing should be guided by age, site, multifocality, associated precursor changes, and syndromic clinical findings. Pancreatic NET multifocality and adjacent islet dysplasia/microtumors may indicate MEN1, MEN4, or von Hippel–Lindau syndrome. Do not diagnose paraganglioma solely from neuroendocrine marker positivity; epithelial keratin expression and GATA3/sustentacular-cell pattern are useful in context. Do not apply a single grading system across all anatomic sites; use site-specific criteria. For pancreatic NETs, evaluate non-neoplastic pancreas for islet dysplasia, microtumors, ductuloinsular complexes, and other clues to hereditary disease. Thyroid epithelial Encapsulated follicular-cell neoplasm No capsular/vascular invasion; no PTC-type nuclei Follicular-cell carcinoma with characteristic nuclei PTC-type nuclear features across diverse patterns Cribriform growth and squamoid morules Diffuse nuclear β-catenin; assess APC/FAP Thyroid C-cell/neuroendocrine Invasive C-cell neoplasm Calcitonin, CEA, and neuroendocrine phenotype Biphasic spindle and glandular tumor Diffuse keratin; p40/p63; thyroglobulin-negative Parathyroid Hypercellular, fat-depleted parathyroid PTH/GATA3; correlate with hyperparathyroidism Adrenal cortical Noninvasive cortical neoplasm No necrosis, invasion, or atypical mitoses Malignant cortical neoplasm Integrate invasion, necrosis, mitoses, and Ki-67 Paraganglionic Extra-adrenal sympathetic paraganglion tumor Zellballen; neuroendocrine; site is extra-adrenal Head and neck paraganglion tumor Carotid body, jugulotympanic, or vagal site Adrenal medullary chromaffin-cell tumor Zellballen; adrenal origin; hereditary workup Chromaffin tumor plus neural/nerve-sheath component Each component well developed; minor component ≥5% Epithelial neuroendocrine Well-differentiated epithelial NET Site-specific lineage, grade, and hormone profile All groups Pediatric Pathology Endocrine Tumors Diagnostic classification of pediatric endocrine neoplasms, integrating anatomic site, cellular lineage, defining morphology, immunophenotype, hereditary predisposition, and diagnostically relevant molecular findings. Tumor Classification at a Glance First establish the organ and cell lineage; then use the defining architecture, invasion, immunophenotype, and syndrome associations to classify the tumor. Entity Category Typical pattern Key diagnostic point Practical Diagnostic Framework 1. Establish the organ and lineage. Separate follicular-cell, C-cell, parathyroid, adrenal cortical, chromaffin/paraganglionic, and epithelial neuroendocrine tumors. 2. Identify the defining architecture. Evaluate encapsulation and invasion in follicular lesions; papillary-type nuclei; Zellballen pattern; and biphasic or composite components. 3. Apply lineage-directed immunohistochemistry. Use thyroglobulin/TTF1, calcitonin/CEA, PTH/GATA3, SF1/inhibin, and neuroendocrine/sustentacular markers in a targeted panel. 4. Assess hereditary risk. Pediatric endocrine tumors may be sentinel manifestations of MEN syndromes, FAP, Li-Fraumeni syndrome, VHL, or SDHx-related disease. 5. Separate diagnosis from risk assessment. Integrate invasion, proliferation, stage, biochemical findings, and molecular results without relying on a single marker. 6. Sample adequately. Examine the entire capsule/periphery of follicular and adrenal cortical tumors and sample distinct components of composite tumors. Search entities, criteria, morphology, markers, or genes... title: Eye Tumors
content: use client Epibulbar Choristoma Conjunctival and Epibulbar Lesions Congenital ectopic mature tissue at the ocular surface; identify the tissue components and exclude atypia. A benign developmental lesion composed of mature tissues in an abnormal epibulbar location. Subtypes include epibulbar dermoid, dermolipoma, and complex choristoma. Present at birth or recognized in early childhood; no sex predilection is established. Typically arises in the superior or inferior temporal epibulbar conjunctiva, often inferotemporally at the limbus. Dermoids are firm, whitish, well-circumscribed limbal lesions and may contain cilia; dermolipomas are soft, yellow, superotemporal lesions. Large lesions may involve the cornea, impair lid closure, or cause amblyopia. Confirm conjunctival, limbal, or corneal localization. Identify mature ectopic tissue without cytologic atypia or destructive growth. Classify as dermoid, dermolipoma, or complex choristoma according to the tissue components. Dermoid: dermal-type collagen with squamous epithelium and variably present skin appendages. Dermolipoma: abundant mature adipose tissue in addition to dermal-type tissue. Complex choristoma: two or more heterotopic mature tissue types, commonly lacrimal gland and cartilage. Dermoid contains interweaving dermal-type collagen bundles covered by squamous epithelium. Cilia with sebaceous and sweat glands may be present in dermoids. Dermolipoma contains a prominent component of mature adipose tissue. Complex choristoma may contain lacrimal acini, cartilage, smooth muscle, nerve bundles, bone, or other mature tissues. Immunohistochemistry is generally unnecessary for conventional lesions. Use lineage-directed markers only when an unusual component requires confirmation. Epibulbar osseous choristoma Composed predominantly of mature compact lamellar bone rather than dermal, adipose, or mixed heterotopic tissues. Phakomatous choristoma Typically arises in the medial lower eyelid or anterior orbit and contains lens-like epithelial islands surrounded by a PAS-positive capsule-like membrane. Do not use a neoplastic term such as dermoid tumor for this developmental choristoma. Bilateral lesions are uncommon and may occur in syndromic settings, including Goldenhar syndrome. Epibulbar Osseous Choristoma Firm epibulbar mass composed of mature compact lamellar bone. A benign developmental choristoma composed of mature bone, usually in the superotemporal conjunctiva. Usually congenital and recognized in childhood or adolescence, although later incidental diagnosis occurs. Reported slight female predominance. Typically unilateral and superotemporal in the conjunctiva; temporal and rarely inferotemporal sites occur. Presents as a firm yellow-white, orange, pink, or white subconjunctival nodule; CT may show calcification. Confirm an epibulbar conjunctival location. Identify compact lamellar bone with morphologically normal osteocytes. Assess for additional heterotopic tissues that would support a complex choristoma. Exclude an infiltrative or cytologically atypical bone-forming neoplasm. Mature compact lamellar bone contains normal osteocytes in lacunae. Haversian canals may be present. Dense fibrous tissue forms a periosteal covering with an internal osteogenic layer. Hematopoietic marrow is usually absent. Additional cartilage, lacrimal tissue, nerves, or adipose tissue may indicate a complex choristoma. Immunohistochemistry is not routinely required; morphology establishes the diagnosis. Epibulbar choristoma Contains dermal, adipose, lacrimal, cartilaginous, or other mature heterotopic tissues rather than a lesion composed predominantly of compact lamellar bone. Avoid the term osteoma when the lesion is a congenital epibulbar choristoma. Phakomatous Choristoma Congenital medial lower-eyelid mass with lens-like epithelial islands and a thick PAS-positive capsule. A rare benign developmental lesion derived from lens placode tissue, occurring outside the globe. Present at birth as a slowly enlarging, smooth, firm subcutaneous mass. No consistent sex predilection is established. Typically involves the deep medial lower eyelid; rare cases are confined to the inferior anterior orbit. May measure up to 2 cm. Confirm a medial lower-eyelid or inferior anterior orbital location. Identify islands of cuboidal to polygonal epithelial cells in desmoplastic stroma. Demonstrate a thick eosinophilic, PAS-positive basement membrane-like material surrounding epithelial islands. Correlate with lens differentiation; malignant features are absent. Epithelial islands are composed of cuboidal to polygonal cells. A thick, amorphous, eosinophilic PAS-positive membrane surrounds the epithelial islands. Bladder cells and psammomatous calcifications may be present. The intervening stroma is densely collagenous and desmoplastic. Lesional cells express vimentin and S100. Lens crystallin proteins support lens differentiation. Cytokeratins are typically negative. Contains mature dermal, adipose, or other heterotopic tissues and lacks the characteristic lens-like epithelial islands with PAS-positive capsule. Medulloepithelioma Arises intraocularly, usually from the ciliary body, and forms multilayered neuroepithelial cords, ribbons, and cystic spaces. The historical term Zimmerman tumor is not recommended. Simple excision is generally curative; recurrence has not been reported. Conjunctival Junctional, Compound, and Subepithelial Nevi Conjunctival Melanocytic Lesions Symmetric melanocytic nests with maturation and/or epithelial inclusion cysts; architecture defines the subtype. Benign acquired conjunctival melanocytic nevi classified by the location of nevus cells as junctional, compound, or subepithelial (stromal). Junctional nevi are usually diagnosed in childhood or adolescence; compound nevi have a median diagnostic age in the early twenties, and subepithelial nevi occur at an older age. Compound and subepithelial nevi show an approximately equal sex distribution. Usually involve the juxtalimbal or bulbar conjunctiva; plica and caruncle involvement is less common. Typically well-circumscribed, tan to brown, mobile lesions; compound and subepithelial nevi are often elevated and may contain epithelial cysts. Growth during childhood may occur; new growth in adulthood warrants evaluation for melanoma. Identify a nested intraepithelial and/or subepithelial proliferation of cytologically bland melanocytes. Junctional nevus: nests are confined predominantly to the epithelial-subepithelial junction. Compound nevus: melanocytic nests involve both epithelium and substantia propria. Subepithelial nevus: melanocytes are confined to the substantia propria. Look for symmetry, maturation with depth, epithelial inclusion cysts, and low proliferative activity. Absence of extensive pagetoid spread, significant atypia, and mitoses in the subepithelial component supports benignity. Junctional nests contain type A epithelioid and/or type B smaller nevus cells along the epithelial-subepithelial junction. Compound nevi contain symmetric junctional and subepithelial components. Epithelial inclusion cysts are common in compound nevi and may be surrounded by stromal nevus cells. Maturation may progress from type A to type B and type C cells with depth, although it is not universal. Subepithelial nevi resemble the stromal component of compound nevi. Inflammation and occasional multinucleated cells may occur without establishing malignancy. Nevus cells express S100, SOX10, MITF, and Melan-A. HMB45 is often negative or only weakly and focally positive, particularly in the junctional component. Ki-67 is low and usually limited to the junctional component. Inflamed juvenile conjunctival nevus Occurs in children and adolescents and shows prominent lymphoplasmacytic and eosinophilic inflammation, rapid apparent growth, and sometimes disordered or reverse maturation. Conjunctival melanoma Favored by destructive or asymmetric growth, significant cytologic atypia, pagetoid spread, mitotic activity in the stromal component, ulceration, and/or molecular copy-number abnormalities. BRAF p.V600E and NRAS p.Q61 mutations are common in conjunctival nevi but do not distinguish nevus from melanoma. FISH panels assessing RREB1, MYB, MYC, and CCND1 copy-number changes may help classify melanocytic lesions of uncertain malignant potential. Corneal involvement is characteristically absent in conventional conjunctival nevi. Prominent inflammation or growth in a child does not by itself establish melanoma. Inflamed Juvenile Conjunctival Nevus Juvenile compound nevus with prominent inflammation, epithelial inclusions, and often alarming clinical vascularity or growth. A distinctive inflamed compound conjunctival nevus of children and adolescents that may show architectural and cytologic features mimicking melanoma. Occurs in children and adolescents, with a mean age around 13 years; many series show male predominance. Usually perilimbal and may involve the limbus. Presents as an elevated, well-circumscribed, often amelanotic or variably pigmented nodule. May enlarge rapidly and appear vascular, with congested feeder vessels and epithelial cysts. Atopic dermatitis, asthma, and allergic conjunctivitis may coexist. Preserve the overall compound nevus architecture, often triangular or V-shaped at low power. Identify a junctional component extending beyond the stromal component. Find epithelial inclusion cysts or solid epithelial rests within the stroma. Demonstrate a prominent inflammatory infiltrate, typically lymphocytes, plasma cells, and eosinophils. Exclude convincing malignant features such as atypical mitoses, destructive invasion, ulceration, or necrosis. Interpret apparent atypia in the context of patient age, architecture, inflammation, and immunostaining pattern. The lesion often has a triangular or V-shaped configuration. Confluent junctional nests may extend horizontally beyond the subepithelial component. Epithelial inclusions are common and may contain goblet cells and mucin. Dense lymphocytic inflammation is prominent, often with germinal centers. Plasma cells and eosinophils are frequent; eosinophils may infiltrate the superficial epithelium. Maturation may be incomplete or paradoxical, with larger cells in the deeper component. Mitoses are rare and the Ki-67 proliferation index remains low. HMB45 highlights the intraepithelial component and superficial stromal nevus cells. Ki-67 is low despite the sometimes alarming morphology. CD3 and CD20 demonstrate a mixed T-cell and B-cell inflammatory population. Plasma cells may express IgG4, but this alone does not establish IgG4-related disease. Conjunctival junctional, compound, and subepithelial nevi Conventional nevi lack the marked inflammatory infiltrate and prominent eosinophils characteristic of the juvenile inflamed variant. Usually shows destructive growth, significant atypia, atypical mitoses, ulceration, or pagetoid spread; the preserved nevus architecture and low proliferation favor an inflamed juvenile nevus. Conjunctival lymphoma May present as a salmon-colored patch but consists of a lymphoid proliferation rather than a melanocytic nevus with epithelial inclusions. Rapid growth, vascularity, and cytologic atypia can be misleading; correlate with the characteristic architecture and inflammatory background. IgG4-positive plasma cells may be numerous but do not independently diagnose IgG4-related disease. Diffuse Choroidal Neurofibroma and Ganglioneuroma Uveal and Iris Lesions Diffuse or multifocal choroidal expansion by Schwannian and fibroblastic elements, usually in an NF1 setting. Benign diffuse choroidal lesions comprising neurofibroma and, when numerous mature ganglion cells are present, choroidal ganglioneuroma. May occur in pediatric patients with NF1; frequency appears to increase with age. Typically diffuse or multifocal, with a predilection for the posterior pole; ciliary nerve involvement may occur. Often detected incidentally on modern imaging or in an enucleated blind, painful, buphthalmic eye. May be associated with congenital iris ectropion, glaucoma, or anterior displacement of ciliary processes. Identify diffuse or multifocal thickening of the choroid. Demonstrate a haphazard proliferation of Schwann cells and fibroblasts. Classify as choroidal ganglioneuroma when conspicuous mature ganglion cells accompany the neurofibromatous component. Correlate with clinical features of NF1 and evaluate for associated uveal abnormalities. Exclude a discrete melanocytic neoplasm when the lesion is mass-forming or pigmented. The choroid is diffusely expanded by Schwann cells and fibroblasts. Mast cells are often present in the neurofibromatous component. Choroidal melanocytes may be admixed with the proliferating Schwannian cells. Tactile corpuscle-like ovoid bodies with lamellated Schwann cells may be present. Numerous mature ganglion cells support the designation of ganglioneuroma. Schwannian cells typically express S100 and SOX10. Neuronal markers may highlight mature ganglion cells in ganglioneuromatous lesions. Lisch nodule (iris hamartoma) A Lisch nodule is a discrete, minimally elevated melanocytic hamartoma on the anterior iris surface, not a diffuse choroidal proliferation. Uveal melanoma Usually forms a discrete melanocytic mass with cytologic and architectural features of a melanocytic neoplasm rather than diffuse Schwannian and fibroblastic expansion. NF1 inactivation is expected in NF1-associated lesions. Rare reported cases associated with Cowden syndrome may harbor PTEN alterations. Ganglion cells may be a normal constituent of the choroid; their presence alone should not prompt a ganglioneuroma diagnosis without the appropriate diffuse stromal lesion. Lisch Nodule (Iris Hamartoma) Bilateral small iris surface nodules composed of bland spindle melanocytes in a patient with NF1. A benign melanocytic hamartoma of the iris, strongly associated with neurofibromatosis type 1. Usually appears in early childhood and becomes more prevalent with age. No sex predilection is established. Occurs on the anterior iris surface, predominantly in the inferior half; lesions are often bilateral. Small tan-to-cream, minimally elevated nodules; two or more are a diagnostic clinical criterion for NF1. Confirm localization to the anterior surface of the iris. Identify a plaque-like proliferation of cytologically bland melanocytes. Correlate with NF1 clinical criteria and the often bilateral distribution. Exclude cytologic atypia and mitotic activity. A dome-shaped plaque is composed predominantly of bland spindle-shaped melanocytes. Melanocytes are arranged haphazardly with indistinct borders. Ovoid or rounded melanocytes and melanophages may be present. The underlying iris stroma may contain similar melanocytes. Nucleoli are inconspicuous and mitotic figures are absent. Lesional melanocytes express S100. Melan-A and SOX10 may support melanocytic lineage when needed. Diffuse choroidal neurofibroma and ganglioneuroma These lesions expand the choroid diffusely and are composed of Schwannian and fibroblastic elements, sometimes with ganglion cells. Iris mammillations Mammillations are multiple regularly distributed, smooth, mound-like elevations of the iris pigment epithelium rather than a melanocytic stromal plaque. NF1 alterations underlie the syndromic association; no specific molecular test is required for diagnosing a Lisch nodule. Two or more Lisch nodules are one of the clinical diagnostic criteria for NF1; a solitary lesion is less specific. Retinocytoma Retinal Neuroepithelial Tumors Well-differentiated retinal lesion composed of photoreceptor-like fleurettes, with calcification and gliosis but no active malignant growth. A rare, differentiated and generally benign retinal tumor considered related to retinoblastoma; similar morphology may occur in treated retinoblastoma. Age at diagnosis ranges from infancy to middle age, with a mean around 29 years; no sex predilection is established. Most lesions are unilateral, although bilateral or multifocal lesions may occur in patients with germline RB1 alterations. Arises in the neurosensory retina and may be unilateral or bilateral. Typically appears semitranslucent with mild-to-moderate surrounding pigmentary changes; intralesional cysts and calcification are common. Identify a retinal lesion composed predominantly or entirely of differentiated photoreceptor-like cells. Find fleurette formation and bland nuclei without brisk mitotic activity or significant necrosis. Look for calcification, gliosis, and retinal pigment epithelial alterations. Distinguish a primary retinocytoma from retinocytoma-like differentiation in a previously treated retinoblastoma. Correlate with clinical and family history because the relationship to retinoblastoma is not fully resolved. Photoreceptor differentiation forms fleurettes resembling bouquets of flowers. Elongated cells have bland nuclei with powdery chromatin. Mitoses and apoptosis are absent or inconspicuous. Calcification and gliosis may be present. Retinal pigment epithelial hyperplasia and degenerative changes may accompany the lesion. Photoreceptor differentiation may be supported by retinal neuronal markers. Immunophenotype should be interpreted with morphology and clinical history; no single marker independently establishes retinocytoma. Retinoblastoma Shows primitive small round blue cells, frequent mitoses and apoptosis, geographic necrosis, and often Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes; retinocytoma is composed of bland differentiated photoreceptor-like cells. Retinocytoma generally harbors biallelic RB1 loss but has fewer secondary mutations and less aneuploidy than retinoblastoma. A second retinocytoma or a concurrent retinoblastoma in either eye strongly raises concern for a germline RB1 alteration. Ki-67 and p53 are typically not expressed; p16 and p130 may be increased, supporting a senescence-associated phenotype. Treated retinoblastoma may develop retinocytoma-like differentiation; treatment history is essential. Primitive retinal small round blue cell tumor with frequent mitoses, apoptosis, necrosis, and often calcification. The most common primary intraocular malignancy of childhood, driven in most cases by biallelic RB1 inactivation; a small subset is associated with MYCN amplification. More than 90% are diagnosed before 5 years of age; bilateral disease presents at a younger median age than unilateral disease. No sex predilection. Arises in the retina; unilateral or bilateral, with rare trilateral disease in heritable cases. Typically presents with leukocoria or strabismus; advanced disease may cause glaucoma, buphthalmos, hyphema, proptosis, or orbital extension. Endophytic tumors seed the vitreous; exophytic tumors extend into the subretinal space and may cause retinal detachment. In a young child, identify an intraocular retinal mass, commonly unilateral or bilateral. Histology shows a primitive small round blue cell neoplasm with scant cytoplasm and frequent mitoses and apoptosis. Geographic necrosis and dystrophic calcification are common. Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes support retinal differentiation; Homer Wright rosettes may also occur. Assess degree of differentiation, anaplasia, necrosis, choroidal invasion, optic nerve invasion, and extraocular extension. Document the depth and extent of choroidal and optic nerve invasion and the status of the optic nerve margin in enucleated specimens. Do not perform routine biopsy of a suspected intraocular retinoblastoma because of the risk of extraocular dissemination. Primitive neuroblastic cells have basophilic nuclei and scant cytoplasm. Numerous mitotic figures and apoptotic bodies are characteristic. Geographic necrosis occurs between viable perivascular tumor cuffs. Dystrophic calcification is common and may be prominent after treatment. Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes have central lumina and resemble retinal differentiation. Homer Wright rosettes contain central neuropil rather than a true lumen. Fleurettes indicate photoreceptor differentiation and may occur focally. Severe anaplasia features enlarged pleomorphic hyperchromatic nuclei and numerous mitoses. Choroidal invasion, postlaminar optic nerve invasion, meningeal involvement, and extraocular extension are critical high-risk findings. Synaptophysin and neuron-specific enolase highlight tumor cells when confirmation of invasion is needed. RB1 immunostaining is lost in most conventional retinoblastomas. Immunohistochemistry is not routinely required when morphology and clinical findings are classic. Composed of bland photoreceptor-like cells and fleurettes without the brisk mitotic activity, apoptosis, and geographic necrosis of retinoblastoma. Usually arises from the ciliary body and forms multilayered neuroepithelial cords, ribbons, and cysts in a myxoid matrix; LIN28A is commonly positive. Coats disease Shows retinal telangiectasia and exudation without a true retinal tumor mass; calcification is not a typical feature. Persistent fetal vasculature Typically produces a retrolental fibrovascular stalk and microphthalmia rather than a primitive retinal neoplasm. Biallelic RB1 inactivation is the central molecular event in nearly all cases; germline RB1 alterations are present in approximately 40% of affected children. A small subset, especially unilateral tumors in very young children, shows high-level MYCN amplification without RB1 alteration. Additional recurrent changes include gains of 1q and 6p and loss of 16q. Germline testing and genetic counseling are important for identifying heritable disease and at-risk relatives. A friable tumor may disperse during grossing and mimic invasion; artifact typically forms irregular aggregates admixed with necrotic and viable cells rather than true infiltrative sheets. Anterior chamber involvement alone is not equivalent to high-risk metastatic invasion. Careful orientation and sampling of the optic nerve, pupil-optic nerve section, and choroid are essential for risk assessment. Retinal and Ciliary Body Neuroepithelial Tumors Ciliary body tumor composed of multilayered polarized neuroepithelial cords and ribbons, often with cysts and myxoid matrix. A rare embryonal neuroepithelial neoplasm, usually arising from the inner surface of the ciliary body. Teratoid tumors contain heteroplastic tissues. Usually occurs in children aged 2–5 years; rare adult cases are reported. Female predominance has been reported. Typically arises from the inner surface of the ciliary body; rare retinal and optic nerve examples occur. Presents with visual loss, leukocoria, strabismus, red painful eye, secondary glaucoma, or iris neovascularization. Intratumoral cysts, lens notching, lens coloboma, or a neoplastic cyclitic membrane may provide diagnostic clues. Identify a tumor centered on the inner surface of the ciliary body. Demonstrate anastomosing cords, bands, or ribbons of polarized multilayered neuroepithelial cells. Look for hyaluronic acid-rich myxoid pools and intratumoral cystic spaces. Classify as teratoid when heteroplastic cartilage, muscle, or brain-like tissue is present; otherwise classify as non-teratoid. Assess cellular atypia, mitotic activity, necrosis, local invasion, and extraocular extension. Use LIN28A immunoreactivity as supportive evidence in the appropriate morphologic setting. Polarized multilayered neuroepithelial cells form anastomosing cords, bands, and ribbons. A delicate net-like or diktyomatous architecture may be present. Neuroepithelial structures are often surrounded by hyaluronic acid-rich myxoid material. Intralesional cysts are common. Rosettes may be present in poorly differentiated areas. Teratoid tumors contain heteroplastic elements, most commonly hyaline cartilage, but may also contain muscle or brain-like tissue. Malignant features include primitive basophilic sheets, increased mitotic activity, pleomorphism, necrosis, and invasion of uvea, cornea, sclera, optic nerve, or extraocular tissues. LIN28A is positive in most intraocular medulloepitheliomas and is typically negative in retinoblastoma. Vimentin and neuron-specific enolase may be positive. Cytokeratin and CK18 expression has been reported; other neural markers show variable results. Usually arises in the retina and consists of primitive small round blue cells with frequent mitoses, apoptosis, and geographic necrosis; LIN28A is generally negative. Is an extraocular medial lower-eyelid developmental lesion with lens-like epithelial islands and a PAS-positive capsule, not an intraocular ciliary body neuroepithelial tumor. Germline DICER1 alterations are associated with a small subset and may indicate DICER1-related tumor predisposition syndrome. Somatic DICER1 and KMT2D mutations have been reported. LIN28A expression is diagnostically useful; C19MC amplification characteristic of some CNS embryonal tumors is absent. Histologic criteria for benign versus malignant behavior correlate imperfectly with clinical outcome; document invasion and extraocular extension carefully. Metastatic disease is associated with extraocular extension. Pilocytic Astrocytoma and Other Optic Pathway Gliomas Optic Nerve and Pathway Tumors Childhood optic pathway glioma, usually pilocytic astrocytoma, with piloid cells, Rosenthal fibers, and MAPK pathway activation. Optic pathway gliomas involve the optic nerve, chiasm, tracts, or radiations. Most are pilocytic astrocytomas; less common patterns include pilomyxoid astrocytoma and ganglioglioma. NF1-associated tumors are typically diagnosed in early childhood; sporadic tumors occur throughout the first two decades. Involve the optic nerve, chiasm, optic tracts, or radiations; may extend to the hypothalamus. Present with visual loss, proptosis, endocrinopathy, or hypothalamic dysfunction. NF1-associated tumors are often indolent; sporadic tumors more frequently progress and require treatment. Identify an expansile glioma involving the optic nerve or optic pathway in a child or young adult. Pilocytic astrocytoma shows piloid astrocytes with bipolar processes and a variable biphasic pattern. Look for Rosenthal fibers and eosinophilic granular bodies. Pilomyxoid astrocytoma shows monomorphic piloid cells in a prominent myxoid background and is often more cellular. A distinct ganglion cell component supports ganglioglioma. Correlate with imaging and NF1 status; biopsy is generally reserved for atypical clinical or radiologic presentations. Pilocytic astrocytoma contains bipolar piloid cells with long processes. A biphasic pattern may alternate compact piloid areas with loose microcystic areas rich in oligodendrocyte-like cells. Rosenthal fibers are frequent. Eosinophilic granular bodies may be present. Myxoid change, microcysts, calcification, hyalinized vessels, and hemorrhage may occur. Pilomyxoid astrocytoma is more monomorphic and typically has a diffusely myxoid background. Ganglioglioma contains a well-defined neoplastic ganglion cell component. GFAP and OLIG2 support glial differentiation. Synaptophysin and neuronal markers highlight the ganglion cell component in ganglioglioma. IHC findings should be integrated with morphology and molecular results. Pilomyxoid astrocytoma Shows monomorphic piloid cells in a diffuse myxoid background and tends to have a higher recurrence and CSF dissemination risk than conventional pilocytic astrocytoma. Ganglioglioma Contains a distinct neoplastic ganglion cell component in addition to the glial component. MAPK pathway activation is characteristic. NF1-associated tumors commonly show biallelic NF1 inactivation. Sporadic pilocytic astrocytomas frequently harbor KIAA1549::BRAF fusion resulting from a 7q34 tandem duplication. BRAF p.V600E mutations occur in a minority of cases. Optic pathway gliomas are often diagnosed radiologically; tissue sampling may risk additional optic nerve injury. Marked nuclear atypia alone may be degenerative; brisk mitotic activity should prompt careful assessment for more aggressive behavior. Tumor Classification at a Glance Anatomic location and defining architecture are the most useful first steps in narrowing the differential diagnosis. Entity Category Typical pattern Key diagnostic point Practical Diagnostic Framework 1. Start with the anatomic compartment. Distinguish conjunctiva/epibulbar surface, eyelid/orbit, uvea/iris, retina/ciliary body, and optic pathway. 2. Define the tissue lineage. Separate choristomatous mature tissues, melanocytic proliferations, Schwannian lesions, and neuroepithelial tumors. 3. Evaluate architecture and cytology. Assess symmetry, maturation, inclusion cysts, rosettes, necrosis, mitotic activity, and invasion. 4. Use ancillary studies selectively. Apply lineage markers and molecular testing when they resolve a specific differential or identify a hereditary tumor predisposition. Search entities, criteria, markers, or differentials...
