title: Female Genital Tract Tumors
content: use client Ovarian Fibroma Ovarian Sex Cord-Stromal Tumors Bland spindle-cell fascicles in collagenous or hyalinized stroma; sex cord elements, if present, comprise less than 10%. A benign fibroblastic stromal neoplasm composed of bland spindle cells in variably collagenous stroma; cellular and mitotically active variants are recognized. Usually occurs in adults, most often after age 30; uncommon in children and adolescents. No consistent sex issue applies; the tumor occurs in the ovary. Usually unilateral; bilateral tumors should raise consideration of nevoid basal cell carcinoma syndrome (Gorlin syndrome), particularly in young patients. Presents as an ovarian mass; hormonal manifestations and Meigs syndrome (ascites with pleural effusion) are less common. Intersecting fascicles of bland spindle-to-ovoid fibroblastic cells are present. The stroma is variably collagenous or hyalinized. Any sex cord component is minor and comprises less than 10% of the tumor. Mitoses are usually absent or inconspicuous; assess cellular and mitotically active areas carefully. Exclude significant atypia, destructive invasion, and tumor cell necrosis before classifying a cellular lesion. Spindle or ovoid cells with scant cytoplasm form intersecting fascicles. Nuclei are bland and elongated. Collagenous and hyalinized stroma is variable in amount. Calcification may be present, particularly in syndromic cases. Cellular fibroma shows increased cellularity; mitotically active cellular fibroma has increased mitotic activity without the features of fibrosarcoma. Infarct-type necrosis or hemorrhage may occur with torsion and should not be mistaken for coagulative tumor cell necrosis. Rare tumors contain luteinized cells or a minor sex cord component. Tumor cells commonly express SF1 and WT1. FOXL2, CD56, and hormone receptors are often positive. Inhibin and calretinin may be positive, usually focally or weakly. Ovarian fibrosarcoma Shows significant cytologic atypia, increased mitotic activity, and often tumor cell necrosis; conventional fibroma is bland. Sclerosing stromal tumor Has pseudolobular architecture, alternating cellular and hypocellular zones, and prominent thin-walled vessels. Sex cord-stromal tumors Usually show a recognizable sex cord pattern and a more convincing sex cord immunophenotype; sex cord elements in fibroma remain under 10%. Young patients, bilateral tumors, or multiple calcified fibromas warrant clinical consideration of Gorlin syndrome (PTCH1 or SUFU) or, less commonly, other predisposition syndromes; molecular testing is not routinely required for diagnosis. Do not overcall infarct-type necrosis associated with torsion as tumor cell necrosis. In a young patient, especially with bilateral tumors, consider an underlying predisposition syndrome. Sclerosing Stromal Tumor Pseudolobules of epithelioid and spindle cells separated by hypocellular stroma, with prominent thin-walled vessels. A benign ovarian stromal neoplasm characterized by pseudolobular architecture, a prominent vascular network, and mixed epithelioid and spindle-cell populations. Typically affects adolescents and young women, but can occur in premenarchal children and rarely in infants. Occurs in the ovary; paraovarian examples are rare. Usually unilateral. May present with menstrual abnormalities, abnormal uterine bleeding, or abdominal pain; precocious puberty, virilization, and Meigs syndrome are occasional presentations. Pseudolobular architecture is present. Cellular pseudolobules contain a mixture of epithelioid and spindle cells. Pseudolobules are separated by hypocellular edematous, collagenous, or occasionally myxoid stroma. Prominent thin-walled, branching, hemangiopericytoma-like vessels are characteristic. The immunophenotype supports sex cord-stromal differentiation. Cellular nodules are arranged in a pseudolobular pattern. Thin-walled, dilated vessels are prominent within and between pseudolobules. Epithelioid cells have clear to eosinophilic, often vacuolated cytoplasm. Spindle cells are admixed with epithelioid cells. Hypocellular intervening stroma is edematous, collagenous, or occasionally myxoid. Luteinization may be prominent, particularly during pregnancy. Mitotic activity is usually low but may be increased in a small subset. Inhibin and calretinin support sex cord-stromal differentiation. SF1 and FOXL2 are commonly expressed. Cytokeratins and EMA are typically negative. Ovarian fibroma Shows uniform intersecting fascicles of bland spindle cells and collagenous stroma without the characteristic pseudolobular pattern and prominent vascularity. Juvenile granulosa cell tumor Shows irregular follicles and primitive granulosa cells rather than the characteristic pseudolobular, vascular pattern. Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor Shows Sertoli cell tubules or cords with Leydig cells; androgenic manifestations and DICER1 alterations may support this diagnosis. GLI2 rearrangements occur in more than 80% of cases; FHL2::GLI2 is a recurrent fusion. This finding can support the diagnosis in difficult cases. Prominent vascularity and vacuolated cells may mimic other ovarian stromal or perivascular tumors; interpret the complete pseudolobular architecture and sex cord markers. Juvenile Granulosa Cell Tumor of the Ovary Primitive granulosa cells in diffuse or nodular growth with irregular follicles; nuclei lack the grooves typical of adult-type granulosa cell tumor. A sex cord-stromal tumor composed of primitive granulosa cells arranged in solid and follicular patterns, usually arising in children and young women. Usually occurs in the first three decades; mean age is approximately 13 years, and about half of patients are prepubertal. Arises in the ovary and is overwhelmingly unilateral. Often presents as a pelvic mass; estrogenic effects may cause precocious pseudopuberty or menstrual disturbance. Virilization and tumor rupture with hemoperitoneum are less common presentations. Primitive granulosa cells show diffuse or nodular growth. Irregularly shaped follicles of variable size are interspersed within the tumor. Follicles may contain basophilic secretions and are lined by variable numbers of tumor-cell layers. Tumor cells have round, vesicular, non-grooved nuclei. Sex cord-stromal immunomarkers support the diagnosis. Do not require a FOXL2 mutation; the characteristic adult-type FOXL2 p.C134W mutation is not a defining feature. Growth is diffuse, nodular, or mixed. Follicles are irregular in shape and variable in size. Follicular lumina often contain basophilic secretions. Tumor cells have round vesicular nuclei without the longitudinal grooves typical of adult granulosa cell tumor. Cytoplasm is usually abundant and pale or eosinophilic. Nuclear atypia and mitotic activity are variable. The stroma may be inconspicuous, sclerotic, or myxoid. Luteinized or spindle-shaped theca cells may be present. SF1, inhibin, and calretinin commonly support sex cord-stromal differentiation. WT1, CD99, and CD56 are often positive. FOXL2 immunoreactivity may occur but does not establish an adult-type granulosa cell tumor. Adult-type granulosa cell tumor Typically shows grooved coffee-bean nuclei, microfollicular Call-Exner bodies, and a FOXL2 c.402C>G (p.C134W) mutation; juvenile tumors have round nongrooved nuclei and irregular follicles. Shows Sertoli cell tubules, cords, or sheets with Leydig cells; retiform architecture and DICER1 mutation support this entity. Has pseudolobules, prominent hemangiopericytoma-like vessels, and alternating cellular and hypocellular zones. Gynandroblastoma Contains distinct or admixed Sertoli-Leydig and juvenile granulosa cell tumor components rather than a pure juvenile granulosa cell tumor. Activating AKT1 alterations occur in approximately 60% and GNAS alterations in approximately 30% of tumors. Somatic mosaic IDH1 or IDH2 mutations may be present in tumors associated with Ollier disease or Maffucci syndrome. Somatic DICER1 mutations are rare; germline predisposition testing may be considered when clinical features suggest a syndrome. Do not diagnose adult-type granulosa cell tumor based on FOXL2 immunostaining alone; morphology and, when needed, FOXL2 mutation testing are more discriminating. Assess rupture, positive peritoneal cytology, and extraovarian spread because these affect recurrence risk. Sex Cord Tumor with Annular Tubules Rounded nests of ring-like tubules surrounding hyaline basement membrane-like material; tall cells show antipodal nuclear orientation. A sex cord-stromal tumor defined by simple or complex annular tubules surrounding basement membrane-like material; it may be associated with Peutz-Jeghers syndrome. Can occur at any age. Arises in the ovary; Peutz-Jeghers syndrome-associated lesions are often bilateral, multifocal, and small. Approximately one third of cases are associated with Peutz-Jeghers syndrome; non-syndromic tumors are usually unilateral. May be incidental; estrogenic effects can cause precocious pseudopuberty or menstrual disturbance. Tumor is composed of rounded nests of simple or complex ring-like tubules. Tubules encircle central hyaline basement membrane-like material. Tumor cells are tall, with pale cytoplasm and basally located round nuclei. Nuclei show an antipodal arrangement within the tubules. Correlate with clinical features of Peutz-Jeghers syndrome, especially in bilateral or multifocal lesions. Rounded nests contain simple or complex annular tubules. Hyaline basement membrane-like material is encircled by the tubules and may also surround them. Tall cells have pale cytoplasm and round basally located nuclei. Nuclei often show antipodal orientation. Peutz-Jeghers-associated lesions may show intratubular calcification and solid areas of indifferent sex cord cells. Non-syndromic tumors may show focal granulosa-cell or Sertoli-cell morphology. Calretinin, WT1, inhibin, and SF1 commonly support sex cord-stromal differentiation. FOXL2 and CD56 are typically positive. EMA and CD10 are typically negative. Shows irregular follicles with primitive granulosa cells rather than annular tubules encircling hyaline material. Shows Sertoli tubules or cords with Leydig cells; annular tubules and antipodal nuclei are not the defining pattern. Contains a composite Sertoli-Leydig and granulosa-cell component rather than a uniform annular-tubule pattern. Is composed predominantly of bland spindle cells in collagenous stroma and lacks annular tubules. Peutz-Jeghers syndrome-associated tumors are linked to germline STK11 alterations. SCTAT is not associated with DICER1 mutations. Syndromic and non-syndromic tumors may differ in size, laterality, and behavior; document the clinical context. Papillary Cystadenoma Ovarian and Paraovarian Epithelial/ Mesonephric-Type Tumors Benign cystic or lobulated mass with complex tubulopapillary growth of nonciliated cuboidal cells; often associated with von Hippel-Lindau syndrome. A benign papillary-cystic neoplasm, usually arising in the uterine ligaments, with features suggesting mesonephric origin and a strong association with von Hippel-Lindau syndrome. Reported predominantly in adults older than 20 years; pediatric cases are exceptional. Usually arises in the uterine ligaments rather than the ovary proper. Most patients have von Hippel-Lindau syndrome. May cause abdominal pain or be detected incidentally. A cystic or lobulated mass is present. Complex tubulopapillary architecture is formed by nonciliated cuboidal epithelial cells. Stromal hyalinization and prominent subepithelial vessels may be present. The immunophenotype supports mesonephric-type differentiation. Consider germline VHL assessment in the appropriate clinical setting. Complex tubulopapillary structures show broad-based and delicate branching papillae. Stromal hyalinization is often prominent. Focal tubular or solid growth may occur. The lining cells are nonciliated and cuboidal with scant clear-to-eosinophilic cytoplasm. Prominent subepithelial blood vessels are common. CK7 and PAX8 are commonly positive. PAX2 and CD10 support mesonephric-type differentiation. WT1 and calretinin are variably positive. ER and PR are typically negative. Müllerian papilloma Is a mucosal papillary lesion lined by bland cuboidal or columnar Müllerian epithelium, usually in the cervix or vagina; papillary cystadenoma is a cystic/lobulated ligament-associated mass with mesonephric phenotype. Mesonephric remnants and hyperplasia Consist of small bland tubules, usually in the lateral cervical wall, without the complex cystic and tubulopapillary mass-forming pattern. Allelic loss or germline mutation of VHL may support the diagnosis, particularly in patients with von Hippel-Lindau syndrome. Confirm the anatomic site: this lesion is typically ligament-associated, not a conventional ovarian epithelial cystadenoma. Sertoli-Leydig Cell Tumor Admixture of Sertoli-cell and Leydig-cell components; classify differentiation and assess for retiform or heterologous elements. A sex cord-stromal tumor composed of variable proportions of Sertoli and Leydig cells, with well-, moderately, and poorly differentiated forms and recognized retiform and heterologous patterns. Occurs across a wide age range; pediatric patients have a median age of approximately 14 years. Arises in the ovary and is usually unilateral. Often presents with pelvic pain or a mass; androgenic manifestations such as hirsutism, clitoromegaly, menstrual irregularity, or amenorrhea occur in about half of patients. Most pediatric cases are moderately or poorly differentiated and may show retiform or heterologous elements. Identify Sertoli-cell and Leydig-cell components within a sex cord-stromal tumor. Grade as well, moderately, or poorly differentiated based on Sertoli-cell tubular differentiation and cytologic features. Search for retiform architecture, particularly in younger patients. Document heterologous elements, especially mucinous epithelium or mesenchymal differentiation. Use sex cord markers to support lineage and consider DICER1 testing, particularly in pediatric cases. Well-differentiated tumors contain open or compressed Sertoli-cell tubules with minimal atypia and low mitotic activity. Leydig cells occur singly, in clusters, or in cords and may contain lipofuscin or Reinke crystals. Moderately differentiated tumors show compressed tubules, cords, or diffuse sheets of Sertoli cells with mild-to-moderate atypia. Poorly differentiated tumors consist of diffuse sheets of immature sarcomatoid Sertoli cells with conspicuous mitoses. Retiform areas form anastomosing slit-like spaces, sieve-like cysts, or papillary structures. Heterologous elements may include intestinal- or gastric-type mucinous epithelium, cartilage, skeletal muscle, neuroendocrine tissue, or hepatocyte-like cells. Sertoli cells commonly express inhibin, calretinin, SF1, WT1, and FOXL2. Vimentin and pancytokeratin may be positive in Sertoli cells. CK7 and EMA are typically negative, helping distinguish the tumor from epithelial ovarian neoplasms. Leydig cells typically express inhibin and melan-A, with little or no FOXL2 and WT1. Shows irregular follicles and primitive granulosa cells without a convincing Sertoli-Leydig cell admixture; SLCT often has androgenic manifestations and DICER1 alterations. Contains both Sertoli-Leydig and juvenile granulosa cell tumor components; identify the distinct granulosa-cell component. Shows pseudolobules and prominent hemangiopericytoma-like vessels rather than Sertoli tubules and Leydig cells. Sex cord tumor with annular tubules Shows annular tubules surrounding hyaline basement membrane-like material and antipodal nuclei. DICER1 RNase IIIb hotspot missense mutations are frequent, particularly in moderately and poorly differentiated pediatric tumors. A subset of tumors has FOXL2 c.402C>G (p.C134W); this molecular subtype is associated with older/postmenopausal patients. Pediatric patients should be considered for germline DICER1 evaluation and genetic counseling when appropriate. Do not overlook small Leydig-cell clusters in moderately differentiated tumors. Retiform architecture and heterologous elements should be specifically documented because they may affect prognosis. Composite sex cord-stromal tumor with both Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor and granulosa-cell tumor components, commonly juvenile granulosa cell type. A rare composite ovarian sex cord-stromal tumor containing Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor and granulosa-cell tumor elements. Reported age range is approximately 13–80 years, with a median in the mid-to-late twenties. May present with abdominal pain, distension, or androgenic symptoms. Most reported tumors are low stage at diagnosis. Demonstrate both Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor and granulosa-cell tumor components. Identify Sertoli-cell areas, Leydig cells, and a distinct granulosa-cell component with follicular structures. Specify whether the granulosa-cell component is juvenile or adult type. Use immunohistochemistry and molecular testing to characterize the components when morphology is ambiguous. Do not classify as gynandroblastoma when only heterologous differentiation is present in an otherwise typical Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor. Sertoli-cell areas form solid lobules, nests, or cords. Leydig cells occur in small clusters and have abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm. Granulosa-cell areas form pale nodules with small cell clusters and follicles of variable size. Juvenile granulosa-cell areas may contain follicles with pink or basophilic flocculent material. The relative proportions of the two components vary. Both components may express sex cord markers including inhibin, calretinin, and SF1. Interpret FOXL2 in conjunction with morphology and mutation status; immunoreactivity alone does not establish adult granulosa-cell differentiation. Component-directed staining may help map Sertoli, Leydig, and granulosa-cell areas. May show heterologous elements and varied architecture, but lacks a distinct juvenile or adult granulosa-cell tumor component. Lacks a convincing Sertoli-Leydig component with Sertoli tubules/cords and Leydig cells. Shows annular tubules encircling hyaline material rather than a composite Sertoli-Leydig and granulosa-cell pattern. A subset of tumors with Sertoli-Leydig and juvenile granulosa-cell components harbors DICER1 RNase IIIb hotspot mutations in both components. Most reported tumors with an adult granulosa-cell component are FOXL2 wildtype, unlike conventional adult-type granulosa cell tumors, which commonly harbor FOXL2 c.402C>G (p.C134W). Extensively sample the tumor to identify both components. Distinguish a true granulosa-cell tumor component from focal heterologous or nonspecific follicle-like differentiation. Small Cell Carcinoma of the Ovary, Hypercalcemic Type Other Ovarian Tumors Aggressive undifferentiated ovarian tumor, usually composed of monomorphic small cells with follicle-like spaces; typically SMARCA4-deficient. A highly aggressive ovarian carcinoma occurring predominantly in adolescents and young adults, characterized by small-cell morphology, frequent hypercalcemia, and loss of SWI/SNF complex proteins. Almost exclusively affects adolescents and young adults, although older patients can be affected. Arises in the ovary and is usually unilateral and large. Often presents with a pelvic or abdominal mass and hypercalcemia; serum calcium may be normal in a minority. A substantial proportion of young patients have a germline SMARCA4 pathogenic variant. Undifferentiated ovarian tumor is composed predominantly of monomorphic small cells. Follicle-like spaces containing eosinophilic or basophilic secretions are often present. A large-cell component may be present; when predominant, classify as the large-cell subtype. Demonstrate loss of SMARCA4 and/or SMARCA2 in tumor cells with retained internal controls. Correlate with serum calcium and consider germline SMARCA4 testing, particularly in young patients. Tumor cells grow in sheets, nests, cords, and trabeculae with scant intervening stroma. Small cells have round, ovoid, or occasionally spindle-shaped nuclei, fine or vesicular chromatin, small nucleoli, and scant cytoplasm. Follicle-like spaces with eosinophilic or basophilic secretions are common. Mitotic activity is brisk. Large cells may have eccentric nuclei, prominent nucleoli, and abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm with a rhabdoid appearance. Focal mucinous differentiation may occur. Rare tumors contain teratomatous or yolk sac tumor-like foci. SMARCA4 (BRG1) expression is lost in almost all tumors. SMARCA2 (BRM) is also commonly lost. WT1 is often diffusely positive. Epithelial markers, CD10, and calretinin are variably expressed. SALL4 may be positive; OCT3/4, inhibin, and TTF1 are typically negative. Malignant rhabdoid tumor May share SWI/SNF deficiency and rhabdoid morphology; integrate ovarian site, clinical setting, SMARCA4/SMARCA2 profile, and broader molecular findings. Yolk sac tumor Usually expresses SALL4 and often shows characteristic reticular/microcystic or other yolk sac patterns; SMARCA4 loss supports hypercalcemic-type small cell carcinoma. Dysgerminoma Shows large cells with clear cytoplasm and lymphocyte-rich septa and is typically positive for OCT3/4 and SALL4. Shows sex cord differentiation with irregular follicles and usually expresses inhibin and SF1; SMARCA4 loss is not typical. Poorly differentiated Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor Usually retains sex cord marker expression and may show DICER1 alterations; assess for Sertoli/Leydig differentiation. Inactivating SMARCA4 mutations occur in almost all tumors. SMARCA2 loss may accompany SMARCA4 deficiency. Germline SMARCA4 variants are clinically important because of rhabdoid tumor predisposition syndrome. A normal serum calcium level does not exclude the diagnosis. SALL4 positivity can occur and should not by itself lead to a diagnosis of germ cell tumor. Use internal non-neoplastic cells as controls when interpreting loss of SMARCA4 or SMARCA2. Mesonephric Remnants and Hyperplasia Lower Female Genital Tract Benign Epithelial Lesions Small bland tubules with dense eosinophilic intraluminal secretions, typically in the lateral cervical wall. Embryonic mesonephric duct remnants and their benign proliferations, most often encountered incidentally in the lateral wall of the uterine cervix. Usually identified in adults as an incidental microscopic finding; can occur in patients of any age. Most often located in the lateral cervical wall; may occur along the lateral urogenital tract. Usually asymptomatic; hyperplasia rarely presents as abnormal cervical cytology or cervical wall expansion. Mesonephric remnants are relatively common and may be present in up to 20% of cervixes. Small-to-medium tubules are lined by bland cuboidal cells with scant eosinophilic cytoplasm. Round-to-ovoid nuclei are bland, and mitoses are inconspicuous. Dense eosinophilic, often PAS-positive intraluminal secretions are characteristic. The typical location is the lateral wall of the cervix, vagina, or uterus. Hyperplasia shows a more extensive proliferation of otherwise similar mesonephric tubules. Tubules occur in clusters or linear arrays. The lining cells are cuboidal with scant eosinophilic cytoplasm. Nuclei are round to ovoid with fine chromatin. Dense eosinophilic PAS-positive intraluminal secretions are usually present. Lobular hyperplasia is most common; diffuse, ductal, and mixed patterns also occur. Ductal hyperplasia may show cleft-like spaces and associated peripheral tubules. CD10 often highlights the luminal/apical surface. GATA3 and PAX8 are frequently positive. Calretinin and TTF1 may be positive. ER, PR, and p16 are typically negative. Shows branching papillae lined by bland Müllerian epithelium rather than small mesonephric tubules with eosinophilic secretions. Papillary cystadenoma Forms a cystic/lobulated mass with complex tubulopapillary growth, often in the uterine ligaments and associated with VHL syndrome. Mesonephric adenocarcinoma Shows infiltrative malignant glands, cytologic atypia, and often destructive growth; benign remnants/hyperplasia lack invasion and significant atypia. No molecular test is routinely required for diagnosis; molecular testing is not clinically relevant in typical remnants or hyperplasia. In a cervical biopsy, distinguish benign mesonephric tubules from mesonephric adenocarcinoma by assessing atypia, infiltrative growth, and destructive invasion. Müllerian Papilloma Benign branching papillae with fibrovascular cores lined by bland cuboidal or columnar Müllerian epithelium. A benign papillary lesion of the cervix or vagina, most often seen in prepubertal girls and unrelated to HPV infection. Typically occurs in prepubertal girls aged 2–5 years; reported age range extends from infancy to young adulthood. Arises in the cervix and/or vagina; some vaginal lesions are intramural. Most patients present with vaginal bleeding. May appear as a friable mucosal polyp or, when intramural, a solid-cystic vaginal wall mass. Papillary architecture with branching fibrovascular cores is present. Papillae are lined by bland cuboidal or columnar epithelium. Cytologic atypia and significant mitotic activity are absent. There is no stromal atypia or cambium layer. The lesion is not associated with HPV infection. Branching papillae contain fibrovascular stromal cores. The lining epithelium is cuboidal or columnar and resembles Müllerian epithelium. Nuclei are bland with fine chromatin. Hobnail morphology and cytologic atypia are absent. Mitoses are usually absent. Squamous metaplasia may be present. Stromal atypia or a cambium layer should prompt evaluation for embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma. The lining epithelium expresses Müllerian epithelial markers such as cytokeratins. Interpret immunostains in conjunction with the benign papillary morphology; no specific immunophenotype is required for diagnosis. Condyloma acuminatum Shows squamous papillomatosis, acanthosis, and koilocytosis associated with HPV rather than bland Müllerian-type glandular epithelium. Consist of bland tubules with eosinophilic secretions, usually in the lateral cervical wall, without branching papillary fibrovascular cores. Embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma Shows malignant stromal cells and often a cambium layer; Müllerian papilloma has bland stroma without atypia. No diagnostic molecular alteration is established; molecular testing is not clinically relevant. Do not mistake the lesion for condyloma based on papillary architecture alone; identify the epithelial lineage and assess for koilocytosis. A cambium layer or stromal atypia is not a feature of Müllerian papilloma. Condyloma Acuminatum Exophytic squamous papillomatosis with acanthosis and koilocytosis, usually associated with low-risk HPV types 6 and 11. A benign HPV-associated verrucous papillary lesion of anogenital skin and mucosa, including the lower female genital tract. Occurs in children, adolescents, and adults; HPV infection is common in young women. Involves anogenital skin and mucosa, including the vulva, vagina, and cervix. Often asymptomatic and detected as one or more papillary or verrucous lesions. In children, transmission may be sexual or nonsexual; histology alone cannot establish the route of transmission. Squamous epithelium shows acanthosis and papillomatosis with papillary architecture. Koilocytic atypia is present to a variable degree. Hyperkeratosis and/or parakeratosis may be present. Low-risk HPV, particularly types 6 and 11, is commonly implicated. Block-type p16 staining should prompt evaluation for high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion rather than routine condyloma. The epithelium shows acanthosis, papillomatosis, and thickened rete ridges. Hyperkeratosis and parakeratosis are variable. Koilocytes show nuclear enlargement, hyperchromasia, irregular nuclear membranes, and perinuclear halos. Basal/parabasal-like proliferation is generally limited to the lower third of the epithelium in LSIL-pattern lesions. Mitoses are generally confined to the lower epithelial zone. Immature papillary squamous metaplasia may occur. Marked basal atypia or abnormal mitotic figures should raise concern for HSIL. p16 is generally non-block or patchy in low-grade condylomatous lesions. Block-positive p16 involving a substantial contiguous epithelial thickness supports HSIL in the appropriate morphologic context. Is lined by bland cuboidal or columnar Müllerian epithelium over fibrovascular cores; condyloma is a squamous lesion with acanthosis and koilocytosis. High-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion Shows marked basal/parabasal atypia, increased N:C ratio through a greater epithelial thickness, abnormal mitoses, and often block-positive p16. Verrucous squamous carcinoma Shows broad pushing invasive fronts and destructive stromal invasion; condyloma lacks invasion. Low-risk HPV types 6 and 11 are most commonly associated with condyloma acuminatum. HPV typing by sequencing may be useful in selected cases; HPV genome generally remains episomal in condyloma. Histology cannot reliably distinguish sexually transmitted anogenital HPV types from common cutaneous wart types, particularly in children. A block-positive p16 pattern is not typical of simple condyloma and should prompt assessment for HSIL. Peritoneal Inclusion Cyst Peritoneal Mesothelial Lesions One or more cysts lined by bland mesothelial cells, without invasion; BAP1 expression is retained. A benign mesothelial-lined cystic lesion of the peritoneum, sometimes congenital and sometimes reactive to surgery, inflammation, or hemorrhage. Occurs from the prenatal period through adolescence; there is a slight female predominance. Usually arises in the peritoneum but may involve the spleen, liver, or testis. May be incidental or present with abdominal/pelvic pain, distension, or an inguinal hernia. Some cases are associated with prior surgery, inflammation, bleeding, or developmental abnormalities. Single or multiple unilocular or multilocular cysts are lined by bland mesothelial cells. No destructive invasion into adjacent tissue is present. Septa consist of fibroconnective tissue without smooth muscle bundles. Mesothelial markers support the diagnosis. Retained BAP1 expression is typical; interpret in the context of morphology and internal controls. Cysts are lined by a single layer of flat or cuboidal mesothelial cells. Reactive or metaplastic changes, including hobnail cells, may occur. Adenomatoid areas may be present. Septa are composed of fibroconnective tissue without smooth muscle bundles. Destructive invasion is absent. Calretinin and CK5/6 support mesothelial differentiation. PAX8, ER, and PR may be variably positive. BAP1 expression is retained. Multicystic mesothelioma The term is historically used for overlapping lesions; classify according to current terminology and carefully exclude atypia, invasion, and features of malignant mesothelioma. Lymphatic malformation Shows endothelial-lined spaces and expresses endothelial markers such as ERG and CD31 rather than mesothelial markers. Cystic metastatic or primary epithelial neoplasm Shows epithelial atypia or tumor-specific epithelial markers and may demonstrate destructive invasion; peritoneal inclusion cysts are lined by bland mesothelium. CDKN2A (p16) deletion is not identified by FISH in typical peritoneal inclusion cysts; molecular testing is not routinely required. Do not use the discouraged term benign cystic mesothelioma as a synonym in the diagnostic heading. Careful sampling is required to exclude an atypical or invasive mesothelial neoplasm. Compare the dominant spindle-cell fascicles, collagen content, and absence of a defining sex cord pattern. Look for pseudolobules, alternating cellularity, and prominent thin-walled vessels. Look for primitive granulosa cells and irregular follicles; assess for estrogenic manifestations. Look for annular tubules encircling hyaline basement membrane-like material and antipodal nuclei. Look for Sertoli-cell tubules/cords and Leydig cells; assess differentiation, retiform pattern, and DICER1 status. Requires a composite Sertoli-Leydig and granulosa-cell tumor pattern. A ligament-associated cystic/lobulated mass with complex tubulopapillary growth and mesonephric phenotype. Small bland tubules with eosinophilic secretions, usually in the lateral cervical wall. Branching fibrovascular papillae lined by bland Müllerian epithelium. Squamous papillomatosis with acanthosis and koilocytosis, usually HPV-associated. All groups Pediatric Pathology Female Genital Tract Tumors Diagnostic overview of pediatric and adolescent non-germ cell tumors of the female genital tract, emphasizing sex cord-stromal differentiation, defining architecture, immunophenotype, and diagnostically relevant molecular alterations. Tumor Classification at a Glance Use the dominant architecture, cell type, anatomic site, and defining molecular findings to narrow the differential diagnosis. Entity Category Typical pattern Key diagnostic point Practical Diagnostic Framework 1. Confirm the anatomic compartment. Separate ovarian sex cord-stromal tumors from lower genital tract epithelial lesions and peritoneal mesothelial lesions. 2. Identify the dominant architecture. Look for spindle-cell fascicles, pseudolobules, follicles, annular tubules, Sertoli tubules, papillae, or squamous papillomatosis. 3. Establish lineage with a focused panel. Use sex cord markers, epithelial markers, mesonephric markers, HPV-associated findings, or mesothelial markers as indicated by morphology. 4. Apply molecular testing selectively. Consider DICER1, STK11, VHL, SMARCA4/SMARCA2, and GLI2-related alterations when they resolve classification or identify a tumor predisposition syndrome. Try a different search term or category. Diagnostic interpretation should integrate patient age, anatomic site, imaging, clinical findings, and adequately sampled tissue. Molecular testing is most useful when it resolves a morphologic differential or identifies a clinically relevant tumor predisposition syndrome.

title: Genetic Tumor Syndromes
content: use client Neurofibromatosis Type 1 (NF1) Neural tumor predisposition NF1 RAS–MAPK signaling (neurofibromin, a RAS GTPase-activating protein) Autosomal dominant; approximately 50% de novo Neurofibromas (including plexiform neurofibromas), optic pathway glioma, other gliomas, and additional neoplasms. Clinical diagnosis is based on established clinical criteria; mosaic forms occur. Neurofibromas may progress through atypical neurofibroma / ANNUBP to MPNST. Loss of p16 and H3K27me3 can support progression in the appropriate setting; molecular confirmation identifies NF1 alterations. Neurofibromatosis Type 2 (NF2) NF2 Hippo signaling / merlin-mediated contact inhibition; cytoskeletal and growth regulation Autosomal dominant; mosaicism is common in apparently sporadic cases Bilateral vestibular schwannomas, other schwannomas, meningiomas, and spinal ependymomas; ocular and other hamartomatous lesions may occur. Multiple or bilateral nerve-sheath tumors and meningiomas at a young age are important clues. Molecular testing helps distinguish NF2-related disease from LZTR1- or SMARCB1-related schwannomatosis. Tuberous Sclerosis Complex (TSC) TSC1, TSC2 TSC1–TSC2 complex; negative regulation of mTORC1 signaling Autosomal dominant; many cases are de novo Multisystem hamartoma syndrome with cortical tubers, subependymal nodules / giant cell astrocytoma, renal angiomyolipomas, cardiac rhabdomyomas, and skin lesions. Subependymal giant cell astrocytoma and characteristic multisystem findings should prompt consideration. TSC1/TSC2 loss activates mTOR signaling. Nevoid Basal Cell Carcinoma Syndrome (Gorlin Syndrome) PTCH1; less commonly SUFU Hedgehog signaling (PTCH1–SMO–SUFU axis) Autosomal dominant; de novo variants occur Predisposition to basal cell carcinomas, odontogenic keratocysts, and characteristic skeletal and intracranial findings; medulloblastoma risk is particularly associated with SUFU. Multiple or early-onset basal cell carcinomas, jaw keratocysts, and characteristic skeletal findings are clues. PTCH1 or SUFU testing supports diagnosis. Hereditary Retinoblastoma Syndrome RB1 RB1–E2F cell-cycle checkpoint (G1/S transition) Autosomal dominant cancer predisposition with a highly penetrant inherited allele; de novo germline variants occur Hereditary predisposition to unilateral or bilateral retinoblastoma, multifocal disease, and second primary malignancies. Bilateral, multifocal, or familial retinoblastoma strongly suggests a germline RB1 alteration. Tumors show biallelic RB1 inactivation. Hereditary Pheochromocytoma–Paraganglioma Syndromes Endocrine tumor predisposition SDHA, SDHB, SDHC, SDHD, SDHAF2; SDHC promoter hypermethylation in some cases Succinate dehydrogenase / mitochondrial complex II; pseudohypoxia and impaired α-ketoglutarate-dependent dioxygenase activity Gene-dependent; generally autosomal dominant. SDHD and SDHAF2 show parent-of-origin effects; SDHC epimutation is not a conventional Mendelian sequence variant Pheochromocytoma and paraganglioma, sometimes multifocal, with additional SDH-deficient tumors including GIST, renal cell carcinoma, pituitary neuroendocrine tumors, and pulmonary chondromas. Loss of SDHB immunoreactivity is a useful screen for SDH deficiency; add SDHA when appropriate. Germline testing defines the syndrome and informs family testing. WAGR Syndrome Wilms tumor predisposition Contiguous deletion at 11p13 involving WT1 and PAX6 (sometimes extending to BDNF in WAGRO) WT1-related renal / genitourinary development and nephrogenesis; PAX6-related ocular development Usually de novo contiguous-gene deletion; not typically inherited as a single-gene Mendelian trait Wilms tumor predisposition with aniridia, genitourinary anomalies, and developmental differences; WAGRO includes obesity related to BDNF deletion. Aniridia should prompt evaluation for a 11p13 deletion including both PAX6 and WT1. Wilms tumors may be bilateral and associated with intralobar nephrogenic rests. Beckwith–Wiedemann Spectrum 11p15.5 imprinting region: CDKN1C, IGF2, H19, KCNQ1OT1; mechanisms include paternal uniparental disomy and imprinting defects Genomic imprinting / IGF2 growth signaling and CDKN1C cell-cycle restraint Usually sporadic and epigenetic; a subset is due to inherited or de novo CDKN1C variants (autosomal dominant with parent-of-origin effects) Overgrowth spectrum with macroglossia, omphalocele, lateralized overgrowth, hyperinsulinism, and predisposition to Wilms tumor and hepatoblastoma. Use the clinical scoring system and molecular testing of 11p15.5. Mosaicism may require testing tissues other than blood; perilobar nephrogenic rests are a relevant renal finding. Familial Adenomatous Polyposis (FAP) Gastrointestinal tumor predisposition APC WNT/β-catenin signaling (APC destruction complex) Numerous colorectal adenomas with risk of colorectal carcinoma; gastric and duodenal polyps, desmoid tumors, and other extracolonic manifestations may occur. Attenuated FAP is a recognized phenotype. Adenomatous polyposis, especially in adolescence, should prompt APC evaluation. Somatic second-hit APC inactivation drives adenoma formation. Lynch Syndrome MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2; EPCAM deletions can silence MSH2 DNA mismatch repair (MMR) Autosomal dominant; cancer risk reflects a heterozygous germline pathogenic variant with somatic second-hit inactivation Predisposition to colorectal and endometrial carcinoma and other cancers, often at younger ages and with a characteristic tumor spectrum. Tumor MMR immunohistochemistry and/or microsatellite instability testing guide evaluation; germline testing establishes Lynch syndrome. Distinguish from constitutional mismatch repair deficiency, which is biallelic. Xeroderma Pigmentosum (XP) Other cancer predisposition syndromes XPA, ERCC3 (XPB), XPC, ERCC2 (XPD), DDB2 (XPE), ERCC4 (XPF), ERCC5 (XPG); POLH (XPV) Nucleotide excision repair (XPA–XPG); translesion DNA synthesis (POLH / XPV) Autosomal recessive Marked UV sensitivity, early freckling, and very high risk of multiple cutaneous and ocular malignancies; internal tumors and neurologic abnormalities occur in subsets. Clinical findings plus molecular testing identify the complementation group. XPV has intact nucleotide excision repair but defective translesion polymerase η. Rothmund–Thomson Syndrome (RTS) RECQL4 (RTS type 2); ANAPC1 (a subset of RTS type 1) DNA replication and repair / RECQ helicase; APC/C-mediated cell-cycle regulation Poikiloderma beginning in infancy, short stature, sparse hair, and skeletal abnormalities; RTS type 2 carries an increased osteosarcoma risk. Poikiloderma is the hallmark. Biallelic RECQL4 variants establish RTS type 2; a negative RECQL4 result does not exclude clinically convincing RTS type 1. Li–Fraumeni Syndrome (LFS) TP53 p53 DNA-damage response: cell-cycle arrest, apoptosis, and senescence Autosomal dominant; de novo germline variants occur Early-onset, broad-spectrum cancer predisposition including sarcomas, breast cancer, brain tumors, and adrenocortical carcinoma. A pathogenic germline TP53 alteration is essential. Childhood tumors in the LFS spectrum should raise suspicion; radiation exposure may increase the risk of secondary malignancies. DICER1 Syndrome DICER1 MicroRNA biogenesis / RNA interference (RNase III processing) Autosomal dominant with reduced/incomplete penetrance; de novo variants and postzygotic mosaicism occur Predisposition to pleuropulmonary blastoma, cystic nephroma, thyroid neoplasia, ovarian Sertoli–Leydig cell tumor, cervical embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma, and selected CNS tumors. Most syndrome-associated tumors carry a germline loss-of-function variant plus a somatic RNase IIIb hotspot mutation. Mosaic RNase IIIb variants may produce an earlier, more extensive phenotype. BAP1 Tumor Predisposition Syndrome BAP1 Ubiquitin-mediated protein regulation / deubiquitination; chromatin regulation and DNA-damage response Autosomal dominant; most cases are inherited, with de novo variants reported Predisposition to uveal and cutaneous melanoma, mesothelioma, renal cell carcinoma, and other tumors; BAP1-inactivated melanocytic tumors may be an early clue. Loss of nuclear BAP1 by immunohistochemistry identifies BAP1-deficient tumors but does not alone prove a germline syndrome; confirm with germline testing. Constitutional Mismatch Repair Deficiency (CMMRD) Biallelic pathogenic variants in MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, or PMS2 Autosomal recessive; parents are typically heterozygous carriers Childhood-onset brain tumors, hematologic malignancies, gastrointestinal polyposis and cancers, often with café-au-lait-like skin macules. Loss of the relevant MMR protein in both tumor and normal tissues is a key clue. Tumors may be ultrahypermutated despite limited MSI; confirm biallelic germline variants or appropriate functional criteria. Rhabdoid Tumor Predisposition Syndrome (RTPS) SMARCB1 (RTPS1); SMARCA4 (RTPS2) SWI/SNF (BAF) chromatin-remodeling complex Autosomal dominant cancer predisposition; de novo and postzygotic mosaic variants occur Predisposition to malignant rhabdoid tumors, including atypical teratoid/rhabdoid tumor, often at very young ages; synchronous or metachronous tumors may occur. Loss of INI1 (SMARCB1) or BRG1 (SMARCA4) supports the corresponding tumor pathway defect; germline testing is required to establish predisposition syndrome. title: Germ Cell Tumors
content: use client Intratubular Germ Cell Neoplasia (GCNIS) Noninvasive Germ Cell Neoplasia Atypical OCT4-positive germ cells arranged along the spermatogonial niche of seminiferous tubules. The common precursor of postpubertal type II testicular germ cell tumors. Postpubertal males; may be asymptomatic or present with infertility or mild testicular discomfort. Occurs in the testis; risk is increased with cryptorchidism, gonadal dysgenesis, and a contralateral testicular germ cell tumor. Atypical gonocytes line the basal spermatogonial niche in a characteristic string-of-beads pattern. Cells have abundant clear cytoplasm and enlarged, angulated nuclei. Confirm with an appropriate germ cell immunohistochemical panel; morphology alone is insufficient. Distinguish from delayed-maturing gonocytes in prepubertal testes. Large atypical germ cells lie between Sertoli cells along the tubular basement membrane. Affected tubules may show pagetoid spread and impaired spermatogenesis. GCNIS may extend into the rete testis along the epithelial-basement membrane interface. Tumor cells express OCT4, PLAP, SOX17, and KIT. Additional supportive markers include podoplanin, NANOG, AP-2γ, and LIN28A. Gonadoblastoma Contains both neoplastic germ cells and sex cord cells with hyaline basement membrane deposits, usually in a dysgenetic gonad. Intratubular seminoma Shows luminal expansion by cohesive seminoma cells rather than a single basal layer of GCNIS cells. Gain or overrepresentation of chromosome 12p supports progression to invasive type II germ cell tumor; it is not required to diagnose GCNIS. Germ cells and immature sex cord cells form nests or cords around hyaline basement membrane material. An in situ germ cell neoplasm arising predominantly in dysgenetic gonads and capable of progression to invasive germ cell tumors. Usually presents in neonates or children with a disorder of sex development; occasional delayed presentation occurs in young adults. Affects gonads; patients may have ambiguous genitalia, primary amenorrhea, an abdominal mass, or an intra-abdominal gonad. Often associated with Y-chromosome material, including in phenotypic females. Identify nests or cords containing neoplastic germ cells admixed with small sex cord cells. Hyaline basement membrane deposits, often calcified, are a key architectural feature. Establish germ cell and sex cord differentiation with immunohistochemistry. Evaluate the clinical and cytogenetic context for a disorder of sex development. Round nests and cords contain large pale germ cells and smaller Sertoli/granulosa-like cells. Sex cord cells may form peripheral palisades or rosettes around hyaline deposits. Hyaline material may show laminated calcification or coalesce into mulberry-like structures. Germ cells express OCT4, PLAP, KIT, and podoplanin. Sex cord cells typically express FOXL2 and inhibin; SOX9 may be weak and calretinin/SF1 may be positive. Leydig-like cells, when present, express inhibin and calretinin. Lacks the characteristic sex cord cell component and hyaline basement membrane deposits. Sertoli cell nodule colonized by GCNIS Sertoli cells are strongly SOX9-positive and FOXL2-negative, unlike the sex cord component of gonadoblastoma. FISH or cytogenetic testing for Y-chromosome material may support the diagnosis in phenotypic females. Germinoma / Dysgerminoma / Seminoma Germinoma-Family Tumors Large uniform germ cells with clear cytoplasm, prominent nucleoli, and a lymphocyte-rich septal pattern. Malignant primordial germ cell tumors with shared morphology and phenotype; termed seminoma in testis, dysgerminoma in ovary, and germinoma at extragonadal sites. Germinoma most often affects adolescents, particularly boys, and arises in the pineal or suprasellar region; basal ganglia/thalamus are additional sites. Seminoma typically affects postpubertal men in the fourth decade and presents as a testicular mass. Dysgerminoma predominantly affects adolescents and young women and presents as a rapidly enlarging ovarian mass. Mediastinal tumors usually arise in the anterior mediastinum and may cause chest pain, cough, dyspnea, or superior vena cava syndrome. Identify large, relatively uniform tumor cells with clear to pale cytoplasm and prominent nucleoli. Tumor cells are arranged in sheets or nests separated by fibrous septa containing lymphocytes. Use immunohistochemistry to confirm germinoma-family differentiation and exclude nonseminomatous components. Serum AFP elevation argues against a pure germinoma-family tumor; mild β-hCG elevation may occur with syncytiotrophoblast cells. Large polygonal cells have distinct borders, clear or glycogen-rich cytoplasm, and central nuclei. Fibrous septa with lymphocytes divide the tumor into lobules. Syncytiotrophoblast cells may be scattered and can produce β-hCG. Tumor cells are typically positive for OCT4, SALL4, KIT, D2-40, and SOX17. SOX2 is generally negative in conventional seminoma/germinoma-family cells. Syncytiotrophoblast cells are β-hCG-positive. Embryonal Carcinoma Shows more pleomorphism, epithelial/glandular or papillary patterns, and expression of SOX2 and broad-spectrum cytokeratins. Yolk Sac Tumor Shows reticular, microcystic, glandular, or other yolk sac patterns and is typically AFP/glypican-3 positive. Contains sex cord cells and hyaline basement membrane deposits in addition to germ cells. Malignant Mixed Germ Cell Tumors Contain a second malignant or teratomatous component; thorough sampling and serum markers are important. Chromosome 12p gain or i(12p) supports a postpubertal gonadal germ cell tumor when the site or morphology is equivocal. KIT/RAS pathway alterations may occur; molecular testing is not usually required for routine diagnosis. Mature Cystic Teratoma Teratomas Mature somatic tissues from at least two germ layers without immature or malignant germ cell components. A benign teratoma composed exclusively of mature tissues; in the testis, this pattern is classified as prepubertal-type teratoma when appropriate. Most commonly arises in the ovary in children and young adults; testicular examples occur predominantly in prepubertal boys. Usually presents as an adnexal or testicular mass; ovarian lesions may cause pain or torsion. Demonstrate mature tissues representing at least two germ layers. Exclude immature neuroepithelial tissue and other malignant germ cell tumor components. In testicular tumors, assess for GCNIS, dysgenetic parenchymal changes, scar, and chromosome 12p abnormalities to distinguish prepubertal- from postpubertal-type teratoma. Mature squamous epithelium, skin appendages, cartilage, bone, respiratory or gastrointestinal epithelium, and other mature tissues may be present. Ovarian lesions are commonly cystic and lined by keratinizing squamous epithelium. Immunohistochemistry is directed by any unusual or suspicious component rather than by a single teratoma-specific profile. Immature Teratoma (Female Gonadal) Contains immature neuroepithelial tissue, often as primitive neuroectodermal tubules or rosettes. Postpubertal-Type Teratoma Often associated with GCNIS, scarred/dysgenetic testicular parenchyma, and chromosome 12p gain; may show atypia or somatic-type malignancy. Extragonadal Teratoma Classification depends on site and absence of a gonadal primary; most pediatric extragonadal lesions are prepubertal-type. Fetus in Fetu Shows organized axial development and metameric segmentation/vertebral structures rather than disorganized mature tissues. Monodermal Teratomas (Female Gonadal) Are composed predominantly or exclusively of a specialized single tissue type, such as thyroid or neuroendocrine tissue. Prepubertal-Type Testicular Teratoma Testicular teratoma in a child without GCNIS, dysgenetic parenchymal changes, or chromosome 12p amplification. Ovarian mature cystic teratomas are generally diploid and lack the chromosome 12p abnormalities characteristic of postpubertal-type testicular teratoma. Teratoma arising outside the gonads, typically along the midline, without evidence of a gonadal primary. An extragonadal teratoma, particularly common in infants and young children, arising along the embryonic midline migration pathway of primordial germ cells. Predominantly affects neonates, infants, and young children; sacrococcygeal and mediastinal sites are characteristic. May present as a palpable mass, respiratory compromise, or an antenatally detected lesion. Confirm a teratoma composed of somatic tissues and document mature versus immature elements. Exclude a gonadal primary by clinical examination and imaging. Interpret histology in the context of age and site; malignant germ cell components must be actively sought. Mature and/or immature derivatives of multiple germ layers are present. Immature neuroepithelial tissue may be present, particularly in immature lesions. Sampling should target solid, hemorrhagic, or necrotic areas to exclude yolk sac tumor or other malignant components. Use component-directed markers when a suspicious focus raises concern for yolk sac tumor, embryonal carcinoma, or another malignant element. Usually gonadal, particularly ovarian; extragonadal classification requires exclusion of a gonadal primary. Is defined by immature neuroectodermal tissue and occurs in the ovary. Shows axialization and metameric segmentation with organized organ development. Contain one or more malignant germ cell components in addition to teratoma. Ovarian teratoma composed predominantly or exclusively of a specialized tissue type, including thyroid or neuroendocrine tissue. Testicular teratoma associated with GCNIS and chromosome 12p gain; mature morphology does not imply benign behavior. No single molecular alteration is required for diagnosis; chromosome 12p assessment may help when a postpubertal-type germ cell tumor is in the differential. A group including struma ovarii, ovarian carcinoid, neuroectodermal-type tumors, and monodermal cystic teratoma. Occurs in the ovary, generally in adolescents and adults; clinical presentation depends on the dominant tissue component. Struma ovarii may cause symptoms of a pelvic mass and, rarely, thyroid hormone excess; carcinoid may cause hormone-related symptoms. Identify the dominant specialized tissue and determine whether it is benign or shows malignant features. Struma ovarii consists of thyroid tissue alone or as the predominant component of a dermoid cyst. Ovarian carcinoid shows characteristic neuroendocrine architecture and cytology. Neuroectodermal-type tumors require distinction from a primary ovarian or metastatic CNS-type neoplasm. Struma ovarii is composed of mature thyroid follicles, sometimes with colloid. Carcinoid shows insular, trabecular, strumal, or mucinous/goblet cell patterns. Neuroectodermal-type components may resemble primitive or differentiated CNS tumors. Monodermal cystic teratoma may be lined by benign keratinizing squamous epithelium or neuroectodermal tissue. Thyroid follicles express thyroglobulin, TTF-1, and PAX8. Carcinoid expresses synaptophysin, chromogranin, and INSM1. Use component-specific markers to distinguish primary ovarian neuroectodermal tumors from other neoplasms. Contains a broader mixture of mature tissues from multiple germ layers rather than a dominant specialized monodermal component. Contains immature neuroepithelial tissue, not simply a mature specialized monodermal component. Shows malignant yolk sac patterns and AFP/glypican-3 expression rather than mature thyroid or neuroendocrine tissue. No recurrent molecular alteration is required for routine classification; test a somatic-type malignant component according to its phenotype. Ovarian teratoma containing immature neuroectodermal tissue, with grading based on the amount of immature neuroepithelium. A malignant-potential ovarian teratoma containing variable amounts of immature and mature tissue. Predominantly affects children, adolescents, and young women. Arises in the ovary and often presents as a rapidly enlarging pelvic or abdominal mass. Identify immature neuroectodermal tissue, typically primitive neuroepithelial tubules or rosettes. Grade according to the quantity of immature neuroepithelium in the sampled tumor. Extensively sample solid areas to exclude yolk sac tumor or other malignant germ cell components. Immature neuroepithelium forms primitive tubules, rosettes, or cellular ribbons. Mature tissues from ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm are variably admixed. Immature mesenchymal and other fetal-type tissues may accompany the neuroepithelium. Neuroepithelial components express neural markers such as synaptophysin and other markers according to differentiation. AFP and glypican-3 positivity should prompt evaluation for an associated yolk sac tumor component. Contains mature tissues only and lacks immature neuroepithelial elements. Contain predominantly mature specialized tissue, such as thyroid or carcinoid, rather than immature neuroepithelium. Shows primitive malignant epithelial cells with OCT4, SOX2, and cytokeratin expression rather than differentiated immature neuroepithelium. Shows yolk sac differentiation, often with reticular/microcystic architecture and AFP/glypican-3 expression. In ovarian immature teratoma, chromosome 12p gain is not the defining feature; assess for molecular evidence of a postpubertal-type germ cell tumor when morphology/site warrants. A distinct testicular teratoma type that is usually benign and biologically unrelated to GCNIS-derived postpubertal-type tumors. Occurs predominantly in prepubertal boys, usually as a painless testicular mass. Typically lacks the clinical and pathologic setting of GCNIS. Identify mature and/or immature teratomatous tissues. No associated GCNIS or characteristic dysgenetic tubular changes should be present. No scar or other evidence of a regressed postpubertal-type germ cell tumor should be identified. Absence of chromosome 12p amplification supports prepubertal-type classification. Teratomatous tissues may be mature or show limited immaturity. Adjacent testicular parenchyma lacks GCNIS and the dysgenetic tubular pattern associated with postpubertal-type tumors. No GCNIS immunophenotype should be identified in adjacent seminiferous tubules. Use OCT4 and PLAP when GCNIS is suspected. Associated with GCNIS, dysgenetic/scarred parenchyma, and chromosome 12p gain; biologically malignant despite mature morphology. Overlaps morphologically; age, testicular background, and molecular findings establish the testicular subtype. Arises outside the gonad and requires exclusion of a gonadal primary. Lacks chromosome 12p amplification, which supports distinction from postpubertal-type teratoma. A GCNIS-derived testicular germ cell tumor composed of somatic-type tissues and classified as a malignant germ cell tumor. Occurs in postpubertal and adult men, often as a testicular mass. May occur as a component of a mixed germ cell tumor and may persist after chemotherapy. Identify teratoma in a postpubertal testis and assess adjacent parenchyma for GCNIS. Look for dysgenetic tubules, scar, or other evidence of a GCNIS-derived tumor. Chromosome 12p gain or i(12p) supports postpubertal-type classification. Search extensively for somatic-type malignancy and other germ cell tumor components. Mature somatic tissues may resemble those in a benign teratoma. Immature tissues and somatic-type malignancies may occur. Adjacent parenchyma may show GCNIS, tubular dysgenesis, atrophy, or scarring. OCT4 and PLAP highlight associated GCNIS when present. IHC is directed at any somatic-type malignant component to classify its lineage. Lacks GCNIS, dysgenetic parenchymal changes, scar, and chromosome 12p amplification. Mature morphology overlaps, but postpubertal-type testicular teratoma is a malignant GCNIS-derived tumor. Somatic-Type Malignancy Arising in Teratoma Represents a specific malignant somatic component within the teratoma; classify and report the component separately. Gain of chromosome 12p or i(12p) is a key molecular feature supporting postpubertal-type teratoma. Nonseminomatous Germ Cell Tumors Primitive malignant epithelial cells with marked atypia, frequent mitoses, and OCT4/SOX2 expression. A highly malignant, pluripotent germ cell tumor and a defining component of many mixed postpubertal germ cell tumors. Usually affects postpubertal adolescent and adult men; most commonly arises in the testis. Often presents as a testicular mass and may be associated with elevated AFP or β-hCG when mixed with other components. Identify primitive malignant epithelial cells in solid, glandular, papillary, or other patterns. Tumor cells show marked nuclear atypia, prominent nucleoli, and brisk mitotic activity. Confirm with OCT4, SOX2, SALL4, and cytokeratin expression. Exclude seminoma and yolk sac tumor by morphology and immunophenotype. Tumor cells form solid sheets, glands, papillae, or alveolar structures. Cells have scant to moderate cytoplasm, overlapping nuclei, and prominent nucleoli. Geographic necrosis and brisk mitotic activity are common. Tumor cells express OCT4, SOX2, SALL4, and broad-spectrum cytokeratins. CD30 is commonly positive, often with membranous/Golgi staining. SOX17 is generally negative, helping distinguish from seminoma. Has uniform clear cells, lymphocyte-rich septa, and SOX17 expression; SOX2 and CD30 are typically negative. Shows yolk sac patterns and AFP/glypican-3 expression; OCT4 is negative. Choriocarcinoma (Non-gestational) Contains cytotrophoblast and syncytiotrophoblast with strong β-hCG expression and extensive hemorrhage. Contains multiple distinct components; embryonal carcinoma may be one component rather than the entire tumor. Chromosome 12p gain or i(12p) supports a postpubertal-type germ cell tumor. KIT/RAS pathway alterations may occur but are not specific to embryonal carcinoma. Variable yolk sac-like patterns with AFP and glypican-3 expression; Schiller-Duval bodies may be present. A malignant germ cell tumor recapitulating extraembryonic yolk sac, allantoic, and mesenchymal structures. Common in infants and young children; also occurs in postpubertal patients, particularly as a component of mixed testicular germ cell tumors. Occurs in gonads and extragonadal midline sites, including sacrococcygeal, mediastinal, and intracranial locations. Often presents as a rapidly growing mass with elevated serum AFP. Identify epithelioid tumor cells in one or more characteristic patterns, often reticular/microcystic, glandular, papillary, or solid. Schiller-Duval bodies, hyaline globules, or hepatoid differentiation are supportive but not required. AFP and glypican-3 expression support the diagnosis; interpret serum AFP in the context of age. Reticular/microcystic architecture is common; other patterns include endodermal sinus-like, papillary, glandular, solid, and hepatoid. Schiller-Duval bodies consist of a central vessel surrounded by tumor cells within a space. Eosinophilic hyaline globules may be present and can be PAS-positive. Tumor cells express SALL4, glypican-3, AFP, and cytokeratins. LIN28A is commonly positive. OCT4 and SOX2 are typically negative. Shows OCT4, SOX2, CD30, and cytokeratin expression; AFP and glypican-3 are usually negative. Shows OCT4, SOX17, KIT, and D2-40; AFP is not elevated in a pure tumor. Shows biphasic trophoblastic differentiation with syncytiotrophoblasts and strong β-hCG. May contain a yolk sac tumor component admixed with other malignant or teratomatous elements. Chromosome 12p gain supports a postpubertal-type germ cell tumor in the appropriate setting; it is not specific to yolk sac differentiation. Developmental and Mixed Lesions Highly organized fetiform structure with axialization and metameric segmentation/vertebral organization. A rare developmental anomaly in which a parasitic twin is enclosed within the body of its co-twin; it is distinguished from teratoma by organized body plan. Usually detected prenatally or in neonates and young children as an intra-abdominal mass. Most often retroperitoneal/intra-abdominal; rare sites include gonad, sacrum, oropharynx, orbit, and thorax. Demonstrate advanced organoid development with axialization. Identify metameric segmentation, typically with vertebral organization. Correlate with imaging and gross examination for recognizable fetal anatomy and a surrounding sac. Shows organized, mature organs and tissues, often including bowel and multiple organ systems. Tissue organization is more advanced and anatomically coordinated than in a conventional teratoma. No specific immunophenotype is diagnostic; ancillary studies are generally not required. Contains mature tissues in a disorganized arrangement without axialization or vertebral segmentation. Shows differentiated tissues but lacks the organized fetal body plan and metameric segmentation. Genotypic identity between the host and the fetiform mass supports monozygotic twin origin; this is not routinely required. Biphasic trophoblastic tumor with cytotrophoblast/intermediate trophoblast and syncytiotrophoblast in a hemorrhagic background. A highly aggressive malignant germ cell tumor showing extraembryonic chorionic differentiation. Rare in children except in patients with disorders of sex development; occurs in gonads, mediastinum, and CNS. Often presents with symptoms of hematogenous metastases, hemorrhage, or a rapidly enlarging mass. Serum β-hCG is markedly elevated; gynecomastia or thyrotoxicosis may occur. Identify both mononuclear trophoblastic cells and multinucleated syncytiotrophoblasts. Extensive hemorrhage and necrosis are characteristic. Confirm trophoblastic differentiation with β-hCG; exclude other germ cell components and gestational origin as clinically appropriate. Cytotrophoblasts and intermediate trophoblasts form aggregates capped by syncytiotrophoblasts. Syncytiotrophoblasts are multinucleated with dense eosinophilic cytoplasm. Vascular invasion, hemorrhage, and necrosis are common. β-hCG highlights syncytiotrophoblasts; hPL may be positive. Cytokeratin is positive; GATA3 and p63 may highlight mononuclear trophoblasts. AFP, OCT4, KIT, and D2-40 are typically negative. Shows yolk sac architecture and AFP/glypican-3 expression rather than a biphasic trophoblastic pattern. Shows primitive epithelial tumor cells with OCT4, SOX2, CD30, and cytokeratin; lacks the characteristic syncytiotrophoblast-rich pattern. May contain scattered syncytiotrophoblasts but lacks a true biphasic choriocarcinoma pattern and extensive hemorrhagic trophoblastic tumor. May contain a choriocarcinoma component alongside other germ cell elements; identify and quantify all components. Chromosome 12p gain or i(12p) supports germ cell tumor origin and helps distinguish from non-germ cell poorly differentiated malignancies. Two or more distinct germ cell tumor components; classify as nonseminomatous even when a seminoma-like component is present. A malignant germ cell tumor composed of multiple histologic elements, often including embryonal carcinoma, yolk sac tumor, teratoma, seminoma, or choriocarcinoma. Occurs in gonads, mediastinum, and CNS; prepubertal cases are rare. Most common in postpubertal males in gonadal sites; CNS mixed tumors often affect children and adolescents and show male predominance. Serum AFP and/or β-hCG may be elevated depending on the components. Identify and document every distinct histologic component. Estimate the percentage of each component, particularly in testicular tumors. Classify any tumor containing a nonseminomatous component as a nonseminomatous germ cell tumor. Extensively sample interfaces and hemorrhagic/necrotic areas to avoid missing a small yolk sac or choriocarcinoma component. Each component recapitulates the morphology of its corresponding pure tumor. Embryonal carcinoma and yolk sac tumor are frequently closely admixed. Distinguish true choriocarcinoma from scattered syncytiotrophoblasts in seminoma. Use component-directed panels: OCT4/SOX2/CD30 for embryonal carcinoma; AFP/glypican-3 for yolk sac tumor; β-hCG for choriocarcinoma; OCT4/SOX17/KIT for seminoma. Immunohistochemistry can help map and quantify components when morphology is ambiguous. A pure germinoma-family tumor lacks a second malignant or teratomatous component; any nonseminomatous component changes classification. A pure embryonal carcinoma lacks the additional distinct components required for a mixed tumor. A pure yolk sac tumor lacks other germ cell tumor components; search carefully for an associated embryonal carcinoma or teratoma. A pure choriocarcinoma lacks additional germ cell components; identify all components in mixed lesions. A pure teratoma is composed of somatic-type tissues; a mixed tumor contains additional malignant germ cell components. Chromosome 12p gain or i(12p) supports postpubertal-type germ cell tumor origin. For CNS tumors, molecular findings should be interpreted with the histologic component and site; component-specific testing may be useful in selected cases. Tumor Classification at a Glance Classification depends on developmental lineage, anatomic setting, maturation, and recognition of malignant components. Entity Category Typical pattern Key diagnostic point Practical Diagnostic Framework 1. Establish the developmental and anatomic context. Consider patient age, gonadal versus midline extragonadal site, and whether a precursor lesion is present. 2. Assess the dominant morphologic pattern. Separate germinoma-family tumors, teratomas, and nonseminomatous components. 3. Identify each tumor component. In mixed tumors, document the percentage and distribution of every component. 4. Use a focused immunohistochemical and molecular panel. Use OCT4, SALL4, SOX17/SOX2, AFP, glypican-3, β-hCG, and cytokeratins according to morphology; assess chromosome 12p when classification requires it. Children, with a peak before age 5 years for juvenile recurrent respiratory papillomatosis; no pediatric sex predilection. Oral cavity (especially palate and tongue) or larynx; multifocal laryngeal disease may extend along the respiratory tract. Painless papillary oral nodule; laryngeal disease causes hoarseness, stridor, cough, or dysphagia. Exophytic, multilayered benign squamous epithelial proliferation. Arborizing fibrovascular cores support the papillary fronds. No significant epithelial dysplasia in most cases; report dysplasia if present. Papillary fronds are covered by nonkeratinizing to variably keratinized squamous epithelium. Koilocytosis may be present. Trauma or inflammation may increase mitotic activity. Low-risk HPV6/11 are associated with most recurrent respiratory papillomatosis cases; genotyping is not required for diagnosis. Verruca vulgaris Often shows prominent hyperkeratosis, papillomatosis, and characteristic viral cytopathic changes; clinical context and site help. Condyloma acuminatum Usually has broader, blunter papillae and may show HPV-related koilocytosis; correlate with clinical setting. Squamous cell carcinoma Shows destructive invasion, cytologic atypia, and often atypical mitoses rather than bland fibrovascular papillae. In contrast, White Sponge Nevus is characterized by bilateral, persistent white corrugated plaques with eosinophilic perinuclear condensation in spinous cells. Bilateral, persistent white corrugated plaques with eosinophilic perinuclear condensation in spinous cells. Usually begins in infancy or early childhood and becomes more conspicuous during adolescence; equal sex distribution. Most often bilateral buccal mucosa; may involve ventral tongue, labial mucosa, palate, or other mucosal sites. Asymptomatic, non-wipeable white spongy plaques; may become tender after trauma. Bright eosinophilic perinuclear condensation in spinous epithelial cells. Acanthosis and shaggy hyperparakeratosis with spinous-layer vacuolation support the diagnosis. Intact basement membrane and minimal inflammation. Acanthotic epithelium shows vacuolated spinous cells. Prominent eosinophilic perinuclear keratin condensation is characteristic. Autosomal dominant pathogenic variants in KRT4 or KRT13 support the diagnosis in selected cases. In contrast, Squamous Papilloma and Papillomatosis is characterized by exophytic papillary squamous proliferation with fibrovascular cores; recurrent respiratory disease is usually hpv6/11-associated. Present at birth or within the first weeks of life; marked female predominance (female-to-male ratio approximately 7–10:1). Usually anterior maxillary alveolar ridge, less often mandibular ridge; rarely tongue or multifocal. Polypoid or pedunculated mucosa-colored gingival mass; may interfere with feeding or respiration. Neonatal presentation with a gingival/alveolar ridge mass. Sheets and nests of bland polygonal cells with abundant eosinophilic granular cytoplasm. Tumor cells are negative for S100 and SOX10. Granular cells have eccentric small uniform nuclei and distinct cell borders. Prominent capillary network may traverse the tumor. Overlying epithelium is attenuated and lacks pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia. Tumor cells are typically negative for S100 and SOX10 and positive for CD68 and vimentin. Granular cell tumor Usually strongly positive for S100 and SOX10 and often shows pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia. Congenital epulis-like lesions Clinical timing and gingival location plus the characteristic S100-negative granular-cell phenotype support congenital granular cell epulis. Central Giant Cell Granuloma Jaw and Fibro-Osseous Lesions Jaw-centered osteoclast-like giant-cell lesion in hemorrhagic vascular stroma, without cyst formation or systemic cause. Usually occurs in the first two decades; slight female predominance. Anterior maxilla or mandible, commonly anterior to the mandibular first molars. Often incidental radiolucency; may cause jaw expansion, pain, paresthesia, tooth displacement, or root resorption. Jaw-centered lesion composed of numerous osteoclast-like multinucleated giant cells in hemorrhagic vascular stroma with bland spindle cells. No cyst formation. Exclude hyperparathyroidism and consider syndromic/multifocal disease. Giant cells are unevenly distributed, often in loose clusters. Background is hemorrhagic and vascular with bland mononuclear spindle cells. Osteoid or woven bone may be present; scattered conventional mitoses may occur. No specific immunophenotype is required for diagnosis. Brown tumor of hyperparathyroidism Clinical and biochemical evidence of hyperparathyroidism; evaluate calcium, phosphate, and PTH. Aneurysmal bone cyst Shows blood-filled cystic spaces with septa; central giant cell granuloma is solid and lacks cystic spaces. Peripheral giant cell granuloma Arises in gingival/peripheral soft tissue rather than centrally within jaw bone. Cherubism Typically bilateral/multifocal jaw lesions with characteristic clinical distribution and SH3BP2-associated syndrome. Giant cell tumor of bone Usually epiphyseal/metaphyseal long-bone lesion; distinct clinical and molecular context. Ossifying Fibroma Central Giant Cell Granuloma is distinguished by jaw-centered osteoclast-like giant-cell lesion in hemorrhagic vascular stroma, without cyst formation or systemic cause. In contrast, Ossifying Fibroma is characterized by well-demarcated fibro-osseous neoplasm with a cellular spindle-cell stroma and variable bone/cementum-like mineralization. Reported somatic alterations include TRPV4, KRAS, and FGFR1; PTPN11 alterations may occur in Noonan-like multiple giant cell lesion syndrome. Molecular testing is not routinely required. Usually adolescents and young adults; pediatric cases occur in the second decade. Most often posterior mandible; maxillary lesions also occur. Slow-growing jaw swelling, expansion, facial asymmetry, tooth displacement, or incidental radiographic lesion. Odontogenic epithelial islands, sheets, or anastomosing strands with peripheral ameloblast-like cells. Peripheral palisading with reverse nuclear polarity and subnuclear vacuolation. Correlate with imaging; unicystic ameloblastoma requires a single cystic lesion without a mural tumor component. Follicular pattern shows epithelial islands with central stellate-reticulum-like cells. Plexiform pattern shows anastomosing epithelial strands. Cystic change is common; infiltrative islands may extend beyond the radiographic margin. IHC is usually not necessary; BRAF V600E immunohistochemistry or molecular testing may support selected cases. In contrast, Ameloblastic Fibroma is characterized by biphasic odontogenic neoplasm with small epithelial islands/strands in a cellular primitive mesenchymal stroma. Adenomatoid Odontogenic Tumor Ameloblastoma is distinguished by odontogenic epithelial neoplasm with peripheral ameloblast-like palisading and reverse nuclear polarity. In contrast, Adenomatoid Odontogenic Tumor is characterized by usually encapsulated odontogenic epithelial lesion with duct-like structures, rosettes, and variable mineralization. In contrast, Odontoma is characterized by hamartomatous odontogenic lesion showing enamel and dentin in compound tooth-like structures or a complex disorganized mass. In contrast, Odontogenic Myxoma is characterized by infiltrative gelatinous jaw lesion composed of bland stellate/spindle cells in abundant myxoid matrix.
