title: Renal And Male Genital Tumors
content: use client Pediatric Cystic Nephroma Nephroblastic and Related Tumors Multilocular cystic renal neoplasm with bland epithelial lining and fibrous septa; no blastema. A benign pediatric renal cystic neoplasm strongly associated with DICER1 syndrome. Usually affects infants and children younger than 2 years (median, 16 months). Slight male predominance; approximately one quarter of cases are bilateral. Presents as an abdominal mass or is detected during surveillance in a child with a DICER1 alteration or pleuropulmonary blastoma. A well-circumscribed, multilocular cystic renal neoplasm. Cysts are separated by fibrous septa containing bland mesenchymal cells. No blastemal component or expansile solid nodule is present. Consider germline evaluation in the appropriate clinical setting. Cysts are lined by flattened, cuboidal, or hobnail epithelium. Septa are usually thin and hypocellular, with focal cellular condensations and well-differentiated tubules. Blastema is absent; its presence favors cystic partially differentiated nephroblastoma. The epithelial lining may show variable epithelial marker expression. ER and PR may be absent, unlike in adult cystic nephroma. Nephroblastoma Blastema and/or immature epithelial or stromal components support nephroblastoma; cystic nephroma lacks blastema. DICER1 alterations are identified in approximately 90% of cases; assess for a germline pathogenic variant. Thoroughly sample septa and any solid areas to exclude blastemal or sarcomatous components. Nephroblastoma (Wilms Tumor) Embryonal renal tumor with blastemal, epithelial, and stromal differentiation; assess anaplasia and treatment effect. A malignant renal tumor recapitulating developing kidney, most often occurring in young children. Most often presents at 3–4 years of age; slight female predominance. Usually unilateral; bilateral disease occurs in approximately 5–10%. Typically presents as an abdominal mass; pain, hematuria, hypertension, and anemia occur in a minority. Associated with predisposition syndromes including WAGR, Denys–Drash, Beckwith–Wiedemann, and DICER1 syndromes. Identify at least two of the three components: blastemal, epithelial, and stromal. Document the relative proportions and any heterologous differentiation. Assess for anaplasia; diagnosis requires nuclear enlargement, hyperchromasia, and atypical multipolar mitotic figures. Distinguish focal from diffuse anaplasia using the applicable COG or SIOP criteria. Interpret viable tumor and treatment effect in the context of preoperative chemotherapy. Blastema comprises primitive small-to-medium cells with frequent mitoses. Epithelial differentiation ranges from primitive rosettes to tubules and glomeruloid structures. Stromal differentiation ranges from primitive mesenchyme to rhabdomyoblastic, cartilaginous, or adipocytic elements. Anaplasia may occur in any component and is defined by marked nuclear enlargement, hyperchromasia, and atypical mitoses. Blastemal cells typically express nuclear WT1 and PAX8. Epithelial components express cytokeratins and EMA; WT1 and PAX8 are variable. Stromal components express vimentin; desmin may be variable. Use a panel guided by morphology to exclude mimics in monophasic tumors. Metanephric Adenoma Usually occurs in older patients and shows monotonous small epithelial cells, low mitotic activity, WT1/CD57 expression, and often BRAF p.V600E. Clear Cell Sarcoma of the Kidney Shows arborizing fibrovascular septa and diffuse BCOR/cyclin D1 expression; molecular alterations involve BCOR or YWHAE. Malignant Rhabdoid Tumor of the Kidney Typically affects infants and shows rhabdoid cells with loss of SMARCB1 (INI1) or, rarely, SMARCA4. WT1, CTNNB1, IGF2/11p15, TP53, and MYCN alterations occur in subsets. TP53 alterations are associated with anaplasia. Chromosome 1q gain is associated with increased risk of relapse and adverse outcome. A biopsy may miss focal or diffuse anaplasia; nephrectomy sampling is essential for definitive assessment. Blastemal predominance in an untreated tumor is not equivalent to the post-chemotherapy blastemal-type high-risk category. TFE3-Rearranged Renal Cell Carcinoma Molecularly Defined Renal Cell Carcinomas Renal epithelial neoplasm with TFE3 nuclear expression and a TFE3 gene fusion; often papillary with clear cells and psammoma bodies. A MiT family translocation-associated renal cell carcinoma that is disproportionately represented in children and young adults. Occurs in children, adolescents, and adults; younger age is typical compared with conventional adult RCC. No consistent sex predilection is established. Presents as a renal mass; clinical features are otherwise nonspecific. Establish renal epithelial differentiation, including PAX8 expression. Demonstrate a TFE3 rearrangement or fusion for definitive classification. Strong diffuse nuclear TFE3 staining is a useful screening finding but should be confirmed molecularly when possible. Consider RNA sequencing when morphology and immunophenotype are convincing but break-apart FISH is negative. A characteristic pattern is papillary architecture lined by epithelioid clear cells. Psammoma bodies may be numerous. Other patterns may mimic clear cell RCC, papillary RCC, oncocytoma, or epithelioid angiomyolipoma. Rare tumors contain melanin pigment. TFE3 shows strong nuclear staining in many cases. PAX8 and other renal epithelial markers are retained. Cytokeratin and EMA may be weaker than in conventional RCC. Cathepsin K is positive in a subset; melan-A and HMB45 are variably expressed. TFEB-Rearranged Renal Cell Carcinoma Often shows a biphasic large-cell/small-cell pattern and TFEB nuclear expression; confirm the specific rearrangement. Epithelioid PEComa Typically lacks PAX8 and epithelial architecture and expresses melanocytic and smooth muscle markers. Eosinophilic Solid and Cystic Renal Cell Carcinoma Shows eosinophilic cells with basophilic cytoplasmic stippling and patchy CK20; TSC1/TSC2 alterations are characteristic. TFE3 fusions involve partners such as ASPSCR1, PRCC, SFPQ, NONO, and others. Xp11 paracentric inversions may be missed by conventional break-apart FISH; RNA-based testing can resolve selected cases. Biphasic nests of large epithelioid cells and smaller cells around basement membrane material; TFEB rearrangement. A MiT family translocation-associated RCC characterized by TFEB rearrangement, classically t(6;11). Occurs in children and adults, with a tendency toward younger patients than conventional RCC. Presents as a renal mass with nonspecific symptoms. Identify a renal epithelial neoplasm with compatible morphology. Strong nuclear TFEB immunoreactivity supports the diagnosis. Confirm TFEB rearrangement by FISH or sequencing. Classic tumors show nests of large epithelioid cells and smaller cells clustered around basement membrane material. Native renal tubules may be entrapped at the tumor periphery. The small-cell component may be inconspicuous or absent, broadening the differential diagnosis. TFEB shows nuclear immunoreactivity. PAX8 and renal epithelial markers are expressed. Melan-A, HMB45, and cathepsin K are commonly positive. Cytokeratin and EMA expression may be limited. Shares MiT-family features but is defined by TFE3 rather than TFEB rearrangement; papillary clear-cell morphology is common. Clear Cell Renal Cell Carcinoma Usually shows diffuse membranous CAIX and lacks the characteristic biphasic architecture and TFEB rearrangement. Oncocytic Renal Neoplasms May overlap when the small-cell component is absent; use TFEB testing and the melanocytic marker profile. The characteristic alteration is MALAT1::TFEB fusion from t(6;11)(p21;q12). TFEB amplification is a distinct mechanism of TFEB overexpression and is more often encountered in adults. ALK-Rearranged Renal Cell Carcinoma Renal carcinoma with an ALK fusion, including VCL::ALK in patients with sickle cell trait. A rare molecularly defined RCC requiring demonstration of an ALK rearrangement. Reported age range is 3–85 years; cases occur in children and adults. Sex distribution is approximately equal. VCL::ALK tumors are associated with young patients with sickle cell trait; other cases have no distinctive clinical profile. Identify a renal carcinoma with compatible morphology and ALK immunoreactivity. Confirm an ALK rearrangement or fusion by FISH or sequencing; immunohistochemistry alone is insufficient. VCL::ALK tumors are often well circumscribed and composed of polygonal cells with abundant eosinophilic, markedly vacuolated cytoplasm. Other fusion subtypes show heterogeneous patterns, including papillary or cribriform architecture and mucinous stroma. Some cases mimic metanephric adenoma or mucinous tubular and spindle cell carcinoma. ALK immunohistochemistry is a useful screening tool. SMARCB1 (INI1) expression is retained, helping distinguish VCL::ALK RCC from renal medullary carcinoma. TFE3 immunoreactivity may occur with some staining protocols but does not establish TFE3 rearrangement. SMARCB1-Deficient Renal Medullary Carcinoma Usually occurs with sickle cell trait, shows high-grade infiltrative carcinoma and loss of INI1; ALK-rearranged RCC retains INI1. Requires TFE3 fusion; ALK-rearranged RCC is defined by an ALK fusion. Shows uniform embryonal epithelial cells, WT1/CD57 expression, and often BRAF p.V600E rather than an ALK fusion. ALK fusions involve partners including VCL, TPM3, EML4, STRN, and HOOK1. Demonstration of an ALK fusion is required for diagnosis. Solid and cystic tumor with voluminous eosinophilic cells, basophilic cytoplasmic stippling, and often patchy CK20. A renal carcinoma frequently associated with somatic TSC1 or TSC2 alterations and mTOR pathway activation. Reported age range is 14–75 years. Originally described predominantly in women, but also occurs in men and children. Usually presents as a renal mass; multifocality and metastases are uncommon but reported. Identify a renal epithelial neoplasm with solid and cystic architecture and eosinophilic cytoplasm. Look for basophilic cytoplasmic stippling and hobnail cyst lining. Patchy CK20 expression is a key immunophenotypic clue. Correlate with TSC1/TSC2 alterations when needed. Tumor cells are polygonal with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm and basophilic stippling. Cysts are often lined by hobnail cells, sometimes multinucleated. Cytoplasmic vacuoles may create a clear-cell appearance. Psammoma bodies and binucleated cells are common. PAX8 is typically positive. CK20 is patchy in many cases. Cathepsin K is often patchy positive. CK7 and CD117 are usually negative. May show papillae, psammoma bodies, and cathepsin K; confirm TFE3 rearrangement and assess the distinctive cytoplasmic stippling of ESC-RCC. Chromophobe Renal Cell Carcinoma May show binucleation and perinuclear halos but typically expresses CK7 and CD117 and lacks the characteristic CK20 pattern. High-Grade Oncocytic Renal Tumor May overlap morphologically and molecularly; integrate CK20, TSC/mTOR pathway alterations, and current classification criteria. Biallelic somatic TSC1 or TSC2 mutations are present in a majority of cases and activate mTOR signaling. High-grade infiltrative renal medullary carcinoma with loss of SMARCB1 (INI1), usually in a patient with sickle cell trait or disease. An aggressive renal carcinoma strongly associated with sickling hemoglobinopathies and SMARCB1 inactivation. Typically affects adolescents and young adults; median age is approximately 21 years. Male predominance (approximately 2:1). Almost all patients are symptomatic, commonly with hematuria, flank pain, abdominal pain, or a mass. Strongly associated with sickle cell trait or hemoglobin SC disease. High-grade infiltrative renal carcinoma, usually centered in the medulla. Loss of nuclear SMARCB1 (INI1) in tumor cells with intact internal controls. Clinical or laboratory evidence of a sickling hemoglobinopathy is supportive but not absolutely required. Infiltrating cords, nests, sheets, tubules, and microcysts are typical. Individual cell necrosis may create a cribriform pattern. Prominent myxoid desmoplasia and chronic inflammation are common. Tumor cells may have rhabdoid cytology and brisk mitotic activity. Sickled erythrocytes may be present, especially in extravasated blood. SMARCB1 (INI1) nuclear expression is lost. PAX8, broad-spectrum cytokeratins, EMA, and vimentin are typically positive. OCT3/4 may be positive and can mimic germ cell tumor in metastatic sites. Usually affects infants and young children and shows rhabdoid morphology with INI1 loss; clinical age and overall morphology are key. May occur in patients with sickle cell trait but retains INI1 and is defined by an ALK fusion. High-Grade Urothelial Carcinoma May show INI1 loss; urothelial carcinoma in situ and CK20 expression support urothelial origin. SMARCB1 inactivation occurs through mutation, deletion, or translocation, often with biallelic loss. Metanephric Tumors Cellular renal epithelial neoplasm of uniform embryonal cells, usually mitotically inactive, often BRAF p.V600E-mutated. A benign epithelial metanephric neoplasm that can mimic epithelial-predominant nephroblastoma or papillary RCC. Most patients are adults, often in the fifth or sixth decade; reported range is 5–83 years. Female predominance. About half are incidental; others present with abdominal pain or hematuria. Polycythemia occurs in approximately 10% due to erythropoietin production. A highly cellular epithelial neoplasm composed of small, uniform embryonal cells. Mitotic activity is absent or very low. WT1 nuclear expression and CD57 expression support the diagnosis. BRAF p.V600E mutation strongly supports the diagnosis in the appropriate morphology. Small uniform cells form crowded acini and branching, elongated tubules. Hyalinized or edematous stroma is typically scant. Vascular invasion is absent and mitoses are rare. WT1 shows diffuse nuclear staining. CD57 is typically positive. CK7 is negative or patchy; EMA and AMACR are typically negative. BRAF VE1 is positive in most cases. Nephroblastoma, Epithelial-Predominant Usually occurs in younger children and shows a pseudocapsule, more elongated nuclei, and greater mitotic activity. Papillary Renal Cell Carcinoma Usually has more abundant cytoplasm, diffuse CK7/EMA, absent WT1, and chromosome 7/17 gains. Metanephric Adenofibroma Contains both metanephric adenoma-like epithelium and metanephric stromal tumor-like spindle stroma. BRAF p.V600E is present in approximately 90% of cases; rare KANK1::NTRK3 fusions occur. Biphasic renal neoplasm combining metanephric adenoma-like epithelium and metanephric stromal tumor-like stroma. A rare benign biphasic metanephric neoplasm. Reported from infancy to adulthood (approximately 13 months to 36 years). No established sex predilection. May present with hematuria or polycythemia; some tumors are incidental. A biphasic renal neoplasm with epithelial and spindle-cell stromal components. Epithelial areas resemble metanephric adenoma. Stromal areas resemble metanephric stromal tumor and entrap native tubules and glomeruli. BRAF p.V600E supports the diagnosis. The proportions of epithelial and stromal components vary. The stromal component may entrap native tubules and glomeruli. Epithelial components show small uniform cells forming acini and tubules. The tumor-kidney interface is often irregular. Stromal cells frequently express CD34. Epithelial elements show an immunophenotype similar to metanephric adenoma, including WT1 and CD57. Purely epithelial without a substantial metanephric stromal tumor-like component. Metanephric Stromal Tumor Predominantly spindle-cell stromal neoplasm without the characteristic metanephric adenoma-like epithelial component. BRAF p.V600E has been identified in reported cases and is shared with other metanephric neoplasms. Bland spindle-cell neoplasm with concentric onion-skin-like collars around native tubules and vessels; often BRAF-mutated. A benign renal stromal neoplasm with a characteristic interaction with entrapped native renal structures. Usually occurs in infants and young children; mean age approximately 24 months, although adult cases occur. Presents with an abdominal mass; hematuria, hypertension, or hemorrhage from extrarenal vasculopathy may occur. A bland, predominantly spindle-cell renal neoplasm. Concentric collars of tumor cells surround and entrap native tubules and blood vessels. Angiodysplasia of entrapped arterioles and juxtaglomerular cell hyperplasia are supportive. No vascular invasion. Spindle or stellate cells have thin hyperchromatic nuclei and indistinct cytoplasmic processes. Concentric onion-skin-like collars surround tubules and vessels in a myxoid background. Angiodysplasia and juxtaglomerular cell hyperplasia may be present. Heterologous glial or cartilaginous differentiation occurs in a subset. Necrosis is unusual; mitoses are usually rare. CD34 is typically positive, often accentuated in peritubular and perivascular collars. Desmin, cytokeratins, PAX8, and S100 are generally negative. Heterologous glial areas may express GFAP and S100. BCOR is typically negative. Contains a substantial metanephric adenoma-like epithelial component in addition to the stromal component. Cellular Mesoblastic Nephroma Often shows ETV6::NTRK3 fusion and lacks the characteristic concentric peritubular/perivascular collars. Typically expresses BCOR and cyclin D1 and has characteristic arborizing fibrovascular septa. BRAF p.V600E is present in most cases and supports the diagnosis. ETV6::NTRK3 fusion is absent, helping distinguish it from cellular mesoblastic nephroma. Ossifying Renal Tumor of Infancy Mesenchymal Renal Tumors Benign intracalyceal lesion composed of osteoid, osteoblast-like cells, and peripheral spindle cells. A rare benign renal pelvic neoplasm of infancy with a characteristic osteoid-forming pattern. Occurs in neonates and infants, from 6 days to approximately 2.5 years. Marked male predominance (approximately 7:1). Often presents with gross hematuria and a calcified mass protruding into the renal pelvis. A renal pelvic/intracalyceal lesion with osteoid, osteoblast-like cells, and spindle cells. Cytologic features are bland, without malignant osteoid or overt sarcomatous atypia. Osteoblast-like cells are located between and around osteoid deposits. A bland spindle-cell component is usually peripheral. Both cellular components lack significant malignant atypia. Osteoblast-like cells are usually positive for EMA and vimentin. Shows concentric collars around native tubules and vessels rather than a dominant osteoid-forming intracalyceal lesion. Mesoblastic Nephroma Forms an infiltrative spindle-cell renal mass and lacks the defining combination of osteoid and osteoblast-like cells. Anaplastic Sarcoma of the Kidney Shows malignant spindle-cell sarcoma, diffuse anaplasia, and often heterologous cartilage or rhabdomyoblastic differentiation. Clonal trisomy 4 has been reported in a small number of cases. Spindle-cell renal tumor of infancy; classic, cellular, and mixed patterns have distinct molecular profiles. A renal spindle-cell neoplasm that predominantly occurs in the first year of life. Most cases occur in the first year, especially the first 3 months; rare after age 3 years. Usually presents as an abdominal mass; hypertension and hematuria may occur. May be detected prenatally and associated with polyhydramnios. A renal spindle-cell neoplasm in an infant, usually younger than 3 years. Classify as classic, cellular, or mixed based on morphology. Classic tumors are infiltrative and relatively hypocellular; cellular tumors are more cellular with increased mitotic activity. Use molecular testing when needed to distinguish cellular mesoblastic nephroma from other spindle-cell tumors. Classic type shows interlacing spindle-cell fascicles, collagen, low mitotic activity, and dilated thin-walled vessels. Cellular type shows sheets of plump cells with vesicular nuclei, increased mitotic activity, and sometimes necrosis or hemorrhage. Mixed type contains both patterns. Entrapped renal elements, cartilage, and extramedullary hematopoiesis may occur. SMA and cyclin D1 are typically positive. Desmin is usually negative. Nuclear pan-TRK staining supports cellular tumors with ETV6::NTRK3 fusion. Shows characteristic concentric collars around native tubules and vessels, CD34 positivity, and usually BRAF p.V600E. Shows arborizing fibrovascular septa and BCOR/cyclin D1 expression rather than typical mesoblastic nephroma architecture. Shows diffuse anaplasia and a multipatterned malignant sarcoma, often with DICER1 alterations. Cellular type commonly harbors ETV6::NTRK3 fusion. Classic type is associated with EGFR internal tandem duplication. Mixed tumors may show either alteration. Malignant renal tumor with arborizing fibrovascular septa and BCOR/cyclin D1 expression. A malignant pediatric renal sarcoma with a broad morphologic spectrum and characteristic BCOR-related molecular alterations. Usually occurs in young children; mean age approximately 3 years. Presents with abdominal distension, pain, a palpable mass, or gross hematuria. Metastases may involve bone, brain, and orbit. Identify characteristic arborizing fibrovascular septa separating nests or trabeculae of tumor cells. Tumor cells often show at least focal nuclear or cytoplasmic clearing. Diffuse nuclear BCOR and cyclin D1 support the diagnosis. Confirm BCOR or YWHAE-related molecular alteration in atypical cases. Classic pattern shows plump ovoid cells separated by arborizing fibrovascular septa. Additional patterns include cellular, myxoid, sclerosing, epithelioid, palisading, and spindle-cell patterns. Tumor cells have monomorphic nuclei with dispersed chromatin and inconspicuous nucleoli. Post-treatment recurrences may resemble myxoma or fibromatosis. BCOR and cyclin D1 show diffuse nuclear staining in most cases. Vimentin, BCL2, TLE1, p75-NGFR, and SATB2 may be positive. CD34, S100, desmin, cytokeratins, and EMA are generally negative. Cyclin B3 is expressed in BCOR::CCNB3-fused tumors. Typically CD34-positive and BCOR-negative, with concentric collars around entrapped renal tubules. Occurs in infants and shows classic or cellular spindle-cell patterns; cellular type may harbor ETV6::NTRK3. Nephroblastoma, Stromal-Predominant Usually contains other nephroblastomatous components and may show heterologous differentiation; integrate WT1 and clinical context. Characteristic mutually exclusive alterations include BCOR exon 15 internal tandem duplication, YWHAE::NUTM2 fusion, and BCOR::CCNB3 fusion. Aggressive renal tumor with rhabdoid cells and loss of SMARCB1 (INI1); usually affects infants. A highly malignant renal tumor defined by loss of SWI/SNF complex function, most often through SMARCB1 inactivation. Usually affects infants and children younger than 2 years (median age approximately 1 year). No strong sex predilection is established. Presents with hematuria or an abdominal mass. A synchronous or metachronous atypical teratoid/rhabdoid tumor of the brain occurs in a subset. Typical rhabdoid morphology in a renal malignancy. Loss of nuclear SMARCB1 (INI1) with intact internal controls. If INI1 is retained but morphology is convincing, assess SMARCA4 (BRG1). Consider germline testing and genetic counseling when SMARCB1 or SMARCA4 alterations are identified. Discohesive sheets of large cells grow in a diffuse infiltrative pattern. Tumor cells have eccentric vesicular nuclei and prominent eosinophilic nucleoli. Eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusions are characteristic but may be focal or absent. Necrosis is often extensive; architecture may be solid, sclerosing, epithelioid, spindle-cell, cystic, vascular, or myxoid. Tumor cells lose nuclear SMARCB1 (INI1) in most cases. Rare SMARCA4-deficient tumors lose nuclear BRG1. Normal stromal, endothelial, and inflammatory cells provide internal positive controls. Typically occurs in older patients with sickle cell trait and shows epithelial differentiation with PAX8 and keratin expression. Shows arborizing fibrovascular septa and BCOR/cyclin D1 expression rather than classic rhabdoid morphology. Usually shows blastemal, epithelial, and/or stromal differentiation and retains SMARCB1. Biallelic SMARCB1 inactivation is characteristic; a small subset has biallelic SMARCA4 inactivation. Germline SMARCB1 alterations occur in a substantial minority and indicate rhabdoid tumor predisposition syndrome. Multipatterned cystic and solid sarcoma with diffuse anaplasia, often associated with DICER1. A rare malignant renal sarcoma within the DICER1 tumor spectrum. Reported age ranges from 10 months to 41 years; median age approximately 9 years. Usually presents as a large renal mass, sometimes with flank pain or hematuria. A multipatterned renal sarcoma with spindle-cell areas and diffuse anaplasia. Malignant cartilage and/or embryonal rhabdomyosarcomatous areas may be present. Residual cystic nephroma may be identified at the tumor periphery. Biallelic DICER1 alterations support the diagnosis. Spindle-cell sarcoma is the predominant pattern. Scattered large cells show hyperchromatic irregular nuclei and atypical multipolar mitotic figures. Malignant cartilage nodules and embryonal rhabdomyosarcomatous areas may occur. Residual cystic nephroma may be present. Immunophenotype is variable and reflects the divergent sarcomatous components. Use lineage-specific markers to characterize rhabdomyoblastic or cartilaginous differentiation. Usually occurs in infants and lacks diffuse anaplasia and the multipatterned malignant sarcomatous component. Defined by rhabdoid morphology and SMARCB1/SMARCA4 deficiency rather than DICER1-associated multipatterned sarcoma. A benign purely cystic lesion without malignant spindle-cell sarcoma, cartilage, or diffuse anaplasia. Biallelic DICER1 alterations, typically including a loss-of-function variant and an RNase IIIb hotspot mutation, are characteristic. Renal Ewing Sarcoma Small round cell renal sarcoma with diffuse membranous CD99 and a FET::ETS-family fusion. An extraosseous Ewing sarcoma arising in the kidney; molecular confirmation is recommended. Often affects adolescents and young adults; reported median age approximately 27 years. Slight male predominance. Presents with hematuria, pain, or a palpable renal mass; symptoms are nonspecific. A highly cellular small round cell tumor, sometimes with rosette formation. Diffuse strong membranous CD99 expression supports the diagnosis. Confirm a FET::ETS fusion by molecular testing. Sheets of uniform small round cells with scant cytoplasm are typical. Rosettes may be present. Keratin expression can occur and does not exclude Ewing sarcoma. CD99 shows strong diffuse membranous staining. NKX2-2 is often nuclear positive but is not fully specific. Use a broad panel to exclude nephroblastoma, neuroblastoma, rhabdoid tumor, and desmoplastic small round cell tumor. Nephroblastoma, Blastemal-Predominant WT1 and PAX8 expression and other nephroblastomatous components support nephroblastoma; molecular testing distinguishes Ewing sarcoma. Shows rhabdoid cytology and loss of INI1 or BRG1. Shows arborizing fibrovascular septa and BCOR-related alterations rather than a FET::ETS fusion. Approximately 90% harbor EWSR1::FLI1; other EWSR1::ETS or FUS::ETS fusions account for most remaining cases. Juvenile Granulosa Cell Tumor of the Testis Non-Germ Cell Testicular Tumors Infantile intratesticular sex cord-stromal tumor with variably sized follicles and cysts. A usually benign testicular sex cord-stromal tumor that occurs almost exclusively in neonates and infants. Usually congenital or diagnosed within the first 6 months of life; cases after 1 year are exceptional. Occurs in male infants; no established later-life sex distribution applies. Presents as a testicular mass or enlargement; hormonal manifestations are very rare. Occasional associations with karyotypic abnormalities or cryptorchidism have been reported. An intratesticular, partially macrocystic or microcystic neoplasm. Primitive granulosa cells show diffuse or lobular growth with variably sized follicles. A sex cord-stromal immunophenotype supports the diagnosis. Interpret serum AFP cautiously in neonates and young infants because physiologic elevation is expected. Lobulated architecture with macrocystic and microcystic areas is characteristic. Follicles contain eosinophilic or basophilic fluid. A solid component is usually present. Tumor cells are polygonal with vacuolated or eosinophilic cytoplasm and ovoid nuclei without grooves. Fibrous or fibromyxoid stroma is present; mitotic activity may be high. Tumor cells express SF1, inhibin, calretinin, SOX9, WT1, and FOXL2. Low-molecular-weight cytokeratins may be focally positive. SALL4, AFP, and glypican-3 are typically negative, helping exclude yolk sac tumor. Yolk Sac Tumor Usually occurs beyond infancy and expresses SALL4, AFP, and glypican-3; follicular structures are not characteristic. Sertoli Cell Tumor, NOS Usually lacks the characteristic follicular architecture; CTNNB1 mutation with nuclear beta-catenin may support Sertoli cell tumor. FOXL2 mutations have not been systematically demonstrated in juvenile granulosa cell tumor; available data are limited. All groups Pediatric Pathology Renal and Male Genital Tumors Diagnostic overview of pediatric renal and non-germ cell testicular neoplasms, emphasizing defining morphology, immunophenotype, molecular alterations, and practical differential diagnosis. Tumor Classification at a Glance Use age, architecture, lineage markers, and defining molecular alterations to classify pediatric renal and testicular tumors. Entity Category Typical pattern Key diagnostic point Practical Diagnostic Framework 1. Start with age and site. An infant renal mass raises mesoblastic nephroma and rhabdoid tumor; a renal mass in an older child or adolescent requires consideration of RCC and sarcoma. 2. Define the dominant pattern. Determine whether the lesion is cystic, triphasic/blastemal, epithelial, spindle-cell, small round cell, or rhabdoid. 3. Apply a focused immunohistochemical panel. Use WT1/PAX8 for renal epithelial or nephroblastic differentiation, INI1/BRG1 for SWI/SNF deficiency, and lineage-specific markers for sarcomas. 4. Confirm defining molecular alterations. Consider DICER1, BRAF, TFE3/TFEB, ALK, TSC1/TSC2, BCOR/YWHAE, ETV6::NTRK3, and FET::ETS fusions as appropriate. Search entities, criteria, markers, or differentials... Collapse all Expand all − + Clinical Profile Essential Diagnostic Criteria Histopathology Immunohistochemistry and Immunophenotype Differential Diagnosis Molecular Pathology Diagnostic Pitfalls No matching entities. Try a different search term or category. Interpret morphology and ancillary studies in the context of patient age, tumor location, treatment history, and clinical findings. Molecular confirmation is recommended when required to define an entity.

title: Skin Tumors
content: use client BAP1-Inactivated Melanocytic Nevus/Tumor Melanocytic Neoplasms Dermal epithelioid melanocytes with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm and loss of nuclear BAP1. A usually indolent melanocytic proliferation characterized by BAP1 inactivation, often arising in association with a conventional nevus and sometimes occurring in the setting of BAP1 tumor predisposition syndrome. Usually presents during the first two decades, but can occur at any age. No established sex predilection. Usually a solitary or multiple cutaneous papule, often on trunk or extremities; lesions may be skin-colored, reddish, or light brown. Typically a well-circumscribed dome-shaped or pedunculated papule, averaging approximately 5 mm; some show sudden change in size or color. Identify a dermal proliferation containing large epithelioid melanocytes with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm. Demonstrate loss of nuclear BAP1 staining in the epithelioid component in most cases. Look for an associated conventional nevus component. Interpret cytologic atypia in context; a subset has intermediate-grade features and requires exclusion of melanoma. Consider germline BAP1 testing in patients with multiple lesions or a suggestive personal/family history. The lesion is predominantly dermal and well circumscribed. Epithelioid nevomelanocytes have abundant, well-defined eosinophilic cytoplasm. Tumor nuclei are vesicular with prominent nucleoli. A conventional nevus component is frequently present. Some lesions show marked atypia and fall within the intermediate-grade spectrum. The epithelioid component typically shows loss of nuclear BAP1 expression. The conventional nevus component, when present, retains nuclear BAP1. Melanocytic markers confirm melanocytic lineage. BRAF V600E immunohistochemistry may support the common initiating pathway alteration but does not establish the diagnosis. Most cases have an initiating BRAF mutation, followed by biallelic BAP1 mutation and/or deletion. NRAS-mutated cases have been reported. Molecular demonstration of BAP1 and BRAF alterations is desirable in difficult cases. Multiple lesions warrant evaluation for germline BAP1 variants and BAP1 tumor predisposition syndrome. Rare cases retain nuclear BAP1 staining despite a BAP1 mutation; sequencing may be informative. Rare progression to melanoma has been reported; do not equate every BAP1-inactivated lesion with melanoma. Congenital Melanocytic Nevus Usually shows deep band-like and single-file nevomelanocytes with adnexal involvement; BAP1-inactivated lesions have a distinct epithelioid component with nuclear BAP1 loss. Junctional, Compound, and Dermal Nevi Conventional nevi are composed of bland melanocytes with maturation; BAP1-inactivated lesions contain large epithelioid cells with loss of nuclear BAP1. Blue Nevus Shows dermal dendritic melanocytes in a fibrous background and usually retains BAP1. Spitz Nevus / Spitz Melanocytoma Shows epithelioid/spindle nests with Spitz-type architecture; BAP1 loss in a large epithelioid dermal component favors BAP1-inactivated nevus/tumor. Pigmented Spindle Cell Nevus (Reed Nevus) Shows heavily pigmented junctional spindle-cell nests rather than a dermal epithelioid proliferation. Melanoma Look for destructive growth, marked pleomorphism, necrosis, atypical mitoses, and multiple genomic alterations; BAP1 loss alone does not establish melanoma. Cutaneous Hamartomas Developmental proliferation of native cutaneous components, with the dominant abnormality involving dermal connective tissue or smooth muscle. A group of benign developmental lesions, often related to postzygotic mosaicism. The major patterns include connective tissue nevus, congenital smooth muscle hamartoma, and Becker nevus. Usually congenital, although some lesions become apparent during early childhood or adolescence. Congenital smooth muscle hamartoma and Becker nevus show a slight or marked male predominance, respectively; connective tissue nevi have no defined sex predilection. Connective tissue nevi favor the back, buttocks, arms, and thighs; smooth muscle hamartomas involve trunk or extremities; Becker nevi favor the shoulder and trunk. Connective tissue nevi are flesh-colored plaques with peau d’orange or cobblestone texture; smooth muscle hamartomas are hyperpigmented, hairy plaques with a pseudo-Darier sign; Becker nevi are large unilateral hyperpigmented patches with hypertrichosis. Correlate the clinical distribution and texture with the dominant dermal component. For connective tissue nevus, identify increased collagen, elastic fibers, glycosaminoglycans, or fibroblasts. For congenital smooth muscle hamartoma, identify disorganized bundles of mature dermal smooth muscle. For Becker nevus, identify smooth muscle hyperplasia with epidermal hyperpigmentation and variable hypertrichosis. Consider syndromic associations when lesions are multiple, patterned, or accompanied by extracutaneous findings. Collagenoma shows poorly demarcated thickening of dermal collagen bundles. Elastoma shows increased elastic fibers; mixed lesions contain both collagen and elastic alterations. Proteoglycan-type lesions show increased dermal mucin; cellular lesions show increased fibroblasts. Congenital smooth muscle hamartoma shows disorganized fascicles of mature smooth muscle extending into deep dermis and sometimes subcutis. Becker nevus shows dermal smooth muscle fascicles, elongated rete ridges, and increased basal and suprabasal melanin. Smooth muscle bundles can be highlighted by smooth muscle actin and desmin. Elastic stains and mucin stains can help characterize the dominant connective tissue component. Immunohistochemistry is generally supportive rather than required for diagnosis. Many lesions are mosaic; the alteration may be detectable only in lesional skin. LEMD3 loss-of-function is associated with dermatofibrosis lenticularis disseminata in Buschke–Ollendorff syndrome. Tuberous sclerosis–associated shagreen patches and Proteus-associated cerebriform connective tissue nevi are collagenomas. Molecular testing of affected skin may help classify atypical lesions; normal skin may be negative. A negative blood test does not exclude a mosaic alteration confined to lesional skin. Recognize shagreen patch, Buschke–Ollendorff syndrome, Proteus syndrome, and Becker nevus syndrome in the appropriate clinical setting. Angiokeratoma Cutaneous Vascular Lesions Ectatic thin-walled superficial dermal vessels with overlying epidermal hyperplasia. A superficial cutaneous vascular lesion in which dilated capillaries are the primary abnormality and epidermal hyperplasia is secondary. Angiokeratoma circumscriptum often presents at birth or in infancy; other forms may arise in childhood or adolescence. No uniform sex predilection; Mibelli type is more frequent in females and Fordyce type in males. Mibelli lesions affect digits; Fordyce lesions involve external genitalia and upper thighs; circumscriptum favors lower extremities; corporis diffusum has a bathing-trunks distribution. Presents as solitary or multiple 2–5 mm red, violaceous, or black papules, sometimes with a scaly or verrucous surface. Identify ectatic, thin-walled vascular channels in the papillary or very superficial reticular dermis. Epidermal acanthosis, papillomatosis, rete ridge elongation, and hyperkeratosis are supportive but may be absent, particularly in corporis diffusum. Assess for a deeper dermal or subcutaneous vascular component to exclude vascular malformations. In diffuse bathing-trunks lesions, evaluate for an associated lysosomal storage disorder. Thin-walled ectatic vessels occupy the papillary and superficial reticular dermis. Overlying epidermis may show acanthosis, papillomatosis, elongated rete ridges, and hyperkeratosis. Congestion or thrombosis may produce dark clinical coloration. In angiokeratoma corporis diffusum, lipid accumulates in endothelial cells, vessel-wall smooth muscle, and arrector pili. Endothelial cells express CD31 and ERG. Solitary pediatric lesions may express PROX1 and D2-40 and lack WT1. In diffuse forms, PAS and Sudan Black B can highlight lipid accumulation. The epidermal changes are secondary; focus on the depth and architecture of the vascular channels. Angiokeratoma corporis diffusum should prompt clinical correlation for Fabry disease and other lysosomal storage disorders. Verrucous venous malformation Shows a deeper dermal and subcutaneous vascular component rather than vessels confined to the superficial dermis. Lymphangioma circumscriptum Has dilated lymphatic channels extending into deeper dermis or subcutis. Acral pseudolymphomatous angiokeratoma of children Shows a prominent lymphocytic infiltrate. Epidermal Nevi Epidermal Hamartomas Persistent mosaic epidermal or adnexal hamartomas, often following the lines of Blaschko. A heterogeneous group of cutaneous hamartomas caused by postzygotic mosaic alterations. The principal patterns are common keratinocytic nevus, nevus sebaceus, nevus comedonicus, and porokeratotic eccrine nevus. Usually congenital, although some types have delayed onset in childhood. No consistent sex predilection is established. Common keratinocytic nevi can occur anywhere but favor Blaschko lines; nevus sebaceus favors scalp and face; nevus comedonicus favors face, neck, upper arm, and chest; porokeratotic eccrine nevi often involve palms and soles. Common keratinocytic nevi are brown, velvety plaques; nevus sebaceus is a hairless yellow-orange plaque; nevus comedonicus shows linear comedones; porokeratotic eccrine nevus shows keratotic papules with punctate pits. Recognize a segmental or Blaschkoid distribution supporting mosaicism. For common keratinocytic nevus, identify acanthosis, papillomatosis, elongated rete ridges, and hyperkeratosis. For nevus sebaceus, identify coordinated abnormalities of epidermis, sebaceous glands, hair follicles, and sweat glands. For nevus comedonicus, identify multiple dilated, keratin-filled follicular infundibula. For porokeratotic eccrine nevus, identify cornoid lamellae overlying dilated acrosyringia and acrotrichia. Common keratinocytic nevus shows well-demarcated acanthosis, papillomatosis, elongated rete ridges, and hyperkeratosis. Nevus sebaceus shows epidermal hyperplasia, superficial hyperplastic sebaceous glands, reduced or abortive hair follicles, and often ectopic apocrine glands. Nevus comedonicus shows dilated, keratin-filled follicular infundibula with atrophy or acanthosis of the overlying epidermis. Porokeratotic eccrine nevus shows multiple dermal invaginations capped by cornoid lamellae corresponding to dilated acrosyringia and acrotrichia. Ruptured comedonal cysts may elicit a foreign-body reaction. No routine immunohistochemical panel is required. Ancillary stains may be selected to characterize adnexal structures or exclude a mimicker; diagnosis is primarily architectural. Postzygotic mosaic mutations commonly affect PI3K or RAS/MAPK pathway genes. FGFR3 alterations can help classify selected lesions, particularly in epidermal nevus syndromes. The mutation may be confined to affected skin and absent from blood or unaffected skin. Nevus sebaceus may develop secondary benign adnexal neoplasms, especially syringocystadenoma papilliferum and trichoblastoma-like proliferations. Multiple or extensive lesions should prompt assessment for an epidermal nevus syndrome. Pilomatricoma Cutaneous Adnexal Tumors Dermal nodule with peripheral basaloid matrical cells transitioning to central anucleate shadow cells. A benign hair-matrix tumor that differentiates toward the hair cortex and commonly affects children. Nearly half of cases are diagnosed during the first two decades of life; it can occur at any age. There is a modest female predominance. Most commonly arises in the head and neck, followed by upper extremities, trunk, and lower extremities. Usually a solitary, firm-to-hard, slow-growing, asymptomatic 1–3 cm dermal or subcutaneous nodule; overlying skin may be red or blue. Identify a dermal or subcutaneous nodule composed of basaloid matrical cells and shadow cells. Demonstrate transition from peripheral basaloid cells through intermediate cells to central anucleate shadow cells. Dense keratin and calcification or ossification may be present. Assess circumscription, symmetry, cytologic atypia, mitotic activity, and lymphovascular invasion to exclude pilomatrical carcinoma. Peripheral basaloid cells are small, deeply basophilic, and mitotically active. Basaloid cells transition through intermediate cells to central shadow (ghost) cells with eosinophilic cytoplasm and absent nuclei. Calcification and, in older lesions, ossification are common. The surrounding dermis is often fibrotic with a foreign-body granulomatous reaction. Proliferating variants may be predominantly basaloid; pigmented variants also occur. Nuclear and cytoplasmic β-catenin expression supports matrical differentiation. Basaloid cells may show nuclear β-catenin accumulation. IHC is usually not necessary when classic morphology is present. Most cases harbor activating CTNNB1 mutations, commonly involving exon 3. Trisomy 18 has been reported in basaloid cells. Calcification and ossification may make the lesion extremely hard clinically. Multiple pilomatricomas may be associated with familial adenomatous polyposis, myotonic dystrophy, and other genetic syndromes. Pilomatrical carcinoma Poor circumscription, asymmetry, frequent atypical mitoses, and lymphovascular invasion favor carcinoma. Basal cell carcinoma Shows basaloid nests with peripheral palisading and stromal retraction; true shadow-cell differentiation is absent. Trichoblastoma Shows follicular germinative differentiation and specialized stroma rather than prominent matrical shadow cells. Melanocytic matricoma Contains matrical differentiation admixed with melanocytes and melanin pigment. Deep, band-like and single-file nevomelanocytic proliferation with adnexal and subcutaneous involvement and frequent neurotization. A benign melanocytic proliferation arising in utero and present at birth or during the first years of life; large and multiple lesions carry increased melanoma and neurocutaneous melanocytosis risk. Present at birth or recognized during the first few years of life; small lesions occur in approximately 1% of newborns, whereas giant lesions are rare. May occur anywhere; large lesions often involve the trunk or scalp and may have satellite nevi. Hyperpigmented, variably hairy, flat-to-rugose or nodular lesions; classify by projected adult diameter from small to giant. Clinical onset is at birth or within the first few years of life. Nevomelanocytes extend deeply through the dermis and may involve subcutis, adnexa, and subendothelial spaces. A band-like or single-file pattern and neurotization are common. Maturation with depth and overall bland cytology support nevus; interpret atypia and mitoses cautiously in neonatal and large lesions. Atypical proliferative nodules require extensive sampling and may need comparative genomic hybridization or FISH. Deep dermal and subcutaneous type C spindle nevomelanocytes often show neuroid differentiation. Intermediate dermis contains type B cells in single files between collagen bundles and around adnexa and vessels. Superficial dermis contains larger epithelioid type A cells, sometimes with melanin. Wagner–Meissner or Masson-like neuroid structures may be present. A grenz zone, band-like growth, papillomatosis, and variable epidermal changes may be seen. Large lesions may contain proliferative nodules with increased cellularity, atypia, pagetoid spread, or mitoses. Melanocytic markers such as SOX10, S100, Melan-A, and HMB45 label nevomelanocytes. Neurotized areas may show reduced melanocytic marker expression and neural differentiation markers. IHC alone cannot reliably distinguish a proliferative nodule from melanoma. Large congenital nevi commonly harbor somatic NRAS p.Q61 mutations. BRAF p.V600 mutations occur in a minority and are relatively more frequent in small lesions. RAF1 and other MAPK-pathway rearrangements have been reported. Comparative genomic hybridization or FISH may help assess atypical proliferative nodules. Pagetoid spread, mitoses, ulceration, and cytologic atypia may occur in neonatal congenital nevi and proliferative nodules; do not diagnose melanoma from one feature alone. A deep expansile nodule with pleomorphism, necrosis, and atypical mitoses raises concern for melanoma. Large or multiple lesions warrant clinical assessment for neurocutaneous melanocytosis. Acquired nevi are usually smaller and lack the deep single-file infiltrative growth, neurotization, and adnexal involvement typical of congenital nevi. Blue nevus is a dermal dendritic proliferation with fibroplasia and G-protein pathway alterations, not a deep band-like congenital-pattern nevus. Spitz lesions are composed of large epithelioid/spindle cells in nests; congenital nevi show deep single-file growth, neurotization, and adnexal involvement. Reed nevus is a heavily pigmented junctional spindle-cell proliferation, usually superficial and sharply circumscribed. Atypical proliferative nodules may mimic melanoma; expansile deep growth, marked pleomorphism, necrosis, and atypical mitoses are more concerning than isolated pagetoid spread or mitoses in a neonate. BAP1-inactivated lesions show large dermal epithelioid melanocytes with loss of nuclear BAP1 rather than the typical deep band-like, neurotized congenital nevus pattern. Symmetric, circumscribed proliferation of bland melanocytes with maturation and no significant deep mitotic activity. Common acquired melanocytic nevi classified by the anatomic distribution of nevomelanocytes at the dermoepidermal junction and within the dermis. Usually develop in early childhood and peak around adolescence; number and size decline during adulthood. Can occur at any site but predominate on the trunk. Usually small (<5 mm), symmetric, uniformly pigmented macules or papules; junctional nevi are often flat, whereas compound and dermal nevi are raised. Demonstrate a symmetric, circumscribed proliferation of cytologically bland melanocytes. Junctional nevus is confined to the dermoepidermal junction; compound nevus has junctional and dermal components; dermal nevus is confined to dermis. Dermal nests show maturation with depth, often progressing to smaller type B and spindle-shaped type C cells. Significant pleomorphism, deep mitoses, and destructive growth are absent. Pagetoid spread is absent or limited to an irritated focus. Junctional component may be lentiginous or nested along the dermoepidermal junction. Compound and dermal nevi show central dermal nests that become smaller and less pigmented with depth. Deep cells may become lymphocyte-like or spindled, reflecting maturation or senescence. Mitoses are usually absent, especially in deep portions. A congenital-type growth pattern may occur in acquired nevi and does not establish congenital onset. S100 and SOX10 highlight melanocytes throughout the lesion. Melan-A and HMB45 may show a maturation gradient, with reduced deep HMB45 staining. p16 is typically strongly retained; Ki-67 is low. Senescence-associated markers are commonly expressed. BRAF mutations are frequent; NRAS mutations occur in a subset. Conventional acquired nevi generally lack chromosomal copy-number alterations. Progression requires additional alterations such as CDKN2A loss or TERT promoter mutation. A congenital-type histologic pattern in an acquired nevus does not prove the lesion was present at birth. Limited pagetoid spread may occur in an irritated nevus; assess the overall symmetry, maturation, and cytology. Congenital nevi show deep single-file infiltration, adnexal involvement, band-like growth, and neurotization. Blue nevus is dermal, dendritic, and fibrosing, often with melanophages and GNAQ/GNA11-pathway alterations. Spitz lesions show larger epithelioid or spindle cells, often with Kamino bodies and characteristic nest architecture. Reed nevus shows heavily pigmented spindle-cell nests with vertical or whorled orientation. Melanoma shows asymmetry, poor circumscription, cytologic atypia, destructive growth, and/or deep mitotic activity rather than bland maturation. BAP1-inactivated lesions contain large epithelioid dermal melanocytes with nuclear BAP1 loss, unlike conventional bland acquired nevi. Dermal dendritic melanocytes in a fibrous stroma, with cellular blue nevus showing additional dense nests and deep expansile growth. A benign dermal melanocytic proliferation comprising dendritic and cellular patterns, typically driven by G-protein pathway alterations. Most frequent in children and young adults. Dendritic blue nevi favor dorsal hands and feet; cellular blue nevi favor buttocks and scalp; congenital lesions are often on the scalp. Dendritic lesions are small blue papules; cellular lesions are often larger (>10 mm), indurated blue nodules. For dendritic blue nevus, identify a poorly circumscribed dermal proliferation of bland dendritic melanocytes with fibroplasia. For cellular blue nevus, identify dense nests and sheets of bland melanocytes superimposed on a dendritic blue nevus pattern. Assess for symmetry, cytologic blandness, absence of necrosis, and lack of significant mitotic activity. Atypical cellular blue nevus or blue-nevus-like melanoma requires assessment for expansile growth, atypia, mitoses, and molecular progression. Dendritic melanocytes are dispersed in a fibrosing dermal background, often with perivascular and periadnexal distribution. Melanophages are common and intracytoplasmic melanin is variable. Cellular blue nevus shows dense nests and sheets of medium-sized melanocytes, often extending deeply into subcutis. Cellular areas may form vertical expansile nodules; large lesions may show central myxoid or cystic change. Conventional lesions lack significant atypia, mitotic activity, and necrosis. S100 and SOX10 label lesional melanocytes. Melan-A and HMB45 are typically positive in melanocytic components. BAP1 is generally retained in conventional blue nevi; loss raises concern for a blue-nevus-like melanoma in the appropriate context. Activating mutations in GNAQ, GNA11, PLCB4, or less commonly CYSLTR2 occur in a largely mutually exclusive pattern. Conventional blue nevi typically lack BRAF, NRAS, NF1, and BAP1 mutations. Molecular testing may help in difficult cases or when melanoma is considered. Cellular blue nevus may extend deeply into subcutis but remains cytologically bland and lacks necrosis. Do not confuse the intermediate-grade atypical cellular blue nevus (melanocytoma) with conventional benign blue nevus or overt melanoma. Congenital nevi show band-like deep nevomelanocytes, single-file growth, adnexal involvement, and neurotization rather than a fibrosing dendritic dermal proliferation. Common nevi are usually more circumscribed and show junctional nests and dermal maturation; blue nevi are poorly circumscribed and dendritic with melanophages. Spitz lesions show plump epithelioid/spindle nests and often Kamino bodies; blue nevi show dendritic melanocytes in fibrous stroma. Reed nevus is a superficial junctional proliferation of heavily pigmented spindle cells, not a deep dermal dendritic lesion. Blue-nevus-like melanoma shows atypia, mitotic activity, necrosis, and expansile growth; conventional blue nevus is bland and lacks necrosis. BAP1-inactivated lesions show epithelioid melanocytes and nuclear BAP1 loss; conventional blue nevi are dendritic/fibrosing and usually retain BAP1. Symmetric, sharply circumscribed nests of large epithelioid and/or spindle melanocytes with maturation and low proliferative activity. A spectrum of melanocytic neoplasms ranging from benign Spitz nevus to Spitz melanocytoma (atypical Spitz tumor); diagnosis requires integration of clinical, histologic, immunophenotypic, and molecular findings. Spitz nevi commonly occur in children; approximately 40% of patients are younger than 15 years. Both sexes are affected similarly. In children, lesions favor head and neck and lower extremities; mucosal lesions are very rare. Usually a solitary, rapidly growing then stable pink-red to brown dome-shaped papule, generally <5–6 mm; atypical Spitz tumors may be larger and asymmetric. For Spitz nevus, identify large epithelioid and/or spindle nevomelanocytes in a symmetric, sharply circumscribed lesion. Deep maturation and single-cell dispersion at the base support benign Spitz nevus. Rare mitoses may occur but are usually superficial; deep or atypical mitoses are concerning. Kamino bodies, clefting around junctional nests, epidermal hyperplasia, and stromal edema are supportive. Spitz melanocytoma has one or more atypical histologic features but insufficient findings for melanoma; integrate molecular and clinical data. Nests of plump epithelioid and/or spindle melanocytes form a symmetric, sharply circumscribed lesion. Most are compound; junctional and dermal forms also occur. Deep maturation is present, with single-cell dispersion at the base. Kamino bodies, clefting around junctional nests, stromal edema, vascular ectasia, and lymphocytic aggregates may be present. Pagetoid migration can be prominent in young children. Atypical Spitz tumors may show asymmetry, poor circumscription, lack of maturation, deep mitoses, ulceration, or marked pleomorphism. S100, SOX10, Melan-A, tyrosinase, and MITF support melanocytic differentiation. S100A6 is typically diffuse. p16 is usually retained in benign Spitz nevi. HMB45 is often top-heavy, and Ki-67 is low with a gradient and little or no staining at the base. ALK immunohistochemistry can support an ALK fusion; pan-TRK may screen for NTRK rearrangement but requires molecular confirmation. Most Spitz nevi harbor kinase fusions or structural rearrangements involving ROS1, ALK, BRAF, NTRK1, NTRK3, MET, RET, or MAP3K8. HRAS mutations define a separate subset and are common in many agminated or eruptive lesions. Atypical Spitz tumors may acquire CDKN2A alterations and chromosomal copy-number changes. FISH or RNA-based next-generation sequencing can help in equivocal cases; no single alteration is fully diagnostic. Multiple copy-number changes, homozygous CDKN2A deletion, or TERT promoter alteration raise concern for Spitz melanoma but must be interpreted with morphology. Spitz nevi can mimic melanoma clinically and histologically; pagetoid spread alone is not sufficient for malignancy in young children. Spitz melanocytoma is an intermediate-grade lesion, not synonymous with melanoma. Molecular abnormalities overlap among Spitz nevus, Spitz melanocytoma, and Spitz melanoma. Congenital nevi show deep single-file infiltration, neurotization, and adnexal involvement rather than symmetric nests of large Spitz cells. Common nevi are composed of smaller bland melanocytes with maturation; Spitz nevi contain large epithelioid and/or spindle cells and may have Kamino bodies. Blue nevus is a dermal dendritic/fibrosing proliferation, usually without Spitz-type nests or Kamino bodies. Reed nevus is a heavily pigmented junctional spindle-cell Spitz variant with vertical/whorled nests. Melanoma shows greater asymmetry, poor circumscription, absent maturation, deep/atypical mitoses, ulceration, and often genomic complexity. BAP1-inactivated lesions typically show a conventional nevus with an epithelioid dermal component lacking nuclear BAP1, rather than classic Spitz-cell nests. Symmetric junctional nests of uniform, heavily pigmented spindle melanocytes, without atypia. A benign pigmented spindle-cell subtype of Spitz nevus that may clinically and histologically mimic melanoma. Usually affects children and young adults, although reported ages range widely. Female predominance is reported. Most often involves extremities, particularly the thigh, followed by trunk and head and neck. Typically an acquired, asymptomatic, dark-brown or black, well-circumscribed macule or papule smaller than 10 mm. Identify junctional nests of uniform spindle-shaped nevomelanocytes. Lesional cells are heavily pigmented and lack significant cytologic atypia. Nests are vertically oriented, whorled, or concentric and are usually confined to epidermis or papillary dermis. Kamino bodies and pagetoid melanocytosis may be present but should be interpreted with the overall symmetry and bland cytology. Symmetric, well-circumscribed junctional proliferation of uniform spindle melanocytes. Nests are heavily pigmented and vertically oriented, whorled, or concentric. Lesional cells lack significant atypia and mitotic activity. Dermal melanophages are usually present. Adnexal extension and limited papillary dermal involvement may occur. S100, SOX10, and other melanocytic markers support melanocytic lineage. HMB45 may show superficial predominance. Use an immunohistochemical panel and molecular studies when morphology is atypical or melanoma is a concern. Reed nevus is a molecular subtype of Spitz nevus and is driven by structural rearrangements producing kinase fusions. NTRK3 fusions are reported in more than half of cases. NTRK3 break-apart FISH or RNA sequencing can confirm a rearrangement in selected cases. Marked pigmentation and pagetoid growth can mimic melanoma; symmetry, uniform spindle cells, and lack of atypia favor Reed nevus. Atypical pigmented spindle-cell tumors require careful evaluation for melanoma. Congenital nevi show deep band-like infiltration, neurotization, and adnexal involvement rather than superficial pigmented junctional nests. Common nevi lack the dense, heavily pigmented, vertically oriented spindle-cell nests characteristic of Reed nevus. Blue nevus is predominantly dermal and dendritic with fibroplasia; Reed nevus is a junctional spindle-cell proliferation. Reed nevus is a pigmented spindle-cell Spitz subtype; conventional Spitz nevi are often less pigmented and may contain epithelioid cells. Melanoma shows asymmetry, cytologic atypia, deep mitoses, and lack of maturation; Reed nevus is symmetric and cytologically uniform. BAP1-inactivated lesions show dermal epithelioid cells and nuclear BAP1 loss, not the heavily pigmented junctional spindle-cell nests of Reed nevus. Malignant melanocytic proliferation with atypical epithelioid, spindle, or small round-cell morphology and destructive or expansile growth. A rare but important pediatric malignancy encompassing congenital nevus-associated melanoma, Spitz melanoma, conventional low-CSD melanoma, and melanoma arising in blue nevus. Rare in children; prepubertal melanoma is particularly uncommon. Both sexes are affected equally. Congenital nevus-associated melanoma may arise at any site, often as a rapidly growing deep nodule within a large congenital nevus; Spitz melanoma favors limbs and head; conventional low-CSD melanoma favors torso and legs. Spitz melanoma may present as a rapidly growing amelanotic nodule and mimic pyogenic granuloma or xanthogranuloma. Conventional melanoma may present as an evolving asymmetric, irregularly bordered, variegated pigmented macule or papule. Demonstrate a malignant melanocytic proliferation composed of epithelioid, spindle, or occasionally lymphoblast-like cells. Assess architecture for asymmetry, poor circumscription, expansile growth, destructive invasion, and lack of maturation. Assess cytology for pleomorphism, prominent nucleoli, atypical mitoses, and necrosis. For congenital nevus-associated melanoma, distinguish a deep expansile nodule from a proliferative nodule within the background nevus. For Spitz melanoma, integrate clinical, histologic, immunohistochemical, and molecular findings; no single test is definitive. Congenital nevus-associated melanoma often forms a deep dermal or subcutaneous nodule distinct from the background nevus. Worrisome features include sharp demarcation, expansile growth, pleomorphism, necrosis, and mitotic figures, interpreted in age-specific context. Spitz melanoma shows confluent, vertically oriented aggregates of large epithelioid and fusiform melanocytes, often with asymmetry, poor circumscription, lack of maturation, deep mitoses, and ulceration. Conventional low-CSD melanoma may show superficial spreading or nodular growth with pagetoid scatter of enlarged melanocytes. Pagetoid spread in children must be interpreted cautiously because it may occur in benign and atypical lesions. Melanocytic markers support lineage but are not independently diagnostic of melanoma. Spitz melanoma often shows diffuse HMB45 expression and loss of p16. Immunohistochemistry has limited utility in distinguishing melanoma from proliferative nodules in congenital nevi. Interpret Ki-67 and melanocytic marker distribution with morphology and molecular findings. Congenital nevus-associated melanoma frequently harbors NRAS mutations; amplification of mutated NRAS has been reported. Spitz melanoma may retain Spitz-type kinase fusions or HRAS alterations and acquire CDKN2A inactivation and TERT promoter alterations. Conventional low-CSD melanoma frequently has BRAF p.V600 mutations, CDKN2A inactivation, and TERT promoter mutations. Melanoma arising in blue nevus commonly involves GNAQ or GNA11 pathway alterations. Multiple chromosomal copy-number changes support melanoma; homozygous CDKN2A loss and TERT promoter alterations are concerning in Spitz lesions. In neonatal congenital nevi and proliferative nodules, atypia, mitoses, ulceration, and pagetoid spread can occur without melanoma. Spitz melanoma overlaps with Spitz melanocytoma and conventional melanoma with spitzoid morphology; use integrated assessment. Nodal melanocyte deposits in Spitz melanoma do not carry the same prognostic implications as nodal metastasis in conventional melanoma. Congenital nevus is usually bland and maturing; melanoma forms a distinct expansile nodule with pleomorphism, necrosis, and atypical mitoses. Common nevi are symmetric, bland, and show maturation with low proliferation; melanoma is asymmetric and cytologically malignant. Conventional blue nevus is bland and lacks necrosis; blue-nevus-like melanoma shows atypia, mitoses, necrosis, and expansile growth. Spitz melanoma shows asymmetry, poor circumscription, absent maturation, deep mitoses, and often genomic complexity; Spitz melanocytoma has atypia insufficient for melanoma. Reed nevus is symmetric with uniform pigmented spindle cells and low mitotic activity; melanoma shows atypia, deep mitoses, and destructive growth. BAP1 loss alone does not establish melanoma; assess for destructive growth, pleomorphism, necrosis, atypical mitoses, and genomic complexity. All groups Pediatric Pathology Skin Tumors Diagnostic overview of pediatric cutaneous hamartomas, vascular and adnexal lesions, melanocytic nevi, and melanoma, emphasizing clinical context, essential morphologic criteria, immunophenotype, and diagnostically useful molecular findings. Tumor Classification at a Glance Use the dominant architecture, maturation pattern, and clinical distribution to narrow the diagnosis. Entity Category Typical Pattern Key Diagnostic Point Practical Diagnostic Framework 1. Establish the clinical pattern. Record age, congenital versus acquired onset, anatomic site, lesion size, pigmentation, and growth behavior. 2. Identify the dominant compartment. Separate epidermal/adnexal hamartomas, superficial vascular ectasia, hair-matrix differentiation, and melanocytic proliferations. 3. Evaluate melanocytic architecture. Assess symmetry, circumscription, nesting, maturation with depth, pagetoid spread, cytologic atypia, mitotic activity, necrosis, and subcutaneous extension. 4. Use ancillary studies selectively. Apply lineage markers and targeted molecular testing to resolve specific differentials; interpret results with morphology and clinical context. Search entities, criteria, markers, or differentials... Diagnostic interpretation should integrate clinical history, lesion distribution, age, complete architectural assessment, and appropriately selected ancillary studies. Adequate sampling is particularly important when melanoma or an atypical melanocytic proliferation is considered.

title: Soft Tissue Bone Tumors
content: use client Lipomatosis Adipocytic Tumors Lipomatoses have previously been subclassified according to their clinical findings and anatomical distribution. Although molecular studies are transforming the way we think about these lesions, some of these clinicopathological terms remain useful in classification. CILF manifests at birth or in early childhood as unilateral facial swelling with hyperplasia of the underlying bone and (in some cases) the teeth, tongue, brain, and parotid gland. Essential: mature adipose tissue infiltrating regional tissues, occasionally arising in specific, relevant clinical contexts or syndromes. Desirable: alterations in PIK3CA (in CILF, PROS, FAVA, and LN), PTEN (in PHOST), related PI3K/PTEN/AKT/TSC/mTORC1 pathway genes, or FGFR1 in relevant clinical contexts. These tumors all show overgrowth of mature adipose tissue, typically infiltrating regional tissues, without lipoblasts or features of malignancy. CILF lesions are infiltrative and incorporate nerve, blood vessels, and hypertrophy of adjacent bone. PHOST shows a distinctive multinodular combination of mature adipose tissue, fibrous tissue, vascular component (often with dilated, back-to-back clustered veins and thick-walled, tortuous arteries), lymphoid follicles, bone, and hypertrophic nerves with onion bulb–like features. FAVA is characterized by abundant, dense, fibrous adipose tissue, vascular malformation, and lymphoplasmacytic aggregates in skeletal muscle. Germline, mosaic, or somatic mutations in PIK3CA, PTEN, other genes in the PI3K/PTEN/AKT/TSC/mTORC1 pathway, and FGFR1 are implicated in a subset of these lesions, as described above. Lipomatosis is a broad term encompassing the infiltrative overgrowth of mature adipose tissue occurring in a wide spectrum of clinical contexts, sometimes in hamartomatous arrangements with other mesenchymal tissue types. Lipoblastoma/lipoblastomatosis Superficial, circumscribed lipoblastoma clinically simulates lipoma or a vascular malformation, whereas lipoblastomatosis originates in deep soft tissue and is more infiltrative. Truncal tumors may infiltrate into the thoracic cavity from extrathoracic locations, or into the spine, with reports of neuroforaminal or intraspinal invasion. Because both types recur, the distinction between circumscribed and infiltrative forms is not clinically relevant. Essential: a lobulated mass in early childhood, composed of sheets of variably mature adipocytes separated by fibrovascular septa. Desirable: molecular confirmation is recommended in older children and adults to rule out liposarcoma. Lipoblastoma is a lobulated tumor comprising sheets of adipocytes showing a spectrum of maturation, ranging from primitive stellate or spindled mesenchymal cells to multivacuolated or small signet-ring lipoblasts through to mature adipocytes, separated by fibrovascular septa. Myxoid areas display a plexiform vascular pattern with primitive mesenchymal cells. The proportion of these cell types varies, and there is sometimes a zonal pattern of maturation, with more immature myxoid cells at the periphery (adjacent to fibrous septa) and mature adipocytes in the center of the lobule. Myxoid regions can occasionally show pooling of matrix similar to myxoid liposarcoma. The adipocytes of lipoblastoma demonstrate reactivity for S100, CD56, and CD34. The primitive mesenchymal cells are often reactive for desmin. In selected cases, the finding of PLAG1 rearrangements / copy-number gain can support the diagnosis; HMGA2 alterations are less common. Lipoblastoma is a benign neoplasm of embryonal white fat, which may be a localized or diffuse tumor with a tendency for local recurrence if incompletely excised. Liposarcoma Liposarcomas of all types generally manifest as large (> 50 mm), deep-seated, painless soft tissue masses. Liposarcomas represent < 2% of all pediatric soft tissue malignancies. Nearly 90% occur in the second decade of life, with a female predominance; > 70% are of myxoid type. ALT/WDLPS Essential: mature fat transected by irregular fibrous septa containing enlarged hyperchromatic cells and (less commonly) lipoblasts. Desirable: nuclear expression of MDM2 and/or CDK4, or evidence of MDM2 and/or CDK4 gene amplification. DDLPS Essential: ALT/WDLPS with abrupt transition to (usually) high-grade pleomorphic sarcoma. The morphological features of pediatric ALT/WDLPS, DDLPS, and conventional PLPS are identical to those seen in older patients. MDM2 and/or CDK4 nuclear immunopositivity is present in most cases of ALT/WDLPS and DDLPS , with the exception of Li–Fraumeni-associated cases, which overexpress p53. The morphological features of MLPS in children and adults are identical. However, unlike in adults, progression to high-grade MLPS (round cell) is not clearly associated with a worse prognosis (probably owing to the rarity of such tumors) in children. Amplification of MDM2 and CDK4 distinguishes ALT/WDLPS from benign mimics. DDIT3 rearrangement and the absence of PLAG1 rearrangement help in the differential diagnosis of MLPS from extensively myxoid lipoblastomas. Liposarcomas are a heterogeneous group of mesenchymal neoplasms with adipocytic differentiation and varying biological behavior ranging from locally aggressive to metastasizing. Fasciitis/myositis Fibroblastic and Myofibroblastic Tumors Both nodular fasciitis and proliferative myositis may simulate sarcoma owing to their rapid growth. Nodular fasciitis usually measures ≤ 20 mm and is always < 50 mm in maximum dimension, whereas cranial fasciitis may be larger. Myositis ossificans manifests as a rapidly growing, painful mass in its early stage, with a plateau in growth after 2 weeks, when flocculent mineralization appears on imaging. Essential: for nodular fasciitis: a bland myofibroblastic proliferation with a tissue culture–like growth pattern, extravasated red cells, and myxoid stroma; for proliferative myositis: a myofibroblastic/fibroblastic proliferation with ganglion-like cells, variable collagenous/myxoid stroma, and an intramuscular checkerboard growth pattern; for myositis ossificans: fascicles of benign-appearing fibroblasts and… Desirable: for nodular fasciitis and myositis ossificans: demonstration of a USP6 gene rearrangement. Nodular fasciitis is composed of loose intersecting fascicles of plump, bland myofibroblasts with fine chromatin and small nucleoli. Lesions may be highly cellular with a high mitotic count. Abundant myxoid stroma, a feathery tissue culture–like appearance, microcysts, osteoclast-like giant cells, and extravasated erythrocytes are common features. Later lesions contain more collagen and may show keloidal hyalinization. By immunohistochemistry, nodular fasciitis and cranial fasciitis are usually positive for SMA and MSA; desmin positivity is occasionally found. Myofibroblasts are positive for SMA and MSA, and negative for desmin. Recurrent USP6 gene rearrangements have been identified in nodular fasciitis, cranial fasciitis, and myositis ossificans. Nodular fasciitis is a self-limiting myofibroblastic neoplasm typically occurring in subcutaneous tissue. Fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva FOP is usually associated with congenital malformations of the great toes (bilateral hallux valgus, malformed first metatarsal bone) and cervical–vertebral fusions. Episodes of painful soft tissue swelling occur during the first decade of life, accompanied by relentless and progressive ossification of soft tissues. Traumas can accelerate the process, so the suspicion of FOP is a contraindication to biopsy. Essential: congenital great toe malformations and rapidly progressive soft tissue masses preceding heterotopic ossification; demonstration of an ACVR1 mutation. Early lesions of FOP are nonspecific vascular loose fibrous tissue proliferations with variable inflammation, which over time become more collagenized. As the lesions mature, cartilage appears, followed by endochondral ossification. FOP cannot be distinguished histologically from localized myositis ossificans. Molecular testing is necessary to demonstrate a germline mutation of ACVR1. Fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva (FOP) is a heritable condition of progressive soft tissue metamorphosis to bone, resulting in immobility and premature death. Fibroma of tendon sheath FOTS is a slow-growing, painless nodule, measuring < 30 mm. FOTS usually occurs in young or middle-aged adults, but cases in infants and children have been reported. FOTS usually occurs on the finger tendons (most commonly in the thumb, index finger, and middle finger) and rarely in the knee, elbow, or wrist. Essential: a firm nodule consisting of a paucicellular proliferation of fibroblasts/myofibroblasts in a collagenous background with slit-like blood vessels, attached to tendon. Histological examination of FOTS reveals a circumscribed arrangement of bland fibroblasts and myofibroblasts in a densely collagenous or hyalinized stroma. Characteristic slit-like blood vessels are often prominent at the periphery of the tumor. Fibroma of tendon sheath (FOTS) is a benign fibroblastic/myofibroblastic, nodular, bland proliferation that attaches to tendon. Gardner fibroma GF is usually diagnosed in young children (aged < 10 years), including neonates, but it can be seen in older children. In contrast, nuchal-type fibroma, which has many overlapping features with GF, occurs mainly in middle-aged men, and as many as 50% of nuchal-type fibroma patients have diabetes mellitus. GF arises in the superficial and deep soft tissues of the torso (most commonly in the back or paraspinal region), head/neck, and rarely other non-visceral sites (e. g. the mesentery). Essential: a poorly defined, bland and paucicellular, densely collagenized, CD34-positive tumor occurring in a child; often associated with FAP and APC mutations. GF exhibits haphazardly arranged coarse collagen bundles interspersed with bland spindled fibroblasts and prominent clefts (cracking artefact). A helpful diagnostic feature is the entrapment of fat and neurovascular bundles at the edge of the lesion. These tumors are CD34-positive, SMA-negative, and often show nuclear β-catenin staining, reflective of their association with FAP. GF is associated with germline and somatic APC mutations. An aggressive phenotype has been described with a specific c. Gardner fibroma (GF) is a benign fibroblastic/myofibroblastic, plaque-like lesion composed of dense collagen bundles with sparse fibroblasts, usually associated with familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP). Fibrous hamartoma of infancy Patients with FHI present with a painless solitary subcutaneous mass, sometimes with overlying skin discoloration, edema, hypertrichosis, and tethering. Large lesions and multiple tumors in the same patient can be encountered. FHI has been reported in patients with tuberous sclerosis and William syndrome. Essential: characteristic triphasic morphology with bundles of bland fibroblastic/myofibroblastic cells, nodules of primitive mesenchyme, and mature adipose tissue. FHI has a characteristic triphasic organoid pattern with fascicles of bland fibroblastic/myofibroblastic cells admixed with mature adipose tissue and myxoid nodules containing primitive mesenchymal cells with rounded to stellate nuclei. One quarter of cases can show areas resembling giant cell fibroblastoma and composed of hyalinized zones containing collagen with cracking artefact forming slit-like spaces lined by flattened tumor cells. Mitotic figures are infrequent, and necrosis is typically absent. Interspersed inflammatory cells can be seen. By immunohistochemistry, FHI shows variable expression of SMA in the fibroblastic areas and in primitive mesenchyme. S100 is expressed in the adipocytic component. Primitive mesenchyme and areas with giant cell fibroblastoma–like morphology are CD34-positive. EGFR exon 20 insertion/duplication mutations have been identified cases of FHI by targeted next-generation sequencing and Sanger sequencing. Fibrous hamartoma of infancy (FHI) is a soft tissue neoplasm of infants and young children, showing a characteristic organoid, triphasic morphology with bundles of bland fibroblastic/myofibroblastic cells, nodules of primitive mesenchyme, and mature adipose tissue. Lipofibromatosis LPF typically manifests as a slowly growing subcutaneous mass. LPF occurs more often in boys than in girls, with a wide age range (birth to 14 years). As many as 20% of reported cases have been congenital.
