Essential: histology showing an admixture of mature fat, short fascicles of bland spindled cells, and lipoblast-like cells; exclusion of other entities with an LPF-like pattern (e. g. calcifying aponeurotic fibroma, infantile fibrosarcoma). LPF is composed of fascicles of mature fibrous tissue with bland, uniform, elongated nuclei and eosinophilic cytoplasm traversing mature adipose tissue. The adipose tissue may form a major proportion of the lesion. In newborn patients, the fat lobules may have an immature appearance with a myxoid matrix. Small collections of univacuolated cells may be present in the fibroblastic component, where melanin-laden cells have been occasionally documented. Immunohistochemically, the fibroblasts show variable expression of CD34 and SMA, and the fat is S100-positive. Detection of the FN1::EGF gene fusion may be helpful in cases of calcifying aponeurotic fibromas lacking calcification , although this is not required for routine diagnosis. Lipofibromatosis (LPF) is a rare pediatric soft tissue tumor with a distinctive admixture of mature fat, fascicles of bland spindled cells, and lipoblast-like cells. Inclusion body infantile digital fibromatosis The typical presentation is a painless, dome-shaped to polypoid cutaneous lesion that can occur multiply (multinodular or metachronous on ipsilateral digits). Tumors arise equally in boys and girls aged < 5 years; most occur during the first year of life and about 30% are congenital, although adult tumors are rare. Classically, these tumors arise from the dorsal/dorsolateral distal to mid portion of the fingers and toes, although they rarely involve the thumb, great toe, hand, or foot; extra-digital locations (extremities, tongue, breast) are rare. Essential: a bland, dermal-based, myofibroblastic spindle cell tumor with intracytoplasmic pink-red inclusions. These are dermal-based lesions composed of spindled myofibroblastic cells arranged in short to medium-length fascicles, sometimes with a whorled or storiform arrangement. The fascicles are often arranged perpendicularly to the epidermis, surrounding skin adnexal structures, with variable collagen content. The nuclei are cytologically bland and there are typically intracytoplasmic pale-pink to red inclusions that may be paranuclear and can indent the nucleus. Trichrome and Movat’s pentachrome stains can help highlight these inclusions, staining them red and pink, respectively. The inclusions are composed of actin-rich myofilaments that stain for SMA, calponin, and sometimes caldesmon. Inclusion body fibromatosis is a benign myofibroblastic tumor with recurrent potential, characterized by intracytoplasmic eosinophilic inclusions. Juvenile hyaline fibromatosis (hyaline fibromatosis syndrome) HFS manifests in infancy or later in childhood as slow-growing papular and nodular skin lesions. Patients affected by juvenile hyaline fibromatosis show joint contractures (in 85–95% of cases), gingival hyperplasia, osteopenia, and osteolytic lesions. Infantile systemic hyalinosis frequently manifests with extreme pain at minimal handling. Essential: subcutaneous nodules and gingival hypertrophy with prominent hyaline-like material. Desirable: germline sequencing of ANTXR2. HFS lesions are characterized by plump to spindled uniform fibroblasts, often arranged in cords simulating vascular spaces, admixed with abundant extracellular eosinophilic, non-fibrillar hyaline material, obliterating normal structures. The hyaline-like extracellular matrix deposits stain strongly with PAS and are diastase-resistant. Molecular testing is necessary to demonstrate a germline mutation of ANTXR2. Hyaline fibromatosis syndrome (HFS) is a rare autosomal recessive disease characterized by abnormal deposits of amorphous substance in the dermis, subcutaneous soft tissues, gingiva, and visceral sites, with clinical manifestations varying from very severe (infantile systemic hyalinosis) to milder (juvenile hyaline fibromatosis). Fibromatosis colli Fibromatosis colli manifests as a mass in the sternocleidomastoid muscle, most often congenitally or within 2–4 weeks of birth. The mass may continue to grow over several weeks, then stabilize and spontaneously resolve in most cases. Approximately 10–20% of patients develop torticollis; such patients show head tilt towards the involved sternocleidomastoid muscle (chin directed towards the contralateral shoulder). Essential: a fusiform mass associated with the sternocleidomastoid muscle of an infant; biopsy or FNAB (if performed) shows a bland fibroblastic proliferation with associated atrophic skeletal muscle. Surgical specimens are uncommon; only a minority of patients require tenotomy for persistent torticollis. Histology demonstrates a paucicellular, scar-like, fibroblastic proliferation entrapping skeletal muscle. Fibromatosis colli is a benign, self-limiting fibrous proliferation in the sternocleidomastoid muscle of infants. Calcifying aponeurotic fibroma Patients with CAF typically present with a slowly growing, superficially located painless mass. The age range is wide, with a peak in incidence at 5–15 years. Patients are more commonly male than female. Essential: an infiltrative fibromatosis-like fibroblastic lesion with variable chondroid foci with possible calcification. Desirable (in selected cases): demonstration of FN1::EGF fusion. Lesions are infiltrative into the surrounding fat, muscle, fascia, tendons, and neurovascular bundles. They consist of fascicular, fibromatosis-like spindle cells and less cellular chondroid zones, often with calcification, bordered by rounded epithelioid cells. Both components are variably present, and early lesions show only a fibromatosis-like pattern. Osteoclast-type giant cells may be present. By immunohistochemistry, lesional cells variably express SMA, MSA, and CD99, while S100 is positive in the chondroid areas. Demonstration of an FN1::EGF fusion may be helpful. Calcifying aponeurotic fibroma (CAF) is a benign tumor of children and adolescents, with a predilection for the distal extremities, characterized by bland spindle cells and zones of calcification with plump epithelioid fibroblasts. Sinonasal angiofibroma The classic triad of nasal obstruction, epistaxis, and nasopharyngeal mass is seen in most patients, often over a prolonged symptom duration. Biopsy is contraindicated because of potentially profuse bleeding. With tumor progression, facial deformity, deafness, diplopia, and proptosis may be seen. Essential: male patient; nasopharynx/posterior nasal cavity location; numerous vessel types and sizes, some with muscular walls; stromal stellate fibroblasts with variably collagenized stroma. Desirable: stromal cell nuclear β-catenin and AR immunoreactivity. There are numerous blood vessels of various sizes, from slit-like capillaries to irregularly dilated and branching vessels. The vascular walls may be thin to focally or continuously thickened and muscular. No elastic tissue is identified in the vessels except in the feeding arteries. The stroma is composed of bipolar or stellate fibroblastic cells with plump, vesicular, spindled nuclei and indistinct nucleoli. Vascular markers highlight the vessels and SMA in the smooth muscle vascular wall, while the stromal cells only show strong nuclear expression of AR and β-catenin. Aberrant nuclear β-catenin expression is seen in most tumors. Sinonasal angiofibroma is a locally aggressive, variably cellular fibrovascular neoplasm arising in the nasopharynx of boys and young men. Plantar/palmar fibromatoses The clinical presentation of palmar fibromatosis includes contractures, swelling, or a painless nodular mass. Patients with plantar fibromatosis usually present with asymptomatic nodules. A subset of patients have synchronous or metachronous lesions. Essential: long fascicles of bland fibroblasts and myofibroblasts; variably collagenous stroma. Microscopically these tumors are composed of a nodular, sometimes plexiform, arrangement of spindle cells. Three phases of growth (proliferative, involutional, and late-stage) have been described, with progression from cellular lesions composed of parallel fascicles of fibroblasts and myofibroblasts to tumors with increased collagen deposition and low cellularity. Mitotic activity can be prominent, but atypical mitoses are absent. Perivascular chronic inflammation, microhemorrhage, and multinucleated giant cells may be appreciated. Palmar/plantar fibromatoses are benign fibroblastic and myofibroblastic proliferations that involve the volar aspects of the hands or the plantar aponeuroses. Dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans DFSP and GCF typically occur as painless, single, red-blue, slowly growing skin plaques or nodules. Other forms exist, including atrophic plaques and morpheaform lesions. The lesion rarely extends beyond 50 mm. Essential: for classic DFSP: a dermal-hypodermal tumor; monotonous spindle cells arranged in a storiform pattern; infiltration of the subcutaneous fat with a honeycomb pattern; CD34 expression; for fibrosarcomatous DFSP: atypical cells with increased mitotic activity arranged in intersecting fascicles producing a herringbone pattern. Desirable: one of the following translocations: COL1A1:: PDGFB, COL6A3::PDGFD, or EMILIN2::PDGFD. Classic DFSP Classic DFSPs are poorly defined tumors invading the dermis and the hypodermis. In the subcutis, the tumor cells entrap fat cells, forming a classic honeycomb pattern. The overlying epidermis can be normal, acanthotic, or ulcerated. DFSP consists of non-atypical spindle cells arranged in a storiform pattern. CD34 is positive in a majority of DFSPs and frequently negative in fibrosarcomatous areas. The identification of the translocation involving PDGFB or PDGFD is useful in non-classic cases. Dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans (DFSP) and giant cell fibroblastoma (GCF) are superficial fibrohistiocytic, locally aggressive, rarely metastasizing tumors harboring a specific fusion gene involving PDGFB or (less often) PDGFD. Desmoid fibromatosis Patients with desmoid fibromatosis present with a slow-growing deep-seated mass. Desmoid fibromatosis is rare, affecting < 4 patients per 1 million person-years and accounting for approximately 2–3% of soft tissue tumors in children. The peak incidence in childhood is between the ages of 6 and 15 years. Essential: infiltrative long, sweeping fascicles of bland fibroblasts and myofibroblasts. Desirable: nuclear β-catenin expression; CTNNB1 mutation (in challenging cases or small biopsies). Histological examination reveals bland (myo)fibroblasts arranged in long, sweeping fascicles with an infiltrative growth pattern. Approximately 20% have an associated Gardner fibroma. The lesional cells typically show tram-track staining for SMA, and the majority (80%) show nuclear β-catenin expression. β-catenin mutation analysis may be helpful in small biopsies and/or when β-catenin immunostaining is difficult to interpret. Desmoid fibromatosis is a locally aggressive, non-metastasizing (myo)fibroblastic neoplasm with a high propensity for local recurrence. EWSR1::SMAD3-rearranged fibroblastic tumor Patients present with a superficially located, often slow-growing lesion at the distal extremities, mainly in acral sites. The tumor in the tibia caused pain and diffuse swelling. There is a strong female preponderance. Essential: a superficially located infiltrating tumor, commonly in the distal extremities / acral sites, consisting of monomorphic spindle cells with central hyalinization; nuclear ERG expression; detection of an EWSR1::SMAD3 fusion gene. Lesions are located in the dermis and subcutis. They show a nodular or multinodular growth pattern with infiltrative margins. There is commonly a biphasic appearance, with high cellularity at the periphery and variable central hyalinization. The spindle cells are arranged in intersecting fascicles. ERG expression is a consistent immunohistochemical finding, unlike in other fibroblastic lesions, and other markers are negative (CD34, SMA, desmin, caldesmon, S100, SOX10, MUC4, β-catenin). Detection of a fusion of EWSR1 (exon 7) with SMAD3 (exon 5), usually by RT-PCR, next-generation sequencing techniques, or FISH (the latter commonly for EWSR1), is required for diagnosis. EWSR1::SMAD3-rearranged fibroblastic tumor is a benign, locally recurring fibroblastic tumor with a characteristic clinical, morphological, immunohistochemical, and genetic profile. Infantile fibrosarcoma Patients typically present with a painless mass or exophytic nodule; rapid growth may occur. Approximately one third of cases are congenital. Imaging, typically ultrasound in young children, demonstrates a heterogeneous enhancing mass with relatively nonspecific characteristics. Essential: a primitive ovoid/round cell or spindle cell tumor, often arranged in sheets or fascicles; hemangiopericytoma-like vessels and/or mixed chronic inflammation. Desirable: ETV6::NTRK3 or other reported fusions or activating alterations of receptor tyrosine kinase pathway genes (e. g. NTRK1, NTRK2, NTRK3, RET, MET, BRAF). IFS may demonstrate a spectrum of histological patterns across cases and within a given case. Most frequently, IFS is a cellular, monomorphic neoplasm composed of primitive, ovoid/round to spindled cells, arranged either in compact, haphazard sheets or in long fascicles. Often tumors demonstrate a prominent ectatic or hemangiopericytoma-like vascular pattern. The background stroma may range from myxoid to heavily collagenous. The IFS immunoprofile is nonspecific, with variable expression of SMA, S100, CD34, and (rarely) desmin. Those tumors harboring NTRK gene rearrangements typically show expression for pan-TRK antibodies. Gene fusions or activating alterations involving receptor tyrosine kinase (e. g. ETV6::NTRK3) or the downstream effector molecule (BRAF) fusions or activating alterations may be demonstrated by various molecular modalities. Infantile fibrosarcoma (IFS) is a fibroblastic tumor, most frequently occurring in infancy, that is often locally aggressive but infrequently metastasizes. Pediatric NTRK-rearranged spindle cell neoplasm Patients with these tumors most frequently present with a palpable mass. The largest series combined demonstrate a wide age distribution (range: 0–77 years; overall median: 19 years). In the pediatric population, > 55% of cases occur in the first year of life. Essential: haphazardly arranged monomorphic primitive spindle cells; characteristic histological pattern(s) as summarized in 6. 04 ; fusions or activating alterations of receptor tyrosine kinase pathway genes (e. g. NTRK1, NTRK2, NTRK3, RET, RAF1, BRAF); exclusion of well-established pathological entities such as inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor and infantile fibrosarcoma. Desirable: expression of CD34 and/or S100. A broad morphological spectrum has been described, including tumors reminiscent of infantile fibrosarcoma, inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor, lipofibromatosis, and malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumor. The main histological patterns are summarized in 6. The most consistent feature is haphazardly arranged primitive/monomorphic spindle cells. Some cases have distinctive stromal and/or perivascular hyalinization. By immunohistochemistry, many tumors show variable coexpression of CD34 and S100. In those tumors with NTRK gene fusions, pan-TRK expression is also present. Testing for NTRK gene or downstream effector molecule (BRAF) fusions or alterations may be useful. This is an emerging family of rare spindle cell tumors showing a wide morphological spectrum, from lipofibromatosis-like lesions (lipofibromatosis-like neural tumor) to infantile fibrosarcoma–like lesions, and harboring NTRK1, NTRK2, or NTRK3 gene rearrangements or other gene alterations (such as RAF1, BRAF, or RET) implicated in receptor tyrosine kinase pathway activation. Low-grade fibromyxoid sarcoma / sclerosing epithelioid fibrosarcoma Patients typically present with a painless mass. In patients aged < 21 years, most LGFMSs are < 50 mm at presentation and typically localized, without evidence of nodal or distant metastases. LGFMS typically occurs in young adults, with a wide age range. LGFMS Essential: alternating fibrous/myxoid areas; bland spindle cells in whorls / short fascicles; diffuse strong MUC4 (in nearly all cases). Desirable: demonstration of FUS gene rearrangement (in selected cases). SEF Essential: epithelioid cells in cords, nests, or trabeculae, in a dense sclerotic stroma; diffuse strong MUC4; keratin-negative. Desirable: demonstration of EWSR1::CREB3L1 or other rearrangements (in selected cases). LGFMS comprises hypocellular collagenous areas and cellular myxoid nodules, with abrupt transition. The cells are spindled or angulated, with even chromatin and indiscernible or fibrillary cytoplasm (usually minimally atypical), and arranged in short fascicles or whorls. Mitoses are generally inconspicuous. Vessels are arteriole-sized with perivascular sclerosis, or hemangiopericytic. Strong diffuse cytoplasmic expression of MUC4 is seen in about 99% of LGFMSs and 90% of SEFs and is highly sensitive and specific for these among fibroblastic and neural neoplasms. MUC4-negative SEF can show histological features similar to those of MUC4-positive SEF and hybrid LGFMS/SEF with fusions of FUS or EWSR1 with CREB3L1 or CREB3L2, and prominent epithelioid cellular morphology. However, MUC4-negative SEF shows a spectrum of morphological features. If MUC4 is negative or unavailable, identification of any of the fusion genes, or identification of FUS or EWSR1 rearrangement, supports the diagnosis. LGFMS typically harbors FUS::CREB3L2 or FUS::CREB3L1 fusions; these also occur in SEF, but EWSR1::CREB3L1 is more common. Low-grade fibromyxoid sarcoma (LGFMS) and sclerosing epithelioid fibrosarcoma (SEF) are malignant fibroblastic neoplasms showing morphological and molecular overlap. Inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor Abdominal tumors may cause vague abdominal pain, gastrointestinal obstruction, or bleeding. Pulmonary IMTs are associated with cough, chest pain, and dyspnea. Some patients develop a constitutional inflammatory syndrome of fever, malaise, weight loss, anemia, thrombocytosis, polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia, and elevated ESR and C-reactive protein. Essential: loose or compact fascicles of spindle cells with a prominent inflammatory infiltrate and a variable fibrous or myxoid stroma; expression of ALK (in as many as 60% of cases) Desirable: demonstration of rearrangements of ALK, ROS1, NTRK3, or other genes. IMT is characterized by a proliferation of spindled and elongated fibroblastic-myofibroblastic cells, with variation in cellularity, stroma, and inflammatory infiltrate, featuring three basic patterns that are often combined in a single tumor ( 6. Scattered ganglion-like cells with abundant cytoplasm, vesicular nuclei, and prominent nucleoli are frequent. Dystrophic calcification and osseous metaplasia may be present. Necrosis is uncommon and mitotic activity is variable. IMT displays variable staining for SMA, MSA, calponin, and desmin. Focal keratin immunoreactivity is seen (in ~30% of cases). ALK immunohistochemistry is positive (membranous, cytoplasmic, perinuclear, or dot-like) in 50–60% of cases and correlates with the presence of ALK gene rearrangement. Molecular assays are recommended for diagnosis. FISH for ALK gene rearrangements is widely used; however, occasional false negative results occur in the setting of abundant inflammation or in the presence of intrachromosomal inversions, such as EML4::ALK fusion. Inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor (IMT) is a rarely metastasizing neoplasm composed of myofibroblastic and fibroblastic spindle cells with an infiltrate of plasma cells, lymphocytes, and/or eosinophils. Low-grade myofibroblastic sarcoma Patients typically present with an enlarging mass. Pain and associated symptoms are rare. Radiologically, the tumors show destructive growth. Essential: infiltrative cellular fascicles of myofibroblastic spindle cells; at least focal nuclear atypia; variable SMA and/or desmin expression. Tumors are diffusely infiltrative, often growing between skeletal muscle fibers, and typically comprise cellular, loosely fascicular, or storiform proliferations of spindle cells with elongated vesicular nuclei, small pinpoint nucleoli, and poorly defined and palely eosinophilic cytoplasm, in a collagenous stroma. Rarely, neoplasms are hypocellular, with extensive collagenous/hyalinized matrix. LGMS can mimic benign or intermediate myofibroblastic neoplasms (e. g. nodular fasciitis or fibromatosis), and although the cells of LGMS can be bland in areas, there is at least focal atypia (typically mild to moderate) with enlarged, hyperchromatic, irregular nuclei. Mitotic activity is typically low, and necrosis is infrequent. Tumors express SMA at least focally (frequently with subplasmalemmal accentuation) and calponin. Some express desmin; most lack h-caldesmon. About 30% express nuclear β-catenin. No recurrent molecular alterations have been described. Low-grade myofibroblastic sarcoma (LGMS) is a rarely metastasizing tumor of cells with myofibroblastic differentiation, typically with mild to moderate atypia, that has a predilection for head and neck sites in childhood. Fibrous histiocytoma Cutaneous FHs (dermatofibromas) are elevated or pedunculated red-brown or blue-black lesions measuring < 10 mm to a few centimetres in diameter. Rarely, they may form a depressed area in the skin (atrophic dermatofibroma). Deep FH manifests as a slow-growing, painless mass. Desirable: for epithelioid FH: demonstration of ALK overexpression by immunohistochemistry or of ALK gene rearrangements by FISH (in selected cases). Cutaneous FH (dermatofibroma) is composed of short spindle cells arranged in a haphazard manner. Tumor cellularity is often higher in the center and reduced in the periphery, where the tumor interdigitates with dermal collagen (collagen trapping). Variable numbers of foamy histiocytes, multinucleated (including Touton) giant cells, and chronic inflammatory cells may be present. Dermatofibroma is mostly centerd in the dermis, but minimal penetration of the subcutis may be seen. A subset of tumors express SMA and desmin, whereas CD34 (often patchy and at the periphery of the tumor) is seen in 5% of cases. Fibrous histiocytoma (FH) is a neoplasm composed of fibroblastic and histiocytic cells arranged in sheets or short fascicles, often accompanied by a varying number of inflammatory cells, foam cells, and siderophages. Plexiform fibrohistiocytic tumor Patients with PFHT present with a slow-growing tumor or plaque measuring about 25 mm (range: 5–80 mm). PFHT shows a wide age range, with a predilection for children and young adults (mean age: ~15 years, range: 1–77 years); 50–70% of cases occur in patients aged < 20 years. There is a slight female predominance. Essential: nodules of histiocytoid cells and often osteoclastic-like giant cells; fascicles of (myo)fibroblastic spindle cells; plexiform architecture. PFHT is localized to the dermal–subcutaneous junction, with infiltration of subcutaneous adipose tissue and skeletal muscle. The tumor is characterized by a plexiform or multinodular arrangement of nodules of histiocytoid cells with a variable number of admixed multinucleated, osteoclastic-like giant cells, connected by fascicles of spindled fibroblastic/myofibroblastic cells. Other histological changes include chronic inflammation, metaplastic bone, hemorrhage, and hemosiderin deposition. Mild to moderate cytological atypia may be present; marked pleomorphism is rare. SMA is expressed in the (myo)fibroblastic component. Those tumors with an overabundance of the (myo)fibroblastic component (e. g. fibroblastic PFHT) may mimic fibromatosis, the recently described plexiform myofibroblastoma , plexiform neurofibroma, and fibrous hamartoma of infancy. A prominent fibrohistiocytic pattern may be reminiscent of dermatofibroma, which lacks the plexiform pattern. Plexiform fibrohistiocytic tumor (PFHT) is a rare dermal and subcutaneous neoplasm composed of biphasic nodules of histiocytoid cells and spindled myofibroblasts arranged in a plexiform architecture. Tenosynovial giant cell tumor Patients with these tumors generally present with swelling and pain, as well as a reduced range of motion in intra-articular disease or a soft tissue mass in extra-articular disease. Radiographically, most tumors appear as poorly defined periarticular masses. On MRI, these tumors show decreased signal intensity in both T1- and T2-weighted images, with artefacts from hemosiderin deposition. Essential: an intra- or extra-articular location; varying proportions of small histiocytic cells, large amphophilic cells, foam cells, and multinucleated giant cells. Desirable: demonstration of CSF1 rearrangement (in selected cases). The microscopic appearance of tenosynovial giant cell tumors is variable and depends on the proportions of mononuclear cells, multinucleated giant cells, foamy macrophages, inflammatory cells, and hemosiderin, as well as the degree of collagenization of the stroma. Two principal cell types are identified within the mononuclear component: small histiocyte-like cells with pale cytoplasm and round or reniform nuclei, and larger epithelioid cells with amphophilic cytoplasm and rounded vesicular nuclei. The larger cells often contain a peripheral rim of hemosiderin granules. Osteoclast-like giant cells are less common in the diffuse form than in the localized form, and they may be absent or extremely rare in as many as 20% of cases. The larger mononuclear cells express clusterin, and in 45–80% of cases a small subset of these cells stain for desmin, which highlights their dendritic processes. The smaller, histiocyte-like cells are positive for CD68, CD163, and CD45. Correlation of histological features with immunohistochemistry and (in selected cases) molecular characterization can help in the distinction of tenosynovial giant cell tumor from juvenile xanthogranuloma (the latter of which has prominent xanthomatous cells and eosinophils, factor XIIIa-positive); giant cell tumor of soft tissue (absence of clefts and presence of metaplastic bone formation); soft tissue aneurysmal bone cyst (desmin-negative, USP6 fusion); and tendon sheath fibroma (absence of mononuclear histiocytoid and epithelioid cells). The term “tenosynovial giant cell tumor” encompasses a group of lesions most often arising from the synovium of joints, bursae, and tendon sheaths and showing synovial differentiation. Capillary malformations Vascular Tumors and Malformations NS comes to clinical attention at birth as one or more pink to red macules that fade with time; if it persists, it is called a CM. Those in the central forehead, cervical, and lumbosacral regions may be associated with underlying abnormalities of the CNS or spine. The best-known CM is the facial port-wine stain, which manifests usually unilaterally in one or more trigeminal sensory dermatomes and is sometimes accompanied by overgrowth of adjacent mucosa, soft tissue, and bone. Essential: dilated capillaries and/or postcapillary venules in an appropriate clinical setting. Desirable: detection of alterations in GNAQ, PIK3CA, and occasionally other genes is helpful in selected cases. Involved skin shows dispersed small channels with the appearance of dilated capillaries, postcapillary venules, and sometimes also small veins. At a young age, in the classic facial port-wine stain, only minimal vascular changes are present, but over time in some patients, channels become larger, with thicker (mostly fibrous) walls, and are accompanied by stromal fibrosis and appendageal hyperplasia. Cutaneous stains in lymphatic, venous, or lymphatic-venous malformations consist of dilated capillaries and/or postcapillary venules. GNAQ or PIK3CA mutations are the most commonly encountered findings. A capillary malformation (CM) is a defect in vasculogenesis resulting in the dilatation of cutaneous capillaries and/or postcapillary venules, affecting the skin and mucosa with frequent extension to the hypodermis and occasionally to deeper structures. Venous malformations CVM is a soft, compressible mass, frequently with a cutaneous bluish blush, involving the subcutaneous fat and (often) the dermis and underlying soft tissue. BRBNS manifests as multiple raised blue papules that increase in number over time; rarely, a congenital large mass may additionally be present. GVM is single or multiple, nodular or plaque-like, and pink to bluish-purple. Essential: for CVM: dysmorphic venous channels; for BRBNS: dysmorphic venous channels; for VVM: predominant capillary-type channels with focal or diffuse endothelial immunopositivity for GLUT1 and focal immunopositivity for GLUT1 and D2-40. Desirable: for CVM: somatic TEK or PIK3CA mutation; for BRBNS: somatic TEK mutation; for VVM: somatic MAP2K1 mutation. In CVM, abnormal venous channels vary in number, caliber, shape, and muscularization; they are often anastomotic, and they contain organizing thrombi. BRBNS typically has closely apposed, small, abnormal and often spongiform veins and organizing thrombi. VVM has dispersed or clustered channels with the morphology of large capillaries or venules involving the dermis and hypodermis; rarely, it is predominantly or wholly restricted to the hypodermis. In VVM the endothelium is focally or diffusely immunopositive for GLUT1 and focally immunopositive for D2-40 and PROX1. In certain cases, demonstration of mutations in TEK, PIK3CA, or MAP2K1 may be useful for confirming the type of malformation. Venous malformations are malformed and/or excessive venous channels of any caliber, resulting from an error in vasculogenesis. Arteriovenous malformations Patients with AVM commonly present with a warm, red lesion, which may be complicated by pain, ulceration, and bleeding. Significant arteriovenous shunting can produce high-output cardiac failure. Patients with PWS present with a warm overgrown extremity and a variable capillary stain. Sporadic AVM Essential: malformed arteries and veins and an increase in a microvascular component; correlation with supportive clinical and imaging features. Desirable: demonstration of somatic MAP2K1 mutations. AVM in PWS, CM-AVM, and HHT Essential: a diffuse minimal enlargement of small arteries, capillaries, venules, and small veins. Desirable: for PWS: demonstration of germline and somatic mutations in RASA1 or EPHB4; for HHT: demonstration of germline mutations in ENG, ACVRL1, GDF2, or SMAD4, or genomic involvement of 5q31 or 7p14. AVMs vary in appearance, but important features are disproportionately large arteries and veins, and vessels that often appear indeterminate in lineage. Arteries show focal dissolution of their internal elastic lamina and neointimal cushions; veins show thickened walls with neointimal hyperplasia, although some may have thinned fibrous walls. There is a generalized increase in small vessels whose appearance approximates that of small arteries, capillaries, and veins. Many AVMs have small foci or lobules of small vessels of mostly capillary caliber, which can mimic lesions such as lobular capillary hemangioma (pyogenic granuloma), infantile or congenital hemangioma, or the pseudokaposiform proliferation associated with Stewart–Bluefarb syndrome. AVM has somatic MAP2K1, KRAS, HRAS, or BRAF mutations. PWS has germline and/or somatic mutations in RASA1 or EPHB4. An arteriovenous malformation (AVM) is an error in morphogenesis resulting in arteriovenous communications and malformed arteries, veins, and capillaries. Intramuscular vascular anomalies Localized discomfort is a prime symptom, particularly with FAVA. VM and FAVA have slow flow, whereas IFVA, AVM, and PHOST demonstrate fast flow on imaging. Multifocal small capillary stains are seen anywhere in capillary malformation–arteriovenous malformation disorders (CM-AVM1 and CM-AVM2), which also frequently manifest as Parkes Weber syndrome. VM Essential: abnormally formed venous channels including a spongiform pattern. Desirable: demonstration of somatic TEK or PIK3CA mutation. FAVA Essential: nodular aggregates of back-to-back thin-walled venous channels; abnormal veins; abundant fibroadipose tissue. Desirable: demonstration of somatic PIK3CA mutation. VM is an admixture of spongiform, variably sized, dysmorphic venous channels and minimal interposed skeletal muscle or fibroadipose tissue. FAVA has abundant fibroadipose tissue with nodular aggregates of back-to-back thin-walled venous channels sometimes seen as diverticula of larger dysmorphic veins. Nerves are often encased by fibrous tissue and infiltrated by abnormal venous channels. Lymphoid aggregates are common and some lesions have metaplastic bone, small foci of dysmorphic lymphatic channels, and clusters of vessels of indeterminate lineage with coiling, thick walls, concentric muscular layers, and tiny lumina. Identification of somatic mutations (TEK, PIK3CA, MAP2K1, KRAS) and germline and/or somatic mutations (RASA1, EPHB4, PTEN) may be helpful in diagnosing some patients. Intramuscular vascular anomalies are composed of abnormal capillary and venous channels and/or of channels with arteriovenous communications, sometimes extending beyond the muscular compartment. Lymphatic anomalies CLM usually manifests as a localized or regional swelling, sometimes with cutaneous vesicles, or as one component of a combined vascular anomaly or syndrome. GLA often manifests as serous cavity effusions; thoracic duct abnormalities may be present. Patients with CCLA may present with serous cavity effusions, enteric protein loss, and/or organ dysfunction, and dysmotility or obstruction of major lymphatic channels including the thoracic duct may be seen. Essential: malformed and usually excessive lymphatic channels; correlation with clinical features and imaging. Desirable: immunopositivity for D2-40 and PROX1; molecular evidence of various gene alterations associated with lymphatic malformations, particularly in KLA if biopsy samples are not diagnostic. CLM, GLA, CCLA, and KLA display malformed lymphatic channels (often excessive in number) with irregularly muscularized walls. Large channels or cysts usually have predominantly fibrous walls with occasional strands of smooth muscle. The lymphatic endothelium is flat without atypia and is immunopositive for D2-40, PROX1, CD31, ERG, and FLI1. Endothelial cells often display only focal immunopositivity for CD34 and faint or focal immunopositivity for D2-40 in larger channels or cysts. Identification of mutations, most commonly in PIK3CA or NRAS, may help to assess the diagnosis. Lymphatic anomalies are localized or generalized malformations of the lymphatic system. Congenital hemangioma RICH with fetal involution is virtually regressed by birth, leaving only a cutaneous stain. RICH, PICH, and NICH are well-circumscribed lesions usually measuring several centimetres in diameter. They are raised and pink, blue-red, or purple, with superficial telangiectasia and sometimes a pale halo. Essential: a lobular capillary lesion in RICH, PICH, and NICH, supported by clinical and imaging features. Desirable: detection of GNAQ or GNA11 mutations. All congenital hemangiomas involve skin and hypodermis. In RICH with fetal involution, a few small clusters of capillaries, enlarged dysmorphic veins, arteries with intimal fibrosis, and dilated lymphatic channels are present within a fibrotic dermis and hypodermis. At an early age, RICH, PICH, and NICH are usually similar, with lobules of capillaries with round or stellate lumina, and bland endothelial cells and pericytes. In RICH, regression is accompanied by smaller lobules; apparent loss of lobules; dysmorphic veins; extensive fibrous stroma; and occasionally hemosiderin, calcifications, and cystic spaces. Most RICHs and NICHs have GNAQ or GNA11 mutations. Congenital hemangiomas are benign vascular tumors that are fully grown at birth, with the exception of a subgroup having undergone involution during fetal life. Infantile hemangioma IH affects approximately 5% of infants, usually manifests in the newborn period, reaches its apogee at about 10 months of age, and gradually involutes over several years. IH may be solitary, segmental, indeterminate, or multifocal. The most common appearance is a solitary bright-red raised tumor; less commonly, it is a patch-like lesion. Essential: lobular capillary growth with endothelial cytoplasmic immunoreactivity for GLUT1. IH in the proliferative phase is a lobular capillary lesion involving the dermis, hypodermis, or both. The closely approximated capillaries have neatly configured round and (at times) inconspicuous lumina, and the endothelium and pericytes are uniform, plump without atypia, and mitotically active. Extension into the perineurium and nerves themselves is sometimes seen. Involution brings about larger lumina, a flattened endothelium, a thickened basement membrane, karyorrhectic forms, and intervascular fibrous stroma. Infantile hemangioma (IH) is the most common vascular tumor of infancy and is characterized by a rapid proliferative phase during infancy followed by gradual involution. hemangioma of placenta Placental hemangiomas occur more frequently in patients with multiple gestations; maternal age ≥ 30 years; and with maternal hypertension, pre-eclampsia, or diabetes mellitus. hemangioma of the placenta is the most common placental tumor. It is often found incidentally, occurring in as many as 1% of placentas. Essential: discrete lesion(s); well circumscribed; subchorionic or peripheral location; bulging above the fetal surface; numerous capillaries in a stroma surrounded by trophoblastic cells. Placental hemangiomas arise from stem villi, and usually a layer of trophoblast is seen surrounding the nodule. The angiomatous pattern is the most common, composed of numerous capillaries embedded in a fibroconnective stroma composed of fibroblasts, macrophages, and scant collagenized tissue , resembling cutaneous capillary malformation. Cellular and degenerative subtypes have been described. Degenerative changes, such as necrosis, hyalinization, hemosiderin, and calcification, may be seen. The endothelial lining stains for usual vascular markers such as CD31, CD34, GLUT1, and von Willebrand factor (factor VIII–related antigen). hemangioma of placenta is a benign nodular lesion composed of numerous capillaries. Lobular capillary hemangioma (pyogenic granuloma) Most patients with LCH present with rapidly growing, solitary, erythematous, dome-shaped or pedunculated papules that bleed easily. Lesions can arise in port-wine stains and other vascular malformations. A congenital form, manifesting as multiple cutaneous and visceral lesions, has been reported. Essential: lobules of capillary vessels; edematous stroma. LCH is an exophytic lesion with frequent ulceration, crusting, and neutrophilic inflammation that is usually restricted to the ulcerated area. An epidermal collarette is present in most cases. LCH is composed of lobules of capillaries in an edematous stroma. Focal epithelioid change may be seen. Vessels are lined by bland endothelial cells that are positive for CD31, CD34, and ERG. Capillaries are surrounded by a layer of SMA-positive pericytes. Lobular capillary hemangioma (LCH, also known as pyogenic granuloma) is a common acquired vascular neoplasm of the skin and mucosae composed of lobules of capillary blood vessels. Epithelioid hemangioma Patients with cutaneous tumors present with one or sometimes multiple erythematous to violaceous papule(s) or nodule(s). In children, the lower extremities are commonly involved and may be multifocal. In children, the mean patient age is 14 years (range: 2–18 years). Essential: well-formed vessels lined by epithelioid endothelial cells with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm. Desirable: variable eosinophilic infiltrate; immunohistochemical expression of panendothelial markers and FOSB; FOS or FOSB rearrangement in selected cases. Epithelioid hemangioma is composed of a lobular proliferation of well-formed blood vessels lined by endothelial cells with enlarged vesicular nuclei, small nucleoli, and abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm. Intracytoplasmic vacuoles may be present. There is no multilayering, and vessels have a pericyte layer. The stroma is variably edematous and may have a lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate with eosinophils. They express CD31, CD34, ERG, and frequently FOSB (in ~50% of cases). EMA and keratin immunoreactivity is common. Identification of FOS or FOSB rearrangement is useful in a subset. Epithelioid hemangioma is a benign tumor of well-formed blood vessels lined by epithelioid endothelial cells with abundant cytoplasm and a variable eosinophilic infiltrate. Tufted angioma and kaposiform hemangioendothelioma Patients with TA present with a pink or red-purple cutaneous macule or infiltrated plaque, whereas those with KHE present with a poorly defined, large, bulging, indurated purple-red tumor. Both may be painful and/or associated with hypertrichosis or hyperhidrosis. KMP usually occurs in the setting of large congenital or early infantile TA/KHE lesions and is characterized by profound thrombocytopenia due to intratumoral platelet trapping, frequently accompanied by petechiae, ecchymoses, and a sudden increase in tumor size. Essential: for TA: a cannonball-like distribution of multiple small and discrete intradermal lobules of tightly packed small capillaries; for KHE: poorly defined coalescing vascular nodules containing fascicles of plump spindled endothelial cells. Desirable: for TA and KHE: a background of variably dilated lymphatic vessels; dual positivity of spindled endothelial cells for panendothelial and lymphatic markers; presence of platelet-rich microthrombi. Classic TA histology shows multiple small, well-circumscribed vascular tufts dispersed in a cannonball-like fashion within the dermis, sometimes extending into the subcutis. The tufts are composed of closely packed capillaries with compressed lumina, occasionally accompanied by subtle fascicles of delicate spindled endothelial cells. Dilated thin-walled lymphatic vessels focally form crescentic clefts at the tuft periphery. Classic KHE histology includes the presence of vascular tufts equivalent to those of TA but accompanied by larger, less-defined, coalescing nodules composed of fascicles of spindled endothelial cells forming elongate slit-like lumina containing erythrocytes and curving around epithelioid, pericyte-rich nodules with central microthrombi. TA/KHE endothelial cells are strongly positive for the panendothelial markers CD31, CD34, and ERG, and the spindled forms are also positive for lymphatic markers including podoplanin, LYVE1, and PROX1. Tufted angioma (TA) and kaposiform hemangioendothelioma (KHE) are related (probably biologically synonymous) vascular tumors, usually pediatric in presentation. Papillary intralymphatic angioendothelioma and retiform hemangioendothelioma PILA and RHE manifest as slow-growing, cutaneous, pink-violaceous nodules or plaques. With both PILA and RHE, a concurrent lymphatic malformation (lymphangioma) or lymphedema may be observed. With < 50 cases of each reported, PILA occurs predominantly in children and young adults, whereas RHE occurs mainly in adolescents and young adults. Essential: for PILA: poorly defined dissecting lymphatic spaces with intraluminal papillary columnar cell tufting, with no atypia or mitoses; the lymphatic phenotype is evidenced by morphological intraluminal proteinaceous fluid and stromal and intraluminal lymphocytes or by VEGFR3 or D2-40 immunoreactivity; for RHE: retiform arborizing vascular channels lined by hobnail endothelial cells, with no atypia or… PILA is composed of columnar, matchstick-like endothelial cells. Papillary tufts of these hobnail endothelial cells surrounding hyaline cores protrude into the lumen of dilated lymphatic spaces; lymphatics may be slit-like with intraluminal glomeruloid endothelial proliferations. Proteinaceous fluid and intraluminal and stromal lymphocytes support the lymphatic phenotype and association. There should not be significant endothelial atypia or mitoses; such cases would instead be classified as angiosarcoma. Both PILA and RHE stain for lymphatic markers (PILA stains for podoplanin [recognized by D2-40], PROX1, VEGFR3, or VEGFR2; RHE stains for PROX1 and occasionally D2-40) as well as endothelial markers (CD31, CD34, and ERG). SMA should be positive around the larger lymphatic spaces and may be absent within the papillary tufting. The presence of SMA also separates these entities from angiosarcoma. Papillary intralymphatic angioendothelioma (PILA) and retiform hemangioendothelioma (RHE) are locally aggressive, rarely metastasizing lymphatic tumors with hobnail endothelia, which may represent a spectrum rather than different types. Pseudomyogenic hemangioendothelioma The typical presentation is painful or painless cutaneous and subcutaneous nodules that may be multifocal in approximately 60% of patients. Multiple tissue planes are usually affected, with 50% of patients having intramuscular lesions and about 20% having lytic bony lesions. The tumors are highly avid on FDG-PET, a technique used to identify multifocal lesions. Essential: plump spindle or epithelioid cells with vesicular nuclei and eosinophilic cytoplasm; fascicular or sheet-like growth; expression of ERG, FOSB, and keratins (AE1/AE3). Desirable: demonstration of FOSB fusion. The tumor is composed of sheets and fascicles of plump spindle cells with abundant bright eosinophilic cytoplasm resembling rhabdomyoblasts (hence the term “pseudomyogenic”). A minor component of epithelioid cells is present and rarely predominates. Intraosseous tumors are often dominated by epithelioid cells with cytoplasmic eosinophilia, associated with reactive woven bone, hemorrhage, and osteoclast giant cell reaction. The tumor cells contain vesicular nuclei with small nucleoli. The tumor cells show diffuse expression of keratins (AE1/AE3) and endothelial markers (FLI1 and ERG). CD31 is positive, while CD34 is negative. FOSB immunohistochemistry shows diffuse nuclear staining. Detection of FOSB rearrangements may be helpful in the diagnosis. Pseudomyogenic hemangioendothelioma is a rarely metastasizing endothelial neoplasm occurring in adolescents and young adults, with a propensity for occurring as multiple discontiguous nodules in different tissue planes, mimicking myoid neoplasms and epithelioid sarcoma. Kaposi sarcoma In children, KS may be disseminated and rapidly progressive. Clinical manifestations in children differ from those seen in adults. Iatrogenic/transplantation-related KS is variable, with lymph node, visceral, and mucocutaneous involvement, as well as cytopenia and fast progression. Essential: appropriate clinical context; bland spindle cell proliferation containing small slit-like vessels lined by mildly atypical cells; extravasated erythrocytes; detection of nuclear KSHV/HHV8 expression by immunohistochemistry or PCR. KS lesions start with a proliferation of spindle cells with no or mild atypia, where lumen formation is not quite evident; then slit-like spaces become more obvious, with intraluminal erythrocytes, sparse lymphocytes, plasma cells, and hemosiderin. Spindle cells form short fascicles in between vessels. Central areas with necrosis are rich in tiny vessels, erythrocytes, hyaline globules, and eosinophilic debris. Vascular visceral dissemination reaches different organs, forming multiple enlarging unencapsulated nodules. Immunohistochemically, endothelial and spindle cells express CD31, CD34, ERG, and lymphatic markers (podoplanin, LYVE1). KSHV/HHV8 detection by PCR is a well-established approach for the confirmation of viral infection. EBV-associated smooth muscle tumors occur in the context of organ transplantation or immunodeficiency. They can develop in any organ, at single or multiple sites, and are EBV-positive by in situ hybridization for EBV-encoded small RNA (EBER). Bacillary angiomatosis often occurs in HIV-positive patients. Kaposi sarcoma (KS) is an aggressive angiogenic tumor associated with the herpesvirus KSHV/HHV8. Epithelioid hemangioendothelioma Presentation varies depending on location. Patients with soft tissue EHE usually present with a painful mass. A high incidence of multiorgan disease is reported in children. Essential: cords and nests of epithelioid cells in a myxohyaline stroma; immunoreactivity for endothelial markers, CAMTA1, or TFE3. Desirable: molecular confirmation of WWTR1::CAMTA1 or YAP1::TFE3. EHE is an infiltrative tumor composed of cords and nests of bland epithelioid tumor cells with round nuclei, eosinophilic cytoplasm, and variable intracytoplasmic vacuoles in a myxohyaline stroma. Angiocentric growth, which can be occlusive, is seen in some cases. A small subset of tumors have nuclear atypia and more mitotic activity. Immunoreactivity for cytokeratin is seen in a minority. By immunohistochemistry, they are typically positive for ERG, CD31, and CAMTA1, and they are variably positive for keratins, SMA, CD34, and podoplanin. Identification of the WWTR1::CAMTA1 or YAP1::TFE3 fusions. Epithelioid hemangioendothelioma (EHE) is a malignant vascular neoplasm composed of epithelioid endothelial cells in a myxohyaline stroma. Angiosarcoma The clinical presentation is variable, depending on location. Cutaneous pediatric angiosarcomas tend to be unifocal, rapidly enlarging masses that can ulcerate, although some are multifocal. Pediatric angiosarcoma is extremely rare. Essential: a vasoformative or sheet-like growth pattern; nuclear atypia; mitotic activity; immunoreactivity for CD31 and ERG. Angiosarcomas are infiltrative lesions, variably composed of anastomosing vessels or sheets of epithelioid to spindled cells. Vasoformative channels are usually scarce in pediatric cases and often exhibit multilayering of endothelial cells and papillary projections. Most have high-grade nuclear features; well-differentiated tumors may have small hyperchromatic nuclei. Epithelioid angiosarcoma often has a sheet-like growth pattern, with atypical cells exhibiting vesicular nuclei and abundant cytoplasm. Most are immunoreactive for CD31 and ERG and variably positive for CD34 and GLUT1 (50%). Epithelioid angiosarcoma may be positive for EMA and cytokeratin. Detection of MYC amplification in lymphedema- and radiation-associated angiosarcomas may help for the diagnosis. Angiosarcoma is an aggressive malignant vascular tumor showing morphological and immunohistochemical endothelial differentiation. Myofibroma and myopericytoma Perivascular and Smooth Muscle Tumors Patients with MF or MP present with one or more painless, superficial or deep, often reddish nodule(s). MF is the most frequent fibroblastic tumor in children and adolescents. MF is diagnosed in patients of all ages, from birth to adulthood, but most frequently occurs within the first 2 years of life. Essential: for MF: a biphasic pattern with myoid cells forming fascicles and more primitive cells associated with vascular structures; no atypia; for MP: condensation of tumor cells around numerous vessels. Desirable: for MF: identification of PDGFRB mutation in challenging cases, and SRF rearrangement in cellular cases; for MP: identification of PDGFRB mutation in challenging cases. MF has a nodular growth pattern and is characterized by a biphasic zonation appearance associated with a biphasic cell population. Some areas consist of fascicles and whorls of spindle-shaped cells with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm and elongated nuclei with fine chromatin; these areas alternate with areas showing a hemangiopericytoma-like vascular pattern composed of more primitive, round to polygonal cells, with small amounts of amphophilic cytoplasm, hyperchromatic nuclei, and indistinct cell borders. These cells often form nodules bulging into vascular lumina. There is no marked atypia, and the rate of mitosis is variable. MF and MP cells express SMA and may stain for desmin and h-caldesmon. Identification of SRF rearrangement is helpful in the diagnosis of cellular MF. Myofibroma (MF) and myopericytoma (MP) are spindle cell neoplasms with perivascular myoid features. Glomus tumor and glomuvenous malformation cGTs are benign, but well-documented cases of mGT have been reported in adults and (rarely) in children. Cutaneous cGTs manifest as single small blue-red nodules with paroxysmal pain, which is elicited by cold exposure or even by minor tactile stimulation. In deeply located tumors, symptoms are related to compression of surrounding structures. Essential: for cGT: a solid proliferation of monomorphic glomus cells; for GVM: dilated vein-like channels surrounded by one or more layers of glomus cells. Desirable: expression of SMA, MSA, and h-caldesmon by the glomus cells; pericellular collagen IV deposition. cGTs are composed of sheets, nests, and trabeculae of monomorphic glomus cells in a hyalinized or myxoid stroma with branching capillary-sized vessels. Symplastic GTs display prominent nuclear pleomorphism, probably representing a degenerative phenomenon, but have very low mitotic activity. mGTs can be either spindle cell type or round cell type. Features frequently seen in mGT include atypical mitotic figures, increased mitotic activity, high cellularity, necrosis, infiltrative growth, and moderate to high nuclear grade. GVMs show vein-like dysplastic channels of variable size surrounded by one or more layers of glomus cells. Glomus cells in cGTs and GVMs stain positively for α-SMA, MSA, h-caldesmon, and vimentin. Most GTs are diagnosed by morphology and immunohistochemistry. GLMN mutations can be detected in the lesional tissue of GVMs. Glomus tumor (GT) is a mesenchymal neoplasm composed of cells resembling the perivascular modified smooth muscle cells of the normal glomus body. EBV-associated smooth muscle tumor The symptoms are usually related to the site of involvement by the tumor: neurological symptoms in cases of intra-axial or extra-axial CNS tumors; abdominal pain caused by bleeding or obstruction in intestinal cases; and cyanosis or infection caused by obstruction in endobronchial cases. Three groups of EBV-SMT are recognized: HIV-associated, posttransplant (solid organs or hematopoietic stem cells), and congenital immunodeficiency–associated. Essential: a tumor with smooth muscle differentiation; a clinical history of immunosuppression; positivity of EBER in situ hybridization or equivalent. The tumors show short interlacing fascicles of spindle cells with eosinophilic cytoplasm and blunt-ended nuclei. Areas containing more primitive round cells are frequent. Cellular atypia or necrotic foci (i. e. sarcoma-like features) may be seen, especially in HIV-related smooth muscle tumors. Intratumoral T lymphocytes are present. Immunohistochemically, the spindle cells are diffusely positive for SMA and h-caldesmon. Diagnosis is confirmed by EBER in situ hybridization or any other molecular analysis revealing EBV infection. EBV-associated smooth muscle tumors (EBV-SMTs) are spindle cell neoplasms that show smooth muscle differentiation and are associated with EBV infection, usually in the setting of immunosuppression. Rhabdomyoma Skeletal Muscle Tumors A growing mass may cause proptosis, decreased vision, airway obstruction, or hoarseness. 06 for a description of the subtypes listed above. Fetal rhabdomyomas occur at all ages, with two peaks (< 3 years and 60 years). Essential: a well-circumscribed mass with mature rhabdomyoblasts lacking atypia or necrosis; mitotic activity may be present. The classic fetal (myxoid) type contains primitive spindle cells with indistinct cytoplasm arranged in irregular bundles within a myxoid background, interspersed with immature skeletal muscle fibers that resemble fetal myotubes. The intermediate fetal type (juvenile or cellular) shows greater cellularity, less myxoid stroma, and a wide spectrum of skeletal muscle differentiation including differentiated rhabdomyoblasts or ganglion-like rhabdomyoblasts. Mitoses can be relatively frequent (as many as 5 mitoses per 50 mm2), but tumors lack substantial nuclear atypia, infiltrative margins, atypical mitoses, and necrosis. Myogenin and MYOD1 are positive in primitive spindle cells and rhabdomyoblasts. Tumor cells are positive for desmin, MSA, focal SMA, and occasional S100. Fetal rhabdomyoma occurs in association with inherited or sporadic inactivating germline mutations in PTCH1. Extracardiac rhabdomyomas are benign mesenchymal tumors with skeletal muscle differentiation. Rhabdomyosarcomas Patients with ERMS often present with site-specific symptoms (e. g. orbital tumors result in proptosis; genitourinary tumors result in bladder obstruction). ARMS is highly aggressive, typically manifesting as a rapidly growing soft tissue mass with distant or locoregional metastases present at diagnosis in 25–30% of patients. Patients with ARMS may also present primarily with bone marrow involvement mimicking leukemia. Essential: for ERMS: primitive spindle to round cell morphology with differentiating rhabdomyoblasts; heterogeneous nuclear staining for myogenin; for ARMS: monomorphic round cells; homogeneous strong nuclear staining for myogenin; presence of PAX3, PAX7, or FOXO1 rearrangement; for SCSRMS: purely spindled morphology with intersecting fascicles or admixed sclerosing patterns with round cells and abundant… Desirable (in selected cases): MYOD1 mutations or VGLL2::NCOA2 gene rearrangements in SCSRMS; diffuse nuclear staining for MYOD1 in SCSRMS. ERMS recapitulates embryonic skeletal muscle development with primitive mesenchymal cells in various stages of myogenesis. ERMS is variably cellular, ranging from stellate cells in an abundant myxoid stroma to sheets of poorly differentiated, densely packed cells with round to slightly angulated nuclei. ERMS may have a prominent spindle cell morphology, although foci of typical ERMS are usually present. Heterologous cartilage may be seen, particularly in tumors associated with DICER1 syndrome. MYOD1-mutated SCSRMS may be spindled or sclerosing. For all rhabdomyosarcomas, skeletal muscle differentiation is confirmed by immunohistochemical expression of desmin, myogenin (MYF4), and/or MYOD1. ARMS with FOXO1 rearrangements shows strong diffuse nuclear staining for myogenin, whereas ERMS shows variable myogenin expression (10–80% of tumor nuclei). PAX3::FOXO1 or PAX7::FOXO1 translocations are present in approximately 85% of morphological ARMS. L122R mutations or VGLL2::NCOA2 rearrangements. Rhabdomyosarcomas are a family of sarcomas with morphological and/or immunophenotypic evidence of skeletal muscle differentiation, comprising embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma (ERMS), alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma (ARMS), spindle cell / sclerosing rhabdomyosarcoma (SCSRMS), and pleomorphic rhabdomyosarcoma. Ectomesenchymoma Patients with ectomesenchymoma present with a deep or superficial soft tissue mass. Ectomesenchymoma has a predilection for infants or children aged < 5 years (range: birth to 15 years) and an M:F ratio of 1. Ectomesenchymoma appears most frequently in the pelvis, urogenital organs, and intra-abdominal or retroperitoneal soft tissue, but the head and neck, extremities, and mediastinum may be affected. Essential: composite growth of histologically recognizable rhabdomyosarcomatous and neuronal/neuroblastic elements, which are evident by immunohistochemistry. The prototypical morphology is a combined tumor with areas resembling embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma and neuroectodermal elements. The latter cover the entire spectrum of neuroblastic phenotype, ranging from scattered ganglion cells to mature ganglioneuroma, intermediate ganglioneuroblastoma, and primitive neuroblastoma. The appearances of embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma can be botryoid , classic fascicular spindle cell with alternating myxoid/cellular areas , and the so-called dense pattern of primitive round cells. Rare cases originally diagnosed as rhabdomyosarcoma revealed a ganglioneuromatous component in residual tumor after chemotherapy. There are correspondent immunophenotypic patterns of MSA, desmin, MYOD1, and myogenin expression in the rhabdomyosarcomatous area, and synaptophysin and chromogranin A staining in the neuroblastic components, with or without S100-positive Schwannian or satellite cells. Ectomesenchymoma is an exceedingly rare multiphenotypic sarcoma composed of both mesenchymal and neuroectodermal components, and it mostly exhibits intermingled cells recapitulating rhabdomyosarcomatous and ganglionic/neuroblastic differentiation. Pediatric gastrointestinal stromal tumor Gastrointestinal Stromal Tumors Unlike adults, children with GIST are seldom asymptomatic. The most common presentations include symptoms related to gastric mucosal ulceration (e. g. acute and chronic gastrointestinal bleeding, abdominal pain, an abdominal mass, and weight loss). Multifocal tumors may be seen at presentation. Essential: an intramural, submucosal, or subserosal mass; epithelioid, spindle cell, or mixed morphology; KIT and/or DOG1 immunopositivity; SDHB loss in SDH-deficient GIST. Desirable: SDH mutations, SDHC epimutation, or (rarely) KIT mutations. Microscopically, SDH-deficient GISTs are characteristically organized in a multinodular architecture separated by bands of muscularis propria, creating a plexiform pattern of mural involvement. The tumor cells are usually epithelioid or mixed epithelioid and spindle cell; the rare KIT-mutant GISTs in children may show spindle cell morphology. Cytoplasmic vacuolation may be seen. Unlike in conventional GISTs, lymphovascular invasion and lymph node metastases are common. Immunophenotypically, most show strong and diffuse expression of KIT (CD117), which appears as cytoplasmic, membrane-associated, or sometimes perinuclear dot-like staining. CD34 is also commonly expressed; however, the muscle markers SMA and desmin are only rarely expressed, as is S100. Pediatric SDH-deficient GISTs lack the KIT and PDGFRA mutations associated with conventional GIST, as well as BRAF and NF1 mutations and other rare alterations. Molecular subtyping to distinguish between SDH-mutant or SDHC-epimutant tumors should be pursued; in the former category, patients with germline SDH-mutant tumors should be referred for cancer predisposition risk assessment and clinical management and surveillance considerations, whereas patients with SDHC-epimutant tumors need screening only for other Carney triad tumors. Gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST) is a mesenchymal neoplasm characterized by differentiation towards the interstitial cells of Cajal; most GISTs in children are succinate dehydrogenase (SDH)-deficient. Schwannoma Peripheral Nerve Sheath Tumors and Related Lesions Schwannomas are slow-growing tumors, often manifesting as asymptomatic masses or incidental findings on imaging studies. Spinal schwannomas may elicit sensory or, less frequently, motor symptoms. Patients with vestibular schwannomas often present with hearing loss and vertigo. Essential: classic schwannoma histopathology (e. g. Antoni A or Antoni B areas); extensive S100 or SOX10 expression. Desirable: Verocay bodies; hyalinized blood vessels; for epithelioid schwannoma: absence of lattice-like CD34 staining; loss of SMARCB1 (INI1) expression; for syndrome-associated schwannoma: a mosaic pattern of SMARCB1 (INI1) expression. Conventional schwannoma is usually an encapsulated spindle cell tumor that is composed nearly entirely of well-differentiated Schwann cells. Schwannomas have a broad morphological range. The large majority are biphasic tumors with compact areas (Antoni A tissue) showing occasional nuclear palisading (Verocay bodies), alternating with loosely arranged foci (Antoni B tissue). Antoni A areas are the predominant component in the majority of pediatric schwannomas. Diffuse nuclear and cytoplasmic staining for S100, which is more prominent in Antoni A areas than in Antoni B areas, is found in all tumors and subtypes. Similarly, SOX10 immunoreactivity is usually extensive. CD34 is commonly positive only in subcapsular areas, in contrast to the lattice-like staining pattern in neurofibromas, although a small subset of cases show more extensive positivity. Loss of chromosome 22q and/or mutation of NF2 are frequent but nonspecific molecular alterations. Schwannomas exhibit a distinct DNA methylation pattern. Schwannoma is a benign nerve sheath tumor composed entirely or nearly entirely of differentiated neoplastic Schwann cells. Neurofibroma Cutaneous neurofibromas are usually asymptomatic and most commonly manifest as a mass. They are mobile soft lesions without a particular anatomical predilection. Deep tumors often occur with motor or sensory symptoms in the distribution of the affected nerve. Essential: an infiltrative, low-cellularity spindle cell neoplasm associated with a variably myxoid to collagenous stroma and a mixed cell population. Desirable: S100 positivity in the Schwann cell population, with a lattice-like CD34 pattern, highlighting the stromal component; intraneural localization; a patient with NF1; for AN/ANNUBP in the setting of NF1: atypical histological features (nuclear enlargement, hypercellularity, architectural loss, mitoses), often with loss of p16 expression. Neurofibromas are characterized by cytologically bland spindle cells with thin, wavy nuclei representing the neoplastic Schwann cell, immersed in a variably loose myxoid stroma. The tumor cells are typically smaller than those of schwannoma. Stromal collagen is characteristic, colorfully likened in classic pathology descriptions to shredded carrots. A variety of other cells are also identifiable in neurofibroma, including perineurial and perineurial-like cells, fibroblasts, and mast cells. The individual fascicles are recognized by the outlining perineurium that is composed of EMA-positive cells. They appear as delicate round, layered structures and are strongly labeled by S100 immunohistochemistry. Other histological features that may be identifiable in individual neurofibromas include Schwann cell nodules, S100-positive onion bulb–like Schwann cell proliferations, melanin pigment, metaplastic bone, epithelioid change, and even glandular differentiation. Molecular analyses do not have an established role in the diagnosis of neurofibroma. However, chromosomal copy-number profiling may be helpful for the evaluation of AN/ANNUBP (CDKN2A or CDKN2B deletion) and its differentiation from MPNST (complex highly rearranged genome). Neurofibroma is a benign peripheral nerve sheath tumor consisting of mature but neoplastic Schwann cells intermixed with non-neoplastic cell types. Perineurioma In intraneural perineurioma, progressive muscle weakness (with or without atrophy) is more frequent than sensory disturbances. Patients with soft tissue perineurioma present with nonspecific mass effects. Both intraneural and soft tissue perineuriomas have been described in patients with neurofibromatosis type 1 and type 2; however, these are rare cases and it is unclear if there is a true association. Intraneural perineurioma Essential: a pseudo–onion bulb pattern on cross-section, with axons in the center; tumor cells are positive for at least one perineurial antigen (EMA, claudin-1, GLUT1) and negative for S100. Soft tissue perineurioma Essential: slender spindle cells with bipolar cytoplasmic processes; storiform and/or whorled architecture; tumor cells are positive for at least one perineurial antigen (EMA, claudin-1, GLUT1) and negative for S100. Intraneural perineurioma consists of concentric layers of perineurial cells around axons, forming characteristic pseudo–onion bulbs. This distinctive architectural feature is best seen on cross-section, wherein fascicles vary in cellularity. Perineurial cells accumulate in the endoneurium, but the perineurium is often affected as well. Particularly large whorls can envelop numerous nerve fibers. Immunohistochemically, tumor cells of intraneural and soft tissue perineurioma are consistently positive for EMA, which ranges from weak and focal to strong and diffuse , and claudin-1 and GLUT1 are also often positive. CD34 is expressed in about 60% of soft tissue perineuriomas. Staining for S100, SOX10, and GFAP is negative. Molecular analyses do not have an established role in the diagnosis of perineurioma. Because of the rareness of perineurioma, a reference group for its DNA methylation–based classification is not currently available. Perineurioma is a benign tumor composed of neoplastic perineurial cells. Hybrid nerve sheath tumor Hybrid nerve sheath tumors occur as painless masses in subcutaneous tissue or dermis. When large peripheral nerves or spinal nerves are involved, the tumors may be associated with pain or neurological deficit. Hybrid nerve sheath tumors are rare. Essential: intermingled features of two types of benign nerve sheath tumors; appropriate immunohistochemical staining for each component. Hybrid schwannoma/perineurioma shows a storiform or fascicular growth and is composed of an admixture of Schwann cells with plump nuclei and eosinophilic cytoplasm and perineurial cells with slender nuclei and delicate elongated cytoplasmic processes. The Schwann cell component is often prominent. The tumors may show degenerative nuclear atypia (ancient change). Rare cases show a biphasic appearance and a lobulated growth pattern, either with separate schwannomatous and perineurial nodules or with schwannomatous nodules surrounded by a perineurial component with a reticular growth pattern and myxoid stroma. The two components can be highlighted by immunohistochemistry: S100-positive Schwann cells and EMA-positive perineurial cells. Immunostaining highlights the mixed population of cells in the neurofibromatous component, including fibroblasts (CD34), Schwann cells (S100 and SOX10), and perineurial cells (EMA, claudin-1, and GLUT1), whereas there is a monomorphic Schwann cell population in the schwannomatous component (diffuse expression of S100 and SOX10). The perineuriomatous areas are immunopositive for EMA, GLUT1, and claudin-1, and the neurofibroma areas show a mixed population of cells including fibroblasts (CD34), Schwann cells (S100 and SOX10), and perineurial cells (EMA, claudin-1, and GLUT1). Hybrid nerve sheath tumors are benign peripheral nerve sheath tumors with combined features of more than one conventional type (neurofibroma, schwannoma, perineurioma). Granular cell tumor Although usually asymptomatic, granular cell tumors can be pruritic to painful in the skin and tongue. Cutaneous lesions are firm, flesh-colored to reddish brown, and 5–30 mm in size. Granular cell tumors usually occur in adults in their fourth to sixth decade of life, but they can be encountered at any age. Essential: nests and sheets of epithelioid to polygonal cells; abundant, intensely eosinophilic, granular cytoplasm; S100 and SOX10 positivity by immunohistochemistry. Granular cell tumor has poorly defined borders and is composed of sheets, nests, and trabeculae of large, monotonous epithelioid to polygonal cells with intensely eosinophilic, granular cytoplasm. Cell borders may be indistinct, producing a syncytial appearance. Nuclei are usually centrally situated and range from uniformly small and mildly hyperchromatic to larger and vesicular with distinct nucleoli. Mitoses are variable in number but usually not prominent. Granular cell tumors are generally reactive for S100, SOX10, nestin, inhibin, and calretinin. Tumors are also positive for CD68, CD63 (NKI/C3 clone), and NSE. MITF and TFE3 (in the absence of gene rearrangements) show diffuse nuclear reactivity in most cases, but HMB45 is uniformly negative, and only very rarely is there focal reactivity for melan-A. A granular cell tumor is a tumor showing neuroectodermal differentiation and composed of epithelioid to polygonal cells with copious eosinophilic, distinctively granular cytoplasm. Solitary circumscribed neuroma Patients with SCN usually present with a slow-growing, firm, painless, circumscribed dermal-based nodule. SCN is mostly solitary, but rare examples of multiple SCNs have been reported, with no evidence of any associated systemic disease. SCN is most common in the fifth to seventh decades of life, but it can occur in patients of any age. Essential: a circumscribed cutaneous lesion of Schwann cell–rich fascicles of nerve fibers with or without partial encapsulation; focal palisading and artefactual clefting; S100 positivity with focal NFP staining; the peripheral capsule is highlighted by perineurial markers (EMA, GLUT1). SCN is a circumscribed dermal-based tumor composed of bland spindle-shaped cells with wavy nuclei in a background of hyalinized collagen. The cells often form well-developed fascicles, and some palisading of nuclei within the tumor is characteristically present. A thin perineurial-derived fibrous capsule may surround the lesion, but it is often incomplete at the superficial aspect. Artefactual clefting is a frequent finding, and extension into the subcutis may be present on occasion. The spindle cells are strongly and diffusely positive for S100. Perineurial cells in the capsule stain for EMA, claudin-1, and GLUT1. No diagnostic molecular findings have been described. Solitary circumscribed neuroma (SCN) is a benign, often cutaneous, nodular proliferation of nerve fibers with Schwann cells predominating over axons, showing a strong predilection for the face. Ectopic meningioma and meningothelial hamartoma The presenting signs and symptoms of ectopic meningiomas vary greatly, with the most common pattern being that of a painless, slow-growing mass. Meningothelial hamartoma is typically detected as an incidental scalp mass or dimple, sometimes with alopecia and/or tenderness. It may be associated with underlying or distant skeletal anomalies or congenital melanocytic nevus. Essential: a meningothelial rest or neoplasm located entirely outside of, and with no connection to, the CNS. The same range of histological appearances and grades encountered intracranially may be seen in ectopic meningiomas, with benign meningothelial tumors being most common. In the scalp, hamartomas usually show slit-like spaces resembling lymphatics. However, they are lined by meningothelial (rather than endothelial) cells. Well-formed meningothelial clusters and psammoma bodies can also be encountered. Highly sensitive and specific immunohistochemical markers are generally lacking, with coexpression of vimentin, EMA, and progesterone used most consistently. Ectopic meningioma is a meningothelial neoplasm occurring entirely outside intracranial and intraspinal cavities. Benign triton tumor / neuromuscular choristoma Patients present most often with progressive pain or features of peripheral neuropathy/plexopathy. There may be atrophy of the involved limb, as well as superimposed desmoid fibromatosis (NMC-fibromatosis) in as many as 80% of cases, with the latter seen mostly after biopsy. On MRI, NMC features T1- and T2-weighted signals similar to those of adjacent skeletal muscle, with no interfascicular fat (unlike fibrolipomatous hamartoma) and minimal contrast enhancement. Essential: skeletal muscle intercalated between intraneural elements; immunohistochemical validation of both endoneurial myogenic and neural elements; intact perineurium surrounding individual fascicles; the presence of nuclear β-catenin expression either in NMC alone or in NMC-fibromatosis. Haphazardly arranged bundles of mature skeletal muscle with cross-striations are intercalated between intraneural elements; smooth muscle elements have also been encountered rarely. In some cranial nerve examples adipose tissue has been reported as well, although this probably represents a different entity. Residual nerve includes NFP-positive axons surrounded by S100-positive Schwann cells. In terms of immunostains, the myogenic component expresses markers of mature skeletal muscle, including desmin. Diffuse expression of myogenin has been recently reported. S45F) mutations supports the diagnosis of NMC with or without associated desmoid fibromatosis. Benign triton tumor / neuromuscular choristoma (NMC) is an expansile intraneural mass characterized by the intimate interposition of mature skeletal muscle and nerve fibers within the endoneurium. Malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumor Like in adults, MPNSTs in children occur as enlarging soft tissue masses, often causing pain, dysesthesia, or other neurological symptoms. Most tumors are large (> 50 mm) and often extend into adjacent structures. MRI features that help distinguish MPNST from benign nerve sheath tumors include peripheral enhancement, peritumoral edema, intratumoral heterogeneity or lobulation, and infiltrative margins, but their sensitivity is about 60%. Essential: a sarcoma arising from a peripheral nerve or in the context of a pre-existing neurofibroma or in a patient with NF1; a sarcoma consisting of fascicles of monomorphic spindle cells with alternating hypercellular and hypocellular areas, geographical tumor necrosis, and numerous mitoses; a spindle cell sarcoma with heterologous elements; a spindle cell sarcoma with nerve sheath differentiation… K27me3 or with MPNST molecular signature; for epithelioid MPNST: a tumor consisting of epithelioid cells with prominent nucleoli showing diffuse expression of S100, absence of melanocytic markers, and SMARCB1 loss. Desirable: for epithelioid MPNST: an associated schwannoma. The majority of MPNSTs consist of fascicles of spindle cells with pale cytoplasm and tapered, wavy, hyperchromatic nuclei. Densely cellular areas alternate with myxoid hypocellular areas, creating a distinctive marbled pattern. Perivascular cell condensation forming cuffs, sometimes with endoluminal protrusions, is characteristic. Geographical necrosis (often with a perivascular-sparing pattern) and numerous mitoses are present. Immunostaining for S100 is patchy or focal in about 50% of conventional MPNSTs, with higher expression in low-grade tumors. SOX10 is expressed in 70–84% of MPNSTs. Myogenic markers, including desmin, MSA, MYOD1, and myogenin, can be used to verify the presence of rhabdomyoblasts. It is important to exclude the entities that enter into the differential and have recurrent molecular alterations (e. g. SS18 [SYT] rearrangement, kinase fusions). Malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumor (MPNST) is a spindle cell sarcoma arising from a peripheral nerve or from a pre-existing benign nerve sheath tumor, or in patients with neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1). Intramuscular/juxta-articular myxoma Myxoid Tumors Overall these tumors occur sporadically, as slow-growing, solitary, painless or painful masses. On MRI, myxoma is bright in T2-weighted images and shows low signal intensity compared with skeletal muscle in T1-weighted images. Intramuscular myxomas are mainly sporadic but may occur in combination with fibrous dysplasia, a condition called Mazabraud syndrome. Essential: bland-looking spindled to stellate cells set in a myxoid stroma. Desirable: sparse capillary-like blood vessels. Intramuscular and juxta-articular myxomas share a common morphological theme: uniform, bland-looking, spindled to stellate cells with round/ovoid nuclei and palely eosinophilic cytoplasm, haphazardly embedded in an abundant myxoid stroma with sparse capillary-like blood vessels. Stromal cystic and frothy changes, sometimes mimicking univacuolated lipoblasts, may be seen. Both lesions may infiltrate, at least focally, into the surrounding tissues.
