Hypercellularity, sometimes associated with a more collagenous stroma and/or increased vascularity, internal fibrous septa, hemorrhage, chronic inflammation, and/or hemosiderin/fibrin deposition are focally observed. Immunohistochemically, the neoplastic cells are variably stained with CD34 and SMA. Intramuscular/juxta-articular myxomas are rare pediatric myxomatous lesions occurring in the muscles of the head and neck and adjacent to large joints, with morphological and immunohistochemical features similar to those of their counterparts in adults. Superficial angiomyxoma Superficial angiomyxomas produce a painless cutaneous or subcutaneous papule or nodule. Superficial angiomyxoma is rare in children. Superficial angiomyxomas have been reported at different sites, including the genital and head/neck regions. Essential: dermal myxoid tumor with a lobular/multinodular configuration. Desirable: arborizing/plexiform capillary-like vessels. Superficial angiomyxoma is composed of bland-looking spindled to stellate cells set in an abundant myxoid stroma with capillary-like vessels that exhibit, at least focally, an arborizing/plexiform configuration. A lobular/multinodular appearance, due to the presence of fibrous septa, is a typical feature. Entrapped cystic epithelial structures may be seen. Superficial angiomyxoma is a bland-looking myxoid dermal tumor with a lobular/multinodular configuration. Deep angiomyxoma Vulvar tumors may mimic a labial cyst or clitoromegaly. In male patients, enlargement of the spermatic cord or a scrotal protruding mass, mimicking a hernia or a hydrocele, is seen. Deep angiomyxoma is rare in children and both sexes are affected, with a wide age range (from infancy to adolescence). Essential: a bland-looking myxoid tumor with numerous thin- to thick-walled blood vessels. Desirable: bundles of smooth muscle cells variably interspersed in the stroma; diffuse desmin immunoreactivity. Deep angiomyxoma is composed of bland-looking, short, spindled and stellate cells set in an abundant myxoid stroma with numerous capillary-like and medium-sized to large blood vessels. Perivascular hyalinization, hypercellular areas, and/or fibrous areas are often seen. Bundles of mature smooth muscle cells, sometimes radiating from the wall of the larger vessels, are variably interspersed in the stroma. Infiltration of the surrounding tissues is common. Immunohistochemically the neoplastic cells often express desmin and variably express CD34 and SMA. Deep angiomyxoma is a bland-looking myxoid tumor occurring in the deep soft tissues, typically of the lower genital tract. Angiomatoid fibrous histiocytoma Tumors of Uncertain Differentiation Typically, patients present with a superficial, painless, slow-growing, and variably fluctuant soft tissue mass. Occasional patients have an associated paraneoplastic syndrome of anemia, fever, and weight loss, related to tumor cytokine production. AFH can occur in adults, but it is most common in the first two decades of life and may occur congenitally. Essential: a small, painless subcutaneous nodule; nodules of epithelioid to ovoid cells arranged in syncytial-like sheets; pseudoangiomatoid spaces; peripheral rims of lymphoplasmacytic cells, including germinal centers; variable desmin, CD99, and EMA immunoreactivity. Desirable (in selected cases): molecular studies confirming EWSR1 gene rearrangement. These tumors are usually well circumscribed and lobulated, with several morphological components. These include (1) sheets or fascicles of spindled or histiocytic-like cells arranged in nodules, containing a moderate amount of eosinophilic cytoplasm and bland vesicular nuclei; (2) non-endothelial lined and blood-filled pseudoangiomatous spaces surrounded by tumor cells; (3) a thick, fibrous pseudocapsule with hemosiderin deposition; and (4) a pericapsular lymphoplasmacytic cell cuff with germinal centers. Nearly one third of tumors lack pseudoangiomatous spaces and are solid, simulating a lymph node. Mitotic figures are usually few, although atypical mitotic figures may be present. Most are positive for SOX9 and are often focally or diffusely immunoreactive for desmin. Perimembranous CD99 staining is common. Tumor cells are consistently negative for MYOD1, myogenin, cytokeratins, S100, and CD34. Demonstration of EWSR1::CREB1, EWSR1::ATF1, or FUS::ATF1 fusion is supportive of the diagnosis. Angiomatoid fibrous histiocytoma (AFH) is a rare mesenchymal tumor of uncertain lineage and with low to intermediate malignant potential. Clear cell sarcoma of soft tissue Most patients present with a palpable mass that grows insidiously over months or years, with a reported median of 10 months between the onset of symptoms and diagnosis in pediatric patients. It may be associated with pain or tenderness in approximately one third to half of the patients. CCS most commonly affects young people, with a peak incidence in the third to fourth decades of life. Essential: nests and short fascicles of plump spindle cells with pale cytoplasm and prominent nucleoli, admixed with occasional wreath-like giant cells; the tumor cells express melanocytic markers including S100, SOX10, melan-A, and HMB45. Desirable: demonstration of EWSR1 rearrangement or EWSR1::ATF1 fusion. CCS is composed of short fascicles and nests of relatively uniform epithelioid or plump spindle cells with vesicular nuclei, prominent central nucleoli, and pale eosinophilic cytoplasm. Despite the name, clear cell features are uncommon. The nests are separated by dense fibrous stroma. Occasional distinctive wreath-like multinucleated giant cells are observed in more than half of all cases. By immunohistochemistry, S100, SOX10, HMB45, melan-A, and MITF are consistently expressed. Demonstration of EWSR1 rearrangement or EWSR1::ATF1 fusion may be helpful to differentiate CCS from melanoma. Clear cell sarcoma (CCS) of soft tissue is a malignant mesenchymal neoplasm with melanocytic differentiation and a distinctive nested growth pattern, most often characterized by EWSR1::ATF1 fusion. Alveolar soft part sarcoma Patients with ASPS present with a slow-growing, painless, intramuscular mass with hemorrhage. MRI is notable for flow voids, large vessels, and moderate to intense postcontrast enhancement. ASPS accounts for < 1% of all soft tissue sarcomas. Essential: eosinophilic polygonal cells in an organoid/nested pattern often encircled by rich sinusoidal capillaries; strong and diffuse nuclear TFE3 expression by immunohistochemistry. Desirable: intracytoplasmic PAS-positive, diastase-resistant crystals; demonstration of TFE3 gene rearrangement or ASPSCR1::TFE3 fusion (in selected cases). ASPS is composed of large polygonal cells with eosinophilic granular cytoplasm, an eccentric vesicular nucleus with a cookie-bite indentation, and a prominent nucleolus, arranged in an alveolar pattern of organoid nests with central discohesion. A rich sinusoidal capillary vasculature encircles tumor nests. Cytoplasmic clearing, rhabdoid cells, a pseudoglandular pattern, central necrosis, and cystic change may be observed. A solid pattern is observed in very young patients, with more alveolar growth in older children and young adults, especially in lingual tumors. Rod-like/rhomboid intracytoplasmic crystalline structures may be identified by PAS with diastase resistance and may stain for MCT1 and CD147. Cathepsin K and occasional calretinin or desmin may be observed. TFE3 rearrangement or ASPSCR1::TFE3 fusion transcripts may be diagnostically helpful. The presence of the ASPSCR1::TFE3 fusion appears to be highly specific and sensitive for ASPS among sarcomas; the same gene fusion can be identified in Xp11. Alveolar soft part sarcoma (ASPS) is a rare tumor of uncertain histogenesis predominantly affecting the deep soft tissues of the extremities, featuring variably discohesive epithelioid cells arranged in nests, resulting in a distinct alveolar appearance. Extrarenal rhabdoid tumor Most patients present with a rapidly enlarging soft tissue mass; the associated clinical symptoms depend on the primary organ involvement. Occasional patients present with multiple cutaneous nodules. Some cases, particularly in infants, manifest as disseminated disease without an obvious primary tumor – such cases are often associated with rhabdoid tumor predisposition. Essential: primitive undifferentiated or rhabdoid cell morphology; loss of expression of SMARCB1 (INI1). The tumor is characterized by rhabdoid cells with large vesicular rounded to bean-shaped nuclei, prominent nucleoli, and abundant cytoplasm, arranged in sheets or in a solid trabecular pattern. Many tumor cells have juxtanuclear eosinophilic, PAS-positive, diastase-resistant hyaline inclusions or globules. At the periphery, tumor cells infiltrate the surrounding tissue. Nuclear pleomorphism is not evident, whereas mitoses are frequent. Immunohistochemically, most of these tumors show expression of epithelial markers such as keratins and EMA. The expression of neural or neuroectodermal markers such as CD99 and synaptophysin is also frequently observed in soft tissue tumors. Less commonly, the cells express MSA and focal S100. Extrarenal rhabdoid tumor is a highly malignant soft tissue tumor that mainly affects infants and children. PEComa Clinical presentation depends on the site. Intra-abdominal tumors may cause acute abdominal symptoms. A few cases of pediatric PEComas, especially in the prepubertal age group, show associations with other malignancies such as neuroblastoma, rhabdomyosarcoma, and acute lymphoblastic leukemia. Essential: a variable proportion of spindle and/or epithelioid cells with abundant clear to eosinophilic cytoplasm, round nucleoli, and pinpoint nucleoli in intimate association with thin-walled capillary vessels; coexpression of melanocytic and smooth muscle markers. Desirable: TFE3 expression (if smooth muscle markers are negative). Histologically, these tumors consist of epithelioid cells with a clear to granular cytoplasm, a round to oval centrally located nucleus, an inconspicuous nucleolus, and a typical perivascular location. In some areas, spindle cells with clear, elongated cytoplasm and distinct cell borders arranged in fascicles are present; in a few tumors (20%), these areas can represent the predominant component, especially in younger patients. Neither adipocytes nor thick-walled blood vessels are observed. Melanin pigment has been identified in the epithelioid and spindle cells in 25% of the tumors. A variable percentage of neoplastic cells consistently stain for melanogenetic markers (e. g. HMB45 and melan-A [MART1]), cathepsin K (a lysosomal papain-like cysteine protease), and muscle markers (especially actin and calponin, and less commonly desmin). Immunoreactivity for vimentin is usually inconspicuous. In childhood, the diagnosis of PEComa may be extremely challenging because of a relatively large differential diagnosis, which differs depending on the tumor site and can include clear cell sarcoma of soft tissue (also known as melanoma of soft parts), alveolar soft part sarcoma, smooth muscle tumors, MiT-family translocation renal cell carcinoma, clear cell sarcoma of the kidney, gastrointestinal stromal tumor, and metastatic melanoma. Perivascular epithelioid cell tumors (PEComas) are mesenchymal tumors composed of perivascular epithelioid cells (PECs), which are characterized by the coexpression of muscle and melanogenetic markers. Synovial sarcoma SS may occur as a longstanding and slow-growing mass, with or without pain. Initial presentation as a small, circumscribed tumor may give the erroneous clinical impression of a benign lesion. SS is most common in adolescents and young adults. Essential: monomorphic spindle cell sarcoma with or without gland formation, showing variable histological and/or immunohistochemical epithelial differentiation; diffuse and strong nuclear immunostaining for TLE1. Desirable: diffuse and strong nuclear immunostaining for SS18::SSX fusion protein or demonstration of an SS18::SSX gene fusion. There are three main histological patterns of SS: monophasic (most common), biphasic (second most common, accounting for as many as a third of cases), and poorly differentiated. Monophasic SS is composed of dense cellular sheets and fascicles of uniform spindle cells. The tumor cells have high N:C ratios and ovoid, hyperchromatic nuclei with regular granular chromatin and inconspicuous nucleoli. Collagen is usually scant, but there may be areas of dense fibrosis or hyalinization. In addition, TLE1 shows diffuse nuclear staining in most cases of SS, although it is not specific and is also expressed in histological mimics such as malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumor and solitary fibrous tumor. Epithelial differentiation can be demonstrated with EMA and cytokeratins. In most cases of SS there is expression of BCL2 and CD99 (which may be perimembranous). Approximately two thirds of SSs carry SS18::SSX1 fusion, one third carry SS18::SSX2, and rare cases carry SS18::SSX4 or SS18L1::SSX1 fusion. Almost all tumors with SS18::SSX2 fusion show monophasic histology, whereas those with SS18::SSX1 fusion show an approximate 2:1 ratio of monophasic to biphasic histology. Synovial sarcoma (SS) is a malignant mesenchymal neoplasm showing variable epithelial differentiation and characterized by a specific SS18::SSX fusion gene. Epithelioid sarcoma C-ES occurs as solitary or multiple slow-growing, painless, firm, superficially located nodules. Lesions often result in non-healing skin ulcers that can clinically mimic ulcerative non-neoplastic dermal processes. Recurrences can involve deep soft tissue, mimicking P-ES. Essential: superficial or deep soft tissue mass; epithelioid to spindled cytomorphology; infiltrative growth; loss of SMARCB1 (INI1, BAF47) expression; staining for vimentin, EMA, and keratins. C-ES consists of cellular nodules of epithelioid and spindled cells with central degeneration and/or necrosis, with a vaguely granulomatous appearance (pseudogranulomatous pattern). Confluent necrotizing nodules result in a serpiginous mass with central geographical necrosis. Deeply situated lesions spread along the fascia as undulating bands of cells punctuated by foci of necrosis. Tumor cells vary from large ovoid/polygonal epithelioid cells to peripheral plump spindle-shaped cells with deeply eosinophilic cytoplasm and mildly atypical nuclei possessing vesicular chromatin and small nucleoli. Both C-ES and P-ES show immunoreactivity for epithelial markers, including low- and high-molecular-weight cytokeratins (CK8 and CK19, whereas CK5/6 is negative or weakly positive) and EMA, in addition to vimentin. Expression of CD34 (50%) and ERG (40–67%, predominantly in C-ES) can cause confusion with vascular tumors. Loss of nuclear expression of SMARCB1 occurs in the vast majority of cases. Epithelioid sarcoma (ES) is a malignant mesenchymal neoplasm characterized by partial or complete epithelioid cytomorphology, expression of epithelial markers, and loss of SMARCB1 (INI1) expression in the majority of cases. Myoepithelial tumors of soft tissue Most patients present with a painless, palpable mass. Patients with visceral or deep-seated tumors may have fever, cough, chest pain, respiratory distress, and paresthesias or weakness due to spinal cord or nerve compression. Overall, 20% of myoepithelial tumors arise in children, and they are more likely to be malignant in this age group. Essential: myoepithelial tumors show trabecular, reticular, nested, and/or solid growth, with a frequent myxoid or hyalinized stroma; mixed tumors show ductal differentiation (which may be focal); myoepithelial carcinomas show increased cytological atypia and mitotic activity; an immunophenotype supporting myoepithelial differentiation is also essential (positivity for EMA and/or keratin and for S100, SOX10, or… Desirable (in selected cases): demonstration of EWSR1 rearrangements (these occur in ~50% of myoepithelial neoplasms, with a wide range of fusion partners). Myoepithelial tumors show marked architectural and cytological heterogeneity, both within a given tumor and between tumors. Most appear multinodular at low power, with variably myxoid, collagenous, or hyalinized stroma. Growth patterns are commonly reticular and trabecular, but they may be nested, fascicular, and solid. Tumor cells are typically spindled or epithelioid, with uniform round or ovoid nuclei and palely eosinophilic, occasionally clear, cytoplasm. Confirmation of myoepithelial differentiation is necessary for diagnosis, although immunophenotypes can be variable. The vast majority (90%) of cases express both epithelial markers (broad-spectrum keratins and/or EMA) and S100. SOX10 is positive in 80%, although in malignant tumors is it less frequent (30%). p63 is positive in a subset of cases (as many as 40%). FISH can be used to detect rearrangements of EWSR1 in myoepithelioma/myoepithelial carcinoma or PLAG1 in mixed tumors. However, RNA or DNA sequencing panels that identify the fusion partner may be needed, because EWSR1 FISH alone may not be sufficient to distinguish myoepithelial neoplasms from other tumors with EWSR1 fusions. Myoepithelial tumors of soft tissue are rare in children. Phosphaturic mesenchymal tumor Longstanding osteomalacia is the most frequent manifestation. Laboratory studies show severe hypophosphatemia and increased levels of FGF23, which can also be demonstrated by RT-PCR in tissue sections of PMTs, even before the development of tumor-induced osteomalacia. PMTs are notoriously difficult to identify because of their tendency to occur as small and inconspicuous lesions in unsuspected places, requiring a meticulous clinical and imaging exploration. Essential: bland spindle cells embedded in a hyalinized matrix with coarse calcification; rich vascularity; phosphaturic wasting and/or osteomalacia, which are cured by tumor removal. Desirable: elevated FGF23 expression in serum or in tumor tissue; demonstration of FN1::FGFR1 or FN1::FGF1 fusion. Most PMTs feature fibroblast-like spindle mesenchymal cells embedded in a hyalinized matrix, which may show coarse calcification. Poorly differentiated chondroid and areas of osseous metaplasia are frequent. Rich vascularization, with capillaries and larger vessels arranged in a pericytomatous or cavernous hemangioma pattern, is characteristic. An array of cells (including osteoclasts, fibrohistiocytic elements, and adipose tissue), frequently surrounded by woven bone, is frequently present. The immunophenotype of most PMTs includes the expression of CD56, ERG, FGFR1, SATB2, and/or SSTR2A. FN1::FGFR1 or FN1::FGF1 fusions are confirmatory ancillary diagnostic techniques. Phosphaturic mesenchymal tumors (PMTs) are neoplasms with a distinctive morphology that usually secrete FGF23, inducing phosphaturic oncogenic osteomalacia in most patients. Desmoplastic small round cell tumor Patients usually present with widespread abdominal/peritoneal involvement. Clinical features (e. g. pain, abdominal distention, a palpable mass, an acute abdomen, ascites, and organ obstruction) are usually related to the primary site of presentation. DSRCT primarily affects children and young adults. Essential: primitive-appearing tumor cells that are immunopositive for cytokeratin and desmin and immunonegative for skeletal muscle–associated markers (e. g. myogenin and MYOD1). Desirable: identification of a t(11;22)(p13;q12) translocation or an EWSR1::WT1 fusion transcript; tumor cell immunoreactivity for a C-terminal WT1-targeted antibody; desmoplastic stroma. DSRCTs often comprise sharply demarcated nests of undifferentiated small cells and a surrounding desmoplastic stroma. The nests can vary in size and shape from tiny cords to large, irregularly shaped confluent sheets. Necrosis is common in the center of larger nests. hemorrhage and cystic degeneration can also be present. Most tumors are positive for desmin, cytokeratins, and EMA, but they are consistently negative for myogenin and MYOD1. Desmin expression is cytoplasmic and distinctly dot-like. The stromal cells frequently express SMA. DSRCT diagnosis is confirmed by detecting the EWSR1::WT1 fusion transcript. Fusion detection is especially useful for identifying DSRCTs disguised by atypical clinical or histological features. Desmoplastic small round cell tumor (DSRCT) is a malignant mesenchymal neoplasm composed of small round tumor cells associated with prominent stromal desmoplasia, polyphenotypic differentiation, and EWSR1::WT1 gene fusion. Undifferentiated sarcomas Undifferentiated sarcomas have no characteristic clinical features that allow their distinction from other sarcoma types. Because most tumors are high-grade, rapid growth is often reported. Pediatric undifferentiated sarcomas are currently regarded as exceedingly rare, and their proportion among pediatric sarcomas has in fact decreased as a consequence of improved diagnostic techniques and the identification of distinct tumor entities. Essential: spindle cell, pleomorphic, and epithelioid morphology in the absence of immunohistochemical or molecular features of specific differentiation. Undifferentiated sarcomas may be broadly divided into pleomorphic, spindle cell, and epithelioid subsets, but the only common denominator is the lack of an identifiable line of differentiation. Pleomorphic undifferentiated sarcoma is composed of a patternless proliferation of pleomorphic, often multinucleated, bizarre giant cells. Spindle cell undifferentiated sarcoma is composed of spindle cells featuring tapering nuclei, organized most often in a fascicular growth pattern. The epithelioid subtype can mimic metastatic carcinoma or melanoma and is composed of neoplastic cells featuring abundant polygonal cytoplasm harboring large vesicular nuclei. Undifferentiated sarcomas are characterized by numerous complex genomic alterations without a recurrent genetic abnormality that could be used for diagnostic purposes. Diagnostic molecular techniques such as cytogenetics and next-generation DNA and RNA sequencing play an important role in identifying specific molecular entities with round or spindle cell morphology – tumors that would otherwise have been classified as undifferentiated sarcoma. Undifferentiated soft tissue sarcomas show no identifiable line of differentiation when analysed using currently available technology. Ewing sarcoma Ewing sarcoma usually manifests with localized pain followed by a palpable mass. Bony tumors may be associated with pathological fracture. B symptoms (fever, night sweats, loss of appetite) are rare except in advanced or metastatic disease. Essential: diffuse infiltrates of small round tumor cells; diffuse and strong membranous CD99 immunoreactivity; exclusion of morphological mimics. Desirable: identification of a FET::ETS gene fusion. Ewing sarcoma features solid sheets of small round tumor cells with round nuclei containing finely granular chromatin; inconspicuous nucleoli; and scant, indistinct, clear to palely eosinophilic cytoplasm. The tumor cells may be highly uniform or show some degree of cytological atypia, in which tumor cells are larger with nuclear contour irregularities and greater nucleolar prominence. Some cases may display neuroectodermal differentiation with well-formed pseudorosettes that feature cells radially oriented towards a central fibrillar core. Necrosis is a frequent finding and may be focal or extensive. CD99 immunohistochemistry typically shows strong diffuse membranous reactivity, but this is not specific for Ewing sarcoma. FLI1 and ERG are often expressed in cases with the corresponding gene fusions. Other markers that may be positive include neuroendocrine antigens, S100, and TRK proteins. The certainty of a diagnosis of Ewing sarcoma is significantly strengthened by molecular confirmation of a gene fusion involving a FET gene (FUS, EWSR1, or TAF15) and an ETS gene. The most common gene fusion is EWSR1::FLI1, resulting from a t(11;22)(q24;q12) translocation, present in about 85% of cases. Ewing sarcoma is a small round cell sarcoma with gene fusions involving a FET-family gene (usually EWSR1) and a member of the ETS family of transcription factors. Round cell sarcoma with EWSR1::non-ETS fusions EWSR1/FUS::NFATC2 sarcomas typically manifest as painful, locally destructive bone lesions or as primary soft tissue tumors. EWSR1::PATZ1 sarcomas manifest as isolated soft tissue masses. EWSR1/FUS::NFATC2 sarcomas occur rarely in children, with only 5 pediatric cases reported (age range: 12–16 years). Essential: spindled to rounded cytomorphology; abundant stromal changes (in most cases), e. g. fibrohyaline, osteogenic, cartilaginous; identification of a fusion transcript remains the gold standard. Desirable: exclusion of a myoepithelial neoplasm (negativity for keratin and SOX10); for NFATC2-rearranged sarcomas: location in the bone (in most cases); positive staining for aggrecan and/or NKX3-1; for PATZ1-rearranged sarcomas: round/spindled cells with a divergent immunophenotype (myogenic and neurogenic). EWSR1/FUS::NFATC2 sarcomas are composed of small to medium-sized round and/or spindled cells with limited eosinophilic or clear cytoplasm, predominantly arranged in cords, nests, trabeculae, and pseudoacinar structures in a fibrohyaline or myxohyaline background. Small round monotonous to markedly pleomorphic nuclei featuring smooth or irregular nuclear contours, dense hyperchromatic or vesicular chromatin, and small or prominent nucleoli have been reported. Tumor necrosis and mitotic activity are variable. Tumor cells diffusely express CD99 (in 50% of cases); NKX2-2 may be expressed, as well as dot-like keratin AE1/AE3 and CD138. Coexpression of myogenic (desmin, myogenin, MYOD1) and neurogenic (S100P, SOX10, MITF, GFAP) markers is seen. EWSR1::NFATC2, FUS::NFATC2, and EWSR1::PATZ1 fusions are best detected by sequence-based fusion assays. The EWSR1::PATZ1 fusion is easily missed using EWSR1 break-apart FISH. Round cell sarcomas with EWSR1::non-ETS fusions are round and spindle cell sarcomas with EWSR1 or FUS fusions involving partners unrelated to the ETS gene family, excluding EWSR1-rearranged myoepitheliomas. CIC-rearranged sarcoma CIC-rearranged sarcomas usually manifest as mass lesions with or without pain; some patients present with symptoms due to visceral involvement, and some present with symptoms of metastatic disease. CIC-rearranged sarcomas occur over a wide age range, with as many as 22% of cases occurring in the pediatric age group. The peak incidence is between 25 and 35 years of age, and there is a slight male predominance. Essential: predominant round cell phenotype; mild nuclear pleomorphism; epithelioid and/or spindle cell components; variably myxoid stroma; immunoprofile with variable CD99 staining and frequent WT1 and ETV4 positivity. Desirable: demonstration of CIC gene rearrangements. CIC-rearranged sarcomas have similar morphological features regardless of the fusion partner. The tumor exhibits a diffuse or vaguely lobular or nodular architecture. Tumor cells are round to oval, small to intermediate in size, and exhibit focal spindling. There can be a moderate degree of nuclear pleomorphism and intratumoral heterogeneity. Immunohistochemistry shows positivity for CD99 (diffuse or patchy, membranous and/or cytoplasmic), WT1 (nuclear with or without cytoplasmic in as many as 95% of cases) and ETV4. BCOR, NKX2-2, keratin, S100, and myogenic markers are generally negative. CIC gene rearrangements can be detected by a variety of molecular methods , with next-generation sequencing assays being the most sensitive. CIC-rearranged sarcomas are high-grade sarcomas composed of primitive round cells harboring rearrangements of the CIC gene (19q13. Sarcoma with BCOR genetic alterations Pain (in 65% of cases) and swelling (in 40%) are the most common symptoms of BCOR::CCNB3 sarcoma. PMMTIs and infantile undifferentiated sarcomas manifest as soft tissue masses of variable size. Sarcomas with BCOR alterations are uncommon. Essential: primitive round to spindle cells arranged in nests or sheets or with a fascicular growth pattern; variably myxoid stroma with delicate vasculature; immunohistochemical positivity for BCOR, SATB2, and cyclin D1. Desirable: molecular confirmation of a BCOR genetic abnormality (fusion or ITD). BCOR::CCNB3 sarcoma is variably cellular and composed of primitive, small, round to slightly elongated cells with poorly defined eosinophilic cytoplasm, arranged in solid sheets or a vague nesting pattern, surrounded by a rich capillary network. Less cellular areas can be seen, with plump or spindled discohesive cells in a prominent myxoid matrix rich in thin-walled branching vessels, and with microcystic areas. Cells arranged in short fascicles reminiscent of poorly differentiated synovial sarcoma (in short, cord-like structures and in clusters) have also been described. The nuclei have finely dispersed chromatin, and nucleoli are generally inconspicuous. BCOR ITD soft tissue tumors (infantile undifferentiated sarcoma and PMMTI) show variable cellularity ranging from solid sheets of small primitive ovoid cells to hypocellular areas of dispersed stellate cells within a myxoid matrix with delicate vasculature. Immunohistochemically, all sarcomas with BCOR alterations display strong and diffuse nuclear BCOR positivity and in most cases also express SATB2, TLE1, and cyclin D1. BCOR gene rearrangements can be detected by FISH break-apart assays; RT-PCR for BCOR::CCNB3 transcripts can also be performed. BCOR ITD can be detected by targeted Sanger sequencing or fragment length analysis. Sarcomas with BCOR genetic alterations are clinically distinct sarcomas arising in soft tissues and bone, characterized by oncogenic BCOR fusion genes (BCOR fusion sarcomas) or internal tandem duplications (ITDs) in BCOR (BCOR ITD sarcomas). Subungual exostosis Bone Tumors Most patients present with painful subungual lesions involving a distal phalanx, of a few months’ to years’ duration. The toenail may be eroded and elevated at presentation, and ulceration and infection may occur. On imaging, a small bony protuberance is seen attached to the dorsum or side of a distal phalangeal bone surface, with no continuity between the lesion and the medullary cavity of the native bone. Essential: a small osteocartilaginous lesion on the surface of a distal phalangeal bone, with no continuity between the lesion and the medullary cavity of the underlying bone. Subungual exostosis is composed of a central core of trabecular bone surrounded by a thin cap composed of hyaline cartilage and focally by fibrocartilage or fibrous tissue. A hypertrophic zone is often thin or lacking within the hyaline cartilage, and columniation is poor. Enchondral ossification with gradual progression to woven and lamellar bone is typically observed; however, the cartilaginous cap may be absent, and bone may form directly from spindle cells. The cellularity of the cartilage and fibrocartilage is variable and minor focal atypia may be identified, including binucleation and a high N:C ratio. Subungual exostosis is a benign osteocartilaginous tumor of the bone surface occurring in the distal phalanx of a digit, underlying the nail bed. Bizarre parosteal osteochondromatous proliferation Patients typically present with a painless mass of a few months’ to several years’ duration. Pain and rapid growth have been reported. Radiologically, BPOP is a well-marginated ossified mass arising from the cortical bone without periosteal reaction, flaring of the underlying cortex, or corticomedullary continuity with affected bone. Essential: an exophytic bone lesion composed of disorganized, hypercellular cartilage containing atypical chondrocytes, spindle cells, and bone (including characteristic blue bone). BPOP is composed of three distinct components with varying degrees of representation: (1) hypercellular cartilage containing frequently enlarged, bizarre, binucleated chondrocytes; (2) cancellous bone undergoing maturation via enchondral ossification, with calcified cartilage having a characteristic basophilic tinctorial quality (known as blue bone); and (3) spindle cell stroma without cytological atypia. Myxoid and fibrocartilaginous tissue may be seen. Bizarre parosteal osteochondromatous proliferation (BPOP) is a benign lesion of the bone surface, composed of an admixture of cartilage, bone, and spindle cells. Osteoid osteoma The usual presenting symptom is pain. At first intermittent and mild with nocturnal exacerbation, the pain eventually becomes relentless to the point of interfering with sleep. In about 80% of patients, NSAIDs, even in small doses, completely (albeit temporarily) relieve the pain. Essential: radiographic demonstration of a small (< 20 mm) central nidus, often surrounded by reactive sclerosis; histological evidence of a bone-forming tumor composed of microtrabeculae of woven bone rimmed by plump osteoblasts in a vascularized stroma. Desirable: evident abrupt transition between a central nidus and peripheral sclerotic bone; typical nocturnal pain relieved by NSAIDs. The central portion (nidus) of the lesion contains differentiated plump osteoblasts present as a single layer around trabeculae of woven osteoid or mineralized bone. Vascularized connective tissue, within which are fibroblast-like stromal cells and cells differentiating into osteoblasts, separates the trabeculae. The osteoid matrix may be microscopically disposed in a sheet-like configuration, but very often it is organized into microtrabecular arrays. Osteoclasts may also be seen engaging in remodeling. FOS gene rearrangement may be found in osteoid osteomas, but it is also found in osteoblastomas and epithelioid hemangiomas. Osteoid osteoma is a benign bone-forming tumor characterized by its small size (< 20 mm), limited growth potential, and disproportionate pain that is usually responsive to NSAIDs. Chondromesenchymal hamartoma of the chest wall Infants may be asymptomatic or present with respiratory distress as a result of rib deformation and involvement of the chest cavity. The mass may be palpable, or it may be detected incidentally on a chest radiograph for an upper respiratory tract infection. Chondromesenchymal hamartoma of the chest wall is extremely rare, with approximately 100 cases reported in the literature ; it is usually congenital and almost all cases are diagnosed in infants. Essential: a well-defined solid-cystic lesion arising from the rib, composed of hyaline cartilage, blood-filled cystic spaces, woven bone, benign spindle cells, and scattered osteoclastic giant cells. Desirable: presentation during infancy or early childhood. The tumor is composed of nodules of hyaline cartilage, often with enchondral ossification, surrounding blood-filled spaces. The walls of the cystic spaces contain reactive bone, spindle cells, and osteoclastic giant cells, reminiscent of an aneurysmal bone cyst. The spindle cells lack cytological atypia and nuclear hyperchromasia. Chondromesenchymal hamartoma of the chest wall is a benign tumor composed of cartilage, spindle cells, bone, and blood-filled cystic spaces. Osteosarcoma Patients usually present with a painful mass that has been growing for several weeks or months. The skin overlying the mass may be warm and erythematous. A pathological fracture through the mass heralds about 15% of cases. Conventional osteosarcoma Essential: a pleomorphic, intramedullary, bone-producing tumor; a permeative/destructive growth pattern; compatible radiographs. Telangiectatic osteosarcoma Essential: a bone tumor with empty or blood-filled cystic spaces; fibrous septa containing malignant cells. Small cell osteosarcoma Essential: a bone tumor with small blue round cells; mineralized osteoid. Parosteal osteosarcoma Essential: a low-grade spindle cell tumor; woven bone formation; surface location; compatible radiographs. Conventional osteosarcomas grow in a permeative pattern, replace the marrow space, surround and destroy pre-existing trabeculae, and fill and expand the Haversian systems. The morphological spectrum of conventional osteosarcoma is broad. The neoplastic cells may be polygonal, round, epithelioid, plasmacytoid, spindled, fusiform or small. The cytoplasm is most often eosinophilic but sometimes clear. Immunohistochemical profiling has limited diagnostic value for osteosarcoma because these tumors do not consistently express any specific markers. However, FOS immunostaining may help differentiate osteoblastomas (which commonly express FOS owing to FOS rearrangement) from osteoblastoma-like osteosarcomas (which do not typically express FOS). Also, immunostaining for SATB2, which is a very sensitive osteoblastic differentiation marker, can help distinguish small cell osteosarcomas from Ewing sarcomas. No specific diagnostic molecular tests are available. FISH for detecting MDM2 amplification may help to differentiate parosteal or low-grade central osteosarcomas from their benign mimics. Osteosarcoma is a family of primary bone sarcomas formed from bone-producing tumor cells. Chondroblastoma The most common symptom is pain, which may be longstanding. Local tenderness, joint effusion, impaired movement, and muscle atrophy may be found as presenting symptoms. Chondroblastomas account for < 1% of all bone tumors. Essential: sheets of chondroblastic cells; islands of eosinophilic chondroid matrix; osteoclast-like giant cells. Desirable: imaging features compatible with an epiphyseal/apophyseal lesion; H3. K37M (K36M) immunoreactivity (for confirmation of cases with unusual features). Histologically, chondroblastomas are composed of sheets of ovoid to polygonal cells with distinct cytoplasmic borders, grooved nuclei, and eosinophilic cytoplasm. There are interspersed osteoclast-like giant cells and islands of eosinophilic chondroid matrix. Basophilic hyaline cartilage is infrequent. Pericellular lace-like or chicken-wire calcification is a common finding in non-decalcified specimens. Immunohistochemistry using an antibody against H3. K37M [K36M]) shows diffuse nuclear expression in > 96% of cases and is helpful in small biopsies or in cases with extensive aneurysmal bone cyst–like change. SOX9, S100, cytokeratin, and DOG1, although not specific, may be positive. The vast majority of chondroblastomas harbor a c. K37M (K36M) substitution on one of the genes that encode histone H3. The differential diagnosis includes aneurysmal bone cyst, giant cell tumor of bone, clear cell chondrosarcoma, chondromyxoid fibroma, Langerhans cell histiocytosis, and an extremely rare subtype of osteosarcoma: chondroblastoma-like osteosarcoma. Chondroblastoma is a benign tumor of bone that typically affects epiphyseal or apophyseal regions, composed of chondroblastic cells and islands of eosinophilic chondroid matrix. Osteochondroma Osteochondroma can be solitary or multiple as part of the hereditary multiple osteochondromas syndrome. They develop and increase in size during the first decade of life, and they stop growing at around puberty, when the growth plates close. Osteochondromas are usually found incidentally. Essential: compatible imaging; a cartilaginous cap (< 20 mm) with a growth plate–like architecture; underlying stalk, the cortex and medulla of which are continuous with underlying bone. The tumor has three layers: perichondrium, cartilage, and bone. The perichondrium is continuous with the periosteum of the underlying bone. The cartilage cap mimics the growth plate, with disorganized endochondral ossification: the superficial chondrocytes are clustered, whereas the ones close to the bone interface become larger, like the hypertrophic cells of the growth plate. In children, the cartilaginous cap can be highly cellular, and cellularity decreases with age, sometimes with extensive calcification. Molecular analyses are not required for the diagnosis. Osteochondroma is a benign cartilaginous neoplasm arising on the surface of bone and consisting of a bony projection covered by a cartilage cap. Chondromyxoid fibroma Pain, usually mild, is the most common symptom and is sometimes present for several years. Swelling is infrequent and is most commonly observed in the bones of the hands and feet. Chondromyxoid fibroma is a rare tumor, accounting for approximately 2. Essential: a lytic, metaphyseal, eccentric, lobulated lesion with sharp margins on conventional radiography; zonal architecture (chondroid and stellate cells within a chondroid and/or myxoid matrix in the center of lobules; spindle-shaped myofibroblast-like cells admixed with osteoclast-like giant cells at the periphery). Chondromyxoid fibroma is sharply demarcated from the surrounding bone. Lobules of tumor may be separate from the main lesion. A lobular pattern with stellate or spindle-shaped cells in a myxoid background is evident. Lobules demonstrate hypocellular centers with hypercellular peripheries. The cartilaginous nature of this tumor is reflected by immunopositivity for S100. Molecular analysis is generally not needed for diagnosis. In selected cases, identification of the exceedingly specific upregulation of GRM1 expression in chondromyxoid fibroma could be a strong diagnostic adjunct in distinguishing this entity from its mimics. Chondromyxoid fibroma is a benign lobulated neoplasm with a zonal architecture composed of chondroid, myxoid, and myofibroblastic areas. Enchondroma and enchondromatosis Enchondromas of the small bones may cause swellings, pain, and fracture, whereas long bone tumors are often asymptomatic. Ollier disease is non-hereditary and usually manifests in early childhood. Maffucci syndrome is also non-hereditary and manifests with cavernous and spindle cell hemangiomas at birth or in early childhood. Essential: an abundance of cartilaginous matrix; an absence of cytological atypia, mitoses, cortical invasion, and soft tissue extension; tumors arising in small bones and/or in patients with enchondromatosis may show more cellularity and atypia. Enchondromas are hypocellular tumors with abundant hyaline matrix and a multinodular or confluent architecture. The cells are embedded within evenly dispersed lacunae. The cytoplasm is barely visible and the nuclei are small and round with condensed chromatin. Cytological atypia and mitoses are absent. Molecular pathology is rarely used for diagnosis. Enchondroma is an intramedullary, benign hyaline cartilaginous neoplasm. Chondrosarcoma Chondrosarcoma is the third most common primary malignancy of bone, usually arising in the fifth to seventh decades of life, with < 5% occurring in patients aged < 18 years. There appears to be a slight male predominance. Patients with chondrosarcoma usually experience localized pain in the affected region, and some report soft tissue swelling. Essential: intramedullary localization with cortical erosion or thickening (for central long bone forms); soft tissue extension; mature hyaline cartilage tumor with variable amounts of myxoid matrix and cellularity dependent upon histological grade; presence of mitotic figures among higher-grade tumors; permeation of bone with entrapment of bone trabeculae. Conventional chondrosarcoma is a hyaline cartilage neoplasm that may be significantly myxoid but is not associated with osteoid production. The morphological features depend in part on the histological grade, according to a three-tiered system based predominantly on cellularity, which is inversely related to the quantity and quality of matrix, and (to a lesser extent) on nuclear features. Mitotic figures are generally only seen in the higher-grade forms. Björnsson and colleagues reported that among 338 patients of all ages with chondrosarcoma of the pelvic girdles and long bones of the extremities, most examples (61%) were grade 1 lesions, approximately 36% were grade 2, and only 3% were grade 3. Molecular analysis is not helpful for the distinction of benign cartilaginous tumors (enchondroma) from chondrosarcoma, because both frequently harbor mutations in the genes encoding the metabolic enzymes IDH1 and (less commonly) IDH2. However, on rare occasions, the presence of these mutations may help distinguish chondrosarcoma from chondroblastic osteosarcoma, which lacks IDH1 and IDH2 mutations. Chondrosarcoma of bone is a malignant intramedullary (central) or surface (peripheral) cartilage-producing neoplasm. Mesenchymal chondrosarcoma Common symptoms are pain and/or swelling. Lesions of the head and neck may be associated with headaches, visual disturbances, and vomiting. Radiologically, intraosseous lesions appear lytic, destructive, and permeative, sometimes with soft tissue extension. Essential: an undifferentiated small cell malignancy juxtaposed to mature hyaline cartilage islands. Desirable: a background staghorn vascular pattern; HEY1::NCOA2 gene fusion. The lesion has a characteristic bimorphic pattern, consisting of a hypercellular round to slightly spindled undifferentiated cell population, alternating with islands of benign to low-grade hyaline cartilage. A background hemangiopericytoma-like vascular pattern is common in these more cellular regions. Rarely, the stroma may be hyalinized/myxoid, with neoplastic cells arranged as cords and in single file. Lace-like osteoid is generally absent, although bone formation may occur, mimicking osteosarcoma. The undifferentiated cells typically exhibit strong membranous CD99 and nuclear NKX2-2 immunoexpression, but they also may display aberrant desmin and myogenin positivity. The vast majority of mesenchymal chondrosarcomas contain a relatively specific gene fusion between HEY1 (8q21. 3), which are separated by only 10 Mb on chromosome 8. Mesenchymal chondrosarcoma is a biphasic, high-grade sarcoma composed of primitive undifferentiated cells admixed with islands of well-differentiated hyaline cartilage. Vascular tumors of bone hemangiomas in children are usually symptomatic and manifest with pain and pathological fracture; tumors in the axial skeleton may cause neurological symptoms. Gorham–Stout syndrome is a rare, non-hereditary disorder, in which lesions are often composed of lymphatic-like vessels, that tends to involve one bone but readily crosses joints to involve adjacent bones, resulting in progressive bony destruction over the course of months. It may be associated with lesions in the soft tissues and thoracic cavity and as a component of a generalized lymphatic anomaly. Essential: for hemangioma: compatible imaging; thin-walled blood vessels lined by a single layer of bland endothelial cells; for EH: large epithelioid endothelial cells with densely eosinophilic cytoplasm and evidence of vasoformation with tombstone pattern; for EHE: cords and nests of epithelioid cells within a myxohyaline stroma lacking vasoformation, with an endothelial immunophenotype; well-formed vascular… Desirable: for EHE: CAMTA1 expression by immunohistochemistry and/or WWTR1::CAMTA1 fusion; TFE3 overexpression by immunohistochemistry and/or TFE3 gene rearrangement. hemangiomas have a lobular architecture and are composed of thin-walled, blood-filled, capillary-like vessels lined by a single layer of flat, uniform, cytologically bland endothelial cells. Some tumors are cellular, and the endothelial cells are plump and obscure the lumina. EH is a lobulated lesion composed of epithelioid cells that line well-formed vascular spaces and grow in cords, aggregates, and sheets. The tumor cells are large and polyhedral, with oval or kidney bean–shaped nuclei that may be hyperlobated, cleaved, and grooved. Endothelial markers (CD31, CD34, ERG, FLI1) are expressed. Keratin and EMA are often positive in EH and EHE. FOS or FOSB rearrangements can be detected in the majority of EHs of bone. WWTR1::CAMTA1 fusion can be detected in 89–100% of EHEs with classic histological features, whereas YAP1::TFE3 fusions are found in < 5% of cases with distinct histology. hemangioma is a benign endothelial tumor of bone composed of vascular channels of varying caliber. Aneurysmal bone cyst The most common signs and symptoms are pain and swelling, which are rarely due to fracture. In the vertebrae, ABC can compress nerves or the spinal cord and cause neurological symptoms. ABC affects patients of all ages, but 80% of cases occur during the first two decades of life. Essential: a multicystic lesion with fluid-fluid levels on imaging; histology showing a cyst wall composed of fibroblasts, osteoclast-like giant cells, hemosiderin, and new bone formation. Desirable: demonstration of USP6 rearrangement. ABC contains blood-filled cystic spaces separated by fibrous septa. The fibrous septa are composed of a moderately dense cellular proliferation of bland fibroblasts, with scattered osteoclast-type giant cells and reactive woven bone rimmed by osteoblasts. The woven bone frequently follows the contours of the fibrous septa. Mitoses are present and can be numerous; however, atypical mitoses are absent. USP6 rearrangement in ABC can be detected by FISH. The percentage of lesional cells carrying the rearrangement can sometimes be low. Aneurysmal bone cyst (ABC) is a benign neoplasm of bone containing multiloculated blood-filled cystic spaces. Giant cell tumor of bone GCTB manifests with pain, swelling, and occasionally restricted joint movement, lasting weeks to months. GCTB represents 4–5% of all primary bone tumors and 20% of benign bone tumors. Although the peak incidence is between the ages of 20 and 45 years, approximately 10% of cases occur in the second decade of life. Essential: compatible imaging; an osteolytic circumscribed tumor involving the epiphysis, generally in a skeletally mature individual; numerous large osteoclasts with a mononuclear cell neoplastic component without atypia. GCTB is a highly cellular lesion dominated by numerous non-neoplastic, osteoclast-like giant cells with intermingled mononuclear cells. The giant cells have a variable number of nuclei, some with > 50 per cell. The neoplastic mononuclear cells have a variety of morphological appearances, including round to oval cells in a non-fibrotic background and spindled cells associated with a fibrous matrix. Atypical mitoses should raise suspicion for malignancy. Histone H3 G34W immunohistochemistry is a reliable surrogate marker for underlying H3-3A:c. H3-3A gene mutation is detected in the neoplastic stromal cells in about 96% of GCTBs ; 90% of these are the H3-3A:c. Giant cell tumor of bone (GCTB) is a locally aggressive, rarely metastasizing neoplasm composed of neoplastic mononuclear stromal cells admixed with macrophages and osteoclast-like giant cells. Non-ossifying fibroma NOF arises in skeletally immature individuals, with a peak incidence in the second decade of life. Although usually asymptomatic and discovered incidentally, larger tumors can be painful (probably related to microfractures) and/or cause pathological fracture. Although the true incidence of NOF is unknown, it is estimated to occur in 30–40% of children, rendering it the most common tumor of bone. Essential: a bone tumor with compatible imaging findings. Desirable: storiform proliferation of plump spindle cells; metaphyseal location in long bones in skeletally immature patients; intermingled giant cells, hemosiderophages, and clusters of foamy histiocytes. Tumors consist of bland, spindle-shaped cells that are arranged in a storiform growth pattern. Osteoclast-type giant cells are scattered throughout the lesion. Reactive features include hemosiderin deposition and collections of foamy macrophages. Reactive woven bone formation and cystic change may occur focally. KRAS and FGFR1 mutation testing can be considered in ambiguous cases. Non-ossifying fibroma (NOF) is a benign and generally self-limiting spindle cell tumor of bone, containing osteoclast-like giant cells. Notochordal tumors Patients with chordomas most commonly present with pain and site-related neurological symptoms. On imaging, chordoma is typically a lytic, destructive lesion arising in the midline. It grows slowly, expanding the bone, and is frequently associated with a large soft tissue mass. Essential: for BNCT: compatible imaging; notochordal differentiation without atypia; typical immunoprofile; for conventional chordoma: compatible imaging; physaliphorous cells with myxoid matrix; typical immunoprofile; for poorly differentiated chordoma: compatible imaging; a poorly differentiated malignant neoplasm with typical immunoprofile plus loss of SMARCB1 expression; for dedifferentiated chordoma:… BNCTs consist of solid sheets of adipocyte-like cells with bland nuclei. Cystic spaces filled with colloid-like material may be present. The involved bone is viable and mildly remodeled. BNCTs lack a lobular architecture, fibrous septa, capsule, myxoid matrix, and tumor vasculature. Notochordal tumors, except the dedifferentiated component, express cytokeratin and brachyury. There is variable expression of S100 and EMA. Loss of SMARCB1 (INI1) expression is seen in poorly differentiated chordoma. Deletion in SMARCB1 can be detected by FISH in poorly differentiated chordoma. Notochordal tumors are a group of neoplasms with variable clinical behavior ranging from benign to highly malignant, usually arising in bones of the axial skeleton with a phenotype that recapitulates the notochord. Simple bone cyst Symptoms associated with SBC are pain, swelling, limitation of motion, and pathological fracture. SBCs affect patients during the first two decades of life. SBCs generally arise in the appendicular skeleton (proximal humerus: 50%, proximal femur: 25%) and rarely in the pelvis, calcaneus, or acral bones. Essential: a simple, usually unilocular, fibrous-walled cyst. Desirable: fibrin-like deposits that may organize and mineralize, resulting in cementum-like structures. SBC is composed of a thin wall of fibrous tissue. Fibrin-like collagenous deposits can be seen on the cyst surface and within the wall, often mineralized and organized in cementum-like structures; chronic inflammation, multinucleated giant cells, hemosiderin, cholesterol clefts, and reactive woven bone can also be present, especially if there has been a pathological fracture. Simple bone cyst (SBC) is an intramedullary, usually unilocular, cystic bone lesion filled with serous or serosanguineous fluid. Adamantinoma Adamantinoma causes pain, swelling, or bowing deformity. At imaging, adamantinoma appears as an intracortical, well-circumscribed, multilobulated lytic lesion, with a soap-bubble appearance. Multifocality, involvement of the medullary cavity, and cortical destruction with infiltration into the soft tissues can occur. Essential: for OFD-like adamantinoma: histology similar to that of OFD but with inconspicuous clusters of epithelial cells embedded within fibrous stroma; almost exclusively in the tibia and/or fibula, always involving cortex; for classic adamantinoma: epithelial malignancy with variable morphology arising within a fibro-osseous stromal background; almost exclusively in the tibia and/or fibula, always involving… Desirable: for OFD-like adamantinoma: may extend into the medullary cavity or adjacent soft tissues; for classic adamantinoma: often extends into the medullary cavity or adjacent soft tissues; variable morphology of epithelial component. OFD-like adamantinoma morphologically overlaps with OFD but contains clusters of epithelial cells readily identifiable by H&E. Classic adamantinoma is dominated by epithelial elements, with only a minor OFD component. Epithelial cells in classic adamantinoma may be tubular, squamous, basaloid, or spindle-shaped. Dedifferentiated adamantinoma shows areas of classic adamantinoma merging with a high-grade sarcoma. Epithelial cells are positive in both subtypes for cytokeratin (typically CK14, CK19, CK5, and CK17) , as well as for p63. Adamantinoma is a biphasic, locally aggressive or malignant tumor characterized by an epithelial neoplastic component within a bland osteofibrous background. Osteofibrous dysplasia OFD can cause pain, swelling, or bowing deformity. OFD is an extremely rare bone tumor, accounting for 0. OFD typically affects patients in the first two decades of life (rarely those aged > 15 years). Essential: imaging consistent with OFD; almost exclusive involvement of the cortex of the tibia and/or fibula; a fibro-osseous tumor with prominent osteoblastic rimming of irregular trabeculae of woven bone; absent/single cytokeratin-positive cells. OFD shows irregular trabeculae of woven bone with prominent osteoblastic rimming surrounded by a fibrous stroma similar to that of fibrous dysplasia. Towards the periphery of the lesion, the woven bone typically merges with pre-existing lamellar bone, giving the tumor a zonal architecture. OFD may show scattered single cells positive for cytokeratin (typically CK14, CK19, CK5, and CK17) , p63, and S100. Compared with OFD, fibrous dysplasia displays a highly cellular and collagenous stroma with woven bone lacking prominent osteoblastic rimming; immunohistochemically, keratin-positive epithelial cells are absent. GNAS gene mutations, present in most cases of fibrous dysplasia, are absent in OFD. The distinction of OFD from OFD-like adamantinoma depends on the more prominent extent of the epithelial component in OFD-like adamantinoma. Osteofibrous dysplasia (OFD) is a benign fibro-osseous tumor of long bone that typically arises in the anterior cortex of the tibia and/or fibula during childhood. Fibrous dysplasia Osseous deformity with associated pain and pathological fractures can occur in fibrous dysplasia; rare cases produce excess FGF23, causing paraneoplastic osteomalacia. In McCune–Albright syndrome, fibrous dysplasia is associated with endocrinopathies and abnormalities of cutaneous pigmentation; in Mazabraud syndrome it is associated with intramuscular myxomas. Fibrous dysplasia appears in standard radiographs as a well-defined, non-aggressive geographical lesion with a ground-glass matrix; in the proximal femur, shepherd’s crook deformity is characteristic. Essential: a fibro-osseous lesion consisting of variable amounts of irregular curvilinear trabeculae of woven bone without osteoblastic rimming embedded within a fibrous component composed of bland fibroblastic cells and abundant collagenous stroma. Desirable: activating missense mutations in GNAS (p. Fibrous dysplasia is composed of a variably cellular proliferation of bland fibroblastic cells with irregular curvilinear trabeculae of woven or (rarely) lamellar bone without conspicuous osteoblastic rimming. Rounded psammomatous calcifications resembling cementum are much more often seen in craniofacial lesions than in appendicular lesions. Nodules of benign hyaline cartilage (also with endochondral ossification), degenerative aneurysmal bone cyst–like changes, and/or fibrohistiocytic replacement with numerous foam cells (mimicking fibroxanthoma) can be seen. The detection of GNAS mutations can be useful to confirm a diagnosis of fibrous dysplasia. Fibrous dysplasia is a benign intramedullary fibro-osseous neoplasm that can be multifocal and is characterized by distorted, poorly organized, and inadequately mineralized woven bone and intervening fibrous tissue. All groups Pediatric Pathology Pediatric Soft Tissue and Bone Tumors A practical diagnostic reference covering pediatric mesenchymal tumors, vascular lesions, peripheral nerve sheath tumors, round cell sarcomas, and primary bone tumors. Emphasis is placed on defining morphology, immunophenotype, and diagnostically relevant molecular alterations. Classification at a Glance Browse the major diagnostic groups represented in this pediatric soft tissue and bone tumor chapter. Diagnostic group Entities ; Practical Diagnostic Framework 1. Establish the anatomic and radiologic context. Determine soft tissue versus bone origin, compartment, depth, relationship to fascia, tendon, nerve, and growth plate, and whether the lesion is circumscribed or infiltrative. 2. Identify the line of differentiation. Assess adipocytic, fibroblastic/myofibroblastic, vascular, smooth or skeletal muscle, neural, myxoid, and round cell patterns. 3. Apply a morphology-directed immunohistochemical panel. Use lineage markers to confirm differentiation and exclude major mimics; interpret staining in the context of architecture and cytology. 4. Use molecular testing to resolve defined entities. Prioritize entity-associated fusions, mutations, or amplifications when morphology and immunophenotype indicate a specific differential. title: Thoracic Tumors
content: use client Fetal Lung Interstitial Tumor Primary Pediatric Lung Tumors Well-circumscribed neonatal lung mass with uniformly expanded alveolar septa containing bland, evenly distributed mesenchymal cells. A benign mesenchymal tumor of the lung interstitium presenting as a solid or spongy microcystic mass in early infancy. Usually presents during the first 3 months of life. No established sex predilection. Arises in the lung parenchyma. Most infants have respiratory distress; some lesions are detected prenatally or incidentally. Well-circumscribed, solid or spongy microcystic intraparenchymal lung mass in an infant. Alveolar septa are diffusely widened by uniform, bland mesenchymal cells. Mesenchymal cells are evenly distributed along the septa rather than forming a subepithelial cambium-like layer. Cytologic atypia, significant mitotic activity, and tumor necrosis are absent. Immature-appearing airspaces are separated by widened alveolar septa. Septal cells are uniform, with round to oval nuclei and dispersed chromatin. Tumor cells have a rim of clear or pale-pink cytoplasm and well-defined cell borders. Airspaces are lined by flattened or cuboidal epithelial cells with clear cytoplasm. Some lesions contain fibroblastic or myofibroblastic areas that expand septa and overgrow airspaces. Inflammatory cells, including plasma cells, may be present in fibroblastic areas. The tumor is well demarcated from adjacent lung, sometimes with a thin fibrous capsule. Compared with type I pleuropulmonary blastoma, septal cells are more uniformly distributed and airspaces are smaller. Mesenchymal tumor cells are positive for vimentin. SMA and desmin show variable expression. Glycogen is abundant in both interstitial mesenchymal cells and the lining epithelial cells. The bland cytology and low proliferative activity contrast with the primitive mesenchymal cells of pleuropulmonary blastoma. Congenital Peribronchial Myofibroblastic Tumor Shows interlacing fascicles of mitotically active spindle cells with peribronchial growth and characteristic islands of benign cartilage; fetal lung interstitial tumor instead expands alveolar septa with bland, evenly spaced cells. Pleuropulmonary Blastoma Type I shows focal subepithelial primitive mesenchymal cells or cartilage in cyst walls; type II/III shows a malignant, often heterogeneous sarcoma. Fetal lung interstitial tumor has bland, uniformly distributed septal cells without hyperchromasia or mitotic activity. A subset harbors ALK fusions, including A2M::ALK; this finding is supportive in the appropriate morphologic context. Do not diagnose type I pleuropulmonary blastoma based only on infant age and a spongy or microcystic lung mass; assess septal cell distribution, cytology, and mitotic activity. Fibroblastic areas may resemble inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor but can occur within fetal lung interstitial tumor. Peribronchial spindle-cell fascicles with brisk but bland mitotic activity and islands of benign bronchial cartilage. A rare congenital or infantile fibroblastic/myofibroblastic lung tumor composed of mitotically active but cytologically bland spindle cells, typically arranged around bronchi. May be detected antenatally or present at birth or during infancy. Arises in the lung with a peribronchovascular distribution; large unilateral lesions are typical. Presentation ranges from fetal hydrops or neonatal respiratory distress to an incidental mass in an asymptomatic infant. Interlacing fascicles of uniform, histologically bland spindle cells with mitotic activity. Peribronchial accentuation of tumor growth, with extension along interlobular septa and pleura. Associated proliferation of benign-appearing bronchial cartilage, often as large peribronchial islands. No diagnostic epithelial-lined cysts with subepithelial primitive mesenchymal nodules. Interlacing fascicles are composed of uniform spindle cells with eosinophilic cytoplasm and indistinct cell borders. Nuclei are mitotically active but generally bland; rare atypical mitoses have been reported. Tumor growth surrounds bronchi and extends along interlobular septa and pleura. Alveolar septal extension may also be present. Large islands of benign cartilage are characteristic and are usually located in peribronchial regions. Unlike type II/III pleuropulmonary blastoma, there is no cambium-like subepithelial condensation, marked cellularity, overt myogenic differentiation, or anaplasia. Spindle cells are generally positive for SMA. Desmin may be positive. S100 may be positive. The immunophenotype supports myofibroblastic differentiation but is not independently diagnostic. Shows diffusely widened alveolar septa containing small, delicate, bland cells with variably clear cytoplasm; it lacks the peribronchial fascicular growth and large benign cartilage islands characteristic of congenital peribronchial myofibroblastic tumor. Type I has epithelial-lined cysts with focal subepithelial primitive cells and/or cartilage; types II/III show dense malignant sarcomatous areas, possible rhabdomyoblastic differentiation, and anaplasia. Congenital peribronchial myofibroblastic tumor has bland spindle cells and benign peribronchial cartilage. No firm molecular diagnostic criteria are established. ETV6::NTRK3 rearrangement has been reported in a small number of cases, but its significance and the distinction from primary pulmonary infantile fibrosarcoma remain unsettled. Mitotic activity alone does not establish malignancy; interpret it with cytologic blandness, peribronchial distribution, and benign cartilage. An ETV6::NTRK3 fusion should prompt careful consideration of infantile fibrosarcoma and other NTRK-rearranged mesenchymal tumors rather than automatic classification as this entity. DICER1-associated embryonal lung tumor spanning purely cystic (type I/Ir), cystic-solid (type II), and solid (type III) patterns. An embryonal mesenchymal malignancy of infancy and early childhood, classified by its cystic and solid components into types I, Ir, II, and III. Type I typically presents in infancy, with a median age of approximately 9 months; types II and III present in older children, with median ages of approximately 36 and 42 months, respectively. No consistent sex predilection is established. Arises in lung or subpleural mesenchyme. Type I may present with dyspnea or pneumothorax from cyst rupture, or as an incidental cyst; types II/III may cause dyspnea, weight loss, and fever. A personal or family history of DICER1-associated tumors may be present. Young child with a cystic, cystic-solid, or solid intrapulmonary mass. Type I: multilocular cyst with subepithelial primitive mesenchymal cell collections and/or nodules of cartilage after adequate sampling. Type Ir: type I-like cystic architecture without an identifiable primitive mesenchymal component; diagnosis may remain difficult. Types II/III: primitive sarcoma with variable blastemal, rhabdomyosarcomatous, spindle-cell, and cartilaginous components; type II retains cystic areas, whereas type III is solid. Pathogenic DICER1 alterations in tumor tissue, particularly loss-of-function and RNase IIIb hotspot variants, strongly support the diagnosis. Type I shows expanded airspaces with widened septa lined by alveolar- or bronchiolar-type epithelium. Type I contains focal or multifocal subepithelial collections of primitive mesenchymal cells in cyst walls. Primitive cells may show rhabdomyoblastic differentiation with eosinophilic cytoplasmic tails and cross-striations. Small nodules of immature cartilage or mature spindle cells may occur in septa. Type Ir has a type I-like cystic architecture but lacks identifiable primitive mesenchymal elements. Type II shows primitive cells extending beyond the subepithelial zone, expanding septa and forming solid sarcomatous nodules. Type III is a purely solid sarcoma resulting from overgrowth of the cystic component. Types II/III may show blastemal nests, embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma-like areas, spindle-cell/fibrosarcomatous areas, and immature or malignant cartilage. Anaplasia is common in types II and III. Rhabdomyoblastic areas may express desmin, myogenin, and MyoD1. Immunophenotype varies with the sarcomatous lineages represented and is not by itself specific for pleuropulmonary blastoma. When synovial sarcoma is considered, epithelial markers may support that diagnosis rather than pleuropulmonary blastoma. A well-circumscribed spongy neonatal mass with bland, uniformly distributed septal mesenchymal cells, smaller airspaces, and no mitotic activity; pleuropulmonary blastoma has focal primitive subepithelial cells/cartilage or a malignant sarcomatous component. Shows bland but mitotically active fascicular spindle cells, peribronchial growth, and large benign cartilage islands; pleuropulmonary blastoma has cyst-wall primitive cells or a more overtly malignant, heterogeneous sarcoma. Cystic Synovial Sarcoma An important consideration in older children or adolescents with a cystic mass and spindle-cell component; epithelial marker expression and an SS18-related fusion support synovial sarcoma. Chest Wall or Mediastinal Rhabdomyosarcoma A primary mass centered in the chest wall, diaphragm, or mediastinum favors rhabdomyosarcoma; pleuropulmonary blastoma is centered in lung parenchyma and may show DICER1 alterations. Germline pathogenic DICER1 loss-of-function variants underlie DICER1 tumor predisposition syndrome in many patients. Tumors typically acquire a second somatic DICER1 RNase IIIb hotspot missense variant, commonly involving p.E1705, p.D1709, p.G1809, p.D1810, or p.E1813. Tumor testing for pathogenic DICER1 loss-of-function and RNase IIIb missense variants is diagnostically useful. TP53 mutation or loss is also common. Extensively sample type I cysts because primitive mesenchymal foci and cartilage may be focal. Type Ir lacks a primitive component and may be difficult to distinguish from blebs or postinfectious cysts; correlate with age, family history, and DICER1 status. A limited biopsy may sample only one sarcomatous pattern in type II/III disease; the tumor is often heterogeneous. For a cystic spindle-cell lesion in an older child or adolescent, actively exclude synovial sarcoma with epithelial markers and SS18 fusion testing. Cardiac Rhabdomyoma Pediatric Cardiac Tumors Usually multiple, well-demarcated myocardial nodules composed of enlarged vacuolated myocytes with characteristic spider cells; strongly associated with tuberous sclerosis. A benign hamartomatous proliferation of developing striated cardiac myocytes and the most common cardiac neoplasm in children. Most often detected prenatally or during infancy and childhood; no specific sex predilection is stated. Occurs most frequently in the ventricular myocardium but may also involve the atria. Usually multiple and intramural; intracavitary pedunculated or sessile masses may occur. Prenatal findings may include arrhythmia, hydrops, or impaired fetal growth; a family history of tuberous sclerosis may be present. Children may be asymptomatic or present with a murmur, arrhythmia, conduction abnormality, or hemodynamic obstruction. A strong association with tuberous sclerosis complex is reported; cardiac rhabdomyoma may be its earliest recognized manifestation. Well-demarcated, often multiple myocardial nodules composed of enlarged vacuolated cardiac myocytes. Abundant glycogen-rich clear sarcoplasm with radial cytoplasmic extensions from the centrally located nucleus to the cell membrane (spider cells). Clinical or imaging evidence of a cardiac mass, often homogeneous and echogenic on echocardiography, supports the diagnosis. A diagnosis of tuberous sclerosis complex is supportive but is not required for the histologic diagnosis. Well-defined but unencapsulated nodules are readily distinguished from surrounding myocardium. Lesional cells are enlarged myocytes with abundant clear, vacuolated sarcoplasm due to glycogen accumulation. Characteristic spider cells show radial sarcoplasmic strands extending from a central nucleus to the cell membrane. Electron microscopy may show abundant glycogen, rare mitochondria, and peripherally distributed intercalated discs. Lesions are typically multiple and white-yellow on gross examination. Tumor cells express striated muscle markers, including myoglobin and desmin. Actin and vimentin are also reported as positive. Do not interpret the clear cytoplasm as epithelial or adipocytic differentiation; it reflects abundant intracellular glycogen. The characteristic spider-cell morphology is the key histologic clue. Cardiac rhabdomyomas often regress spontaneously; clinical management is usually conservative unless significant obstruction or arrhythmia is present. Solid or spongy microcystic mass Uniform bland mesenchymal cells expanding alveolar septa Solid peribronchial mass Bland mitotically active spindle-cell fascicles with benign cartilage islands Cystic (I/Ir), cystic-solid (II), or solid (III) Primitive subepithelial mesenchyme or malignant heterogeneous sarcoma; DICER1-associated Usually multiple intramural myocardial nodules Glycogen-rich vacuolated myocytes with characteristic spider cells; association with tuberous sclerosis All groups Pediatric Pathology Thoracic Tumors Diagnostic overview of pediatric thoracic tumors, including primary lung and cardiac entities, emphasizing clinical presentation, growth pattern, cytology, immunophenotype, and diagnostically useful molecular findings. Tumor Classification at a Glance The chapter includes three primary pediatric lung entities and one cardiac entity; classify each by its characteristic anatomic and histologic pattern. Entity Typical Pattern Key Diagnostic Point Practical Diagnostic Framework 1. Establish the anatomic compartment. Separate intraparenchymal lung masses from myocardial masses; prenatal detection is common in both fetal lung lesions and cardiac rhabdomyoma. 2. For lung lesions, map the architecture. Look for uniformly expanded alveolar septa (fetal lung interstitial tumor), peribronchial fascicles with benign cartilage (congenital peribronchial myofibroblastic tumor), or cystic/solid embryonal tumor (pleuropulmonary blastoma). 3. For cardiac masses, look for spider cells. Glycogen-rich vacuolated myocytes with radial sarcoplasmic extensions strongly support cardiac rhabdomyoma; assess for tuberous sclerosis complex. 4. Use molecular testing selectively. ALK fusions may support fetal lung interstitial tumor; reported ETV6::NTRK3 findings in congenital peribronchial myofibroblastic tumor are not definitive; DICER1 alterations are diagnostically useful in pleuropulmonary blastoma. Molecular testing is not clinically relevant for cardiac rhabdomyoma. Search entities, criteria, markers, or differentials... Try a different search term or category. Interpret morphology and molecular findings in conjunction with patient age, imaging, clinical history, and adequate tumor sampling. For pleuropulmonary blastoma, assess DICER1 status and consider genetic counseling when appropriate; evaluate patients with cardiac rhabdomyoma for tuberous sclerosis complex.

title: Adnexal Tumors
content: use client Hidrocystoma/cystadenoma Benign Sweat gland — apocrine/eccrine (ductal; often overlapping) Most hidrocystomas occur on the face, with a predilection for the eyelids, but they can also affect the ears, vulva, and fingers. Hidrocystomas are solitary, asymptomatic, bluish, cystic, and translucent lesions, usually located on the face. They typically measure 5–10 mm but can reach 70 mm in size. Multiple lesions (Robinson-type hidrocystomas) are rare . Hidrocystoma affects middle-aged adults of both sexes . Etiology Hidrocystomas usually increase in size during the summer or after exposure to heat; they decrease in size or disappear in winter. Essential: a unilocular or multilocular cystic lesion lined by columnar cells with or without decapitation secretion and surrounded by a layer of myoepithelial cells. Staging Not relevant Hidrocystomas typically present as round to oval solitary cystic structures. They are lined by columnar epithelium, often showing decapitation secretion, surrounded by myoepithelial cells and a basement membrane. Mucin may be present in the columnar cells. Most cases contain abundant mucin in the lumen, but the content is sometimes homogeneous and eosinophilic. Accumulation of secretion material can compress and flatten the epithelium. Immunohistochemically, luminal cells are positive for EMA and CEA; the myoepithelial elements are immunoreactive for S100, SOX10, and p63. Other markers include GCDFP-15, as well as various keratins in a pattern similar to that seen in the secretory portion of the eccrine glands . lacrimal gland cysts. Cytology Insufficient information available Syringoma Sweat gland — eccrine Most syringomas arise in the lower eyelids and periorbital area . Eruptive lesions tend to occur on the neck, chest, axillae, pubic area, umbilicus, and genital region. Syringoma manifests as skin-colored or slightly yellow smooth papules. Eruptive syringoma manifests as several scattered small papules (mostly on the anterior chest wall and flexural areas of the limbs), which may coalesce to form plaques . They can have a linear and one-sided distribution. Syringomas most commonly affect elderly women, but the eruptive pattern is most common in young women . Clear cell syringoma, which is more common in people with diabetes, is histopathologically characterized by ducts and solid aggregates of epithelial cells with optically clear cytoplasm. Essential: skin-colored or slightly yellow smooth papules; ductal structures embedded in a sclerotic stroma. Syringomas are well-circumscribed lesions more frequently located in the upper half of the dermis. Syringoma has two components: epithelial cells forming ducts, cords, tubules, and cysts; and a homogeneous and sclerotic stroma. The lumina of the ductal and tubular structures are lined by a double layer of cuboidal cells, sometimes containing granular basophilic material. The ducts often show characteristic extensions resembling a tadpole tail. Solid collections of epithelial cells are also observed, often containing multiple confluent cytoplasmic vacuoles. In superficial biopsies, the differential diagnosis includes microcystic adnexal carcinoma, sclerosing/morphoeic basal cell carcinoma, and columnar trichoblastoma (formerly desmoplastic trichoepithelioma), from which distinction may be impossible without complete removal and clinicopathological correlation. Ductal proliferations in cicatricial alopecia, alopecia areata, and prurigo nodularis may resemble syringoma; however, in such cases, the stroma is different. Eruptive hamartomas of clear cells of the eccrine duct (or so-called clear cell metaplasia of the eccrine duct) resemble clear cell syringomas , but these lesions affect only the excretory ducts of pre-existing eccrine glands. Cytology Not relevant Poroma Sweat gland — eccrine / poroid (apocrine-pattern variants occur) Intraepidermal poroma commonly involves the extremities, but it can affect other sites.
