Pilomatrical carcinoma is poorly circumscribed and infiltrative, and it involves the deep dermis, subcutaneous tissue, and even skeletal muscle and fascia. The lesion is composed of solid aggregates of immature basaloid matrical cells with scant cytoplasm, a vesicular nucleus, a prominent nucleolus, and numerous mitoses. Atypical mitoses may be seen. Shadow cells are less abundant in pilomatrical carcinoma than in pilomatricoma, but they are characteristic and useful in the diagnosis . In some cases, inner root sheath differentiation (including trichohyalin granules and nests of bluish-grey cornified material) can be seen. Pilomatrical carcinomas show both nuclear and cytoplasmic staining for β-catenin in the basaloid matrical cells, as well as nuclear expression of CDX2 and LEF1 ; BerEP4 is negative . Pilomatrical carcinoma should be distinguished from pilomatricoma and basal cell carcinoma with matrical differentiation. Pilomatricoma is a benign cystic neoplasm that appears as a symmetrical, well-circumscribed lesion with regular and smooth borders; it usually does not show any areas of necrosis en masse or the cytological atypia seen in pilomatrical carcinoma. Basal cell carcinoma with matrical differentiation is a neoplasm with all the architectural and cytological features of a basal cell carcinoma, and focal aggregates of shadow cells; rarely, areas with matrical differentiation predominate and display some degree of cytological atypia . Trichoblastic carcinoma/carcinosarcoma The reported lesions have occurred in the head and neck and the trunk. These neoplasms appear to affect elderly patients and present as a solitary nodule. Both neoplasms are very rare and probably underrecognized. Fewer than 10 cases of bona fide trichoblastic carcinosarcoma have been reported . Essential: an invasive tumor with dual differentiation towards follicular stroma and follicular epithelium; for trichoblastic carcinoma: a benign stromal component identical to that of trichoblastoma, and an atypical basaloid component; for trichoblastic carcinosarcoma: a biphasic tumor in which both the epithelial (basaloid) and mesenchymal components resembling specific follicular mesenchyme… Trichoblastic carcinoma is an invasive but well-circumscribed neoplasm composed of a stromal component identical to that of trichoblastoma and a basaloid component that shows moderate to severe atypia. In trichoblastic carcinosarcoma, both the epithelial and the mesenchymal components are malignant, with pleomorphic cells, abnormal mitotic figures, crowding, and hyperchromasia. Each epithelial nodule is intimately associated with the stroma, which recapitulates specific follicular mesenchyme by virtue of papilla-like aggregations that are often aligned across a broad front, resembling continuous papillae. Despite their close association throughout the tumor, the epithelial and stromal cells are sharply separated, with no gradual transition between the two elements; this is an important feature distinguishing this neoplasm from sarcomatoid (metaplastic) basal cell carcinoma. Trichoblastic carcinoma is distinguished from trichoblastoma by atypia in the epithelial component. Basal cell carcinoma lacks the specialized follicular stroma and is composed of basaloid epithelial cells that are less atypical than those seen in trichoblastic carcinoma/carcinosarcoma. In basal cell carcinoma with sarcomatoid differentiation, the transition between the epithelial and mesenchymal components is gradual, and the mesenchymal component appears as pleomorphic sarcoma rather than resembling follicular papillae . Trichoblastic carcinoma should be differentiated from benign plaque-like trichoblastomas that occur around the mouth and frequently involve the underlying skeletal muscle, which is a normal constituent of the deep dermis in this area . Trichilemmal carcinoma Trichilemmal carcinoma involves sun-exposed areas, most commonly the face, scalp, and neck, and less frequently the back of the hands. Trichilemmal carcinoma manifests as an erythematous, tan, or flesh-colored papule; a keratotic nodule; or an indurated plaque mimicking squamous or basal cell carcinoma. It is frequently ulcerated. Trichilemmal carcinoma may arise in patients exposed to chronic actinic damage, receiving radiotherapy treatment with long latency periods, or affected by xeroderma pigmentosum. Trichilemmal carcinoma has a predilection for elderly individuals; the majority of cases occur between the seventh and ninth decades of life. There is no sex predominance . Essential: a cutaneous nodule on a sun-exposed, hair-bearing anatomical site; a lobular proliferation of atypical, glycogen-rich clear cells lacking mucin and palisading around a follicular unit. Trichilemmal carcinoma is characterized by a proliferation of tumoral lobules (composed of large atypical cells with clear cytoplasm) with a sharply defined border and pushing margins continuous with the epidermis or pilosebaceous structures. The tumor cells give a positive PAS reaction, and there are prominent nucleoli, frequent mitoses, and foci of trichilemmal keratinization. At the periphery of the lobules, the keratinocytes show palisading and are surrounded by a prominent connective tissue sheath. The tumor is more commonly associated with an invasive component centerd on a pilosebaceous unit and may show pagetoid spread in the overlying epidermis. The tumor cells are strongly positive for p53 and focally positive for CD34 (My10), which is a marker of differentiation from the outer root sheath. The main differential diagnosis of trichilemmal carcinoma is clear cell squamous cell carcinoma, although these tumors are considered by some authors to be the same entity . Squamous cell carcinoma with clear cells lacks trichilemmal keratinization and lobular proliferation. Trichilemmal carcinoma must be distinguished from other skin cancers with clear cell changes. The identification of ductal differentiation with CEA and EMA staining is useful for differentiating hidradenocarcinoma from trichilemmal carcinoma. Desmoplastic trichilemmoma may rarely exhibit an infiltrative growth pattern but lacks pleomorphism and mitoses. Sebaceoma Sebaceous gland Sebaceomas arise most commonly on the face and scalp, and rarely on the trunk or extremities . Sebaceomas are solitary, yellow-tan papules/nodules . They may rarely arise in a pre-existing sebaceous nevus . Lesions associated with Muir–Torre syndrome may be multifocal . Sebaceomas may be associated with Muir–Torre syndrome , part of Lynch syndrome (see the Digestive System Tumors and Genetic Tumor Syndromes volumes of this series ). The mean patient age at diagnosis is 70 years , and there is a female predominance . Essential: a solitary, yellow-tan papule/nodule; well-circumscribed cellular lobules composed mostly of small, monomorphic, immature but cytologically benign basaloid cells admixed with fewer mature sebocytes (< 50%), haphazardly distributed throughout the tumor. Sebaceoma consists of well-circumscribed cellular lobules composed mostly of small monomorphic immature basaloid cells admixed with fewer mature sebocytes (< 50%), haphazardly distributed throughout the tumor. Mature sebocytes have abundant cytoplasmic vacuoles that produce scalloped nuclei. Duct-like structures and cystic areas may be seen, which often show an eosinophilic cuticle and occasionally contain holocrine secretions . Infundibulocystic structures, squamous metaplasia, and apocrine differentiation can also be observed . Mitotic figures may be common in the immature component, but atypical forms and necrosis are not expected. Diagnostic molecular pathology is not relevant for individual tumors. Germline sequencing may be indicated in some cases. Sebaceous carcinoma and sebaceous adenoma are the most common differential diagnoses. BerEP4 negativity may help in the distinction from basal cell carcinoma . Some other cutaneous neoplasms, such as squamous cell carcinomas and basal cell carcinomas, may show very focal sebaceous differentiation. Many reported cases of so-called “ripple-pattern” trichoblastomas are in fact sebaceoma. Sebaceous adenoma Sebaceous adenoma is principally seen in the skin of the head and neck. Sebaceous adenoma is a well-circumscribed yellow-tan nodule (5–15 mm) . Lesions associated with Muir–Torre syndrome may be multifocal and can have a central cystic area or a papillomatous morphology resembling keratoacanthoma . Mismatch repair (MMR)-deficient sebaceous neoplasms occur more commonly outside of the head and neck area than do MMR-stable sebaceous neoplasms . Sebaceous adenomas are principally seen as solitary lesions in people aged > 40 years . They are usually located in sun-damaged skin of the head and neck area. Essential: a well-circumscribed yellow-tan nodule; well-circumscribed lobular aggregates consisting mostly of mature sebocytes, with a variable rim of immature, cytologically benign basaloid cells; direct connection to the overlying epidermis. Sebaceous adenomas are well-circumscribed lobular aggregates composed mostly of mature sebocytes, with a variable rim of immature basaloid cells, recapitulating normal sebaceous glands . The mature sebocytes are characterized by an abundant vacuolated, “bubbly” cytoplasm and a central scalloped nucleus, and these sebocytes predominate (> 50% of all tumor cells) over the small monomorphic immature basaloid cells. Sebaceous adenoma may show a direct connection to the overlying epidermis, which may be covered by keratin and cellular debris. MMR-deficient sebaceous neoplasms show cystic change, intratumoral mucin, squamous metaplasia, ulceration, a lymphocytic infiltrate, and intertumoral heterogeneity more often than do MMR-stable sebaceous neoplasms . The vacuolated cytoplasm of the mature sebocytes expresses EMA and adipophilin . The principal differential diagnosis for sebaceous adenoma is sebaceous hyperplasia, in which sebaceous lobules are arranged around a central follicle that is connected to the epidermis, but sebaceous hyperplasia shows a clear association with a central hair follicle, whereas sebaceous adenoma does not. Sebaceoma is another benign nodular lesion composed of a more equal admixture of basaloid epithelial cells and small groups of vacuolated sebocytes . Considerable morphological overlap may exist between sebaceous adenoma and sebaceoma . Sebaceous carcinoma Sebaceous carcinoma can occur anywhere but shows a predilection for the head and neck and occurs most commonly around the eyelids : 75% of all cases arise in a periocular (eyelid) location . They may involve the conjunctival and/or skin surface. Extraocular sebaceous carcinomas occur most commonly on the skin of the head and neck, followed by the trunk, genitals, and extremities. Rare cases occur in the oral cavity, salivary gland, lung, and breast . Patients with sebaceous carcinoma present with a tan-pink-yellow, firm, occasionally nodular lesion measuring 10–30 mm. Periocular sebaceous carcinoma may be mistaken clinically for benign inflammatory or neoplastic conditions, leading to a delay in diagnosis and to higher morbidity and mortality . Pagetoid sebaceous carcinoma may resemble chronic blepharoconjunctivitis . Sebaceous carcinoma develops in older adults, with no sex predilection. The median age at diagnosis is 73 years. Essential: a firm, tan-pink-yellow, occasionally nodular lesion, sometimes resembling inflammation; an invasive or intraepithelial tumor showing sebaceous differentiation, manifesting as multivesicular cytoplasmic clearing with nuclear scalloping. Desirable: immunohistochemical confirmation of sebaceous differentiation in cases lacking obvious histopathological evidence of sebaceous differentiation. Staging The eighth edition of the Union for International Cancer Control (UICC) / American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) TNM system forms the basis for staging. The application of the eighth edition of the AJCC system was found to be useful in predicting nodal metastasis; however, local recurrence and distant metastasis were not significantly correlated to the T classification . Well-differentiated sebaceous carcinoma consists of lobules of polygonal tumor cells with atypical, oval vesicular nuclei and abundant intracytoplasmic vacuoles that impart a foamy appearance and impinge on the nucleus, creating scalloping. Central comedo-type necrosis may be seen. More poorly differentiated tumors show a higher N:C ratio, nuclear pleomorphism, prominent nucleoli, basophilic cytoplasm with fewer intracellular vacuoles , and brisk mitotic activity. Sebaceous carcinoma may show basaloid, squamoid (often with keratin pearl formation), spindle cell / sarcomatoid, or neuroendocrine (rippled or organoid growth) features . Invasive tumors can adopt various architectural patterns, including well-circumscribed lobules with pushing borders and variable comedonecrosis, papillary architecture, and highly infiltrative cords; combinations of these patterns are often observed. Sebaceous carcinoma shows immunoreactivity for pancytokeratin (and also CK7), adipophilin, EMA, BerEP4, AR, p40, and p63 . EMA labelling may enhance the cytoplasmic vacuolization of the tumor cells, but it is often only positive in well-differentiated tumors and lacks specificity. Adipophilin is a more sensitive and specific marker of sebaceous differentiation . Positivity for CD10, DOG1, KIT (CD117), p16, p53, perforin, and factor XIIIa has also been reported in sebaceous carcinoma . Sebaceous carcinoma should be excluded when examining basaloid, squamoid, and clear cell epithelial tumors in periocular locations. The differential diagnosis includes sebaceoma, balloon cell melanoma, clear cell squamous cell carcinoma, basal cell carcinoma, Merkel cell carcinoma, and metastatic clear cell carcinomas from visceral organs. Hidradenoma papilliferum Anogenital mammary-like gland — apocrine-type Most cases affect the vulva; less frequently, the perianal and perineal skin is involved. The lesion occurs as a solitary asymptomatic nodule or cyst-like lesion measuring 2–20 mm . Hidradenoma papilliferum is the most common benign glandular neoplasm of the vulva. It almost exclusively affects White women aged 20–89 years; it occurs rarely in children and in Black populations . Essential: a solitary asymptomatic nodule or cyst-like lesion; complex growth of branching and anastomosing epithelial papillae and tubules with a myoepithelial cell layer. Staging Not clinically relevant Hidradenoma papilliferum appears as a well-circumscribed intradermal solid-cystic nodule with a complex pattern of branching and anastomosing tubules interconnected in a labyrinthine manner, focally forming papillae. The tubules and papillae consist of a central axis of fibrous tissue lined by a luminal layer of epithelial cells surrounded by a layer of myoepithelial cells. Decapitation secretion is common. Cystic change, sclerosing adenosis–like and mammary-type ductal changes, and necrosis have been identified. Oxyphilic metaplasia, especially in areas with solid growth with nuclear polymorphism, may simulate adenocarcinoma. Fibroadenoma and phyllodes tumor of anogenital mammary-like glands Anogenital mammary-like gland — mammary-type Most cases occur in the vulva and perianal area . Rare patients also present with mammary fibroadenoma, similar lesions in the axilla , and bilateral anogenital tumors . Fibroadenoma and phyllodes tumor occur as solitary nodules measuring 8–60 mm (mean size: 30 mm). In the reported cases, the age at diagnosis was 20–69 years (mean: 39 years) . Both tumors are very uncommon, with < 80 cases reported to date. Most patients are female . Essential: biphasic histology (for both lesions); for fibroadenoma: round or elongated, often branching and anastomosing glandular structures surrounded by usually paucicellular stroma; for phyllodes tumor: leaf-like projections and hypercellular stroma. Fibroadenoma is a well-circumscribed neoplasm composed of round or elongated, often branching and anastomosing glandular structures surrounded by a paucicellular stroma containing bland spindled or stellate cells, showing low or practically no mitotic activity. When the glandular lumina maintain round or oval configurations, the image is that of a pericanalicular growth pattern, whereas abundant stroma compressing the glandular elements into slit-like structures produces an intracanalicular pattern . Phyllodes tumor shows a growth pattern with leaf-like projections into glandular lumina. The stroma is usually hypercellular, typically with periglandular condensation; cellularity commonly varies within a given neoplasm . Three categories are delineated: benign, low-grade, and high-grade; the grade is defined by stromal atypia. The epithelial component stains for ER, PR, and GATA3, whereas ERBB2 (HER2) is negative. Stromal cells, including those in PASH areas, are positive for vimentin and CD34 and variably positive for actins . Vascular markers are negative in PASH . Fibroadenoma and benign phyllodes tumor manifest overlapping features; in some cases, distinguishing between them can be difficult. Generally, phyllodes tumors have more-cellular stroma (with variation within a lesion), less regular outlines, and leaf-like projections. Focal connection to the epidermal surface with numerous plasma cells may resemble syringocystadenoma papilliferum. Fibroepithelial foci resembling fibroadenoma may rarely be found in other complex lesions of anogenital mammary-like glands . Fibrocystic disease and other lesions with prominent ductal hyperplasia may be differential diagnoses in a limited specimen . Mammary Paget disease Mammary gland / nipple epidermis — Paget-type intraepidermal spread MPD involves the nipple and areola; in advanced cases, it may extend to the adjacent skin of the breast. One breast is typically involved, but there may be both synchronous and metachronous involvement . A supernumerary nipple (or ectopic breast tissue adjacent to a supernumerary nipple) can also very rarely be involved . There is usually an eczematous scaly or crusted lesion confined to the nipple or areola, sometimes associated with ulceration or inversion of the nipple and discharge. Rare cases are pigmented, resembling a melanocytic lesion. MPD accounts for 1–4% of all breast carcinomas. It almost exclusively affects women; < 1% of reported cases occurred in men . Essential: large intraepidermal atypical cells with abundant pale cytoplasm and large nuclei with prominent nucleoli; single cells or small clusters typically leaving a single layer of basal keratinocytes; positivity for low-molecular-weight cytokeratins and ERBB2. Staging If no underlying carcinoma or ductal carcinoma in situ is present, MPD is staged as Tis according to the eighth edition of the Union for International Cancer Control (UICC) TNM classification. If there is invasive carcinoma, it is staged according to the invasive component . The neoplastic cells (Paget cells) have abundant weakly eosinophilic or pale-staining cytoplasm and large vesicular nuclei. They are scattered in the epidermis (pagetoid spread) in the form of solitary units, clusters, or (rarely) acinar/glandular structures. Skin adnexa can also be involved. Paget cells contain intracellular mucin in 40% of cases, and they may contain melanin due to phagocytosis (a possible diagnostic pitfall ). The epidermis is often hyperkeratotic and acanthotic, especially in longstanding lesions. There is no known association with a specific gene mutation, although it has been suggested that the MSI1/mTOR pathway may drive the pathogenesis of mammary and extramammary Paget disease . Genetically, Paget cells are similar to the underlying carcinoma cells in most cases . Clinically, MPD must be distinguished from eczema and nipple adenoma. The histological differential diagnosis includes spongiotic dermatoses, candidiasis/dermatophytes, squamous cell carcinoma in situ (Bowen disease), and superficial spreading melanoma. Rare cases of clinically pigmented MPD contain melanin pigment, usually in isolated dendritic melanocytes, thus raising the possibility of melanoma. These isolated cells express melanocytic markers (melan-A [MART1], SOX10), while the surrounding Paget cells express CK7, EMA, and ERBB2 (HER2) . In some cases, hyperplasia of Toker cells, a normal component of the nipple, may present a diagnostic dilemma . Extramammary Paget disease Cutaneous apocrine / anogenital mammary-like gland-associated (often secondary) The labium majus of the vulva is the most common site, followed by the labium minus and clitoris. The perineum, perianal area, scrotum, penis, lower abdomen, and inguinal folds can also be affected. Outside the anogenital region, EMPD can very rarely affect non-genital regions . The most common presentation is a relatively well-demarcated flat or slightly elevated, scaly, oozing, erythematous patch or plaque accompanied by pruritus or burning; thus, these lesions often clinically resemble eczema. They generally cover a large area (median: 20.5 cm2) . Rare forms include lesions with hyperpigmentation or hypopigmentation and multicentric lesions (e.g. genital lesions associated with unilateral or bilateral axillary involvement, occurring synchronously or metachronously) . EMPD accounts for about 1% of all neoplasms in the anogenital area. It mostly occurs in White postmenopausal women, with a median age of about 70–75 years. Essential: presence of atypical epithelial cells involving the epidermis; confirmation by immunohistochemistry (low-molecular-weight cytokeratin, CK7, CEA). Desirable: clinical/imaging evaluation to help distinguish primary from secondary; additional immunohistochemistry (uroplakin, CK20, p63, CDX2, NKX3-1, ERBB2). Staging Staging depends on the subtype, primary versus secondary EMPD, and the location; for example, invasive vulval Paget disease is staged the same way as other vulval cancers. There is a proposal for TNM staging . The intraepithelial neoplastic cells (Paget cells) have vesicular nuclei with prominent nucleoli and abundant basophilic to amphophilic cytoplasm. They occur as solitary cells or well-demarcated solid nests or gland-like structures. Many cases also involve underlying skin adnexa, especially hair follicles and eccrine ducts . Occasionally, there is focal dermal invasion by single cells, glands, or small groups of cells (invasive Paget disease). Less common morphological changes include epidermal hyperplasia resembling syringocystadenocarcinoma papilliferum, syringoma-like structures, melanin pigment within the cytoplasm of the neoplastic cells simulating a melanocytic lesion, signet-ring cell morphology, and association with other vulvar lesions . Primary EMPD is consistently positive for CK7 and GATA3 and with CAM5.2, and it often expresses CEA, GCDFP-15, ERBB2, CA125, and AR . ER and PR may be positive or negative . The most important issue is the distinction between primary and secondary EMPD. Coexpression of CK20 and CDX2 by the Paget cells and dirty necrosis (although the latter is unusual) support a colorectal origin. Uroplakin-3 expression is typical for urothelial carcinoma, whereas coexpression of PSA and NKX3-1 suggests an underlying prostatic carcinoma. Potential mimics of EMPD are vulvar Toker cells, vulvar and penile analogues of cervical stratified mucin-producing intraepithelial lesion , high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion, melanoma, pagetoid dyskeratosis, and clear cell papulosis. In addition to immunohistochemistry, clinicopathological correlation is essential for correct diagnosis. Adenocarcinoma of mammary gland type The most common location is the labia majora . Most patients are postmenopausal and present with a vulval mass. These are rare vulval neoplasms. Etiology Unknown Pathogenesis Adenocarcinoma of mammary gland type is proposed to arise from anogenital mammary-like glands located in the anal and vulval area . Essential: a solitary nodule with a fibrous cut surface, similar to breast carcinoma; histology consistent with that of invasive breast carcinoma. Desirable: location usually the labia majora; association with lobular structures consistent with mammary differentiation; immunohistochemical expression of ER, PR, and ERBB2. The most common type is adenocarcinoma, which is identical to mammary invasive ductal carcinoma and may (uncommonly) have an identifiable in situ component in the adjacent glands. Rare types include lobular, tubulolobular, mixed ductal and lobular, and mammary analogue secretory carcinoma. There is commonly expression of ER, PR, GATA3, and ERBB2 . Based on the immunoprofile, they can be classified like their breast counterparts into luminal A, luminal B, HER2-enriched, and basal-like subtypes . Cytology No data available Diagnostic molecular pathology is not clinically relevant in most cases. Secretory carcinoma harbours the characteristic ETV6::NTRK3 fusion. All PathologyGPS / Skin / Adnexal Tumors Skin Adnexal Tumors A site-oriented, morphology-first reference to cutaneous adnexal neoplasms, emphasizing essential diagnostic criteria, immunophenotype, and practical differential diagnosis. Core diagnostic principle Location narrows the field; architecture and cytology establish the diagnosis. Adnexal tumors show substantial morphologic overlap. Correlate anatomic site, depth, clinical pattern, and the relationship to native epidermal and adnexal structures. Diagnostic GPS: start with anatomic location Head and neck / eyelid Hidrocystoma, syringoma, poroma, spiradenoma, cylindroma, trichoblastoma, pilomatricoma, sebaceous tumors, and most periocular sebaceous carcinomas. Palms and soles / digits Poroma; digital papillary adenocarcinoma; consider acral-specific clinical and histologic context. Scalp Proliferating trichilemmal tumor, cylindroma, trichilemmoma, trichofolliculoma, and pilomatrical lesions. Vulva / anogenital skin Hidradenoma papilliferum, syringoma, mammary-like gland tumors, extramammary Paget disease, and mammary-type adenocarcinoma. Trunk and proximal limbs Hidradenoma, mixed tumor, tubular adenoma, poroma, and many nonspecific adnexal carcinomas. Periorificial / central face Microcystic adnexal carcinoma and trichoblastoma; assess infiltrative growth and perineural invasion. Perianal / genital skin Extramammary Paget disease, syringocystadenoma papilliferum variants, and site-specific glandular lesions. Any site with multiple lesions Consider inherited syndromes, particularly CYLD-associated Brooke–Spiegler syndrome and other syndrome-linked adnexal proliferations. Tumor classification by differentiation and biologic behavior Each entity is assigned to its principal differentiation category as organized in the supplied WHO excerpt. Several sweat gland tumors show overlapping apocrine and eccrine features; the table preserves that overlap rather than implying a lineage that morphology cannot reliably separate. Differentiation / tissue type Behavior Tumor / entity bg-white bg-slate-50 bg-emerald-50 text-emerald-800 bg-rose-50 text-rose-800 bg-amber-50 text-amber-800 Classification note: “Apocrine/eccrine” indicates the WHO sweat-gland grouping or recognized morphologic overlap; it does not mean every tumor has two demonstrable lineages. Poroma-family tumors are classified as poroid/sweat duct neoplasms. Behavior note: “Intermediate” is retained where the page uses that category. Phyllodes tumors span benign, borderline, and malignant grades; proliferating trichilemmal tumors also require grading and clinicopathologic correlation. Naming guide: Greek and Latin roots adnexal Latin adnexus, “attached” — skin appendages attached to the skin: hair follicles and sebaceous/apocrine/eccrine glands. hidro- / hidr- Greek hydōr, “water” — historically used for sweat-gland lesions (e.g., hidrocystoma, hidradenoma). syringo- Greek syrinx, “pipe or tube” — refers to duct-like structures (syringoma, syringocystadenoma). poroma / poro- Greek poros, “passage or pore” — poroid tumors show sweat-duct differentiation. adenoma / adeno- Greek adēn, “gland” — glandular differentiation; carcinoma denotes malignant epithelial behavior. spiradenoma Combines spir- (coil/spiral, referring to the coiled sweat apparatus) and adēn (“gland”). cylindroma Greek kylindros, “cylinder” — named for the characteristic jigsaw-puzzle arrangement of tumor islands. tricho- / pil- Greek thrix/trichos and Latin pilus, both meaning “hair” — follicular differentiation. matricoma From hair matrix — matrical differentiation recapitulates the hair bulb matrix. trichilemmal From the hair follicle outer root sheath (the trichilemma); often associated with abrupt keratinization. sebaceous Latin sebum, “fat/grease” — sebocyte differentiation with lipid-rich cytoplasm. apocrine / eccrine Greek apo- + krinein (“separate/secrete”) and ekkrinein (“secrete out”) — historical glandular secretion terms. Etymology is a memory aid, not a reliable predictor of lineage or behavior. Historical names do not always map cleanly to current concepts. Interpretive cautions Benign adnexal tumors are much more common than carcinomas; clinical irregularity, ulceration, or pain is not independently diagnostic of malignancy. Many adnexal tumors overlap morphologically. A descriptive diagnosis such as “atypical adnexal tumor” or “adnexal tumor of uncertain malignant potential” may be appropriate when benign versus malignant behavior cannot be resolved. For adnexal carcinoma, exclude metastasis from an extracutaneous primary with clinical evaluation and a directed immunohistochemical panel. Assess depth, infiltrative growth, perineural invasion, lymphovascular invasion, mitotic activity, necrosis, and any adjacent benign component. Multiple adnexal neoplasms should prompt consideration of a hereditary syndrome; correlate with clinical history and family history. Scope note: This reference is based on the supplied WHO excerpt. Molecular findings are included only where the excerpt identifies diagnostic or potentially useful alterations. Site and clinical associations should be interpreted in clinicopathologic context.

title: Cutaneous Genetic Tumor Syndromes
content: use client Familial Melanoma Usually autosomal dominant in high-risk families; polygenic susceptibility also occurs CDKN2A (most common); CDK4; rare high-penetrance genes: BAP1, POT1, ACD, TERF2IP, TERT, ATM, EBF3. Moderate-risk genes include MC1R, MITF, and SLC45A2. Generally defined by melanoma in two or more first-degree relatives. Melanoma often develops approximately 10 years earlier than in the general population in CDKN2A- or CDK4-associated families. Multiple primary melanomas are common. Atypical (dysplastic) nevi may be present, but are not required. CDKN2A families may also show increased pancreatic cancer risk; smoking-related cancers have been reported in some founder-variant families. Cutaneous melanoma; familial uveal melanoma is less common and may be associated with BAP1 or MBD4. CDKN2A is also associated with pancreatic cancer. Familial melanomas in CDKN2A carriers often show superficial spreading melanoma morphology. Increased pigmentation and pagetoid scatter have been described. Spindle-cell morphology in the vertical growth phase was a strong negative predictor of CDKN2A carrier status in one study. Acral and mucosal familial melanoma has not been reported in the cited source. No syndrome-specific immunophenotype is established; evaluate the melanoma using the usual site- and subtype-directed panel. Germline CDKN2A variants are the most common established cause of familial clustering; CDKN2A encodes p16INK4a, which binds CDK4. Activating germline CDK4 variants also confer melanoma susceptibility. CDKN2A or CDK4 variants are identified in approximately 30–40% of families with at least three melanoma cases. Rare susceptibility genes include BAP1, POT1, ACD, TERF2IP, TERT, ATM, and EBF3; each is found in fewer than 1% of familial melanoma families in the source. MC1R, MITF, and SLC45A2 contribute moderate-penetrance pigmentation-related susceptibility; multiple low- and medium-risk loci contribute polygenic risk. Establish a detailed pedigree, including the number and relationship of affected relatives, age at diagnosis, multiple primary melanomas, and associated cancers. The usual clinical definition is melanoma in two or more first-degree relatives. Consider germline testing when the family history and geographic/family-specific criteria support inherited susceptibility. Germline sequencing is often required; the source notes that diagnostic criteria vary by geography and patient age. BAP1-related tumor predisposition syndrome Consider when multiple BAP1-inactivated melanocytic tumors, uveal melanoma, mesothelioma, or renal cell carcinoma occur in the family. Xeroderma pigmentosum Usually presents in childhood with marked UV sensitivity, early freckling, ocular findings, and multiple UV-related skin cancers; autosomal recessive DNA-repair disorder. Sporadic multiple primary melanoma A family history may be absent; assess age, nevus phenotype, UV exposure, and germline risk factors. The supplied source does not provide a single characteristic histologic pattern or syndrome-specific IHC profile. The source reports no large histopathologic/outcome series for familial melanoma. Do not equate a family history alone with a confirmed germline syndrome. BAP1-Related Tumor Predisposition Syndrome Autosomal dominant BAP1 (heterozygous germline loss-of-function variant or deletion; chromosome 3p21) Multiple BAP1-inactivated melanocytic nevi/tumors often begin in the second decade. Skin lesions are typically multiple, subtle, skin-colored to reddish-brown, dome-shaped papules measuring approximately 4–12 mm, often on sun-exposed skin. The number of cutaneous lesions ranges from a few to more than 50. Associated tumors include uveal and cutaneous melanoma, pleural/peritoneal mesothelioma, clear cell renal cell carcinoma, and basal cell carcinoma. Patients tend to develop associated tumors at a younger age than the general population. BAP1-inactivated melanocytic nevi/tumors; uveal and cutaneous melanoma; pleural and peritoneal mesothelioma; clear cell renal cell carcinoma; basal cell carcinoma. Additional reported tumors include meningioma, cholangiocarcinoma, and hepatocellular carcinoma. BAP1-inactivated melanocytic lesions are predominantly intradermal, with occasional junctional involvement. Most lesions contain conventional small nevus cells admixed with larger epithelioid melanocytes. Epithelioid cells range from mildly atypical to markedly pleomorphic cells with abundant amphophilic cytoplasm, vesicular nuclei, and prominent nucleoli. Some lesions show increased cellularity, nuclear pleomorphism, or increased mitotic activity. The spectrum ranges from BAP1-inactivated melanocytic nevus to BAP1-inactivated melanocytoma with uncertain clinical behavior. Mitotic activity is usually low, and tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes are frequent. Loss of nuclear BAP1 expression supports BAP1 inactivation in the melanocytic lesion. BAP1 loss in a tumor is not by itself proof of a germline syndrome because somatic BAP1 inactivation also occurs. The syndrome is caused by heterozygous germline BAP1 loss-of-function variants or deletions. Associated tumors commonly show biallelic BAP1 loss, with loss of nuclear BAP1 by IHC. Cutaneous BAP1-inactivated melanocytic tumors commonly harbor MAPK-pathway activation, most often BRAF p.V600E; NRAS mutations or RAF1 fusions are less common. Confirm the syndrome by germline DNA testing; tumor IHC alone is insufficient. Suspect the syndrome in patients with multiple BAP1-inactivated melanocytic nevi/tumors or a young-onset combination of associated tumors. Confirm by identifying a pathogenic loss-of-function BAP1 germline variant or a germline deletion involving BAP1. Correlate tumor BAP1 IHC with personal and family history. Conventional melanocytic nevus Lacks the characteristic epithelioid component and BAP1 loss in the lesional cells. Spitz nevus / Spitz melanocytoma Can show epithelioid cytology; integrate architecture, cytologic spectrum, BAP1 IHC, and germline context. Sporadic BAP1-deficient tumor Somatic BAP1 loss may occur without germline predisposition; germline testing is required to establish BAP1-TPDS. BAP1-inactivated melanocytic nevi generally have a good prognosis and rarely metastasize. The exact lifetime risks for individual associated tumors remain uncertain in the supplied source. UV exposure and asbestos exposure may modify melanoma and mesothelioma risk, respectively. Xeroderma Pigmentosum Autosomal recessive XPA, ERCC3 (XPB), XPC, ERCC2 (XPD), DDB2 (XPE), ERCC4 (XPF), ERCC5 (XPG), and POLH (XPV) Marked UV sensitivity; approximately half have severe sunburn after minimal exposure, while the remainder may tan relatively normally. Freckle-like hyperpigmented macules develop on sun-exposed skin, usually before age 2 years. Multiple basal cell carcinomas, squamous cell carcinomas, and melanomas occur at unusually young ages. Ocular findings include photophobia, conjunctival inflammation, keratitis, corneal scarring, and eyelid abnormalities. Neurologic abnormalities occur in approximately 25% of cases and may include sensorineural hearing loss, microcephaly, spasticity, and seizures. Multiple cutaneous basal cell carcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, and melanoma; increased risks of CNS tumors, myelodysplasia/acute myeloid leukemia, gynecologic tumors, and thyroid tumors. Skin cancers in XP have the same histologic morphology as their sporadic counterparts. The syndrome is recognized clinically and genetically rather than by a unique tumor histology. No syndrome-specific IHC profile is described in the supplied source. XP results from defective nucleotide excision repair (XPA–XPG) or defective translesion DNA synthesis (POLH/XPV). XPC and DDB2/XPE impair global-genome repair while transcription-coupled repair is preserved; neurologic involvement is generally absent in these groups. XPA, XPB/ERCC3, XPD/ERCC2, XPF/ERCC4, and some XPG cases may have defects in both global-genome and transcription-coupled repair and may develop neurologic abnormalities. DNA sequencing identifies the complementation group; cultured fibroblasts show hypersensitivity to UV-induced cell killing. Clinical abnormalities of skin and eyes, together with family history, are the essential clinical basis for diagnosis. Confirm with DNA sequencing and/or specialized cellular testing for UV hypersensitivity and DNA-repair deficiency. Chromosomal breakage studies and cultured fibroblast UV-sensitivity assays may support the diagnosis. Identify the specific complementation group when possible. Constitutional photosensitivity disorders Use the characteristic early freckling, ocular involvement, skin-cancer burden, and nucleotide-excision-repair testing to support XP. Familial melanoma Familial melanoma is defined by melanoma clustering and does not produce the characteristic childhood UV sensitivity and early freckling of XP. Sporadic UV-related skin cancer The extreme early-onset and multiplicity of cancers, with ocular and sometimes neurologic findings, favor XP. In patients younger than 20 years, the risk of skin cancer at UV-exposed sites is reported to be more than 1000-fold higher than in the general population. The median age of non-melanoma skin cancer onset in the US source cohort was 9 years. The source emphasizes lifelong photoprotection and early detection of cutaneous and internal malignancies. Nevoid Basal Cell Carcinoma Syndrome (Gorlin Syndrome) PTCH1 (most common), SUFU, and rarely GPR161 Multiple basal cell carcinomas may arise on both sun-exposed and non-sun-exposed skin, often after age 10 years. Odontogenic keratocysts commonly arise in the posterior mandibular ramus, often beginning in adolescence; mean reported onset is approximately 15.5 years. Palmar and plantar pits, macrocephaly, falx/tentorium/sella calcification, and bifid or fused ribs are characteristic findings. Medulloblastoma typically occurs in early childhood, often before age 5 years and frequently before age 2 years. Other findings include ovarian fibroma, facial/skeletal anomalies, and additional CNS tumors. Multiple basal cell carcinomas; odontogenic keratocysts; desmoplastic/nodular medulloblastoma; ovarian fibroma and other less common tumors. Basal cell carcinomas show conventional BCC morphology; no unique syndrome-specific subtype is required. Basaloid nests may show peripheral palisading, stromal clefting, stromal mucin, and infundibulocystic differentiation. Nearly all associated medulloblastomas show nodular histology, usually desmoplastic/nodular medulloblastoma or medulloblastoma with extensive nodularity. Odontogenic keratocysts show a thin epithelial lining without rete ridges, corrugated parakeratin, and palisaded hyperchromatic basal cells. Basal budding and microcysts in the cyst wall are more frequent in syndrome-associated odontogenic keratocysts. No syndrome-specific IHC profile is described; evaluate each associated neoplasm according to its tumor-specific diagnostic workup. Constitutional inactivating variants in PTCH1 or SUFU cause most cases; GPR161 variants are reported exceptionally. PTCH1 and SUFU are tumor suppressors in the sonic hedgehog pathway; loss of the remaining normal allele activates SHH signaling. PTCH1/SUFU sequencing and deletion/duplication analysis identify most constitutional variants; a subset remains molecularly unexplained. SUFU-associated disease carries a substantially higher medulloblastoma risk than PTCH1-associated disease in the cited source (approximately 20% versus 1–2%). Assess the combination of multiple BCCs, odontogenic keratocysts, palmar/plantar pits, skeletal anomalies, and intracranial calcifications. Desmoplastic/nodular medulloblastoma in a very young child should prompt evaluation for Gorlin syndrome. Confirm with constitutional PTCH1 and SUFU sequencing plus deletion/duplication analysis. Consider genetic counseling and testing in young children with extensive nodular/desmoplastic medulloblastoma. Multiple sporadic basal cell carcinomas Usually lack the combination of jaw keratocysts, palmar/plantar pits, skeletal anomalies, and characteristic family history. Other hereditary BCC predisposition Correlate age, associated developmental findings, and PTCH1/SUFU pathway testing. Sporadic medulloblastoma Desmoplastic/nodular morphology in a child younger than 5 years raises suspicion; constitutional PTCH1/SUFU testing is required. Radiation treatment for medulloblastoma may induce multiple secondary BCCs and other tumors in the radiation field. Avoid unnecessary radiation exposure when syndrome status can influence treatment planning. The source notes substantial cumulative BCC burden and recommends surveillance. Carney Complex PRKAR1A (germline inactivating alterations in approximately 62%); less commonly PDE8B, PDE11A, and PRKACA amplification; PRKACB copy testing may be relevant in selected cases Often diagnosed in the early 20s; manifestations and tumors accumulate over time. Spotty pigmentation/lentigines commonly involve the lips, periocular skin, conjunctiva, and genital region. Cardiac myxomas may be an early and clinically important manifestation. Endocrine findings include primary pigmented nodular adrenocortical disease with ACTH-independent Cushing syndrome, acromegaly, and multiple thyroid nodules. Other manifestations include cutaneous/mucosal myxomas, melanocytic nevi, pigmented melanotic schwannoma, and gonadal tumors. Cardiac and cutaneous/mucosal myxomas; melanocytic nevi; psammomatous melanotic schwannoma; primary pigmented nodular adrenocortical disease; pituitary, thyroid, and gonadal tumors; osteochondromyxoma and selected breast/pancreatic/liver tumors. The supplied source does not provide a syndrome-specific histologic description; associated tumors generally resemble their sporadic counterparts. Cutaneous and cardiac myxomas, melanocytic lesions, and psammomatous melanotic schwannomas are important pathology-associated manifestations. Pigmented melanotic schwannoma is an important exception because it may metastasize and be lethal. No single syndrome-specific IHC profile is described; apply tumor-specific immunohistochemistry to the individual lesion. Germline inactivating PRKAR1A alterations are identified in approximately 62% of cases. Less common alterations involve PDE8B or PDE11A; germline PRKACA amplification is also reported. PRKAR1A inactivation increases protein kinase A activity through the cAMP signaling pathway. Molecular diagnosis may include PRKAR1A/PDE8B/PDE11A sequencing and PRKACA/PRKACB copy-number testing. The source requires at least two major diagnostic criteria, confirmed by laboratory testing, histopathology, or imaging. In the presence of one supplemental criterion, a single clinical manifestation is sufficient. Major criteria include characteristic spotty pigmentation, myxomas, specified endocrine tumors/hyperactivity, pigmented melanotic schwannoma, osteochondromyxoma, and breast adenomas. Supplemental criteria include an affected first-degree relative or a pathogenic inactivating germline PRKAR1A variant. Isolated cardiac myxoma A single myxoma does not establish Carney complex; assess characteristic pigmentation, endocrine lesions, other tumors, and family history. Other lentiginosis syndromes Carney complex is supported by the combination of lentigines with myxomas, endocrine abnormalities, and pigmented melanotic schwannoma. Sporadic melanotic schwannoma Evaluate for additional Carney complex manifestations and germline PRKAR1A-pathway alterations. Most associated tumors are benign and slow-growing. Cardiac myxomas can cause catastrophic complications because of their location, despite benign histology. Pigmented melanotic schwannoma is the major malignant-behavior exception. Muir–Torre Syndrome Autosomal dominant; a cutaneous phenotype within Lynch syndrome MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, or PMS2; MSH2 is most commonly associated. A similar phenotype may occur with inherited MUTYH pathogenic variants. Characterized by sebaceous neoplasms and/or keratoacanthomas in association with visceral malignancy. Sebaceous adenoma is the strongest cutaneous indicator; sebaceoma and sebaceous carcinoma are also associated. Multiple sebaceous neoplasms or sebaceous tumors outside the head and neck are particularly suspicious. Cystic keratoacanthomas may be multiple, occur in younger patients, and arise at sites without chronic sun exposure. Associated visceral cancers include colorectal, endometrial, gastric, small bowel, ovarian, hepatobiliary, pancreatic, urinary tract, renal, brain, and prostate tumors. Sebaceous adenoma, sebaceoma, sebaceous carcinoma, and keratoacanthoma; visceral malignancies, especially colorectal adenocarcinoma (reported in approximately 50% of patients in the source). The source does not describe a unique syndrome-specific histology; sebaceous neoplasms and visceral tumors are morphologically evaluated by their usual criteria. Sebaceous hyperplasia is not considered an Muir–Torre-associated neoplasm in the source. Keratoacanthomas may show sebaceous differentiation. Assess nuclear expression of MLH1, PMS2, MSH2, and MSH6 in the tumor. Loss of MSH2 alone or with MSH6 suggests an MSH2 pathway defect. Loss of MLH1 alone or with PMS2 suggests MLH1 inactivation or acquired MLH1 promoter methylation. Retained MMR protein expression does not completely exclude functional MMR deficiency. The syndrome is caused by a constitutional pathogenic variant in an MMR gene; definitive diagnosis requires germline testing. Biallelic somatic inactivation produces MMR deficiency and microsatellite instability. Tumor MSI testing by PCR correlates with MMR IHC, but colorectal-derived MSI markers may be less sensitive in sebaceous neoplasms. MMR deficiency in a sebaceous tumor is a screening clue, not proof of a germline syndrome; integrate age, personal/family history, and multiplicity. Suspect Muir–Torre syndrome in patients with multiple sebaceous neoplasms and one or more visceral malignancies. Demonstrate tumor MMR deficiency by IHC and/or MSI testing when indicated. Confirm the Muir–Torre/Lynch syndrome diagnosis by identifying a constitutional/germline pathogenic variant in an MMR gene. Interpret MMR IHC in the context of personal history, family history, age, number of sebaceous tumors, and tumor site. Sporadic sebaceous neoplasm Many sebaceous tumors are sporadic; MMR loss alone has limited positive predictive value for a germline defect. Lynch syndrome without Muir–Torre phenotype Muir–Torre is the cutaneous sebaceous-neoplasm/keratoacanthoma phenotype within the Lynch spectrum. MUTYH-associated phenotype The source notes that inherited MUTYH variants can produce a similar phenotype; germline testing distinguishes the underlying syndrome. Sebaceous hyperplasia should not be counted as a Muir–Torre-associated sebaceous neoplasm. Approximately one half to two thirds of unselected sebaceous neoplasms may show deficient MMR protein expression, most of which are sporadic. The source reports that MMR deficiency rates vary by site and tumor type; clinical correlation and germline testing are essential. Brooke–Spiegler Syndrome and Related CYLD Cutaneous Syndromes Autosomal dominant; mosaic presentations may occur CYLD (heterozygous germline pathogenic variants; chromosome 16q12–q13) Multiple cutaneous spiradenomas, cylindromas, spiradenocylindromas, and/or trichoepitheliomas typically begin around puberty. Spiradenomas, cylindromas, and spiradenocylindromas commonly affect the head and neck and may number dozens to hundreds. Trichoepitheliomas often present as bilateral small papules on the nasolabial folds and face. Lesion number and size increase over time; unilateral clustering may indicate genetic mosaicism. Rapid growth, ulceration, or bleeding, particularly in older patients, raises concern for malignant transformation. Salivary gland tumors occur in approximately 1–2% of cases, usually as membranous basal cell adenoma of the parotid. Cutaneous spiradenoma, cylindroma, spiradenocylindroma, and trichoepithelioma; rare salivary gland membranous basal cell adenoma; rare malignant transformation and pulmonary metastasis. Spiradenoma is composed of basaloid cells in trabecular, reticular, or solid patterns, admixed with pale cells and conspicuous lymphocytes. Spiradenoma may contain tubular structures and PAS-positive hyaline basement membrane droplets. Cylindroma shows a characteristic jigsaw-puzzle arrangement of basaloid islands surrounded by thick eosinophilic basement membrane material. Cylindroma nests often show peripheral palisading of darker cells and paler central cells; intratumoral lymphocytes are absent or sparse. Spiradenocylindroma combines the histologic patterns of spiradenoma and cylindroma. Salivary gland membranous basal cell adenoma is often multicentric/bilateral, with basaloid nests, peripheral palisading, and dense hyaline stroma. Salivary gland membranous basal cell adenomas express epithelial and myoepithelial markers. The source does not define a single IHC panel for the cutaneous CYLD-associated tumors. Germline heterozygous pathogenic CYLD variants cause Brooke–Spiegler and related CYLD cutaneous syndromes. Most variants are frameshift or nonsense changes; splice-site variants, missense variants, and large deletions are also reported. Cutaneous tumors frequently acquire loss of heterozygosity or a second inactivating CYLD alteration. Biallelic pathogenic CYLD variants support the diagnosis. ALPK1 hotspot mutations are characteristic of sporadic spiradenomas and related malignant tumors and are not seen in BSS skin tumors in the supplied source. The diagnosis is established in a proband with multiple histologically confirmed inherited cutaneous cylindromas, spiradenomas, spiradenocylindromas, and/or trichoepitheliomas. Germline heterozygous pathogenic CYLD testing is desirable for confirmation. A small cluster of lesions without family history may reflect mosaicism; testing affected skin tumors may be necessary. Consider the syndrome in patients with membranous-type multicentric salivary gland basal cell adenoma and a personal history of a cylindroma, trichoepithelioma, or spiradenoma. Sporadic spiradenoma/cylindroma Usually solitary; multiple tumors beginning around puberty and a family history support a CYLD-associated syndrome. Membranous basal cell adenoma versus basal cell adenocarcinoma Basal cell adenoma lacks invasion; basal cell adenocarcinoma is invasive. Cellular pleomorphic adenoma Membranous basal cell adenoma has a consistently basaloid pattern, peripheral palisading, and thick hyaline basement membranes. Approximately 80–85% of classic Brooke–Spiegler phenotype and 40–50% of multiple familial trichoepithelioma phenotype cases harbor germline CYLD variants in the source. The offspring of an affected individual have a 50% chance of inheriting the variant. Rapid clinical change warrants careful sampling to exclude malignant transformation.
