title: Cutaneous Hematopoietic Lymphoid Tumors
content: use client Cutaneous mastocytosis Myeloid / mast cell Maculopapular disease favors trunk and proximal extremities; palms, soles, and central face are usually spared. Diffuse cutaneous mastocytosis involves the entire skin surface; mastocytomas may occur anywhere, especially trunk and scalp. Childhood-onset disease is usually skin-limited; most adult-onset cutaneous mastocytosis is associated with systemic mastocytosis. Lesions may urticate, redden, swell, itch, or blister after stroking (Darier sign) or temperature change. Typical cutaneous lesions with increased dermal mast cells, preferably confirmed by KIT and tryptase. Distinguish cutaneous from systemic mastocytosis clinically; skin histology alone cannot establish or exclude systemic involvement. Mast cells are scattered or clustered around vessels and adnexa, or form small/band-like upper-dermal infiltrates in maculopapular disease. Diffuse cutaneous disease shows a marked increase in mast cells; mastocytoma forms nodular aggregates. Cells may appear inconspicuous and histiocytoid on H&E; Giemsa/toluidine blue highlights metachromatic granules. Mast cells coexpress tryptase and KIT (CD117). CD2, CD25, and/or CD30 aberrancy supports clonality but may be absent in skin, particularly in adults. Activating KIT mutations are characteristic; KIT p.D816V occurs in >90% of adult cases and approximately 35–40% of pediatric cases. KIT mutation testing in lesional skin supports diagnosis; adult evaluation generally requires bone marrow assessment when mastocytosis is suspected. Reactive mast-cell increase Basal hyperpigmentation, interstitial distribution, and clusters of ≥3 mast cells favor maculopapular cutaneous mastocytosis. Mast cell sarcoma Requires a destructive mass of highly atypical mast cells, not simply pleomorphic/promastocyte forms in childhood cutaneous disease. Can arise in any organ; bone and gastrointestinal tract are most often involved. Primary cutaneous and oral mucosal cases are exceedingly rare. Usually arises de novo; adults predominate, but children can be affected. May present as a destructive mass with mast-cell mediator symptoms and increased serum tryptase. Localized infiltrative, destructive tumor composed of highly atypical mast cells expressing tryptase and usually KIT. Criteria for systemic mastocytosis are not fulfilled. Destructive sheets of immature mast cells with medium-to-large pleomorphic or epithelioid cells and oval/bilobed nuclei. Multinucleated cells, mitotic activity, eosinophils, and metachromatic cytoplasmic granules may be present. Tryptase is positive; KIT (CD117) is positive in most cases. CD2, CD25, and CD30 are variable; CD68, CD45, CD43, and MITF may be nonspecific pitfalls. KIT p.D816V is uncommon; approximately half of reported cases are KIT wild type. Whole-gene KIT sequencing is recommended because non-D816V mutations may occur. ALK-negative anaplastic large cell lymphoma Use a broad lineage panel; mast-cell tryptase and KIT support mast-cell differentiation. Histiocytic/myeloid neoplasm, melanoma, carcinoma, sarcoma Integrate lineage-specific markers with morphology; CD68 alone is not specific. Cutaneous involvement by myeloid neoplasms / myeloid sarcoma Myeloid Most often trunk, extremities, and head/neck; dermis and subcutis are involved. May occur with AML, MDS, MPN, or MDS/MPN, including CMML; skin lesions can precede AML in approximately 10% of myeloid sarcomas. Violaceous or hemorrhagic papules, plaques, or nodules; infants may show blueberry-muffin lesions. Architectural effacement by a tumor of myeloid blasts, with or without maturation, defines myeloid sarcoma regardless of blast percentage. Without architectural effacement, use a descriptive diagnosis of cutaneous involvement by a myeloid neoplasm; if blasts are ≥20%, diagnose AML involving skin. Myeloid sarcoma forms diffuse sheets in dermis/subcutis, often sparing epidermis with a grenz zone. Blasts are medium to large with fine chromatin and inconspicuous nucleoli; monocytic differentiation may show folded nuclei/promonocytes. Non-mass-forming infiltrates may be perivascular, periadnexal, patchy nodular, or interstitial. Common markers: CD13, CD33, CD43, CD68, and MPO. Monocytic differentiation often expresses CD4, CD11c, CD14 (variable), CD56, and lysozyme; CD34 and KIT are often absent. Granulocytic blasts may express CD34 and KIT; cytoplasmic NPM1 can indicate an NPM1 mutation. No skin-specific molecular test is required; perform systemic cytogenetic and molecular classification for therapy. Shared AML/MS abnormalities include monosomy 7, trisomy 8, KMT2A/11q23 abnormalities, and NPM1, FLT3, or RAS-pathway mutations. Blastic plasmacytoid dendritic cell neoplasm CD4, CD56, CD123, CD303, TCL1, and TCF4; MPO and lysozyme are absent. Large-cell lymphoma Expresses lineage-defining lymphoid markers such as CD3, CD19, or CD20. Sweet syndrome / inflammatory infiltrate Maturing or mature cells without architectural effacement or blast excess require clinical and hematologic correlation. Mature plasmacytoid dendritic cell proliferation associated with myeloid neoplasm Plasmacytoid dendritic cell Cutaneous lesions may accompany CMML and other myeloid neoplasms; skin, blood, and bone marrow correlation is important. Occurs in the setting of an underlying myeloid neoplasm, particularly CMML. May appear as papules, nodules, or plaques; can be scattered or nodular. Recognize a mature pDC proliferation in association with a myeloid neoplasm rather than automatically classifying it as BPDCN. pDCs may be scattered singly or form nodular aggregates within a myeloid infiltrate. Use a pDC panel including CD123, CD303, TCL1, and TCF4, interpreted with morphology and clinical context. The supplied source does not specify a defining molecular alteration for this proliferation. BPDCN is a blastic neoplasm; correlate cytology, phenotype, and underlying myeloid disease. Reactive pDC infiltrate Interpret distribution and density in the context of the associated myeloid neoplasm. Blastic plasmacytoid dendritic cell neoplasm (BPDCN) Skin is a frequent presenting site; lesions may be multifocal and can precede or accompany bone marrow/blood involvement. Typically presents with bruise-like or violaceous papules, plaques, and nodules. Systemic staging is essential because skin disease may be the first manifestation. Blastic neoplasm with a plasmacytoid dendritic cell phenotype; establish lineage with a coordinated marker panel. Dense dermal and/or subcutaneous infiltrate of monomorphic blastic cells; epidermis is often spared by a grenz zone. Typical phenotype includes CD4, CD56, CD123, CD303, TCL1, and TCF4. MPO and lysozyme are absent, helping separate BPDCN from myeloid sarcoma. The supplied excerpt emphasizes immunophenotypic classification and does not identify a single defining molecular alteration. Myeloid sarcoma Usually expresses MPO and/or lysozyme; monocytic lesions often express CD68 and CD33. Mature pDC proliferation Occurs with a myeloid neoplasm and lacks the overt blastic morphology of BPDCN. Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH) Langerhans cell / dendritic Skin involvement commonly affects scalp, flexures, trunk, and intertriginous areas; disease may be single-system or multisystem. Occurs in infants, children, and adults; clinical behavior depends on extent and organs involved. Cutaneous lesions may be papules, crusted plaques, or ulcerated lesions. Large grooved or convoluted epithelioid cells in the appropriate context, expressing CD1a and CD207 (langerin). Assess extent of disease; cutaneous biopsy does not establish whether disease is skin-limited. Large round-to-oval cells with grooved/folded nuclei and moderate eosinophilic cytoplasm. Upper dermis is expanded, often with epidermotropism, scale-crust, or ulceration. Eosinophils, lymphocytes, multinucleated cells, and occasional neutrophils/plasma cells form the inflammatory background. CD1a and CD207 (langerin) are defining; S100 is nuclear and cytoplasmic. CD68 shows a Golgi-dot pattern; Ki-67 is usually low (<10% in cited double-stain studies). MAPK-pathway alterations are common; BRAF p.V600E is clinically relevant and associated with increased relapse risk in the source. Sensitive assays may be needed for low variant allele fractions; BRAF and other MAPK alterations may guide targeted therapy. Reactive CD1a-positive dendritic-cell hyperplasia Branched cells, tight perivascular distribution, and low/negative CD207 favor reactive hyperplasia. Juvenile xanthogranuloma / ECD / ALK-positive histiocytosis Use macrophage-lineage markers and molecular testing; these are usually CD1a/CD207 negative. Langerhans cell sarcoma Moderate-to-severe atypia, prominent nucleoli, atypical mitoses, and increased proliferation. Xanthelasma Histiocytic / macrophage Usually eyelids, especially medial canthi; may be solitary or multiple. Yellow-orange soft papules or plaques; may be associated with dyslipidemia but can occur with normal lipid levels. Clinical yellow plaque with dermal lipid-laden macrophages; correlate with lipid status when appropriate. Superficial dermal sheets or clusters of foamy histiocytes, often with accompanying inflammatory cells. Macrophage markers such as CD68 and CD163 support histiocytic lineage; no unique immunophenotype is specified. No diagnostic molecular alteration is established in the supplied source. Juvenile/adult xanthogranuloma Look for Touton giant cells and a more developed xanthogranulomatous infiltrate. Erdheim–Chester disease Consider systemic, often periocular, disease and characteristic clinical/radiologic findings. Juvenile xanthogranuloma (JXG) Most often head and neck, followed by trunk and extremities; may be solitary or multiple. Usually affects infants and young children; adult-onset lesions also occur. Typical lesions are yellow-orange to red-brown papules or nodules. Bland xanthogranulomatous histiocytic proliferation in the appropriate clinical setting. Early lesions may be monomorphic histiocytes; mature lesions show foamy histiocytes and Touton-type giant cells. Mixed inflammatory cells, including lymphocytes and eosinophils, may be present. CD68, CD163, and factor XIIIa are typically positive; CD1a and CD207 are negative. S100 is usually negative or only focal. MAPK-pathway alterations have been reported in the broader xanthogranuloma family; no routine molecular test is required in typical cutaneous JXG. LCH LCH is CD1a+/CD207+ and shows grooved Langerhans cells with eosinophils. ALK-positive histiocytosis ALK immunoreactivity and ALK rearrangement support that entity. ECD / adult xanthogranuloma Use clinical distribution and systemic/radiologic findings. Reticulohistiocytosis Skin and joints; multicentric disease typically involves hands, face, and periarticular skin. Includes solitary, multifocal, and multicentric forms; multicentric reticulohistiocytosis is associated with destructive polyarthritis. Epithelioid histiocytes with abundant eosinophilic, ground-glass cytoplasm; correlate with joint and systemic findings. Sheets or nodules of large histiocytes with abundant finely granular eosinophilic ground-glass cytoplasm. Multinucleated giant cells may be present; nuclei are often vesicular. CD68 and CD163 are positive; factor XIIIa is often positive. CD1a is negative; S100 is usually negative or rarely positive. No recurrent diagnostic molecular alteration is established in the supplied source. Rosai–Dorfman disease RDD shows emperipolesis and S100/OCT2 expression. ALK positivity/rearrangement distinguishes this entity. LCH expresses CD1a and CD207. Rosai–Dorfman disease (RDD) Classically cervical lymph nodes; extranodal disease may involve skin, upper respiratory tract, orbit, and other organs. Cutaneous RDD may be skin-limited. May present as solitary or multiple red-brown to yellowish papules, plaques, or nodules. Systemic disease often presents with painless lymphadenopathy; cutaneous-only cases are recognized. Histiocytes with emperipolesis and a characteristic S100-positive macrophage phenotype in the appropriate clinical setting. Large pale histiocytes in a dense lymphoplasmacytic background. Emperipolesis—intact lymphocytes/plasma cells within histiocyte cytoplasm—is a key clue, although it may be focal or inconspicuous. Histiocytes express S100, CD68, CD163, and OCT2; fascin is often positive. CD1a and CD207 are negative. A subset has MAPK-pathway mutations; testing may be useful in selected cases, particularly systemic/refractory disease. Ground-glass eosinophilic cytoplasm; typically lacks the classic S100/OCT2-positive emperipolesis pattern. JXG / ECD Usually CD163/CD68 positive but S100 negative or only focal; correlate with systemic distribution. CD1a and CD207 are positive in LCH. Erdheim–Chester disease (ECD) Systemic disease with characteristic long-bone, retroperitoneal/perirenal, cardiovascular, and CNS involvement; skin and periocular tissues may be involved. Usually adults; chronic multisystem disease with variable symptoms based on organ involvement. Cutaneous lesions may be xanthomatous or xanthogranulomatous. Bland foamy CD68/CD163-positive histiocytes in the appropriate radiologic and clinical context; evaluate for systemic disease. Foamy histiocytes in fibrotic or xanthogranulomatous infiltrates; Touton giant cells may occur. Fibrosis can be prominent; morphology overlaps with JXG and other xanthogranulomatous disorders. CD163, CD68, CD14, and CD4 are positive; factor XIIIa, fascin, and S100 may be at least partially positive. CD1a and CD207 are negative; phospho-ERK is frequently positive. BRAF p.V600E or other MAPK-pathway mutations are frequent; BRAF variant allele fraction may be very low. Sensitive molecular assays are important; BRAF/MEK inhibitors are therapeutically relevant. JXG / adult-onset xanthogranuloma Clinical-radiologic evidence of multisystem ECD is decisive. RDD RDD is typically S100+/OCT2+ with emperipolesis. LCH is CD1a+/CD207+; mixed histiocytosis can occur. May be skin-limited or multisystem; cutaneous lesions are solitary or multiple papules, nodules, or plaques. Occurs in children and adults; multisystem disease may occur in infancy. Clinical course varies with disease distribution; skin lesions may regress. Sheets/aggregates of histiocytes without high-grade atypia, with ALK immunoreactivity and at least two macrophage markers. Non-epidermotropic, non-circumscribed dermal infiltrate of histiocytes, sometimes with fibrosis. Cells range from epithelioid/foamy to spindle or multinucleated forms; irregular nuclear contours, emperipolesis, and Touton cells may occur. Morphology may closely resemble JXG. ALK is positive, sometimes weak/focal; CD68, CD163, CD14, CD4, and lysozyme show variable positivity. Fascin and factor XIIIa are commonly positive; CD1a, CD207, and CD30 are negative. ALK rearrangement is characteristic; KIF5B is the most common partner, with several less common partners reported. Demonstration of an ALK fusion supports diagnosis and may guide ALK-inhibitor therapy. JXG Can be morphologically indistinguishable; ALK IHC/rearrangement is decisive. RDD / reticulohistiocytosis Compare S100/OCT2, emperipolesis, ground-glass cytoplasm, and lineage markers. Histiocytic sarcoma High-grade cytologic atypia and destructive growth favor histiocytic sarcoma. Can involve skin as primary or secondary disease; also occurs in lymph nodes and extranodal organs. Very rare aggressive neoplasm; skin lesions may be solitary or multiple nodules/plaques. Malignant tumor with convincing histiocytic differentiation and exclusion of epithelial, melanocytic, lymphoid, myeloid, and dendritic-cell neoplasms. Diffuse destructive sheets of large pleomorphic cells with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm. Marked nuclear atypia, prominent nucleoli, atypical mitoses, and necrosis may be present; hemophagocytosis can occur. CD163, CD68, lysozyme, and PU.1 support histiocytic differentiation; expression may be variable. Exclude lineage mimics with broad keratin, melanocytic, lymphoid, myeloid, and dendritic-cell markers. RAS/MAPK-pathway alterations and other mutations may occur; no single alteration is defining in the supplied source. Anaplastic large cell lymphoma Use CD30, T-cell markers, and ALK as appropriate; histiocytic markers alone are insufficient. Melanoma / carcinoma Exclude with melanocytic markers and broad-spectrum keratins. MPO and other myeloid-lineage markers support myeloid differentiation. Indeterminate dendritic cell tumor (IDCT) Other dendritic cell Usually skin-limited; solitary, multifocal, or generalized papules, nodules, or tumors. Clonal disorder with variable clinical course; most cutaneous cases are indolent, but progression is reported. Infiltration by Langerhans-like cells expressing CD1a and S100 but lacking CD207 (langerin). Exclude LCH, ECD, ALK-positive histiocytosis, and other defined histiocytoses. Dermis/subcutis contains sheets of monomorphic Langerhans-like cells with kidney-shaped or deeply grooved nuclei and abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm. Epidermis is usually spared; peripheral lymphocytes and eosinophils may be present. S100 and CD1a are positive; CD207 is negative and Birbeck granules are absent. Reactive macrophages may express CD68/CD163; do not mistake them for tumor cells. BRAF analysis may help exclude other histiocytoses; no defining recurrent alteration is specified. LCH is CD207-positive. Interdigitating dendritic cell sarcoma Lacks CD1a; IDCT is CD1a-positive. Reticulohistiocytoma Macrophage markers positive; CD1a negative and S100 rarely positive. Reactive B-cell-rich lymphoid proliferation Reactive lymphoid / B cell Cutaneous lesions may occur at sites of arthropod bites, infection, tattoo, medication exposure, or other antigenic stimuli. Benign reactive process with a broad range of infectious and noninfectious triggers. Polymorphous B-cell-rich infiltrate with clinical/pathologic evidence supporting a reactive process; exclude primary cutaneous B-cell lymphoma. Nodular or diffuse lymphoid infiltrate with a mixed population and reactive germinal centers in some cases. Preserved compartmental organization and cytologic polymorphism favor a reactive process. Use CD20/PAX5, CD3, CD21/CD23, BCL6, CD10, BCL2, and light-chain studies to assess architecture and clonality. Clonality studies may be supportive but must be interpreted cautiously; no single molecular alteration defines reactive proliferation. Primary cutaneous marginal zone lymphoma Assess plasma-cell distribution, class switching, light-chain restriction, and clinical course. Primary cutaneous follicle centre lymphoma Neoplastic follicle-centre cells show a coherent B-cell phenotype and altered follicular architecture. Primary cutaneous marginal zone lymphoma (PCMZL) B-cell lymphoma Usually trunk and upper extremities; primary disease is confined to skin at diagnosis. Indolent course with excellent prognosis despite frequent cutaneous recurrence. Class-switched and IgM-positive non-class-switched subtypes are recognized. Primary cutaneous B-cell lymphoproliferation with marginal-zone/plasmacytic differentiation; exclude extracutaneous lymphoma. Dense nodular or diffuse dermal infiltrate, often with reactive germinal centers and marginal-zone-like B cells. Plasma cells may be prominent and often cluster at the periphery of nodules. B cells express CD20/PAX5; plasma cells express CD138/MUM1 with light-chain restriction in many cases. Class-switched subtype often shows class-switched immunoglobulin; IgM-positive subtype retains IgM and may have a different phenotype. No single defining molecular alteration; clonality and selected genetic findings may support classification but are not stand-alone. Reactive B-cell-rich proliferation Reactive architecture and polytypic plasma cells favor a reactive process; correlate clinically. Follicle-centre phenotype and architecture rather than marginal-zone/plasmacytic differentiation. Primary cutaneous follicle centre lymphoma (PCFCL) Most often scalp, forehead, and trunk; primary disease is skin-limited at diagnosis. Usually adults; solitary or grouped erythematous papules, plaques, or tumors. Indolent course and excellent prognosis; extracutaneous spread is uncommon. Follicle-centre B-cell neoplasm arising primarily in skin; staging is required to exclude systemic follicular lymphoma. Nodular, follicular, and/or diffuse dermal infiltrate of centrocytes and variable centroblasts. Epidermis is usually spared; follicular dendritic-cell meshworks may be present. CD20/PAX5 and BCL6 are positive; CD10 is variable. BCL2 is often negative or weak; strong diffuse BCL2 and systemic findings prompt evaluation for systemic follicular lymphoma. BCL2 rearrangement is uncommon compared with systemic follicular lymphoma; molecular findings may help in selected difficult cases. Systemic follicular lymphoma involving skin Strong BCL2 and/or BCL2 rearrangement and extracutaneous disease support systemic lymphoma. PCMZL Plasmacytic/marginal-zone differentiation rather than follicle-centre phenotype. Primary cutaneous diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, leg type (PCDLBCL-LT) Typically lower legs, often bilateral; may occur at other sites. Usually older adults, with female predominance in many series; rapidly enlarging red-blue tumors. Aggressive clinical course compared with PCFCL and PCMZL. Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma with characteristic phenotype arising primarily in skin; exclude systemic DLBCL. Diffuse sheets of centroblast- and immunoblast-like large cells throughout dermis and subcutis. Epidermis is often spared; mitoses are frequent. CD20/PAX5 positive; BCL2, MUM1/IRF4, and FOXP1 commonly positive; BCL6 variable; CD10 usually negative. MYC may be expressed; interpret with morphology and molecular findings. MYD88 and CD79B mutations are characteristic recurrent findings and help distinguish from PCFCL. PCFCL Usually more centrocytic, less monomorphic; BCL2/MUM1 profile differs. Systemic DLBCL involving skin Clinical staging is essential to establish primary cutaneous origin. Intravascular large B-cell lymphoma (IVLBCL) Neoplastic cells are confined predominantly to small-vessel lumina in skin and other organs; cutaneous variant often involves legs. Usually older adults; cutaneous lesions may be erythematous or violaceous patches, plaques, or nodules. Systemic disease may involve CNS, lungs, kidneys, and other organs; hemophagocytic variant is recognized. Large atypical B cells predominantly or exclusively within vascular lumina. Large atypical lymphoid cells distend dermal/subcutaneous small vessels. Perivascular or extravascular tumor growth is usually limited in classic cases. CD20, PAX5, and other B-cell markers are positive; endothelial markers outline involved vascular lumina. Assess CD5, CD10, MUM1, and proliferation index as appropriate. No single molecular alteration is defining in the supplied excerpt; systemic lymphoma workup guides classification. Vasculitis / thrombotic vasculopathy Neoplastic large B cells fill vessel lumina rather than inflammatory destruction or bland thrombi. Other large B-cell lymphoma Demonstrate intravascular growth pattern and exclude systemic/extravascular disease. Reactive T-cell-rich lymphoid proliferation Reactive lymphoid / T cell Can arise in association with arthropod bites, infection, medication, vaccination, tattoo, and other inflammatory stimuli. Benign reactive process; clinical history and distribution are important. Polymorphous T-cell-rich infiltrate without convincing cytologic or phenotypic evidence of lymphoma. Variable superficial/deep perivascular, nodular, or diffuse lymphocytic infiltrate; admixed histiocytes, eosinophils, and B cells may occur. CD3-positive T cells predominate; assess CD4/CD8 balance and pan-T-cell antigens (CD2, CD5, CD7). Retained pan-T-cell markers and mixed populations favor reactive proliferation. T-cell receptor clonality may occur in reactive lesions and is not independently diagnostic. CTCL Look for epidermotropism, atypia, antigen loss, and clinicopathologic persistence/progression. CD4-positive small/medium T-cell LPD Localized clinical presentation and characteristic follicular-helper T-cell phenotype require consideration. Primary cutaneous CD4-positive small/medium T-cell lymphoproliferative disorder T-cell lymphoproliferative disorder Usually solitary lesion on face, neck, or upper trunk. Typically adults; localized slow-growing papule, plaque, or nodule. Generally indolent behavior. Localized dermal proliferation of small/medium CD4-positive T cells with a follicular-helper T-cell phenotype; exclude systemic disease. Dense nodular or diffuse dermal infiltrate of small-to-medium pleomorphic lymphocytes, often with admixed B cells, plasma cells, and histiocytes. Epidermotropism is usually absent. CD3+, CD4+; follicular-helper markers such as PD-1, ICOS, BCL6, and CXCL13 may be expressed. CD8 and cytotoxic markers are usually absent; assess CD30 and proliferation in large-cell subsets. Clonal T-cell receptor rearrangement may be present but is not sufficient alone for diagnosis. Mycosis fungoides Usually epidermotropic and clinically patch/plaque based. Primary cutaneous peripheral T-cell lymphoma, NOS More atypical/aggressive and lacks the characteristic localized indolent pattern. Mycosis fungoides (MF) T-cell lymphoma / CD4 predominant Classically buttocks, trunk, and proximal extremities (bathing-trunk distribution); folliculotropic variant favors head and neck. Usually adults; patches progress to plaques and tumors over time; erythrodermic disease may occur. Clinical evolution and distribution are essential to diagnosis. Epidermotropic atypical T-cell infiltrate with compatible clinical presentation and evolution. Epidermotropism by atypical lymphocytes with irregular/cerebriform nuclei, often disproportionate to spongiosis. Pautrier microabscesses may be present; plaque/tumor stages show denser dermal infiltrates. Folliculotropic MF shows follicular epitheliotropism and may cause alopecia. Usually CD3+, CD4+, with loss of one or more pan-T-cell antigens (often CD7); CD8-positive variants occur. CD30 may be expressed in transformed disease. Clonal T-cell receptor rearrangement supports diagnosis in context; genomic abnormalities involve T-cell signaling and epigenetic pathways. Chronic spongiotic dermatitis More spongiosis, less atypical epidermotropism, and no convincing aberrant T-cell phenotype. Pityriasis lichenoides / inflammatory dermatoses Integrate clinical course, cytology, epidermal pattern, and T-cell phenotype. Lymphomatoid papulosis (LyP) T-cell lymphoma / CD30-positive Typically trunk and extremities; lesions occur in crops and may be widespread. Recurrent papules/nodules that spontaneously regress, often leaving varioliform scars. Clinical course is essential; histology alone may overlap with primary cutaneous ALCL. Recurrent self-healing papulonodular lesions with a CD30-positive atypical T-cell infiltrate. Several histologic patterns (A–E) with variable wedge-shaped infiltrates, large atypical cells, epidermotropism, or angiocentric/angiodestructive features. Large atypical cells are typically scattered or clustered in an inflammatory background. Atypical cells are strongly CD30-positive; T-cell markers are variable and may be partially lost. ALK is generally negative in primary cutaneous cases. Clonal T-cell receptor rearrangements may be detected but do not distinguish LyP from other CD30-positive disorders. Primary cutaneous ALCL Persistent tumor rather than recurrent self-regressing crops; clinical behavior distinguishes. Reactive CD30-positive infiltrate Correlate with lesion evolution and exclude infection/drug reaction. Primary cutaneous anaplastic large cell lymphoma (PCALCL) Commonly trunk, face, and extremities; usually solitary or localized tumors. Persistent rapidly growing red-brown nodules or tumors; ulceration may occur. Skin-limited disease has a generally favorable prognosis, unlike systemic ALCL. Dense dermal tumor of large pleomorphic/anaplastic CD30-positive T cells; exclude systemic ALCL. Cohesive sheets of large anaplastic cells with hallmark horseshoe/kidney-shaped nuclei; epidermal involvement may be variable. At least 75% of tumor cells typically express CD30. Strong diffuse CD30; T-cell markers variably retained; ALK usually negative. EMA may be positive in a subset; broad panel and staging distinguish systemic ALCL. DUSP22 and TP63 rearrangements occur in subsets; not required for diagnosis. Lymphomatoid papulosis Recurrent self-healing lesions versus persistent tumor. Systemic ALK-negative ALCL Clinical staging and extracutaneous disease determine classification. Transformed MF Background MF and clinical history support transformation. Subcutaneous panniculitis-like T-cell lymphoma (SPTCL) T-cell lymphoma / αβ cytotoxic Subcutaneous fat of trunk and extremities; usually spares dermis and epidermis. Usually adults; multiple tender subcutaneous nodules/plaques, sometimes with fever and hemophagocytic syndrome. αβ phenotype generally has a more favorable course than γδ lymphoma. Atypical cytotoxic T cells rimming individual adipocytes in a predominantly lobular panniculitis; αβ phenotype. Lobular panniculitis with atypical lymphocytes rimming adipocytes and karyorrhexis. Fat necrosis and histiocytes are common; hemophagocytosis may be present. CD3+, CD8+, βF1+, cytotoxic markers (TIA1, granzyme B, perforin); usually CD4−, CD56−, and EBV−. CD30 is generally negative. Clonal T-cell receptor rearrangement supports diagnosis; no single defining recurrent mutation specified. Lupus panniculitis Lymphoid follicles, plasma cells, hyaline fat necrosis, and interface change favor lupus. Primary cutaneous γδ T-cell lymphoma Usually βF1-negative with γδ TCR expression and more aggressive epidermal/dermal involvement. T-cell lymphoma / γδ cytotoxic Involves dermis and subcutis; may also show epidermotropic disease. Aggressive lymphoma with ulcerated plaques, nodules, or tumors; systemic symptoms may occur. Clonal cytotoxic T-cell neoplasm expressing γδ T-cell receptor, with appropriate clinical and morphologic findings. Variable epidermotropic, dermal, and subcutaneous infiltrates; angioinvasion, necrosis, and cytotoxic injury may be prominent. Cells range from small/medium to pleomorphic; panniculitic pattern can mimic SPTCL. CD3+, βF1−, TCRγ/δ+; cytotoxic markers positive. CD4 and CD8 are variable; CD56 may be positive; EBV is negative. Clonal T-cell receptor rearrangement supports diagnosis. SPTCL SPTCL is αβ/βF1-positive and usually confined to subcutis. Primary cutaneous CD8-positive aggressive epidermotropic lymphoma Typically αβ phenotype with marked epidermotropism. Primary cutaneous acral CD8-positive T-cell lymphoproliferative disorder T-cell lymphoproliferative disorder / CD8 Acral skin, especially ear, nose, and distal extremities. Usually adults; solitary slowly growing papule or nodule. Indolent behavior and excellent prognosis; terminology reflects its lymphoproliferative rather than aggressive lymphoma behavior. Localized dermal CD8-positive T-cell proliferation in an acral site, with indolent clinical course. Dense nodular dermal infiltrate of monomorphic small-to-medium cells, often with a grenz zone. Epidermotropism is absent or minimal. CD3+, CD8+, often TIA1+; CD4−; CD30 usually negative or limited. Granzyme B and perforin are generally absent or limited compared with aggressive cytotoxic lymphomas. Clonal T-cell receptor rearrangement may be present; no defining molecular alteration specified. Marked epidermotropism, cytotoxic phenotype, and aggressive clinical course. PCALCL Large pleomorphic CD30-positive cells and persistent tumors. Primary cutaneous CD8-positive aggressive epidermotropic cytotoxic T-cell lymphoma T-cell lymphoma / CD8 cytotoxic Widespread skin; epidermis, adnexa, dermis, and sometimes subcutis may be involved. Aggressive course with multiple ulcerated papules, plaques, and tumors; mucosal involvement may occur. Atypical CD8-positive cytotoxic T-cell infiltrate with prominent epidermotropism and destructive epithelial injury. Pagetoid epidermotropism by atypical lymphocytes, often with epidermal necrosis/ulceration. Adnexal epitheliotropism and dermal/subcutaneous involvement may be present. CD3+, CD8+, βF1 often positive; cytotoxic markers TIA1, granzyme B, and perforin positive. CD4−; CD30 variable; EBV negative. Clonal T-cell receptor rearrangement supports diagnosis; no single defining molecular alteration specified. Primary cutaneous acral CD8-positive T-cell LPD Acral, localized, dermal, indolent lesion without destructive epidermotropism. γδ T-cell lymphoma TCRγ/δ positive and βF1 negative; distribution and phenotype differ. T-cell lymphoma Skin; no defining anatomic predilection. Very rare; diagnosis of exclusion for cases not fitting a defined cutaneous T-cell entity. Primary cutaneous T-cell lymphoma that does not meet criteria for another specific entity; exclude systemic lymphoma. Usually atypical pleomorphic lymphoid infiltrate with variable dermal/subcutaneous distribution. T-cell phenotype with variable antigen loss; characterize CD4/CD8, cytotoxic markers, CD30, and EBV as indicated. T-cell receptor clonality may support a clonal process but is not entity-defining. Specific CTCL entities Exclude MF, CD30-positive LPD, SPTCL, γδ lymphoma, and CD8-positive entities. Systemic peripheral T-cell lymphoma Clinical staging is required to establish primary cutaneous disease. Sézary syndrome T-cell lymphoma / leukemic CTCL Generalized skin involvement (erythroderma) with circulating malignant T cells and often lymphadenopathy. Usually adults; erythroderma, severe pruritus, palmoplantar keratoderma, alopecia, and ectropion may occur. Blood involvement is defining; distinguish from erythrodermic MF. Erythroderma with a clonal circulating atypical T-cell population meeting blood criteria for Sézary syndrome. Skin may show a superficial band-like or lichenoid infiltrate with epidermotropism; findings can be subtle and overlap with MF. Usually CD3+, CD4+, with loss of CD7 and/or CD26; assess aberrant phenotype by flow cytometry. T-cell receptor clonality should be demonstrated in blood and correlated with skin. Clonal T-cell receptor rearrangement in blood; genomic abnormalities overlap with CTCL signaling and epigenetic pathways. Erythrodermic mycosis fungoides Blood tumor burden and circulating clone distinguish Sézary syndrome. Reactive erythroderma No matching aberrant clonal circulating T-cell population. Severe mosquito bite allergy EBV-associated T/NK-cell LPD Usually exposed skin at mosquito-bite sites; may involve multiple body regions. Typically occurs in children or adolescents, often in association with chronic active EBV infection and systemic symptoms. Marked local reactions may include ulceration, necrosis, fever, lymphadenopathy, and hepatosplenomegaly. Exaggerated mosquito-bite reaction with EBV-positive cytotoxic T/NK-cell proliferation in the appropriate clinical setting. Dense dermal infiltrate with atypical lymphocytes, often admixed with eosinophils and other inflammatory cells. Angiocentricity, vascular injury, and epidermal necrosis may be present in severe lesions. T-cell or NK-cell phenotype; cytotoxic markers are expressed. EBER in situ hybridization is positive; determine T-cell versus NK-cell lineage with an appropriate panel. EBV association is central; T-cell receptor gene rearrangement may help establish T-cell lineage. Ordinary arthropod-bite reaction Usually lacks EBV-positive atypical cytotoxic lymphoid proliferation and systemic manifestations. Hydroa vacciniforme lymphoproliferative disorder Photosensitivity-associated vesicles on sun-exposed skin and varioliform scarring are characteristic. Sun-exposed skin, especially face, ears, and hands; systemic form may involve extracutaneous sites. Usually children/adolescents; recurrent photosensitivity-associated vesicles that heal with varioliform scarring. Classic and systemic forms are recognized; systemic disease may be more severe. Hydroa vacciniforme-like lesions with EBV-positive cytotoxic T/NK-cell proliferation in the appropriate clinical setting. Epidermal necrosis, vesiculation, and reticular degeneration with dense lymphocytic infiltrate. Atypical lymphocytes may show angiocentricity and cytotoxic injury. T-cell or NK-cell phenotype; cytotoxic markers are expressed; EBER in situ hybridization is positive. EBV is central; demonstrate EBER. T-cell receptor clonality may help establish T-cell lineage in selected cases. Polymorphous light eruption / classic hydroa vacciniforme EBV-positive atypical cytotoxic infiltrate and systemic features support the lymphoproliferative disorder. Extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma Clinical course, EBV-associated phenotype, and extent of disease differ. EBV-positive mucocutaneous ulcer EBV-positive B-cell lymphoproliferative disorder Oral cavity, skin, and gastrointestinal tract; typically sharply circumscribed mucocutaneous ulcer. Often older or immunosuppressed patients; may arise with immunosenescence or iatrogenic immunosuppression. Usually localized and may regress when immunosuppression is reduced. Localized sharply circumscribed ulcer with EBV-positive atypical B cells in a polymorphous inflammatory background. Well-demarcated ulcer with a polymorphous infiltrate and scattered large atypical immunoblasts/Hodgkin-like cells. A rim of small T lymphocytes often demarcates the lesion. Large cells express B-cell markers (CD20, PAX5, CD79a) and often CD30; EBER is positive. Background T cells form a peripheral rim. EBV positivity by EBER is essential; clonality may be detected but does not imply systemic lymphoma. EBV-positive DLBCL Usually mass-forming or disseminated rather than a sharply circumscribed localized ulcer. Classical Hodgkin lymphoma Integrate architecture, clinical setting, and full phenotype. Inborn error of immunity-associated lymphoproliferative disorders Immune deficiency-associated T-cell LPD Often generalized skin with multiple papulonodular lesions; may involve extracutaneous tissues. Associated with inborn immunodeficiency; chronic, protracted course with slow/limited growth and variable prognosis. The source highlights CD8-positive T-cell-rich and histiocyte-rich infiltrates not associated with EBV. Cutaneous T-cell-rich/histiocyte-rich proliferation in a patient with a defined inborn error of immunity; exclude EBV-associated disease. Papulonodular infiltrates rich in CD8-positive T cells and histiocytes; cytologic atypia and distribution vary. Characterize CD3, CD8, CD4, cytotoxic markers, and histiocytic markers; assess EBV by EBER. No single defining molecular alteration is specified; correlate with the underlying germline immune disorder. EBV-positive T/NK-cell LPD EBER positivity and clinical context support EBV-associated disease. Primary CTCL Underlying immune deficiency and chronic indolent pattern are important context. Core diagnostic rule Classify the lineage first; then integrate site, architecture, cytology, phenotype, and clinical distribution. For histiocytic and dendritic-cell lesions, clinicopathologic correlation is essential. For primary cutaneous lymphomas, exclude extracutaneous disease at diagnosis. Lineage-based classification and diagnostic map Myeloid lineage Cutaneous mastocytosis; mast cell sarcoma; cutaneous myeloid neoplasms / myeloid sarcoma. Dendritic-cell lineage Plasmacytoid dendritic cell neoplasms; Langerhans cell neoplasms; indeterminate dendritic cell tumor. Histiocytic lineage Xanthelasma, JXG, reticulohistiocytosis, RDD, ECD, ALK-positive histiocytosis, histiocytic sarcoma. Lymphoid lineage Reactive B/T-cell proliferations; primary cutaneous B-cell lymphomas; CTCLs; EBV-associated and immune-deficiency-associated LPDs. Primary cutaneous lymphoma is defined by absence of extracutaneous disease at diagnosis. Similar histology or immunophenotype does not make a systemic lymphoma a primary cutaneous lymphoma. Establish context Age, lesion distribution, systemic history, immune status, blood counts, imaging, and whether disease is truly skin-limited. 2. Map the compartment Epidermotropic, dermal, perivascular/periadnexal, nodular, diffuse, intravascular, or panniculitic. 3. Identify lineage Start with morphology and a focused screening panel; avoid interpreting CD68, CD4, CD56, or CD30 in isolation. 4. Apply entity-specific tests CD1a/CD207 for LCH; ALK for ALK-positive histiocytosis; KIT for mast cells; EBER for EBV-associated LPD; targeted molecular testing when indicated. 5. Stage and classify Exclude systemic lymphoma or myeloid disease where relevant; distinguish primary cutaneous entities from secondary skin involvement. Biopsy and reporting checklist Record exact anatomic site, lesion number, distribution, and whether disease is clinically skin-limited. Describe the dominant compartment and growth pattern: epidermotropic, dermal, subcutaneous, intravascular, nodular, diffuse, or destructive. State the lineage-defining immunophenotype and identify any aberrant antigen expression or antigen loss. Use molecular tests selectively: KIT, BRAF/MAPK, ALK rearrangement, and entity-directed studies; a negative low-sensitivity assay does not exclude low-allele-fraction variants. For suspected lymphoma, correlate with clinical staging and prior/current extracutaneous disease before using a primary cutaneous designation. For histiocytic lesions, explicitly distinguish macrophage-lineage tumors from Langerhans, plasmacytoid, and indeterminate dendritic-cell neoplasms. content: use client Nevus Lipomatosus Superficialis Adipocytic tumors Benign / hamartomatous Classic NLS is more common in the gluteal region and neighbouring skin 13858911 ; 4648802 ; 6629609 ; 7430482 , and it manifests with multiple lesions. There may be a linear or zosteriform distribution that does not cross the midline 1235780 ; 1219048 . Solitary NLS has a wider anatomical distribution, including in the head and neck 9248887 ; 16268886 ; 3273051 ; 5647029 , upper extremities 1235780 ; 22607282 ; 34494674 ; 31452824 , distal lower extremities 13858911 ; 1235780 ; 18474480 , and external genitalia 12974709 . NLS manifests as slow-growing, skin-colored to yellow, dome-shaped plaques formed by confluent papules and nodules. The overlying skin is wrinkled or cerebriform, sometimes with comedones 1235780 ; 1219048 . The plaques vary in size from 3 mm to 200 mm 13858911 ; 1219048 . There are usually no associated clinical abnormalities 13858911 . Rarely, NLS can be associated with generalized folded skin (Michelin tyre baby syndrome) 464627 ; 25424205 . NLS is rare. In the classic form, lesions arise at birth or develop in the first two decades of life 1235780 . Solitary NLS has been reported in a wider age group (birth to 88 years) 23113758 ; 12974709 . There is no sex predilection 17223884 . nevus lipomatosus superficialis (NLS) is a rare cutaneous hamartoma characterized by dermal ectopic adipose tissue. NLS is composed of aggregates of mature adipocytes at the level of the papillary and upper reticular dermis, typically around blood vessels 13858911 ; 1219048 . Accompanying connective tissue changes in the dermis include increased dermal capillaries inversely proportional to the fat content, irregularly distributed and sometimes thickened collagen, reduction of elastic fibres, and increased numbers of fibroblasts 13858911 ; 11277956 . The epidermis may show irregular acanthosis, follicular plugging 13858911 ; 4648802 ; 1219048 , and (rarely) various abnormalities of folliculosebaceous units 12031036 ; 14721781 ; 16029355 ; 33223741 ; 15649197 ; 17224390 . The pathogenesis is unknown. It has been suggested that lesional adipocytes arise from precursor cells lying close to the blood vessels, analogous to the sequence of events in fetal adipogenesis 7430482 . NLS must be differentiated from lipoma and soft tissue fibroma with lipomatous stroma. Lipoma is typically a well-circumscribed subcutaneous nodular lesion composed mostly of mature adipocytes. Although thin connective tissue septa may separate lobules of adipocytes in lipomas, there is no dermis between the adipocytes like in NLS. Soft tissue fibroma contains groups of mature adipocytes in the stroma, but the lesion has a pedunculated silhouette. Soft tissue fibromas with fatty metaplasia are considered by some to be a solitary form of NLS. Essential: aggregates of mature adipocytes at the level of the papillary and upper reticular dermis; dermal connective tissue changes. Fibroma of tendon sheath Fibroblastic, Myofibroblastic, and Fibrohistiocytic Tumors Benign Fibroblastic Tumors Benign The most common sites are the tendons of the fingers, hands, and wrists. Less common sites include the forearm, foot, and knee 27125357 ; 91424 . Most tumors present as an asymptomatic to mildly painful, small (< 20 mm), slow-growing, and solitary mass, although multiple nodules have also been reported 23212985 ; 91424 ; 22028571 . Fibroma of tendon sheath is rare, with a predilection to occur in middle-aged men 23212985 ; 27125357 ; 91424 . Fibroma of tendon sheath is a rare benign tumor, presumably of (myo)fibroblastic origin, that arises in the tenosynovial soft tissue, usually attached to a tendon, and occurs predominantly in the upper extremities. Fibroma of tendon sheath is composed of small to medium-sized bland fibroblastic spindle and stellate cells arranged in fascicles or a storiform pattern, set within a dense fibrocollagenous hyalinized matrix with slit-like spaces and dilated vascular channels. Some myxoid change, extravasated red blood cells, mononuclear inflammatory cells, and (rarely) giant cells can be seen 26729987 . Cellular areas may also be present 91424 . tumors with unusual histological findings such as a palisading growth pattern, epithelioid cells, and osteoclast-like multinucleated giant cells may have PKM or ASPN as a gene fusion partner 32661296 . USP6 rearrangement may support diagnosis in challenging cases. These tumors have been found to have gene fusions involving USP6 and a variety of partners, including PKM, RCC1, ASPN, COL1A1, COL3A1, MYH9, MIR22HG, CTNNB1, SPARC, CAP1, EMP1, CYTOR (LINC00152), NR1D1, RAB1A, and TNC 34088995 ; 34520696 . They may be a tenosynovial form of nodular fasciitis 32661296 . The differential diagnosis includes nodular fasciitis, myofibroma, and benign fibrous histiocytoma. Essential: a well-circumscribed lobulated nodule on tendon; usually hypocellular, with spindle cells in a collagenous background and slit-like vascular spaces. Desirable: USP6 rearrangement (in selected or challenging cases). 0 Calcifying aponeurotic fibroma CAF most commonly involves aponeurotic soft tissue of the palms and feet. Other sites include the thigh, arm, elbow, and knee 9865839 . CAF typically presents as a solitary painless mass. Multiple lesions are exceptional 9865839 . CAF is rare. It shows a predilection for male children, although adults can also (more rarely) be affected 9865839 . Calcifying aponeurotic fibroma (CAF) is a benign, locally infiltrative fibroblastic tumor with chondro-osseous foci, predominantly occurring in the distal extremities of children. CAF is infiltrative and composed of bland spindled cells arranged in parallel fascicles with fibrous stroma. Chondroid foci can be seen, with or without calcification, surrounded by epithelioid cells 9865839 ; 13032926 . Chondroid cells, multinucleated giant cells, and calcific debris may be seen 11335964 . There is variable expression of MSA, SMA, CD99, S100, and CD68. Rare cases also label for CD34, CD57, PR, and EMA. β-catenin is negative 18939887 . Detection of FN1::EGF fusion may be helpful in challenging cases. CAFs have a recurrent translocation involving the promoter region of FN1 (exon 23, 27, or 42) on 2q35 and EGF (exon 17 or 19) on 4q25, resulting in the aberrant overexpression of EGF, which can be detected immunohistochemically 26691015 . This fusion can also be seen in a subset of lipofibromatosis cases, which may represent CAF lacking calcifications 30310176 . The differential diagnosis includes infantile digital fibromatosis (inclusion body fibromatosis), fibromatosis, and lipofibromatosis. Essential: an infiltrative bland spindle cell proliferation in parallel fascicles and fibrous background (fibromatosis-like); epithelioid/chondroid cells with or without calcification. Desirable: FN1::EGF fusion in challenging cases. Sclerotic fibroma Sclerotic fibroma is most common in the head and neck region and in the arms 2029087 . tumors are solitary or multiple, typically slow-growing, longstanding, painless, white to skin-colored papules or nodules 2029087 ; 2464630 . Sclerotic fibroma has a predilection for middle-aged adults. Cases associated with Cowden syndrome occur predominantly in men 2029087 , while sporadic cases occur predominantly in women 2464630 . Sclerotic fibroma is a benign cutaneous fibrous tumor with a prominent storiform pattern and clefting. The tumors can be sporadic or associated with Cowden syndrome. Sclerotic fibromas are polypoid, well-circumscribed, hypocellular lesions with abundant collagen with plywood-like clefting, admixed with banal small spindle cells arranged in a storiform pattern. Myxoid change can be seen 2029087 ; 2464630 . The tumors express CD34 10698210 . Loss of PTEN by immunohistochemistry may suggest Cowden syndrome. tumors that arise in association with Cowden syndrome have loss of PTEN (10q23.3), resulting in loss of its expression. Dermatofibroma is the main differential diagnosis. Sclerosing dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans may also mimic a sclerotic fibroma, especially on partial biopsies 28134725 . Essential: hypocellular banal spindle cells arranged in a storiform pattern; abundant collagen with plywood-like clefting. Desirable: for Cowden syndrome: loss of PTEN expression by immunohistochemistry. Nuchal-type fibroma The most common site is the posterior neck 9921988 , but other sites can be involved. Nuchal-type fibroma most often involves the subcutaneous soft tissue, sometimes with dermal and skeletal muscle involvement. Patients typically present with a long history of a solitary, superficial to deep, painless swelling; rarely, lesions can be multiple 7872429 ; 21950671 ; 9921988 . Nuchal-type fibroma has a male predilection and a peak incidence between the third and fifth decades of life. Nuchal-type fibroma is a benign fibroblastic tumor characterized by abundant thick collagen bundles, most commonly arising in the posterior neck. Nuchal-type fibromas are poorly circumscribed, hypocellular, and characterized by thick collagen fibres and small fibroblasts. Entrapped islands of fat, skeletal muscle, and nerves with traumatic neuroma–like changes can be seen. This feature is usually absent from Gardner fibroma, which is often otherwise indistinguishable from nuchal-type fibroma. Elastic fibres and small blood vessels are present between the collagen fibres. Immunohistochemistry is not specific; the tumors are negative for desmin, actin, S100, and EMA 7872429 ; 9921988 . There may be nuclear expression of β-catenin. Some cases may have mutations in APC or MUTYH; however, mutation analyses are usually unnecessary for the diagnosis. A few tested cases were found to have APC mutations. One case had a mutation in MUTYH, which encodes a base excision repair protein and has also been implicated in familial adenomatous polyposis 21752055 . The differential diagnosis includes desmoid-type fibromatosis and Gardner fibroma (which may be related). Essential: poorly circumscribed hypocellular tumors with small fibroblasts and thick collagen fibres; entrapped fat and nerves. Pleomorphic fibroma Pleomorphic fibroma affects the extremities, trunk, and head and neck 23506010 ; 2916726 ; 33534206 . The tumors are painless, single, slow-growing, fleshy polyps or papules 23506010 ; 2916726 ; 33534206 . This fibroma occurs in middle-aged adults 23506010 ; 2916726 ; 33534206 . Pleomorphic fibroma is a benign, often polypoid, fibroblastic dermal neoplasm characterized by bizarre pleomorphic cells. These tumors are hypocellular and composed of dense, haphazardly arranged collagen bundles admixed with spindle cells and large pleomorphic cells that have hyperchromatic multilobulated nuclei with smudgy chromatin 23506010 ; 2916726 . They are positive for CD34 and show loss of RB1 expression 28543636 ; 33534206 . There is aberrant p53 expression in Li–Fraumeni syndrome–associated cases 32187703 . Not clinically relevant These tumors have RB1 deletion and are negative for MDM2 amplification 28543636 ; 2916726 . Cases associated with Li–Fraumeni syndrome harbour TP53 germline mutations 32187703 . The differential diagnosis includes superficial atypical lipomatous tumor, pleomorphic lipoma, and atypical fibroxanthoma. Essential: dermal dome-shaped to polypoid tumors; dense, haphazardly arranged collagen bundles; hypocellular spindle cells and large pleomorphic cells with hyperchromatic, smudgy chromatin. Desirable: loss of RB1 expression by immunohistochemistry. Elastofibroma Elastofibroma is most often subscapular. It sometimes involves the chest wall but can occur anywhere. These tumors are slow-growing, typically solitary, and usually asymptomatic, but they can cause pain, limitation of movement, or scapular snapping/impingement. Elastofibroma most commonly affects elderly adults, with a female predominance. Elastofibroma is a benign soft tissue tumor characterized by abnormal elastic fibres, bland fibroblasts, and myxoid stroma. Elastofibromas are large and have poorly defined borders. They are often hypocellular with degenerative collagen fibres that are fragmented, thickened, and globular; these can be highlighted with Verhoeff elastic staining. Variable proportions of bland uniform small spindle cells, aggregates of mature adipocytes, and myxoid stroma are present 7116305 . Elastofibromas have a variety of chromosomal abnormalities. Copy gains (including gains of Xq) 12165800 , alterations to chromosome 1, and t(8;12)(q22;q24.3) 11343783 and/or t(2;19) and (X;1) rearrangements 11458949 have been found in some of the cases. Essential: fragmented, thickened, and globular collagenous fibres; bland spindle cells; admixed mature adipocytes and myxoid stroma. Desmoplastic fibroblastoma Desmoplastic fibroblastoma has a predilection for the upper extremities, although it may occur anywhere 7661281 ; 9670823 ; 8832562 . This tumor is a painless, solitary, slow-growing mass and predominantly subcutaneous, although it may involve skeletal muscle 9670823 . Desmoplastic fibroblastomas are rare. They predominantly affect adults (median age: 50–60 years) and show a male predominance 7661281 ; 9593348 ; 9670823 ; 8832562 . Desmoplastic fibroblastoma is a benign soft tissue tumor characterized by stellate fibroblasts in a fibromyxoid background. Desmoplastic fibroblastomas are hypocellular tumors with bland, spindled to stellate fibroblasts and a fibromyxoid to delicate collagenous background 7661281 ; 9670823 ; 8832562 . Immunohistochemistry is nonspecific; desmin, keratin, and CD34 are negative 8832562 . The differential diagnosis includes desmoid-type fibromatosis. Desmoplastic fibroblastomas have been reported to have translocations involving 11q12, including t(2;11)(q31;q12) and t(11;17)(q12;p11.2) 15036892 ; 19596257 . The FOSL1 gene is located nearby (at 11q13.1), and the FOSL1 protein is overexpressed in these tumors 27442992 ; 22411068 . Essential: a hypocellular tumor with a fibromyxoid collagenous background; bland spindled to stellate fibroblasts. Fibrous papule The most common sites include the nose and central face 30028760 . Fibrous papule typically manifests as a dome-shaped, sessile papule that is solitary and sporadic in the vast majority of cases. Multiple (syndromic) fibrous papules may be associated with tuberous sclerosis, and less commonly with Birt–Hogg–Dubé syndrome or multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 30246432 ; 16021156 ; 9236523 . There is a tendency for multiple fibrous papules to occur in early childhood in tuberous sclerosis, whereas those associated with Birt–Hogg–Dubé syndrome or multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 are usually seen in adults 30246432 . Fibrous papules are most commonly seen in middle-aged adults 30028760 . Fibrous papule is a benign lesion, presumably of fibroblastic origin, that most commonly occurs on the nose or central face. Classic fibrous papule has a dome-shaped configuration with dilated blood vessels within the dermis, surrounded by fibrotic or collagenized stroma with spindle-shaped or stellate fibroblasts 15953376 . The overlying epidermis may show melanocytic hyperplasia 32496596 . Histological patterns of fibrous papule may be hypercellular, pigmented, pleomorphic, clear cell, granular cell, epithelioid, or inflammatory 15953376 . Multiple fibrous papules in tuberous sclerosis are thought to occur due to constitutional activation of the mTOR pathway due to germline mutations in TSC1 or TSC2 (tuberous sclerosis), and similar mechanisms have been suggested for the pathogenesis of sporadic fibrous papules 24558502 . The differential diagnosis includes fibroma, melanocytic nevus (pigmented or epithelioid pattern), atypical fibroxanthoma (hypercellular or pleomorphic pattern), balloon cell nevus or xanthoma (clear cell pattern), and granular cell tumor (granular pattern). Essential: small papular lesions, usually occurring on the centrofacial skin; dilated dermal blood vessels within a collagenous stroma with prominent stellate or spindle-shaped fibroblasts. Fibroblastic connective tissue nevus Most lesions arise on the trunk, head and neck, and limbs 22892597 ; 22014540 ; 28632950 ; 26268513 ; 30024070 . FCTN typically manifests as a solitary, slowly growing, painless plaque-like or nodular skin lesion 22892597 ; 28632950 . Some agminate cases have been described 31469926 ; 27296971 , as well as atrophic plaques 28543313 and exophytic tumors 30024070 . FCTN has a slight female predominance and usually affects young patients (median age: 10 years). Congenital cases have been described 30187166 ; 28067672 , especially on the trunk, as large infiltrated plaques. Fibroblastic connective tissue nevus (FCTN) is a benign dermal-based mesenchymal lesion of fibroblastic/myofibroblastic lineage composed of short intersecting fascicles of bland spindled cells. FCTN is a poorly circumscribed lesion localized in the reticular dermis and commonly extending into the superficial subcutis. It is composed of bland spindle-shaped and ovoid cells arranged in a short intersecting fascicular pattern and entrapping appendages that are preserved. Cellularity is variable. Mitotic activity is absent. A storiform pattern may be observed. Epidermal papillomatosis and ectopic dermal adipose tissue are commonly observed 22892597 . Elastic fibres may be decreased in number. Expression of CD34 and SMA is described 28632950 . KHDRBS1::NTRK3 rearrangement has been reported in 1 case 30187166 . FCTN overlaps clinically and morphologically with plaque-like CD34-positive dermal fibroma 34449590 ; 30811625 and dermatomyofibroma 26268513 . Essential: short intersecting fascicles of bland spindled cells in the reticular dermis. Desirable: often associated with adipocytes in the dermis and epidermal papillomatosis; absence of COL1A1::PDGFB fusion (to rule out plaque-stage dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans). Fibro-osseous tumor of digits FOT affects the subcutaneous tissues of the proximal phalanx of the fingers and, less frequently, the toes 3463398 ; 29787930 ; 19678826 ; 30946936 . FOT of the digits is a rapidly growing and often painful lesion. Random calcifications are often present on imaging studies. Over time, the lesion becomes hard and well demarcated 12894350 . The lesions have a broad age distribution, from infancy to late adulthood, but most patients are young adults 3463398 ; 29787930 ; 19678826 ; 32635781 . Fibro-osseous tumor (FOT) of digits, arising in the soft tissues of the digits, is a localized, self-limiting, benign neoplasm composed of proliferating spindle cells and osteoblasts. The lesion has areas resembling nodular fasciitis with bone in various stages of formation. It is hypercellular and composed of proliferating spindle cells that are oriented randomly or in short intersecting fascicles. The spindle cells have eosinophilic cytoplasm and plump fusiform nuclei with fine chromatin and conspicuous nucleoli. Normal mitoses may be numerous. The stroma is richly vascular and myxoid, and it contains fibrin, extravasated erythrocytes, scattered lymphocytes, and osteoclast-like giant cells. The spindle cells merge with poorly defined trabeculae and sheets of unmineralized woven bone that are rimmed by prominent osteoblasts with amphophilic cytoplasm and harbour large osteocytes 12894350 ; 18384209 . Molecular studies for USP6 rearrangement may be useful in the appropriate clinicopathological context. USP6 fusion genes are present in FOT 29787930 ; 33000481 . USP6 fusion genes are also encountered in nodular fasciitis, a tumor with overlapping morphology. FOT and myositis ossificans are histologically similar, except that in the former there is usually no zonation pattern and the bone is located randomly throughout the tumor. Essential: densely cellular fascicles of spindle cells; numerous typical mitoses; abundant admixed woven bone formation that is random or most mature at the periphery. Desirable: detection of USP6 rearrangement may help in selected cases. Dermatofibroma (fibrous histiocytoma) The classic dermatofibroma is seen most frequently on the legs, followed by the arms and trunk. Rare sites of involvement include the hands, feet, and head and neck 2171878 ; 19054841 ; 33893133 . Dermatofibroma presents as an isolated, asymptomatic, dome-shaped papule or nodule that usually measures from a few millimetres to 10–20 mm; very rarely, it reaches 100 mm (giant dermatofibroma). It is hyperpigmented, but in early growing lesions and in individuals with lightly pigmented skin it may appear erythematous. Classic dermatofibroma usually exhibits a dusky brown color. The aneurysmal subtype may show a red cut surface, whereas tumors with abundant lipid may be tan to yellow. It is firm and, when squeezed, exhibits a central dimple (“dimple sign”). Dermatofibroma can be eroded or crusted. Occasionally, numerous dermatofibromas in a widespread distribution or in an agminated pattern can be seen. The latter has no clinical significance. Eruptive dermatofibromas can be associated with autoimmune disorders (e.g. lupus erythematosus) 16334865 or in the setting of immunosuppression (e.g. HIV, immunosuppressive drugs) 31625625 . Dermatofibroma is the most common mesenchymal neoplasm in the skin. It arises over a wide age range but is most common in the third and fourth decades of life. The classic subtype is seen most frequently in the lower extremities of younger female patients. The other subtypes have a more equal sex distribution. Dermatofibroma (fibrous histiocytoma) is a common benign papular or nodular skin lesion composed of a combination of (myo)fibroblasts with surrounding reactive dendrocytes and macrophages in between collagen bundles. The tumor grows in the reticular dermis, but superficial infiltration of the subcutaneous tissue, along with perivascular lymphocytic inflammation, is frequent. Classic dermatofibroma is polymorphous, composed of spindled to rounded neoplastic cells with surrounding reactive dermal dendrocytes and macrophages 20520936 . There is characteristic, albeit nonspecific, entrapment of collagen bundles at the periphery, forming collagen balls. A storiform growth pattern may be seen. The epidermis typically exhibits hyperplasia with elongated hyperpigmented rete ridges. Follicular and/or sebaceous gland induction and junctional melanocytic hyperplasia may be present 32767564 ; 19955877 ; 25727075 . Early lesions are more cellular, whereas older lesions appear more fibrotic with less macrophages. Numerous histological patterns have been described in the literature (fibrocollagenous, lipidized, clear cell, granular cell, halo, osteoclastic, myofibroblastic, keloidal, palisading, and atrophic, among others) 24937822 ; 10770432 ; 22576077 ; 10231403 ; 9354896 , which have no clinical significance, unlike the subtypes described below; however, one or more patterns or subtypes can overlap in the same tumor. In tumors that are significantly lipidized, the histiocytoid and giant cells contain abundant vacuolated cytoplasm 10770432 . Cellular dermatofibroma exhibits a fascicular growth pattern, composed of relatively monotonous spindle cells with fine chromatin and pale eosinophilic cytoplasm 30741794 ; 31074502 . Entrapment of superficial subcutaneous tissue is common, whereas approximately 10% of cases exhibit small foci of necrosis, which is not indicative of malignancy 8017561 . Aneurysmal dermatofibroma contains blood-filled spaces and hemosiderin occupying much of the lesion and mimicking a vascular tumor. It is polymorphous in composition, like the classic subtype, containing neoplastic spindle cells, Touton-type giant cells, lymphocytes, and macrophages 30868503 ; 7607620 . Overlying epidermal hyperplasia and peripheral entrapment of collagen bundles is characteristic. Atypical dermatofibroma contains scattered atypical and pleomorphic cells. Atypical mitoses and necrosis can be seen 11756767 . The background cells can be uniform or polymorphous, like in cellular or classic dermatofibroma, respectively. Deep fibrous histiocytoma arises entirely within the subcutaneous or deep soft tissue. It is well circumscribed, in contrast to its superficial counterparts, with a uniform cellularity and storiform growth pattern 2167613 ; 20804915 ; 18300816 . Immunohistochemistry is not particularly helpful in reaching the correct diagnosis. CD68 highlights interspersed histiocytes. Multifocal staining for SMA (more pronounced in the cellular subtype) supports myofibroblastic differentiation. Desmin and CD34 can be focally positive (in 30% and 5% of cases, respectively) 22775584 . Factor XIIIa is not a specific stain, highlighting interspersed reactive dendrocytes. Recurrent gene fusions involving PKC isoforms (PRKCA, PRKCB, and PRKCD) with various genes encoding membrane-associated proteins (e.g. LAMTOR1, PDPN, CD63, and KIRREL family genes) have been identified in a minority of cases 26121314 ; 24721208 ; 30094855 ; 26432191 . As a result, the catalytic domain of PKC in the chimeric protein localizes to the cell membrane 24721208 . These data provide proof of the neoplastic, clonal nature of dermatofibroma. Dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans infiltrates the subcutaneous tissue in a honeycomb fashion, is diffusely positive for CD34, and harbours PDGFB/PDGFD rearrangements. Angiomatoid fibrous histiocytoma is an unrelated tumor of intermediate malignancy and should not be confused with the aneurysmal subtype. Superficial pseudomyogenic hemangioendothelioma (PMHE), spindle cell melanoma, squamous cell carcinoma, and superficial leiomyosarcoma are all in the differential with cellular dermatofibroma. They can be distinguished easily with the help of immunohistochemical studies. In approximately half of PMHE cases, interspersed neutrophils can serve as a helpful clue. PMHE expresses keratin and vascular markers (most consistently ERG) and harbours FOSB rearrangements with various partners (most commonly WWTR1 and ACTB). FOSB immunohistochemical stain can serve as a surrogate marker. Melanoma is positive for SOX10, squamous cell carcinoma for keratin markers, and leiomyosarcoma for desmin and caldesmon. Atypical dermatofibroma can be potentially confused with atypical fibroxanthoma / pleomorphic dermal sarcoma. Background findings of classic dermatofibroma would be critical to secure the correct diagnosis. Epithelioid fibrous histiocytoma (see section Epithelioid fibrous histiocytoma) is now considered a separate entity with characteristic ALK protein overexpression due to ALK rearrangements or, very rarely, due to alternative transcription activation mechanisms 35289445 . Nevertheless, fibrous histiocytomas with epithelioid features and ALK negativity have occasionally been found to harbour PRKCB rearrangements 31653978 . Essential: ovoid to spindled cells; peripheral entrapment of dermal collagen bundles. Desirable: epidermal hyperplasia; follicular/sebaceous induction. Superficial fibromatosis Intermediate, locally aggressive Palmar fibromatosis affects the volar surface of the hands and the flexor aspects of the fingers. In adults, plantar fibromatosis occurs in non–weight-bearing surfaces of the foot, such as the medial plantar arch, from the navicular bone to the base of the first metatarsal 6507097 . In the pediatric population, plantar fibromatosis most commonly involves the anteromedial heel pad 11123783 . About 50% of cases of palmar fibromatosis and as many as 25% of cases of plantar fibromatosis are bilateral 6507097 ; 29310463 . Penile fibromatosis involves the tunica albuginea, on the dorsal aspect of the penis 32681945 . Palmar fibromatosis develops gradually and manifests as small, painless coalescing nodules forming cords or bands in the subcutaneous tissue and underlying fascial plane. Plantar fibromatosis is often asymptomatic and does not cause contractures, but pain may be present after periods of standing or walking. Penile fibromatosis manifests as firm nodules or plaques, causes abnormal curvature of the penis, and may elicit pain during erection and intercourse 6507097 ; 32681945 . Palmar fibromatosis shows a prevalence of 1–2% in the population, affecting mainly adults, with a male predominance (M:F ratio: 3:1). Prevalence increases with age and is higher in populations of northern European descent, reaching 30% in age groups > 60 years 10760640 ; 19145463 . Plantar fibromatosis is less common and affects younger patients, including the pediatric population, where it shows a female predominance 8989694 ; 16006806 . Penile fibromatosis affects predominantly White populations of middle-aged adults, with a mean age of 55 years 32681945 . Superficial fibromatoses (palmar, plantar, and penile) are nodular, locally recurrent fibroblastic/myofibroblastic proliferations. Superficial fibromatoses are characterized by three phases of growth (proliferative, involutional, and late stage). The proliferative stage consists of a cellular, bland proliferation of long fascicles of fibroblasts/myofibroblasts blending into tendons and aponeuroses. Neoplastic cells are elongated cells with tapering vesicular nuclei, small inconspicuous nucleoli, and pale eosinophilic cytoplasm. Mitotic figures may be increased, especially in children. In the background, a collagenous matrix (which increases in the late stages) is seen. Rarely, multinucleated giant cells and osseous or cartilaginous metaplasia are seen. Neoplastic cells may be positive for SMA and focally for desmin. Rare cases display nuclear expression of β-catenin 11455002 ; 17711447 ; 16006806 despite the absence of CTNNB1 or APC mutations Although the pathogenesis of superficial fibromatosis is driven at least in part by the WNT/β-catenin signalling pathway, this tumor lacks the CTNNB1 and APC mutations characteristic of desmoid fibromatosis 11455002 ; 30774465 ; 29310463 . Hyperplastic scars may resemble fibromatosis but tend to be non-infiltrative and lack β-catenin expression. Sclerotic fibromas have “plywood”-type collagen and usually express CD34. Nodular fasciitis has a more myxoid background resembling tissue culture. Essential: a cellular fascicular proliferation of spindle cells embedded in collagenous stroma; involvement of aponeurosis and tendons and (variably) the subcutis and dermis. 1 Inclusion body fibromatosis The classic subtype occurs in the hands or feet and involves the dorsal/dorsolateral aspect of the distal or middle second, third, and fourth digits most frequently, followed by the fifth digit, while typically sparing the first digit 840560 ; 3892466 ; 18830128 . Non-classic tumors are reported to occur on the extremities, tongue, and breast 3740876 ; 8209857 ; 6496846 ; 7377793 ; 2836293 . Patients with the classic subtype present with an asymptomatic, dome-shaped/polypoid cutaneous nodule, typically no larger than 20 mm 840560 ; 3835952 ; 18830128 . Synchronous and/or metachronous lesions occur, sometimes affecting multiple digits 4344937 ; 840560 ; 3835952 , but simultaneous involvement of both the fingers and the toes is rare 840560 . Patients with the non-classic subtype present with solitary masses/nodules 18830128 . The classic subtype accounts for 2% of pediatric fibroblastic tumors 1946077 . More than 80% of cases present by 3 years of age, with about 30% found at birth 3892466 ; 840560 . No sex predilection exists. Rare cases occur in adults 11069537 ; 7377793 ; 2836293 ; 8209857 . Inclusion body fibromatosis is a benign myofibroblastic tumor characterized by eosinophilic intracytoplasmic inclusions and the potential for local recurrence. Spindled cells have lightly eosinophilic cytoplasm and an elongated, cytologically bland nucleus, with low mitotic activity. Cells proliferate in whorls, interlacing short fascicles, or storiform arrays within a collagenous dermis, and they characteristically grow perpendicularly to the epidermis and around adnexa, occasionally infiltrating deeper tissues 4344937 ; 3892466 . A variable number of cells harbour a rounded, pale pink, intracytoplasmic (frequently paranuclear), 1.5–24 μm inclusion 14322942 ; 3892466 highlighted by trichrome (red), phosphotungstic acid–hematoxylin (dark purple), and Movat’s (pink) stains 18830128 . Cells express vimentin, muscle actin(s) in a peripheral “tram-track” pattern, calponin, desmin, and CD99 1310240 ; 18830128 . Inclusions mark with calponin-1 24117680 and occasionally with caldesmon 18830128 . Unknown Essential: a dermal-based, cytologically bland, spindled cell proliferation; eosinophilic intracytoplasmic inclusions. Plexiform fibrohistiocytic tumor Intermediate, rarely metastasizing There is a marked predilection for the arms, particularly the forearms, followed by the lower limbs, trunk, and head and neck area 17870015 ; 10366148 ; 1723956 ; 2847569 . The tumors present as slowly enlarging nodules and plaques, typically measuring about 20–30 mm 2847569 . Children, adolescents, and young adults are most commonly affected, with a reported median age ranging from 14.5 to 20 years (overall age range: 1–77 years). There may be a female predilection 17870015 ; 10366148 ; 1723956 ; 2847569 . Plexiform fibrohistiocytic tumor (PFHT) is a plexiform tumor within the dermis and subcutis, showing a biphasic morphology characterized by a nodular growth of histiocytoid cells and fascicles of myofibroblastic spindle cells. PFHT is a fibroblastic-fibrohistiocytic, dermal–subcutaneous interface tumor composed of small to medium-sized, cannonball-like nodules of whorling, histiocyte-rich foci with osteoclast-like giant cells and/or fascicular spindled myofibroblastic fascicles in the subcutis. PFHT has a plexiform to poorly circumscribed architecture. Three histological patterns are based on the predominant cell type: myofibroblastic, histiocytoid, and mixed 17870015 . Features of hemorrhage (to which the osteoclast-like giant cells are attracted), myxoid change, chronic inflammation (mostly in the pure myofibroblastic pattern), fat or adnexal trapping with perineural or peri-Pacinian corpuscle growth, stromal hyalinization, rare metaplastic bone, and pseudogranulomatous patterns may be observed. Mitotic activity is low, and cytological atypia, vascular invasion, and atypical mitoses are exceedingly rare 2847569 ; 1723956 ; 17870015 ; 17617005 ; 10366148 . There is expression of SMA in the spindled myofibroblastic foci and CD68 in the histiocytic cannonballs with osteoclast-type giant cells. The tumors are generally negative for CD34, desmin, EMA, keratin, and S100. There are no known consistent, reproducible molecular signatures. Single case reports have documented cytogenetic findings that include 46,X,del(X)(q13)[3]/46,XX[23], 46,XY,t(4;15)(q21;q15), and 46,XY,-6,-8, del(4)(q25q31),del(20)(q11.2) with additional der (8) and (p22) 9973942 ; 2164878 ; 21261704 . This tumor can be confused with other dermal or subcutaneous reactive or neoplastic processes, including granulomata, fibromatosis, lipofibromatosis, myofibromatosis, fibrous hamartoma of infancy, nodular fasciitis, giant cell tumor of soft parts, so-called plexiform myofibroblastoma (which may be identical to pure myofibroblastic PFHT) 34449590 ; 32618598 , and cellular neurothekeoma 17325474 ; 19342943 ; 17870015 . Essential: a fibrohistiocytic tumor in dermis and subcutis; plexiform growth pattern; fascicular fibroblastic and/or cannonball-like histiocytic proliferation; osteoclast-like giant cells. Superficial acral fibromyxoma The great majority arise in the periungual/subungual region of the fingers and toes, with occasional cases involving the hands, feet, ankles, wrists, lower legs, and thighs 11486169 ; 19236516 ; 18537858 ; 18764846 ; 22367301 ; 27825811 . Acral fibromyxomas are slowly growing and often painful, and they range in size from 10 to 50 mm (mean: ~20 mm) 11486169 ; 18537858 ; 22367301 . Associated nail deformities and lytic lesions of underlying bone may be seen 22367301 ; 18327578 ; 29423724 . The age range is wide, but most cases occur in middle-aged adults, with a male predilection 11486169 ; 22367301 . Superficial acral fibromyxoma is a benign fibroblastic neoplasm typically restricted to acral sites with a marked predilection for the periungual region of the digits and potential for local recurrence. Acral fibromyxomas are lobulated dermal and subcutaneous lesions, sometimes with an epidermal collarette. Most have infiltrative borders and the underlying bone may be involved. Most are relatively hypocellular, composed of bland spindled to stellate cells in a loose growth pattern that can be vaguely fascicular to storiform. tumor cells are embedded in a variably collagenous to myxoid stroma, and a thin-walled vasculature may be present in myxoid areas. Multinucleated cells may be present. Mitotic figures are rare 11486169 ; 18537858 ; 18764846 ; 22367301 ; 28045748 . A subset may have increased cellularity 19236516 . Cartilaginous and osseous metaplasia is rare 29360681 . The tumor cells are positive for CD34, CD99, and nestin and may express EMA and SMA in a minority; they are negative for MUC4 and BCL2 11486169 ; 28045748 ; 22367301 . Loss of RB1 expression is seen in most tumors 27825811 . The tumors show deletion of RB1 27825811 , but this is not required for diagnosis. RB1 deletions have been reported 27825811 . The stromal component of onychomatricoma is identical to that of acral fibromyxoma, but acral fibromyxoma lacks an epithelial component. Myxoid neurofibroma is less cellular and the tumor cells are positive for S100. Myxoid dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans is very rare on the digits and lacks the collagen component, and the tumor cells display a storiform pattern. Essential: acral location, usually periungual; a lobulated dermal and subcutaneous tumor with bland spindled to stellate cells; variably myxoid to collagenous stroma. Desirable: CD34 positivity; frequent loss of RB1 expression by immunohistochemistry. Cutaneous myxoma (superficial angiomyxoma) Solitary lesions, which are not associated with Carney complex, are usually located on distal areas of the limbs or the head 3389450 ; 7615884 .
