Multiple cutaneous myxomas in patients with Carney complex are particularly frequent in the external auditory canal and on the eyelids 8116795 . Cutaneous myxomas manifest as slow-growing nodules with a translucent appearance due to abundant mucin content. In patients with multiple lesions, the possibility of Carney complex should be investigated. The syndrome is inherited as an autosomal dominant trait and consists of the association of endocrine hyperactivity (Cushing syndrome, testicular tumors, and acromegaly); spotty skin pigmentation; epithelioid blue naevi; psammomatous melanotic schwannoma; and multiple cutaneous, cardiac, and mammary myxomas 7640202 ; 3729510 ; 11174387 ; 1571257 ; 18804312 . Multiple cutaneous myxomas in the absence of any other anomalies associated with Carney complex have also been described 9747204 ; 8835175 . Cutaneous myxoma is an uncommon neoplasm occurring mostly in adults. The sex distribution is equal. Most cases are sporadic, but multiple lesions can arise in the setting of Carney complex. Cutaneous myxoma (superficial angiomyxoma) is a benign multilobular lesion composed mostly of myxoid material with an arborizing vascular network and spindled or stellate cells. Cutaneous myxoma (superficial angiomyxoma) manifests as a well-circumscribed multilobular lesion with abundant vascular component. Collagenous septa compartmentalize the lesion, and the vascular component is more prominent at the periphery 10435560 . Each lobule is composed of abundant myxoid material, with sparse cellularity. The stromal cells have a fusiform or stellate morphology. Adnexal induction in the epidermis covering the lesion is frequently seen in myxomas of patients with Carney complex 22588545 . A prominence of scattered neutrophils in the stroma is also characteristic of cutaneous myxoma 10435560 . There is positivity for α-SMA. The spindle and stellate cells are negative for CD34, S100, factor XIIIa, CD57, CD68, and desmin 10435560 ; 7615884 . Immunohistochemically, loss of expression of PRKAR1A has been found in sporadic superficial angiomyxomas 34532875 ; 34889853 . In cases associated with Carney complex, there are mutations of the PRKAR1A gene 15371594 . Focal mucinosis lacks the cellular and vascular components seen in cutaneous myxoma. Cutaneous myxomas may involve the genital area 9421071 ; therefore, the histopathological differential diagnosis must be established with aggressive angiomyxoma. Aggressive angiomyxoma is a larger lesion that extends deeply to subcutaneous structures and displays a vascular component characterized by variably sized vessels, from small thin-walled capillaries to large thick-walled vessels with perivascular hyalinization. Essential: a nodular myxoid tumor with an arborizing vascular network and spindled to stellate cells. Dermatomyofibroma Predilection sites are the upper trunk and upper arm, shoulder, axillary folds, and neck, followed by the abdominal wall and thigh 8468425 ; 1597573 ; 19155724 . DM manifests as an asymptomatic, erythematous, reddish-brown or hypopigmented, longstanding or slowly growing, slightly indurated, flat, plaque-like lesion, or (less often) a nodule 33059951 ; 19155724 . Linear and annular presentations have also been reported. Rarely, the tumor may be congenital, multicentric, or of considerable size 34152037 ; 18801097 . DM most frequently occurs in young females 8468425 ; 19155724 . DM in young children is rare 21752049 ; 28318057 . Dermatomyofibroma (DM) is a rare benign cutaneous mesenchymal neoplasm of fibroblastic/myofibroblastic differentiation. Throughout the dermis, there is a horizontally oriented plaque-like arrangement (except in the deep dermis / subcutis where the arrangement is usually perpendicular to the epidermis) of densely packed slender bundles and long fascicles of cytologically bland fusiform spindle cells showing fibroblastic and myofibroblastic differentiation. The epidermis is generally unaffected. The papillary dermis is typically spared. The adnexal structures are surrounded by the tumor but are usually not disrupted. Elastic fibres are preserved or even slightly increased. DM extension into the superficial subcutis is rare. DM usually expresses vimentin and calponin, while α-SMA and CD34 show variable positivity. Desmin, h-caldesmon, and S100 are negative 33059951 ; 19155724 . The absence of COL1A1::PDGFB rearrangement may help in challenging cases. DM is a myofibroblastic tumor 1597573 ; 8872155 . The main differential diagnosis includes dermatofibroma and plaque-stage dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans 31908825 . Unlike in dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans, there is no COL1A1::PDGFB rearrangement 31090131 . Essential: a benign myofibroblastic proliferation limited to the reticular dermis; groups of spindle cells arranged in fascicles and parallel to the epidermis. Multinucleate cell angiohistiocytoma Multinucleate cell angiohistiocytoma shows a predilection for the dorsal hands and fingers, lower extremities, and trunk or back 8615046 . The head and neck are rarely involved. Multinucleate cell angiohistiocytoma presents as solitary or multiple smooth erythematous papules and nodules. This relatively uncommon lesion arises in middle age. Some studies have demonstrated a female predisposition 25140659 , whereas others have shown equal incidence between sexes 30927287 . Multinucleate cell angiohistiocytoma is a benign acquired lesion of fibrohistiocytic and vascular lineage. Multinucleate cell angiohistiocytoma consists of a triad of multinucleated cells, stromal fibrosis, and vascular changes. The multinucleated cells are angulated and stellate, with elongated cytoplasmic extensions. They may be few in number and revealed by deeper tissue levels 30927287 . Stromal fibrosis is often parallel to the epidermis. Increased numbers of small-calibre vessels within the papillary and reticular dermis show thickened walls with prominent endothelial cells. The multinucleated cells may express CD68 (variable) and factor XIIIa, yet they are generally negative for CD163, CD34, and factor VIII 19336021 ; 30927287 . The vascular proliferation is highlighted by conventional vascular markers (CD31, CD34, ERG, factor VIII). Its pathogenesis has not fully been elucidated. Several mechanisms have been hypothesized, including a role for fibroblasts, ERα overexpression, and mast cells 33180332 ; 20644465 . Fibrous papule (angiofibroma) of the nose is a close mimic but affects the head and neck and shows concentric perifollicular fibrosis. The atrophic pattern of dermatofibroma can resemble multinucleate cell angiohistiocytoma but shows storiform rather than parallel fibrosis and favours the lower extremities. Telangiectasia macularis eruptiva perstans can also display multinucleated stromal cells but usually presents with eosinophils and increased mast cells. Multinucleate cell angiohistiocytoma should be distinguished from reactive multinucleate cell angiohistiocytoma–like changes that may present as a focal histological finding or within another dermatological lesion 31070801 . Essential: solitary or multiple smooth erythematous papules and nodules; multinucleated and angulated stromal cells; dermal fibrosis (often parallel to the epidermis); thickened stromal blood vessels, increased in number and with dilated lumina. Plaque-like CD34-positive dermal fibroma The tumor has a broad site distribution but shows a predilection for the proximal limbs, upper trunk, and neck 15337977 ; 20061935 . The tumor typically presents as a solitary, slowly growing, asymptomatic, well-demarcated, round to oval or medallion-shaped, erythematous to brown-yellow plaque, or (less often) as a nodular or protuberant growth 26645569 , measuring several centimetres in diameter 15337977 ; 20061935 . The surface is often wrinkled, depressed, and pliable 20061935 . Some proliferations can be pruritic and painful 24003290 . The tumor can be either a congenital or an acquired proliferation 15337977 ; 20061935 ; 30635930 . It has a wide age distribution but most commonly develops in children and young adults 15337977 ; 20061935 ; 28750558 and shows a female predominance 15337977 ; 20061935 ; 30635930 . Plaque-like CD34-positive dermal fibroma is a benign tumor of fibroblastic origin characterized histologically by a band-like proliferation of bland CD34-positive spindle cells in the upper dermis, typically sparing the papillary dermis and adnexal structures. The tumor is distinguished by a band-like proliferation of variably cellular and fairly uniform fibroblasts in the upper and mid dermis, characteristically sparing the papillary dermis 15337977 ; 20061935 . Extension into the subcutaneous fatty tissue is rare 15337977 ; 20061935 . Some proliferations display a zonation pattern with perpendicular growth towards the surface and more storiform arrangements of tumor cells in the lower parts 20061935 . Concentric growth of tumor cells around adnexal structures, vascular channels, and nerves is often seen. The tumor cells are bland, with small nuclei, inconspicuous nucleoli, and rare mitoses 20061935 . Multiple dilated venules are present throughout the neoplasm 20061935 . Elastic fibres are often fragmented and reduced in number. The tumor cells are diffusely positive for CD34 and fascin 15337977 ; 20061935 ; 30635930 . Staining for factor XIIIa is inconsistent. Plaque-like CD34 positive dermal fibroma must be distinguished from dermal dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans, dermatomyofibroma, and fibroblastic connective tissue nevus. Essential: a band-like proliferation of uniform fibroblasts in the upper and mid dermis; diffuse CD34 positivity; multiple dilated venules throughout the neoplasm. Nodular fasciitis Nodular fasciitis can arise from the superficial fascia, from the subcutaneous septa, or (rarely) in the dermis, and it usually bulges into the subcutis. Intramuscular, intra-articular, and visceral lesions are rare 20716998 ; 16434899 ; 27686647 ; 8311183 ; 10380041 . The most common sites are the forearm, thigh, and upper arm, which account for more than half of all cases 6462780 ; however, nodular fasciitis can involve any part of the body 19469872 . Well-described rare subtypes include intravascular fasciitis and cranial fasciitis 7351023 ; 7246849 ; 9923933 . Nodular fasciitis presents clinically as a relatively rapidly growing subcutaneous mass that enlarges (typically over the course of 3–6 weeks, but in some cases over a period as long as 3 months) and then regresses. It is typically smaller than 20–30 mm in maximal diameter, although an exceptional 100 mm case has been reported 6279273 ; 31355033 . The mass may be tender or painless 6462780 . Nodular fasciitis can occur at any age but has a peak incidence in the third and fourth decades of life, with equal distribution between the sexes 5675403 ; 13737962 . Nodular fasciitis is a self-limited benign myofibroblastic/fibroblastic neoplasm, classically occurring in the subcutis, arranged in a disorganized tissue culture–like pattern; it usually harbours USP6 rearrangement. Nodular fasciitis is composed of fibroblasts and/or myofibroblasts without overt cytological atypia. Mitotic activity can be frequent, but the mitoses are not atypical. Cellularity varies between and within lesions. Feathery tissue culture–like areas are typical of the lesion, but more-cellular areas can form fascicles. The stroma can be myxoid and/or collagenous, even keloidal. The vasculature is rich and fine, resembling granulation tissue. Extravasated red cells are usually seen, often in the tissue culture–like areas. Osteoclastic giant cells and chronic inflammatory cells can be present. Strong expression of SMA by the neoplastic cells is characteristic. Molecular testing is usually unnecessary in clinically and histologically typical cases. However, in challenging cases, detection of USP6 rearrangement may be useful to confirm the diagnosis 28752842 ; 29623468 ; 30139549 . Nodular fasciitis has been shown to harbour a translocation between chromosomes 17 and 22, t(17;22) (p13;q13), which results in MYH9::USP6 fusion and subsequent overexpression of USP6 21826056 . USP6 encodes a deubiquitinating enzyme with roles in cell trafficking, cell signalling, protein breakdown, and inflammation. MYH9 encodes a non-muscle myosin heavy chain that has roles in cell motility, shape, adhesion, and differentiation. A study of p16, CDK4, MDM2, and p53 implicated the possible involvement of cell-cycle arrest and presumed senescence by p16 in lesional myofibroblastic cells in nodular fasciitis, resulting in its self-limited growth and regression 31933915 . In addition, USP6 expression creates a negative feedback via TNFSF10 (TRAIL) and interferon-β, resulting in apoptosis and senescence of tumor cells 34381187 . Rearrangements in USP6 have been shown in approximately 90% of nodular fasciitis cases, and > 65% of these are MYH9::USP6 gene fusions 21826056 . These are most often detected in earlier (younger) lesions, while the detection of USP6 rearrangements in older lesions can be as low as 20% because of the negative feedback from USP6 expression in tumor cells 34381187 . Other gene promoters can be substituted for MYH9, sometimes with atypical features 28752842 : PPP6R3::USP6 and CALD1::USP6 have been reported in exceptional malignant cases 31538390 ; 34213575 , EIF5A::USP6 fusion has been described in a dermal nodular fasciitis of the left forearm with atypical mitosis 31880592 , and CTNNB1::USP6 fusion was seen in an intraneural nodular fasciitis 35175167 . USP6 rearrangements have also been reported in aneurysmal bone cyst, fibro-osseous tumor of the digits, and a subgroup of fibroma of tendon sheaths. tumors in this group (including nodular fasciitis) have morphological and clinical overlap, and it has been suggested that they may represent a spectrum of manifestations of the same disease process in different locations 32635781 ; 30758758 . The histological differential diagnosis depends on the location, the proportion of collagen and myxoid stroma, and cellularity. Collagenous patterns can be mistaken for fibromatosis, collagenous fibroma (desmoplastic fibroblastoma), or granulation tissue. The differential diagnosis also includes neural tumors, nerve sheath tumors, myositis ossificans, proliferative fasciitis, proliferative myositis, and inflammatory myofibroblastic tumors. Large and/or mitotically active nodular fasciitis can be mistaken for sarcoma 11601130 . Essential: bland, typically cellular myofibroblastic spindle cells with a tissue culture–like pattern, variable myxoid stroma, extravasated red blood cells, and lymphocytes. Desirable: USP6 rearrangement is useful in challenging cases, such as small biopsies or atypical presentations. EWSR1::SMAD3-rearranged fibroblastic tumor The tumors are superficially located within the dermis and/or subcutaneous fat. Dermal involvement may abut the epidermis. The large majority occur in the hands and feet 29957732 ; 29309308 , while the lower extremity represents the most common non-acral site 32901982 . Patients usually present with a small, painless, superficial tumor in an acral site. EWSR1::SMAD3-rearranged fibroblastic tumors are rare, with < 20 cases reported to date. Patients have a wide age range (1–68 years, median: 39 years), and most are female (M:F ratio: 1:4) 32901982 . EWSR1::SMAD3-rearranged fibroblastic tumor is a distinctive benign fibroblastic neoplasm with strong predilection for the hands and feet. These tumors are typically well demarcated, but they can infiltrate subcutaneous fat. In particular, in adults, the acellular center of the tumor appears hyalinized, which can resemble collagen rosettes. The peripheral zones consist of intersecting cellular fascicles of fibroblastic spindle cells within collagenous to more myxoid stroma. However, about half lack this zonation pattern. Lesional cells lack nuclear pleomorphism, hyperchromasia, prominent nucleoli, and mitotic activity. Myopericytomatous growth is rare. There may be focal stippled dystrophic calcification 29309308 ; 29957732 ; 32901982 . By immunohistochemistry, the fibroblastic tumor cells consistently show strong diffuse nuclear ERG expression, whereas SMA and CD34 are negative. When EWSR1 rearrangement is detected by FISH, a myoepithelial tumor may be considered in the differential diagnosis. However, immunohistochemistry for cytokeratins, EMA, S100, and SOX10 is negative. The tumor type is defined by a fusion of exon 7 of EWSR1 with exon 5 or exon 6 of SMAD3, which may be confirmed by next-generation sequencing or validated by break-apart FISH assays 29309308 ; 32901982 . SMAD3 is an important signal transducer in the TGF-β/SMAD signalling pathway, which is involved in extracellular matrix synthesis by fibroblasts. Essential: clinical presentation as a small dermal and subcutaneous acral nodule; intersecting hypercellular fascicles comprising bland monomorphic spindle cells lacking mitotic activity, admixed with centrally located acellular hyalinized areas; diffuse strong ERG immunopositivity; molecular studies by FISH or next-generation sequencing confirming EWSR1::SMAD3 fusion. Dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans Intermediate Fibroblastic Tumors DFSP is most common on the trunk, followed by the proximal extremities and the head and neck region 10870053 ; 27806849 . Rare cases involving the distal extremities and acral sites have been reported 29240584 . Patients with DFSP typically present with a painless, firm, slow-growing plaque or nodule. Discolouration (brown, reddish-blue, or violaceous) may be seen. Longstanding lesions may develop a multinodular or protuberant appearance. Rapid growth in a longstanding lesion may indicate fibrosarcomatous transformation. Rarely, cases can be subcutaneous; in such cases there is a possible association with PDGFD rearrangement or with head and neck locations 35034038 ; 28420485 . PDGFD-rearranged DFSPs have also been described in tumors in the breast 30014607 . DFSP occurs most often in young to middle-aged adults, but it can arise at any age and can even be congenital 32558231 ; 21429521 ; 17310000 ; 12502925 . Dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans (DFSP) is a superficial fibroblastic mesenchymal tumor with storiform architecture. The majority of cases harbour a COL1A1::PDGFB translocation. Classic DFSP The classic form is characterized by a proliferation of uniform, medium-sized spindle cells with a storiform or cartwheel pattern of growth centred in the dermis. It is separated from the epidermis by a grenz zone and infiltrates the subcutaneous adipose tissue in a lace-like or honeycomb pattern. It lacks the overlying epidermal hyperplasia of a dermatofibroma. The periphery is poorly defined and the tumor can show subtle tentacle-like extension along tissue planes and around lobules of subcutaneous adipose tissue. Less commonly, it can be centred in the subcutis, with minimal or no dermal involvement. Mitotic figures are infrequent. There is minimal atypia. Diffuse strong staining for CD34 is characteristic. Giant cell fibroblastoma This subtype is most commonly seen in childhood (and is considered a pediatric subtype of DFSP). Giant cell fibroblastoma has a similar localization to the classic form and shows storiform spindle cell morphology, but it also shows additional features including numerous multinucleated giant cells with a wreath-like arrangement of nuclei around pseudovascular spaces and prominent myxoid change 17349565 ; 12502925 . Myxoid DFSP This uncommon subtype is defined as DFSP with > 50% myxoid change. The tumors show multinodular growth with abundant pale myxoid stroma; frequently branching, small, thin-walled vessels; and scattered mast cells 17890911 ; 17721193 . This subtype is diagnostically challenging, because the storiform pattern can be obscured by myxoid stroma. Pigmented DFSP This subtype contains numerous dendritic cells containing melanin pigment. The pigmented cells can show positive staining for S100. Myoid DFSP This subtype is characterized by pale nodules of spindle-shaped cells with eosinophilic cytoplasm. It has well-defined margins and is often centred on a blood vessel and associated with stromal hyalinization. The nodules are positive for SMA and negative for CD34 and desmin 26076821 . Plaque-like DFSP This subtype is characterized by a poorly circumscribed cellular dermal spindle cell tumor with wavy nuclei, a horizontal to fascicular arrangement of cells, and a myxoid stroma 20061935 . Other morphological patterns Granular cell, sclerosing, and atrophic tumors have also been described; hybrids of these and all of the above-mentioned forms can also be encountered. DFSP with fibrosarcomatous transformation Fibrosarcomatous transformation, which is seen in approximately 10% of DFSP cases, is characterized by (often abrupt) transition to a herringbone or fascicular growth pattern with increased cellularity, increased atypia, and increased mitotic activity. This subtype may form a discrete nodule in a background of DFSP and often shows diminished or lost CD34 expression. Fibrosarcomatous transformation can occur de novo or in recurrent tumor 9591728 . DFSP shows strong diffuse staining for CD34 in most cases (80–90%). CD34 positivity can be lost in fibrosarcomatous areas. Rarely, these tumors can have pleomorphic to even round cell morphologies 21478726 . The majority of cases will harbour a COL1A1::PDGFB rearrangement, sometimes cryptic by FISH, with rare cases harbouring alternative rearrangements with PDGFD and partners such as COL6A3, EMILIN2, or TNC. The tumor is considered to be fibroblastic in origin. Supernumerary ring chromosomes containing the centromere from chromosome 22 and material from chromosomes 22 and 17 is the characteristic cytogenetic finding 2208065 ; 8076341 ; 7757993 . Another alteration, unbalanced t(17;22)(q21.3;q13.1), is more common in pediatric cases. Both aberrations bring the PDGFB gene under the control of the COL1A1 promoter 8988177 . There are numerous breakpoints in the COL1A1 gene (which consists of 52 exons), whereas the PDGFB breakpoint is restricted and always allows expression of PDGFB exon 2 9739023 ; 17950782 . After proteolytic processing that removes the COL1A1 protein leader sequence, there is massive overexpression of normal PDGFB ligand, which ignites downstream pathways, probably in an autocrine fashion. Gains in genomic copies of COL1A1::PDGFB and alterations in the mTOR signalling pathway can be seen in fibrosarcomatous transformation 16980946 ; 28711648 . Rare cases can have cryptic COL1A1::PDGFB or alternative PDGFD rearrangements with COL6A3, EMILIN2, or TNC 34628665 ; 29955147 ; 30014607 ; 35034038 ; 34256767 . The distinction from dermatofibroma can be difficult on a small or superficial biopsy. Dermatofibroma has less-uniform cytology, with variability of the spindle cell morphology and admixture with other cell types, including macrophages, lymphocytes, and multinucleated giant cells. Dermatofibroma is usually associated with overlying epidermal hyperplasia. Entrapment of collagen is seen peripherally; it is usually CD34-negative. tumors in the differential diagnosis of DFSP lack rearrangement of PDGFB, but morphology and immunohistochemistry are most often sufficient 17950782 ; 21484928 . Essential: a cellular, predominantly dermal-based tumor with monotonous, short spindle cells with a storiform pattern, typically with infiltrative growth and honeycomb subcutis involvement; diffuse CD34 reactivity; the fibrosarcomatous subtype has a fascicular growth pattern with increased mitoses, sometimes with decreased CD34 labelling. Desirable: rearrangements involving COL1A1::PDGFB (common) or PDGFD (rare). Myxoinflammatory fibroblastic sarcoma Intermediate, locally aggressive; rare metastasis MIFS usually affects the acral dorsal extremities, particularly the hands 9578090 ; 9706971 ; proximal examples amount to 5% of cases 12376919 ; 24121178 . The hand, finger, and wrist account for about 60% of cases, and the foot and ankle for 20% 24121178 . MIFS usually manifests as a painless mass. On imaging, it is centred in the subcutis (in about two thirds of cases) or deeper and typically displays infiltration into adjacent tissues, often mimicking infection, tenosynovial giant cell tumor, or ganglion cysts 27560024 ; 17449774 ; 15908525 . MIFS is rare. It has a peak incidence in the fourth to sixth decades of life and no sex predilection 24121178 ; 18190444 ; 9706971 ; 9578090 ; 9779486 . Myxoinflammatory fibroblastic sarcoma (MIFS) is an infiltrative, locally aggressive fibroblastic neoplasm with a predilection for acral soft tissue, characterized by prominent inflammation, a myxohyaline stroma, and pleomorphic fibroblastic cells with macronucleoli. MIFS is infiltrative and multinodular, being centred in the subcutaneous tissue in most cases. Especially in acral sites, these lesions tend to be superficial and to involve the dermis. They are characterized by dense inflammation merging with stroma varying from myxoid to hyalinized and containing sheets and small foci of epithelioid and spindled cells. Some lesions contain foamy histiocytes, giant cells, and hemosiderin. Within the inflammatory background, scattered bizarre cells with large vesicular nuclei and macronucleoli reminiscent of Reed–Sternberg cells are present. Many cells show degenerated (smudged) chromatin. Pseudolipoblasts with cytoplasmic mucopolysaccharide matrix may be seen. The inflammatory infiltrate is mixed, consisting of lymphocytes, plasma cells, histiocytes, and eosinophils in varying proportions. Emperipolesis, often subtle, is a common feature 9779486 ; 32514165 ; 25886867 . Mitotic activity is minimal. Immunohistochemistry is unhelpful. The majority of cases exhibit expression of cyclin D1 (BCL1), factor XIIIa, D2-40, and CD10 9706971 ; 24121178 ; 25886867 ; 32514165 . Variable expression of CD34, CD163, and PRAME is also observed, as well as focal expression of keratin, KIT (CD117), CD68, and actin 18190444 ; 24121178 ; 9706971 ; 25886867 . Amplification of VGLL3 on 3p11-p12, resulting in a supernumerary ring chromosome, is reported in > 50% of cases 31898851 . A t(1;10) with breakpoints around OGA on 10q24 and TGFBR3 on 1p22 is documented in 13% of cases 31898851 ; 32514165 and is also found in pure hemosiderotic fibrolipomatous tumors, in examples with mixed MIFS morphology (where the translocation appears to be more prevalent) 21717526 ; 26980036 , and in pleomorphic hyalinizing angiectatic tumor 24705316 . BRAF fusions or amplifications are also found 28692601 ; 32514165 ; 31898851 . Essential: typical distal extremity location; atypical fibroblastic cells with macronucleoli; variably myxoid and hyalinized matrix with a mixed inflammatory infiltrate. Desirable: pseudolipoblasts. Myxofibrosarcoma Malignant Fibroblastic Tumors Malignant Myxofibrosarcomas usually involve the extremities, especially the thigh. The trunk, head and neck, and acral sites are rare locations. Approximately half of the cases occur in dermal/subcutaneous tissues; the remainder involve deeper compartments 8604805 ; 15138937 ; 26759307 ; 29065228 . Myxofibrosarcoma is an often slow-growing and painless tumor with frequent local recurrence. Low-grade cases may develop histological progression to higher grades upon recurrence, thus acquiring an increased risk of metastasis. Myxofibrosarcoma, with a slight male predominance, is a rather common sarcoma of elderly patients, occurring usually in the sixth to eighth decades of life; it is rare in patients aged < 30 years 8604805 ; 20878245 ; 26759307 . Myxofibrosarcoma is a nodular spindle-to-pleomorphic sarcoma with wide variations in cellularity, nuclear atypia, and a myxoid stroma with curvilinear vasculature. As the histological grade increases, myxofibrosarcoma exhibits increased cellularity, pleomorphism, and proliferative activity but decreased myxoid stroma 8604805 ; a minimum of myxoid stroma (optimally 5%) is required to distinguish undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcomas 26759307 . Subcutaneous lesions often have extensive infiltration beyond what can be clinically detected 15138937 . Low-grade myxofibrosarcoma is hypocellular, prominently myxoid, and composed of mildly atypical spindle-to-stellate cells featuring nuclear hyperchromasia and perivascular cellular condensation with some mucin-containing pseudolipoblasts 27591498 . The intermediate-grade lesions become more cellular and pleomorphic but lack the solid areas characteristic of high-grade cases. The latter often show necrosis, atypical mitoses, and overlap with undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma. The rare epithelioid subtype typically shows cohesive clusters and/or sheets of epithelioid cells with abundant cytoplasm and vesicular nuclei, simulating carcinoma or melanoma 17197925 . SMA and/or CD34 reactivity is occasionally seen in myxofibrosarcoma 23600956 ; 34326362 , whereas desmin and S100 are negative. Myxofibrosarcomas harbour frequent chromosomal structure rearrangements and copy-number alterations, even in low-grade cases, and they exhibit increasing genomic complexity in recurrent lesions with histological progression 16415793 ; 20601955 ; 29100075 ; 30018380 . Myxofibrosarcomas are predominated by somatic copy-number alterations, where several oncogenes (TRIO, RICTOR, SKP2, and AMACR) on frequently gained 5p are variably coamplified and associated with increased grade 22322669 ; 25384383 ; 27577794 . In half of myxofibrosarcomas, the pathogenetic aberrations converge on p53 signalling and the G1/S cell-cycle checkpoint. tumor suppressor mutations that inactivate TP53 (46%, most frequent), RB1 (18%), and/or CDKN2A/CDKN2B (16%) occur more frequently than oncogene amplifications of CDK6, CCND1, or MDM2 30018380 . RB1-inactivated and TP53-inactivated myxofibrosarcomas critically rely on SKP2 for survival 32161142 , while amplifications of TRIO and RICTOR activate the RAC/PAK and AKT/mTOR pathways, respectively 27577794 . The differential diagnosis includes superficial angiomyxoma, myxoid spindle cell lipoma, nerve sheath myxoma, myxoid dermatofibrosarcoma, low-grade fibromyxoid sarcoma, and other higher-grade sarcomas with a myxoid matrix. Essential: a multinodular tumor with infiltrative margins; myxoid stroma; variably pleomorphic cells; curvilinear vessels; hypercellular areas in higher-grade lesions. 3 Cherry hemangioma Vascular Tumors Hemangiomas The most common location is the trunk, followed by the upper limbs and (less commonly) the lower limbs. The lesions are multiple, tiny, bright red, asymptomatic papules that increase in number with age. This hemangioma affects middle-aged to elderly adults, with no sex predilection. Cherry hemangioma is a common benign superficial dermal capillary proliferation with a lobular architecture, appearing in adulthood. The papillary dermis is expanded by a slightly polypoid lobular proliferation of small congested and dilated capillaries with surrounding loose stroma, often with an epithelial collarette. HRAS and KRAS somatic mutations are found in a small proportion of cases 26802240 , and frequent somatic mutations of GNA14, GNA11, and GNAQ have also been described 34040639 ; 31189994 . Essential: a lobular proliferation of capillaries in the papillary dermis associated with an epidermal collarette. Sinusoidal hemangioma The most common location is the trunk. Subcutaneous tissue of the breast and extremities can be affected. The lesion is a small, asymptomatic, well-demarcated acquired dermal or subcutaneous bluish nodule. These relatively rare lesions occur primarily in middle-aged women. In men, they frequently develop in the setting of gynaecomastia. Sinusoidal hemangioma is a histologically distinctive benign vascular lesion consisting of thin-walled vascular channels with scant smooth muscle in a sinusoidal or sieve-like pattern, and with features resembling those of anastomosing hemangioma (a lesion seen mainly in the kidney). The lesions are lobular and relatively well circumscribed. They are composed of irregular, dilated, congested, thin-walled vascular channels with scant smooth muscle in a sinusoidal or sieve-like pattern, with little intervening stroma 1746680 ; 26945338 ; 19606014 . The endothelial cells are uniform and mitotically quiescent. Thrombosis and dystrophic calcification are often present. A similar sinusoidal vascular pattern is commonly seen focally in venous malformations. In the breast, the differential diagnosis includes well-differentiated angiosarcoma. However, angiosarcoma shows multilayering of endothelial cells, cytological atypia, and mitotic activity. Essential: a lobular proliferation of dilated vascular channels with a sinusoidal or sieve-like pattern. Microvenular hemangioma This lesion affects the trunk and extremities, with a predilection for the forearms. The lesion is a single, small (or occasionally larger), red, asymptomatic papule or plaque. Exceptional eruptive or multiple lesions have been reported 22722465 ; 25263662 ; 20881833 . This rare hemangioma arises mainly in young adults, with no sex predilection. Microvenular hemangioma is a mitotically quiescent vascular lesion, likely to be a type of venous malformation. The lesions are poorly defined, usually involve superficial and deep reticular dermis, and consist of elongated (often irregular) small vascular channels resembling venules. The vessels dissect somewhat hyalinized-looking collagen bundles. Extension of channels into arrector pili muscles is common. A single layer of pericytes, which can be highlighted by SMA staining, is consistently present and often conspicuous. The endothelial cells are bland and lack mitotic activity; they are positive for ERG, CD31, and CD34 but negative for podoplanin (recognized by D2-40) 23169416 ; 25263662 . The dissection of collagen may prompt consideration of angiosarcoma or Kaposi sarcoma. Microvenular hemangioma lacks atypia and multilayering; each vessel is surrounded by a pericyte layer, and it is KSHV/HHV8-negative 1939781 ; 25263662 . Essential: a poorly defined dermal proliferation of small, elongated, and irregular venule-like vascular channels. Hobnail hemangioma This lesion affects the trunk and extremities. Most lesions arise as a small, nondescript erythematous papule. Uncommonly, the lesion is a small reddish-brown or purple papule surrounded by concentric ecchymotic haloes, hence the original name “targetoid hemosiderotic hemangioma”. This relatively rare hemangioma occurs mainly in young and middle-aged adults, with a male predilection. Hobnail hemangioma is a benign vascular malformation of lymphatic lineage, with hobnail endothelial cells and a delayed presentation. The lesions are wedge-shaped and consist of scattered, thin-walled, irregular vascular channels lined by bland endothelial cells with a hobnail appearance and focal intraluminal papillary projections. Vessels deeper in the lesion become smaller, flattened, and inconspicuous, without hobnail endothelial cells. Red blood cell extravasation, hemosiderin deposition, and perivascular lymphocytes are common. The endothelial cells are strongly positive for podoplanin (recognized by D2-40) and usually negative or weakly positive for CD34, suggesting a lymphatic lineage 15059220 ; 9888709 ; 10472756 ; 24601986 ; 26475078 ; 21821311 . Expression of lymphatic markers and negativity for WT1 and mitotic markers supports the conclusion that these are superficial lymphatic malformations that undergo delayed perilesional bleeding and hemosiderin deposition 21798621 ; 21821311 . Atypical vascular lesions occurring after radiotherapy may be identical, but they usually lack the wedge-shaped architecture. Papillary intralymphatic angioendothelioma (Dabska tumor) and retiform hemangioendothelioma have hobnail endothelial cells but have a distinctive pattern and are larger and more infiltrative. Essential: a superficial dermal, wedge-shaped collection of irregular, thin-walled lymphatic vascular channels lined by hobnail endothelial cells. Desirable: perilesional deposits of hemosiderin. Glomeruloid hemangioma The lesions are multiple erythematous papules. This rare hemangioma shows no sex predilection. Examples occurring outside the setting of multicentric Castleman disease or POEMS syndrome are likely to in fact be papillary hemangioma (see Differential diagnosis, below) 18001423 ; 19077091 ; 18805868 ; 17927585 . A rare association with Erdheim–Chester disease has been reported 30563806 . Glomeruloid hemangioma is a reactive vascular proliferation associated with multicentric Castleman disease and POEMS syndrome (polyradiculoneuropathy, organomegaly, endocrinopathy, clonal plasma cell disorder, and skin changes). There is dermal proliferation of dilated vascular channels containing clusters of capillaries that resemble renal glomeruli. The endothelial cells often contain intracytoplasmic inclusions that give a positive PAS reaction; these inclusions may be immunoglobulins, enlarged lysosomes, or thanatosomes 2173428 ; 19614998 ; 8030771 . Raised serum levels of VEGF have been described in one study, suggesting that this may play in a role in the development of the vascular lesions 30563806 . Papillary hemangioma has a predilection for the head and neck and manifests as a single lesion consisting of dermal dilated channels lined by endothelial cells with frequent papillary projections and lacking glomeruloid architecture 18805868 . Essential: dilated dermal vascular channels with intraluminal proliferation of small blood vessels mimicking renal glomeruli. Papillary hemangioma Papillary hemangioma occurs almost exclusively on the head and neck 17927585 ; 31592865 . Papillary hemangioma appears as a solitary, longstanding, bluish-red papule as large as 11 mm in diameter. It is most common in adult men. Papillary hemangioma is a distinctive vascular proliferation consisting of dilated vascular channels with prominent intraluminal papillary projections lined by endothelial cells, many of which contain intracytoplasmic globules. Papillary hemangioma is characterized by dermal, widely dilated, thin-walled vascular channels with numerous luminal papillary projections containing capillaries lined by plump endothelial cells, surrounded by pericytes, and displaying frequent intracytoplasmic eosinophilic globules. These globules, known as thanatosomes, represent dilated lysosomes containing debris and fat vacuoles. Endothelial cells are positive for CD31, CD34, and ERG and are negative for lymphatic markers. The lesions are histologically similar to glomeruloid hemangiomas, which differ in their typical multifocally, involvement of the trunk and extremities, and association with POEMS syndrome. Essential: a nodule consisting of ectatic dermal vascular channels with prominent papillary projections lined by endothelial cells with frequent intracytoplasmic eosinophilic globules. Spindle cell hemangioma This lesion affects the distal extremities and occasionally the neck. The lesions are multiple asymptomatic bluish nodules developing over many years, with little tendency for regression. There is a strong association with Maffucci syndrome, and less common associations with lymphedema, early-onset varicose veins, and Klippel–Trénaunay syndrome 7661276 ; 2071088 ; 23485734 ; 8827025 . This rare hemangioma is more common in the second and third decades of life, with no sex predilection. Spindle cell hemangioma is a benign neoplasm composed of spindled cells, ectatic vascular spaces, and vacuolated endothelial cells. The tumors are relatively well circumscribed, often partially intravascular, or sometimes poorly defined. They occupy the dermis, with frequent extension into the subcutis, and they consist of irregular, dilated, thin-walled, congested, cavernous-like vascular channels mixed with solid areas of vacuolated epithelioid endothelial cells scattered among bland spindle-shaped cells with pericytic and fibroblastic features and poorly defined eosinophilic cytoplasm. The cavernous vascular channels are lined by a single layer of bland endothelial cells. Thrombi, with or without dystrophic calcification, are common. Smooth muscle cells may be seen focally. Degenerative cytological atypia is sometimes present. The endothelial cells within the vascular channels and the epithelioid vacuolated cells show positive immunostaining for endothelial markers. Spindle cells may show focal positivity for SMA 2071088 ; 23485734 ; 8827025 ; 3740350 . Sporadic lesions and lesions associated with Maffucci syndrome are associated with IDH1 p.R132C hotspot mutations 23485734 ; 22057234 ; 28845532 . Frequent somatic alterations in 2p22.3, 2q24.3, and 14q11.2 are also found in spindle cell hemangiomas and enchondromas occurring in patients with Maffucci syndrome 25565925 . Nodular Kaposi sarcoma lacks cavernous vascular channels and epithelioid vacuolated cells and is positive for KSHV/HHV8. Essential: a well-circumscribed dermal/subcutaneous tumor composed of dilated, cavernous-like vascular channels intermixed with solid areas composed of vacuolated epithelioid endothelial cells. Epithelioid hemangioma Cutaneous lesions have a predilection for the head and neck and the trunk 4008683 . EHs manifest as single or multiple, persistent, skin-colored to erythematous papules and nodules. Peripheral eosinophilia is seen in 15% of patients 4008683 . Similar lesions may occur in deeper soft tissue, internal organs, and bone. Lesions occur most commonly in young adults (with a slight male predilection), but people of all ages and ethnic groups are affected 4008683 . Epithelioid hemangioma (EH) is a benign vascular proliferation with vessels lined by epithelioid endothelial cells, often with an associated inflammatory component. There is a lobular proliferation of vascular channels lined by bland epithelioid endothelial cells with abundant eosinophilic or amphophilic cytoplasm and vesicular nuclei that protrude into the lumen. A focal intravascular component may be seen, and rare examples are entirely intravenous 32094426 . Inflammation is typically prominent, consisting of lymphocytes, histiocytes, plasma cells, and numerous eosinophils. Fibrosis occurs in late-stage lesions, which are also characterized by less inflammation and less prominent epithelioid endothelial cells. In many cases, mural damage in a medium-sized to large artery is present. Immunohistochemically, the endothelial cells are positive for blood vascular markers, lack lymphatic markers, and are accompanied by an SMA-positive pericyte layer. The epithelioid endothelial cells do not express EMA or keratins and usually display nuclear staining for FOSB 29527734 . FOS or FOSB gene rearrangements are commonly present in bone and soft tissue EHs, but they are rare in cutaneous lesions and absent in histologically classic examples of angiolymphoid hyperplasia with eosinophilia, although these are positive for FOSB by immunohistochemistry 26135557 ; 29527734 . EH must be distinguished from Kimura disease, which occurs mainly in Asian males, presents with larger and deeper lesions and involvement of lymph nodes, and is often associated with systemic symptoms. Histologically, although the composition of the inflammatory cell infiltrate of Kimura disease is similar to that of EH, germinal centres may be seen and the vascular channels are not lined by epithelioid endothelial cells 6718071 . Essential: a lobular proliferation of small vascular channels lined by epithelioid endothelial cells often associated with prominent inflammation (namely, eosinophils and lymphocytes). Tufted hemangioma These lesions have a predilection for the neck and upper trunk. Tufted hemangiomas manifest as slow-growing, poorly defined macules, papules, nodules, and plaques, with rare focal regression 12383094 ; 20644037 . Patients with large cutaneous lesions may develop Kasabach–Merritt syndrome 10642677 ; 27607323 . This and other features, including genetic evidence of a homogeneous methylation pattern, support the widely held opinion that tufted hemangioma is a smaller, more superficial clinical presentation of kaposiform hemangioendothelioma 31887709 . This rare hemangioma has a strong predilection for infants and children, with no sex predilection 2644316 ; 20644037 . Congenital cases have been reported 30318642 , and presentation in adult life is exceptional 17186794 . Tufted hemangioma is a benign cutaneous vascular tumor sometimes associated with Kasabach–Merritt syndrome and now widely considered part of the kaposiform hemangioendothelioma spectrum. Multiple scattered, tightly packed lobules of capillaries are present throughout the dermis and (more rarely) the subcutis, in a cannonball pattern. The lumina of vascular channels are often difficult to discern, and pericytes are prominent. The endothelial cells are flat and occasionally contain intracytoplasmic hyaline structures. A distinctive feature is the presence of a crescent-like lymphatic channel around many individual tumor lobules. The stroma between tumor lobules may be desmoplastic and contain lymphatic-like channels. Focal fascicles of spindled endothelial cells, which are positive for podoplanin (recognized by D2-40), CD31, ERG, and CD34, may be seen within the capillary lobules. Nodular Kaposi sarcoma lacks a cannonball architecture and is positive for KSHV/HHV8. Essential: tufts of capillaries scattered throughout the dermis, with frequent crescent-like lymphatic vessels around tumor lobules. Angiokeratoma ACD is characterized by lesions in a bathing-trunk distribution. AF occurs on the scrotum and vulva 6069899 ; 6019084 . AM occurs on the dorsum of fingers and toes 8993949 . SA occurs mainly on the lower limbs 8993949 . Patients with ACD present with numerous asymptomatic pinpoint papules with minimal epidermal change. Patients with AF or AM present with single or multiple small red keratotic papules. Patients with SA present with a single keratotic (often crusted) papule or nodule. Four clinicopathological types of angiokeratomas have been described 6018992 . ACD is associated with Fabry disease and arises in late childhood. AF most commonly occurs in adult men. AM most commonly occurs in adults, with no sex predilection. SA or angiokeratoma circumscriptum also occurs in adults, with no sex predilection. Angiokeratoma is a superficial vascular ectasia associated with variable overlying epidermal changes. ACD shows dilated, congested vascular channels in the papillary dermis, with minimal epidermal change. Endothelial cells, pericytes, and fibroblasts show cytoplasmic vacuoles representing lipid. AF, AM, and SA show dilated, thin-walled vascular channels in the papillary dermis associated with overlying epidermal changes consisting of acanthosis and hyperkeratosis 6018992 . SA must be distinguished from verrucous venous malformation (see section Verrucous venous malformation). Essential: a papillary dermal proliferation of dilated thin-walled vascular channels with variable overlying epidermal changes and lacking a deep component. Infantile hemangioma These lesions are most common on the head and neck and the extremities, but they also occur on the trunk, genitals, and in some viscera (notably, the liver and intestines). Nascent tumors may be evident at birth but typically appear in the first 2–6 weeks of life, as a bright-red or blue nodule or plaque, often with a strawberry-like appearance. There is initial rapid growth over a period of months, transitioning to a longer involuting phase of a few years 18429772 ; 24641194 . Lesions arising at certain locations may be associated with underlying malformations and multiple lesions; usually, the presence of > 5 lesions is associated with liver hemangiomas 34419524 . This hemangioma, which occurs in about 4% of the population, is the most common tumor of infancy. It shows a female predilection and is more common in White populations 18429772 ; 24641194 . Infantile hemangioma is a benign tumor characterized by a proliferation of lobules of capillaries with a distinctive immunophenotype arising exclusively in infancy and showing spontaneous slow regression. The histology of infantile hemangioma defines the three stages of the lesion: proliferation, partial involution, and complete involution. These stages form an overlapping continuum. Early proliferative lesions consist of cellular dermal and/or subcutaneous masses of tightly packed capillaries with small lumina, lined by plump endothelial cells rimmed by pericytes. The capillaries are interspersed with immature dendritic-type cells and arranged in lobules separated by delicate fibrous septa or normal intervening stroma. Perineural extension is common 7737662 , and the feeding and draining vessels may be quite large. During active involution, the lesional capillaries become variably dilated and congested, and gradually disappear. The basement membranes thicken and show apoptotic dust, and the pericapillary mast cells increase in number. Nearing end-stage, the tumor lobules are replaced by loose fibrous or fibrofatty stroma containing a few residual ghost capillaries composed of thickened multilayered rinds of basement membrane material with little or no cellular lining. The endothelial cells show a complex immunophenotype shared only by placental capillaries, including positivity for GLUT1, LeY, CD15, CCR6, IDO1, and IGF2 11735711 . The fact that infantile hemangioma’s immunoreactivity for GLUT1, LeY, and other markers is identical to that of placental microvessels suggests that this tumor results from embolization of placental cells or stem cells differentiating towards placental vascular cells 11346333 . Cultured infantile hemangioma endothelial cells are clonal, a finding consistent with a neoplastic process 11254674 . No underlying genetic abnormalities have been identified. Infantile hemangioma must be distinguished from congenital non-progressive hemangiomas on the basis of careful clinicopathological correlation and GLUT1 immunohistochemistry. All infantile hemangiomas have endothelial GLUT1 positivity, whereas congenital non-progressive hemangioma endothelial cells are negative for this marker 10665907 . Essential: an acquired vascular tumor developing after birth and composed of lobules of capillaries lined by GLUT1-positive endothelial cells. Congenital non-progressive hemangiomas: Rapidly involuting congenital hemangioma and non-involuting congenital hemangioma The most common location is the head, followed by the extremities. The lesions are usually fully formed at birth, typically following either a persistent clinical course (NICH) or a very rapidly regressive course through infarction (RICH) during the first 6 months of life 15018449 . Initial lesions vary in size and consist of a vascular red or bluish mass with overlying telangiectasia, occasionally associated with ulceration. Rare tumors regress incompletely (PICH) 24176519 . NICH increases in size proportionally as the patient grows, and it does not regress 11391180 . Exceptional cases show limited postnatal growth. Congenital non-progressive hemangiomas arise at birth, with no sex predilection. They are less common than infantile hemangioma. Congenital non-progressive hemangiomas are a distinct group of vascular lesions that arise in utero and are fully formed at birth. There are two clinical subtypes: rapidly involuting congenital hemangioma (RICH) and non-involuting congenital hemangioma (NICH). For cases that regress incompletely, the term “partially involuted congenital hemangioma (PICH)” has been proposed. RICH, PICH, and NICH vary along a histopathological spectrum, largely dependent on the degree of infarction. All are composed of variably well-circumscribed capillary lobules within the dermis and/or subcutis. The interlobular stroma is often fibrotic and may contain arteries, veins, and sometimes lymphatic channels of moderate size. Intralobular capillary endothelial cells and pericytes can be plump, but they lack the increased mitotic activity, GLUT1 positivity, and basement membrane multilamination of infantile hemangioma. Persistent lesions (NICHs and PICHs) are more likely to display arteriovenous shunts, hobnail endothelial cells, and a large vessel in the center of the vascular lobules 11391180 . The endothelial cells of all subtypes are negative for GLUT1 15153887 . Somatic activating mutations in GNAQ and GNA11 at Q209 have been identified in both NICH and RICH 27058448 . The distinction from infantile hemangioma is usually straightforward, on the basis that congenital non-progressive hemangiomas arise at birth and lack endothelial positivity for GLUT1 8774499 ; 9551150 ; 15153887 ; 24176519 . Essential: a congenital lesion; dermal and/or subcutaneous lobules of capillaries lined by endothelial cells that are negative for GLUT1. Lobular capillary hemangioma Lesions have a predilection for the fingers and the head and neck, in particular the nasal and oral mucosae. Gingival lesions occur in pregnant women (granuloma gravidarum). Involvement of internal organs is rare 17922196 . The lesion is a rapidly growing, polypoid, hemorrhagic, and frequently ulcerated blue or red nodule. Multiple lesions occasionally develop; in children, recurrences may be associated with multiple satellites 12423439 ; 3777375 ; 5647967 . Lesions can occur in association with port-wine stain and other vascular malformations. They are also associated with many medications and biological agents, including retinoids and BRAF inhibitors 22134277 ; 6225396 ; 27116335 ; 16958814 . Rare tumors arise in deep dermal / subcutaneous or intravenous locations 575269 . A congenital disseminated aggressive lobular capillary hemangioma with a predilection for the skin, brain, viscera, and musculoskeletal system has been described 32622671 . This hemangioma (including rare congenital cases) occurs over a wide age range, with no sex predilection 5220911 ; 10827405 ; 1792196 . Lobular capillary hemangioma is a common vascular cutaneous and mucosal neoplasm that consists of a proliferation of capillaries with a lobular architecture. The tumors are polypoid and have an epidermal collarette, and show frequent ulceration with prominent inflammation consisting of neutrophils, usually restricted to the superficial aspect of the lesion. Variably dilated capillaries lined by plump endothelial cells rimmed by a pericyte layer are arranged in lobules within edematous stroma. Mitotic activity is common, and focal cytological atypia may be noted, in particular in mucosal lesions. Older lesions show variable fibrosis. Deep-seated and intravenous lesions are identical but lack inflammation 1792196 ; 5220911 . Sporadic lobular capillary hemangiomas and those occurring within port-wine stain may be associated with RAS-family and BRAF mutations (mainly c.1799T>A p.V600E) 26802240 . Nodular Kaposi sarcoma shows a similar architecture but consists of bundles of spindle-shaped cells with clefting, intracytoplasmic eosinophilic globules, and KSHV/HHV8 positivity. Bacillary angiomatosis (an infectious vascular proliferation caused mainly by Bartonella henselae, formerly called Rochalimaea henselae) is histologically similar, but the vascular channels are lined by pale epithelioid endothelial cells and aggregates of neutrophils, and nuclear dust and amorphous basophilic or amphophilic material consisting of Warthin–Starry stain–positive bacteria are identified. Essential: a polypoid tumor with an epithelial collarette and lobules of capillaries associated with an edematous stroma. Poikilodermatous plaque-like hemangioma Almost all lesions arise in the lower extremities 30930084 ; 32362008 . Patients present with asymptomatic, slowly growing, erythematous or violaceous scaly plaques varying in size between 20 and 70 mm that are often described as poikilodermatous. The plaques are typically solitary, rarely multiple. Although clinically the lesions raise concern for poikilodermatous mycosis fungoides, on histology these two entities share no common features. Most of the patients are elderly men. Poikilodermatous plaque-like hemangioma is an acquired band-like vascular proliferation involving the superficial dermis. There is a band-like proliferation of small-calibre blood vessels lined by bland endothelium in the papillary and superficial reticular dermis, with no grenz zone and with a concomitant loss or decrease of elastic fibres in the affected area. Most cases exhibit a certain degree of hyperkeratosis or acanthosis and mild lymphocytic inflammation between the vessels. The differential diagnosis includes other vascular neoplasms, such as acquired elastotic hemangioma (smaller and with a similar pattern but with the presence of solar elastosis), microvenular hemangioma (involves the superficial and deep dermis, no absence of elastic fibres, and an absence of a plaque-like architecture), and hobnail hemangioma (wedge-shaped architecture, irregular lymphatic-like channels, lined by hobnail endothelial cells and hemosiderin deposits) 30930084 . Essential: a proliferation of numerous small blood vessels with bland endothelium in the superficial dermis; concomitant loss or attenuation of elastic fibres. Desirable: a lower-extremity, slowly growing erythematous or violaceous plaque. Acquired elastotic hemangioma AEH has a predilection for the forearms and the lateral aspect of the neck. The lesion manifests as an asymptomatic, small papule or plaque developing in sun-exposed skin 12196746 ; 31268926 . Multiple lesions are exceptional 35170476 . AEH is rare. It occurs in middle-aged and elderly adults, with a slight female predilection. Acquired elastotic hemangioma (AEH) is a superficial band-like proliferation of small vascular channels arising in sun-exposed skin and associated with solar elastosis. AEH shows a band-like proliferation of capillaries, each surrounded by a layer of pericytes and oriented parallel to the epidermis in the upper reticular dermis. There is background solar elastosis. Microvenular hemangioma involves the mid to deep dermis and is poorly defined and not associated with solar elastosis. Poikilodermatous plaque-like hemangioma is also a superficial plaque-like proliferation but the lesions are larger, the stroma is edematous, elastic fibres are missing, and there is no solar elastosis. Essential: a superficial dermal plaque-like proliferation of capillaries in association with solar elastosis. Verrucous venous malformation These lesions have a predilection for the distal extremities; occasionally they occur on the trunk. The lesions are slightly raised singular, grouped, or confluent red to purple plaques that become more hyperkeratotic and may ulcerate, bleed, and slowly enlarge over time. Linear lesions have been reported 10688730 . Local tissue hypertrophy is not a feature. This is a rare congenital lesion with no sex predilection. Verrucous venous malformation is a distinctive localized vascular malformation associated with overlying prominent epidermal changes. An epidermis with prominent acanthosis, papillomatosis, hyperkeratosis, parakeratosis, and crusting overlies an expanded papillary dermis with numerous dilated and congested capillaries and venules, often extending into the investing dermis of the skin adnexa while sparing the reticular dermis. The subcutaneous tissue displays an increased density of variably congested capillaries and venules, with occasionally admixed larger veins. Mitotic activity is rare to absent. There may be focal light endothelial positivity for GLUT1, but the full placenta-like vascular phenotype of infantile hemangioma is lacking. Small dilated lymphatic vessels also may be present but the predominant differentiation is clearly blood vascular 10886755 ; 6038751 ; 25263605 . Verrucous venous malformation is non-familial. A somatic missense mutation in MAP3K3 has been identified in some cases 25728774 . The superficial dermal changes closely resemble angiokeratoma. Histological distinction relies on the identification of a deep dermal / subcutaneous component. Essential: plaques with verrucous epidermal hyperplasia overlying dilated vascular channels in the dermis, with an associated subcutaneous component. Arteriovenous malformation AVM can involve the skin, subcutis, bone, and viscera and has a marked predilection for the head, neck, and limbs. Small, superficial vascular lesions with a predilection for the lips, perioral skin, nose, and eyelids of middle-aged to elderly men, traditionally called acral arteriovenous tumor, may not be true AVMs. AVMs involving skin and deep soft tissue are characterized by a poorly defined bluish or red mass that may be pulsatile, with variably severe arteriovenous shunting, sometimes leading to local tissue necrosis, hemorrhage, or high-output heart failure. The superficial subtype is typically a small red or blue papule. Deep-seated and cutaneous clinical subtypes have been described 17582945 ; 23125071 . AVMs have no sex predilection. They are congenital but may not become clinically evident until later in life. Most are solitary and sporadic. Arteriovenous malformation (AVM) is a congenital vascular anomaly characterized by abnormal arteriovenous connections and high-flow arteriovenous shunting. The lesions are histologically heterogeneous but primarily show beds of arterioles, capillaries, and venules set within a fibromyxomatous background, intermixed with larger-calibre arteries and thick-walled veins. In lesions with high-grade shunting, the arteries are tortuous, with fragmented mural elastic laminae, and the veins show irregular intima and/or mural fibrosis, reflective of elevated venous pressure and turbulence. The overlying skin often contains a small-vessel proliferation similar to that seen in ischemia and stasis. Superficial scalp AVMs, which are limited in depth by cranial bone, are histologically similar. Diagnosis typically requires careful clinicopathological correlation and radiological studies, particularly in small samples. Focal cellular small-vessel proliferations in AVM can mimic infantile hemangioma but are GLUT1-negative 28552538 . Essential: superficial or deep vascular proliferation consisting of capillaries, arterioles, and venules associated with larger-calibre arteries and veins. Lymphangioma (superficial lymphatic malformation) Other Benign Vascular Tumors SLMs may be found in any area of the body surface, but they have a predilection for the axillary folds, shoulders, neck, proximal limbs, genital region, and tongue 831620 ; 5484713 ; 1268059 . Lesions appear as multiple small translucent or yellowish vesicles grouped in a plaque (with a frogspawn appearance). Frequently, there is a wart-like surface. Purpuric areas due to the presence of a blood vessel component are sometimes seen inside the lesion. The net-like SLMs consist of red to purplish macules with a finely reticulated pattern 26800314 . Most SLMs are accompanied by deeper malformed lymphatic vessels in the subcutis 629576 , and rare cases are associated with visceral involvement 8763441 ; 9563054 . SLM may also be associated with Maffucci syndrome 5440820 and Cobb syndrome 8864618 . Cystic hygroma (cystic lymphangioma) is a subtype of subcutaneous macrocystic lymphatic malformation located in the neck, armpits, and groin folds 14259790 . Lesions involving the posterior triangle of the neck may be associated with hydrops fetalis, Turner syndrome (45,X0 karyotype), diverse congenital malformations, several chromosomal aneuploidies, and fetal death 6888468 . Lymphangiomatosis is a rare disorder characterized by abnormal lymphatic vessels diffusely distributed within an anatomical region. Cases of lymphangiomatosis with bone and visceral involvement have a poor prognosis and high mortality 8494102 , whereas lesions involving only soft tissues and bone have an indolent course 5484713 . The recently described multifocal lymphangioendotheliomatosis with thrombocytopenia consists of an association of congenital SLM, gastrointestinal lymphatic malformations, and coagulopathy. Severe cases may evolve to massive consumptive coagulopathy (i.e. Kasabach–Merritt syndrome) 15148106 . SLMs are present at birth or appear during the first few months of life. There is no sex predilection. Lymphangiomas are benign vascular lesions composed of a localized collection of dilated lymphatic channels and may represent superficial lymphatic malformations (SLMs). SLMs involve the papillary dermis, although they sometimes extend to the reticular dermis and even subcutaneous tissue. Lesions consist of dilated thin-walled vascular structures lined by a single discontinuous layer of flattened endothelial cells 7316423 ; 831620 . Lumina of these vessels either appear empty or are filled with eosinophilic homogeneous lymphatic fluid and sometimes erythrocytes. Small delicate valves are a clue to the diagnosis. Foamy macrophages, multinucleated giant cells, and discrete lymphocytic infiltrate are sometimes present in the underlying dermis. Macrocystic and deeper lymphatic malformations appear as interconnected, irregular, dilated vessels in the subcutaneous fat, some with a thick muscular wall 6025577 . Endothelial cells lining SLM express CD31 and ERG as well as the lymphatic-specific endothelial markers podoplanin (D2-40), LYVE1, and PROX1 19013877 ; 15376314 ; 12853470 . Lymphangioma circumscriptum, also called microcystic lymphatic malformation, occurs as plaques of clear or hemorrhagic cystic spaces said to resemble frogspawn and consisting of superficial dilated lymphatic vessels up to 10 mm in diameter, with acanthosis of the overlying epidermis 26374361 ; 35739629 . It may be associated with deeper lymphatic malformations 35250235 . VEGFR3 and its ligands VEGF-C and VEGF-D seem to be involved in lymphangiogenesis. Transgenic mice with VEGF-C hyperexpression have been shown to develop lymphatic hyperplasia 9162011 . Families with Milroy disease, a congenital inherited lymphatic disorder transmitted in an autosomal dominant fashion, show mutations in FLT4 (encoding VEGFR3) on chromosome 5q 12543715 ; 9817924 . Mutations in PROX1 10499794 and FOXC2 11078474 ; 17372167 ; 19760751 are also involved in the development of SLM. Classically, SLMs and angiokeratomas have been considered as separate entities. However, endothelial cells lining angiokeratoma vessels also have a lymphatic endothelial cell immunophenotype 25243395 ; 24666194 . Essential: dilated thin-walled vascular structures lined by a single discontinuous layer of flattened endothelial cells involving superficial dermis. Cutaneous epithelioid angiomatous nodule Cutaneous epithelioid angiomatous nodule affects a wide range of anatomical sites, with a predilection for the trunk and extremities. Mucosal surfaces may also be involved 14726818 ; 18212538 ; 25728975 . The lesions appear as solitary papules and nodules with erythematous to bluish discolouration, measuring < 15 mm (median: 5 mm). Rarely, the tumors are multiple. An eruptive presentation has also been reported 14726818 ; 21931284 ; 18212538 . The age of presentation has a wide range, with peak incidence in young to middle-aged adults (median age: 37 years) 14726818 ; 18212538 . There is no strong sex predilection. Cutaneous epithelioid angiomatous nodule is a distinctive benign cutaneous vascular proliferation with prominent epithelioid cell morphology. The tumors occur as well-circumscribed nodules in the superficial to mid dermis. They are composed of solid sheets of large polygonal epithelioid cells with abundant cytoplasm containing vesicular nuclei with small eosinophilic nucleoli. Intracytoplasmic vacuoles are frequently observed. Mitotic figures are seen, but atypical mitoses and nuclear pleomorphism are absent. Intralesional vascular channels are a focal feature. The tumors show hemosiderin deposition; an inflammatory cell infiltrate composed of lymphocytes, plasma cells, and eosinophils; and variable perilesional fibrosis. The overlying epidermis may be acanthotic with collarette formation. Rarely, there is involvement of deep dermis and superficial subcutis. Immunohistochemically, the tumor cells express endothelial cell markers (CD31, CD34, and factor VIII), and intralesional SMA-positive pericytes are present. Immunohistochemistry for FOSB is negative 28009608 . The tumors are endothelial cell neoplasms. Differentiation from epithelioid angiosarcoma is important because of its aggressive behavior, and both tumors can occur in a similar clinical context. Epithelioid angiosarcoma is larger and involves deeper structures, with infiltrative margins; it is characterized by nuclear pleomorphism with numerous and atypical mitotic figures. tumor necrosis may also be present. Epithelioid hemangioendothelioma is characterized by epithelioid endothelial cells arranged in cords and strands in a chondromyxoid stroma rather than the solid sheet-like growth seen in epithelioid angiomatous nodule. Epithelioid hemangioma is multinodular and shows more vasoformative elements lined by epithelioid endothelial cells in a fibrous stroma; there is also a variably prominent inflammatory cell infiltrate with eosinophils and lymphoid follicles. Essential: small bluish nodule or papule; nodular proliferation of epithelioid endothelial cells; lack of nuclear pleomorphism and atypical mitotic activity; preserved SMA-positive pericytic layer. Postradiation atypical vascular lesion Most lesions appear on the anterior chest, but identical lesions may also occur at irradiation sites for cervical cancer, endometrial cancer, ovarian cancer, Hodgkin lymphoma, myeloma, melanoma, or vascular malformations 16006792 , which has resulted in multiple names for this lesion 2311281 ; 10564386 ; 3771862 ; 12360056 . Patients typically present with papules, small vesicles, or erythematous ecchymotic plaques with prominent telangiectasia. Most patients are elderly women. The latency period varies, but it is usually 2–3 years after radiotherapy 16006792 . Postradiation atypical vascular lesion (AVL) is a benign vascular proliferation arising in irradiated skin, with histopathological features mimicking angiosarcoma. AVL involves the upper and mid dermis and, rarely, the deep dermis. However, in contrast to radiation-induced angiosarcoma, the subcutis is spared. At scanning magnification, an inverted V-shaped architecture is the most common pattern. Less commonly, lesions are poorly defined, lacking the V-shaped pattern and involving only the mid dermis. The proliferation is composed of irregular, branching, anastomosing, thin-walled, empty lymphatic-like vascular channels lined by a single discontinuous layer of endothelial cells with little or no cytological atypia and often displaying hobnail morphology. In places, the vascular channels are back-to-back. Small intravascular papillae are frequently seen. Two histopathological patterns of AVL have been described: the lymphatic type (described above) and the very rare vascular type 18551753 . In the vascular type, there is proliferation of small capillaries usually lacking a lobular arrangement. Endothelial cells are positive for ERG, CD34, and CD31. They are also positive for podoplanin (D2-40), PROX1, and LYVE1, which gives support to a lymphatic lineage. The Ki-67 proliferation index is low 11859204 . In lesions of vascular type, endothelial cells express CD31 and CD34, but not lymphatic markers. KSHV/HHV8 is negative. AVL can coexist or progress to radiation-induced angiosarcoma, and superficially sampled radiation-induced angiosarcomas can be indistinguishable from AVLs (see below) 16006792 ; 16359542 ; 11442250 ; 24943869 ; 18551753 . Radiation-induced angiosarcoma shows endothelial MYC expression and a high Ki-67 proliferation index (> 10%), whereas AVLs are MYC-negative and show no substantial proliferation. AVL is caused by radiation-induced endothelial cell proliferation, the mechanism for which is uncertain. Mutation analysis has demonstrated that AVLs show a low number of HRAS and TERT mutations, whereas postradiotherapy angiosarcomas show a high frequency of EGFR, TP53, HRAS, and TERT mutations 32043616 . MYC and FLT4 gene amplifications are not found in AVL. The main differential diagnosis is with radiation-induced angiosarcoma. In the latter there is cytological atypia, multilayering, mitotic activity; tumor cells are positive for MYC, and FISH shows MYC amplification 22121953 ; 20949568 ; 20008140 ; 21909081 ; 30251277 . Furthermore, strong cytoplasmic VEGFR3 (FLT4) staining and FLT4 gene amplification by FISH is more frequent in radiation-induced angiosarcoma that in AVL 25864386 . Hobnail hemangioma can be identical to AVL but the clinical presentation is different and the former is usually associated with prominent hemosiderin deposition. Other differential diagnoses include lymphatic malformations, benign lymphangioendothelioma, and Kaposi sarcoma. Essential: postirradiation appearance of papules, vesicles, or plaques; irregular, branched, anastomosing, thin-walled vascular channels lined by a single discontinuous layer of endothelial cells with little or no cytological atypia and frequent hobnail appearance; involving predominantly the upper dermis. Pseudomyogenic hemangioendothelioma Intermediate Vascular Neoplasms Intermediate / uncertain Pseudomyogenic hemangioendothelioma most commonly involves the lower extremities (55%); the upper extremities and trunk are less commonly affected (20% each), and the head and neck are rarely involved (5%) 12502927 ; 1371711 ; 23381465 ; 21263239 . Patients present with painless or painful nodules; ulceration may be present. In about 60% of cases the disease is multifocal, involving multiple tissue planes, most commonly the skin and subcutis, but it may also involve skeletal muscle and bone 12502927 ; 21263239 ; 1371711 ; 23381465 . Young men (mean age: 30 years) are most commonly affected (M:F ratio: 3.5:1) 21263239 . Pseudomyogenic hemangioendothelioma is a rarely metastasizing endothelial neoplasm that often presents as multiple nodules in different tissue planes and histologically mimics a myoid tumor or epithelioid sarcoma. Pseudomyogenic hemangioendotheliomas are variably composed of infiltrative sheets and fascicles of spindled (most commonly) to epithelioid cells with dense, eosinophilic cytoplasm 21263239 ; 12502927 . Atypia is usually mild, and tumor nuclei are vesicular with small nucleoli. Significant nuclear atypia may be seen in about 10% of cases 21263239 . Admixed neutrophils are seen in approximately 50%. By immunohistochemistry, they are positive for keratins (most often with AE1/AE3 clones, less often MNF116), FLI1, ERG, and FOSB, but negative for CD34 21263239 ; 12502927 ; 27515856 ; 28009608 . About 50% are positive for CD31, and focal expression of SMAs is seen in as many as one third of cases. SMARCB1 expression is retained 21263239 . Detection of FOSB rearrangement may be helpful. Pseudomyogenic hemangioendothelioma has rearrangements of FOSB, including SERPINE1::FOSB, ACTB::FOSB, WWTR1::FOSB, CLTC::FOSB, and EGFL7::FOSB 24374978 ; 30459475 ; 30256258 ; 31243110 ; 32749039 ; 33550637 . This results in upregulation, with FOSB acting as an active transcription factor capable of its own regulation 24374978 ; 29511030 . tumors with ACTB::FOSB fusions are more likely to be solitary 30256258 . tumors with EGFL7::FOSB may be more aggressive 33550637 . Essential: fascicles or sheets of spindled to epithelioid cells with dense eosinophilic cytoplasm, vesicular nuclei, and expression of ERG and AE1/AE3. Desirable: demonstration of FOSB expression or FOSB rearrangement. Epithelioid hemangioendothelioma Malignant (intermediate-grade spectrum) EHE rarely involves the skin, with no site predilection 9855348 ; 9130982 . Most are nondescript nodules, sometimes with a thickened epidermis 25782038 ; 9855348 ; 25386269 or ulceration 24354555 . EHE most often arises in middle-aged adults, with a slight female predominance 25782038 ; 9130982 ; 9855348 ; 25386269 . Epithelioid hemangioendothelioma (EHE) is a malignant endothelial neoplasm composed of epithelioid cells within a myxohyaline stroma; almost all have a WWTR1::CAMTA1 fusion. A distinctive subtype composed of epithelioid cells with abundant cytoplasm and solid, nested, and/or vasoformative growth has a YAP1::TFE3 fusion. EHE is composed of relatively bland epithelioid cells, often with intracytoplasmic vacuoles, arranged in cords and nests, embedded in a variably myxohyaline stroma 7093931 . Vasoformative architecture is not seen in conventional EHE. The EHE subtype with YAP1::TFE3 fusion has tumor cells with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm, arranged in a solid or nested growth pattern, often forming vascular spaces 23737213 ; 34381186 . Immunohistochemically, EHE is positive for CD31, FLI1, ERG, and (less often) CD34. Low-molecular-weight cytokeratins are expressed in 20–30% of cases 11014572 ; 24986479 ; 34381186 . Composite hemangioendothelioma (CHE) is a locally aggressive, rarely metastasizing endothelial neoplasm composed of an admixture of components, each resembling other vascular lesions. Neuroendocrine marker expression may be present. There is a complex and variable admixture of histological patterns, including retiform, spindle cell, epithelioid, lymphangioma, hemangioma, and even well-differentiated angiosarcoma–like components 10716148 . They most often consist of areas identical to retiform hemangioendothelioma, juxtaposed to foci somewhat resembling epithelioid hemangioendothelioma 17895759 . Neuroendocrine CHE is characterized by a distinctive admixture of retiform hemangioendothelioma–like areas, epithelioid hemangioendothelioma–like areas, and a component with a striking nested appearance, as well as by expression of neuroendocrine markers (typically synaptophysin).
