Kaposi sarcoma Malignant, often indolent The skin is the principal site of involvement. Lesions occur most commonly on the lower limbs, followed by the face and the genitalia. However, mucosal involvement (especially of the oral cavity) is common. Classic KS tends to affect the lower extremities of elderly non–HIV-infected men. Visceral KS in the absence of cutaneous lesions is encountered more frequently among AIDS-related cases [[Pantanowitz L, Stebbing J, Dezube BJ. Overview of Kaposi sarcoma. In: Pantanowitz L, Stebbing J, Dezube BJ, editors. Kaposi sarcoma: a model of oncogenesis. Kerala (India): Research Signpost; 2010. pp. 1–40.]]. Four clinicopathological subtypes are recognized: classic KS, endemic African KS, AIDS-associated KS, and iatrogenic (transplant-related) KS. The spectrum of conventional cutaneous lesions among all four of these clinicopathological groups encompasses patches, plaques, and nodules; these tend to have a purplish appearance, and their sizes can range from small to several centimetres. Lower limb involvement may be accompanied by painful lymphedema. Smaller ulcerated nodules closely resemble pyogenic granulomas. Rarely, verrucous or bullous lesions occur. KS flare may develop when HIV-positive patients are first introduced to antiretroviral therapy. KS can affect individuals of any age or sex, but it occurs most commonly in adults and shows a predilection for men. However, a high proportion of children and women are affected by AIDS-associated KS in Africa [[Pantanowitz L, Stebbing J, Dezube BJ. Overview of Kaposi sarcoma. In: Pantanowitz L, Stebbing J, Dezube BJ, editors. Kaposi sarcoma: a model of oncogenesis. Kerala (India): Research Signpost; 2010. pp. 1–40.]] 28324233 . The estimated worldwide crude and age-standardized incidence rates of KS are both 0.6 cases per 100 000 person-years, with an M:F ratio of 1.9:1. However, there are striking geographical differences, with the highest crude and age-standardized incidence rates (of 8.8 and 11.2 cases per 100 000 person-years, respectively) seen in eastern Africa. The incidence of KS is highest among men who have sex with men (5.7 per 100 person-years) 15385736 . Kaposi sarcoma (KS) is a locally aggressive KSHV/HHV8-associated vascular proliferation. It usually manifests with multiple cutaneous lesions, but it may also involve mucosal sites, lymph nodes, and visceral organs. Patch-stage lesions are characterized by abnormal vessels or subtle endothelial cell proliferation with dermal collagen dissection, in particular around the skin adnexa; the promontory sign may also be seen 549492 . Plaque-stage KS is characterized by abnormal vessels, greater cellularity, and a spindle cell proliferation. Additional features include slit-like spaces containing erythrocytes, surrounding spindled cells, siderophages, and occasional cells containing small intracytoplasmic hyaline globules. Subcutaneous extension can occur. Nodular KS lesions show greater cellularity and resultant tumor formation, with haphazardly intersecting fascicles of spindled cells, often accompanied by a plasma cell–predominant inflammatory infiltrate. Mitoses and mild atypia can be seen. The lesional cells show immunoreactivity for the KSHV/HHV8-associated protein LANA1, as well as CD34, CD31, and podoplanin (recognized by D2-40). Lesions that have regressed after chemotherapy or antiretroviral therapy show increased microvascular density around native dermal vessels 18655700 . Numerous less-common histopathological patterns have been described (see #34362Table 7.01), including lymphangioma-like KS and anaplastic KS 18655700 ; 20075709 . Rare AIDS-associated cases can harbour an opportunistic pathogen or concomitant pathology (e.g. intravascular lymphoma) 21789262 ; 29532696 ; 31361614 . KSHV/HHV8 is detectable in lesional tissue by PCR and in situ hybridization 7489408 . Whether KS qualifies as a true sarcoma is still a matter of debate 17623796 . There is increasing evidence that early stages are oligoclonal and can regress, while later clonal selection leads to progression 35267506 . KSHV/HHV8 infection alone is insufficient for KS oncogenesis; host immune dysfunction, genetic factors, and environmental factors also play a role. Initially, there is infection by KSHV/HHV8 of resident and circulating endothelial cells and mononuclear inflammatory cells. LANA1 upregulates viral homologues of FLICE inhibitory protein (vFLIP) and cyclin D (viral cyclin). Viral oncoproteins (e.g. vIL6) and antiapoptotic proteins (e.g. LANA1, vIAP, and vBCL2) potentiate the proliferation of infected endothelial cells and immune evasion, while expression of matrix metalloproteinases and proangiogenic molecules leads to migration of infected endothelial cells. An inflammatory phase follows, with secretion of proinflammatory cytokines and chemotaxis of T helper 2 (Th2) inflammatory cells. Subsequent tumorigenesis involves activation of autocrine and paracrine pathways, secretion of stimulatory molecules by inflammatory cells, induction of angiogenesis (e.g. via vGPCR-induced upregulation of VEGF), and spindle cell proliferation. There is reprogramming of blood vessel endothelial cells and a resultant expression profile more akin to that of lymphatic endothelium 17623796 ; 17623793 . In one study, comparative genomic hybridization revealed a recurrent gain at 11q13, with amplification of FGF4 and FGF3 (INT2) identified on subsequent interphase FISH 10786811 . Early disease is associated with clonal Y chromosome loss, while copy-number changes involving chromosomes 16, 17, 21, X, and Y occur during the development of late (nodular) KS lesions 16954721 . A wide differential diagnosis exists [[Wadee R, Grayson W. Cutaneous Kaposi sarcoma and its mimics. Diagn Histopathol. 2022 Jan;28(1):38–52. doi:10.1016/j.mpdhp.2021.10.005.]]. The differential diagnoses of the more conventional histopathological patterns of cutaneous KS and the less common histopathological patterns are listed in #34125Table 7.02 and #34362Table 7.01 , respectively. Most cutaneous glomus tumors come to clinical attention as solitary, small (< 10 mm), painful nodules or plaques, with a pink to blue hue 28163461 ; 28435574 ; 28116265 ; 34953423 ; 34900456 . Glomuvenous malformations are often multiple or familial 30677819 . Most glomus tumors occur in the skin 21187877 ; 28203512 . Glomus tumors are mesenchymal neoplasms composed of cells resembling the modified smooth muscle cells of the normal glomus body. Glomus cells are small, uniform, and round, with a central round nucleus, amphophilic to lightly eosinophilic cytoplasm, and a sharp cellular outline with peripheral basal lamina. Oncocytic, epithelioid, myxoid, and hyalinized patterns are recognized 7672784 ; 3038728 . Solid glomus tumors, which account for approximately 75% of all cases, are composed of nests of glomus cells surrounding capillary-sized vessels. Small cuffs of glomus cells are often seen around small vessels located outside the main mass. Glomuvenous malformations, which account for 20% of cases, feature dilated vascular channels with intervening small clusters of glomus cells. Glomus tumors may also contain spindled cells resembling smooth muscle (glomangiomyoma) or a branching, haemangiopericytoma-like vasculature (glomangiopericytoma) 9591720 . Glomangiomatosis is an extremely rare pattern of glomus tumor with an overall architectural resemblance to diffuse angiomatosis 11145243 ; 15372213 ; 19267531 , but containing nests of glomus cells within vessel walls. Symplastic tumors show striking nuclear atypia in the absence of other worrisome features 11145243 ; 19602065 ; 25051107 . Histologically and/or clinically malignant glomus tumors are extremely rare 11145243 ; 22228777 ; 27772590 . The diagnosis of malignant glomus tumor should be reserved only for tumors showing marked nuclear atypia (with any level of mitotic activity) and/or atypical mitotic figures. A component of pre-existing benign-looking glomus tumor is often present. Malignant glomus tumors may retain an overall architectural resemblance to normal glomus tumor (but with malignant-looking round cells), or they may consist of a spindled component resembling leiomyosarcoma or fibrosarcoma. In the absence of a clear-cut benign precursor, immunohistochemical demonstration of SMA and pericellular collagen IV is required for diagnosis of round cell forms of malignant glomus tumor, in the absence of a clear-cut benign precursor. Glomus tumors that show atypical features but lack severe nuclear atypia or atypical mitotic activity should instead be classified as glomus tumors of uncertain malignant potential. Glomus tumors of all types typically express SMA, h-caldesmon, and pericellular collagen IV 11145243 . Demonstration of MIR143::NOTCH1, MIR143::NOTCH2, or MIR143::NOTCH3 fusions may be helpful in selected cases. Myopericytoma The distal extremities are the main sites of involvement, followed by the proximal extremities, head and neck (including the oral cavity), and trunk. Most lesions are dermal-based or subcutaneous, while deep lesions are rare, and visceral and intracranial involvement is very rare 16330949 ; 26068635 . Myointimoma of the glans penis may fall within the spectrum of these lesions. Most arise as solitary painless dermal or subcutaneous nodules. The tumor may occur over a wide age range, from childhood to old age. Multifocal lesions affecting the same or different anatomical sites are uncommon 16330949 . Rare intravascular lesions may be painful 21355959 . No epidemiological data are available. Myopericytoma is a benign neoplasm with perivascular myoid cell differentiation. Myopericytoma is a well-circumscribed but unencapsulated nodule of cytologically bland, oval to spindled cells with concentric multilayered perivascular growth. The cytoplasm is eosinophilic, with myoid features. The nuclei are round to ovoid. The cellularity varies greatly, as does the vasculature. The presence of thin-walled communicating vessels may mimic solitary fibrous tumor, while lesions with thicker vessels result in an appearance reminiscent of angioleiomyoma. Cellular solid patterns are similar to myofibroma 16330949 . Rare subtypes include diffuse plexiform growth (myopericytomatosis), intramural growth (within vascular walls), and intravascular myopericytoma. Uncommon features include hyalinization, metaplastic bone, ischemic necrosis, and degenerative atypia. Myopericytoma usually stains for α-SMA and h-caldesmon, and occasionally for MSA, but desmin immunoreactivity is usually absent or focal 27047931 ; 16330949 . Myopericytoma was considered to form a spectrum with myofibroma, angioleiomyoma, and glomus tumor, but recent studies suggest these are rather distinct at the molecular level, albeit having significantly overlapping morphological and phenotypic features 26558691 . The differential diagnosis includes myofibroma, angioleiomyoma, and solitary fibrous tumor. Myopericytoma probably differentiates towards myopericytes, intermediate cells between pericytes of Zimmermann and true smooth muscle cells 16330949 . The solitary form of the disease has a male predilection, whereas the multicentric form predominantly affects females. Angioleiomyoma is a benign mesenchymal tumor that typically arises in the dermis or subcutis. tumors are composed of thick-walled vessels surrounded by well-differentiated perivascular bundles of smooth muscle. It is a member of the perivascular myoid family of tumors and is on a morphological continuum with myopericytoma. All angioleiomyomas are composed of bundles of bland, well-differentiated smooth muscle surrounding blood vessels of varying calibre. Mitotic activity is inconspicuous. Three subtypes of angioleiomyoma have been described based on predominant vascular morphology: solid, venous, and cavernous. The solid subtype is composed of compact bundles of smooth muscle surrounding compressed, slit-like vessels. Venous-subtype tumors are made up of thick-walled vessels, with smooth muscle from blood vessel walls blending with intervascular smooth muscle bundles. Cavernous-subtype lesions are composed of dilated vascular channels, with a proliferation of smooth muscle within intervascular spaces. Hybrid lesions have been described. Some tumors share features with myopericytoma, with concentric whorling of less spindled to ovoid myoid cells around vessels 17270242 . Desmin expression is variable and may be very focal or completely absent in a small subset of tumors 8025650 ; 17270242 . Melanocytic markers such as HMB45 and melan-A are negative in tumors with adipocytic metaplasia, thus enabling distinction from angiomyolipoma 6722737 ; 17270242 ; 26047608 . Similarly to glomus tumors and myopericytomas, angioleiomyomas demonstrate diffuse immunoreactivity for the pericytic antigen RGS5 26558691 . Angioleiomyomas are thought to arise from vascular smooth muscle 6722737 . Reported cytogenetic abnormalities include monosomy of chromosome 13 and loss of 6p, 21q, and 13q 20471520 ; 14654964 . Smooth muscle hamartoma Smooth Muscle Tumors Benign Smooth Muscle Tumors The majority of cases occur on the trunk or extremities; the head and neck region and external genitalia are less common sites of involvement 32804407 . There is a slightly indurated and pigmented or flesh-colored plaque, ranging from millimetres to several centimetres in size, with or without perifollicular papules and hypertrichosis. A positive pseudo–Darier sign is present in 80% of congenital SMHs (CSMHs). Most CSMHs are solitary; however, rare multiple, familial, and non-familial cases have been documented 22630577 . Diffuse CSMH has been described as a component of Michelin tyre baby syndrome 8436660 , and cases of combined SMH with congenital or blue naevi have also been reported 18544054 ; 8436660 . SMH has a slight male predominance. CSMH is uncommon, affecting approximately 1 in 2600 births 2356798 . Acquired SMH is extremely rare, with < 20 cases reported to date. Age at presentation ranges from 12 to 64 years 29774573 ; 34637157 . Smooth muscle hamartoma (SMH) represents an anomalous proliferation of haphazardly arranged smooth muscle bundles in the dermis. SMH demonstrates haphazardly arranged, mature smooth muscle bundles in the dermis, often in close proximity to the pilosebaceous units 2658846 . This is in contrast to pilosebaceous leiomyoma, which demonstrates more orderly smooth muscle bundles arranged in ramifying fascicles. Atypia/pleomorphism and mitoses are absent. Focal retraction artefact may be observed around the smooth muscle bundles. Expression of smooth muscle markers is seen. Overlying epidermal hyperkeratosis, acanthosis, and basal hyperpigmentation, reminiscent of Becker nevus, may be encountered. A subset of CSMHs result from postzygotic ACTB mutations. These mutations have been previously reported in Becker naevi, suggesting that CSMHs and Becker naevi are biologically related 32170967 . Essential: haphazardly arranged muscle bundles within the dermis; absent atypia. Cutaneous leiomyomas The extensor surfaces of the extremities are most commonly affected, followed by the trunk and the head and neck region 11907496 . Genital leiomyomas can involve the scrotum, vulva, nipple, or areola. Cutaneous leiomyomas are flesh-colored to reddish-brown, firm, dome-shaped papules or nodules. Multiple leiomyomas are more often painful and may be distributed in linear, segmental, or zosteriform patterns 27584971 . Solitary leiomyomas are usually no larger than 20 mm 25605645 . Genital leiomyomas are usually solitary raised to pedunculated papules or nodules, usually < 20 mm but occasionally larger, and asymptomatic. Vulvar tumors may enlarge during pregnancy 25605645 . Cutaneous leiomyomas are rare. Cases involving multiple tumors typically have an earlier onset than do solitary leiomyomas 25605645 . Solitary tumors show a female predominance. Cutaneous leiomyomas are benign dermal smooth muscle tumors derived from intrinsic dermal arrector pili smooth muscle (pilar leiomyomas) or dartoic/vulvar/areolar smooth muscle (genital leiomyomas). Pilar leiomyomas are poorly circumscribed dermal nodules of intersecting, well-differentiated smooth muscle bundles composed of spindle cells with elongated, blunt-ended nuclei, perinuclear vacuoles, and eosinophilic cytoplasm 11907496 ; 21430885 ; 25605645 . Rare mitotic figures may be seen 9056647 . Enlarged, hyperchromatic cells similar to those seen in symplastic uterine leiomyomas may be encountered 23550704 ; 11481520 ; 26981742 . SMA, desmin, and caldesmon are typically expressed. Demonstration of loss of fumarate hydratase (FH) expression and enhanced expression of 2-succinocysteine (2SC) is useful in identifying possible cases of hereditary leiomyomatosis and renal cell cancer syndrome 26945337 ; 28288038 ; 27097334 ; 25292446 . Molecular testing is not required in sporadic cases. In the familial setting, although FH and 2SC immunohistochemistry identify FH-deficient neoplasms, they do not replace genetic testing, because biallelic FH mutation/inactivation can occur as a purely somatic phenomenon. For sporadic tumors, the pathogenesis is unknown. For familial leiomyomas, see the Urinary and male genital tumors volume of this series [[WHO Classification of tumors Editorial Board. Urinary and male genital tumors. Lyon (France): International Agency for Research on Cancer; 2022. (WHO classification of tumors series, 5th ed.; vol. 8). https://publications.iarc.who.int/610.]]. Essential: well-differentiated smooth muscle closely resembling normal pilar smooth muscle; occasional mitotic figures and enlarged, hyperchromatic cells may be present; infiltration of subcutaneous fat is absent. Desirable: expression of SMAs, desmin, and caldesmon (in most cases); absent FH expression and enhanced 2SC expression in hereditary leiomyomatosis and renal cell carcinoma syndrome–associated tumors. EBV-associated smooth muscle tumor Intermediate / uncertain; multifocal potential The commonest site of involvement is the CNS, followed by the liver, lung, and subcutaneous tissues of the limbs and trunk 15844077 ; 16330945 ; 21437186 ; 27362573 ; 31700854 ; 22175892 ; 25027306 . When arising in the subcutis, the tumor manifests as a skin-colored nodule. Occasionally, there may be associated pain 22175892 ; 12207602 ; 33245561 ; 33627249 . Multiple tumors may evolve concurrently or sequentially at different anatomical sites 15844077 ; 12207602 . EBV-SMT is a rare neoplasm. It occurs in approximately 1–5% of patients with immunosuppression 25027306 . The age range varies widely, but most patients are adults. There is a slight female predominance 21437186 ; 31700854 ; 2217589 ; 25318810 . EBV-associated smooth muscle tumor (EBV-SMT) is an EBV-driven benign smooth muscle neoplasm occurring in the clinical setting of immunosuppression. Irrespective of site, the majority of EBV-SMTs show circumscription and interlacing fascicles of spindled myoid cells in a background of collagenous matrix 31700854 ; 22175892 ; 33627249 ; 3324556 . Typically, there is an admixed population of smaller rounded cells and intratumoural lymphocytes. Some tumors show focal myxoid change. Mitotic activity is generally low. However, tumors with leiomyosarcoma-like features showing nuclear atypia and necrosis in addition to high mitotic activity have been described 22175892 ; 7990860 ; 25318810 . Some may mimic myopericytoma or angioleiomyoma 25027306 ; 21437186 ; 18199115 ; 22175892 . EBV-SMTs show expression of h-caldesmon, desmin, SMA, and MSA. Important differential diagnoses include Kaposi sarcoma, leiomyoma, leiomyosarcoma, and a pseudotumour secondary to mycobacterial or fungal infection. None of these entities show nuclear reactivity by in situ hybridization for EBV-encoded small RNA (EBER). EBV infection of neoplastic myoid cells is usually demonstrated by in situ hybridization for EBER. It is postulated that EBV gains entry into a progenitor smooth muscle cell of vascular origin through CD21 receptor function or interaction with an EBV-infected lymphocyte 16330945 ; 7990860 ; 19706821 . There is aberration of the mTOR/AKT pathway 19706821 . Overexpression of MYC has been reported 9890420 ; 22420456 . Multiple tumors represent separate clonal events 16330945 . Essential: demonstration of EBV infection in the constituent myoid cells of a smooth muscle tumor arising in an immunosuppressed patient. Atypical intradermal smooth muscle neoplasm Intermediate Smooth Muscle Neoplasms The tumors most commonly involve the trunk and lower extremities 21358302 ; 20102404 . The tumors typically manifest as small (5–30 mm), solitary, and occasionally painful nodules. Cutaneous leiomyosarcomas are rare, with an age-adjusted incidence of roughly 0.2 cases per 100 000 person-years 31729020 . They most often occur in older men, with a mean patient age of 56 years and an M:F ratio of 3:1 to 4:1 21358302 ; 20102404 . Atypical intradermal smooth muscle neoplasm is a primary dermal neoplasm composed of generally well-differentiated spindled cells closely resembling normal arrector pili smooth muscle but showing nuclear enlargement, hyperchromatism, and mitotic activity. Atypical intradermal smooth muscle neoplasms are typically well differentiated, consisting of fascicles of relatively uniform, eosinophilic spindled cells with perinuclear vacuoles and cigar-shaped nuclei. Compared with normal pilar smooth muscle, these tumors show greater cellularity, nuclear enlargement, and hyperchromatism, and they show mitotic activity. Marked nuclear pleomorphism and necrosis are rare; the presence of such features should raise concern for metastasis from a deeply situated tumor, which may be regarded as cutaneous leiomyosarcoma 21989966 . Atypical intradermal smooth muscle neoplasms typically grow in an infiltrative fashion into the surrounding dermis, and they may show limited involvement of the subcutaneous fat. Immunohistochemically, these tumors are essentially always positive for SMA and desmin, and almost always positive for caldesmon 21358302 ; 20102404 . Expression of keratins may be seen in as many as 45% of cases 21358302 . The genetic events underlying the development of atypical intradermal smooth muscle neoplasm are unknown. Germline FH mutation does not appear to be a predisposing factor 20618355 . Essential: a dermal-based tumor with an infiltrative growth pattern; fascicles of relatively uniform, eosinophilic spindled cells with perinuclear vacuoles and cigar-shaped nuclei; variable SMA, desmin, and caldesmon expression; limited involvement of the subcutaneous fat. Dermal hyperneury / epithelial sheath neuroma Neural Tumors Benign Neural Tumors Periorificial and mucosal lesions (lips, eyelid, tongue) appear in multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2B (MEN2B) 30660595 . Cutaneous nerves are enlarged in patients with MEN2B, even in the absence of visible lesions 6127365 . Outside a syndromic setting, there is a slight predilection for the trunk 31216366 . Epithelial sheath neuroma shows a predilection for the back 10680886 . The lesions are single or multiple and asymptomatic. Rarely, patients may experience itching, intermittent burning, or pain. Mucocutaneous neural proliferations have been described in syndromic patients as young as 5 years old 16702501 . Most of the patients in the sporadic setting are in their seventh decade of life. There is a slight female preponderance. Dermal hyperneury represents a form of small nerve hypertrophy characterized by unusually large and prominent dermal nerve fibres. Epithelial sheath neuroma has similar histological features, with the added finding of mature squamous epithelium surrounding the perineurium. Increase in nerve fibre–aggregated neural tissue is observed within the dermis or the dermal/subcutaneous interface. Histological changes are identical in syndromic and non-syndromic cases. Nerve fibres are 1.5–4 times as large as normal nerves. Mild neuroma-like internal nerve fibre disorganization can be seen. Lymphoplasmacytic and histiocytic perineurial inflammation or intraneural mucin accumulation may be seen. In epithelial sheath neuroma, enlarged nerve fibres are ensheathed by squamous epithelium. Subcutaneous extension is exceptional 29797343 . Occasionally, dermal hyperneury presents incidentally to other lesions such as actinic keratosis, basal cell carcinoma, and nodular prurigo. Multiple lesions in younger patients should prompt investigation for genetic syndromes and pertinent molecular alterations. Not entirely elucidated but may involve PTEN-regulated and RET-regulated signalling pathways 26604880 , particularly in syndromic cases. Essential: enlarged and prominent dermal nerve fibres; nerve sheath squamous cells in epithelial sheath neuroma. Desirable: mild neuroma-like internal disorganization (in some cases). Solitary circumscribed neuroma SCN commonly occurs on the face (90%), often near mucocutaneous junctions 2660609 or in oral mucosa 20237984 . SCN can involve any cutaneous site, including acral skin 19614730 . SCN usually manifests as a small, solitary, asymptomatic, firm, skin-colored papule. Rare examples of multiple SCNs have been reported in the absence of systemic disease 26460241 . SCN can occur at any age, most commonly in the fifth to seventh decades of life. There is no sex predilection. Solitary circumscribed neuroma (SCN) is a benign nodular proliferation of nerve fibres, typically arising as an asymptomatic papule on the face. SCN is a dermal-based nodule composed of fascicles of bland spindled cells encased in a delicate, often incomplete, fibrous capsule. Artefactual clefting at the tumor–stroma interface is characteristic 4639250 . Focal palisading of nuclei within the tumor is usually present but Verocay bodies are less common 30834800 . Multilobular and plexiform growth patterns are well described 19614730 ; 8468415 . No cytological atypia or conspicuous mitotic activity is seen. Tumoural Schwann cells are strongly and diffusely positive for S100. Tiny axons throughout the tumor can be identified by staining for NFP 1705947 . The capsular perineural cells stain for EMA, claudin-1, and GLUT1 20237984 . SCN is a benign tumor with slow growth of nerve fibres, unrelated to trauma 2660609 . SCN, especially the plexiform subtype, can be mistaken for other benign neural neoplasms, some of which have associations with systemic disease. Neurofibromas are hypocellular tumors with a loose, delicate matrix that are unencapsulated (except in the plexiform subtype). Schwannomas tend to have a more variable cell density (Antoni A and B areas), prominent palisading (Verocay bodies), and hyalinization of vessel walls, and they lack clefting artefact. Essential: a nodular, multinodular or plexiform circumscribed dermal nodule composed of fascicles of Schwann cells and axons without significant atypia or mitotic activity. Desirable: at least partial encapsulation highlighted by perineural markers (e.g. EMA); artefactual clefting. Dermal nerve sheath myxoma Dermal nerve sheath myxoma occurs in the distal extremities, particularly the fingers (36% of cases), toes, and lower extremities 16327434 ; 11070116 . It rarely involves the spinal canal 23306964 . The tumors manifest as small, superficial, slow-growing asymptomatic masses; some are painful 16327434 . Dermal nerve sheath myxomas are rare. The two largest modern series describe 68 tumors arising over a wide age range (8–72 years), with a peak in the mid-thirties and a slight male predominance 16327434 ; 11070116 . Dermal nerve sheath myxoma is a benign peripheral nerve sheath tumor. Dermal nerve sheath myxoma characteristically shows a multinodular growth pattern, abundant myxoid matrix, and a dense fibrous border in the dermis, subcutis, or both; it rarely extends to skeletal muscle. Neoplastic cells are small, epithelioid, ring-like, stellate, and spindled Schwann cells in cords, nests, and syncytial-like aggregates, with mild nuclear atypia. Some show ring-like morphology, resembling lipoblasts; rarely, multivacuolated cells with spider-like cytoplasmic processes, nuclear palisading, or Verocay body–like structures are seen. Scattered moderate pleomorphism, similar to that seen in ancient schwannomas, may be present. Mitoses are absent to very few 16327434 . S100 is diffusely positive, and GFAP and CD57 are also often positive 6365307 ; 2645040 ; 16327434 ; 11070116 . Rare cells are positive for AE1/AE3, and the fibrous capsule may show scattered EMA-positive cells. Dermal nerve sheath myxoma was previously called “classic or myxoid variant of neurothekeoma” 7446487 . However, pathological 11070116 ; 17592278 ; 16327434 ; 17325474 and molecular data 21297585 demonstrated the Schwann cell derivation of dermal nerve sheath myxoma, which is clinically and biologically distinct from neurothekeoma. Thus, the gene signature of dermal nerve sheath myxomas is similar to that of dermal schwannomas, whereas cellular neurothekeomas more closely resemble cellular fibrous histiocytomas 21297585 . Essential: a small, superficial tumor in a distal extremity (especially the fingers); a multilobular, myxoid neoplasm with S100-positive bland spindled and epithelioid cells. Perineurioma Perineurioma has a wide distribution, occurring most commonly on the lower limbs, followed by the upper limbs and trunk 15958848 . Rarely, it arises on the head/neck, in visceral organs (intestinal mucosa 15958849 ), and also in nerves 7785653 , soft tissues, and central body cavities. Sclerosing perineurioma usually occurs on fingers and palms 9414186 , rarely elsewhere 27845943 . Perineuriomas manifest as well-circumscribed, painless, skin-colored papules, nodules, or tumors. Ten per cent are dermal, and subcutaneous tissue is more commonly involved than deep soft tissue 11012740 . They are rarely multiple 19187114 . Perineuriomas are rare. They have a slight female predilection and a wide age range, with a peak incidence in middle-aged adults 15958848 . Children are rarely affected. The sclerosing subtype is more common in young men 9414186 ; 12836021 . Perineurioma is a usually benign perineural neoplasm occurring in skin, intestinal mucosa, nerves, and soft tissue. Perineuriomas typically show a storiform to fascicular growth pattern, with a lamellar arrangement, perivascular whorls, and a collagenous to myxoid stroma. Plexiform 10936896 ; 16133356 or lipomatous 18496437 patterns have rarely been reported. The tumor cells are slender and spindled, with wavy, tapering nuclei and delicate bipolar cytoplasmatic processes. Occasionally, ancient features with degenerative nuclear changes, multinucleated giant cells, and nuclear pseudoinclusions may be seen 15958848 . The sclerosing subtype shows strands of small epithelioid to spindle cells, rarely showing granular cell changes 18360122 , in dense collagen. The reticular subtype shows anastomosing cords of elongated spindle cells with reticulate architecture 11257623 . Malignant perineuriomas have a similar architecture but also show hypercellularity, hyperchromasia, pleomorphism, and a high mitotic count 9808129 . EMA is positive, from weak and focal to strong and diffuse 15958848 . Collagen IV, laminin 14507408 , claudin, and GLUT1 are often positive 12459629 ; 12836021 , and 60% of tumors express CD34 20849453 . Sclerosing perineurioma shows limited keratin expression 9414186 . tumor cells are negative for S100, SOX10, and GFAP. Perineuriomas share pathogenetic mechanisms with other nerve sheath tumors, similar to schwannoma and meningioma, such as deletion of 22q12, monosomies, and mutations in NF2 9042282 ; 11290539 ; 17122521 ; 30303818 . Deletion of 17q11 (including NF1) is common in soft tissue perineurioma; other alterations include a three-way chromosome 2, 9, and 4 translocation involving ABL1. Rearrangement involving 10q24 frequently occurs in the sclerosing subtype 16096405 . Malignant perineuriomas have been reported with loss of chromosome 13q and small deletions of chromosomes 3, 6, and 9 18844938 ; 30303818 . The differential diagnosis includes epithelioid fibrous histiocytoma, fibroma of tendon sheath, sclerotic fibroma, extracranial meningioma, and low-grade fibromyxoid sarcoma 9414186 . Essential: painless, skin-colored papules, nodules, or tumor; storiform, whorled, and lamellar architecture; elongated, slender spindle cells with bipolar cytoplasmatic processes; EMA positive; variable expression of claudin-1, GLUT1, CD34. Neurofibroma Sporadic neurofibromas occur characteristically on the trunk; diffuse neurofibromas localize on the head and neck 6638406 . Sporadic neurofibromas are solitary, slow-growing, painless, soft, skin-colored papules or nodules. Subcutaneous (including diffuse) neurofibromas form nodules or deep plaques. Plexiform neurofibromas are congenital, irregular, tortuous, multinodular masses. Diffuse and plexiform neurofibromas usually affect children or young adults 6638406 ; 12789188 ; 3068997 . All demographic groups are affected, with no sex predilection and with peak incidence in the third decade of life [[Antonescu CR, Scheithauer BW, Woodruff JM. Tumors of the peripheral nervous system. Washington, DC: Armed Forces Institute of Pathology; 2013. (AFIP atlas of tumor pathology, series 4; fascicle 19).]]. Neurofibroma is a benign tumor of axons, Schwann cells, fibroblasts, and perineurial cells in a collagenous matrix containing mast cells and mucin. Neurofibromas are unencapsulated tumors composed of spindle cells, collagen fibres, lymphocytes, and mast cells 2479359 ; skin appendages are usually preserved. Neurofibromas are composed of spindle cells with thin, wavy, hyperchromatic nuclei and delicate, pale, eosinophilic cytoplasm. Several patterns have been described: interstitial mucin is prominent in myxoid neurofibroma 11558882 ; 10564384 ; 7528474 . Sclerotic neurofibroma has scant spindle cells in a collagenous matrix 16441412 ; 18496433 . Lipomatous neurofibroma has admixed adipocytes 12142613 ; 15769276 ; 12140442 . Diffuse neurofibroma infiltrates dermis and subcutis, entrapping adnexa or adipocytes 7528474 ; 7695017 ; 12789188 . Plexiform neurofibroma consists of tortuous nerves distended by axons, Schwann cells, and fibroblasts 3068997 ; multivacuolated, mucin-filled cells express CD34 and GLUT1 27816720 . Melanotic neurofibroma contains variable melanin 3049734 ; 10716146 . Some cells are positive for S100 and SOX10 1693425 ; 7695017 , and for peripherin in thin axons 9414188 . EMA is negative 3169685 except in plexiform neurofibroma. A characteristic “fingerprint” pattern consists of CD34-positive perineurial fibroblasts anastomosing around Schwann cells 20849453 ; 21457155 ; 24033860 . Even non-pigmented diffuse neurofibromas may express melanocytic markers 23715161 ; 9414187 . Molecular analyses do not have an established role in the diagnosis of neurofibroma. However, chromosomal copy-number profiling (showing CDKN2A/CDKN2B deletion) may be helpful for the evaluation of atypical neurofibroma / atypical neurofibromatous neoplasm of uncertain biological potential (see the relevant section in the WHO classification of tumors of soft tissue and bone [[WHO Classification of tumors Editorial Board. Soft tissue and bone tumors. Lyon (France): International Agency for Research on Cancer; 2020. (WHO classification of tumors series, 5th ed.; vol. 3). https://publications.iarc.who.int/588.]]) and its differentiation from MPNST (which shows a complex, highly rearranged genome). Of note, conventional dermal and plexiform neurofibromas, atypical neurofibroma / atypical neurofibromatous neoplasm of uncertain biological potential, and MPNST all exhibit distinct DNA methylation profiles 26857854 . The originating cell and nosological classification are controversial 5354040 ; 7528474 ; 6798835 ; 9504678 ; 20233971 . Most neurofibromas are sporadic and solitary. Multiple tumors or the plexiform and diffuse subtypes suggest neurofibromatoses (NF1 and NF2), autosomal dominant disorders caused by genetic alterations in the neurofibromin gene (NF1) on chromosome 17 or in NF2 (encoding merlin [NF2, schwannomin]) on chromosome 22. Many affected patients’ disease reflects new mutations. NF1 encodes neurofibromin (NF1), a negative regulator of the RAS/MAPK pathway. NF1 mutations cause loss of neurofibromin function, resulting in RAS signalling and MAPK activation. Germline plus somatic mutations (NF1−/−) cause loss of functional neurofibromin 22155606 . Detailed genotype–phenotype correlations have been documented 32771543 . Subsequent loss of CDKN2A on chromosome 9p21.3 eventuates in atypical neurofibromatous tumor of uncertain biological potential, which may progress to malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumor (MPNST) 31091306 . The differential diagnosis includes schwannoma, perineurioma, dermatofibroma, sclerotic fibroma, neurotized and sclerotic/desmoplastic melanocytic nevus, dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans, fibromatosis, and desmoplastic melanoma. Essential: an infiltrative, low-cellularity spindle cell neoplasm associated with a variably myxoid to collagenous stroma. Desirable: S100 positivity in the Schwannian cell population and CD34 positivity in the stromal component. Note: For diagnosis of NF1 and NF2, see the related sections in the pediatric tumors volume of this series [[WHO Classification of tumors Editorial Board. pediatric tumors. Schwannoma Schwannomas occur in the soft tissues of the extremities, head and neck, and trunk. Subcutaneous localization is more common than dermal. Schwannomas of the skin are thought to arise from small peripheral nerves in subcutaneous soft tissue or, less commonly, in nerve twigs of the dermis. Schwannomas are slow-growing and occasionally painful 5796779 . They are typically solitary, except in patients with neurofibromatosis type 2 (NF2) or schwannomatosis 19545378 . Sporadic schwannomas typically arise in the fourth to sixth decades of life 5796779 . Schwannoma is a benign neoplasm composed entirely or nearly entirely of mature neoplastic Schwann cells. Antoni A areas containing spindle cells with wavy nuclei alternate with hypocellular Antoni B areas, which contain a myxoid matrix and a variable lymphohistiocytic infiltrate. Within the Antoni A areas, parallel rows of nuclei (Verocay bodies) may be seen. Mitoses are rare. In ancient schwannoma, there is degenerative nuclear atypia. Rare subtypes include plexiform, epithelioid, cellular, neuroblastoma-like, and microcystic/reticular schwannoma 3557324 ; 3096870 ; 28368924 ; 18520439 ; 8116794 ; 2493641 ; 26350054 ; 9508344 . Schwannomas are strongly positive for S100 and SOX10 and have an EMA-positive perineurial capsule. Chromosome 22q deletion and/or NF2 mutation are frequent but nonspecific alterations. Schwannomas have a distinct DNA methylation pattern, although in the vast majority of cases, molecular testing is not needed 33479225 . Conventional schwannomas typically harbour somatic loss-of-function mutations in NF2 and complete or partial loss of chromosome 22, including the wildtype NF2 allele 8889506 . Other recurrently mutated tumor suppressors include ARID1A/ARID1B (mutated in 29% of cases) and TSC1/TSC2 (in 15%). SH3PXD2A::HTRA1 fusions (found in 10% of cases) activate the MAPK pathway and are mutually exclusive with mutations in the receptor tyrosine kinase gene DDR1 (found in 11% of cases) 27723760 . Germline pathogenic mutations in NF2, LZTR1, SMARCB1, and DGCR8, all located on chromosome 22q, are associated with schwannoma susceptibility. Vestibular schwannomas are the hallmark of NF2. Schwannomatosis 1 and schwannomatosis 2 are due to germline mutations of SMARCB1 (INI1) and LZTR1, respectively 17357086 ; 24362817 . Schwannomas in these patients typically demonstrate loss of two tumor suppressors (NF2 and either LZTR1 or SMARCB1) 27921248 . DGCR8 point mutations are associated with familial multinodular goitre with schwannomatosis 31805011 . The differential diagnosis includes neurofibroma, although this often has a lattice-like CD34 staining pattern not seen in schwannomas, as well as a smaller proportion of S100/SOX10-positive cells. It also includes solitary circumscribed neuroma. Epithelioid schwannoma should be distinguished from melanoma, myoepithelioma, and ossifying fibromyxoid tumor; roughly 40% of epithelioid schwannomas show loss of SMARCB1 (INI1) expression 28368924 . Cellular schwannomas with increased atypia and/or mitotic activity may raise concern for malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumor (MPNST). However, schwannomas typically show diffuse S100/SOX10 staining (unlike MPNST) and express p16 and H3 p.K27me3, which are lost in most MPNSTs 26990975 . Essential: a well-circumscribed spindle cell tumor with classic Antoni A and/or Antoni B regions. Desirable: Verocay bodies, encapsulation, hyalinized blood vessels; diffuse S100 immunoreactivity; extensive SOX10 positivity; lack of a lattice-like CD34 staining pattern. Granular cell tumor Granular cell tumors preferentially affect the deep dermis and subcutaneous and mucosal tissues, with a predilection for the head and neck, trunk, and proximal extremities 26637199 ; 6246310 . The most frequently affected anatomical sites include the tongue, oesophagus, and breast. Granular cell tumors are most frequently solitary; however, 7–29% of patients may display multiple lesions, of which as many as 30% affect the skin and subcutaneous tissues 24082205 . Granular cell tumors typically manifest as solitary, firm, skin-colored to reddish-brown painless nodules that are not always well defined 26637199 . At times, however, these lesions can be pruritic and/or painful. The lesions vary in size, but they are slow-growing and commonly 5–30 mm in diameter. Granular cell tumors can be diagnosed in all age groups; however, they predominantly occur in the fourth to sixth decades of life 26637199 . Although they have been reported to occur more frequently in women than in men (M:F ratio ranging from 1:1.8 to 1:2.4) 11314193 , large retrospective studies have suggested a higher frequency in men 10089680 ; 6246310 . These tumors are most prevalent in African Americans 6246310 . The vast majority of granular cell tumors are benign. The malignant form is vanishingly rare (1–2%); this subtype has an age distribution of 3–87 years (median: 53 years) and is reported to be more prevalent in women (65% of cases) and in White populations (70%), affecting the trunk in as many as one third of the cases 28989104 . Granular cell tumor is a benign neuroectodermal tumor derived from Schwann cells and composed of epithelioid cells with abundant lysosome-rich granular eosinophilic cytoplasm. Granular cell tumors have an infiltrating growth pattern with poorly defined borders and are composed of sheets, nests, and trabeculae of large epithelioid to polygonal cells with abundant eosinophilic and distinctly granular cytoplasm. Cell borders are sometimes not distinctive, resulting in a syncytial growth pattern. Nuclei are usually centrally located, ranging from small, uniform, and mildly hyperchromatic to larger and vesicular with prominent nucleoli 10410172 ; 26637199 ; 9669341 . The finely granular cytoplasm is composed of granules of varying sizes and morphology, which are the result of a massive accumulation of lysosomes; larger intracytoplasmic granules surrounded by clear haloes (pustulo-ovoid bodies of Milian), which can be PAS-positive/diastase-resistant, are commonly observed 17448196 ; 26637199 . Perineural and perivascular involvement is frequent 26637199 . Mitotic figures are generally scant. When affecting the skin, granular cell tumors often elicit exuberant pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia, which may result in the consideration of a diagnosis of squamous cell carcinoma 6246310 ; 26637199 . The vanishingly rare malignant form of granular cell tumor is recognized by overt features of malignancy, including increased cellularity, prominent spindling, high N:C ratio, marked pleomorphism, increased mitotic activity (including aberrant mitotic figures), and necrosis 9669341 ; 21282016 ; 26637199 . It should be noted, however, that malignant granular cell tumors may display bland histological features, and neither mitotic figures nor necrosis alone can identify all tumors with metastatic potential 11584326 ; 19734486 ; 21745132 ; 24617529 . The immunohistochemical profile of granular cell tumors includes strong and diffuse positivity for S100, SOX10, inhibin, and calretinin 22495377 ; 22804786 ; 26637199 . CD68 and CD63 (NKI/C3) are also common expressed, and NSE can also be positive 26637199 . Nuclear expression of TFE3 and MITF, in the absence of rearrangements of these genes, is common 26009539 ; 31788112 ; 17284958 , whereas melan-A, GFAP, keratins, and NFP are largely negative. HMB45, however, has been reported to be uniformly negative in these tumors 17284958 ; 26637199 . The Ki-67 proliferation index is typically low (< 2%) 26637199 ; 15214825 , but it is often higher in atypical and malignant forms 17227124 . Given that loss-of-function mutations affecting ATP6AP1 and ATP6AP2 are probably pathognomonic of granular cell tumors, being detected in < 0.3% of other tumor types analysed to date 30166553 , sequencing analyses of these genes may provide additional confirmatory evidence for a diagnosis of granular cell tumors. In 72% of cases, whole-exome and targeted sequencing analyses of these cancers have revealed mutually exclusive loss-of-function mutations affecting ATP6AP1 and ATP6AP2, which encode accessory components of the vacuolar ATPase and play pivotal roles in the regulation of endosomal pH and vesicle trafficking 30166553 . In a subset of granular cell tumors with wildtype ATP6AP1 and ATP6AP2, loss-of-function mutations affecting other genes encoding components of the vacuolar H+-ATPase have been detected 30597645 ; 33289181 . These mutations are not only oncogenic but also shown to result in impaired vesicular acidification and altered distribution of endosomes – and consequently, in a massive intracytoplasmic accumulation of early and recycling endosomes 30166553 . The mechanistic basis for the oncogenic properties of these loss-of-function mutations remains to be fully characterized. These tumors have a low mutation burden and appear not to harbour recurrent oncogenic fusion genes 30166553 . Non-neural granular cell tumor (NNGCT) is a rare, low-grade neoplasm of mesenchymal cells of unknown lineage with prominent cytoplasmic granularity. NNGCTs can be polypoid. Some lesions are gently domed. The lesional cells often extend to the base of the dermis or into the subcutis. The overlying epidermis is usually thin, with epithelial collarettes defining the lateral edges. The granular cells form sheets and are large and oval, with coarse eosinophilic granules. The cellular granularity is due to the accumulation of lysosomes in the cytoplasm of the affected cells. The largest granules are surrounded by clear haloes (pustulo-ovoid bodies of Milian). The nuclei can vary from moderately sized and monomorphic to large, pleomorphic, and heterochromatic. Mitoses can range from few to many (as many as 6 mitoses/mm2), and atypical mitoses can occur. Most cases arise on sun-damaged sites in elderly individuals. The diagnosis requires the evaluation of multiple immunostains. A circumscribed dermal tumor is present with no involvement of the subcutis. The neoplasm is typically highly cellular, with striking nuclear enlargement, pleomorphism, and atypia. Mitoses are frequent, with atypical forms. Enlarged spindle or epithelioid cells are seen, some with histiocyte-like appearances. Irregular fascicles may be present with scattered inflammatory cells and occasional hemorrhage. Ulceration is common, sometimes with an epidermal collarette or atrophy. Necrosis is absent in AFX. Plaque-like growth is occasionally seen with a band of cells parallel to the epidermis. These plaque-like lesions may be less well circumscribed 20526171 . AFX with a spindle cell pattern shows exclusively spindle-shaped cells in fascicles with eosinophilic cytoplasm, vesicular nuclei, and prominent nucleoli 26098709 . Sometimes the cytological features of this pattern are relatively bland. AFX with a clear cell pattern exhibits cells with clear to foamy cytoplasm and hyperchromatic, pleomorphic nuclei 26848640 . Glycogen is of limited extent or absent. Further patterns include granular cell, keloidal, myxoid, and sclerotic forms. Regression is sometimes seen, which can be extensive, making diagnosis on a partial biopsy challenging. Pigmented AFX show hemosiderin deposition and hemorrhage 9870148 ; 24080496 . Some AFXs contain osteoclast-like giant cells, which may be multinucleated tumor cells (demonstrating nuclear atypia) or background histiocytes (CD163-positive with bland nuclei). Immunohistochemistry is vital to exclude other malignancies, especially melanoma, leiomyosarcoma, and poorly differentiated squamous cell carcinoma. A metastasis should always be considered. A broad panel of immunostains is essential. In particular, melanocyte markers (e.g. SOX10, S100) and keratinocyte markers (e.g. MNF116, AE1/AE3, 34βE12, p63, p40) should be negative 20526171 ; 19807823 ; 19476522 ; 25029117 . Many AFXs are MITF-positive, and occasionally there may be focal expression of melan-A 25238448 ; 22050092 . Desmin positivity has been reported in AFX, but these tumors may represent leiomyosarcoma, particularly if staining is prominent. CD10 is almost invariably strongly and diffusely expressed in AFX and may be the only positive stain. Although this is nonspecific and can be seen in some melanomas and squamous cell carcinomas, for example, AFX should be diagnosed with great caution if CD10 is absent. Rarely, myxoid stroma and metaplastic bone are reported in PRDM10-rearranged soft tissue tumors 34121219 . These tumors invariably express CD34, and they are focally immunoreactive for keratins in close to 70% of cases (most often with the AE1/AE3 clones). SMARCB1 (INI1) expression is retained, and p53 expression shows a wildtype pattern. The Ki-67 (MIB1) proliferation index is very low (< 5%) 23887307 ; 27636918 ; 34121219 ; 34969957 . PRDM10 immunohistochemistry is consistently positive 30570551 . CADM3 (SynCam3) immunopositivity is reported in 95–100% of cases 34121219 ; 34969957 . Demonstration of PRDM10 rearrangement is useful in selected cases. The morphological, immunohistochemical, and molecular genetic features of SCD34FT and tumors referred to as “PRDM10-rearranged soft tissue tumor” are identical, strongly supporting their unity 30570551 ; 34121219 ; 34969957 . The terminology “superficial CD34-positive fibroblastic tumor” is preferred, because not all tumors harbour demonstrable PRDM10 rearrangements. PRDM10 rearrangements have been identified and have been reported in close to 60% of cases previously classified as SCD34FT or PRDM10-rearranged soft tissue tumor 30570551 ; 34969957 . Specific identified fusions have included MED12::PRDM10, CITED2::PRDM10, PRDM10::ARHGAP32, and PRDM10::RAB30 30570551 ; 34121219 ; 34969957 . The differential diagnosis of SCD34FT includes pleomorphic dermal sarcoma, dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans, plaque-like CD34-positive dermal fibroma, myxoinflammatory fibroblastic sarcoma, superficial solitary fibrous tumors, inflammatory myofibroblastoma, superficial myxofibrosarcoma, fibrous histiocytoma, and epithelioid sarcomas 33969057 . It may also include atypical fibrous histiocytoma, atypical fibroxanthoma, and undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma. Essential: superficial location; large eosinophilic cells with granular to glassy cytoplasm, marked nuclear pleomorphism, and a low mitotic rate; diffuse CD34 expression. Desirable: CADM3 expression; keratin immunoreactivity; PRDM10 rearrangement. Pleomorphic dermal sarcoma The primary location is the head and neck region, with a preference for the hairless scalp 34202213 ; 35099104 . This malignancy typically manifests as a rapidly growing nodule with a diameter of 5–50 mm (median: 25 mm). Ulceration is observed in at least 50% of the lesions 35099104 . PDS occurs on severely sun-damaged skin of White patients in their seventh or eighth decade of life 22510760 ; 26264237 , with a male predominance 22510760 . Pleomorphic dermal sarcoma (PDS) is a rare tumor occurring in elderly patients, in chronically ultraviolet (UV) radiation–exposed skin. It is genetically, morphologically, and clinically related to atypical fibroxanthoma, but subcutaneous invasion and lymphovascular/perineural invasion are not features of atypical fibroxanthoma and confer an increased risk of aggressive behavior. The tumors are centred within the dermis, with an expansile nodular or plaque-like growth pattern, poor demarcation, and irregular borders. Ulceration is frequently seen (> 50% of cases). A diffusely infiltrative growth with invasion of subcutaneous adipose tissue, skeletal muscle, or fascia is common and may be relevant for local relapse risk 32583897 . The tumor cells vary in size and shape. Most frequent are pleomorphic spindle cells with hyperchromatic or vesicular nuclei and prominent nucleoli. In addition, epithelioid, spindled, and multinucleated giant cells may be admixed. Mitotic activity is brisk and includes atypical forms. tumor necrosis, perineural infiltration, and lymphovascular invasion may also be seen. The next most common morphological pattern shows atypical spindle cells in a fascicular arrangement. Other less common features include myxoid, desmoplastic, or keloidal stromal change; pseudoangiomatous features; a storiform growth pattern; and admixed osteoclast-like multinucleated giant cells. The tumor cells are consistently negative for S100, SOX10, PMEL (gp100), cytokeratins, CD34, ERG, and desmin 22510760 ; 24080496 . SMA and CD31 may be focally positive, and aberrant melan-A expression is occasionally seen 22510760 ; 22050092 ; 24080496 ; 35099104 . Immunoreactivity for CD10, CD99, and PDGFRB is typically detected. PDS is an undifferentiated tumor of uncertain histogenesis that does not express epithelial, melanocytic, vascular, or muscle differentiation markers. Similarly to atypical fibroxanthoma, PDS occurs in chronically UV radiation–exposed skin, frequently with or after UV radiation–dependent cutaneous epithelial malignancies including actinic keratosis or squamous cell carcinomas, sometimes on chronic radiodermatitis. Next-generation sequencing consistently showed a high mutation load, with a UV radiation signature; mutations in TP53, NOTCH family genes, and the TERT promoter; and alterations in CDKN2A and CDKN2B responsible for cell-cycle control 34202213 ; 29099504 . This mutation profile widely overlaps with that of cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma. The differential diagnosis includes atypical fibroxanthoma, desmoplastic melanoma, poorly differentiated carcinoma, leiomyosarcoma, and angiosarcoma. Negative staining for ERG can be useful for excluding angiosarcoma in diagnostically difficult cases. Essential: a pleomorphic dermal-based neoplasm; invasion of the subcutis, necrosis, perineurial infiltration, or lymphovascular invasion; exclusion of epithelial, vascular, smooth muscle, and melanocytic tumors by immunohistochemistry. Epithelioid sarcoma Classic ES arises in the distal extremities, predominantly on the volar surfaces of the hands and feet 4014539 ; 26645461 . Proximal-type ES arises in deep soft tissues, most often at truncal locations or in the buttock or hip 9042279 ; 11454997 . Classic ES manifests as superficial, slow-growing, painless, firm nodules. Sporotrichoid spread is characteristic. Non-healing skin ulcers mimic other processes 33247494 . Soft tissue ES is larger and more infiltrative 9042279 ; 11454997 . ES may metastasize to lymph nodes and distant sites. ES represents < 1% of adult soft tissue sarcomas 19224301 and 4–8% of childhood non-rhabdomyosarcomatous soft tissue sarcomas 16353216 . Classic ES is reported twice as often as proximal ES 19141382 ; 18607629 . The M:F ratio is 2:1 for classic ES 26645461 and 1.6:1 for proximal-type ES 9042279 ; 11454997 . Classic ES occurs mainly in adolescents and young adults. Proximal-type ES affects a somewhat older population of young to middle-aged adults 26645461 . Epithelioid sarcoma (ES) is a malignant soft tissue tumor with hybrid mesenchymal and epithelial morphological and immunophenotypic features. Two subtypes are described: classic ES tends to arise in acral skin, with a palisading, pseudogranulomatous growth pattern; proximal ES occurs in deep truncal locations as nests and sheets of larger epithelioid cells. Classic ES consists of infiltrative, pseudogranulomatous nodules of epithelioid and spindled tumor cells palisading around foci of necrobiosis 3717528 . Constituent cells are large, with deeply eosinophilic cytoplasm and atypical nuclei with vesicular chromatin and small nucleoli. Mitoses are inconspicuous. Dystrophic calcification and metaplastic bone are seen in 20% of cases 4014539 . Proximal ES is characterized by sheet-like growth of larger epithelioid cells with vesicular nuclei with nucleoli 9042279 ; 11454997 . tumor necrosis is frequently seen. Rhabdoid cells occur in both forms but are more frequent in proximal ES 9042279 . ES is high-grade by definition. Both subtypes show immunoreactivity for cytokeratins and EMA 10452506 . Most express CK8/19 10452506 but are negative for CK5/6 12946229 . CD34 is expressed in > 50% of cases. Loss of nuclear SMARCB1 expression occurs in the vast majority of ESs 19033866 ; 18973917 ; 21357725 . ERG expression is observed in 40–67% of ESs 23774169 ; 24072183 ; 25479928 . In challenging cases, panel sequencing may detect mutations inactivating SMARCB1 30652038 . The SMARCB1 gene (also known as BAF47, INI1, and SNF5) encodes a component of the SWI/SNF chromatin-remodelling complex present in normal cells. SWI/SNF has ATPase activity and functions to shift the position of nucleosomes modulating transcription of genes involved in cell differentiation 28945250 . Loss of nuclear SMARCB1 protein expression is characteristic of ES, but an extreme minority retain SMARCB1 (INI1) expression, instead exhibiting abnormal expression of other SWI/SNF chromatin-remodelling complex members, such as SMARCA4 (BRG1), SMARCC1 (BAF155), or SMARCC2 (BAF170) 29309303 . Genomic analysis has revealed complex copy-number aberrations and relatively high mutation burden 26365879 . RNA sequencing shows a unique profile that does not cluster with any particular tissue type or other SWI/SNF-aberrant system 26365879 ; 26343384 . This includes granulomatous processes, carcinomas, and epithelioid vascular tumors. Essential: a tumor presenting as a soft tissue mass (termed distal or proximal presentations); epithelioid to spindled cytomorphology with infiltrative growth; diffuse loss of SMARCB1 (INI1, BAF47); staining for EMA and keratin. CRTC1::TRIM11 cutaneous tumor Malignant potential not fully established CTCT shows a broad anatomical distribution, although it occurs most commonly in the extremities (upper extremity 40%, lower extremity 30%), followed by the trunk (15%), head, and mucosa (oral and nasal reported) 35993578 ; 29240581 ; 31237704 . The tumors occur as a discrete, slowly growing, skin-colored nodule. Mild pain and tingling have been noted 35993578 ; 29240581 ; 31237704 . Nearly 50 cases have been reported in the literature 29240581 ; 30676334 ; 31237704 ; 31276279 ; 33586183 ; 35993578 ; 35751643 ; 36177516 , without an obvious sex bias and across a broad age range (11–87 years, median: 44 years) 35993578 . CRTC1::TRIM11 cutaneous tumor (CTCT) is a dermal spindled and epithelioid cell tumor with partial melanocytic differentiation and CRTC1::TRIM11 translocation. The morphology is highly uniform and resembles that of clear cell sarcoma. tumors are dermal-based, well-circumscribed, unencapsulated nodules with a pushing border and no pigment. They can abut, but only very rarely involve, the epidermis. Cells are arranged in nests and streaming long and short intersecting (at times herringbone to vaguely palisaded) fascicles with intervening thin fibrous bands; they are fusiform with abundant pale cytoplasm, smooth nuclear membranes, vesicular chromatin, and prominent nucleoli. Mitoses are typical, although not conspicuous 35993578 ; 29240581 ; 31237704 ; 35751643 . All tumors express diffuse SOX10. Diffuse S100 staining is seen in only 50% of cases; melan-A (MART1) and HMB45 are only focally expressed. Pan-TRK expression can be observed (60% diffuse). TRIM11 immunohistochemistry is typically positive in nuclei at the periphery of the nodule 35993578 ; 29240581 ; 31237704 . Demonstration of CRTC1::TRIM11 fusion is necessary for the diagnosis. Although the precise molecular function of the CRTC1::TRIM11 fusion protein has not been proved, CRTC1 (CREB-regulated transcription coactivator 1, 19p) is thought to enhance cell proliferation, differentiation, and expression of the oncogene MITF through activation of CREB1 (the cAMP response element-binding transcription factor) 14506290 ; 14536081 ; 28263292 . The main differential diagnosis includes clear cell sarcoma and metastatic melanoma 35993578 . Essential: a circumscribed, non-pigmented dermal tumor comprising intersecting bundles of epithelioid to fusiform cells with pale cytoplasm and vesicular nuclei; expression of SOX10, with at least partial loss of other melanocytic markers; no demonstrable EWSR1 rearrangement. Desirable: demonstration of TRIM11 rearrangement. Dermal clear cell sarcoma Dermal CCS predominantly affects the extremities, especially the distal extremities 20087159 ; 31688004 , but it can also occur elsewhere, including in the head and neck region. Most superficial cutaneous (i.e. primary dermal) tumors manifest as small amelanotic nodules. They may be confused with melanocytic neoplasms, such as Spitz naevi 23228147 . CCS tends to affect young adults, most often during the third to fourth decade of life 14332545 ; 6614306 ; 20087159 . Very rarely the tumor may also occur in children 32324602 or older individuals. Dermal clear cell sarcoma (CCS) is a malignant neoplasm of uncertain histogenesis displaying melanocytic differentiation and associated with a gene fusion involving EWSR1 and ATF1 or CREB1. The tumor is characterized by fascicles and nests of usually amelanotic spindle and epithelioid cells. A few cells may display clear cytoplasm. Multinucleate wreath-type giant cells are often seen. The degree of nuclear atypia and number of mitoses are variable. The tumor often displays collagenous septa separating tumor cell aggregates. Most tumors have a grenz zone 20087159 . On rare occasion a tumor may involve both the dermis and the epidermis (compound CCS), often as junctional nests, and is therefore more likely to be confused with a primary cutaneous melanoma or a melanocytic nevus 20087159 ; 23228147 ; 23980901 ; 31688004 . The tumor cells express S100, SOX10, and melanocyte differentiation antigens such as PMEL (gp100), TYRP1 (gp75), melan-A, and MITF 23228147 . In contrast to cutaneous melanomas, PRAME expression is usually absent or only focal 32681554 ; 34991102 . Identification of EWSR1 gene rearrangement and/or documentation of an EWSR1::ATF1 or EWSR1::CREB1 gene fusion may be helpful, in particular to differentiate CCS from malignant melanoma. The majority (70–90%) of CCSs harbour an EWSR1::ATF1 fusion secondary to the reciprocal translocation t(12;22)(q13;q12). The oncogenic fusion constitutively activates the promoter of MITF (microphthalmia-associated transcription factor), resulting in melanocytic differentiation and tumor growth. A variant translocation, t(2;22)(q32.3;q12), which results in an EWSR1::CREB1 fusion, is rare, accounting for approximately 5% of tumors 19561568 ; 17227118 . CCS may be associated with additional chromosomal aberrations, such as extra copies of chromosomes. Dermal CCS may be confused with spitzoid melanocytic tumors, cellular blue nevus, primary nodular or metastatic melanoma, epithelioid sarcoma, or other sarcomas. Essential: characteristic nested or fascicular architecture; plump spindle or ovoid cells with palely eosinophilic cytoplasm and prominent nucleoli; spindle and epithelioid neoplasm with melanocytic differentiation confirmed by immunohistochemistry. Desirable: documentation of an EWSR1 gene rearrangement and/or EWSR1::ATF1 or EWSR1::CREB1 fusion. Ewing sarcoma Ewing sarcoma most commonly involves the lower limbs (38% of cases), followed by the upper extremities (26%), head (20%), and trunk (16%). Extraskeletal Ewing sarcoma occurs in approximately 12% of patients and has a wide anatomical distribution, including superficial / primary cutaneous sites 22098102 ; 33635948 ; 29977059 ; 9363452 ; 21649689 ; 19783720 ; 18820660 ; 9500772 . Ewing sarcoma manifests as dermal or subcutaneous nodules that may be painful, polypoid, and/or ulcerated. The median tumor size is 23 mm (range: 5–120 mm) 9363452 ; 9500772 ; 19783720 ; 18820660 . Cutaneous Ewing sarcoma tends to occur in children and young adults, but it has been reported in older individuals. The median age at diagnosis is 17 years (range: 2–77 years); 67% of patients are female, and 33% are male 22098102 ; 33635948 ; 29977059 ; 9363452 ; 21649689 ; 19783720 ; 18820660 ; 9500772 . Ewing sarcoma is a small round cell sarcoma showing gene fusions involving one member of the FET family of genes (usually EWSR1) and a member of the ETS family of transcription factors. Superficial / primary cutaneous lesions are rare but well described. tumors are composed of sheets of mitotically active, uniform small blue round cells with indistinct cell borders and round nuclei with fine stippled chromatin and inconspicuous nucleoli. Constituent cells have a high N:C ratio and scant, lightly eosinophilic to clear glycogenated cytoplasm that gives a positive PAS reaction 9363452 ; 9500772 ; 19841938 . Membranous CD99 immunoreactivity is a highly sensitive but nonspecific finding in nearly all cases. Neural markers (e.g. NSE, S100, PGP9.5, and CD57) 2163356 and epithelial markers (AE1/AE3, CAM5.2) may occasionally be expressed, but desmin positivity is rare and typically only very focal 11176079 ; 16006796 ; 10716155 ; 19841938 . FLI1 and ERG are often expressed in cases with the corresponding translocation; some cross-reactivity has been reported 22766791 . NKX2-2 is sensitive but imperfectly specific 26847175 ; 22446943 ; 29661713 . Molecular confirmation is often required for a diagnosis of Ewing sarcoma, as round cell morphology is common to other sarcomas, carcinomas, and lymphomas. All cases of Ewing sarcoma harbour FET::ETS fusions. The EWSR1::FLI1 fusion is seen in > 95% of cutaneous and superficial Ewing sarcomas 8022439 ; 9500772 ; 8834175 ; 9121764 . Rarely, an EWSR1::ERG fusion is present 7700648 ; 27526022 ; 8162068 ; 18820660 . As with their deeper counterpart, the pathogenesis of cutaneous Ewing sarcomas is driven by transcription factors encoded by chimeric FET::ETS gene fusions, most commonly EWSR1::FLI1 and EWSR1::ERG 24680181 ; 30709443 ; 9500772 ; 7493136 ; 21649689 . Chimeric fusion genes encode transcription factors that serve as master regulators that activate and repress thousands of genes. Expression of these transcription factors in the correct tumor microenvironment is ostensibly required for the development of Ewing sarcoma. Proteins bind both GGAA microsatellites and canonical ETS binding sites in the genome and recruit chromatin regulators. Binding of the fusion proteins to GGAA microsatellites results in transition from a closed to open chromatin state that establishes de novo enhancers which activate genes. Conversely, binding to canonical ETS binding sites displaces wildtype ETS factors and represses gene expression. In combination, these events establish an oncogenic gene expression programme that underlies tumor initiation 10623711 ; 29977059 . The differential diagnosis includes a very rare subset of superficially located Ewing-like undifferentiated small blue round cell sarcomas such as CIC-rearranged and BCOR-rearranged sarcomas, representing distinct entities. Essential: small blue round cell cytomorphology; membranous CD99 immunoreactivity. Desirable: detection of a FET::ETS fusion. intermediate uncertain low metastatic risk rarely metastasizing locally aggressive malignant potential not fully established malignant No specific information provided in the source. — $1§ . All Intermediate PathologyGPS / Skin / Cutaneous Soft Tissue Tumors Cutaneous Soft Tissue Tumors A morphology-first reference organized by tumor family, with side-by-side comparison tables followed by complete diagnostic profiles. Intermediate neoplasms receive dedicated emphasis. WHO entities intermediate / uncertain behavior profiles American English Diagnostic principle Integrate architecture, cytology, anatomic level, clinical context, and targeted ancillary studies. Atypia, mitotic activity, or necrosis must be interpreted in the context of the specific entity; none is independently synonymous with malignancy. Diagnostic GPS: practical approach Define the setting Age, sex, site, size, depth, growth pattern, prior radiation, lymphedema, and immune status. Classify the lineage Adipocytic, fibroblastic, vascular, perivascular, smooth muscle, neural, or uncertain differentiation. Assess behavior Separate benign, locally aggressive intermediate, rarely metastasizing intermediate, and malignant categories. Select targeted tests Use IHC and molecular assays to answer a defined differential; avoid broad, non-directed panels. Check sampling Large, deep, heterogeneous, or ulcerated lesions require representative sampling and clinical-radiologic correlation. WHO behavior categories Benign: usually cured by local excision; recurrence, if present, is generally non-destructive. Intermediate, locally aggressive: may infiltrate or recur locally but has little or no metastatic potential. Intermediate, rarely metastasizing: has a low but definite metastatic risk; the WHO introduction cites a risk below 2% for this category. Malignant: infiltrative tumors with local recurrence and meaningful metastatic potential; risk varies by histotype, grade, size, and depth. Important general diagnostic cautions Benign lesions can show atypia (e.g., pleomorphic fibroma and atypical fibrous histiocytoma) or frequent mitoses (e.g., nodular fasciitis). FNCLCC grading is rarely applicable to cutaneous sarcomas; some histotypes are considered high grade by definition. Complete excision is a major factor in preventing local recurrence. Large (>50 mm) superficial lesions and all deep or subfascial tumors warrant specialist multidisciplinary assessment before biopsy or surgery. Intermediate neoplasms: focused review These entities are highlighted throughout the family tables and their complete diagnostic profiles are shown directly below each table. Behavior is not interchangeable across this group: local aggressiveness, rare metastasis, uncertain malignant potential, and low-grade malignancy must be distinguished.
