title: Epidermal Tumors
content: use client Actinic keratosis Premalignant keratoses Intraepidermal squamous dysplasia; potential precursor of SCC Usually affects fair-skinned adults older than 40 years; incidence increases with age. Occurs on chronically sun-exposed face, ears, scalp, neck, lips, forearms, and dorsal hands. Presents as multiple scaly erythematous patches or plaques, typically 2–10 mm, on photodamaged skin. Squamous dysplasia involves the basal to mid-spinous epidermis but is not full thickness. Adnexal epithelium is generally spared, although atypical cells may extend along pre-existing adnexal structures. Solar elastosis is usually present in the superficial dermis. Atypical keratinocytes show enlarged, irregular, hyperchromatic or vesicular nuclei. Mitotic figures, including atypical forms, are common. The granular layer is typically reduced or absent, with overlying parakeratosis. Lichenoid, hypertrophic, proliferative, atrophic, acantholytic, and pigmented patterns may occur. SCC in situ Full-thickness epidermal atypia favors SCC in situ; AK is limited to the lower epidermis. Seborrheic keratosis Usually shows orderly maturation and lacks convincing keratinocyte dysplasia. Arsenical keratosis Potential precursor of SCC Follows chronic environmental, medicinal, or occupational arsenic exposure, often with a latency of decades. Palms and soles are favored; diffuse or localized hyperpigmentation and raindrop pigmentation may involve the trunk. Presents as yellowish hyperkeratotic papules or confluent verrucous plaques. Squamoproliferative lesions with or without squamous dysplasia occur in the setting of chronic arsenic exposure. The dysplasia does not involve the full thickness of the epidermis. Acanthosis, papillomatosis, and hyperkeratosis form a spectrum of changes. Dysplastic keratinocytes may show vacuolization, multinucleation, and atypical mitotic activity. Verruca Viral cytopathic change and typical wart architecture favor verruca; exposure history and dysplasia support arsenical keratosis. Full-thickness epidermal atypia supports SCC in situ. PUVA keratosis Treatment-associated keratosis; increased subsequent nonmelanoma skin cancer risk Occurs in patients receiving prolonged psoralen plus UVA therapy, often for psoriasis. Develops in treated, typically sun-protected skin of the trunk and thighs. Presents as multiple warty, hyperkeratotic, scaly papules with a broad base. Well-circumscribed squamoproliferative lesion with up to mild squamous dysplasia in the setting of prolonged PUVA treatment. Well-demarcated acanthosis with overlying hyperkeratosis is characteristic. Papillomatous growth and focal parakeratosis may be present. Mild keratinocyte dysplasia occurs in approximately half of biopsies. A superficial chronic inflammatory infiltrate may be present. Koilocytosis, hypergranulosis, and characteristic papillomatous architecture support verruca. Marked full-thickness atypia is not a feature of uncomplicated PUVA keratosis. TP53 and HRAS mutations with UV-signature changes have been reported; no routine diagnostic molecular test is indicated. Squamous cell carcinoma in situ (Bowen disease) SCC and precursors Intraepidermal carcinoma Usually occurs in adults older than 60 years, particularly older White patients with cumulative sun exposure. Common sites include lower limbs, head, neck, and hands; both sun-exposed and protected skin may be involved. Usually presents as a solitary, slowly growing scaly erythematous patch or plaque that may persist for years. Full-thickness epidermal replacement by atypical keratinocytes with loss of maturation. No invasion into the underlying dermis. Superficial adnexal epithelium may be involved. Atypical pleomorphic keratinocytes involve the full epidermal thickness and often show loss of polarity. Mitoses are increased and may extend to the epidermal surface. Hyperparakeratosis and loss of the granular layer are common. Pagetoid single-cell or nested growth may occur. The basal layer may be retained (eyeliner sign). Ki-67 labeling extending through the full epidermal thickness can support the diagnosis in subtle cases. p16 may help assess dysplasia in genital lesions; interpret in the appropriate clinical setting. Atypia is limited to the lower epidermis; adnexal epithelium is generally spared. Paget disease / melanoma in situ Pagetoid lesions may require epithelial, glandular, and melanocytic markers to establish lineage. Microinvasive SCC Look for jagged invasive nests crossing the dermoepidermal junction. TP53 and NOTCH1 alterations are frequent, but molecular testing is not routinely required for diagnosis. Verruca vulgaris Benign keratoses and simulants Benign HPV-associated squamoproliferation Common in children and less frequent in adults; immunosuppression is a risk factor. Hands and fingers are common sites; elbows, knees, face, flexures, and genital skin may also be affected. Presents as single or multiple verrucous, keratotic papules or nodules. Papillomatosis, hyperkeratosis, hypergranulosis, and parakeratotic columns. Koilocytosis is desirable but may be absent, particularly in older lesions. Prominent inwardly proliferating rete ridges create a papillomatous architecture. Coarse keratohyalin granules and hypergranulosis are characteristic. Dilated tortuous capillaries occupy the papillary dermis. Koilocytes may be present in the superficial epidermis. Verruca shows papillomatosis, hypergranulosis, and often koilocytosis. Verrucous SCC Deep, broad, club-shaped endophytic tongues with pushing borders favor verrucous SCC. Routine HPV subtyping is not indicated. Verruca plantaris / palmaris Occurs on the soles or palms; children are affected more often than adults. Lesions may be single or multiple and are often painful. Myrmecial lesions are hard, slightly elevated keratotic papules; mosaic lesions are superficial and confluent. Marked hyperkeratosis, acanthosis, and hypergranulosis. Koilocytosis supports the diagnosis. Myrmecial lesions show endophytic growth and vacuolated keratinocytes with coarse eosinophilic keratohyalin granules. Mosaic lesions show more superficial confluent growth and usually milder papillomatosis. Hemorrhage may be seen in regressing lesions. Callus/corn Warts may show thrombosed capillaries and viral cytopathic change; calluses lack these features. Deep infiltrative/pushing growth and clinical persistence raise concern for carcinoma. Verruca plana Benign HPV-associated lesion Typically affects children and young adults. Commonly involves the face, dorsal hands, and lower legs. Presents as multiple flat-topped, smooth, skin-colored to light-brown papules. Acanthosis with a relatively flat surface and viral cytopathic changes. Mild acanthosis and hyperkeratosis with a broad, flattened epidermal surface. Koilocytosis may be present in the upper epidermis. Lichen planus-like keratosis Interface inflammation and basal vacuolar change favor lichen planus-like keratosis. Horn cysts and more pronounced papillomatosis favor seborrheic keratosis. Benign keratinocytic neoplasm Very common in adults; frequency increases with age. May occur on almost any skin surface but typically favors the trunk, face, and extremities. Often presents as a sharply demarcated, waxy, 'stuck-on' papule or plaque; lesions may be pigmented or inflamed. Acanthotic, papillomatous, or reticulated proliferation of bland basaloid keratinocytes. Horn cysts or pseudohorn cysts are characteristic in many cases. Architectural patterns include acanthotic, hyperkeratotic, and reticulated forms. Horn cysts and pseudohorn cysts are common. Melanin pigmentation and squamous eddies may be present. Inflamed lesions may show lichenoid inflammation and obscure the underlying architecture. Significant full-thickness atypia and disordered maturation favor SCC in situ. Melanocytic lesion Use melanocytic markers when a clonal or pigmented lesion is equivocal. Solar lentigo Benign UV-associated epidermal lesion Usually occurs in middle-aged and older adults with chronic sun exposure. Favors sun-exposed face, dorsal hands, and forearms. Presents as a sharply demarcated tan-to-brown macule. Basal epidermal hyperpigmentation with elongated rete ridges and increased basal melanocytes, without significant melanocytic atypia. Elongated, often club-shaped rete ridges extend into the dermis. Basal keratinocytes contain increased melanin. Solar elastosis is often present in the underlying dermis. Lentigo maligna Confluent atypical melanocytes and adnexal extension favor lentigo maligna; use melanocytic IHC when needed. Pigmented seborrheic keratosis Horn cysts and basaloid proliferation favor seborrheic keratosis. Benign inflammatory regression of a keratinocytic lesion Usually occurs in middle-aged or older adults. Commonly affects sun-exposed trunk and extremities. Presents as a solitary erythematous, violaceous, or pigmented papule or thin plaque. Lichenoid/interface inflammatory reaction associated with regression of a pre-existing keratinocytic lesion. Band-like lichenoid lymphocytic infiltrate obscures the dermoepidermal junction. Basal vacuolar alteration, apoptotic keratinocytes, and pigment incontinence may be present. Residual features of solar lentigo or seborrheic keratosis may be identified. Melanocytic neoplasm Prominent interface inflammation can obscure melanocytic lesions; use SOX10/Melan-A when indicated. Lichen planus Clinical context and residual keratinocytic architecture support lichen planus-like keratosis. Clear cell acanthoma Benign epidermal neoplasm Usually affects middle-aged and older adults. Most often occurs on the lower legs. Presents as a solitary, well-circumscribed, red or brown, dome-shaped papule or nodule. Well-demarcated epidermal proliferation of glycogen-rich clear keratinocytes. Acanthotic epidermis is sharply demarcated from adjacent epidermis. Keratinocytes have abundant pale, glycogen-rich cytoplasm and small uniform nuclei. Neutrophils may be present within the epidermis. Psoriasis Clear cell acanthoma is sharply circumscribed and composed of glycogen-rich clear cells. SCC Significant cytologic atypia and infiltrative growth are absent in clear cell acanthoma. Large cell acanthoma Benign keratinocytic lesion Typically occurs in older adults on chronically sun-exposed skin. Often affects the face and extremities. Presents as a small, sharply demarcated scaly macule or thin plaque. Sharply circumscribed epidermal proliferation composed of enlarged keratinocytes without significant atypia. Keratinocytes are larger than those in adjacent epidermis and show abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm. Acanthosis and hyperkeratosis may be present. Solar elastosis is common. Actinic keratosis shows genuine dysplasia rather than uniform cellular enlargement. Full-thickness cytologic atypia and loss of maturation favor SCC in situ. Warty dyskeratoma Benign follicular infundibular lesion Usually affects adults, often as a solitary lesion. Commonly occurs on the head and neck. Presents as a small umbilicated papule or nodule. Cup-shaped or crateriform epidermal invagination with acantholysis and dyskeratosis. Acantholysis and prominent dyskeratosis produce corps ronds and grains. A central keratin-filled cup may communicate with a follicular infundibulum. A suprabasal cleft may be present. Acantholytic SCC Invasive atypical squamous nests and destructive growth favor carcinoma. Darier disease Usually multiple lesions and a broader clinical distribution. Other benign keratoses / acanthomas Benign; pattern-based group Clinical presentation and site vary by subtype. May occur as solitary or multiple papules or plaques. Classify by the dominant histologic pattern and exclude dysplasia or invasion. Patterns include acantholysis, epidermolytic hyperkeratosis, hypergranulosis, glycogen deposition, and melanocyte hyperplasia. Verrucae may overlap morphologically with benign and malignant keratinocytic proliferations. Look for cytologic atypia, disordered maturation, and infiltrative growth. Correlate the specific architectural and cytologic pattern. Superficial basal cell carcinoma Basal cell carcinoma Lower recurrence-risk BCC subtype Usually occurs on the trunk and extremities, often in younger adults than other BCC patterns. Presents as a slowly enlarging erythematous, scaly patch or thin plaque; multiple lesions may occur. Multifocal or broad-based basaloid buds arise from the epidermis and extend superficially into the papillary dermis. Peripheral palisading and stromal retraction support BCC. Tumor nests are attached to the epidermis and extend horizontally along the dermoepidermal junction. Peripheral palisading and stromal clefting are usually present. The tumor does not show the deep, narrow infiltrative strands of high-risk patterns. BerEP4 is typically positive and can support BCC in difficult cases. BCC shows basaloid nests with palisading and retraction; SCC in situ shows full-thickness squamous atypia. Trichoepithelioma Follicular differentiation and specialized stroma favor trichoepithelioma. Hedgehog pathway dysregulation, commonly involving PTCH1 or SMO, is central to BCC pathogenesis; routine molecular testing is not required. Nodular basal cell carcinoma Most often occurs on the head and neck, especially the face. Usually presents as a slowly growing pearly papule or nodule, sometimes with ulceration or telangiectasia. Rounded, relatively large basaloid tumor nests with peripheral palisading and stromal retraction. No significant micronodular, infiltrative, or morphoeic component. Nodules of basaloid cells extend into the dermis. Peripheral palisading and clefting from the surrounding stroma are characteristic. Cystic, keratotic, pigmented, or nodulocystic patterns may occur. BerEP4 is typically positive. Papillary mesenchymal bodies, follicular germ-like structures, and specialized stroma favor trichoepithelioma. Squamous maturation and keratinization favor SCC. PTCH1 loss or SMO activation drives Hedgehog pathway signaling in many cases. Micronodular basal cell carcinoma Higher recurrence-risk BCC subtype Usually occurs on the head and neck. May present as an ill-defined, slowly enlarging plaque or nodule; clinical borders may underestimate tumor extent. Numerous small, deeply infiltrative basaloid nests, typically smaller than those in nodular BCC. Small nests extend into deeper dermis and may involve subcutis. Tumor is composed of compact, small basaloid nests with limited peripheral palisading. Nests infiltrate between collagen bundles and may extend deeply. Clefting may be less conspicuous than in nodular BCC. Nodular BCC Micronodular BCC has smaller, more deeply infiltrative nests. Desmoplastic trichoepithelioma Follicular differentiation and specialized stroma favor a benign follicular tumor. Hedgehog pathway alterations are characteristic of BCC; no subtype-specific molecular test is established. Infiltrating basal cell carcinoma Usually arises on the head and neck, particularly the central face. Often presents as an ill-defined indurated plaque or scar-like lesion. Narrow, angulated strands and small nests of basaloid cells infiltrate between dermal collagen bundles. Tumor extends beyond the clinically apparent borders. Thin cords and irregular nests infiltrate a fibrotic stroma. Peripheral palisading and stromal retraction may be inconspicuous. Perineural invasion may occur. Sclerosing/morphoeic BCC Both are high-risk; morphoeic BCC shows more prominent dense sclerosis and narrow infiltrative strands. Benign follicular differentiation and specialized stroma favor trichoepithelioma. Hedgehog pathway dysregulation is central to BCC; molecular testing is not routinely needed. Sclerosing / morphoeic basal cell carcinoma Typically affects the central face and other sun-exposed head and neck sites. Presents as a firm, scar-like, poorly defined plaque. Thin strands and small nests of basaloid cells infiltrate a dense sclerotic stroma. Tumor strands are often difficult to identify at low magnification. Narrow cords of basaloid cells are embedded in densely collagenized stroma. Tumor borders are poorly circumscribed and may extend well beyond the visible lesion. Perineural invasion may be present. BerEP4 is typically positive and may help identify subtle infiltrating tumor strands. Scar / morphea Basaloid tumor strands and BerEP4 positivity support BCC. Follicular structures and specialized stroma favor trichoepithelioma. Hedgehog pathway dysregulation, particularly PTCH1 or SMO alterations, is central to BCC. Basosquamous carcinoma Higher recurrence-risk carcinoma with BCC and SCC differentiation Usually occurs on sun-exposed head and neck skin. Clinical appearance overlaps with other BCCs and SCCs; often presents as an enlarging or ulcerated lesion. Malignancy showing unequivocal features of both BCC and SCC. Transition between basaloid and squamous components may be present. Basaloid nests show BCC-type peripheral palisading and stromal retraction. Squamous areas show eosinophilic cytoplasm, intercellular bridges, and/or keratinization. A transition zone between the two components supports the diagnosis. BerEP4 typically highlights the BCC component and is reduced or absent in the squamous component. Squamous markers such as p40 and CK5/6 highlight squamous differentiation. BCC with focal squamous metaplasia Require convincing malignant squamous differentiation rather than limited metaplasia. SCC with basaloid features Look for a genuine BCC component with characteristic palisading, retraction, and BerEP4 expression. BCC-associated Hedgehog pathway alterations may be present; no routine molecular test is required. Basal cell carcinoma with sarcomatoid differentiation Rare malignant BCC variant Usually occurs in older adults on sun-exposed skin. Clinical presentation resembles conventional BCC. Conventional BCC component with an associated malignant spindle-cell or other sarcomatoid component. Basaloid carcinoma is associated with a malignant spindle-cell component. The sarcomatoid component may show loss of epithelial morphology and may require extensive sampling. Epithelial markers may be retained in the conventional BCC component and variably lost in the sarcomatoid component. BerEP4 can help identify the conventional BCC component. Spindle cell SCC Look for an SCC component and squamous marker expression. Pleomorphic dermal sarcoma / AFX A conventional BCC component supports sarcomatoid BCC. No specific diagnostic molecular test is established in the supplied source. Basal cell carcinoma with adnexal differentiation Rare BCC variant Usually arises on sun-exposed skin, particularly the head and neck. Clinical findings are not reliably distinctive from conventional BCC. Basal cell carcinoma with morphologic differentiation toward an adnexal structure. Basaloid carcinoma shows areas of follicular, sebaceous, or other adnexal differentiation. The overall malignant BCC architecture and cytology should be established. Use a morphology-directed panel to characterize the suspected line of adnexal differentiation; no single marker is definitive. Primary adnexal carcinoma Look for a conventional BCC component and integrate architecture, stromal relationship, and immunophenotype. Benign follicular neoplasm Infiltrative growth and malignant cytology support carcinoma. Fibroepithelial basal cell carcinoma (fibroepithelioma of Pinkus) Often occurs on the lower trunk, especially the lower back. Usually presents as a small, skin-colored or pink papule or plaque. Anastomosing strands of basaloid cells extend into a fibrous stroma. The characteristic fibroepithelial architecture supports the diagnosis. Thin, branching basaloid cords are embedded in a prominent fibrous stroma. The pattern may resemble a fenestrated network. Fibroepithelioma / trichoblastoma Correlate the overall architecture and infiltrative features; avoid relying on a single stain. Other BCC patterns The distinctive branching cords and fibrous stroma define this pattern. Hedgehog pathway alterations are implicated in BCC; no routine subtype-specific molecular test. Keratoacanthoma Low-grade squamous proliferation; biological relationship to SCC remains debated Usually occurs in older adults on sun-exposed skin, particularly the face and extremities. Presents as a rapidly growing crateriform nodule with a central keratin plug. Some lesions undergo spontaneous regression. Symmetric crateriform architecture with a central keratin-filled crater. Lobules of well-differentiated squamous epithelium have a pushing rather than destructive interface. Adequate sampling of the base is essential. A central keratin-filled crater is flanked by epithelial lips. Squamous lobules show glassy eosinophilic cytoplasm and relatively bland nuclei. Inflammation and partial regression may be present. Well-differentiated SCC Asymmetry, infiltrative tongues, significant atypia, and destructive invasion favor SCC. Verruca shows papillomatosis and viral cytopathic change rather than classic crateriform architecture. Conventional cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma Malignant; metastatic potential Most common in older adults with cumulative UV exposure; incidence is markedly increased in chronically immunosuppressed patients. Usually affects sun-exposed head, neck, ears, lips, and dorsal hands; may arise in scars or chronic ulcers. Presents as a rapidly growing, firm, hyperkeratotic or ulcerated papule, plaque, or nodule. Infiltration of dermis by atypical squamous cells, with variable keratinization. An in situ component may be present. Assess differentiation, depth, perineural invasion, lymphovascular invasion, and other high-risk features. Irregular nests, tongues, and individual atypical squamous cells infiltrate the dermis. Keratinization ranges from individual cell dyskeratosis to keratin pearls. Well-differentiated tumors show abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm and intercellular bridges. Poorly differentiated tumors may show minimal overt squamous maturation. p40, p63, CK5/6, MNF116, and 34βE12 support squamous differentiation. SOX10 helps exclude melanoma in poorly differentiated or spindle-cell lesions. BCC shows basaloid nests, peripheral palisading, stromal retraction, and BerEP4 expression. Adnexal carcinoma Look for ductal/luminal differentiation and use CEA/EMA or other directed markers. Melanoma Use SOX10 and other melanocytic markers when morphology is poorly differentiated. UV-signature mutations are common; TP53 and NOTCH pathway alterations are frequent. Molecular testing is not routinely required for conventional diagnosis. Verrucous squamous cell carcinoma Locally aggressive; low metastatic potential Predominantly affects older men; most patients in cited series were at least 60 years old. Cutaneous sites include palms, soles, distal digits, and anogenital skin; chronic ulcers and scars may be involved. Presents as a slowly growing hyperkeratotic plaque or exophytic condylomatoid lesion. Complex exophytic and endophytic architecture with deep, broad, club-shaped tongues. Pushing borders and minimal cytologic atypia. Exclude reactive/infectious verruciform proliferations. Marked hyperkeratosis overlies complex exophytic and endophytic growth. Broad bulbous tongues extend deeply into the dermis with pushing borders. Cytologic atypia is usually minimal and may be concentrated near the advancing interface. Verruca / callus Deep club-shaped endophytic tongues and pushing invasion favor verrucous SCC. Reactive pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia Correlate with infection, ulceration, and deep interface; reactive processes lack the characteristic pushing tumor architecture. Verruciform xanthoma Foamy macrophages in papillary dermis support verruciform xanthoma. Acantholytic squamous cell carcinoma Invasive SCC; prognostic significance of acantholysis alone is debated Usually affects older men and sun-exposed head, neck, face, and ears. Clinical appearance resembles conventional invasive SCC. May be more frequent in organ transplant recipients. Invasive SCC with tumor-cell acantholysis producing variably sized spaces within tumor lobules. Pseudoglandular architecture may be present. Acantholysis separates tumor cells and creates pseudoglandular or pseudovascular spaces. Individual rounded tumor cells may float within the spaces. The overall architecture resembles conventional invasive SCC. Adnexal / metastatic adenocarcinoma True gland formation and luminal differentiation favor adenocarcinoma; acantholytic SCC forms pseudoglandular spaces. Angiosarcoma Endothelial markers and true vasoformative growth distinguish angiosarcoma. Adenosquamous carcinoma True ducts/glands and a distinct glandular component favor adenosquamous carcinoma. p40, p63, and CK5/6 support squamous differentiation; use glandular and endothelial markers when needed. Lymphoepithelial carcinoma of skin Poorly differentiated SCC; intermediate metastatic potential Exceedingly rare; typically occurs on sun-exposed head and neck skin. Often grows rapidly but has no distinctive clinical appearance. Poorly differentiated SCC with tumor islands surrounded and infiltrated by lymphocytes and plasma cells. Poorly differentiated epithelial islands are surrounded and infiltrated by lymphocytes and variable plasma cells. The appearance may resemble undifferentiated nasopharyngeal carcinoma. Pancytokeratin, CK5/6, and p63 highlight epithelial elements that may be obscured by the lymphoid infiltrate. Cutaneous lymphoid infiltrate / lymphoma Cytokeratin-positive epithelial nests establish carcinoma. Inflamed SCC The prominent lymphoplasmacytic background and characteristic tumor-cell pattern support lymphoepithelial carcinoma. Clear cell squamous cell carcinoma Invasive or in situ SCC variant Usually occurs in older men on sun-damaged skin, especially the head and neck. Clinical appearance is generally indistinguishable from conventional SCC. Squamous carcinoma with clear-cell differentiation in at least 25% of neoplastic cells (proposed threshold). PAS-positive glycogen is a desirable feature. Malignant squamoid cells have abundant clear cytoplasm with cytoplasmic vacuolation. Focal keratinization may be present. Intracytoplasmic vacuoles are usually unilocular; clear material is often PAS-positive glycogen. Trichilemmal carcinoma Often deeply seated without epidermal connection; peripheral palisading, basement membrane prominence, and pilar keratinization may be present. Sebaceous carcinoma Multivacuolated cytoplasm and adipophilin/perilipin expression support sebaceous differentiation. Clear cell BCC BerEP4 expression and basaloid architecture support BCC. Porocarcinoma / hidradenocarcinoma Ductal differentiation highlighted by CEA and EMA supports adnexal carcinoma. Use p40/p63 and CK5/6 to support squamous differentiation; PAS with and without diastase can demonstrate glycogen. Spindle cell squamous cell carcinoma Poorly differentiated SCC; potentially aggressive Usually affects elderly men, most often older than 70 years. Occurs on sun-exposed face, head, neck, chest, and upper extremities. Presents as a rapidly growing raised or exophytic plaque or nodule, often ulcerated or bleeding. Closely packed fascicles of pleomorphic spindle cells with frequent mitoses. Establish epithelial differentiation, particularly when no conventional squamous component is present. Pleomorphic spindle cells form closely packed fascicles in the dermis. Keratinization is often absent. Severe solar elastosis and an overlying actinic keratosis or SCC in situ may provide clues. Tumor may extend into subcutis and along interlobular fat septa. p40, p63, 34βE12, CK5/6, and/or MNF116 support squamous differentiation. SOX10 helps exclude spindle-cell melanoma; CD45 helps exclude lymphoma. Atypical fibroxanthoma / pleomorphic dermal sarcoma These lack convincing epithelial marker expression; assess depth, necrosis, and perineural/vascular invasion. Spindle-cell melanoma SOX10 and other melanocytic markers support melanoma. Leiomyosarcoma SMA, desmin, and h-caldesmon support smooth-muscle differentiation. Squamous cell carcinoma with sarcomatoid differentiation Rare malignant SCC variant Usually occurs on sun-exposed face, head, neck, chest, and upper extremities. Typically presents with rapid growth; no unique clinical appearance is established. SCC with recognizable sarcomatoid differentiation, often chondroblastic, osteoblastic, rhabdomyosarcomatous, or myoid. A conventional keratinizing SCC component is usually present alongside a sarcomatous component. Heterologous elements may include cartilage, bone, skeletal muscle, or smooth-muscle-like differentiation. Extensive sampling may be required to identify the conventional SCC component. Epithelial markers may be retained in the conventional SCC component; the sarcomatoid component may show limited expression. Primary cutaneous sarcoma Identification of a conventional SCC component supports sarcomatoid SCC. Sarcomatoid SCC has specific heterologous differentiation rather than only spindle-cell morphology. Merkel cell carcinoma Other epidermal malignancies Aggressive primary cutaneous neuroendocrine carcinoma Predominantly affects elderly White patients; median age at diagnosis is approximately 75 years. Most often occurs on sun-damaged head and neck, followed by extremities and trunk. Presents as a rapidly growing flesh-colored or violaceous nodule or plaque; immunosuppression is a risk factor. Dermal small-blue-cell tumor with neuroendocrine cytology. Neuroendocrine immunophenotype with characteristic perinuclear dot-like cytokeratin staining. Exclude metastatic neuroendocrine carcinoma from another primary site. Dermal and/or subcutaneous tumor forms sheets, nests, or trabeculae of small-to-intermediate cells. Nuclei show finely stippled chromatin; mitoses and apoptotic bodies are numerous. Lymphovascular invasion is frequent. INSM1 and other neuroendocrine markers are positive. Cytokeratin 20 typically shows a perinuclear dot-like pattern. TTF1 is generally negative in Merkel cell carcinoma and helps distinguish many pulmonary small-cell carcinomas. Metastatic small-cell carcinoma Correlate clinically and use CK20, TTF1, neuroendocrine markers, and site-directed evaluation. Lymphoma Cytokeratin positivity supports carcinoma. SOX10 and melanocytic markers support melanoma. Clonal Merkel cell polyomavirus integration is present in approximately 80% of cases in regions with lower sun exposure. Virus-negative tumors commonly show TP53 and RB1 alterations and a UV-signature mutation profile. MCPyV large T-antigen IHC or molecular testing supports virus-positive MCC. Lower recurrence risk Superficial Broad-based buds attached to epidermis; superficial horizontal growth. Nodular Large rounded dermal nests with peripheral palisading and stromal retraction. Fibroepithelial Branching basaloid cords in prominent fibrous stroma (fibroepithelioma of Pinkus). Higher recurrence risk Micronodular Small compact nests with deeper infiltrative growth. Infiltrating Narrow angulated strands and irregular nests between collagen bundles. Sclerosing / morphoeic Thin strands and small nests in dense sclerotic stroma; poorly defined borders. Malignancy with unequivocal BCC and SCC differentiation. Rare variant With sarcomatoid differentiation BCC component associated with a malignant sarcomatoid component. With adnexal differentiation BCC showing morphologic differentiation toward adnexal structures. In situ SCC in situ (Bowen disease) Full-thickness epidermal atypia without dermal invasion. Conventional invasive Conventional SCC Invasive atypical squamous nests/tongues with variable keratinization. Well differentiated / low metastatic potential Deep, broad, club-shaped pushing tongues; minimal atypia. Histologic subtype Acantholysis creates pseudoglandular spaces within invasive tumor lobules. Lymphoepithelial carcinoma Poorly differentiated epithelial islands with dense lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate. Clear cell SCC Squamous carcinoma with clear-cell differentiation, proposed threshold ≥25%. Predominantly pleomorphic spindle cells; confirm epithelial differentiation. SCC with sarcomatoid differentiation SCC with chondroblastic, osteoblastic, rhabdomyosarcomatous, or myoid differentiation. All Risk / category Type Defining classification feature PathologyGPS / Skin / Epidermal Tumors Epidermal Tumors A morphology-first diagnostic reference to keratinocytic lesions, basal cell carcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, and primary cutaneous neuroendocrine carcinoma. Core rule Classify by architecture, cytologic differentiation, invasion, and recurrence or metastatic risk. For BCC and SCC, the histologic subtype is clinically consequential. Identify high-risk growth patterns and document invasion-related risk features. Diagnostic GPS: from epidermal pattern to classification Start with the clinical setting Age, site, sun exposure, immunosuppression, prior radiation/PUVA, arsenic exposure, and growth rate. Assess epidermal architecture Intraepidermal dysplasia, crateriform growth, basaloid nests, squamous nests, or a small-blue-cell pattern. Determine invasion Evaluate the dermoepidermal junction, depth, infiltrative pattern, perineural invasion, and lymphovascular invasion. Assign the subtype Separate low- and high-recurrence-risk BCC patterns; classify SCC in situ and invasive histologic variants. Use targeted ancillary tests BerEP4 for BCC in selected differentials; p40/p63/CK5/6 for SCC; neuroendocrine markers and CK20 for MCC. Basal cell carcinoma: histologic classification and recurrence risk The classification emphasizes recurrence risk. Superficial, nodular, and fibroepithelial BCCs are lower-risk patterns; micronodular, infiltrating, and sclerosing/morphoeic BCCs are higher-risk. Basosquamous carcinoma is also considered higher risk. Rare differentiation patterns are listed separately. Squamous cell carcinoma: classification by invasion and histologic subtype SCC classification distinguishes intraepidermal disease from invasive carcinoma and recognizes variants with distinctive architecture, differentiation, or clinical behavior. High-risk features in cutaneous SCC Tumor thickness greater than 2 mm. Clark level IV or V invasion. Perineural invasion; involvement of nerves ≥0.1 mm is associated with higher disease-specific mortality. Primary site on the ear or lip. Poor differentiation. Additional clinical risk factors include poorly defined borders, recurrence, immunosuppression, prior radiation or chronic inflammation, rapid growth, and neurologic symptoms. Lymphovascular invasion and high-risk histologic subtype should also be documented. Targeted immunohistochemistry and molecular findings BCC BerEP4 supports basaloid differentiation; Hedgehog pathway dysregulation (PTCH1/SMO) is central. p40/p63/CK5/6 and broad-spectrum keratins help establish epithelial lineage; SOX10 excludes melanoma. MCC INSM1/neuroendocrine markers and perinuclear dot-like keratin staining; CK20 is typically dot-like. Virus-positive MCC MCPyV large T-antigen IHC or molecular testing supports viral association. Virus-negative MCC TP53/RB1 alterations and UV-signature mutations are common. Entity reference Clinical profiles and diagnostic criteria Search by entity, site, morphology, immunophenotype, or molecular alteration. e.g. BerEP4, palisading, p40, acantholysis... bg-teal-700 text-white border border-slate-300 bg-white text-slate-600 Collapse View diagnostic profile − + Clinical profile Essential diagnostic criteria Histopathology Immunophenotype Differential diagnosis Molecular pathology No matching entity. Practical sampling and reporting checklist For BCC, identify and report all growth patterns, particularly micronodular, infiltrating, and sclerosing/morphoeic components; mixed patterns may occur. For basosquamous carcinoma, document unequivocal BCC and SCC differentiation and assess the transition between components. For SCC, document differentiation, tumor thickness/depth, anatomic level, perineural invasion (including nerve caliber), lymphovascular invasion, and margins. Sample the deep interface in crateriform and verruciform lesions to distinguish keratoacanthoma, verruca, verrucous SCC, and conventional invasive SCC. In spindle-cell lesions, search for an in situ or conventional squamous component and use a focused epithelial/melanocytic/mesenchymal panel. For suspected MCC, use neuroendocrine and keratin markers and exclude a metastatic neuroendocrine carcinoma from another primary site. Scope note: Content is based on the supplied WHO excerpt. Molecular findings are included only when diagnostically relevant; supportive immunostains should be interpreted with morphology and clinical context.

title: Melanocytic Tumors
content: use client Junctional, Compound, and Dermal Nevi Benign Benign; progression is very rare Common acquired nevi; widely distributed, especially trunk. Usually acquired during childhood through adulthood. Multiple small, symmetric, uniformly pigmented macules or papules are typical. Localized clonal proliferation of melanocytes forming nests of at least three nevus cells. Classify by anatomic distribution: junctional, compound, or dermal. Junctional nevus: nests are confined to the dermoepidermal junction. Compound nevus: junctional nests extend into the superficial dermis. Dermal nevus: melanocytes are confined to the dermis, often with maturation with depth. Cytologic atypia and mitotic activity are absent or minimal in ordinary nevi. SOX10, S100, Melan-A, and HMB45 highlight melanocytes; maturation with depth may be reflected by diminishing HMB45. Usually a single initiating MAPK-pathway alteration; BRAF p.V600E is common in acquired nevi. Dysplastic nevus Architectural disorder and cytologic atypia are greater; evaluate symmetry, circumscription, and lamellar fibroplasia. Melanoma Confluent growth, pagetoid spread, asymmetry, significant atypia, and lack of maturation raise concern. Nevus cells may mature with depth; assess the entire lesion and its symmetry. Simple Lentigo and Lentiginous Melanocytic Nevus Sun-exposed skin; lentiginous nevi may occur in various cutaneous sites. Small, flat, uniformly pigmented macule; simple lentigo is often associated with sun exposure. Increased basal epidermal melanocytes without the atypical confluent proliferation of melanoma in situ. Lentiginous nevus shows a benign junctional melanocytic proliferation. Simple lentigo: increased single melanocytes along the basal layer, often with elongated rete ridges. Lentiginous nevus: increased junctional melanocytes, sometimes with small nests; cytology remains bland. Melanocytic markers highlight the increased basal melanocytes; IHC is rarely needed in a typical lesion. No routine molecular testing; source describes benign nevi as generally carrying an initiating alteration without additional progression events. Melanoma in situ Confluent atypical melanocytes, pagetoid spread, and cytologic atypia favor melanoma. Pigmented actinic keratosis Keratinocyte atypia and solar damage, rather than a primary melanocytic proliferation. Clinical and histologic correlation is important in chronically sun-damaged skin. Dysplastic Nevus Benign nevus with atypical features; low progression risk Often trunk; may be multiple in patients with atypical mole phenotype. Usually acquired in adolescents or adults. Often larger and more irregularly pigmented than common acquired nevi. Junctional or compound nevus with architectural disorder and cytologic atypia. Assess symmetry, circumscription, bridging of rete ridges, and degree of melanocytic atypia. Irregular junctional nests and lentiginous melanocytic hyperplasia may be present. Bridging of adjacent rete ridges and lamellar fibroplasia are characteristic architectural clues. Cytologic atypia ranges from mild to severe; grading terminology varies. PRAME may be useful in selected difficult cases but is not independently diagnostic; interpret with morphology. Common initiating MAPK alterations may be present; progression-associated alterations are not a routine diagnostic assay. Marked confluent growth, extensive pagetoid scatter, significant atypia, and asymmetry favor melanoma. Common acquired nevus Lacks the architectural disorder and cytologic atypia. Atypia alone does not establish melanoma; interpret architecture and cytology together. Halo Nevus Benign; immune-mediated regression Usually trunk; can occur at multiple sites. Often occurs in children and young adults. A pigmented nevus is surrounded by a symmetric depigmented halo. Pre-existing nevus with a surrounding lymphocytic inflammatory response and melanocyte loss. Dense lymphocytic infiltrate may obscure nevus cells. Regressive lesions show fibrosis and reduced or absent melanocytes. SOX10 or Melan-A can help identify residual nevus cells in heavily inflamed lesions. No routine molecular testing. Melanoma with regression Asymmetry, atypical residual melanocytes, and an irregular rather than symmetric regressive pattern are concerning. Lichen planus-like keratosis Usually lacks a pre-existing melanocytic nevus. A halo phenomenon can occur around melanoma; evaluate the underlying melanocytic lesion carefully. Meyerson Nevus Benign nevus with eczematous inflammation Usually trunk or extremities. Eczematous, scaly erythematous halo around a pre-existing nevus. Benign melanocytic nevus accompanied by spongiotic dermatitis. Underlying nevus retains benign architecture and cytology. Overlying epidermis shows spongiosis, parakeratosis, and superficial inflammation. Melanocytic markers may outline the underlying nevus; no specific IHC profile. Halo nevus Prominent lymphocytic regression and depigmentation rather than spongiotic dermatitis. Inflamed melanoma Look for atypical melanocytes and architectural disorder independent of the inflammation. Do not let the inflammatory reaction obscure assessment of the underlying nevus. Recurrent Nevus Benign proliferation after partial removal At a prior biopsy or excision site, often trunk. Repigmentation within a scar after partial removal of a nevus. Residual/recurrent nevus proliferation associated with scar tissue and prior procedure history. Junctional melanocytic proliferation overlies dermal fibrosis. Melanocytes may extend over the scar but are generally confined to the scarred area. Cytologic atypia is usually limited; maturation may be present in residual dermal component. PRAME may assist in selected cases but does not replace comparison with the prior specimen. Recurrent melanoma Melanocytic proliferation extending beyond the scar, marked atypia, and lack of maturation favor melanoma. New primary melanoma Clinical mapping and comparison with the prior biopsy are essential. Always obtain the prior pathology report and correlate the exact biopsy site. Combined Nevus Benign combined melanocytic proliferation Commonly trunk and extremities. Usually a pigmented papule or plaque with variable color. Two or more morphologically distinct nevus components within one lesion. Common combinations include conventional nevus with blue nevus or deep penetrating component. Each component should retain its characteristic cytology and architecture. Use SOX10, S100, Melan-A, and HMB45 selectively to map components; staining patterns vary by component. Components may carry distinct initiating alterations; molecular comparison can clarify selected cases. Melanoma arising in a nevus Look for destructive growth, significant atypia, mitoses, and a malignant component. Melanocytoma Atypical component with additional pathogenic alterations may represent an intermediate neoplasm. Do not mistake juxtaposition of two benign components for tumor progression. WNT-Activated Deep Penetrating / Plexiform Melanocytoma Intermediate Intermediate melanocytic neoplasm; low but non-zero progression/metastatic concern Usually skin; may arise in association with a common acquired nevus. Often presents as a pigmented papule or nodule; age range is broad. Deep penetrating or plexiform melanocytic proliferation with characteristic morphology and WNT-pathway activation. Classify as melanocytoma when additional pathogenic alterations distinguish it from a conventional deep penetrating nevus. Symmetric, wedge-shaped or plexiform proliferation extends into deep dermis or subcutis. Pigmented spindle and epithelioid melanocytes may be arranged around adnexa and neurovascular structures. Cytologic atypia and mitotic activity are variable; assess deep component and maturation. Nuclear β-catenin supports WNT pathway activation. LEF1 may be positive; interpret in the morphologic context. WNT pathway activation through CTNNB1 or related alterations; secondary alterations may include ID1 activation. Deep penetrating nevus Usually lacks additional progression-associated alterations and has bland cytology. Marked atypia, destructive growth, brisk/atypical mitoses, and metastasis support melanoma. The term melanocytoma denotes an intermediate biological category, not a synonym for melanoma. Pigmented Epithelioid Melanocytoma Intermediate; regional nodal deposits may occur, with generally indolent behavior Usually skin; may occur at various cutaneous sites. Often a heavily pigmented papule or nodule in younger patients, but can occur at any age. Pigmented epithelioid/spindle melanocytic neoplasm with characteristic morphology and PRKAR1A pathway inactivation. Sheets and nests of heavily pigmented epithelioid and/or spindle melanocytes. Cells may have abundant cytoplasm and variable nuclear atypia. Melanophages and pigment may be prominent. Loss of PRKAR1A expression supports the diagnosis in an appropriate lesion. Melanocytic markers are positive; HMB45 expression may be retained. PRKAR1A inactivation is characteristic; often arises in a BRAF-mutated nevus background. Blue nevus Usually dendritic/spindle-cell morphology without the epithelioid component and PRKAR1A loss. Greater cytologic atypia, destructive growth, and high mitotic activity favor melanoma; nodal deposits alone do not automatically establish conventional melanoma. Regional lymph node involvement can occur; interpret behavior in the context of this intermediate entity. BAP1-Inactivated Melanocytoma Intermediate; generally low risk but warrants complete evaluation Cutaneous; may be associated with a conventional nevus. Often a skin-colored to pink papule or dome-shaped nodule; may be multiple in BAP1 tumor predisposition syndrome. Biphasic melanocytic lesion with a conventional nevus component and a population of large epithelioid cells showing BAP1 loss. Biphasic architecture: conventional nevus cells admixed with large epithelioid melanocytes. Large cells have abundant amphophilic or eosinophilic cytoplasm and vesicular nuclei with prominent nucleoli. Loss of nuclear BAP1 in the epithelioid component, with retained staining in internal controls. Melanocytic markers highlight both components. Biallelic BAP1 inactivation; a subset is associated with germline BAP1 tumor predisposition syndrome. Spitzoid melanoma BAP1 loss and characteristic biphasic morphology support BAP1-inactivated melanocytoma; assess for additional malignant features. Conventional nevus Lacks the distinct BAP1-deficient epithelioid component. Consider genetic counseling/testing when multiple lesions or relevant personal/family history is present. Spitz Nevus Benign Spitz-lineage tumor Can arise anywhere on the skin; often extremities or head and neck. Most common in children and adolescents; typically a rapidly growing pink, red, or pigmented papule. Symmetric, circumscribed proliferation of large spindle and/or epithelioid melanocytes with Spitz-lineage features. Symmetric wedge-shaped or dome-shaped lesion with maturation and Kamino bodies in some cases. Large spindle and/or epithelioid melanocytes form nests; epidermal hyperplasia may be present. Mitoses may occur but deep or atypical mitoses are concerning. p16 is usually retained; Ki-67 is generally low. ALK, ROS1, pan-TRK, or other fusion-directed IHC may be useful as screening in selected cases. Initiating HRAS mutation or kinase fusion involving ROS1, NTRK1, NTRK3, ALK, BRAF, MET, MAP3K8, or RET. Spitz melanocytoma Additional atypical features and secondary genetic events support intermediate classification. Spitz melanoma Marked atypia, destructive growth, deep/atypical mitoses, and progression-associated alterations support malignancy. Spitzoid conventional nevus/melanoma Morphologic resemblance alone does not establish Spitz lineage; defining molecular alterations are required. Do not use 'Spitzoid' as a synonym for a molecularly defined Spitz tumor. Spitz Melanocytoma (Atypical Spitz Tumor) Intermediate; metastatic risk is low but not zero Any cutaneous site; common in adolescents and young adults. Usually a papule or nodule; age range overlaps with Spitz nevus and Spitz melanoma. Spitz-lineage melanocytic neoplasm with atypical features beyond a conventional Spitz nevus but insufficient criteria for Spitz melanoma. Core rule Classify the lesion by its evolutionary state, not by cytologic atypia alone. A nevus generally carries an initiating driver; a melanocytoma has additional pathogenic alterations; melanoma shows malignant progression. WHO terminology in the supplied source reserves nevus for lesions with features of a single initiating alteration and uses melanocytoma for genetically intermediate lesions. Uveal melanocytoma is retained as a traditional exception, although biologically it has nevus-like features. Practical melanoma assessment and reporting checklist Document anatomic site, laterality, clinical size, and whether the lesion is on chronically sun-damaged, intermittently sun-exposed, acral, mucosal, or ocular skin. For invasive cutaneous melanoma, report Breslow thickness, ulceration, mitotic rate per mm², microsatellites, lymphovascular invasion, neurotropism, and margins as applicable. Distinguish radial growth phase from vertical growth phase; nodular melanoma has no identifiable radial growth phase. For melanocytomas and lesions of uncertain significance, describe the pathway and the specific intermediate entity; avoid using 'melanocytoma' without a qualifier. Use PRAME, p16, Ki-67, HMB45, BAP1, and molecular assays selectively; no single ancillary test replaces morphology and clinicopathologic correlation. For indeterminate lesions, consider descriptive terminology such as SAMPUS, IAMPUS, or MELTUMP when appropriate, and state the leading differential and staging-relevant findings. Correlate with prior biopsies, clinical photographs, imaging, and relevant personal/family history. Scope note: Based on the supplied WHO melanocytic neoplasm excerpt. Intermediate lesions have variable reproducibility and should be classified using integrated morphology, clinical context, and molecular findings. Ancillary tests are not stand-alone diagnostic criteria.

title: Nail Bed Epithelial Tumors
content: use client Onychomatricoma Fibroepithelial nail matrix tumor Benign Usually the nail matrix of fingers; toes are less commonly involved. Rare cases arise in the proximal nail fold or nail bed. Typically affects middle-aged adults, with a female predominance; pediatric cases are rare. Presents as a proximal subungual nodule with sharply demarcated nail plate thickening. The nail plate is often yellow, transversely overcurved, and associated with splinter hemorrhages. End-on inspection of the distal nail plate may reveal cavities; avulsed nail plate shows proximal honeycomb-like or wormwood-like channels. Pigmented lesions may present with longitudinal melanonychia; dorsal pterygium can occur. Matrical fibroepithelial proliferation that interdigitates with the thickened nail plate. A proximal stromal component is covered by reduplicated nail matrix epithelium. The epithelial-stromal projections form a characteristic finger-and-glove configuration. When available, the attached nail plate demonstrates multiple cavities and V-shaped keratogenous zones. The proximal component arises in the nail matrix and consists of variably fibrocellular, occasionally myxoid stroma. The stroma contains CD34-positive spindle cells. Reduplicated matrical epithelium interdigitates with the nail plate in a finger-and-glove pattern. Numerous V-shaped keratogenous zones are present. The nail plate is thickened and may contain loculated serum and hemorrhage. Papillated epithelium and dilated blood vessels may be present. Pleomorphic and proliferative patterns have been described; pigmented lesions may contain melanin in the epithelium and nail plate. CD34 highlights the stromal spindle cells. IHC is generally supportive rather than independently diagnostic; the characteristic architecture is decisive. Diagnostic molecular pathology is not relevant according to the supplied source. Superficial acral fibromyxoma May also express CD34, EMA, and CD99; lacks the characteristic matrical epithelial projections interdigitating with the nail plate. Angiofibroma Usually lacks the defining finger-and-glove matrical epithelial component. Neurofibroma Neural morphology and immunophenotype differ; it does not produce the characteristic nail plate channels. Perineurioma Perineurial differentiation does not reproduce the matrical fibroepithelial architecture. A nail clipping may contain diagnostic features, including a thickened plate, loculated serum, hemorrhage, and attached epithelium. Onychomycosis may occur secondarily and does not exclude an underlying onychomatricoma. The relationship of reported nail bed–based lesions to conventional onychomatricoma remains uncertain. Onychopapilloma Nail matrix / nail bed epithelial proliferation Benign; a single malignant case has been reported Most often affects fingernails. Originates in the distal nail matrix and extends along the nail bed to the hyponychium. Usually occurs in adults; pediatric cases are rare. Typically presents with longitudinal erythronychia or yellow discoloration, sometimes beginning as a wedge-shaped distal matrix lesion. Splinter hemorrhage and distal subungual hyperkeratosis, often forming a spicule, are common. May cause distal nail plate splitting, fissuring, notching, or onycholysis. Pigmented and leukonychic clinical patterns are recognized. Nail bed epithelial hyperplasia with proximal matrical metaplasia, interpreted in the appropriate longitudinal clinical pattern. The distal nail bed is often papillated and shows hypergranulosis. Characteristic distal subungual parakeratosis and hyperkeratosis may indent the undersurface of the nail plate. Subungual hemorrhage and multinucleated nail bed keratinocytes are desirable but not required findings. A full-thickness longitudinal nail unit specimen best demonstrates the diagnostic architecture. Proximally, slight nail matrix epithelial hyperplasia may be present. Matrical metaplasia of the nail bed shows matrix-like maturation with retained keratinocyte nuclei over eosinophilic superficial keratinocytes. Distally, the nail bed is hyperplastic and often papillated, with hypergranulosis. Multinucleated keratinocytes may occur in the mid to distal nail bed. Distal subungual parakeratosis and hyperkeratosis are characteristic and may indent the overlying nail plate. Subungual hemorrhage may be present. The supplied source does not identify a diagnostic immunohistochemical profile. Verruca vulgaris The main differential diagnosis; onychopapilloma shows a longitudinal nail unit pattern with matrical metaplasia and characteristic distal subungual hyperkeratosis. Squamous cell carcinoma in situ A single malignant onychopapilloma-like case has been reported; evaluate for significant cytologic atypia and full-thickness epithelial atypia. Subungual keratosis Correlate with the longitudinal erythronychia/yellow streak and the characteristic proximal-to-distal epithelial changes. A longitudinal specimen is important; tangential or fragmented sampling may obscure the proximal-to-distal pattern. Diagnostic epithelium may remain attached to the nail plate during avulsion or reflection. Do not equate multinucleated keratinocytes alone with malignancy. Ungual Fibrokeratoma Periungual fibrous / fibrokeratotic lesion Usually periungual; less often intraungual or subungual. Toenails are affected more often than fingernails, especially the hallux and thumb. An uncommon acquired lesion; epidemiologic data are limited. May occur sporadically or as multiple lesions in tuberous sclerosis, where it is termed a Koenen tumor. Presents as a rod-shaped, dome-shaped, flat, or branching periungual growth; dome-shaped and branching forms are most common. A longitudinal nail plate groove is a frequent associated finding. Trachyonychia, chromonychia, onycholysis, subungual hyperkeratosis, nail plate splitting, or hemorrhagic crust may occur. A periungual or nail-associated lesion composed of fibrovascular tissue with a fibrous core. A sausage-shaped configuration at low power is a useful clue. Epidermal hyperplasia with hyperkeratosis is desirable but may vary. Serum at the distal pole of the specimen is a supportive gross/microscopic finding. The lesion is composed of fibrovascular tissue. Low-power examination often shows a sausage-shaped tumor, sometimes with serum at its distal tip. The overlying epidermis may show hyperkeratosis, acanthosis, focal hypergranulosis, and irregular rete ridges. Reported stromal patterns include densely collagenous, fibroblast-rich, and edematous/hypocellular forms. In tuberous sclerosis–associated lesions, angiomatous, mixed, and fibrous patterns reflect the relative vascular and fibrous components. Immunohistochemistry is generally not required. CD34 expression in cellular angiofibroma and superficial acral fibromyxoma may complicate the differential diagnosis; interpret staining with morphology. Diagnostic molecular pathology is not clinically relevant according to the supplied source. Often CD34-positive and may be more myxoid and cellular; correlate with the characteristic site and architecture. Cellular angiofibroma Can be CD34-positive; assess the overall vascular and stromal pattern rather than relying on CD34 alone. Other periungual fibrous lesions The clinical distribution and fibrovascular core with epidermal hyperkeratosis support ungual fibrokeratoma. CD34 positivity is not specific and should not override the characteristic morphology. Multiple periungual fibrokeratomas should prompt clinical correlation for tuberous sclerosis. Onychocytic Matricoma Nail matrix epithelial / nail plate–producing tumor Localized within a single nail unit, with matrix epithelium and nail plate production. An unusual lesion with no established epidemiologic profile. Most reported cases present as longitudinal pachymelanonychia: a longitudinal hyperpigmented streak with nail plate thickening. Rare hypopigmented cases present as longitudinal pachyxanthonychia, with yellow discoloration and nail plate thickening. Nail plate thickening is present in at least part of the lesion. The nail matrix epithelium shows hyperplasia in one of the described patterns. A dermal or stromal component is absent; this is a key distinction from onychomatricoma. Depending on the pattern, look for epithelial whorls, papillomatous projections, or an expanded keratogenous zone. The acanthotic pattern shows matrix epithelial acanthosis and epithelial whorls that may differentiate into onychocytes. The papillomatous pattern shows papillomatous projections of matrix-derived epithelium associated with a thickened nail plate and intraplate cavities. The keratogenous pattern shows an expanded keratogenous zone that forms a channel along the nail plate. In the keratogenous pattern, maturation into onychocytes is delayed and occurs in the distal channel. All described patterns lack a dermal component. Onychomatricoma has a CD34-positive stromal component with reduplicated matrical epithelium interdigitating with the nail plate; onychocytic matricoma lacks a dermal component. Onychopapilloma is centered on distal nail matrix/nail bed with distal nail bed hyperplasia and subungual hyperkeratosis. Other nail plate–producing lesions Use the presence or absence of a stromal component and the specific matrix epithelial growth pattern. The absence of a dermal component is an important diagnostic discriminator. Clinical pigmentation is common but not obligatory; hypopigmented/yellow cases are reported. Subungual Keratoacanthoma Squamoproliferative nail bed tumor Uncertain behavior (ICD-O /1) Usually distal nail bed; may arise in the proximal nail fold and present as paronychia. Any digit may be involved, predominantly fingers. Rare tumor, usually in middle-aged adults; reported cases are more common in light-skinned individuals. Presents as a painful nodule with subungual hyperkeratosis and/or a nail spicule. May be solitary, multiple, eruptive, or familial; bone erosion or osteolysis can occur. Unlike conventional cutaneous keratoacanthoma, spontaneous resolution is uncommon and surgical treatment is often required. The subungual tumor of incontinentia pigmenti (STIP) occurs in women, typically at 15–35 years, in the late verrucous phase; nail dystrophy, destruction, or paronychia may be the presenting feature. A nodular or nodulocystic lesion with a lobular to cystic proliferation of eosinophilic keratinocytes. Numerous dyskeratotic keratinocytes, often clustered, are present. Adjacent and central hyperkeratosis is characteristic. A more vertical growth orientation and fewer eosinophils/neutrophils than conventional cutaneous keratoacanthoma are useful clues. Calcification of individual keratinocytes or corneocytes is a desirable, uncommon feature. Lobular proliferation of eosinophilic keratinocytes with a crateriform to cystic contour. Adjacent and central hyperkeratosis is present. Dyskeratotic keratinocytes are numerous and often form clusters, particularly in hyperkeratotic areas. The lesion may show a more vertical orientation than conventional cutaneous keratoacanthoma. Eosinophils and neutrophils are less prominent; fibrosis at the base may be absent. Rare cases show calcifying keratinocytes and corneocytes. In STIP, the tumor may displace the nail plate and cause dystrophy. Subungual squamous cell carcinoma may show higher p53 and Ki-67 expression than subungual keratoacanthoma; these findings are adjunctive and require morphologic correlation. NFKB1 amplification-associated protein expression was reported in a small series; it is not established as a routine diagnostic assay. STIP occurs in the setting of incontinentia pigmenti, which is caused by an X-linked IKBKG mutation affecting NEMO and NF-κB activation. HPV15 has been implicated in a small series of STIP cases. A small study reported NFKB1 and CTTN (formerly EMS1) amplification in subungual keratoacanthoma but not digital/subungual SCC; this finding is based on limited evidence and is not a routine test. Digital/subungual squamous cell carcinoma May show greater p53 and Ki-67 expression; assess cytologic atypia, infiltrative growth, and overall malignant features. Subungual epidermoid inclusion cyst A cystic lesion lined by squamous epithelium lacks the characteristic lobular keratoacanthoma-like proliferation with clustered dyskeratosis. Onycholemmal carcinoma A malignant nail unit epithelial tumor; distinguish by its cytologic and architectural features rather than the clinical appearance alone. STIP Histologically indistinguishable from subungual keratoacanthoma in the supplied source; young women with compatible findings warrant evaluation for incontinentia pigmenti. Subungual keratoacanthoma and STIP are histologically indistinguishable; clinical context is essential. Do not assume spontaneous regression as in conventional cutaneous keratoacanthoma. Severe pain and possible bone erosion make clinical and radiologic correlation important. The reported NFKB1/CTTN amplification data derive from a small study and should not be treated as a validated routine discriminator. All Uncertain behavior Uncertain PathologyGPS / Skin Tumors / Nail Unit Nail Bed Epithelial Tumors A morphology-first reference to nail matrix and nail bed epithelial lesions, emphasizing anatomic origin, longitudinal architecture, essential criteria, and practical differential diagnosis. Core diagnostic principle Identify the anatomic level and follow the lesion along the nail unit. Matrix-derived lesions may produce or alter the nail plate; distal nail bed lesions often create longitudinal streaks, hyperkeratosis, or nail plate changes. Anatomic orientation: where does the lesion arise? Proximal nail matrix Onychomatricoma; onychocytic matricoma. Look for matrical epithelium and nail plate production. Distal nail matrix → nail bed → hyponychium Onychopapilloma. A longitudinally oriented lesion; full-thickness longitudinal sampling is preferred. Periungual soft tissue Ungual fibrokeratoma. Usually periungual, especially toes/hallux; intraungual and subungual examples are less common. Distal nail bed / proximal nail fold Subungual keratoacanthoma and STIP. Painful nodular or nodulocystic squamoproliferation; proximal fold lesions may mimic paronychia. High-yield diagnostic distinctions Entity Anatomic origin / component Key clue Nail matrix + fibrous stroma Finger-and-glove epithelial projections; nail plate cavities Distal matrix / nail bed Matrical metaplasia, distal papillated hyperplasia, subungual hyperkeratosis Ungual fibrokeratoma Periungual fibrovascular tissue Sausage-shaped fibrovascular core Onychocytic matricoma Nail matrix epithelium Matrix epithelial hyperplasia without a dermal component Subungual keratoacanthoma Distal nail bed / occasionally proximal nail fold Lobular/cystic squamoproliferation with clustered dyskeratosis Sampling and orientation For suspected onychopapilloma, a full-thickness longitudinal nail unit excision best demonstrates the proximal-to-distal diagnostic pattern. For suspected onychomatricoma, submit the nail plate when possible; proximal cavities and attached interdigitating epithelium are diagnostically useful. For onychocytic matricoma, preserve the relationship between matrix epithelium and the thickened nail plate and assess for absence of a stromal component. For ungual fibrokeratoma, orient the lesion to identify the fibrovascular core and distal tip. For painful subungual nodules, correlate with imaging for possible bone erosion or osteolysis. Onychomatricoma vs. onychocytic matricoma Feature Stromal component Present; fibrocellular, CD34-positive spindle-cell stroma Absent Epithelium Reduplicated matrical epithelium Hyperplastic matrix epithelium with acanthotic, papillomatous, or keratogenous pattern Nail plate Interdigitating finger-and-glove projections with multiple cavities Thickened; may contain cavities or a longitudinal channel depending on pattern Key diagnostic clue Fibroepithelial architecture Matrix epithelial proliferation without dermal component Biopsy, reporting, and clinical correlation checklist Document the involved digit, exact nail unit compartment, longitudinal extent, and clinical nail plate change. State whether the specimen includes nail plate and whether the matrix, nail bed, hyponychium, or periungual tissue is represented. For longitudinal lesions, preserve and describe proximal-to-distal orientation. For subungual keratoacanthoma, correlate pain, growth rate, imaging, and possible bone erosion; assess carefully for SCC. When STIP is considered, recommend clinical correlation for incontinentia pigmenti, particularly in a young woman with compatible nail disease. Report margins and completeness of excision when assessable; complete excision is associated with low recurrence for onychomatricoma and onychopapilloma. Scope note: This page is based on the supplied WHO excerpt on nail bed epithelial tumors. The source describes five entities; no additional nail unit tumors have been added. Molecular findings reported in small series are identified as limited evidence and are not presented as routine diagnostic tests.
