title: Genetic Tumor Syndromes
content: use client Li-Fraumeni Syndrome (TP53-Associated Cancer Predisposition) Core Thoracic Tumor-Predisposition Syndromes A germline pathogenic TP53 variant in a patient or family with early-onset, multiple primary cancers, especially sarcoma, breast cancer, brain tumor, or adrenocortical carcinoma. Autosomal dominant cancer predisposition with a broad tumor spectrum and important implications for radiation exposure, surveillance, and family testing. Usually presents in childhood, adolescence, or young adulthood, although cancers may occur at any age. Affects both sexes; lifetime cancer risk is higher in females, partly because of breast cancer. Thoracic manifestations include lung adenocarcinoma (often in nonsmokers), thymic carcinoma, and mediastinal or cardiac sarcoma; these are uncommon relative to the core tumor spectrum. Patients may present with multiple primary malignancies or a striking family history of early-onset cancers. Identify a constitutional pathogenic or likely pathogenic TP53 variant by germline testing. Assess personal and family history against established LFS/Chompret clinical criteria; clinical criteria guide testing but do not replace molecular confirmation. Distinguish a germline variant from a somatic tumor variant or clonal hematopoiesis, particularly when variant allele fraction is low or testing uses blood-derived DNA. A variant of uncertain significance does not establish the syndrome. Thoracic tumors arising in LFS generally show the same histopathology as their sporadic counterparts. No syndrome-specific histologic pattern is established; the diagnostic clue is the clinical context of early-onset or multiple primary cancers. Tumor p53 immunohistochemistry may show aberrant overexpression or complete loss, but neither pattern establishes germline LFS. A tumor p53 abnormality must be followed by constitutional testing; somatic TP53 alterations are common in many cancers. Germline pathogenic variants in TP53 establish the molecular diagnosis. Tumor-only sequencing may identify a TP53 variant, but constitutional status requires confirmatory germline testing using an appropriate non-tumor specimen. EGFR activating alterations have been reported in LFS-associated lung adenocarcinomas, but they are not diagnostic of LFS. Do not diagnose LFS from tumor-only TP53 sequencing or p53 immunohistochemistry alone. Consider clonal hematopoiesis and mosaicism when a TP53 variant is detected in blood at an atypical allele fraction. Radiation-associated second malignancies are a relevant management concern; the syndrome itself does not change histologic classification of an individual tumor. BAP1 Tumor Predisposition Syndrome TP53-associated broad early-onset cancer spectrum, especially sarcoma and breast/brain/adrenocortical tumors, rather than the BAP1-associated combination of mesothelioma, melanocytic tumors, and RCC. Carney Complex LFS is defined by germline TP53 and early-onset malignancies; Carney complex is recognized by lentigines, myxomas, and endocrine manifestations, usually with PRKAR1A involvement. Germline BAP1 pathogenic variant with mesothelioma, uveal/cutaneous melanoma, renal cell carcinoma, or characteristic cutaneous melanocytic tumors, often at a younger age. Autosomal dominant predisposition to mesothelioma and several melanocytic and epithelial malignancies; confirmation requires germline testing. Typically recognized in adults; BAP1-associated mesothelioma is diagnosed at a younger median age (approximately 55–58 years) than sporadic mesothelioma. Affects both sexes. Thoracic hallmark is pleural mesothelioma; peritoneal mesothelioma also occurs. Other associated tumors include uveal and cutaneous melanoma, clear cell renal cell carcinoma, cholangiocarcinoma, basal cell carcinoma, and melanocytic BAP1-mutated atypical intradermal tumors (MBAITs). Demonstrate a heterozygous germline pathogenic or likely pathogenic BAP1 variant. Consider testing in patients with multiple BAP1-associated tumors or one such tumor plus a first- or second-degree relative with a BAP1-associated tumor. Loss of nuclear BAP1 expression in a tumor supports BAP1 pathway inactivation and may prompt germline evaluation, but does not by itself prove a hereditary syndrome. A variant of uncertain significance is not diagnostic. Mesotheliomas and other tumors arising in this syndrome are histologically similar to their sporadic counterparts. Cutaneous MBAITs are benign melanocytic neoplasms and may be a useful clinical clue to the syndrome. Loss of nuclear BAP1 staining in tumor cells, with retained staining in internal non-neoplastic controls, supports somatic BAP1 inactivation. BAP1 loss in mesothelioma or a melanocytic tumor is a screening clue for germline evaluation, not a substitute for germline testing. Confirm with germline BAP1 sequencing and deletion/duplication analysis on peripheral blood or another appropriate constitutional specimen. Most reported pathogenic germline variants are sequence variants; copy-number changes are less common. BAP1 loss in a tumor is not synonymous with BAP1 tumor predisposition syndrome; sporadic tumors may also lose BAP1. Do not use tumor IHC alone to classify a patient or relatives as germline carriers. BAP1 syndrome is characterized by mesothelioma, uveal/cutaneous melanoma, RCC, and MBAITs; LFS has a broader TP53-associated spectrum dominated by early-onset sarcomas and breast cancer. BAP1 syndrome is associated with mesothelioma and melanocytic/renal tumors; Carney complex features myxomas, lentigines, and endocrine tumors. Spotty lentiginous pigmentation plus cardiac or extracardiac myxomas, endocrine overactivity/neoplasia, or characteristic associated tumors. Autosomal dominant multisystem syndrome most often caused by PRKAR1A inactivation, with cardiac myxomas, pigmented lesions, and endocrine manifestations. Manifestations often begin around puberty; primary pigmented nodular adrenocortical disease commonly presents in the second or third decade. Affects both sexes; large cell calcifying Sertoli cell tumors occur in boys and men. Cardiac myxomas occur across the age spectrum and are present in more than half of affected individuals. Other sites include skin and mucosa, endocrine organs, testes, thyroid, breast, bone, and peripheral nerve sheath. Establish at least two major diagnostic criteria, or one major criterion plus a supplemental criterion, using accepted Carney complex criteria. Major manifestations include spotty pigmentation, cardiac/cutaneous/breast myxomas, primary pigmented nodular adrenocortical disease, acromegaly from GH-producing pituitary adenoma, large cell calcifying Sertoli cell tumor, thyroid tumors, psammomatous melanotic schwannoma, and osteochondromyxoma. A germline pathogenic PRKAR1A variant supports the diagnosis; absence of an identified variant does not exclude clinically established Carney complex. Evaluate for affected relatives and de novo disease. Cardiac and extracardiac myxomas have the same histologic features as their sporadic counterparts. Other associated neoplasms retain their site-specific morphology; the syndrome is recognized by the constellation of lesions rather than a single pathognomonic histologic pattern. Loss of PRKAR1A expression in a tumor may raise suspicion for Carney complex and should prompt germline evaluation. PRKAR1A immunohistochemistry is supportive rather than independently diagnostic. Germline inactivating PRKAR1A variants account for approximately two thirds of cases; sequencing detects most, with targeted deletion/duplication analysis identifying additional cases. A second susceptibility locus at 2p16 has been implicated, but the responsible gene remains unidentified. Do not confuse Carney complex with Carney triad, which is non-hereditary and comprises GIST, pulmonary chondroma, and paraganglioma. A cardiac myxoma, particularly if recurrent, multiple, or occurring in a young patient, should prompt assessment for Carney complex. Carney complex is defined by myxomas, spotty pigmentation, and endocrinopathy; LFS is defined by germline TP53 and a broad early-onset malignancy spectrum. Carney complex features cardiac/cutaneous myxomas and endocrine disease; BAP1 syndrome features mesothelioma, melanocytic tumors, and clear cell RCC. Germline EGFR p.T790M-Associated Lung Cancer Predisposition Additional Hereditary Thoracic Tumor-Predisposition Conditions A pretreatment lung adenocarcinoma or family history of lung adenocarcinoma with EGFR p.T790M detected before exposure to an EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor. Emerging autosomal dominant lung cancer predisposition associated with constitutional EGFR p.T790M; penetrance and lifetime risk remain incompletely defined. Reported across adulthood; the precise age distribution and lifetime penetrance are not established. Affects both sexes; lung adenocarcinoma may occur in never-smokers. Primarily involves the lung, often with adenocarcinoma. A family history of lung cancer or an EGFR p.T790M variant in a pretreatment specimen should raise suspicion. Identify EGFR p.T790M in a tumor or other specimen obtained before EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor therapy. Confirm constitutional status with germline testing; approximately half of de novo EGFR p.T790M findings have been estimated to be germline. Interpret p.T790M in the context of treatment history because it is a well-known acquired resistance mutation after EGFR inhibitor therapy. Familial penetrance and lifetime risk are not sufficiently characterized to use a definitive clinical threshold. Associated lung cancers are generally lung adenocarcinomas and are not defined by a unique histologic pattern. The tumor may harbor an additional EGFR-activating mutation. No syndrome-specific immunohistochemical profile is established; classify the lung tumor by conventional morphologic and immunophenotypic criteria. Germline EGFR p.T790M is the best-characterized variant in this emerging hereditary lung cancer predisposition. Other germline EGFR variants within or adjacent to the kinase domain have been reported as potential predisposition variants. Germline ERBB2 mutations have also been associated with rare familial lung cancer predisposition, but the clinical spectrum is less well characterized. Do not interpret EGFR p.T790M as germline without constitutional confirmation, particularly after EGFR inhibitor exposure. Do not infer a defined penetrance estimate or surveillance threshold from the limited available data. Peutz-Jeghers Syndrome Distinguish by the defining clinical tumor spectrum and confirmatory molecular finding. DICER1 Tumor Predisposition Syndrome Tuberous Sclerosis Complex Carney Triad Mucocutaneous pigmentation and gastrointestinal hamartomatous polyps with a germline STK11 pathogenic variant; lung carcinoma is an uncommon associated malignancy. Autosomal dominant STK11-associated syndrome with gastrointestinal polyposis, characteristic pigmentation, and increased risk of multiple carcinomas. Often recognized in childhood or adolescence because of pigmentation and gastrointestinal polyps; cancer risk increases with age. Thoracic manifestation is an increased risk of lung carcinoma, although it is not the defining tumor of the syndrome. Clinical presentation commonly includes perioral/buccal pigmentation and gastrointestinal polyps. Demonstrate a germline pathogenic STK11 variant, or establish the syndrome using accepted clinical criteria. Integrate characteristic mucocutaneous pigmentation and gastrointestinal hamartomatous polyposis with personal and family history. Do not diagnose the syndrome from lung carcinoma alone. Gastrointestinal polyps classically show arborizing smooth muscle extending into the lamina propria beneath the epithelium. Associated lung carcinomas are classified and evaluated according to their usual histologic criteria. No thoracic tumor-specific immunophenotype establishes Peutz-Jeghers syndrome. STK11/LKB1 loss in a tumor may support pathway inactivation but requires germline confirmation for hereditary classification. Germline pathogenic variants in STK11 (LKB1) establish the molecular basis of the syndrome. Do not confuse Peutz-Jeghers syndrome with other pigmentary or gastrointestinal polyposis syndromes; the STK11 result and characteristic polyp morphology are useful discriminators. Pleuropulmonary blastoma or lung cysts in a child, particularly with cystic nephroma, Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor, or thyroid neoplasia. Autosomal dominant predisposition caused by germline loss-of-function DICER1 variants, with a characteristic spectrum of pediatric and young-adult tumors. Most characteristic thoracic presentation is in infancy or childhood. Thoracic manifestations include pleuropulmonary blastoma and lung cysts. Associated tumors include cystic nephroma, Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor, and thyroid neoplasms. Identify a germline pathogenic loss-of-function DICER1 variant in an appropriate clinical context. Recognize pleuropulmonary blastoma as a major sentinel tumor and assess for associated neoplasms in other organ systems. A second, acquired DICER1 variant is commonly present in the tumor, often a missense alteration affecting the RNase IIIb domain. Pleuropulmonary blastoma has cystic, solid, or mixed patterns depending on tumor type and stage; interpret in the context of age and associated lesions. Lung cysts may be an early manifestation and warrant clinical correlation. No single immunohistochemical marker establishes DICER1 tumor predisposition syndrome; diagnosis is molecular and clinicopathologic. The typical mechanism is a germline loss-of-function variant with a second somatic hit in the tumor. The acquired second hit is often a missense variant in the DICER1 RNase IIIb domain. Do not assume every pediatric lung cyst is pleuropulmonary blastoma; integrate imaging, histology, age, and DICER1 status. Multisystem hamartomatous disease with characteristic skin, brain, kidney, cardiac, and pulmonary findings; consider TSC in pulmonary LAM or PEComa. Autosomal dominant disorder caused by TSC1 or TSC2 loss-of-function variants, resulting in mTOR pathway activation. Often recognized in infancy or childhood, although manifestations vary widely and may be diagnosed in adulthood. Thoracic manifestations include pulmonary lymphangioleiomyomatosis and PEComa; cardiac rhabdomyomas are strongly associated, especially in children. Other common sites include brain, skin, and kidneys. Establish clinical diagnosis using accepted major and minor features and/or identify a germline pathogenic TSC1 or TSC2 variant. Consider TSC in patients with LAM, pulmonary PEComa, or cardiac rhabdomyoma, particularly when additional multisystem findings are present. A pathogenic variant in either TSC1 or TSC2 is sufficient for molecular diagnosis. Pulmonary LAM shows proliferation of abnormal smooth muscle-like cells along lymphatics, vessels, and airways, often with cystic lung destruction. Pulmonary PEComas show perivascular epithelioid cell differentiation and may express melanocytic and smooth muscle markers. Cardiac rhabdomyomas are often multiple and may regress during childhood. LAM and PEComa typically express melanocytic markers (such as HMB45 or Melan-A) and smooth muscle markers, interpreted as a panel. No tumor immunostain alone establishes germline TSC. Germline loss-of-function variants in TSC1 or TSC2 disrupt the hamartin–tuberin complex and activate mTOR signaling. Tumor-specific second-hit inactivation may occur in TSC-associated lesions. LAM and PEComa can occur sporadically as well as in TSC; assess for clinical criteria and germline findings. Do not mistake the presence of a single TSC-associated tumor for a confirmed hereditary syndrome. The characteristic combination of gastrointestinal stromal tumor, pulmonary chondroma, and paraganglioma; this is not a hereditary syndrome. Non-hereditary tumor association, classically affecting young women, with SDHC promoter hypermethylation in associated tumors. Usually presents in adolescents or young adults; predominantly affects females. Pulmonary chondroma is the characteristic thoracic lesion. Associated tumors are gastrointestinal stromal tumor and paraganglioma. The complete triad may develop metachronously; not all components are necessarily present at initial diagnosis. Recognize the association of pulmonary chondroma, GIST, and paraganglioma; any two components strongly support the diagnosis in the appropriate setting. Establish each component by its own morphologic and immunophenotypic criteria. Do not require a germline pathogenic variant; Carney triad is non-hereditary. Pulmonary chondroma is a benign cartilage-forming tumor, often well circumscribed. GIST and paraganglioma show their respective conventional morphologic patterns. Use site-specific immunohistochemical panels for chondroma, GIST, and paraganglioma; no single immunophenotype defines the triad. SDHC promoter hypermethylation has been identified in the tumors; this is an epigenetic event rather than evidence of a germline SDHC mutation. Do not confuse Carney triad with Carney complex: the former is non-hereditary and features GIST, pulmonary chondroma, and paraganglioma; the latter is associated with PRKAR1A, myxomas, pigmentation, and endocrinopathy. All PathologyGPS · Thoracic Pathology Genetic Tumor-Predisposition Syndromes of the Thorax A practical diagnostic reference to hereditary and familial tumor-predisposition conditions with thoracic manifestations, emphasizing clinical recognition, essential diagnostic criteria, tumor morphology, immunohistochemistry, molecular confirmation, and key differential diagnoses. Diagnostic Approach: Recognize the Pattern, Confirm the Germline Finding 1. Identify the tumor pattern Consider age, multiplicity, unusual tumor combinations, and personal/family history. A thoracic tumor may be the first clue to a multisystem syndrome. 2. Separate tumor phenotype from syndrome diagnosis Histology and tumor IHC characterize the neoplasm; constitutional testing establishes a hereditary predisposition when indicated. 3. Interpret tumor sequencing cautiously A pathogenic variant detected in tumor-only sequencing may be somatic. Confirm constitutional status using an appropriate germline specimen. 4. Use IHC as a screening clue BAP1 or PRKAR1A loss may prompt germline evaluation, but neither alone establishes a hereditary syndrome. 5. Recognize non-hereditary associations Carney triad is non-hereditary and must be distinguished from PRKAR1A-associated Carney complex. 6. Refer for genetic counseling A confirmed germline pathogenic variant has implications for relatives, surveillance, and sometimes treatment selection. Critical principle: A tumor-associated alteration or abnormal IHC result does not by itself establish a germline syndrome. title: Heart Tumors
content: use client Papillary Fibroelastoma Benign Cardiac Neoplasms Small mobile endocardial lesion with branching avascular fibroelastic fronds. Usually adults aged 60–70 years; reported from neonates to older adults. No clear sex predilection. Usually arises on a left-sided valve, especially the aortic valve; may involve other endocardial surfaces. Often incidental; may cause embolic events, syncope, valvular obstruction, or sudden death. Endocardial-based papillary lesion composed of avascular fibroelastic fronds. Each frond is covered by a single layer of endothelium. Fibroelastic core is essential; papillary architecture may be obscured by fibrosis or thrombus. Delicate, branching papillary fronds have collagenous and elastic cores. Fronds may be fused by fibrosis or coated by surface thrombus. Grossly, the lesion may unfurl in fluid into a sea-anemone-like configuration. Surface endothelial cells express CD31, CD34, and factor VIII-related antigen. S100 may label scattered deeper dendritic cells; it is not a defining marker. Lambl excrescence Simple, usually nonbranching filiform strands on the valve closure line; fibroelastoma has more complex branching and may arise away from the closure line. Cardiac myxoma Myxoma contains stellate or spindle myxoma cells in myxoid matrix; fibroelastoma has avascular fibroelastic fronds and is usually valvular. Infective or nonbacterial thrombotic vegetation Vegetations are composed of fibrin, platelets, inflammation, and/or organisms rather than orderly endothelial-covered fibroelastic fronds. Valvular calcification Calcification is mineralized and lacks branching endothelial-covered fronds. Cardiac Fibroma Bland fibroblasts in dense collagenous stroma, often with microcalcifications and ventricular location. Cardiac Rhabdomyoma Glycogen-rich cardiac myocytes with spider cells, commonly in infants and associated with TSC1/TSC2. Adult Cellular Rhabdomyoma Adult-type proliferation of granular eosinophilic mature striated muscle cells without classic spider cells. Cardiac Lipoma and Lipomatous Hypertrophy of the Atrial Septum Mature adipose lesion; distinguish circumscribed lipoma from nonencapsulated septal fat expansion sparing the fossa ovalis. Lipomatous Hamartoma of the Atrioventricular Valve Nonencapsulated mature adipose tissue admixed with native AV valve fibroconnective tissue and thin-walled vessels. KRAS exon 2 or 3 driver mutations occur in a subset (reported in up to approximately 80%); testing is not required for diagnosis. Do not use 'giant Lambl excrescence' as a synonym when the lesion has complex branching fibroelastic fronds. Cardiac Myxoma Intracavitary myxoid neoplasm, usually attached to the left atrial side of the fossa ovalis. Most common in adults in the fourth to seventh decades; may occur at any age. Approximately twice as common in women as men in sporadic cases. Usually arises in the left atrium near the fossa ovalis; right atrial, ventricular, and multicentric tumors occur. May cause obstruction, embolization, constitutional symptoms, or sudden death. Appropriate intracavitary endocardial location, usually with a stalk. Bland stellate, ovoid, or plump spindle myxoma cells in abundant myxoid stroma. Perivascular rings or cords of myxoma cells and calretinin reactivity are desirable supportive findings. Myxoma cells occur singly or in cords, nests, rings, or perivascular cuffs. Abundant mucopolysaccharide-rich myxoid matrix is Alcian blue positive. Hemorrhage, hemosiderin-laden macrophages, Gamna–Gandy bodies, fibrosis, calcification, and thrombosis may occur. Villiform tumors may be friable and embolize; solid tumors are more smooth and globular. Calretinin is positive in most myxoma cells. SMA, desmin, S100, synaptophysin, and NSE may show variable staining. Loss of PRKAR1A expression should prompt evaluation for Carney complex. Organizing thrombus Thrombus shows laminated fibrin, organization, and recanalization without characteristic myxoma cells in myxoid matrix; calretinin supports myxoma. Papillary fibroelastoma Usually valvular with avascular endothelial-covered fibroelastic fronds; myxoma is typically chamber-based with myxoid matrix and myxoma cells. Calcified amorphous tumor Predominantly calcified nodules in fibrinous material rather than myxoma cells in myxoid stroma. Metastatic adenocarcinoma involving a myxoma True infiltrative malignant glands with epithelial markers differ from rare bland entrapped or heterotopic glands; correlate clinically. Cardiac fibrin-associated DLBCL Atypical large B cells are confined to fibrin/thrombus within or on a myxoma rather than forming the myxoma itself. PRKAR1A alterations occur in Carney complex-associated tumors and in a subset of sporadic myxomas. Germline PRKAR1A testing is appropriate when clinical features suggest Carney complex. A non-left atrial or multiple myxoma should raise suspicion for Carney complex. Do not mistake a fibrin-associated lymphoma arising in a myxoma for diffuse lymphoma involving the heart. Well-circumscribed, often calcified ventricular mass composed of bland fibroblasts in collagenous stroma. Approximately 90% occur in children; one third present before age 1 year. No sex predilection. Usually involves the ventricular septum or ventricular free wall, more often left than right. May cause arrhythmia, obstruction, murmur, or heart failure. Nodular collection of bland fibroblasts in variably collagenized stroma. Ventricular location and microcalcifications are supportive. Entrapment or infiltration of adjacent cardiac muscle may occur and does not by itself imply malignancy. Bland spindle fibroblasts are embedded in dense collagenous or hyalinized stroma. Cellularity tends to decrease and collagen increase with patient age. Microcalcifications and elastic fibers may be present. Adjacent myocardium may be entrapped at the periphery. Lesional cells show myofibroblastic SMA expression. Desmin is generally absent or limited; interpret in conjunction with morphology. Cardiac rhabdomyoma Rhabdomyoma is composed of glycogen-rich myocytes with spider cells and is often multiple; fibroma is collagen-rich and commonly calcified. Hamartoma of mature cardiac myocytes Hamartoma contains enlarged disorganized striated cardiomyocytes; fibroma is a fibroblastic/collagenous mass. Mesenchymal cardiac hamartoma Hamartoma is a disorganized admixture of multiple mature tissue types rather than a predominantly collagenous fibroblastic nodule. Cardiac leiomyosarcoma Leiomyosarcoma shows atypical intersecting smooth-muscle fascicles, mitoses, and often necrosis; fibroma is cytologically bland. Avascular, endothelial-covered branching fibroelastic fronds on an endocardial surface. Bland stellate or spindle myxoma cells in abundant myxoid matrix, usually attached near the fossa ovalis. PTCH1 alterations may occur in sporadic tumors or in the setting of germline PTCH1-associated Gorlin syndrome. Myocardial entrapment at the edge of an otherwise bland fibroma is not equivalent to destructive malignant invasion. Most common cardiac tumor of infancy and childhood; often multiple and associated with tuberous sclerosis. Usually detected prenatally, in infancy, or early childhood. No consistent sex predilection. Usually arises in ventricular myocardium; atrial and intracavitary lesions also occur. May cause arrhythmia, conduction abnormalities, outflow obstruction, or heart failure; many regress spontaneously. Benign proliferation of cardiac striated myocytes with characteristic glycogen-rich spider cells. Often multiple and associated with tuberous sclerosis complex. Intramyocardial or intracavitary location and typical imaging support the diagnosis. Large polygonal myocytes have clear or vacuolated cytoplasm with radiating strands extending to the cell membrane (spider cells). Cells may be arranged in sheets or nodules within myocardium. Glycogen-rich cytoplasm is PAS positive and diastase sensitive. Regression with age may produce residual fibrous tissue. Desmin, muscle-specific actin, myoglobin, and other skeletal/cardiac muscle markers are positive. HMB45 and melanocytic markers are not expected; use a focused panel if PEComa is considered. Cardiac fibroma Fibroma is collagen-rich with bland fibroblasts and often calcification; rhabdomyoma contains spider cells and glycogen-rich myocytes. Adult cellular rhabdomyoma Adult cellular rhabdomyoma is a distinct adult-type lesion with granular eosinophilic cells, usually without classic spider cells. Hamartoma shows enlarged bizarre mature myocytes with disorganization and vacuolization, but lacks the characteristic spider-cell population. Conduction system hamartoma Conduction system hamartoma comprises histiocytoid/Purkinje-type cells tracking along conduction tissue and often involves valve cusps. Contains multiple mature mesenchymal and cardiac tissue types rather than a relatively uniform rhabdomyocyte proliferation. TSC1 or TSC2 loss activates mTORC1 and underlies the association with tuberous sclerosis complex. Consider germline evaluation when clinical features or family history suggest tuberous sclerosis. Do not confuse spontaneous regression with sampling-related disappearance; correlate with age, imaging, and TSC status. Rare adult cardiac mass of large granular eosinophilic striated muscle cells, often atrial or ventricular. Predominantly adults; reported in both sexes. May arise in atrial or ventricular myocardium. May be incidental or present with obstruction, arrhythmia, or heart failure. Well-circumscribed or infiltrative proliferation of mature striated muscle cells with abundant granular eosinophilic cytoplasm. Cells show skeletal/cardiac muscle differentiation and lack the classic spider-cell pattern of childhood rhabdomyoma. Large polygonal cells have abundant granular eosinophilic cytoplasm and centrally located nuclei. Cross-striations may be demonstrable. Mature muscle cells are arranged in sheets or bundles; cytologic atypia and mitotic activity are not prominent. Desmin, myoglobin, and muscle-specific markers are positive. Mitochondrial markers may highlight granular cytoplasm. Childhood rhabdomyoma typically shows glycogen-rich spider cells, often multiple and TSC-associated; adult cellular rhabdomyoma has granular eosinophilic cells. Hamartoma shows bizarre enlarged myocytes, disorganized whorls, and interstitial fibrosis rather than a relatively uniform granular-cell proliferation. Cardiac granular cell tumor Granular cell tumor is S100/SOX10 positive and lacks convincing striated muscle differentiation. Fibroma is composed of fibroblasts in collagen and lacks myocyte marker expression. No defining recurrent molecular alteration is established. Distinguish a circumscribed mature-fat neoplasm from nonencapsulated fat expansion of the atrial septum. Usually adults; lipomatous hypertrophy is most often recognized in older or overweight adults. Lipoma may occur in any cardiac chamber, myocardium, or pericardium; lipomatous hypertrophy characteristically involves the interatrial septum while sparing the fossa ovalis. Often incidental; large lesions may cause obstruction or arrhythmia. Lipoma: circumscribed mass of mature adipocytes, usually with a capsule or discrete border. Lipomatous hypertrophy: nonencapsulated, unencapsulated accumulation of mature and brown fat in the interatrial septum, classically sparing the fossa ovalis and producing a dumbbell configuration. Exclude atypical stromal cells, lipoblasts, and infiltrative atypical lipomatous tumor/well-differentiated liposarcoma. Lipoma consists of mature adipocytes with uniform size and no atypical stromal cells. Lipomatous hypertrophy shows mature adipose tissue admixed with hypertrophic cardiac myocytes and brown-fat cells. Lipomatous hypertrophy is nonencapsulated and centered in the atrial septum. S100 highlights adipocytes; desmin and myoglobin highlight admixed cardiomyocytes in lipomatous hypertrophy. MDM2 and CDK4 should be negative in ordinary lipoma/lipomatous hypertrophy; amplification testing is appropriate if atypical lipomatous tumor is suspected. Lipomatous hamartoma of the atrioventricular valve Valve hamartoma contains adipocytes mixed with native valve mesenchymal elements and lacks a capsule; it is localized to an AV valve. Lipoma A circumscribed, usually encapsulated mature-fat mass contrasts with nonencapsulated septal lipomatous hypertrophy. Well-differentiated liposarcoma Atypical hyperchromatic stromal cells, lipoblasts, and MDM2 amplification support well-differentiated liposarcoma; these are absent in benign lipomatous lesions. Contains a heterogeneous mixture of myocardium, vessels, nerves, smooth muscle, and fat rather than predominantly adipose tissue. Lipomatous hypertrophy may harbor molecular alterations similar to those in lipoma; molecular findings support a clonal process in some cases but are not required for diagnosis. Rare nonencapsulated valve lesion composed of mature fat admixed with native atrioventricular valve mesenchymal tissues. Reported across a wide age range, approximately 2–76 years. No established sex predilection. Arises in an atrioventricular valve, usually as a localized valvular lesion. May be incidental or cause valvular dysfunction or obstruction. Mature adipocytes admixed with native AV valve components, including fibroconnective tissue and thin-walled vessels. Absence of a fibrous capsule is a useful distinguishing feature. No atypical stromal cells, lipoblasts, or malignant features. Mature adipose tissue is intermingled with fibrous connective tissue and thin-walled vasculature native to the valve. The lesion lacks a discrete fibrous capsule. Cytologic atypia and mitotic activity are absent. Adipocytes express S100. Native valve stromal and vascular components show their expected lineage markers; no specific IHC profile is required. Cardiac lipoma Lipoma is usually a circumscribed/encapsulated mature-fat neoplasm; lipomatous valve hamartoma is nonencapsulated and contains native valve mesenchymal elements. Lipomatous hypertrophy of the atrial septum Occurs in the interatrial septum, classically sparing the fossa ovalis, and contains brown fat and hypertrophic cardiomyocytes. Shows atypical stromal cells and often MDM2 amplification; these are absent in lipomatous hamartoma. Shows a broader admixture of cardiac muscle, nerves, smooth muscle, vessels, and adipose tissue, usually in ventricular myocardium. No clinically useful defining molecular alteration is established. Hamartoma of Mature Cardiac Myocytes Cardiac Hamartomatous and Developmental Lesions Discrete nodular collection of enlarged, disorganized mature cardiomyocytes with vacuolization and bizarre nuclei. Usually occurs in younger patients; median age approximately 24 years, reported from infancy to 76 years. Approximately two thirds occur in men. Usually ventricular; atrial lesions are reported. Often incidental, but may cause palpitations, syncope, chest pain, arrhythmia, or sudden death. Discrete nodular collection of enlarged, disorganized cardiac myocytes forming a myocardial mass. Myocytes show striations, sarcoplasmic vacuolization, and nuclear enlargement/atypia without proliferative activity. Interstitial fibrosis is characteristic. Enlarged striated cardiomyocytes are arranged in disorganized whorls or a herringbone-like pattern. Sarcoplasmic vacuolization and bizarre nuclei are common. Interstitial fibrosis is present; fat and nerves may be intermixed. Ki-67 proliferation is very low or absent. Desmin, troponin, actin, and myosin highlight cardiac muscle differentiation. Ki-67 is very low, supporting a nonproliferative hamartomatous lesion. Rhabdomyoma shows spider cells with glycogen-rich clear cytoplasm, often in infants and with TSC; mature myocyte hamartoma shows enlarged bizarre myocytes and fibrosis. Fibroma is a fibroblastic collagenous mass and lacks a dominant population of striated myocytes. Mesenchymal hamartoma contains a complex mixture of multiple mature tissues, not predominantly disorganized hypertrophic cardiomyocytes. Adult cellular rhabdomyoma has uniform granular eosinophilic muscle cells rather than bizarre, vacuolated myocytes in disorganized whorls. Conduction System Hamartoma Multifocal subendocardial proliferation of histiocytoid/Purkinje-type cells tracking along the cardiac conduction system. Cystic Tumor of the Atrioventricular Node Endodermal inclusion cyst centered in the atrioventricular septum within the triangle of Koch. No established diagnostic molecular alteration; a nonproliferative profile is characteristic. Mesenchymal Cardiac Hamartoma Benign disorganized admixture of mature cardiac and mesenchymal tissues within ventricular myocardium. Reported in adults of both sexes; age range is not well defined. Occurs in ventricular septum and free walls. May cause dyspnea, fatigue, syncope, ventricular arrhythmia, or sudden death. Admixture of mature cardiac myocytes and multiple mesenchymal components in a disorganized architecture. Low mitotic activity, absence of necrosis, and lack of significant cytologic atypia support benign behavior. Mature cardiomyocytes, smooth muscle, fibroblasts, vessels of varying caliber, nerves, fibrous tissue, and adipose tissue are variably admixed. Cardiomyocytes may show hypertrophy, myocytolysis, and haphazard arrangement. Vessels may show intimal myxoid narrowing. Inflammatory cells may be scattered; necrosis and significant atypia are absent. Desmin, myoglobin, and other muscle markers label cardiomyocytes. SMA highlights smooth muscle and myofibroblastic components. CD31 and ERG highlight vascular endothelium; S100/SOX10 may highlight neural elements. Predominantly enlarged, disorganized cardiomyocytes with vacuolization and fibrosis, without the broad mesenchymal admixture. Predominantly bland fibroblasts in collagenous stroma, often calcified; lacks the diverse mature tissue components. Cardiac lipoma / lipomatous hypertrophy Predominantly mature adipose tissue; does not show the complex admixture of myocardium, smooth muscle, vessels, and nerves. Glycogen-rich spider cells, often in infants and associated with TSC, rather than a polymorphic mature-tissue hamartoma. No established diagnostic molecular alteration is known. Cardiac Hemangiomas Benign Vascular Tumors Benign vascular tumor with capillary, cavernous, or arteriovenous architecture. Can occur from fetal life through old age; approximately 10% occur in children and some are diagnosed prenatally or in infancy. Slight male predominance. May arise in endocardium, myocardium, or pericardium; ventricular free walls are common, while congenital lesions often involve the right atrium. Usually incidental; may cause dyspnea, palpitations, arrhythmia, effusion, hemopericardium, or tamponade. Benign proliferation of vascular channels lined by bland endothelial cells. Recognize capillary, cavernous, and arteriovenous patterns; mixed patterns occur. No significant endothelial atypia, destructive growth, or atypical mitotic activity. Capillary type: small thin-walled vessels clustered around a larger feeder vessel. Cavernous type: dilated blood-filled vascular spaces separated by fibrous septa. Arteriovenous type: admixture of thick-walled arteries and veins with intervening vascular channels. Thrombosis, hemorrhage, and secondary fibrosis may occur. Endothelial cells express CD31, CD34, ERG, and factor VIII-related antigen. ERG and CD31 are useful to confirm endothelial differentiation. Cardiac angiosarcoma Angiosarcoma shows infiltrative anastomosing vascular channels or solid atypical endothelial cells, pleomorphism, mitoses, and often necrosis. Epithelioid hemangioendothelioma Shows cords/nests of epithelioid endothelial cells in myxohyaline stroma and characteristic molecular fusions; hemangioma is cytologically bland. Endocardial papillary fronds with fibroelastic cores rather than a true vascular proliferation. Contains multiple mature tissue types, including vessels, myocardium, nerves, and fat, rather than a predominantly vascular neoplasm. No defining molecular alteration is required for diagnosis. Usually presents in infancy; more than 60% are diagnosed in the first year and it is extremely rare after age 2 years. Female predominance (male-to-female ratio approximately 1:3). Involves the sinoatrial and atrioventricular conduction systems, predominantly subendocardially; valve cusps may also be involved. Arrhythmias, conduction abnormalities, sudden death, or presentation initially labeled as sudden infant death syndrome. Collections of pale eosinophilic Purkinje-type cells distributed along the endocardium and cardiac conduction system. Multifocal distribution and involvement of valve cusps support the diagnosis. Exclude rhabdomyoma and other histiocytoid lesions. Large polygonal histiocytoid cells have granular eosinophilic sarcoplasm containing glycogen and lipid. Lesional cells are interspersed among conduction system fibers. Ultrastructurally, abundant abnormal mitochondria displace myofibrils to the cell periphery. Muscle markers including desmin and muscle-specific actin are positive. Mitochondrial stains may highlight the abundant abnormal mitochondria. NDUFB11-related immunohistochemical/genetic findings may support selected cases but are not routine. Rhabdomyoma forms discrete myocardial nodules with spider cells and is often TSC-associated; conduction system hamartoma tracks along conduction tissue and may involve valve cusps. Usually an adult mass-forming lesion of granular eosinophilic striated muscle cells, not an infantile conduction-system proliferation. Shows enlarged disorganized striated myocytes with bizarre nuclei and fibrosis rather than histiocytoid Purkinje-type cells along conduction tissue. Contains diverse mesenchymal tissues and usually forms a ventricular mass. NDUFB11 or other NDUF-family gene mutations have been reported and may support the diagnosis in selected cases; testing is not widely used clinically. Mean age approximately 38 years; reported from birth to 95 years. More common in women. Located in the triangle of Koch/AV septum. May cause palpitations, syncope, dizziness, partial or complete heart block, or sudden cardiac death. Endodermal inclusion forming a cystic lesion within the atrioventricular septum. Cyst lining is bland and may be columnar, transitional, or squamous. No significant cytologic atypia and mitoses are rare. Cysts are lined by columnar, transitional, or squamous epithelium; goblet and sebaceous cells may occur. Lining cells are bland, with rare mitoses. Mucin is demonstrable by Alcian blue and PAS stains. Cytokeratin AE1/AE3, CK5, and CEA are positive in the epithelial lining. Scattered cells may express serotonin, chromogranin, or calcitonin. Mesothelial, endothelial, and lymphatic markers are negative. Mesothelial cyst Mesothelial cysts express calretinin, WT1, and D2-40; AV node cyst lining is epithelial and typically cytokeratin/CEA positive. Lymphangioma Shows endothelial-lined lymphatic spaces with D2-40/ERG positivity rather than epithelial cyst lining. Myxoma is a solid intracavitary myxoid neoplasm with calretinin-positive myxoma cells, not a bland epithelial cyst. Composed of histiocytoid Purkinje cells tracking along conduction tissue, not an epithelial-lined cyst. Nodular enlarged, disorganized striated cardiomyocytes with vacuolization, bizarre nuclei, and interstitial fibrosis. No clinically relevant molecular alteration is established. Cardiac Angiosarcoma Primary Cardiac Sarcomas High-grade malignant endothelial tumor, usually arising in the right atrium and often associated with hemorrhagic pericardial effusion. Usually adults in the fourth to sixth decades; broad reported age range. More common in men. Most often arises in the right atrium/atrioventricular groove, with frequent extension into adjacent chambers and pericardium. Dyspnea, chest pain, syncope, right-sided heart failure, arrhythmia, hemopericardium, or tamponade; metastases often involve lung, liver, brain, and bone. Malignant neoplasm with vascular differentiation demonstrated morphologically and/or immunophenotypically. Infiltrative vasoformative channels or solid epithelioid/spindle-cell growth with significant atypia. Endothelial lineage must be established and metastatic angiosarcoma excluded clinically. Anastomosing irregular vascular channels lined by pleomorphic hyperchromatic endothelial cells are typical. Vascular spaces may become slit-like or inconspicuous, producing solid spindle-cell areas. Epithelioid areas contain plump polygonal cells in cords, nests, or papillae. Hemorrhage and necrosis are common; biphasic conventional and epithelioid patterns may coexist. CD31 and ERG are the most useful endothelial markers; CD34 and factor VIII-related antigen may also be positive. Cytokeratin may be expressed, particularly in epithelioid areas, and does not exclude angiosarcoma. Cardiac hemangioma Hemangioma has bland endothelial cells and well-formed benign vascular channels without destructive invasion, marked atypia, or necrosis. Usually has cords/nests of epithelioid cells in myxohyaline stroma and defining fusion; angiosarcoma is more overtly high grade and vasoformative. Metastatic angiosarcoma Exclude a cutaneous, breast, hepatic, or other primary by clinical history and imaging. Undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma UPS lacks convincing endothelial differentiation; angiosarcoma expresses ERG/CD31 and may show vasoformation. Shows smooth-muscle fascicles and desmin/SMA/h-caldesmon expression rather than endothelial differentiation. Cardiac Undifferentiated Pleomorphic Sarcoma High-grade pleomorphic spindle/epithelioid sarcoma, usually a left atrial mass, diagnosed only after excluding definable lines of differentiation. No single defining molecular alteration is required for diagnosis. POT1 alterations have been reported in a subset of familial/Li–Fraumeni-like contexts; assess clinical/family history when appropriate. Cardiac Leiomyosarcoma Malignant smooth-muscle tumor, most often arising in the left atrium. Median age approximately 48 years; reported from infancy to older adulthood. Usually arises from the left atrial free wall; right atrial and ventricular tumors occur. Left-sided tumors may cause dyspnea, hemoptysis, and atrial fibrillation; right-sided tumors may cause edema and ascites. Malignant spindle-cell neoplasm with intersecting fascicles of eosinophilic cells and blunt-ended nuclei. Moderate-to-marked nuclear atypia, mitotic activity (including atypical forms), and often necrosis. Smooth-muscle differentiation must be confirmed immunohistochemically. Long intersecting fascicles of spindle cells have pale to brightly eosinophilic fibrillary cytoplasm. Nuclei are plump and blunt-ended with variable pleomorphism. Tumors are usually hypercellular; myxoid, hyalinized, or fibrotic areas may occur. Mitotic figures and tumor necrosis are common in high-grade tumors. SMA, desmin, and h-caldesmon support smooth-muscle differentiation. Calponin may be positive; use a panel because SMA alone is nonspecific. UPS lacks a convincing specific line of differentiation; leiomyosarcoma shows smooth-muscle fascicles and diffuse desmin/h-caldesmon. Synovial sarcoma May show spindle-cell fascicles but is supported by SS18::SSX fusion and TLE1/keratin expression. Angiosarcoma Shows malignant endothelial channels or epithelioid vascular differentiation with ERG/CD31 positivity. Bland fibroblasts in collagenous stroma without significant atypia, mitoses, or smooth-muscle phenotype. No defining recurrent molecular alteration is established; molecular testing is mainly used to exclude mimics such as synovial sarcoma. Mean age approximately 50–55 years; no sex predilection. Most often arises in the left atrium, commonly posterior or lateral wall; may involve atrial appendage, septum, or mitral valve. Presents with dyspnea, pulmonary congestion, arrhythmia, heart failure, fever, constitutional symptoms, or metastatic disease. High-grade pleomorphic spindle and/or epithelioid sarcoma involving the heart. No convincing morphologic, immunophenotypic, or molecular evidence of a specific sarcoma such as leiomyosarcoma or synovial sarcoma. Exclude pulmonary artery intimal sarcoma extending into the heart and metastatic sarcoma. Markedly pleomorphic spindle and epithelioid cells in sheets, fascicles, or haphazard arrays. Mitotic activity is usually brisk and necrosis is common. Myxoid areas with curvilinear vessels may mimic myxofibrosarcoma. Heterologous malignant bone or cartilage may be present. Surface fibrin and hemorrhage may be prominent. No lineage-specific immunophenotype; broad panel should exclude endothelial, smooth-muscle, epithelial, melanocytic, and hematolymphoid differentiation. ERG/CD31, desmin/h-caldesmon, broad-spectrum keratin, and lymphoid markers are selected according to morphology. Leiomyosarcoma shows intersecting eosinophilic fascicles, blunt-ended nuclei, and smooth-muscle marker expression. Angiosarcoma shows vasoformative growth and endothelial markers such as ERG and CD31. SS18::SSX fusion establishes synovial sarcoma; TLE1 and keratin may support it. Myxoma is composed of bland myxoma cells in myxoid matrix and usually attaches near the fossa ovalis; UPS is destructive and high grade. Metastatic sarcoma Clinical history and imaging should exclude an extracardiac primary. Molecular testing may identify alterations characteristic of intimal sarcoma, including MDM2 amplification; such cases may be better classified as intimal sarcoma when criteria are met. Use targeted molecular testing to exclude specific sarcoma entities rather than treating UPS as a molecularly defined tumor. Cardiac Diffuse Large B-Cell Lymphoma Cardiac Hematolymphoid Neoplasms Large B-cell lymphoma involving the heart, usually the right atrium, with no or only minor extracardiac disease. Usually older adults; median age approximately 63 years, with reported pediatric cases. Male predominance (approximately 2:1). Right atrium is the most common site; pericardial involvement occurs in about one third. Dyspnea, chest pain, heart failure, arrhythmia, pulmonary embolism, or sudden cardiac death. Large B-cell lymphoma involving the heart/pericardium with no or only minor extracardiac component. Large atypical lymphoid cells with a mature B-cell phenotype. Classify by cell of origin, MYC/BCL2 expression, and EBV status as appropriate. Diffuse sheets or aggregates of large discohesive lymphoid cells with vesicular nuclei and prominent nucleoli. Immunoblastic or centroblastic morphology may occur. Necrosis and apoptosis may be prominent. CD20, PAX5, CD79a, and other B-cell markers establish B-cell lineage. CD10, BCL6, and MUM1/IRF4 help assign cell-of-origin phenotype. EBER in situ hybridization assesses EBV association. Assess MYC and BCL2 protein expression and perform rearrangement studies when indicated. Primary effusion lymphoma PEL is HHV8/LANA positive and presents predominantly as a serous cavity effusion, often without a solid cardiac mass; conventional B-cell markers are often absent. Fibrin-associated DLBCL Tumor cells are confined to fibrin/thrombus in a cyst, myxoma, or prosthetic material without invasion of normal tissue. Pyothorax-associated DLBCL Arises in a chronically inflamed pleural space, usually as a solid mass, and is EBV positive; cardiac DLBCL is not defined by this setting. Metastatic/systemic DLBCL involving heart Systemic nodal or extranodal disease is present; primary cardiac lymphoma has no or only minimal extracardiac disease. Cardiac myxoma with reactive lymphoid infiltrate Myxoma has characteristic bland myxoma cells and myxoid matrix; lymphoma forms sheets of clonal large B cells. Cardiac Fibrin-Associated Diffuse Large B-Cell Lymphoma EBV-associated large B-cell proliferation confined to fibrin or thrombus in a cardiac cyst, myxoma, graft, or prosthetic valve. MYC and BCL2 FISH and EBER in situ hybridization assist classification. IGH clonality and broader molecular subtyping may be useful in selected cases. Adults, reported age range approximately 25–91 years; median about 56.5 years. Reported more often in men, partly reflecting associated cardiac lesions and devices. Occurs in chronic fibrin deposits, including atrial myxomas, intracardiac thrombi, prosthetic valves, and endovascular grafts. Often incidental; presentation is usually determined by the underlying lesion, although embolic events may occur. Atypical large B-cell population associated with fibrin/thrombus and the characteristic immunophenotype. Lymphoma cells remain confined to fibrinous material and do not infiltrate histologically normal surrounding tissue. EBV positivity is characteristic; assess the full clinical and morphologic context. Loose aggregates of large atypical lymphoid cells are embedded in fibrin and cellular debris. Cells often have immunoblastic morphology, irregular nuclei, prominent nucleoli, and amphophilic cytoplasm. Mitoses and apoptosis are frequent; inflammation is usually sparse. Focal extension into myxomatous stroma or a fibrous capsule may occur, but invasion into normal tissue is absent. CD20 and other B-cell markers are usually positive; plasmablastic differentiation may alter the phenotype in some cases. EBER is typically positive in tumor cells. CD30 and MUM1/IRF4 may be expressed; interpret with B-cell markers and morphology. Cardiac DLBCL Conventional cardiac DLBCL forms a mass infiltrating cardiac tissue; fibrin-associated DLBCL is restricted to fibrin/thrombus without invasion of normal tissue. PEL is HHV8/LANA positive and effusion-based; fibrin-associated DLBCL is generally HHV8 negative and attached to fibrinous material. DLBCL associated with chronic inflammation This forms a destructive mass in a longstanding chronically inflamed space; fibrin-associated DLBCL remains noninvasive and localized to fibrin. Reactive lymphoid proliferation in thrombus Reactive cells lack the cytologic atypia and EBV-associated clonal large B-cell proliferation characteristic of fibrin-associated DLBCL. Myxoma is a myxoid mesenchymal neoplasm; fibrin-associated lymphoma consists of atypical B cells confined to overlying fibrin. EBER is usually positive; clonal IGH rearrangement is common but not required. No specific recurrent genetic abnormality is established; MYC and BCL2 rearrangements are generally absent, with rare BCL6 rearrangements reported. All Pathology GPS Thoracic Pathology Home / Heart Tumors Heart Tumors Morphology-first diagnostic reference for primary cardiac neoplasms and tumor-like lesions, integrating clinical presentation, anatomic site, histopathology, immunophenotype, and diagnostically relevant molecular findings. Because even histologically benign cardiac lesions can cause major hemodynamic or electrical complications, location and clinical correlation are essential. Diagnostic approach • Metastatic involvement of the heart is substantially more common than a primary cardiac tumor. • Establish the anatomic compartment: endocardial, myocardial, valvular, or pericardial. • Correlate morphology with age, imaging, multiplicity, and clinical setting. • Consider syndromic associations, including TSC, Carney complex, Gorlin syndrome, and selected familial sarcoma predispositions. heart-search Search diagnoses and differential points Search: myxoma, spider cells, ERG, PRKAR1A, TSC... heart-group Category Collapse All Expand All of diagnostic entities Open a diagnosis for criteria, histology, IHC, and differential diagnosis.
