title: Pleural Pericardial Tumors
content: use client Adenomatoid Tumor of the Pleura Benign and Preinvasive Mesothelial Tumors A small, circumscribed mesothelial nodule with bland tubules, slit-like spaces, and vacuolated cells. Usually incidental; reported age range approximately 40–70 years. May arise on visceral or parietal pleura; fewer than 20 cases have been reported. Often discovered during surgery or at autopsy; asbestos association is uncertain. Circumscribed, focal proliferation of tubular spaces, pseudoglands, or vacuoles lined by flattened or cuboidal mesothelial cells in fibrous stroma. Bland cytology without tumor necrosis or a sarcomatoid component. No diffuse or multifocal pleural spread; exclude destructive invasion by thorough sampling of the entire lesion. Mesothelial differentiation supported by cytokeratins and markers such as calretinin, D2-40, and WT1. Interanastomosing pseudoglands, pseudovascular spaces, tubules, signet-ring-like spaces, and papillae may coexist. Cells are flat to cuboidal with scant epithelioid or vacuolated cytoplasm and bland nuclei. Vacuolated cells may contain bridging cytoplasmic strands forming a delicate network within tubular or slit-like lumina. Basophilic luminal material and lymphoid aggregates may be present. The lesion is usually circumscribed and nodular; limited adjacent soft-tissue entrapment can occur, so evaluate the overall interface. Cytokeratins are positive. Calretinin, D2-40, and WT1 support mesothelial differentiation. BAP1 expression is retained in reported cases. L1CAM may be useful as a surrogate marker in the context of TRAF7 alterations, but its role in pleural tumors is not fully established. Diffuse pleural mesothelioma Usually shows diffuse pleural involvement, destructive invasion, cytologic atypia, necrosis, or sarcomatoid morphology; sample the entire adenomatoid lesion. Localized pleural mesothelioma A malignant mesothelial tumor forming a circumscribed mass; look for malignant cytology and invasion beyond the mass. Well-differentiated papillary mesothelial tumor Shows true papillae with bland surface mesothelium and myxoid/fibrovascular cores rather than the characteristic tubular and vacuolated network. Mesothelioma in situ A surface-based single-layer neoplastic proliferation with BAP1 and/or MTAP loss or CDKN2A homozygous deletion in the appropriate clinical setting. Lymphangioma / epithelioid hemangioendothelioma Use endothelial markers and morphology to establish vascular rather than mesothelial differentiation. Metastatic signet-ring cell carcinoma Usually expresses epithelial/site-specific carcinoma markers and lacks a convincing mesothelial profile; correlate clinically. Well-Differentiated Papillary Mesothelial Tumor (WDPMT) of the Pleura Shows bland papillae with no stromal invasion. No established diagnostic molecular alteration is defined for pleural adenomatoid tumor. TRAF7 mutations are described in genital-tract adenomatoid tumors; their significance in thoracic lesions remains uncertain. Do not diagnose mesothelioma from focal entrapment alone; assess the entire lesion and the presence or absence of malignant features. Do not assume that a mesothelial immunophenotype alone establishes malignancy. Bland papillae with paucicellular myxoid or fibrovascular cores and no stromal invasion. Median age approximately 62 years; broad age range and no apparent sex predilection. Arises from visceral and/or parietal pleura; extremely rare, with fewer than 50 reported cases. May present with dyspnea and recurrent unilateral pleural effusion or be discovered incidentally. Papillary stromal formations covered by a single layer of bland flattened-to-cuboidal mesothelial cells. No stromal invasion; examination of the entire lesion is required to exclude focal invasion. Mesothelial immunophenotype supports the diagnosis; BAP1 is usually retained. Papillae range from thin to broad and contain paucicellular myxoid or fibrovascular cores. Surface cells are bland, with inconspicuous nucleoli and rare or absent mitoses. Inflammation is typically absent from papillary cores; occasional hyalinization, foamy macrophages, or rare psammomatous calcifications may occur. Crowded back-to-back papillae can simulate invasion; keratin staining may demonstrate preserved papillary architecture. Multifocal millimeter-sized pleural nodules may impart a granular or velvety pleural surface; a solitary arborescent mass may reach 5 cm. Mesothelial markers are positive. BAP1 is usually retained; retention does not independently establish benign behavior. Diffuse pleural mesothelioma, epithelioid type Shows invasion into deep pleural connective tissue or beyond, often with diffuse pleural thickening; papillary architecture alone does not exclude invasion. Usually presents with persistent unexplained effusion and a single-layer surface proliferation; BAP1 and/or MTAP loss or CDKN2A deletion supports neoplasia. Reactive mesothelial hyperplasia / reactive papillary mesothelial proliferation Papillae are generally stubby and accompanied by inflammation and reactive cytologic features; no defining molecular loss pattern. Adenomatoid tumor of the pleura Usually a circumscribed tubulocystic/vacuolated nodule rather than a surface-based papillary proliferation. Forms a circumscribed malignant mass with mesothelioma morphology and invasion within or beyond its borders. Molecular data are limited; BAP1 is usually retained. CDKN2A homozygous deletion has not been observed in reported pleural WDPMT. Do not use the historical term well-differentiated papillary mesothelioma as the preferred diagnostic name. Do not diagnose WDPMT on cytology alone because invasion cannot be assessed. Focal invasion in a WDPMT-like lesion remains a difficult category; invasion criteria and biological classification are not fully established. Mesothelioma in Situ A noninvasive surface mesothelial proliferation with BAP1 and/or MTAP loss or CDKN2A homozygous deletion in a carefully selected clinical setting. Reported pleural cases are very rare, predominantly in men aged approximately 67–79 years. Usually presents with persistent, unexplained pleural effusion without a mass on imaging or thoracoscopy. Risk context may include heavy asbestos exposure, prior irradiation, or familial predisposition. Persistent, nonresolving pleural effusion with no mass or gross tumor identified by imaging or thoracoscopy. Single-layer surface proliferation of mesothelial cells, with or without cytologic atypia, and no histologic evidence of invasion. Demonstration of BAP1 nuclear loss and/or MTAP cytoplasmic loss and/or CDKN2A homozygous deletion by validated assays with appropriate controls. Adequate, preferably multisite thoracoscopic pleural biopsies; ideally 100–200 mm² of tissue from different pleural areas. Clinicoradiologic correlation and multidisciplinary review; small biopsies and cytology alone are insufficient. Flat or cuboidal mesothelial cells line the pleural surface in a single layer. Cytologic atypia may be absent or minimal; nuclei may be bland with occasional prominent nucleoli. Mitoses are typically absent. Small papillary projections or tiny nodules may occur and can show moderate-to-severe atypia. No stromal invasion should be identified; exclude surface spread from an adjacent invasive mesothelioma. Loss of nuclear BAP1 expression is a useful marker of neoplastic mesothelial proliferation. Loss of cytoplasmic MTAP is a surrogate for CDKN2A homozygous deletion. CDKN2A homozygous deletion can be demonstrated by FISH. Interpret all stains with intact internal controls; isolated marker loss is not a diagnosis without the appropriate clinical, imaging, and morphologic context. Reactive mesothelial proliferation Usually retains BAP1 and MTAP and lacks CDKN2A homozygous deletion; correlate with inflammation and clinical context. Diffuse pleural mesothelioma with surface spread May be indistinguishable in a limited surface sample; imaging, thoracoscopic findings, and adequate multisite sampling are essential to exclude an invasive mass. Often forms multiple millimeter-sized papillary nodules and a granular/velvety pleural surface; papillary stromal cores are characteristic. A circumscribed tubulocystic/vacuolated nodule rather than a single-layer surface proliferation. Presents as a discrete mass with malignant mesothelial morphology rather than a purely preinvasive surface lesion. BAP1 inactivation and CDKN2A homozygous deletion are early events in mesothelioma development. MTAP immunohistochemistry can serve as a surrogate for deletion involving the CDKN2A/MTAP region. The diagnosis is not based on molecular testing alone; clinical, imaging, and histologic criteria are required. Do not diagnose mesothelioma in situ in an effusion specimen or small biopsy alone; invasion cannot be excluded. BAP1/MTAP loss or CDKN2A deletion in isolation does not establish mesothelioma in situ. Do not overlook surface spread from an unsampled invasive tumor. Localized Pleural Mesothelioma Malignant Mesothelial Tumors A solitary, circumscribed mesothelial malignancy without clinical or histologic evidence of diffuse serosal spread. Mean age approximately 59 years; reported range 6–82 years, with male predominance (M:F approximately 2.7:1). Usually an intrathoracic mass involving pleura, chest wall, lung, or mediastinum; most cases are pleural in origin. May be asymptomatic or cause chest pain, dyspnea, or symptoms from compression of adjacent structures. A solitary, localized, circumscribed mass established by imaging, operative findings, and histology. Resection specimen demonstrates no diffuse serosal spread and no invasion beyond the circumscribed tumor border. Histology is that of mesothelioma, with epithelioid, sarcomatoid (including desmoplastic), or biphasic morphology. Immunohistochemistry confirms mesothelial differentiation. Pleural fluid cytology should be negative for malignant cells by definition; multidisciplinary clinicoradiologic correlation is desirable. Approximately 55% are epithelioid; the remainder include biphasic and sarcomatoid tumors. Rare epithelioid tumors may show pleomorphic, microcystic, or rhabdoid features. Sarcomatoid tumors may show desmoplastic or lymphohistiocytoid differentiation. Histologic and immunophenotypic features otherwise parallel diffuse mesothelioma. Use a panel of at least two mesothelial markers and two carcinoma markers, interpreted with morphology. Calretinin, WT1, D2-40, and CK5/6 support mesothelial differentiation in epithelioid tumors. Claudin-4, BerEP4/MOC31, CEA, and other carcinoma markers help exclude metastatic carcinoma. Sarcomatoid tumors are usually at least focally positive for pancytokeratin, although rare keratin-negative examples occur; D2-40 may be more sensitive than calretinin. BAP1 loss, MTAP loss, or CDKN2A homozygous deletion may support malignant mesothelial proliferation but do not distinguish localized from diffuse growth. Shows diffuse pleural thickening or rind-like spread rather than a solitary circumscribed mass. Solitary fibrous tumor Usually STAT6 nuclear positive and lacks a mesothelial immunophenotype. Metastatic carcinoma to pleura Often expresses claudin-4 and epithelial/site-specific markers; mesothelial markers are absent or limited. Primary pleural or pulmonary sarcoma, including synovial sarcoma Use lineage markers and molecular testing; SS18 rearrangement supports synovial sarcoma. Bland, small, circumscribed tubulocystic lesion without malignant cytology or destructive invasion. WDPMT Bland papillary surface lesion without invasion, not a malignant mass-forming mesothelioma. Surface-confined preinvasive proliferation without a gross mass. Diffuse Pleural and Pericardial Mesothelioma Shows diffuse serosal involvement and invasion rather than a circumscribed or preinvasive pattern. Potential pathogenetic alterations include BAP1 and TRAF7 mutations and genomic near-haploidization. Ancillary molecular studies used for diffuse mesothelioma may support mesothelial malignancy but do not define localized growth. A circumscribed appearance alone is insufficient; confirm mesothelioma histology and absence of diffuse serosal disease. Do not confuse localized mesothelioma with solitary fibrous tumor or metastatic sarcoma. Diffuse serosal malignancy with epithelioid, sarcomatoid, or biphasic morphology; invasion is the most robust criterion of malignancy. Usually affects older adults, with a strong male predominance related in part to asbestos exposure. Pleural disease is more common on the right; bilateral disease at diagnosis is unusual. Presents with unilateral pleural effusion, dyspnea, chest pain, cough, weight loss, or circumferential pleural thickening. Primary pericardial mesothelioma is exceptionally rare and may cause pericardial effusion, cardiac compression, or tamponade. Diffuse pleural or pericardial involvement by a malignant neoplasm with epithelioid, sarcomatoid, or biphasic morphology. Unequivocal invasion into adjacent adipose tissue, skeletal muscle, lung parenchyma, or other structures; alternatively, convincing malignant tumor nodules or tumor necrosis in the appropriate context. Immunohistochemical panel supports mesothelial differentiation and excludes carcinoma and other mimics. Biphasic mesothelioma in a definitive resection contains at least 10% epithelioid and at least 10% sarcomatoid components; any demonstrable proportion of both components may be diagnosed as biphasic in a small biopsy. Desmoplastic mesothelioma requires dense collagenized tissue with malignant mesothelial cells in storiform or patternless arrays in at least 50% of a definitive resection; in small biopsies, report desmoplastic features. BAP1 and/or MTAP loss or CDKN2A homozygous deletion are desirable ancillary findings, not mandatory in every case. Epithelioid mesothelioma: tubulopapillary, trabecular, acinar, solid, micropapillary, and other patterns may occur; cells range from bland to markedly pleomorphic. Sarcomatoid mesothelioma: infiltrative spindle cells in intersecting fascicles or haphazard arrays, often with marked atypia and desmoplastic stroma. Desmoplastic mesothelioma: dense hyalinized collagen with sparse malignant spindle cells in storiform or patternless architecture; bland necrosis and invasion are important clues. Biphasic mesothelioma: unequivocal epithelioid and sarcomatoid components; report the percentage of sarcomatoid component. Pericardial mesothelioma is usually diffuse and is classified as epithelioid, sarcomatoid, or biphasic. Report architectural, cytologic, and stromal features with prognostic relevance, including solid, micropapillary, pleomorphic, transitional, rhabdoid, lymphohistiocytoid, and myxoid features where present. Invasion of adipose tissue is particularly useful in distinguishing sarcomatoid/desmoplastic mesothelioma from organizing pleuritis. For epithelioid tumors, use at least two mesothelial markers (calretinin, WT1, D2-40, CK5/6) and at least two carcinoma markers (claudin-4, BerEP4/MOC31, CEA, or others). Claudin-4 is a sensitive and specific marker supporting carcinoma over mesothelioma in the appropriate context. Pancytokeratin is usually positive in epithelioid mesothelioma; a negative result should prompt consideration of non-epithelial mimics. Sarcomatoid mesothelioma is generally at least focally positive for pancytokeratin, but occasional tumors are keratin negative. D2-40 is more often positive than calretinin in sarcomatoid mesothelioma; WT1 and CK5/6 are relatively insensitive in this subtype. Loss of nuclear BAP1, loss of cytoplasmic MTAP, and CDKN2A homozygous deletion support malignant mesothelial proliferation over benign reactive mesothelium. Strong diffuse GATA3 may favor sarcomatoid/desmoplastic mesothelioma over sarcomatoid carcinoma, with important exceptions including breast and urothelial carcinoma. TTF1 and/or p40 expression supports sarcomatoid carcinoma; interpret with a broad panel and clinical/radiologic findings. Reactive mesothelial hyperplasia / organizing pleuritis Reactive lesions lack unequivocal destructive invasion; organizing pleuritis may show zonation and capillaries. BAP1/MTAP retention and absence of CDKN2A deletion support a benign process but do not replace morphology. Metastatic lung adenocarcinoma or squamous cell carcinoma Usually expresses claudin-4 and lineage/site-specific carcinoma markers; use at least two carcinoma markers and two mesothelial markers. Metastatic carcinoma from breast, kidney, ovary, prostate, pancreas, or gastrointestinal tract Use morphology-directed site-specific markers and clinical correlation; mesothelial markers alone are insufficient. Sarcomatoid carcinoma Carcinoma markers, TTF1 or p40, and/or molecular findings such as MET exon 14 alterations may support carcinoma; strong diffuse GATA3 can favor sarcomatoid mesothelioma in context. STAT6 nuclear expression supports solitary fibrous tumor; mesothelioma typically shows keratin and mesothelial marker expression. Synovial sarcoma SS18 rearrangement / t(X;18) supports synovial sarcoma; TLE1 alone is not sufficiently specific. Epithelioid hemangioendothelioma / angiosarcoma Endothelial markers and characteristic CAMTA1::WWTR1 or YAP1::TFE3 fusions support epithelioid hemangioendothelioma; vascular morphology and endothelial markers support angiosarcoma. Melanoma SOX10, S100, HMB45, and Melan-A support melanocytic differentiation; BRAF p.V600E may be supportive in selected cases. Desmoid-type fibromatosis Usually keratin negative with nuclear beta-catenin and/or CTNNB1 alteration; can mimic desmoplastic mesothelioma. Same mesothelial morphology and immunophenotype but a solitary circumscribed mass without diffuse pleural spread. Adenomatoid tumor / WDPMT / mesothelioma in situ These mesothelial lesions are separated by architecture, absence of invasion, and clinical/radiologic setting; BAP1/MTAP/CDKN2A results should be interpreted in context. BAP1 inactivation, NF2 alterations, and CDKN2A homozygous deletion are recurrent events; BAP1 loss and CDKN2A/MTAP loss are useful diagnostic adjuncts. CDKN2A homozygous deletion can be detected by FISH; MTAP loss by immunohistochemistry is a surrogate for deletion involving the 9p21 region. Blood biomarkers such as soluble mesothelin-related peptide, HMGB1, fibulin-3, and calretinin are not recommended for routine diagnosis or monitoring because sensitivity and specificity are inadequate. For selected mimics, molecular testing is useful: SS18 rearrangement for synovial sarcoma, CAMTA1::WWTR1 or YAP1::TFE3 for epithelioid hemangioendothelioma, and IDH1/2 mutations in selected chondrosarcoma differentials. BAP1/MTAP loss or CDKN2A deletion distinguishes malignant from benign mesothelial proliferation but does not distinguish mesothelioma from other malignant tumors. Do not diagnose sarcomatoid mesothelioma from D2-40 or calretinin alone; confirm keratin/mesothelial differentiation and exclude sarcoma. Do not mistake organizing pleuritis for desmoplastic mesothelioma; invasion of adjacent tissue, especially adipose tissue, is the most reliable criterion. Before diagnosing primary pericardial mesothelioma, exclude direct extension from a pleural primary. Primary Effusion Lymphoma (PEL) Hematolymphoid Tumors HHV8-positive large B-cell lymphoma presenting predominantly as a serous cavity effusion, usually without a solid mass or nodal disease. Most often affects immunosuppressed patients, particularly HIV-positive men in the fifth decade with low CD4 counts. Involves pleural, pericardial, or peritoneal cavities; classic disease presents as an effusion without a tumor mass or lymphadenopathy. Kaposi sarcoma or multicentric Castleman disease may coexist; extracavitary PEL forms solid tumors in sites such as lung, gastrointestinal tract, skin, or CNS. Large malignant lymphoid cells in a serous effusion or an appropriate extracavitary mass, with plasmablastic, immunoblastic, pleomorphic, or anaplastic morphology. HHV8 positivity in tumor cells, usually demonstrated by LANA immunohistochemistry, is required. Plasmablastic/terminally differentiated phenotype, commonly expressing CD38, CD138, MUM1/IRF4, VS38c, EMA, and HLA-DR, with frequent absence of conventional B-cell markers. Classic PEL usually lacks surface and cytoplasmic immunoglobulins and may lack CD45. EBV is supportive but is neither required nor sufficient for diagnosis. Effusion cytology commonly shows large immunoblastic or plasmablastic cells with pleomorphic or anaplastic nuclei and prominent nucleoli. Cytoplasm is abundant, basophilic to amphophilic, and may show a perinuclear hof or vacuoles. Some cells resemble Reed–Sternberg cells. Extracavitary tumors form sheets of large malignant cells, often with apoptosis and necrosis; sinusoidal growth may mimic carcinoma or anaplastic large cell lymphoma. LANA (HHV8) nuclear positivity in tumor cells is required for diagnosis. Plasma cell/activation markers commonly include CD38, CD138, MUM1/IRF4, VS38c, EMA, HLA-DR, CD30, and PD-L1. Conventional B-cell markers CD19, CD20, PAX5, OCT2, BOB1, and CD79a are usually absent in classic PEL. Surface and cytoplasmic immunoglobulins are usually absent. EBER is positive in most cases, particularly in HIV-associated PEL, but EBV is not required. Aberrant CD4 or CD7 expression may occur; T-cell marker expression should not override the required HHV8 result. Effusion-based large B-cell lymphoma / HHV8-negative PEL-like lymphoma Usually HHV8 negative, often CD20 positive with a mature B-cell phenotype, occurs in older immunocompetent patients with fluid overload, and generally has a more favorable prognosis. DLBCL associated with chronic inflammation (pyothorax-associated lymphoma) Forms a solid pleural mass in longstanding chronic inflammation, is EBV positive but HHV8 negative, and commonly expresses B-cell markers. Primary mediastinal (thymic) large B-cell lymphoma Usually expresses B-cell markers and lacks HHV8; often presents as a mediastinal mass with secondary pleural/pericardial involvement. HHV8-positive DLBCL associated with multicentric Castleman disease Often involves lymph nodes, is usually EBER negative and CD138 negative, and commonly expresses IgM. Anaplastic large cell lymphoma Can show large pleomorphic cells and CD30 expression but is HHV8 negative and has a T-cell/null-cell phenotype; assess ALK and T-cell markers. ALK-positive large B-cell lymphoma May have plasmablastic morphology and plasma-cell phenotype but is ALK positive and HHV8/EBV negative; immunoglobulin is often expressed. Diffuse Large B-Cell Lymphoma Associated with Chronic Inflammation (Pyothorax-Associated Lymphoma) Arises in longstanding chronic inflammation as a solid pleural mass, is EBV-positive, and is HHV8-negative. HHV8 detection by LANA immunohistochemistry is required; EBER in situ hybridization is supportive. PEL is clonal with somatic hypermutation of IGH variable-region genes; complex karyotypes may include trisomies 7 and 12 and 1q abnormalities. MYC, BCL2, and BCL6 translocations are generally absent, although MYC protein may be deregulated. Do not diagnose PEL based on effusion cytology and plasmablastic phenotype without demonstrating HHV8. EBV positivity alone does not establish PEL. Classic PEL may be negative for CD20 and other B-cell markers; their absence does not exclude B-cell lineage. EBV-positive mass-forming large B-cell lymphoma arising after decades of chronic inflammation in a confined pleural space; HHV8 negative. Typically affects older adults, with median age approximately 65–70 years and male predominance. Usually arises in the pleural cavity after longstanding pyothorax, classically following artificial pneumothorax for tuberculosis treatment decades earlier. Presents with chest or back pain, fever, chest-wall swelling, productive cough, hemoptysis, or dyspnea; serum LDH is often elevated. Mass-forming pleural tumor in the setting of longstanding chronic inflammation or pyothorax. Large-cell lymphoma with B-lineage differentiation, usually CD20 and/or CD79a positive. EBV positivity in tumor cells, typically EBER positive with type III latency (LMP1 and EBNA2 expression). HHV8 negative. Exclude PEL, which is typically HHV8 positive and effusion-based rather than a solid pleural mass. Morphology resembles DLBCL-NOS, most often centroblastic or immunoblastic with large round nuclei and prominent single or multiple nucleoli. Extensive necrosis and angiocentric growth may be present. Tumor forms a fleshy pleural mass, often larger than 10 cm. Most cases express CD20 and CD79a. A subset shows plasmacytic differentiation with loss of CD20 and/or CD79a and expression of MUM1/IRF4 and CD138. Usually has an activated B-cell/non-germinal-center phenotype; CD30 may be positive. EBER is positive in tumor cells; type III latency is characteristic, with LMP1 and EBNA2 expression. HHV8 is negative. Occasional aberrant T-cell marker expression (CD2, CD3, CD4, or CD7) may complicate lineage assignment. Primary effusion lymphoma PEL is HHV8 positive and typically presents as an effusion without a solid tumor mass; classic cases often lack CD20/CD79a. Usually presents as a cavity effusion without a solid mass, is HHV8 negative, and often retains a mature B-cell phenotype; chronic pyothorax history and EBV latency III favor chronic-inflammation-associated DLBCL. Other DLBCL, including DLBCL-NOS Requires correlation with the characteristic confined-site chronic inflammatory background and EBV association; the morphology may otherwise be indistinguishable. Fibrin-associated DLBCL Occurs in association with fibrin in confined spaces and is a separate entity; it is not synonymous with DLBCL associated with chronic inflammation. Is HHV8-positive and predominantly effusion-based, usually without a solid mass. EBER in situ hybridization is useful and usually positive; EBV latency is typically type III. Clonal IG gene rearrangements and somatic hypermutation are present. TP53 mutations occur in a substantial proportion; MYC amplification and TNFAIP3 deletion may occur; complex karyotypes are common. Do not classify this tumor as PEL: the defining clinical pattern is a solid pleural mass after chronic inflammation, with EBV positivity and HHV8 negativity. Do not confuse fibrin-associated DLBCL with chronic-inflammation-associated DLBCL; they are distinct entities. title: Thymic Tumors
content: use client Type A Thymoma (Including Atypical Type A Thymoma) Thymomas Bland spindle/oval epithelial cells with very few immature T cells; classify as type AB if a substantial TdT-positive lymphocyte-rich component is present. Usually adults in the sixth to seventh decades; slight female predominance. Anterior (prevascular) mediastinum; may be incidental or cause mass symptoms. Myasthenia gravis occurs in a minority. Thymic epithelial neoplasm composed predominantly of bland spindle and/or oval cells, occasionally polygonal. Fascicular, storiform, or hemangiopericytoma-like growth; rosettes, glandular structures, microcysts, or whorls may occur. Immature lymphocytes are absent or very sparse; no lymphocyte-dense component that meets criteria for type AB. Conventional cases have low mitotic activity and usually lack necrosis. Atypical type A may show hypercellularity, increased mitoses, and focal necrosis; these features alone do not establish carcinoma. Fibrous capsule may be complete or incomplete, with lobulation and thick fibrous bands. Tumor cells have bland nuclei, finely dispersed powdery chromatin, and inconspicuous nucleoli. Perivascular spaces are less frequent than in other thymoma types; Hassall corpuscles are absent. Tumor cells express cytokeratins and p63/p40; FOXN1 and CD205 are supportive. CD5 and KIT (CD117) are generally negative in epithelial cells. Aberrant focal CD20 expression by neoplastic epithelial cells is a useful clue. TdT highlights absent or very sparse immature T cells; use it when type AB is a consideration. Type AB thymoma Type AB contains a lymphocyte-rich component with numerous TdT-positive immature T cells; even focal dense areas or a meaningful moderate infiltrate favor AB. Solitary fibrous tumor STAT6 and usually CD34 are positive; epithelial markers are negative. Synovial sarcoma SS18::SSX fusion or surrogate immunostaining supports synovial sarcoma; thymoma retains thymic epithelial differentiation. Metaplastic thymoma Metaplastic thymoma is biphasic, with anastomosing squamoid epithelial islands and a vimentin-positive spindle-cell stroma. Type AB Thymoma Distinguish from Type AB Thymoma by its defining pattern: A mixture of lymphocyte-poor type A-like areas and lymphocyte-rich areas containing immature T cells. Type B1 Thymoma Distinguish from Type B1 Thymoma by its defining pattern: Organotypic thymic cortex-like architecture with dispersed epithelial cells and conspicuous medullary islands. Type B2 Thymoma Distinguish from Type B2 Thymoma by its defining pattern: Lymphocyte-rich tumor with more numerous, clustered polygonal epithelial cells than type B1. Type B3 Thymoma Distinguish from Type B3 Thymoma by its defining pattern: Predominantly epithelial sheets of mildly to moderately atypical polygonal cells with sparse immature T cells. Micronodular Thymoma with Lymphoid Stroma Distinguish from Micronodular Thymoma with Lymphoid Stroma by its defining pattern: Multiple epithelial nodules separated by abundant lymphoid stroma rich in B cells and follicles. Metaplastic Thymoma Distinguish from Metaplastic Thymoma by its defining pattern: Biphasic tumor with anastomosing squamoid epithelial islands and bland spindle-cell stroma. GTF2I p.L424H is highly characteristic, particularly in type A/AB thymoma, and can support the diagnosis in difficult cases; it is not independently diagnostic. Do not classify a tumor as type A if a lymphocyte-rich component meets type AB criteria. Anaplasia or focal necrosis in an otherwise conventional thymoma does not, by itself, justify a diagnosis of thymic carcinoma. A mixture of lymphocyte-poor type A-like areas and lymphocyte-rich areas containing immature T cells. Adults, mean age approximately 57 years, with slight female predominance. Anterior mediastinum; myasthenia gravis occurs in approximately one fifth of cases. Lobulated thymic epithelial tumor with variable proportions of spindle-cell, lymphocyte-poor type A-like areas and lymphocyte-rich type B-like areas. The two components may form separate lobules or be intricately intermingled. The lymphocyte-rich component contains a significant population of immature TdT-positive T cells and a keratin-positive epithelial network. The lymphocyte-rich areas are not simply type B1, B2, or B3 thymoma. Type A-like areas may show fascicular, storiform, or other patterns typical of type A thymoma. Lymphocyte-rich areas contain small oval, plump spindle, or polygonal epithelial cells among abundant lymphocytes. Medullary islands and Hassall corpuscles are usually absent or inconspicuous. Pancytokeratin, CK19, and p63/p40 highlight the epithelial network, particularly in lymphocyte-rich areas. TdT and CD3 highlight immature T lymphocytes. Epithelial CD5 is absent; aberrant epithelial CD20 may be present. Ki-67 should be assessed in epithelial cells separately from proliferating thymocytes. Type A thymoma Type A lacks a lymphocyte-rich component; TdT staining helps quantify immature T cells. Micronodular thymoma with lymphoid stroma Micronodular thymoma has epithelial nodules separated by lymphoid stroma that is largely devoid of keratin-positive epithelial cells and contains abundant B cells. Type B1 thymoma B1 recapitulates thymic cortex with dense lymphocytes, dispersed epithelial cells, and obligatory medullary islands; AB has distinct type A-like areas. Metaplastic thymoma has a true biphasic epithelial/spindle-cell pattern rather than type A-like and immature-T-cell-rich compartments. Distinguish from Type A Thymoma (Including Atypical Type A Thymoma) by its defining pattern: Bland spindle/oval epithelial cells with very few immature T cells; classify as type AB if a substantial TdT-positive lymphocyte-rich component is present. GTF2I p.L424H is recurrent and supports the A/AB molecular family; molecular testing is not required for routine diagnosis. Organotypic thymic cortex-like architecture with dispersed epithelial cells and conspicuous medullary islands. Typically adults; anterior mediastinum, with occasional ectopic tumors in the neck and other sites. Myasthenia gravis is a common presentation. Lobulated tumor recapitulating non-involuted thymic cortex, with accompanying medullary differentiation. Dense small lymphocytes dominate; epithelial cells are individually dispersed and not clustered. Pale medullary islands are obligatory; Hassall corpuscles and myoid cells are optional. Epithelial cell clusters or increased epithelial density favor type B2 rather than B1. Lobules are separated by delicate collagenous septa and are often larger than normal thymic lobules. Epithelial cells have pale cytoplasm, round-to-oval nuclei, clear chromatin, and small nucleoli. Medullary islands contain less densely packed lymphocytes; poorly formed perivascular spaces are common. Pancytokeratin highlights sparse, dispersed epithelial cells and the medullary epithelial network. TdT and CD3 highlight abundant immature T cells. Cytokeratin staining helps identify epithelial clusters that would favor B2. Type B2 thymoma B2 has increased epithelial density and clusters of polygonal epithelial cells; medullary islands are less consistently conspicuous. AB contains recognizable spindle-cell, lymphocyte-poor type A-like areas. T-lymphoblastic lymphoma Lymphoblastic lymphoma is a destructive lymphoid neoplasm without a preserved thymic epithelial network; cytokeratin stains reveal the epithelial framework of B1 thymoma. Normal or hyperplastic thymus Thymoma typically forms an expansile, lobulated mass with enlarged lobules and altered epithelial density; correlate with imaging and gross findings. Lymphocyte-rich tumor with more numerous, clustered polygonal epithelial cells than type B1. Usually adults in midlife; anterior mediastinum. Myasthenia gravis is frequent. Lymphocyte-rich thymic epithelial tumor with epithelial cells present at a density greater than normal thymus or type B1 thymoma. Polygonal neoplastic epithelial cells occur singly and in clusters among numerous immature T cells. Lobulated thymic architecture and perivascular spaces support thymoma. Anaplastic foci do not establish carcinoma if thymoma architecture, immature T cells, and absence of epithelial CD5/KIT are retained. Polygonal epithelial cells have vesicular nuclei and conspicuous nucleoli, with pale-to-eosinophilic cytoplasm. Epithelial clusters are readily identified at low or intermediate power. Medullary islands may be present but are less defining than in B1. Pancytokeratin highlights increased epithelial cells and clusters. TdT and CD3 highlight abundant immature T lymphocytes. Epithelial CD5 and KIT are generally negative; positivity should prompt careful consideration of thymic carcinoma. B1 has fewer, individually dispersed epithelial cells and conspicuous medullary islands. Type B3 thymoma B3 is epithelial-cell rich and lymphocyte poor, producing a pink rather than blue appearance on H&E. Thymic squamous cell carcinoma Carcinoma shows overt malignant cytology and destructive growth; thymoma retains lobulation, perivascular spaces, immature TdT-positive T cells, and usually lacks epithelial CD5/KIT. Lymphoblastic lymphoma lacks the organized keratin-positive thymic epithelial network. At the B2/B3 boundary, acknowledge a morphologic continuum and sample extensively rather than forcing an artificial distinction. Predominantly epithelial sheets of mildly to moderately atypical polygonal cells with sparse immature T cells. Usually adults; anterior mediastinum. Myasthenia gravis may occur but is less characteristic than in B1/B2. Lobulated thymic epithelial tumor composed predominantly of polygonal neoplastic cells in sheets. Small numbers of non-neoplastic immature T cells are usually scattered among tumor cells. Perivascular spaces with epithelial palisading are prominent. The diagnosis requires distinction from thymic squamous cell carcinoma, particularly when cytologic atypia is marked. Tumor is usually pink on H&E because epithelial cells predominate over lymphocytes. Cells have eosinophilic or clear cytoplasm and mildly to moderately atypical round, elongated, grooved, or raisinoid nuclei. Intercellular bridges are generally absent; sparse immature T cells are usually present. Lymphoid follicles may accompany perivascular spaces, especially in tumors associated with myasthenia gravis. Pancytokeratin and p63/p40 highlight epithelial sheets. TdT highlights the sparse immature T-cell population, when present. Epithelial CD5 and KIT are usually absent in thymoma; their expression supports carcinoma in the appropriate context. B2 is lymphocyte rich, with numerous immature T cells and epithelial cells in a less dominant population. Carcinoma shows destructive invasion, more overt malignant cytology, and often epithelial CD5 and/or KIT; thymoma retains thymic architecture and immature T cells. Type A is composed of bland spindle/oval cells with very few immature lymphocytes. Metaplastic thymoma has a biphasic pattern with bland spindle-cell stroma and anastomosing squamoid epithelial islands. Type B3 thymoma shows greater chromosomal instability than type A/AB tumors; TP53 alterations are more frequent toward the B2/B3 and carcinoma spectrum. Multiple epithelial nodules separated by abundant lymphoid stroma rich in B cells and follicles. Typically middle-aged to older adults; anterior mediastinum. Often discovered as a localized mass; myasthenia gravis is uncommon. Thymic epithelial tumor composed of multiple discrete micronodules or islands of bland epithelial cells. Nodules are separated by abundant lymphoid stroma, often with reactive follicles and germinal centers. The lymphoid stroma is largely devoid of a keratin-positive epithelial network and contains numerous B cells. Atypia and destructive invasion are not features of the conventional lesion. Epithelial nodules may be spindle, oval, or polygonal and may show type A-like or other thymoma morphology. Lymphoid stroma contains mature lymphocytes, plasma cells, and reactive germinal centers. Perivascular spaces may be present. Pancytokeratin highlights epithelial nodules and helps demonstrate separation from lymphoid stroma. CD20 highlights abundant B cells and germinal centers; CD3 highlights background T cells. TdT-positive immature T cells are not a dominant feature of the lymphoid stroma. AB lymphocyte-rich areas contain a keratin-positive epithelial meshwork and predominantly immature TdT-positive T cells; micronodular stroma is B-cell rich and epithelial-poor. Thymic carcinoma with micronodular/lymphoid pattern Carcinoma shows malignant epithelial cytology and destructive invasion; assess epithelial atypia, mitoses, necrosis, and invasion. Reactive lymphoid hyperplasia Reactive thymic tissue retains normal corticomedullary organization rather than discrete neoplastic epithelial micronodules. Biphasic tumor with anastomosing squamoid epithelial islands and bland spindle-cell stroma. Usually adults, often middle-aged; anterior mediastinum. Usually localized and indolent. Biphasic thymic neoplasm composed of anastomosing islands or cords of polygonal squamoid epithelial cells and a background of bland spindle cells. Epithelial component may show variable nuclear atypia but lacks the high-grade features of sarcomatoid carcinoma. Spindle-cell component is cytologically bland and typically low proliferative. TdT-positive immature T cells are usually absent. Epithelial islands form complex anastomosing networks within a spindle-cell-rich stroma. Spindle cells are bland, often with elongated nuclei and a fibromyxoid background. Rare high-grade sarcomatoid transformation has been reported; evaluate any abrupt atypical spindle-cell component. Epithelial islands express cytokeratins and p63/p40. Spindle cells express vimentin and may show focal EMA or actin; keratin and p63/p40 are absent or only focal. Both components are generally negative for CD5, CD20, CD34, and KIT. Ki-67 is typically low in both components. Type A may show varied growth patterns but is essentially monophasic; it lacks anastomosing squamoid epithelial islands and its spindle cells retain epithelial keratin expression. Sarcomatoid carcinoma / carcinosarcoma Sarcomatoid carcinoma has a high-grade spindle component with marked atypia, frequent mitoses, necrosis, and sometimes heterologous elements. Biphasic thymic tumor, NOS Metaplastic thymoma is the defined biphasic entity with anastomosing squamoid epithelial islands and bland spindle stroma.
